metadata_title: The effectiveness and feasibility of the new Forest parenting programme for Chinese children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and their families
pages: The effectiveness and feasibility of the new Forest parenting programme for Chinese children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and their families Yongchang Zhang a,1, Caiyan Liu a,1, Bingxiao Li b,1, Xiangzhen Fu a, Hin Fong c, Ziqing Yu d, Sisi Wang a, Wenting Jin d, Lingling Shi a,d,e,* a Department of Psychiatry, the First Affiliated Hospital of Jinan University, Guangzhou, China b Department of Pediatrics, the First Affiliated Hospital of Jinan University, Guangzhou, China c Faculty of Medicine, International School, Jinan University, Guangzhou, China d Key Laboratory of CNS Regeneration (Ministry of Education), Guangdong Key Laboratory of Non-human Primate Research, GHM Institute of CNS Regeneration, Jinan University, Guangzhou, China e Co-innovation Center of Neuroregeneration, Nantong University, Nantong, China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: ADHD Parent training New forest parenting programme Feasibility Effectiveness A B S T R A C T Background: The New Forest Parenting Programme (NFPP) is a therapist-delivered parent training intervention aimed at improving behavioral difficulties in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) by promoting positive parenting practices. Although NFPP has shown effectiveness in several Western countries, evidence regarding its feasibility and effectiveness in the Chinese context remains limited. This study aims to evaluate its feasibility and effectiveness in China. Methods: Thirty Chinese children with ADHD and their families were enrolled and sequentially allocated to the NFPP intervention group (n = 15) or control group (n = 15). Parent-report measures, including the Chinese Version of Swanson Nolan and Pelham, Version IV Scale-parent Form (SNAP-IV), Chinese Parenting Sense of Competence (C-PSOC), and Parenting Styles Dimensions Questionnaire (PSDQ), were used to assess quantitative outcomes and analyzed using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). Finally, semi-structured interviews were con ducted with the intervention group after completing the NFPP, and the qualitative data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Results: Based on parent-report, compared with the control group, the intervention group showed significant reductions in inattention, hyperactivity/impulsivity, and oppositional defiant scores after the NFPP intervention. Parents reported increased parenting efficacy and satisfaction, along with increased use of an authoritative parenting style. The qualitative analysis offered insights into driving factors of NFPP's effectiveness, participant motivation, adherence barriers, limitations, and acceptability. Conclusions: This non-randomized controlled trial suggests that NFPP is effective and feasible for Chinese chil dren with ADHD and their families. Further validation in larger-scale randomized controlled trials is warranted. 1. Introduction Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is one of the most common psychiatric disorders in children. It's characterized by persis tent and developmentally inappropriate symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity/impulsivity (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). The worldwide prevalence of ADHD is 5.29% (Polanczyk et al., 2007), while epidemiological studies report a higher prevalence among chil dren in China (6.4%) (Li, Cui, et al., 2022). Children with ADHD often experience significant impairments in academic performance, social functioning, and executive processes such as working memory and organizational planning. often face many challenges, including elevated levels of parenting stress, frequent family conflicts, greater reliance on harsh or coercive disci pline, and less effective parenting practices (Johnston & Mash, 2001). Research suggests that these adverse parenting and family environments influence ADHD symptom expression and may be associated with an increased likelihood of an ADHD diagnosis (Claussen et al., 2024). Stimulants are recommended as the first-line medication for treating ADHD. However, medication adherence is often suboptimal, with adverse effects and perceived lack of efficacy being among the most frequently reported reasons for discontinuation (Ferrin et al., 2025; Gajria et al., 2014). Compared to medication treatment, parents seem to have a higher acceptance of psychosocial interventions (Adler & Nier enberg, 2010; Shen et al., 2021). In addition, all clinical practice guidelines also emphasize the importance of non-pharmacological in terventions (Coghill et al., 2023). Notably, parent training is recom mended as first-line treatment for preschool-aged children with ADHD (Wolraich et al., 2019). In China, evidence-based parent training pro grams remain scarce. Some research groups have found that non- pharmacological interventions such as Integrated Brain, Body, and So cial intervention and Executive Function Training have shown only limited effectiveness in improving ADHD symptoms (Shuai et al., 2021; Smith et al., 2020). A recent randomized controlled trial conducted in China demonstrated that a mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) programme effectively alleviated stress levels among parents of children with ADHD; however, it did not produce significant improvements in the children's ADHD symptoms (Law et al., 2025). Although a parent edu cation program conducted in Hong Kong presented positive effects on preschool children with developmental disabilities, including ADHD (Leung et al., 2016), it was not specifically designed as ADHD-focused parent training. Similarly, a Multiple Family Therapy for ADHD fam ilies conducted in China failed to show significant treatment effects (Ma et al., 2018). In summary, the interventions currently available for ADHD in China are not empirically supported. Therefore, there is an urgent need to introduce evidence-based, ADHD-specific parent training programs in the Chinese context. The New Forest Parenting Programme (NFPP) originated in the United Kingdom and is a well-established, evidence-based parent training intervention (Russell et al., 2022; Thompson et al., 2009). Generic parenting programs such as Incredible Years (Webster-Stratton et al., 2008) and Triple P (Nowak & Heinrichs, 2008) are based on universal behavior modification principles. They are primarily effective in reducing oppositional behaviors with limited impact on core ADHD symptoms, the NFPP was specifically developed for children with ADHD. Drawing on key aetiological theories of ADHD, the NFPP directly targets ADHD-related behavioral characteristics and underlying psy chological deficits, particularly impairments in executive functioning, with the aim of achieving sustained improvements in core symptoms across multiple settings (Sonuga-Barke et al., 2008; Thompson et al., 2009). Building on traditional behavior management strategies, the NFPP further incorporates interventions targeting neurocognitive defi cits and, through parents' use of constructive parenting, ultimately promotes the development of self-control and self-regulation in children with ADHD. Randomized controlled trials in multiple countries, including the UK, the United States, and Denmark, have demonstrated that NFPP significantly improves ADHD symptoms, providing robust evidence of its efficacy (Abikoff et al., 2015; Daley & O'Brien, 2013; H ̈age et al., 2018; Lambek et al., 2023; Sonuga-Barke et al., 2001; Thompson et al., 2009). In recent years, the NFPP has been introduced to China. It is pri marily delivered as an individual therapist-led intervention. However, the high costs associated with therapist training and ongoing supervi sion, together with practical barriers such as parents' work commit ments, may limit participation. To improve accessibility and reduce barriers to engagement, a self-help version of the NFPP (NFPP-SH) based on self-help materials has been proposed as an alternative approach. To date, only one study in China has evaluated NFPP-SH (Thompson et al., 2017). The NFPP-SH study targeted both parents and grandparents of children with ADHD. Although NFPP-SH was generally well received, its implementation encountered challenges, as grandparents experienced difficulties in fully understanding and consistently applying the rec ommended parenting strategies, which may have constrained the overall effectiveness of the intervention. Accordingly, the authors highlighted the potential value of therapist-led NFPP interventions in facilitating caregivers' understanding, adaptation, and implementation of the intervention strategies. Given the limited evidence for NFPP-SH in China and the potential challenges faced by caregivers in compre hending and applying intervention strategies, we therefore conducted a therapist-led NFPP intervention. To our knowledge, no study has sys tematically evaluated the therapist-led NFPP in Chinese families using both quantitative and qualitative approaches. Therefore, we conduct a small therapist-led trial to objectively assess its effectiveness using quantitative data. In addition, because NFPP was originally developed in the United Kingdom, its feasibility in the Chinese context remains un certain. To address this, we conduct semi-structured interviews to further explore its feasibility by examining the following research questions: (a) the driving factor of NFPP's effectiveness; (b) participation motivations; (c) adherence barriers; (d) program limitations; (e) acceptability. 2. Methods 2.1. Study design The participants in this study were recruited from the outpatient clinics of the hospital. Informed consent was obtained for all parents and children, and all consent forms were signed by the parents. The reporting of the quantitative research part of this study was in accor dance with the Transparent Reporting of Evaluations with Non randomized Designs, while the reporting of the qualitative part adhered to the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research. In this study, we employed quantitative and qualitative approaches. This approach enables a more thorough evaluation of an intervention (Campbell et al., 2000). Fig. 1 shows a conceptual diagram outlining the framework of our study. 2.2. Participants Children included in this study met the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria for ADHD, were under 12 years of age, and had primary caregivers who were able to understand and complete the relevant questionnaires. Families that met these criteria were included in the study. To ensure sample homo geneity and minimize potential confounding factors, families were excluded if any of the following applied to the child: (a) current use of ADHD medications or engagement in behavioral therapy; (b) comorbid intellectual disability; (c) comorbid other psychiatric disorders; (d) co morbid neurological disorders, organic brain diseases, or other neuro developmental disorders (such as autism spectrum disorder). During the study period, no children with ADHD received medication treatment. We initially obtained informed consent from 32 families. However, two families met the exclusion criteria—one child had comorbid tic disorder, and the other was currently taking ADHD medication. There fore, a total of 30 families of children with ADHD were included, with one parent from each family serving as a participant in this study. At baseline, information on the gender, age, and educational level of both the children with ADHD and their parents was collected. The participants were non-randomly assigned to the intervention and control groups due to practical constraints. Specifically, only two therapists were qualified to deliver the NFPP intervention, while the number of families interested in participating exceeded our intervention capacity. To manage this limitation and maintain participant satisfac tion, families were assigned to groups based on the order of recruitment: Y. Zhang et al. Acta Psychologica 264 (2026) 106492 2

the first 15 families were assigned to the intervention group to receive the NFPP intervention, while the remaining 15 families were placed on a waitlist and assigned to the control group (scheduled to receive the NFPP intervention six months later). The intervention and control groups were assessed on ADHD core symptoms, parenting styles, and parenting sense of competence both at baseline and post-intervention (week 8). In addition, semi-structured interviews were conducted with the 15 parents in the intervention group. It should be noted that, due to limitations in the study design, the recruitment and data collection for the control group were conducted after a certain delay compared to the intervention group. In addition, during the implementation of the study, participants completed their assessments in separate rooms to prevent sharing of information between the two groups, thereby ensuring data independence. Fig. 2 shows the flowchart of subject recruitment, se lection, and study process. 2.3. Intervention The NFPP is a parent training program developed for parents of children with ADHD. In our study, the NFPP intervention was conducted by two experienced therapists who had received standardized training, supervision, and assessment from the original NFPP team in the UK. Each therapist worked individually with one ADHD family, providing NFPP sessions once a week for eight consecutive weeks, with each ses sion lasting approximately 1.5 h. All sessions were conducted in a comfortable, purpose-designed room, specifically arranged for NFPP implementation. The NFPP program mainly includes ADHD health ed ucation, behavior management techniques, scaffolding support, parent- child interaction, and strategies for predicting future behavioral and emotional problems in children (DC et al., 2014). During the 8-week intervention period, parents applied the strategies and skills learned in the sessions to their own children. Supplementary Table 1 presents the weekly content of the NFPP intervention. These are designed to help develop abilities in ADHD children such as sitting still, focusing, taking turns, waiting, negotiating, and compromising. 2.4. Outcome measures All measures used in this study were based on parent-report. The intervention and control groups were evaluated using the following scales at baseline and after 8 weeks of NFPP: the Chinese Version of Swanson Nolan and Pelham, Version IV Scale-parent form (SNAP-IV) (Swanson et al., 2001; Zhou et al., 2013)was employed to assess the core symptoms improvement of children diagnosed with ADHD, which has satisfactory measurement properties regarding test-retest reliability and validity. Parenting efficacy and satisfaction were assessed using the Chinese Parenting Sense of Competence (C-PSOC) (Ngai et al., 2007) and parenting style was measured with the Parenting Styles Dimensions Questionnaire (PSDQ) (Alagla et al., 2019). Li (Li et al., 2021) and Fu (Fu et al., 2013) conducted reliability and validity analyses of the C-PSOC and PSDQ, and the findings showed that both instruments exhibited satisfactory psychometric properties. All of the above scales were administered by the same researcher. The primary outcome measure in this study was the SNAP-IV scale. The C-PSOC and PSDQ were included as secondary outcome measures. 2.5. Statistical analysis 2.5.1. Quantitative The data were analyzed using IBM SPSS 26.0 software. The Shapiro- Fig. 1. Wilk test and homogeneity of variance test were performed to assess data normality and variance homogeneity, respectively. Fisher's Exact Test, Chi-square test, and independent samples t-test were used to compare age, gender, and education level between the two groups. A two-tailed P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Quantitative data with a normal distribution were described as mean ± SD, and group comparisons were performed using independent- samples t-tests. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was performed to compare post-intervention scores on the SNAP-IV, PSDQ, and C-PSOC between the intervention and control groups, adjusting for baseline or pre-intervention scores as covariates. To control for the inflation of Type I error associated with multiple comparisons, Bonferroni correction was applied separately to each scale. Cohen's d of 0.8 indicates a “large” effect, while a Cohen's d of 1.2 indicates a “very large” effect (Sawilowsky, 2009). For quantitative data that were not normally distributed, results were summarized as the median [P25, P75]. Between- group comparisons were performed using the Mann–Whitney U test, and effect sizes were reported as |r|. A total of 30 families participated in this study. Among the 15 fam ilies undergoing the NFPP intervention, one parent had to withdraw from the intervention two weeks early due to a change in her work schedule. Following the intention-to-treat principle, we included her in the original intervention group for analysis, applying last observation carried forward by using the sixth-week data as a substitute for the missing data from the end of the 8-week intervention. 2.5.2. Qualitative Two trained researchers (L. Shi and B. Li) conducted individual, face- to-face semi-structured interviews with parents who completed the NFPP intervention (intervention group). All 15 parents were interviewed individually. The interview guide included seven open- ended questions and three structured questions (Tarver et al., 2022). With parental consent, all interviews were audio-recorded and tran scribed verbatim. The duration of the interviews ranged from 26 to 40 min (mean [SD], 32.40[4.31]), and all interviews were conducted in a comfortable, private room. Two researchers independently conducted thematic analysis of the qualitative data using NVivo 12 software. They continuously discussed and revised the coding results to reach agreement. Thematic analysis, a fundamental method for qualitative research, is widely used in quali tative research. It seeks to uncover key themes and patterns within the data to gain a profound understanding. This method allows for the ex amination of both inductive themes (emerging from the data) and deductive themes (derived from existing theories), offering flexibility in identifying and exploring central themes relevant to the research ques tion, while capturing naturally occurring themes within the dataset (Clarke & Braun, 2013). The analysis process followed the six-stage approach to thematic analysis proposed by Braun & Clarke (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Data collection was guided by the principle of data saturation, indicating that information from all interviews was adequate. This allowed the generation of rich, nuanced, and multifaceted insights into the phenomenon under investigation. (Ruan et al., 2025). The research team held multiple rounds of in-depth discussions and deliberations on various themes during group meetings to ensure that the findings re flected a collective perspective rather than that of a single researcher, thereby strengthening the rigor and credibility of the analysis. 3. Results 3.1. Quantitative analysis A total of 30 ADHD children and 30 parents participated in this study (Table 1). There were no statistically significant differences between the intervention and control groups in demographic characteristics of the children and parents. Participants who attended all eight sessions were considered to have completed the intervention. Among the 15 families participating in the NFPP intervention, 14 successfully completed it, resulting in a completion rate of 93.3%. At baseline, no significant differences were observed between the intervention and control groups on any parent-report scale measures (all P > .05). After completing the 8-week NFPP intervention, according to parent-report outcomes, the intervention group showed significantly lower scores for inattention (F = 12.593; P = .004; d = 0.647), hyper activity/impulsivity (F = 12.200; P = .005; d = 0.686), and oppositional defiant (F = 7.011; P = .040; d = 0.880) compared with the control group. In addition, compared with the control group, parents in the inter vention group reported higher levels of parenting efficacy (F = 9.263; P = .010; d = 0.874) and parenting satisfaction (F = 7.149; P = .025; d = 0.950) after the NFPP intervention, along with improvements in parenting style — characterized by increase authoritative parenting (F = 12.046; P = .005; d = 1.058) and decreased authoritarian (F = 20.543; P < 0.001; d = 1.122) and permissive parenting styles (F = 9.264; P = .015; d = 0.863). These results are presented in Tables 2–4. 3.2. Qualitative analysis A total of 15 parents participated in semi-structured interviews, including 2 males (13.3%) and 13 females (86.7%). The interviews identified six themes: (a) motivation, (b) knowledge and theoretical parenting skills acquisition, (c) understanding and respect: reshaping parental beliefs, (d) active participation in parenting practices, (e) bar riers, and (f) limitations. Each theme was further subdivided into several subthemes as follows: (a) teacher complaints, concerns about the child's future development, and difficulty in management; (b) illness-related knowledge, parenting skills-related knowledge; (c) capacity development, parenting styles; (d) communication and sharing, changing parenting styles, and putting knowledge into practice; (e) time cost, spousal involvement; (f) hope for ongoing follow-up in the future, literal translation of some terms. The themes, subthemes, and their frequencies are summarized in Sup plementary Table 2, while Table 5 presents the themes and subthemes along with representative supporting quotations. 3.2.1. Theme 1—Motivation When asked why they participated in the NFPP program, parents expressed concerns about their children's difficulties in school, at home, and in their daily lives. This theme has been organized into three subthemes: teacher complaints, concerns about the child's future development, and difficulties in behavior management. 3.2.1.1. Teacher complaints. Parents reported that the primary reason for participating in NFPP stemmed from teachers' complaints regarding classroom discipline, emotional management, and academic progress of their children. Observations of unusual behaviors by some profession ally trained teachers also helped identify potential symptom and encouraged parents to seek medical help. 3.2.1.2. Concerns about the child's future development. Furthermore, parents aimed to effectively support their children's development, hoping to see improvements in their abilities to face challenges at school and in life. And they hoped to see their children grow into better individuals. 3.2.1.3. Difficulty in management. These children often experienced emotional dysregulation, learning difficulties, and social challenges. Undoubtedly, these issues undoubtedly increased parental stress and anxiety, which also diminished their confidence and satisfaction in parenting to some extent. 3.2.2. Theme 2—Knowledge and theoretical parenting skills acquisition At the beginning of the NFPP program, parents received a compre hensive introduction to ADHD, as gaining knowledge about the disorder is often the first step to effective intervention. In the interviews, parents reported significant improvement in their understanding of ADHD characteristics and parenting skills. 3.2.2.1. Illness-related knowledge. All parents reported that they previ ously had little understanding of ADHD. Throughout the intervention, they gradually developed a deeper understanding of the causes, symp toms, and functional impairments associated with ADHD. 3.2.2.2. Parenting skills–related knowledge. As the intervention pro gressed, parents acquired tailored parenting skills for ADHD to support the development of their children's emotional regulation, organization, and time perception abilities. 3.2.3. Theme 3—Understanding and respect: Reshaping parental beliefs The NFPP provided participants with ADHD-related theoretical knowledge at the beginning to enhance the overall understanding of the disorder. Based on this foundation, parents' perspectives on their chil dren's issues were changing. 3.2.3.1. Capacity development. Additionally, several parents mentioned the importance of setting appropriate goals and tasks for their children based on their developmental level, rather than solely assessing their abilities based on academic performance. This also reflected parents' comprehensive acceptance of their children, offering them more understanding and compassion. 3.2.3.2. Parenting styles. Moreover, changing parenting styles is crucial, as they profoundly impact children's developmental processes. Parents noted a positive shift in their attitudes toward their children, no longer resorting to simple punishment or neglecting issues but attempting to interact with them more patiently, showing more attention to their emotional needs. 3.2.4. Theme 4—Active participation in parenting practices Parents actively engaged in parenting practices and most parents integrated them into daily lives. This theme is divided into three sub themes: communication and sharing, changing parenting styles, and putting knowledge into practice. 3.2.4.1. Communication and sharing. Throughout the intervention pro cess, the support of partners and family members was crucial, with almost all parents mentioning sharing their NFPP-acquired knowledge with family, friends, or colleagues, and exchanging parenting experi ences. This facilitated parenting consistency and alleviated individual parenting pressures. 3.2.4.2. Changing parenting styles. Additionally, the most obvious change mentioned by parents was the shift in their parenting approach. They ceased resorting to scolding or reacting negatively, but instead strove to understand, respect, and support their children, fostering a harmonious parent-child atmosphere. 3.2.4.3. Putting knowledge into practice. Parents learned coping strate gies and techniques through NFPP, enabling them to approach their children with greater confidence and apply these strategies in their daily routines. They continuously reflected on experiences, leading to im provements in their children's behavior throughout this process. 3.2.5. Theme 5—Barriers Obstacles parents encountered during the implementation of stra tegies would reduce their execution and impact the effectiveness of the intervention. 3.2.5.1. Time cost. The lack of available time for implementing strate gies was reported as the biggest issue by parents. They acknowledged being frequently occupied with work, which indeed posed significant difficulties. Parents expressed a desire for dedicated one-to-one time with their child with ADHD, but interruptions from siblings frequently occurred. Consequently, it became difficult for parents to dedicate their full attention and energy to the child with ADHD. 3.2.5.2. Spousal involvement. Parents' comprehension of the curriculum content was important, as it influenced their strategy choices in specific situations. Another obstacle was the frequent disagreement between parents in using different strategies to deal with their children's behavioral and emotional issues, making it difficult at times to reach a consensus on motivating the children to exhibit the expected behavior. Additionally, fathers seemed to show less patience than mothers in parenting matters. 3.2.6. Theme 6—Limitations Although parents generally expressed positive attitudes toward the NFPP and acknowledged its benefits, they also articulated their expec tations for ongoing support and program improvement. 3.2.6.1. Hope for ongoing follow-up in the future. Many parents strongly hoped to maintain long-term contact with the therapists after the course ended, believing that continued follow-up would help reinforce what they had learned and sustain positive parenting behaviors. Although the NFPP enhanced parents' confidence and skills, they still felt a need for continuous guidance to maintain behavioral change. This expectation for ongoing support also revealed an active learning attitude—parents no longer regarded themselves as passive recipients of knowledge but as active participants seeking continuous improvement. 3.2.6.2. Literal translation of some terms. Some noted that certain terms translated from English into Chinese were occasionally confusing, although therapists' explanations could partly resolve this issue. These reflections underscored the need for cultural and linguistic adaptation of NFPP to ensure that parents fully comprehend and effectively apply its strategies. Beyond practical concerns, such reflections revealed a pro cess of meaning-making—parents actively interpreted program concepts and sought to integrate them within their own cultural and familial contexts. 3.2.7. Structured questions All parents indicated that they would recommend NFPP to friends, expressed a desire for it to be a part of their usual care from their clinician, and believed that the intervention should be routinely offered to parents seeking care for their child with ADHD. 3.3. Comparison of quantitative and qualitative findings The quantitative and qualitative findings were generally consistent and mutually reinforcing. The quantitative analysis showed that after the 8-week NFPP intervention, parents reported significant reductions in children's inattention, hyperactivity/impulsivity, and oppositional be haviors, along with notable improvements in parenting efficacy, satis faction, and authoritative parenting style. In the semi-structured interviews, many parents described the posi tive impact of the NFPP on both their children and families. They re ported reduced time spent on homework, fewer classroom restlessness behaviors, fewer complaints from teachers, and enhanced competence in managing children's behavioral problems. Consequently, many par ents expressed a willingness to recommend the NFPP to other families, further supporting the program's effectiveness and acceptability from a subjective perspective. Moreover, quantitative data indicated an increase in authoritative parenting style. Qualitative findings supported this by showing that parents regarded a better understanding of ADHD as one of the most valuable outcomes of NFPP participation. This deeper understanding enhanced their overall cognitive insight and contributed to a more empathetic and tolerant attitude toward their children. Parents consis tently applied the parenting skills learned during the program in their daily routines, which reduced the use of harsh discipline, improved their ability to cope with the challenges of raising a child with ADHD, and ultimately facilitated a shift toward a more authoritative and supportive parenting style. Discussion This study examined the effectiveness and feasibility of the NFPP among families of children with ADHD in China. The results indicate that the NFPP effectively improves parent-report core ADHD symptoms, and both the attendance rate and semi-structured interview findings suggest that NFPP is feasible and well-accepted in the Chinese context. This study reveals that NFPP is effective for Chinese children with ADHD. Compared with the control group, the intervention group showed significant reductions in parent-report inattention, hyperactiv ity/impulsivity, and oppositional defiant scores after the NFPP inter vention. In addition, parents demonstrated improved parenting efficacy and satisfaction, along with an increased use of an authoritative parenting style. These findings are consistent with those reported by Daley et al., who also found that the NFPP improved ADHD symptoms while enhancing parenting efficacy and satisfaction (Daley & O'Brien, 2013). Sonuga-Barke et al. further compared the effectiveness of NFPP with treatment-as-usual and found that NFPP produced notable im provements in oppositional defiant behaviors but only minimal effects on inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity. A plausible explanation is that the study adopted broad inclusion and exclusion criteria to maxi mize recruitment of children with ADHD, without applying strict diag nostic standards. As a result, many children presented with comorbid difficulties and developmental delays, which may have led to an un derestimation of NFPP's true therapeutic effects (Sonuga-Barke et al., 2018). Deng et al. (Deng et al., 2024) also conducted a quantitative study on the effectiveness of the NFPP among Chinese children with ADHD. Although their findings suggested that NFPP significantly improved core ADHD symptoms, the control group in their study received routine health education, and the hyperactivity and impulsivity scores of the control group also showed significant improvement after the intervention, indicating that health education itself might have contributed to certain behavioral improvements. Therefore, the study may not have accurately isolated the specific effects of NFPP. Compared with other nonpharmacological interventions imple mented in China, the NFPP appears to offer broader benefits for both parents and children. The MBSR program delivered to parents of chil dren with ADHD in Hong Kong, as reported by Law et al., showed that MBSR can effectively reduce parental stress; however, it had no sub stantial impact on improving ADHD symptoms in children (Law et al., 2025). One likely reason is that the MBSR intervention focused primarily on cultivating awareness of emotions, thoughts, and bodily sensations to enhance parental well-being, but did not deeply address child-related issues or parenting strategies. Consequently, the benefits for children with ADHD were limited. In contrast, NFPP places a stronger focus on improving parenting styles, strengthening positive parenting behaviors, and promoting constructive parent–child interactions. These changes help improve the parent–child relationship and lead to more effective reductions in ADHD-related behaviors. Importantly, improvements in parenting behaviors function as a key mediator linking the intervention to changes in child behavior, thereby indirectly contributing to the meaningful behavioral improvements observed in children (R et al., 2014). Consequently, when compared with other non-pharmacological interventions conducted in Chinese cultural contexts, NFPP may pro vide more comprehensive and targeted support for both parents and children. Among the 15 families in the intervention group, all completed the baseline assessment (100%), 14 families completed the eight-week NFPP intervention (93.3%), and all 15 families completed both the post-intervention assessment (100%) and the semi-structured interviews (100%). Parents in the intervention group showed strong motivation to participate, mainly due to concerns raised by teachers and worries about their children's future. They hoped that NFPP could help improve their child's behavior and enhance the parent–child relationship. Despite obstacles such as busy work schedules, overall adherence remained high, with 93.3% of families completing all sessions. Parents reported that they learned useful knowledge and skills, became more under standing and respectful toward their children, and actively applied parenting strategies in daily life. Although minor challenges related to the Chinese translation of NFPP materials existed, the therapists' ex planations mitigated these effects. Furthermore, all parents indicated that they would recommend NFPP to friends, expressed a desire for it to be part of routine clinical care, and believed that the intervention should be regularly offered to parents of children with ADHD. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that NFPP shows high acceptability and good feasibility among Chinese families of children with ADHD. The semi-structured interviews indicated that Chinese parents' motivation to participate in the NFPP was primarily driven by teacher complaints, difficulties in managing their child's behavior, and concerns about the child's future development. In contrast, Daley's qualitative study of families in the United Kingdom identified a different pattern: UK parents mainly joined the NFPP to learn more knowledge. Different motivations may stem from cultural differences between East and West. Influenced by traditional Confucianism, Chinese parents prioritize social norms, interpersonal harmony, and the importance of hard work (du Prel Carroll et al., 2012; Fu et al., 2022). Additionally, academic achievement remains highly valued. Therefore, Chinese parents priori tize evaluation metrics that may influence their children's future development, ultimately driving their healthcare-seeking behavior. In the interviews, parents consistently reported gaining a deeper understanding of ADHD and relevant parenting strategies, suggesting a meaningful improvement in their knowledge. With this enhanced un derstanding, many parents began to reflect on the underlying causes of their children's behavioral difficulties. Their attitudes gradually shifted from blame and punishment toward greater understanding, acceptance, and support. They also reported applying the strategies learned in NFPP to everyday parenting, reducing the use of harsh discipline and adopting more positive approaches. These changes, in turn, appeared to contribute to improvements in their children's ADHD symptoms. Pre vious research has shown that emotional maltreatment, as well as negative, overprotective, or overly controlling parenting practices, are risk factors for ADHD, whereas NFPP emphasizes enhancing paren t–child relationships and improving child behavior through promoting positive parenting strategies (Gau, 2007; Johnston, 1996). The KAP theory, proposed by Dr. Gcust in the 1960s, posits that individuals first acquire information about specific behaviors, then undergo attitude changes toward these behaviors, resulting in behaviors consistent with these attitudes (Bettinghaus, 1986). Thus, the KAP framework may partially explain the patterns observed in our study: improvements in parental knowledge and attitudes may have facilitated positive changes in parenting behavior, thereby contributing to symptom improvement in children. However, it should be noted that although parents reported improved understanding in the interviews, this study did not quantify parental knowledge levels before the intervention. Therefore, the role of the KAP model in explaining the mechanisms of NFPP requires further evaluation in future research. Parents' and caregivers' understanding of the disorder plays a crucial role in the primary healthcare of children and adolescents (Gajria et al., 2014; Khan & Aslani, 2020). Insufficient parental understanding of ADHD may lead to delays in identification and treatment (Park et al., 2018). The European ADHD Guidelines Group (EAGG) suggests that most treatment goals for ADHD can be achieved by providing high- quality psychoeducation at the outset of treatment, helping families better understand ADHD and its management, and considering their concerns, attitudes, and beliefs about ADHD (Coghill et al., 2023). Additionally, parents' understanding of their children's challenging be haviors determines their treatment needs (Bussing et al., 2012; dosReis et al., 2007); therefore, we emphasize the significant role of parental Y. cognition, as acquiring knowledge is often the first step in ADHD treatment and can significantly influence treatment outcomes. Many parents in China may lack adequate awareness and understanding of ADHD (Li, Wang, et al., 2022). Therefore, we recommend providing high-quality psychoeducation for Chinese ADHD families to enhance parental awareness, thereby promoting positive treatment outcomes. Although our study demonstrates that NFPP is effective for Chinese children with ADHD, as NFPP originates from the UK, the differences in understanding and cultural contexts between China and the UK may limit some of its therapeutic potential. Therefore, it is crucial to make cultural adaptations to NFPP to better suit the Chinese context. In addition, although parents clearly expressed a need for continued sup port during the interviews, the design of the present study does not permit an assessment of the long-term impact or sustainability of NFPP. Future research should incorporate randomized controlled trials with extended follow-up periods to determine whether the short-term bene fits observed can be maintained over time. In summary, this study offers preliminary evidence supporting the use of NFPP among Chinese families of children with ADHD, showing meaningful improvements in parent-report child symptoms and parental parenting competence. The findings further indicate that NFPP is both feasible and acceptable in Chinese context. Together, these results sug gest that NFPP could serve as a valuable complement to routine clinical services, providing more structured support for families of children with ADHD and offering clinicians a practical, evidence-based framework for delivering parent-training interventions. 5. Limitations Our study has some limitations. Firstly, this study employed both quantitative and qualitative methods to address two distinct research aims: quantitative data were used to evaluate the effectiveness of NFPP, while qualitative data focused on its feasibility. As a result, the quanti tative and qualitative findings could not be integrated into a compre hensive conclusion as traditional mixed-methods research. In the future, we plan to design a rigorous mixed-methods framework to fully leverage the complementary strengths of quantitative and qualitative research, thereby enhancing our understanding of the research questions. Sec ondly, child behavioral outcomes in the present study were assessed primarily through proximal informant reports, namely parent-report measures. Although parent reports are commonly used and clinically meaningful outcomes in parent training research, they may be influ enced by changes in parental perceptions, expectations, or reporting bias following the intervention. Therefore, the observed improvements in child behavior should be interpreted with caution. Future studies should incorporate multiple informants, such as teacher reports, as well as more objective behavioral assessments, to evaluate the consistency of intervention effects across different contexts and reduce potential informant bias. Thirdly, we assessed participants only before and after the intervention, which limits the ability to evaluate the long-term ef fects and sustainability of NFPP. Future research should incorporate randomized controlled trials with extended follow-up periods to deter mine whether the short-term benefits of NFPP can be sustained over time. Fourthly, the participants in this study were recruited from hos pital outpatient clinics, which may introduce a degree of selection bias. Families actively seeking clinical services often display stronger moti vation for intervention and greater concern regarding their children's symptoms. As a result, the current sample may not fully represent the broader population of families of children with ADHD. This motivation- related bias could have positively influenced both intervention engagement and perceived benefits. Future research should consider recruiting participants from community settings, schools, or broader population-based samples to enhance representativeness and external validity. Fifthly, we did not use random methods for group assignment. Although there were no significant differences in baseline characteristics between the two groups, we cannot guarantee that there were no other potential confounding factors affecting the final results. In addition, the delayed recruitment and data collection of the control group may have introduced influences other than the NFPP intervention. Future ran domized controlled trials are needed to further validate the conclusions of this study. Finally, the relatively small sample size may limit the generalizability of our findings. To improve the robustness and appli cability of future results, we plan to include larger samples in subsequent studies. 6. Conclusion This non-randomized controlled trial demonstrates the effectiveness of NFPP in reducing parent-report core symptoms of ADHD in children and enhancing parents' parenting competence and use of authoritative parenting styles. Although parents encountered some challenges in implementing the strategies, NFPP was generally considered feasible and acceptable. In addition, some cultural adaptations may be needed to better tailor NFPP to Chinese families. metadata_title: Educational robotics and augmented reality for improving social skills of children with ADHD: A scoping review
pages: Educational robotics and augmented reality for improving social skills of children with ADHD: A scoping review Maria Koukounara a,* , Korina Hatzinikolaou a a Child Psychology and Education Lab., School of Early Childhood Education, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Thessaloniki, Greece A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Educational robotics Social robotics Augmented reality ADHD Social skills Scoping review A B S T R A C T Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is the most common childhood neurodevelopment disorder that is characterized by symptoms of inattention, distractibility, impulsivity, and hyperactivity. To support children with ADHD to overcome developmental challenges, innovative technologies such as Educational Robotics and Augmented Reality have been introduced. The use of these technologies can contribute to enhancing cognitive and social skills. This scoping review aims to map how both technologies have been applied to support social skills in children with ADHD and summarize reported outcomes. A comprehensive literature search was con ducted in Springer Link, IEEE, MDPI, ERIC, PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and PsycINFO for studies published in either Greek or English from 2015 to the present. The review identified seven studies meeting the inclusion criteria, with sample sizes ranging from 1 to 59 participants. Findings indicate that robots and AR systems can enhance children's engagement, attention, concentration, motivation, positive behaviors, and emotional recognition. Despite these promising results, the limited number of studies and small sample sizes highlight the need for further research to confirm these effects. 1. Introduction 1.1. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neuro developmental disorder that emerges early in childhood and often per sists across development, affecting multiple domains of functioning (Franke et al., 2018). Beyond its core symptoms of inattention, hyper activity, and impulsivity, ADHD is consistently associated with signifi cant difficulties in social functioning, particularly during the preschool and early school years, when peer interactions play a central role in socio-emotional development (Barkley, 2015). Children with ADHD frequently experience challenges in forming and maintaining peer relationships, interpreting social cues, regulating emotional responses, and adapting their behavior to social contexts (Gardner & Gerdes, 2015). These difficulties often result in peer rejec tion, negative social feedback, and reduced opportunities for social learning, which in turn contribute to lower self-esteem and increased emotional distress (Meinzer et al., 2021). Consequently, the enhance ment of social skills has been identified as a critical target for early intervention in children with ADHD. ADHD is characterized by heterogeneous symptom profiles, commonly classified into inattentive, hyperactive/impulsive, and com bined presentations (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Regard less of subtype, impairments in executive functioning, emotion regulation, and behavioral inhibition are central features that directly interfere with children's ability to engage effectively in social in teractions (Barkley, 2015). Empirical evidence indicates that children with ADHD often struggle with turn-taking, maintaining reciprocal conversations, managing frus tration, and responding appropriately to peers' emotional expressions (Christiansen et al., 2019; McKay et al., 2023). Difficulties in emotion recognition and regulation are particularly salient, with a substantial proportion of children with ADHD demonstrating deficits that exacer bate social misunderstandings and interpersonal conflict (Çiray et al., 2022). These challenges are especially pronounced in structured envi ronments such as classrooms, where sustained attention, self-regulation, and cooperation are required. * Corresponding author at: Child Psychology and Education Lab., School of Early Childhood Education, Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, 54124, Thessaloniki, Greece. 1.2. Social skills in children with ADHD: Conceptual framework In the context of the present study, social skills are defined as the set of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral processes that enable children to perceive social information, regulate their responses, and engage in socially appropriate and goal-directed interactions (Elliott & Gresham, 2008). This definition is anchored primarily in the Social Information Processing (SIP) model (Crick & Dodge, 1994), and emotion regulation frameworks, which have been widely applied to understand social dif ficulties in children with ADHD (Eisenberg et al., 2010). According to the SIP model, effective social behavior depends on a sequence of processes, including the encoding of social cues, interpre tation of social intentions, generation of possible responses, and behavioral enactment (Crick & Dodge, 1994). Children with ADHD often exhibit disruptions at multiple stages of this process, particularly in cue interpretation and response selection, due to impulsivity and limitations in executive control (Barkley, 2015). Similarly, emotion regulation models emphasize the role of attentional control and inhibitory pro cesses in managing emotional reactions during social inter actions—domains in which children with ADHD commonly experience deficits (Christiansen et al., 2019). Social skills in children with ADHD are typically assessed using a combination of standardized rating scales completed by parents and teachers, structured behavioral observations, and performance-based tasks that evaluate social problem-solving abilities, emotional under standing, and peer interaction patterns (Gresham et al., 2011). Estab lishing a clear operationalization of social skills is essential for the design, implementation, and evaluation of targeted interventions. 1.3. Educational robotics and augmented reality in general and special education In recent years, educational technologies have gained increasing attention as tools for supporting learning and development in both general and special education contexts. Educational Robotics, in particular, has been shown to actively engage children in the learning process while fostering problem-solving, collaboration, and social interaction (Di Battista et al., 2020; Evripidou et al., 2020). In early childhood education, robotics-based activities have been associated with improvements in cognitive engagement, motivation, and founda tional social skills (Zviel-Girshin et al., 2020). Augmented Reality (AR) complements these approaches by over laying digital elements onto real-world environments, creating interac tive and potentially immersive learning experiences (Lorusso et al., 2018). AR may support attention, emotional engagement, and concep tual understanding, particularly for learners with special educational needs (Dhaas, 2024; Mikropoulos et al., 2020). Importantly, AR envi ronments allow for the visualization and manipulation of social sce narios in a controlled and adaptable manner, thereby facilitating targeted practice of social behaviors. The integration of Educational Robotics with AR has recently emerged as a promising instructional approach, offering multimodal interaction, immediate feedback, and opportunities for repeated prac tice in structured yet engaging contexts (Chen et al., 2020). These fea tures align closely with the learning profiles of children with ADHD, who benefit from predictability, active participation, and reduced cognitive load. 1.4. Contribution of educational robotics in ADHD treatment Non-pharmacological interventions that target social and emotional competencies are strongly recommended for young children with ADHD, particularly in educational settings (Danielson et al., 2018). Educational Robotics has been increasingly explored as a medium for such interventions, as robot-mediated activities can support attention regulation, sustained engagement, and social learning (Fridin & Yaakobi, 2011). Social robots, in particular, provide consistent, non-judgmental interaction partners and can simulate everyday social situations, enabling children with ADHD to practice social behaviors in a safe and structured environment. Research suggests that interactions with robots may facilitate the development of empathy, emotional awareness, and socially appropriate behavior, while also supporting emotion recogni tion and self-regulation (Bakola & Drigas, 2020; Berrezueta-Guzman, Robles-Bykbaev, et al., 2021). By combining Educational Robotics with Augmented Reality, in terventions can further enhance the realism and flexibility of social scenarios, allowing children to engage in meaningful, context-rich in teractions that directly target the social skill deficits associated with ADHD. This integrated technological approach represents a promising avenue for supporting social functioning in children with ADHD and constitutes the central focus of the present study. The purpose of this study is to present a scoping review of the sci entific literature examining the contribution of Educational Robotics and Augmented Reality to the enhancement of social skills in children with ADHD. Specifically, the review aims to identify existing interven tion approaches, describe how they have been implemented, summarize reported outcomes, highlight gaps in the current literature, and propose directions for future research. The study is guided by the following research questions: 1. What types of interventions using Educational Robotics have been implemented to support social skills in children with ADHD, and what outcomes have been reported? 2. What Augmented Reality applications have been used to support social skills in children with ADHD, and what outcomes have been reported? 3. Have any interventions integrated both Educational Robotics and Augmented Reality, and what patterns of reported outcomes emerge from these studies? 2. Methods 2.1. Selection of publications For this study, a scoping review was deemed the most appropriate method to systematically map and analyze the available literature regarding the use of Educational Robotics and Augmented Reality (AR) to enhance social skills in children with ADHD. Scoping reviews are particularly suitable for emerging fields, where research is limited and heterogeneous, allowing the identification of key concepts, research gaps, and directions for future studies (Munn et al., 2018). To ensure a comprehensive and interdisciplinary coverage, the literature search was conducted across seven major databases: Spring erLink, IEEE Xplore, MDPI, ERIC, PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, and PsycINFO. These databases were selected to encompass both educational/technological research and psychological/clinical studies. The search included studies published from 2015 to the present, reflecting the period when Educational Robotics and AR applications in education began to expand significantly. The search was limited to publications in English and Greek. English- language studies were included to ensure international comprehen siveness, while Greek-language studies were intentionally included to capture local research and applications in educational and clinical contexts within Greece. This dual-language approach ensures that the review reflects both global evidence and region-specific insights, which are particularly relevant given that some interventions are developed and tested locally. A systematic search strategy was applied using the following key words: (“Educational Robotics” OR “Social Robotics” OR “Social Assis tive Robotics”) AND (“Augmented Reality”) AND (“Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder” OR “ADHD”) AND (“Social Skills”). strategy yielded 248 articles, which were imported into Mendeley reference management software to identify and remove duplicates. After deduplication, inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied. Inclusion criteria required studies to: (a) involve children with ADHD, (b) inves tigate the use of Educational Robotics and/or AR, (c) target the enhancement of social skills, and (d) be primary research studies pub lished in peer-reviewed journals or conference proceedings. Exclusion criteria ruled out studies: (a) focusing on populations other than chil dren with ADHD, (b) using technologies other than Educational Robotics or AR, (c) being reviews rather than primary research, or (d) involving participants over 18 years old. (See Table 1.) Following these procedures, seven primary studies were included in the final analysis. The PRISMA 2020 framework was applied to ensure transparency and replicability, and a flow diagram (Flow Diagram 1) summarizing the selection process has been included in the manuscript. Detailed reasons for exclusion at each stage of the selection process are summarized in Supplementary Table 1, enhancing transparency and reproducibility of the review. Additionally, a Table 2 summarizing the characteristics of the included studies—including sample size, inter vention type, duration, setting, outcome measures, and key fin dings—was added to facilitate comparison and clarity. 2.2. Data synthesis and analysis Data were analyzed using thematic analysis, which allows flexible and in-depth exploration of qualitative and quantitative findings (Braun & Clarke, 2006). This approach enabled the identification of common patterns, intervention characteristics, psychological mechanisms tar geted, and observed outcomes related to the use of Educational Robotics and AR in children with ADHD. 2.3. Study characteristics and data extraction A standardized data extraction template was used to systematically collect key characteristics of the included studies. These characteristics included sample size, participant demographics, intervention type and setting, duration, outcome measures, and main findings. Only peer- reviewed primary studies were included to ensure methodological rigor. While no formal risk-of-bias or quality appraisal was conducted, the extracted methodological details allow readers to evaluate potential limitations regarding reliability, generalizability, and replicability of the findings. This approach is consistent with the scoping review method ology, which emphasizes mapping and describing existing evidence rather than formal quality assessment. 3. Results The current scoping review analyzed seven primary studies exam ining the use of Educational Robotics (ER) and Augmented Reality (AR) to support social skills in children with ADHD, published from 2015 to the present. Four studies employed ER interventions, while three focused on AR applications. Across the included studies, sample sizes were small (ranging from 1 to 59 participants), the majority of partici pants were male, and interventions were conducted predominantly in therapeutic or alternative settings rather than mainstream classrooms. The outcomes assessed varied across studies and included social skills (e. g., collaboration, communication, emotion recognition), cognitive abilities (e.g., attention, concentration, self-regulation), and behavioral measures (e.g., adherence to rules, motivation for learning). Regarding ER, two studies reported outcomes explicitly related to social skills, such as emotion recognition, positive social behavior, and collaborative engagement (Amato et al., 2021; Berrezueta-Guzman, Pau, et al., 2021). Interaction with social-assistive robots, including the hu manoid Pepper, LEGO WeDo 2.0 kits, the Ozobot robot, and custom- designed robots such as Atent@, provided structured contexts in which children engaged with social behaviors. In these studies, ER provided a predictable and emotionally simpler interface than human interaction, supporting children in practicing social behaviors without fear or anxiety. For example, Amato et al. (2021) reported outcomes related to emotional recognition and engagement in five children interacting with Pepper, while Berrezueta-Guzman, Pau, et al. (2021) observed adherence to tasks and positive behaviors during home-based activities with 12 children using Atent@. The remaining two ER studies primarily targeted cognitive outcomes but also reported secondary social-related outcomes. Fern ́andez-Bata nero et al. (2022) conducted a four-year intervention with a single 11- year-old student using LEGO WeDo 2.0, reporting engagement, atten tion, fine motor skills, logical-mathematical reasoning, and social participation. Similarly, Periba ̃nez et al. (2023) implemented Ozobot activities with nine children with neurodevelopmental disorders (including ADHD, ASD, and DLD), observing engagement, attention, and task-related social interactions. Regarding AR, all three studies primarily focused on cognitive skills but reported social-related outcomes. Avila-Pesantez et al. (2018) applied the AR game ATHYNOS with 11 children aged 7–10 years, reporting outcomes in attention, concentration, frustration tolerance, time management, and social participation during gameplay. Fraggista et al. (2023) evaluated AR-enhanced History lessons with 10 children in a classroom setting, reporting engagement, motivation, attention, and peer interaction. De Luca et al. (2024) developed AR-based serious games on the BRAVO platform, reporting outcomes related to self- regulation, rule adherence, attention, and social-emotional participa tion over a six-month period. No studies were identified that integrated both ER and AR for chil dren with ADHD, highlighting a gap in the literature. Some ER in terventions combined robotics with other technologies, such as Virtual Reality, but these focused on other neurodevelopmental disorders, including Autism Spectrum Disorder (Lled ́o et al., 2024). Across all included studies, several patterns were observed, including small sample sizes, pilot designs, and heterogeneous outcome measures, which limit generalizability. Multiple studies reported engagement, motivation, participation, and social skill–related outcomes; however, these findings are preliminary and context-dependent. Cognitive out comes were often reported alongside social outcomes but were consid ered separately. Interventions mainly occurred outside mainstream educational settings, indicating a need for school-based research to assess ecological validity and practical applicability. A summary table presents the key characteristics of the included studies, including sample size, setting, intervention type, comparison conditions (if any), outcome measures, key reported outcomes, and limitations. This synthesis maps similarities and differences across studies and provides a descriptive overview of the current evidence base regarding interventions for social skills in children with ADHD. In conclusion, the results describe the types of ER and AR in terventions used, the contexts and participants involved, and the out comes reported. Evidence regarding potential effects is preliminary and highly context-dependent, underscoring the need for larger, controlled, and school-based studies, the use of standardized social skills in struments, and systematic examination of long-term outcomes. 4. Discussion The present scoping review examined studies investigating in terventions using Educational Robotics (ER) and Augmented Reality (AR) aimed at supporting social skills in children with ADHD. Seven primary studies were included, four employing ER and three employing AR. Overall, the evidence base is limited and preliminary, reflecting the emerging nature of research in this area. Across the reviewed studies, reported outcomes were related to attention, executive functioning, emotion regulation, social information processing, and social participation. ER interventions were described as providing structured and engaging interactions that enabled children to practice social behaviors, such as turn-taking, cooperation, and emotion recognition, while sus taining attention and focus. AR environments were reported to offer immersive and controllable scenarios, enabling repeated observation and practice of social behaviors in safe, adaptive contexts. Both tech nologies were designed to target cognitive and emotional processes relevant to social competence, supporting children in processing social cues and regulating emotional responses, though the reported findings remain preliminary and context-dependent. However, across the reviewed studies, several common intervention features were identified that may represent the “active ingredients” underlying the reported positive outcomes associated with both ER and AR technologies on social skill development in children with ADHD. Identifying these shared elements is important for understanding po tential mechanisms of change and for informing the design of future interventions, regardless of the specific technology employed. The first “active ingredient” identified is reduced social complexity; both ER and AR interventions simplify the social environment compared to naturalistic human interactions. Robots offer predictable, consistent responses without the subtle and rapidly changing cues characteristic of human communication. Similarly, AR presents controlled social sce narios where variables can be isolated and manipulated. For children with ADHD, who often struggle to process multiple social cues simul taneously due to attentional and executive function deficits (Barkley, 2015), this reduction in complexity may reduce cognitive demands and may allow focused practice on specific skills. The second “active ingredient” relates to the predictability and consistency provided by both technologies. A hallmark of both tech nologies is the delivery of predictable, repeatable interactions. Unlike human partners, whose responses vary based on mood, context, and history, robots and AR systems respond consistently to the same inputs. M. Koukounara and K. Hatzinikolaou Acta Psychologica 266 (2026) 106882 4

This predictability may help reduce anxiety associated with social un certainty and may support the development of stable expectations about interaction sequences, which is a foundation for social learning that may be disrupted in children with ADHD due to difficulties with pattern recognition and anticipation in social contexts (Christiansen et al., 2019). The third “active ingredient” concerns the immediate and consistent feedback provided by both technologies. Both ER and AR interventions typically provide immediate feedback on children's responses, whether through robotic reactions, visual cues, or game-based reward systems. Immediate feedback is particularly important for children with ADHD, who show reduced sensitivity to delayed reinforcement and benefit from proximal consequences that strengthen the association between behavior and outcome (Luman et al., 2005). This feature may support learning by helping to make the connection between social behavior and its effects explicit and timely. The fourth “active ingredient” refers to high engagement through novelty and interactivity ensured by both technologies. The novelty of robots and immersive AR environments may capture and sustain attention, which provides a potential advantage for children with ADHD who struggle with sustained engagement in conventional learning con texts. The interactive nature of both technologies requires active participation rather than passive observation, which may enhance encoding and retention of social skills. Several reviewed studies reported increased motivation, engagement, and willingness to participate when children interacted with ER or AR systems compared to traditional ac tivities (Avila-Pesantez et al., 2018; Fern ́andez-Batanero et al., 2022). The fifth “active ingredient” is the provision of a safe environment for practice and error. Both technologies create low-stakes environments where children can practice social behaviors without fear of negative social consequences. Mistakes made with a robot or in an AR scenario do not result in peer rejection, embarrassment, or damaged relationships. This psychological safety may encourage experimentation and risk- taking that children with ADHD might avoid in real social situations due to histories of negative peer feedback (Meinzer et al., 2021). Repeated practice in such contexts may contribute to building confi dence and automaticity before skills are transferred to more complex real-world interactions. Finally, both technologies can allow controlled pacing and adaptive difficulty. Unlike real-time human interactions that proceed at a pace determined by social partners, both ER and AR allow for pacing that can be adapted to the child's needs. AR systems can pause, repeat, or slow down scenarios, while robotic interactions can be structured to allow processing time. Some interventions also incorporated adaptive diffi culty, adjusting task complexity based on child performance (De Luca et al., 2024). This scaffolding aligns with established principles of skill acquisition and may be particularly supportive for children with ADHD who require additional processing time due to executive function difficulties. These shared features suggest that the potential value of ER and AR interventions may be related not only to the technologies themselves but also to how interventions incorporate these design principles. Future intervention design may benefit from explicitly incorporating these active ingredients, and research should investigate which features are most relevant for different social skill outcomes and for children with varying ADHD presentations. 4.1. Mechanisms linking technology features to social skill outcomes: A theoretical hypothesis To advance understanding beyond descriptive synthesis, we propose conceptual models grounded in Social Information Processing (SIP) theory (Crick & Dodge, 1994) and emotion regulation frameworks (Eisenberg et al., 2010) that illustrate the potential mechanisms through which Educational Robotics and Augmented Reality may support social skills in children with ADHD. These models aim to clarify how each technology targets distinct psychological processes and SIP stages, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for interpreting the reviewed findings and guiding future intervention design. 4.2. Educational robotics pathway Fig. 1 presents the proposed pathway through which ER in terventions may support social skill development. The key features of ER, specifically predictable interaction patterns, embodied physical presence, reduced social complexity, immediate and consistent feed back, and a non-judgmental interaction partner, are hypothesized to influence several psychological mechanisms relevant to social func tioning in children with ADHD. Specifically, interaction with robots may reduce social anxiety by providing a safe practice environment free from the fear of rejection or negative evaluation. The novelty and interactivity of robots may help sustain attention and motivation, addressing core attentional difficulties associated with ADHD. Furthermore, the consistency of robotic re sponses allows for repeated behavioral rehearsal without the unpre dictability inherent in human interaction. From a SIP perspective, ER interventions may primarily support later processing stages, specifically Response Selection and Response Enactment. It should be emphasized that the idea that ER facilitates Response Enactment through embodied interaction remains theoretical and has not been empirically tested in the reviewed studies. Children can practice selecting appropriate social responses and executing social behaviors (e.g., turn-taking, cooperation, verbal communication) with a predictable partner, potentially reducing the cognitive load typically associated with real-time social monitoring. This may allow children to focus on skill execution rather than simultaneously managing the interpretation of rapidly changing social cues. However, ER may provide less direct support for earlier SIP stages (Cue Encoding and Interpreta tion), as robotic interactions, while valuable for practice, do not fully replicate the complexity and subtlety of human social cues. 4.3. Augmented reality pathway Fig. 2 presents the proposed pathway through which AR in terventions may support social skill development. AR technologies offer distinct features, such as immersive visual scenarios, controlled and repeatable practice opportunities, multimodal engagement, real-world overlay, and adaptive difficulty, that may target different psychologi cal mechanisms than ER. AR environments may enhance sustained attention through visual immersion and novelty. Critically, AR allows for controlled exposure to social cues without the time pressure of live interaction, enabling chil dren to practice identifying and interpreting facial expressions, body language, and contextual information at their own pace. AR also pro vides opportunities for emotion regulation practice within safe, simu lated scenarios where the consequences of errors are minimized. From a SIP perspective, AR interventions may primarily support earlier processing stages, namely Cue Encoding, Cue Interpretation, and Response Selection. By presenting social scenarios in a controlled, repeatable format, AR enables observational learning and deliberate practice of cue identification and interpretation. Children can repeat edly view and analyze social situations, potentially supporting the development of schemas for recognizing emotional expressions and so cial intentions. However, AR may provide less direct opportunities for Response Enactment, as the virtual nature of AR interactions limits opportunities for embodied behavioral practice with a physically pre sent social partner. 4.4. Proposed integrated model: Synergistic potential of combined ER and AR interventions The complementary strengths identified above suggest a theoretical M. Koukounara and K. Hatzinikolaou Acta Psychologica 266 (2026) 106882 5

rationale for integrating ER and AR within combined interventions. Fig. 3 presents a proposed integrated model illustrating how such a combination could potentially address the full SIP sequence. In this framework, AR components would target earlier processing stages by providing immersive scenarios for observational learning, cue identification, and interpretation practice. ER components would target later processing stages by offering embodied, interactive opportunities for response selection and behavioral enactment with a predictable ro botic partner. The integration point, namely Response Selection, rep resents a stage where both technologies may contribute, with AR supporting cognitive rehearsal of response options and ER enabling physical practice of selected responses. This integrated approach may offer several potential advantages. First, it provides comprehensive coverage of the SIP sequence, addressing social skill development from initial perception through behavioral execution. Second, multimodal learning—combining visual- observational practice (AR) with embodied-interactive practice (ER)— may reinforce skill acquisition through complementary encoding path ways. Third, scaffolded complexity could be achieved by progressing from AR-based observation and interpretation to ER-based enactment, allowing children to build competence incrementally. However, it is essential to emphasize that this integrated model represents a theoretical hypothesis requiring empirical validation. No studies included in the present review tested combined ER and AR in terventions for children with ADHD. The proposed synergistic effects are extrapolated from the separate mechanisms identified in individual ER and AR studies. Future research should examine whether combined in terventions yield additive or synergistic benefits compared to single- technology approaches, and identify optimal sequencing and dosage of each component. 4.5. Limitations Several limitations were identified across the reviewed studies. Most interventions involved small sample sizes, pilot designs, and, in several cases, the absence of control groups, which limits the reliability and generalizability of findings. The measures employed to assess social skills were heterogeneous, including parent- and teacher-rated Fig. 1. Conceptual Model: Educational Robotics Pathway to Social Skill Enhancement in Children with ADHD. M. Koukounara and K. Hatzinikolaou Acta Psychologica 266 (2026) 106882 6

questionnaires, observational tools, and performance-based tasks, complicating cross-study comparisons. Given the limited number of studies and small sample sizes, the reported outcomes should be inter preted cautiously. The current evidence provides preliminary insights and highlights directions for future research. Additionally, interventions were primarily conducted in therapeutic or alternative settings, with only one study implemented within a mainstream educational context. This limits understanding of the ecological validity and practical applicability of these technologies in typical classroom environments. Furthermore, although combined ER and AR interventions have been proposed as potentially beneficial, no empirical studies have yet tested this integration specifically for children with ADHD. Consequently, claims regarding synergistic effects of ER and AR remain hypothetical, highlighting the need for empirical validation. 4.6. Future research Future research should focus on addressing these limitations through methodologically rigorous designs. Larger, controlled trials with diverse samples are necessary to strengthen the evidence base and allow for more robust conclusions. Employing standardized and validated mea sures of social skills will facilitate cross-study comparisons and ensure reliable assessment of intervention outcomes. Investigating the integration of ER and AR in combined interventions represents a particularly promising avenue, as it may capitalize on the complementary strengths of both technologies to support attention, emotion regulation, and social learning. Furthermore, implementing interventions in mainstream classroom settings is crucial to evaluate feasibility, engagement, and broader educational impact. Longitudinal research is also recommended to examine the sustain ability of cognitive, emotional, and social outcomes over time. By addressing these research gaps, future studies may contribute to the development of more robust, ecologically valid, and scalable in terventions for children with ADHD. Fig. 2.
