5. Conclusion This scoping review synthesizes the current state of research on ER and AR interventions aimed at supporting social skills in children with ADHD. Despite the limited number of studies and the preliminary nature of the evidence, the reviewed studies reported outcomes related to attention, self-regulation, and social functioning. ER interventions were described as providing structured, interactive opportunities for prac ticing social behaviors, while AR was reported to offer immersive, adaptive scenarios that enable rehearsal of social skills in safe and controlled contexts. The review highlights both the characteristics of the interventions and the gaps in the field. Few studies specifically targeted children with ADHD, no empirical research has yet tested combined ER–AR in terventions, and most interventions were conducted outside mainstream classrooms. Additionally, heterogeneity in study designs, outcome measures, and settings limits comparability and generalizability. By framing these interventions within the context of psychological models of social information processing and emotion regulation, this review provides a conceptual foundation for future research and a descriptive overview of intervention characteristics. In conclusion, although research in this area remains at an early stage, the results describe the types of ER and AR interventions imple mented, the contexts and participant characteristics, and the reported outcomes. Evidence regarding potential effects is preliminary and highly context-dependent, highlighting the need for larger, controlled, school- based studies, standardized social skills measures, and systematic investigation of long-term outcomes before drawing conclusions regarding efficacy. metadata_title: The relationship between ADHD, OCD, and problematic social media use
pages: The relationship between ADHD, OCD, and problematic social media use Nazir S. Hawi a, Maya Samaha a,*, Emma Shaffu a a Notre Dame University-Louaize, Zouk Mosbeh, Lebanon A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Problematic social media use Inattentive symptoms Obsessive-compulsive symptoms Social media addiction Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder University students A B S T R A C T Problematic social media use (PSMU) has increasingly been conceptualized as an addiction-like pattern of online engagement characterized by impaired control and continued use despite negative consequences. This cross- sectional study examined whether inattentive symptoms and OCD symptoms were associated with PSMU, and whether inattentive symptoms mediated or moderated the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU, in a sample of 403 Lebanese university students who completed validated self-report measures of all three constructs. Analyses included Pearson correlations, linear regression, and PROCESS-based mediation and moderation models. Inattentive symptoms showed the strongest association with PSMU, and OCD symptoms were indirectly associated with PSMU through inattentive symptoms. Together, OCD symptoms and inattentive symptoms explained 35.98% of the variance in PSMU. Mediation analyses indicated partial mediation of the OCD–PSMU association by inattentive symptoms, whereas moderation analyses provided no evidence that inattentive symptoms altered the strength of the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU. These findings are consistent with the view that attentional dysregulation may represent an important indirect pathway linking OCD symptoms with PSMU. 1. Introduction The marked increase in social media and other digital platforms has reshaped communication, information seeking, and social interaction, while also being accompanied by maladaptive patterns, such as compulsive checking, mood modification, withdrawal-like experiences, and social conflict, that echo key features commonly discussed within behavioral addiction frameworks (Bhukya & Lakshmana, 2025; Wartberg et al., 2025). The rapid proliferation of these platforms has therefore intensified concerns regarding mental health and well-being, particularly among adolescents and emerging adults (Baltaci, 2019; Hawi & Samaha, 2019; Hussain & Griffiths, 2018; Nguyen et al., 2020; Senturk et al., 2021). Recent research emphasizes that adolescents and students may be especially susceptible to problematic social media use (PSMU) given developmental, social, and psychological vulnerabilities (Kang et al., 2025). In addition, solitary online experiences and limited offline social engagement may further increase the risk of problematic use (Pezzi et al., 2024). For some users, social media engagement can shift from routine use to a dysregulated pattern (i.e., PSMU). This behavior is characterized by diminished control, compulsive engagement, and persistent preoccu pation with social platforms, which in turn is associated with functional impairment, distress, and social disruption (B ́anyai et al., 2017; Guazzini et al., 2022). Importantly, high levels of social media use do not necessarily indicate problematic use. Emerging evidence suggests that time spent on social media, in isolation, may not be inherently mal adaptive, and that problematic use is better characterized by impaired control, compulsive engagement, and functional impairment. For example, recent large-scale research indicates that prolonged use may not be associated with negative outcomes when it occurs in the absence of dysregulation or distress. This distinction underscores the importance of focusing on qualitative aspects of use rather than duration alone (Zsila et al., 2026). Consistent with this profile, research associates PSMU with broader personal, interpersonal, and educational/occupational diffi culties, including withdrawal-like experiences and other adverse out comes (Cheng et al., 2021; Hawi & Samaha, 2017; Werling et al., 2022), often driven by distinct cognitive, emotional, and behavioral responses that may undermine well-being (Ansari et al., 2024). Beyond these internalizing symptoms, other psychiatric vulnerabilities have also been linked to dysregulated online social engagement (Griffiths et al., 2024). The potentially compulsive nature of PSMU, often expressed as re petitive, habitual engagement reinforced by immediate social or infor mational rewards (Dolan et al., 2016; Hussain & Shabir, 2020; Whiting & Williams, 2013), has drawn comparisons to other behavioral * Corresponding author at: Notre Dame University-Louaize, Zouk Mosbeh, P.O. addictions (D'Arienzo et al., 2019), highlighting the need to clarify its psychological and clinical correlates. One vulnerability that has received increasing attention is attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by develop mentally inappropriate patterns of inattention and/or hyper activity–impulsivity that interfere with functioning. Evidence suggests that ADHD symptoms are associated with higher susceptibility to PSMU, with adolescents and emerging adults showing heightened emotional and behavioral difficulties that may amplify problematic engagement (Dekkers & van Hoorn, 2022; Shuai et al., 2021). In particular, inattention may be associated with increased vulner ability by undermining sustained attention, task persistence, and self- regulation, which may be associated with increased susceptibility to compulsive checking and difficulty disengaging from rewarding digital environments (Dekkers & van Hoorn, 2022). Consistent with this ac count, multiple studies indicate that inattention is among the strongest predictors of PSMU, associating it with prolonged screen time, diffi culties disengaging from platforms, and excessive online multitasking (Boer et al., 2020; Deasley, 2016; Settanni et al., 2018; Thorell et al., 2024). Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) may add another layer of complexity to understanding PSMU. Characterized by intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviors (compulsions) intended to reduce distress, OCD shares behavioral parallels with PSMU, including compulsive checking, reassurance-seeking, and difficulties regulating use (Guazzini et al., 2022; van Bennekom et al., 2018). Social media platforms, through rapid feedback and intermittent reinforcement, may further maintain these patterns and may be associated with greater vulnerability to PSMU among individuals with elevated anxiety and dependence-prone traits (James et al., 2017; Senturk et al., 2021). Fear of missing out (FOMO) may also intensify repetitive engagement, potentially contributing to fatigue and burnout among individuals with OCD (Fontes-Perryman & Spina, 2022). From this perspective, social media platforms are not viewed as inherently addictive. Rather, problematic use may emerge when these platforms are used to manage underlying psychological distress, thereby reinforcing maladaptive engagement over time (Griffiths, 2005; Hussain & Griffiths, 2018). Within cognitive-behavioral accounts of problematic online behavior, psychopathological vulnerabilities may function as distal risk factors that shape maladaptive cognitions and reinforce dys regulated patterns of use (G ́amez-Guadix et al., 2013, 2012). In this context, inattentive symptoms and OCD symptoms may be especially relevant. Inattention may be associated with greater vulnerability to PSMU through difficulties in sustained attention, self-regulation, and disengagement from salient digital cues (Arness & Ollis, 2023; Dekkers & van Hoorn, 2022; Liu et al., 2024), whereas OCD symptoms may be associated with repetitive checking, reassurance-seeking, and compul sive patterns of online engagement (Fontes-Perryman & Spina, 2022; van Bennekom et al., 2018). Despite growing evidence linking both inattentive symptoms and OCD symptoms to problematic online behaviors (Arness & Ollis, 2023; Fontes-Perryman & Spina, 2022; Liu et al., 2024), the nature of their joint association with PSMU remains insufficiently understood. In particular, it remains unclear whether inattentive symptoms operate primarily as an indirect pathway through which OCD symptoms are associated with PSMU, as a vulnerability factor that changes the strength of that association, or both. Addressing this question may help clarify the cognitive and clinical correlates of PSMU among university students (Awad et al., 2022; Fekih-Romdhane et al., 2024). University students represent a particularly relevant population for examining problematic social media use, as emerging adulthood is characterized by increased autonomy, academic demands, and heightened reliance on digital communication (Nguyen et al., 2020; Whiting & Williams, 2013). In the Lebanese context, where social media platforms play an important role in communication and information exchange, and maintaining social connections, these behaviors are highly integrated into students' daily lives (Awad et al., 2022; Fekih-Romdhane et al., 2024). Prior research among Lebanese university students has also reported elevated technology-related addictive behaviors, including excessive social media use (Samaha & Hawi, 2016), and has linked these behaviors with psychological and behavioral difficulties (Sabbah et al., 2019). Accordingly, examining the psychological correlates of PSMU in Leb anese university students may contribute to a more contextually grounded understanding of problematic digital engagement. Accordingly, the present study examined the association between inattentive symptoms, OCD symptoms, and PSMU among Lebanese university students. First, it was expected that higher levels of inatten tive symptoms would be positively associated with PSMU (H1). Second, it was hypothesized that inattentive symptoms would partially mediate the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU, such that higher OCD symptom severity would be associated with greater inattentive symptoms, which in turn would be associated with higher PSMU (H2). Third, it was hypothesized that inattentive symptoms would moderate the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU, such that the asso ciation between OCD symptoms and PSMU would be stronger at higher levels of inattention (H3). To test these hypotheses, mediation and moderation analyses were conducted using the PROCESS macro for SPSS. In doing so, the study examined whether inattentive symptoms functioned more strongly as an indirect pathway or as a moderator of the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU. Clarifying these relationships may contribute to a more precise understanding of the psychological factors associated with problematic social media use in student populations. 2. Method 2.1. Participants and procedure The present study employed a cross-sectional, online survey design to examine the relationships among OCD symptoms, ADHD symptoms, and PSMU among a sample of Lebanese university students. Approval for the study was obtained from the university institutional review board (IRB Reference number: IRB 202428). Participants were recruited via convenience sampling using mailing lists and social media platforms between December 2024 and January 2025. Before starting the survey, participants were given an overview of the study's purpose and assur ances of confidentiality and anonymity regarding data collection, stor age, and reporting. All participants provided written informed consent to participate in the study before being given access to the survey. A total of 403 undergraduate students from a private university completed the survey (Mage = 20.11 years, SD = 1.83), with ages ranging from 18 to 26 years. The sample included students from sophomore to senior year. The sample size was determined using an a priori power analysis conducted in G*Power 3.1 for multiple linear regression. Assuming a medium effect size (f2 = 0.15), α = 0.05, power = 0.95, and 3 predictors, the minimum required sample size was 119. The final sample of 403 participants exceeded this requirement. Of the 403 par ticipants, 181 were female (44.9%) and 222 were male (55.1%). Par ticipants were recruited from a range of broad academic disciplines. Typically, participants completed the survey within 25 min. No missing data were observed for age or gender. 2.2. Measures The survey comprised four sections: demographic questions, PSMU assessment, OCD assessment, and ADHD assessment. The demographic section collected data on age and gender. PSMU was assessed using the eight-item Social Media Addiction Questionnaire (SMAQ; Hawi & Samaha, 2017). Items (e.g., “I have been unable to reduce my use of social media”) are rated on a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). Following the standard SMAQ scoring procedure, items endorsed at the threshold level (ratings of 6 or 7) were coded as 1, with Items 1 and 2 contributing N.S. Hawi et al. Acta Psychologica 267 (2026) 107134 2

a maximum combined score of 1 and Items 4 and 5 contributing a maximum combined score of 1, yielding a total score range of 0 to 6. In the present study, PSMU was operationalized as this threshold-scored SMAQ total, with higher scores indicating greater problematic social media use. Although a total score of 5 or 6 is used to indicate probable social media addiction, this classification was used only for descriptive purposes. The continuous SMAQ total score was used in all correlational, regression, mediation, and moderation analyses. The SMAQ demon strated very good internal consistency in the present study (Cronbach's α = 0.851; McDonald's ω = 0.844). ADHD symptoms were assessed using the 18-item Adult ADHD Self- Report Scale (ASRS-v1.1), developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) based on DSM-IV criteria (American Psychiatric Association, 2000; Kessler et al., 2005). The ASRS assesses core ADHD symptoms, specifically inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity, among adult populations (Kessler et al., 2007). Although the scale is not intended for diagnostic purposes, the ASRS serves as a validated screening instru ment for identifying individuals whose symptom patterns may warrant further clinical evaluation. The ASRS-v1.1 comprises two subscales: the Inattention subscale and the Hyperactivity/Impulsivity subscale. The nine-item Inattention subscale assesses inattentive symptoms (i.e., self- reported attentional difficulties), including difficulties related to sus tained attention, organization, and concentration. Items (e.g., “How often are you distracted by activity or noise around you?”) are scored dichotomously (0 or 1), with total scores ranging from 0 to 9. The nine- item Hyperactivity/Impulsivity subscale assesses motor symptoms (five items) and verbal impulsivity (four items). Items (e.g., “How often do you interrupt others when they are busy?”) are also scored dichotomously (0 or 1), with total scores ranging from 0 to 9. Scoring followed the standard ASRS scoring procedure, whereby each item was assigned either 0 or 1. For Items 1–3, 9, 12, 16, and 18, responses of “sometimes”, “often,” or “very often” were scored as 1, whereas “never” or “rarely” were scored as 0. For the remaining items, only “often” or “very often” were scored as 1, and “never”, “rarely” or “sometimes” were scored as 0. In the present study, the ASRS Inattention subscale was used to assess inattentive symptoms dimensionally in a non-clinical sample and was analyzed as a continuous symptom variable. Although ASRS subscale scores can be used for screening purposes, screening classifications were not used in the inferential analyses. The ASRS-v1.1 demonstrated very good internal consistency in the present study (Cronbach's α = 0.855; McDonald's ω = 0.852). OCD symptoms were assessed using the 18-item Obsessive- Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI-R) (Foa et al., 2002). The scale comprises six dimensions common to OCD: checking, ordering, neutralizing, washing, obsessing, and hoarding. Items (e.g., “I check things more often than necessary”) are rated on a five-point Likert scale from 0 (Not at all) to 4 (Extremely), with total scores ranging from 0 to 72. In the present study, OCD symptoms were analyzed as a continuous total OCI-R score, with higher scores indicating greater obsessive- compulsive symptom severity. Although a cutoff score has been pro posed in prior research for screening purposes, the continuous total score was used in all inferential analyses. The OCI-R demonstrated very good internal consistency in the present study (Cronbach's α = 0.884; McDonald's ω = 0.881). 2.3. Data analysis Data analysis was conducted using SPSS (Version 27), except for McDonald's omega, which was calculated using R (Version 4.4.2) and the psych package to assess the internal consistency of the OCI-R, ASRS- v1.1, and SMAQ. Descriptive statistics were computed for demographic characteristics and study variables. Pearson's correlation coefficients were used to assess the associations among OCD symptoms, inattentive symptoms, and PSMU. All inferential analyses treated PSMU as a continuous outcome variable, operationalized as the threshold-scored SMAQ total score (range = 0–6), and treated inattentive symptoms as a continuous variable, operationalized as the ASRS Inattention subscale total score. OCD symptoms were operationalized as the continuous total OCI-R score. No demographic covariates were included in the inferential models. A simple linear regression analysis was conducted to examine whether inattentive symptoms were associated with PSMU. Mediation and moderation analyses were conducted using the PROCESS macro for SPSS (Version 5.0). PROCESS Model 4 was used to test whether inat tentive symptoms mediated the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU. PROCESS Model 1 was used to test whether inattentive symp toms moderated the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU by including the product term between OCD symptoms and inattentive symptoms. For the moderation analysis, conditional effects were examined at low, moderate, and high levels of inattentive symptoms (values of 1.0, 4.0, and 6.0, respectively). Indirect effects were estimated using bias-corrected bootstrapping with 5000 resamples, and statistical significance was determined using 95% confidence intervals that did not include zero. Unstandardized regression coefficients, standard errors, p values, and confidence intervals were reported for the regression-based analyses. Prior to conducting the regression-based analyses, assumptions relevant to linear regression were evaluated. Linearity between the predictor variables and PSMU was assessed through visual inspection of scatterplots. Homoscedasticity was examined by inspecting plots of standardized residuals against standardized predicted values. Normality was evaluated by examining the distribution of standardized residuals and normal probability plots. Multicollinearity between OCD symptoms and inattentive symptoms was assessed using tolerance and variance inflation factor values. Because mediation effects were estimated using bias-corrected bootstrapping with 5000 resamples, inference for the indirect effect did not rely on the assumption of normality of the sam pling distribution of the indirect effect. Missing data were handled using listwise deletion, with participants who had missing values on any study variable excluded from the relevant analyses. 3. Results 3.1. For descriptive purposes, 36.70% of participants screened positive for OCD symptoms (OCI-R ≥28), 29.31% screened positive for ADHD symptoms (ASRS Total score ≥9), and 8.00% met the cutoff for probable PSMU (SMAQ ≥5). Scores on the ASRS Inattention subscale (M = 3.60, SD = 2.26) were higher than scores on the ASRS Hyperactivity/ Impulsivity subscale (M = 2.75, SD = 2.21). In addition, 28.78% of participants met the screening threshold for inattention (≥5), compared with 20.54% for hyperactivity/impulsivity (≥5). Pearson product-moment correlations among the continuous study variables are presented in Table 2. PSMU was positively correlated with OCD symptoms and with overall ADHD symptoms and all ADHD sub scales. Among the ADHD-related variables, the strongest correlation with PSMU was observed for inattentive symptoms. OCD symptoms were also positively correlated with overall ADHD symptoms and all ADHD subscales, with the strongest association observed for inattentive symptoms. Although inattentive symptoms showed the strongest correlation with PSMU, motor and verbal impulsivity symptoms were also positively associated with PSMU. This indicates that broader ADHD-related symptom dimensions may also be relevant. 3.2. Regression analysis Given the strongest correlation between PSMU and inattentive symptoms in Table 2, a simple linear regression analysis was conducted to examine whether inattentive symptoms were associated with PSMU. The model was statistically significant, F(1, 401) = 216.509, p < .001, explaining 35.1% of the variance in PSMU (R2 = 0.351, adjusted R2 = 0.349). Higher inattention scores were associated with higher PSMU scores, B = 0.428, SE = 0.029, β = 0.592, t = 14.714, p < .001 (see Table 3). 3.3. Mediation analysis Mediation analysis using the PROCESS macro (Model 4) examined whether inattentive symptoms mediated the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU (Table 4). OCD symptoms were significantly associated with inattentive symptoms (B = 0.0691, p < .001, 95% CI [0.0533, 0.0849]), accounting for 15.56% of the variance in inattentive symptoms (R2 = 0.1556). In the outcome model, OCD symptoms and inattentive symptoms jointly explained 35.98% of the variance in PSMU (R2 = 0.3598). The direct effect of OCD symptoms on PSMU was statistically sig nificant but small (B = 0.0130, p = .0188). In addition, inattentive symptoms were significantly associated with PSMU (B = 0.3987, p < .001), and the indirect effect of OCD symptoms on PSMU through inattentive symptoms was significant (B = 0.0276, 95% CI [0.0194, 0.0358]), indicating partial mediation (Fig. 1). The total effect of OCD symptoms on PSMU was 0.0406, with approximately 68% of the total effect represented by the indirect pathway through inattention. Overall, this pattern is consistent with a statistically significant indirect associ ation between OCD symptoms and PSMU through inattentive symptoms. Multicollinearity diagnostics for the outcome model indicated no evidence of problematic collinearity between OCD symptoms and inat tentive symptoms, with VIF values of 1.21 and tolerance values of 0.83 for both predictors. To further examine the robustness of the mediation findings to demographic variation, we re-estimated the mediation model while including gender as a covariate in both the mediator and outcome equations. The adjusted model showed that OCD symptoms remained significantly associated with inattentive symptoms (b = 0.071, 95% bootstrap CI [0.056, 0.087], p < .001), and inattentive symptoms remained significantly associated with problematic social media use (b = 0.316, 95% bootstrap CI [0.243, 0.383], p < .001). The indirect effect of OCD symptoms on problematic social media use through inattentive symptoms remained significant after adjustment for gender (b = 0.023, 95% bootstrap CI [0.016, 0.030], p < .001), while the direct effect remained small but statistically significant (b = 0.012, 95% bootstrap CI [0.001, 0.024], p = .043). Gender was not a significant covariate for inattentive symptoms (b = 0.066, p = .784) or problematic social media use (b = 0.126, p = .335). These findings indicate that the observed mediation pattern was robust to adjustment for gender. 3.4. Moderation analysis The moderation analysis examined whether inattentive symptoms moderated the relationship between OCD symptoms and PSMU (Table 5). The overall model was significant (R2 = 0.3598, p < .001), indicating that approximately 36% of the variance in PSMU was explained by the predictors. Consistent with prior analyses, inattentive symptoms showed a significant association with PSMU (B = 0.3772, p < .001). However, neither the main effect of OCD symptoms (B = 0.0096, p = .3406) nor the interaction effect (OCD × inattentive symptoms) was significant (B = 0.0009, p = .6871). The non-significant interaction indicated that inattentive symptoms did not moderate the OCD-PSMU relationship (i.e., the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU did not vary across levels of inattention). Taken together, these findings indicate that while inattentive symptoms were a significant predictor of PSMU, they did not alter the strength of the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU. Thus, the moderation hypothesis was not supported. Table 2 Pearson product-moment correlation coefficients between research variables. 4. Discussion The present study examined the associations among inattentive symptoms, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and problematic social media use (PSMU) in a sample of Lebanese university students. Three main findings emerged. First, inattentive symptoms were strongly associated with PSMU. Second, inattentive symptoms partially mediated the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU. Third, no evidence was found for a moderating effect of inattentive symptoms on the OCD–PSMU association. Taken together, these findings are most consistent with a partial mediation model in which attentional dysre gulation may represent a potential pathway linking obsessive- compulsive symptomatology with problematic social media use. These findings suggest that the association between OCD symptoms and problematic social media use may operate, in part, through atten tional processes. Individuals with higher levels of obsessive-compulsive symptoms may experience greater difficulties in attentional control and disengagement, which may be associated with increased vulnerability to repetitive and cue-driven patterns of social media engagement. In contrast, the absence of a moderating effect indicates that inattention does not amplify the strength of the OCD-PSMU association across different levels of symptom severity but may instead function as a pathway through which this association is expressed. The present findings also have tentative applied implications. Attentional difficulties and obsessive-compulsive tendencies may be associated with increased vulnerability to problematic social media use, suggesting that interventions targeting attentional regulation, cognitive flexibility, and compulsivity-related processes may be relevant. Ap proaches such as cognitive-behavioral and mindfulness-based in terventions, along with digital well-being strategies (e.g., structured screen-time management), may therefore be worth examining in future research. In addition to reducing problematic use, emerging research highlights the importance of promoting adaptive forms of so cial media engagement, such as mindful use. Mindful engagement em phasizes intentional, present-focused interaction with digital platforms and has been associated with improved well-being and lower levels of compulsive use patterns (Shabahang et al., 2024). These approaches may complement interventions focused solely on reducing usage. However, these implications should be interpreted cautiously, as the present study did not directly examine intervention effects. Inattentive symptoms showed the strongest association with PSMU, supporting H1. However, the significant correlations between PSMU and the motor and verbal impulsivity subscales indicate that impulsivity- related symptoms may also contribute to problematic social media use. These associations may reflect difficulties inhibiting urges to check social media, respond to notifications, or disengage from immediately rewarding online cues. Therefore, the present findings should not be interpreted as excluding the role of impulsivity. Rather, future research should examine inattentive and impulsivity-related symptoms simulta neously to clarify their unique and shared contributions to PSMU. Consistent with prior research, the strong association between inatten tion and PSMU may reflect difficulties in self-regulation, sustained attention, and disengagement from salient digital cues (Arness & Ollis, 2023; Werling et al., 2022). The pattern of findings also suggests that the association between ADHD-related symptoms and PSMU may be more strongly linked to inattention-related processes than to broader ADHD symptomatology. The observed association between inattentive symptoms and PSMU also provides context for the mediation findings involving OCD symp toms. Supporting H2, inattentive symptoms partially mediated the as sociation between OCD symptoms and PSMU, suggesting that attentional processes may play a role in linking obsessive-compulsive symptomatology with problematic social media use. This interpreta tion is consistent with executive dysfunction accounts, which propose that individuals with elevated OCD symptoms may experience diffi culties in cognitive control, attentional disengagement, and the regula tion of repetitive or habit-driven responses. In digital contexts, such difficulties may contribute to more persistent checking and greater dif ficulty disengaging from reinforcing social media cues, which may in turn be associated with PSMU (Abramovitch et al., 2019). These supplementary analyses strengthen confidence in the robust ness of the mediation findings. First, the low VIF and high tolerance values indicate that the observed associations were not attributable to problematic multicollinearity between OCD symptoms and inattentive symptoms. Second, the indirect pathway from OCD symptoms to prob lematic social media use through inattentive symptoms remained sig nificant after adjusting for gender, while gender itself was not a significant covariate in the model. This pattern suggests that the medi ating role of inattentive symptoms is substantive rather than an artifact of demographic variation. The subgroup analyses were consistent with this interpretation, as the indirect effect was evident in both males and females, although the residual direct association appeared more pro nounced in males. In the present study, approximately 68% of the total association between OCD symptoms and PSMU was represented by the mediated association through inattentive symptoms. These findings suggest that attentional processes may account for a substantial portion of this as sociation. vulnerability to repetitive, cue-driven online behaviors, which may be associated with greater difficulty regulating problematic social media use. In turn, problematic online engagement may become negatively reinforced as a maladaptive coping response to distress and may contribute to the maintenance of PSMU over time (Choudhury & Ali, 2020; Ioannidis et al., 2018; Thorell et al., 2024). By modeling inat tentive symptoms as a mediator, the present study offers a more nuanced perspective on the associations among OCD symptoms, inattention, and PSMU. However, contrary to H3, inattentive symptoms did not moder ate the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU, indicating that the strength of this relationship did not vary significantly across levels of inattention. Thus, although inattention was strongly associated with PSMU, it did not function as a risk amplifier of the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU. In addition to the mediation findings, the regression-based analyses indicated that inattentive symptoms were consistently associated with PSMU across models. The proportion of explained variance ranged from 15.56% in the model predicting inattentive symptoms to 35.98% in the model predicting PSMU from OCD symptoms and inattentive symptoms. Taken together, these findings suggest that inattention is more relevant to the OCD-PSMU association as a mediator than as a moderator. More specifically, OCD symptoms showed a small but significant direct asso ciation with PSMU, while a larger portion of the overall association was represented by the indirect association through inattentive symptoms. This pattern is broadly consistent with prior research linking obsessive- compulsive symptoms, attentional difficulties, and problematic online behaviors, including findings relating OCD symptoms to fear of missing out and digital fatigue, and ADHD symptoms to emotional dysregulation and addictive online behaviors (Fontes-Perryman & Spina, 2022; Liu et al., 2024). Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the pre sent findings. First, the sample consisted of Lebanese university students from a private university, which may limit the generalizability of the results to other cultural, demographic, or educational contexts. Second, all variables were assessed using self-report measures, which may be influenced by recall bias and social desirability. Although gender was collected as a demographic variable, the study did not assess sexual orientation, gender identity beyond the available response categories, or LGBTQ status. This limits the ability to examine whether patterns of PSMU differ across diverse gender and sexual identity groups. Future research should include more inclusive demographic measures to better understand these potentially important differences. Third, OCD and inattentive symptoms were operationalized as continuous dimensions rather than clinical diagnoses, which constrains the applicability of the findings to clinical populations. Fourth, de mographic covariates were not initially included in the inferential models, and thus the possibility of residual confounding cannot be ruled out. Finally, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference and limits conclusions regarding the directionality of the observed associations. Future research should adopt longitudinal and multi-method ap proaches to clarify the temporal ordering and underlying mechanisms linking OCD symptoms, inattentive symptoms, and problematic social media use (PSMU). Additionally, examining contextual moderators, such as peer influences, platform-specific features, and broader aspects of the digital environment, may provide a more nuanced understanding of these relationships, particularly within emerging adult populations. Incorporating comorbid conditions, including anxiety and depression, may further enhance understanding of the broader psychological context in which these variables interact. 5. Conclusion The present study suggests that inattentive symptoms may represent a theoretically informed indirect pathway statistically linking OCD symptoms with problematic social media use (PSMU), with approximately 68% of the total association between OCD symptoms and PSMU represented by the indirect pathway through inattention. Overall, the findings are consistent with the view that OCD symptoms are asso ciated with PSMU partly through attentional dysregulation, alongside a smaller direct association. Contrary to H3, inattentive symptoms did not moderate this relationship, indicating that the association between OCD symptoms and PSMU did not vary significantly across levels of inat tention. Taken together, these findings highlight the potential relevance of attentional regulation and compulsivity-related processes in under standing problematic social media use. Future research should use lon gitudinal and multi-method designs to clarify temporal ordering and causal direction, and should also examine the roles of psychiatric co morbidity and demographic factors in shaping these associations. metadata_title: Cognitive behavioral therapy effects on global functioning, domain-specific functioning, and quality of life in adult ADHD: A comprehensive meta-analysis
pages: Cognitive behavioral therapy effects on global functioning, domain-specific functioning, and quality of life in adult ADHD: A comprehensive meta-analysis Carlos L ́opez-Pinar a , Benjamin Selaskowski b, Marcel Schulze c, Martin Oscarsson d, Javier Fenollar-Cort ́es a, Margaret H. Sibley e, Alexandra Philipsen c, Tatja Hirvikoski f,* a Department of Psychology, European University of Valencia, Valencia, Spain b Institute for Network Stimulation, Department of Stereotactic and Functional Neurosurgery, University Hospital Cologne, Germany c Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, University of Bonn, Bonn, Germany d Department of Psychology, Stockholm University, Stockholm, Sweden e Department of Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences, University of Washington School of Medicine, Seattle, United States f Center of Neurodevelopmental Disorders at Karolinska Institutet (KIND), Center for Psychiatry Research, Department of Women's and Children's Health, Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Cognitive behavioral therapy Adult ADHD Functional impairment Quality of life Meta-analysis A B S T R A C T Background: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for adult ADHD provides adaptive coping strategies targeting executive dysfunction and emotion regulation, processes underlying functional impairment. However, most research has prioritized symptom reduction over functional outcomes. This meta-analysis quantified CBT effects on global functioning, quality of life (QoL), and domain-specific functioning (social, occupational, educational), while examining moderators and the role of ADHD symptom change. Method: We included 70 studies (5152 participants): 38 RCTs, four non-randomized trials, 24 single-arm trials, and four single-case designs. Random-effects meta-analyses estimated standardized mean differences for between-group and within-subject outcomes at post-treatment and follow-up. Risk of bias was formally assessed, and GRADE assessed evidence certainty. Results: CBT produced moderate effects on global functioning at post-treatment (SMD = 0.47) that increased at follow-up (SMD = 0.67). QoL effects were smaller and non-significant at follow-up. Strongest effects were found for occupational functioning, effects on social functioning were moderate, and academic benefits were limited. Individual format and longer duration were associated with better outcomes. ADHD symptom improvement predicted QoL but not functioning. Conclusions: CBT was associated with improvements in functioning (often the primary treatment concern), with moderate effects observed at post-treatment and some evidence of sustained effects at follow-up, particularly in directly targeted domains. The dissociation between symptom change, QoL, and functioning suggests that functional gains may not be fully explained by symptom reduction alone, although the mechanisms underlying these effects remain unclear. These findings support a more process-oriented perspective on CBT, while high lighting the potential relevance of directly targeting everyday functioning within psychological interventions. Risk of bias, self-report reliance, Western sample concentration, and short follow-ups (typically 3 months) warrant cautious interpretation. 1. Introduction Attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neuro developmental disorder characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with func tioning (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). It often persists into adulthood, affecting approximately 3% of adults (Popit et al., 2024). Its main clinical characteristics are symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, * Corresponding author. and/or impulsivity that cause functional impairment in important areas of life, reflecting disruptions in the psychological processes that regulate goal-directed behavior. Beyond these core symptoms, emotional dysre gulation is increasingly recognized as a central feature of adult ADHD and one of the symptoms that causes the most functional impairment (Beheshti et al., 2020). Moreover, it often co-occurs with other psychi atric disorders, including anxiety, depression, and substance use disor ders, among others (Choi et al., 2022). Additionally, it is significantly associated with a wide range of somatic conditions, including obesity, sleep disorders, asthma, and metabolic diseases (Libutzki et al., 2024). 1.1. Functional impairment and quality of life in adults diagnosed with ADHD This clinical presentation is characterized not only by a broad range of core symptoms but also by marked impairment in everyday func tioning (Cherkasova et al., 2022; Kosheleff et al., 2023). In fact, this impairment is often the main reason for consultation in adults rather than the ADHD symptoms per se (CADDRA, 2020). These symptoms also affect specific domains, including educational (DuPaul et al., 2021), occupational (Holst & Thorell, 2020), and social/familial (French et al., 2024) functioning, among others. In the academic domain, ADHD in adulthood has been linked with lower grade point averages (GPAs, Gormley et al., 2019), less frequent use of study skills (DuPaul et al., 2021), a lower academic level (Holst & Thorell, 2020), and a higher risk of educational dropout (Uchida et al., 2018). Regarding occupational functioning, adults diagnosed with ADHD are at an increased risk of having lower work performance (French et al., 2024), unemployment (Uchida et al., 2018), being fired (Fuermaier et al., 2021), and more frequent job changes (Helgesson et al., 2023). Regarding social and fa milial functioning, adult ADHD has been linked to smaller social net works, with fewer family members and friends (Holst & Thorell, 2020; Michielsen et al., 2015), as well as greater feelings of loneliness (Kosheleff et al., 2023), lower emotional connectedness (Montejo et al., 2019), and difficulties in establishing and maintaining friendships and achieving intimacy with others (French et al., 2024). Another relevant finding is that social network size has been shown to moderate the relationship between ADHD symptoms and functional impairment, with larger networks providing a protective effect (Reeble et al., 2023). Regarding sex differences, emerging evidence suggests that men diag nosed with ADHD may experience greater impairment in educational functioning, while women may experience greater impairment in social functioning (Faheem et al., 2022). Additionally, stronger predictors of functional impairment in adulthood include the persistence of ADHD symptoms from childhood and the presence of comorbidities (Cherkasova et al., 2022). The quality of life (QoL) is significantly and negatively affected by symptoms and diagnosis of ADHD in adulthood, even when controlling for other demographic variables (French et al., 2024; Orm et al., 2023). This impact persists over time (Agnew-Blais et al., 2018). QoL captures an individual's perceived subjective well-being in their context (World Health Organization, 1995). In contrast, functional impairment refers to more objective limitations in life domains such as education, work, or social relationships. Reduced QoL applies not only to adults with a formal ADHD diagnosis, but also to those presenting with subclinical ADHD symptoms (Adamis et al., 2024). All dimensions of QoL (e.g., health-related, physical, emotional, and social QoL) are affected in adults with ADHD (Krauss & Schellenberg, 2022). It seems that higher comorbidities increase the risk of having a reduced QoL (Quintero et al., 2019). Furthermore, the QoL of friends and family members of in dividuals with ADHD is decreased as well (Zeides Taubin et al., 2024). Overall, the need for effective evidence-based treatments and rigorous evaluation of their impact on broader functional outcomes beyond the core symptoms is underscored by these functional impairments and reduced QoL in adults with ADHD. 1.2. Treatment of QoL and functioning in adults with ADHD Both pharmacotherapy—primarily stimulant medication—and psy chotherapy, particularly cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), have been shown to improve core symptoms and comorbidities in adults with ADHD (Ostinelli et al., 2025). However, despite their clinical relevance, functional and QoL outcomes are often understudied, underreported, and overshadowed by symptom outcomes in ADHD clinical trials (Young et al., 2017). Since adults with ADHD present more negative automatic thoughts (Knouse et al., 2019) and greater behavioral avoidance (Torrente et al., 2014), CBT targets maladaptive cognitions and provides behavioral compensatory skills to address executive dysfunction (Ramsay, 2010), focusing on domain-specific functional impairment rather than core symptoms reduction. Additionally, third-wave behavioral approaches (e.g., acceptance and commitment therapy, mindfulness, and dialectical behavior therapy [DBT]) com plement and broaden goals beyond symptom reduction toward valued-focused behaviors (Champ et al., 2021), which may further improve QoL and functioning. Despite this theoretical rationale, the evidence base for CBT's impact on functional outcomes and QoL remains limited and methodologically heterogeneous. Coghill et al. (2017) found that effect sizes (ESs) were larger for stimulants than non-stimulants and for core symptoms than for QoL and functioning. Several meta-analytic reviews have explored CBT effects on functional outcomes. Knouse et al. (2017) found mod erate post-treatment effects compared to controls on global functioning, which increased to moderate-to-large at follow-up according to L ́opez-Pinar et al. (2018). Other meta-analyses reported improvements in specific functioning domains, such as occupational (Lauder et al., 2024) and social functioning, even when delivered online (Shou et al., 2022). Moreover, combined CBT and pharmacotherapy may be more effective than pharmacotherapy alone for improving social functioning (Li & Zhang, 2024). Regarding QoL, Liu et al. (2023) found small-to-moderate effects at post-treatment, and L ́opez-Pinar et al. (2020) reported that these effects were sustained at follow-up. Zhang et al. (2025) reported similar findings for variants such as DBT. However, previous reviews present several limitations, such as the inclusion of heterogeneous psychosocial interventions beyond CBT, focused exclusively on specific variants such as DBT, or examined only comparisons with pharmacotherapy. Notably, none comprehensively examined CBT effects on both QoL and functional impairment across specific functioning domains, limiting the clinical picture available to inform practice. Furthermore, given the substantial growth of the evi dence base in recent years, previous reviews may have omitted a sig nificant number of more recent studies. Overall, while research has largely focused on symptom improvement, existing findings suggest that CBT may benefit this population by improving functioning and QoL. Nevertheless, symptom reduction provides only an indirect indicator of change in everyday behavioral functioning, underscoring the need for a comprehensive synthesis focused on functional outcomes. 1.3. The present study Functional impairment and QoL are central to the everyday chal lenges faced by adults with ADHD, yet research and previous reviews have largely focused on core and comorbid symptoms, often overlooking these broader outcomes. As a result, the field lacks a comprehensive understanding of how CBT influences real-world functioning, the mechanisms through which these changes may occur, and which treat ment characteristics optimize functional outcomes. Addressing this gap requires moving beyond symptom-based evaluations toward a function- centered perspective that can inform both clinical decision-making and theoretical models of impairment. Accordingly, examining functional outcomes offers a unique opportunity to clarify how psychological in terventions translate into real-world behavioral change in adult ADHD. The present study addresses this gap by: (1) quantitatively C. L ́opez-Pinar et al. Behaviour Research and Therapy 201 (2026) 105026 2

synthesizing the existing literature on the efficacy of CBT interventions in improving functional impairment and QoL in adults with ADHD; (2) examining the effects on specific domains of functioning (social, occu pational and educational); (3) exploring how sample and study char acteristics moderate these effects and may reveal underlying treatment processes; and (4) examining whether improvements in core ADHD symptoms predict changes in functional outcomes. 2. Method This review was pre-registered in PROSPERO (CRD42024590094) and conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines (Page et al., 2021). No funding was received from public, commercial, or nonprofit sources. The PRISMA checklist, the full screening and selection process, the codebook, and the extracted data can be found in the Open Science Framework (OSF) associated link. 2.1. Eligibility criteria Studies were included if they met the following criteria: • Participants: Adults (≥18 years) formally diagnosed with ADHD according to DSM-5 or ICD-11 criteria, by the research team or a community clinic, or reporting clinically elevated ADHD symptoms on validated ADHD symptom measures. Both formally diagnosed participants and those with clinically elevated ADHD symptoms were included to maximize the comprehensiveness of the review and capture the full breadth of available evidence in the field; subgroup analyses comparing these two groups were conducted to examine whether diagnosis status moderated treatment effects. Comorbidities (e.g., substance use disorder, depression, anxiety disorders, high- functioning autism) were allowed. • Intervention: Eligible interventions included any structured psy chological treatment grounded in behavioral or cognitive-behavioral principles, encompassing second-wave CBT (e.g., cognitive restruc turing, metacognitive therapy), third-wave approaches (e.g., mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, dialectical behavior therapy), and psychoeducation programs explicitly aimed at developing cognitive or behavioral skills. All eligible interventions were required to explicitly introduce at least one specific cognitive or behavioral skill and to be adapted to the needs of adults with ADHD. These intervention types were subsumed under the CBT umbrella given their shared theoretical foundations in behavioral and cogni tive principles (Hofmann & Asmundson, 2008). The intervention could be delivered alone or in combination with pharmacotherapy. • Control: For RCTs, at least one arm did not receive a CBT-based intervention and therefore served as a control group. Controls could be active (e.g., other psychological treatment, medication alone, support groups, treatment as usual) or inactive (e.g., waitlist, no intervention). RCTs in which all arms received CBT were also eligible for within-subject analyses. • Outcomes: Studies reported a measure of functional impairment and/or QoL, assessed by self-report (e.g., Sheehan Disability Scale, AAQoL) or by clinician/researcher rating. • Study design: To provide a comprehensive synthesis of the litera ture, eligible designs included randomized controlled trials, single- arm trials, and single-case designs. Between-group and within- subject analyses were conducted and reported separately to distin guish controlled from uncontrolled treatment effects. Only articles published in peer-reviewed journals in English, German, Swedish, Dutch, or Spanish were considered. Language restrictions were applied based on the languages natively spoken by or proficient to the research team. 2.2. Information sources and search strategy We conducted the primary search in MedLine (via PubMed), Scopus, and PsycInfo, without date restrictions. The last search was conducted on October 4, 2025. The search combined terms for population (ADHD, attention deficit) and intervention (CBT, cognitive behavioral therapy, dialectical behavior therapy). The full search strings are available at the OSF link. In addition, we performed backward and forward citation searches of all included studies (in Scopus) and screened the reference lists of relevant prior reviews. 2.3. Selection process The first author conducted the initial screening of titles, abstracts, and keywords. Full-text screening was subsequently performed by the second and third authors. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. Interrater agreement was substantial (κ = 0.75). Screening was con ducted using an online form, with reviewers not blinded to study characteristics. 2.4. Data collection and data items Data extraction was carried out using a pre-defined template and codebook. The second and third authors independently extracted and coded the following variables: (A) number of study arms and arms receiving CBT; (B) country(es) in which the study was conducted; (C) number of participants at baseline; (D) dropouts in the CBT group(s); (E) sample characteristics (diagnosis, percentage of participants with at least one comorbidity, mean age, and percentage of males); (F) inter vention characteristics (psychotherapy type [second-wave CBT, DBT, mindfulness, psychoeducation, or others], number of sessions or weeks, provider, delivery and format, type of medication, percentage of par ticipants on ADHD medication); and (G) type of comparison group. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. The first author extracted the data required for computing effect sizes (number of participants, pre-treatment standard deviation, and pre-, post-, and follow-up means where available). We contacted the corre sponding authors for missing data. To ensure accuracy, a randomly selected 33% of these data points were independently verified by the fourth author. 2.5. Assessment of risk of bias Risk of bias was assessed using study-design-specific tools: the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 2 for RCTs (Sterne et al., 2019), with the Metapsy adaptation for psychotherapy trials (Miguel et al., 2025), ROBINS-I for nonrandomized controlled trials (Sterne et al., 2016), and the NIH Tool for before-after studies with no control group for single-arm trials (National Institutes of Health, 2021). Risk of bias assessment was conducted independently by the first and fourth authors, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Publication bias was exam ined through visual inspection of funnel plot symmetry, the trim-and-fill method (Duval & Tweedie, 2000), and Egger's test (Egger et al., 1997). 2.6. Assessment of certainty of evidence The certainty of evidence for each outcome was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) framework (Guyatt et al., 2008), evaluating risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias to rate evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low certainty. GRADE assess ments were conducted by the first author and reviewed by the fourth author, with disagreements resolved by consensus. C. L ́opez-Pinar et al. 2.7. Data analysis Post-treatment and follow-up changes in QoL and global functional impairment were defined as the primary outcomes. Domain-specific functioning (academic, occupational, and social) was examined as a secondary outcome. For the meta-analysis, standardized mean differences (SMDs) and their variances were calculated using Morris's formulas for within- subject (Morris, 2000) and between-group outcomes (Morris, 2008), which include a small sample factor correction (cp): d = cp [ ( MpostT −MpreT ) − ( MpostC −MpreC ) ] SDprePooled For estimating the variances of both effect size indices, as the pre- post correlation was not reported in the studies, a value of 0.70 was assumed for r, as recommended by Rosenthal (1991). Sensitivity ana lyses with r values of 0.50 and 0.90 were also conducted. Standard errors were derived from the square root of the estimated variance for each SMD. Following Cohen (1988), SMDs of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 were inter preted as small, moderate, and large effects, respectively. Given the expectation of high heterogeneity and the assumption that true effects could vary across studies (Borenstein et al., 2010), random-effects models were used in all meta-analyses, with a 95% confidence inter val. Heterogeneity was quantified with the I2 index, following stan dardized interpretation, i.e., 25% = small, 50% = moderate, and >75% high heterogeneity, and with Cochrane's Q (Higgins et al., 2003). A meta-analysis of the included SCDs was attempted, but no study included enough measures (<3 observations) to compute the ES or the associated standard error. Therefore, a narrative review approach was adopted for these studies. 2.7.1. Additional analyses Potential moderators were examined, including sample characteris tics (dropouts, diagnosis, proportion with comorbidities, mean age, and proportion of males), intervention features (type of psychotherapy, number of sessions or weeks, provider, delivery format, type of medi cation, proportion of participants on ADHD medication), and control group type. Subgroup analyses were conducted for categorical moder ators, and meta-regressions for continuous moderators. They were restricted to subgroups with >5 studies and meta-regressions to out comes with >10 studies, as fewer studies yield unstable estimates and increase the risk of spurious findings (Borenstein et al., 2009). We conducted sensitivity analyses using a leave-one-out approach to eval uate the influence of individual studies on the pooled effects. Additional sensitivity analyses excluding studies with high risk of bias were con ducted for all outcomes. Studies were classified as high risk if rated as high risk of bias (RoB 2), critical/serious risk (ROBINS-I), or poor quality (NIH tool). To evaluate statistical power, we calculated minimum detectable effects (MDEs) for each meta-analysis, defined as the smallest standardized mean difference detectable with 80% power at a two-tailed α of 0.05, given the observed standard errors. All the analyses were performed in R (R Core Team, 2025) using the meta package (Balduzzi et al., 2019). The full R code and database are available in OSF at this link. 3. Results Of the 2484 records reviewed, 70 studies were included (Table 1, Fig. 1): 38 randomized controlled trials (RCTs), four nonrandomized controlled trials, 24 single-arm trials, and four SCDs with 5152 partici pants. Full references for included studies are shown in Supplementary Materials. Most of the controlled trials (69.1%) used an active comparator (e.g., standard clinical management, parallel loosely struc tured discussion group, treatment as usual, among others). Over half of the studies (55%) were conducted in Europe, with most of those (33%) in Sweden. Thirty percent were conducted in the Americas, primarily in the United States (90%), and 15% were conducted in Asia, with half of those in China. Participants were, on average, 32.6 years old, and 47.8% were male. Of these participants, 84.5% were formally diagnosed with ADHD, and 57.4% had at least one comorbidity. Interventions were primarily stand-alone second-wave CBT (53.5%), followed by third- wave approaches, such as DBT or mindfulness (8.4% each). These in terventions were typically delivered by therapists in face-to-face (74.6%) vs remote (15.7%), and individual (44%) vs group (34.2%) or combined (9.8%) formats across an average of 12 sessions. The mean dropout rate was 14.9%, and 62.1% of participants received ADHD medication. 3.1. Risk of bias assessment results Of the RCTs, 36% were assessed as having high risk of bias, 31% low risk, and 33% some concerns (Fig. 2). All non-randomized trials (100%) had serious or critical risk of bias. Among single-arm trials, 46% had good methodological quality, 46% fair, and 8% poor quality. One of the most frequent issues among the RCTs was the insufficient reporting of allocation concealment. The main concerns for nonrandomized controlled trials were inadequate control of confounding variables, se lection bias in assigning participants to groups, and deviations from intended interventions. Common issues among single-arm trials included non-representative samples (e.g., high-functioning participants and unbalanced sex ratios) and small sample sizes. Across all study de signs, issues such as inappropriate handling of missing data and lack of pre-registration could introduce bias in the findings. Publication bias analyses (see Supplementary Table 1) revealed po tential bias in the following outcomes only: between-group QoL, aca demic functioning, and social functioning at follow-up; and within- subject global functioning. This is suggested by significant Egger's tests and trim-and-fill adjustments that rendered the effects nonsignifi cant. On the other hand, visual inspection of the funnel plots did not reveal asymmetry clearly. For all other outcomes, the tests were non- significant, suggesting the absence of publication bias. 3.2. Meta-analyses results Full results are in Table 2; forest plots for primary outcomes in Figs. 3–4; remaining forest plots and funnel plots in Supplementary Figs. 1–29. The pooled estimates reported below should be interpreted in light of the risk of bias assessment results, which indicate that a substantial proportion of included studies carried methodological limitations. Global functioning improved with moderate effects that increased over time (k = 16, n = 1,164, SMD = 0.47, 95% CI [0.32, 0.62] at post- treatment; k = 8, n = 703, SMD = 0.67, 95% CI [0.52, 0.82] at follow- up). QoL effects were smaller: small-to-moderate improvements at post- treatment (k = 25, n = 2,249, SMD = 0.28, 95% CI [0.14, 0.42]) did not persist at follow-up (k = 10, n = 993, SMD = 0.18, 95% CI [−0.03, 0.40]). Heterogeneity was moderate (I2 = 30.3-77.9%). Cochrane's Q was significant for most outcomes, especially the primary ones, con firming the presence of variability beyond chance. Additionally, forest plots revealed considerable spread in study-level effects, including several near-zero and negative effects, indicating that pooled estimates should not be interpreted as reflecting a uniform benefit across all studies. Across specific domains, occupational functioning showed the largest effects. The follow-up SMD was also large, although it was only based on two studies and must be considered preliminary. Social func tioning improved with small-to-moderate effects that persisted at follow-up, whereas academic functioning showed short-term gains that were not maintained at follow-up. Within-subject effects were moderate for global functioning and QoL. At follow-up they remained stable for QoL and increased to large for global functioning. Leave-one-out sensitivity analyses showed that results were robust across all outcomes. All results were robust to sensitivity analyses using r values of 0.50 and 0.90. Sensitivity analyses excluding high risk of bias studies revealed no significant differences in effect sizes between high and non-high risk studies. Effects remained statistically significant when analyzing only non-high risk studies, except for between-group aca demic functioning. Achieved statistical power was generally high except for QoL and academic functioning at follow-up. GRADE certainty for between-group outcomes was high for global functioning and moderate for most other outcomes, but low to very low for academic and occu pational functioning at follow-up due to small sample sizes. For within- subject outcomes, certainty was high for social functioning at post- treatment, moderate for most primary and secondary outcomes, and low to very low for outcomes with limited evidence or concerns about publication bias. 3.3. Subgroup analyses results Statistically significant subgroup analyses are reported in Supple mentary Table 2. Few significant moderator effects emerged. Individual format (k = 7) was more effective than group format (k = 7) for global functioning in both between-group and within-subject analyses. For within-subject global functioning, second-wave CBT (k = 24) was significantly more effective than mindfulness (k = 5). Additionally, remote delivery (k = 7) outperformed face-to-face (k = 16) interventions for between-group QoL, although this finding should be interpreted with caution given the small number of studies in each subgroup and the potential for unexamined differences between them. All other subgroup comparisons were nonsignificant or could not be conducted due to insufficient studies (k < 5), including study design (RCT vs. non-RCT), diagnostic status (formal diagnosis vs. high symptomatology), pro vider (therapist vs. self-delivered), medication type (stimulant vs. combination), or comparator type (active vs. inactive control). 3.4. Meta-regression analysis results Significant meta-regressions are shown in Supplementary Table 3. For QoL, two consistent predictors emerged. Higher psychiatric co morbidity rates were associated with poorer within-subject outcomes at post-treatment (R2 = 13.7%, k = 27). Greater ADHD symptom re ductions predicted better QoL outcomes between-group (R2 = 29.0%, k = 23) and within-subject (R2 = 22.7%, k = 17) at post-treatment, and at follow-up (R2 = 68.1%, k = 11; Fig. 5). For global functioning, several study characteristics were significant. Higher male proportions predicted greater within-subject improvements at post-treatment (R2 = 19.2%, k = 36) and follow-up (R2 = 47.7%, k = 10). Longer treatment duration predicted larger within-subject post- treatment effects (R2 = 28.7%, k = 36). Additionally, greater ADHD symptom reductions predicted stronger post-treatment improvements (R2 = 20.4%, k = 35; Fig. 6). For specific domains, findings were limited. Older age predicted larger within-subject academic functioning effects (R2 = 87.4%, k = 12), while higher medication rates predicted larger between-group social functioning effects (R2 = 89.2%, k = 13). However, these very high R2 values should be interpreted cautiously given the small number of studies and potential overfitting. More generally, all meta-regression findings should be interpreted with caution, as high R2 values in the context of a limited number of studies may reflect instability or leverage from individual trials rather than robust moderating effects. All other meta-regressions were non-significant. 3.5. In college populations, both face-to-face (Eddy et al., 2015) and online delivery (L ́opez-Pinar & Vicente-Gispert, 2023) reduced impairment and improved organization, time management, and social/academic engagement (e.g., better grades, more time with friends), with the online cases showing QoL gains that increased up to 6-month follow-up. A community SCD (Puente & Mitchell, 2016) also found enhanced functioning and QoL post-treatment, but partial relapse and interpersonal difficulties at 2-month follow-up. Finally, in cases with co-occurring substance use disorder (van Emmerik-van Oortmerssen et al., 2015), CBT improved ADHD symptoms, substance use, and QoL, although sustained benefits were observed only in the participant who remained engaged. Together, these findings suggest CBT can yield meaningful improvements in functioning and QoL across settings but highlight the need for strategies to maintain gains over time. 4. Discussion Traditionally, literature on interventions for adults with ADHD has focused on improving core symptoms, with moderate effects for CBT (Liu et al., 2023) and stimulants (Gosling et al., 2025). This meta-analysis summarizes the evidence on how CBT effects in adult ADHD relate to changes in everyday behavioral functioning beyond symptom reduction. Specifically, we quantified the impact of CBT on global functioning and QoL, examined effects across specific functional domains (social, occupational, and educational), explored potential moderators of treatment effects, and assessed whether improvements in core ADHD symptoms predict functional outcomes. Compared to previous studies, this review substantially expands the evidence base by including 70 studies with 5152 participants, surpassing the 32 studies with 896 participants in Knouse et al. (2017) and the 28 RCTs with 2190 participants in Liu et al. (2023). The continued growth of this literature may reflect the increasing recognition of CBT's potential for adults with ADHD. The characteristics of the included sample align with epidemiological data on adults with ADHD, showing comparable rates of comorbidity (Faraone & Larsson, 2019) and a higher proportion receiving medication (62.1%), which is typical of treatment-seeking samples included in clinical trials (Garcia-Argibay et al., 2025). The interventions predominantly represented the most commonly imple mented model to date: face-to-face, second-wave CBT delivered over an average of 12 sessions. Average dropout rates (14.9%) were lower than those typically reported in CBT trials (Fernandez et al., 2015), which may suggest favorable treatment acceptability in this population. This expanded evidence base provides the most comprehensive assessment of CBT's effects on functioning and QoL in adults with ADHD to date. 4.1. CBT effect on QoL and global functioning Across the different outcomes examined, CBT showed the most consistent effects on global functioning, with moderate effects at post- treatment that increased at follow-up, with GRADE ratings indicating moderate-to-high certainty of evidence. These results should nonethe less be interpreted in light of the methodological limitations identified across studies. These findings build upon and extend those of previous reviews (Knouse et al., 2017; L ́opez-Pinar et al., 2018). The observed effects may reflect clinically relevant improvements in functioning, Fig. 1. PRISMA flow diagram. C. L ́opez-Pinar et al. Behaviour Research and Therapy 201 (2026) 105026 9

which is noteworthy given that adults with ADHD typically seek treat ment for functional impairment rather than symptom severity per se (Kosheleff et al., 2023). Given that ADHD symptoms typically persist across the lifespan (Cherkasova et al., 2022), CBT's focus on developing adaptive coping skills rather than eliminating symptoms may make it particularly suited for addressing the functional difficulties that Fig. 2. characterize adult ADHD (French et al., 2024). Our results are broadly consistent with previous literature suggesting that CBT may improve functional outcomes across disorders characterized by executive and emotional regulation deficits, including emotional disorders (Kambeitz-Ilankovic et al., 2022) and other neurodevelopmental disor ders (Schweizer et al., 2023). Although the mechanisms underlying these effects were not directly tested in this meta-analysis and remain speculative, the consistency of functioning improvements across ADHD, emotional, and other neurodevelopmental disorders suggests that CBT's benefits may operate through transdiagnostic mechanisms, such as improved emotion regulation and cognitive flexibility, rather than disorder-specific pathways (Sloan et al., 2017), although this interpre tation should be considered tentative. In contrast, between-group effects on QoL were smaller and did not persist at follow-up. These results differ from L ́opez-Pinar et al. (2020), who found sustained follow-up effects on QoL, but align with Liu et al.'s (2023) post-treatment findings. This discrepancy may reflect differences in sample size and methodological characteristics across reviews, Fig. 2. (continued). C. L ́opez-Pinar et al. although this explanation should be interpreted cautiously. However, within-subject QoL effects were moderate and appeared stable over time, supporting previous studies (L ́opez-Pinar et al., 2020). These dif ferential effects between the two primary outcomes may reflect several factors, though these explanations were not directly tested and should be considered speculative. First, the more specific and objective nature of functioning versus the more subjective well-being nature of QoL (World Health Organization, 1995). Second, temporal factors: func tioning is more directly targeted and may improve rapidly, while QoL may require longer to emerge as functional changes accumulate. Most studies' short follow-up periods (approximately 3 months) may be insufficient to capture delayed QoL benefits. Third, adults with ADHD often hold negative self-schemas and maladaptive cognitions (Knouse et al., 2019; Philipsen et al., 2017), which may make them more critical when evaluating their overall life satisfaction, even when they experi ence objective functional improvements. Fourth, CBT skills are designed to target functioning domains (e.g., time management for improving academic or work performance). In contrast, QoL may be influenced by many factors beyond CBT's direct targets (e.g., financial situation, physical health), which are often impaired in adults with ADHD (French et al., 2024; Libutzki et al., 2024). Fifth, the high rate of psychiatric comorbidity may explain differential effects. CBT targeting ADHD may improve functioning without fully addressing QoL when depression, anxiety, or other conditions also contribute to reduced life satisfaction. This interpretation is tentatively supported by our meta-regression finding that higher comorbidity rates predicted poorer QoL outcomes. Taken together, these modest QoL effects are consistent with broader transdiagnostic CBT research showing similar small-to-moderate im provements across multiple conditions (Fordham et al., 2021), although the extent to which ADHD-specific versus transdiagnostic factors ac count for these patterns remains unclear. SCDs provided case-level observations consistent with these findings. They also suggest that sustained improvements may depend on continued skill application (van Emmerik-van Oortmerssen et al., 2015), and that reduced engagement was associated with partial relapse (Puente & Mitchell, 2016). Although not directly tested, this pattern aligns with the within-subject findings and is consistent with the pos sibility that CBT may produce skill-dependent gains rather than stable trait changes, which may have implications for long-term skills main tenance, as supported by recent literature (L ́opez-Pinar et al., 2023). Detailed case-level data also suggested specific improvement mecha nisms, such as enhanced organization and time management, which may be associated with better academic performance and social engagement (Eddy et al., 2015; L ́opez-Pinar & Vicente-Gispert, 2023). 4.2. CBT effect on specific functioning domains Across specific domains, CBT showed statistically significant effects on all outcomes except for between-group academic functioning at follow-up. Among them, the most favorable quality of evidence was for social functioning outcomes. Although different instruments were used, studies generally assessed similar aspects of social functioning including interpersonal relationships, social activities/leisure participation, social support, and sexual life/intimacy. CBT produced small-to-moderate ef fects for social functioning with some evidence of maintenance at follow-up for both controlled and uncontrolled outcomes. These results are consistent with previous meta-analyses showing that CBT combined with medication may improve social functioning compared to pharma cotherapy alone (Li & Zhang, 2024), with the novel finding that these gains appear to be sustained at follow-up. The apparent stability of ef fects at follow-up could be particularly noteworthy given that social impairments are among the most distressing consequences of adult ADHD (Holst & Thorell, 2020), though this interpretation remains speculative.
