immune activation, which can result in inflammation that crosses the placenta and potentially alters fetal neurodevelopment (Bouwland et al., 2015; Suter et al., 2012). Despite these biological hypotheses, the strength of the association between maternal smoking and ADHD re mains debated, with some studies suggesting a robust link, while others report that the association diminishes after adjusting for genetic and familial factors (Thapar et al., 2009; Joelsson et al., 2016). In contrast, paternal smoking has received less attention in the literature, although it may also contribute to the risk of ADHD through both direct and indirect pathways. Direct effects could include second- hand smoke exposure to the mother and fetus, while indirect effects may involve epigenetic changes in sperm caused by smoking, leading to altered gene expression in the offspring (Langley et al., 2012; Joehanes et al., 2016). Moreover, the shared genetic predisposition between fa thers who smoke and their children could confound the relationship, making it unclear whether the observed associations are due to smoking itself or underlying familial traits (Gustavson et al., 2017). Although numerous cohort and case-control studies have investi gated the relationship between prenatal smoking and ADHD, the evi dence is fragmented across various populations, study designs, and outcomes. Systematic reviews (SRs) and meta-analyses have been con ducted to synthesise these findings, yet they often present conflicting conclusions (Thapar et al., 2009; Joelsson et al., 2016; He et al., 2020). Additionally, the methodological quality of these reviews, including the handling of confounding factors, the rigor of statistical methods, and the assessment of heterogeneity, has not been consistently evaluated. This lack of a comprehensive synthesis makes it challenging to draw defini tive conclusions about the true strength and credibility of the association between prenatal smoking and ADHD risk. Against this background, an umbrella review offers an opportunity to systematically evaluate the existing SRs and meta-analyses to determine the overall strength of evidence on this topic. Umbrella reviews, which are overviews of SRs and meta-analyses, provide a higher-level synthesis that can help to identify whether the evidence base is consistent or contradictory, and whether the conclusions drawn from individual re views are reliable. This approach allows for a more robust assessment of the quality of the evidence and the strength of the associations reported across studies. Therefore, the aim of this umbrella review is to provide a compre hensive overview of the breadth and validity of the associations between maternal and paternal smoking during pregnancy and attention-deficit/ hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in offspring. Specifically, we seek to synthesise the magnitude, consistency, and credibility of these associa tions across the existing evidence base, including an assessment of het erogeneity and potential biases using established umbrella review criteria (Ayano et al., 2024; Belbasis et al., 2015; Ioannidis and Trika linos, 2007). By doing so, this umbrella review aims to clarify whether prenatal smoking should be considered an important, potentially modifiable risk factor for ADHD and to identify priority targets for future clinical, preventive, and policy interventions. 2. Methods 2.1. Study design and eligibility criteria We employed an umbrella review methodology to systematically identify, appraise, and synthesise all available systematic reviews (SRs) and meta-analyses on this topic. An umbrella review is a systematic overview of SRs and meta-analyses that provides a high-level synthesis of a broad and heterogeneous evidence base and enables formal grading of the strength and consistency of associations across studies. (Aromataris et al., 2015; Slim and Marquillier, 2022). The review pro tocol was prospectively registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; CRD42022361466). Eligible SRs were those that assessed the association between pre natal smoking exposure (maternal or paternal) and ADHD outcomes, and that conducted a quantitative meta-analysis of cohort or case- control studies. Included reviews were required to report study-level effect sizes (ESs) with corresponding 95 % confidence intervals (CIs). SRs that did not include a meta-analysis, lacked extractable ESs, or synthesised evidence narratively only were excluded. When multiple SRs covered overlapping primary studies, the review with the largest and most comprehensive dataset was retained, consistent with recom mended umbrella review methods (Ioannidis, 2009). 2.2. Literature search, systematic review selection, and data extraction We systematically searched the following databases from inception to September 21, 2024: Medline, Scopus, PsychINFO, and Web of Sci ence. The search strategy was designed to capture SRs and meta- analyses related to maternal and paternal smoking exposure and ADHD in offspring, with no language restrictions. The search was sup plemented by manual screening of reference lists from included studies. The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Re views and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines for the selection of SRs (Moher et al., 2009). Two reviewers (GA and DZ) independently screened titles and ab stracts for eligibility, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer through discussion. Full-text reviews were conducted for articles that could not be definitively included or excluded based on title and abstract review. From the included SRs, two investigators independently extracted data, including first author, year of publication, number of included studies, outcomes, and summary meta-analytic estimates. 2.3. Quality assessment of included systematic reviews The methodological quality of the included SRs was assessed using the AMSTAR-2 tool (A Measurement Tool to Assess Systematic Reviews), a 16-point checklist used to evaluate the rigor of SRs (Shea et al., 2017). Two independent reviewers applied the AMSTAR-2 tool to each SR, with discrepancies resolved by discussion. The assessment included key criteria such as protocol registration, comprehensive search strategies, and appropriate methods for assessing risk of bias (Shea et al., 2017). 2.4. Statistical analysis Summary odds ratios (ORs) with 95 % CIs were re-estimated using a common metric and random-effects models, anticipating high hetero geneity among studies (DerSimonian and Laird, 1986). Heterogeneity was quantified using Cochran’s Q test and the I2 statistic, with p-values <0.10 considered statistically significant (Higgins et al., 2003). The 95 % prediction interval (PI) was calculated to account for between-study heterogeneity and estimate the range of effects expected in a new study (IntHout et al., 2016). Egger’s test was applied to evaluate pub lication bias and small-study effects, with p-values ≤0.10 indicating potential bias (Egger et al., 1997). We also tested for excess significance bias, comparing the number of studies with statistically significant results (O) to the expected number (E), based on power calculations for each study (Ioannidis and Trikali nos, 2007). Associations were classified according to strength of evi dence as “convincing,” “highly suggestive,” “suggestive,” or “weak,” based on statistical criteria, including heterogeneity, sample size, and significance (Schmid et al., 2020). Statistical analyses were performed using Stata version 12.0 (Stata Corp, College Station, TX, USA), and all p-values were two-tailed (Schmid et al., 2020; Furukawa and Leucht, 2011). 3. These meta-analyses focused on ADHD as the outcome, with a total of 172,987 ADHD cases (159,765 cases for maternal smoking and 13,222 cases for paternal smoking). The median number of ADHD cases per meta-analysis was 16,000 (IQR 2500 to 85, 000), and the median total population per meta-analysis was 198,000 (IQR 50,000 to 925,000). Four of the six meta-analyses were based on cohort studies, while two included a combination of cohort, case-control, or cross-sectional studies. The median number of study estimates per meta-analysis was 7 (IQR 5 to 9, range 3–15). Both associations, for maternal and paternal smoking, were statistically significant under the random-effects model. For maternal smoking, the random effects summary estimate was OR 1.71 (95 % CI: 1.46–2.00), with a p-value of 3⋅8E-21. The heterogeneity was high, with I2 = 79 %, and the 95 % prediction interval ranged from 1.05 to 2.75. For paternal smoking, the random effects summary esti mate was OR 1.36 (95 % CI: 1.17–1.59), with a p-value of 1⋅6E-29. The heterogeneity was moderate, with I2 = 47 %, and the 95 % prediction interval ranged from 1.08 to 2.24 (Table 1). The Egger test for publication bias showed a significant effect for maternal smoking (p = 0.004) but was non-significant for paternal smoking (p = 0.42). Both associations were robust under a 10 % cred ibility ceiling, with maternal smoking showing high heterogeneity and paternal smoking showing moderate heterogeneity. The level of evi dence for maternal smoking was classified as Highly Suggestive (Class II), while paternal smoking was classified as Convincing (Class I) (Table 1). Fig. 1. 3.1. Quality of the studies The quality of the six meta-analyses included in this umbrella review was assessed using the AMSTAR 2 tool. Three of the studies were clas sified as high quality, as they met most of the AMSTAR 2 criteria, including having clear research questions, comprehensive literature search strategies, and appropriate methods for study selection and data extraction (Appendix 2). These studies also conducted thorough risk of bias (RoB) assessments, reported heterogeneity, and performed adequate analyses of publication bias, such as small study effects. Two studies were categorized as moderate quality, as they lacked important elements such as protocol registration, detailed exclusion criteria, and, in some cases, assessments of RoB and publication bias. Additionally, some deviations from the protocol were noted without sufficient justi fication, which impacted their overall quality rating. One study was rated as low quality, as it failed to meet several key AMSTAR 2 criteria, including duplicate study selection, data extraction, risk of bias assess ment, and heterogeneity analysis. Furthermore, this study lacked transparency in reporting funding sources and potential conflicts of in terest. Overall, 50 % of the meta-analyses were rated as high quality, while 33 % were moderate, and 17 % were low quality (Appendix 2). These findings reflect a range of methodological rigor across the included reviews, from robust to weaker standards. 3.2. Level of evidence for the associations The hierarchical grading of evidence from the six meta-analyses on maternal and paternal smoking exposure during pregnancy in relation to ADHD in offspring was based on statistical significance, heterogeneity, and robustness of the associations. Paternal smoking during pregnancy was graded as convincing evidence (Class I). This association had a random effects summary estimate of OR 1.36 (95 % CI: 1.17–1.59), with a p-value of 1⋅6E-29, moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 47 %), and a 95 % prediction interval of 1.08–2.24, which did not cross the null. The strength of evidence was supported by its large sample size, absence of small study effects, and the exclusion of excess significance bias. Maternal smoking during pregnancy was graded as highly suggestive evidence (Class II). The random effects summary estimate was OR 1.71 (95 % CI: 1.46–2.00), with a p-value of 3⋅8E-21, but the heterogeneity was high (I2 = 79 %). The 95 % prediction interval ranged from 1.05 to 2.75, indicating that the association remained statistically significant. While maternal smoking showed large heterogeneity, it retained sig nificance under a 10 % credibility ceiling, but small study effects and excess significance bias were present, which contributed to the classi fication as Class II evidence (Table 1). 3.3. Sensitivity analysis by study design and adjustment for psychiatric history The sensitivity analysis, stratified by both study design and adjust ment for psychiatric history, showed consistent associations between both maternal and paternal smoking exposure and the risk of ADHD in offspring. For maternal smoking, the pooled odds ratio (OR) from cohort studies was 1.84 (95 % CI: 1.34–2.53) based on 25 studies, while case- control studies showed a pooled OR of 1.92 (95 % CI: 1.47–2.44) from 18 studies. Similarly, for paternal smoking, cohort studies had a pooled OR of 1.36 (95 % CI: 1.15–1.61) from 4 studies, while case-control studies yielded a higher pooled OR of 1.88 (95 % CI: 1.24–2.81) from 2 studies. Discussion This umbrella review systematically and quantitatively synthesised the hierarchy of evidence for maternal and paternal smoking as risk factors for ADHD in offspring. Overall, prenatal smoking was associated with an increased risk of ADHD, but the strength and consistency of evidence differed by parental source. Paternal smoking during preg nancy showed convincing evidence (Class I) of association with offspring ADHD (OR 1.36, 95 % CI 1.17–1.59; I2 = 47 %), whereas maternal smoking was supported by highly suggestive evidence (Class II; OR 1.71, 95 % CI 1.46–2.00) with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 79 %). Taken together, these findings indicate that prenatal smoking is a robust marker of ADHD risk in offspring, but they also highlight important uncertainty regarding causality and the specific contribution of maternal versus paternal pathways. The convincing evidence for paternal smoking suggests a moderate but reliable increase in ADHD risk. Several mechanisms may underlie this association, including epigenetic alterations in sperm (e.g. DNA methylation changes affecting neurodevelopmental genes), oxidative stress–related sperm DNA damage, and increased second-hand smoke exposure of pregnant partners and fetuses (Agarwal et al., 2014; Jaak kola and Gissler, 2004) (Ernst et al., 2001). In addition, the association may partly reflect shared familial liability: fathers who smoke are more likely to share genetic and environmental risk factors with children who develop ADHD, including impulsivity, externalising traits, or broader familial psychopathology (Thapar et al., 2009). Thus, paternal smoking may act both as a potential biological exposure and as a proxy marker for intergenerational genetic and environmental risk. By contrast, maternal smoking during pregnancy showed a stronger point estimate but marked between-study variability. Biologically, maternal smoking is highly plausible as a risk factor: nicotine and other tobacco constituents can disrupt fetal brain development through effects on the cholinergic system, fetal hypoxia, epigenetic modifications, and immune activation, all of which may interfere with neural circuits un derlying attention, impulse control, and emotion regulation (Lewis et al., 2022; Lopes, 2019; Dietert and Zelikoff, 2008; Sussman, 2002; Ekblad et al., 2015). However, the substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 79 %) suggests that the size—and possibly the presence—of the association varies meaningfully across contexts and study designs. This variability is likely driven by multiple factors, including differences in how smoking exposure (timing, intensity, cessation) and ADHD outcomes (diagnostic criteria, informants, age at assessment) are measured; variation in adjustment for key confounders such as maternal ADHD, depression, socioeconomic status, and co-occurring substance use; and differences in underlying population risk profiles. Importantly, studies using more rigorous causal designs (e.g. sibling comparisons or negative control analyses) often report attenuated associations, implying that part of the observed link between maternal smoking and ADHD may be explained by shared familial or genetic factors rather than a purely intrauterine causal effect. These nuances have important conceptual and practical implica tions. Conceptually, our findings support the view that prenatal smoking is not simply an isolated teratogenic exposure but part of a broader intergenerational risk context for ADHD. The stronger and more consistent evidence for paternal smoking, together with heterogeneous evidence for maternal smoking, points towards a combination of genetic liability, shared environmental factors (e.g. family stress, socioeconomic disadvantage), and direct toxic effects of tobacco smoke. Clinically and from a public health perspective, this underscores the importance of addressing smoking as a family-level risk factor, rather than focusing solely on pregnant women. Integrating smoking cessation support for both parents into preconception and antenatal care may therefore be a pragmatic strategy to reduce a cluster of adverse outcomes, including ADHD, even if the causal fraction attributable to intrauterine exposure remains uncertain. In practice, these findings reinforce existing recommendations for universal smoking cessation during the perinatal period, but add nuance by emphasising paternal involvement. For clinicians, prenatal smo king—maternal or paternal—may serve as a useful marker of elevated developmental risk, prompting closer monitoring of child behaviour, early identification of attentional and behavioural difficulties, and timely referral to support services. At the policy level, our results sup port continued investment in tobacco control measures and targeted cessation programs in reproductive-age populations, particularly in families with known ADHD or other psychiatric vulnerabilities. This umbrella review also highlights key gaps and priorities for future research. First, there is a need for more high-quality, causally informative designs—such as sibling-comparison studies, negative control parent designs, adoption studies, and Mendelian random isation—to better disentangle intrauterine effects from shared familial liability.45,49 Second, future meta-analyses should systematically stratify by key methodological features (e.g. degree of confounder adjustment, exposure timing and intensity, ADHD assessment method) to clarify sources of heterogeneity in maternal smoking results and identify subgroups or contexts where the association is strongest. Third, mechanistic studies integrating epigenetic, neuroimaging, and longitu dinal phenotypic data could help link prenatal smoking exposures to specific neurodevelopmental pathways implicated in ADHD. Finally, more work is needed in diverse populations and low- and middle-income settings, where patterns of smoking, co-exposures, and healthcare access may differ substantially, to ensure that inferences and prevention stra tegies are globally relevant. This umbrella review has limitations inherent to synthesising observational evidence, including the possibility of residual confound ing, exposure misclassification, and publication or small-study bias.48–50 Our evidence grading did not fully account for biological plausibility or explicitly reward quasi-experimental designs, which may lead to conservative classification of some associations. Nonetheless, by applying a structured hierarchy of evidence across multiple SRs and meta-analyses, this review provides a comprehensive and nuanced assessment of the links between maternal and paternal smoking and offspring ADHD. The findings highlight prenatal smoking as an impor tant intergenerational risk marker for ADHD and underscore the need for both more rigorous causal research and family-focused smoking cessation strategies during the preconception and antenatal periods (Krieger et al., 2010). 5. Conclusion In conclusion, both maternal and paternal smoking during preg nancy were identified as significant risk factors for ADHD in offspring, with paternal smoking showing convincing evidence (Class I) and maternal smoking showing highly suggestive evidence (Class II). These findings, while robust, underscore the need for cautious interpretation and further research, particularly with regard to potential confounding factors and the mechanisms underlying these associations. pages: A systematic review of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) for adults with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) Tianran Zhang a, Dimitrios Adamis b,* a Department of Health & Nutritional Sciences, Atlantic Technological University, Sligo, F91 YW50, Ireland b HSE Sligo Mental Health Services, University of Galway, University of Limerick, University College Dublin, Ireland A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: ADHD Transcranial direct current stimulation Systematic review cognitive enhancement Neuromodulation A B S T R A C T Background: Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) has been proposed as a potential non- pharmacological intervention for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). While evidence from pedi atric populations is growing, the effects of tDCS in adults with ADHD remain insufficiently characterized, increasing recognition of ADHD as a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition with persistent functional impairments. Objective: This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effects of tDCS in adults with ADHD across clinical, cognitive, and neurophysiological outcome domains. Methods: Six electronic databases were systematically searched to identify peer-reviewed controlled trials eval uating tDCS interventions in adults with clinically diagnosed ADHD through May 2025. Data extraction encompassed clinical symptom outcomes, cognitive task performance, neurophysiological findings, adverse events, medication status, and stimulation protocols. Study quality was assessed using the Downs and Black checklist. Where sufficient data were available, an exploratory random-effects meta-analysis was conducted for clinical symptom outcomes; all other outcomes were synthesized narratively. Results: Eleven controlled studies (n = 415) met inclusion criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis. Two randomized controlled trials provided sufficient data for exploratory meta-analysis of clinical symptoms. Pooled results suggested a possible beneficial effect of tDCS on inattention symptoms, accompanied by sub stantial heterogeneity (I2 = 79.95 %), while no significant effect was observed for hyperactivity/impulsivity. Cognitive outcomes were heterogeneous and domain-specific, with some evidence of post-stimulation im provements in inhibitory control, working memory, and attentional measures. Two studies reported tDCS- induced modulation of frontal neurophysiological markers associated with cognitive control. Stimulation pro tocols varied considerably across studies, with no consistent association between specific parameters and out comes. Adverse events were generally mild and transient, and follow-up data were limited. Conclusions: Current evidence suggests that tDCS may exert domain-specific effects on inattention and selected cognitive functions in adults with ADHD. However, conclusions remain tentative due to methodological het erogeneity, small sample sizes, and limited quantitative evidence. Future research should prioritize standardized protocols, adequately powered trials with extended follow-up periods, integration of neurophysiological bio markers, and systematic evaluation of individual difference factors to clarify the therapeutic potential and mechanisms, and advance precision neuromodulation approaches for adult ADHD. 1. Introduction Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neuro developmental condition characterized by persistent patterns of inat tention, and/or hyperactivity, and impulsivity that significantly impair functioning (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Once considered primarily a childhood disorder, accumulating evidence demonstrates its persistence into adolescence and adulthood, often resulting in substan tial academic, occupational, and social difficulties (Sibley et al., 2017; Turgay et al., 2012). individuals with ADHD, including altered activity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), the anterior cingulate cortex, and the basal ganglia, regions implicated in executive function, attention regulation, and impulse control (Marcos-Vidal et al., 2018; Passarotti et al., 2009; Seidman et al., 2005; Samea et al., 2019; Rapport et al., 2013; Kasper et al., 2012; Keune et al., 2015; Krain and Castellanos, 2006). These cognitive domains also represent core features of ADHD pathophysi ology and are central to most theoretical models of the disorder (Barkley, 1997; Willcutt et al., 2005; Rubia, 2018). These neural features offer a neurobiological rationale for targeting cortical regions through brain-based interventions. Current ADHD treatment strategies primarily comprise pharmaco logical interventions, including stimulant and non-stimulant medica tions, and psychological therapies, particularly cognitive-behavioural approaches (Sibley et al., 2014; Fullen et al., 2020). While pharmaco therapy demonstrates robust short-term efficacy, adverse effects, non adherence, potential misuse, and contraindications limit its utility in certain populations (Hsu et al., 2017). Behavioural interventions, though effective for skill-building and behavior management, often require sustained therapeutic engagement, trained personnel, and structured environments, which may be less accessible to adults or insufficient for addressing core neurocognitive deficits (Daley et al., 2014). These limitations have sparked interest in alternative and adjunctive interventions that can directly modulate underlying neural dysfunction. Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques, particularly transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), have emerged as promising neuro modulatory treatments for ADHD (Westwood et al., 2021; Salehinejad et al., 2019, 2020). tDCS modulates cortical excitability through weak direct current applied via scalp electrodes, with polarity-dependent ef fects such that anodal stimulation is generally associated with increased neuronal excitability, while cathodal stimulation is associated with relative reductions in excitability at the cortical level. Although these effects are context-dependent and influenced by baseline neural state, stimulation parameters, and task engagement, this basic neurophysio logical framework has guided the design of most tDCS protocols tar geting prefrontal regions. Its portability, favourable safety profile, and low cost make it an attractive candidate for clinical implementation (Polanía et al., 2018; Imburgio and Orr, 2018; Bikson et al., 2016). Emerging evidence suggests that tDCS may enhance cognitive perfor mance and reduce core symptoms in individuals with ADHD by influ encing prefrontal networks involved in attention and executive control (Salehinejad et al., 2019; Rubia, 2018; Nejati et al., 2017; Breitling et al., 2016), with a substantial proportion of existing research focusing on pediatric or mixed-age populations. Although research on tDCS in children and adolescents with ADHD has expanded, evidence in adult populations remains comparatively limited (Courr`eges et al., 2025). This imbalance is notable given the growing recognition of ADHD as a chronic condition with persistent cognitive and functional impairments across the lifespan (Wender et al., 2001). While core symptom domains are shared across age groups, developmental changes in brain organization and cognitive control systems suggest that findings derived from pediatric samples may not be directly generalizable to adults. These considerations underscore the need for focused synthesis of the adult literature, rather than reliance on extrapolation from child and adolescent studies. Adults with ADHD face elevated risks of educational underachieve ment, occupational instability, interpersonal difficulties, and comorbid psychiatric disorders (Kooij et al., 2010). Epidemiological data indicate an average adult ADHD prevalence of 2.8 % across 10 countries in the WHO World Mental Health Surveys (Fayyad et al., 2016), while meta-analytic evidence reveals prevalence rates of 27 % in psychiatric outpatient populations when screening tools are used, decreasing to 14.61 % with formal diagnostic assessment (Adamis et al., 2022). Despite these substantial figures, adult ADHD remains significantly underdiagnosed and undertreated, creating considerable socioeconomic burden and unmet clinical need. Within this context, tDCS has been investigated as a potential yet underexplored intervention for adult ADHD. However, the more modest and heterogeneous effects reported in adult studies, relative to pediatric samples, raise questions about age-related factors that may influence responsiveness to neuromodulation. One plausible consideration is that adults typically exhibit reduced experience-dependent cortical plasticity and greater reliance on established functional networks compared with children, which may constrain the magnitude or durability of stimulation-induced effects. Importantly, this interpretation remains tentative, as the adult tDCS literature is characterized by substantial variability in stimulation protocols, target brain regions, outcome measures, and participant characteristics. Furthermore, how stimulation parameters (site, polarity, intensity, duration) and individual factors (medication status, symptom subtype) influence treatment outcomes is not yet well characterized (Salehinejad et al., 2020). To address these gaps, we conducted a systematic review of controlled studies investigating tDCS effects in adult ADHD. In contrast to broader neuromodulation reviews and syntheses that include mixed- age populations or focus on narrower outcome domains, the present review focuses specifically on adults and considers clinical, cognitive, and neurophysiological outcomes alongside medication status and stimulation parameters. Our objectives were to: (1) examine whether tDCS improves cognitive functions, neural activity, or clinical symptoms in adults with ADHD; (2) identify the cognitive domains and neuro physiological measures most responsive to stimulation; and (3) explore how stimulation parameters and participant characteristics modulate treatment effects. This synthesis aims to clarify current findings and identify priorities for future research and clinical applications. 2. Methods 2.1. Search strategy This systematic review adhered to PRISMA 2020 guidelines (Page et al., 2021) and was pre-registered on PROSPERO (2025 CRD420251070474; available from https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/ PROSPERO/view/CRD420251070474). We conducted comprehensive searches across six electronic databases: PubMed, MEDLINE (via Ovid), EBSCO (including PsycINFO), Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane CENTRAL, covering all records through May 2025. The search strategy combined terms related to “ADHD,” “attention deficit hyperactivity disorder,” “transcranial direct current stimulation,” “tDCS,” and “adult,” utilizing both keywords and database-specific subject headings. Full search strategies for each database are provided in Supplementary Ma terial (Search Strategy). 2.2. Selection process Following duplicate removal based on titles and publication details, records underwent manual screening in three sequential phases: title review, abstract screening, and full-text assessment. Two independent reviewers applied predefined eligibility criteria, with discrepancies resolved through a consensus process. Inclusion criteria: Studies were eligible if they (1) involved adults aged 18 years and older with formal ADHD diagnoses using established criteria (DSM or ICD), (2) applied tDCS as a primary or standalone intervention, (3) employed a control or comparison group (sham stim ulation, waitlist, or baseline condition), (4) reported quantitative out comes for clinical symptoms (inattention, impulsivity, hyperactivity) or cognitive performance (e.g., executive functioning, working memory, attention), and (5) were peer-reviewed primary studies. Exclusion criteria: We excluded (1) studies conducted exclusively with children or adolescents, (2) animal studies, (3) case studies, re views, conference abstracts without full text, or editorials, (4) studies where tDCS effects could not be isolated (e.g., combined interventions T. Data extraction and statistical analysis Data extraction employed a structured template that captured the study design, participant characteristics, diagnostic criteria, stimulation parameters (including montage, intensity, duration, and session num ber), control conditions, primary and secondary outcomes, adverse events, and medication status. Medication status was categorized as unmedicated, medicated-withdrawn, stable medication, medication- naïve, or partially medicated. Additional variables included ADHD subtype and exclusion criteria for comorbidities. Two reports by Cosmo et al. (2015a, 2015b), although derived from the same participant sample, were retained as separate studies because they reported non- overlapping outcome domains (cognitive task performance vs. EEG measures), and therefore did not result in duplication within the quan titative synthesis. Statistical analyses were performed using the “meta” package in R software (version 4.5.1). For clinical symptoms, we conducted an exploratory random-effects meta-analysis using post-intervention symptom scores from two eligible trials, which employed closely matched ADHD rating scales (ASRS and CASRS) with comparable item structure and scoring direction. Standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) with 95 % confidence intervals were calculated, and heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic. Given the limited number of eligible studies and minor differences in rating source (self-report vs. clinician- rated), the meta-analytic results were interpreted cautiously, with remaining clinical findings synthesized narratively. Cognitive outcomes underwent structured narrative synthesis. First, we extracted and coded all reported tasks per study based on statistical significance at the post-intervention time point (p < .05), prioritizing between-group comparisons when available. Second, tasks were cate gorized into five predefined cognitive domains: inhibitory control, working memory, attention, executive function, and social/emotional cognition. For each domain, we summarized the number of tasks employed, proportion showing significant improvement, and available effect sizes. When multiple dependent measures were derived from the same task (e.g., multiple Tower of London indices), these were treated as a single task to maintain consistency in domain-level aggregation. Neurophysiological outcomes from two studies using electroen cephalography (EEG) were synthesized narratively. Neural correlates included spectral power (delta, theta, beta bands), resting-state EEG changes, and event-related potential (ERP) components (P200, P300) during cognitive or emotional tasks. Methodological heterogeneity precluded pooled analysis. Additional narrative synthesis examined stimulation protocols, adverse events, and potential effect moderators, including medication status, participant demographics, and ADHD subtypes. These elements were analysed descriptively to assess the consistency of tDCS effects across methodological variations. Given design heterogeneity and var iable reporting standards, all subgroup and moderator analyses remained exploratory. 2.4. Risk of bias assessment Risk of bias and methodological quality were assessed using the Downs and Black checklist (Downs and Black, 1998), which allows structured appraisal across reporting quality, external validity, internal validity (bias and confounding), and statistical power. All included studies were assessed independently by two reviewers, with discrep ancies resolved through discussion to achieve consensus. Item-level scores for each study are provided in Supplementary Table S1. Across the eleven included studies, total Downs and Black scores ranged from 17 to 28 (out of a possible 32), indicating overall moderate to high methodological quality. Reporting quality was generally strong, with most studies scoring between 9 and 10 out of 10, reflecting clear descriptions of objectives, interventions, outcomes, and statistical ana lyses. External validity scores were consistently moderate to high (2–3 out of 3), suggesting reasonable generalizability within clinical and research settings. Internal validity related to bias was also rated highly across studies (typically 7 out of 7), indicating appropriate randomization procedures, outcome assessment, and control of measurement bias. Similarly, in ternal validity concerning confounding was generally strong (5–6 out of 6), reflecting adequate control of key confounders and appropriate an alytic strategies in most trials. In contrast, statistical power emerged as the most consistently limited domain, with power scores ranging from 0 to 2, and the majority of studies scoring 0 or 1. This reflects the absence of formal power cal culations and the small sample sizes characteristic of many included trials, particularly those assessing clinical symptom outcomes. Lower overall scores were therefore primarily driven by limitations in power rather than deficiencies in study design or reporting. Taken together, this quality assessment suggests that while the included studies were generally well conducted and clearly reported, limitations related to sample size and statistical power constrain the strength and precision of effect estimates. These methodological fea tures are considered further in the Discussion when interpreting the robustness and clinical implications of the synthesized evidence. 3. Results Database searches identified 1176 records. Following screening and full-text assessment, 11 studies met inclusion criteria and were included in the final review (Leffa et al., 2022; Cachoeira et al., 2017; Basiri and Hadianfard, 2023; Allenby et al., 2018; Barham et al., 2022; Beiman et al., 2025; Cosmo et al., 2015; Cosmo et al., 2015b; Dubreuil-Vall et al., 2021; Weinberg et al., 2023; Jacoby and Lavidor, 2018). The study se lection process is summarized in the PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 1). 3.1. Study characteristics Among the 11 included studies, 3 assessed clinical symptoms as primary outcomes, 9 evaluated various cognitive functions, and 2 included EEG-based neurophysiological measurements. Across studies, tDCS protocols varied substantially, with stimulation intensities ranging from 1 to 2 mA, session durations from 20 to 30 min, and the number of sessions ranging from single-session designs to multi-session in terventions (up to 28 sessions), reflecting considerable heterogeneity in intervention parameters. Study details are presented in Table 1. Medication status categories: Unmedicated: Participants not taking medication during study period or discontinued for ≥1 month (sufficient washout). Stable medication: Participants remained unmedicated or maintained stable regimen for defined duration (≥4 weeks). Medica tion-naïve: Participants never received prior ADHD pharmacological treatment. Medicated (withdrawn): Participants unmedicated or with held medication on experimental days (24-h discontinuation). Partially medicated: Mixed sample with no medication status control or standardization. 3.2. Exploratory meta-analysis of clinical outcomes We conducted an exploratory random-effects meta-analysis of clin ical symptom outcomes using post-intervention scores from two ran domized controlled trials (RCT) (Leffa et al., 2022; Cachoeira et al., 2017) across two domains: inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity. Given the limited number of eligible studies reporting sufficiently comparable clinical outcomes, this analysis was undertaken to provide a quantitative summary of available data rather than a definitive estimate of treatment effects. RCT (N = 80) compared Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) alone, tDCS alone, combined DBT and tDCS, and a control condition, employing a stimulation protocol that differed in both dosage and electrode polarity from other studies. The tDCS group received 1.5 mA stimulation (20 min/session, 10 sessions with 72-h intervals) targeting F3 (anodal) and F4 (cathodal), a reversal from other studies. Results indicated tDCS alone significantly improved inattention symptoms (η2 = .467, p = .001) but not hyperactivity/impulsivity. Conversely, DBT showed stronger effects on hyperactivity, while the combined group demonstrated moderate improvements in both domains (η2 = .448 for hyperactivity, .062 for inattention). While tDCS alone was also associated with sig nificant improvements in inattention symptoms, the study's design and reporting structure precluded inclusion in the pooled analysis, high lighting substantial methodological diversity across the clinical evi dence base. Collectively, the available evidence suggests that tDCS may exert differential effects across symptom domains, with more consistent sig nals observed for inattention than hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms. However, the extremely small number of studies, substantial methodo logical heterogeneity, wide confidence intervals, and inability to assess publication bias severely limit the interpretability of pooled estimates. Accordingly, these exploratory findings should be viewed as hypothesis- generating rather than confirmatory, highlighting the need for adequately powered trials with standardized outcome measures and longer follow-up periods. 3.3. Cognitive performance outcomes We synthesized cognitive effects by categorizing outcomes into five domains based on the primary cognitive process targeted by each task, as defined in established neurocognitive models and task validation literature: inhibitory control, working memory, attention, executive function, and social/emotional cognition. This domain-based classifi cation was intended to accommodate heterogeneity in task design while enabling structured comparison across studies. Tasks were assigned to domains according to their dominant cogni tive demands rather than their surface characteristics or outcome labels. For example, the Trail Making Test Part A (TMT-A) was classified under attention due to its emphasis on sustained attention, visual scanning, and processing speed, whereas the Trail Making Test Part B (TMT-B) and the Tower of London (ToL) were classified under executive function given their reliance on cognitive flexibility, set-shifting, and planning processes. Therefore, inhibitory control was measured using the Stop Signal Task (SST), Go/No-Go Task (GNG), Stroop Task, and Emotional Flanker Task (EFT), evaluating the capacity to suppress automatic or prepotent responses —a core impairment of ADHD. Working memory was assessed using N-back tasks and Digit Span (forward and backward), with a focus on temporary storage and information manipulation. Attention was measured using Continuous Performance Test (CPT), CPT variants (Conners' CPT, MOXO-CPT), and Trail Making Test Part A (TMT-A), targeting sustained attention and vigilance. Study mapping according to assessed domains and corresponding outcomes is detailed in Table 2, summarizing cognitive tasks, study arms compared, and reported sig nificance at post-intervention. Reported significance classifications reflect outcomes as described within individual studies; due to incon sistent reporting of effect sizes across studies, these indicators are pre sented descriptively rather than as comparative measures of effect magnitude. To further examine patterns across studies, we aggregated task-level results by domain (Table 3), reporting the number of task applications, the proportion of tasks showing benefit, and the contributing studies and their corresponding effect sizes. Across 23 cognitive task applications from eight studies, 10 tasks (43.5 %) demonstrated positive effects post- tDCS. The overall pattern revealed modest benefits in selected domains. Effect size information in Table 3 is reported where available to char acterize individual study findings, but was not used for cross-study quantitative comparison given heterogeneity in task design, outcome metrics, and reporting practices, and the limited control of practice or fatigue effects across studies. Inhibitory control was most frequently assessed (10 tasks), with four tasks showing significant improvements and generally small to moder ate effect sizes. Working memory was examined through three tasks, two of which demonstrated positive effects with small to moderate effect sizes. Attention was assessed in seven tasks, with three showing signif icant benefit. Executive function outcomes were mixed, with only one of two tasks reporting significant improvement. No beneficial effects were found for the single social-emotional task employed. When single tasks produced multiple outcome indices within the same domain (e.g., the Tower of London yielded five measures or multiple Continuous Perfor mance Test indices), these were treated as a single task in both the total count and positive effect tally for the purposes of domain-level synthesis. This approach was adopted to avoid outcome inflation and to provide conservative estimates of domain-level effects while preserving consistency across studies. 3.4. Neurophysiological outcomes Two studies investigated neurophysiological outcomes using EEG- based measures to assess changes in brain function following tDCS. Cosmo et al. (2015b) examined cortical connectivity using a Func tional Cortical Network (FCN) model, reporting increased EEG-based functional connectivity following single-session 1 mA anodal stimula tion over left DLPFC. Connectivity enhancements extended beyond the stimulated frontal site to occipital, bilateral temporal, and centro-parietal regions, suggesting diffuse modulatory effects across large-scale brain networks. Dubreuil-Vall et al. (2021) analysed event-related potentials (ERPs) during cognitive control tasks, finding that 2 mA left DLPFC stimulation increased P300 amplitude and reduced reaction time in the Eriksen Flanker Task, indicating improved conflict monitoring and attentional control. However, no significant effects were observed on ERP markers during the Stop Signal Task. The authors noted potential state-dependent effects, as baseline P300 amplitude appeared to predict treatment response. These findings provide preliminary, mechanistic indications that prefrontal tDCS may influence neural markers of attention and cognitive control in adults with ADHD. However, given limited studies and methodological heterogeneity, neurophysiological mechanisms under lying tDCS effects remain inconclusive and warrant further investigation. 3.5. Medication status and moderators of effect Among included studies, medication status varied considerably: 3 recruited only unmedicated participants (medication-free or ≥1 month washout), 4 recruited participants withdrawing medication on stimu lation days, 1 included only medication-naïve individuals, 1 maintained stable medication status, 1 involved partially medicated participants without medication control, and 1 did not report medication details. Medication categories are reported here according to the predefined definitions outlined in Table 1. Given the small number of studies and substantial heterogeneity in medication definitions and study designs, no formal moderator analyses were performed. Only Allenby et al. (2018) systematically explored differential tDCS effects between medicated and unmedicated participants. They found CPT false positive errors significantly improved following tDCS only among participants currently using ADHD medication (χ2 = 12.15; p < .001), with no comparable effect in the unmedicated group. Medication status significantly predicted CPT performance across conditions (β = −.69; p = .001), though three-way interaction testing was limited by sample size. These findings suggest concurrent psychostimulant use may modulate tDCS-related behavioural effects on attentional control; however, this observation is based on a single study and requires confirmation in adequately powered samples. Additional potential moderators include age, sex, psychiatric comorbidities, and ADHD subtype. Participant age ranged widely (mean 22–38 years), with male proportions varying substantially (21.3 %–70 %). All studies excluded psychiatric comorbidities. Regarding ADHD subtypes, three studies included combined and inattentive subtypes, two included all three subtypes, and six did not specify subtype information. Despite sample composition differences, no studies conducted subgroup analyses based on demographic or clinical characteristics. The potential moderating role of medication status and other sample characteristics on tDCS efficacy remains unclear and represents a key priority for future, adequately powered studies. 3.6. Dubreuil-Vall et al., 2021; Jacoby et al., 2018) reported no adverse ef fects. Among them, only Cosmo et al. (2015a; 2015b) used a formal tDCS Adverse Events Questionnaire to confirm the absence of discomfort, while the remaining two studies (Dubreuil-Vall et al., 2021; Jacoby et al., 2018) did not specify how adverse effects were assessed. Three studies provided more detailed evaluations. Leffa et al. (2022) and Cachoeira et al. (2017) systematically monitored adverse effects using the Comfort Rating Questionnaire and a tDCS Adverse Events Questionnaire, respectively. Both found mild and transient effects, such as tingling, itching, burning, and scalp discomfort, with higher fre quency in the active stimulation group. No participants withdrew in Leffa et al. but in Cachoeira et al. one participant discontinued after experiencing acute mood changes post-stimulation. Allenby et al. (2018) also administered the tDCS Effects Questionnaire and reported only mild side effects. Additionally, Beiman et al. (2025) conducted follow-up phone assessments at 5 and 24 h post-session, with no major concerns identified. Overall, the evidence indicates that tDCS is generally safe and well- tolerated in adults with ADHD. However, adverse event assessment methods were not standardized across studies, limiting comparability of safety profiles and constraining interpretation of tolerability outcomes, which underscore the need for more systematic and longitudinal assessment in future studies. Future studies would benefit from the use of standardized adverse event reporting tools to improve consistency across trials. 3.7. Stimulation parameters Included studies employed heterogeneous tDCS protocols varying across electrode montage, intensity (1–2 mA), session duration (10–30 min), total sessions (single session to 28 sessions), and stimulation schedule (daily vs. weekly). The most common approach was anodal DLPFC stimulation, with five studies targeting left DLPFC (F3), three targeting right DLPFC (F4), one applying bilateral anodal stimulation over F3 and F4, and one using an anode over the F4-F8 crossing point. Details are provided in Table 1. Substantial variability in montage, po larity, and session structure precludes firm conclusions regarding optimal stimulation parameters. No clear pattern emerged linking spe cific parameter combinations with treatment efficacy. Only Dubreuil-Vall et al. (2021) employed crossover design to directly compare left and right DLPFC stimulation, reporting that right-sided stimulation (F4) led to significantly greater commission error reductions, suggesting potential lateralized effects on attention-related outcomes. However, these findings are preliminary and have not been replicated. No studies used individualized protocols or adapted parameters based on participant-specific neurocognitive or neurophysiological profiles. Given methodological heterogeneity and limited sample sizes, current evidence does not support clear conclusions regarding optimal stimulation parameters. Further trials are needed to systematically evaluate electrode placement, polarity, intensity, and potential person alized tDCS approaches in adult ADHD populations. 4. Discussion This systematic review synthesized current evidence regarding the efficacy and tolerability of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) in adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Across the eleven included studies, considerable methodological heterogeneity was observed, limiting the strength of inferences that can be drawn. Nevertheless, patterns within the available evidence allow tentative observations regarding the domains in which effects have been exam ined, while acknowledging that the strength and consistency of these effects remain uncertain. 4.1. Clinical efficacy: differential effects on core symptoms Findings from the exploratory meta-analysis suggested a differential response pattern between ADHD symptom domains. While pooled esti mates indicated a potential reduction in inattention symptoms following tDCS, no statistically significant benefit was observed for hyperactivity/ impulsivity. Given the limited number of studies contributing to the quantitative synthesis and the substantial heterogeneity observed, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Nonetheless, the directional pattern is broadly consistent with reports from pediatric populations (Salehinejad et al., 2020), suggesting that observed effects may vary across symptom domains rather than indicating uniform clinical benefit. This apparent differential pattern may reflect differences in the neurobiological substrates underlying ADHD symptom domains. Inat tention has been closely linked to dysfunction within prefrontal cortical networks involved in executive control, the brain regions that are rela tively accessible to superficial cortical stimulation techniques such as tDCS. In contrast, hyperactivity and impulsivity are thought to involve more distributed cortico-subcortical circuits, including deep structures such as the basal ganglia, which are less directly targeted by conven tional tDCS protocols. From a mechanistic perspective, these consider ations are consistent with the possibility that tDCS effects in adult ADHD may be more readily detectable in cognitive-attentional domains than in behavioural symptom domains, although this interpretation remains tentative given current evidence limitations. 4.2. Cognitive outcomes: task-specific improvements Cognitive assessments revealed a nuanced pattern of improvements that extended beyond simple domain-level analyses. Working memory and inhibitory control tasks, particularly the N-back and Stop Signal Task, were associated with the most consistently reported task-level improvements following tDCS. However, effects were often confined to specific task indices rather than global performance improvements. For instance, significant reductions in omission errors occurred without corresponding changes in commission errors on both the N-back and CPT tasks (Beiman et al., 2025), highlighting the precision with which tDCS may influence distinct cognitive processes. This granular pattern of improvement underscores the importance of moving beyond broad cognitive domains toward more refined outcome measures. Rather than aggregating effects at the task level, future studies should identify which specific cognitive processes, sustained attention versus inhibitory speed, for example, are most responsive to prefrontal stimulation. Such precision would not only enhance mecha nistic understanding but also facilitate the development of personalized treatment protocols tailored to individual cognitive profiles. The relatively modest effects observed in adult populations, compared to more pronounced benefits reported in studies including pediatric populations (Salehinejad et al., 2019), may reflect develop mental differences in neural plasticity and cortical network organiza tion. These findings suggest that therapeutic expectations and protocols may need to be adjusted for adult populations, with greater emphasis on sustained treatment regimens or alternative stimulation approaches. 4.3. Neurophysiological insights: an underexplored frontier Only two included studies incorporated neurophysiological assess ments, both using EEG and reported alterations in neural oscillatory activity following tDCS. Specifically, observed changes in spectral power and event-related potential components (e.g., P200/P300) are consis tent with modulation of attentional allocation, stimulus evaluation, and cognitive control processes, which align with the cognitive domains assessed behaviourally in this review. Similarly, reported changes in functional connectivity and frontal oscillatory patterns may reflect engagement of prefrontal control networks implicated in executive functioning and sustained attention. However, both EEG studies employed single-session stimulation designs, limiting the extent to which these findings can be interpreted as markers of sustained neurophysiological change or long-term clinical benefit. As such, while these results provide preliminary mechanistic indications of tDCS-related modulation of neural processes relevant to ADHD, conclusions regarding enduring neuroplastic effects remain constrained. The limited integration of objective neurobiological markers in adult tDCS research therefore represents a significant gap in the literature. In contrast, pediatric tDCS research has increasingly integrated EEG and neuroimaging modalities to link neural changes with cognitive and clinical outcomes (Westwood et al., 2021b), enabling more sophisti cated mechanistic insights and personalized treatment approaches. Future adult studies should prioritize the inclusion of neurophysio logical assessments, such as event-related potentials (ERPs), resting- state EEG, and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), which are feasible, cost-effective, and well-tolerated in adult populations, within multi-session and longitudinal designs. These tools can serve dual purposes: providing mechanistic insights into how tDCS modulates neural activity, and identifying biomarkers of treatment response to support stratified or adaptive intervention models. For instance, EEG- based indices of frontal theta activity or connectivity patterns may help identify individuals most likely to benefit from prefrontal stimu lation, while longitudinal changes in these signals could offer early in dicators of treatment efficacy. These approaches would allow examination of whether acute neural changes (e.g., P300 amplitude modulation or connectivity shifts) translate into sustained cognitive improvement or clinical symptom reduction over time. Embedding neurophysiological monitoring into tDCS protocols may therefore sup port both mechanistic understanding and the development of stratified or adaptive intervention models in adult ADHD. 4.4. Stimulation parameters: the challenge of optimization The substantial variability in stimulation protocols across studies, including electrode placement, current intensity, session duration, and treatment frequency, precluded clear conclusions about optimal pa rameters. While most studies targeted the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC, F3) with anodal stimulation, systematic comparisons of montages, intensities, and dosing schedules remain limited. Only one study (Dubreuil-Vall et al., 2021) used a within-subject crossover design to compare left and right DLPFC stimulation, reporting no statistically significant differences in outcomes. The question of treatment durability emerged as particularly important. The single study (Allenby et al., 2018) including follow-up assessment found that cognitive benefits did not persist after stimula tion discontinuation, suggesting that sustained or booster protocols may be necessary for long-term efficacy. This finding has important impli cations for clinical implementation, as it suggests that tDCS for adult ADHD may require ongoing maintenance therapy rather than discrete treatment courses. 4.5. Clinical implications and future directions These findings have several important clinical implications. First, tDCS may be more appropriately considered as a potential adjunctive approach targeting specific cognitive-attentional processes, rather than a comprehensive ADHD intervention. Second, the need for sustained treatment protocols has important cost-effectiveness considerations that warrant systematic evaluation. Third, the safety profile reported across studies suggests that extended treatment regimens may be feasible, although standardized adverse event reporting remains necessary. Several critical research priorities emerge from this review. Large- scale, adequately powered trials with harmonized protocols are ur gently needed to establish definitive efficacy and identify optimal stimulation parameters. Long-term follow-up studies should evaluate treatment durability and establish guidelines for maintenance therapy. Critically, future studies must incorporate stratified analyses by ADHD subtype, sex, age, and medication status to identify individual difference factors that moderate treatment response. Moreover, head-to-head comparisons with established non- pharmacological interventions, such as cognitive behavioural therapy or neurofeedback, would help position tDCS within the broader treat ment landscape for adult ADHD. Economic evaluations comparing tDCS to standard care approaches would inform implementation decisions and healthcare policy. 4.6. Limitations Several limitations constrain the interpretation of these findings. The small number of included studies and substantial methodological het erogeneity limited our ability to conduct robust quantitative syntheses, where quantitative pooling was possible, it was restricted to an exploratory meta-analysis based on two trials. Most studies employed small sample sizes and lacked long-term follow-up, which restricted generalizability and precluded evaluation of treatment durability. The wide variability in outcome measures, coupled with limited consider ation of potential moderator variables, further constrains the strength of conclusions. Methodological quality was variable and generally mod erate to high, although statistical power was frequently limited, reflecting small sample sizes across trials. Additionally, the risk of publication bias and selective reporting cannot be excluded, particularly given the early stage of this research field and the predominance of pilot studies, which often involve narra tive reporting of results. metadata_title: Gut-brain axis in Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD): A narrative review of the links between gut microbiota and ADHD pathophysiology
pages: Gut-brain axis in Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD): A narrative review of the links between gut microbiota and ADHD pathophysiology Barbara Luyens a,b,c,d,* , Francisco Felgueroso-Bueno d,e, Amandine Everard b,f,1, Isabelle Massat a,c,d,g,h,1 a Department of Infant, Child, Adolescent and Young Adult Psychiatry, Hopitaux Universitaires de Bruxelles (HUB), Brussels, Belgium b Metabolism and Nutrition Research Group, Louvain Drug Research Institute, UCLouvain, Universit ́e Catholique de Louvain, Brussels, Belgium c Laboratory of Developmental Psychiatry, Universit ́e Libre de Bruxelles (ULB), Brussels, Belgium d UNI, ULB Neuroscience Institute, Universit ́e Libre de Bruxelles (ULB), Brussels, Belgium e Department of General Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, Universit ́e Libre de Bruxelles (ULB), Brussels, Belgium f Walloon Excellence in Life Sciences and BIOtechnology (WELBIO) Department, WEL Research Institute, 6 Avenue Pasteur, Wavre, Belgium g National Fund for Scientific Research (FNRS), Brussels, Belgium h Center for Research in Cognition and Neurosciences (CRCN), Universit ́e Libre de Bruxelles (ULB), Brussels, Belgium A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) Neurodevelopment Gut microbiota Gut-brain axis Neuroinflammation A B S T R A C T Characterized by developmentally inappropriate levels of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, Attention- Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is the most prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder, posing a significant public health concern. Its etiopathogenesis is considered multifactorial with complex determinism but remains unclear. Recent research highlights the gut microbiota and the gut-brain axis as promising avenues for under standing and potentially treating ADHD, with a growing number of studies exploring alterations in gut micro biota composition among affected individuals. This narrative review examines the current literature on the role of the gut microbiota in ADHD and focuses on key findings about bacterial composition, how it may be linked to ADHD symptomatology, and the possible mechanisms involved. While studies consistently report changes in microbial composition and diversity in individuals with ADHD, results remain heterogeneous across taxonomic levels. Some compelling evidence also suggests a link between gut microbial profiles and ADHD symptom severity. The involvement of microbiota in influencing neuro development is proposed to be mediated through mechanisms related to SCFA production, immune modulation, and neurotransmitter synthesis. These findings pave the way for microbiota-targeted interventions as adjunct therapies for ADHD. This review evaluates areas of consensus and discrepancies between studies, while addressing the methodo logical limitations present in this field of research. Although the gut microbiota appears to play a meaningful role in the complex and multifactorial origins of ADHD, more rigorous and comprehensive studies are needed to confirm these findings and translate them into effective clinical applications. This could ultimately improve both our understanding and treatment of this heterogeneous disorder. 1. Attention Deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) 1.1. Prevalence and symptomatology Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is the most common neurodevelopmental disorder in child psychiatry (Polanczyk et al., 2014) with a worldwide prevalence in children and adolescents around 8 % (Ayano et al., 2023; Thomas et al., 2015) and an estimated male-to-female ratio of 2–4:1 (APA, 2013; Bitsko, 2022; Dalsgaard et al., 2020). These symptoms negatively affect daily functioning, social interactions, aca demic performance, as well as physical and mental health (Ayano et al., 2023; Fenollar-Cort ́es and Fuentes, 2016). Associated with comorbid disorders, such as conduct disorders, anxiety, depression and autism spectrum disorders (ASD), ADHD is actually an undeniable public health priority (Akmatov et al., 2021; Vasileva et al., 2021). ADHD is also associated with a range of executive and attentional deficits (Khaledi et al., 2019; Kofler et al., 2013; Pievsky and McGrath, 2018), predom inant in the symptomatology of ADHD associated with structural and functional brain variations (Martella et al., 2020; Samea et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2023). Its symptoms persist into adulthood in 60 % cases and are associated with social and occupational impairment (Sibley et al., 2017). 1.2. Etiology The etiopathogenesis of ADHD is widely considered multifactorial, arising from complex interactions between genetic and environmental factors (Akutagava-Martins et al., 2016; Faraone et al., 2015). Its etiol ogy remains incompletely understood, suggesting that the factors are interchangeable and no single factor can be identified as an isolated and direct trigger of ADHD. This heterogeneity reflects the phenotypic variability observed in ADHD and continues to hinder diagnosis and treatment (Klein et al., 2019; Thapar et al., 2013). Twin studies consistently demonstrate a genetic contribution, with heritability esti mates between 60 % and 90 % (Faraone et al., 2005; Larsson et al., 2014). Large-scale genomic association research (GWAS) identified genes involved in neuronal plasticity and dopaminergic, noradrenergic, and serotonergic systems (Demontis et al., 2019, 2023; Faraone and Larsson, 2019; Franke et al., 2009). Environmental factors, including prenatal, perinatal, and postnatal conditions (pollutant exposure, psychological stress, ...) have been suggested to contribute to ADHD (Kim et al., 2020; Thapar et al., 2013). Their effects, however, appear modest and often intertwined with ge netic vulnerability. Individuals genetically predisposed may be more sensitive to specific environmental risks (Dunn et al., 2019; Rutter et al., 2006). Prenatal exposure to certain environmental factors may initiate immune-related processes that interfere with neurodevelopment and increase the risk of ADHD (Razaz and Ananth, 2024). Among these in fluences, dietary and nutritional factors during gestation and early childhood appear particularly relevant (Lebovitz et al., 2018; Mathee et al., 2020; O'Mahony et al., 2017). Increasing evidence suggests that certain dietary patterns can promote inflammation, oxidative stress, altered gut permeability, changes in microbiome composition, and altered metabolite production, each capable of influencing neuro development (Lebovitz et al., 2018). These findings raise the possibility that gastrointestinal dysregulation contributes to ADHD (Dunn et al., 2019; Verlaet et al., 2014). The gut microbiome may be the missing piece of the neurodevelopmental puzzle, linking early-life stress to brain function and behavior (O'Mahony et al., 2017). In parallel, accumulating evidence implicates immune-related mechanisms in ADHD pathophysiology. Neuroinflammation, defined as inflammatory activity within neural tissue involving microglia, as trocytes, cytokines, and related molecular processes in the central ner vous system (CNS), is now widely considered to be a key factor in ADHD (Dunn et al., 2019; Turiaco et al., 2024). Consistent with this view, ADHD has been linked to elevated inflammatory and immune markers (R.-Y. Zhou et al., 2017), as well as to higher prevalence of immune-related conditions such as eczema, asthma, psoriasis, allergic rhinitis, and type 1 diabetes (Chua et al., 2021; van der Schans et al., 2017). In addition, several susceptibility genes associated with neuro developmental risk in ADHD have also been implicated in immune pathways (Chang et al., 2021; Dunn et al., 2019; Leffa et al., 2018; Saccaro et al., 2021; Zayats et al., 2015). These findings support the existence of a pro-inflammatory state in ADHD, which could be a cause, effect, or related phenomenon of the condition (Saccaro et al., 2021). Immune-related inflammatory processes are consistent with well- established neurobiological models of ADHD that involve dysregula tion of the dopaminergic and noradrenergic systems, which underlie impulsivity, behavioral control, and attention (Dunn et al., 2019; Stan ford and Sciberras, 2022; Wu et al., 2012). These catecholaminergic pathways are also targeted by ADHD treatments, which modulate catecholamine release and uptake to normalize neurotransmission (Faraone and Glatt, 2009; Verlaet et al., 2018). At the cerebral level, these catecholaminergic disturbances correspond to structural and functional alterations observed in ADHD, suggesting a global delay in brain maturation. These differences include cortical and subcortical activation abnormalities, particularly in prefrontal regions involved in cognitive control, motor planning, and attentional processes (Martella et al., 2020; Samea et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2023). Recent work has proposed that gut microbes may influence neuro inflammation and catecholamine regulation in reward-related brain regions (Huwart et al., 2025). This suggests a possible connection be tween diet, the gut microbiome, immune signaling, and neurotrans mitter systems relevant to ADHD. Despite ongoing debate, diet has emerged as a relevant area of investigation, with dietary interventions increasingly explored for their potential to alleviate ADHD symptoms, possibly through the modulation of allergic or inflammatory responses that are more prevalent in children with ADHD (Bull-Larsen & Mohajeri, 2019; Lewis et al., 2025; Turiaco et al., 2024). Given the broad influence of the gut on human physiology, and growing evidence that the intes tinal microbiota contributes to health across many medical domains (Armour et al., 2019), attention has turned to its communication with the brain. The gut–brain axis, a bidirectional system in which the gut microbiota plays a central role, is now considered a promising frame work for understanding neurodevelopment and behavior (Bundgaard-Nielsen et al., 2020; Cryan and Dinan, 2012; McMath et al., 2023; Soltysova et al., 2022). As described in depth in this review, only a handful of studies have investigated the gut-brain axis in ADHD. 2. Gut microbiota and the gut-brain axis The gut microbiota represents the community of microorganisms including bacteria, viruses, fungi and archaea that are inhabiting the gastrointestinal tract of the host. The term gut microbiome describes the collective genomes of the microorganisms that reside in the gut and the microorganisms themselves. Among these microorganisms, bacteria have been larger investigated whereas more recent research also focused on viruses and fungi. The last estimation evaluated around 3.9 × 1013 the total number of bacteria within human body, a number approx imatively equivalent to human eucaryotic cells (Sender et al., 2016). Importantly, these estimates do not consider the viruses and phages also present in our bodies, which could equal the bacterial estimates (Liang and Bushman, 2021). The interaction between gut bacteria and the host is qualified as a symbiotic relationship since both microbes and the host benefit from this mutually beneficial relationship. Importantly, this host–microbe sym biosis is essential to health and well-being whereas disruption of this symbiotic state, the so-called dysbiosis and transition from symbiosis to dysbiosis have been implicated in human disease (Malard et al., 2021). Importantly, the gut is also densely innervated by hundreds of mil lions of neurons that comprise the enteric nervous system (ENS), inter acting with the gut microbiota (Geng et al., 2022). This system cooperates with intestinal microbes, intestinal immune system, and endocrine systems to form a complex network that is required to maintain a stable intestinal microenvironment (Geng et al., 2022). Interestingly, the ENS contains integrative neural circuitry with simi larities to the CNS of mammals and arising before and independently of the CNS from an evolutionary point of view (Furness and Stebbing, 2018). Therefore, the ENS can be seen as the first brain developed independently of the CNS. Moreover, reciprocal connections between ENS and CNS occur in mammals and are part of the gut-brain axis B. For the past two decades there has been growing evidence supporting the roles of gut microbiota as one of the key regulators of gut-brain function which leads to the microbiota gut brain axis concept (Blair et al., 2025). Indeed, bidirectional communi cations between gut microbes and the brain are supported through the immune system, vagus nerve system, neuroendocrine system, circula tory system and enteric nervous system (Yuan et al., 2023). Specifically, a distinct microbiota-gut-brain axis across the lifespan, especially during neurodevelopment, has been highlighted (Cryan, 2025). In line with this, germ free mice have been reported to present altered neurogenesis processes that are not restored by postweaning microbial colonization (Ogbonnaya et al., 2015). Moreover, a role of the microbiome in neu rodevelopmental disorders ranging from ASD to ADHD has also been delineate in animal models (Wright, 1985). Even if this mechanistic perspective should still be supplemented with more translational studies to evaluate the applicability of findings from animal models to human subjects, some preliminary human studies also support a link between gut microbiome and ADHD. 3. Gut microbiota in ADHD 3.1. State of the art: available studies on gut microbiota in ADHD Current human studies on gut microbiota in ADHD remain limited but are rapidly increasing, using diverse methodological approaches and research questions. To date, 12 studies have compared the gut micro biota of individuals with ADHD to age-matched controls or unaffected siblings (see Table 1). The majority of these studies involve children and adolescents, although a few have focused on adult patients (Aarts et al., 2017; Richarte et al., 2021; Szopinska-Tokov et al., 2020). In addition, most studies use 16S rRNA sequencing to analyze bacterial populations, with more recent works applying shotgun metagenomics for higher taxonomic resolution (Wan et al., 2020; N. Wang et al., 2024). ADHD is highly heterogeneous, with substantial variability in symptoms and severity, contributing to inconsistent findings related to gut microbiota. Therefore, rather than solely comparing individuals with ADHD to unaffected controls, investigating gut microbiota varia tions in relation to symptom profiles may be more informative. Seven clinical studies have examined associations between gut microbiota composition and ADHD symptomatology, assessing how specific taxa or diversity patterns relate to symptom severity. Additional work has linked gut microbiota profiles in ADHD with brain imaging (Aarts et al., 2017) and dietary habits (L.-J. Wang et al., 2020). Although growing interest, existing studies on the gut microbiota in ADHD show significant methodological variability: from study design and analytical techniques to participant age, geographic location, medication status, and assessment tools. This heterogeneity likely con tributes to the inconsistent findings across studies and complicates direct comparisons, as noted in other research contexts (Rodriguez et al., 2024).
