autism and ADHD do not overlap, but homotypic co-occurrence has been evidenced, as autistic individuals commonly present ADHD symptoms and vice versa (Berenguer et al., 2018; Khachadourian et al., 2023; Rong et al., 2021). Socio-emotional difficulties manifest differently in autism and ADHD. In autism, these range from simpler forms of social interactions (e.g., joint attention) to more complex processes (e.g., establishing and maintaining friendships) as they are unable to respond to their peers (e. g., lack of social smiling), have challenges in eye contact, body language, and speech production (APA, 2022). Contrarily, social problems in ADHD result rather from rejection by their peers, as their impulsive behaviour is perceived as upsetting or disruptive in social interactive contexts (Chiang and Gau, 2014). The functioning heterogeneity observed in autism and ADHD may be explained by differences in executive function (EF) and emotion regu lation (ER) in these conditions, which are crucial for social cognition and communication (Moriguchi and Hiraki, 2013). Therefore, a possible approach to the early identification and differential diagnosis of autism, ADHD and autism/ADHD co-occurrence (autism/ADHD) may be related to particularities in the association between EF and ER in these conditions. EF consists of a set of top-down, higher-order cognitive processes that enable individuals to manage and regulate their thoughts, actions, and emotions to achieve goals (Diamond, 2013; García-Molina, 2018). Key components of EF include working memory (the ability to tempo rarily hold and manipulate information), inhibitory control (the ability to control impulses, resist distractions, and refrain from behaviours that may interfere with goal attainment), and cognitive flexibility/shifting (the ability to adapt to changing circumstances and adjust one’s thinking in response to new information and problem solving) (Diamond, 2013; Friedman and Miyake, 2017; García-Molina, 2018; Miyake et al., 2000). EF challenges have been proposed to be associated with autistic traits, including social domains and repetitive and restricted behaviours (Demetriou et al., 2018; Jones et al., 2018; Leung et al., 2016; Lopez et al., 2005; Pugliese et al., 2016), as well as with core ADHD symptoms (i.e. impulsivity) (Burgess et al., 2010; Craig et al., 2016; Tillman et al., 2011). Challenges in planning and flexibility are particularly prominent in autism, with the latter being associated with repetitive behaviours and social difficulties (Leung et al., 2016; Lopez et al., 2005). Difficulties in response inhibition and working memory are more characteristic of ADHD, contributing to impulsivity and hyperactivity (Alderson et al., 2012; Craig et al., 2016; Rapport et al., 2009; Antshel and Russo, 2019). Individuals with co-occurring autism and ADHD may have more severe executive dysfunctions, especially in flexibility, inhibition, and attention (Benallie et al., 2021). ER refers to the ability to monitor, evaluate, and modulate emotional experiences in response to internal or external/environmental stimuli, as well as how they are processed and expressed (Carver and Johnson, 2018; Gross, 2015). ER contributes to the organisation of cognitive ac tivity, emotional responses, and overt behaviour (Gioia et al., 2002; Zelazo and Cunningham, 2007). It is important to note that ER strategies are neither inherently adaptive nor maladaptive, but depend on flexi bility and contextual appropriateness (Gross, 2015). Individuals with NDDs often have difficulty using ER strategies flexibly, which can result in heightened emotional reactivity, tantrums, irritability, or aggressive behaviour (Mazefsky et al., 2013; Graziano and Garcia, 2016). Altered ER ability has been linked to key processes during develop ment in both autism (Cai et al., 2019; Conner et al., 2020; Reyes et al., 2020) and ADHD (Barkley, 2010; Faraone et al., 2019; Groves et al., 2020; Shaw et al., 2014), particularly in relation to social maladjust ment, language (Çiray et al., 2022; Jaisle et al., 2023), and behavioural problems (R ̈oll et al., 2012; Tse, 2020). For example, Tye et al. (2014) found that autistic, ADHD and autistic/ADHD children (8–13 years) showed atypical emotion processing: autism showed reduced early re sponses to anger, ADHD altered contextual processing for fear and joy, and co-occurring autism/ADHD combined difficulties. These results suggest ER difficulties may underlie social challenges, especially in autism/ADHD (Walter et al., 2023). EF and ER are closely linked across the lifespan in non-clinical populations (Hendricks and Buchanan, 2016; Schweizer et al., 2017; Sperduti et al., 2017; Wante et al., 2017). Neuroanatomically, ER is associated with activation in the prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex, regions also involved in EF (Buhle et al., 2014; Kohn et al., 2014; Niendam et al., 2012). This overlap supports models suggesting that EF is central to emotional modulation (Makowski et al., 2015; Ochsner et al., 2012; Ochsner and Gross, 2005). As both EF and ER depend on the maturation of the prefrontal and subcortical-cortical regions, which is often disrupted in NDDs, this disruption may account for the observed difficulties (Shaw et al., 2014). Inhibition and flexibility difficulties have been related to maladaptive ER strategies and emotional dysregulation in both autism (Mazefsky et al., 2013) and ADHD (Banaschewski et al., 2012). Likewise, in autism/ADHD, poorer cognitive functioning has been associated with maladaptive ER strategies and pronounced func tional impairments (Rao and Landa, 2014). Overall, the evidence suggests that EF and ER are dynamically interconnected processes that jointly influence social adjustment and mental health outcomes (Hendricks and Buchanan, 2016; Nigg, 2017). EF appears to provide the cognitive control necessary for implementing ER strategies, and ER can, in turn, modulate the efficient use of EF re sources (Camacho et al., 2025; Bridgett et al., 2013). Therefore, clari fying how these domains interact in autism, ADHD, and autism/ADHD is crucial to understanding the mechanisms underlying shared socio-emotional and behavioural difficulties. Building on this, research in clinical populations has proposed EF and ER as potential trans diagnostic mechanisms that are particularly relevant in the context of autism, ADHD and their co-occurrence (Astle et al., 2022; England-Mason, 2020). Thus, understanding the relationship between EF and ER may contribute to a more integrated model of neuro developmental functioning that moves beyond categorical diagnostic boundaries towards dimensional, mechanism-based frameworks (Insel et al., 2010; Cuthbert, 2014). Furthermore, identifying the nature and strength of the association between EF and ER in autism, ADHD, and autism/ADHD has significant implications for clinical practice. Identifying similarities and differences in these associations and outlining potential cognitive–emotional pro files, may help clinicians differentiate between autism, ADHD, and their overlap. This could facilitate differential diagnosis, reduce the number of clinical hypotheses, and shorten the diagnostic process. An accurate and timely diagnosis is also essential for accessing appropriate in terventions, which can prevent more severe behavioural and emotional difficulties (Ozonoff, 2015; Simon et al., 2023). An early diagnosis has been shown to lead to better functional independence, cognition, and adaptation in autism (Pickles et al., 2016) and ADHD (Agnew-Blais et al., 2018). In contrast, delayed identification can limit access to support and has been linked to negative psychosocial outcomes, including loneliness, lower self-esteem, or substance use (Gabbay-Dizdar et al., 2022). Examining shared and distinct cognitive –emotional profiles across autism and/or ADHD can therefore enhance diagnostic precision and support the development of more personalised and effective early interventions. 1. Current study This study aimed to comprehensively investigate the relationship between executive function and emotion regulation in autism, ADHD, and co-occurring autism/ADHD and answer the following research questions: 1) How does executive functioning relate to emotion regu lation in autism?, 2) How does executive functioning relate to emotion regulation in ADHD?, and 3) How does executive functioning relate to emotion regulation in autism/ADHD co-occurrence? 2. Method The methods and protocol for the present systematic review were established and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420250652223) prior to the implementation of this study. We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) checklist guidelines (Moher et al., 2015) to conduct this systematic review. 2.1. Literature search strategy The electronic databases PubMed, Web of Science, PsychInfo and Scopus were searched for empirical articles published in English be tween January 2013 (to reflect the latest diagnostic criteria for autism and ADHD, as the DSM-5 was published this year) and October 2024. The following search terms were used: (("autism" OR "autistic” OR "asd" OR "autism spectrum disorder" OR "asperger") OR (“attention deficit hyperactivity disorder” OR “adhd”) AND (“executive functions” OR “executive functioning” OR “updating” OR “working memory” OR “planification” OR “planning” OR “shifting” OR “cognitive flexibility” OR “inhibitory control” OR “inhibit*” OR “decision making”) AND ("emotion dysregulation" OR “emotional dysregulation” OR "emotion regulation" OR “emotional regulation” OR "emotion control" OR “emotional control”)). Studies were considered if they i) enrolled people with a diagnosis of ASD, autism or Asperger’s syndrome, and/or ADHD, according to the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th (ICD-10) and 11th (ICD-11) revisions or the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th Edition, Text Revision (DSM-IV-TR), 5th Edi tion (DSM-5) or 5 th Edition Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) diagnostic criteria; and ii) focused on the association between EF and ER in ASD, ADHD, and/or ASD/ADHD. Titles and abstracts were screened for eligible studies. The full text of the selected studies was then examined according to the inclusion and exclusion criteria, as described below. The eligibility of all records (title and abstract and full texts) was assessed independently by two re searchers. Cohen’s kappa coefficient was calculated at each stage to measure interrater reliability and ensure that the included data accu rately reflected the assessed variables (McHugh, 2012). Any discrep ancies or doubts were resolved at a consensus meeting conducted by a third researcher who acted as a consultant in case of conflict. It should be noted that a manual search of the reference lists of the included studies was conducted to identify further studies. However, this search did not result in the inclusion of any additional studies. 2.2. Procedure and eligibility criteria The initial database search resulted in 1593 articles of which 713 were duplicated. Hence, the title and abstract of 880 articles were screened for the inclusion criteria (k = 0.67). Studies were excluded based on the following exclusion criteria: i) different format than empirical paper (i.e., book chapters, congress abstracts, letters to the editor, meta-analysis or reviews) (n = 272), ii) not using human samples (n = 5), iii) not focused on ASD, Asperger’s diagnosis and/or ADHD (n = 280), iv) not focused on the study of executive functions and/or emotional regulation (n = 137). Two additional studies were excluded as they were written in languages other than English. Thus, the title and abstract screening resulted in 184 potentially relevant articles. After a thorough and comprehensive examination of the full text of these articles for inclusion criteria, 162 were additionally excluded (k = 0.76). The following eligibility/selection criteria were applied i) participants with a diagnosis of ASD, autism, Asperger's syn drome and/or ADHD according to the ICD-10, ICD-11, DSM-IV-TR, DSM-5 or DSM-5-TR, or whose diagnosis has been confirmed by a standardised ASD questionnaire or diagnostic interview (Autism Diag nostic Interview-Revised [ADI-R; Rutter et al., 2003], Autism Diagnostic Observational Schedule-2 [ADOS-2; Lord et al., 2012]) or by a standardised ADHD questionnaire or diagnostic interviews (KiddieSchedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia - Present and Life time DSM-5 Version [K-SADS-PL; Kaufman et al., (2016)], ADHD Rating Scale - IV [ADHD-RS-IV; DuPaul et al., (1998)], ADHD-RS-5 (DuPaul et al., 2016), Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale [ASRS; Kessler et al., (2005)]) (n = 57); and ii) studies analysing the relationship between EF and ER in autism, ADHD and/or autism/ADHD (n = 104). In addition, one study (S ́aez-Suanes et al., 2020b) was excluded because it reported the same results regarding EF and ER associations as another earlier study – S ́aez-Suanes et al. (2020a), the latter being included in this review. A total of 22 articles were included in this review. These articles were divided into three groups according to the diagnosis of the participants: autism (participants with a diagnosis of ASD, autism or Asperger Syn drome only), ADHD (participants with a diagnosis of ADHD only), and autism/ADHD (participants with a co-occurring diagnosis of ASD, autism or Asperger and ADHD). Four articles were included in the autism group, 16 in the ADHD group, and two in the autism/ADHD group. Fig. 1 depicts the flowchart of the selection procedure. 2.3. Data selection and extraction In addition to study descriptors (e.g. authors, year of publication), the following information was extracted from the full-text documents: i) sample size, ii) age of participants, iii) gender distribution, iv) diagnosis, v) instruments used to assess EF and ER, and vi) results regarding the association between EF and ER. The quality and risk of bias of the included studies were assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklist for cross-sectional analytical studies (Moola et al., 2017). Supplementary Material Table 1 provides information on the quality of the studies. Interrater reliability was excellent (k = 0.95). 3. Results Table 1 summarises the methodological characteristics and results of the studies included in this review. Results are presented according to the three groups: autism, ADHD and autism/ADHD. 3.1. EF and ER in Autism Four studies reporting on the relationship between EF and ER in autism were included. S ́aez-Suanes et al. (2020a) used informant-report questionnaires to assess both EF and ER in autistic individuals aged 18–62 years with co-occurring intellectual disability (ID) – the Dysexecutive Question naire (DEX) to assess EF, and the Emotional Regulation Checklist (ERC; Shields and Cicchetti, 1997) to assess ER. The DEX is a general measure of executive dysfunction assessed through 20 items rated on a 5-point Likert-scale. The ERC is a 24-item questionnaire comprising two sub scales: emotion regulation (assessing the appropriate expression and modulation of emotions) and lability/negativity (measuring emotional dysregulation characterised by rapid and intense mood fluctuations). The lability/negativity subscale was used as an indicator of emotional dysregulation. Therapists completed the questionnaires as participants had limited ability to independently complete them, attributed to their co-occurring ID. Results indicated that executive dysfunction was posi tively and significantly associated with emotional dysregulation (r = 0.648, p < .01). DeLucia et al. (2022) and Jahromi et al. (2019) used the Day/Night Task to assess inhibitory control in autistic and non-autistic (i.e., control group) preschoolers. In this task two types of cards are shown with the illustration of a sun or a moon and stars. Children were then asked to say "day" if a moon and stars card was shown, and "night" if a sun card was shown. In addition to the Day/Night Task, Jahromi et al. (2019) assessed inhibitory control also using the Hand Game Task, which required children to initially mimic the experimenter's hand movements and M. Pozo-Rodríguez et al. In addition, effortful control (i.e., ability to focus attention on task-relevant information and switching between tasks, while inhibiting unwanted responses; Chevalier, 2018) was measured using the Chil dren’s Behaviour Questionnaire–Short Form (CBQ-SF; Putnam and Rothbart, 2006; Rothbart et al., 2001), a parent-reported instrument assessing temperament, with effortful control scores derived from sub scales measuring inhibitory control, low-intensity pleasure, perceptual sensitivity, and attention focusing. Both studies assessed ER abilities using the parent-report ERC, with Jahromi et al. (2019) also using observation to rate behaviours during a gratification delay task, with positive and negative affect behaviour being rated on a 7-point scale (1- ‘no negative/positive emotion displayed’; 7- ‘three or more intense, heightened, or prolonged displays of negative/positive emotion’). DeLucia et al. (2022) found no significant relationships between inhibitory control, measured by the Day/Night Task, and the Labili ty/Negativity or Emotion Regulation subscales of the ERC, in autistic preschool children aged 4–6 years and in the non-autistic comparison group. Similarly, Jahromi et al. (2019) found no significant associations between inhibitory control, assessed using the Day/Night Task or Hand Game Task, and the ERC or the observed behaviours (i.e., reflecting negative or positive affect) in autistic and non-autistic children aged 40–77 months. However, the authors observed that ER was significantly associated with effortful control (r = 0.58, p < .05) in the autistic group. In contrast, in the non-autistic group, ER was significantly related to joint attention (r = 0.51, p < .05). Finally, Zantinge et al. (2017) assessed EF using the parent-report (preschool questionnaire) version of the Behaviour Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF; Gioia et al., 2002). This questionnaire as sesses EF across nine clinical scales – Inhibit, Self-Monitor, Shift, Emotional Control, Initiate, Working Memory, Plan/Organise, Organi sation of Materials, and Monitor – which are further grouped into three high-level executive domains, each represented by a regulatory index: behavioural, emotional, and cognitive regulation. ER was evaluated using the Locked Box task, a performance-based task from the preschool Laboratory Temperament Assessment Battery (Lab-TAB). This task was aimed at inducing frustration by denying children access to a chosen toy for 4 min using incorrect keys, followed by 1 min of playing after unlocking the box giving access to the toy. While performing this task, the authors observed the behaviour of 43- to 79-month-old preschoolers, measured their physiological arousal (i.e., heart rate activity), and cat egorised their emotional coping strategies as constructive, venting, and avoidance. The results showed no statistically significant association between EF (inhibitory control or shifting abilities) and ER strategies in autistic children. The study also included a group of non-autistic pre schoolers but did not report on the association between EF and ER strategies in this group. 3.2. Addi tional regression analysis showed that children’s difficulties in regu lating negative emotional states were being explained in part by reduced EF. Additionally, these inhibition diffi culties were related to the composite score of emotional dysfunctions (r = 0.69, p < .001), which the authors computed by combining the lability/negative emotionality and ER subscales of the ERC and the emotional control subscale from the BRIEF. (2015) used an Emotional n-back task to measure EF and ER in children aged 8–15 years with and without ADHD. This task consisted of a pseudorandom sequence of letters that were presented to children who were asked to respond to a pre-specified letter, assessing working memory abilities. Two memory load conditions were created: a 0-back condition (that required no working memory) and a 1-back condition (which required a response when the same letter was pre sented in two successive trials). In each memory load condition, four different backgrounds with different pictures were used – a black screen (no picture), a neutral (e.g., spoon), an emotionally positive (e.g., chocolate), and an emotionally negative (e.g., snake). Children were asked to ignore the pictures presented in the background, while per forming the task. Although children with ADHD exhibited slower reac tion times (treated as proxy for emotional interference in the working memory task) to both negative and positive images compared to neutral stimuli, these differences did not reach statistical significance. In addi tion, a greater interference effect was observed for ADHD when comparing neutral to no picture conditions (F(1,62) = 4.35, p = .041). Accordingly, these results suggested a general difficulty in managing emotional interference while performing the working memory task in ADHD, indicating a relationship between emotional dysregulation and poorer working memory performance. No significant differences across conditions were observed in the non-ADHD group, which indicated a relationship between ER and inhibitory control in both ADHD and non-ADHD. One study (Colonna et al., 2022) used a clinical interview to assess ER and a performed-based task to assess EF, and another study (Linca et al., 2022) used a performance-based task to assess ER and neuro psychological tests to measure EF. Colonna et al. (2022) assessed the relationship between irritability (treated as an indicative of enhanced emotionality and thus as a proxy of poorer ER) and cool (processes such as working memory or inhibition) and hot (processes such as delay aversion or risky decision making) EF in ADHD adolescents aged 10–18 years. Irritability was measured using a composite score derived from five items of the Child and Adolescent Psychiatric Assessment interview. Cool EFs were assessed using the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST), which measures set-shifting by requiring participants to categorise cards based on evolving rules, and a Go/No-Go task, which assesses motor inhibition by instructing participants to respond to "go" stimuli while suppressing responses to "no-go" stimuli. Hot EFs were examined through the Card Playing Task, which evaluates perseverance under loss conditions; the Temporal Discounting Task, which measures impulsivity by presenting choices between immediate and delayed rewards; the Choice under Risk Task assesses risk-taking and impulsivity by evalu ating an individual's tendency to opt for short-term gains despite po tential long-term benefits; and the Ultimatum Game, an economic decision-making paradigm in which participants respond to monetary split proposals, often rejecting unfair offers due to emotional responses, despite the potential financial gain. The authors observed that irrita bility was not associated with hot or cool EFs in adolescents with ADHD. Linca et al. (2022) investigated the moderating role of ER in the relationship between problem-solving abilities (along with visuomotor precision and visuospatial integration) and school results in children aged 72–120 months with and without ADHD. In this study, the authors measured problem-solving and working memory abilities, using the Tower task and the Face Memory task, respectively, both part of the Neuropsychological Development Assessment. ER was assessed using an imaging system of pictures and children were asked to identify the facial expressions, emotions and emotional responses. Results showed that ER significantly moderated the relationship between school outcomes and both problem-solving (ADHD group: Z = 9.07, SE = 9.93), p < .01; non-ADHD group: Z = 4.46, SE = 0.001, p < .01), and working memory (ADHD group: Z = 10.9, SE = 6.08, p < .05; non-ADHD group: Z = 3.53, SE = 0.001, p < .01) in both groups. Stronger effects were observed in the ADHD group. Seven studies used performance-based tasks to assess EF and informant-report questionnaires to assess ER (Anker et al., 2022; Dir et al., 2020; Imanipour et al., 2021; Inci Izmir et al., 2024; Jensen et al., 2018; Tarle et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023). Jensen et al. (2018) used the parent-report version of the Emotional Control subscale of the BRIEF to measure ER, conceptualising this subscale as a measure of emotional lability, and the Shift subscale of the BRIEF, as well as the backward conditions of the Digit Span and Spatial Span tasks, along with the Letter-Number Sequencing subtest from the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children – Fourth Edition (WISC-IV), to measure EF in children aged 8–12 years with and without ADHD. These tests have been widely used to assess working memory abilities as participants are required to recall sequences of digits, block figures, and number-letter combinations, respectively, in reverse order. Results showed a negative correlation between children's working memory, as assessed by the letter–number sequencing task, and parent-reported emotional lability, indicating that lower working memory scores (i.e., more impairments) were associated with heightened emotional lability symptoms (i.e., greater ER diffi culties; r = -0.37, p < .01). This association was consistent across chil dren with and without ADHD, suggesting that diagnostic status did not affect the relationship. Dir et al. (2020), comparing school-aged children aged 11–12 years with ADHD and co-occurring Disruptive Behaviour Disorder with and without suicidal ideation, used the parent-report version of the ERC to assess ER, and the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART) to measure decision-making abilities. The BART task involves participants to inflate a virtual balloon to earn increasing rewards while balancing the growing risk of the balloon exploding. The authors did not find a significant relationship between ER and decision-making in both groups. Anker et al. (2022) assessed working memory and processing speed using corresponding indices from the third edition of the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale in adults aged 18–65 years with ADHD. Working memory was measured through the Arithmetic, Digit Span, and Let ter–Number Sequencing tests, while processing speed was evaluated using Digit Symbol-Coding and Symbol Search tests. Emotional dysre gulation was assessed using the CBS. The authors did not find associa tions between self-reported emotional dysregulation severity and performance-based working memory or processing speed. Zhang et al. (2023) used the WCST to assess set-shifting and the Attention Network Test for attentional capacity and inhibition by requiring children aged 7–11 years to redirect their gaze away from a stimulus rather than follow its trajectory. Emotional dysregulation was measured in relation to neuroticism, assessed by the Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ). EPQ is a self-reported questionnaire consisting of 88 items that assesses three dimensions of personality, psychoticism, extraversion, and neuroticism. Neuroticism was conceptualised as a variable related to emotional dysregulation or a diminished capacity for ER (Gross and John, 2003; Wang et al., 2009). This study compared cognitive flexibility and ER difficulties, as measured by neuroticism in children with and without ADHD. Children with ADHD demonstrated more significant impairments in both areas, along with significant cor relations between the two. Specifically, neuroticism was significantly positively associated with perseverative responses (B = 1.115, β = 0.305, p < .05), perseverative errors (B = 1.151, β = 0.320, p < .05), and significantly negatively associated with the number of categories completed on the WCST (B = −0.120, β = −0.327, p < .05), suggesting that higher neuroticism scores or greater ER challenges were linked to increased difficulties in cognitive flexibility in ADHD children. Tarle et al. (2021) used an observational approach to measure ER strategies or behaviours during a phonological working memory task and a control task, which involved drawing in Microsoft Paint, in chil dren aged 8–12 years with and without ADHD. ER behaviours were coded according to the following - Self-Praise/Positive Self-Talk, Self-Criticism/Negative Self-Talk, Solicitations, Emotion Ventilation, Positive Emotion Expression, Shuts Down, and Total Emotion Expres sion. The Phonological Working Memory Task required children to reorder numbers and place a letter at the end of the sequence. The findings indicated that increased working memory demands generally heightened emotional expression in children. However, the effect was more pronounced in those with ADHD than in their non-ADHD peers (F (1,66) = 26.56, p < .001, ηp2 = 0.29). Specifically, children with ADHD experienced more difficulty with ER under higher cognitive load, particularly in the form of increased self-criticism (t(42.24) = -2.91, p = .006, d = 0.69) and heightened positive emotion expression (t (66) = -2.62, p = .011, d = 0.64). (2024) assessed ER using the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), a 36-item self-report questionnaire, and EF using the CNS Vital Signs (CNSVS) in children aged 8–12 years with ADHD. The study indicated that lower EF levels were associated with heightened emotional dysregulation (F(1174) = 4.78, p < .05), with EFs accounting for about 3 % of the variation in ER dif ficulties (R2 = 0.0267). Imanipour et al. (2021) assessed ER using the 10-item Emotion Regulation Questionnaire for Children and Adolescents (ERQ-CA). This questionnaire evaluates the tendency to regulate emotions according to two strategies: cognitive reappraisal, generally considered to be adap tive, and expressive suppression, generally considered to be maladap tive. Working memory was measured using the Digit Span, Letter–Number Sequencing, and Arithmetic subtests of the Working Memory Index of the WISC-IV. The study included children aged 7–12 years with an ADHD diagnosis, as well as an age- and sex-matched group without an ADHD diagnosis. The authors reported no significant asso ciation between working memory and ER in either group. One study (Leib et al., 2023) assessed EF using both performance-based and informant-reported tasks in children and ado lescents aged 6–16 years with ADHD. The authors used the BRIEF Emotional Control and Shift subscales (parent and teacher versions) to assess ER, and two tasks of the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children – Fifth Edition, the forward and backward conditions of the digit span, and the Picture Span Task, which involves observing a sequence of images and recalling them in the presented order to assess working memory – to measure EF. Participants were then categorised as emotionally averaged or emotionally dysregulated, based on the Emotional Control subscale scores of the BRIEF. The results revealed a negative association between higher working memory performance (better-developed working memory) and elevated parent-reported ER difficulties (Digit Span, r = -0.08, p < .05; Picture Span, r = -0.11, p < .001). However, this relationship was not observed in teacher-reported measures of ER. These findings suggest that poorer working memory abilities are associated with greater ER impairments in children with ADHD. Lastly, the study of Sj ̈owall and Thorell (2019) used both performance-based and informant-reported tasks to assess both EF and ER in children aged 48–72 months with ADHD. The authors used a Go/No-Go task to measure inhibitory control and, to assess working memory, the authors used the digit span task and the Find the Phone task, which measures spatial memory by requiring participants to sequence phones that had rung. To assess delay aversion, the authors used the Flower task, and quantified the frequency of selecting between rewards, and the Gift Delay task, to assess self-regulation by observing whether children waited to receive a reward. Additionally, teacher-reported EFs were assessed using the Childhood Executive Functioning Inventory, a 24-item questionnaire measuring working memory and inhibition. To measure ER, four performance-based tasks were used: the Facial Emotion Recognition task; the Deception Para digm, which evaluated emotional expressions following a simulated disappointment; the Puzzle Cheating Task and the Impossible Lego Task, which assessed self-regulation during frustration when failing to com plete a puzzle or a figure. Teacher-reported ER was assessed using the Emotion Questionnaire, a 40-item instrument rated on a 5-point Likert scale. The authors reported significant positive associations between ER and EF, as assessed using performance-based tasks (r = 0.45, p < .001) or parent/teacher reports (r = 0.75, p < .001). This suggests that greater EF impairment was linked to increased difficulties in ER. 3.3. EF and ER in Autism/ADHD Two studies reporting on the relationship between EF and ER in autism/ADHD were included. Barnes et al. (2025) used informant-report questionnaires to assess EF and ER – the Flexibility Scale-Revised, a 29-item parent-report questionnaire measuring daily cognitive flexibility and the Emotional Dysregulation Inventory a 13-item parent-report questionnaire designed to assess dysfunctional ER, in autistic/ADHD and non-autistic/ADHD children and adolescents aged 5–18 years. Results revealed a significant effect of cognitive inflexibility on emotional dysregulation in both groups (autistic/ADHD: β = 0.62, p = .000; non-autistic: β = 0.88, p = .000). Conner et al. (2023) used a self-report questionnaire to assess ER and performance-based tasks to measure EFs, in autistic/ADHD adolescents and young adults aged 16–25 years. The authors used the DERS to assess ER, while EF was measured using three tests of the Delis-Kaplan Exec utive Function System: the Number-Letter Switching task of the Trail-Making Test, which evaluates cognitive flexibility by alternating between numbers and letters; the Colour-Word Interference Test, which assesses inhibition through discrepancies between text and colour; and the Card Sorting Test, which examines cognitive flexibility and con ceptual reasoning through repeated sorting based on different charac teristics. No significant associations were observed between cognitive flexibility, inhibition, and the total DERS score or any of its subscales, except for the relationship observed between inhibitory control and the DERS Goals subscale. 4. Discussion This systematic review aimed to formally investigate the relationship between executive function (EF) and emotional regulation (ER) in neurodevelopmental disorders, specifically autism, ADHD, and autism/ ADHD co-occurrence. We systematically analysed studies published since 2013 that examined this relationship in autistic, ADHD, and autism/ADHD individuals. 4.1. Executive functions and emotional regulation in autism Of the four studies that examined the relationship between EF and ER in autism, three focused on preschool children, and one investigated autistic adults with intellectual disability. The findings were mixed. While two studies reported an association between EF difficulties and ER problems (S ́aez-Suanes et al., 2020a; Jahromi et al., 2019), the other two found no significant relationship (DeLucia et al., 2022; Zantinge et al., 2017). The broader literature highlights a strong association between autistic traits – such as restricted behaviours and socialisation diffi culties – and emotional dysregulation (Berkovits et al., 2017; Samson et al., 2014), as well as significant EF difficulties (Demetriou et al., 2018; Jones et al., 2018; Lopez et al., 2005; Leung et al., 2016; Pugliese et al., 2016). Executive dysfunction impacts cognitive development, language abilities (Ellis Weismer et al., 2018), and academic performance (Dijkhuis et al., 2020). Emotional dysregulation is also linked to social difficulties and behavioural problems (Berkovits et al., 2017; Mazefsky et al., 2013). According to Cai et al. (2018c), the use of both regulatory strategies and flexibility in their application are crucial for ER in autism, with adaptive strategies serving as protective factors for psychological well-being (Cai et al., 2018a, 2018b). However, difficulties in regulating emotions flexibly may be related to reduced attentional shifting and working memory, which are associated with cognitive reappraisal and rumination (Beckw ́e et al., 2014; McRae et al., 2012). The findings of S ́aez-Suanes et al. (2020a) and Jahromi et al. (2019) align with this evidence, showing that greater EF dysfunction is linked to more mal adaptive ER strategies (e.g., lability/negativity). Additionally, higher effortful control (i.e., cognitive control) is associated with greater ER abilities, but only when assessed through informant reports (parents or therapists). However, when EF are assessed using task-based measures, this relationship is not observed. For example, DeLucia et al. (2022) and Jahromi et al. (2019), using the Day/Night task, and Zantinge et al. (2017), using the Laboratory Temperament Assessment Battery (LabTAB), did not find a significant relationship between EF and ER. A po tential explanation for these discrepancies is the reliance on verbal instructions in EF tasks, which may pose challenges for autistic pre schoolers, who often exhibit communication difficulties (Petrolo et al., M. Pozo-Rodríguez et al. Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews 183 (2026) 106570 8

2025). For instance, the Day/Night task has been questioned as a reli able measure of inhibition in autistic children, as it requires verbal re sponses. Therefore, observed difficulties may reflect challenges in using internal language for self-regulation rather than true challenges in in hibition (Jahromi et al., 2013; Russell et al., 1999). Additionally, the ERC, used in these studies, has been validated for children aged 6–12 years (Shields and Cicchetti, 1997), a developmental period in which ER mechanisms are still maturing (Riediger and Bellingtier, 2022; Silvers, 2022). Studies suggest that ER strategies are less effective in preschool-aged children than in older children, improving progressively into adulthood (Sch ̈afer et al., 2017). Consequently, the assessment of ER in children aged 3–6 years may not fully capture the relationship between these processes. Although task characteristics may have contributed to the absence of significant relationships between the EF and ER, the lack of significant findings cannot be attributed to a po tential floor effect in the measurement of the constructs. This is because the scores reported by DeLucia et al. (2022) and Jahromi et al. (2019) were not near the lower bound of the possible scoring range for either autistic or non-autistic participants. Moreover, the three included studies (also Zantinge et al., 2017, which used parent-report measure ments) found no significant associations between EF and ER in either autistic or non-autistic preschoolers. This pattern suggests that the absence of a relationship may reflect a lack of association between these processes in young children, regardless of diagnostic status. The studies of autistic individuals have used neuropsychological tasks and informant measures to assess cognitive and emotional pro cesses. Christoforou et al. (2023) identified distinct EF impairments patterns across different types of assessment, particularly in working memory and planning. Similarly, Demetriou et al. (2018) reported greater executive dysfunction in informant ratings than in task perfor mance. Comparable discrepancies in methodology have also been observed in self-regulation measures (Eisenberg et al., 2019). These inconsistencies likely arise because performance-based tasks are con ducted under structured conditions that enable children with NDDs to perform optimally, thereby reducing ecological validity (Toplak et al., 2013). In contrast, informant-based assessments capture difficulties observed in real-life contexts, which may explain why greater severity is often reported than is reflected in task performance (Hendry et al., 2016; Sj ̈owall and Thorell, 2019). Therefore, combining multiple assessment methods can provide a more comprehensive and ecologically valid evaluation of these processes. This approach leverages the strengths of each method while compensating for their limitations. Moreover, these methodological differences highlight the impor tance of considering the potential influence of shared measurement sources on the observed associations. For example, in studies that rely solely on parent-report questionnaires, the consistent correlations be tween EF and ER may partly reflect shared method variance. This is a bias that occurs when data on two or more variables are obtained from the same source and/or using the same measurement method (Karimi and Meyer, 2019). This issue may partly explain why significant asso ciations are more frequently observed in informant-report measures, particularly parent-report, than in task-related assessments. Therefore, using multiple assessment methods can help to confirm the presence of genuine relationships and prevent overestimation or underestimation due to task-specific methodological biases, particularly in domains where inconsistent findings have been reported. It is also important to consider the wide age range of autistic par ticipants across the included studies. While three studies focused on preschool-aged children (DeLucia et al., 2022; Jahromi et al., 2019), only one study (S ́aez-Suanes et al., 2020a) examined autistic adults. This age variability limits the ability to identify consistent patterns of EF and ER across development, as childhood and adolescence are critical pe riods marked by substantial changes in executive and emotional pro cesses (Berkovits et al., 2017; Best and Miller, 2010; Cibralic et al., 2019; Van Den Bergh et al., 2014), which may influence the association be tween EF and ER. Future research should address underrepresented age groups, particularly middle childhood and adolescence, and ideally employ longitudinal designs to track EF and ER trajectories in autism over time. This approach could help identify sensitive periods for intervention and target specific cognitive–emotional profiles at stage of development. Taken together, factors such as participant age and methodological differences (task-based vs. report-based assessments) may limit the identification of clear relationships between EF and ER. However, findings from informant-based measures consistently indicate that autistic individuals – both children and adults – with greater EF diffi culties also exhibit poorer ER abilities, suggesting that these difficulties persist across the lifespan. 4.2. Executive functions and emotional regulation in ADHD Of the 16 included studies on ADHD, 12 examined children, three focused on adults, and one investigated adolescents. While four studies did not find significant associations between EF and ER, ten reported links between greater EF difficulties and poorer ER outcomes. These associations were observed across both task-based and report-based measures in children and adults with ADHD. The relationship between EF and ER is well-established in the liter ature, with EF problems recognised as a core feature of ADHD. Impair ments in inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory have been linked to emotional impulsivity and heightened emotional reactivity – hallmark features of ADHD (Kooij et al., 2019) – with sig nificant implications for social functioning (Bullard et al., 2024; Tamm et al., 2021). Difficulties in inhibitory control hinder the regulation of immediate emotional reactions, often leading to impulsive emotional outbursts, challenges in delaying gratification, and struggles in suppressing inap propriate emotional expressions in social contexts (Singh et al., 2023). Accordingly, it has been suggested that reduced inhibitory control dis rupts the ability to regulate emotional responses, which affects behav iour and in turn contributes to increased emotional lability (Sonuga-Barke, 2003). Similarly, impaired cognitive flexibility affects the ability to adapt to changing social environments, contributing to emotional difficulties (Roshani et al., 2020). This is particularly evident in children, who often experience heightened frustration and anger, leading to interpersonal conflicts (Aydın et al., 2022; Groves et al., 2022). Additionally, working memory difficulties may impair the ability to recall and apply previously learned coping strategies, contributing to emotional dysregulation (Zhao and Zhang, 2024; Marx et al., 2011). Four studies did not find an association between EF and ER. Anker et al. (2022) specifically investigated the relationship between ER and working memory in adults with ADHD. Similarly, Imanipour et al. (2021) found no association between ER and working memory in chil dren with or without ADHD. This suggests that the absence of a rela tionship is not specific to ADHD. However, this finding contrasts with the results of other studies, which reported significant associations be tween these constructs in ADHD (Jensen et al., 2018; Linca et al., 2022; Tarle et al., 2021). Of note, all of these studies assessed working memory using performance-based tasks, which may limit the detection of diffi culties in everyday functioning. This may reflect challenges related to the ecological validity of these assessments, as traditional neuropsy chological tasks often fail to capture real-world variability in executive performance (Chaytor and Schmitter-Edgecombe, 2003). Age differ ences may also contribute, as working memory difficulties tend to become less pronounced as individuals with ADHD mature (Ramos et al., 2020). Similarly, Dir et al. (2020) and Colonna et al. (2022) did not find a significant relationship between EF and ER. Dir et al. (2020) assessed decision-making in children with ADHD, a cognitive process known to be influenced by age. Research indicates that older individuals demonstrate more effective and deliberative decision-making strategies (Paulsen et al., 2011; Peters et al., 2007), suggesting that the absence of a significant association with ER in this study may be due to the ongoing M. development of decision-making processes in children. On the other hand, Colonna et al. (2022) examined this relationship in adolescents but used irritability as a proxy for ER. This may have limited their findings, as irritability may not fully capture ER difficulties in this population. For instance, while school-aged children with ADHD often exhibit ER difficulties through aggressive behaviours and irritability, such as kicking or pinching (King and Waschbusch, 2010), adolescents with ADHD tend to display more hostility-driven behaviours (Yoo et al., 2021). These developmental differences highlight the importance of selecting appropriate ER measures across different age groups. The inclusion of a control group in some studies revealed that the associations between cognitive and emotional dimensions were present in participants with and without ADHD, suggesting a pattern indepen dent of diagnostic status (Jensen et al., 2018; Linca et al., 2022). How ever, other studies have indicated diagnostic specificity, showing that these associations are stronger, or only significant, among individuals with ADHD (Al-Yagon et al., 2020; Cavallet et al., 2016; Tarle et al., 2021; Van Cauwenberge et al., 2015). Of the included studies, seven have used self-report measures, particularly to assess ER (Al-Yagon et al., 2020; Anker et al., 2022; Biederman et al., 2020; Imanipour et al., 2021; Inci Izmir et al., 2024; Leib et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023). Only one study has also used self-reports to evaluate EF (Biederman et al., 2020). The results should be interpreted with caution and ideally contrasted with those from other sources (e.g., caregiver reports), since individuals with ADHD often overestimate their academic, cognitive, and social abilities. This phe nomenon is known as ‘positive illusory bias’ (Evangelista et al., 2008; Hoza et al., 2004, 2013; Swanson, Owens, and Hinshaw, 2012). This bias reflects a discrepancy between self-perceived and actual performance and has been associated with the psychosocial challenges commonly experienced by individuals with ADHD (Jia et al., 2016; Ohan and Johnston, 2011). EF may partly explain this discrepancy, as lower EF has been associated with less accurate self-assessment, even in individuals without ADHD, suggesting that EF difficulties may amplify this bias in ADHD (Chan and Martinussen, 2016). Similarly, Beer (2012) proposed that EF integrate positive and negative information to form a realistic self-concept. Thus, executive dysfunction may lead to inaccurate self-knowledge. While no studies have directly examined this bias in relation to ER, existing evidence suggests that EF difficulties could distort such self-evaluations. Two of the included studies used self-reports with adult participants (Anker et al., 2022; Biederman et al., 2020), in which this bias appears to be less evident. However, Nelson (2013) found that young adults with ADHD also tend to overestimate their self-concept. Studies using self-reports in children or adolescents (Al-Yagon et al., 2020; Imanipour et al., 2021; Inci Izmir et al., 2024; Leib et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023) should also be interpreted cautiously due to the greater likelihood of this bias. Therefore, future research should carefully select assessment tools that consider the possible influence of this bias. Ideally these tools should combine self-reports with informant-based measures to validate the reliability of responses provided by individuals with ADHD, as Leib et al. (2023) did. Overall, despite some studies not supporting this line of evidence, the broader body of research indicates a robust association between EF and ER difficulties in individuals with ADHD across various developmental stages. 4.3. Executive Functions and Emotional Regulation in Autism/ADHD Only two studies examining the relationship between EF and ER in individuals with autism/ADHD co-occurrence were included. Barnes et al. (2025) reported a significant association between cognitive flexi bility challenges and poorer ER abilities in both autistic and non-autistic children and adolescents. This pattern was observed regardless of diagnostic status, suggesting that the relationship between these con structs is not specific to autism. In contrast, Conner et al. (2023) found no significant relationship between EF (specifically shifting and inhibi tion) and ER in adolescents and young adults. These discrepancies may be due to methodological differences. Barnes et al. (2025) relied on parent-report measures, whereas Conner et al. (2023) used self-reports for ER and task-based assessments for EF. As seen in autism and ADHD research, parent-reported measures tend to show stronger associations between EF and ER than performance-based tasks. Contextual factors may play a role, as symptom severity often varies across different settings (Hwang-Gu et al., 2021), and parents may perceive greater impairments due to the disruptive nature of behaviours in daily life (Hartman et al., 2007). However, the association between the EF and ER reported by Barnes et al. (2025) should be interpreted with caution, given that a single informant was used to assess both constructs. While findings align with the broader autism and ADHD literature, conclusions should be drawn cautiously due to the limited number of studies. Nonetheless, current evidence suggests that reduced cognitive flexibility is associated with ER difficulties in co-occurring autism/ ADHD, highlighting the need for further research in this area. 5. General discussion This systematic review highlights the complex relationship between EF and ER in autism, ADHD, and autism/ADHD co-occurrence. Across these neurodevelopmental conditions, EF and ER appear to be closely related, yet the strength and nature of this association seem to vary depending on methodological approaches and developmental factors. A key dimension that may be influencing findings is age. The rela tionship between EF and ER in autism is less consistently observed in preschool-aged children, possibly due to ongoing neurodevelopmental maturation and the limitations of verbal task-based assessments. In contrast, in ADHD, EF difficulties appear to be linked to ER difficulties across childhood and adulthood, with emotional impulsivity emerging as a core feature of the condition. Limited research on autism/ADHD co- occurrence suggests that cognitive flexibility plays a crucial role in ER difficulties, particularly in children and adolescents, but further studies are needed to clarify these associations across different life stages. Methodological differences may also be contributing to in consistencies in findings. Informant-based measures, such as parent re ports, tend to reveal a stronger association between EF and ER than task- based assessments, suggesting that real-world executive difficulties may be more predictive of ER challenges than standardised cognitive tests (Rosenthal et al., 2013). Additionally, EF tasks that rely on verbal in structions may not accurately capture the executive profiles of autistic individuals, particularly in early childhood, when language difficulties are common. These factors underlie the importance of using multimodal assessments that integrate performance-based and ecological measures when examining EF and ER relationships. Despite these methodological and developmental considerations, some patterns emerge across conditions. Both autism and ADHD are characterised by executive dysfunction and emotional dysregulation, but the nature of these difficulties differs. In autism, ER challenges appear to be often linked to cognitive rigidity, difficulties in attentional control, and a reliance on maladaptive regulatory strategies, potentially associated with impairments in cognitive flexibility and working mem ory. However, the limited number of studies may reflect the fact that research on ER is still in its early stages within this population. To date, most research has focused on broader behavioural processes, such as irritability, anxiety and depressive symptoms, and social difficulties (Kim et al., 2024; Macintosh and Dissanayake, 2006; Mayes et al., 2011; McGuire et al., 2016), rather than investigating the underlying capacity to regulate emotions directly, which may contribute to these behav ioural challenges. In ADHD, emotional impulsivity, heightened reac tivity, and difficulties in inhibitory control seem to be a key contributor to ER dysfunction, reflecting a more immediate and reactive emotional dysregulation profile. The limited evidence on autism/ADHD M. Pozo-Rodríguez et al. Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews 183 (2026) 106570 10

co-occurrence suggests that these individuals may experience height ened EF and ER difficulties, particularly in flexibility-related domains, although findings remain inconclusive. Importantly, these differences in the associations between EF and ER may be partly explained by the increased attention given to ADHD in the last decade, which seems to be supported by the unbalanced number of articles included in the autism (n = 4), ADHD (n = 16), and co-occurring autism/ADHD (n = 2) sec tions of this review. In fact, the prevalence of ADHD has increased over the years, due to the broadening of the diagnostic criteria for ADHD over time, and to increased awareness of the condition by clinicians and the public, particularly among underrepresented minorities (Abdelnour et al., 2022). Overall, this review highlights the need for further research to address the relationship between EF and ER across these conditions, particularly in autistic individuals and those with co-occurring autistic/ ADHD, where evidence is limited. Future studies should prioritise lon gitudinal designs, incorporate diverse assessment methods, and consider developmental trajectories to provide a more comprehensive under standing of the relationship between EF problems and ER difficulties in neurodivergent populations. 5.1. Limitations of the included studies The limitations of the included studies can be broadly categorised into three domains: generalisability, comorbidities, and methodological issues. Generalisability is limited by the small sample sizes commonly re ported in studies on autism (DeLucia et al., 2022; Jahromi et al., 2019; Zantinge et al., 2017), ADHD (Cavallet et al., 2016; Dir et al., 2020; Imanipour et al., 2021; Jensen et al., 2018; Marques et al., 2024; Tarle et al., 2021; Van Cauwenberge et al., 2015), and autism/ADHD (Barnes et al., 2025; Conner et al., 2023). Small samples reduce statistical power and hinder the extrapolation of findings to broader clinical populations. This limitation is further compounded by the underrepresentation of females. Some studies excluded women entirely (Cavallet et al., 2016), while others presented marked gender imbalances in autism (DeLucia et al., 2022; Zantinge et al., 2017), ADHD (Colonna et al., 2022; Jensen et al., 2018; Leib et al., 2023; Linca et al., 2022; Marques et al., 2024; Sj ̈owall and Thorell, 2019; Tarle et al., 2021; Van Cauwenberge et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2023), and co-occurring autism/ADHD (Barnes et al., 2025; Conner et al., 2023). Additionally, two studies (Al-Yagon et al., 2020; Jahromi et al., 2019) did not report participants’ sex/gender distribution, further constraining the interpretation and comparability of results. Comorbidities also represent a major challenge. Several studies included participants with additional diagnoses such as ID (S ́aez-Suanes et al., 2020a), Disruptive Behaviour Disorders (DBD, e.g., oppositional defiant or conduct disorder) (Dir et al., 2020; Tarle et al., 2021; Van Cauwenberge et al., 2015), cognitive disconnection syndrome (Inci Izmir et al., 2024), or specific learning disorders (Tarle et al., 2021). These co-occurring conditions likely amplified cognitive and emotional difficulties, particularly in cases involving DBD, which have been consistently linked to increased irritability and emotional dysregulation (APA, 2022), as well as greater executive impairments (Flores et al., 2022). Consistent with this, Hernandez et al. (2024) found that children with ADHD with co-occurring DBD exhibited more pronounced emotional problems than those with ADHD alone. Methodological limitations further constrain interpretation. Many studies relied solely on caregiver-reported questionnaires, which, although ecologically valid (Diercks et al., 2022; Wallisch et al., 2018), would benefit from the inclusion of multiple informants to strengthen reliability and provide a more comprehensive perspective (Al-Yagon et al., 2020; Barnes et al., 2025; Marques et al., 2024). Likewise, studies using self-report measures (Al-Yagon et al., 2020; Anker et al., 2022; Biederman et al., 2020; Inci Izmir et al., 2024; Leib et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023) could be complemented with additional sources to minimise self-perception bias. Another frequent limitation is the absence of control groups, reported in studies on autism (S ́aez-Suanes et al., 2020a), ADHD (Anker et al., 2022; Biederman et al., 2020; Colonna et al., 2022; Dir et al., 2020; Inci Izmir et al., 2024; Leib et al., 2023), and autism/ADHD (Conner et al., 2023). While the present review focuses on within-diagnosis associations between cognitive and emotional di mensions, including control groups would clarify whether such re lationships are disorder-specific or reflect general developmental patterns. Finally, intellectual functioning was not consistently controlled across studies. Some works on autism (DeLucia et al., 2022; Jahromi et al., 2019) and ADHD (Al-Yagon et al., 2020; Biederman et al., 2020; Marques et al., 2024) did not account for intelligence quotient (IQ), whereas others used it for sample characterisation, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or as a covariate for cognitive and emotional functioning (Jensen et al., 2018; Linca et al., 2022; Van Cauwenberge et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2023). For example, Zantinge et al. (2017) found that autistic participants had a lower IQ, which was linked to greater reliance on avoidance strategies. Similarly, Jensen et al. (2018) found significant differences in IQ between ADHD and control groups, which could explain poorer performance in working memory (Antshel et al., 2010; Jepsen et al., 2009). Conner et al. (2023) found that, in autistic/ADHD participants, higher IQ was linked to poorer ER but better EF. Together, these findings suggest that IQ may act as a moderating factor in the relationship between EF and ER, influencing the strength and direction of their association by shaping individuals’ cognitive resources and ca pacity to implement effective ER strategies. 5.2. Limitations and Future Directions Despite providing valuable insights into the relationship between EF and ER in autism, ADHD, and co-occurring autism/ADHD, this review has several limitations. The included studies varied widely in methodological approaches, particularly in how EF and ER were assessed. Studies using informant- reported measures (e.g., parent or teacher questionnaires) generally found associations between EF and ER compared to those using task- based measures. This discrepancy may be due to the ecological val idity of standardised tasks, which often fail to capture real-world EF and ER challenges (Chaytor and Schmitter-Edgecombe, 2003). Future research should prioritise standardising EF and ER questionnaires and performance tasks to increase reporting consistency and improve the reliability of results, thereby facilitating data integration across studies. Using standardised methodologies would also allow for more accurate, potentially quantitative, comparisons of these relationships across diagnostic groups. From a methodological perspective, it is possible that the findings of studies that used a single informant to assess both con structs were influenced by shared method variance (Barnes et al., 2025; Marques et al., 2024; S ́aez-Suanes et al., 2020a). Therefore, to reduce the potential bias introduced by this method-related effect and increase the reliability of the results, it is recommended that future research use multiple informants. In addition, given the key role that age seems to play in the association between EF and ER, longitudinal studies are needed to clearly understand the developmental trajectory of EF and ER interactions over time, to clarify whether early EF difficulties predict later ER challenges. The small number of studies investigating autism and co-occurring autism/ADHD limits the ability to draw conclusions about the interac tion between EF and ER in these populations. In autism, the relationship between EF and ER appears to vary across studies. In the case of autism/ ADHD, however, evidence suggests that the association between altered cognitive flexibility and ER problems may be particularly pertinent. A possible explanation for the limited number of studies examining this relationship in autism/ADHD is that simultaneous diagnosis of both conditions only became permissible following the publication of the DSM-5, as previous diagnostic frameworks did not allow for this (APA, M. Pozo-Rodríguez et al. Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews 183 (2026) 106570 11

2013; Harris, 2014). This has likely contributed to the scientific litera ture predominantly focusing on examining each condition separately. Indeed, the proportion of participants with dual diagnoses in the two studies included in this review was very small. This represents a sig nificant limitation that restricts the validity and generalisability of their findings. Consequently, the current evidence is insufficient to clearly understand the relationship between EF and ER in individuals with co-occurring autism and ADHD. Addressing this gap should be a priority for future research, as this could inform the development of more tar geted and effective clinical interventions. Additionally, more research is needed to understand how the overlapping and distinct characteristics of autism and ADHD influence these processes, given the high rates of co-occurrence between these conditions. Moreover, further studies are required to determine whether additional factors, such as the presence of camouflaging behaviours, may influence the nature of this relationship. In conclusion, although the current review highlights the critical role of EF and ER relationship difficulties among autistic, ADHD and autistic/ ADHD individuals, further investigation is essential to clarify both the shared and distinct patterns of this relationship across these diagnostic profiles. Considering this association as a potential transdiagnostic mechanism offers important clinical implications. This systematic re view provides a valuable synthesis of the literature that can inform everyday practice, particularly in the domains of assessment, differen tial diagnosis, and intervention planning. Recognising how EF diffi culties may underlie ER challenges can facilitate the early identification of neurodevelopmental conditions and support the implementation of targeted cognitive interventions. These may promote emotional self- regulation, adaptive functioning, and overall therapeutic outcomes. In this context, developing a deeper understanding of the shared and disorder-specific cognitive and emotional characteristics is essential for creating more personalised and effective treatment approaches. Addi tionally, a broader neuropsychological profile of the autism/ADHD co- occurrence group could lead to more precise and individualised treat ment approaches, ultimately contributing to more effective clinical de cision-making. pages: Systematic review of virtual reality therapy in the treatment of visual dysfunction in children with ADHD and dyslexia Kei See Chung a, Ka Yi Lee a, Yuk Ming Tang a,d,* , Cynthia Y.Y. Lai b,d, Chi-Wai Do c, Kenneth N.K. Fong b,d a Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong, China b Department of Rehabilitation Sciences, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong, China c School of Optometry, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong, China d Research Centre for Assistive Technology, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong, China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Visual Dysfunction Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder Dyslexia Binocular dysfunction Virtual Reality Virtual Reality Therapy A B S T R A C T Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and dyslexia are prevalent neurodevelopmental disorders that significantly impact educational and social functioning. Both conditions are frequently associated with comorbid visual dysfunction, which can further exacerbate learning and attentional difficulties. Virtual reality therapy (VRT) has emerged as a promising intervention for addressing visual impairments such as convergence insuf ficiency and binocular dysfunction in affected children. This systematic review evaluates the effectiveness of VRT in treating visual dysfunction in children with ADHD and/or dyslexia. 20 studies published between 2015 and 2025 were analyzed. VRT improved visual acuity (0.89–1.32 lines) and stereoacuity in amblyopia, reduced omission/commission errors (14.75/4.75 errors) in ADHD, and enhanced reading speed (r = 0.992) and visual perception (d = 0.93) in dyslexia, with gains comparable to patching for binocular dysfunction. VRT is an effective intervention for improving visual acuity, binocular function, visual attention, and processing speed in children with ADHD and/or dyslexia, with effect sizes ranging from moderate to large. Key strengths include its engaging, gamified design, which improves treatment adherence. However, the literature remains fragmented: most studies examine ADHD or dyslexia in isolation, with limited research on their comorbidity. Heterogeneity in study designs also constrains definitive conclusions. Future research should prioritize longitudinal studies with large, well-designed randomized controlled trials with longitudinal follow-up to evaluate sustained efficacy. 1. Introduction Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a highly prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder, affecting 5–8% of children and adoles cents worldwide (Ayano et al., 2023; Polanczyk et al., 2014; Thomas et al., 2015). This disorder is characterized by symptoms including inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, which can hinder a child's ability to focus on tasks and control their impulses, causing educational and social challenges. ADHD can be classified into three subtypes: pre dominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, and combined (Nú ̃nez-Jaramillo et al., 2021). Dyslexia is a learning disability characterized by difficulties in decoding (reading), writing, and spelling (Snowling et al., 2020). Children with dyslexia have impaired phonological abilities, leading to difficulties in decoding words, reading fluently, and comprehending written text. While ADHD and dyslexia are distinct conditions, they frequently occur together, with a high, bidirectional comorbidity rate of 25–40% (McGrath and Stood ley, 2019). This high rate of co-occurrence underscores the need for transdiagnostic interventions that can simultaneously address the overlapping visual and cognitive challenges in children with ADHD and dyslexia. Importantly, both ADHD and dyslexia are associated with visual dysfunction, a broad term encompassing impairments in the efficient processing of visual information. In the present review, “visual dysfunction” and “visual processing deficits” are defined consistently with the neurodevelopmental literature (Kibby et al., 2015; Raghuram et al., 2019; Stein, 2019).
