dysfunction (e.g., convergence insufficiency), stereopsis deficits, and accommodative disorders, as well as (2) higher-order visual processing domains, including visual attention and vigilance, visual processing speed, visuospatial working memory, visual perceptual skills (e.g., discrimination, figure-ground perception), and resistance to visual crowding. These higher-order domains are not general cognitive func tions but modality-specific visual-cognitive processes that are frequently impaired in ADHD and dyslexia and directly contribute to academic difficulties such as poor reading fluency, inefficient visual search, and sustained attention problems during visual tasks (Cunha et al., 2023; Facoetti et al., 2001; Kibby et al., 2015). The prevalence of these visual issues is substantial. For instance, 79% of children with dyslexia had a clinically diagnosed deficit in at least one domain of visual function, including accommodation and ocular motor tracking (Raghuram et al., 2018), while children with ADHD show sig nificant impairments in convergence function, including reduced near point of convergence (NPC), compared to their typically developing peers (Bellato et al., 2023). These visual dysfunctions are not merely co-occurring conditions but can play a significant role in the clinical profile. For children with dyslexia, deficits in the magnocellular visual system can lead to unstable binocular control, poor fixation, and visual crowding, directly affecting reading fluency and accuracy while contributing to visual stress, discomfort, and reading avoidance (Stein, 2019). In ADHD, impairments in oculomotor control (Lee et al., 2023) and processing speed (Lee, 2023) have been documented, and such deficits may exacerbate core inattention symptoms, hindering the ability to follow instructions or complete visual tasks efficiently. Current treatments for visual dysfunction include vision therapy and colored lenses, which offer benefits but often struggle with compliance, engagement, and variable efficacy, especially in pediatric populations (Smaakjær et al., 2022; Suttle and Conway, 2025). Virtual reality ther apy (VRT) has emerged as a promising alternative, utilizing computer-generated three-dimensional simulations to create immersive environments for users. This technology has found applications across various fields, including rehabilitation and mental health (Freeman et al., 2024; Lau et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2025). Recent research suggests that VRT effectively treats visual dysfunc tions, improving binocular vision and alleviating symptoms associated with conditions like convergence insufficiency and accommodative dysfunction (Li et al., 2022). Additionally, it holds potential for addressing visual impairments, such as binocular dysfunction, stereop sis, myopia, and strabismus (Backus et al., 2018; Cepeda-Zapata et al., 2019; Fortenbacher et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2024; Yaramothu et al., 2019). In the context of neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD and dyslexia, VRT also offers innovative avenues for intervention. For chil dren with ADHD, VRT extends beyond merely minimizing distractions. It enables targeted cognitive training through gamified tasks delivered in immersive virtual classrooms or real-world simulations. This approach has been shown to improve sustained attention, working memory, and executive function by providing controlled, engaging en vironments where users can practice self-regulation strategies without real-world consequences (Bashiri et al., 2017; Corrigan et al., 2023), though the existing evidence is based on studies with methodological limitations and small sample sizes (Corrigan et al., 2023). Recent meta-analytic evidence confirms that VR-based interventions produce a moderate reduction in attention deficit symptoms (SMD = −0.33), with immersive VR showing particular promise for enhancing ecological validity in assessment and training (Zheng et al., 2025). Similarly, for children with dyslexia, VRT offers multisensory, embodied learning experiences that target both phonological and visual-spatial processing deficits. By using immersive, interactive exercises, VR reduces perfor mance anxiety, facilitates the visualization of texts, and fosters greater motivation, while also allowing for customizable, intensive practice that can be tailored to individual needs (Maresca et al., 2022). Emerging evidence indicates that VR-based neurorehabilitation can produce sig nificant gains in reading fluency and processing speed that are sustained over time (Maresca et al., 2024). Thus, VRT presents innovative avenues for treatment, potentially increasing the effectiveness of interventions for children facing these challenges. Previous systematic reviews have examined VR interventions either for isolated visual conditions (e.g., amblyopia or strabismus) or for broad cognitive outcomes in ADHD/dyslexia, without specifically syn thesizing evidence on the full spectrum of visual processing deficit s—including both low-level binocular/oculomotor functions and higher- order visual-cognitive domains—in children with ADHD and/or dyslexia. Most studies have investigated VRT either for general (pri marily low-level) visual dysfunctions or for the core symptoms of ADHD and dyslexia independently, leaving a critical synthesis gap at the intersection of these areas. To bridge this gap, this systematic review aims to consolidate the current state of knowledge, evaluate the effectiveness of VRT in treating visual dysfunctions in children with ADHD and/or dyslexia, and identify methodological limitations and underexplored areas in the literature. This review not only provides an updated synthesis of evidence but also highlights directions for future research to advance the clinical appli cation of VRT in this complex patient group. Specifically, this research focuses on the following research questions: RQ1. What visual processing domains are targeted by virtual reality therapy (VRT) interventions in children with ADHD and/or dyslexia? RQ2. What VRT methodologies and outcome measures are currently employed in treating visual dysfunction in children? RQ3. What is the effectiveness of VRT in treating visual dysfunctions in children with comorbid ADHD and/or dyslexia? 2. Literature review 2.1. Visual dysfunction in ADHD Beyond the core symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, children with ADHD frequently experience co-occurring visual dysfunction that may exacerbate academic and attentional chal lenges. A growing body of evidence indicates that ADHD is associated with impairments in multiple visual domains, including convergence (e. g., reduced near point of convergence), accommodation, and visual processing speed (Alqahtani et al., 2019; Bellato et al., 2023; DeCarlo et al., 2016). These visual deficits are well-documented in children with ADHD and are not merely secondary symptoms. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis confirmed a significant association between ADHD and vision problems, including convergence insufficiency and accommodative dysfunction (Bellato et al., 2023). Importantly, conventional ADHD treatments—including medication, cognitive training, and behavioral therapies—rarely target these visual deficits directly (Jones et al., 2020; Marx et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2019). This oversight is significant because impairments in visual attention, processing speed, and oculomotor control can directly hinder a child's ability to follow visual instructions, complete worksheets efficiently, and sustain focus on academic tasks (Cunha et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024). Consequently, addressing visual dysfunction may represent an underexplored but potentially valuable avenue for improving functional outcomes in children with ADHD, which is where VRT offers promise through its ability to deliver engaging, adaptive, and ecologically valid visual training. 2.2. Visual dysfunction in dyslexia Dyslexia, characterized by persistent difficulties in reading, spelling, and decoding, is fundamentally linked to phonological processing defi cits (Snowling et al., 2020). Primary interventions, such as phonological-based training and transcranial direct current stimulation K.S. Chung et al. Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews 187 (2026) 106723 2

(tDCS), aim to address these core linguistic weaknesses (Costanzo et al., 2016; Pasqualotto and Venuti, 2020). However, the role of visual dysfunction in dyslexia has been a persistent and evolving area of in quiry. Several influential theoretical frameworks have been proposed. The magnocellular theory posits a deficit in the visual pathway responsible for timing, motion perception, and binocular control, which may lead to unstable visual perception and reading difficulties (Stein, 2019). The visual attention span deficit hypothesis argues for a reduced capacity to process multiple visual elements simultaneously, affecting orthographic processing (Bosse et al., 2007). Additionally, research has identified increased susceptibility to visual crowding, where letters become difficult to recognize when surrounded by other letters, which can directly impair reading speed and accuracy in individuals with dyslexia (Gori and Facoetti, 2015). While the causal role of these visual factors remains debated, empirical studies consistently demonstrate their elevated prevalence in dyslexic populations. Consistent with these models, a significant subset of individuals with dyslexia also experiences pronounced visual stress and dysfunction. Raghuram et al. (2019) reported that vision-related symptoms including tired eyes, double vision, intermittent blurring of words, uncomfortable eyes, headaches, and words moving on the page are more frequent in children with dyslexia. While coloured lenses or filters may offer symptomatic relief, they do not constitute rehabilitative treatment for the underlying visual processing inefficiency (Suttle and Conway, 2025). This highlights a potential treatment gap where visual aspects of dyslexia are managed palliatively rather than therapeutically. 2.3. Visual-based differences and similarities of ADHD and dyslexia Kibby et al. (2015) demonstrated that children with ADHD and dyslexia show visual processing defects that differ in the specific pathway affected, yet also overlap substantially. Children with ADHD exhibit impairments primarily in the visual-spatial processing pathway, including visual-spatial storage and the visual-spatial central executive domains of working memory (Shiels et al., 2008). In contrast, children with dyslexia show deficits in visual discrimination and sequential short-term memory (Kibby et al., 2015). Importantly, visual attention and visuospatial working memory are not separate general cognitive functions but integral components of vi sual processing in both disorders (Kibby et al., 2015). Deficits in sus tained visual attention, visual search efficiency, and visuospatial working memory are associated with impaired reading fluency, text comprehension, and difficulty maintaining focus on visual tasks. These higher-order visual processing impairments frequently co-occur with low-level deficits such as binocular visual dysfunction (BVD), oculo motor instability, and increased susceptibility to visual crowding (Mukhtar et al., 2024; Sol ́e Puig et al., 2015; Stevens et al., 2012). Studies have also shown prolonged reaction times in the left visual field in both ADHD and dyslexia, possibly due to asymmetric hemispheric control of visual attention (Facoetti et al., 2001; Jones et al., 2008; Mohamed et al., 2016). The convergence of these specific visual processing deficits—BVD, crowding, left visual field asymmetries, inefficient visual attention, and visuospatial working memory overload—provides a compelling ratio nale for interventions that target these overlapping neural and func tional pathways (Kibby et al., 2015; Mukhtar et al., 2024; Stein, 2019). Traditional approaches to these issues—such as prism lenses, patching, or specific visual training (Aleci et al., 2015; Barton and Ranalli, 2021; Doble et al., 2010; Smaakjær et al., 2022)—can be effective but often lack the engagement needed for consistent adherence in pediatric pop ulations. This context creates a strong opportunity for immersive tech nologies like VRT. VRT can deliver engaging, personalized, and intensive training of both low-level binocular/oculomotor functions and higher-order visual processing skills (visual attention, processing speed, and visuospatial working memory) in ecologically valid environments, which is particularly promising for children with ADHD and/or dyslexia. 2.4. Existing systematic reviews on VR interventions Previous reviews have synthesized evidence on VRT, but their scopes remain segmented, failing to address the specific intersection that is the focus of this study. As summarized in Table 1, existing systematic re views have predominantly investigated one of two avenues: (1) the ef ficacy of VRT for general visual dysfunctions such as amblyopia and strabismus in mixed or non-specified populations (Chan et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2022), or (2) the application of VRT for managing the core neu rodevelopmental symptoms of ADHD or dyslexia, such as inattention or reading accuracy (Corrigan et al., 2023; Romero-Ayuso et al., 2021). Even reviews encompassing both disorders have focused on broad learning or cognitive outcomes rather than visual dysfunction (Lozano- ́Alvarez et al., 2023). Other relevant reviews have examined specific aspects such as the use of AR/VR games for ADHD (Sinha et al., 2023), VR-assisted mindfulness interventions for ADHD (Mitsea et al., 2023), and the challenges of VR in developmental disorders (AbdelMassih et al., 2024). A critical synthesis gap remains: no systematic review has yet consolidated evidence to explicitly evaluate the role of VRT in treating visual dysfunction within the clinically complex, comorbid ADHD- dyslexia population. This gap limits the translation of VRT’s potential into targeted clinical guidance for this group. Therefore, this review directly addresses this omission by posing research questions that bridge the segmented literature, aiming to evaluate the methodologies, appli cations, and effectiveness of VRT specifically for visual dysfunctions in children with ADHD and/or dyslexia. 3. Research objective and methodology This systematic review aims to synthesize and critically evaluate the current evidence on the application of VRT for managing visual dysfunction in children diagnosed with ADHD and/or dyslexia. The re view methodology was designed to identify, select, and analyze relevant studies in a structured and reproducible manner. 3.1. Research questions To achieve the primary objective, this review is guided by three specific research questions (RQs), each formulated to address a distinct aspect of the literature. The rationale for each RQ is detailed in Table 2. 3.2. Search strategy This systematic review was not preregistered in a prospective reg istry such as PROSPERO or Open Science Framework. The authors acknowledge this as a limitation, as preregistration helps prevent reporting bias, selective outcome reporting, and unplanned changes to analysis methods. To mitigate potential bias, the authors adhered to PRISMA guidelines, prespecified the research questions and all eligi bility criteria, and fully documented the search strategy and screening process (see Fig. 1). Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers, with any disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. 3.2.1. Search strings and source searched A systematic search was performed across five major electronic da tabases: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Science Direct. The search timeframe spanned from January 1, 2015, to December 31, 2025, to capture the most recent decade of technological and clinical advancements. The search strategy employed a combination of keywords and controlled vocabulary terms (e.g., MeSH in PubMed) related to three core concepts: 1. Population: "ADHD", "Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder", "Dyslexia", "Reading Disorder". K.S. Chung et al. Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews 187 (2026) 106723 3

2. Intervention: "Virtual Reality". 3. Condition/Outcome: "Visual Dysfunction", "Binocular Dysfunction", "Convergence Insufficiency", "Visual Processing", "Amblyopia". Boolean operators (AND, OR) were used to combine these concepts. The specific search strings for each database are detailed in Table 3. To ensure completeness, the reference lists of retrieved articles and relevant systematic reviews were manually screened to identify any further eligible studies. 3.2.2. Study selection process and eligibility criteria All retrieved records (n = 1406) were imported into EndNote 20.4.1 for reference management. After removing 421 duplicates using auto mated and manual checks, 985 unique records remained for screening. The study selection involved two sequential phases: For title or abstract screening, two reviewers independently screened the 985 records against the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Discrep ancies were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. For full-text screening, the full text of 166 potentially eligible articles was retrieved and assessed independently by two reviewers. During full-text screening, each study was required to explicitly report at least one quantitative or qualitative outcome measure in one of the following predefined visual domains: (1) low-level visual function (e.g., best-corrected visual acuity, amblyopia, stereoacuity, near point of convergence, positive fusional vergence, accommodation, binocular dysfunction, or visual crowding); or (2) higher-order visual processing (e.g., sustained visual attention, selective visual attention, visual search efficiency, visual processing speed, visuospatial working memory, or visual perceptual skills such as discrimination and figure-ground perception). Studies were included if they reported VRT outcomes in any of these visual domains (low-level visual function or higher-order visual processing). This approach captures both primary visual in terventions (with potential applicability to ADHD and dyslexia) and those targeting the visual-cognitive deficits that are commonly embedded in ADHD and dyslexia symptoms. Purely non-visual cognitive outcomes (e.g., verbal memory alone or general executive function without a clear visual processing component) were excluded. For this review, VRT was defined as any intervention delivered through a computer-generated three-dimensional virtual environment with real-time user interaction. This included immersive VR (e.g., Oculus Quest, HTC Vive), semi-immersive VR (e.g., Kinect-based sys tems), and non-immersive VR (e.g., tablet-based 3D applications). Purely two-dimensional screen-based tasks without a virtual environ ment component were excluded. Ultimately, 20 studies satisfied all criteria and were included for data extraction and synthesis (Fig. 1). The established eligibility criteria were crucial for ensuring a sys tematic examination of the selected articles. The inclusion criteria required that articles be published between 2015 and 2025, written in English, directly related to VRT, and report at least one outcome mea sure in the domains of visual function defined above. Conversely, arti cles were excluded if they fell into any of the following categories: review articles, book chapters, or conference papers; irrelevant to the use of VR; unrelated to the treatment or management of ADHD, Dyslexia, or visual dysfunction; or when the full text could not be ob tained after reasonable efforts, defined as attempting retrieval via institutional subscriptions and contacting corresponding authors by email (two follow-up attempts over three weeks). For records where the full text remained unavailable, the reviewers screened the abstract; if the abstract suggested potential eligibility, the study was recorded as 'full text not retrievable' and excluded. 3.3. Non- randomized studies, including single-group pre-post interventions, case- control studies, and two-group quasi-experimental designs, were eval uated using appropriate tools based on their design: the Newcastle- Ottawa Scale (NOS) for case-control studies (maximum 9 stars), the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Quasi-Experimental Studies for single-group pre-post and two-group quasi-experimental designs, and the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) for mixed-methods studies. Two reviewers independently performed the quality assessments, with disagreements resolved by discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Overall, the quality of evidence was moderate. Most RCTs were rated as having "some concerns" or "low risk" of bias, primarily due to challenges with blinding participants and personnel (inherent to VR interventions) and small sample sizes. Result This section provides a comprehensive overview of VRT in relation to ADHD, dyslexia, and visual dysfunction. It also addresses the research questions outlined in the previous section. The summary of the included studies is shown in Table 5. 4.1. Research trends and characteristics A total of 20 studies met the inclusion criteria, providing a contemporary snapshot of VRT research intersecting visual dysfunction, ADHD, and dyslexia. The publication trend (Fig. 2) reveals a marked increase in research activity, with 17 studies (85%) published since 2021, peaking in 2024 (6 studies). Notably, only 1 study from 2025 was included in the final analysis. This is not indicative of a decline in research interest but is primarily attributable to the inherent time lag in the academic publication and indexing cycle. Research conducted or submitted in 2025 is unlikely to have completed peer review, been published in final form, and been fully indexed in the databases searched by the time. Most 2025 records retrieved during the search were excluded upon full-text screening, typically because they were confer ence proceedings, study protocols, or articles that did not meet the specific population-intervention-outcome criteria. Therefore, the con centration of included studies from 2021 to 2024 accurately reflects the most recent completed and accessible body of empirical work, under scoring the growing recognition of VRT’s potential in these clinical domains. To highlight the research landscape, a visual depiction of the dis tribution of disorders examined across all included studies is presented in Fig. 3. The review analysis showed that most studies are directed toward ADHD (45%), followed by attention to dyslexia (35%), and amblyopia (15%). The results emphasize the current research priorities and point out potential gaps in exploring comorbid conditions. The technological landscape was diverse, employing a range of VR hardware (Fig. 4). PC/Console-Powered VR headsets (e.g., HTC Vive) were the most prevalent (n = 7), followed by mobile-powered VR so lutions, including smartphone-based and tablet-based systems (n = 5) and standalone VR headsets (e.g., Meta Quest, Oculus Quest 2) (n = 4). This diversity highlights the parallel use of accessible, consumer-grade VR and higher-fidelity, immersive systems for therapeutic applications. 4.2. RQ1: What visual processing domains are targeted by virtual reality therapy (VRT) interventions in children with ADHD and/or dyslexia? The 20 included studies recruited children and adolescents with ADHD, dyslexia, or specific learning disabilities in whom VRT interventions targeted visual processing deficits as part of their clinical profile. This synthesis reveals that VRT interventions were deliberately designed to address the overlapping visual dysfunction profiles commonly observed in ADHD and dyslexia. Table 6 summarizes the most frequently reported or implied visual processing domains that were explicitly targeted (or strongly implied as targets) across the included studies. The results show that VRT interventions in the included studies primarily targeted a range of overlapping visual processing domains in children and adolescents with ADHD and/or dyslexia. The most consistently addressed domain was visual attention and vigilance, with multiple studies focusing on difficulties sustaining visual focus, impaired visual search efficiency, and reduced accuracy/speed on visual tasks (Alobidi et al., 2024; Di Giusto et al., 2023; Fang et al., 2019; Flores-Gallegos et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2024; Skalski et al., 2021). Visual processing speed emerged as another key target, with in terventions addressing slower and more erratic processing of visual in formation, as well as inefficient visual information-seeking strategies (Cunha et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Pedroli et al., 2017). Challenges in oculomotor and binocular control were also frequently targeted, including inefficient visual scanning, poor fixation control, and oculo motor instability (Flores-Gallegos et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2024). Visuospatial working memory and visual perceptual challenges, such as visual discrimination, figure-ground perception, and visual crowding, were targeted in several studies, often as part of broader efforts to reduce cognitive overload during academic tasks (K ̈ose et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2024; Lozano- ́Alvarez et al., 2025). A key finding is the substantial overlap in the visual processing do mains targeted across both ADHD and dyslexia populations. In terventions frequently addressed shared impairments in sustained visual attention, visual search, processing speed, oculomotor control, and vi sual perception. These converging deficits extend beyond the core diagnostic criteria of each disorder and contribute significantly to functional academic difficulties, particularly in reading fluency, text comprehension, and overall school performance (Maresca et al., 2022). In summary, VR-based visual rehabilitation interventions predomi nantly target multiple integrated visual processing domains—spanning low-level, such as processing speed, binocular/oculomotor control, and higher-order, such as attentional vigilance, visuospatial working mem ory functions in children with ADHD and/or dyslexia. By focusing on these overlapping visual impairments, VRT offers a promising, trans diagnostic approach to reducing visual-related academic disability. 4.3. RQ2: What VRT methodologies and outcome measures are currently employed in treating visual dysfunction in children? VRT methodologies and outcome measures employed in the included studies reflect the multifaceted nature of visual processing deficits in ADHD and dyslexia. Across the reviewed papers, VRT applications can be usefully categorized along a continuum rather than as entirely separate approaches. For primary visual dysfunctions (e.g., amblyopia and convergence insufficiency), VRT predominantly utilizes dichoptic stimulation and vergence/accommodation training to target low-level binocular and oculomotor deficits. In contrast, interventions addressing ADHD- and dyslexia-related visual processing deficits employ gamified, adaptive, immersive platforms to train higher-order visual skills—such as sus tained visual attention, visual search efficiency, perceptual discrimina tion, visuospatial working memory, and resistance to visual crowding—that are specifically impaired in these neurodevelopmental disorders (see Table 5 for domain-specific manifestations). This distinction is meaningful: although all VR experiences have a visual component, the studies in this review deliberately target the precise visual processing pathways shown to be dysfunctional in ADHD and dyslexia, rather than generic cognitive training. VRT methodologies for primary visual dysfunction For amblyopia, VRT predominantly utilizes dichoptic stimulation to reduce interocular suppression. Studies by Meqdad et al. (2024) and Rajavi et al. In treatments targeting primary visual conditions, measures often included best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) and stereoacuity for amblyopia, and near point of convergence (NPC), positive fusional vergence (PFV), and the Convergence Insufficiency Symptom Survey (CISS) for convergence insufficiency and accommodative dysfunction (Li et al., 2022; Meqdad et al., 2024; Rajavi et al., 2021). For interventions addressing visual processing deficits in ADHD, dyslexia, and related learning disabilities, outcome measures were more diverse, encompassing both cognitive-behavioral and performance- based metrics. These included standardized tools such as the Italian Battery for ADHD (BIA), which assesses auditory and visual attention, working memory, and inhibition; the Visual Motor Integration (VMI) test for visual-perceptual and motor coordination; the Language Battery (BVL) for verbal fluency and working memory; and the Motor-Free Vi sual Perception Test-3 (MVPT-3) for visual perception independent of motor output (De Luca et al., 2024; Di Giusto et al., 2023; K ̈ose et al., 2022). Studies also employed neuropsychological batteries tailored to specific visual-cognitive domains; for instance, Di Giusto et al. (2023) used the Visual Attention and Design Fluency subtests of NEPSY-II to quantify gains in visual scanning speed, accuracy, and visuospatial planning following VR training in children with SLD. Additionally, studies frequently incorporated neuropsychological tests (e.g., South western Assessment of Processing Speed, WAIS-III subtests), behavioral rating scales (e.g., IVA-CPT, CBCL, CPRS), and in-game performance metrics (e.g., task completion time, error rates, accuracy) to capture changes in visual attention, processing speed, and executive function (Cunha et al., 2023; Fang et al., 2019; Flores-Gallegos et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2024). This multi-method approach allows for a comprehensive evaluation of VRT’s impact on both low-level visual functions and higher-order cognitive processes. 4.4. RQ3: What is the effectiveness of VRT in the treatment of visual dysfunctions related to ADHD and dyslexia? Although few studies directly examined children with comorbid ADHD and dyslexia, the included trials targeting ADHD or dyslexia consistently evaluated VRT effects on shared visual processing outcomes (low-level and higher-order). This provides indirect yet valuable evi dence for the potential utility of VRT in the comorbid population. Research on VRT has shown the effectiveness of VRT in addressing a range of visual dysfunctions associated with ADHD, dyslexia, and spe cific learning disorders, with benefits observed across multiple func tional domains. Summary of the review on the effectiveness of VRT in treating visual dysfunctions related to ADHD and dyslexia is shown in Table 7. The systematic review reveals a range of functional domains, including best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), stereoacuity, visual attention, visual perception, reading, motor coordination, binocular functions and processing time. For amblyopia, VRT has demonstrated efficacy in improving BCVA and stereoacuity, often comparable to traditional patching therapy. For instance, Meqdad et al. (2024) reported BCVA gains of 0.89 lines after 10 weeks of VRT, increasing to 1.32 lines after 20 weeks, with no sta tistically significant difference compared to patching. Rajavi et al. (2021) similarly found significant BCVA improvements in both VRT and patching groups, though VRT showed greater gains in letter-count as sessments (P = 0.002). Notably, Elhusseiny et al. (2021) observed no significant BCVA change after 8 weeks of VRT but documented mean ingful improvements in stereoacuity, underscoring VRT’s potential to enhance binocular function even when monocular acuity remains stable. For convergence insufficiency and accommodative dysfunction, VRT has proven to be a viable alternative to office-based vision therapy (OBVAT). Li et al. (2023) found that a 6-week VR program significantly improved visual attention (p = 0.006) in children with SLD, with gains in attention and inhibition largely maintained at 6-month follow-up. (2019) demonstrated that VR-based performance metrics strongly correlated with traditional neuropsychological tests and parent-reported behav ioral scales. In summary, VRT demonstrates multifaceted effectiveness across visual dysfunction subtypes, with consistent evidence supporting its utility in improving visual acuity, binocular function, attention, pro cessing speed, and perceptual skills in children with ADHD, dyslexia, and related conditions. 5. Discussion This systematic review synthesizes evidence on virtual reality ther apy (VRT) for the full spectrum of visual processing deficits in children with ADHD and/or dyslexia. By defining visual dysfunction to include both low-level visual functions (e.g., binocular control, accommodation, and stereopsis) and higher-order visual-cognitive domains (e.g., visual attention, visual processing speed, and visuospatial working memory), the review reveals VRT’s distinctive advantage: immersive environ ments enable targeted, simultaneous training of the precise visual pathways that are dysfunctional in these disorders, unlike traditional therapies that often address symptoms in isolation. In addressing RQ1, the synthesized evidence demonstrates that VRT interventions systematically target a shared profile of visual processing impairments common to ADHD and dyslexia. These impairments extend beyond the core diagnostic criteria of each disorder and significantly contribute to academic difficulties. Across studies, interventions most strongly targeted visual attention and vigilance—improving sustained visual focus, visual search efficiency, and attentional control—while also addressing visual processing speed, oculomotor/binocular control (e.g., fixation stability and scanning), and, in some cases, visuospatial working memory and broader visual perceptual deficits. Although most included studies examined ADHD or dyslexia sepa rately rather than in comorbid samples, the substantial overlap in tar geted visual processing domains identified in RQ1 and Table 5 suggests shared neurobiological underpinnings that VRT is particularly well- suited to address in a transdiagnostic manner. Dyslexia is consistently associated with inefficiencies in the magnocellular-dorsal visual pathway, which supports rapid temporal processing, motion detection, and precise oculomotor control—functions essential for stable fixation and fluent reading— though this remains debated (Gori and Facoetti, 2015; Stein, 2019). In ADHD, similar behavioral deficits in oculomotor control and processing speed have been documented (Bellato et al., 2023), though the magnocellular theory originates from dyslexia research. In contrast to behavioral and cognitive overlaps, a large-scale meta-analysis by McGrath and Stoodley (2019) found that the gray matter correlates of dyslexia and ADHD are largely distinct. Only a single region of subtle convergence was identified in the right caudate, and this was observed only under a lenient statistical threshold, poten tially implicating shared mechanisms in procedural learning rather than widespread attentional networks. VRT offers a distinct advantage here because its immersive and ecologically valid environments allow simultaneous training of these shared low-level (e.g., binocular stability and oculomotor control) and higher-order (e.g., sustained visual attention, visual processing speed, and visuospatial working memory) deficits within a single adaptive platform. By providing gamified tasks with real-time feedback and dy namic difficulty adjustment, VRT may promote neuroplastic changes along the dorsal stream and attentional networks, thereby reducing the visual-cognitive load that underlies academic impairments common to both disorders. This transdiagnostic mechanism distinguishes VRT from traditional unimodal interventions and supports its potential as an in tegrated rehabilitation approach, particularly for children with comor bid ADHD and dyslexia. Future studies should explicitly test these shared visual pathways in comorbid populations to evaluate additive therapeutic benefits. Regarding RQ2, the review maps a diverse yet coherent methodo logical landscape. The distinction noted in RQ2—dichoptic and ver gence training for primary visual conditions versus gamified visual- perceptual training for neurodevelopmental disorders—highlights VRT’s versatility rather than a conceptual weakness. Primary visual studies provide important mechanistic proof-of-concept (e.g., improving binocular control), while ADHD- and dyslexia-focused studies demon strate real-world transfer to academically relevant visual processing outcomes such as reading fluency and sustained visual attention. This integration is novel; prior meta-analyses of VR for ADHD have focused primarily on broad cognitive outcomes without specifically emphasizing visual processing, and reviews on visual dysfunction have rarely addressed neurodevelopmental comorbidity. For RQ3, the analysis demonstrates that VRT is effective in improving specific visual dysfunctions associated with these conditions. For amblyopia, studies such as Meqdad et al. (2024) and Rajavi et al. (2021) report significant gains in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) and stereoacuity, with efficacy comparable to traditional patching. For convergence insufficiency, VRT has proven a viable alternative to office-based vision therapy, improving binocular functions like near point of convergence and positive fusional vergence (Li et al., 2022). In the realm of neurodevelopmental disorders, VRT shows positive effects on core domains such as visual attention, processing speed, and visual perception in children with ADHD and dyslexia (Cunha et al., 2023; Flores-Gallegos et al., 2022; K ̈ose et al., 2022). This is further supported by Di Giusto et al. (2023), whose VR intervention led to significant and sustained improvements in visual attention and inhibitory control in children with SLD, underscoring VRT’s potential to target shared visual-cognitive deficits across learning disorders. One of the key advantages of VRT lies in its capacity to address both low-level and higher-order visual processing deficits within the same intervention platform. The engaging, adaptive, and ecologically valid characteristics of immersive VR make it especially suitable for children who often struggle with traditional therapy adherence. The gamified elements of VR tools not only captivate users but also encourage consistent participation in therapy sessions, as indicated by Rajavi et al. (2021). This is particularly beneficial for children and young adults, who may find traditional methods less motivating. The ability to use VR at home also facilitates earlier detection of visual changes and promotes ongoing engagement, which is crucial for effective treatment outcomes. However, it is important to note that not all studies included in this review measured both low-level and higher-order visual outcomes simultaneously. Consequently, the degree to which VRT interventions exert distinct or synergistic effects across these two levels of visual processing remains unclear. Future research should explicitly incorpo rate outcome measures from both domains within the same study design to empirically validate the integrated framework proposed here. While several studies reported limited improvements in visual acu ity, notable gains in stereoacuity and other binocular functions highlight VRT's capacity to address complex visual processing issues. For instance, Elhusseiny et al. (2021) highlight VRT's capacity to address higher-order visual integration and depth perception. This suggests that VRT may operate through mechanisms that enhance visual integration and depth perception, which are critical for overall visual function. However, the review for RQ3 also reveals a significant synthesis gap: very few studies specifically investigated VRT for visual dysfunction within the comorbid ADHD-dyslexia population. Most existing research examines each disorder or general visual conditions in isolation. This limits definitive conclusions regarding VRT’s tailored efficacy for this complex, high-need group and represents a critical avenue for future clinical research. Moreover, the versatility of VRT, as demonstrated across different studies, indicates its applicability for various visual dysfunctions, from amblyopia to convergence insufficiency. The tailored approaches out lined in the studies, ranging from dichoptic stimulation to vergence training, and from gamified attention training (e.g., Di Giusto et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024) to integrated neurofeedback systems (De Luca et al., 2024), emphasize the technology's flexibility to meet heteroge neous patient needs. This adaptability is essential for addressing the individual variability seen in conditions like ADHD and dyslexia, where symptoms can manifest differently across individuals. Looking forward, the integration of AI with VRT promises to move beyond a universal therapeutic approach. AI can enable real-time per formance monitoring and dynamic adjustment of difficulty, creating a truly personalized treatment protocol. This approach not only optimizes the therapeutic dosage for each individual but also increases patient engagement by maintaining an optimal challenge level. The combina tion of personalized, data-driven therapy with the inherently engaging nature of VRT could significantly improve the management of visual dysfunction associated with ADHD and dyslexia. The evidence from these studies suggests that VRT is a valuable tool in the diagnosis and treatment of various visual conditions, and further exploration of its long-term benefits and broader clinical applications is needed. 6. Limitations and future works This systematic review is subject to several key limitations that reflect the current state of the literature and outline important directions for future research. A primary limitation is the scarcity of studies directly addressing the comorbid ADHD-dyslexia population in the context of visual dysfunction, a significant gap identified while answering RQ3. The existing literature remains fragmented and imbal anced, with most research focusing on either ADHD or dyslexia in isolation and few studies targeting the shared visual dysfunction profile outlined in RQ1 within a truly comorbid sample. This restricts definitive conclusions about VRT's tailored efficacy for this clinically complex group. Beyond the scarcity of comorbid samples, the overall quality of the available evidence also presents a challenge. While the findings suggest that VRT may improve visual attention and processing speed in children with ADHD and dyslexia, the overall low to moderate quality of the evidence—characterized by small sample sizes, lack of blinding, and methodological heterogeneity—limits the strength of conclusions regarding its definitive effectiveness. Larger, well-designed RCTs are needed to confirm these preliminary observations. A further limitation is the conceptual breadth of visual processing, which necessarily includes both low-level (e.g., binocular and oculo motor functions) and higher-order domains (e.g., visual attention, pro cessing speed, and visuospatial working memory). This heterogeneity, while firmly grounded in the neurodevelopmental literature, compli cates direct comparisons and meta-analytic synthesis across studies. Additionally, methodological heterogeneity presents a substantial challenge, as considerable variability exists across studies in VRT pro tocols, hardware platforms, and outcome measures—diversity that was mapped in RQ2 but complicates synthesis. Frequent small sample sizes and a general lack of long-term follow-up in the reviewed studies further limit robust conclusions regarding optimal treatment parameters and the sustainability of therapeutic benefits. While every effort was made to obtain full texts through interlibrary loans and author contact, some potentially relevant studies could not be retrieved and were excluded, introducing possible availability bias. In light of these limitations, future research should prioritize several interconnected avenues. First, studies must directly address the identi fied synthesis gap by recruiting children with comorbid ADHD and dyslexia and designing VRT interventions explicitly tailored to their common visual dysfunctions. Second, to strengthen the evidence base, researchers should pursue larger, more methodologically rigorous studies employing standardized protocols, core outcome sets, and lon gitudinal designs to evaluate lasting effects. Finally, future work should explore the integration of artificial intelligence for adaptive, personal ized therapy and investigate hybrid models that combine VRT with other evidence-based interventions. Such advances would move the field to ward more comprehensive and effective treatment strategies for this K.S. Chung et al. Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews 187 (2026) 106723 13

population. 7. Conclusion This systematic review synthesizes studies on the use of VRT for treating visual dysfunctions in children with ADHD and dyslexia. The findings confirm that VRT interventions target a common profile of vi sual impairments affecting domains such as visual attention and vigi lance, visual processing speed, oculomotor and binocular control, visuospatial working memory, and visual perceptual challenges in children with ADHD and/or dyslexia, establishing a clear therapeutic target. The review further maps the diverse yet converging methodol ogies of VRT, which leverage engaging, adaptive, and often gamified platforms to address these dysfunctions. Importantly, the analysis demonstrates that VRT is an effective intervention for improving specific visual outcomes—including visual acuity, stereoacuity, and visual attention—with efficacy comparable or superior to traditional therapies, particularly in terms of user engagement and compliance. The engaging, flexible, and increasingly personalized nature of VRT positions it as a highly promising tool for pediatric neurovisual reha bilitation. However, its full potential for the comorbid ADHD-dyslexia population remains underexplored due to a lack of targeted research, and the evidence base is currently constrained by methodological vari ability and short-term study designs. Therefore, while VRT represents a significant advancement in treatment modality, future research must prioritize well-controlled, longitudinal studies that directly address vi sual dysfunction in children with comorbid ADHD and dyslexia, employ standardized methods, and explore integrated, technology-enhanced therapeutic models to translate this promise into optimized clinical practice. metadata_title: Independent and joint associations of physical activity and sleep with ADHD in a population-based sample of children: A cross-sectional study
pages: Independent and joint associations of physical activity and sleep with ADHD in a population-based sample of children: A cross-sectional study Beibei Shi a, Hong Mou b, Zhiduo Chen c, Changshuang He a, Meng Zhang a, Zimeng Zhang a, Huakun Zheng a, Jing Wang d,*, Minghui Quan a,** a Key Laboratory of Exercise and Health Sciences of Ministry of Education, School of Exercise and Health, Shanghai University of Sport, Shanghai, 200438, China b School of Psychology, Shanghai University of Sport, Shanghai 200438, China c School of Physical Education, Shandong University, Jinan, 250061, China d School of Sports Science and Engineering, East China University of Science and Technology, Shanghai 200237, China A B S T R A C T Background: This study examines the independent and joint associations of physical activity (PA) and sleep with ADHD prevalence and severity. Methods: Data from the 2016–2023 National Survey of Children's Health were used in this population-based, cross-sectional study. All measures were parent-reported. PA was categorized by weekly guideline-meeting days (≥60 min/day). Sleep duration, regularity, and ADHD severity were classified as short/optimal/long (age- specific), four-level, and three-level, respectively. Weighted multivariable logistic and ordinal regression models were used to examine the associations of PA and sleep with ADHD prevalence and severity. Results: This study analyzed 98,182 adolescents aged 13–17, including 13,258 with ADHD. PA, sleep duration, and sleep regularity were independently associated with ADHD (all P < 0.05). Significant interactions between PA and sleep duration/regularity were observed for ADHD prevalence (P < 0.05), but not for ADHD severity. Compared to children with long sleep and 0 weekly PA days, those with optimal sleep and ≥1 weekly PA days had lower ADHD odds, with the lowest in the “optimal sleep and daily PA” group (OR = 0.32, 95% CI:0.21–0.51). Better sleep regularity plus more PA-meeting weekly days was linked to lower ADHD odds, with the lowest in the “always regular sleep and daily PA” group (OR = 0.25, 95% CI:0.18–0.36). Conclusion: Even occasional engagement in regular PA was associated with lower odds of ADHD in children. Improving sleep regularity is as important as ensuring optimal sleep duration. Combining sufficient PA with healthy sleep habits showed the strongest association, underscoring the value of an integrated lifestyle approach to understanding childhood health risks. 1. Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) represents one of the most prevalent neurodevelopmental disorders in childhood, affecting an estimated 2%–7% of children worldwide[49,52], with evi dence of a rising prevalence[48]. ADHD in childhood predicts the sub sequent development of psychiatric disorders as well as impairments in academic, occupational, and social functioning, and in adulthood it is further associated with reduced life expectancy, decreased work pro ductivity, and substantial socioeconomic burden[1,20,37]. Although medication and behavioral interventions have demonstrated some evidence-based support in alleviating ADHD symptoms[41,57], their limitations remain significant, including limited efficacy, short duration of effect, and potential side effects[4,50]. These limitations further un derscore the necessity of exploring interventions targeting modifiable risk factors and highlight the importance of proactively managing such factors in the prevention and treatment of ADHD. In recent years, physical activity (PA) has gained attention as a non- pharmacological intervention to improve cognitive and mental health outcomes in children with ADHD[17,57]. PA is defined as any bodily movement that increases energy expenditure above resting levels[9]. The World Health Organization (2020) recommends that children and children engage in at least 60 min of moderate-to-vigorous PA daily, primarily aerobic in nature[6]. Compared to their non-ADHD peers, children with ADHD are less likely to meet the recommended 60 min of MVPA per day, and they generally engage in lower levels of PA. A nationwide prospective study has shown that lower levels of physical health, particularly in terms of cardiovascular and muscular fitness, are independently associated with a higher risk of ADHD in children and adolescents[12]. These findings support the notion that promoting PA * Corresponding author at: J. and improving fitness may be reliable ways to prevent ADHD. Further more, an increasing body of research suggests that modifiable factors such as PA, ST, and SLP are positively correlated with mental health and social competence indicators in children with ADHD, significantly alleviating ADHD symptoms. For example, children who regularly participate in extracurricular physical activities have significantly lower levels of ADHD symptoms, with a more pronounced effect in girls[45]. Intervention studies also show that exercise can improve executive function and attention in ADHD, alleviating core symptoms[22,27,28], particularly when cognitive engagement in the activity is higher. These findings suggest that PA may play a protective role in the onset and intervention of ADHD. Sleep is another modifiable lifestyle factor that is crucial for ADHD management, and the relationship between the roles of sleep and ADHD is interactive. Approximately 25% to 50% of children with ADHD experience sleep disorders[61], which impair attention, behavior, and daytime functioning, thereby affecting school, social, and family life [16]. Research indicates that sleep adequacy (i.e., sleep duration with age-recommended sleep duration[23] and bedtime regularity[43] are critical factors influencing ADHD. However, prior studies have often failed to distinguish between “long sleep” and “short sleep,” where sleep duration deviates from the recommended guidelines, a distinction that warrants further investigation. Research has shown that children with ADHD typically experience shorter sleep duration or insufficient sleep compared to healthy controls[2,34,53]. Furthermore, longitudinal studies indicate that early childhood sleep problems may serve as pre dictive factors for the future development of ADHD[29,63]. Insufficient sleep may be an underlying risk factor for ADHD symptoms[53,59]. For example, studies indicate that shorter sleep duration in early childhood correlates with symptoms of inattention at age 5[29]. Further research demonstrates that inadequate sleep duration is closely associated with the severity of ADHD symptoms. Insufficient sleep exacerbates ADHD symptoms such as inattention, whereas by contrast, extending sleep duration improves attention and behavioral functioning in children with ADHD[2,51]. A recent study reported that longer sleep duration (>8.5 h) was associated with a decreased risk of ADHD symptoms in children [8]. While fewer studies have explored bedtime regularity, existing research indicates that children with ADHD exhibit greater variability in bedtime compared to controls[33]. However, given the small sample sizes (n 〈1000), larger-scale studies are needed to explore the relation ship between sleep duration, bedtime regularity, and ADHD prevalence and severity. PA and sleep are essential components of daily life and may exert joint or combined effects on health risks. Evidence from both children [25,62] and adults[11] has demonstrated these joint effects across a variety of health outcomes and all-cause mortality[5,26]. However, most existing studies focus on the association between a single factor (e. g., whether recommended levels of PA are met) and the prevalence of ADHD, while research on the relationship between this factor and ADHD symptom severity remains scarce[24,46]. More importantly, there is still a lack of in-depth analysis of the association between the interaction of multiple factors (e.g., PA and sleep duration/regularity) and ADHD prevalence and severity. Therefore, this study aims to use large-scale cross-sectional data to examine the associations between PA, sleep, and the prevalence and severity of ADHD, and further explore their combined effects, so as to provide new research perspectives and evidence support for the pre ventive intervention and clinical treatment of ADHD. 2. Methods 2.1. Data source This study utilized the combined database of the National Survey of Children's Health (NSCH) from 2016 to 2023, comprising 334,708 cases. The NSCH is a nationwide survey conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau designed to assess American children's physical and mental health sta tus, healthcare access, and social determinants of health. The survey employed a multi-stage data collection approach: first sending screening questionnaires to households to identify whether children aged 0–17 years were present, then randomly selecting one child from each household with children, followed by completion of an age-specific topical questionnaire by a caregiver (typically a parent) familiar with the child's health status. The sampling strategy covered all 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia, using stratified sampling to ensure repre sentation across states, particularly in high-poverty communities. Par ticipants could complete the survey via web, paper, telephone, or email. Informed consent was obtained from all participating children's parents or guardians. The survey design and procedures are publicly available and described in more detail in documents provided at the following website: https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/data/datase ts.html. Ethical approval was obtained for the original data collection [64]. This study is based on existing, publicly available, de-identified data, and therefore does not involve human subjects research re quirements. In conducting and writing this study, we strictly adhered to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemi ology (STROBE) guidelines[60] (Supplementary Table 1). 2.2. Measures 2.2.1. ADHD and ADHD severity Parents reported on their child's lifetime and current attention deficit disorder or ADHD, “Has a doctor or other health care provider ever told you that this child has [condition]? If yes, does this child currently have the condition?” Only current psychiatric conditions were included as indicators for this study. Parents endorsing that their child had current ADHD rated the severity as ‘mild’ (1), ‘moderate’ (2), or ‘severe’ (3). 2.2.2. PA PA was assessed by the question: “During the past week, how many days did this child exercise, play a sport, or participate in PA for at least 60 min?” Response options included: “0 days”, “1–3 days”, “4–6 days”, and “every day”. 2.2.3. Sleep duration Parents reported child's weeknight sleep duration via the question: “During the past week, how many hours of sleep did this child get on most weeknights (6–17 years)?” Response options ranged from “less than 6 hours” to “11 or more hours.” While the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 9–12 h for ages 6–12 and 8–10 h for ages 13–18, the NSCH questionnaire design prevented accurate identification of prolonged sleep (>12 h) in younger children[47]. Therefore, only children aged 13–18 were included, with sleep categorized as optimal (8–10 h), short (<8 h), or long (>10 h). 2.2.4. Bedtime irregularity Parents reported on their child's weeknight bedtime irregularity with, “How often does this child go to bed at about the same time on weeknights?” Parents rated this item using the following response op tions: ‘always’ (1), ‘usually’ (2), ‘sometimes’ (3), ‘rarely’ or ‘never’ (4). 2.2.5. Measurements of other variables Considering the effect of other factors on result, we collected data of potential confounding factors, which were shown to be associated with the dependent variable[19,35]. Participants reported on their child's age, sex, race, annual household income, highest level of education among reported adults, insurance status, premature birth, number of kids, BMI, ADHD medication currently and ADHD behavioral treatment. Household poverty level was categorized into four groups based on total family income relative to the U.S. Census Bureau's poverty threshold. Highest level of adult education was determined by the question “What is the highest grade or year of school you have completed?” and B. Shi et al. BMI is categorized into three classes based on percentile rankings: underweight (<5th percentile), healthy weight (5th–84th percentile), and overweight/obese (≥85th percentile). ADHD medication use was assessed by the question: “Is this child currently taking medication for ADD or ADHD?” Behavioral treatment was measured through the item: “At any time during the past 12 months, did this child receive behavioral treatment for ADD or ADHD, such as training or an intervention that you or this child received to help with his or her behavior, age 3-17 years?” 2.3. Statistical analysis Following NSCH analysis guidelines, all statistical analyses in this study employed complex sampling methods with sample weights to generate accurate national estimates for the United States. Continuous variables were summarized as mean ± SD, while categorical variables were presented as frequencies with weighted percentages (%). Between- group differences were assessed using t-tests and χ2 tests. Weighted bi nary logistic regression examined associations between PA, sleep dura tion, sleep regularity, and ADHD. Weighted ordinal logistic regression analyzed relationships with ADHD severity. For independent association analyses, 0 days/week of ≥60-min PA, long sleep duration, and highly irregular sleep served as reference groups. We constructed two sequential adjustment models for our ana lyses. Model 1 adjusted for demographic characteristics (age, sex, race), socioeconomic factors (household income, caregiver education, insur ance status), and health indicators (premature birth, number of children, BMI). Model 2 extended Model 1 by additionally adjusting for sleep duration or PA to assess their independent effects. When analyzing ADHD severity, we further adjusted for ADHD medication and behav ioral treatment in addition to the covariates in Model 1. To evaluate joint effects, interaction terms were introduced and considered significant at p < 0.05 (Wald test). We examined combina tions of: (1) sleep duration (three categories) with PA levels (four cat egories); and (2) sleep regularity (four categories) with PA levels. Groups with bad sleep and 0 days/week of ≥60-min activity served as references. The joint effect analyses were based on Model 1. The same approach was applied to ADHD severity analyses within the ADHD subpopulation. We also performed sensitivity analyses to evaluate the robustness of our findings. First, sleep duration was reclassified into two categories (suboptimal and optimal sleep) by merging participants with long sleep duration into the short sleep group due to limited statistical power in the long sleep group. Second, to address potential selection bias due to participant exclusion, we applied propensity score adjustment by including the estimated propensity score for inclusion as a covariate in the fully adjusted models. Third, inverse probability weighting analyses were conducted to account for participant exclusion, using inclusion weights combined with the study design survey sampling weights. Fourth, multiple imputation analyses were performed to address missing covariate data. All analyses were performed using R 4.2.1, with two-sided p < 0.05 considered statistically significant. 3. Results 3.1. Participant characteristics From 334,708 NSCH participants (aged 0–17 years, 2016–2023), we applied a series of exclusion criteria to refine our sample. The participant selection process is shown in Supplementary Fig. 1. The basic characteristics of included and excluded participants are shown in Supplementary Table 2. After these exclusions, the final analytic sample comprised 98,182 participants. According to ADHD status, participants were classified into ADHD (n = 13,258) and non-ADHD (n = 84,924) groups, whose baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Sig nificant differences were observed between groups in sex, race, care giver highest education level, insurance status, premature birth, number of children in the household, and BMI (all P < 0.05). However, age (P = 0.40) and household poverty level (P = 0.80) did not differ significantly between the two groups. Children with ADHD exhibited higher rates of physical inactivity (20.0% vs. 12.1%, P < 0.001) and lower rates of daily PA (12.8% vs. 15.1%). Additionally, ADHD participants demonstrated poorer sleep behaviors, with a greater proportion reporting irregular bedtimes (11% vs. 6.1%, P < 0.001) and non-optimal sleep duration (35% vs. 30%, P < 0.001) compared with their non-ADHD counterparts. 3.2. Association between PA, sleep and ADHD prevalence and severity 3.2.1. Association between PA and ADHD prevalence and severity Higher levels of PA were associated with lower ADHD odds (See Fig. 1). Compared with children reporting 0 days per week of ≥60-min PA, those engaging in PA 7 days per week had 54% lower odds of ADHD (Model 1: OR = 0.45, 95% CI: 0.34–0.52; Model 2: OR = 0.46, 95% CI: 0.40–0.53). Intermediate PA levels also showed inverse associations with ADHD, with 4–6 days per week (Model 2: OR = 0.54, 95% CI: 0.47–0.62) and 1–3 days per week (Model 2: OR = 0.66, 95% CI: 0.59–0.73) both associated with lower odds of ADHD compared with inactivity. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 2, 1–3 days/week of PA (Model 2: OR = 0.73, 95% CI: 0.60–0.88) and 4–6 days/week of PA (Model 2: OR = 0.73, 95% CI: 0.56–0.96) were associated with lower odds of greater ADHD severity, whereas daily PA (7 days/week) was not significantly associated (Model 2: OR = 0.92, 95% CI: 0.71–1.18). 3.2.2. Association between sleep duration and ADHD prevalence and severity As shown in Table 1, the independent associations between sleep duration and ADHD prevalence and severity are presented. Compared with long sleep, optimal sleep was significantly associated with lower odds of ADHD in both models (Model 1: OR = 0.54, 95% CI: 0.41–0.70; Model 2: OR = 0.57, 95% CI: 0.43–0.75). Similarly, short sleep duration showed inverse associations with ADHD (Model 1: OR = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.53–0.91; Model 2: OR = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.54–0.95). However, when examining ADHD severity among affected individuals, neither optimal sleep (Model 2: OR = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.48–1.36) nor short sleep (Model 2: OR = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.49–1.40) showed significant associations with greater ADHD severity compared with long sleep duration. 3.2.3. Association between sleep regularity and ADHD prevalence and severity For sleep regularity, more consistent bedtime routines were associ ated with lower odds of ADHD. Compared with children who rarely or never had regular bedtimes, those who always maintained regular bedtimes had significantly lower odds of ADHD (Model 1: OR = 0.47, 95% CI: 0.39–0.57; Model 2: OR = 0.53, 95% CI: 0.44–0.64). Children who usually maintained regular bedtimes showed a comparable inverse association (Model 1: OR = 0.46, 95% CI: 0.39–0.53; Model 2: OR = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.44–0.59), while those who sometimes maintained reg ular bedtimes also had moderately lower odds of ADHD (Model 2: OR = 0.70, 95% CI: 0.59–0.83). Among children with ADHD, sleep regularity was also inversely associated with ADHD severity (Supplementary Fig. 2.). Compared with those who rarely or never had regular bedtimes, children who always maintained regular bedtimes had lower odds of greater ADHD severity (Model 2: OR = 0.59, 95% CI: 0.41–0.85), and those who usually maintained regular bedtimes demonstrated a B. Association of PA and sleep joint with and ADHD prevalence After incorporating interaction terms into Model 1, significant joint associations of sleep duration with PA and sleep regularity with PA were observed for ADHD prevalence (P < 0.001). However, none of these interactions reached statistical significance in the analysis of ADHD severity. Therefore, joint association analyses were conducted only for ADHD prevalence. The sample-weighted ADHD prevalence across combinations of PA and sleep behaviors is presented in Fig. 2. In Panel A, long sleep com bined with 0 days per week of PA showed the highest prevalence (18.0%), whereas optimal sleep with 7 days per week of PA showed the lowest (9.0%). In Panel B, rarely regular sleep combined with 0 days per week of PA had the highest prevalence (21.2%), while always regular sleep with 7 days per week of PA had the lowest (8.3%). When sleep duration was reclassi fied into two categories—suboptimal and optimal sleep by merging participants with long sleep duration into the short sleep group—results were consistent with the main analyses (Supplementary Table 3 and 4). Similar results were obtained using the propensity score adjustment method, inverse probability weighting accounting for participant exclusion, and multiple imputation analyses addressing missing covar iate data (Supplementary Table 5–8). 4. Discussion This study revealed independent associations between higher weekly PA frequency, optimal sleep duration, and greater sleep regularity with lower ADHD prevalence. In addition, both PA frequency and sleep reg ularity were inversely associated with ADHD severity. Further analyses identified significant joint associations of PA with both sleep duration and sleep regularity for ADHD prevalence, although these interactions were not significant for ADHD severity. Specifically, within the PA–sleep combinations, adequate levels of either behavior appeared to attenuate the higher odds of ADHD associated with insufficient levels of the other. These findings suggest that PA and sleep behaviors are jointly associated with ADHD prevalence, highlighting the value of considering their combined influence in future research and in the broader context of child health. Our analysis demonstrated a significant inverse association between PA and ADHD prevalence in children. Compared with children who did not meet the PA guideline on any day, those who met the recommen dation of at least 60 min of PA on one or more days per week had lower odds of ADHD, with the inverse trend strengthening as PA frequency increased, and even 1–3 days per week showed potential benefits. These findings extend previous evidence. For instance, Ning Pan et al.[46] reported that children who did not meet the recommended PA level on any day had a 12% higher risk of ADHD. Regarding ADHD severity, meeting the PA guidelines on 1–3 days or 4–6 days per week was associated with approximately 27% lower odds of being in a higher ADHD severity category. This aligns with prior studies showing that PA is inversely related to ADHD symptom severity and can improve exec utive function[17,54,58]. The results raise the possibility of a non-linear association between PA frequency and ADHD severity in children; however, this inference is speculative and drawn by analogy to U-shaped patterns reported in adults[10]. Future studies using more detailed PA measurements (e.g., duration and intensity) and multidimensional ADHD assessments are needed to clarify whether such a pattern exists in children. populations and health outcomes[14,21,55]. Compared with long sleep duration, short sleep was associated with lower odds of ADHD. How ever, This does not imply that shorter sleep may be better. This finding likely reflects characteristics captured by the long-sleep category, as previous studies have shown that children with ADHD tend to report longer sleep durations[3,7,15,30,39]. In addition, children with long sleep duration may experience prolonged sleep latency, which has been associated with greater odds of ADHD[44,56]. Given the cross-sectional design, few long sleepers, and limited sleep parameters, associations with short sleep should be interpreted cautiously. No significant asso ciation was observed between sleep duration and ADHD severity. Notably, Sleep duration in our study reflected weekday sleep only, potentially underestimating weekend compensatory sleep, consistent with a meta-analysis showing shorter sleep in ADHD primarily on weekends[40]. Additionally, the impact of sleep duration may vary across ADHD subtypes[13], underscoring the need for future research employing objective and multidimensional sleep assessments, as well as refined evaluations of ADHD symptom domains. With respect to bedtime, previous studies have primarily focused on sleep timing rather than regularity[33]. Our findings suggest that bedtime regularity may be more strongly associated with both ADHD prevalence and severity than sleep duration. Maintaining regular bed times was associated with lower odds of ADHD, and the inverse asso ciation strengthened with increasing regularity. However, the estimates for the “always regular” and “usually regular” groups were nearly identical, suggesting a potential ceiling effect in the association between bedtime regularity and ADHD. Importantly, sleep regularity in this study reflects broader family and behavioral patterns rather than biological sleep mechanisms alone, making it a more modifiable factor. Extensive evidence indicates that sleep and PA exert synergistic in fluences on multiple health outcomes, including mental health[25,62], cardiovascular disease[26], and all-cause mortality[36]. To our knowl edge, this study is the first to systematically examine the combined as sociations of PA and sleep behaviors with ADHD prevalence in a pediatric population. Our results showed that the inverse association between PA and ADHD was most evident among children with optimal or short sleep duration, whereas no significant association was observed in the long-sleep group. Moreover, the elevated odds of ADHD associ ated with PA (0 days per week) persisted even among those with optimal sleep duration. These findings are consistent with previous experimental studies and time-substitution models, which indicate that PA may partially compensate for the adverse health correlates of inadequate sleep[36,62]. Given that modifying sleep duration can be challenging, improving sleep regularity may represent a more feasible behavioral target. In our study, children with more regular bedtimes exhibited substantially lower odds of ADHD compared with those with irregular bedtimes. Furthermore, higher PA frequency was associated with lower odds of ADHD even among children with irregular sleep patterns. Another notable finding was that within any level of sleep regularity, engaging in PA 4–6 days per week was associated with a similar reduction in ADHD odds as daily activity (7 days per week), suggesting a potential threshold effect. These results indicate that maintaining moderate-to-high PA frequency across the week, rather than daily ex ercise, was associated with similarly lower odds of ADHD. This pattern may have implications for promoting achievable, consistent PA routines in efforts to support behavioral and mental health in children. Fig. 4. This study did not detect a significant joint effect of PA and sleep on ADHD severity. A substantial body of evidence indicates that ADHD is clinically heterogeneous, with systematic differences across subtypes in symptom presentation, comorbidity patterns, cognitive function, and neuropsychological underpinnings[38,65]. For instance, the combined subtype is often associated with more severe cognitive impairment and substance misuse[18], whereas the predominantly inattentive subtype is closely linked to social anxiety[32]. Given this heterogeneity, relying on a single global severity score may not adequately capture the potential relationships between PA, sleep, and specific ADHD symptom di mensions. Additionally, parents often lack a frame of reference for their own child's behavior, parent ratings may be influenced by treatment, expectations, or caregiver burden[31]. Strengths of this study include the integration of data from multiple survey cycles, yielding a large, nationally representative sample of U.S. children and adolescents. Sample-weighted and multivariable-adjusted analyses were applied across all regression models to enhance the reli ability and robustness of the findings. Furthermore, This study examined sleep duration and regularity together to better assess their associations with PA and ADHD. However, this study also had several limitations. First, cross-sectional analyses are limited to describing associations, not proving causation. It is also possible that ADHD symptoms influence both sleep and PA. Second, reliance on parent-reported measures may intro duce measurement error[42]. Third, PA and sleep variables were cate gorical, limiting the ability to examine dose-response relationships or identify precise behavioral thresholds. Future research should integrate multi-informant and multidimensional ADHD assessments (e.g., teacher reports, executive function tests), employ objective sleep monitoring (e.g., actigraphy), and adopt longitudinal designs to clarify temporal relation ships and better understand these interactions. 5. Conclusion This cross-sectional study provides valuable insights into the associ ations of PA and sleep habits with ADHD. Meeting PA recommendations and maintaining healthy sleep (including adequate duration and regular bedtime) were independently associated with lower ADHD prevalence and milder symptoms, with partially overlapping effects. From a public health perspective, supporting children in improving multiple behaviors concurrently while recognizing the value of partial changes may hold practical relevance. These lifestyle factors serve as supportive adjuncts rather than substitutes in ADHD management, a role that requires further validation through longitudinal or mechanistic research.
