metadata_title: Meta-analysis of the association between prenatal antibiotic exposure and risk of childhood attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
pages: Review Article Meta-analysis of the association between prenatal antibiotic exposure and risk of childhood attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Jiali Fan a,b,c, Shanshan Wu a,b, Chengshuang Huang a,b,c, Dongqiong Xiao a,b,c, Fajuan Tang a,b,c,* a Department of emergency, West China Second University Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, 610041, China b Key Laboratory of Birth Defects and Related Diseases of Women and Children (Sichuan University), Ministry of Education, Chengdu, 610041, China c Department of Emergency, Chengdu Hi-Tech Zone Hospital for Women and Children, Sichuan University, Chengdu, China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Pregnancy Antibiotics ADHD Meta-analysis A B S T R A C T Background: Studies examining the association between maternal antibiotic use during pregnancy and the risk of childhood attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) have yielded inconsistent results. This meta-analysis synthesizes available evidence to establish a more comprehensive understanding of this association. Methods: Observational studies published through October 2, 2024, were systematically searched from Cochrane Library, EMBASE, Web of Science, and PubMed databases. The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale was used to assess the quality of the included studies, and statistical analyses were performed using Stata version 15.0. Results: Nine studies encompassing 6,180,434 participants were included. Prenatal antibiotic exposure was associated with an increased risk of childhood ADHD (HR = 1.15; 95 % CI = 1.09–1.22, P < 0.0001; OR = 1.28; 95 % CI = 1.21–1.35, P < 0.001). Both mid-pregnancy (HR = 1.11; 95 % CI = 1.02–1.22, P = 0.282) and late- pregnancy (HR = 1.07; 95 % CI = 1.02–1.12, P = 0.521) antibiotic exposure was associated with an increased risk of ADHD. Repeated antibiotic exposures was associated with an increased risk further (twice: HR = 1.13; 95 % CI = 1.10–1.16, P = 0.856; ≥3 times: HR = 1.21; 95 % CI = 1.17–1.24, P = 0.166). Conclusion: This analysis identified a link between maternal antibiotic use during pregnancy and an increased risk of childhood ADHD. Large-scale, multicenter, well-designed prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings and adjust for potential confounders in evaluating the relationship between prenatal antibiotic exposure and childhood ADHD. 1. Introduction Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is the most preva lent neurodevelopmental disorder and frequently coexists with other neurodevelopmental conditions, including autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, and tic disorders (Thapar and Cooper, 2016). This disease is characterized by inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity, and its prevalence continues to rise, imposing substantial burdens on individuals, families, and society (Posner et al., 2020). ADHD has mul tiple etiological factors. Although genetic factors are crucial in ADHD etiology, mounting evidence indicates the significance of environmental factors (Thapar et al., 2013). Among these, prenatal risk factors are significant contributors. Despite extensive research, its risk factors remain inconclusive (Kian et al., 2022). Notably, studies examining prenatal antibiotic exposure remain limited and yield conflicting results regarding the risk of ADHD in offspring, partly due to the inherent un controllability of exposure conditions. Antibiotics are the primary therapeutic agents for the prevention and treatment of infections. While most antibiotics demonstrate minimal adverse effects during administration, they alter gut microbiota composition, which may result in short- and long-term health conse quences (Ramirez et al., 2020). Antibiotic use during pregnancy remains common, accounting for 80 % of prescription medications in Western countries. Beyond disrupting maternal microbiota (Kuperman and Koren, 2016), prenatal antibiotic exposure also modifies the composi tion of gut microbiota in infants (Grech et al., 2021). Substantial evidence demonstrates a complex interplay between gut microbiota and the nervous system (He et al., 2024). Alterations in gut microbiota can affect behavior through gut-brain axis mechanisms, potentially contributing to neurodevelopmental disorders (Wang et al., 2023) including ADHD. Studies have identified distinct gut microbial * Corresponding author at: Department of emergency, West China Second University Hospital, Sichuan University, Chengdu, Sichuan, 610041, China. compositions in ADHD patients compared with healthy controls (Liang- Jen et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2018). Furthermore, gut microbiota from patients with ADHD affects brain function in mice (Tengeler et al., 2020), suggesting that microbial alterations may drive structural and functional brain changes. However, investigations into the relationship between prenatal antibiotic use and offspring neurodevelopmental dis orders have yielded inconsistent results. Given the increasing use of antibiotics, this meta-analysis aimed to synthesize available evidence to examine the link between maternal antibiotic use during pregnancy and the risk of childhood ADHD, providing evidence-based guidance for clinical practice. 2. Methods This meta-analysis was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (In ternational Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews) under regis tration number CRD42024539313. 2.1. Search strategy The systematic review followed PRISMA and Cochrane guidelines. A comprehensive database search was performed across Cochrane Library, EMBASE, Web of Science, and PubMed through October 2, 2024. Med ical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and free-text keywords were com bined to design search terms, including pregnancy, antibiotics, and childhood ADHD. Reference lists of relevant articles were manually screened for completeness. The search strategy is illustrated in Supple mentary Materials. 2.2. Eligibility criteria Eligibility criteria were established following the PECOS framework: 1. Population (P): Pregnant women; 2. Exposure (E): Antibiotic use; 3. Comparison (C): Pregnant women without antibiotic exposure; 4. Outcome (O): Childhood ADHD; 5. Study design (S): Cohort studies. Exclusion criteria included: (1) animal studies or abstracts with incompatible study types, (2) non-pregnant populations, (3) pregnant women without antibiotic exposure, (4) no relevant outcome measures, and (5) non-English literature. 2.3. Literature screening Two investigators independently examined the retrieved literature against predetermined criteria. Reports were imported to EndNote 20 to remove duplicates, and subsequently, titles and abstracts were checked to exclude irrelevant studies. The full texts of the remaining studies were downloaded and screened to determine eligibility. Disagreements dur ing the literature screening process, if any, were addressed by a third investigator. 2.4. Data extraction Two investigators independently extracted data from eligible studies, including first author, publication year, country, sample size, follow-up duration, gender ratio of children with ADHD, and age at diagnosis. Extracted data were cross-verified, with disagreements resolved through discussion with a third investigator. 2.5. Quality assessment Two investigators independently assessed the study quality. The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) was leveraged to appraise the quality of non-randomized studies based on the selection of study groups, comparability between groups, and outcome assessment. Studies could achieve a maximum score of 9 points. Those scoring ≥8 points were considered high quality, those with 6–7 points were at a moderate risk of bias, and those scoring ≤5 points were considered at a high risk of bias. Disagreements were addressed through team discussion. 2.6. Data synthesis Statistical analyses were performed using Stata version 15.0. Effect measures included odds ratios (OR), risk ratios (RR), or hazard ratios (HR), with 95 % confidence intervals (CI). Results were presented using forest plots. Heterogeneity was evaluated via Cochran's Q test and I2 values. Fixed-effects models were applied in the absence of significant heterogeneity; random-effects models were employed otherwise. Sensitivity analyses were executed to evaluate the stability of the results. Publication bias was assessed through funnel plots and Egger's test. For significant publication bias, trim-and-fill methods were employed to evaluate its impact on the results. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05. 3. Results 3.1. Literature search From databases, 781 articles were retrieved. After removing 58 du plicates, 723 articles remained. Following exclusion based on animal studies, incompatible populations or outcomes, 15 potentially eligible studies were identified. Six studies were eliminated due to inaccessible full texts (n = 3) or infeasible data extraction (n = 3). Finally, nine studies were ultimately included (Fig. 1). 3.2. Study characteristics This analysis included nine studies (Lavebratt et al., 2019; Hamad et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020; Aversa et al., 2021; Straughen et al., 2023; Njotto et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2023; Holmgaard et al., 2024; Jiyeon et al., 2024) encompassing 6,180,434 participants. Seven studies reported HR or RR (Lavebratt et al., 2019; Hamad et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020; Aversa et al., 2021; Straughen et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2023; Jiyeon et al., 2024), while two reported OR (Njotto et al., 2023; Holmgaard et al., 2024). Two studies were conducted in Asian populations (Lin et al., 2023; Jiyeon et al., 2024), and seven in non-Asian populations (Lavebratt et al., 2019; Hamad et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020; Aversa et al., 2021; Straughen et al., 2023; Njotto et al., 2023; Holmgaard et al., 2024). Publication dates ranged from 2019 to 2024. The baseline characteristics of the included studies are provided in Table 1. Quality scores of included studies ranged from 6 to 9 points, indi cating moderate to high methodological quality. 3.3. HR analysis 3.3.1. Association between prenatal antibiotic exposure and childhood ADHD risk Seven cohort studies providing HR or RR data (Lavebratt et al., 2019; Hamad et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020; Aversa et al., 2021; Straughen et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2023; Jiyeon et al., 2024) were meta-analyzed using a random-effects approach due to substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 90.5 %). Results revealed prenatal antibiotic exposure was associated with increased risk of ADHD in offspring (HR = 1.15; 95 % CI = 1.09–1.22, P < 0.001, Fig. 2). Subgroup analysis by geographic region showed no heterogeneity (I2 = 0) in Asian populations (Fig. 3), suggesting geographic location as a potential source of heterogeneity. 3.3.2. Association between ADHD risk and antibiotic exposure during different gestational periods Five studies examined specific gestational periods of antibiotic exposure. One study (Jiyeon et al., 2024) was excluded due to con founding psychiatric conditions in its outcomes. The meta-analysis was performed using fixed-effects models (I2 < 50 % for all periods). The results showed that antibiotic exposure during mid-pregnancy (HR = 1.11; 95 % CI = 1.02–1.22, P = 0.282) and late pregnancy (HR = 1.07; 95 % CI = 1.02–1.12, P = 0.521) was associated with an increased risk of ADHD. Early pregnancy exposure (HR = 1.03; 95 % CI = 0.94–1.13, P = 0.791) was not associated with ADHD (Fig. 4). 3.3.3. Association between frequency of prenatal antibiotic exposure and childhood ADHD risk Three studies (Hamad et al., 2020; Straughen et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2023) assessed how prenatal antibiotic exposure frequency influenced the risk of childhood ADHD. For single exposure, due to substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 55.4 %), a random-effects model was used (Fig. 5). For two or more exposures, heterogeneity was low (I2 < 50 %), and fixed-effects models were applied (Figs. 6, 7). The analysis showed that Fig. 1. Flow chart of the literature research. J. Fan et al. repeated antibiotic exposures were associated with increased risk of ADHD: two exposures (HR = 1.13; 95 % CI = 1.10–1.16, P = 0.856) (Fig. 6) and three or more exposures (HR = 1.21; 95 % CI = 1.17–1.24, P = 0.166) (Fig. 7). Single exposure showed no statistically significant association (HR = 1.04; 95 % CI = 0.97–1.11, P = 0.106) (Fig. 5). 3.4. OR analysis Meta-analysis of two studies reporting OR (Njotto et al., 2023; Holmgaard et al., 2024) showed no heterogeneity (I2 = 0). The fixed- effects model was used. The results revealed that prenatal antibiotic exposure was associated with increased risk of childhood ADHD (OR = 1.28; 95 % CI = 1.21–1.35, P < 0.001) (Fig. 8). 3.5. Sensitivity analysis Sensitivity analysis by sequentially excluding individual studies unraveled that the pooled HR estimates did not substantially change (Fig. 9), confirming the statistical robustness of the results. Additionally, Fan et al. (Fan et al., 2020) included infection among the adjusted confounders while other studies did not. After excluding this study and conducting sensitivity analysis, the results showed an HR of 1.16 (95 % CI = 1.09–1.23) (Fig. 11), with no significant difference compared to the original analysis. This finding suggests that inclusion of infection among the adjusted confounders may not substantially affect our results. However, given the limited data available for this analysis, these find ings should be interpreted with caution and require further confirmation. 3.6. Publication bias Funnel plots were used to assess potential bias for the seven studies reporting HR Funnel plots were asymmetrical (Fig. 10). Egger's test indicated no significant publication bias (P = 0.630). However, considering the small number of studies, the results of Egger's test should be interpreted with caution. 4. Discussion This meta-analysis evaluated data from nine studies (6,180,434 participants) exploring whether prenatal antibiotic exposure influences the development of ADHD in offspring. The findings confirmed an Table 1 Basic characteristics and quality evaluation of included studies. Author, year Country Sample size Exposure assessment Age at ADHD assess NOS Lavebratt et al. association between prenatal antibiotic exposure and an elevated risk of ADHD. Specifically, antibiotic exposure during either mid- or late pregnancy was associated with increased risk of ADHD. Repeated anti biotic exposures (≥2 times) also were associated with increased risk. Previous meta-analyses (Ai et al., 2021; Tao et al., 2022; Otten et al., 2022) have investigated how prenatal antibiotic exposure (Hamad et al., 2020) affects offspring psychiatric disorders. The current analysis, incorporating recent cohort studies, corroborates these findings. More over, our study includes a larger sample size, adds Asian populations, focuses exclusively on ADHD without confounding psychiatric condi tions, and additionally analyzes the association between (Fan et al., 2020) ADHD and exposure timing and frequency. Ai et al. (Ai et al., 2021) reported associations between antibiotic exposure across different gestational periods and an increased risk of ADHD in offspring. The present analysis yielded slightly different re sults, showing no association between early pregnancy exposure and ADHD risk. Among the studies included in our analysis, five (Hamad et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020; Straughen et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2023; Jiyeon et al., 2024) stratified antibiotic exposure by gestational period. Three studies (Hamad et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020; Straughen et al., 2023) found no significant association between gestational antibiotic exposure and offspring ADHD risk, whereas two studies (Lin et al., 2023; Jiyeon et al., 2024) found that exposure during any pregnancy stage was associated with increased risk. The inconsistent results may be related to differences in sample size, geographical region, control of confounding factors, antibiotic classes used, and study outcomes. When pooling the relevant results, no association was observed between early pregnancy antibiotic exposure and ADHD risk, whereas mid-to-late pregnancy exposure was associated with increased risk. The study by Jiyeon et al. (Jiyeon et al., 2024) had a large sample size and greater statistical power, potentially enabling detection of subtle but significant associa tions and thus exerting greater influence on the pooled results. It should be noted that studies by Fan et al. and Lin et al. (Fan et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2023) used incomplete classification of antibiotic exposure pe riods, which may have influenced our findings. The absence of a sig nificant association between early pregnancy antibiotic exposure and ADHD risk raises questions regarding the influence of such exposure during critical neurodevelopmental windows. Future research should consider maternal stress, nutritional status, and mode of delivery (ce sarean versus vaginal birth) as potential influencing factors, and further explore antibiotic use in early pregnancy. The mechanisms underlying the association between gestational antibiotic exposure and increased offspring ADHD risk may involve antibiotic-induced dysbiosis effects on the gut–brain axis (GBA). Antibiotic-induced dysbiosis can influence brain cognition and function through several pathways: modulating neurotransmitter synthesis (Chen et al., 2021), short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) (Steckler et al., 2024), and tryptophan metabolism (Cavaleri et al., 2024); disrupting intestinal and blood–brain barrier integrity, leading to increased systemic inflamma tion affecting the central nervous system (Lewis et al., 2025); and modulating vagal nerve function, thereby influencing brain activity (Kim et al., 2020). Germ-free animal experiments have demonstrated that maternal microbiota changes during pregnancy can influence neonatal brain development (Castillo-Ruiz et al., 2023), and that germ- free animals exhibit marked alterations in brain function during devel opment (Delgado-Oca ̃na and Cuesta, 2024), resulting in abnormal neurodevelopment and behavior. Similar patterns have been observed in antibiotic-treated mice compared to germ-free mice (Li et al., 2022), suggesting that dysbiosis can affect the nervous system. Some studies have found that maternal infection during pregnancy is Fig. 3. Forest plot of subgroup analysis of the association between antibiotic use during pregnancy and childhood ADHD. J. associated with increased offspring ADHD risk (Ayubi and Mansori, 2022), potentially through maternal inflammatory responses and im mune activation that affect fetal neurodevelopment. However, other studies have reported no overall association between maternal infection and offspring ADHD (Werenberg Dreier et al., 2016), with observed associations possibly attributable to inadequately controlled confound ing (Zhu et al., 2022). In our review of included studies, Lavebratt et al. (Lavebratt et al., 2019) reported that adjusting for maternal infection during pregnancy did not substantially alter the estimated risk of psy chiatric disorders in offspring following gestational antibiotic exposure (HR ≈1.16), suggesting that antibiotics may exert an independent ef fect. However, the outcome in that study encompassed psychiatric disorders beyond ADHD. Animal studies have shown that antibiotic exposure alone can alter offspring behavior, further supporting an in dependent role of antibiotics (Otten et al., 2022). Other included studies could not fully disentangle the direct effects of antibiotics from those of infection on ADHD risk. Future prospective studies should incorporate stratification by infection type, severity, and treatment modality to differentiate the independent effects of antibiotics and infection. Jiyeon et al. demonstrated that the number of prenatal and postnatal antibiotic exposure is associated with an associated with of neuropsy chiatric disorders in children (Jiyeon et al., 2024). Similarly, Z. Aversa et al. found that girls who received three to four antibiotic courses during childhood had an increased risk of ADHD compared to those with Fig. 4. fewer courses, while children who received five or more antibiotic courses showed significantly higher risks of hyperactivity disorder (Aversa et al., 2021). The current analysis confirms that repeated anti biotic exposures (≥2 times) are associated with an increased risk of ADHD. Multiple exposures may cumulatively disrupt the microbiota; however, the precise mechanisms require further experimental and clinical investigation. These findings suggest that clinicians should consider potential long-term neurodevelopmental effects when pre scribing repeated courses of antibiotics in pregnant woman. 5. Strengths and limitations This meta-analysis has several strengths. First, we included broader and more recent literature and extracted comprehensive data. Second, this study additionally included Asian populations. Third, stratified analyses of exposure timing and frequency were performed. However, several limitations should be noted. Notably, due to limited primary data, it is impossible to analyze antibiotic types, expo sure duration, or spectrum (broad vs. narrow) and frequency during different pregnancy periods. The absence of data on antibiotic class/type Fig. 6. Forest plot of the association between antibiotic two exposures during pregnancy and childhood ADHD. Fig. 7. Forest plot of the association between antibiotic three or more exposures during pregnancy and childhood ADHD. Fig. 8. is a major gap. Future studies should differentiate the effects of various antibiotic classes, such as macrolides and β-lactams, on the microbiota. Second, heterogeneity was found in our results. We tried to identify the sources of heterogeneity from antibiotic types, administration timing, population characteristics, and study design. We attempted to perform meta-regression analyses (e.g., by sample size, publication year, and confounder adjustment); however, these could not be conducted due to the limited number of studies. Nonetheless, no source of heterogeneity was determined. Additionally, only English-language publications are included in our study, which may have led to selection bias. Future research should provide more comprehensive information and apply meta-regression to investigate the influence of different factors on outcomes. 6. Conclusion This meta-analysis unveils that prenatal antibiotic exposure is asso ciated with an increased risk of childhood ADHD, especially exposure during mid- or late pregnancy periods Repeated antibiotic exposures is associated with an increased risk. These findings indicate that antibiotic use during pregnancy should be carefully evaluated to avoid adverse effects on gut microbiota and unnecessary use. Future research should comprehensively record prenatal antibiotic use, including indications, precise timing, classes (macrolides, beta- lactams, etc.), dosage, and duration. This comprehensive approach would facilitate the distinction between the effects of antibiotic use versus underlying conditions and enable dose-response analyses. metadata_title: Alterations in gray matter volume and cortical thickness in medication-naive offspring with ADHD and a parental history of bipolar disorder
pages: Research paper Alterations in gray matter volume and cortical thickness in medication-naive offspring with ADHD and a parental history of bipolar disorder Rui Lu a,b,*,1, Yu Deng a,1, Yuchun Qin b, Yuanju Lou a, Hehua Zeng a, Songtao Tan a, Lvqin Xu a, Guiyun Xu c,d, Yuanyuan Lv a,b,* a Department of Psychology, Jiangmen Maternity and Child Health Care Hospital, Jiangmen, China b Women's Health Center, Jiangmen Maternity and Child Health Care Hospital, Jiangmen, China c Department of Affective Disorders, The Affiliated Brain Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University, Guangzhou, China d Laboratory of Emotion and Cognition, The Affiliated Brain Hospital of Guangzhou Medical University, Guangzhou, China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Bipolar disorder Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Gray matter volume Cortical thickness A B S T R A C T Background: Bipolar disorder (BD) is a high heritability rate mental disorder. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in offspring of individuals with BD may manifest as a prodromal stage of BD and have distinct neuroimaging features compared to typical ADHD. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional involving 101 medication-naive participants aged 8 to 15 years dividing into three groups: BD offspring with ADHD (n = 21), non-BD offspring with ADHD (n = 36), and healthy controls (n = 44). Voxel-based morphometry and Surface-based morphometry methods were used to calculated gray matter volume and cortical thickness of three groups. After conducting the aforementioned analyses, we pooled all ADHD patients into a single cohort and conducted correlation analyses between the SNAP-IV subscale scores and the mean values of differential brain regions. Results: Significant reductions in gray matter volume were observed in BD offspring within the limbic system compared to both other groups. Cortical thickness thinning was found in bilateral precentral gyri, bilateral fusiform gyri, bilateral parahippocampal gyri, bilateral temporal pole in BD offspring compared to both other groups. Non-BD offspring showed decreased cortical thickness in the bilateral precentral gyrus when compared to HCs. The severity of ADHD hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms is negatively correlated with cortical thickness in the precentral gyrus. Conclusions: Offspring of individuals with BD diagnosed with ADHD exhibit more pronounced brain structural alterations than those with typical ADHD, suggesting these changes may represent the genetic abnormalities underlying bipolar disorder. 1. Introduction Bipolar disorder (BD) is a chronic mood disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of depression and mania/hypomania with a world wide prevalence of approximately 1 % (Merikangas et al., 2011). BD is one of the top 20 causes of global burden of diseases, which causes great morbidity and disability (Vigo et al., 2016). BD imposes a significant global health burden in 2019, contributing 6.2 million disability- adjusted life-years (DALYs), primarily due to years lived with disability (YLDs), with an age-standardized DALY rate of 14.9 per 100,000 population (GBD 2019 Adolescent Mortality Collaborators, 2021). BD is a type of mental disorder with a high genetic predisposi tion, with a heritability rate ranging from 60 % to 85 % (Song et al., 2015; Mullins et al., 2021; Bienvenu et al., 2011). Having a first-degree relative with BD significantly elevates the likelihood of developing the condition (Doucette et al., 2016). Children born to parents with BD exhibit heightened susceptibility to developing psychiatric disorders, particularly BD itself (Türk ̈ozer et al., 2025). The developing from a genetic high-risk status to the full-blown BD in offspring of individuals with BD represents a developmental * Corresponding authors at: Department of Psychology, Jiangmen Maternity and Child Health Care Hospital, Jiangmen, China. continuum (Wiltink et al., 2015). The later phase of this prodromal period is often referred to as the ultra-high-risk (UHR) stage, charac terized by the presence of subthreshold symptoms that precede a definitive BD diagnosis. Commonly reported prodromal symptoms include irritability, sleep disturbances, hyperactivity, anxiety, and sub threshold manic or depressive episodes (Axelson et al., 2011; Howes and Falkenberg, 2011). There is a significant association between attention- deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and the subsequent development of BD in offspring of individuals with BD (Duffy et al., 2014). Notably, childhood ADHD is more prevalent among individuals at high familial risk for BD and has been proposed as a potential early marker or even a prodromal feature of BD in some cases (Raouna et al., 2018). This overlap contributes to the frequent misdiagnosis of BD in its early stages, particularly when symptoms such as inattention — commonly associ ated with ADHD — dominate the clinical presentation (Lubl ́oy et al., 2020; Vieta et al., 2018). Such diagnostic ambiguity often leads to delays in appropriate intervention, underscoring the importance of identifying specific neurobiological markers that can differentiate between these conditions and aid in early detection among genetically vulnerable populations. Neuroimaging has increasingly been recognized as a promising source of objective biomarkers in psychiatry. Morphometric studies have identified widespread gray matter (GM) alterations in individuals with BD. For instance, reductions in gray matter volume (GMV) have been consistently reported in the right prefrontal cortex, right temporal cortex, right insula, and limbic structures among BD patients (Long et al., 2023; Selvaraj et al., 2012). Additionally, cortical thickness (CT) analyses have revealed significant thinning in BD compared to healthy controls, particularly in frontoinsular regions such as the left insula, the orbital part of the left inferior frontal gyrus, the medial portion of the left superior frontal gyrus, and the bilateral anterior cingulate cortex (Zhu et al., 2022).In contrast, individuals with ADHD also show reduced GM volume relative to healthy controls, with the most consistent findings observed in subcortical structures, particularly the basal ganglia (Albajara S ́aenz et al., 2019; Samea et al., 2019). Cortical thickness abnormalities, most commonly cortical thinning, have been reported across various brain regions, including the frontal, prefrontal, parietal, and temporal cortices; however, these findings tend to be less consistent than those observed in BD (Albajara S ́aenz et al., 2019; Samea et al., 2019; You et al., 2024). Importantly, accumulating evidence suggests that structural brain alterations in BD may reflect a progressive neuro developmental process. Studies indicate a gradual reduction in gray matter volume within key brain regions such as the limbic system and prefrontal cortex, showing a continuum of decreasing GMV from healthy individuals to those at high genetic risk, and further to those at ultra- high risk for BD (Lin et al., 2015). These findings support the hypothe sis that neuroanatomical changes may serve as early indicators of dis ease progression and could inform early intervention strategies. Notably, studying medication-naive offspring of individuals with BD in the prodromal phase offers important advantages, as it minimizes po tential confounding effects of psychotropic medications and comorbid psychiatric conditions on the observed neuroimaging outcomes (Goff et al., 2017; Lai, 2021). Based on the above studies, we hypothesize that ADHD in offspring of individuals with BD patients may exhibit distinct neuropathological features compared to typical ADHD. The gray matter volume and cortical thickness abnormalities in medication-naive offspring of in dividuals with BD with ADHD show pattern differences when compared to those observed in individuals with typical ADHD. Specifically, compared to typical ADHD, offspring of individuals with BD with ADHD may exhibit more pronounced structural abnormalities in the brain structures. 2. Methods 2.1. Participants This study employed a cross-sectional design. Participants included children diagnosed with ADHD who were recruited from the Jiangmen Maternity and Child Health Care Hospital, as well as healthy controls recruited from the local community in Jiangmen City. Three groups of participants were recruited: (1) BD offspring with ADHD group (BDO): Offspring of individuals with BD who were themselves diagnosed with ADHD; (2) Non-BD offspring with ADHD group (NBDO): Children diagnosed with ADHD who had no family history of BD, schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, or major depressive disorder; (3) Healthy control group (HC): Typically developing children without any DSM-5 diagnosis. The inclusion criteria for BD offspring were as follows: 1. Diagnosis of ADHD based on DSM-5 criteria; 2. At least one biological parent diagnosed with BD; 3. No prior exposure to neuroleptics, mood stabilizers, or psychostimulant medications. The inclusion criteria for Non-BD offspring were as follows: 1. Diagnosis of ADHD based on DSM-5 criteria; 2. No family history of BD, schizophrenia, schizoaffective dis order, or major depressive disorder; 3. No prior exposure to neurolep tics, mood stabilizers, or psychostimulant medications. The inclusion criteria for healthy controls were: 1. No current or history DSM-5 diagnosis; 2. No family history of mental illness. All participants were aged between 8 and 15 years and were free from thyroid dysfunction, and neurological conditions such as cranioencephalic injuries or other central nervous system diseases. Comorbid diagnoses including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, anxiety disorders, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and substance use disorders were excluded. The diagnosis of ADHD was based on the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age Children-Present and Lifetime version 5 (K-SADS-PL-5). All participants underwent clinical assessments using the following scales: Hamilton Depression/Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM- D/A), Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS), 18-Item Swanson, Nolan and Pelham-IV Rating Scale (SNAP-IV). This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Jiangmen Maternity and Child Health Care Hospital. Written informed consent was obtained from the legal guardians of all participants. 2.2. MRI data acquisition MRI data were collected using a 1.5 T Philips MRI scanner with a standard head coil. Structural brain image data of T1-weighted images were obtained using a magnetization-prepared rapid gradient echo (MPRAGE) sequence. The sequence parameters were as follows: TR = 1035 ms, TE = 5.2 ms, flip angle = 15◦, field of view = 256 × 256, voxel size = 1 × 1 × 1 mm3. Participants were instructed to remain still with their eyes closed during the scan. After the MRI examination comple tion, radiologists reviewed the image quality and excluded images with significant head motion. 2.3. MRI data processing Gray matter volume and Cortical thickness were calculated using Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and Surface-based morphometry (SBM) methods, respectively. Statistical Parametric Mapping 12 pack age (SPM12, https://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/) and Computational Anatomy Toolbox 12 (CAT12, http://dbm.neuro.uni-jena.de/cat) both integrated with MATLAB Software were used for VBM and SBM data analysis. Default templates provided by those tools were utilized to normalize the images into Montreal Neurological (MNI) space. After normalization, structural image data were segmented into gray matter (GM), white matter and cerebrospinal fluid. For VBM analyses, GM data were smoothed using an 8 mm full- width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) Gaussian Kernel. For SBM analyses, R. Lu et al. Journal of Aρective Disorders 393 (2026) 120322 2

brain surfaces were reconstructed using the projection-based thickness method, an automated surface-preprocessing algorithms implemented in CAT12 (Gaser et al., 2024). Cortical thickness was calculated as the distance between the inner and outer surfaces at each point on the mesh. Prior to further analyses the cortical thickness data were smoothed with a 15 mm FWHM Gaussian Kernel. 2.4. Statistical analysis Statistical analyses of demographic and clinical data were conducted using R version 4.1.3 (https://cloud.r-project.org/). Parametric (one- way analysis of covariance, ANCOVA) and/or non-parametric (Kruskal- Wallis test or Chi-square test) tests were applied to assess group differ ences after evaluating the normality of continuous variables. Scheff ́e method was used for post-hoc pairwise comparisons with a significance level at p < 0.05 to adjust for multiple comparisons. For VBM and SBM data, statistical analyses were performed using SPM12 and CAT12. One-way analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was employed to examine cross-group differences, with age, sex, and total intracranial volume (TIV) included as covariates. To control the family- wise error rate (FWER), threshold-free cluster enhancement (TFCE) was applied with 5000 random permutations, and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05 for family wise error correction (FWE) to correct for multiple comparisons. The anatomical locations of significant clusters showing gray matter volume (GMV) and cortical thickness (CT) differ ences were determined with reference to the AAL and Desikan-Killiany atlases respectively. After ANCOVA analysis, significant cluster values of individuals were extracted. Group differences were further analyzed using R software, with post-hoc pairwise comparisons conducted via the Scheff ́e method with a significance level at p < 0.05 to control for multiple comparisons and identify specific differences between groups. Correlation analyses were conducted using R (version 4.1.3). All individuals with ADHD were pooled into a single group, and brain re gions showing significant differences in prior group comparisons were defined as regions of interest (ROIs). Within these ROIs, we examined associations between cluster-level values and clinical symptom severity as measured by the SNAP-IV subscales, including inattention and hy peractivity/impulsivity. To control for Type I error due to multiple comparisons, the Bonferroni correction was applied, with the signifi cance threshold set at p < 0.05 divided by the total number of correla tion tests performed. 3. Result 3.1. Demographics and clinical measures A total of 101 participants were included in the study, comprising 21 BD offspring with ADHD, 36 individuals with ADHD and no family history of mental disorders, and 44 healthy controls (HC). The de mographic and clinical characteristics are presented in Table 1. No significant differences were found in Hamilton Depression Scale (HAMD) or Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) scores among the three groups (p > 0.05). Both the BD offspring group and the non-BD offspring group showed significantly higher SNAP-IV inattention subscores and hyperactivity/impulsivity subscores compared to the HC group (p < 0.05, Scheff ́e corrected). Additionally, the BD offspring group exhibited higher hyperactivity/impulsivity subscores than the non-BD offspring group (p < 0.05, Scheff ́e corrected) (Table 1). 3.2. Gray matter volume difference Results of the one-way ANCOVA (corrected for age, sex, and total intracranial volume) revealed significant gray matter volume differ ences among the three groups after correction (p < 0.05, TFCE-FWE corrected). As shown in Fig. 1, these differences were observed in brain regions in the bilateral limbic system (right parahippocampal & amygdala and left amygdala) (Table 2). Post-hoc tests revealed that the BD offspring group exhibited greater lower gray matter volumes compared to both the non-BD offspring group and healthy controls (p < 0.05, Scheff ́e corrected). No significant differences in gray matter volume were found between the non-BD offspring group and the HC group (Fig. 1) (Supplementary Table 1). 3.3. Cortical thickness analysis For cortical thickness, our results revealed significant differences in the bilateral precentral gyri, bilateral fusiform gyri, bilateral para hippocampal gyri, bilateral temporal pole after correction (p < 0.05, TFCE-FWE corrected) (Table 3) (Fig. 2). Post-hoc analyses demonstrated that the BD offspring group exhibi ted significantly reduced cortical thickness in these regions compared to both the non-BD offspring group and healthy controls (p < 0.05, Scheff ́e corrected). Furthermore, the non-BD offspring group also showed decreased cortical thickness in the bilateral precentral gyri when compared to HCs (p < 0.05, Scheff ́e corrected). However, no significant differences in cortical thickness were found between the non-BD offspring group and HCs in the bilateral fusiform gyri, bilateral para hippocampal gyri, or left temporal pole (Fig. 3) (Supplementary Table 2). 3.4. Correlations between ROI region and SNAP-IV subscales score A total of 20 correlations were conducted between the ROI regions and the SNAP-IV subscales and to account for multiple comparisons, we applied the Bonferroni correction, setting the adjusted significance threshold at 0.0025 (0.05/20) for the 20 correlations. As show in the Supplementary Table 3, our study revealed a significant negative cor relation between right precentral gyrus cortical thickness and Hyper activity/Impulsivity scores (p = 0.001), while the left precentral gyrus exhibited a trend toward negative association with the same subscale, though this did not survive multiple comparisons correction (p = 0.013) (Supplementary Table 3, Supplementary Fig. 1). 4. Discussion This study investigated medication-naïve BD offspring with ADHD using structural neuroimaging and compared them to individuals with ADHD but without familial risk for BD. Our results indicate significant group differences in both gray matter (GM) volume and cortical thick ness. Specifically, patients with ADHD who have a genetic predisposi tion to BD exhibited more pronounced reductions in GM volume and cortical thickness, even in the absence of overt BD symptoms. Our study found that BD offspring with ADHD, compared to non-BD offspring and healthy controls (HCs), exhibited decreased gray matter (GM) volume primarily in the right parahippocampal gyrus, left amyg dala. The hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and amygdala are all components of the limbic system, a network of interconnected cortical and subcortical brain structures that plays a central role in integrating visceral states, emotions, cognition, and behavior (Rolls, 2019). This system is involved in key functions such as memory formation and retrieval, emotional regulation, and spatial orientation. Additionally, it contributes significantly to social interactions, motivation, and mood regulation (Catani et al., 2013). The parahippocampal gyrus and hippocampus have been identified as critical regions in the interaction between emotion and memory. These areas not only support the encoding of memories related to emotional events but also facilitate the development and contextual learning of fear responses (Lang and Bradley, 2010; Phillips et al., 2008; Rich et al., 2008). The amygdala plays a pivotal role in processing emotions closely tied to survival, forming the core foundation of human motivation and emotional reac tivity (LeDoux, 2000). Interestingly, the brain regions showing gray matter (GM) volume reductions in our study bear a strong resemblance to those reported in studies of individuals at ultra-high risk for bipolar disorder, who also exhibit GM loss in the limbic system and adjacent areas (Lin et al., 2015). Collectively, these regions are strongly associated with emotional regulation and processing (Rolls, 2015), suggesting that they may represent neuroimaging markers of genetic vulnerability to bipolar disorder. In contrast, this study did not detect significant differences in GM volume between the non-BD offspring group and healthy controls (HCs). This lack of findings may be related to the relatively young age of the participants. Research suggests that ADHD is characterized by delayed brain maturation (Shaw et al., 2007), and structural differences between individuals with ADHD and typically developing controls tend to diminish with age (Hoogman et al., 2017). Moreover, several meta- analyses have failed to identify consistent structural abnormalities in the brains of individuals with ADHD, leading to the hypothesis that ADHD may reflect a dysconnectivity disorder rather than localized structural deficits in specific brain regions (Samea et al., 2019). In the cortical thickness analysis, our study found reduced cortical thickness in the bilateral parahippocampal gyri — a finding consistent with our VBM results. The SBM analysis further revealed cortical thickness differences between the BD offspring group and both the non- BD offspring group and healthy controls (HCs) in several brain regions not identified by the VBM analysis. These included significant cortical thinning in the bilateral precentral gyri, bilateral fusiform gyri, bilateral temporopolar. hyperactivity/impulsivity subscale of the SNAP-IV, which may reflect poorer motor control and more pronounced cortical thinning in the precentral gyrus. The fusiform gyrus, part of the inferior temporal cor tex, is critically involved in visual cognition and facial recognition (Axmacher et al., 2008; Pierce et al., 2001). Cortical thinning in this region may contribute to altered social and emotional processing in high-risk populations. In addition, the temporopolar region integrates exteroceptive sensory information with interoceptive states, playing a crucial role in social cognition by linking external stimuli with internal affective states (Mesulam, 2023). Recently, there has also been studies on ADHD patients with a family history of bipolar I disorder (Qin et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2023). Inter estingly, they found that patients of ADHD with a family history of bi polar disorder showed lower gray matter volumes in the limbic system, as well as cortical thickness thinning in the parahippocampal cortex, temporal pole cortex, and fusiform cortex, compared to typical ADHD patients. However, in their study, these patients additionally exhibited cortical thinning in the superior frontal, temporal, orbitofrontal, and cingulate cortices, as well as in striatal regions strongly implicated in emotional regulation which were not observed in our study. We spec ulate that the discrepancies between the two studies may be related to the fact that the BDO group in our study had not previously experienced mood symptoms. Alternatively, it is possible that our relatively small sample size limited our ability to detect such differences. Notably, our findings are consistent with those studies that also reported abnormal cortical thickness in the parahippocampal gyrus, fusiform gyrus, tem poral regions, among individuals with bipolar disorder. Our finding further supports our perspective that offspring of individuals with BD who have ADHD differ from typical ADHD patients, and these neuro structural differences may serve as potential biomarkers of elevated risk for BD. Finally, we also found that cortical thickness in the precentral gyrus was negatively correlated with hyperactivity/impulsivity scores in ADHD. Studies have indicated that cortical thinning in the precentral gyrus of individuals with ADHD leads to reduced GABA levels in this region, contributing to ADHD-related symptoms (Edden et al., 2012). Treatment with stimulant medications may alleviate this cortical thin ning, suggesting that the persistent neurochemical and neurophysio logical alterations in ADHD may be associated with this abnormality (Shaw et al., 2009). However, why offspring of individuals with both ADHD and bipolar disorder exhibit more severe cortical thinning in the precentral gyrus remains to be further investigated. Our study has several limitations that should be considered. First, the sample size was relatively small, which may limit the ability to detect subtle differences and suggests the need for replication in larger cohorts. However, the high consistency with prior research findings supports the reliability of our results. Second, as this is a cross-sectional study, lon gitudinal studies are necessary to further investigate the relationship between our findings and the risk of BD progression over time. Longi tudinal designs could provide more insight into the developmental tra jectories and potential predictive markers of BD onset. Third, our study did not include a matched group of patients diagnosed with bipolar disorder. The inclusion of such a control group would have enhanced the validity of our data analysis and improved the clinical interpretability of our conclusions. Future research incorporating individuals with BD could offer valuable comparisons and deeper insights into the neurobi ological underpinnings of genetic risk for BD among ADHD patients. 5. Conclusion Our findings indicate that offspring of individuals with bipolar dis order who have ADHD but who have not yet exhibited mood symptoms or even subthreshold mood symptoms show brain structural alterations similar to those observed in BD, and more pronounced than those typically associated with ADHD alone. These abnormalities are pri marily characterized by reduced gray matter volume in the limbic system, as well as cortical thinning in the precentral gyrus, fusiform gyrus, temporal pole, and parahippocampal gyrus. The severity of ADHD hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms is negatively correlated with cortical thickness in the precentral gyrus. This study suggests that ADHD in the offspring of individuals with BD may differ from typical ADHD. The identified neuroanatomical changes may serve as potential bio markers with significant clinical implications. These findings identify promising candidate biomarkers that may facilitate early identification and targeted intervention in individuals at genetic risk for BD. metadata_title: The effects of computerized executive function training on the youth with ADHD: A systematic review and meta-analysis
pages: Review Article The effects of computerized executive function training on the youth with ADHD: A systematic review and meta-analysis Shibo Yan a,1, Xiaoxiang He a,1, Yifan Zhang a, Jing Yang a, Xiang Xu a, Xinyu Liang a, Ting Xu a, Wenjie Dou a, Baoming Li a,b, Zhenghan Li a,b,c,* a Institute of Brain Science and Department of Physiology, School of Basic Medical Sciences, Hangzhou Normal University, Hangzhou, 311121, China b Zhejiang Philosophy and Social Science Laboratory for Research in Early Development and Childcare, Hangzhou Normal University, Hangzhou, 311121, China c Department of Psychology, Jing Hengyi School of Education, Hangzhou Normal University, Hangzhou, 311121, China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Executive function Cognitive training Youth ADHD Meta-analysis A B S T R A C T Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is one of the most prevalent neurodevelopmental disorders among the youth, imposing significant stress and economic burdens on so many countries and families. With the widespread adoption of computers, computerized executive function training (CEFT) has emerged as a poten tially safer, more convenient, and accessible treatment of ADHD. However, the efficacy of CEFT on the youth with ADHD is debated. To evaluate the efficacy of CEFT for youth with ADHD, we examined its immediate, transfer (including near transfer to other cognitive functions and far transfer to ADHD symptoms, academic performance, and quality of life), and sustained effects. We systematically searched four databases: PubMed, Web of Science, CNKI (China National Knowledge Infrastructure), and Wanfang Data, with search terms encompassing ADHD, CEFT, and youth. After screening, thirty-six articles with 1798 participants have been identified. In the included studies, participant sample sizes varied from 17 to 104 individuals, with mean age spanning from 5 to 15.6 years. Study quality and risk of bias were assessed using the EPHPP tool, with 22 % of studies (n = 8) at low risk, 56 % (n = 21) at moderate risk, and 22 % (n = 8) at high risk. The meta-analysis results revealed significant immediate effects, near transfer effects, far transfer effects, and sustained effects. The meta-regression was conducted but no significant moderator was found. Our study indicates considerable efficacy of CEFT to youth with ADHD, and further exploration of potential moderators may be beneficial to refine its application. 1. Introduction Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is one of the most prevalent neurodevelopmental disorders among the youth (Perou et al., 2013), with a global prevalence estimated between 2 % and 7 % (Chan et al., 2024; Elia et al., 2018). ADHD is characterized by symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, which can have detrimental effects on children's academic performance and social interactions. Beyond the physical and psychological distress experienced by those diagnosed, ADHD also entails a substantial economic burden on fam ilies. Research conducted in Germany revealed that patients with ADHD incur an average of 1500 euros more in annual medical expenses than their non-ADHD peers (Libutzki et al., 2019). They also documented that, for children with co-occurring conditions, such as mood disorders, substance abuse, and obesity, the additional costs can amount to 2800 euros per year. The primary treatments currently employed for the youth with ADHD consist of pharmacotherapy, widely regarded as the cornerstone of treatment for ADHD due to its robust efficacy and safety (Bellato et al., 2025; Ching et al., 2019; Storebø et al., 2015), and cognitive- behavioral therapies (Sibley et al., 2023). Although these in terventions effectively ameliorate ADHD's core symptoms, issues such as low medication adherence and parental concerns regarding potential side effects pose significant challenges (Meyer et al., 2020). Moreover, cognitive-behavioral therapies can be prohibitively expensive due to a lack of qualified professionals, further complicating access to effective treatment for ADHD. Meanwhile, cognitive rehabilitation methods have emerged as an accessible and potentially safer alternative for treating * Corresponding author at: Institute of Brain Science and Department of Physiology, School of Basic Medical Sciences, Hangzhou Normal University, Hangzhou, 311121, China. ADHD and other psychiatric disorders. For instance, Buonocore et al. (2015) evaluated a combined intervention of computerized cognitive remediation and metacognitive training in adults with schizophrenia, demonstrating significant improvements in cognitive flexibility and so cial functioning. Hoorelbeke et al. (2015) investigated a computerized cognitive training (CCT) program targeting cognitive control in patients with depression, finding reductions in stress reactivity and rumination alongside enhanced cognitive control. Recent systematic reviews further support the efficacy of cognitive remediation in psychiatric disorders. For instance, Vita et al. (2021) analyzed 130 studies from 2011 to 2020 involving 8851 participants, confirming that cognitive remediation significantly improves cognition and functioning in schizophrenia. Similarly, Mokhtari et al. (2023) emphasized the value of integrating cognitive rehabilitation into clinical practice, demonstrating notable reductions in core symptoms of major depressive disorder (MDD), highlighting its potential as an adjunctive approach for youth with MDD and other mental disorders. With a notable focus on executive functions training, CCT may serve as a potentially effective treatment for patients with ADHD (Westwood et al., 2023). Executive functions (EFs) encompass the cognitive processes through which individuals regulate and manage their thoughts and behaviors, incorporating higher-order cognitive functions, including working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and sustained atten tion (Ferreri et al., 2022). Extensive literature supports a robust asso ciation between ADHD symptoms and deficits in executive functioning (Kofler et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2022). Computerized executive functions training (CEFT) involves utilizing software and hardware technologies to design systematic, individualized, and quantifiable tasks and inter vention programs that address the EFs weaknesses in children with ADHD (Luo et al., 2022; Rapport et al., 2013). Through repeated training, these interventions aim to enhance self-control, working memory, cognitive flexibility, and thereby improve issues related to attention deficits, hyperactive behavior, social adaptation, and learning difficulties. CEFT for youth with ADHD targets four key domains: working memory, cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control, and sustained atten tion (Barkley, 1997; Gibson et al., 2011; Sergeant et al., 2002; Willcutt et al., 2005). For instance, Mawjee et al. (2017) randomized 38 children with ADHD into three groups: standard-duration (45 min/session, 25 sessions), short-duration (15 min/session, 25 sessions), and control. Both intervention groups showed significant improvements in working memory and hyperactivity compared to controls. Similarly, Dentz et al. (2020) used Cogmed software for working memory training, reporting enhanced attention and overall functioning. Meyer et al. (2020) adapted a Stop-Signal Task to improve inhibitory control, with Electroencepha logram (EEG) data showing reduced ADHD symptoms, linked to changes in theta band energy and N200 component latency/amplitude. Tamm et al. (2014) conducted an eight-week training with 24 children, improving cognitive flexibility and reducing attentional issues. Korpa et al. (2020) implemented a 20-session protocol targeting working memory, inhibitory control, and sustained attention, yielding improve ments in EFs and ADHD symptoms. Rosa et al. (2020) used Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to compare brain activation in children with ADHD and typically developing peers, finding that training enhanced sustained attention, associated with changes in pa rietal cortex and striatal-limbic activation. Although numerous studies suggest that CEFT can effectively enhance EF deficits and behavioral outcomes in children with ADHD, some research reports inconsistent results. Dongen-Boomsma et al. (2014) trained 47 children with ADHD using Cogmed working memory tasks over five weeks, employing the ADHD Rating Scale IV (ADHD-RS) alongside assessments of neurocognitive function, daily EFs, and clinical functioning, but found no significant effects on behavior, neuro cognition, or daily executive abilities. Similarly, Woltering et al. (2021) randomized 89 children with ADHD into long-duration (45 min/session, 25 sessions), short-duration (15 min/session, 25 sessions), or control groups, finding no notable improvements in neurocognitive or behav ioral transfer effects compared to controls. Bikic et al. (2021) evaluated 70 children with ADHD, noting that an eight-week CEFT combined with standard treatment did not significantly improve sustained attention. Likewise, Dovis et al. (2015) found no ADHD symptom improvements in 89 children after game-based CEFT. With respect to the effectiveness of CEFT on the youth with ADHD, researchers not only debate the immediate effects of these interventions but also lack consensus regarding their transferability and sustainability. Transferability refers to the ability of intervention effects to generalize to other contexts (Saccardo et al., 2024), while sustainability denotes the durability of effects over time (Stanford et al., 2023), both of which are critical indicators of intervention efficacy. In terms of transferability, Bigorra et al. (2016) found evidence of far transfer effects from CEFT, whereas Ackermann et al. (2018) reported that cognitive intervention effects did not extend beyond the targeted domains. Furthermore, Jones et al. (2020), in their n-back computerized intervention study, observed that while training effects were transferable within similar tasks, they failed to translate into broader contexts. Regarding sustainability, Donk et al. (2015) found no enduring effects from computerized executive function interventions, while Kofler et al. (2020) reported that im provements from inhibitory control training were maintained at a 2–4 months follow-up. Dentz et al. (2020) similarly noted that the effects of computerized working memory interventions persisted for up to 6 months after intervention. In light of the variability in findings across studies, recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses of this growing literature have provided preliminary evidence that CEFT can improve various outcomes of chil dren and adolescents with ADHD, including working memory, reading comprehension, and some clinical symptoms (Dhir et al., 2021; West wood et al., 2023). However, these meta-analyses primarily focused on the impacts of training on specific EF components without delineating differences among various forms of executive function training. Furthermore, there has been insufficient examination of the sustain ability of intervention effects, and the impact of critical moderating variables, such as whether the intervention is gamified or the intensity of the intervention, remains to be clarified. Therefore, the present study aims to address the ongoing debate regarding the efficacy of CEFT on youth with ADHD, and explore po tential factors influencing the effectiveness of training. Specifically, we will systematically review existing trials of CEFT on the youth (< 18 years old) with ADHD, and apply meta-analytic techniques to establish the effects of CEFT on the youth with ADHD and the impact on training effects of potential moderators, such as the training target, training in tensity, gamification, and so on. We also sought to investigate 1) the transfer effect (general cognitive function, clinical symptoms, academic performance, and quality of life), and 2) the sustained effect of CEFT on the youth with ADHD. Based on previous research, we propose the following hypotheses. First, CEFT can effectively enhance cognitive abilities of the youth with ADHD. Second, CEFT can significantly alleviate ADHD symptoms, thereby improving their academic performance and quality of life (transfer effect). Third, the intervention effects of CEFT on the youth with ADHD would exhibit a degree of sustainability (sustained effect). Fourth, the effectiveness of CEFT may be influenced by various moderating factors, particularly the EF components of the training program. 2. Methods 2.1. Search Strategy The current study is in accordance with the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines (Liberati et al., 2009). Articles in both English and Chinese from PubMed, Web of Science, CNKI (China National Knowledge S. Yan et al. Journal of Aρective Disorders 395 (2026) 120730 2

Infrastructure), and Wanfang Data (a comprehensive Chinese-language database) were searched until May 2025. The following search terms were utilized in titles, abstracts, table of contents, indexing, and key concepts: (ADHD OR attention deficit hyperactivity disorder OR hy peractivity disorder) AND (children OR child OR adolescent OR ado lescents OR development OR developmental OR school-age OR underage OR lifespan) AND (computer OR computerized OR digital OR digitized) AND (cognitive control OR executive control OR executive function OR working memory OR inhibition control OR cognitive flex ibility OR sustained attention) AND (training OR intervention). 2.2. Exclusion criteria Among all the retrieved studies, those meeting the following criteria were excluded from this meta-analysis: 1) duplicates; 2) review or meta- analysis studies; 3) case studies; 4) studies not involving computer-based training or interventions; 5) studies not including an ADHD group; 6) studies only including adults (age ≥18); 7) studies with effect sizes that could not be extracted or calculated; 8) studies not in English or Chinese; 9) non-peer-reviewed articles; 10) studies including comorbid condi tions (other mental disorders); 11) studies not targeting executive function training. Two authors independently reviewed the titles and abstracts of identified studies, as well as any eligible full-text articles. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion with a third researcher to achieve consensus on the final coding. 2.3. Data extraction The overall quality of all studies was evaluated using the Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP) Quality Assessment Tool for Quantitative Studies (Effective Public Health Practice Project, 1998). The EPHPP Quality Assessment Tool evaluates study quality based on eight components: 1) selection bias; 2) study design; 3) confounders; 4) blinding; 5) data collection methods; 6) withdrawals and dropouts; 7) intervention integrity; and 8) analysis. A positive rating for each component indicates a low risk of bias, while a negative rating suggests a high risk. The EPHPP tool was chosen for its established framework for systematically assessing the quality of included studies. The data extracted from the articles and the coding of study char acteristics included: the first author, publication year, language of article, mean age (years) of participants, sample size, gamification of training program, training target, training intensity, type of control group, near transfer effects, ADHD symptoms, assessment format of ADHD symptoms, academic achievement, quality of life, and sustained effects (follow-up). Following the recommendations of Higgins (2009), two authors of the present study preliminarily coded the literature and verified their results independently. Any discrepancies were resolved through consultation with a third researcher to reach a consensus on the final coding. 2.4. Outcomes For outcomes, we adopted a three-tiered approach to examine the intervention effects, which included the immediate effects, transfer ef fects, and sustained effects of CEFT in youth with ADHD. Specifically, we first distinguished the performance of EFs, which effectively reflected the immediate effects of the intervention. Regarding secondary out comes, we examined the transferability of the intervention's impacts. We hypothesized that other cognitive functions of participants, as well as academic performance, ADHD symptoms, and quality of life, would improve if the intervention effects were transferable. Furthermore, we regarded the sustainability of the intervention effects as an important outcome of interest. When multiple intervention outcomes were available in a study, we prioritized EF outcomes as the primary outcome for effect size calcula tion. If the primary outcome did not adequately reflect the intervention effect, we combined the multiple intervention outcomes using a hier archical method (Borenstein et al., 2021) to create a synthetic variable and subsequently included the combined effect size in the overall analysis. 2.5. Statistical analysis The analyses were conducted using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA) Version 3.3 (Borenstein, 2022). We performed a random-effects meta-analysis using the standardized mean difference, specifically Hedges' g (Hedges and Olkin, 1985), as the effect size for the experi mental group compared to the control group. Effect sizes were inter preted as follows: 0.2 indicates a small effect size, 0.5 indicates a medium effect size, and 0.8 indicates a large effect size. The effect size Hedges' g was calculated using the sample sizes of the control and experimental groups, as well as the post-test means and standard de viations. In cases where means or standard deviations were unavailable, the data were transformed or selected for computation using χ2, t, or F statistics. To assess whether heterogeneity was due to sampling error, between- study heterogeneity was measured using Cochran's Q and Higgins' I2 statistics. Here, I2 indicates the proportion of variance among studies relative to the total variance (I2 = 25 %, 50 %, 75 % signifies low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively). A significant Q and I2 ≥75 % indicated substantial heterogeneity between studies, suggesting that the use of a random-effects model was appropriate (Huedo-Medina et al., 2006). 2.6. Publication bias Several methods were utilized to evaluate potential publication bias. Funnel plots and Egger's test were used first to test for publication bias. An intercept close to 0 and non-significant in Egger's linear regression indicated a lower likelihood of publication bias (Egger et al., 1997). Furthermore, the fail-safe N method was used if both Egger's test and funnel plots indicated significant publication bias (Khoury et al., 2013; Rosenthal and Bulletin, 1979). The fail-safe N, the minimum number of studies with non-significant results needed to overturn the meta-analysis conclusions, was then calculated. A larger fail-safe N indicated a lower likelihood of bias; however, a fail-safe N less than 5 k + 10 (where k is the number of original studies) suggested that publication bias was a concern (Rothstein et al., 2006). 2.7. Robustness and sensitivity analysis Considering the results of the meta-analysis were potentially influ enced by factors such as inclusion criteria, data extraction methods, and handling of missing values, we performed a sensitivity analysis on the overall effect size estimate by re-evaluating effect sizes after excluding outliers. 2.8. Moderator analysis We followed the PICO principle (Akobeng, 2005), focusing on three aspects: 1) participant characteristics, 2) intervention, and 3) outcomes. Based on evidence-based medicine principles, we identified moderators which might affect the effectiveness of computer-based interventions for EFs in youth with ADHD. These included: first, participant characteris tics, such as age and sample size; second, intervention factors, including gamification of the training program, control group type, training target, and training duration; and third, outcomes, specifically the number of EFs targeted by the intervention. The meta-regression analysis using linear mixed-effects models was conducted to further examine the impact of potential moderators on S. Yan et al. Journal of Aρective Disorders 395 (2026) 120730 3

intervention effectiveness. Before including categorical variables in the regression analysis, one level of each variable was chosen as the refer ence group, while other levels were automatically generated as dummy variables by CMA Version 3.3 (e.g., if the regional variable was divided into east or west categories, west could be designated as the reference group, with east transformed into a dummy variable); the choice of reference variable was not expected to affect the model's results. 3. Results 3.1. Study selection Systematic searches of peer-reviewed databases up to May 2025 yielded 1639 articles. After removing duplicates, 1311 articles were screened. The characteristics of final included studies are as follows: Overall, 36 articles (with 37 studies) including 1798 participants were suitable for meta-analysis (Fig. 1). In the 37 studies, sample sizes ranged from 17 to 104, mean ages ranged from 5 to 15.6 years, and the pro portion of female participants ranged from 0 to 1. Studies in English (92 %, n = 34) outnumbered those in Chinese (8 %, n = 3), and Western studies (65 %, n = 24) outnumbered Eastern studies (35 %, n = 13). Active control groups were used in 16 studies (43 %), non-active control groups in 15 studies (41 %), and other alternative control groups in 6 studies (16 %). Most interventions (73 %, n = 27) were gamified, while 27 % (n = 10) were non-gamified. Most interventions (81 %, n = 30) lasted less than 10 weeks, 16 % (n = 6) lasted 10 to 20 weeks, and 3 % (n = 1) exceeded 20 weeks, with an average duration of 7.27 weeks. Among studies, 8 % (n = 3) addressed all four EF aspects (working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and sustained atten tion), 24 % (n = 9) addressed three, 19 % (n = 7) addressed two, and 49 % (n = 18) focused on one. Study details are in Supplementary Table S1. Over half of the studies were rated “Moderate” (n = 21), with “Strong” and “Weak” ratings each at 22 % (n = 8). Quality assessment details are in Supplementary Table S2. 3.2. Immediate effects A total of 35 effect sizes comprising 1618 participants were included in the meta-analysis of immediate effects. The pooled effect size was moderate and statistically significant (g = 0.488, 95 % CI [0.371, 0.606], p < 0.01) (Fig. 2), with non-significant between-study heterogeneity (Q = 45.759, τ2 = 0.031, p > 0.05, I2 = 25.697 %). The funnel plot showed no significant asymmetry (Supplementary Fig. S1), indicating negligible publication bias. Egger's test was also non-significant (Z = 0.630, p > 0.05). Meta-regression analyses exploring potential moderators yielded no significant findings. A leave-one-out sensitivity analysis confirmed the robustness of the results, identifying no outliers. 3.3. Sustained effects Sustained effects were evaluated through EFs measures, with eight effect sizes involving 428 participants. The pooled effect size was moderate (g = 0.541, 95 % CI [0.308, 0.774], p < 0.01) (Fig. 5). Between-study heterogeneity was not significant (p > 0.05), so moder ator analysis was not conducted. Effects of moderators Meta-regression analyses employing mixed-effects model were per formed to investigate the influence of potential moderators on training outcomes. Specifically, we evaluated the effects of age, gender, control group type, training program, and assessment methods. None of these moderators exhibited statistically significant effects, suggesting a limited impact on the overall training outcomes. 4. Discussion To examine the effectiveness of CEFT for youth with ADHD, we conducted a meta-analysis and systematic review focusing on three primary outcomes: immediate effects, transfer effects, and sustained effects. Our findings demonstrate that CEFT significantly improves ADHD symptoms, enhances quality of life, and bolsters general EFs among youth with ADHD. Furthermore, the training effects appear to persist over extended periods, suggesting that CEFT has considerable potential for broader applications, including clinical therapy, educa tional training, and preventive interventions. The current study confirms that CEFT improves EFs in youth with ADHD, aligning with prior findings (Sonuga-Barke et al., 2013). How ever, CEFT's impact varies across EFs domains. Cortese et al. (2015) found no significant improvements in inhibitory control or cognitive flexibility, though working memory and sustained attention benefited. Similarly, Gates et al. (2019) reported modest short-term EFs gains, noting that low methodological quality in studies warrants cautious interpretation. Notably, CEFT appears more effective for children from lower socioeconomic backgrounds than higher ones (Scionti et al., 2019), supporting Hackman et al. (2015) framework and highlighting the potential of CEFT to promote equitable educational outcomes. Significant transfer effects of CEFT were also identified in the present meta-analysis. Previous studies have consistently reported robust near transfer effects (Melby-Lervag et al., 2016; Scionti et al., 2019), and our results corroborate these findings. In contrast, far transfer effects are less frequently observed. Cortese et al. (2015) noted transfer to EFs and mathematical ability, though with a small effect size for the latter. Similarly, Luis-Ruiz et al. (2020) reported near transfer effects but noted that these benefits did not extend to more complex, real-life scenarios. Although our meta-analysis revealed a significant and moderate far transfer effect (g = 0.515, 95 % CI [0.129, 0.901], p < 0.01), this finding should be interpreted with caution due to limitations, including small sample sizes and a limited number of included studies. Consequently, the far transfer effects of CEFT require further investigation to establish their robustness. Stronger near transfer compared to far transfer in CEFT may arise from the interplay of general and specific EF mechanisms. Fu et al. (2022) found similar single-neuron activation patterns and overlapping geometric representations in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) across Stroop, task-switching, and working memory tasks. Similarly, Morales et al. (2018) showed cross-task activation in the anterior Fig. 4. The forest plot of far transfer effects. Note. CEFT = Computerized Executive Functions Training. S. Yan et al.
