strategy was intentionally restricted to the terms malingering and feigning because the review specifically focused on the detection of intentionally fabricated or exaggerated ADHD symptoms in adult diag nostic settings, particularly when such presentations may be associated with external incentives. Broader or conceptually distinct terms, including constructs related to factitious presentations, were not included because they reflect different motivational frameworks and are used less consistently in the adult ADHD literature, which would have reduced the specificity of the search. Records published up to December 13, 2024, were considered. Eligible studies were required to present original empirical data, focus on malingering in adult ADHD, provide full-text availability in English or in a version allowing reliable trans lation, and report a clear methodological framework for assessing malingering. Studies exclusively addressing pediatric populations under 18 years of age, non-original research formats such as reviews, editorials, or abstracts only, investigations not primarily focused on malingering in ADHD, and non-peer-reviewed or inaccessible articles were excluded during the study selection process. Accordingly, studies were retained only when they empirically manipulated, classified, measured, or validated feigned, malingered, exaggerated, or otherwise noncredible ADHD presentation in an adult or transition-age ADHD assessment context. A total of 305 records were initially identified. After the removal of 163 duplicates, 142 records remained for title and abstract screening. At this stage, 72 records were excluded because they did not meet the in clusion criteria, and 70 reports were sought for full-text retrieval. Of these, 7 could not be obtained despite attempts through major online repositories, leaving 63 articles for full-text assessment. populations, and 21 because they did not primarily address malingering in ADHD. Ultimately, 29 studies met all inclusion criteria and were included in this review. The final set of articles provides a comprehen sive basis for analyzing methodologies and findings relevant to the detection and characterization of malingering in adult ADHD. Fig. 1 presents the PRISMA flow diagram of the study selection process. 3. Results Table 1 summarizes the characteristics of the 29 studies included in the review. 3.1. Validity tests and indices used to detect malingering Most of the reviewed studies used a range of ADHD symptom mea sures and methodological approaches to detect malingering or other forms of noncredible performance. Across the 29 included studies, TOMM was used in 6 studies (20.7%), WMT in 5 studies (17.2%), LMT in 4 studies (13.8%), DMT in 4 studies (13.8%), and NV-MSVT in 4 studies (13.8%). When MSVT and NV-MSVT were considered together as related memory-based PVTs, they appeared in 5 studies (17.2%). PAI or PAI-A validity indicators were examined as focal validity measures in 5 studies (17.2%). Reported diagnostic performance varied substantially by instrument, cut-off, sample composition, and study design. Among studies reporting explicit classification values, sensitivity estimates ranged from 47.5% to 94%, whereas specificity estimates ranged from 80.1% to 100%. For example, Jasinski et al. (2011) reported that failure of two or more validity tests produced sensitivity of 0.475 and specificity of 1.00. Aita et al. (2018) reported sensitivity of 54% and specificity of 92% for a scale-based PAI algorithm and sensitivity of 85% and speci ficity of 97% for an item-level PAI algorithm. Ramachandran et al. (2019) reported sensitivity of 90.3% and specificity of 80.1% for the Subtle ADHD Malingering Screener (SAMS), whereas Quinn (2003) re ported sensitivity of 94% and specificity of 91% for the IVA CPT impairment index. A WMT-specific sensitivity range could not be sum marized consistently because WMT was often used as part of a broader validity battery, as a criterion measure, or as a cross-check rather than as an isolated index with separately reported classification accuracy. Nevertheless, WMT-related findings were clinically relevant: Suhr et al. (2008) reported a WMT failure rate of 31% in adults referred for ADHD evaluation, and Marshall et al. (2016) included WMT within validity- based criteria used to classify suspect effort in archival adult ADHD assessments. Thus, for WMT, the review could quantify frequency of use but not derive a valid instrument-specific sensitivity range from the available studies without mixing different analytic roles, including stand-alone PVT use, criterion classification, and inclusion within broader validity batteries. Among stand-alone PVTs, TOMM and WMT were the most frequently represented measures, although frequency of use should not be inter preted as evidence of definitive superiority. These memory-based PVTs include tasks expected to be performed adequately by most individuals with genuine cognitive difficulties. Markedly poor performance on such tasks may therefore suggest noncredible cognitive performance rather than true ADHD-related impairment, although PVT failure should not automatically be equated with malingering. The TOMM, for example, assesses visual recognition memory and was among the most frequently used stand-alone performance validity measures across studies. The WMT similarly compares performance across easier and more difficult memory conditions to detect improbable response patterns. Spenceley et al. (2022) also highlighted the potential value of embedded validity indicators derived from the Woodcock-Johnson IV Tests of Cognitive Abilities, suggesting that such measures may provide useful adjunctive information within a broader validity-oriented assessment framework. Other measures included the Medical Symptom Validity Test (MSVT), the Nonverbal Medical Symptom Validity Test (NV-MSVT), and the Amsterdam Short Term Memory Test (AKGT), along with psychological validity indicators from the Personality Assessment In ventory (PAI), including Negative Impression Management (NIM), the Malingering Index (MAL) and the Rogers Discriminant Function (RDF), the latter originally developed in forensic settings. Taken together, these findings suggest that performance validity tests and psychological val idity indicators may provide an important validity-oriented complement to ADHD symptom scales. Musso et al. (2016) reported that standard PAI validity cutoffs showed limited sensitivity for detecting feigned ADHD, whereas alter native cutoffs for NIM, MAL, and RDF improved detection while main taining high specificity. Similarly, Young and Gross (2011) showed that standard ADHD rating scales can be easily manipulated by individuals instructed to simulate symptoms, raising important concerns about the validity of self-reported data in diagnostic settings. Marshall et al. (2016) further observed that the absence of effort testing during initial evaluations may contribute substantially to diagnostic error. Several studies also support the value of multi-method validity assessment. Williamson et al. (2014) showed that combining TOMM, the Nonverbal Medical Symptom Validity Test (NV-MSVT), and the Letter Memory Test (LMT) improved the differentiation of genuine and simu lated ADHD presentations. This approach appears particularly impor tant because no single measure is sufficient on its own. Instead, combining ADHD symptom scales, SVTs, PVTs, collateral developmental information, behavioral observations, and cognitive data may improve interpretive confidence and may reduce the likelihood that current diagnostic protocols are exploited through coached or exaggerated self- presentation. 3.2. ADHD symptom measures and diagnostic information A wide range of instruments was used to assess ADHD, each with different functions. Among the most frequently used ADHD symptom measures were the Conners' Adult ADHD Rating Scales (CAARS), the Barkley Adult ADHD Rating Scale (BAARS-IV), the Wender Utah Rating Scale (WURS), and related self-report instruments. The Personality Assessment Inventory (PAI) was also used in several studies, not as an ADHD symptom measure, but as a measure of personality, psychopa thology and response style. The CAARS assesses core ADHD symptoms such as inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Smith et al. (2017) reported that participants simulating ADHD scored higher on negative response distortion indices and lower on PIM than genuine ADHD groups, underscoring the vulnerability of self-report scales to non credible responding. Similarly, Aita et al. (2018) showed that the PAI may contribute useful specificity in the assessment process, although it should not be considered a stand-alone ADHD measure. Other in struments included the Brown Attention-Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), used to assess cognitive and organizational difficulties, and the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS), often used for initial screening because of its brevity and ease of administration. Some studies also included continuous performance tests and related computerized measures. Together, these scales show that most studies relied on established instruments to assess ADHD symptomatology. At the same time, several of these measures, particularly self-report scales such as the CAARS and BAARS-IV, are susceptible to malingered responses. Furthermore, accurate diagnosis requires information from multiple sources, not only from the patient, but also, when possible, from parents or other informants, even in adulthood. This helps reduce the impact of subjective distortion and improves developmental reconstruction. 3.3. Geographic distribution of studies Most of the included studies were conducted in the United States, reflecting the strong emphasis of this literature on North American adult ADHD assessment and college-based evaluations. A substantial propor tion of these studies were also conducted in college settings, a pattern that was less common outside the United States. Outside the United G. Ratti et al. Although this group of studies provides some international perspective, the overall geographic distribution still highlights the need for broader global representation to better understand patterns of malingering in adult ADHD assessment. 3.4. Overview of participants Across the collected studies, sample sizes varied substantially, although this aggregate includes several large normative, standardiza tion, and baseline datasets, as well as some multi-phase samples. Re ported ages ranged from 17 to 78 years, and mean ages were generally in the early 20s, indicating a marked emphasis on young adult samples. The lower end of this range reflects the inclusion of one transition-age study judged conceptually relevant to late-adolescent and early-adult assessment contexts (Rios and Morey, 2013). This focus is particularly relevant because ADHD diagnosis and related incentives, such as aca demic accommodations, are often salient in post-secondary education settings. Gender representation was variable across studies. Many sam ples were relatively balanced, but the proportion of male participants ranged from 20% to 84.8%. 3.5. Types of study design The methods used to investigate malingering were varied, although the most frequent approach consisted of comparing participants with ADHD and participants instructed to feign or exaggerate ADHD symp toms. This design was particularly common in experimental, analogue, or simulation studies, which accounted for more than half of the included studies (Smith et al., 2017; Walls et al., 2017; Tucha et al., 2009; Williamson et al., 2014). The widespread use of this approach suggests that many authors considered simulated presentations a useful model for understanding how ADHD symptoms can be intentionally reproduced and how such presentations differ from genuine cases. Other approaches included retrospective clinical and archival analyses (Leppma et al., 2018; Hoelzle et al., 2019; Marshall et al., 2016; Ord et al., 2021a; Shura et al., 2017), cross-sectional studies (Ramachandran et al., 2020; Ramachandran et al., 2019), and meth odological or psychometric studies focused on scale development and validation. Overall, archival data analyses, experimental designs, simulation studies, and comparative studies each contributed comple mentary findings, although each also had specific limitations. Archival studies allowed the examination of large pre-existing datasets, but they were at times constrained by incomplete or non-uniform data. Experi mental studies were useful for isolating variables, although they often relied on smaller samples. Simulation and comparative designs were particularly relevant for the present review because they directly addressed the distinction between genuine ADHD and feigned pre sentations. By contrast, Marshall et al. (2016) belongs to the archival clinical literature and provides evidence that suspect effort occurs in real-world adult ADHD referrals, rather than serving as an example of a simulation study. Taken together, these methodological approaches illustrate the multifaceted nature of ADHD malingering research and suggest that greater integration of methods may improve diagnostic accuracy and reliability. 3.6. Reported comorbid conditions As noted earlier, ADHD diagnosis is frequently complicated by the co-occurrence of other psychiatric conditions. In the studies analyzed, when comorbidities were reported, mood and anxiety disorders were the most frequently described, whereas substance-related conditions, personality disorders, and learning disorders were reported less often (Musso et al., 2016; Hoelzle et al., 2019; Williamson et al., 2014; Shura et al., 2017). These conditions may obscure the clinical picture, increase diagnostic uncertainty, and complicate the assessment process for cli nicians, particularly when differentiating genuine ADHD from malin gering or from symptoms better explained by other disorders. They may also affect effort, fatigue, processing speed, working memory, and test engagement, thereby complicating the interpretation of SVT and PVT findings. For this reason, SVT or PVT failure should not be equated automatically with malingering (Hirsch and Christiansen, 2018; Shura et al., 2017). 3.7. Further considerations Across the 29 studies, results were heterogeneous and context dependent, with supportive findings for selected validity indicators or algorithms in some settings and mixed or limited generalizability in others (Ramachandran et al., 2019; Ramachandran et al., 2020; Harrison et al., 2022). An important issue in the reviewed studies was the role of incentives. Explicit study incentives were reported inconsis tently. In several simulation studies, participants received monetary compensation, performance-contingent bonuses, course credit, or com binations of these. The strongest recurring message is not that a single test resolves validity uncertainty, but that defensible detection of non credible adult ADHD presentations depends on convergence across developmental history, impairment evidence, collateral data, ADHD measures, and explicit SVT/PVT assessment tailored to the clinical context (Williamson et al., 2014; Marshall et al., 2016; Ord et al., 2021a; Harrison et al., 2022). 3.8. Findings concerning ADHD and malingering Most of the reviewed studies cautioned against relying on any single measure to distinguish genuine ADHD from simulated presentations, thereby highlighting the complexity of the relationship between ADHD symptom presentation and malingering. When the 29 included studies were considered according to their overall conclusions regarding utility for malingering detection in adult ADHD, the evidence remained het erogeneous. A subset of studies supported selected validity indicators or multi-test approaches, a smaller group found specific methods insuffi cient, and several studies yielded mixed or context-dependent findings. This distribution should not be interpreted as evidence that detection is straightforward. Rather, it indicates that the literature is divided be tween studies showing that some measures can identify noncredible adult ADHD presentations under specific conditions and studies showing that these effects become weaker, less specific, or less transportable in more heterogeneous clinical settings. Broadly supportive findings were concentrated in two partially overlapping groups. First, several studies supported the use of stand- alone performance validity tests or multitest approaches, particularly when multiple failures were interpreted conjointly rather than in isolation. Jasinski et al. (2011), Sollman et al. (2010), Williamson et al. (2014), Marshall et al. (2016), and Suhr et al. (2008) each showed that stand-alone PVTs or multi-test validity approaches, including TOMM, WMT, LMT, DMT, and NV-MSVT, improved discrimination between genuine ADHD and malingered or suspect presentations. Quantitatively, the clearest extracted estimate came from Jasinski et al. (2011), where failure of two or more validity tests yielded sensitivity of 0.475 and specificity of 1.00. This pattern is clinically important: conservative multi-test rules may strongly reduce false-positive classification of genuine ADHD as noncredible, but their modest sensitivity means that many feigned presentations may still pass validity testing. Clinically, these findings support an asymmetric interpretation. Multiple failed PVTs or convergent validity failures across PVTs, SVTs, and embedded indicators should substantially increase concern for a noncredible presentation, especially when developmental corroboration G. is weak and external incentives are present. Conversely, passing validity tests should not be interpreted as proof of genuine ADHD, because sensitivity was modest or variable across several measures and study designs. Validity testing should therefore be used to determine whether symptom reports and cognitive findings are interpretable, not as a stand- alone diagnostic substitute. Edmundson et al. (2017) similarly suggested that multiple PVT failures improved discrimination even when symptom coaching was introduced, reinforcing the value of multi-method validity assessment. Quinn (2003) and Berger et al. (2021) further suggested that selected CPT-derived indices may add discriminatory value when interpreted within a validity-oriented framework. Second, a number of studies suggested that embedded, personality-inventory, or ADHD-specific validity indicators may provide clinically useful information, espe cially when calibrated for this diagnostic context rather than transferred unchanged from general malingering models. This pattern was reported by Aita et al. (2018), Musso et al. (2016), Smith et al. (2017), Walls et al. (2017), Spenceley et al. (2022), Rios and Morey (2013), and Young and Gross (2011). The quantitative pattern was not uniform across measure types. Aita et al. (2018) reported specificity above 90% for both PAI- derived algorithms, with sensitivity increasing from 54% for the scale- based algorithm to 85% for the item-level algorithm. Ramachandran et al. (2019) reported higher sensitivity for SAMS (90.3%) but lower specificity (80.1%), suggesting greater screening potential but also a higher risk of false positives. Quinn (2003) reported sensitivity of 94% and specificity of 91% for the IVA CPT impairment index in an analogue design, although this finding requires clinical replication. Spenceley et al. (2022) found that several WJ-IV embedded indices identified at least 50% of simulators while maintaining specificity of at least 90%, suggesting useful adjunctive value but not stand-alone sufficiency. Importantly, however, even these supportive studies generally empha sized high specificity more than high sensitivity and did not support the use of any single measure as a definitive detector of malingering. The extracted data instead suggest a recurring trade-off: conservative PVT or multi-test rules tend to increase specificity, whereas sensitivity remains modest or variable; broader self-report or screening indices may improve sensitivity but may reduce specificity and require external corroboration. Real-world clinical and archival studies were especially important because they showed that invalid responding is not rare in ADHD referral contexts. Marshall et al. (2016) classified 115 of 554 adult ADHD assessments as involving suspect effort, and Suhr et al. (2008) reported WMT failure in 31% of adults referred for ADHD evaluation. Shura et al. (2017) found that 19.3% of veterans assessed for ADHD failed TOMM Trial 1, 44.7% showed MMPI-2-RF over-reporting, and 8.8% showed both. These findings support routine validity assessment in adult ADHD evaluations, while also showing that invalid performance, symptom over-reporting, and ADHD diagnosis do not map onto each other in a simple one-to-one manner. Predominantly non-supportive findings were less frequent but methodologically important. Bryant et al. (2018) showed that WHODAS 2.0 was readily inflated under malingering instructions and should not be used as a stand-alone measure when external incentives are present. Tucha et al. (2009) found that BADDS alone did not adequately distin guish malingered from genuine ADHD, and Niesten et al. (2017) showed that moral reminders or contracts did not reliably reduce symptom over- reporting. These studies are especially informative because they converge on a common point: face-valid self-report measures and simple pre-test deterrence strategies appear insufficient when symptom exag geration is intentional and contextually motivated. The largest remaining group of studies yielded inconclusive, mixed, or context-dependent findings. Fuermaier et al. (2018), Ord et al. (2021a), and Harrison et al. (2022) found that some indices or com bined scores were informative, but not accurate enough to function as stand-alone detectors across settings. Hoelzle et al. (2019), Hirsch and Christiansen (2018), and Shura et al. (2017) further showed that validity-test failure or invalid responding can complicate interpretation of symptom and neuropsychological profiles, while also demonstrating that noncredible performance does not map neatly onto ADHD diagnosis itself. Other studies in this group were relevant mainly because they highlighted vulnerability to distortion, heterogeneity of presentation, or limitations in generalizability rather than validating a specific detection method, including Harrison et al. (2007), Booksh et al. (2010), and Ramachandran et al. (2019, 2020). This point is particularly relevant from a psychiatric research perspective, because several of the most encouraging findings were generated in analogue studies with instructed simulators, whereas real-world referral samples were more heteroge neous, more comorbid, and less cleanly separable. In this sense, the gap between analogue detection and clinical applicability remains one of the central unresolved issues in the field. Taken together, these findings suggest that the major contribution of the literature is not the identification of a single best test, but the pro gressive clarification of a more defensible diagnostic strategy. Detection appears more credible when adult ADHD assessment integrates devel opmental corroboration, collateral history, symptom scales, stand-alone and embedded validity measures, and cautious interpretation of neu ropsychological data only after response validity has been addressed (Williamson et al., 2014; Marshall et al., 2016; Harrison et al., 2022; Suhr et al., 2008). Therefore, the main novel insight emerging from this review is that malingering in adult ADHD should be conceptualized less as a problem solvable by one instrument and more as a problem of diagnostic architecture. The more the assessment relies on isolated self- report and poorly corroborated symptom narratives, the more vulner able it becomes to distortion. By contrast, the more the evaluation is structured, longitudinally informed, and methodologically plural, the greater the likelihood of distinguishing genuine ADHD from noncredible presentations in a clinically meaningful way. 4. Discussion 4.1. Clinical features suggestive of genuine ADHD versus malingering Individuals with genuine ADHD generally show a more coherent pattern of impairment across tasks and areas of daily life, consistent with their developmental and clinical history (American Psychiatric Association, 2022; Faraone et al., 2024). By contrast, individuals simulating ADHD may report selective or exaggerated deficits while preserving broader overall functioning and may present in contexts in which obtaining a diagnosis rather than clarifying longstanding diffi culties, appears to be the primary objective (Harrison et al., 2007; Marshall et al., 2016; Sadek, 2022). Although such features are not sufficient on their own, they may indicate the need for a more in-depth assessment. Personality disorders, mood disorders, and affective temperaments should also be carefully evaluated (Asherson et al., 2014). Some patients may identify more readily with a less stigmatized condition such as ADHD than with a mood or personality disorder, which makes differ ential diagnosis a central task for the specialist (Harrison and Armstrong, 2016; Lovett and Harrison, 2021). The clinician must therefore distinguish ADHD from alternative explanations and, when necessary, provide appropriate feedback to the patient. At the same time, this process must be conducted carefully so as not to alienate or stigmatize individuals who may have genuine difficulties, thereby pre serving the therapeutic relationship and trust in the healthcare system. 4.2. Practical recommendations for assessment When malingering is possible, the assessment should rely on struc tured clinical judgment and multiple independent sources of informa tion rather than on any single symptom scale, SVT, or PVT. 1. the integration of ADHD symptom scales, collateral developmental information, behavioral observations, cognitive data, SVTs, and PVTs, which may improve interpretive confidence (Nelson and Lovett, 2019); 2. the interpretation of validity findings in relation to individual his tory, symptom course, comorbidities, external incentives, and de mographic context, which may help adapt the diagnostic process to the patient's clinical profile (Lovett and Harrison, 2021); 3. longitudinal follow-up, when feasible, because observing symptom stability and functional impairment over time may help distinguish persistent ADHD from noncredible or situational presentations (Faraone et al., 2024; Roor et al., 2024). Given the challenges highlighted in this review, standard ADHD as sessments should be supplemented with explicit validity assessment, including SVTs, PVTs, and embedded validity indicators when clinically appropriate (Nelson and Lovett, 2019; Sweet et al., 2021; Ovsiew et al., 2023). Performance validity tests such as the TOMM, WMT, LMT, DMT, NV-MSVT and MSVT should be considered useful adjuncts not because they were frequently used, but because several studies found that stand- alone PVTs and multi-test validity approaches showed high specificity and moderate or variable sensitivity in detecting feigned or noncredible ADHD presentations (Suhr et al., 2008; Sollman et al., 2010; Jasinski et al., 2011; Williamson et al., 2014; Spenceley et al., 2022). The strongest quantitative example was Jasinski et al. (2011), where failure of two or more validity tests produced specificity of 1.00 but sensitivity of 0.475. This means that multiple validity-test failures may strongly increase suspicion of noncredible performance, whereas pass ing validity tests does not exclude feigning or symptom exaggeration. Other studies were consistent with this interpretation: Sollman et al. (2010) reported moderate sensitivity and high specificity for TOMM, DMT, LMT, and NV-MSVT, Williamson et al. (2014) found that TOMM, LMT, and NV-MSVT differentiated malingered ADHD from ADHD with and without comorbidity, and Spenceley et al. (2022) reported that embedded WJ-IV indices detected at least 50% of simulators while maintaining specificity of at least 90%. Stand-alone PVTs are relevant because they assess performance on tasks that are generally easy even for individuals with genuine cognitive difficulties, so markedly poor performance may suggest noncredible cognitive performance rather than true ADHD, although PVT failure should not automatically be equated with malingering (Hirsch and Christiansen, 2018; Shura et al., 2017; Sweet et al., 2021). The clinical interview must also extend beyond the patient's imme diate report and explore developmental history, behavioral patterns, functional impairment, and the motivation for seeking a diagnosis (American Psychiatric Association, 2022; Nelson and Lovett, 2019; Lovett and Harrison, 2021). SVTs and self-report validity indicators also showed clinically useful but heterogeneous performance. PAI-derived ADHD-specific algorithms showed high specificity, especially at item level, whereas SAMS showed high sensitivity but lower specificity (Aita et al., 2018; Ramachandran et al., 2019). CAARS, BADDS, WHODAS 2.0, and other face-valid self-report instruments were vulnerable to inflation or insufficient as stand-alone credibility indicators (Harrison et al., 2007; Tucha et al., 2009; Bryant et al., 2018; Walls et al., 2017). Therefore, SVTs, PVTs, and embedded validity indicators should be interpreted as convergent evidence rather than as definitive classifica tion tools. Whenever possible, collateral information from family members, teachers, or colleagues should also be obtained (American Psychiatric Association, 2022; Nelson and Lovett, 2019). This multi-method approach is particularly important because it allows the clinician to compare self-report, observed behavior, cognitive performance, validity findings, and developmental history across sources. In this way, it be comes more difficult for coached or exaggerated presentations to remain undetected, especially when current protocols rely too heavily on self- report measures alone. Although this approach is more resource- intensive, it appears necessary when malingering is suspected. Clini cally, the most defensible interpretation is therefore asymmetric: mul tiple failed PVTs or convergent SVT/PVT abnormalities increase concern for noncredible presentation, whereas normal validity findings do not by themselves establish that the ADHD presentation is genuine. Most of the reviewed studies focused on psychological and behav ioral assessment, whereas biometric and neurophysiological markers remain only marginally explored. Fuermaier et al. (2018) explored the utility of vigilance tasks and motion tracking in detecting malingering, although motion tracking offered only limited additional value. Outside formal testing, clinicians may also attend to features such as response latency, repetitive symptom descriptions, excessive emphasis on defi cits, or discrepancies between declared difficulties and observed behavior during assessment. These indicators are not diagnostic evi dence, but they may justify deeper evaluation (Sansone and Sansone, 2011; Sadek, 2022). 4.3. Unraveling the tangle: motivations underlying malingering in adult ADHD assessment It is essential to understand the motivations that may underlie malingering in ADHD assessment (Sansone and Sansone, 2011; Sadek, 2022). Identifying these motives is complex, because they vary across individuals and contexts. However, the literature reviewed here suggests several recurrent external incentives, including academic accommoda tions, access to stimulant medications, and the avoidance of academic or occupational demands (Harrison et al., 2007; Marshall et al., 2016; Ramachandran et al., 2020). These motivations are particularly relevant in adult ADHD assessment because they may directly influence how symptoms are described and emphasized during the diagnostic process. A further contemporary concern is the increasing accessibility of online ADHD-related information and self-assessment material (Abdelnour et al., 2022; Karasavva et al., 2025). Social media content, commercial screening tools, and online questionnaires may encourage self-diagnosis or provide individuals with symptom descriptions that can later be reproduced during clinical evaluation. In this context, the role of the specialist is pivotal, because the clinician must distinguish between genuine ADHD symptoms, symptoms shaped by other psychiatric con ditions, and presentations influenced by social pressures, expectations, or external gain (American Psychiatric Association, 2022; Lovett and Harrison, 2021). The broader social context should also be considered. In environments in which performance demands are high, an ADHD diagnosis may at times be perceived as a way to explain academic or occupational difficulties, gain access to accommodations, or obtain medication (Harrison and Rosenblum, 2010; Sadek, 2022). For this reason, misdiagnosis is clinically consequential and may lead to inap propriate treatment, unnecessary exposure to stimulant medication and its adverse effects, and inefficient allocation of clinical resources (Abdelnour et al., 2022; Faraone et al., 2024). At the same time, it may undermine the legitimacy of individuals who genuinely require support. Specialists therefore play a central role not only as diagnosticians, but also as guides in ensuring that diagnoses are evidence-based, clinically grounded, and not driven by uncorroborated self-report or external in centives, in accordance with the principle of “first, do no harm”. metadata_title: Effects of video game intervention on attention deficit in children with ADHD: A systematic review and meta-analysis
pages: Review article Effects of video game intervention on attention deficit in children with ADHD: A systematic review and meta-analysis Pengwei Ma a,b , Zhuolin Xue a,b, Kun Yuan a,b, Peiyun Zheng a,b, Junfeng Li c,*, Jindong Chang a,b,* a School of Physical Education, Southwest University, Chongqing, China b Institute of Motor Quotient, Southwest University, Chongqing, China c Ministry of Sports, Shandong Technology and Business University, Yantai, China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: children with ADHD Video game Meta-analysis B R I E F C O M M U N I C A T I O N S Purpose: To explore the effects of a video game intervention on children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Methods: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were systematically searched in PubMed, Web of Science, Scien ceDirect, and X-MOL databases. Studies were screened based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Assessment Tool. Relevant data were analyzed using RevMan 5.3.5 software, and publication bias was assessed using Stata 17.0. Results: A total of 10 RCTs involving 820 subjects were included. Meta-analysis indicated that the video game intervention had a positive effect on reducing attention deficit symptoms in children with ADHD (SMD=-0.19, 95 % CI [-0.34, -0.03]). Egger’s test confirmed that the included studies were free from publication bias. Conclusion: Findings indicate that video game interventions show statistically significant but not clinically meaningful benefits on attention and may be therapeutic when added to other evidence-based therapies. 1. Introduction 1.1. ADHD Inattention, one of the core symptoms of children with attention deficits hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), is a primary cause of these negative effects (Bental and Tirosh, 2007; Greven et al., 2014; Skalski et al., 2021; Trane and Willcutt, 2023), making it one of the most pressing issues for these children. Currently, there are both pharmaco logic and non-pharmacologic approaches to the treatment of ADHD (S. Cortese et al., 2018; Mechler et al., 2022; Fridman et al., 2015). But there are some side effects of such drugs, such as insomnia, dry mouth, loss of appetite, and syncope (S. Cortese et al., 2018), and even affect children’s growth and development (Greenhill et al., 2020). With the continuous advancements in this field, more pharmacological treat ments have emerged, such as polyunsaturated fatty acids (Gillies et al., 2023). Non-pharmacological approaches mainly involve psychosocial interventions (Zwi et al., 2011), including cognitive-behavioral therapy, family therapy, and interpersonal psychotherapy (Correll et al., 2021). Other non-pharmacological treatments include neurofeedback (Cortese et al., 2016), video game therapy (Jaklevic, 2020), and brain stimulation (Rubia et al., 2021). 1.2. Video games and ADHD Inattention in children with ADHD is primarily due to abnormal central nervous system function, characterized by poor inhibition and inadequate secretion of dopamine and norepinephrine due to dysfunc tion in the frontal-striatal circuitry (Christiansen et al., 2019). This dysfunction leads to attentional selection and maintenance issues when external stimuli are present. Studies have shown that video games can promote striatal dopamine release, which may improve attention deficit symptoms (Koepp et al., 1998). Video games as an emerging digital therapy method, are increasingly used to diagnose and intervene in clinical symptoms in children with ADHD (Pe ̃nuelas-Calvo et al., 2022). virtual reality video game models have been employed to assess chil dren’s attention, impulsivity, and processing speed, effectively dis tinguishing children with ADHD from controls (Areces et al., 2018). Additionally, video games have been utilized to differentiate between ADHD subtypes, revealing a positive correlation between reaction time measured by the video game and inattentiveness subtypes (Delgado-Gomez et al., 2017). Studies indicate that video games have a high accuracy rate in diagnosing ADHD symptoms, with a 78 % accuracy rate for the inattentive subtype and a 75 % accuracy rate for the com bined subtype of ADHD (Heller et al., 2013). Interventions using video games for ADHD symptoms primarily focus on cognitive training and neurofeedback. One study conducted a 10- week, thrice-weekly PC video game intervention for children with ADHD, resulting in improvements in life skills and a reduction in ADHD symptoms (Bul et al., 2016). Attention deficit, a core symptom of ADHD, has been the primary target of video game interventions due to their potential ameliorative effects. However, with increased research, some studies have found that while video games may improve impulsivity, they do not significantly enhance attention in ADHD patients (Bul et al., 2018). Furthermore, some studies are limited by sample size, making their results less reliable. This paper reviews related studies and employs meta-analysis to investigate whether video games have a significant effect on attention in children with ADHD. 2. Methods This study adheres to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Liberati et al., 2009) for selecting and employing research methods. The review protocol was registered in the PROSPERO database (registration number CRD42024554539). 2.1. Search strategy A systematic literature search was performed in four databases: PubMed, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, X-MOL. The final search date was May 10, 2024. The following search terms were used: ("attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity"[MeSH Terms] OR ("attention"[All Fields] AND "deficit"[All Fields] AND "disorder"[All Fields] AND "hyperactivity"[All Fields]) OR "attention deficit disorder with hyper activity"[All Fields] OR "adhd"[All Fields]) AND ("child"[MeSH Terms] OR "child"[All Fields] OR "children"[All Fields] OR "child s"[All Fields] OR "child s"[All Fields] OR "children’s"[All Fields] OR "children"[All Fields]) AND ("video games"[MeSH Terms] OR ("video"[All Fields] AND "games"[All Fields]) OR "video games"[All Fields] OR ("video"[All Fields] AND "games"[All Fields]) OR "video games"[All Fields]). Addi tionally, references from identified articles were screened for inclusion. 2.2. Inclusion and exclusion criteria Subjects were patients aged 12 years and younger with a clinical diagnosis of ADHD; (2) implemented video games-based interventions; (3) reported the effects of video games on ADHD symptoms of attention deficit in children; (4) were randomized controlled trials (RCTs); (5) were published in peer-journals. Studies were excluded if they met the following criteria: (1) included participants with other types of disabilities or failed to provide data specific to children with ADHD; (2) did not involve video games in terventions; (3) were observational in nature (e.g., cross-sectional, case- control, or cohort); (4) were review articles, case/government reports, conference papers, book chapters, or policy documents. 2.3. Study selection The literature was examined to ensure consistency with the research questions and to meet sufficient methodological quality standards. The included studies were assessed for risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool. Two authors (PM and ZX) independently assessed the included studies, and any inconsistencies were resolved by involving the third (KY) and fourth (PZ) authors. Intraclass correlation coefficients were used to measure consistency. 2.4. Data extraction Data were identified, examined, and mined by two independent authors (PM and ZX), after which both authors received systematic training and developed a data extraction form. Variables collected included authors, country, year of publication, design, age of sample, sample size, gender distribution of the sample, mean, standard devia tion, and measures. The primary outcome was the effectiveness of the video game intervention on attention in children with ADHD. 2.5. Risk of bias assessment Adoption of the Cochrane quality assessment handbook (Higgins et al., 2011). Risk of bias assessment of the literature was used to identify random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete data, selective reporting and other biases. The process was completed independently by two authors, and upon completion was reviewed by two researchers, with a third reviewer consulted in case of disagreement. 2.6. Data analysis and synthesis The study was conducted using RevMan 5.3.5 software and Stata 17.0 software for data analysis, and continuous outcomes were expressed as standardized mean difference (SMD) with 95 % confidence interval (CI). Heterogeneity was tested by p values and I2. Heterogeneity was considered low enough for meta-analysis using a fixed-effects model if p > 0.10 and I2〈50 %. If p < 0.10 and I2〉50 %, heterogeneity was high, and a random effects model was used. Sensitivity analyses were per formed for individual studies using a case-by-case exclusion method. If heterogeneity was excessive (I2 > 85 %), meta-regression analysis was performed. The included studies were tested for bias using funnel plots and Egger’s test. 3. Results 3.1. Search results The search and screening process is shown in Fig. 1. A total of 1983 studies were retrieved from the database. After excluding duplicates, 929 studies remained. A total of 366 articles were excluded for not being RCTs, 33 articles were excluded due to missing data, and 532 articles were excluded because the subjects did not match. Additionally, 28 articles were drawn from the references, of which 11 articles were excluded for non-empirical literature, 5 articles were excluded due to missing data, and 9 articles were excluded because the subjects did not match. In the end, a total of 10 articles were included in the review and all were included in the meta-analysis. 3.2. Characteristics of the included studies A total of 10 studies were included in this meta-analysis (Benzing and Schmidt, 2019; Dovis et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2023; Kollins et al., 2020; Lim et al., 2012, 2019, 2023; Medina et al., 2021; Qian et al., 2018), including 820 children with ADHD. The publication years of these studies ranged from 2012 to 2023, and the age range of the subjects was 6–12 years. The basic characteristics, experimental results, experimental design, and measurement methods of the included RCTs are shown in Table 1. P. Ma et al. Psychiatry Research 356 (2026) 116884 2

3.3. Risk of bias Six of the included studies described the method of randomized allocation, while the remaining studies referred to "randomization" without providing specific details. Five studies concealed the allocation scheme, while the others could have described it in detail. Four studies employed blinding, with the rest lacking specific descriptions of blinding procedures. Four studies reported outcome data comprehensively; two had missing data, and the others needed to provide detailed information. All ten studies reported primary and secondary outcomes, as illustrated in Figs. 2 and 3. Fig. 1. Flow diagram of the literature search. 3.4. Results of meta-analysis A meta-analysis was conducted on the included studies, and the re sults are illustrated in Fig. 4-A. The test for heterogeneity among the included studies yielded X2=9.97, P = 0.35, and I2=10 %, indicating low heterogeneity. The combined effect size of the standardized mean dif ference (SMD) was −0.19, with a confidence interval (95 % CI) ranging from −0.34 to −0.03. The test for the combined effect size showed Z = 2.40, p = 0.02. The analysis results indicated homogeneity among the included studies (X2 = 9.97, P = 0.35, I2 = 10 %). Therefore, a fixed-effects model was used to determine the combined effect sizes. The combined effect size for the standardized mean difference was −0.18, with confidence interval (95 % CI) ranging from −0.31 to −0.04 (Fig. 4-B) These results suggest that video game interventions effectively improve attention in children with ADHD. 3.5. Bias test The funnel plot of this study, shown in Fig. 5, appears to be sym metrical, indicating minimal bias. The Egger test was used to assess bias in the included articles quantitatively, and the p-value of the Egger test was 0.13, which was greater than 0.05, indicating no publication bias in this study. 4. Discussion Results suggest that videogame interventions can provide a statisti cally significant but not clinically meaningful improvement in the attention of children with ADHD. These findings validate previous studies and provide a reference for using video games to enhance attention in children with ADHD. In the study, a human-computer interaction motor game was designed, and an 8-week intervention was conducted three times a week for 30 min per session (Benzing and Schmidt, 2019). The mean differ ence between the baseline and endpoint data of the experimental and control groups was 91.11 and 80.34, respectively, demonstrating an improvement in attention in children with ADHD. Similarly, In addition, there are also study used a motion-based video game, the mean differ ences between the baseline and endpoint data of the experimental and control groups were 5.6 and 4.1, respectively, showing the effectiveness of the video game intervention (Dovis et al., 2015). In the study, an 8-week experiment using the ACTIVAT video game was conducted. The mean difference between the baseline and endpoint data for the experimental and control groups was 2.85 and 0.76, respectively, indicating a positive effect of the video game intervention (Bikic et al., 2018). Conversely, in the study, the AKL-T01 video game was used in a 4-week, 5-day-a-week experiment. The results showed that the video game did not significantly improve attention in children with ADHD (Kollins et al., 2020). This suggests that the duration of the intervention may affect the improvement in attention, which could be explored in future studies. Additionally, analyzing the intervention designs used in the studies included in the meta-analysis revealed that video games combined with exercise had a more significant improvement in attention for children with ADHD compared to video game-only interventions. Previous studies have shown that physical activity alone can improve attention in children with ADHD (Kang et al., 2011). Therefore, combining video games with exercise may yield a more substantial improvement in attention for children with ADHD. In this study, the effect size of video game intervention was 0.19, which was lower than that of stimulant drug intervention (0.5 - 0.8) and non-stimulant drug intervention (0.6 - 0.9) (Catal ́a-L ́opez et al., 2017). This indicates that video game intervention may not be a first-line intervention method, but it can be used as a complementary approach to drug intervention. Additionally, improvements in the video game intervention approach may be beneficial for enhancing the intervention effect and increasing the effect size. Furthermore, while video game interventions have been associated with negative effects such as game addiction, exercise can bidirection ally modulate dopamine and its receptors. This neurotransmitter is associated with pleasure and reward mechanisms and has a significant impact on game addiction intervention (Ma and Liang, 2022). Fig. 2. Risk of bias graph. Fig. 3. Risk of bias summary. P. Ma et al. Psychiatry Research 356 (2026) 116884 4

Therefore, future studies on video game interventions for children with ADHD should consider incorporating exercise to enhance the effective ness of the intervention and mitigate the negative effects of game addiction. Even though this study suggests the benefits of videogame in terventions, certain limitations of this report should be kept in mind. The authenticity and reliability of the results of this meta-analysis may be affected by several factors: (1) The studies included in this meta-analysis were published only in Chinese and English, which introduces a lan guage bias. (2) Few studies specifically described the concealment of random assignment and blinding of subjects, researchers, and outcome assessors. (3) The lack of large-sample, multicenter, and long-term RCTs may affect the reliability of this meta-analysis. 5. Conclusion Although the improvement from these interventions is statistically significant, it has not yet reached the level of clinical treatment efficacy, suggesting that video game interventions may only produce therapeutic effects when used in conjunction with other evidence-based therapies. This systematic review and meta-analysis provide supporting evidence for the feasibility of future video game intervention programs and sug gest that future studies should focus on the intervention intensity, type, and optimal dose when combined with physical exercise. metadata_title: Non-suicidal self-injury in individuals with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A systematic review and Meta-analysis with Age- and Sex-stratified findings
pages: Review article Non-suicidal self-injury in individuals with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A systematic review and Meta-analysis with Age- and Sex-stratified findings Liliane Smaniotto , Arthur Tolentino * , Felipe M.R. Barros , Eduardo Barreto , Barbara Colnaghi , Lais Ker , Eloisa Helena Rubello Valler Celeri , Osmar Della-Torre , Renata C.S. Azevedo Department of Psychiatry, Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP), Campinas, Brazil A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Non-suicidal self-injury Gender differences Meta-analysis A B S T R A C T Background: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is a significant mental health concern that often co-occurs with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Although growing evidence suggests a link between ADHD and NSSI, the prevalence and moderating factors of this association remain unclear. Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to quantify the prevalence of NSSI in individuals with ADHD and to examine age- and sex-stratified differences across studies conducted in clinical, community, convenience, and population-based samples. A comprehensive search was performed across MEDLINE, EMBASE, and PsycINFO. Fourteen studies met inclusion criteria. Pooled prevalence estimates and odds ratios (ORs) were calculated using random-effects models. Subgroup analyses were performed by age group (adolescents vs. adults) and sex. Results: The overall pooled prevalence of NSSI among individuals with ADHD was 27% (95% CI: 19%–37%), with similar rates among adolescents (28%) and adults (25%). Compared to individuals without ADHD, those with ADHD had twice the odds of engaging in NSSI (OR = 2.26, 95% CI: 1.69–3.00). Sex-stratified analysis, based on three eligible studies, suggested a higher risk in females with ADHD compared to males with ADHD (OR = 4.07, 95% CI: 3.09–5.36). High heterogeneity was observed across studies, potentially attributable to differences in diagnostic criteria, assessment tools, sample characteristics, and sociocultural contexts. Conclusions: Individuals with ADHD show elevated rates of NSSI across developmental stages, with preliminary evidence indicating a potentially greater risk among females. However, these sex-specific findings should be interpreted cautiously due to the limited number of studies. Future research should investigate underlying mechanisms and longitudinal trajectories to better inform targeted interventions and prevention strategies. PROSPERO: CRD420251017948. 1. Introduction Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a childhood- onset neurodevelopmental disorder that frequently persists into adolescence and adulthood. It is clinically characterized by core symp toms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity (Drechsler et al., 2020). Globally, the prevalence of ADHD among children and adoles cents is estimated to range between 5 % and 7 %, with a higher diag nostic rate in males (Thomas et al., 2015). Beyond these core symptoms, individuals with ADHD often exhibit difficulties in emotional regulation, impaired executive functioning, and high rates of psychiatric comor bidities, such as mood disorders, conduct disorders, and substance use disorders (Gnanavel et al., 2019). These factors contribute to significant impairments in quality of life, academic performance, and social re lationships (Danckaerts et al., 2010; French et al., 2024). Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) is defined as any deliberate act of self- inflicted bodily harm without the explicit intention to die (Cipriano et al., 2017). This behavior is particularly prevalent during adolescence, * Corresponding author at: Department of Psychiatry, Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP), 80 Vital Brasil Street, University City, Campinas, S ̃ao Paulo 13083-888, Brazil. with reported rates ranging from 13 % to 20 % across various pop ulations (Farkas et al., 2024; Muehlenkamp et al., 2012). Common methods of NSSI include superficial cutting, scratching, burning, or ingestion of non-lethal substances (Klonsky et al., 2014). In the litera ture, this phenomenon is also referred to using a range of terminologies, such as self-injurious behavior, deliberate self-harm, and non-fatal self-injury. Adolescents who experience emotional dysregulation, impulsivity, or psychiatric comorbidities such as depression are at increased risk of engaging in NSSI (Andover and Morris, 2014; Niu et al., 2024). Given the overlap between the clinical features of ADHD and the risk factors associated with NSSI, a potential association between these conditions has been proposed (Allely, 2014). Although several studies have reported an association between ADHD and self-injurious behaviors, particularly among adolescents with clinical or subthreshold symptoms, the evidence remains scattered and inconclusive (Austgulen et al., 2024; Bal ́azs et al., 2018; Mulraney et al., 2021; Ojala et al., 2022). Many investigations are based on clinical or convenience samples, which may limit the generalizability of their findings. Moreover, there is a lack of comprehensive, quantitative syn thesis regarding the frequency of NSSI in individuals with ADHD across developmental stages and by sex. This gap hinders the development of targeted prevention and intervention strategies. To address these limi tations, the present study aims to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to estimate the pooled frequency of NSSI among in dividuals with ADHD, across studies conducted in clinical, community, convenience, and population-based samples; and to examine potential moderating factors, including age and sex, where data are available. 2. Methods We conducted a systematic review with meta-analysis, following the guidelines set by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) (Page et al., 2021). 2.1. Eligibility criteria Studies were considered for inclusion if they assessed patients with an ADHD diagnosis and reported the frequency of NSSI. ADHD had to be identified through DSM- or ICD-based diagnostic criteria, structured or semi-structured clinical interviews, clinician-confirmed diagnoses, or validated rating scales applying established clinical cutoffs. NSSI was defined as any deliberate act of self-inflicted bodily harm without the explicit intention to die. Examples of NSSI included superficial cutting, scratching, burning, among others. We included cross-sectional studies, cohort studies, and secondary analyses of randomized controlled trials when they reported the proportion or frequency of NSSI among in dividuals with ADHD. Case reports, posters, and review articles were excluded, as were studies that did not clearly distinguish between NSSI and suicidal intentionality. 2.2. Search strategy We conducted a systematic search of three electronic data bases—MEDLINE, EMBASE, and PsycINFO—for articles published up to March 2025. Only studies published in English were considered for in clusion. The search strategy combined two main clusters of terms: one related to attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (e.g., “attention deficit hyperactivity disorder”, “ADHD”) and the other encompassing non-suicidal self-injury and its related constructs. To ensure compre hensive retrieval, the NSSI cluster included a range of synonymous and closely related terms such as “non-suicidal self-injury”, “self-injurious behavior”, “self-harm”, “deliberate self-harm”, and “non-fatal self- injury”. For example, the search strategy used in MEDLINE can be found in the supplementary material. Additionally, the reference lists of the included articles were manually reviewed to identify any additional relevant studies. 2.3. Study selection Three reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts of the retrieved articles. Full-text articles were reviewed when the eligi bility criteria were unclear. Following this, each article selected in the screening phase was independently assessed in full by three reviewers for inclusion in the narrative analysis. In both phases, any disagreements were resolved through discussion. For inclusion in the quantitative analysis, studies were selected by consensus among the three reviewers. 2.4. Data extraction Data from each selected article were independently extracted by three reviewers using a standardized spreadsheet developed by the au thors. Any discrepancies in the extracted data were reviewed by the reviewers, and disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus. 2.5. Statistical analysis We conducted random-effects meta-analyses to estimate the pooled frequency of non-suicidal self-injury among individuals with ADHD and the corresponding 95 % confidence intervals (CI). A random-effects framework was selected a priori because substantial clinical and meth odological heterogeneity was expected across studies, including differ ences in sampling frames (clinical, community, and population-based samples), diagnostic criteria for ADHD, assessment tools for NSSI, age composition, and sociocultural context. Under this model, true effect sizes are assumed to vary between studies, and both within-study and between-study variance are incorporated into the pooled estimates, allowing for more conservative and generalizable inferences compared to fixed-effect approaches (Barili et al., 2018). For studies that included a comparison group without ADHD, we performed separate random-effects meta-analyses to estimate the odds of NSSI in individuals with ADHD relative to non-ADHD participants. To further explore potential sources of heterogeneity, we conducted pre defined subgroup meta-analyses stratified by age group (adolescents versus adults) and by sex within the ADHD population, following established recommendations for subgroup analyses in meta-analytic research (Borenstein and Higgins, 2013; Choi and Kang, 2025). Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran’s Q test, with a significance threshold of P < 0.10, and quantified using the I2 statistic, which describes the proportion of total variability attributable to between-study heterogeneity rather than sampling error. Potential publication bias and small-study effects were evaluated only for meta- analytic models including more than ten studies, in accordance with methodological guidelines. These assessments involved visual inspec tion of funnel plot asymmetry and formal testing using Egger’s regres sion intercept (Page et al., 2021). All analyses were conducted using R statistical software. 3. Results A total of 1514 articles were identified using our search strategy across the three databases. After removing duplicates, 1280 titles and abstracts were screened. At this stage, the primary reasons for exclusion were inappropriate outcomes, study populations, and study designs (e. g., case reports, case series, reviews, and guidelines). Following this process, 99 articles were selected for full-text review, of which 14 were included in the systematic review and meta-analysis. The study selection flowchart, along with reasons for exclusion, is presented in Fig. 1. Most of the included studies had a cross-sectional design (8 studies), while 5 were longitudinal in nature and 1 study was a secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial. Sample sizes varied widely, ranging from 74 to 10,957 participants, and included both adolescent and adult populations. The mean age ranged from 10 to 44.8 years, and the L. Smaniotto et al. proportion of female participants varied substantially, from 11.8 % to 100 %. ADHD diagnosis was established through structured clinical in terviews, validated self-report measures, or formal diagnostic criteria. NSSI was assessed using standardized instruments, clinical rating scales, or specific self-report questions regarding self-injurious behavior, with recall periods ranging from lifetime history to the past 12 months. The methodological characteristics of the included studies are summarized in Table 1. 3.1. Frequency of NSSI in adolescents with ADHD Hurtig et al. (2012), using the Northern Finland Birth Cohort, found that adolescents with ADHD (n = 104) had significantly higher rates of NSSI (69 %) than controls (31 %, n = 169), based on K-SADS-PL) item “non-suicidal physical self-damaging acts,” which captures behaviors such as cutting or burning without suicidal intent (Hurtig et al., 2012). Similarly, Kılıç et al. (2017), applying the SIBQ in Turkish adolescents, reported that 30 % of those with ADHD (n = 30) engaged in NSSI and 6.7 % attempted suicide, with higher trauma and dissociation scores than controls (Kılıç et al., 2017). Bal ́azs et al. (2018) examined 202 psychiatric inpatients in Hungary and showed that among those with ADHD (n = 52), 67.3 % engaged in NSSI. The association was statistically accounted for by co-occurring conditions, including affective disorder, suicidality, psychosis, and alcohol abuse in girls (Bal ́azs et al., 2018). In line with these findings, Gamli and Tahiroglu (2018) studied 82 treatment-naïve ADHD adoles cents and reported baseline NSSI frequency of 58.5 % (mean onset age 11.4). Adolescents with NSSI showed higher impulsivity scores, and those receiving methylphenidate exhibited scores in a more favorable direction compared with those not receiving medication, although impulsivity levels remained elevated (Gamli and Tahiroglu, 2018). Population-based studies also confirmed increased risk, including the Northern Finland Birth Cohort reported by Hurtig et al. (2012), as well as studies by Austgulen et al. (2024); Kazda et al. (2022), and Mulraney et al. (2021). Mulraney et al. Frequency of NSSI in adults with ADHD Hinshaw et al. (2012) followed 140 girls with childhood ADHD and 88 controls over 10 years, finding significantly higher self-injury rates in early adulthood (50.6 % in ADHD-C vs. 19.0 % in controls). Risk was particularly elevated in the combined subtype and persisted after adjustment for comorbidities, IQ, and socioeconomic factors (Hinshaw et al., 2012). Extending to male populations, Kimbrel et al. (2017) studied 140 Iraq/Afghanistan-era veterans and reported that ADHD remained strongly associated with NSSI (AOR = 3.51, p = 0.031) even after adjusting for PTSD, depression, and demographic variables, with alcohol use disorder as the only other significant factor (Kimbrel et al., 2017). Further evidence in adults highlights the role of impulsivity and comorbidities. Olsson et al. (2022), in a six-month follow-up of 804 adults, found that those with ADHD were more likely to engage in impulsive self-harm, particularly linked to emotional dysregulation and relationship difficulties, though lethality did not differ from controls (Olsson et al., 2022). Smari et al. (2023), focusing on women with cardiometabolic conditions, showed that co-occurring ADHD was asso ciated with markedly higher rates of depression (PR = 2.38), bipolar disorder (PR = 4.81), and PTSD (PR = 2.78), as well as increased risk of self-harm (PR = 1.47) and suicide attempts (PR = 2.37) (Smari et al., 2023). Finally, Di Salvo et al. (2024) assessed suicidality in ADHD adults using the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS). Lifetime frequency was high in this adult sample (mean age of approximately 30 years), with 59.5 % reporting suicidal ideation, 16.2 % severe ideation, 9.5 % suicidal behavior, and 10.8 % engaging in NSSI, underscoring the chronic vulnerability to self-injury across the lifespan [28]. 3.3. The pooled frequency of NSSI was estimated at 27 % (95 % CI: 19 %–37 %, I2 = 95 %) (Fig. 2). The funnel plot suggested visual asymmetry, and Egger’s regression was statistically significant (p = 0.02), indicating potential publication bias or small-study effects (Fig. 3). Nine studies, comprising approximately 28,600 participants, allowed for comparisons between individuals with ADHD and control groups. The meta-analysis revealed that patients with ADHD exhibited a higher frequency of NSSI compared to controls (pooled OR = 2.26, 95 % CI: 1.69–3.00, I2 = 80 %). In subgroup analyses, five studies allowed for this comparison in adolescent populations, yielding a pooled OR of 2.40 (95 % CI: 1.64–3.53, I2 = 74 %), while four studies focused on adult populations, with a pooled OR of 2.08 (95 % CI: 1.26–3.43, I2 = 69 %) (Fig. 4). 3.4. Sex Across the reviewed studies, sex was examined as a potential factor in the association between ADHD and self-injurious outcomes. Kılıç et al. (2017) identified female sex as a significant predictor of suicide at tempts, but not of non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) (Kılıç et al., 2017). Bal ́azs et al. (2018) reported higher rates of NSSI among girls with ADHD, with 71.4 % of those presenting both conditions being female (Bal ́azs et al., 2018). Austgulen et al. also found that female adolescents in the ADHD group were more likely to engage in self-harm, particularly those with severe inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms, as well as higher levels of depressive symptoms (Austgulen et al., 2024). In contrast, Lin et al. (2024) observed higher rates of suicidal thought s/attempts and self-harm among boys with ADHD, with no increased risk identified among girls with the condition (Lin et al., 2024). A meta-analysis was conducted using data from three studies that reported NSSI frequency by sex in adolescents with ADHD. The pooled OR was 4.07 [95 % CI: 3.09–5.36], indicating higher odds of NSSI among girls compared to boys within the ADHD population. Heteroge neity was low (I2 = 0 %, τ2 = 0.00, p = 0.5), indicating consistency in effect estimates across the included studies (Fig. 5). 4. Discussion In this study, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to explore the frequency of NSSI among individuals with ADHD. Across fourteen studies including adolescents and adults, approximately 27 % of individuals with ADHD reported a history of NSSI, notably higher than the 18–22 % typically found in the general population (Lim et al., 2019; Swannell et al., 2014). Moreover, in a comparative analysis comprising over approximately 28,600 participants, individuals with ADHD demonstrated roughly twice the odds of engaging in NSSI compared to those without the disorder (pooled OR = 2.10, 95 % CI: 1.65–2.67). These findings suggest a meaningful association between ADHD and self-injurious behaviors and highlight the importance of systematically evaluating NSSI risk in clinical settings when working with this population. The heterogeneity observed across the included studies was sub stantial, particularly in the pooled frequency estimates (I2 > 90 %). This variability likely reflects a combination of methodological and contex tual differences among the studies. Variations in the diagnostic pro cedures for ADHD were evident, with some studies relying on structured clinical interviews (such as the K-SADS-PL or DISC-IV), others using self- Fig. 2. report instruments like the ASRS. Similarly, assessments of NSSI differed considerably, encompassing both validated instruments (e.g., DSHI, ISAS) and less standardized measures such as single-item self-reports or clinical interviews with differing recall periods. Cultural and contextual factors may also have played a role, given that the studies were con ducted in a wide range of sociogeographic settings, potentially influ encing how self-injurious behaviors are reported, perceived, and interpreted. Additionally, differences in sample character istics—particularly between clinical populations and community-based cohorts—could have contributed to the variability, as clinical samples often include individuals with greater symptom severity, higher rates of comorbidity, and more pronounced functional impairment. Further more, although funnel plot inspection and Egger’s regression suggested asymmetry, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to the limited number of studies and the high degree of heterogeneity, which may produce apparent asymmetry independent of publication bias or small-study effects. The association between ADHD and NSSI likely reflects a complex clinical scenario shaped by multiple interacting psychopathological mechanisms. Rather than a direct or singular pathway, several under lying factors may contribute to the increased vulnerability to self-injury observed in individuals with ADHD. Impulsivity and emotional dysre gulation, both core features commonly associated with ADHD, have been consistently implicated as proximal risk factors for NSSI (Cassels et al., 2022; Wolff et al., 2019). These traits may impair an individual's ability to tolerate distress, leading to maladaptive coping strategies such as self-injury. Additionally, interpersonal difficulties, including peer rejection, social isolation, and family conflict, are frequently reported in youth with ADHD (Sodano et al., 2021) and may further heighten emotional distress and contribute to NSSI as a form of affect regulation or social signaling (Muehlenkamp et al., 2013). Academic under achievement and school failure, often experienced by individuals with ADHD, can erode self-efficacy and fuel a sense of hopelessness (Polderman et al., 2010). Finally, low self-esteem and negative selfconcept—which may develop over time through repeated experiences of failure and criticism—have been identified as important psychological vulnerabilities associated with both ADHD and NSSI (Forrester et al., 2017; Mazzone et al., 2013). These converging pathways underscore the need for a multidimensional and developmentally informed under standing of risk in this population. An additional and particularly novel finding emerging from this re view is the association between Cognitive Disengagement Syndrome (CDS) and NSSI among adolescents with ADHD (Ergül and Ers ̈oz Alan, 2024). CDS, characterized by symptoms such as mental fogginess, day dreaming, and slowed cognition, represents a non-traditional atten tional profile that is partially distinct from the classical inattention symptoms captured in standard ADHD criteria (Becker et al., 2023). The observed link between CDS and self-injurious behavior suggests that attentional disengagement and cognitive hypoactivity may constitute an underrecognized pathway to emotional dysregulation and maladaptive coping strategies, including NSSI. However, recent evidence from a community-based sample of early adolescents found that CDS was not independently associated with NSSI after adjusting for ADHD symptom severity (Thornton et al., 2025), suggesting that the contribution of CDS to self-injury may not extend beyond its overlap with core ADHD symptoms. Taken together, these divergent findings highlight that the role of CDS in self-injury remains uncertain and may vary according to population characteristics, measurement methods, or co-occurring psy chopathology, reinforcing the need for further research to clarify whether CDS represents an independent risk factor or reflects broader attentional and emotional vulnerabilities within ADHD. Psychiatric comorbidities appear to play a crucial moderating role in the relationship between ADHD and NSSI.
