For executive functions, all intensity subgroups showed sta tistically significant beneficial effects, including LPA (SMD = 0.46, 95% CI: 0.17 to 0.75), MPA (SMD = 0.58, 95% CI: 0.47 to 0.68), MVPA (SMD = 0.50, 95% CI: 0.40 to 0.59), and VPA (SMD = 0.54, 95% CI: 0.18 to 0.89). The subgroup difference by intensity was not statistically signif icant (P = 0.630). 3.4.4. Exercise session duration For session duration, both shorter and longer sessions were associ ated with significant improvements in ADHD core symptoms (<60 min: SMD = 0.36, 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.60; ≥60 min: SMD = 0.41, 95% CI: 0.15 to 0.68), with no significant subgroup difference (P = 0.777). For ex ecutive functions, significant effects were observed for both session durations (<60 min: SMD = 0.58, 95% CI: 0.52 to 0.65; ≥60 min: SMD = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.50 to 0.94). The subgroup difference was not statisti cally significant (P = 0.327). 3.4.5. Exercise type Regarding exercise type, both aerobic exercise and cognitively engaging exercise showed significant beneficial effects on ADHD core symptoms. Cognitively engaging exercise showed a numerically larger effect (SMD = 0.65, 95% CI: 0.39 to 0.92) than aerobic exercise (SMD = 0.48, 95% CI: 0.11 to 0.84), but the subgroup difference was not sta tistically significant (P = 0.499). For executive functions, cognitively engaging exercise showed a significantly larger effect (SMD = 0.64, 95% CI: 0.56 to 0.72) than aerobic exercise (SMD = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.25 to 0.42), with a significant subgroup difference (P < 0.001). 3.4.6. Exercise length For total intervention length, significant effects on ADHD core symptoms were observed for both shorter and longer interventions (<12 weeks: SMD = 0.32, 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.52; ≥12 weeks: SMD = 0.40, 95% CI: 0.10 to 0.71). The subgroup difference by intervention length was not statistically significant (P = 0.484). For executive functions, signif icant effects were also observed for both intervention lengths (<12 weeks: SMD = 0.58, 95% CI: 0.48 to 0.63; ≥12 weeks: SMD = 0.60, 95% CI: 0.48 to 0.71), with no significant subgroup difference (P = 0.573). 3.5. Fig. 5 provided a visual summary of the direction and magnitude of pooled effects together with the corresponding certainty ratings, whereas Supplementary Material S7 presented the detailed GRADE evidence profile, including the num ber of included meta-analyses, pooled effect estimates, heterogeneity, initial certainty ratings, downgrading reasons, and final certainty ratings Fig. 5. for each outcome. ADHD core symptoms and executive functions were rated as low-certainty evidence. Although both outcomes showed sta tistically significant beneficial effects, the certainty was downgraded mainly because the pooled analyses included mixed-design meta-ana lyses and showed moderate heterogeneity. Mental health and motor skills were also rated as low certainty, largely due to variability in outcome constructs, measurement approaches, and the underlying evi dence base. Evidence for social problems was rated as low certainty because, although the pooled effect was statistically significant and heterogeneity was low, the evidence was based on only three meta- analyses. Evidence for sleep quality, BMI, and academic achievement was rated as very low certainty, primarily because these outcomes were supported by only one or two meta-analyses, had wide confidence in tervals crossing the null, or showed substantial heterogeneity where applicable. Overall, the findings suggest potential benefits of physical exercise interventions for several ADHD-related and functional out comes, but the certainty of evidence remains limited and should be interpreted cautiously. 4. Discussion This umbrella review synthesized evidence from 45 meta-analyses on physical exercise interventions for children and adolescents with ADHD. The findings suggest that structured physical exercise may improve ADHD core symptoms and executive functions, and may also benefit selected broader functional outcomes, including mental health, motor skills, and social problems. In contrast, no statistically significant effects were found for sleep quality, academic achievement, or BMI. Based on the GRADE assessment, however, the certainty of evidence was low for ADHD core symptoms, executive functions, mental health, motor skills, and social problems, and very low for sleep quality, BMI, and academic achievement. Thus, the present findings should be interpreted as sup portive but not definitive evidence for the adjunctive role of exercise in ADHD management. The observed benefits for ADHD core symptoms and executive functions are biologically and clinically plausible. ADHD is character ized not only by behavioral symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, but also by deficits in executive control, including inhibi tory control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory. Structured ex ercise may influence these domains through several pathways, including increased arousal regulation, enhanced catecholaminergic activity, improved cerebral blood flow, and neurotrophic processes relevant to prefrontal and fronto-striatal functioning (Benzing and Schmidt, 2017; Herold et al., 2018; Fang et al., 2024; Peng et al., 2024). These mech anisms may partly explain why exercise interventions were associated with improvements in both symptom-level and cognitive outcomes. Nevertheless, the low certainty of evidence indicates that these effects should be interpreted with caution, particularly given the heterogeneity in intervention protocols, participant characteristics, and outcome measures across the included reviews. A closer examination of the effects on specific executive function subdomains reveals a nuanced pattern. The largest pooled effect sizes were observed for cognitive flexibility and inhibitory control, followed by a small effect on working memory. This hierarchy of responsiveness may reflect the distinct neuroanatomical substrates and cognitive de mands engaging by different exercise modalities (Zhu et al., 2023). Cognitively engaging exercise, which showed superior efficacy overall, inherently require rapid task-switching, adaptive rule application, and response inhibition, which processes directly taxing cognitive flexibility and inhibitory control. These activities may preferentially enhance prefrontal cortex (PFC) connectivity and dopamine neurotransmission in associated circuits (e.g., dorsolateral and inferior frontal cortices). The relatively smaller effect on working memory aligns with some prior hypotheses that its neural underpinnings (e.g., dorsolateral PFC and parietal networks) might require more specific or prolonged interven tion to manifest change measurable at the behavioral level (Song et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2023). Furthermore, methodological heterogeneity in working memory assessment (e.g., simple vs. complex span tasks) across primary studies could have contributed to a more attenuated pooled estimate. The subgroup findings should be interpreted as exploratory, but they provide useful clues regarding intervention design. For ADHD core symptoms, no statistically significant subgroup differences were observed across age, exercise frequency, intensity, session duration, exercise type, or intervention length, suggesting that current evidence is not sufficient to identify a clearly superior exercise parameter for symptom reduction. For executive functions, however, significant sub group differences were found for exercise frequency and exercise type. Interventions delivered at least three sessions per week showed larger effects than less frequent interventions, which aligns with principles of neuroplasticity, indicating that regular stimulation may be necessary to induce and maintain neural adaptations (Li et al., 2025; Christiansen et al., 2019). Cognitively engaging exercise also showed larger effects than aerobic exercise, suggesting that concurrent cognitive-motor de mands may be particularly relevant for executive function improve ment. However, because these subgroup analyses were based on aggregate data from included meta-analyses, these findings should not be interpreted as definitive exercise prescriptions. The findings for broader functional outcomes were more mixed. Improvements in mental health may be related to both biological and psychosocial mechanisms, including stress regulation, increased self- efficacy, better emotional regulation, and enhanced social participa tion (Wong et al., 2026). Improvements in motor skills are also plausible, because repeated physical practice directly targets coordination, bal ance, and movement control, while improved attention and executive control may further support motor learning (Bi et al., 2023). The observed benefit for social problems may reflect the structured and interactive nature of many exercise programs, particularly those involving group activities, rules, cooperation, and peer engagement. These findings suggest that exercise may have effects extending beyond core ADHD symptoms, but the low certainty of evidence means that these broader benefits remain provisional. In contrast, the absence of statistically significant effects on sleep quality, academic achievement, and BMI may reflect a mismatch between general exercise interventions and the mechanisms required to change these outcomes. Sleep is influ enced by multiple factors, including bedtime routines, circadian rhythm, medication use, family environment, and comorbid emotional symp toms. Academic achievement depends not only on attention and exec utive function, but also on curriculum exposure, learning support, school context, and long-term educational engagement. BMI is affected by diet, total energy expenditure, growth stage, metabolic factors, and intervention duration. Therefore, exercise programs designed primarily to improve ADHD symptoms or cognitive functioning may not be suf ficiently targeted or intensive to produce measurable changes in these domains. Moreover, sleep quality and academic achievement were each supported by only one meta-analysis, and BMI by only two meta-analyses, which further limits confidence in these findings. These results should therefore be interpreted as insufficient evidence rather than evidence that exercise has no effect on these outcomes. Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the influence of comorbidity could not be fully examined. Although reviews involving comorbid neurological disorders were excluded when ADHD-specific data were unavailable, information on psychiatric, developmental, or behavioral comorbidities was not consistently reported. Given the high comorbidity burden in ADHD, this may have affected intervention re sponses. Second, the age criterion of ≤21 years may have introduced developmental heterogeneity. Although this cutoff was adopted to include late-adolescent populations and to remain consistent with several included meta-analyses, participants aged 18–21 years may differ from younger children and adolescents in symptom profiles, neurodevelopmental stage, exercise capacity, and responsiveness to exercise interventions. More refined developmental subgroup analyses F. Zhu et al. Psychiatry Research 364 (2026) 117267 14

were not feasible because individual participant data were unavailable and age categories were inconsistently reported across reviews. Third, substantial variability existed in exercise protocols and outcome mea sures, including exercise type, intensity, frequency, duration, setting, and assessment tools, which may have contributed to heterogeneity and reduced comparability across reviews. Fourth, the evidence base for several secondary outcomes was limited. Sleep quality and academic achievement were each based on only one meta-analysis, and BMI was based on two meta-analyses; none of these pooled effects reached sta tistical significance. In addition, subgroup analyses were not conducted for secondary outcomes because the number of available meta-analyses was small and intervention characteristics were not consistently re ported across reviews, which would have resulted in unstable and potentially misleading subgroup estimates. Finally, although primary study overlap was assessed using the corrected covered area and was considered moderate, overlap may still have influenced the precision and interpretation of pooled estimates. These limitations should be considered when applying the findings to clinical practice or public health recommendations. 5. Conclusion Structured physical exercise may be considered a promising adjunctive component of multimodal ADHD management for children and adolescents, particularly for improving core symptoms and execu tive functions. Subgroup findings suggest that cognitively engaging ex ercise and interventions delivered at least three times per week may be especially relevant for executive function improvement. However, ex ercise should not be viewed as a replacement for established pharma cological, behavioral, educational, or psychosocial interventions. Given the low to very low certainty of evidence across outcomes, exercise- based interventions should be implemented with appropriate clinical judgment and tailored to individual needs. Further high-quality studies with standardized protocols, clearly defined exercise prescriptions, and longer follow-up are needed to clarify the optimal intervention charac teristics and long-term benefits for this population. metadata_title: Intellectual achievement and cognitive functioning in children and adolescents with ADHD-affected siblings: A systematic literature review and meta-analysis
pages: Intellectual achievement and cognitive functioning in children and adolescents with ADHD-affected siblings: A systematic literature review and meta-analysis Ari Alex Ramos a,b,*, Vinícius Boaventura c, Alanis Aparecida Nascimento d, Luana Lopes Rocha Leite d, Liana Machado a a University of Otago, Department of Psychology, William James Building 275 Leith Walk, Dunedin, New Zealand, 9016 b Universidade Federal de S ̃ao Carlos, Department of Gerontology, Rodovia Washington Luis, km 235, S ̃ao Carlos (SP), Brazil, 13.565-905 c Universidade Federal de S ̃ao Paulo, Department of Psychiatry, Rua Marjor Maragliano, 241 - Vila Mariana, S ̃ao Paulo (SP), Brazil, 04.017-030 d Pontifícia Universidade Cat ́olica do Paran ́a, Department of Psychology, Rua Imaculada Conceiç ̃ao, 1155 - Prado Velho, Curitiba (PR), Brazil, 80.215-901 A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Cognition Cognitive dysfunction Risk factors Neuropsychological tests Family members A B S T R A C T Background: Emerging literature suggests that neurocognitive traits commonly observed in children and ado lescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are present, albeit to a lesser degree, in their non- ADHD siblings. This meta-analytic review aimed to quantitatively summarize intellectual and cognitive per formance differences between children and adolescents without ADHD and both their ADHD-diagnosed siblings and unrelated peers without ADHD. Methods: We implemented strategic search algorithms in four indexing databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and ProQuest) to retrieve potentially eligible reports published up to 5th June 2025. Meta- analyses were conducted using three-level hierarchical models to account for the dependency among effect sizes derived from the same study. Between-group differences in intellectual and cognitive scores were quantified using standardized mean differences (SMD). Moreover, we assessed the robustness of the findings by testing for potential small-study effects. Results: Based on 404 unique effect sizes derived from 32 studies, involving a total of 8873 participants, the current results demonstrate that the overall cognitive-intellectual performance of siblings surpasses their ADHD- affected siblings (SMD = 0.30, 95 % CI [0.23, 0.38]), but falls short of unrelated peers (SMD = −0.28, 95 % CI [−0.35, −0.21]). This suggests that non-ADHD siblings exhibit an intermediate neurocognitive profile between their ADHD-affected siblings and peers without ADHD. Notably, we observed this pattern of results consistently across the major cognitive categories examined (intellectual functioning, attention and perceptual-temporal processing, memory, and executive functions). Importantly, no evidence of small-study effects was found. Conclusion: The current findings provide robust support for cognitive-intellectual vulnerabilities in siblings of ADHD-diagnosed children and adolescents, possibly accounted for by genetic inheritance, shared environmental influences, and gene-environment interactions. 1. Introduction Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a childhood- onset neuropsychiatric condition characterized by non-adaptative (developmentally age-inappropriate) levels of inattention, impulsivity, and/or hyperactivity, often accompanied by neuropsychological (e.g., difficulty sustaining attention when managing and completing school work) and social (e.g., tendency to interact in a manner that does not lead to peer acceptance) difficulties (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Based on over three decades of family studies, the heritability of ADHD has been estimated at 74 % (Faraone & Larsson, 2019), and a previous systematic review documented that the prevalence of ADHD among siblings of children and adolescents affected by the condition ranges from 26 % to just over 45 % (Hidalgo-L ́opez et al., 2019). This is in line with past research suggesting that siblings of children and ado lescents with ADHD are at a ninefold increased risk of developing ADHD * Corresponding author at: Department of Gerontology, Rodovia Washington Luis, km 235, S ̃ao Carlos (SP), CEP: 13.565-905. compared to control siblings (Chen et al., 2008). From a genetic standpoint, biological siblings of probands with ADHD share on average 50 % of their genetic information, and hence non-proband siblings are vulnerable to ADHD-related neurobiological characteristics, including the developmental structure of genetic risk factors that contribute to ADHD-related cognitive difficulties. This is particularly relevant in light of accumulating evidence indicating that ADHD-diagnosed children and adolescents exhibit inferior test performance relevant to a number of important cognitive processes such as working memory (Ramos et al., 2020), time perception (Marx et al., 2022), and response inhibition (Lipszyc & Schachar, 2010), in addition to higher chances of academic underachievement (Loe & Feldman, 2007). Collectively, these findings provide strong motivation to profile cognitive and intellectual perfor mance in siblings without ADHD to determine any difficulties. The literature on cognition in siblings of ADHD-affected children and adolescents has gained increasing attention in recent decades but has yielded inconclusive findings. While some studies suggest that non- ADHD siblings perform similarly to peers without ADHD on most neu ropsychological measures (Durston et al., 2004; Fan et al., 2018; Goos et al., 2009), a growing body of evidence indicates that siblings of ADHD-diagnosed children and adolescents share neurocognitive vul nerabilities (Kuntsi et al., 2010), including significant difficulties in neuropsychological measures designed to assess cognitive inhibition, working memory, and intellectual functioning (Albrecht et al., 2010; Bidwell et al., 2007; Doyle et al., 2005; Nikolas & Nigg, 2015; Rom melse, Altink, Oosterlaan, Buschgens, et al., 2008). These mixed findings may be attributed to differences in study designs, including variations in the cognitive-intellectual measures employed across studies. Another factor that may be driving these inconsistencies relates to how siblings are deemed to not have ADHD. In scientific literature, substantial vari ability exists across studies in how this classification is operationalized, and in many cases, the extent of behavioral characteristics below the diagnostic threshold (i.e., subthreshold ADHD traits) is not clearly re ported, thereby preventing analysis. Throughout this meta-analytic synthesis, therefore, “unaffected siblings” and “non-ADHD siblings” refer to child or adolescent biological siblings who did not meet full diagnostic criteria for ADHD. Importantly, an evidence-based understanding of the intellectual and cognitive profile of siblings of ADHD-diagnosed children and adoles cents holds critical implications for both research and clinical practice. By aggregating data across studies, a meta-analytic approach helps clarify whether non-ADHD siblings exhibit an intermediate neuro cognitive profile between ADHD probands and unrelated peers without ADHD, as suggested by some previous research (e.g., Faraone et al., 1993; Gau & Shang, 2010; Leon et al., 2024; Rommelse, Altink, Oos terlaan, Buschgens, et al., 2008). Furthermore, as individual studies often report inconsistent findings due to variations in design, sampling, statistical power and measurement tools (Button et al., 2013; Harris & Smith, 2009; Ramos et al., 2020), the meta-analytic approach offers a robust strategy to (at least partially) address such inconsistencies by examining whether pre-specified moderators (e.g., age, sex, cognitive domain) contribute to the heterogeneity of the pooled effect sizes. The outcomes have stronger potential to inform more clearly on intellectual- cognitive performance differences in siblings without ADHD, thus providing invaluable information relevant to early identification of at- risk family members (e.g., by informing early cognitive screening pro tocols) and for guiding support services and educational programs for caregivers and stakeholders. Considering all mentioned above, this quantitative review aimed to meta-analyze intellectual and cognitive performance differences in the following groups of children and adolescents: (a) unaffected vs. ADHD- diagnosed siblings; and (b) non-ADHD siblings vs. unrelated controls without ADHD. In addition, we explored potential moderators that may play critical roles in between-group performance differences by means of subgroup and meta-regression analyses. Note that we initially also intended to investigate the neurocognitive profile of unaffected offspring of ADHD-affected individuals, but no study meeting the eligibility criteria was found. 2. Methods 2.1. Guideline and data availability The present research synthesis was reported in accordance with the 2020 Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta- Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Page et al., 2021). In the spirit of Open Science, statistical coding and spreadsheets containing the collected data are available at the Open Science Framework (https://osf. io/sjwf3/). Although this systematic review was not pre-registered, and hence no protocol is available, all procedures (e.g., search strate gies, eligibility criteria, and analytic methods) were conducted accord ing to established meta-analytic standards, were fully reported to support reproducibility, and investigated a priori research questions that were theoretically grounded in the literature. 2.2. Eligibility criteria Randomized controlled trials and cross-sectional, cohort, and case- control studies published in English, Spanish, or Portuguese were eligible for inclusion. In addition, studies had to meet the following criteria. First, the diagnosis of participants with ADHD had to be based on established diagnostic criteria according to the Diagnostic and Sta tistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM). Second, consistent with a previous ADHD meta-analysis (Vertessen et al., 2022), we considered only studies reporting on at least one intellectual or cognitive outcome for children and adolescents aged ≥5 and ≤18. Third, studies had to report the statistics needed to calculate standardized effect sizes (e.g., sample size, mean and standard deviation). In cases where a study provided only variance-based effect sizes (e.g., partial eta-squared, Cohen’s f) for between-group differences, we converted these statistics to standardized mean differences (SMD) before quantitatively summa rizing results. Fourth, all meta-analyzable outcomes had to be derived from objective neurocognitive testing, either using validated measure ment tools for cognition and/or academic achievement (e.g. Digit Span, Peabody Individual Achievement Test [PIAT]), or in cases of non- standard measures, the study had to detail the test design and the methodology followed in administering the test (or cite the relevant reference containing these details); if not, the measure was excluded from the meta-analyses. Studies relying solely on questionnaires or rating scale data (e.g., parent or teacher reports) were not considered in the quantitative syntheses. Moreover, we excluded publications based on the following additional criteria: duplicated literature, single case studies, conference proceedings and abstracts, and qualitative or theo retical research. 2.3. Information sources and search strategy The systematic literature search was initially carried out on 13th December 2022, in four indexing databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection, PsycINFO, and ProQuest), without applying date restrictions. Subsequently, we updated this literature search on 30th June 2024 and further on 5th June 2025 using the same search terms. In addition, the reference lists of articles deemed relevant were cross- checked for further eligible studies. In the Supplementary Online Con tent, the Appendix details the search algorithms (strategic syntax) for each database. The search string for cognitive outcomes implemented in all databases stemmed from a comprehensive umbrella review (Pievsky & McGrath, 2018) that provided an extensive list of cognitive measures commonly administered in ADHD research. 2.4. Selection process EndNote 20 (Thomson Reuters) software managed citations and removed duplicate reports. Unique references were uploaded to the online platform Ryyan (www.rayyan.ai) for title/abstract and full-text screening. The third and fourth authors independently screened the retrieved reports for eligibility; in cases of disagreement at the level of title/abstract screening, a consensus was reached after discussion with the first author. The first and second authors assessed the full-texts and determined the final study eligibility. 2.5. Data collection process Based on a pre-defined Microsoft Excel template, we extracted the following information from each included study: the country where the study took place, first author, year of publication, study design (e.g., cross-sectional or cohort), demographic data (percentage of boys, and sample mean age and range), and the meta-analyzable statistics from each included outcome measure (e.g., sample size, mean and standard deviation, t or F test results). For children and adolescents with ADHD, we further collected information on methylphenidate pharmacology (coded as naïve, else medicated or not medicated during the cognitive testing), ADHD presentation (combined, predominantly inattentive, or predominantly hyperactive/impulsive), and diagnosis criteria (i.e., edition of DSM). For longitudinal studies with follow-up assessments, only baseline test scores were extracted. Importantly, the first author collected data from the included reports, and the second author cross- screened for inconsistencies and double-checked all extracted data to ensure accuracy. 2.6. Population, intervention/exposure, comparator, and outcome The population of interest consisted of ADHD-unaffected children and adolescents with a child or adolescent sibling diagnosed with ADHD. For the purposes of this quantitative synthesis, any intervention or exposure involving cognitive testing that met the inclusion criteria was considered eligible. As previously noted in the Introduction, we were interested in two comparisons: (a) unaffected vs. ADHD-affected siblings (Meta-Analysis I); and (b) ADHD-unaffected siblings vs. unre lated peers without ADHD (Meta-Analysis II). The measured outcomes of interest were the average scores on intellectual and/or cognitive tests for each of the compared groups. 2.7. Sample overlap In the present quantitative review, we carefully analyzed test scores that came from the same study population. In cases of two or more publications with overlapping sample, we included the test scores from the study with the largest sample size (given the same intellectual/ cognitive test) and test scores from unique intellectual/cognitive tests. This approach allowed us to meta-analyze a single effect size for each test from the included studies. To achieve this, we initially grouped studies with sampling overlap into three subgroups. The first subgroup comprised 27 potentially eligible studies that utilized data from the International Multi-Center ADHD Genetics Project (IMAGE), a research initiative conducted in seven European countries (Belgium, Germany, Netherlands, Ireland, Spain, Switzerland, and United Kingdom) and Israel between 2003 and 2006. In addition, we identified two studies from the NeuroIMAGE project (2009–2012), a follow-up cohort study that collected cognitive test scores from participants at the Dutch site of the IMAGE project. From this subgroup, 10 studies (Albrecht et al., 2008; Banaschewski et al., 2012; Bitsakou et al., 2009; Christiansen & Oades, 2010; Himpel et al., 2009; Jiang et al., 2020; Oades & Chris tiansen, 2008; van der Stigchel et al., 2007; van Lieshout et al., 2019; Wood et al., 2011) were retained in the quantitative analyses. The sec ond subgroup consisted of nine overlapping sample studies conducted at the National Taiwan University Hospital. Following our analysis, five studies (Fan et al., 2018; Faraone et al., 1993; Gau & Huang, 2014; Gau & Shang, 2010; Hwang-Gu & Gau, 2015) from this subgroup were included in the current meta-analyses. The third subgroup encompassed three studies (Slaats-Willemse et al., 2003; Slaats-Willemse et al., 2005; Slaats-Willemse et al., 2007) conducted by Slaats-Willemse et al., and all were retained since they employed different neuropsychological mea sures (albeit involving the same participants). 2.8. Cognitive domain The full list of tests and subtests considered is provided in Table 1. To organize the wide range of intellectual and neuropsychological out comes included in this quantitative review, we employed different ap proaches to classify each test outcome according to a primary neuropsychological domain (e.g., verbal memory, cognitive flexibility) – here referred to as cognitive subdomains. For Performance IQ and Verbal IQ Indexes, both derived from previous editions of the Wechsler Intel ligence Scale for Children (WISC), we followed the classification sum marized in the Encyclopedia of Clinical Neuropsychology (2011). For well-known and widely used tests (e.g., Wisconsin Card-Sorting Test), we followed Strauss et al. (2006). For the cognitive measures that comprise the Cambridge Automated Neuropsychological Test Battery (CANTAB), we employed the classification available on the CANTAB website (https://cambridgecognition.com/digital-cognitive-assess ments/). In cases of non-standard measures from studies that met the inclusion criteria, we relied on detailed test descriptions or referenced publications to determine an appropriate classification. This framework yielded 12 cognitive subdomains (see Table 1). The subdomains were used to structure the subgroup analyses and the presentation of results. Although low statistical power in subgroup analyses is a common drawback in meta-analyses, there is no rule of thumb to determine how many studies should be considered in such analyses (Cuijpers et al., 2021; Jackson & Turner, 2017; Myles et al., 2021). To minimize the risk of power-related bias in interpreting results from subgroup analyses, in the present meta-analytic review we grouped the 12 subdomains into four major cognitive domains as follows: 1) The Intellectual Functioning domain includes tests and subtests designed to measure global intelligence (e.g., Full-Scale IQ and estimated IQ from the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children [WISC]), scholastic achievement (e.g., Wide Range Achievement Test), Performance IQ (e.g., Block Design and Object Assembly from the WISC), and Verbal IQ (e.g., Arithmetic and Similarities from the WISC). 2) The Attention and Perceptual-Temporal Processing domain comprises (sub)tests relevant to the assessment of attention and psychomotor speed (e.g., Part A of the Trail Making Test, Continuous Performance Test) and perceptual-temporal processing (e.g., Motor Timing Task, Time Reproduction Task). 3) The Memory domain was derived from only four studies (Gau & Shang, 2010; Luca et al., 2007; Nikolas & Nigg, 2015; Shang & Gau, 2011) that provided scores on measures designed to assess verbal memory (e.g., Digit Span Forwards) and visuospatial memory (e.g., Delayed Matching to Sample from CANTAB), and hence the sum mary effect size from this major cognitive domain should be inter preted with caution. The limited number of studies and the availability of data precluded a more detailed classification into specific subdomains (e.g., short-term memory, episodic memory). 4) The Executive Function domain is an umbrella category that encom passes a range of tasks purported to assess the constructs of cognitive flexibility (e.g., Wisconsin Card Sorting Test), cognitive inhibition (e. g., Go/No-Go Task, Stop-Signal Task), working memory (e.g., Digit Span Backwards), and planning (indexed only by the Stockings of Cambridge from CANTAB). Note that the systematic review identified two studies (Bidwell et al., 2007; Wood et al., 2011) that assessed delay aversion, a construct used in the ADHD literature to characterize motivational style (Fern ́andez- Martín et al., 2025; Sonuga-Barke, 2002, 2003). Effect size direction Note that we carefully aligned the direction of the average scores before conducting the statistical analyses because the direction (inter pretation) of treatment effects differs across various neuropsychological measures. For instance, scores on the Trail Making Test reflect the time spent to complete the test, with higher scores indicating poorer perfor mance. In contrast, scores on Digit Span Backward reflect the number of items correctly recalled, with higher scores indicating better perfor mance. To aid interpretability of the current results, we computed effect sizes such that positive values reflect better cognitive performance. 2.10. Risk of quality-related bias in individual studies We employed the checklists for analytical cross-sectional, case-con trol, and cohort studies from the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Tools (Moola et al., 2020) to rate the risk of quality-related bias in the individual studies included. Note that no randomized controlled trial met the inclusion criteria. Following best practice criteria related to research design, methodology, and statistical analyses, the JBI templates allow studies to be categorized into levels of quality based on the allotted response for each question (yes, no, unclear, or not applicable [NA]). Consistent with a recent meta-analysis with a design analogous to the current study (Ramos et al., 2022), we used the following cut-off values to rate study quality: ≤49 % yes responses, high risk of bias; 50–69 % yes responses, moderate risk of bias; ≥70 % yes responses, low risk of bias. Note that the second author graded the quality of each study, and the first author cross-checked for in consistencies. Since all but one of the studies met the criteria for low risk of bias (indicating high quality), we did not conduct subgroup analyses including study quality as a moderator variable. 2.11. Age differences In the Supplementary Online Content, eTable 2 shows a detailed study characterization based on the age of the included samples in each group. In both the ADHD and control groups, the sample mean age ranged from 6 to 18 years, whereas in the unaffected sibling group the sample mean age ranged from 5 to 18 years. Note that we initially planned to classify participants in each group as either children (5 ≤ sample mean age ≤12) or adolescents (13 ≤sample mean age ≤18) to determine potential effect size differences between these two age cate gories in subgroup analyses. However, only two studies (Bitsakou et al., 2009; Halperin & Gittelman, 1982) provided sufficient data to catego rize the included participants as either children or adolescents. Hence, we did not perform subgroup analyses by age category and instead included the sample mean age as a continuous predictor covariate in meta-regression analyses. 2.12. Statistical analyses and synthesis methods We performed all the statistical analyses in R (R Core Team, 2022) with R Studio (RStudio Team, 2022). To control for the within-study dependency of effect sizes (correlated outcomes), the metafor package fitted an overall three-level meta-analysis and three-level subgroup and meta-regression analyses for each comparison group, using restricted maximum likelihood estimation and random-effects modeling with the rma.mv function. To improve the robustness of our inference and ac count for potential model misspecification, we applied cluster-robust variance estimation (CRVE) in all fitted meta-analytic models (Hedges et al., 2010). Based on the formula devised by Hedges (Hedges, 1981), the escalc function of the metafor package computed standardized mean differences (SMDs) correspondent to the Hedges’ g effect size – an un biased variance estimator for meta-analyses including small-sized sam ples (N ≤20). Moreover, we plotted the standardized residuals from the three-level meta-analyses to identify influential data points (outliers) that can distort the effect size precision. Residuals < −1.96 or > 1.96 were deemed influential outliers, given that we would expect that 95 % of the residual values would fall within this range under a standard normal distribution (Kutner et al., 2004). All R scripts are available online at https://osf.io/sjwf3/. To characterize the extent of variation in effect sizes, we calculated two indexes of heterogeneity not accounted for by sampling error: τ2, an estimation of absolute effect size dispersion, and I2, an estimation of the average percentage of variation in effect sizes. Given the implementa tion of multilevel analyses, we reported on two levels of random-error- free heterogeneity: τ2 2 and I2 2 for the within-study/cluster variance (level 2) and τ2 3 and I2 3 for the between-study/cluster variance (level 3). In the current quantitative review, I2 statistics of 25 %, 50 %, and 75 % were interpreted as suggesting low, moderate, and substantial levels of het erogeneity, respectively (Higgins & Thompson, 2002). Subgroup ana lyses investigated the influence of the four major cognitive domain category clusters (intellectual functioning, attention and perceptual- temporal processing, memory, and executive functions) on the effect size variance, and the Wald-type test assessed potential statistically significant differences in effect sizes across the major cognitive domain categories. Similarly, univariate meta-regression analyses examined whether numerical demographic data (sample mean age and percentage of boys) and year of publication moderate between-group performance differences. In meta-regression analyses, we applied listwise deletion to handle missing data. 2.13. Small-study effects In the meta-analytic literature, small-study effects are a type of publication bias and reflect the tendency for small-sized studies to es timate different (typically larger) treatment effects than studies with larger samples (Schwarzer et al., 2015). To address this issue, in the current quantitative review we first visually inspected the graphical presentation of the data in funnel plots. In the absence of small-study effects, data points (the SMD of each study) are expected to be roughly symmetrically distributed in upside-down funnel plots. To sta tistically ascertain the risk of small-study effects, we applied a well- known graph-based method of funnel plot asymmetry (Egger’s regres sion test) and a selection model method (the three-parameter selection model [3PSM]) (Coburn & Vevea, 2019; Vevea & Hedges, 1995). The 3PSM assumes that studies are not randomly selected and allows esti mation of the impact of potential missing studies. Note that we imple mented the weight-function model in R using its default two-tailed significance threshold of p = .05 to distinguish between significant and non-significant effects. It is important to mention that both Egger’s regression test and the 3PSM assume independent effect sizes and do not account for the complex hierarchical structure of the data. To partially mitigate this limitation, we applied these tests to study-level pooled effect sizes. The number of effect sizes per study ranged from 1 to 24 (median = 6) in both Meta-Analysis I and II, as most studies reported multiple intellec tual or cognitive outcomes. To calculate study-specific pooled estimates, we first performed a three-level subgroup analysis by study ID (i.e., within clusters of correlated effects at the study level) and then we applied CRVE, as detailed in the R code available at https://osf. io/sjwf3/. This approach yielded a single summary effect size per study, preserved the hierarchical structure of the data, and informed the construction of both forest and funnel plots. 3. Results 3.1. Study selection Fig. 1 illustrates the major steps of the systematic review. The liter ature search in online databases, in addition to the citation searching, identified 3668 publications, of which only 32 studies met the eligibility criteria for inclusion in the quantitative syntheses. Importantly, eTable 3 (Supplementary Online Content) lists the specific reasons for excluding 176 studies initially deemed eligible during the screening phase. 3.2. Study characteristics Table 2 summarizes the relevant characteristics of each included study. Three studies included participants from two or more European countries, and the remaining 29 studies were conducted within a single country: Netherlands (n = 8), Germany (n = 5), Taiwan (n = 5), United States (n = 5), Canada (n = 2), Brazil (n = 1), England (n = 1), India (n = 1) and Israel (n = 1). siblings with the combined presentation, and the remaining studies either reported intermixing different ADHD presentations (n = 10) or did not specify this information (n = 12). Twenty-two studies reported that the ADHD-affected siblings were in the off phase of their stimulant medication during the cognitive assessment, whereas 10 studies did not provide this information. The distribution of DSM versions used for ADHD diagnosis was as follows: DSM-5 (n = 1), DSM-IV (n = 29), DSM- III-R (n = 1), and DSM-II (n = 1). Except for two cases (Halperin & Gittelman, 1982; Oades et al., 2010), in which the applied diagnostic criteria for non-ADHD siblings could not be precisely determined, the included studies used scales based on the same DSM edition to rule out ADHD in unaffected siblings. Overall, we computed 404 unique effect sizes from the 32 studies included, with a total of 8873 participants. 3.3. Quality-related risk of bias in studies As shown in Table 2, critical appraisal of the included studies revealed three types of study designs: cross-sectional (n = 30), pro spective case-control (n = 1), and prospective cohort (n = 1). In the Supplementary Online Content, eTables 4, 5, and 6 detail the outcomes for the assessment of risk of quality-related bias in individual studies. Overall, only one study (Halperin & Gittelman, 1982) showed moderate risk of bias (moderate quality), whereas the other 31 studies met the criteria for low risk of bias (high quality). 3.4. Meta-Analysis I: Unaffected vs. ADHD-affected siblings The forest plot in Fig. 2 displays the pooled SMDs for each included study and highlights the relevant outcomes for the meta-analysis that synthesized data from non-ADHD children and adolescents compared to their ADHD-affected siblings. In total, we computed 216 unique effect sizes from 31 studies, and the final meta-analysis sample consisted of 2400 non-ADHD siblings and 4007 ADHD-affected siblings. The overall pooled SMD (0.30, 95 % CI [0.23, 0.38], p < .001) indicates that non- ADHD siblings achieved average cognitive performance corresponding to 0.30 standard deviations above that of their siblings with ADHD. Low- to-moderate heterogeneity was observed at both level 2 (τ2 2 = 0.0232, I2 2 = 38.03) and level 3 (τ2 3 = 0.0219, I2 3 = 35.90). These I2 values suggest that the within-study variance (level 2) was slightly higher than the between-study heterogeneity (level 3). Although we observed an outlying residual, a sensitivity analysis demonstrated that removing this outlier from the meta-analysis yielded a nearly identical SMD (0.29, 95 % CI [0.23, 0.36], p < .001) and had little impact on the effect size variance (level 2: τ2 2 = 0.0221, I2 2 = 39.38; level 3: τ2 3 = 0.0182, I2 3 = 32.45). Thus, we retained all effect sizes. Table 3 provides the results of subgroup analyses for the outcomes of the two group comparisons we studied (unaffected vs. ADHD-affected siblings, and unaffected siblings vs. unrelated controls), specifying the cognitive subdomains falling under each of the four major cognitive domains we studied. For unaffected vs. ADHD-affected siblings, the pooled SMDs showed that children and adolescents without ADHD outperformed their ADHD-affected siblings in all four major cognitive domains we examined: intellectual functioning (0.29, 95 % CI [0.14, 0.44], p = .001), attention and perceptual-temporal processing (0.31, 95 % CI [0.19, 0.43], p < .001), memory (0.21, 95 % CI [0.04, 0.38], p = .034), and executive functions (0.32, 95 % CI [0.21, 0.43], p < .001). Group differences in all cases showed small-to-medium effect sizes. The Wald-type test (QM[3] = 1.56, p = .668) indicated that there was not enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis of equal effect sizes across the four major cognitive domains analyzed. For the pooled SMDs in Table 3, within-cluster (τ2 2 = 0.0234, I2 2 = 37.21) and between-cluster (τ2 3 = 0.0235, I2 3 = 37.46) variance indicated low-to-moderate levels of heterogeneity. In the Supplementary Online Content, eTable 7 displays the out comes of the univariate meta-regression analyses. For unaffected vs. ADHD-affected siblings, the sample mean age (β = −0.038, 95 % CI [−0.105, 0.029], p = .220), the percentage of boys (β = −0.000, 95 % CI [−0.007, 0.006], p = .805) and the year of publication (β = −0.010, 95 % CI [−0.023, −0.002], p = .080) did not moderate the effect size heterogeneity. 3.5. Meta-Analysis II: unaffected siblings vs. unrelated controls The forest plot in Fig. 3 summarizes the relevant data on perfor mance differences between non-ADHD siblings and unrelated controls, in addition to displaying the pooled SMD for each study included in the meta-analysis. In total, we computed 188 unique effect sizes from 27 studies, and the final meta-analysis sample involved 2094 siblings without ADHD and 2466 unrelated controls. The overall pooled SMD (−0.28, 95 % CI [−0.35, −0.21], p < .001) revealed that the cognitive performance of siblings without ADHD falls 0.28 standard deviations below the average of the control group. The amount of within-study heterogeneity (level 2: τ2 2 = 0.0395, I2 2 = 56.97) was nearly four times greater than the estimated between-study heterogeneity (level 3: τ2 3 = 0.0117, I2 3 = 16.95), meaning that over half of the total variation was attributable to within-study heterogeneity. In the sensitivity analysis, the removal of an outlying residual did not significantly reduce the within-study (τ2 2 = 0.0327, I2 2 = 49.79) or between-study (τ2 3 = 0.0150, I2 3 = 22.80) heterogeneity and yielded a similar SMD (−0.27, 95 % CI [−0.34, −0.20], p < .001). Consequently, the outlying residual was retained in the meta-analysis. Regarding subgroup analyses summarizing data of unaffected sib lings vs. unrelated controls by major cognitive domain categories (Table 3), the pooled SMDs demonstrate that siblings without ADHD exhibited significantly inferior performance relative to the comparison group in all four major cognitive domain categories under study: intel lectual functioning (−0.34, 95 % CI [−0.50, −0.18], p = .002), attention and perceptual-temporal processing (−0.26, 95 % CI [−0.35, −0.16], p < .001), memory (−0.24, 95 % CI [−0.37, −0.10], p = .021), and ex ecutive functions (−0.28, 95 % CI [−0.38, −0.18], p = .001). Together, these effects suggest that siblings without ADHD tend to present with small-to-moderate difficulties in cognition compared to controls. The Wald-type test (QM[3] = 1.66, p = .647) indicated that the difficulties did not appear to differ by major cognitive domain category, resulting in not rejecting the null hypothesis of equal between-cluster effect sizes. The computed within-cluster (τ2 2 = 0.0387, I2 2 = 54.01) and between- cluster (τ2 3 = 0.0149; I2 3 = 20.82) variance indicates that 54 % of the effect size variation was accounted by level-2 heterogeneity. In addition, the robustness to small-study effects was statisti cally confirmed for both unaffected vs. ADHD-affected siblings (Egger’s regression test: z = −0.01, p = .989; 3PSM: χ2 [1] = 0.09, p = .769) and unaffected siblings vs. controls (Egger’s regression test: z = −0.03, p = .972; 3PSM: χ2 [1] = 0.08, p = .779). 4. Discussion To the best of our knowledge, the present quantitative synthesis is the first attempt at summarizing statistical data on intellectual and cognitive performance differences among children and adolescents without ADHD, their ADHD-affected siblings, and unrelated controls without ADHD. The current findings demonstrated that the neuro cognitive profile of siblings without ADHD fell between that of their ADHD-affected siblings and the comparison control group. More pre cisely, siblings without ADHD consistently outperformed their ADHD- affected siblings but achieved significantly lower intellectual and cognitive scores compared to unrelated controls, with just under one- third of a standard deviation differentiating the groups overall. We did not find statistically significant differences among the pooled effect sizes estimated for the major cognitive domain categories (intellectual functioning, attention and perceptual-temporal processing, memory, and executive functions), which each showed significant performance differences between siblings without ADHD and both ADHD-affected siblings and controls. Regarding the lack of significant differences between the major cognitive domain categories, it is important to keep in mind that mul tiple neurocognitive processes are involved in effective performance of complex neuropsychological tasks, and this is especially true for tests designed to assess intelligence and academic achievement (Peng & Kievit, 2020). An inspection of the (sub)tests included in the intellectual functioning category (Table 1) reveals that these measures involve a variety of cognitive processes that can potentially account for the het erogeneity of intellectual performance among unaffected siblings, as noted in the Introduction. For example, the versions of the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC) were designed to assess multiple neuropsychological outcomes, not just overall IQ. Of note, while the Vocabulary and Comprehension subtests from WISC depend heavily upon verbal reasoning and memory, the Block Design and Object As sembly subtests demand visuospatial processing and motor planning. Similarly, performance on scholastic achievement tests engage complex cognitive abilities, including semantic memory, executive functions, temporal information processing, and mathematical reasoning. In this quantitative review, inclusion of tests that tap multiple cognitive func tions, combined with some rather broad major cognitive domain cate gories, may have led to intermixing of performance strengths and performance weaknesses, thereby preventing dissociation and thus identification of particular cognitive difficulties. The intermediate level of intellectual and cognitive performance observed in siblings without ADHD, relative to their siblings with ADHD and unrelated controls, may relate to findings from neurofunctional and neurostructural imaging studies. For instance, a prior neurofunctional analysis revealed that, relative to controls without ADHD, children without ADHD with a positive family history of ADHD showed significantly reduced frontal activation during working memory processing (n-back task) (Li, Motwani, et al., 2023). In addition, siblings of ADHD-affected adolescents and young adults have been reported to have gray matter volumes intermediate between those of their affected siblings and con trols without ADHD, particularly in brain regions relevant to cognition (Bralten et al., 2016). Although conducted with adult samples, another study found that ADHD-affected individuals and their first-degree rela tives without ADHD exhibit shared neurostructural distinctions (Pironti et al., 2014). Relatedly, siblings without ADHD showed lower region- specific and total cortical surface volumes relative to controls without ADHD (Hoogman et al., 2019). Taken together, it may be that the cognitive difficulties in siblings without ADHD across multiple neuro psychological domains as reported here are underpinned by neuro functional and neurostructural imaging distinctions associated with familial ADHD. Importantly, in the literature on ADHD in children and adolescents, several of the brain areas showing distinctions have been implicated in the performance of neuropsychological measures designed to assess response inhibition (Barber et al., 2015; Booth et al., 2005; Huey-Ling et al., 2022) – an executive process for which difficulties are considered a core neuropsychological feature underlying ADHD (Barkley, 1997). In their comprehensive and insightful review of the neuropsycho logical functioning of ADHD, Johnston and Chronis-Tuscano (2015) highlighted that the factors behind the reduced intellectual performance often observed in children with ADHD, compared to peers without ADHD, remain largely unexplained. On the other hand, twin studies suggest that poorer intellectual performance in ADHD, as indexed by lower IQ scores, seems largely driven by genetic influences (Kuntsi et al., 2004; Rommel et al., 2015). In relation to these previous considerations, findings from the current quantitative review add to the literature on intellectual functioning in ADHD by providing compelling evidence that siblings without ADHD are also more likely to achieve lower intellec tual/academic scores compared to unrelated controls, albeit not to the Fig. 3. Other factors that may be relevant to the findings discussed here pertain to the higher likelihood of families with ADHD sharing dysfunctional environments and experiencing more unstable house holds. For instance, an increasing number of studies have shown that children and adolescents with ADHD, and consequently their siblings, present with higher chances of having parents suffering from psycho pathological disturbances, including depression (especially maternal depression), anxiety, conduct problems, antisocial behavior, personality disorders, and alcohol and drug-related abuse (Biederman et al., 1995; Johnston & Chronis-Tuscano, 2015; Kashdan et al., 2004; Margari et al., 2013; Wesseldijk et al., 2018). Compounding matters, coexisting with children and adolescents with ADHD is frequently a stress-generating experience (mainly for their siblings and parents), given that ADHD- related challenges (e.g., poor adherence to rules, difficulties with delayed gratification and routines, overactivity, erratic sleep patterns, and lack of motivation) often contribute to heightened within-family interpersonal conflict that leads to increased maternal distress, sibling rivalry and disrupted parent-child relationships, in addition to marital instability that in numerous circumstances culminates in separation and divorce (Angeline & Rathnasabapathy, 2023; Johnston & Chronis- Tuscano, 2015; Kendall et al., 2005). Regarding the latter, a previous longitudinal analysis showed that parents of children with ADHD are 75 % more likely to dissolve their relationship within 10 years after the ADHD-affected child’s birth (Kvist et al., 2013), while other studies have found that early-life stressful experiences such as neglect, household chaos, and trauma from parents’ separation/divorce are associated with executive dysfunction and rele vant difficulties in attentional processing and self-regulation (Andrews et al., 2021; Claussen et al., 2024; Lengua & Sandler, 1996). Moreover, past research on maternal parenting behavior and family functioning found that children and adolescents with ADHD and their siblings re ported less perceived family support compared to unrelated peers without ADHD (Chang & Gau, 2017), which may be an important factor, given that family support has been shown to have a significant impact on academic performance (Li, Xue, et al., 2023) and also seems to be an important predictor of cognition and behavioral adjustment in child hood (Hughes et al., 2018). Adding further complexity, a less supportive home environment has been linked to higher rates of hyperactivity/ impulsivity behaviors and oppositional problems in siblings without ADHD (Mulligan et al., 2013). Combined with genetic factors, these environmental factors may contribute to cognitive difficulties in siblings without ADHD. Fig. 4. Funnel plots for small-study effects. 4.1. Strengths Notwithstanding that only studies published in English met the in clusion criteria, the comprehensive literature search we undertook considered studies published in English, Portuguese, and Spanish in order to minimize the risk of language-related bias, and thus this approach constitutes an important distinguishing feature of the present quantitative review. In addition, the current meta-analytic synthesis followed best-practice procedures to account for dependencies among effect sizes arising from studies reporting multiple outcomes. Specif ically, we implemented three-level meta-analytic models with CRVE and carefully addressed potential sample overlap to ensure the inclusion of a unique effect size for each cognitive-intellectual test outcome. This thorough methodology is important towards ensuring the robustness of the results reported here. 4.2. Limitations The present meta-analytical review comes with relevant drawbacks that must be pointed out. Regarding the search strategy, despite the multilingual approach strategy employed, we acknowledge that restricting the systematic search to studies published in English, Portu guese, and Spanish may still introduce selection bias. Relevant studies published in other languages may have been inadvertently excluded, particularly those from scientific journals not indexed in the online databases we used (PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection, PsycINFO, and ProQuest). In relation to the study design, although observational studies have enabled relevant meta-analytical conclusions in medical and health sciences (Mueller et al., 2018; Muka et al., 2020; Paul & Leeflang, 2021), the nature of these studies precludes the infer ence of causal relationships. Sample characteristics present additional limitations. First, only 10 studies clearly reported on the inclusion of ADHD siblings with the combined presentation, whereas the remaining studies either inter mixed ADHD presentations or did not provide this information. Thus, we could not investigate whether between-group effect size differences depend on the condition presentation (combined, predominantly inat tentive, or predominantly hyperactive/impulsive). Second, we were unable to conduct the planned investigation of potential effect size dif ferences between children and adolescents due to only two studies (Bitsakou et al., 2009; Halperin & Gittelman, 1982) included in the quantitative syntheses providing sufficient data to distinguish partici pants aged 5 to 12 years (children) from those aged 13 to 18 years (adolescents). Although we did not find any statistically significant as sociation through meta-regression analyses between the sample mean age of the sibling group without ADHD and the effect size variance, it may be that an age-group comparison would have had greater sensitivity to a developmental effect. Third, although the percentage of boys in meta-regression analyses did not show an association with the effect size variance, the well-known high prevalence of ADHD in boys (Arnett et al., 2015) indicates that future studies should further explore the potential influence of sex-based differences in cognition among siblings of ADHD-affected children and adolescents. Fourth, the included studies rarely reported detailed information on unaffected siblings beyond age, sex, and the statistics needed to compute effect sizes, and hence this limited reporting prevented a more nuanced psychosocial character ization of this group. Additional methodological concerns involve heterogeneity in diag nostic and classification procedures. In particular, subthreshold ADHD traits could potentially have had a significant influence on the reported group differences. To shed light on this, ideally we would have included a subgroup analysis; however, the available information was insuffi ciently documented. For instance, only seven studies (Christiansen & Oades, 2010; Hwang-Gu & Gau, 2015; Jiang et al., 2020; Nikolas & Nigg, 2015; Slaats-Willemse et al., 2003; Slaats-Willemse et al., 2005; Slaats-Willemse et al., 2007) explicitly excluded or controlled for participants with subthreshold ADHD traits, and the operational criteria (e.g., number of symptoms/traits) were inconsistent across these studies. Furthermore, three of these seven investigations originated from the same research group (Slaats-Willemse et al., 2003; Slaats-Willemse et al., 2005; Slaats-Willemse et al., 2007), limiting generalizability. Moreover, although most of the included studies employed stan dardized ADHD assessments (e.g., structured clinical interviews or validated rating scales), the specific diagnostic procedures varied considerably. Some studies applied comprehensive psychiatric evalua tions, while others relied on brief screening tools or did not report procedures in detail. Variability in participant classification procedures may have contributed to heterogeneity in the meta-analytic findings and influenced the reported between-group differences. Finally, we feel that it is important to note that although we used the term controls, consis tent with terminology used in most of the studies included in this quantitative review, terms such as neurotypical align better with rec ommendations pertaining to avoiding ableist language (French et al., 2025). One final methodological consideration concerns the exclusion criteria applied across studies. We observed considerable heterogeneity in how these criteria were operationalized for probands with ADHD, unaffected siblings, and control groups, with reporting often too sparse or inconsistent to permit systematic coding. For example, some studies reported applying stringent exclusions for controls – such as prior his tory of neurodevelopmental (e.g., autism), neurological (e.g., head trauma), psychiatric (e.g., clinically significant mood or anxiety diffi culties), and genetic conditions (e.g., fragile X syndrome, Down syn drome) – whereas others provided only a brief statement about excluding individuals with ADHD and with no behavioral problems at school. Such discrepancies could influence observed group differences. Future meta-analyses would benefit from more transparent and stan dardized reporting of exclusion criteria to enable their evaluation as a potential source of variability in effect sizes. 4.3. Implications In line with studies demonstrating that siblings of children and ad olescents with ADHD are at increased risk for psychopathological con ditions and emotional difficulties (Orm & Fjermestad, 2021; Palacios- Cruz et al., 2014; Steinhausen et al., 2012), the neuropsychological outcomes presented in the current meta-analytic review highlight that siblings without ADHD warrant greater attention in future research to better elucidate their intellectual-cognitive profile. Within a family context, the needs of a sibling without ADHD may be overlooked by parents who may allocate more attention to the child with ADHD (King et al., 2016; Steinhausen et al., 2012), and hence identifying (neuro) psychological vulnerabilities in siblings without ADHD could inform and help guide not only parents but also the development of early inter vention strategies. Early support with a family-focused approach could be offered to help mitigate unfavorable outcomes pertaining to the cognitive, academic, and social development of siblings without ADHD. 5. Conclusion Findings from this quantitative review revealed that the intellectual and cognitive profile of children and adolescents not exhibiting clini cally diagnosable behavioral characteristics of ADHD lies between that of their ADHD-diagnosed siblings and unrelated peers without ADHD. This intermediate neurocognitive profile was consistently observed across the four major cognitive domain categories we studied: intellec tual functioning, attention and perceptual-temporal processing, mem ory, and executive functions. Ongoing prospective cohort studies on siblings of ADHD-affected children and adolescents are needed to pro vide insight into the persistence of these cognitive vulnerabilities into adulthood. In addition, the development of strategies and interventions aimed at enhancing the intellectual-cognitive abilities of siblings A.A. Ramos et al. Clinical Psychology Review 123 (2026) 102688 12

metadata_title: Diagnostic stickiness and shifting relevance: Reassessing autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and/or attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) diagnoses. A qualitative interview study
pages: Diagnostic stickiness and shifting relevance: Reassessing autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and/or attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) diagnoses. A qualitative interview study Rose-Marie Lindkvist a,* , Katalin Niklasson b,c , Allan Lidstr ̈om d , Michelle Nilsson e, Sophia Eberhard f,g, Peik Gustafsson g , Sebastian Lundstr ̈om g,h, Maria Råstam c, Lena Eriksson d a Psychiatry, Department of Clinical Sciences Malm ̈o, Lund University, Lund, Sweden b Outpatient Department, Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Clinic, Region Skåne, Lund, Sweden c Department of Clinical Sciences, Faculty of Medicine, Lund University, Lund, Sweden d Department of Philosophy, Linguistics and Theory of Science, University of Gothenburg, Gothenburg, Sweden e Swedish Partnership for Mental Health, Malm ̈o, Sweden f Psychiatry, Habilitation and Aid, Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Regional Inpatient Care, Emergency Unit, Region Skåne, Malm ̈o, Sweden g Department of Clinical Sciences Lund, Division of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, Lund University, Lund, Sweden h Gillberg Neuropsychiatry Centre, Institute of Neuroscience and Physiology, Sahlgrenska Academy, University of Gothenburg, Gothenburg, Sweden A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder Autism spectrum disorder Diagnosis Overdiagnosis Medicalization Reassessment Thematic analysis A B S T R A C T The rising rate of diagnosed autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) has led to more individuals near the diagnostic threshold living with neurodevelopmental diagnoses. While often assigned in childhood to initiate support in medical, school and family contexts, these diagnoses may persist across time and settings, shaping adult life in ways that are unaligned with current functioning. This study explores the perspectives of individuals who actively sought to have ASD and/or ADHD diagnoses reassessed. Within a pilot project in Skåne, Sweden, fourteen individuals aged 17–30 years, originally diagnosed at ages 4–18, participated in semi-structured interviews. Motivations for seeking reassessment, examined using reflexive thematic analysis, clustered around four themes: having capacity, being no different, demanding fairness, and removing barriers. While some initially benefited from resources linked to diagnosis, many described how it had become restrictive—limiting career options, influencing health-care encounters, and shaping identity. Diagnoses were experienced as “sticky”: tied to childhood contexts yet continuing to circulate into adult institutions. Although not representative of all individuals with ASD/ADHD, this group constitutes a critical case, high lighting reassessment as a possible response to the temporal durability and institutional reach of psychiatric labels. The very fact that individuals request, and institutions require, a formal act of removal underscores the enduring power of such classifications as both resources and constraints. The study contributes to debates on overdiagnosis by highlighting the temporal and institutional dimensions of diagnostic expansion, and by examining how proportionality between benefits and burdens may shift over time. 1. Introduction Over the past two decades, diagnoses of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) have increased markedly in Sweden and internationally (Polanczyk et al., 2007; Lundstr ̈om et al., 2015; Arvidsson et al., 2018; Rydell et al., 2018; Hansen et al., 2021; Jablonska et al., 2024). This expansion has been widely discussed in relation to shifting diagnostic thresholds, heightened awareness among professionals and the public, institutional incentives, and changing expectations about behaviour and This article is part of a special issue entitled: Overdiagnosis published in Social Science & Medicine. * Corresponding author. performance in school and work (Garcia-Argibay et al., 2024; Conrad and Bergey, 2014; Duvall et al., 2025). While such developments are often analysed through the lens of medicalization – describing the expansion of medical categories into new domains of life – they have increasingly also been discussed in terms of overdiagnosis. In epidemiological research, overdiagnosis is commonly defined as the identification of conditions that would not have caused symptoms or harm, or situations in which diagnostic expansion does not yield pro portional benefit to patients (Brodersen et al., 2018; Moynihan et al., 2012). This literature has been most extensively developed in relation to cancer screening and other somatic conditions. However, the concept has also informed broader debates about diagnostic expansion, lowered thresholds, and the balance between benefit and harm in mental health (van Dijk et al., 2016; Moynihan et al., 2012). In these discussions, overdiagnosis does not necessarily imply diagnostic error at the time of assessment. Rather, it draws attention to questions of proportionality and to situations in which the overall effects of diagnosis, including treatment, labelling, and institutional consequences, may be limited, ambivalent, or detrimental over time. Much of the literature on overdiagnosis has focused on diagnostic expansion at the point of classification, including changing thresholds, revised criteria, screening practices, and rising prevalence rates (Welch et al., 2011; Brodersen et al., 2018; Glasziou et al., 2020). Less attention has been directed towards what happens over time, once a diagnosis has been recorded and begins to circulate across institutional contexts. Di agnoses, particularly psychiatric ones assigned in childhood, often endure well beyond the clinical contexts in which they were first established. They travel into educational systems, welfare bureau cracies, employment sectors, and licensing authorities, acquiring new meanings and consequences along the way (Jutel, 2009, 2024). In this sense, overdiagnosis may not only concern initial classification, but also the temporal durability of diagnostic labels beyond their clinical and functional relevance. This study explores a group that makes this temporal dimension visible: young adults who actively sought reassessment of previously assigned ASD and/or ADHD diagnoses. Within a pilot project in southern Sweden, individuals who had received neurodevelopmental diagnoses in childhood requested renewed evaluation, often asking whether the diagnosis still applied – and in many cases, whether it could be formally removed. These individuals are not statistically representative of all people with ASD or ADHD. Rather, they constitute a critical case that illuminates how diagnostic categories persist, travel, and are retro spectively contested. By examining participants’ motivations for seeking reassessment, we aim to contribute to social science debates on overdiagnosis and diag nostic expansion. Instead of asking whether particular diagnoses were “correct” or “incorrect,” we analyse how individuals negotiate the continued presence of a classification that may no longer align with their current functioning, identity, or life aspirations. Their reassessment re quests make diagnostic thresholds visible as temporal and institutional boundaries, rather than as one-time clinical decisions. In doing so, we shift attention from the initial act of diagnosis to the afterlives of diag nostic categories, and to the institutional and personal work required to undo them. The marked increase in ASD and ADHD diagnoses illustrates what Conrad and Potter (2000, 2014) describe as the diffusion of medical categories, where diagnostic boundaries extend to new populations and life stages. In parallel, there is growing unease within the scientific community as well as among clinicians regarding the mismatch between observed diagnostic rates and epidemiological expectations. As diag nostic nets widen, more people whose functioning is close to the “typical” range come to live with neurodevelopmental diagnoses. This trend resonates with sociological debates on medicalization, where diagnostic categories expand to include increasing varieties of human experience, and with discussions of overdiagnosis, which draw attention to questions of proportionality and potential unintended consequences when diagnostic expansion does not clearly translate into sustained benefit (van Dijk et al., 2016; Busfield, 2017). Together, these per spectives highlight how expanding diagnostic categories reshape boundaries around what counts as “normal” or in need of care. Our study contributes by examining how such processes may later be reconsidered through renewed assessment of existing diagnoses. Cases at the edge of diagnostic thresholds are analytically important, not because they settle where the diagnostic boundary should be drawn, but because they reveal a paradox at the heart of diagnostic expansion. The same label that can unlock needed support in childhood may later operate as a barrier to full participation in adult life, raising questions about the proportionality between benefits and burdens over time, as diagnoses are taken up by institutions (e.g., education, military, police recruitment, licensing authorities, health-care triage) as sorting devices with durable consequences (Sims et al., 2021). Diagnostic categories become social resources as well as social constraints, shaping access and exclusion across time and institutional domains (Jutel, 2011, 2024). In line with Jutel's (2009, 2011, 2024) work in the sociology of diagnosis, diagnostic categories can be viewed as social as much as medical objects that organise meaning, authority, and responsibility across institutions. Diagnoses are not only clinical judgments but social classifications that carry moral weight and institutional consequences over time. Beyond institutional effects, psychiatric diagnoses also carry social and emotional consequences. As O'Connor et al. (2018) show, diagnostic labels can both undermine and enhance young people's self-concept, producing experiences of alienation and stigma but also self-understanding and belonging. These ambivalent effects show that diagnoses function not only as clinical categories but as social identities negotiated in everyday life. Our study examines individuals who, as young adults, actively re- engage with and challenge earlier diagnostic decisions, addressing a research gap on adult retrospective reflections on childhood diagnoses. We aimed to explore who seeks to have a diagnosis removed, and why. How do they describe their experiences of receiving, living with, and seeking to undo a diagnostic label? 2. Methods Between 2023 and 2025, a pilot project was conducted within child and adolescent psychiatry (CAP) in Skåne, Sweden, in collaboration between the University of Gothenburg, Lund University, and the regional healthcare provider Region Skåne. The project aimed to study the need for and structure of a routine for reassessments of ASD and ADHD. In this descriptive inductive qualitative study interviews with participants in the pilot were analysed by reflexive thematic analysis. In a constructionist approach we aimed to recognize the subjective per spectives of the study participants (Braun and Clarke, 2006, 2019). 2.1. Setting and participants Region Skåne, with a 1.4 million population, is situated in the southern part of Sweden, which in 2022 had an estimated prevalence of ASD/ADHD of about 0.8/2.6 percent among individuals aged 0-19 years (Jablonska et al., 2024). At the time of this study, the region annually received about sixty requests from residents who turned to healthcare and asked about the possibility of having ASD and/or ADHD diagnoses removed. Reassessments of ASD/ADHD were not part of standard healthcare, wherefor our project aimed to assess the need for such a routine. Individuals contacting Region Skåne's child or adult psychiatric units requesting reassessment of ASD and/or ADHD were referred to the project. Inclusion criteria were age >16, residency in Skåne, and a registered ADHD and/or ASD diagnosis. Individuals who had ADHD medication within the previous 12 months were excluded. Seventy-two were included, aged 16-57 years, whereof 80 percent were aged 16-24. Over half had a prior diagnosis of ADHD. Eleven were recommended to R.-M. Lindkvist et al.
