retain their diagnosis. An additional three were awaiting further assessment. The subsample of participants who were qualitatively interviewed, consisting of the first 14 out of the 72, were 17-30 years old, whereof ten males and four females. All except one were in employment or studying. Five had ADHD, four had ASD and five wished to reassess both diagnoses, received at 4-18 years of age by public healthcare providers. One participant had had diagnosis for less than one year, seven for five to nine years, and six for ten to fourteen years. Ten had taken diagnosis-related medication. In clinical evaluations, current and childhood symptomatology among all 72 were assessed through structured interviews, followed by case conferences involving experienced clinicians who jointly assessed whether the individuals currently and at least for the last 1-2 years still met diagnostic criteria for ASD and/or ADHD. Eleven of the 72 were recommended to retain their diagnosis and an additional three were awaiting further assessment. Out of the 14 who were qualitatively interviewed in this specific study, twelve were classified as not to meet criteria for the original diagnosis and as a result had it removed, meaning that it was noted in their medical records that they did not have the diagnosis/-es. One had their ADHD diagnosis first removed, and six months later, ASD. One participant was assessed to have a low level of functioning and significant difficulties, such that a diagnosis and continued contact with habilitation services was deemed relevant. 2.2. Data generation Interviews, performed in Swedish, were conducted June-August 2023 after participants had begun to take part in procedures related to the reassessments of their diagnoses but before reassessments were finalized. A semi-structured interview guide was used, including open- ended questions related to the reasons behind seeking reassessment, meanings of the diagnosis in the participants' lives, experiences related to diagnostic assessments and reflections about the future. A pilot interview, also included in the analysis, was performed by RL and LE together, both experienced in qualitative interviewing. The pilot resul ted in minor changes to the guide, including asking more specifically about circumstances where the diagnosis may turn up or play a role in transitions between institutions, such as the shift from elementary school to high school. The following interviews were performed by RL alone. Recruitment and interviewing continued until the material was judged to provide sufficient depth, variation, and information power in relation to the study aim. At this point, the interviews had captured recurring themes across participants' accounts while still allowing for differences in how reassessment was motivated, experienced, and anticipated. The final sample consisted of 14 interviews. Follow-up questions were asked based on participants' responses, allowing the interviewer to pursue issues of particular relevance and gain depth in each account. Follow-up questions were asked based on the participants’ responses and with the aim of following the participants to gain depth. Seven interviews took place in physical meetings at hospital premises and seven remotely, by video call. Interviews lasting 28-102 min, were audio-recorded and transcribed. 2.3. Analysis Data analysis was performed collaboratively by co-authors RL, KN, AL, and LE. The analytic process combined individual work with joint meetings, including full day analytical sessions and the sharing of notes. We allowed substantial time for reflection on the interview material, making use of our different backgrounds in social science, psychology, theory of science, and medical science. These different disciplinary backgrounds, theoretical orientations, and roles generated productive discussions, enriched our interpretations, and supported reflexivity throughout the analysis, as emerging interpretations, assumptions, and uncertainties were continuously examined among the co-authors. Initially, to become familiar with the data, we listened to recordings and read and re-read the transcripts. To generate the initial codes, we began by individually reading the first ten pages of three interviews, taking notes on preliminary thoughts and ideas, and highlighted data extracts relevant to the aim. We then discussed the highlighted excerpts and drafted a first version of the coding scheme through joint reflection. Text excerpts were coded inductively and close to participants’ own words. NVivo [QSR International Pty Ltd. (2021) NVivo, Version 14] was used to support the analysis. The preliminary coding was expanded and adjusted through analysis of the remaining interviews. Throughout this process, we continued to review interviews individually, and to meet regularly to reflect on content, coding and emerging interpretations. When all interviews had been coded, analytically significant features in relation to the aim were collected into themes and organized into clusters based on meaning. Relevant data excerpts were then collated to develop a concise and coherent account of the data across themes. 2.4. Ethical considerations Study participants were recruited by KN who also conducted the initial clinical assessments. Participation was voluntary and based on informed consent. Interviewers were not involved in the reassessment process, and the clinical team involved in assessments did not gain insight into the data until after the participants had been assessed. To ensure anonymity, data was presented without reference to age, gender, or workplace. The research protocol (reg. number 2022-06213-01) was approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority. 3. Results Our analysis rendered four main themes capturing different impor tant elements related to the participants’ rationale to seek reassessment of ASD and/or ADHD. The themes, illustrated as circles at the centre of Fig. 1, related to who the participants perceived themselves to be (being no different and having capacity) and what they aspired to achieve when asking for reassessment (demanding fairness and removing barriers). Content relating to the themes are presented in Fig. 1 to provide a brief overview of results, which are expanded upon, linked to the themes and exemplified with data excerpts in the text below. Participants gave rich descriptions of how being diagnosed affected them in the past, present, and future. Content is presented chronologi cally with descriptions of receiving the original diagnosis, its effects, followed by a presentation of the themes. Thereby, we hope to provide an easy-to-follow description of the stories, gradually building towards the participants’ rationale to seek reassessment of ASD/ADHD. 3.1. Being diagnosed: a confusing and unfair process with limited influence Participants described the original diagnosis acquired in childhood as a process without control, dominated by the adult world. The process leading to diagnosis had been initiated by parents, sometimes supported by teachers, other school personnel or social services. Participants described how adults had acted due to being alarmed about what they had perceived to be strange or irregular behavior at home, in school or elsewhere, of “something not being right” (Interview 7). Participants reported having displayed characteristics and behaviors at the time which they thought explained being diagnosed. These included having been too lively and unable to sleep, too lazy and un focused, having had difficulties with language, food or getting started or having been unable to adjust to changed circumstances, being hyper active and angry. ” I did everything to just do the opposite. (...) I was very, like, loud and disturbed.” (Interview 5) ”I was awful as a kid. I was aggressive.” (Interview 12) R.-M. Lindkvist et al. Social Science & Medicine 405 (2026) 119549 3

”I was very rowdy och (...) didn’t listen much.” (Interview 11) Participants described how they had had low motivation in school, social difficulties, constantly gotten into fights, and not having wanted or been able to interact. ” In eighth grade, when I really didn't go to school at all, I didn't have any friends to talk to at all. (...) I was at home gaming.” (Interview 2) ”I wasn’t the one who played with the others.” (Interview 14) Some participants’ views on these characteristics and behaviors were that was just who they were at the time, not like everyone else and just different, slow learners, withdrawn or lonely, and that these behaviors had been interpreted as signs of diagnosis. Participants expressed having experienced unfairness in the process of being diagnosed as their re actions to unsafe, stressful or traumatic living conditions had been misinterpreted as diagnostic symptoms, mentioning parental addiction, bullying, deaths in the family, and exposure to abuse. Participants explained that these difficulties in life had made them lose motivation and concentration. “There is so much in my personal life that has affected me at school, which has perhaps led to me receiving this diagnosis.” (Interview 7) ”He (the father) abused my mother so much that he ended up in prison when I was little. (...)I had to sit there with a tape recorder to my ear so that they could record conversations with him, because you never knew what he was capable of. So, that was very scary. (...) There was a lot happening there that made my behavior escalate.” (Interview 4) Several participants described their parents as having been persis tently driving the process towards a diagnosis, in a targeted way. They said they had felt exposed to procedures where adults around them were “fishing for faults” (Interview 14), and teaming up against them. ”Dad said: “Hey? Wanna go somewhere?”, without knowing where we were going. But just to get me out of the house. And then we went to CAP in [city]. And then I had to answer questions. (...) And then, just out of nowhere, it was: “Well, you have this diagnosis”.” (Interview 12) ”Mom said that I would get help by going to school and then a teacher tells me not to go to class, that I was going somewhere else in her car.” (Interview 13) The neuropsychiatric assessments were described by some as blurry and based on information from others. ”They diagnosed me based on what the teachers and my parents said.” (Interview 5) Participants described having felt confused about the meaning of meetings and tests and how they had willingly or with little resistance tagged along filling out papers and doing tests. ” Most of the time I was quite bored. (...) Like, I was just excited to go to the playroom.” (Interview 6) ”A really strange place where I met an even stranger person who said he was a doctor and was going to help me by giving me a math test.” (Interview 13) Participants described different levels of confidence towards those leading the assessments, where some had felt like they had been based on standard checklists. They had been handed a diagnosis, like ‘here you go’, without sensing that the procedure was focusing on them as in dividuals and without looking for alternative explanations for their be haviors. Some participants said that they found it strange and questioned if it was reasonable to, for example, diagnose a child who did not have a safe home environment. Some described being angry and upset about processes they had felt forced to go through. ”He's the one who gave me this diagnosis, he's the one I see as the biggest bad guy in this. Him and the Swedish system. (...) I remember refusing to go there and how I hated him with my whole being.” (Interview 12) Some participants described having completely trusted the pro fessionals and the procedures within psychiatry. Others described that Fig. 1. no matter what they said or did was interpreted as typical signs of diagnosis. ”I felt a bit manipulated (...) Like, I told her: “Yes, but I’m very sensitive, I get easily offended by others”. And they just said: “Yes, but that’s very common among autistic women”, and then it was like this: “Yes, but I’m outgoing and I don’t have a problem with, like, social interactions”, (...) and they just said: “Yes, but that’s also very common in autism in women”, and no matter what I said, they just said: “Yes, but that’s ... it’s not in the book, but it’s common among autistic women.” (Interview 8) Participants commented on how adults around them had motivated the need for and benefits of being diagnosed, mainly to gain access to resources in school, and to receive financial aid. ”They said that I was diagnosed with high-functioning autism, uh, mainly to be able to get help at school if I needed. (...) That it's better to write that I have it than not.” (Interview 2) ”He (the father) wanted to try to get benefits. (...) I know he got a lot of benefits from the social insurance agency after I was diagnosed.” (Interview 14) 3.2. Identity and identification: excitement, recognition – and the opposite Participants described how being diagnosed had led to shifts within themselves and changed self-understanding. One group of participants was clear in that they initially considered their diagnosis to be correct. ”Earlier I've recognized myself a lot in it. When I was in school and had a lot of problems.” (Interview 5) ”I've sat for countless hours just nerding out and checking: Do I really fit into this? When I was younger, absolutely.” (Interview 12) Some described initial feelings of excitement about being diagnosed, indicating that they were special or seen as proof of something not being right. “It sounded cool. (...) I felt a bit unique.” (Interview 9) “I was happy at first because: Yes, there is something wrong with me.” (Interview 8) Another group of participants described having never identified with being diagnosed. ”I never had that feeling where others have said: “Oh, God, how nice, now I have an explanation for why I behave the way I do.” (Interview 4) ”I've met many people with Asperger's. (...) [sighs] And I've never recognized myself. (...) How could they put that diagnosis on me?” (Interview 9) Participants described emotions of being diagnosed, saying that it had made them feel like they were ‘worse than everyone else’ (interview 2). They described having felt frustrated, distressed and disappointed. ” I was devastated, ashamed, and didn't feel like it suited me at all.” (Interview 4) 3.3. Formal and informal effects of diagnosis ranging from crucial help to misdirection Participants said that they had been able to access resources or ad justments in school after having been diagnosed, including changing schools, working in smaller groups, receiving knowledgeable supportive teachers, being admitted despite missing grades and receiving financial aid. Some described these effects as necessary and life changing. ”I was able to come to a different school. (...) The teachers seemed to have experience with people with difficulties. (...) I actually believe that saved me.” (Interview 2) ”Finally, I was one of the top students the year I graduated. I never would have done that without my ADHD boarding school.” (Inter view 13) ”She (mother) needed these care allowances (...) for food or for other things that were really, really needed.” (Interview 7) Participants described experiences of how receiving the diagnosis had improved approaches and understanding from teachers, and that parents had educated themselves because of their diagnosis. These changes improved their well-being and situation in school and at home, making them feel supported and listened to, resulting in higher grades. ”Immediately after I got it (the diagnosis), all the teachers under stood that I wasn't being like that just to mess with them (...) so they changed their attitude (...) and then everything went well, [laughs] really well.” (Interview 5) ”At the habilitation center (...) I had a great supportive contact.” (Interview 8) Participants also gave examples of resources they had been provided with related to the diagnosis which they said had not made any real difference to them or their situation. ”I got this personal assistant; I still wasn't doing any better at school.” (Interview 1) ”I got (...) a kind of mat. So, you sit in a chair and there are (...) thorns all around, uh, but I didn't get anything else. (...) Maybe it helped a little bit, as a kind of distraction.” (Interview 6) Participants testified to changes related to the diagnosis which had been unhelpful. Some participants described how they thought that the diagnosis had drawn attention to the wrong things. Instead of receiving help to, for example, handle difficulties related to parental addiction at home or bullying in school, the diagnosis had resulted in medical in terventions or changes in school which had made them feel worse. Some participants described negative experiences with diagnosis-related medication. ”I’ve never felt like I’ve functioned any better on (...) ADHD medi cation. Did you experience any negative effects from it? Yes, I did. Anxiety, paranoia, decreased appetite, changed personality. (...) And did you tell anyone? Yes, all the time. (...) So, I went through all of them without any improvement. The biggest and best improvement was when I stopped taking it. Strange.” (Interview 9) ”They never brought up the bullying. It was just about me losing interest easily, and their first solution to that was medication. (...) So, in the end I had teachers and parents saying: “Yes, but take medication”. But I didn’t want to.” (Interview 13) Participants reported adverse spatial consequences associated with their diagnosis, including social isolation, and struggles to integrate, as they were separated from classmates, moved to a new school or put in separate rooms, where they had not followed the curriculum, felt lonely and did not feel like they fit in. ”I wasn't allowed to learn regular subjects. I wasn't allowed to learn math and Swedish, English, because we were given something else. So, I was locked in a room and kind of had to do this computer ... computer stuff.” (Interview 7) ”I didn't want to be alone in a different room doing, uh, assignments. I wanted to be in my class.” (Interview 10) R.-M. Lindkvist et al. Social Science & Medicine 405 (2026) 119549 5

”It was too damn awful, because my friends were at the old school. (...) There were only boys at the school I changed to. I think there were one or two girls, but they were also like boys.” (Interview 12) 3.4. Motive and rationale for wanting reassessment Going deeper into the reasons for seeking reassessment below fol lows a description of results organized into the four main themes. Being interrelated and not easily separated the first section covers aspects on motive and rationale related to descriptions of who the participants were (Being no different and Having capacity) and the second to what the participants aspired to achieve (Demanding fairness and Removing barriers). 3.4.1. Being no different and having capacity Participants discussed how they in their current life were able to handle things on their own and lead a normal life, which had made them think about reassessment of the diagnosis. One aspect of realizing that they might not have the diagnosis was related to the discovery of not needing any treatment or support. School results in high school were described by several participants as a turning point, where studies were largely based on individual interests provided in a new context. They described feeling more motivated, able to work and focus on things that interested them based on their own choices, of making friends and no longer experiencing social issues. “When I started high school, I didn't feel like I ... well, I didn't get any special help there, but I managed anyway. Because I made friends and things like that. Who encouraged me and made me want to go to school.” (Interview 2) ”One summer holiday when I didn't take (the medication) anymore (...) I felt like: “Oh, I'm kind of the same with the medicine as I am without it.” (Interview 5) “It's going really well. I can handle things on my own and stuff. And so, I've kind of thought: But does it really fit with me? Like, what was it like when I was younger compared to now? What has changed? Or, like, was it incorrect?” (Interview 7) Different levels of emotional investment behind the initiative to get a reassessment was reported. Some described how it was about taking the opportunity and ‘check to see if it is gone or still there’ (Interview 1), where the true answer was the goal rather than a certain outcome. ”It’ll just be nice to have it confirmed. Whether I actually have ADD or not. I just want to know. Regardless (...) I'll be happy. Because then I’ll know for sure.” (Interview 7) Some participants described having considered the risks of getting a reassessment as persons close to them had warned them about losing access to future support. Others described having wanted diagnosis reassessment for years and how they had tried to have it removed, in some cases going back all the way to the time when they had been diagnosed. Being an adult had given them the means to initiate a reassessment. ”After I got my diagnosis, I felt like, “No, this doesn’t apply to me.” So, I tried to contact CAP. I tried to change schools. I tried to persuade my mother, but without results. (...) Now that I’ve turned 18, I was able to reach out to Lund university and this experiment and ask for help.” (Interview 12) Some participants stated how they had been opposed by parents or others around them who did not support the idea of reassessing the diagnosis. Participants expressed frustration over feeling that they were seen by people close to them as who they once were rather than who they were today. However, more so they described support from others, for example a parent, a teacher, a school nurse or friends who were saying that they saw no signs of them having a diagnosis and encour aging them to have it reassessed. Participants said that when everyone around you says that it makes sense to question the diagnosis, they had begun to feel even more that they did not fit into it. Participants described how they perceived that they had caught up with themselves as they were living a more normal teenage life, looking back on them selves as young and easily impressionable, but since then having grown, making the diagnosis no longer relevant to them. ”The brain develops over time, and I believe that things like that can change. (...) If you learn to find ways to deal with it, you don't have a problem anymore and then there's no diagnosis, right?” (Interview 5) ”Maybe even I thought that it was right, but now I don't. It doesn't make sense.” (Interview 10) ”I want to feel like everyone else. I don't want to feel special.” (Interview 3) Participants described having capacity and influence to initiate a process on their own terms. ”I'm the one who applied here now, eh, and, like, have done it on my own terms. And it's not just one person who gets to talk, but several people are discussing. And that feels really safe.” (Interview 4) 3.4.2. Demanding fairness and removing barriers Looking back on experiences of unfair diagnostic processes and difficult life circumstances, participants were motivated to have the diagnosis reassessed for fairness and rectification. Several participants questioned the diagnosis, pointing toward alternative explanations, such as having been depressed, living with parental addiction or being the victim of controlling parents with an agenda. ”I want to get rid of it because I felt they did so much wrong, so it's almost a little bit about (...) revenge.” (Interview 8) ”Now being adult, I understand that my diagnoses are probably my mother's scapegoat (...) for everything that happened during my childhood. (...) Why should I carry that label when it's obviously so wrong? It's not fair.” (Interview 9) ”I've always felt like this was something my father tried to get through. (...) Now, when I have left my father, I want to get rid of everything I felt wasn't quite right.” (Interview 14) Participants were talking about how seeking reassessment was not only about themselves but also about contributing to change. ”We need to share because it can help others.” (Interview 1) ”There are many who feel the same way I do. (...) I thought about this for so many years, but there was never anywhere to turn. Uh. It is so much easier to receive a diagnosis than to get rid of one.” (Interview 4) Participants were saying that a diagnosis needed to be up to date, that it is unnecessary to go around carrying a diagnosis which they could no longer identify with. They questioned that these diagnoses were not checked upon regularly, with reference to how much they thought their behavior had changed since the time of the first assessment. ”Shouldn't they keep it (the diagnosis) up to date?” (...) It was basically almost nine years ago now, not much of that diagnosis is visible today.” (Interview 6) ”You want to have the right diagnosis. It feels strange to walk around with a diagnosis that you don't have.” (Interview 8) Participants described how the diagnosis had made them feel like they had lost their life's purpose. Realizing that a diagnosis could pre vent them from working towards their dream job had made them lose motivation. The potential effects the diagnosis could have on their R.-M. Lindkvist et al. Social Science & Medicine 405 (2026) 119549 6

future had decreased their functioning in school, creating a downward spiral. Seeking reassessment of the diagnosis was a potential way to remove systemic hurdles and fulfil dreams of applying for military ser vice, becoming a policeman or taking a driver's license without needing a medical permission. ”Oh, what does it take to become a police officer? Yeah, no one with ADHD.” Well, [sighs] almost everything fell apart, because that’s what I wanted. (...) Why should I spend time in school when I can’t even become what I want to?” (Interview 1) While some were quite critical about having received the diagnosis, others were thankful. ”If I hadn't gotten them (the diagnoses), I might not have even made it ... I mean, finished high school, and then I could have completely forgotten about considering joining the military or the police.” (Interview 2) Among the fourteen who were interviewed one participant said they had always and were still identifying themselves with the diagnosis yet wanted to have it removed because it was required by the system to be able to fulfill the dream of becoming a policeman. ”My ADHD isn’t really something I want to get rid of. Because I still want to be able to show that: “Yes, I am a police officer, I have ADHD.” (Interview 13) Participants described that removing the diagnosis could be a way to address limited access to healthcare. ” I hit the famous wall, uh, felt really bad, and sought care for sleeping issues and anxiety, and then it was immediately: “Yes, but you have ADHD, you need to seek psychiatric care.” But (...): “I haven’t received any help with ADHD, I feel like these are two separate things”. But she still sent me to some psychiatric assessment unit (...) And their assessment was that: ‘no, you have nothing to do with psychiatry at all, this is something for the primary care level to handle, you have to go back there’. I went back there, and they said: ‘No, but you need to go to psychiatry.’ So, [laughs] and I just need help, I’m going ... like: “I’m exhausted, I need help for this. Stop talking about ADHD.” (Interview 4) Participants explained that the diagnosis affected their sense of freedom and choice in general terms, making them wish to have it reassessed and hopefully removed. They described the diagnosis as a constant companion which could turn up anywhere, creating a sense of non-transparency. This made them feel trapped, not seen as who they were and set up to fail. They described how they suspected but not al ways knew that the diagnosis had played a role in a situation – and that it would continue to do so unless it was removed. ”But why haven't I received a letter?” And then I called the military. (...) And then she said that it's not possible, like, there's something here that means I can't join. And she refused to say what it was.” (Interview 7) ”It follows you like some bloody cancer that plagues your life in every aspect and I could never feel normal. (...) This is just hard. It adds nothing. (...) It takes away my dignity.” (Interview 9) ”In a way I just want it to be normal. (...) Maybe it doesn't affect me now, but I just want to get rid of it.” (Interview 14) 4. Summary of findings The interviews revealed a wide range of experiences and perspec tives among participants who sought a reassessment of their ASD and/or ADHD diagnoses. Participants described the tension between access to support and restricted opportunities, and how the diagnosis continued to “travel” across systems long after school, affecting decisions in ways that were often opaque to them. Many described how their diagnoses had been initiated by concerned parents, often with support from teachers or other professionals, in response to behaviours perceived as problematic or abnormal. While some accepted their parents' intentions as well-meaning, others recalled feeling confused, unheard, or even coerced into diagnostic procedures that, in retrospect, felt misaligned with their own experiences. A common justification for diagnosis was its instrumental value: it provided access to educational, social or financial support. However, participants also reflected on how behaviours that led to diagnosis—such as restlessness, anger, or social withdrawal—could be understood as responses to difficult life circumstances, including trauma or unsafe home environments. The diagnostic process was often described as adult-driven, with little space for the child's voice, and participants questioned whether their experiences were adequately considered in context. The consequences of receiving a diagnosis were described as both enabling and limiting. Some participants gained access to resources that improved their school situation or well-being. Others described how the diagnosis had misdirected attention away from more pressing issues, led to unwanted interventions (such as medication or school segregation), or contributed to stigmatization. Several described feeling that their diagnosis followed them into adulthood, shaping others’ perceptions and limiting opportunities in education, healthcare, employment, and military service. Participants’ identification with their diagnoses varied. Some had never truly identified with the label, others had only initially embraced it, and one still found it meaningful but sought its removal for practical reasons. The desire for reassessment stemmed from the wish to correct what felt like an inaccurate or unjust categorization, to overcome institutional barriers, personal growth and change, and a hope to gain clarity on current self-understanding. Notably, many emphasized the importance of undergoing reassessment on their own terms—voluntarily, know ingly, and with a greater sense of agency. 5. Discussion 5.1. Diagnostic durability and temporal reach Our findings highlight the durability of neurodevelopmental di agnoses across time and contexts. Several participants described how their ASD and/or ADHD diagnosis/-es continued to “stick,” long after they had ceased to be in contact with psychiatry or in need of treatment or support, raising questions about the proportionality between initial benefits and ongoing consequences over time (van Dijk et al., 2016). Previous research has shown that psychiatric diagnoses can affect how young people understand themselves and relate to others. O'Connor et al. (2018) demonstrate that diagnostic labels can threaten self-concept through experiences of stigma and invalidation but also provide validation and belonging. Our participants' reflections on growing out of or moving beyond childhood diagnoses resonate with this ambivalence, as they negotiated between identification with and rejection of diagnostic identities. The tension between personal development and persistence of diagnostic identity echoes previous qualitative work. Honkasilta et al. (2016) have shown how young people negotiate ADHD as part of their self-concept, oscillating between self-pathologizing and self-liberating understandings of their behaviour. Our participants reveal similar struggles to redefine themselves beyond the diagnostic narratives established in childhood. The label persisted in medical records and institutional registers affecting driver's license applications and military service recruitment. This persistence is not incidental but built into the infrastructures of record keeping and bureaucratic coordination. Turowetz and Maynard (2019) show that diagnostic categories are produced and stabilized through documentation practices that inscribe R.-M. Lindkvist et al. Social Science & Medicine 405 (2026) 119549 7

clinical judgments into durable institutional artefacts. Once entered into medical records, diagnoses become circulating facts that travel across systems and acquire authority independent of the individual's present condition. Attention to the materialities of care helps explain this persistence: records, letters, and forms mediate how diagnostic labels endure and circulate beyond clinical encounters (Buse et al., 2018). In this sense, the diagnosis had a life of its own, shaping opportunities and exclusions irrespective of present functioning. Such temporal durability complicates narrow understandings of overdiagnosis as a matter of initial misclassification, suggesting the need to consider how diagnoses may outlive their clinical relevance. The original diagnostic process was often initiated at the request of parents and teachers in response to behaviors experienced as disruptive or difficult. As several participants reflected, the problem was not necessarily that they had difficulties with school, but rather that school had difficulties with them. This echoes wider sociological concerns of how psychiatric diagnosis can individualize social or relational prob lems. As O'Connor et al. (2018) highlight, diagnostic labelling often redirects attention from contextual or interpersonal difficulties, such as family instability or trauma, toward individual pathology. Such a shift shapes how both professionals and young people understand the source of distress. From this perspective, the original diagnosis served to manage the needs of others - to explain behavior and secure support - more than to reflect the child's own understanding or experience. Similar dynamics are noted in ASD research focusing on children's perspectives. Karni-Visel et al. (2024) show how diagnostic and treat ment encounters often marginalize children's voices, as adults, (pro fessionals and parents), define the problem. Our participants' retrospective accounts can be read as efforts to reclaim interpretive authority over experiences once narrated by others. Today the same individuals navigate workplaces, higher education, the military, and health-care settings. The subject of the diagnosis is thus no longer the child with limited voice but an adult capable of self-advocacy in new institutional arenas. This illustrates how diagnostic categories extend beyond their initial clinical purpose and continue to act as social clas sifications across life (Jutel, 2009, 2024; Conrad, 2007). As Hacking (2006) has argued, categories “make up people” not only at the point of classification but through the trajectories they enable and foreclose. 5.2. Beyond intended support: unintended effects across domains The participants’ accounts also demonstrate how diagnoses, initially intended to provide access to resources, travel into domains far removed from their original purpose. Several participants explained how their diagnosis closed off professional opportunities or introduced additional requirements. Others described how their diagnosis was invoked in health-care settings attributing unrelated problems to the diagnosis. In everyday life, participants reported feeling labelled and perceived as different, even when they no longer identified with the diagnosis. These findings resonate with sociological analyses of medicalization, where diagnoses expand their reach by offering medical explanations for behavioural or cognitive difficulties, often replacing structural or pedagogical critiques (Conrad and Bergey, 2014; Singh, 2002). In line with Sims et al. (2021), our participants’ stories show how a diagnostic label may simultaneously enable support and impose barriers, becoming a sorting device used by institutions to regulate eligibility, access, and participation. This dual function is precisely what makes near-threshold cases analytically salient: they illustrate both the benefits and unin tended burdens of diagnostic expansion (Conrad and Bergey, 2014; Busfield, 2017). From the perspective of overdiagnosis debates, such cases illustrate how the balance between benefit and burden may shift across institutional contexts and life stages, also when initially being perceived as highly validating. Importantly, such effects were visible across some of the most powerful organizing frameworks of society - education, employment, military service, law enforcement, and the family - domains in which participants described their diagnosis as a direct barrier to full participation. In interpreting these findings, it is important to situate them in the Swedish context. Sweden has anti-discrimination legislation covering disability Diskrimineringslag (2008:567), and automatic exclusion from military service or police education on the basis of ADHD or autism has in recent years been challenged and replaced, at least formally, by re quirements for individual assessment. Nevertheless, participants’ ac counts indicate that diagnoses may still become consequential in specific institutional encounters. The issue, then, is not simply whether a diag nosis formally excludes a person from participation, but how it may become a practical barrier, a source of uncertainty, or something requiring explanation, documentation, or reassessment in relation to future opportunities. 5.3. Reassessment as a response to stickiness and unintended effects Participants’ wish for reassessment can be understood as an effort to regain control over classifications that no longer fit their lives and as a potential response to no longer being proportionate to current circum stances. For some, this was framed in terms of fairness: correcting a perceived misdiagnosis, often linked to life circumstances. Others wished to remove practical barriers create by diagnosis, or moving on from an identity they did not recognize. The very fact that individuals actively seek, and institutions often require, a formal act of diagnostic removal is telling. It highlights how psychiatric classifications retain weight long after their clinical rele vance has faded and raises questions of epistemic authority and re sponsibility: What does it mean, ethically and clinically, to acknowledge that a diagnosis once helpful has become a source of limitation or harm? As Jutel (2016) argues, diagnosis is not merely a technical decision but a socially and existentially charged moment that rewrites the patient narrative, shifts identity, and dictates the clinical pathway. The act of removal, or diagnostic reversal, can also be seen as a transformative social event. For our participants, a new clinical assessment reconfig ured how they were seen by institutions and themselves, marking a transition from being defined by a diagnostic past to reclaiming authorship of their present identity. Who has the power to say that a diagnosis no longer applies to individuals who are living with conse quences of a classification made in their name but not necessarily on their terms? To what extent do other institutions accept such reassessments? Another challenge concerns how reassessment requests are perceived within psychiatry. A common critique is that patients arrive with an “agenda”— answering assessments in ways that maximize the likelihood of removal. Yet, in a broader sense, all patients come to healthcare with an agenda: seeking recognition, relief, or change. In our case, the agenda is inverted: the suffering stems not from the absence of a diagnosis, but from living with one. This “patient who wants to be seen as well” raises a different kind of diagnostic dilemma: one that concerns not only the validity of past classifications, but also the limits of insti tutional trust, the distribution of epistemic authority and responsibility, and the evolving relationship between identity and diagnosis over time. 6. Methodological reflection Recruitment based on requests for reassessment without advertising means that our study may add information based on actual needs in the target group. Individuals who proactively request renewed assessment are not intended as a proxy for the ASD/ADHD population. They are informative because they live with, and actively contest, the conse quences of diagnostic classification at the widened edges of these cate gories. Their requests for reassessment make visible how diagnostic thresholds are not settled once and for all at the moment of diagnosis, but may become newly consequential as people move across life stages, institutional settings, and social roles. In this sense, reassessment re quests can be read as empirical signals within broader debates on R.-M. Lindkvist et al. Social Science & Medicine 405 (2026) 119549 8

diagnostic expansion and overdiagnosis. 7. Conclusion In relation to debates about diagnostic expansion and overdiagnosis, we argue that reassessment cases illuminate critical dynamics in the governance of diagnosis today. They show how diagnoses such as ASD and ADHD extend far beyond the clinic, acquire unintended effects across domains, and generate demands not only for classification but also for declassification. In this sense, the group we studied may not be statistically representative, but they exemplify a broader sociological phenomenon: the growing need to negotiate not only the expansion but also the proportionality and temporal durability of psychiatric diagnoses in contemporary society. pages: Review Article Cognitive functioning in children with both epilepsy and ADHD: A systematic review and meta-analysis Steven Wickens *, Persephone Gummersall, Trevor Brown Neurocare Group, Melbourne, VIC, Australia A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Childhood epilepsy Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder Cognition Neuropsychology Cattell-horn-Carroll A B S T R A C T There is a well-known bidirectional association between epilepsy and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children. The aim of the current systematic review and meta-analysis was to investigate neuropsy chological functioning of children with epilepsy (CWE) and ADHD. The systematic search of two databases revealed 22 observational studies that comprised samples of CWE + ADHD and cognitive outcomes as compared to CWE alone, ADHD alone, and/or healthy controls. Neuropsychological data was organised with respect to Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) taxonomy. Random effects meta-analyses across all measured cognitive domains showed small to moderate effect sizes indicating poorer cognitive outcomes in the CWE + ADHD group as compared to either condition alone (standardised mean difference [SMD] -0.30 to -0.72), with moderate to large effect sizes compared to healthy controls (SMD -0.61 to -1.12). Confidence intervals were wide and overlapping, suggesting a broad heterogenous profile of neuropsychological functioning in children with both conditions. These findings underscore the breadth, magnitude and vulnerability of cognitive dysfunction in children with comorbid neurobehavioral conditions, thus highlighting the need for comprehensive assessment and targeted intervention in this vulnerable population. 1. Introduction Epilepsy and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) repre sent the most common neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders in children, affecting up to 1% and 5–7% of the population, respectively [1–2]. There is significant comorbidity among children with epilepsy (CWE) and ADHD, with estimates of up to 30% of CWE meeting diag nostic criteria for ADHD [3] with a higher prevalence inattention (rather than hyperactivity/impulsivity) symptoms [4], and a 2.5-fold higher risk of epilepsy in those with ADHD [5]. Understanding the nature of the combined presentation is complex, and considers shared context at the genetic, biological, and environ mental levels interacting over time [6]. For instance, there are shared genetic factors that may link the conditions which, when interacting with environmental variables may modify developmental trajectories and behavioural vulnerabilities [7]. Complexity increases when there is consideration to the many biological variables that contribute to and/or exacerbate the cognitive and behavioural challenges (e.g., medication effects, impact of seizures, interictal paroxysmal activity etc.; [8]). Research has shown that in many children with both ADHD and epilepsy, challenges with learning, cognition and socio-emotional function antedate the onset of seizures and have been linked with structural brain differences [7,9]. A recent meta-analysis of prevalence studies showed that age (e.g., younger, earlier age of onset), epilepsy type (e.g., absence epilepsy), frequency of seizures and intellectual/ developmental disabilities were significant risk factors for ADHD in epilepsy [3]. There is an extensive body of literature on cognitive outcomes in both childhood epilepsy and ADHD, although historically, there has been a focus on understanding specific profiles of neuropsychological function at the group level across different epileptic syndromes [10], and typical domains of dysfunction in ADHD (e.g., attention and exec utive functioning; [11]). The review literature has revealed significant heterogeneity, and widespread deficits present at the group study level [12–16]. Considering this variability, there has been a movement to wards understanding broad cognitive phenotypes within a personalised medicine approach and a paradigm shift in the understanding of neu ropsychological outcomes and neurobehavioral comorbidities moving towards network-based models of brain function [10,17]. Others have considered the utility of classifying a broader overarching developmental brain disorder with varying topography, as opposed to the consideration of discrete comorbid con ditions [18]. Research has documented a vulnerability to more severe cognitive deficits in the comorbid ADHD/epilepsy presentation [19] although to date, there has been no effort to quantitively synthesize the available research to determine the magnitude and profile of neuropsychological outcomes. The recent systematic review by Leal and colleagues [19] acknowledged the similarities of their review to the present pre- registered review, however they focussed primarily on exploring how ADHD alters neurocognitive outcomes in CWE. While acknowledging the heterogeneity between studies that is often present when consid ering such populations broadly, information from quantitative syntheses may serve to further clarify the comorbid relationship and associated combinatorial and/or overlapping cognitive features. The aim of the current systematic review and meta-analysis was to synthesize current research on neuropsychological functioning of children with both epi lepsy and ADHD, according to a well-defined taxonomy of cognition, and to compare these profiles with those of CWE alone, ADHD alone, and/or healthy controls. 2. Methods 2.1. Search strategy The systematic review protocol was registered with the Inter- national Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO: registration number CRD420251015603). The review was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines [20]. A search for articles was con ducted using Pubmed and ProQuest databases to May 2025. Keywords were entered in terms of epilepsy (epilepsy OR seizures), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and cognitive function (cognitive, cognition, neuropsychology, neuropsychological, intelligence, language, memory, executive function). The reference lists of eligible articles were also searched for additional studies. Further detail regarding search strategy, PRISMA checklist and protocol registration can be found in the supplementary material. 2.2. Selection criteria Study inclusion criteria were all of the following: (a) original research published in a peer-reviewed journal, (b) studies with samples including participants with both childhood epilepsy and ADHD in addition to a control group with either healthy peers, epilepsy without ADHD or ADHD without epilepsy (c) population included children up to 16 years of age (d) any published measure of neuropsychological functioning. Studies were excluded if (a) separate data for a combined epilepsy and ADHD group was not provided (b) epilepsy was in the context of another defined genetic or neurological condition (e.g., stroke, brain injury, trisomy 21 etc.), (c) the control group was absent or some other diagnosable condition; (d) full-text article was not available; (e) means and standard deviations for test data were not available. 2.3. Data Extraction Data extraction was completed by corresponding author, SW. Means and standard deviations from measures of cognitive function were extracted. Based on the methodology of previous systematic reviews in epilepsy [13–14,21], the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) model was used to classify broad cognitive factors for each test. The CHC model of intelli gence is widely regarded as the most comprehensive and empirically supported framework for understanding human cognition [22]. It is structured as a hierarchical, three-stratum model. At the top level is a general intelligence factor (G), which influences a range of broad cognitive abilities and each of these broad domains encompasses numerous more specific, narrow abilities. For the purpose of the present study, the relevant broad abilities included: • Crystallized intelligence (Gc) - acquired knowledge of the language, information and concepts of a specific culture, and/or the application of this knowledge. • Fluid reasoning (Gf) - deliberate and controlled mental operations to solve novel problems that cannot be performed automatically. • Short-term Working memory (Gsm) – limited capacity system for holding and working with information in the immediate situation. • Processing speed (Gs) - the ability to automatically and fluently perform relatively easy or over-learned elementary cognitive tasks. • Decision Speed/Reaction Time (Gt) - the ability to make elementary decisions and/or responses at the onset of simple stimuli. • Long-term storage and retrieval and fluency (Glr / Gr) - the ability to store and consolidate new information in long-term memory and later fluently retrieve the stored information. Regarding neuropsychological test extraction of data, where a single study reported on multiple tests reflecting the same underlying broad CHC factor (i.e. PIQ and Raven's matrices) each test was extracted and pooled within the study for the respective factor (I.e. Gf). Where a test included multiple outcomes for the same set of stimuli, a single repre sentative outcome was chosen (i.e. reaction time variability in contin uous performance tasks). Where separate neuropsychological test data was reported for subgroups within a study (i.e. ADHD or epilepsy sub type), data for each group was extracted and pooled within the study. Where information was reported prospectively across multiple time- points, data was extracted for patients and controls at T0 only (e.g. [9]). Where there were multiple papers containing possible overlapping samples (i.e. [7,9]) papers/outcomes were retained if they provided information on different cognitive measures and/or domains of func tion. There was one full text paper by Fang et al. [23] available in Chinese and unavailable in English, which was included and translated to English using Google Translate. Classifying tests traditionally conceptualised as measures of execu tive function is challenging within the CHC taxonomy, as many mea sures overlap and are subsumed under multiple CHC constructs, including but not limited to Gf, Gs, Gsm, and Gr. Accordingly, tests were categorised based on the factor judged to account for the greatest pro portion of variance in the measurement outcome. For example, execu tive measures of inhibitory control, such as the Stroop task, were classified under processing speed (Gs), as they are considered measures of complex speed due to their primary reliance on response time. This approach has been adopted in previous research [13–14]. In addition to cognitive outcomes, information was extracted from included studies pertaining to study characteristics, demographics and key clinical variables. This included case and control sample sizes; country of study; mean sample age of groups; mean sample age of onset for epilepsy; epilepsy type (e.g., focal/generalised/epileptic syndrome); ADHD and epilepsy diagnostics; and medication status of clinical groups (e.g., antiepileptics and/or stimulants). Meta-regression and/or moderator analyses were considered if there were a sufficient number of studies (k≥10). 2.4. Statistical analysis Meta-analyses were performed using the Metafor package in RStudio 4.3.1. Effect sizes were calculated for each study and then pooled by cognitive domain. Each study contributed an effect size representing the standardised mean difference (SMD) in neuropsychological performance within the domain between children with both ADHD and epilepsy, and S. Standard bench marks were used to interpret effect size magnitude (SMD = 0.20 = small, 0.50 = moderate, 0.80 = large), and interpretations were supported by the corresponding confidence intervals. A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted for each cognitive domain, estimating the overall mean effect size and its 95% confidence and prediction interval. This model assumes that the included studies are independent, and each reflects a true effect size drawn from a normally distributed population. Hetero geneity among studies was assessed using the Q test, where a significant result indicates variability beyond chance. The I2 statistic was also calculated to quantify the proportion of variance due to heterogeneity rather than random sampling error. 2.5. Assessment of methodological quality Methodological quality of studies was completed using the New castle Ottawa Scale (NOS) for case-control studies [24]. The NOS scale assesses each study for risk of bias across three domains of selection, comparability and exposure/outcome, with a total possible score out of nine. Scores are classified as low risk (i.e. 7–9), moderate risk (i.e. 4–6), and high risk (i.e. 0–3) of bias. In the current context of observational, cross sectional neuropsychological outcome data between cases (CWE + ADHD) and controls (CWE, ADHD or healthy controls), all studies were rated according to case-control NOS criteria, as the distinction between case-control and cohort designs was not considered relevant to the current study. It is acknowledged that the registered protocol specified independent quality assessment by two assessors, in practice a second assessor (PG) independently evaluated a randomly selected 30% of studies (7/22) to assess inter-rater reliability (Cohen's κ). Where there were discrepancies between raters, consensus was reached through collaborative discussion. 3. Results Retrieved searches were imported into Rayyan for screening and duplicate search [44]. The initial search identified 1361 records and there were 730 studies after duplicate removal. Among these, 99 full- text papers reviewed for eligibility. Exclusion of 77 studies resulted in 22 studies that met the inclusion criteria (see Fig. 1 for the Prisma Flowchart and Table 1 for characteristics of included studies). Included studies had samples from varied geography, although approximately a third of samples were US based. The average age of study CWE + ADHD samples ranged from 7.6 to 12.1 years old. Studies comprised samples with mixed epilepsy syndromes (57%), focal (30%) or generalised epi lepsy (13%). Across the various cognitive domains, the number of included studies ranged from 3 to 13. For the combined group, the sum number of cases ranged from 50 to 405 children and comparison groups from 77 to 717 children. The G factor comprised tests largely reflective of Full-Scale Intelli gence Quotient from various editions of the Wechsler battery (i.e., WISC- R, WISC-III, WISC-IV, WASI) across different language-editions. Fluid reasoning (Gf) measures were represented by non-verbal performance and perceptual reasoning Wechsler tests, along with other flexible thinking and mental switching tasks that are often considered under the umbrella of executive functioning (e.g., Ravens' Matrices, Wisconsin Card Sorting Test, Mazes, and Tower of Hanoi). Studies examining the short-term working memory construct (Gsm) employed tasks from the Wechsler working memory tasks, or memory batteries (i.e., Wide Range Assessment of Learning and Memory [WRAML], Children Memory Scales [CMS]), examining both verbal and visuospatial short-term working memory abilities. The broad stratum ability of processing speed (Gs) contained standard tasks of speed of information processing of simple visual material, such as the PSI mea sures from the Wechsler scales, Trail Making and Stroop tasks. Reaction and decision time (Gt) comprised tests representing sustained attention and vigilance measures from Continuous Performance Tasks (CPTs), principally attending to measures of Reaction Time Variability. When only accuracy measures of continuous performance tasks were available, these were considered more compatible with Gs over Gt. Given paucity of studies including measures of long-term memory retrieval and fluency independent of encoding, both verbal learning tasks and phonemic and semantic fluency tasks were pooled into a representative Glr construct. A detailed list of neuropsychological tests organised according to broad stratum CHC constructs can be found in the supplementary material. 3.1. Quantitative synthesis Summary statistics for random effects meta-analyses of cognitive outcomes in the combined CWE + ADHD group as compared to either group alone (i.e. CWE or ADHD alone) and healthy controls are demonstrated in Table 2. Pooled standardised mean differences (SMD) with confidence intervals across each cognitive domain and compassion group are visualised in Fig. 2. Compared to children with either ADHD or epilepsy alone, there were small to moderate effect sizes observed across all assessed domains of cognition with overlapping confidence intervals, indicating poorer outcomes in the CWE + ADHD group. In the ADHD alone comparison, the largest effect size was in the Glr domain (k = 3, SMD = −0.72, 95% CI = −0.94 to −0.50, p < 0.001), however this also contained the fewest studies. Smaller effects were seen in domains of short-term working memory (k = 6, SMD = −0.31, 95% CI = −0.59 to −0.03, p = 0.03) and reaction time / attention measures from continuous performance tasks (k = 5, SMD = −0.33, 95% CI = −0.84 to −0.17, p = 0.017) followed by the overarching factor G (k = 7, SMD = −0.44, 95% CI = −0.70 to −0.17, p = 0.001) and fluid intelli gence (k = 8, SMD = −0.38, 95% CI = −0.60 to −0.15, p = 0.001). There were relatively larger, moderate effects noted in verbal language abilities (k = 7, SMD = −0.54, 95% CI = −0.85 to −0.23, p < 0.001) and processing speed (k = 5, SMD = −0.56, 95% CI = −0.94 to −0.17, p = 0.005). Random effects meta-analyses comparing the ADHD+CWE group to CWE alone revealed mostly small effect sizes across domains of Gsm (k = 5, SMD = −0.30, 95% CI = −0.47 to −0.12, p < 0.001), processing speed (k = 6, SMD = −0.32, 95% CI = −0.49 to −0.15, p < 0.001) and reaction time / decision speed (k = 6, SMD = −0.45, 95% CI = −0.84 to −0.06, p = 0.024), Glr (k = 3, SMD = −0.34, 95% CI = −0.55 to −0.12, p = 0.002), fluid intelligence (k = 8, SMD = −0.44, 95% CI = −0.76 to −0.12, p = 0.008) and the overarching G factor (k = 11, SMD = −0.43, 95% CI = −0.68 to −0.18, p < 0.001). There was a moderate effect size for Gc (k = 10, SMD = −0.55, 95% CI = −0.85 to −0.25, p < 0.001). Alternatively, the CWE + ADHD group showed large effect sizes compared to the healthy control group across most cognitive domains (k = 4–8, SMD = −0.70 to −1.12, p < 0.01) except for Glr, where there was an observed moderate effect size (k = 3, SMD = −0.61, 95% CI = −0.82 to −0.41, p < 0.001). Moreover, the effect for Gt compared to healthy controls did not reach significance (p = 0.053). 3.2. Clinical variables and neuropsychological function Among the various analyses, there were two cognitive domains in the CWE control group where there were sufficient studies (i.e. ≥10) for performing meta-regression and subgroup analyses (i.e., G and Gc). Meta-regression was considered for the following variables: age, age of onset, epilepsy subtype (e.g., % of sample focal), AED status, ADHD subtype and NOS quality rating. Overall, no tested variable explained any significant portion of variance, however, there were several missing values across studies severely limiting the analyses. When consulting included study effects across epilepsy variables there were inconsistent effects on cognitive outcomes. An earlier age of onset and a higher number of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) was associated with poorer attention in CWE, both with and without ADHD in one study [41]. However, several other studies failed to show any significant dif ference in cognitive measures based on age of seizure onset or AED usage [9,29,36,38]. Quality assessment and risk of Bias Across the eight NOS items, the mean inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ) was 0.63 (range 0–1), indicating substantial overall agreement. Two items showed lower agreement (κ = 0.30 and 0.00), likely a reflection of the small sample size and limited variability in ratings (e.g., the latter had 100% agreement with all “no” responses). The NOS quality ratings for the 22 studies ranged from 3 to 9, with a mean score of 4.91, indi cating a concentration of studies within the moderate risk of bias range. While a few studies demonstrated higher methodological quality (scores of 7 and 9), several studies scored on the lower end, suggesting notable variability in overall study quality (see supplementary Table S1). Most studies applied the same test batteries across groups and adequately selected and defined control groups. The most common sources of po tential bias related to limited representativeness in the selection domain of the comorbid group, as well as frequent lack of examiner blinding and incomplete reporting of non-response rates in the exposure domain. Funnel plots were inspected for evidence of publication bias. For ana lyses with ≥10 studies (G and Gc for CWE + ADHD vs CWE only), Egger's test was consulted and was non-significant for both ([G, z = 0.86, p = 0.39; Gc, z = 1.85, p = 0.06]). 4. Discussion The present findings revealed that the group of children with both epilepsy and ADHD displayed poorer overall neuropsychological scores compared to either condition alone with small to moderate effect sizes. Compared to healthy controls, the cognitive deficit in the combined group was, unsurprisingly, markedly larger. This compliments and ex tends the recent systematic review and narrative synthesis by Leal et al. [19] by revealing the magnitude of cognitive impairment in the com bined group compared to CWE and ADHD alone, as well as healthy controls. These findings are consistent with previous meta-analytic re views of neuropsychological functioning in both CWE [12–14,21] and ADHD [15–16], indicating widespread and heterogenous cognitive outcomes. The relationship between childhood epilepsy and ADHD is complex and multifaceted, with influences from genetics, disease and treatment variables including specific interactions with localised effects, as well as environmental factors [6]. One interpretation of the present findings at group level is that there may be a dose-response relationship corre sponding to amplified cognitive deficits. Children with both conditions exhibit more widespread and/or increased dysfunction of the underlying developmental brain disorder, with heterogeneity interacting with contextual and specific disease variables (e.g., onset of seizures, epilepsy type, frequency of seizures, ADHD subtype etc.). This more parsimo nious suggestion is that both disorders share domains of impairment and together, are additive to worsen outcomes. Alternatively, there are also indications for unique contributions from each condition affecting cognitive function in different ways and distinct effects combine to produce a broader, more heterogenous profile of widespread cognitive dysfunction. While acknowledging the overlapping confidence intervals across the various cognitive domains, there is some evidence from within the neuropsychological profile comparisons to suggest that there are Fig. 2. perhaps relatively greater contributions arising from certain cognitive constructs from the CWE and ADHD components. Within CHC theory, Executive Functioning (EF) is conceptualised as a conflation of various broad stratum abilities that tend to load more on factors of fluid intel ligence, processing speed and retrieval fluency (e.g., corresponding to tasks such as trail making, Stroop, verbal fluency, and tower of Hanoi among others). Compared to healthy controls, effect size point estimates indicate largest cognitive deficit in the combined group to EF domains of fluid reasoning and speed of information processing. On the other hand, there is data to support that inattention symptoms can be directedly related to processing speed and fluid reasoning organised within CHC taxonomy, not otherwise mediated by test session behaviour [45]. The combined group compared to ADHD alone showed relative effects greatest in domains of memory retrieval and speed, which is cited as a consistent feature in CWE compared to controls [46]. Alternatively, the addition of ADHD to CWE (i.e., in the comparison of the combined group to CWE alone) showed relatively higher effect sizes for verbal intelli gence and language measures as well as reaction time variability, the latter reflecting a common measure of intraindividual variability and sustained attention that holds well-known clinical utility in the neuro psychological assessment of ADHD [16,47]. Although effect sizes were small for processing efficiency domains of short-term working memory and processing speed in the CWE alone comparison, it is noteworthy that prediction intervals and heterogeneity statistics were lower and non- significant, showing that these effected domains were more predict able and stable across studies. Across most cognitive domains, there was substantial heterogeneity between studies. Although the meta-analysis revealed significant pooled effect sizes at the group level, the majority of prediction intervals were wide and included zero, indicating that the observed effects in any future study could plausibly be small, large, or even absent. This sug gests meaningful variability in cognitive outcomes across samples. In general, confidence and prediction intervals were wider for the healthy control comparison compared to the clinical comparisons, which makes sense given the shared clinical features and impact thereof. At the in dividual level, this aligns with the broad spectrum of cognitive strengths and vulnerabilities observed clinically—despite an overall increased risk for cognitive deficits. Thus, the substantial between-study heterogeneity would appear to mirror the variability seen at the level of the individual. Taken together, these findings demonstrating significant variability underscore and support the growing movement towards identifying broad cognitive phenotypes within a personalised medicine framework [10]. The evidence from this study lends weight to the clinical relevance of neuropsychological assessment when seizures co-occur with attention and behaviour challenges in children. This is particularly relevant dur ing the diagnostic assessment of ADHD where cognitive testing is com mon, although not always completed in practice. Given the magnitude of cognitive deficit in the combined group, there is also a need for in terventions that can support cognition while addressing seizures and ADHD symptoms. Reviews have shown that stimulant medication is generally tolerable and safe in CWE [8], although there can be caution exercised when treating comorbidity with multiple medication classes in children. As such, medication alternative psychosocial intervention, such as behavioural therapy, cognitive remediation, and/or targeted neuromodulation therapies should also be considered [48]. For example, EEG biofeedback is a non-invasive biobehavioural technique that provides real-time feedback of brain activity to support self- regulation of cognitive, emotional and behavioural functions and there is a body of evidence investigating EEG biofeedback in both ADHD [49] and epilepsy [50]. There were in fact studies that investigated the effectiveness of neurofeedback in children with both CWE and ADHD, conditioning cortical stability through reinforcing sensorimotor rhythm activity and/or feedback on arousal vigilance states [26,51–52]. These studies went beyond intervention for primary symptoms (e.g., to reduce seizures, inattention, hyperactivity etc.), with some evidence showing improvements in cognitive ability such as short-term working memory, and cognitive flexibility speed [26,51]. While the existing research is scarce and limited to small samples and case studies, there is value in further well-controlled studies exploring individualised biologically- driven, behavioural interventions in this at-risk population. The present study has several limitations. The combining of various childhood epileptic syndromes into a single group limited the ability to examine neuropsychological profiles across epileptic syndromes and may have introduced bias, leading to findings that suggest more wide spread and heterogeneous deficits. However, previous reviews using similar methods in specific focal epilepsy syndromes [14,21] and idio pathic generalised epilepsy [13] have shown comparable findings. Additionally, many of the studies that examine CWE and comorbid ADHD tend to combine epilepsy types together. There is the further limitation of collapsing narrow cognitive abilities into broader CHC constructs, which results in a loss of detail regarding specific cognitive functions. There were also several notable CHC broad stratum abilities either under-represented (e.g., Glr and Gr) or absent (i.e. Gv and Ga) from the current meta-analysis, given the lack of studies including such measures, that limit a more comprehensive appreciation of the cognitive profile. Included studies showed wide variability in exclusion criteria related to IQ which introduces bias in representativeness. Where several studies applied no exclusion based on IQ, others varied exclusion from severe intellectual disability to IQ scores below 80. Given the vulnerability of lower cognitive functioning in this combined population, variability in exclusion criteria will likely lead to an underestimation of the impact of cognitive difficulties. Furthermore, many studies failed to report on the status of stimulant medications at the time of cognitive assessment. Given the well-known positive impact of central nervous system stim ulants on neuropsychological functioning, especially on tests of atten tion and executive function [53], this variability in standardization introduces a potential confound in appreciating the influences of cognitive dysfunction in this population. The present findings support a widespread profile of cognitive dysfunction in children with both epilepsy and ADHD compared to either condition alone or healthy controls, with important consideration to the significant heterogeneity present. Future studies would benefit from more standardised reporting of clinical variables to enable clearer understanding of the complex relationship between neurological and neurobehavioral manifestations. Given the substantial heterogeneity observed at the group level, future research adopting idiographic and contextual approaches may be well suited to elucidate causal factors in the brain-behaviour relationship to inform personalised intervention. In conclusion, CWE who also experience clinically significant issues with attention and behaviour are at an increased risk of neuropsychological dysfunction, and there is a need for further empirical and clinical efforts into targeted interventions for addressing neuropsychological sequelae. E-mail address: s2030444@u.tsukuba.ac.jp (T. Marumoto). Takafumi Monma b, b Institute of Health and Sport Sciences, University of Tsukuba, 1-1-1 Tennodai, Tsukuba-shi, Ibaraki 305-8577, Japan Yukinori Sawae b, Fumi Takeda b a r t i c l e i n f o Article history: Received 9 October 2025 Revised 25 March 2026 Accepted 27 March 2026 Keywords: Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity Mothers Mental Health Social Support Stress, Psychological a b s t r a c t Background: Mothers of children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are known to have a tendency toward poor mental health. This study aimed to identify specific parenting stressors impacting maternal mental health as well as the social support that buffers against those stressors in mothers of children with ADHD. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted with Japanese mothers of children under 18 years of age diagnosed with ADHD. The Questionnaires included attributes of participants and their children with ADHD, parenting stressors assessed by the Developmental Disorder Parenting Stressor Index, social support provided from spouse, parents, peer, friends, school, and medical and welfare institution, and maternal mental health assessed by the K6. A total of 149 responses (mean age 43.1 ± 4.9, children's mean age 10.2 ± 3.3, with 80.5% male) were analyzed. Results: Multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed that the parenting stressor ‘difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs’ was associated with poor maternal mental health. Additionally, social support from medical and welfare institution buffered the impact of this parenting stressor on maternal mental health. Implications to practice: Medical and welfare institution professionals should strength social support reducing parenting stressors of ‘difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs’ among mothers of children with ADHD. Conclusion: The parenting stressor of ‘difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs’ may impact mental health in mothers of children with ADHD and the medical and welfare institution's social support may buffer this stressor. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.
