All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies. Introduction Mothers of children with ADHD often experience depressive symptoms. This has been supported by a meta-analysis showing that mothers of children with ADHD had significantly more severe depressive symptoms than other mothers (Cheung, Aberdeen, Ward and Theule, 2018). Such poor maternal mental health leads to dysfunctional parenting such as corporal punishment, lack of discipline, and overly strict disciplining (Gau & Chang, 2013; Gerdes, Haack and Schneider, 2012; Shin & Stein, 2008), worsening children's ADHD symptoms, behavioral problems, and oppositional defiant disorders (Agha, Zammit, Thapar and Langley, 2017; Brammer, Galán, Mesri and Lee, 2018; Chronis et al., 2007; Walls et al., 2018). Therefore, maintaining the mental health of mothers is important for both mothers and children with ADHD, and identifying factors associated with maternal mental health is crucial for developing effective measures. Regarding factors related to the mental health of mothers of children with ADHD, a few studies have reported maternal attributes such as lower income (Al-Balushi et al., 2019), marital status (Chou, Hsiao, Chang and Yen, 2021), no other caregivers (Al-Balushi et al., 2019) and own ADHD tendencies (Marumoto et al., 2023). Additionally, children's related factors such as severity of ADHD symptoms (Cheung, Aberdeen, Ward and Theule, 2018), hyperactive/impulsive feature (Al-Balushi et al., 2019) and combined feature (Al-Balushi et al., 2019) have also been reported. On the other hand, there has not been examined the relationship between parenting stressors and mental health of mothers of children with ADHD. Although qualitative studies exploring the parenting stressors experienced by mothers of children with ADHD remain limited (Leitch et al., 2019), previous research has identified several unique parenting stressors, including the difficulty in obtaining understanding from others (Laugesen & Groenkjaer, 2015; Leitch et al., 2019;

Mofokeng & van der Wath, 2017) and the emotional struggle to accept their child's disability (Teraoka et al., 2014). There have been several assessment tool of parenting stressor to date. However, the widely used Parenting Stress Index (Abidin, 1983; Abidin, 1990; Abidin, 1995) does not clearly distinguish between parenting stressors and stress responses. In addition, although a stressor scale was developed by Song et al. (2004), and another scale for assessing parental stressor prior to kindergarten entry and school enrollment was developed by Watanabe et al. (2006), both scales were designed for parents of children with high-functioning autism or Asperger's disorder, and their validity has not been examined. On the other hand, The Developmental Disorder Parenting Stressor Index (DDPSI; Yamane, 2013) was designed to assess parenting stressors among mothers with developmental disabilities including ADHD and was demonstrated both reliability and validity. T. Marumoto, T. Monma, Y. Sawae et al. Journal of Pediatric Nursing 89 (2026) 1–8 According to DDPSI, the parenting stressors consist of four factors, ‘difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs,’ ‘anxiety about the child's future and independence,’ ‘inadequate understanding of the child's disorder from others,’ and ‘conflicting emotions with regard to the child's disorder.’ The highest proportion of variance in DDPSI was explained by the ‘difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs.’ However, it is unknown which of these parenting stressors has a negative effect on mental health of mothers of children with ADHD. A study has examined the association between parenting stressors and depressive symptoms in mothers of children with ADHD, but this used the Parenting Stress Index (PSI; Abidin, 1983; Abidin, 1990; Abidin, 1995) for mothers of children in general (Theule et al., 2013), moreover some items of PSI overlap those of depression measurement such as the Beck Depression Inventory (Beck, Ward, Mendelson, Mock and Erbaugh, 1961). Therefore, a study that identifies specific parenting stressors impacting mental health of mothers of children with ADHD is needed. In addition, it has not been identified which provider's social support buffers the negative effects of parenting stressors on mental health of mothers of children with ADHD. In the context of stress and social support theory, a buffering effect refers to the role of social support in reducing the negative impact of stressors on individuals' mental health (Cohen & Wills, 1985). Social support, broadly defined as material and psychological assistance provided by others, is generally be divided into two types: instrumental support and emotional support (Vaux, 1988). In addition to the types of social support, previous research has reported that the effectiveness of social support differs depending on the providers of support (Acoba, 2024; Dakof & Taylor, 1990; Gariépy et al., 2016). In the present study, we focused on the providers of social support to determine which provider's social support are helpful. To date, it has been known that the total social support from husbands, parents, health care providers and peer parents is negatively related to parenting stressors in mothers of children with developmental disabilities (Yamane, 2013) and the total social support is negatively related to the total parenting stressors in parents of children with ADHD (Theule et al., 2011). It has also been known that social support is negatively associated with depressive symptoms in parents of children with ADHD (Lovell, Moss and Wetherell, 2012) and less family support is associated with depressive symptoms in caregivers of children with ADHD (Chou, Hsiao, Chang and Yen, 2021). Intervention studies have suggested that support from medical and welfare institution may contribute to improved maternal mental health. For example, behavioral parent training has been shown to improve child-related outcomes and to enhance mental health in parents of children with ADHD (Mehri et al., 2020a; Mehri et al., 2020b). However, it is unclear which provider's social support buffers the negative effects of parenting stressors on mental health of mothers of children with ADHD. In Japan, various social supports are provided for parents of children with developmental disabilities. For example, developmental disability support centers, which are welfare institutions, mainly provide support for individuals with developmental disabilities, including ADHD, and their families (Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, 2021). In medical institutions, ‘guidance for individual parents’ to discuss how to deal with their children's troubling behaviors and ‘behavioral parent training’ are often conducted for parents of children with ADHD (Makino et al., 2018) based on the guidelines for diagnosis and treatment of the disorder (Saito & Iida, 2022). In schools, individual guidance is provided based on an understanding of the needs of each child with ADHD (Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, 2003), and special support education coordinators are assigned for this purpose (Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology, 2018). Therefore, it is vital to identify the social support that buffers the negative effects of parenting stressors on mental health of mothers of children with ADHD. Hence, this study aims to identify parenting stressors that affect the mental health of mothers of children with ADHD as well as providers of social support that buffer these effects. We hypothesize that the parenting stressor of ‘difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs’ is a risk factor for psychological distress and that social support provided by spouses and parents buffer parenting stressors. Methods Participants Participants were recruited through two peer groups for parents of children with developmental disabilities, a provider of after-school care services, and a support group for children with developmental disabilities in Japan. Inclusion criteria was to be a Japanese mother of children under 18 years of age who had been diagnosed with ADHD by medical professionals. Of 164 study participants, 149 who provided complete responses to the survey and met the eligibility criteria (mean age 43.1 ± 4.9 years, mean age of children with ADHD 10.2 ± 3.3 years, 80.5% male) were included in the analysis. Procedures Online survey was conducted between September 24 and October 19, 2021. Before beginning the survey, participants were presented with an online informed consent form that explained the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of participation, and data confidentiality. Only those who provided consent electronically were allowed to proceed to the questionnaire. This study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Health and Sport Sciences of the University of Tsukuba, Japan (approval number: Tai 021–8; approval date: June 19, 2021). This study was reported in accordance with the STROBE statement (von Elm et al., 2007). Measures Participant attributes The respondents were asked about their age, education, marital status, occupation, household income, ADHD tendencies, number of children, number of children with ADHD, and psychiatric medication status. To measure maternal ADHD tendencies, Part A of the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS; Kessler et al., 2005) was administered. The ASRS has two parts: Part A and Part B. Part A is used to screen adults for ADHD. Threshold-level responses to four or more of the six Part A questions indicate a positive result. The sensitivity and specificity of the Part A screening using the ASRS were 68.7% and 99.5%, respectively (Kessler et al., 2005). Cronbach's alpha coefficient for Part A of the ASRS in this study was 0.831. Mothers with a positive ASRS Part A result were considered as having ADHD tendencies. Regarding psychiatric medication status, data on the mothers' medicine use for mental health problems (antidepressants, anxiolytics and hypnotics) and ADHD symptoms (ADHD medications) were collected. General drug names for antidepressants, anxiolytics, hypnotics, and 2

ADHD medications approved in Japan were provided as references in the questionnaire. The use of any of these medications was itemized as ‘use of any psychiatric medications.’ T. Marumoto, T. Journal of Pediatric Nursing 89 (2026) 1–8 Attributes of participants' children with ADHD The attributes of the children with ADHD included age, sex, diagnosis of comorbid developmental disorders (autism spectrum disorders, learning disorders, developmental coordination disorders, and others), and ADHD symptom severity. In case of having two or more children with ADHD, participants were required to respond with regard to the child with the highest burden. ADHD symptom severity was assessed using the Japanese version of home form of the ADHD-Rating Scale (ADHD-RS; Tani et al., 2010). A higher score indicates greater severity of ADHD symptoms. Cronbach's alpha coefficient of ADHD-RS in this study was 0.878. Parenting stressors We used the DDPSI, which was specifically developed to assess parenting stressors that are universally experienced by mothers of children with developmental disabilities, including ADHD, regardless of the child's age (Yamane, 2013). The18-item questionnaire comprises four factors and respondents were asked to rate the frequency of their experience for each item using a 4-point Likert scale: (1) difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs (six items, score range: 0–18), (2) anxiety about the child's future and independence (five items, score range: 0–15), (3) inadequate understanding of the child's disorder from others (four items, score range: 0–12), and (4) conflicting emotions with regard to the child's disorder (three items, score range: 0–9). A higher score on any factor indicates greater stressor experienced by the respondents. The Cronbach's alpha coefficients of the four factors in this study ranged from 0.721 to 0.868. Social support The Social Support Scale (Yamane, 2013) was used with some modifications. It comprises four items for instrumental and emotional support, such as ‘He/She is willing to talk to me about my child and discuss it with me,’ ‘He/She listens to my worries and complaints about parenting,’ ‘He/She cheers me up,’ and ‘He/She provides guidance, education, treatment, and assistance that is appropriate for my child.’ Providers of social support were established based on previous studies as ‘Spouse,’ ‘Parents (biological parent, parent-in-law),’ ‘Peer (a person met through a parents’ meeting),’ ‘Friends (other than a person met through a parents' meeting),’ ‘School (such as a teacher and a special education coordinator),’ and ‘Medical and welfare institution (such as a doctor and a psychologist).’ For each item, respondents were asked to rank the degree of expected support on a 4-point Likert scale (definitely no/probably no/probably yes/definitely yes). Score range of each social support is 4 to 16 and a higher score indicates a state in which respondents feel they can expect more support. The results of the principal component analysis for each of the six providers' support indicated that all had high loadings (0.80–0.93) and high contribution rates (72.96–83.76) for the first principal component, and all were confirmed to have a one-dimensional structure. The Cronbach's alpha coefficient for our respondents was 0.915 for the scale as a whole and 0.874–0.935 for the six provider's support. Maternal mental health We used the Japanese version of the K6, whose validity and reliability have been verified (Furukawa et al., 2008). The K6 is a scale designed to be sensitive around the threshold for the clinically significant range of the distribution of nonspecific distress (Kessler et al., 2003). Poor mental health was defined as a K6 score ≥9, which is one of the optimal cutoff points corresponding to DSM-IV (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition) mood disorders and anxiety disorders and is typically adopted for the Japanese population (Dhungel et al., 2021; Hamazaki et al., 2016; Miyaki et al., 2012; Takaki & Hibino, 2014; Takehara et al., 2020). The Cronbach's alpha coefficient for K6 in this study was 0.866. Statistical analysis First, the relationships between maternal mental health and participant attributes, attributes of participants' children with ADHD, parenting stressors, and social support were examined using univariate logistic regression analysis with mental health (K6 score ≤8/K6 score ≥9) as the dependent variable. P-value correction applying the Benjamini-Hochberg method was conducted for multiple test problems. Second, multivariate logistic regression analysis (forced entry method) was conducted with mental health as the dependent variable and variables related to mental health in univariate analysis as independent variables. Then, six multivariate logistic regression analyses were conducted with mental health as the dependent variable and the parenting stressors that had a significant association with mental health in the above multivariate logistic regression analysis (forced entry method) and each of six provider's social support as independent variables. In these six multivariate logistic regression analyses, participant attributes, attributes of participants' children with ADHD and parenting stressors which showed significant association with mental health in the univariate analysis were adjusted. In addition to the primary multivariate logistic regression analyses, we conducted sensitivity analyses to examine the robustness of our findings. Specifically, for both the initial multivariate logistic regression analysis and the six subsequent multivariate models, we constructed additional models that included clinically relevant potential confounders— maternal ADHD tendencies, use of any psychiatric medications, and comorbid developmental disorders—regardless of their statistical significance in the univariate analyses. In the analyses, parenting stressors and social support were divided into two categories by median split because none of their ten score distributions followed a normal distribution, as determined by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test (Supplementary Fig. S1). Before the multivariate logistic regression analysis, we examined the interrelationships between the independent variables and confirmed that there was no multicollinearity. IBM SPSS Statistics version 27 for Macintosh was used for all statistical analyses, and reported values were considered statistically significant at p < .05. Results Mean K6 score of all respondents was 8.5 ± 5.3, and 74 (49.7%) respondents had poor mental health (score ≥9). Table 1 shows the result of logistic regression analysis for mental health. In the univariate analysis, mental health showed significant association with parenting stressors of difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs (p < .001, odds ratio = 5.02), anxiety about the child's future and independence (p = .012, odds ratio = 2.92), inadequate understanding of the child's disorder from others (p = .006, odds ratio = 3.31), conflicting emotions with regard to the child's disorder (p = .014, odds ratio = 2.76), use of any psychiatric medications (p = .015, odds ratio = 5.19) and severity of their child's ADHD symptoms (p = .015, odds ratio = 1.05). In the multivariate analysis (forced entry method), parenting stressors of difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs (p = .039, odds ratio = 2.53) and use of any psychiatric medications (p = .005, odds ratio = 4.94) had a significant association with mental health. The overall logistic regression model was statistically significant (χ2(6) = 40.06, p < .001), indicating that the predictors collectively contributed to the model. The six multivariate logistic regression analyses are presented in Table 2. Although all forms of social support had no independent relationship with mental health, only Model 6, with the inclusion of social 3

support from medical and welfare institution, showed the vanishing of the significant association between the ‘difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs’ stressor and mental health (p = .061, odds ratio = 2.35). The results of sensitivity analyses after adjusting for potential confounders were also consistent with the main findings (Supplementary Tables S1 and S2), indicating that the observed associations remained robust. Discussion We aimed to identify parenting stressors which have an impact on maternal mental health as well as social support which buffer these effects in mothers of children with ADHD. First, this study revealed that among parenting stressors measured by DDPSI, ‘difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs’ was associated with maternal mental health. This may be consistent with the fact that this factor explains the highest proportion of the variance in the DDPSI (Yamane, 2013). The factor ‘difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs’ was composed of questionnaire items such as ‘I did not really know what my child was thinking,’ ‘It was difficult for me to understand the needs and desires of my child,’ and ‘I did not know what to do for my child when they caused problems.’ This supports our hypotheses and suggests that reducing the parenting stressor of ‘difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs’ is vital to preventing mental health problems in mothers of children with ADHD. At the 4

same time, it should be noted that the relationship between the parenting stressor and maternal mental health may be bidirectional. While our findings suggest that the parenting stressor contributes to poor mental health, it is also possible that maternal psychological distress exacerbates perceptions of parenting difficulties. In addition to parenting stressors, use of any psychiatric medications showed a strong independent association with poor maternal mental health in the multivariate analysis (odds ratio = 4.94). This variable likely reflects a complex clinical context. On one hand, it may serve as a marker of more severe preexisting or concurrent mental health conditions requiring pharmacological treatment. On the other hand, psychiatric medication use may also be a consequence of unmanaged parenting stress. Given the cross-sectional design of the study, the causal relationships among parenting stressors, psychiatric medication use, and maternal mental health cannot be determined. Nonetheless, the magnitude of this association highlights the importance of considering psychiatric medication use as a key covariate when examining maternal mental health among mothers of children with ADHD. In each analysis, variables related to mental health in univariate analysis such as ‘use of any psychiatric medications,’ ‘child's severity of ADHD symptoms,’ parenting stressors of ‘anxiety about the child's future and independence,’ parenting stressors of ‘inadequate understanding of the child's disorder from others,’ and parenting stressors of ‘conflicting emotions with regard to the child's disorder’ were adjusted. Second, contrary to previous studies (Chou, Hsiao, Chang and Yen, 2021; Yamane, 2013), this study found no direct association between any social support and mental health, but it revealed that only social support from medical and welfare institution buffers the negative impact of the parenting stressor ‘difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs’ on mental health. It should be noted that although a previous intervention study demonstrated improvements in parental mental health through behavioral parent training (Mehri et al., 2020a), the present study clarified that such support appeared to function as a factor buffering the association between the parenting stressor and maternal mental health. The difference between our findings and previous studies should be interpreted with methodological and conceptual differences. Prior studies demonstrating improvements in parental mental health were based on randomized controlled trial designs that evaluated the effects of clearly defined and structured behavioral parent training interventions. In contrast, the present study was conducted in a naturalistic setting using an online survey. Moreover, social support from medical and welfare institution in our study was not limited to behavioral parent training but included broader forms of support such as instrumental support and emotional support. It is well known that pediatricians, psychologists, and staffs of welfare support facilities provide behavioral parent training, which is an educational approach of teaching parenting skills to parents of children with ADHD (Evans, Owens and Bunford, 2014). In Japan, behavioral parent training is the primary social support offered by medical and welfare institution (Makino et al., 2018; Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, 2021). Behavioral parent training has been reported to improve parenting behaviors and mental health in parents of children with ADHD (Mehri et al., 2020a; Rimestad et al., 2019). It should be noted that the change in odds ratio was small (from 2.53 to 2.35), and the shift in pvalue was also marginal (from 0.039 to 0.061). Therefore, further research is needed to validate the findings of the buffering effect of social support provided by medical and welfare institution. In addition, from a clinical perspective, future research should explore the differential impact of various types of support. The social support scale used in this study included both instrumental support (e.g., providing guidance, education, treatment, and assistance tailored to the child's needs) and emotional support (e.g., listening to concerns and offering empathy regarding parenting). However, the scale was not originally designed to distinguish between these two types of support in analysis. Further studies are needed to examine which type of support is more effective in buffering parenting stressors in clinical settings. Strengths and limitations This study has several strengths. First, to our knowledge, this is the first study to identify the specific parenting stressor associated with 5

poor mental health as well as the social support that buffers against parenting stressor in mothers of children with ADHD. Furthermore, beyond clinical settings, these findings may also inform public health and policy strategies. By identifying which parenting stressor affects maternal mental health and which providers' social support are effective in buffering these effects, this study provides evidence to guide the development of parent-focused interventions and the prioritization of support resources. Importantly, such distinctions have not been clearly addressed in previous research. These insights may contribute to the development of more targeted and effective intervention strategies, as well as resource allocation efforts aimed at promoting maternal wellbeing among mothers of children with ADHD. T. Marumoto, T. Monma, Y. Sawae et al. Journal of Pediatric Nursing 89 (2026) 1–8 However, this study has several limitations. First, it was a crosssectional study, and we could not prove causal relationships between mental health, parenting stressors, and social support. Thus, future longitudinal studies are required. Second, the sample size for this study was relatively small. Considering the possibility that the voluntary nature of the online survey and its distribution via support groups may have led to selection bias, we cannot rule out that the respondents are not representative of the population; specifically, these mothers have already reached to support groups, potentially leading to an underestimation of stress and mental health issues in the broader population. Third, in the analyses in this study, parenting stressors and social support were divided into two categories by median split because the distribution of both was bimodal with peaks at both ends of the median. However, this median split has not been clinically validated, there are interpretation limitations for a high vs low comparison based on this samplebased values. Specifically, dichotomizing continuous variables may reduce statistical power, obscure variability, and limit the interpretability of the results. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted with caution. Alternative approaches using standardized continuous scores or quantile regression should be considered in future research to preserve statistical power and information. Fourth, the survey used a self-report questionnaire that may have introduced reporting and recall biases. Further studies using objective measurements such as expert ratings of clinical symptoms would be useful. Fifth, it should be noted that our study is limited to Japanese mothers and may not be generalizable to other countries and contexts. Sixth, although the children in our sample spanned a wide age range, we were unable to conduct detailed analyses stratified by child age due to the limited sample size. Future studies with larger samples are needed. Implications to practice The findings of this study have several implications for clinical practice. First, the results suggest that the parenting stressor of ‘difficulty in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs’ may play a key role in poor maternal mental health among mothers of children with ADHD. Therefore, clinical support for these mothers should not only focus on managing the child's symptoms but also address this parenting stressor. Second, the present findings suggest that social support from medical and welfare institution may buffer the negative impact of the parenting stressor on maternal mental health. In clinical settings, pediatricians working at medical institutions in departments such as child psychiatry, and clinical psychologists working at developmental disability support centers may play an important role in providing such support. In addition to offering behavioral parent training and practical guidance for managing children's behaviors, professionals in medical and welfare institutions should also provide emotional support to mothers of children with ADHD by offering reassurance and encouragement and by listening to their concerns and difficulties related to child rearing. Furthermore, the social support scale used in this study included both instrumental support, such as providing guidance, education, treatment, and assistance tailored to the child's needs, and emotional support, such as listening to concerns and offering empathy regarding parenting. These findings suggest that both types of support may be important components of clinical care for families of children with ADHD. Although the present study was not designed to distinguish their relative contributions, integrating both practical guidance and empathic communication into routine clinical interactions may help improve maternal poor mental health. Conclusion This study showed that the stressor of difficulties in understanding the child and coping with the child's needs was associated with poor maternal mental health and that social support from medical and welfare institution buffered the impact of this parenting stressor on maternal mental health. These findings will contribute to developing measures to improve mental health in mothers of children with ADHD. metadata_title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Predictors of Adult Psychiatric Outcomes of Childhood Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
pages: META-ANALYSIS Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Predictors of Adult Psychiatric Outcomes of Childhood Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Noa E. van der Plasa,b,*, MSc , Siri D.S. Noordermeera,b, PhD , Jaap Oosterlaana,b,c,d, PhD , Marjolein Lumana,b,e, PhD Objective: Psychiatric disorders are highly prevalent in adults with childhood-onset attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Currently, little is known about childhood predictors for these outcomes. Method: PubMed, PsychInfo, Web of Science, and EMBASE were searched until June 2024. Eligible studies investigated childhood predictors of persistent ADHD,substanceusedisorders (SUDs),conductdisorder,antisocialpersonalitydisorder,majordepressivedisorder(MDD),and/oranxietydisordersinadults diagnosed with childhood ADHD (PROSPERO #CRD42022320887). Meta-analytic models were tested when N 3 for a predictor with similar effect measures, otherwise predictors were discussed narratively when N 2. The Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) was used to assess study quality. Results: The selected 36 studies included 119 predictors, with 10 predictors eligible for meta-analyses. History of stimulant treatment (odds ratio [OR] 1⁄4 1.88, 95% CI 1⁄4 1.28-2.75, p 1⁄4 .001) was associated with increased, and higher childhood IQ with decreased (OR 1⁄4 0.99, 95% CI 1⁄4 0.981.00, p 1⁄4.039), risk of ADHD persistence in adulthood. ADHD persistence was associated with increased risk of SUDs (OR 1⁄4 2.12, 95% CI 1⁄4 1.533.17, p 1⁄4.004) and MDD (OR 1⁄4 3.19, 95% CI 1⁄4 1.71-5.95, p <.001). Narratively reviewed predictors of fair/good quality studies showed potential predictors for ADHD persistence (ie, ADHD combined type, hyperactive/impulsive symptoms, anxiety disorders, externalizing problems, social dysfunctioning, and socioeconomic status). Conclusion: We confirmed earlier reported childhood predictors (ie, stimulant treatment history, ADHD persistence) and identified potential new predictors (ie, childhood anxiety disorders, social problems, socioeconomic status) for psychiatric outcomes of ADHD. However, the available literature is hampered by methodological shortcomings. Future studies should focus on studying combined effects of potential predictors. Plain language summary: This study systematically evaluated previous research on risk factors for adult psychiatric outcomes of children diagnosed with ADHD. Results showed that those adults who were treated with stimulant medication were twice as likely to still have ADHD in adulthood. Those adults who still had ADHD were at greater risk for also having a substance use disorder and depressive disorder. Study registration information: Predictors of Long-term Psychiatric Outcomes of Childhood ADHD in Adulthood: a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42022320887 Key words: ADHD; mental disorders; comorbidity; risk factors; cohort studies J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2026;65(2):231-249. ttention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a predominantly childhood-onset neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a persistent pattern of hyperactive-impulsive and/or inattentive behaviors.1 The developmental trajectory of ADHD is highly variable, ranging from full remittance to full persistence. Approximately 75% of individuals with ADHD experience remittance of their ADHD diagnosis at a certain point, but impairing symptoms of ADHD persist in the majority of the cases.2,3 Meta-analyzed point estimations of ADHD persistence rates range between 3.3% and 25.7%, depending on the type of sample (clinical vs populationbased), diagnostic classification system and diagnostic tools used, sex distribution of the sample, and geographic region.4,5 However, in cohort studies with clinical samples, the ADHD persistence rates reported are often higher, up to 77%.3 Although the long-term outcome of childhood ADHD is heterogeneous, many individuals show impairments due to their ADHD symptoms and the development of comorbid problems.6 Childhood ADHD is an early warning sign for later psychopathology, both for adults with persistent ADHD and for those with remitted childhood ADHD.7,8 Childhood ADHD increases the risk for developing psychiatric outcomes by 2.5 times.9 Besides ADHD persistence, the most common psychiatric adult outcomes of childhood ADHD include substance use disorders (SUDs; estimated prevalence 21%-36%), mood disorders (eg, major A Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry www.jaacap.org 231 Volume 65 / Number 2 / February 2026

depressive disorder [MDD]; estimated prevalence 21-22%), anxiety disorders (eg, generalized anxiety disorder [GAD]; estimated prevalence 23%-25%), and disorders involving antisocial behavior (eg, conduct disorder [CD] and antisocial personality disorder [ASPD], estimated prevalence 27%-34%).1,10 These outcomes have a negative impact on global and daily functioning,9,11 including an increased risk for long-term work disability, delinquency, negative life events, suicidality, and premature death.12-16 Identifying predictors of prevalent psychiatric outcomes in adults with childhood ADHD is important,11 as this may open up possibilities for early intervention, enhance outcomes, and reduce health care costs.17 A substantial number of studies have addressed predictors for adult psychiatric outcomes of childhood ADHD. The only available review aggregated 16 studies on predictors for ADHD (symptom) persistence and reported higher ADHD severity, receiving pharmacological treatment for ADHD, comorbid CD, and comorbid MDD to be predictive of ADHD persistence into adulthood.18 There is currently no review or meta-analysis on predictors other than ADHD (symptom persistence) on adult psychiatric outcomes of childhood ADHD.1,18 The current systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to aggregate existing longitudinal studies focusing on childhood predictors for the development of the most common psychiatric outcomes in adults diagnosed with childhood ADHD, including ADHD persistence, SUDs, CD, ASPD, MDD, and anxiety disorders. We critically appraised the current state of evidence, and formulated recommendations for future research. METHOD Design The systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in agreement with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) criteria (PRISMA checklists are outlined in Table S1 and Table S2, available online).19 The study protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; #CRD42022320887). Study Selection Studies were selected if they met the following criteria: (1) contained a sample of adults with a childhood ADHD diagnosis (according to DSM-III, ICD-9, or later versions), where childhood ADHD should have been diagnosed before the age of 18 years, or retrospectively by reliable clinical interviews; (2) investigated childhood (mean age <18 years) predictors of most prevalent (estimated prevalence 20%) adult (mean age 18 years) DSM- or ICD-based psychiatric outcomes (ie, persistent ADHD, SUDs, CD, ASPD, MDD, and/or anxiety disorders [GAD, agoraphobia, social phobia, panic disorder, and specific phobia]); (3) used a retrospective or longitudinal design, where the sample was measured at least at 2 time points, of which at least 1 measurement took place at a mean age of <18 years and at least 1 measurement at a mean age of 18 years; and (4) was published in a peer-reviewed journal (last search May 2024). PubMed, PsychInfo, Web of Science, and EMBASE (including MEDLINE) were searched for relevant studies, combining search terms of ADHD, predictors, and adult psychiatric outcomes (full search strategy in Supplement 1). Reference lists were searched for additional studies. The Web app Rayyan was used to detect duplicates.20 Two raters (NP, and either DJ, ML, SN, or JO) independently judged articles for eligibility based on titles and abstracts. Thereafter, fulltext articles were checked by 2 raters for eligibility. If studies reported on overlapping samples, a hierarchical selection process was used to select one study. Preferably, the study was selected that reported on the largest number of predictors. If multiple studies had the same number of predictors, we the study with the longest follow-up interval (ie, the oldest age at assessment) was selected. Data Extraction The first 60% of the data extraction was done in duplicate (NP, DJ), and the remainder was done by one of the authors (NP). Extracteddataincludedtotalsamplesize,sex distribution,ageat last follow-up, ADHD subgroups and accompanying group size, attrition rates, statistical approach, reported effect sizes of the statistical model, risk factors studied, statistical controls, and psychiatric outcomes. Findings of studies that investigated predictors that assessed highly similar constructs were merged: findings were pooled for the presence/absence of the following: (1) oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) and CD, (2) parental psychiatric problems, (3) maternal psychiatric problems, (4) paternal psychiatric problems, (5) educational difficulties, and (6) family stress factors (Table S3, available online; Table S3 also includes all operationalizations of predictors found in at least 2 studies). Likewise, several outcome measures were merged, including outcomes of (1) SUDs and (2) anxiety disorders (ie, panic disorder, social anxiety disorder, separation anxiety disorder, specific phobia, selective mutism, GAD, and agoraphobia). Study Quality Two raters independently assessed study quality using the Newcastle–Ottawa Quality Assessment Scale (NOS) for cohort studies (Supplement 2, available online).21 232 www.jaacap.org Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Volume 65 / Number 2 / February 2026 VAN DER PLAS et al.

Inconsistencies in ratings were solved by consensus and, if needed, by discussion with a third rater. Studies were classified as poor, fair, or good quality corresponding to the Agency for Health Research and Quality standard.22 Statistical Analyses Multivariate meta-analysis was used to account for studies that included several effect sizes of the same predictor of the studied psychiatric outcomes. This analysis used 3 levels, which included the following: (1) primary study summary statistics (ie, all relevant effect sizes provided by 1 study); (2) nested within study (ie, 1 effect size per study); and (3) nested within 1 effect size (ie, meta-analysis of 1 effect size across all studies) to control for several effect sizes within 1 study. Robust variance estimation was used to provide valid standard errors of the point estimates and valid significance tests.23 All multivariate meta-analyses used a random-effects model to calculate aggregated point estimates using R.24 Where possible, effect sizes were selected that adjusted for the largest number of possible confounding variables of a study, irrespective of the type of confounder (eg, age, sex, ADHD severity) to better approximate the true effect of the specific predictor. The Higgins I2 index was measured and the Cochran Q test was conducted to indicate heterogeneity among studies. Only cases of potential high heterogeneity were reported in the text. If a meta-analysis was not feasible (ie, when there were fewer than 3 studies looking at a specific predictor or when effect sizes were not comparable), a narrative review was provided for those predictors of a particular psychiatric outcome included in at least 2 studies. The narrative systematic review reported terms of evidence as follows: (1) evidence for an association, if all studies found an association; (2) some evidence for an association, if a study/some studies found an association and a study/some studies did not; (3) evidence for no association, if all studies found no association. Figure 1 provides a flowchart of decisions made for our analyses. For the narrative review, multiple effect sizes of the same predictor of the psychiatric outcomes studied were first averaged within studies to have each study contributing a single effect size per predictor to the narrative review, where possible using odds ratios (ORs) or hazard ratios (HRs). When merging was not possible (eg, for studies that did not report effect sizes), we assumed the following: evidence for no association, if all effect sizes or the majority of the effect sizes were nonsignificant; evidence for an association, if all effect sizes or the majority of the effect sizes were significant; some evidence for an association, if the effect sizes were equally divided between significant and nonsignificant. Sensitivity analyses for the multivariate meta-analyses and narrative review were performed excluding poorquality studies. RESULTS The systematic search revealed a total of 2,729 unique studies (Figure S1, available online). Of these, 2,558 studies were excluded at the title/abstract level and 133 after fulltext assessment (Supplement 3). In total, 34 prospective and 2 retrospective longitudinal studies in adults with childhood ADHD were included, with 17 studies looking into ADHD persistence, 19 studies into SUDs, 4 studies into CD, 5 studies into ASPD, 8 studies into MDD, and 4 studies into anxiety disorders (Table 125-59; Tables S4-S9, available online). Studies reported on several predictors for each outcome (Tables S10 and S11, available online). The available data allowed multivariate meta-analyses of 10 predictors of ADHD persistence, SUDs, MDD, and anxiety disorders (Table 2). A narrative review was provided for a subsequent 31 predictors that were studied at least twice. Of 36 studies, 16 were of fair or good study quality (Tables S12-S14, available online). Notably, 53% of studies did not control for any confounding variables. Predictors of ADHD Persistence Five predictors of ADHD persistence were included in the meta-analyses (Table 2). A childhood history of stimulant treatment (OR 1⁄4 1.88, 95% CI 1.28-2.75, p 1⁄4 .001) was associated with an increased risk for a persistent course of ADHD,29,32,36,37 and a higher childhood Full Scale IQ (OR 1⁄4 0.99, 95% CI 1⁄4 0.98-1.00, p 1⁄4 .039) was associated with a decreased risk.7,33,37,53 Severity of childhood ADHD-related impairment was not associated with adulthood ADHD persistence (OR 1⁄4 2.12, 95% CI 1⁄4 0.994.54, p 1⁄4 .054),29,37,44 and findings showed potentially high heterogeneity among studies (Q[2] 1⁄4 10.44, p 1⁄4 .005, I2 1⁄4 76.9%). Furthermore, childhood ODD/CD (OR 1⁄4 1.03, 95% CI 1⁄4 0.87-1.24, p 1⁄4 .564),7,30,32,37,44 and male sex (OR 1⁄4 0.93, 95% CI 1⁄4 0.71-1.23 p 1⁄4 .621)7,32,36,37,53 were not associated with ADHD persistence. Sensitivity analyses excluding poor quality studies for predictors of adulthood ADHD persistence did not change the results for ADHD-related impairment,29,37,44 stimulant treatment history,29,36,37 and male sex,36,37,53 with the single exception that the association for childhood Full-Scale IQ became nonsignificant (Table S13, available online).33,37,53 An additional 25 predictors for ADHD persistence were included in the narrative review (Table 2). Sensitivity analyses excluding poor quality studies (10 of 17 studies) showed some evidence for the following predictors being associated with an increased risk of ADHD persistence: ADHD combined type,37,44 hyperactive/ impulsive symptoms,29,33,36,37 anxiety disorders,29,30 externalizing problems,29,33,36,37,50 social dysfunctioning,29,33 and low socioeconomic status.29,33,36,53 There was evidence for no association for ADHD hyperactiveimpulsive type,37,44 inattention symptoms,29,33,36,37 mood disorders,29,44 internalizing problems,29,33 paternal psychopathology,29,44 maternal psychopathology,29,44 and family stress factors.29,44,53 Too few studies with fair/good quality were left for a narrative review of the remaining predictors. Predictors of SUDs Three predictors were included in the meta-analysis for SUDs in adulthood (Table 2). ADHD persistence was associated with an increased risk of SUDs in adulthood (OR 1⁄4 2.20, 95% CI 1⁄4 1.26-3.85, p 1⁄4 .018),7,30,32,57,59 whereas stimulant treatment (OR 1⁄4 1.41, 95% CI 1⁄4 0.72-2.75, p 1⁄4 .142)45,56,57 and ODD/CD (HR 1⁄4 2.09, 95% CI 1⁄4 0.60-7.30, p 1⁄4 .104)35,55,57 in childhood were not. Findings for ADHD persistence showed moderate-tohigh heterogeneity (Q[2] 1⁄4 25.84, p 1⁄4 .004, I2 1⁄4 59.7%). After exclusion of poor quality studies, too few effect sizes were available for a meta-analysis. In addition, 3 childhood predictors were included in the narrative review (Table 3). There was some evidence for later age at initiation of stimulant treatment being associated with an increased risk of SUDs in adulthood.26,35 For ADHD combined type56,57 and stimulant treatment duration,26,35,49 there was evidence for no association. Sensitivity analyses excluding poor quality studies showed that there was evidence for no association for stimulant treatment duration.26,49 Too few studies were left for a narrative review of the remaining predictors. Predictors of CD No predictors of CD were eligible for meta-analysis. Narratively, there was some evidence that childhood stimulant treatment history was associated with an increased risk of adult CD (Table 3).27,56 Too few studies were left for narrative review after exclusion of the poor quality studies. Predictors of ASPD No predictors of ASPD were eligible for meta-analysis. One predictor was included in the narrative review, showing that persistent ADHD was associated with an increased risk of adult ASPD (Table 3).38,59 However, this result was based on 2 poor quality studies. Predictors of MDD One predictor of MDD was included in the meta-analysis (Table 2), showing ADHD persistence to be associated with an increased risk of MDD in adulthood (OR 1⁄4 3.19, 95% CI 1⁄4 1.71-5.95, p < .001).7,30,54,59 After exclusion of poor quality studies, too few effect sizes were available for a meta-analysis. DISCUSSION This meta-analysis and systematic review is the first to aggregate results on a large variety of childhood assessed predictors of adult psychiatric outcomes of childhood ADHD, including ADHD persistence, SUDs, CD, ASPD, MDD, and anxiety disorders. We identified 36 studies, including 119 unique predictors. Most outcomes were considered in few studies, and 66% of all predictors were studied only once. The available data allowed meta-analyses of 10 predictors, and 31 predictors were narratively reviewed. Only 44% of all included studies were of fair/ good study quality. Our meta-analytic results demonstrated that a history of childhood stimulant treatment was associated with an increased risk for ADHD persistence into adulthood, whereas higher IQ was associated with a decreased risk. ADHD persistence was not associated with childhood assessed ADHD-related impairment, ODD/CD, or sex. Although ADHD persistence was associated with an increased risk of SUDs and MDD in adulthood, ADHD persistence was not associated with an increased risk for adulthood anxiety disorders. Adulthood SUDs were not predicted by childhood ODD/CD or stimulant treatment. Sensitivity analysis excluding poor quality studies replicated most meta-analytic findings for ADHD persistence as outcome, showing an association with stimulant treatment history, and no association with ADHD-related impairment and sex, with the single exception that childhood IQ no longer was associated with an increased risk for ADHD persistence. Limiting the narrative review to fair/good quality studies, our narrative results revealed 7 additional potential childhood predictors (showing some evidence) of ADHD persistence, including ADHD combined type, hyperactive/ impulsive symptoms, anxiety disorders, externalizing problems, social dysfunctioning, and socioeconomic status. Furthermore, fair/good studies showed no evidence that adult ADHD persistence was predicted by childhood ADHD hyperactive-impulsive type, inattention symptoms, mood disorders, internalizing problems, paternal psychopathology, maternal psychopathology, and family stress factors; and no evidence that SUDs in adulthood were predicted by childhood stimulant treatment duration. However, there was large heterogeneity in our findings across studies. Also, some studies provided several effect sizes per potential predictor, which we dealt with by averaging effect sizes to obtain a single conclusion. However, this approach was limited by the assumption of equal weight of each effect size. Therefore, it is important to interpret the narrative results with caution. ADHD Persistence Into Adulthood The meta-analytic results for adult ADHD persistence in relation to childhood stimulant treatment history and sex confirm the findings of an earlier meta-analysis by Caye et al.,18 except that we found an association for childhood IQ and no association for childhood ODD/CD and severity of ADHD-related impairment. A possible explanation for the discrepancy in the findings on ODD/CD is that our systematic review included only clinical samples with an ADHD diagnosis and looked at a persistent diagnosis of ADHD, whereas the meta-analysis of Caye et al.18 also included (subclinical) samples of hyperactive children and included persistent ADHD symptoms as outcome. It is possible that ODD/CD is predictive of ADHD symptom persistence, but not of a diagnosis of ADHD in clinical samples. Furthermore, the results regarding impairment were not significant, despite all individual studies reporting significant odds ratios. Substantial heterogeneity between effect sizes likely contributed to our finding, possibly due to different operationalizations of impairment between studies and differences between studies in the adjustment for possible confounding variables. More specifically, 1 study adjusted for age and residence,37 whereas the other 2 studies did not provide adjusted effect sizes,29,37 which might introduce additional heterogeneity. With regard to our surprising finding on childhood IQ, which reached significance in predicting adult persistent ADHD, the effect was very small, with the confidence interval including a rounded 1. Moreover, IQ was no longer significant after removing 1 poor quality study,18 indicating that this finding may not have been very robust and may warrant further investigation. Furthermore, our meta-analysis showed that a childhood history of stimulant treatment was associated with a doubled risk for a persistent course of ADHD in adulthood. Although stimulant treatment has often been reported as a protective factor for a range of ADHD-related outcomes,60 it is also related to higher symptom severity and level of impairment during time of prescription, suggesting that the most affected children may receive stimulant treatment, which potentially increases the relationship between childhood stimulant treatment and adulthood ADHD persistence.61 Importantly, studies included in our meta-analyses on stimulant treatment did not control for severity of impairment, stressing the need to look at combined effects of predictors in future studies. The narrative results of fair/good quality studies hint toward the relevance of childhood symptom severity (symptoms of ADHD, anxiety, and externalizing problems) in predicting ADHD persistence in adulthood, corresponding to results from a previous narrative review.62 In addition, (low) childhood SES might be a relevant factor. In an earlier meta-analysis, SES was not associated with an increased risk for ADHD persistence18; however, in that study, the investigators disregarded study quality and included 1 poor quality study without an effect (out of 3 studies). Furthermore, participants with lower SES might be more often lost to follow-up,63 and as low SES increases risk for receiving an ADHD diagnosis in childhood,64 SES should be further studied as a potential predictor. Our narrative review of fair/good quality studies showed no specific evidence of childhood maternal or paternal psychopathology as a predictive factor, but 1 good quality study did hint toward the predictive value of parental psychopathology as a risk factor for ADHD persistence. In addition, we found a predictive effect of maternal psychopathology driven by a poor quality study, also hinting toward potential relevance of parental psychopathology. Similarly, the earlier meta-analysis18 remained inconclusive on the role of parental psychopathology for ADHD persistence. Parental psychopathology is an umbrella term for several psychiatric problems and is thought to act as a risk factor for an ADHD diagnosis in childhood.65 Our results suggest that although it may influence ADHD in childhood, it may not be associated with ADHD persistence into adulthood. Potentially, only specific aspects of parental psychopathology may have an impact on persistence.65 In contrast to our findings, Caye et al.18 identified childhood comorbid MDD as a predictor for adult ADHD persistence.18 However, the single study with an effect was excluded in our systematic review, as the sample overlapped66 with another, more recent, included study (without an effect).44 To summarize, childhood stimulant treatment history was associated with an increased risk of adult ADHD persistence, whereas sex was not. The inconsistent findings of childhood ADHD–related impairment, ODD/CD, and IQ warrant further investigation. In addition, potential childhood predictors of adult ADHD persistence that should be further investigated, preferably by meta-analyses, include ADHD combined type, hyperactive/impulsive symptoms, anxiety disorders, externalizing problems, social dysfunctioning, thought problems, parental psychopathology, and socioeconomic status. Psychiatric Outcomes Other Than ADHD Persistence in Adulthood Our meta-analytic results showed that a persistent course of childhood ADHD was associated with an increased risk of SUDs and MDD in adulthood by more than 2 and 3 times, respectively, corroborating previous findings.1 A persistent course of childhood ADHD was defined by a diagnosis of Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry www.jaacap.org 245 Volume 65 / Number 2 / February 2026 ADULT PSYCHIATRIC OUTCOMES OF ADHD

ADHD in childhood that was subsequently confirmed in adulthood, reflecting not only childhood ADHD but also adult ADHD. Therefore, alternatively, SUDs and MDD may also be the result of the presence of adult ADHD. However, the underlying mechanism linking ADHD and SUDs or MDD is likely due to a shared neurobiological and familial/genetic underpinnings of the disorders, suggesting that a persistent course of childhood ADHD may indeed be related to an enhanced risk of SUDs and MDD in adulthood.67,68 Furthermore, in agreement with a recent review, SUDs were not associated with a childhood history of stimulant treatment.69 Finally, our results indicate that childhood ODD/CD was not associated with SUDs in adulthood. Despite the ongoing debate (see, for example, Groenman et al.70), our finding suggests that ODD/CD is not driving the risk for SUDs in individuals with ADHD. Narratively, too few fair/good qualities studies were left to identify potential predictors of SUDs, CD, ASPD, and MDD. For adult anxiety disorder, we found no evidence that ADHD persistence acts as a risk factor. Our findings build upon suggestions based on the results of another review on the relationship between ADHD and anxiety disordeers,71 suggesting that future studies should include other predictors (such as internalizing problems, trauma, childhood aggression, or difficulties making friends) when studying the development of anxiety disorders in individuals with ADHD.72 Clearly, the current meta-analyses were limited by the number of available studies and by the types of predictors and outcomes studied. We suggest that future studies into the psychiatric long-term outcomes of childhood ADHD take the following recommendations into account. First, studies should include a wide range of potential predictors, including genetic, prenatal, perinatal, neuroimaging, neurocognitive, environmental, psychological, and social factors, to gain a better understanding of the mechanisms that play a role in the development of adult psychiatric outcomes.1,73-76 Second, existing studies rely on linear statistical models including single predictors that do not capture the complex (nonlinear) relations between predictors and adult psychiatric outcomes of ADHD. Machine learning might offer promising possibilities, as becomes evident in the wider medical field.77,78 Third, studies should investigate other highly impairing, albeit less prevalent, outcomes, to capture all of the psychiatric outcomes of ADHD, including eating disorders or obsessive-compulsive disorder.79,80 Fourth, studies should improve on the adjustment for confounders, as this was the primary reason for qualifying almost half of the studies as studies of poor quality. No studies controlled for CD, MDD, or anxiety disorders in childhood, whereas they did study the presence of these disorders in adults, thereby complicating identification of causal effects. Also, hardly any studies controlled for ADHD severity in childhood. Ideally, future studies should adjust for a standardized set of covariates, such as sex, age, and severity of ADHD-related impairment in childhood, and childhood presence of the psychiatric outcome at hand to be better able to approximate the true effect. Finally, the current meta-analysis was susceptible to ecological fallacy due to the availability of summary data instead of individual participant data. Therefore, we call for studies to share individual participant data to facilitate individual patient data meta analysis (IPDMA). Ideally, an IPDMA would generate larger sample sizes, increasing the power to detect predictors for psychiatric outcomes of ADHD with lower prevalences (eg, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, schizophrenia), which were not included in the current study. The current meta-analysis and narrative review studied predictors of adult psychiatric outcomes of childhood ADHD, including ADHD persistence, SUDs, CD, ASPD, MDD, and anxiety disorders. Our meta-analysis added to the existing evidence of some earlier reported predictors (ie, history of stimulant treatment as predictor for ADHD persistence), and was the first to meta-analytically identify additional predictors (ie, ADHD persistence as predictor for adult SUD and MDD). Narratively (including only fair/good quality studies), we identified potential new predictors including thought and social problems, anxiety disorders, and socioeconomic status for ADHD persistence. No other predictors of adult psychiatric outcomes were identified, possibly due to limitations in available literature (eg, clinical and methodological heterogeneity, poor study quality) and the statistical approaches used. Finally, we highlighted avenues for future research to deepen our understanding of childhood predictors of adult ADHD psychiatric outcomes. metadata_title: Noninvasive Brain Stimulation in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Treatment Efficacy and Targeting Strategies
pages: META-ANALYSIS Noninvasive Brain Stimulation in Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Treatment Efficacy and Targeting Strategies Qiuxing Chen a,b,c,# , MM , Nanfang Pan a,b,c,d,# , MD , Yajing Long a,b,c,# , MD , Kun Qin e , PhD , Arshiya Sangchooli d , MD, MPhil , Ying Cao a,b,c , MM , Manpreet K. Singh f , MD, MS , Ying Chen a,b,c, *, MD, Qiyong Gong a,b,c,g, *, MD, PhD # Qiuxing Chen, Nanfang Pan, and Yajing Long contributed equally to this work. Objective: Noninvasive brain stimulation (NIBS) has emerged as a promising novel treatment for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, the precise effects of NIBS in ADHD as well as optimal stimulation protocols remain elusive. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to provide a rigorous evaluation and robust quantified evidence on the therapeutic efficacy of NIBS in ADHD. Method: A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase identified 59 studies (repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation [rTMS]: 11; transcranial direct current stimulation [tDCS]: 35; other NIBS: 13). Of these, 33 randomized controlled trial studies (7 for rTMS, 26 for tDCS; 1,049 participants with ADHD) were included in meta-analyses of therapeutic efficacy. Subgroup analyses were performed to investigate the impact of stimulation targets on therapeutic outcomes, and meta-regression analyses were included to evaluate the dose-response relationship. Results: NIBS has favorable tolerability, but evidence for its therapeutic efficacy in ADHD remains inconclusive. Meta-analyses indicated that rTMS was effective in alleviating inattention symptoms (Hedges’ g = − 1.44, p = .002), reducing hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms (Hedges’ g = − 0.95, p = .005), and improving attention-related functions (Hedges’ g = 0.53, p = .023), and tDCS showed therapeutic benefits in reducing hyperactivity/ impulsivity symptoms (Hedges’ g = − 0.28, p = .024) and improving inhibitory control (Hedges’ g = 0.39, p = .028). tDCS positioned over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and right orbitofrontal cortex demonstrated significant effects in improving inhibitory control. No significant doseresponse relationship was found for either tDCS or rTMS in ADHD. Conclusion: This meta-analysis supports the therapeutic potential of NIBS in ADHD, revealing domain-specific benefits across different stimulation devices and sites. Although more data are needed, NIBS shows promise as an intervention for ADHD. Plain language summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis investigated the role of noninvasive brain stimulation in the treatment of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Drawing on data from 33 randomized controlled trial studies with 1,049 participants, the authors found that repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) was associated with improved attention and reduced hyperactivity/impulsivity, while transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) helped enhance inhibitory control and reduce hyperactivity/impulsivity. The effectiveness was linked to which brain region was stimulated. These results suggest that noninvasive brain stimulation may be a valuable treatment option for individuals with ADHD, particularly for those who do not respond well to standard medications. ttention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is characterized by age-inappropriate symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. 1 Pharmacotherapy (eg, psychostimulants) is currently the first-line treatment for ADHD, 2 but it may be associated with potential risks of misuse and addiction. 3 Further, individuals with ADHD may develop therapeutic tolerance following prolonged pharmacological treatment, rendering conventional medications less effective. 4 ADHD medications also have adverse effects that primarily stem from their nonspecific actions in the brain. For example, psychostimulants broadly modulate dopamine and norepinephrine neurotransmission across multiple neural circuits, rather than selectively affecting pathological pathways involved in specific ADHD symptom domains. 5 Noninvasive brain stimulation (NIBS) includes a group of techniques that modulate brain activity externally and target specific brain regions that induce neuroplasticity. 6,7 NIBS has emerged as a promising therapeutic intervention in psychiatry, initially demonstrating efficacy in treating major depressive disorder through targeted stimulation of the left prefrontal cortex to encourage cortical inhibition necessary for adaptive mood regulation. 8 Building on this success, application of NIBS expanded to obsessivecompulsive disorder, where it alleviated symptoms by targeting dysfunction in prefrontal-striatal circuits. 9 Given these encouraging outcomes in modulating prefrontal function and associated neural networks, NIBS has been introduced as a potential therapeutic approach for ADHD. Commonly used methods for ADHD include transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), transcranial electrical stimulation (eg, transcranial direct current stimulation [tDCS]), and external trigeminal nerve stimulation (eTNS). 10 Although preliminary evidence suggests that NIBS may improve clinical symptoms and cognitive deficits in ADHD by targeted modulation of dysfunctional neural circuits, 11,12 empirical testing has yielded inconsistent findings, 13,14 necessitating further systematic investigation. Previous reviews on the application of NIBS in ADHD have also yielded inconsistent conclusions. 15-20 The inconsistency may arise from the heterogeneity of participant characteristics, outcome measures, and experimental designs, which restricts the generalizability and comparability of findings. Moreover, prior research insufficiently explored how stimulus targets and parameters (eg, treatment duration) influence the efficacy of NIBS, limiting its utility in guiding clinical applications. With a notable increase in studies investigating NIBS in ADHD, an up-todate meta-analysis incorporating a broad range of NIBS techniques and comprehensive measures of both clinical and cognitive outcomes is urgently needed. Thus, our study aimed to synthesize the evidence from various NIBS techniques used in the treatment of ADHD and to provide a critical appraisal of their clinical and cognitive effects. Further, we conducted meta-analyses of tDCS and repetitive TMS (rTMS) studies in ADHD to quantitatively synthesize and compare cognitive and clinical outcomes. To elucidate the importance of interventionspecific factors, subgroup analyses stratified by anatomical stimulation site and meta-regression analyses on doseresponse relationships were performed. Thus, this systematic review and meta-analysis will provide a rigorous evaluation and robust quantified evidence on the efficacy of NIBS in ADHD. METHOD Literature Search and Eligibility Criteria The study protocol was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/bmhax). We conducted a comprehensive literature search in PubMed, Web of Science, and Embase for NIBS studies up to July 5, 2024 (detailed search strategy is provided in Supplement 1, available online). In addition, manual searches were performed of the reference lists of previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses. This systematic review and metaanalysis was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Evaluation and MetaAnalysis (PRISMA) criteria. 21 Studies comprising participants with ADHD confirmed by meeting either a clinical criterion of ADHD defined by DSM/ICD or cutoff criteria on validated ADHD rating scales and studies adopting any NIBS techniques were included. Studies were excluded if they did not examine clinical or cognitive outcomes of NIBS, were not original research, were written in nonEnglish languages, or did not provide sufficient details on methods or results. Studies other than randomized controlled trials (RCTs) (for meta-analysis only) were also excluded. For studies with multiple publications from overlapping samples, the study with the largest sample was included in the meta-analysis. Study Selection and Data Extraction The search identified 59 studies (rTMS: 11; tDCS: 35; other NIBS: 13) in systematic reviews and 33 studies (7 for rTMS, 26 for tDCS) in meta-analyses of therapeutic efficacy. The study selection process is shown in Figure 1; details on studies excluded after full-text review are provided in Table S1, available online. We extracted comprehensive data from included studies, as follows: A 370 www.jaacap.org Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Volume 65 / Number 3 / March 2026 CHEN et al.

1. Study characteristics (authors, publication year, research country, sample size, study design) 2. Participant characteristics (age, sex, diagnostic criteria, ADHD subtype, comorbidities, medication status) 3. Intervention parameters (stimulation type, sham protocol, target location, targeting method, frequency/current, treatment duration, washout period for crossover designs) 4. Outcome measures (clinical symptom ratings, cognitive performance measures, neurophysiological indicators, and tolerability/adverse effects) Two authors (Q.C. and Y.L.) separately carried out the search, performed the study selection and data extraction, and discussed discrepancies; a third author (N.P.) crosschecked the results and was consulted if consensus could not be reached. Meta-analysis Given the limited number of included studies (metaanalysis was performed when ≥3 studies were identified), 22 we conducted meta-analyses only on the clinical and cognitive effects of rTMS and tDCS in ADHD (details about calculation of Hedges’ g are provided in Supplement 2, available online). To reduce heterogeneity, we clustered clinical symptoms and cognitive function into different domains and conducted independent meta-analyses for each domain. Specifically, clinical symptoms were divided into inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity domains. Cognitive function consisted of 4 domains: attention, inhibitory control, processing speed, and working memory (categorization of cognitive outcomes is provided in Table S2, available online). We conducted a random-effects meta-analysis to estimate the effect of NIBS by calculating Hedges’ g values as the standardized mean difference in clinical and cognitive measures of ADHD. When multiple indicators were assessed using identical scales or tasks, the indicator that most accurately represented the primary construct was selected as the principal outcome variable based on the research objectives. For outcomes measured by multiple scales, means and standard deviations were pooled to calculate the overall effect size. If the same cohort underwent multiple experiments with different stimulus conditions (stimulation targets, current intensity), all conditions were included in the analysis. To avoid inflating the sample size, the total sample size of the cohort was proportionally divided across the different conditions included in the meta-analysis. The heterogeneity of effects was assessed using the I 2 statistic, which was categorized into low (≤50%), moderate (50%-75%), and high (≥75%) levels. 23 To systematically identify potential sources of heterogeneity among the included studies, we conducted a narrative review highlighting the key variations across studies. In the subgroup analysis stratified by stimulation targets, the stimulation targets were generally assigned to 6 groups: anodal left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), anodal right inferior frontal cortex (IFC), anodal right orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), cathodal right OFC, cathodal right DLPFC, and cathodal left DLPFC. In the subgroup analysis stratified by age group, participants were classified as children (<18 years old) or adults. In the subgroup analysis stratified by trial structure, studies were divided into parallel and crossover trials. The subgroup analyses were conducted only when at least 3 independent studies were available. 22 We also performed a meta-regression analysis to evaluate the dose-response relationship. We defined rTMS dose as number of total stimulus × duration of each stimulus, whereas tDCS dose was defined as session × duration of each session. Given the potential for both linear and nonlinear associations between dose and efficacy, 24 we used both linear and quadratic models and compared their performance with leave-oneout evaluation (Supplement 3, available online). Jackknife sensitivity analyses (ie, repeating the same analysis each time and excluding different studies) were performed to evaluate the reproducibility of the findings. When 2 or more high-risk studies were included, we conducted a sensitivity analysis that excluded all high-risk studies. We used visual inspection of funnel plots and Egger test to assess publication bias. All analyses were 2tailed and performed at α level .05 using Stata version 18.0 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, Texas). Risk-of-Bias Assessment We used the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (RoB 2) to assess the quality of RCTs included in the meta-analyses. 25 The tool has 5 different domains: randomization process, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of outcome, selection of reported result. 26 The overall risk-of-bias assessment was generated after individual evaluation of all 5 quality domains. Studies with low risk of bias for all domains were judged as “low risk.” Studies with at least some concerns of bias in any area, but without high risk of bias for any domain, were judged as “some concerns.” Studies with at least 1 high risk of bias in any area or some concerns for multiple domains were judged as “high risk.” RESULTS Sample Characteristics This systematic review included 59 studies comprising 1,657 participants with ADHD (1,164 male participants, mean [SD] age = 17.08 [11.43] years). A total of 6 NIBS techniques were involved, including rTMS (11 studies), tDCS (35 studies), eTNS (2 studies), transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) (5 studies), transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) (5 studies), and transcranial pulse stimulation (TPS) (1 study) (Figure 2). Study and participant characteristics, intervention parameters, and outcome measures of individual studies are detailed in Table 1 and Table S3, available online. 11-14,27-80 The metaanalyses quantitatively evaluated the clinical and cognitive outcomes of rTMS and tDCS in ADHD, incorporating 7 RCTs of rTMS and 26 RCTs of tDCS, with 1,049 participants with ADHD (727 male participants, mean [SD] age = 19.91 [12.44] years). Results of Systematic Review rTMS Studies. Six studies indicated that rTMS could significantly improve core symptoms of ADHD such as inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity. 27,29-33 In addition, 3 studies found that when rTMS is combined with pharmacotherapy or behavioral training, it can more effectively improve attention, hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms, and sleep disorders. 11,34,35 These studies also observed significant enhancements in executive functions, such as arithmetic performance, coding ability, and emotional decision making. 11,34,35 Functional magnetic resonance imaging studies further revealed that rTMS targeting the right prefrontal cortex during working memory tasks enhanced brain network activity related to attention, including activation in the right DLPFC, right parietal cortex, and right inferior frontal gyrus, and 372 www.jaacap.org Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Volume 65 / Number 3 / March 2026 CHEN et al.

increased activation of the right DLPFC was significantly positively correlated with improvements in inattention and memory symptoms. 33 However, in 2 studies, although there was some improvement in overall clinical symptoms, the difference between the rTMS and sham groups was not statistically significant, and no improvement in attention function was observed (Table 1). 13,28 Among 8 studies that assessed the safety and tolerability of rTMS, 7 showed that rTMS was safe and well tolerated (Table S4, available online). 11,13,27-29,31,35 Common side effects included mild headaches, transient local discomfort, or mild pain in the treated area. Another study reported 1 case of seizures after rTMS. 32 Overall, rTMS has shown therapeutic efficacy for clinical symptoms across multiple studies, but evidence regarding its impact on cognitive function is limited.
