Five studies reported that tDCS significantly alleviated clinical symptoms in individuals with ADHD, primarily inattention symptoms. 40,41,43,55,64 However, 4 studies did not find improvement of clinical symptoms with tDCS. 45,58,62,66 In addition, 2 studies indicated that tDCS targeting the right IFC had an adverse effect on overall clinical symptoms, inattention, and hyperactive/impulsive symptoms in individuals with ADHD. 14,54 In terms of cognitive function, evidence for tDCS efficacy in ADHD emerged across multiple domains: enhancement of attention processes was documented in 7 studies, 37,39,40,46,54,58,64 and improvement in inhibitory control was exhibited in 8 studies. 39,44-47,49,62 Further, 4 studies found significant improvements in processing speed, 12,37,42,49 and 4 found improvements in working memory performance. 47,49,54,59 Some studies also indicated that tDCS showed potential for improving reward processing, verbal fluency, and emotional regulation. 52,60,61,67,68 Seven studies did not observe significant improvements in cognitive functions following tDCS intervention, such as attention, inhibitory control, and working memory in ADHD. 14,38,48,53,55,65,66 Furthermore, 1 study reported that tDCS on the left DLPFC impaired attention function, 42 and another found that stimulation on the right posterior parietal cortex impaired inhibitory control (Table 1). 51 Stimulation targets may influence the therapeutic effects of tDCS. Anodal tDCS targeting the left DLPFC and right OFC, as well as cathodal tDCS targeting the right OFC, has demonstrated improvement in certain cognitive functions across the majority of studies. In contrast, anodal tDCS targeting the right IFC and cathodal tDCS targeting the right and left DLPFC have shown inconsistent effects on cognitive functions. Findings from 5 studies, in which all experimental conditions were controlled except for the stimulation targets, revealed that different stimulation targets have varying impacts on cognitive function. 46,49,52,60,61 For instance, anodal tDCS on the left DLPFC effectively improved verbal fluency, whereas anodal tDCS on the right DLPFC and right IFC improved semantic fluency. 60 Anodal tDCS on the left DLPFC significantly enhanced attention and working memory, whereas anodal tDCS on the right OFC notably improved inhibitory control. 46,49 Among 35 studies, 29 reported the safety and tolerability of tDCS. Among these, 26 studies showed that tDCS was safe and well tolerated (Table S4, available online). 12,37-42,44,45,48-55,57,59-62,65,66,68 Common mild adverse effects include mild skin redness, scalp burning, and tingling pain. However, 3 studies also reported that 5 of these participants experienced serious adverse events after receiving tDCS, including mood swings, decreased appetite, sleep disorders, and severe headaches. 14,43,58 In summary, although tDCS has shown favorable safety and tolerability, definitive evidence for its therapeutic efficacy in improving clinical symptoms and cognitive function in individuals with ADHD remains inconclusive due to mixed results across studies. Moreover, cognitive outcomes appear to be differentially modulated by different stimulation sites. Other NIBS Studies. eTNS (n =2) has shown significant efficacy in reducing inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity symptoms, as well as enhancing inhibitory control of individuals with ADHD. 69,70 Further, the clinical outcomes of eTNS were associated with increased electroencephalography activity in right frontal lobe and midfrontal line regions. 70 tRNS (n = 5) studies suggest potential therapeutic benefits in both reconciling clinical symptoms and enhancing executive functions, particularly inhibitory control and working memory, in individuals with ADHD and showed superior efficacy compared with tDCS. 71-74 tRNS also improves the processing speed of individuals with ADHD when faced with cognitive fatigue and environmental distractions. 72 Among the 5 included tACS studies, 3 confirmed its potential modulating effects on cognitive performance, such as attention, inhibitory control, and working memory. Importantly, observed cognitive enhancement exceeded the therapeutic efficacy of methylphenidate in both magnitude and duration. 75,76,78 However, the remaining 2 studies did not find that tACS can improve attention of individuals with ADHD. 77,79 Only 1 study has explored the effect of TPS, finding that TPS can significantly reduce the severity of symptoms in individuals with ADHD, with improvement effects persisting during the follow-up period of 1 to 3 months (Table 1). 80 These NIBS techniques were safe and well tolerated, and no serious adverse events were reported (Table S4, available online). Sources of Heterogeneity Our included studies exhibited considerable heterogeneity, which mainly arose from differences in stimulation protocols, participant characteristics, and study designs. First, stimulation protocols may serve as a heterogeneity source, with diverse stimulation targets, treatment durations (ranging from a single session to 8 weeks) and intervention sessions (1-56 sessions). Second, variability in participant characteristics, particularly the imbalanced age distribution (67% children, 33% adults), contributes to the heterogeneity. Besides, inconsistency in diagnostic criteria across studies further compounds this variation (90% based on DSM-IV/DSM-5 or the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age Children [KSADS], 5% using the ADHD rating scale, and 5% not specified). ADHD presentations vary, as do comorbidity managing strategies (85% excluded psychiatric comorbidities, 12% included specific comorbidities, and 3% unreported). Medication status differs across studies: 63% required discontinuation of ADHD medications during treatment, 14% included only medication-naïve individuals, 5% allowed continued medication use, and 18% did not report medication status. Third, study design differences further heighten the heterogeneity, including variations in trial structure (40% parallel trials, 53% crossover trials, and 7% single-arm trials), intervention strategies (85% monotherapy treatment, 15% augmented treatment), washout periods in crossover trials (ranging from 1 day to 1 month), and outcome measures. In the subgroup analysis stratified by age groups, rTMS showed significant improvement in hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms in children with ADHD (Hedges’ g = − 1.62, 95% CI [− 2.17, − 1.07], p < .001) (Figure S3B, available online), whereas no significant effect was found in adults. tDCS showed significant enhancement in inhibitory control in children with ADHD (Hedges’ g = .49, 95% CI [0.02, 0.96], p = .039) (Figure S4B, available online), whereas no such enhancement was observed in adults. Conversely, tDCS was effective in alleviating inattention symptoms in adults with ADHD (Hedges’ g = − 1.82, 95% CI [− 2.26, − 1.39], p < .001) (Figure S4A, available online), but no significant effect was observed in children. Additionally, no significant differences were found between children and adults in the effects of tDCS on hyperactivity/ impulsivity symptoms, attention-related function, or processing speed. In the subgroup analysis stratified by trial structure, tDCS showed a significant improvement in inhibitory control in individuals with ADHD in crossover trials (Hedges’ g = 0.28, 95% CI [0.03, 0.54], p = .029) (Figure S5B, available online), but no significant effect was observed in parallel trials. In contrast, tDCS showed a significant improvement in working memory in parallel trials (Hedges’ g = 1.04, 95% CI [0.20, 1.87], p = .015) (Figure S5D, available online), whereas no such effect was observed in crossover trials. No significant differences were found in the effects of study design on tDCS treatment outcomes for attention or processing speed. The meta-regression analysis was performed to evaluate the relation between dose and efficacy in tDCS and rTMS studies on clinical and cognitive outcomes. Analysis of the relation between dose and efficacy using both linear and quadratic modeling yielded nonsignificant results in both rTMS (modulatory effects of dose and model comparisons are provided in Tables S5 and S6, available online) and tDCS studies (Tables S7 and S8, available online). Risk of Bias Among the eligible studies, 54.5% were assessed as having a low risk of bias, 36.4% had some concerns, and 9.1% were at high risk. Owing to lack of relevant information, 21.2% were considered to have some risk of bias in the randomization process, and 39.4% were considered to have some risk in selection bias when reporting results. Overall, the bias was low in the majority of domains (Figure S6, available online). DISCUSSION We provide a comprehensive and systematic review examining the therapeutic efficacy of NIBS techniques in ADHD. Meta-analyses demonstrated distinct therapeutic benefits for different NIBS modalities: rTMS significantly improved core clinical symptoms and enhanced attentionrelated cognitive functions, whereas tDCS effectively reduced hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms and enhanced cognitive aspects of inhibitory control. Notably, tDCS with anodal stimulation over the left DLPFC and cathodal stimulation over the right OFC showed significant enhancement in inhibitory control, although treatment dose did not significantly influence cognitive outcomes. Compared with previous reviews and meta-analyses, 15-20 our study incorporated a larger sample size, more comprehensive outcome measures, and exploratory analyses of stimulation targets and dose-response relationships. These findings support the therapeutic potential of NIBS as a promising nonpharmacological intervention for ADHD and offer valuable insights for optimizing clinical application. Our systematic review indicated that NIBS has the potential to improve clinical symptoms and certain cognitive functions in individuals with ADHD. However, the results of existing studies showed considerable heterogeneity, making it challenging to draw a definitive conclusion. This heterogeneity stems from 3 main factors: stimulation protocols (eg, stimulation targets may have a direct influence on treatment effects 14,41 ), participant characteristics (eg, age may modulate different neuroplasticity responses), and study design differences (eg, potential learning effects in crossover designs may affect the accurate assessment of treatment effects). 45 Despite the observed heterogeneity, our findings indicated that NIBS is well tolerated and safe. Additionally, the therapeutic effects of NIBS on ADHD can persist during the follow-up period. Two rTMS studies indicated that following 3 weeks of 15 treatment sessions, improvements in attention and hyperactivity/impulsivity can be maintained for up to 1 month, though with some attenuation over time. 31,34 Studies on tDCS suggested that short-term interventions (5-10 sessions) can sustain improvements in attention and inhibitory control for 2 to 6 weeks, 43,47,61 with 1 study suggesting that effects may last up to 4 months. 54 However, 1 study reported that the benefits of 5 tDCS sessions on inhibitory control did not persist at the 386 www.jaacap.org Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Volume 65 / Number 3 / March 2026 CHEN et al.

1-month follow-up. 56 Furthermore, other NIBS techniques, such as tACS and TPS, have also demonstrated varying degrees of long-term efficacy. 76,78,80 Based on the current evidence, NIBS may serve as an effective complement to ADHD management, particularly for individuals who may be refractory to or unsuitable candidates for pharmacological interventions. Meta-analyses indicated that rTMS significantly improved core clinical symptoms and enhanced attentionrelated cognitive functions in individuals with ADHD, whereas tDCS can enhance inhibitory control functions and alleviate hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms. rTMS generates a time-varying magnetic field in the targeted region to stimulate the cerebral cortex locally, modulating inhibitory and excitatory synaptic transmission and thereby regulating cortical excitability. 81 In ADHD treatment, the right DLPFC, a neural substrate crucial for attentional control, serves as the primary therapeutic target. 82 A study showed that rTMS intervention significantly enhances right DLPFC activation, with these neurophysiological changes exhibiting robust correlations with improvements in attention and memory functions. 33 This finding further confirms the critical role of the right DLPFC in attention regulation. Some studies have also reported that rTMS improved hyperactive/ impulsive symptoms, especially when stimulation targets are extended to other regions of the prefrontal cortex, such as the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and the left DLPFC. 29,32 In contrast, tDCS applies a constant, low-intensity direct current via electrodes, which influences voltage-gated ion channels and alters the resting membrane potential of neurons, modulating excitability thresholds. 83 tDCS typically employs a dual-electrode system comprising an anode and cathode, which not only modulates local neural activity at the stimulation site but also influences the intrinsic functional connectivity patterns within broader cortical networks. 42 In ADHD intervention, electrode placement primarily targets the prefrontal cortex, specifically engaging the prefrontalstriatal-thalamic circuit—a neural network fundamental to inhibitory control mechanisms. 84,85 This stimulation approach enhances both prefrontal cortical activity and its functional integration with connected neural substrates, thereby strengthening inhibitory control capabilities and subsequently ameliorating hyperactivity and impulsivity symptoms in patients with ADHD. Further subgroup analysis stratified by stimulation targets revealed that tDCS applying anodal stimulation to the left DLPFC and the cathodal stimulation to the right OFC showed significant improvement in inhibitory control. This may be closely related to the roles of these 2 regions within the inhibitory control function. Inhibitory control, a core deficit in ADHD, 86 is primarily regulated by the prefrontal-striatal-thalamic circuit, with the DLPFC playing a crucial role. 87 Research has shown that individuals with ADHD exhibit significant structural and functional deficits in the DLPFC, and during inhibitory control tasks, the activation of the DLPFC is also significantly reduced. 88-91 At the same time, abnormalities in the OFC have been extensively observed in individuals with ADHD, including reduced gray matter volume and altered activation patterns. 92-94 These OFC dysfunctions in ADHD have been associated with impulsivity symptoms, which are closely linked to inhibitory control. 95 In addition, studies suggested that individuals with ADHD display abnormal functional connectivity between the DLPFC and related regions during inhibitory tasks, 96 and such network-level dysregulation may be a key contributor to deficits in inhibitory control. tDCS may enhance functional activity in the DLPFC and OFC while modulating the functional connectivity of relevant neural circuits, thereby enhancing inhibitory control function. Subgroup analysis stratified by age groups revealed an agedependent pattern of NIBS efficacy in the treatment of ADHD. rTMS showed a significant improvement in hyperactive/impulsive symptoms only in children’s samples. Our findings suggest that clinical approaches to neurostimulation should be tailored according to age groups when targeting different symptoms. The efficacy of rTMS primarily in pediatric populations suggests that children’s brains retain greater neuroplasticity in response to electromagnetic stimulation. In contrast, tDCS, with its dual-electrode configuration, likely engages more complex neural pathways, necessitating further research to determine its age-dependent effectiveness. Subgroup analysis stratified by trial structure revealed that study design may influence the effects of tDCS on cognitive function in individuals with ADHD due to heterogeneity in the washout periods across crossover trials, which may have introduced learning effects or carryover effects. 45 Therefore, future studies should prioritize crossover designs with an adequate washout period or consider using parallel-group designs to enhance study reliability. Meta-regression analysis revealed that dose did not significantly impact efficacy in ADHD. The findings carry important clinical implications: rather than focusing on extending treatment dose, clinicians should prioritize other factors, such as the selection of stimulation targets corresponding to clinical profiles and stimulation intensity. Notably, the observed clinical and cognitive improvements even with smaller doses suggest that NIBS offers both enhanced treatment acceptability and clinical flexibility. However, these conclusions should be interpreted with caution. Our study considered only the session number and duration to investigate the dose-response relationship, Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry www.jaacap.org 387 Volume 65 / Number 3 / March 2026 NONINVASIVE BRAIN STIMULATION IN ADHD

which are consistently reported across studies with superior generalizability. This approach, though methodologically sound for meta-analytic synthesis, provides only a partial characterization of dose dimensions. This limitation emphasizes the necessity for future studies specifically designed to investigate the dose-response relationship of NIBS. Our study should be considered in light of some limitations. First, methodological heterogeneity across studies, including unstratified participant characteristics, diverse stimulation protocols, and varying study designs, limits the systematic evaluation of NIBS efficacy across studies conducted in ADHD. Second, the limited number of studies and sample sizes prevented comprehensive subgroup analyses of stimulation targets and made it difficult to establish a reliable dose-response relationship for different NIBS techniques, thus constraining the generalizability of our findings. Finally, the heterogeneity in domain-specific therapeutic outcomes across studies presents an important methodological consideration: these differences may be attributed either to the distinct mechanisms of various stimulation devices or to the differential selection of stimulation sites across devices. This confound limits our ability to determine the precise source of treatment specificity. Future research should aim to reconcile these sources of heterogeneity to enhance the specificity and robustness of the results. 97 Moreover, increased sample sizes and incorporating a broader range of NIBS techniques could facilitate personalized applications 98 and facilitate exploration of the comparative advantages of different NIBS technologies and optimal stimulation pipelines. NIBS is a promising therapeutic approach to alleviating clinical symptoms and enhancing cognitive functions in individuals with ADHD. Specifically, rTMS demonstrates efficacy in improving core clinical symptoms and enhancing attention-related cognitive functions, whereas tDCS shows particular promise in reducing hyperactivity/ impulsivity symptoms and strengthening inhibitory control. The therapeutic efficacy of NIBS interventions is notably influenced by stimulation protocols, with target region selection playing a crucial role. In particular, tDCS protocols incorporating anodal stimulation of the left DLPFC combined with cathodal stimulation of the right OFC have demonstrated significant improvements in inhibitory control among individuals with ADHD. Moving forward, future research should focus on optimizing NIBS protocols and investigating the comparative advantages of different NIBS technologies to establish their relative efficacy in addressing both clinical symptoms and cognitive deficits, ultimately advancing the practical therapeutic application of NIBS for ADHD management. metadata_title: Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis: Moderators of Response to Stimulants for Preschool Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder
pages: META-ANALYSIS Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis: Moderators of Response to Stimulants for Preschool Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Luis C. Farhat a,b , MD, PhD , Luisa Shiguemi Sugaya a , MD, PhD , Michael H. Bloch c , MD, MS , Ann Childress d , MD , Samuele Cortese b,e,f,g,h , MD, PhD , Daniel Fatori a , PhD , Giovanni A. Salum i,j,k , MD, PhD , Luis Augusto Rohde j,k , MD, PhD , Guilherme V. Polanczyk a, *, MD, PhD Objective: This study aimed to identify moderators of efficacy of stimulants against placebo to inform personalized recommendations for treatment in preschool children (<6 years of age) with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Method: We acquired individual-level participant data from 2 randomized placebo-controlled trials (RCTs) of preschool ADHD: namely, MAPPA (8-week methylphenidate, 102 participants, Brazil) and SPD489-347 (6-week lisdexamfetamine, 148 participants, United States). We evaluated the moderator and predictor effects of baseline demographic (age, sex, race, ethnicity, maternal educational level) and baseline clinical (ADHD symptom severity, intelligence quotient, number of psychiatric comorbidities) characteristics, as available, on endpoint ADHD symptom severity scores. Data from each study were analyzed separately with linear mixed-effects model for repeated measures. For categorical variables, we also computed treatment effects (ie, stimulants vs placebo) within subgroups and, when possible, pooled them alongside subgroup data from the Preschoolers with AttentionDeficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Treatment Study (PATS) (5-week methylphenidate, 165 participants, United States) in random-effects meta-analyses. Results: Stimulants had greater efficacy against placebo in White children compared to Black children when considering data from US studies. Older age was not a moderator of greater efficacy of stimulants against placebo, nor was it associated with worse ADHD symptom severity at endpoint. Greater baseline ADHD symptom severity was associated with higher ADHD symptom severity at endpoint independently of the assigned treatment group. Conclusion: Race, but not older age or baseline ADHD symptom severity, may moderate the efficacy of stimulants for preschool ADHD. Given the post hoc nature of subgroup analyses, the findings should be interpreted as exploratory and viewed as hypotheses for confirmation in future studies. Plain language summary: In this individual participant meta-analysis, the authors obtained data from 2 clinical trials of psychostimulants for preschool children (aged 6 years or younger) with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) to investigate associations between demographic, clinical characteristics, and treatment effects. One study was focused on methylphenidate and was conducted in Brazil with 102 participants. The other study focused on lisdexamfetamine and was conducted in the United States with 148 participants. Some analyses also included subgroup data from a study focused on methylphenidate and was conducted in the US with 165 participants. In the US studies, stimulants appeared to work better in White children than in Black children, while older age or clinical severity was not associated with effectiveness of stimulants. The authors emphasize that these findings are exploratory and should be confirmed in future studies before guiding clinical decisions. Clinical trial registration information: Safety and Efficacy Study in Preschool Children Aged 4-5 Years With Attention-deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD); https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03260205; Early Interventions in Children With Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02807870 Key words: randomized controlled trial; amphetamine; methylphenidate J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry 2026;65(6):781-792. ttention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a pervasive, persistent, and developmentally inappropriate pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity– impulsivity that interferes with development and/or functioning. 1 ADHD symptoms usually emerge in the first years of life, 2 and a diagnosis may be possible in children as young as 3 to 4 years. 3 Population-based studies from the United States and Scandinavian countries estimate that around 2 in 100 preschool children (ie, <6 years of age) may receive a diagnosis of ADHD. 4-6 Preschool ADHD has been associated with interference in social and academic development, 7 substantial economic burden, 8 and possibly increased risk of mortality attributed to physical injuries. 9 Treatment could reduce the impact of ADHD early in life. A large body of evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) has shown that stimulants (ie, methylphenidate and amphetamines) lead to large reductions in the A Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry www.jaacap.org 781 Volume 65 / Number 6 / June 2026

severity of ADHD symptoms in school-aged children and adolescents. 10,11 However, less robust evidence base specifically for preschool children is available to guide practitioners and guideline developers. 12 A systematic review with meta-analysis could find only 5 RCTs with a median treatment duration of 4 weeks and approximately 500 participants testing stimulants for this patient group. 13 Those RCTs showed that stimulants, compared against placebo, had only a moderate effect size on the reduction in the severity of ADHD symptoms. In addition, although stimulants have mostly been associated with higher rates of mild adverse events only, 14 longer-term RCTs in the preschool population are lacking, prompting concerns around the safety of those medications, in particular regarding the cardiovascular system, somatic growth, and brain development. 15-17 In this context, clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) more conservatively suggest that stimulants may be an option for preschoolers who continue to experience interference in functioning after a trial of a nonpharmacological intervention. 18,19 Nevertheless, there is concern that, unintentionally, these recommendations may contribute to the delayed initiation of stimulants and the overuse of non–evidence-based interventions, such as use of antipsychotics, for preschoolers in the community. 20-22 Practitioners may be more inclined to prescribe stimulants for those preschool children who are more likely to experience greater benefits with the medication. Additional insights on stimulant treatment in this population are needed to inform such personalized recommendations. Specifically, published analyses of RCTs consider average effects (effects are valid at the group level), but there is substantial individuallevel variability, and some preschoolers may experience greater benefits with stimulants than the average. 23 Demographic and clinical characteristics that are routinely collected at patient intake offer an opportunity to attempt to identify those individuals who may be more likely to benefit from stimulants. However, to date, only one previous study has examined this issue using data from the initial 5-week phase of the landmark National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)–funded Preschoolers with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Treatment Study (PATS). 24 This study reported that the number of comorbid disorders was inversely associated with the efficacy of methylphenidate against placebo in terms of reductions of ADHD symptom severity. 25 Nonetheless, post hoc secondary analyses of RCTs may be particularly prone to both type I and type II errors. 26-28 Therefore, it is critical that findings from moderator analyses based on one RCT be replicated in other samples and show robustness in pooled analyses of studies. 28 Notably, in more recent years, other RCTs of stimulants in preschoolers have been conducted, offering the opportunity to test replicability of the finding from PATS in other samples, as well as to identify other moderators of response to stimulants in preschoolers. To address this critical gap, we conducted, for the first time, moderation analyses using individual participant data from 2 RCTs of stimulants vs placebo for preschoolers with ADHD and pooled findings across studies when possible. METHOD Study Design The current study builds upon a previous systematic review of placebo-controlled RCTs of stimulants for preschool ADHD. In that previously published study, which was preregistered with PROSPERO CRD42022348597, literature searches on 4 online databases (Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials; Embase; PubMed; WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform) were carried out up to July 2022 to identify 5 double-blinded RCTs of stimulants vs placebo including 489 preschoolers with a primary diagnosis of ADHD according to the DSM criteria. 13 In this study, we sought to acquire individual-level participant data (IPD) from the 5 RCTs 24,29-32 that were included in the prior study. By contacting study authors or sponsors, we acquired IPD from 2 RCTs: (1) MAPPA, an 8-week RCT of methylphenidate conducted in a specialist center in S~ao Paulo, Brazil, with participants enrolled from August 2016 to October 2019 (NCT02807870) 30 ; and (2) SPD489-347, a 6-week RCT of lisdexamfetamine conducted in 44 centers in the United States between September 2017 and October 2018 (NCT03260205). 31 Additional details on each study are available in their corresponding published reports 30,31 and ClinicalTrials.gov records, all of which are openly available. We were not able to include IPD from 2 RCTs, as investigators no longer had access to the dataset 32 or did not respond to our inquiry. 29 Also, we were not able to include IPD from PATS because we were unable to identify the variable corresponding to the randomized groups in the dataset from NIMH Data Archive. In fact, we contacted the NIMH Data Archive Help Desk, 6 investigators from PATS, and the data management center for the study, but we were unable to retrieve any other information. This was understandable, as the study was conducted 20 years ago. However, the investigators from PATS had previously conducted moderator analyses and published the group-level statistics (ie, mean, SD) of ADHD symptom severity with methylphenidate or placebo at endpoint for each subgroup of candidate categorical moderators. 25 Therefore, we were able to extract those data and to calculate within-subgroup effect sizes for pooling in meta-analysis alongside information from MAPPA and SPD489-347. 782 www.jaacap.org Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Volume 65 / Number 6 / June 2026 FARHAT et al.

Participants According to the eligibility criteria of the RCTs included in our study, children had to be 5.5 years of age or younger and to have a primary diagnosis of ADHD according to DSM criteria (edition IV onward) with moderate or severe baseline core ADHD symptoms. Children were required to attend school or daycare with same-aged peers and to have an intelligence quotient (IQ) of ≥70 in MAPPA and PATS, or a score of ≥70 on the Peabody Picture Vocabulary in SPD489-347. Children with co-occurring autism or affective or psychotic disorders were not eligible for participation. In addition, in SPD489-347 and PATS, children were eligible only if they had failed a previous adequate trial of a nonpharmacological intervention (in SPD489-347, investigator defined based on patient history; in PATS, parent training administered by PATS investigators) unless their symptoms were judged to be severe enough to skip that step. PATS and SPD489-347 also excluded participants who had evidence of nonresponse or poor tolerability to stimulants, although all but 2 participants from MAPPA were stimulant naive. Interventions In MAPPA, methylphenidate was titrated from 0.3 mg/kg/ d to 0.7 mg/kg/d in the first 4 weeks and then up to 1.25 mg/ kg/d between the 4th and 8th weeks if there was room for improvement and no limiting adverse events (daily dose mean [SD] = 27 [6] mg/d). It was prescribed adjuvant to an educational intervention that focused on typical development and had no active component addressing ADHD symptoms. In SPD489-347, lisdexamfetamine was randomly prescribed at fixed-doses of 5 mg/d, 10 mg/d, 20 mg/d, or 30 mg/d with forced weekly dose escalation. If the assigned dose was not tolerated, participants were required to discontinue treatment. We considered data only from groups assigned to doses of 10 mg/ d through 30 mg/d following the primary efficacy analysis for the RCT, in line with the protocol established a priori. 31 In PATS, methylphenidate was prescribed at multiple fixed doses (3.75, 7.5, 15, 22.5 mg/d) for 1 week each. We considered data only for the dose of 22.5 mg/d, in accordance with the previous study that reported moderation analyses in PATS. 25 Outcome The outcome of this study was ADHD symptom severity at endpoint, without any restrictions on rating scale or informant. When multiple rating scales or informants were available, we chose the study-defined primary outcome measure. Additional details on the rating scales that were used can be found in Supplement 1, available online. From MAPPA, we used the combined parent and teacher Swanson, Nolan and Pelham–IV (SNAP-IV) scores, 33 measured at baseline, week 4, and week 8 (endpoint). From SPD489-347, we considered the clinician ADHD Rating Scale–IV–Preschool (ADHD-RS-IV-PS) scores, 34 measured weekly from baseline through week 6 (endpoint). From PATS, we used the combined parent and teacher Conners, Loney and Milich Rating Scale (CLAM) and Swanson, Conners, Milich and Pelham Scale (SKAMP) scores, 35 measured just once at the end of the week. Putative Moderators and Predictors Candidate variables were selected considering current recommendations from CPGs, potential to inform clinical practice, and data availability across at least 2 RCTs to enable replicability and pooling of data in meta-analyses. We selected both baseline demographic (age, sex, race, ethnicity, maternal educational level) and baseline clinical (baseline ADHD symptom severity, IQ, and number of cooccurring psychiatric conditions) characteristics. Age and ADHD symptom severity were chosen because some CPGs make differential recommendations regarding stimulant treatment for preschool- vs school-aged children and for individuals with mild-to-moderate vs severe ADHD symptoms. 19,36 Both variables were analyzed continuously. However, for baseline age, we also considered a dichotomized variable (<5 years; ≥5 years) to reflect the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) differential treatment recommendations for children under 5 years of age and those 5 years and over. 19 Sex (male participants, female participants), race (Black, White), and ethnicity (Hispanic, non-Hispanic) were analyzed, considering that minorities are underrepresented in ADHD RCTs and clinical research, 37,38 and more research is needed to characterize whether there is differential treatment response based on sex, race, and ethnicity. The number of baseline co-occurring psychiatric conditions (continuous and categorized into none, 1 or 2, and 3 or more) was included because it was the only significant finding from the previous study that reported moderation analyses in PATS. 25 Similarly, we also included maternal educational level (dichotomized into high school vs post– high school education) and children’s IQ (continuous and dichotomized into ≤85 or >85) following the previous study with PATS. 25 Statistical Analyses To analyze IPD from MAPPA and SPD489-347, we initially assessed the distribution of baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of participants across arms and Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry www.jaacap.org 783 Volume 65 / Number 6 / June 2026 MODERATORS OF STIMULANT RESPONSE FOR PRESCHOOL ADHD

then reproduced the primary efficacy analysis as described in the published reports. 30,31 Analyses adhered to the intention-to-treat principle and adopted a linear mixedeffects model for repeated measures (MMRM) using data from all available timepoints and an interaction term visit*group to assess the effect of stimulant vs placebo at endpoint (ie, time treated as a categorical variable). Additional details about the statistical models from each study, as well as covariates that were included in each analysis, are available from their corresponding published reports. 30,31 We compared our results with those from the published reports to ensure that there were no discrepancies. We considered that baseline characteristics were a moderator if the effect size of stimulants against placebo on ADHD symptom severity at endpoint was not the same for all values of the candidate variable. 23,39 To assess the moderator effect of putative variables, we added a 3way interaction term variable*visit*treatment to the MMRM. We considered that baseline characteristics were a predictor if there was a main effect on ADHD symptom severity, but the comparative effect size between interventions was the same for all values of the candidate variable. 23,39 To assess the predictor effect of putative variables, we considered the corresponding main effect coefficient from the model including the 3-way interaction term. We used a type III analysis of variance with the Satterthwaite method to probe statistical significance of putative variables. Candidate variables were tested individually, one at a time. To pool data from MAPPA and SPD489-347 in metaanalyses, we extracted the standardized regression coefficients (ß) and their corresponding standard errors (SE), estimated by using standardized ADHD symptom severity as the outcome. We used the within-study baseline standard deviation across arms for standardization. In addition, to enable pooling within subgroup effect sizes of methylphenidate vs placebo from PATS, for categorical variables we also calculated the within-subgroup effect sizes of methylphenidate and lisdexamfetamine vs placebo at endpoint for MAPPA and SPD489-347, respectively, using the endpoint standard deviation across arms for standardization. We then pooled those data to compute summary standardized mean difference (SMD) of stimulant against placebo within each subgroup in random-effects meta-analyses weighted by the inverse of the variance. We then ran subgroup tests to probe differences in stimulant efficacy across subgroups. Analyses were conducted in R (version 4.4.2) with packages “lme4” (version 1.1-35.5) 40 and “meta” (version 8.0-1). 41 Statistical significance was determined at the level of p < .05. RESULTS In MAPPA, 102 children were randomized to methylphenidate (n = 51) or placebo (n = 51). Of those, 3 participants (1 in methylphenidate, 2 in placebo) discontinued treatment. All 102 participants were included in the analyses. In SPD489-347, 159 children were randomized to lisdexamfetamine (n = 113) or placebo (n = 46). Of those, 41 participants (32 in lisdexamfetamine, 9 in placebo) discontinued treatment. All randomly assigned participants receiving at least 1 dose of lisdexamfetamine and having at least 1 postbaseline assessment (148 of 159, 93%) were included in the analyses. Table 1 lists the baseline demographic and clinical characteristics that were available from each study, stratified by treatment group. In PATS, 165 children enrolled in the crossover titration phase, 24 and the distribution of baseline characteristics has been previously reported. 25 Baseline Demographic Characteristics Age. Age did not moderate response to stimulants in either MAPPA (ß = –0.02 for every year from 3 years of age, 95% CI = –0.66 to 0.62, F = 0.91, p = .41) or SPD489347 (ß = 1.02 for every year from 3 years of age, 95% CI = –0.05 to 2.04, F = 1.28, p = .26). Meta-analysis across the 2 studies similarly did not indicate any differential association between baseline age and ADHD symptom severity at endpoint across treatment arms (ß = 0.41 for every year from 3 years, 95% CI = –0.59 to 1.41, p = .42). When considering subgroups based on a cutoff of 5 years, baseline age similarly did not moderate response to stimulant in either MAPPA or SPD489-347 (Table 2). Meta-analysis with all 3 studies also did not indicate any significant subgroup differences between children under 5 years of age and those 5 years or older (Q = 0.13, p = .72) (Figure 1; Figure S1, available online). Finally, when analyzed either as a continuous or a categorical variable, baseline age was not a significant predictor of ADHD symptom severity at endpoint in either study (Table 3) or in meta-analysis (ß = 0.26 for every year from 3 years, 95% CI = –0.21 to 0.73, p = .27). Sex. Sex did not significantly moderate response to stimulant in either MAPPA or SPD489-347 (Table 2). Metaanalysis with all 3 studies did not indicate subgroup differences between female and male participants (Q = 1.26, p = .26) (Figure 1; Figure S2, available online). Sex was also not a predictor of ADHD symptom severity at endpoint in either study (Table 3) or in metaanalysis (ß = –0.10 for female participants compared to male participants, 95% CI = –0.73 to 0.52, p = .75). 784 www.jaacap.org Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry Volume 65 / Number 6 / June 2026 FARHAT et al.

Race. In SPD489-347, 67 (45%) and 70 (47%) of the 148 individuals included in the analyses self-identified as Black and White, respectively, with the remaining 11 individuals scattered across different categories (1 [0.7%] American Indian, Alaskan Native; 5 [3%] multiple; 4 [3%] “other”; 1 [0.7%] missing). Modeling of race as Black vs White, with the remaining individuals entered in the model as a third category, indicated that race did not moderate response to stimulant in SPD489-347 (Table 2). However, metaanalysis with PATS indicated significant subgroup differences (Q = 7.13, p = .008), with large significant effects of stimulants against placebo on White (SMD = –0.87, 95% CI = –1.18 to –0.56, p < .0001) compared to medium-tosmall non-significant effects on Black (SMD = –0.28, 95% CI = –0.58 to 0.03, p = .08) (Figure 1; Figure S3, available online). There was no evidence that race was a predictor of ADHD symptom severity at endpoint in SPD489-347 (Table 3). Ethnicity. In SPD489-347 there were 25 (17%) Hispanic participants, and modeling of Hispanic vs non-Hispanic participants indicated that ethnicity did not moderate response to stimulant in SPD489-347 (Table 2). Metaanalysis with PATS did not indicate subgroup differences between Hispanic and non-Hispanic participants (Q = 1.62, p = .20) (Figure 1; Figure S4, available online). There was no evidence that ethnicity was a predictor of ADHD symptom severity at endpoint in SPD489-347 (Table 3). Maternal Educational Level. DISCUSSION In this study, we aimed to generate an evidence base that could inform personalized recommendations of treatment for preschoolers with ADHD. For the first time, we analyzed individual-level participant data from 2 placebocontrolled RCTs of stimulants (lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate) for preschool ADHD. 30,31 When possible, we pooled the data from those studies together alongside subgroup-level treatment effects from PATS, 24 extracted from a previous publication reporting on moderator analyses conducted by the PATS investigators. 25 Our findings indicated that race may moderate stimulant efficacy, as White children experienced a larger treatment effect compared to Black children. There were no other variables with a significant moderating effect, including age or baseline ADHD symptom severity. Finally, our results indicated that only baseline ADHD symptom severity was a non-specific predictor, with higher baseline ADHD symptom severity being associated with higher ADHD symptom severity at endpoint independently of the assigned treatment group. Taken together, those findings, which are exploratory given the nature of post hoc subgroup analyses, generate hypotheses that should be examined in future empirical studies. We found smaller effects of stimulants against placebo in Black children compared to White children through pooled subgroup analyses of data from SPD489-347 and PATS. To the best of our knowledge, our study is the first to report such finding for preschoolers with ADHD. overlooked thus far. There are several possible explanations for this finding. Given that race is a social construct, a thorough consideration of factors related to structural racism is important. For example, the diminished efficacy of stimulants on Black vs White preschool children with ADHD could be confounded by larger exposure of minoritized populations to socioeconomic hardship (eg, as shown in the Multimodal Treatment of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder [MTA] study). 43 However, careful consideration about confounding is warranted, as some factors may instead be mediators and may underlie the pathway between race and diminished stimulant efficacy. For instance, previous research has shown that Black individuals may have lower rates of medication use and compliance compared to their White counterparts. 44,45 In turn, decreased adherence may underlie the association between race and stimulant efficacy. The distinction between confounders and mediators is relevant because interventions focused on the latter may contribute to improved outcomes, and the field should focus on this topic to promote equity around stimulant treatment. In addition, future studies should also examine the possible impact of teacher or clinician rater biases on the association between Black children and reduced stimulant efficacy. 46,47 Notably, we did not find any moderating effect of baseline age on stimulant efficacy through pooled subgroup analyses of data from the 3 RCTs. Traditionally, clinical lore considers that stimulants are less efficacious in preschool- than in school-aged children; however, there are no substantiative data to support this claim. Most often, practitioners point to differences in the magnitude of effect sizes of stimulants against placebo across age groups, but comparative evidence across RCTs is limited because of potential residual confounding. For instance, stimulants have been prescribed at relatively low doses in RCTs of preschoolers, but flexible titration until maximum licensed doses has been associated with greater efficacy in RCTs of other pediatric populations. 48 In addition, RCTs of preschoolers typically require a previous trial of a non-pharmacological intervention, 24,29,31 which in turn may contribute to overrepresentation of severe cases that may have worse treatment outcomes. Our findings showed that, within the preschool population, older age was not associated with greater stimulant efficacy compared to placebo. Whether our findings indicate that recommendations from CPGs should separate preschoolers from school-aged children at 6 years as the age cut-off or should simply abolish differences across age groups remains to be established. In addition, we did not find a moderating effect of baseline ADHD symptom severity on stimulant efficacy. Some CPGs (eg, German and Dutch guidelines for ADHD) indicate differential recommendations regarding stimulants for mild-to-moderate vs severe ADHD. Understandably, practitioners may be more inclined to prescribe stimulants in scenarios where ADHD symptoms are more severe to maximize benefits against risks. There is no empirical non-arbitrary ADHD symptom severity threshold regarding impairment, 49 and some individuals with low ADHD symptom severity may still be considered “severe” based on clinical judgment that also accounts for ADHD-related impairment. Therefore, although our findings are not necessarily contrary to current recommendations, they reinforce that assessment of “severe” ADHD should not be based solely on a threshold score in ADHD symptom rating scales, at least in preschoolers. Importantly, although subgroup analyses are appealing, we stress that the overall finding from an RCT usually represents the best estimate of the treatment effect compared with those reported in post hoc subgroup analyses. 50,51 For instance, given the limited number of Black individuals in the RCTs, it remains to be determined whether the lower effect of stimulants vs placebo found in our study is representative of the true comparative effect in the population. In addition, there is risk that the association between race and lower stimulant efficacy represents a spurious significant finding purely by chance, arising from multiple comparisons. At the same time, the absence of differences in stimulant efficacy across age subgroups could merely reflect insufficient statistical power. Altogether, the findings from our study should be interpreted as generating additional hypotheses, which should be directly tested by experimental research in the future. Given that moderation analyses have the potential to inform treatment selection, 52 it would be particularly helpful if the field attempted to confirm the findings of (lack of) subgroup differences through a priori designed RCTs. However, until further evidence is available, the exploratory findings from our post hoc subgroup analyses should not directly affect the current state of treatment for preschoolers with ADHD. Finally, we also found that higher baseline ADHD symptom severity was associated with worse prognosis at endpoint, irrespective of the assigned treatment group. This finding is indicative that preschool children with more severe ADHD symptoms may still require additional interventions after trialing stimulants. Therefore, advancements in the treatment of ADHD in preschool children (eg, development of novel, or improvement of available, pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions) may be particularly warranted for those who are more severely affected by this condition during this important developmental period. Our study does have limitations. First, SPD489-347 had large discontinuation rates, which may introduce bias in their findings. Second, the MAPPA study did not collect information on race or ethnicity from their participants. Given that race is a social construct, we cannot determine whether, and how, our findings translate to different countries. Third, all RCTs included participants with moderate or severe baseline core ADHD symptoms, and we cannot determine how our findings translate to preschoolers with mild ADHD symptoms. Fourth, except for age (categorical) and sex, we had data for only 2 of the 3 RCTs for all putative moderator and predictor variables that were explored in this study. This inconsistency across RCTs from a relatively small field illustrates the wide variability in assessment instruments across studies, which in turn hinders the ability to draw conclusions from their data. We hope that our study underscores the importance of developing core measurement sets for RCTs in the field. 53 Fifth, our meta-analyses at times combined data from different stimulants (lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate) given the small number of studies that were available, and we were unable to evaluate potential differences across medications. Finally, the approach combining subgroup data from PATS allowed adding data only regarding putative categorical variables. Because moderator analyses are exploratory in nature, it is possible that some of the categories were created to enhance discoverability in PATS. Indeed, we failed to replicate the only previous significant finding from PATS for the number of psychiatric comorbidities in MAPPA. Specifically, we showed that a higher number of baseline psychiatric comorbidities was associated with larger, and not smaller, reductions in ADHD symptom severity at endpoint with stimulants vs placebo. Relatedly, for race and ethnicity, the findings are also limited by the data that were collected and reported in PATS, as White, Black, and Hispanic participants were all grouped under the same category “ethnicity.” Furthermore, we could not examine the moderating and predicting effect of individual comorbidities (eg, anxiety or conduct disorder), which would have been more informative clinically, as those data were not examined or reported in PATS. In conclusion, this study collated moderator analyses from the 3 landmark randomized controlled trials of stimulants vs placebo for preschoolers with ADHD and showed that race, but not older age or baseline ADHD symptom severity, may moderate the efficacy of stimulants for preschool ADHD. Given the post hoc nature of subgroup analyses, these findings generate hypotheses that should be examined in future empirical studies. CRediT authorship contribution statement Luis C. metadata_title: Effects of exercise on social dysfunction in children and adolescents with ADHD: A systematic review and network, dose-response meta-analyses
pages: Effects of exercise on social dysfunction in children and adolescents with ADHD: A systematic review and network, dose-response meta-analyses☆ Xiang Gao a,1, Meng Zhang a,1, Changshuang He a, Zongyu Fan a, Keyu Pan a, Huan Huang b, Shanru Jin a, Yiting Wei a, Wanqun Xu a, Minghui Quan a,* a School of Exercise and Health, Shanghai University of Sport, Shanghai 200438, China b Department of Rehabilitation Sciences, Faculty of Education, East China Normal University, Shanghai 200062, China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Social functioning Children Network meta-analysis Dose-response relationship A B S T R A C T Background: Children with ADHD frequently face social dysfunction hindering neurodevelopment. While exercise shows promise, the relative efficacy of specific modalities and precise dose- response relationships remain undefined. This study compares exercise modalities to identify the optimal dose for enhancing social functioning. Methods: Seven databases were systematically searched from inception to March 2025 for ran domized controlled trials of exercise interventions targeting social outcomes in children with ADHD. Exercise interventions were categorized by modality (closed-skill exercise, open-skill exercise, multicomponent exercise and mind-body therapy). Doses were harmonized to MET- min/week. Bayesian network meta-analysis (Hedges’ g) synthesized relative efficacy, while a 4- knot natural-spline model identified the optimal dose-response range. Results: Thirteen trials including 703 participants aged 6–13 years were eligible. Closed-skill exercise produced the largest improvements in social functioning (Hedges’ g = −0.96, 95% CrI: −1.18 to −0.75). Multicomponent exercise (Hedges’ g = −0.74, 95% CrI: −1.13 to −0.34) and mind–body therapy (Hedges’ g = −0.53, 95% CrI: −0.79 to −0.28) showed moderate, clinically meaningful effects, whereas open-skill exercise had small effects (Hedges’ g = −0.16, 95% CrI: −0.36 to −0.04). Dose-response analysis indicated an inverted U-shaped relationship, with a minimum effective dose of 660 MET-min/week and an optimal dose of 1290 MET-min/ week. Both age and gender had a significant impact on the outcomes. Conclusion: Closed-skill and multicomponent exercise appear most effective for improving social functioning in children with ADHD, with benefits maximised at around 1290 MET-min/week. 1. Introduction Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is the most prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder in childhood, affecting approximately 5–7% of school-age children and adolescents worldwide (Salari et al., 2023). Its core symptoms—inattention, impul sivity, and hyperactivity—adversely affect academic performance, psychological development, and social integration. While these symptoms typically emerge in early childhood, research indicates that over 50% of affected individuals continue to experience functional impairments into adulthood (Danielson et al., 2024), often manifested through persistent social dysfunction and diminished quality of life (Samosh et al., 2024). Consequently, the impaired social functioning observed among children and adolescents diag nosed with ADHD, particularly evident in peer interactions, represents a significant clinical concern requiring attention (Faraone et al., 2021). Social dysfunction in ADHD is a multifaceted construct that manifests across three primary domains: (1) social skills performance deficits (the ‘knowing-doing’ gap), (2) impaired social information processing, and (3) diminished social reciprocity and peer rela tionship stability (Bunford et al., 2015; McQuade & Hoza, 2015). Approximately 60% of children and adolescents with ADHD experience significant social impairment, which not only hinders immediate development but also elevates the risk of comorbid internalizing disorders, such as anxiety and depression, in later life (Nijmeijer et al., 2008). These challenges are further compounded by comorbid conditions like Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) or Conduct Disorder (CD), which exacerbate symptom severity and psychosocial impairment (Eskander, 2020), engendering a pernicious cycle that negatively impacts familial harmony and future vocational prospects. At present, pharmacological treatment remains the primary approach for managing ADHD, as evidenced by the utilisation of central nervous system stimulants, including extended-release methylphenidate formulations (Biederman & Faraone, 2005). Non-pharmacological interventions encompass health education, cognitive behavioural therapy (Safren et al., 2005), alongside comprehensive approaches including lifestyle training, mindfulness and meditation, and occupational therapy. Although medication has been demonstrated to be efficacious in the alleviation of core ADHD symptoms (such as attention deficits and impulse control), there is currently no evidence to suggest that it can enhance positive social behaviours or normalize peer status (Hoza et al., 2005). Moreover, parents frequently express concerns regarding its side effects, including reduced appetite and sleep disturbances (Nafees et al., 2014; Stein et al., 2012). Conversely, the focus on exercise intervention as a low-risk, highly feasible, and multifaceted non-pharmacological approach is increasing (Cerrillo-Urbina et al., 2015). Research indicates that exercise not only effectively im proves core symptoms but also positively impacts social functioning by providing structured social settings that enhance teamwork abilities and social skills in children and adolescents with ADHD (Pontifex et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2023). Consequently, exercise is regarded as a potentially effective complementary treatment for ADHD. Despite the exploration of the impact of exercise on the social functioning of children and adolescents with ADHD in existing research, a systematic and quantitative synthesis is warranted for several reasons. First, a substantial body of new evidence has been published since the lats meta-analysis conducted in 2015, requiring an urgent update of the current knowledge base. Second, previous reviews often failed to evaluate social functioning as an independent primary outcome, typically subsuming it under broader "behavioral improvement" without dedicated indicator analyses (Cornelius et al., 2017). Moreover, there remains a paucity of sys tematic comparisons regarding the relative efficacy of different exercise modalities and a lack of evidence concerning the dose-response relationship between intervention parameters (e.g., frequency, intensity, total volume) and social outcomes. To address these gaps, the present study employs network meta-analysis and dose-response modeling to systematically evaluate the efficacy of various exercise types and identify optimal intervention dosages, thereby providing a theoretical foundation and practical guidance for clinical rehabilitation. 2. Method 2.1. Protocol registration This review strictly adheres to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Network Meta-Analyses (PRISMA-NMA) guidelines (Page et al., 2021) and the Cochrane Collaboration manual (Jpt, 2008).The study protocol has been registered with the PROSPERO International Prospective Systematic Reviews Register (Registration number: CRD42025632382). As this study involves only a review and synthesis of published literature without human or animal experimentation, approval from an institutional review board is not required. 2.2. Information and search strategy A comprehensive search strategy was employed, encompassing eight prominent electronic databases, namely MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, SPORT Discus, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and CINAHL. The search was X. Gao et al. Research in Developmental Disabilities 172 (2026) 105276 2

conducted from inception to March 2025, with no restrictions applied to the publication date or language. The search strategy was formulated through the combination of keywords and Medical Subject Headings terms, including 'children', 'adolescents', 'attention- deficit/hyperactivity disorder', 'ADHD', 'physical activity' and 'exercise'. The detailed search strategy is presented in Supplement 1. In addition to conducting database searches, a cross-check was performed on reference lists of key reviews, and Google Scholar was searched using the same search terms to identify relevant citations within included studies. 2.3. Inclusion and exclusion criteria Studies were included if they met all the following criteria: 1) Participants: Children or adolescents aged 6–18 years with ADHD (diagnosed according to DSM (Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders: DSM-5TM, 5th ed, 2013) or ICD (Organization, 2004) criteria); 2) Duration of exercise intervention: ≥4 weeks (Jonsson et al., 2019); 3) Outcomes: It is imperative that assessments of social functioning impairments in children and adolescents be included; 4) Study design: The present study exclusively considers randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Research is required that compares different types or intensities of exercise, or that compares exercise groups with control groups. 5) The publication has been disseminated through the medium of peer-reviewed academic journals, with the written content being presented in either English or Chinese. The following criteria are to be considered as exclusionary: 1) Studies using healthy children as control groups; 2) Interventions based on multimodal approaches, such as exercise combined with psychotherapy or behavioural interventions; 3) Identification of duplicate publications; 4) Studies with erroneous, missing, or unobtainable data. 2.4. Study selection and data extraction We imported the retrieved studies into Endnote X9 and removed duplicate trials. Two reviewers (X.G. and M.Z.) independently screened study titles, abstracts, and full texts, extracting data on study characteristics, participant characteristics, interventions, and study outcomes. For studies reporting two or more measurement time points, we selected only baseline and post-intervention mea surements. Where data were presented graphically, we attempted extraction using GetData Graph Digitizer. For studies where data could not be obtained, we will make three attempts to contact the corresponding author within six weeks to request the data. In the event of disagreement, we will resolve the issue through discussion or by consulting a third independent author (M.H.Q.) until consensus is reached. 2.5. Data coding and management Exercise interventions were categorized into four distinct modalities: closed-skill exercise, open-skill exercise, multicomponent exercise, and mind-body therapy. The classification was based on the predictable nature of the environment and the specific motor demands of each activity. Detailed definitions and the classification criteria for each included study are provided in Supplement 2. The exercise intensity unit is defined as the product of the specific exercise intensity (task metabolic equivalent [MET]), weekly frequency, and single-session duration based on primary intervention time (excluding warm-up and cool-down), expressed as MET-min/week (Li et al., 2025). Duration used in the study was not explicitly defined; mean total duration was calculated using study averages and progressive protocols. MET values were assigned according to A Youth Compendium of Physical Activities (Butte et al., 2018); for unlisted activities, the closest equivalent activity in the guidelines was used (Li et al., 2025). For multi-component interventions, overall intensity was calculated as the duration-weighted average MET value of each component. Exercise intensity ategories were predefined as follows: light (<3.0 MET), moderate (3.0–6.0 MET), and vigorous (>6.0 MET). 2.6. Quality assessment Risk of bias assessment employed the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for randomized controlled trials (RoB) (Higgins et al., 2011), with feasibility evaluation conducted using the Confidence IN Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) tool (Nikolakopoulou et al., 2020). CINeMA is a tool designed to assess the confidence in the results of network meta-analyses (NMAs). It assists researchers in evaluating NMA outcomes and determining their reliability. More specifically, CINeMA employs a series of criteria to assess consistency between direct and indirect evidence, alongside other potential sources of bias, thereby providing an overall confidence assessment for NMA results. The assessment encompasses selection bias, performance bias, attrition bias, detection bias, and reporting bias. Following Cochrane Handbook criteria (Higgins et al., 2011), each bias domain is judged as “yes”, “no”, or “unclear” to indicate whether suf ficient measures were taken to prevent each potential source of bias within each study. Two independent reviewers conducted the risk of bias and credibility assessments independently. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or by arbitration by a third author. X. Gao et al. 2.7. Summary measures and synthesis To measure the magnitude of effects across different interventions, this study employs Hedges’g as a standardized effect size in dicator, interpreted as follows: small effect (~0.2), moderate effect (~0.5), large effect (~0.8) (Cohen, 1988). Hedges’g effectively corrects for bias arising from small sample sizes and facilitates comparisons across studies with varying sample sizes. Effect sizes were calculated based on the standardized mean difference (SMD) and standard deviation (SD) from each study, ensuring a consistent measure of intervention effects. For studies lacking SD data, we estimated the standard deviation using standard error, 95% confidence intervals, p-values, or t-statistics. Following the Cochrane Collaboration's recommended bias risk assessment tool, we employed a correlation coefficient of 0.5 to calculate SD differences (Higgins et al., 2019). Furthermore, referencing prior research, we defined 0.5 SD units as the minimum clinically important difference (MCID) (Norman et al., 2003). The primary analysis employed a Bayesian multilevel network meta-analysis model based on arms, assuming each observed effect size represents a sample from a broader true effect distribution. To account for sampling error and heterogeneity in effect sizes across studies, we utilized a random-effects model to estimate the effect of exercise interventions, thereby enhancing the stability and Fig. 1. reliability of the analytical results. The Bayesian analysis fitted a multilevel random-effects model using the R package ‘brms’ (Bürkner, 2017), with model intercepts specified using weak prior information (population effect size μ ~ [0, 1], between-studies heterogeneity τ ~ [0, 1]). Model convergence was assessed using the potential scale reduction factor (PSRF) (Gelman et al., 1995), with PSRF values below 1.05 indicating good model fit. To address dependency among multiple effect sizes within the same study, we employed a multilevel model to account for intra-study dependence of multiple effect sizes. The ranking of different interventions was assessed by calculating the Sum of Areas Under the Cumulative Rank Curve (SUCRA) values (Salanti et al., 2011). The similarity in the distribution of key effect modifiers between comparison groups was also examined in order to validate the transferability assumptions of network meta-analysis. Furthermore, the consistency between direct and indirect comparisons was evaluated using the node partitioning method within the 'netmeta' software package (Rücker & Schwarzer, 2014), and network consistency was tested using the 'by treatment design' model. All statistical analyses were conducted within the R environment (version 4.4.1). 2.8. Additional analyses A random-effects model was employed, with the brms package (Bürkner, 2017) serving as the underlying framework for con ducting a non-linear dose-response analysis (natural spline, 4 knots). The present analysis modelled the relationship between weekly exercise dose and the duration of the exercise intervention, and social dysfunction in children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD. In addition, participant characteristics (age, gender) and funding availability were considered as potential moderators, with the aim of assessing the robustness of the model. Furthermore, a multilevel Egger's regression test (Rodgers & Pustejovsky, 2020) was conducted in order to examine potential small-study effects. In addition, to incorporate a more state-of-the-art publication-bias-adjusted approach, a supplementary robust Bayesian meta-analysis (RoBMA) was performed (Bartoˇs et al., 2022). RoBMA model-averages across models assuming the presence versus absence of an overall effect, heterogeneity, and publication bias, thereby yielding publication-bias-adjusted pooled estimates. Because some studies reported multiple SFD symptom indicators/tasks, task-specific effect sizes within the same treatment arm were first aggregated at the study-arm level to avoid double-counting. The primary aggregation assumed a within-study correlation of ρ = 0.6, with additional sensitivity analyses using ρ = 0.3 and ρ = 0.8. The resulting study-level pairwise effect sizes and their standard errors were then entered into the RoBMA. 3. Results 3.1. Study selection and characteristics The search process yielded a total of 3759 citations, of which 2600 were retained subsequent to the removal of duplicates (see Fig. 1). Following the rigorous screening process of 2600 titles and abstracts, as well as 137 full texts, 13 randomized controlled trials were identified as meeting the inclusion criteria for this systematic review (Supplement 14). The studies encompassed a total of 703 participants with an average age ranging from 6.83 to 13.85 years, with female participants accounting for only approximately 2.6% of the study population. Six of the included studies originated from high-income countries: two from the United States, two from South Korea, one from Australia, and one from Spain. Furthermore, two studies were conducted in China, one in Egypt, one in Brazil, and one in Iran. The characteristics of the included studies and the features of the participant and treatment groups are detailed in Table 1 and Supplement 3. 3.2. Study bias and quality for evidence Supplement 4 presents the reporting bias tables, risk of reporting bias, and bias items for each study. The studies were then categorized into three risk levels: low risk of bias (0.00%), some risk of bias (84.62%), and high risk of bias (15.38%). The results of the CINeMA study, as outlined in Supplement 12, indicate that the quality of the evidence supporting intervention measures is categorised into three levels: low (40%), moderate (40%), and high (20%). The primary reasons for downgrading the quality ratings are as follows: risk of bias, the small number of direct comparison studies (<10), high heterogeneity, and minimal overlap in CRLs. 3.3. Comparative efficacy of different exercise modalities Fig. 2 presents comparative results across different exercise intervention types. Compared with the control group, the Closed-skill exercises group exhibited the highest number of participants and direct comparisons. The Closed-skill exercises group (Hedges’g = −0.96, 95% CrI: −1.18 to −0.75, k = 4, SCURA = 0.54) demonstrated a clinically significant effect in improving social dysfunction among children and adolescents with ADHD. The Multicomponent exercises group (Hedges’g = −0.74, 95% CrI: −1.13 to −0.34, k = 2, SCURA = 0.63) and Mind-body therapy (Hedges’g = −0.53, 95% CrI: −0.79 to −0.28, k = 3, SCURA=0.80) yielded moderate- effect therapies, likewise achieving clinically significant effects. The open-skill exercises group (Hedges’g = −0.16, 95% CrI: −0.36 to −0.04, k = 4, SCURA = 0.38) exhibited a smaller effect size. I2 was 67.5% (moderate to high), with an overall Q-statistic for Fig. 2.
