heterogeneity of 336.61 (P < 0.001). Conventional assessments of small-study effects at the network level did not indicate clear ev idence of funnel plot asymmetry, and the multilevel Egger’s regression test was not statistically significant (F1,80 = 1.5783, p = 0.2127) (Supplement 11). To further examine the robustness of the overall findings, a supplementary publication-bias-adjusted sensitivity analysis was conducted using RoBMA based on study-level pairwise effect sizes aggregated across task-specific outcomes. Under the primary within-study correlation assumption (ρ = 0.6), RoBMA yielded moderate evidence for publication bias (in clusion BF = 5.64) and strong evidence for heterogeneity (inclusion BF = 18.44), whereas evidence for a non-zero pooled effect was inconclusive (inclusion BF = 0.86). After adjusting for potential bias, the estimated pooled effect size was 0.146 (95% CrI: −0.509,0.820). Sensitivity analyses using alternative within-study correlations (ρ = 0.3 and ρ = 0.8) yielded a broadly similar overall pattern, with evidence for publication bias remaining present and the credible interval of the adjusted pooled effect continuing to include zero. While the primary NMA suggested a significant effect, the bias-adjusted estimate from the RoBMA framework crossed the null value, indicating that the observed significance might be sensitive to potential publication bias (Supplement 13). 3.4. The dose-response relationship and clinical MCID thresholds Fig. 3 illustrates the non-linear relationship between weekly exercise dose and therapeutic efficacy for social dysfunction, revealing a U-shaped dose-response relationship characterized by an inverted U-curve. The MCID dose was determined to be 660 MET-min/week Fig. 3. Dose-response relationship between exercise and improvement in social function disorder symptom in children and adolescents with ADHD. SFD, social function disorder. X. Gao et al. Research in Developmental Disabilities 172 (2026) 105276 7

(Hedges’g = −0.7, 95% CrI = −0.51 to −0.89), equivalent to 16–31 min of moderate-intensity exercise daily. The optimal dose was 1290 MET-min/week (Hedges’g = −1.43, 95% CrI = −0.98 to −1.89), corresponding to 31–61 min of moderate-intensity exercise daily. A detailed investigation into the duration of intervention and its efficacy in treating social dysfunction was conducted, revealing a non-linear relationship that exhibited a positive correlation trend. This relationship demonstrated that as intervention duration increased, therapeutic effectiveness diminished (see Supplement 8). Additionally, the broader 95% credible interval (CrI) in the subsequent phases signifies an elevated degree of uncertainty with protracted intervention. It is recommended that future research incorporate additional studies with a view to further validating and refining these trends. This would enhance the accuracy and reliability of predictions. 3.5. Moderation by participants and study characteristics Analysis of the efficacy of exercise on social functional impairment revealed that compared to models considering activity type alone (R2 = 0.273), both age (R2 = 0.374) and gender (R2 = 0.334) models increased explanatory power, whereas the funded model (R2 = 0.261) showed reduced explanatory power (Supplement 9). Women may experience greater improvements in social functional impairment within the Mind-body therapy group. Conversely, men may achieve greater improvements in social functional impairment within the Multicomponent exercises, Closed-skill exercises, and Open-skill exercises groups (Fig. 4). The relationship between ex ercise intervention effects and age also varied. Treatment efficacy diminished with increasing age in the Multicomponent exercises, Closed-skill exercises, and Mind-body therapy groups, whereas it remained relatively stable in the Open-skill exercises group (Fig. 4). 4. Discussion 4.1. Summary of principal findings The present study indicates that exercise interventions can improve social functioning in children and adolescents with ADHD, with interventions characterized by higher levels of structuralization demonstrating more pronounced effects. Specifically, network meta- analysis reveals that closed-skill exercises possess the most potent efficacy in enhancing social functioning, followed by multicom ponent exercise and mind-body therapy, while open-skill exercise exhibit comparatively diminished effects. Moreover, this research Fig. 4. Moderation by gender and age. SFD, social function disorder. X. Gao et al. Research in Developmental Disabilities 172 (2026) 105276 8

identifies a non-linear, U-shaped dose-response relationship between exercise volume and social function improvement. We estab lished a clinically significant threshold for the Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID) at 660 MET-min/week (equivalent to 16–31 min of daily moderate-intensity exercise) and identified an optimal therapeutic dose at 1290 MET-min/week (equivalent to 31–61 min of daily moderate-intensity exercise). Extrapolated analysis further revealed that gender and age serve as critical moderating factors, suggesting that individual phenotypic characteristics significantly influence treatment responsiveness. Taken together, these findings provide quantitative support for the potential clinical application of exercise interventions in addressing social dysfunction in pediatric ADHD populations. 4.2. Theoretical mechanisms of social impairment The social dysfunction observed in children and adolescents with ADHD is not an isolated phenomenon but is intricately inter twined with core symptomatology and underlying executive function deficits (Nijmeijer et al., 2008). Research has demonstrated that deficits in inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory make it more challenging for these children and adolescents to regulate their emotions, adhere to social norms, and express themselves appropriately in real-world interactions, thereby significantly limiting their social capabilities (Christiansen et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2023). While these neuropsychological mechanisms offer sub stantive explanations for the etiology of social impairment, the enhancement of social functioning is a multidimensional trajectory that extends beyond the mere mitigation of core symptoms. Nevertheless, a disproportionate majority of current intervention research remains narrowly focused on alleviating hyperactivity and inattention, often neglecting the imperative for direct interventions tar geting social integration itself. Consequently, to achieve more holistic and sustainable improvements, future paradigms should pri oritize the cultivation of pragmatic social skills and the application of robust emotion regulation strategies. Against this theoretical backdrop, the present study systematically explored various exercise modalities and identified marked heterogeneities in their ca pacity to improve social outcomes. 4.3. Efficacy comparisons across exercise modalities Among these intervention forms, closed-skill exercise emerged as the most efficacious modality for enhancing social functioning. This superiority may be attributed to the inherent characteristics of closed-skill tasks—specifically their highly structured nature and predictable repetitiveness—which are thought to more potently elicit activation within prefrontal cortex regions. This neural engagement enhances executive control and social coping mechanisms, making it uniquely suited for children and adolescents exhibiting high levels of impulsivity and distractibility (Christiansen et al., 2019). Furthermore, closed-skill exercise have been shown to augment activity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which facilitates the development of sophisticated social cognition, such as empathy and turn-taking awareness (Benzing et al., 2018). Such structured environments are exceptionally conducive to establishing behavioral regulation habits. In stark contrast, open-skill exercises (e.g., football, basketball), while ostensibly offering more inter active opportunities, impose excessive cognitive demands regarding rapid attention switching and perceptual judgment. For children and adolescents with ADHD, these demands may inadvertently trigger anxiety or impulsive reactions. Under certain conditions, the high-pressure team environment may paradoxically hinder the formation of positive peer bonds, increasing the risk of social exclusion and exacerbating feelings of social frustration, thereby attenuating the overall efficacy of the intervention (Hoza et al., 2015). 4.4. Non-linear dose-response relationships Regarding the parameters of the intervention, this study identified a non-linear, U-shaped dose-response relationship. This finding implies that moderate-intensity exercise, when delivered at an appropriately calibrated volume, optimizes social skill acquisition, whereas sub-threshold levels fail to provide the requisite cognitive and situational stimulation. Conversely, suprathreshold volumes may induce physiological fatigue, heightened anxiety, or distractibility, which collectively neutralize the intervention's benefits. This complex relationship underscores the necessity of avoiding the "too much of a good thing" pitfall when prescribing exercise regimens for this clinical population. Specifically, this study proposes 660 MET-min/week as the requisite volume to achieve the MCID. Furthermore, the optimal therapeutic window was identified at approximately 1290 MET-min/week, where social improvements reached their peak. Although this optimal dose is quantitatively lower than the World Health Organization's (WHO) general recommendation of 60 min of daily moderate-to-vigorous activity (Bull et al., 2020), it represents a clinically meaningful milestone for children and adolescents with ADHD. This suggests that even conservative exercise volumes can yield substantial therapeutic dividends, providing a more pragmatic and achievable target for children and adolescents who struggle to meet international physical activity guidelines. Importantly, intervention protocols should be meticulously tailored to individual fitness levels and psychological tolerance, with intensity gradually titrated to maximize efficacy while minimizing the risk of overexertion. 4.5. Influencing factors and research robustness The moderating influence of individual factors, such as gender and age, warrants specific consideration. Our analysis indicates that female participants exhibited a higher sensitivity to mind-body therapies, whereas males demonstrated superior responsiveness to closed-skill and multi-component formats. This divergence may reflect sex-specific preferences in emotional self-regulation and physical engagement, representing a fertile area for future investigation. Concurrently, the diminished efficacy of certain interventions X. Gao et al. Research in Developmental Disabilities 172 (2026) 105276 9

observed with increasing age suggests that developmental stages influence intervention acceptance and cognitive adaptability. Therefore, prioritizing early-stage interventions may be instrumental in achieving the most favorable long-term social outcomes. A discrepancy was observed between the primary network meta-analytic findings and the publication-bias-adjusted estimates derived from the RoBMA framework. Specifically, the primary NMA suggested a favorable overall pattern of exercise effects, whereas the RoBMA-adjusted pooled estimate became statistically uncertain, with the interval including zero. One plausible explanation for this difference lies in the inherently conservative nature of the RoBMA framework. RoBMA applies Bayesian model averaging across competing models that differ with respect to the presence or absence of an overall effect, heterogeneity, and publication bias. Under conditions of substantial between-study heterogeneity and a relatively limited evidence base, the framework may assign greater weight to models closer to the null, thereby yielding a more attenuated pooled estimate. Although the RoBMA findings suggest that the magnitude of the pooled effect should be interpreted with greater caution, they do not necessarily negate the potential clinical relevance of the present findings. Across different sensitivity models, the direction of the effect remained broadly consistent, indicating a potentially beneficial role of exercise interventions for improving social dysfunction in children and adolescents with ADHD. At the same time, the discrepancy between the primary NMA and the RoBMA-adjusted estimates highlights the need for further high-quality, large-scale randomized controlled trials to provide more precise effect estimates and to reduce the influence of small-study effects and reporting bias. 4.6. Strengths and limitations This study offers distinctive contributions regarding both methodological rigor and clinical translatability. First, incorporating the MCID as a criterion for assessing social function improvement enhances the clinical interpretability and practical value of the findings. Second, the application of Bayesian network meta-analysis and nonlinear dose-response modeling not only systematically compared the effects of different exercise interventions but also clearly identified effective and optimal dose ranges. Such findings provide robust, quantitative evidence to inform the development of personalized exercise prescriptions, highlighting the study’s considerable potential for seamless clinical implementation. Despite these contributions, several limitations warrant acknowledgment. First, the omission of granular intervention parame ters—such as real-time heart rate data, precise intensity metrics, or consistent attendance rates—in some primary studies necessitated the use of proxy-based estimations derived from contemporary literature. Although these procedures were based on established guidelines, they may have introduced additional computational uncertainty. Second, the supplementary publication-bias-adjusted sensitivity analysis suggested a more conservative pooled pattern than conventional assessments alone, indicating that the magni tude of the overall pooled effect should be interpreted prudently. Finally, the evidence base remained demographically imbalanced, with female participants representing only a small proportion of the total sample, and detailed reporting of concurrent medication use was often insufficient, limiting our ability to examine potential treatment interactions.These constraints underscore the need for future research to prioritize more gender-inclusive cohorts and standardized reporting of therapeutic interactions to further refine our un derstanding of individualized exercise responses. 5. Conclusions This study demonstrates that exercise interventions can effectively improve social functioning deficits in children and adolescents with ADHD. Specifically, closed-skill exercise yielded the most significant effects, followed by multi-component exercise and mind- body therapy, while open-skill exercise produced relatively limited benefits. Exercise interventions exhibit an optimal dose win dow, with 660 MET-min/week (equivalent to 16–31 min of moderate-intensity exercise daily) representing the minimum effective dose and 1290 MET-min/week (equivalent to 31–61 min of moderate-intensity exercise daily) constituting the optimal dose. These findings provide quantitative evidence for developing individualized exercise prescriptions in clinical practice, holding significant clinical application value. metadata_title: A systematic review on the association between ADHD and procrastination
pages: A systematic review on the association between ADHD and procrastination Rossella Suriano * Department of Cognitive Sciences, University of Messina, Messina 98100, Italy A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: ADHD Procrastination Self-regulation Systematic review PRISMA A B S T R A C T Background: Procrastination is a maladaptive self-regulation behavior frequently observed in in dividuals with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), yet the consistency and under lying mechanisms of this association remain unclear. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic search was conducted in Web of Sci ence, Scopus, PsycINFO, and PubMed. Peer-reviewed quantitative studies examining the rela tionship between ADHD (diagnosis or symptoms) and procrastination using validated measures were included. Results: Eleven studies (N = 2788) met inclusion criteria. Across studies, ADHD symptoms were consistently positively associated with procrastination. Inattention emerged as the most robust correlate. Findings were also consistent with the involvement of executive functioning deficits, emotion dysregulation, and motivational processes, although evidence was primarily based on cross-sectional designs. Conclusion: The available evidence supports a robust association between ADHD symptoms and procrastination. However, methodological limitations, including reliance on cross-sectional data and heterogeneous measures, preclude causal inferences. Future research should employ longi tudinal and multi-method designs to clarify underlying mechanisms. 1. Introduction Procrastination is commonly defined as the voluntary and irrational delay in initiating or completing a planned action, despite awareness of its potential negative consequences ((Klingsieck, 2013a, 2013b; Steel, 2007; Svartdal & Nemtcan, 2022). The construct has been progressively reconceptualized as multidimensional, encompassing different forms (e.g., general, academic, decisional, and behavioral) and distinguishing between functional and dysfunctional configurations (active vs. passive procrastination) (Choi & Moran, (2009); Chun Chu & Choi, (2005); Ferrari, (1992); (Klingsieck, 2013a, 2013b). This theoretical evolution has helped move beyond a unitary view of the phenomenon, instead framing it as the expression of dysfunctional processes of cognitive, emotional, and motivational regulation (Rebetez et al., 2015; Sirois & Pychyl, 2013). More recent theoretical models converge in interpreting procrastination as a failure of self-regulation, arising from the interaction between deficits in executive functions, difficulties in emotion regulation, and alterations in motivational processes (Mohammadi Bytamar et al., 2020; Rebetez et al., 2018; Steel, 2007; Zhang et al., 2019). In particular, the inability to maintain focus on long-term * Correspondence to: Department of Cognitive, Psychological and Pedagogical Sciences and Cultural Studies, University of Messina, Messina 98100, Italy. goals, modulate negative emotional states associated with the task, and resist immediate gratification represents a core feature of the phenomenon (Wu et al., 2016). These perspectives are situated within the framework of Temporal Motivation Theory (Steel & K ̈onig, 2006) and broader models of self-regulatory failure, which highlight the role of impulsivity, delay sensitivity (delay discounting), and emotion regulation processes in the development of procrastinatory behaviors (Steel et al., 2018). Consistent with dual-process models of self-regulation (Hofmann, Friese, & Strack, 2009), procrastination can be further inter preted as the result of an imbalance between controlled (top-down) processes, responsible for maintaining goal-directed behavior, and automatic (bottom-up) processes, driven by impulses, emotional reactivity, and sensitivity to immediate reward. From this perspec tive, procrastinatory behaviors emerge when automatic processes—such as avoidance tendencies triggered by negative emotions associated with the task or a preference for immediate gratification—override executive control mechanisms (Sirois, 2014; Zentall, 2021). Accordingly, procrastination may be understood as a short-term regulatory strategy aimed at reducing immediate distress, although dysfunctional with respect to the pursuit of future goals (Sirois & Pychyl, 2013). Within this theoretical framework, conditions characterized by impairments in self-regulatory processes are particularly relevant. Among these, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) represents a key reference model (Bolden & Fillauer, 2020; Oguchi et al., 2021). ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent and pervasive patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, and is classified into three clinical presentations: predominantly inattentive (ADHD-I), predominantly hyper active/impulsive (ADHD-H), and combined (ADHD-C) (American and Association, 2013; Fabio et al., 2024; Faraone et al., 2021). Within recent theoretical models, ADHD has been conceptualized as a dual-pathway disorder (Sonuga-Barke, 2002), in which deficits in executive control processes coexist with alterations in motivational systems, including delay aversion and heightened sensitivity to reward (Karalunas & Huang-Pollock, 2011; Sonuga-Barke, 2003). Beyond this framework, broader accounts have suggested that in dividuals with ADHD may also exhibit steeper temporal discounting, reflecting a stronger preference for immediate over delayed outcomes (Marx et al., 2021). These motivational characteristics may contribute to difficulties in sustaining effort toward long-term goals and help explain the association between ADHD symptoms and procrastinatory behavior. Individuals with ADHD exhibit significant impairments across multiple domains, including academic, social, emotional, and physical functioning, with substantial consequences for everyday life (French et al., 2024; Kosheleff et al., 2023). A large body of literature has documented a robust association between the core symptoms of the disorder and deficits in executive functions, including working memory, inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and planning ability (Fabio & Suriano, 2021; 2024; Martinussen et al., 2005; Willcutt et al., 2005). These difficulties, together with alterations in motivational and emotional processes (e.g., delay aversion and difficulties in affective regulation), support the conceptualization of ADHD as a disorder of executive and behavioral regulation, as well as a condition characterized by an imbalance between top-down control systems and bottom-up motivational and automatic processes (Fabio et al., 2026; Petrovic & Castellanos, 2016; Sonuga-Barke, 2002). From this perspective, the mechanisms underlying ADHD show substantial overlap with those implicated in procrastination, suggesting the involvement of transdiagnostic self-regulatory processes in the link between the two constructs (Bodalski et al., 2023; Niermann & Scheres, 2014). Consistently, a growing number of empirical studies have investigated the association between ADHD symptoms and procrastinatory behaviors in both clinical and non-clinical populations (Altgassen et al., 2019; Niermann & Scheres, 2014). However, the existing literature remains fragmented and is characterized by marked heterogeneity in the definition and operationalization of both ADHD (e.g., symptoms vs. diagnosis) and procrastination (e.g., global vs. domain-specific measures). In this context, distinguishing among different forms of procrastination is particularly important, because global, academic, decisional, behavioral, active, and passive procrastination may reflect partially distinct self-regulatory processes and may therefore be associated with different patterns of ADHD symptoms. Previous research has used heterogeneous measures of procrastination and has often focused on specific manifestations of the construct, leaving open the question of whether the ADHD–procrastination association is comparable across different forms of procrastinatory behavior. Moreover, the principal shared theoretical mechanisms—such as emotion regulation, delay sensitivity, and the imbalance between automatic and controlled processes—have rarely been considered in an integrated manner. In this regard, a systematic synthesis that critically organizes the empirical evidence within a unified theoretical framework appears crucial for advancing understanding of the phenomenon and clarifying the nature of the relationship between ADHD and procrasti nation. Despite the growing body of empirical research, findings remain fragmented, and no systematic synthesis has yet clarified whether the association between ADHD and procrastination is consistent across different populations and operationalizations, nor which mechanisms most reliably account for this relationship. In light of this, the present systematic review aims to examine the quantitative empirical literature on the relationship between ADHD symptoms (or diagnosis) and procrastination. Specifically, the objectives of the review are to: (a) examine the consistency of the association between ADHD and procrastination across studies; (b) analyze the role of different forms of procrastination; (c) explore the principal cognitive, emotional, and motivational mechanisms underlying this relationship; and (d) identify the main methodological and theoretical gaps in the existing literature. 2. Method 2.1. Search strategy The systematic literature search was conducted across four electronic databases: Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and PubMed. The last search was conducted on March 15, 2026. The general search string was: (ADHD OR "attention deficit" OR inattention OR impulsiv* OR hyperactiv*) AND procrastinat*. The search strategy was adapted to the syntax and indexing systems specific to each R. Suriano Research in Developmental Disabilities 175 (2026) 105342 2

database in order to ensure conceptual equivalence across sources (e.g., title/abstract fields in PubMed and PsycINFO, topic search in Web of Science, and title–abstract–keywords fields in Scopus). The complete database-specific search strategies, including field codes and applied filters, are reported in Supplementary Table S1. Searches were limited to peer-reviewed scientific articles published in English, with no temporal restrictions. No additional hand-searching of reference lists was conducted. 2.2. Eligibility criteria Studies were included in the present systematic review if they met the following criteria. 2.3. Inclusion criteria Only empirical quantitative studies were included, encompassing both cross-sectional and longitudinal designs. Studies were required to assess attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) through either a formal clinical diagnosis or validated psychometric instruments specifically designed to measure ADHD symptoms (e.g., ASRS, CAARS, Conners scales), operationalized either categor ically or dimensionally. Procrastination had to be measured using standardized and validated instruments (e.g., General Procrastination Scale, Procrasti nation Assessment Scale for Students, Pure Procrastination Scale), ensuring construct validity and comparability across studies. Studies were included only if they explicitly and directly examined and statistically tested the relationship between ADHD and procrastination within the main analyses. Eligible analytical approaches included correlations, regression analyses, group compari sons, structural equation modeling, and mediation or moderation analyses, provided that the ADHD–procrastination association was a primary or central component of the main analytical framework. Studies including additional psychological or behavioral variables were retained, provided that the ADHD–procrastination association was explicitly tested within this framework. The reference to a “central role” was not intended to introduce an additional eligibility criterion, but rather to clarify that the ADHD–procrastination association had to be part of the study’s main analytical framework. Specifically, the association was considered central when procrastination was operationalized as a primary outcome, mediator, moderator, or key construct analyzed in relation to ADHD within the main statistical analyses, rather than merely as a descriptive, secondary, or peripheral variable. 2.4. Exclusion criteria Studies were excluded if they met one or more of the following conditions. Studies that did not explicitly examine or statistically test the relationship between ADHD and procrastination were excluded, even when both constructs were measured. Studies were also excluded when ADHD or procrastination was included only as a covariate, control variable, descriptive variable, secondary variable, or marginal predictor in analyses primarily focused on other relationships, without a direct statistical test of the ADHD–procrastination association. Studies were further excluded when ADHD was used only as a moderator of the relationship between procrastination and another outcome, or when procrastination was used only as a predictor, covariate, or associated factor of another outcome, without the ADHD–procrastination association itself being a primary or central component of the main analysis. Studies using non-validated, non-specific, or ad hoc measures of ADHD or procrastination were excluded. This restriction was adopted to preserve the conceptual specificity of the review and to ensure that the included evidence directly addressed the ADHD–procrastination association, rather than only providing ancillary or descriptive information from analyses primarily focused on other constructs. 2.5. Selection procedure The screening of studies was conducted using Microsoft Excel. In an initial phase, the identified records were examined on the basis of title and abstract in order to assess their relevance with respect to the inclusion and exclusion criteria. Subsequently, articles deemed potentially eligible were evaluated at the full-text level. During the screening process, studies were classified as included, excluded or potentially relevant based on the criteria defined previously. Two independent reviewers screened titles and abstracts based on the predefined eligibility criteria. Full-text articles were then assessed independently. Disagreements were resolved through discussion, and when necessary, consultation with a third experienced researcher. Studies that measured both ADHD-related variables and procrastination but did not directly test their association were excluded. Study authors were not contacted to obtain or confirm un reported associations. 2.6. Data extraction For each included study, data were extracted using a standardized extraction form. The extracted information included: authors, year of publication, country, sample characteristics, study design, measurement instruments for ADHD and procrastination, and the main findings. R. 2.7. Quality assessment The methodological quality of the included studies was independently assessed by two reviewers using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross-Sectional Studies. The checklist evaluates eight domains related to sampling procedures, measurement validity, confounding factors, and statistical analysis. Each item was rated as “yes”, “no”, “unclear”, or “not applicable”. 2.8. Data synthesis Due to substantial heterogeneity in study designs, measures, and statistical approaches, a meta-analysis was not conducted. Spe cifically, the included studies differed in the operationalization of ADHD, including clinical diagnosis, screening cut-offs, dimensional symptom scores, and specific symptom dimensions. They also differed in the type of procrastination assessed, including general, academic, passive, active, and behavioral procrastination, as well as in sample characteristics, ranging from clinical adult samples to university, medical student, community, and online samples. In addition, the statistical indices reported across studies were not directly comparable, as they included zero-order and partial correlations, standardized and unstandardized regression coefficients, group comparisons, mediation paths, SEM estimates, and indirect effects. Several studies also did not report confidence intervals or sufficient information to transform all associations into a common standardized effect size without introducing additional assump tions. For these reasons, a formal meta-analysis was not considered appropriate. Instead, a narrative synthesis was performed, while tabulating the main effect estimates and precision information when available. The synthesis focused on (1) the consistency of as sociations between ADHD symptoms and procrastination and (2) the explanatory mechanisms proposed across studies, including executive functioning, emotion regulation, and motivational processes. Particular attention was given to differences in sample characteristics, ADHD operationalization, types of procrastination assessed, and study quality. Studies were grouped narratively ac cording to sample characteristics, ADHD operationalization, type of procrastination assessed, and the explanatory mechanisms examined. The review was not prospectively registered, and no protocol was prepared. Fig. 1. PRISMA diagram for study selection. R. Suriano Research in Developmental Disabilities 175 (2026) 105342 4

3. Results 3.1. Study selection The initial search in the databases yielded a total of 464 records. After the removal of 218 duplicates, 246 articles remained and were subjected to screening based on title and abstract. Subsequently, articles deemed potentially relevant (13) were evaluated through full-text review according to the inclusion and exclusion criteria previously defined. Of the 13 articles assessed for eligibility at the full-text stage, 2 were excluded. Reasons for exclusion are provided in Supplementary Table S2. At the end of this selection process, 11 studies were included in the present systematic review (Fig. 1). 3.2. Characteristics of the included studies The included studies, published between 2014 and 2026, comprised a total of 2788 participants from studies conducted across six countries: Germany, the United States, Iran, Hungary, Israel, Netherlands, and online samples recruited through MTurk or Prolific. Sample sizes ranged from 53 participants (Altgassen et al., 2019) to 640 participants (Netzer Turgeman & Pollak, 2026). Most studies were conducted on non-clinical samples, including university students, medical students, and general adult online samples (Bodalski et al., 2023; Bolden & Fillauer, 2020; Massoodi et al., 2025; Müller et al., 2023; Netzer Turgeman & Pollak, 2023, 2025, 2026; Niermann & Scheres, 2014; Shirdel et al., 2024). A more limited number included clinical or clinically characterized samples, such as adults with a clinical ADHD diagnosis or outpatients evaluated for ADHD (Altgassen et al., 2019; Ashworth & McCown, 2018). All studies adopted a cross-sectional design; several studies additionally employed mediation models or structural equation models (Bodalski et al., 2023; Bolden & Fillauer, 2020; Netzer Turgeman & Pollak, 2023, 2026; Shirdel et al., 2024). ADHD was operationalized both categorically (clinical diagnosis; Altgassen et al., 2019) and dimensionally using validated self-report instruments, predominantly the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) (Ashworth & McCown, 2018; Massoodi et al., 2025; Müller et al., 2023; Netzer Turgeman & Pollak, 2023, 2025, 2026; Shirdel et al., 2024). Procrastination was assessed in all studies using standardized scales, with variations in type (general procrastination, academic procrastination, or specific subtypes). The main characteristics of the included studies are reported in Table 1. 3.3. Association between ADHD and procrastination All included studies reported at least one significant positive association between ADHD symptoms and procrastination, although the magnitude of the effects and the operationalization of both constructs varied across studies (Altgassen et al., 2019; Ashworth & McCown, 2018; Bodalski et al., 2023; Bolden & Fillauer, 2020; Massoodi et al., 2025; Müller et al., 2023; Netzer Turgeman & Pollak, 2023, 2025, 2026; Niermann & Scheres, 2014; Shirdel et al., 2024). Although the heterogeneity of statistical metrics precluded quantitative pooling, the available estimates suggest that the most frequent pattern was a moderate positive association between ADHD symptoms and procrastination. Among studies reporting zero- order correlations, effect sizes generally fell in the moderate range, approximately between r = .42 and r = .51, with one study reporting a stronger association (r = .72). Regression and SEM-based estimates were less directly comparable, but they generally converged in indicating a positive association between ADHD symptoms and procrastination. For example, passive procrastination showed a positive association with ADHD symptoms, whereas active procrastination showed a small negative association, suggesting that the magnitude and direction of effects may vary depending on the specific form of procrastination assessed. Overall, the distri bution of findings therefore points to a predominantly moderate positive association, while also indicating meaningful variability across measures and analytical models. For instance, Massoodi et al. (2025) reported a moderate correlation between ADHD and academic procrastination (r = .478), along with a significant predictive effect (β =.746). This association was also observed in non-clinical populations. Among university students, ADHD symptoms were positively associated with procrastination in both correlational analyses and mediation models (Bodalski et al., 2023; Bolden & Fillauer, 2020). Notably, in the latter study, executive functions statistically mediated the relationship in a cross-sectional model in which procras tination was treated as the predictor and ADHD symptoms as the outcome, limiting conclusions about directional effects. Similarly, Müller et al. (2023) found that passive procrastination was positively associated with ADHD symptoms, whereas active procrastination showed a negative association. Converging evidence also emerged from general adult samples, in which ADHD symptoms were positively associated with pro crastination even after controlling for motivational variables and item overlap (Netzer Turgeman & Pollak, 2023, 2025, 2026; Shirdel et al., 2024). Regarding symptom dimensions, several studies indicated that inattention represents the most robust predictor of procrastination. Specifically, inattention was significantly associated with general procrastination, whereas hyperactivity and impulsivity were no longer significant after controlling for shared variance (Niermann & Scheres, 2014). This pattern was supported by other studies, which also found stronger associations between procrastination and inattentive symptoms compared to other ADHD dimensions (Bolden & Fillauer, 2020; Netzer Turgeman & Pollak, 2023, 2026). 3.4. Explanatory Mechanisms and Functional Correlates Several studies have examined the possible mechanisms underlying the association between ADHD and procrastination, suggesting a multifactorial model involving executive, emotional, and motivational processes. With regard to executive functions, the findings are consistent with their possible role in the link between ADHD and procrasti nation. In particular, Bolden and Fillauer (2020) reported evidence compatible with a mediating role of executive functions, with particular relevance for time management and organization. Consistent findings also emerge from clinical studies, in which poorer attentional performance was associated with greater procrastination (Ashworth & McCown, 2018). In addition, Altgassen et al. (2019) reported findings compatible with a partially mediating role of prospective memory in the relationship between ADHD and procrastination. Emotional processes also emerged as relevant. Bodalski et al. (2023) reported findings consistent with a role of emotion dysre gulation and low self-esteem in the relationship between ADHD symptoms and procrastination, including a significant serial pathway. At the motivational level, Netzer Turgeman and Pollak (2023) found that lower expectancy of success and greater impulsivity were associated with the relationship between ADHD and procrastination, with results compatible with a mediating role. In a subsequent study, the same authors (2026) further highlighted the possible involvement of delay sensitivity, low task value, and flexible goal regulation. Finally, some studies examined procrastination as a possible intermediate process between ADHD and functioning. In particular, the findings are consistent with a role of procrastination in the relationship between ADHD and quality of life (Netzer Turgeman & Pollak, 2025), as well as between ADHD and dysfunctional driving behaviors (Shirdel et al., 2024). Overall, these findings are consistent with the hypothesis that procrastination may represent an important intermediate process through which ADHD symptoms are associated with functional difficulties in everyday life; however, the cross-sectional nature of the included studies does not allow causal conclusions to be drawn. 3.5. Quality assessment The methodological quality of the included studies is presented in Table 2. Overall, the studies demonstrated generally sound methodological characteristics across most domains. All studies clearly defined their inclusion criteria (Q1) and provided adequate descriptions of participants and study settings (Q2). Exposure and outcome variables were assessed using validated and reliable in struments in the majority of studies (Q3, Q7), and appropriate statistical analyses were consistently employed (Q8). However, some limitations were identified in relation to confounding. Although several studies incorporated multivariate statis tical approaches, including regression, mediation, or structural equation modeling (Q6), the explicit identification and conceptual discussion of potential confounding factors (Q5) were not consistently reported across all studies. Overall, these findings indicate variability in specific methodological domains, particularly concerning the identification and handling of confounding variables, which should be considered when interpreting the results of the included studies. 4. Discussion The present systematic review provides converging evidence of a positive and consistent association between ADHD symptoms and procrastination, observed across different populations, contexts, and modes of construct operationalization. This pattern emerges in both clinical and non-clinical samples, suggesting that procrastination represents a relatively stable correlate of the difficulties associated with ADHD, rather than a phenomenon limited to specific contextual conditions. In particular, the inattention dimension emerges as the most robust and consistent correlate of procrastination, whereas the contribution of hyperactivity and impulsivity appears less stable when the shared variance among symptom dimensions is taken into account (Bolden & Fillauer, 2020; Niermann & R. Scheres, 2014). This finding is consistent with the hypothesis that procrastination is more strongly linked to difficulties in sustained attention, planning, and the regulation of goal-directed behavior (Barkley,1997; Willcutt et al., 2005). Overall, the findings are consistent with models that interpret procrastination as an expression of self-regulatory difficulties. The included studies show that ADHD symptoms are associated with patterns characterized by reduced goal-directed control, including difficulties in task initiation, time management, and persistence (Bolden & Fillauer, 2020). At the same time, motivational and emotional variables—such as lower expectancy of success, greater impulsivity, heightened delay sensitivity, stronger preference for immediate rewards, and steeper temporal discounting—may help explain the association between ADHD symptoms and procrasti nation. Rather than pointing to a single explanatory mechanism, the evidence suggests that the relationship between ADHD and procrastination is better understood as the result of the interaction among cognitive, emotional, and motivational processes (Netzer Turgeman & Pollak, 2023; Steel & K ̈onig, 2006). More specifically, several studies reported findings compatible with a possible role of executive functions in this association, particularly with regard to planning, organization, and time management (Altgassen et al., 2019). Similarly, the findings support the involvement of emotion regulation processes, highlighting how procrastination is associated with greater emotional distress and lower self-esteem in individuals with higher levels of ADHD symptoms (Bodalski et al., 2023; Mohammadi Bytamar et al., 2020; Sirois & Pychyl, 2013). Motivational variables, including delay aversion and task valuation, also emerge as relevant correlates (Steel et al., 2018). However, it is important to emphasize that these findings should be interpreted as converging associative patterns rather than evidence of specific causal mechanisms, in light of the cross-sectional nature of the included studies. Taken together, these findings are consistent with a multi-component account in which executive dysfunction, emotion regulation difficulties, and moti vational alterations jointly contribute to procrastinatory behavior in individuals with higher ADHD symptoms. A further element that emerged concerns the possible role of procrastination as an intermediate process between ADHD symptoms and functional outcomes. Some studies have reported associations between procrastination and indicators of functioning, such as quality of life and everyday functioning (Kosheleff et al., 2023). Although these findings are consistent with the hypothesis that procrastination may represent a relevant pathway through which ADHD symptoms are associated with functional difficulties, such interpretations should be considered with caution and cannot be taken as evidence of mediation in a causal sense. At the same time, several important methodological limitations must be considered. First, all included studies adopted cross- sectional designs, which do not allow conclusions to be drawn regarding the directionality of the relationship. It is plausible that this association reflects bidirectional or reciprocal processes, in which ADHD symptoms and procrastination influence each other over time. Moreover, although several studies employed mediation models, these analyses were based on cross-sectional data and therefore cannot be interpreted as evidence of temporal or causal mediation. Second, the predominant use of self-report measures for both ADHD and procrastination introduces the risk of common method variance and subjective reporting biases. In addition, some widely used ADHD symptom scales include items that directly refer to delaying or avoiding cognitively demanding tasks (e.g., difficulty getting started on tasks requiring sustained mental effort), creating potential construct overlap with procrastination measures. Consequently, part of the observed association may reflect shared item content rather than entirely distinct underlying psychological processes. This issue should be considered when interpreting the strength of the reported relationships and highlights the importance of employing multi-method assessment strategies in future research. However, it should also be acknowledged that procrastination is not fully transparent to external observation. By definition, procrastination involves a voluntary delay despite awareness of potential negative consequences, and therefore depends partly on the individual’s subjective judgment, intention, and awareness. For this reason, external informant ratings and behavioral measures may complement self-report instruments, but they cannot fully replace them. Experimental or behavioral tasks may capture delay-related behavior, but they may not always distinguish procrastination from other processes, such as forgetting, poor prospective memory, task misunderstanding, or lack of opportunity. Future research should therefore combine self-report, informant-based, and behavioral indicators while carefully distinguishing intentional delay from other forms of task non-completion. In addition, the role of confounding variables has not been systematically addressed. Factors such as depression, anxiety, and personality traits—particularly low conscientiousness—are associated with both ADHD and procrastination and may contribute to the observed shared variance. Additional limitations concern the predominance of non-clinical samples, particularly university students, which may limit external validity and the generalizability of the findings to clinically diagnosed populations. Furthermore, although the included studies were conducted across multiple countries, the available evidence is derived predominantly from Western, highly educated, or university student samples. Consequently, the extent to which the observed associations generalize across different cultural, socio economic, and educational contexts remains uncertain, highlighting the need to examine the ADHD–procrastination relationship in more diverse and culturally representative populations. Another important limitation concerns the heterogeneity of procrastination assessment. Although all included studies employed validated instruments, these questionnaires capture partially different facets of the construct, including general procrastination, academic procrastination, and active or passive forms of procrastination. Such conceptual and psychometric differences may contribute to variability in the reported associations with ADHD symptoms and complicate direct comparisons across studies. Future research would benefit from greater consistency in measurement practices and from explicitly distinguishing among different forms of procrastination. Longitudinal designs, the use of multi-method assessments (e.g., behavioral measures and external informant ratings), and more systematic control of confounding factors will also be necessary to clarify the nature of the relationship. A further limitation concerns the relatively restrictive eligibility criteria adopted in the present review. We focused on studies in which the ADHD–procrastination association was examined as a main objective or as a central component of the analytical framework. This decision was made to preserve the conceptual focus of the review and to ensure that the included studies provided directly interpretable evidence regarding the association of interest. synthesis, as studies in which ADHD or procrastination was included only as a moderator, covariate, descriptive variable, secondary variable, or ancillary correlate may still provide potentially relevant information about their association. Future reviews may adopt broader eligibility criteria or conduct sensitivity or supplementary analyses including such studies to determine whether they provide convergent or divergent evidence. Despite these limitations, the present review makes several important contributions to the literature. First, it provides a systematic synthesis of an empirically consistent but conceptually fragmented body of evidence. Second, by jointly considering executive, emotional, and motivational processes, it advances a more integrated framework for understanding the association between ADHD symptoms and procrastination. From this perspective, procrastination may be conceptualized as a transdiagnostic self-regulatory difficulty closely associated with ADHD. From a clinical perspective, these findings suggest that procrastination may represent a promising intervention target in individuals with elevated ADHD symptoms, consistent with clinical approaches to adult ADHD that have long emphasized procrastination, task initiation difficulties, and difficulties translating intentions into actions as relevant treatment targets (Safren, 2006; Ramsay, 2020). Future intervention research should evaluate whether treatments specifically targeting procrastinatory behavior - through improve ments in executive functioning, emotion regulation, motivational processes, or time-management strategies - can produce downstream benefits in everyday functioning and quality of life. Longitudinal and randomized controlled studies will be particularly important for determining whether reducing procrastination contributes to improved functional outcomes in individuals with ADHD. In conclusion, the available evidence consistently supports the existence of a robust association between ADHD symptoms and procrastination. Although the underlying mechanisms and the directionality of the relationship require further investigation, the findings underscore the importance of considering procrastination within broader models of self-regulation in ADHD and point to relevant directions for future research. pages: Resting-state functional connectivity alterations in adult ADHD: A systematic review of rs-fMRI studies Jay Kakadiya a,1 , Beatriz A. de Macedo a,1, Neel Vora b, Vidhi Dhaduk c, Dhairya A. Lakhani d, Haris I. Sair a, Licia P. Luna a,* a Department of Radiology, Division of Neuroradiology, Johns Hopkins Medical Center, Baltimore, MD, USA b Department of Cardiovascular Radiology, Cleveland Clinic, Cleveland, OH, USA c Shantabaa Medical College and General Hospital, Amreli, Gujarat, India d Department of Neuroradiology, Rockefeller Neuroscience Institute, West Virginia University, Morgantown, WV, USA A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Resting state-functional MRI Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Adult Resting state networks Functional connectivity ADHD A B S T R A C T Background: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) often persists into adulthood and causes signifi cant functional impairments. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) offers valuable insights into intrinsic brain connectivity; however, connectivity (FC) alterations specific to adults with ADHD remain unclear. This sys tematic review aimed to synthesize rs-fMRI studies comparing adults with ADHD and healthy controls, identify consistent FC patterns, and assess methodological quality. Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched for rs-fMRI studies involving adults diagnosed with ADHD per DSM-IV/DSM-5 criteria. Eligible studies examined FC differences between adults with ADHD and healthy controls. Data extraction included study characteristics, imaging pa rameters, and FC methodologies. Study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Results: Eight studies (n = 529; 264 ADHD, 265 controls) met inclusion criteria. FC analyses employed Seed- Based Analysis (SBA), Independent Component Analysis (ICA), and graph theory methods. Despite methodo logical heterogeneity, consistent FC alterations were observed: increased FC in the default mode (DMN), visual (VN), and central executive (CEN) networks, and decreased FC in the ventral attention (VAN) and somatomotor (SMN) networks. Alterations were predominantly left-hemispheric. Conclusion: Adults with ADHD exhibit distinct rs-FC disruptions, mainly involving DMN, VAN, CEN, and SMN. Standardized analytic approaches and subtype-specific analyses are needed for improved clinical relevance. 1. Introduction Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. While historically consid ered a childhood disorder, ADHD frequently persists into adulthood, affecting approximately 2.5-5% of adults worldwide (Kessler et al., 2006; Kosheleff et al., 2023). Adult ADHD is associated with consider able functional impairments across educational, occupational, and interpersonal domains. Despite increasing clinical awareness, the neurobiological underpinnings of adult ADHD remain incompletely understood (Alexander and Farrelly, 2018). Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) has emerged as a powerful, non-invasive neuroimaging technique to examine the brain's intrinsic functional architecture. By measuring spontaneous fluctuations in the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal, rs-fMRI enables the identification of functional connectivity (FC) patterns between distributed brain regions in the absence of task-related activity (Tang et al., 2022). This modality has been instrumental in revealing atypical connectivity in several large-scale resting state net works (RSNs) implicated in ADHD, including the default mode network (DMN), central executive network (CEN), ventral attention network (VAN), dorsal attention network (DAN), visual network (VN) and sen sory motor network (SMN). This approach is particularly advantageous in ADHD, as task-based evaluation can be difficult in children and may introduce confounding factors related to task performance. fMRI has become a key tool in elucidating the neural underpinnings of ADHD with various analytical approaches offering distinct perspectives on brain connectivity. Independent Component Analysis (ICA), a data-driven method, is commonly used to identify intrinsic connectivity networks without requiring predefined regions. Seed-Based Analysis (SBA), in contrast, is hypothesis-driven and measures FC between a selected seed region and the rest of the brain, allowing for targeted investigation of circuits implicated in ADHD. Region of Interest (ROI)-to-ROI analysis extends this by examining FC between multiple predefined brain regions to map broader network dysfunctions. (Rosazza et al., 2012) Further more, graph-theoretical approaches conceptualize the brain as a network, enabling the quantification of topological properties such as integration, segregation, and centrality—metrics increasingly applied to characterize altered network organization in ADHD. Together, these analytical strategies provide a comprehensive framework for under standing the distributed and network-based nature of ADHD-related brain dysfunction. While there is a growing body of literature examining fMRI con nectivity in ADHD, the majority of studies have focused on children and adolescents or task-based fMRI (Cubillo and Rubia, 2010; Cortese et al., 2021; Tamon et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2023; Cortese et al., 2012; Saletin et al., 2019; Noordermeer et al., 2016; Lei et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2021). Findings of rs-fMRI in adult ADHD are more limited and often inconsistent, reflecting heterogeneity in study populations, imag ing methodologies, and analytic approaches. Furthermore, differences in brain networks between children and adults suggest that FC alter ations in adult ADHD may represent persistent or compensatory neural mechanisms distinct from those observed in younger individuals (Hong et al., 2024). Comprehensive synthesis systematically evaluating the FC findings from rs-fMRI studies specifically focused on adults with ADHD is lack ing. This systematic review addresses this gap by critically appraising and summarizing existing literature comparing rs-fMRI connectivity in adults with ADHD to healthy control (HC) groups. Our objective is to summaries existing literature, identify consistent patterns of altered brain connectivity associated with adult ADHD. 2. Methods 2.1. Inclusion criteria Studies were included if they met all the following criteria: a) orig inal, peer-reviewed articles published in English; b) adult patients (aged ≥18 years) diagnosed with ADHD based on DSM-IV or DSM-5 criteria with a comparable group of HCs; c) use of rs-fMRI; and d) application of any FC analysis method using rs-fMRI. There were no limitations regarding the nationality, race, sex of the participants. 2.2. Exclusion criteria Studies were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: a) animal studies; b) children and adolescents (<18 years); c) absence of HCs, d) insufficient information on FC changes; e) meeting abstracts, comments, summaries, protocols, letters and guidelines; and f) articles not written in English. In case of overlapping cohorts; the most recent study was included. 2.3. Search strategy The systematic review was conducted accordance with a predefined protocol (PROSPERO 2025 CRD420251041135). It was designed ac cording to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines. A systematic search was performed of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus to identify studies investi gating rs-fMRI in neurodegenerative or psychiatric disorders from inception until February 25, 2025, by two independent reviewers (J.K. and B.M.). The detailed search string for each database is provided in the supplementary material. Search results were imported into Covidence, where duplicates were automatically screened and deleted. Two authors (J.K. and B.M.) inde pendently screened the titles and abstracts of the remaining studies. Screening results were examined by a third reviewer (L.P.L., neurora diologist, 15 years of experience), and all discordant evaluations were resolved via discussion to reach a consensus. As this review is a part of larger systematic review, studies involving adult ADHD populations were further categorized. A complete flow chart of the process is shown in the supplementary material. 2.4. Data Extraction Data extraction was performed independently by two investigators (J.K. and B.M.). For each article, we extracted: a) patient and control demographics b) MRI scanner strength, c) software used, d) FC analysis method, e) Number and location of seeds (if seed-based), f) Direction of FC changes (increase/decrease), and g) regions with FC difference, and h) Brain network involved For the analysis of the most frequently involved brain networks, only whole-brain studies were included. To minimize selection bias, studies restricted to predefined regions or specific networks were excluded when reporting results from whole-brain investigations. 2.5. Quality Evaluation Studies were appraised with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), scored on a 0 to 9 scale based on patient selection, comparability of groups and outcome assessment. Studies with a total NOS score of 7 or higher (out of 9) were considered high quality. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion by a third independent reviewer (L.P.L.). J. Kakadiya et al. 3. Results 3.1. Study selection and overview The study selection process and reasons for exclusion during full text screening are described in supplementary material. Out of 4,405 potentially eligible citations, 8 studies met inclusion criteria. Study characteristics are reported in Table 1. In total, the included studies involved 529 participants: 264 adults with ADHD (SBA = 71; ICA = 65; GBA = 128) and 265 HCs (SBA = 73; ICA = 65; GBA = 127). 3.2. Seed-based/ROI to ROI studies Hwang et al. (Hwang et al., 2025) reported increased FC predomi nantly in bilateral lateral parietal (LP) cortex regions when seeded from the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC). Kucyi et al. (Kucyi et al., 2015) investigated cerebellum-cerebral connectivity using a cerebellar seed and observed increased FC in multiple regions, including areas within the DMN, SMN, VAN, VN, and CEN. Zhao et al. (Zhao et al., 2017) examined whole brain FC using six insular subregions as seeds and found increased FC particularly in the right precuneus alongside decreased FC in several regions, spanning multiple networks. (Supplementary material) 3.3. Non-seed based studies Zhang et al. (Zhang et al., 2021) employed ICA to assess FC between eight RSNs, noting increased connectivity in the right fronto-parietal network (FPN) and auditory regions, while decreased connectivity was observed within the anterior medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) compared to HCs. Wu et al. (Wu et al., 2023) applied motif analysis as a graph-theoretical metric and identi fied significant connectivity alterations involving all major large-scale networks. Pretus et al. (Pretus et al., 2019) evaluated stepwise FC changes using integration as a graph metric, observed increased FC in the left calcarine (CAL) and right lingual gyrus (LG), while orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) showed reduced FC in ADHD. Hong et al. (Hong et al., 2017) reported increased nodal centrality in the VN and decreased centrality across multiple areas within the CEN, VAN, SMN, and sub-cortical network (SCN). Fan et al. (Fan et al., 2019) noted increased clustering co-efficient and path length within DMN. (Supplementary material) 3.4. Illustrative brain map of replicated neuroimaging findings Fig. 1 summaries regions with altered FC. we identified regions with consistently increased FC including left AG in the DMN, left LG and medial occipital gyrus in the VN, left superior frontal gyrus (SFG) within the CEN. The left anterior pre-frontal cortex (laPFC) and insula within the VAN also showed increased FC. Decreased FC was observed in the left pre-central gyrus (PreCG) and right superior temporal gyrus (STG) within the SMN, right putamen in the SCN, bilateral Insula in the VAN (Fig. 1; Supplementary material). Overall, increased FC was predominantly observed across DMN, VN, and CEN; while decreased FC was primarily seed in the VAN and SMN. Considering only whole brain studies, most consistently altered net works includes the DMN, VN, and SMN (71%) (Fig. 2). 3.5. Quality of studies Study quality was appraised using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), as illustrated in Fig. 3. Eight case-control studies were included in the quality evaluation. Of these, three were rated as having a low risk of bias, while five demonstrated a moderate risk. No studies were clas sified as high risk. The observed sources of bias primarily stemmed from incomplete reporting of data and suboptimal control group definition or selection procedures. Overall, the methodological quality of the included studies was deemed acceptable for synthesis. 4. Discussion Our study sought to evaluate FC alterations in adults with ADHD using rs-fMRI, an area that remains underexplored compared to pedi atric populations. Prior studies described pattern of widespread but heterogeneous FC alterations across multiple large-scale RSNs. We identified two prior meta-analyses with separate analyses on adult ADHD (Cortese et al., 2012; Lei et al., 2015), both task-based. Addi tionally, two rs-fMRI-based meta-analyses were identified, one focusing on local FC measures in adolescent (Shu et al., 2025), another including Table 1 Characteristics of included studies. Despite heterogenous literature, we observed a consistent pattern of FC changes in adults with ADHD at rest. Regions with consistently altered FC included increased FC in the left AG, LG, laPFC and SFG (involving DMN, VN, and CEN). Decreased FC was observed in the right insula, right putamen, right STG, and left PreCG (involving VAN, SMN). The left insula (VAN) exhibited both increased and decreased FC across studies (Fig. 1; Supplementary material). Moreover, the calcarine sulcus, showed increased FC in non-seed-based studies (Zhang et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2023; Pretus et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2019); but not in seed-based analyses. laPFC FC alteration can be explained by prior literature showed dysfunction and delayed maturation of PFC is a key abnormality in ADHD (Soman et al., 2023). The lingual gyrus and visual cortical areas are essential for sensory integration, visual processing, and attentional control. VN Hyperconnectivity demonstrated in our analysis reflects involvement of occipital lobe in visual attention task in ADHD. (Li et al., 2025; Zarka et al., 2021) Insular cortex dysfunction in ADHD contributes to sensory integration deficits, emotional dysregulation, and impaired cognitive control, reflecting its role as a multimodal integra tive hub within the VAN. (Fateh et al., 2022; Viering et al., 2021) Our findings align with the prior rs-fMRI meta-analyses reporting FC changes in the left precuneus/PCC, left LG, left MFG, and laPFC. (Shu et al., 2025; Sutcubasi et al., 2020) This overlap reinforces the idea that rs-fMRI may capture distinct and consistent patterns compared to task-based approaches. Interestingly, these findings suggest dominant involvement of the left hemisphere, in contrast to previous task-based fMRI meta-analyses reporting right-hemisphere abnormalities in similar regions. The most commonly involved regions with altered FC in prior task- based meta-analyses include the right sided PreCG, insula, and pre cuneus/PCC. (Tamon et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2023; Cortese et al., 2012; Saletin et al., 2019; Lei et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2021; Kowalczyk et al., 2022) In contrast, our review found altered FC in left hemisphere counterparts (PreCG, insula, and precuneus/PCC). This hemispheric discrepancy may reflect the nature of the imaging modality: task-based fMRI studies are inherently influenced by lateralization and handedness, often biasing activation toward the right hemisphere dur ing attention and inhibition tasks. (Toga and Thompson, 2003; Szaflarski et al., 2006; Holland et al., 2007; Leckey and Federmeier, 2017; Tzourio-Mazoyer et al., 2020) In contrast, rs-fMRI captures intrinsic brain activity without task confounds, potentially offering a more stable and generalizable assessment of FC. Literature suggests hemispheric dominance evolves with age, with the left hemisphere becoming increasingly specialized for executive and cognitive control functions, while right hemisphere functions become more lateralized for visuospatial and attentional tasks. Other regions with FC changes that align with our findings include the AG (Cortese et al., 2012); putamen (Tamon et al., 2024; Cortese et al., 2012; Lei et al., 2015); STG (Tamon et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2022; Cortese et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2021); MFG (Tamon et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2023; Cortese et al., 2012; Lei et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2021; Shu et al., 2025); and LG (Tamon et al., 2024; Shu et al., 2025). Prior studies have also reported FC changes in various other re gions not consistently replicated across studies, such as the MOF, IPS, IFG, FG, thalamus, GP, amygdala, and caudate, highlighting high vari ability and the need for more uniform analytic approaches. Conversely, a few meta-analyses reported no significant FC changes. (Cortese et al., 2021; Toga and Thompson, 2003) Detailed findings from prior meta-analyses are summarize in supplementary material. The heterogeneity observed across included studies is due to fundamental differences in FC analysis methodology. SBAs are hypoth esis driven measure in which results are biases toward connectivity patterns involving pre-determined areas identified as a seed region, overlooking alterations in regions not selected a priori. (Joel et al., 2011) Similarly, ICA introduces variability through dimensionality estimation includes alteration in identification of brain network and their connectivity due to extracted components varied. (Joel et al., 2011) Graph-theoretical approaches are particularly sensitive to thresholding and the parcellation scheme utilized; different atlases and threshold values can result in divergent network topology metrics even from identical primary data. (Epstein et al., 2007) These methodological sources of variability likely contribute to the inconsistent and sometimes divergent FC findings reported across studies in this review, and underscore the need for standardized acqui sition and analysis pipelines in future rs-fMRI research. 4.1. Limitations First, our results are based on a limited number of studies (n=8) with small sample sizes, which limits generalizability. Second, due to this limitation, our analysis relied on the identification of overlapping re gions rather than statistical meta-analysis, which reduces the robustness of effect estimates. Third, the included studies employed heterogeneous FC analysis methods (e.g., SBA, ICA, graph theory), introducing vari ability in results and interpretation. Forth, medication status represents a significant potential confounder as stimulant medications are known to modulate BOLD signal and alter FC; included studies varied consid erably in whether participants were medicated, unmedicated, or medication-naive, and stratified analyses was not performed by medi cation status. Fifth, comorbid psychiatric conditions (depression, anxi ety disorders, and substance use disorders) are highly prevalent in adults with ADHD and can independently affect FC pattern; however, comor bidity profiles were rarely used as covariates in studies. Sixth, head motion during rs-fMRI acquisition is a well-established confound, and adults with ADHD tend to demonstrate higher micro-movements than neurotypical controls in scanner; differences in motion correction and censoring thresholds introduce bias in FC estimates. Finally, the age ranges and sex distributions affect resting-state network organization and is varied across included studies. Future studies should focus to wards controlling these variables to improve comparability and inter pretability of rs-fMRI findings in adult ADHD. 5. Conclusion This systematic review synthesizes current evidence on rs-FC alter ations in adults with ADHD, revealing widespread but heterogeneous disruptions across key brain networks predominantly involving left sided DMN, LN, and SMN. These hemispheric differences may reflect developmental shifts and/or task-based nature of earlier studies. Future studies should aim for larger, more diverse samples, incorporate longi tudinal and multimodal designs, and stratify results based on clinical subtypes and comorbidities to explore the utility of resting-state imaging as a diagnostic and monitoring tool in adult ADHD. pages: Review article Are children and adolescents with ADHD less physically fit? Findings from a systematic review and meta-analysis Nerea Blanco-Martíneza,b,*, Jose Carlos Diz-Gomeza,b, Benito Outeda-Monteagudoc, Rocío Carballo-Afonsoa,b, Carlos Ayan-Pereza,b a Departamento de Didacticas Especiais, Universidade de Vigo, 36310 Vigo, Espa~na, Spain b Well-Move Research Group, Galicia Sur Health Research Institute (IIS Galicia Sur), SERGAS-UVIGO, 36310 Vigo, Espa~na, Spain c Facultad de Ciencias de la Educacion y del Deporte, Universidad de Vigo, 36005 Pontevedra, Spain A R T I C L E I N F O Article History: Received 17 June 2025 Revised 23 March 2026 Accepted 22 May 2026 Available online 25 June 2026 A B S T R A C T Background: Health-related physical fitness is critical from early childhood, yet it is unclear whether children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) differ from their typically developing (TD) peers. Objective: To systematically review and meta-analyze differences in health-related physical fitness between children and adolescents with and without ADHD. Methods: and Setting: Seven electronic databases were searched for studies comparing cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength, and flexibility between children and adolescents with ADHD and TD peers. Methodological quality was evaluated using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Results: Thirteen studies including 1,814 participants (560 with ADHD, 1,254 typically developing [TD]) were reviewed. Eleven studies assessed cardiorespiratory fitness. Pooled data from two VO2peak studies (28 ADHD, 33 TD) showed no significant group differences (mean difference = -4.28 mL¢kg−1¢min−1; 95% CI: -10.51 to 1.96; p = 0.18; I2 = 59%). Seven studies using field-based tests revealed mixed outcomes. Pooled data from six studies using the 20-meter Shuttle Run or PACER test (149 ADHD, 949 TD) indicated significantly lower performance in the ADHD group (standardized mean difference = -0.46; 95% CI: -0.78 to -0.14; p = 0.004; I2 = 47%). Five studies examining heart rate variables reported no significant differences (mean difference = 2.23 bpm; 95% CI: -2.72 to 7.19; p = 0.38; I2 = 42%). Muscular strength outcomes (six studies) and flexibility (five studies) showed minimal differences between groups (strength: SMD = -0.07, 95% CI: -0.31 to 0.17; flexibility: SMD = -0.16, 95% CI: -0.65 to 0.33), with low-to-moderate heterogeneity. Conclusion: Children and adolescents with ADHD exhibit comparable levels of muscular strength and flexibility to their TD peers. Evidence on cardiorespiratory fitness is mixed and depends on assessment methods: field-based tests indicate lower performance in ADHD, while laboratory peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) and resting heart rate measures show no significant differences. © 2026 The Author(s). This is an open access article under the CC BY license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) Keywords: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Health-related physical fitness Cardiorespiratory fitness Muscular strength Flexibility Children Adolescents Introduction Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by problematic levels of inattention, disorganization, and impulsivity, which may occur with varying degrees of hyperactivity [1,2]. Despite its marked heterogeneity and interindividual variability, three common presentation types are typically identified: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive/impulsive, and combined presentation [1,2]. In the scientific literature, the prevalence of ADHD in children and adolescents ranges from 5.6% to 7.6%, with a higher incidence in males, showing an approximate ratio of 3:1 [3]. Its etiology is complex and multifactorial, resulting from the interaction between genetic variants and environmental factors, with epigenetics potentially playing a key mediating role [4]. Beyond the core clinical features of the disorder, additional health problems frequently emerge. Children and adolescents with ADHD have shown an increased body mass index (BMI), possibly due to fragmentation of the daily rhythm of activity [5]. In addition, later in adulthood, people with ADHD face an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases, sleep problems, and a greater prevalence of physical and mental health problems, which contribute to reduced longevity * Corresponding author.
