compared with the general population [6]. In this context, promoting physical activity from an early age is essential, as it is associated with improved life expectancy [7]. The beneficial effects of physical activity are mediated through its impact on dimensions of physical fitness that are directly related to health [8]. Physical fitness refers to the ability to perform physical activity and encompasses a wide range of physiological and psychological attributes, serving as a key indicator of health [9]. According to the model proposed by Caspersen et al [10], physical fitness can be divided into health-related physical fitness and motor-related physical fitness. Health-related physical fitness includes five components: cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular endurance, muscular strength, body composition, and flexibility [10]. These components, particularly muscular strength, muscular endurance, and flexibility, are closely associated with various health outcomes, playing a crucial role in maintaining functional capacity, preventing chronic diseases, and enhancing overall quality of life [11]. Systematic reviews with meta-analyses have shown that greater cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength, and flexibility are associated with better health indicators in children and adolescents with typical development (TD) [12,13]. Several studies have examined differences in motor-related physical fitness between children and adolescents with ADHD and their TD peers, consistently reporting poorer performance in those with ADHD [14,15]. In contrast, systematic reviews addressing healthrelated physical fitness have predominantly focused on body composition [16−19], and to date, no systematic review has specifically examined whether differences exist across other components of health-related physical fitness between children and adolescents with and without ADHD. This question is relevant because physical fitness is key to health and quality of life, and children with ADHD are often perceived as less fit. Synthesizing existing studies can clarify if this stigma reflects actual differences. For this reason, the aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to assess the existence of differences in health-related physical fitness among children and adolescents with and without ADHD. Methods This systematic review and meta-analysis adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [20] for transparent and comprehensive reporting. The study protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/P7VEA Search strategy A comprehensive search was performed in seven electronic databases— Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus, Dialnet Plus, SPORTDiscus, ERIC, and the PEDro Database— encompassing all publications up to March 2025. The search strategy utilized the following Boolean operators and term combinations: ("Physical fitness" OR "fitness levels" OR "motor skills" OR "cardiorespiratory fitness" OR "muscular strength" OR "balance" OR "coordination" OR "endurance" OR "physical activity levels") AND ("Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder" OR "ADHD" OR "children with ADHD" OR "adolescents with ADHD"). Eligibility criteria Studies reporting outcomes related to cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength, and flexibility as components of healthy physical fitness in children and adolescents with and without ADHD were considered eligible for inclusion in this review. Investigations were excluded if: a) the studies did not include children or adolescents with ADHD; b) the research involved participants with multiple pathologies, unless separate data for the ADHD subgroup were provided; c) physical fitness data for ADHD and TD groups were reported but comparative statistical analyses were not conducted; d) baseline data was not informed; and e) the full text of the study was not available. Study selection Two researchers independently screened the titles and abstracts of all retrieved studies to assess their eligibility. After completing the review separately, they compared their results and agreed on the final selection. Full texts of studies deemed potentially relevant were then obtained. In cases where eligibility was uncertain, a third reviewer was consulted to resolve discrepancies and reach a final decision. Additionally, Google Scholar was searched for further studies meeting the inclusion criteria. Reference lists of the selected articles and their citing papers were also reviewed to identify any additional relevant studies for inclusion. Data extraction For each included study, data were extracted on the authors, year of publication, country, research objective, participant characteristics (sex and age), outcomes assessed, and main findings. One researcher carried out the data extraction, and a second investigator verified its accuracy to ensure consistency and reliability. Quality appraisal The methodological quality and risk of bias of the studies included in this review were assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) version 2018 [21]. This tool has proven to be useful in systematic reviews that include various study designs [22]. The critical appraisal was conducted independently by two reviewers, with any disagreements resolved through discussion. Item scores may vary as follows: yes (criterion met), no (criterion not met), and unclear (insufficient information provided to assess the criterion). Statistical analysis The data extracted from the articles was processed in an Excel spreadsheet, and the meta-analysis was performed using Review Manager (RevMan) software (version 5.4.1). The mean difference or standardized mean difference, along with their 95% confidence intervals (CI), were utilized to estimate effect sizes for quantitative dependent variables. When variability was expressed as standard error, it was converted to standard deviation. In instances where continuous variables were expressed as median and interquartile range, they were converted to mean and standard deviation. The continuous variables were analyzed using a random effects model and the inverse variance method. The confidence interval for the global effect was determined by employing the weighted variance method. The heterogeneity statistic (I2) was utilized to evaluate heterogeneity. An I2 value of 0% indicates the absence of heterogeneity, whilst a higher value indicates greater heterogeneity. Results Study selection A total of 9985 records were initially identified through the database search. After duplicate removal, 7127 titles and abstracts were screened, leading to the retrieval of 335 articles for full-text review. Finally, 10 studies met the inclusion criteria and were incorporated into the systematic review. Additionally, citation tracking of the N. Blanco-Martínez, J.C. Diz-Gomez, B. Study characteristics The reviewed studies were published between 1997 and 2025. Of the total investigations, six primarily aimed to analyze differences in healthy physical fitness parameters between children and adolescents with and without ADHD. The participants were children and adolescents ranging in age from 4−7 years [23] to 11−16 years [24]. Across all included studies, the combined sample size was 1,814 participants (1,153 males and 661 females). Among them, 560 had a clinical diagnosis of ADHD, with 71.61% being male (n = 401). Only four investigations included exclusively male samples [25−28], while the remaining studies involved mixed-gender samples. Sample sizes in individual studies ranged from 18 participants [27] to 892 [29]. Kang et al [30] and Verret et al. [26] further categorized participants with an ADHD diagnosis based on whether they were receiving medication, with a total of 69 participants undergoing pharmacological treatment. Table 1 provides a summary of the main characteristics of the included studies. Main outcomes Cardiorespiratory fitness Eleven studies examined differences in cardiorespiratory fitness parameters between children and adolescents with and without ADHD diagnoses [24−29,31−35]. Peak oxygen uptake (VO2peak) was assessed by Tantillo et al. [35] and Wigal et al [27] using the Bruce Test and a constant and incremental cycling protocol, respectively. The pooled data from these studies included 28 participants in the ADHD group and 33 in the TD group. The meta-analysis results showed no significant differences between groups (95% CI = -4.28 [-10.51, 1.96]; p = 0.18), with a moderate level of heterogeneity (I2 = 59%) (Fig. 2). Maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) levels were informed by Buker et al. [31] and Huang et al. [33] using the 20-meter Shuttle Run Test and by Tantillo et al [35] using the Bruce Test. Their findings yielded mixed results. Seven studies assessed performance on specific cardiorespiratory fitness tests [24−26,29,32−34]. No significant differences were found in the Shuttle Run Test (in laps or time), the Bruce Test (time), the Leger Test (time) or in endurance time run [26,32,33]. In the physical working capacity at a heart rate of 170 beats/min (PWC170 test), Ludygova et al [24] reported no significant differences, whereas Ludygova et al [34] found significantly lower performance in the ADHD group (p = 0.002), even after adjusting for BMI (p = 0.002). Martinson et al [29] and Pan et al [25] used the Progressive Aerobic Cardiovascular Endurance Run (PACER Test) and observed significantly lower performance in the ADHD group (p < 0.001 and p < 0.01, respectively). The pooled data from six studies that used either the 20-meter Shuttle Run Test (n = 4) or the PACER test (n = 2), including 149 participants with ADHD and 949 TD participants, are presented in Fig. 3. The pooled standardized mean difference was -0.46 (95% CI: -0.78 to -0.14; p = 0.004), indicating a significantly lower cardiorespiratory fitness among children and adolescents with ADHD. Heterogeneity was low to moderate (I2 = 47%). Five studies examined heart rate variables, with resting heart rate being the most frequently analyzed [24,28,35]. None of them reported significant intergroup differences. Tantillo et al [35] and Wigal et al [27] also assessed recovery heart rate and peak heart rate, with no significant differences observed. Muscular strength Six studies compared muscular strength parameters between children and adolescents with and without ADHD [23,25,26,30−32]. Muscular endurance was the most frequently assessed strengthrelated physical fitness component. The tests used included the situp [26,30,34], curl-up [25,32], push-up [26,32], pull-up [32], bentarm hang [31], flexed arm hang [32], and side jumps [23]. Only Colombo-Dougovito et al [32] reported significant differences in favor of the ADHD group in the push-up (p = 0.029) and pull-up (p = 0.012) tests. The meta-analysis results concerning the curl-up and sit-up revealed a standardized mean difference of -0.07 (CI95% -0.31 to 0.17: p=0.58: I2=0%) (Fig. 5). Three studies administered isometric strength tests, including the hand grip strength, back strength test, and isometric push-up [25,30,31], and no significant differences between participants with and without ADHD were reported. Similar findings were reported by Buker et al [31] following an assessment of lower-body explosive strength using the Standing Broad Jump test. Flexibility Flexibility differences were assessed in five studies [25,26,30−32]. For comparative analysis, four investigations used the Sit & Reach test [25,26,31,32], while Kang et al [30] employed the Standing Trunk Flexion test. None of the investigations reported the existence of significant differences. This trend was confirmed by a meta-analysis combining the four studies that assessed flexibility through the Sit & Reach test, for a standardized mean difference of -0.16 (CI 95% -0.65 to 0.33; p= 0.52; I2 = 55%) (Fig. 6). A sensitivity analysis with a different effect size estimate (Hedges’ g) and prediction intervals did not reveal major changes in our results (Supplementary material. Table S1). Methodological quality As shown in Table 2, the quality was highly heterogeneous across studies. Five studies were quantitative non-randomized [23,25,29,32,33]. In general, none of these studies included a sample representative of the target population. In contrast, all of them used appropriate measurements for both the outcome and the intervention. In the case of the quantitative descriptive studies, the most frequent source of bias was related to the relevance of the sampling strategy to the research question, with only one study meeting this criterion [24]. In addition, only those investigations conducted by Buker et al [31], Kang et al [30], Ludygova et al [24], and Ludygova et al [34] included samples representative of the target population. Conversely, all studies employed appropriate tools to assess outcomes and interventions, and the interventions were generally delivered as planned. Discussion This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the existence of differences in health-related physical fitness between children and adolescents with and without ADHD. The obtained findings provide insightful information on healthy fitness in this population, which may guide future interventions and assessment strategies for children and adolescents with ADHD. Cardiorespiratory fitness is a key health indicator in children and adolescents, as low levels have been significantly associated with a higher risk of developing metabolic syndrome [36], as well as other chronic diseases and increased mortality in adulthood [37]. This component of health-related physical fitness was the most frequently analyzed outcome, addressed in eleven of the included investigations, although findings were inconsistent. Studies using field-based tests to estimate VO2max—such as the PACER and Shuttle Run tests, which are widely used for children and adolescents—generally indicated lower cardiorespiratory fitness in ADHD groups compared with TD peers. In contrast, studies that assessed VO2peak in laboratory settings did not show consistent differences between groups. This distinction is important, as laboratory tests are considered the gold standard for assessing cardiorespiratory fitness, and VO2peak is recognized as the most reliable indicator in children [38]. However, evidence from laboratory assessments remains limited, as the metaanalysis included only two investigations. Interestingly, resting heart rate—another validated biomarker of cardiorespiratory fitness [39]— did not differ significantly between groups. In addition, heterogeneity across studies may have played a role in the variability of these findings, as factors such as ADHD subtype, medication status, or sex could have acted as potential moderators. Furthermore, although the included studies generally employed appropriate statistical analyses and assessment methods, their samples presented notable limitations. Specifically, as most studies were not primarily designed to compare cardiorespiratory fitness between participants with and without ADHD, their sampling strategies were not always adequate or representative, thereby restricting the generalizability of the findings. Consequently, the evidence regarding differences in cardiorespiratory fitness between children and adolescents with ADHD and their TD peers remains inconclusive. Muscular fitness during childhood and adolescence is a key health indicator and a protective factor against the development of diseases in adulthood [12,40]. In children with ADHD, greater muscular strength has also been associated with improved cognitive performance and reduced hyperactive-impulsive behaviors in the school setting [41]. In this review, muscular endurance was the most frequently assessed component, with findings from the meta-analysis indicating that no significant differences were observed between the analyzed groups. This result may be due to the fact that these tests Fig. 6. Forest plot of the comparison of flexibility differences between children and adolescents with ADHD and those with TD. involve repetitive movements of short duration and moderate-tohigh intensity in a closed skill context, which may align better with the behavioral profile of children with ADHD, who tend to prefer brief and dynamic tasks over open skills in changing environments [42,43]. In this regard, studies assessing isometric and explosive strength reported no significant differences, indicating that children and adolescents with ADHD generally exhibit comparable strength levels to their TD peers. However, given the methodological weaknesses identified through the MMAT assessment, these null findings should be interpreted with caution, as limitations in sample representativeness and sampling adequacy may have reduced the studies’ ability to detect subtle between-group differences. Flexibility provides essential health benefits, including increased range of motion, injury prevention and reduction, pain relief, and improved coordination—factors that are fundamental throughout the lifespan [44]. In this review, flexibility was the least studied component of physical fitness. The meta-analysis found no significant differences in flexibility between children and adolescents with ADHD and their TD counterparts. These findings suggest that ADHD does not significantly affect flexibility, at least during childhood and adolescence. This may be due to the fact that flexibility largely depends on structural and anatomical factors [45], which are unlikely to be directly influenced by the core symptoms of ADHD. However, given that only two studies were specifically designed to examine between-group differences, these findings should be interpreted with caution, as sampling limitations likely undermined their robustness despite strengths in assessment, statistical analyses, and intervention implementation. This seems to be the first systematic review and meta-analysis to investigate differences in health-related physical fitness between children and adolescents with and without ADHD. While the findings do not provide conclusive evidence regarding differences in cardiorespiratory fitness, they suggest that strength and flexibility levels are largely comparable between the two groups. It should be noted, however, that most included studies involved prepubertal or early pubertal participants, a developmental stage in which differences in physical fitness components tend to be less distinguishable compared with the pubertal years [46]. Despite the novelty of this review, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, only six of the included studies explicitly aimed to assess differences in health-related physical fitness between children and adolescents with and without ADHD. Second, although most studies used valid instruments and procedures, many were constrained by small sample sizes, uneven sex distribution, or poorly defined inclusion criteria, particularly concerning ADHD severity and medication status. Additionally, some of the studies presented significant risks of bias, which may have influenced the reliability of the findings. Third, although meta-analyses were performed, they were based on a small number of studies and exhibited heterogeneity, which precluded a formal assessment of publication bias. Fourth, body composition was not included, despite being a core component of health-related physical fitness, and its omission may have influenced the other outcomes examined. Lastly, the exclusion of grey literature may have narrowed the scope of the review, potentially omitting relevant data that could have strengthened the overall findings. Conclusion The findings of this review suggest that children and adolescents with ADHD exhibit comparable levels of muscular strength and flexibility to their TD peers. However, evidence on cardiorespiratory fitness is mixed: field-based tests suggest lower performance in ADHD, whereas laboratory-based VO2peak measurements and resting heart rate show no significant differences. metadata_title: The influence of existing interventions on sleep of youth with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
pages: Clinical Review The influence of existing interventions on sleep of youth with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials☆ Yuan Fang a,1 , Zixin Wang b,1 , Mengge Zhang c , Fenghua Sun a,* a Department of Health and Physical Education, The Education University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China b Centre for Health Behaviours Research, JC School of Public Health and Primary Care, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China c Department of Educational Psychology, Faculty of Education, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: ADHD Children and adolescents Sleep Interventions Randomized controlled trial Meta-analysis A B S T R A C T Sleep problems are commonly observed among children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorders (ADHD). We completed a literature search by 2025-6-9 on EBSCOhost, PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus to quantify the effects of any existing interventions on sleep outcomes among children/adolescents with ADHD. From a pool of 4081 studies, 40 randomized controlled trials (RCTs; 75% with low-risk-of-bias, 4361 participants and 65.2% attended interventions) were eligible for a pairwise meta-analysis (PWMA). Of these, 28 RCTs were included in a Bayesian network meta-analysis (NMA). Results were yielded from both mean change and post-test measurement of the outcomes if available. In PWMA (moderate-to-high certainty), the examined interventions had small and significant effects on sleep disturbance (standardized mean difference [SMD] by mean change [95% CI]: overall [k = 29]: −0.30 [-0.42, −0.17], p < 0.001; sleeping pills [k = 7]: −0.10 [-0.41, 0.22], p > 0.05; ADHD drugs [k = 6]: −0.25 [-0.52, 0.01], p > 0.05; behavioral sleep [BS] interventions [k = 10]: −0.48 [-0.70, −0.27], p < 0.001) and sleep onset latency (overall [k = 12]: −0.41 [-0.67, −0.14], p < 0.01; sleeping pills [k = 3]: −0.68 [-1.08, −0.27], p < 0.01; ADHD drug [k = 1]: −0.39 [-0.96, 0.18], p > 0.05; BS interventions [k = 5]: −0.36 [-0.88, 0.16], p > 0.05). The examined interventions did not have significant effects on sleep efficacy, sleep duration, latency to persistent sleep or daytime sleepiness. Results of NMA showed that sleeping pills had the best performance in shortening SOL, while BS interventions may be the best choice for reducing sleep disturbance. However, more rigorous evidence is warranted. This review indicates that a multi- component and tailored-designed intervention represents important personalized strategies for improving sleep in youths with ADHD. Introduction Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a commonly diagnosed developmental disorder [1] with a 5.9–7.1 % worldwide prevalence in children and adolescents [2,3]. Besides well-known symptoms such as inattention and/or hyperactivity/impulsiveness [2], sleep problems are also commonly observed in individuals with ADHD. Approximately 70% of children with ADHD present different sleep problems [4,5], and these children have experienced more sleep prob lems than those without this condition [6–8]. These problems [7–9] have been detected using subjectively measured variables such as bedtime resistance, sleep-onset difficulties, night awakening, difficulties in awakening in the morning, sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), and daytime sleepiness, as well as using objectively measured variables (e.g., sleep onset latency [SOL] and latency to persistent sleep [LPS]). Based on the existing evidence, a bidirectional relationship has been established between ADHD symptoms and sleep problems [10,11]. It proposes that sleep problems may be an early predictor of ADHD onset [11,12] and may be negatively associated with poorer child psychoso cial situations [13]. Several associated factors have been identified in the literature. First, children with ADHD were found to have a reduced number of cyclic alternating pattern (CAP) sequences and a lower CAP rate than normal controls, which was due to the low CAP rate during sleep stage 2 non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep [14]. Consistent to this, ADHD population were reported to have a reduction in slow-wave activity across the whole brain, reduced delta power in deep sleep but increased delta/theta activity when they were compared with normal controls [15,16]. These abnormal brain activity during sleep may further aggravate cognitive dysfunction in those with ADHD [15–17]. Second, several neurobiological mechanisms are embedded in sleep problems associated with ADHD, including delayed circadian rhythms [12,18], dopaminergic dysfunction [19], and commencement of mela tonin synthesis [20–22]. Third, sleep disturbances may also correlate with problems in brain morphology and network connectivity in ADHD [23], such as smaller gray matter volumes in the middle and inferior frontal gyri, amygdala, striatum, and insula. Fourth, sleep disorders (such as restless legs syndrome [RLS], periodic limb movements [PLMS], obstructive sleep apnea [OSA]) are observed to associated with ADHD [24–26]. Studies show a high prevalence of PLMS and RLS in individuals with ADHD, with some evidence linking iron deficiency to both ADHD and RLS pathophysiology [27]. As a result, many ADHD symptoms resemble those of sleep deprivation, and children and adolescents with ADHD who experience a lack of sleep may also exhibit hyperactivity and impulsivity [28]. So far, it has been revealed that current drugs for treating ADHD (e. g., stimulant) may cause adverse events such as decreased appetite or even worsening of sleep problems especially if taken later in the day [29]. ADHD medication may interfere the physiological arousal level in those affected by ADHD. Thus, sleep problems in children/adolescents with ADHD can be caused by ADHD drugs [30] or ADHD per se [31,32]. Therefore, the reduction of sleep problems and enhancement of sleep health play important roles in the ADHD management, neuro-development, and well-being of children and adolescents with ADHD. Several types of interventions have been applied to treat sleep problems among children and adolescents with ADHD [9,33], including pharmaceutical treatments (e.g., melatonin, which can regulate circa dian rhythms and inhibit presynaptic dopamine release [34]) and non-pharmaceutical interventions (e.g., behavioral sleep training and sleep hygiene education). Although some sleeping pills [35] and behavioral therapy [9] have been reported to be effective in treating insomnia, a high relapse rate of sleep-onset insomnia when resuming melatonin treatment was also reported in a long-term follow-up study [36]. Thus, the identification of efficient and sustainable strategies is necessary to help children and adolescents with ADHD improve the quality of sleep. Therefore, a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of existing interventions on sleep of children and adolescents with ADHD is warranted; Yet, it is not available. To fill this knowledge gap, the present study aimed to (1) quantify the extent to which the existing interventions influence the sleep of children and adolescents with ADHD, (2) compare the intervention effects on sleep according to various intervention types and subtypes, and (3) calculate the relative effect of existing interventions on participants’ sleep and rank their probable performance. 2. Methods This review was registered in PROSPERO (Ref No.: CRD420251070940). As this review was conducted and analyzed based on published data, internal review board (IRB) approval was not required. Y. 2.1. Search strategy Relevant journal articles were identified by searching PubMed, Web of Science, EBSCOhost, and Scopus databases and platforms covering the published periods of 1966–2025, 1975–2025, 1929–2025, and 1970–2025, respectively; the search was completed on June 9, 2025 (Fig. 1). The Boolean operator was used in the search strategy with “OR” and/or “AND” used to link search terms. The asterisk “*” was used as a wildcard symbol appended at the end of the terms to search for varia tions of those terms. The complete and detailed search strategies for the title, abstract, or topic are presented in Table 1 and Table S1, respectively. 2.2. Inclusion and exclusion criteria Inclusion criteria for the review were studies having to (1) be a true- experiment (i.e., a randomized controlled trial, RCT), (2) be conducted in children or adolescents (age 0-19 years old) diagnosed with ADHD; (3) report the effect of an intervention for children and/or adolescents with ADHD (e.g., the effect of a sleep medicine or a sleep health edu cation program); (4) report the sleep-related continuous variables of children and/or adolescents with ADHD (e.g., mean and standard deviation [SD]); (5) use between-group comparisons to evaluate the effectiveness of the interventions (i.e., comparing the effect between intervention and control group); (6) be published in English, peer- reviewed journals; and (7) have an available full text. Screening process Two authors (YF and ZW) were involved in screening of articles, and a consensus by comparison or discussion was reached between the au thors during the process. As shown in Fig. 1, after initial execution of the search strategy and exclusion using automated tools in each database, the remaining papers were combined and checked for duplicates. After removing duplicates, 4081 articles were screened for relevance by reviewing their titles. Then the abstracts of 1602 articles were reviewed for eligibility, yielding 90 articles for full-text screening. In addition, 22 papers were included after checking the reference lists of 27 previously published systematic reviews in relevant research areas (listed in Table S2). Overall, 112 papers were read in full to determine whether they met the inclusion criteria. Finally, 40 articles were included in the meta-analysis. The inter-rater reliability analyses showed that Cohen's kappa ranged from 0.941 to 0.956 during the article screening process, which indicates almost perfect agreement between two reviewers (see Table S3). These studies provided sufficient data to compare the effect sizes of any primary endpoints, that is, sleep duration (i.e., objectively- measured total sleeping time [TST] and self-reported data), sleeping efficacy (SE), SOL, sleep disturbance, LPS, and daytime sleepiness. Since the majority of included studies provided post-outcome measures (38/ 40) and had a balanced baseline (36/40), the post-test measurements were selected as endpoint outcomes for meta-analysis. 2.4. Assessment for publication quality and risk of bias The risk of bias in the included articles was assessed by risk of bias 2 (RoB 2) in RCTs [37]. The results were categorized as low risk, some concerns, or high risk (Table S4). Each item was assessed by the same authors who had completed the review/screening process, and a consensus was reached through comparison or discussion when necessary. 2.5. Data extraction Relevant information from the included articles was analyzed and summarized using a standardized table with categorized themes of key information (Table S5). This table includes the publication year, coun try, characteristics of participants, intervention content in both the intervention and control groups, and the effectiveness of the designed interventions in terms of the measures utilized and the key results. Two authors (as indicated above) independently completed the review/ screening process and data extraction, with a consensus regarding the final study inclusion, analyses, and summary was achieved via discussion. 2.6. Pairwise meta-analysis RevMan v.5.4.1 (The Cochrane Collaboration, Software Update, Oxford, UK) and Stata v.16 (StataCorp LLC, Texas, US) were used to conduct a pairwise meta-analysis (PWMA). If the mean or SD of an outcome was not provided, it was estimated from the corresponding median, standard error (SE), range, and number of participants in each arm, based on the formula described in the Cochrane handbook [38]. The extracted post-test outcomes (both parallel- and crossover-arm RCTs) and/or mean change of pre-/post-test (for parallel-arm RCTs only, since crossover-arm RCTs had no insufficient data, see Appendix 1) were operationalized as continuous measures for comparison, which may have resulted in a high level of heterogeneity between different studies. Thus, SMD (calculated as Hedge's adjusted g with adjustment for small sample bias [39], Appendix 1) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) was calculated using a random-effects model. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. The SMD (95% CI) was perceived as trivial (0.00–0.19), small (0.20–0.49), medium (0.50–0.79), and large (≥0.80) [40,41]. Subgroup analyses were conducted to detect the potential effect modifiers by using a random-effects model. The potential effect modi fiers were primarily grouped by (1) pharmacological species for sleeping pills (melatonin, Z-drugs, L-Theanine, L-Dopa, and antihistamines) and ADHD drugs (stimulant vs non-stimulant), and (2) intervention content or intensity for non-pharmaceutical interventions (BS vs non-BS, or Hiscock protocol vs other more-intensive-scheduled protocols). For a meta-analysis of a small number of included studies, the Q statistic test, a comprehensive test of the homogeneity of effect sizes and the impact of moderators, was applied [42]. Furthermore, heterogeneity (%) was assessed by the I2 statistic, and the I2 value was interpreted as small (<25%), medium (25-75%), or large (>75%), as per convention [43]. The PWMA results are presented in Table 2 and Table S6. 2.7. Assessment of publication bias The potential publication bias of the selected endpoints was pre sented using funnel plots with SMD on the x-axis and the standard error of SMD on the y-axis. All endpoints were further assessed using Egger's test to detect asymmetry of the funnel plots [44]. Moreover, the trim-and-fill method was used to estimate the true effect sizes, adjusted for potential publication bias and the number of studies needed to bal ance the funnel plot [45]. Significance was set at p < 0.05 for all tests. The results are summarized in Table S7. 2.8. Evidence grading of traditional meta-analytic results For PWMA results, the certainty of evidence was assessed by using the grading of recommendation assessment, development and evalua tion framework (GRADE) [46]. The assessed domains were suggested by the GRADE handbook [47], which includes number of studies, risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias, number of studies, and intervention effects (SMD and 95% CI). Two authors (as indicated above) independently completed the assessment and a consensus was reached by discussion when necessary. The GRADE assessment results are presented in Table S8. 2.9. Network meta-analysis Among the included RCTs, a Bayesian network meta-analysis (NMA) was further applied to 28 parallel-arm, placebo/usual care/sham- controlled RCTs, which allowed the simultaneous comparison of mul tiple arms of the RCTs, including direct and indirect comparisons. Bayesian NMA was conducted using the web-based tool MetaInsight v.6.4.0, which enables users to interactively conduct NMA for both bi nary and continuous outcomes for fixed and random effects models based on R packages and codes [48]. The analyses were applied to each comparison twice as the comparisons were categorized by intervention type or specified intervention. The Bayesian NMA procedures are consistent with the literature with respect to the following steps [49]: First, the network geometry plot consisted of nodes and edges that represented the number of studies that directly examined a treatment and compared two given treatments. Second, a random-effects model based on the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulation method was built to obtain the pooled effect sizes using the Bayesian consistency model. Subsequently, the relative effect Y. Fang et al. Sleep Medicine Reviews 88 (2026) 102303 4

size of each evaluated outcome was calculated using the mean difference (MD) of the continuous variables. The goodness-of-fit of the model was assessed using residual deviance (i.e., deviance information criterion [DIC]). The ranking of the evaluated interventions was completed through MCMC simulations by performing 20,000 sample iterations [50]. The ranking results were obtained using Litmus Rank-O-Gram plots [51]. In these plots, the higher surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) values and cumulative ranking curves near the top left indi cated a probable better performance of the intervention. 3. Results 3.1. Overview of included studies A PRISMA flow diagram describing the search process is shown in Fig. 1. Forty papers published between 1995 and 2025 were included in the meta-analysis. The background information of the included studies is shown in Table S5. A total of 4361 children and/or adolescents with ADHD aged 2–17 years were included in the reviewed RCTs (particu larly, for parallel-RCTs: total n = 3902, intervention n = 2384, control n = 1518; for cross-over RCTs, total n = 459). Apart from four studies with no disclosure of the sex of the participants, 41.7–100% were male. Among the studies with reports of prior status on medication, six studies included drug-naïve participants, two studies included only treatment- naïve participants, and in other studies, 29.0–91.2% of the participants were on prior medication. Furthermore, the reviewed RCTs were con ducted in 13 countries or districts including USA (11 RCTs), Australia (5 RCTs), Canada (4 RCTs), Iran (4 RCTs), the Netherlands (4 RCTs), Brazil (2 RCTs), and 1 RCT was performed in each of the following countries/ districts: Belgium, Egypt, Germany, Hong Kong (China), Spain, Sweden, and Turkey. Moreover, among the 40 included RCTs, 30 were parallel- arm RCTs and 10 were crossover-designed RCTs. 3.2. Risk of bias and study quality Based on the assessment of RoB 2 (Table S4), 75% (30 studies) of the included RCTs showed a low risk of bias, whereas another 10 RCTs were considered to have some concerns. Potential sources of bias included deviations from the intended interventions (e.g., limitations in blind ing), a considerable proportion of missing outcome data, and potential selection bias in reporting the results. 3.3. Design of evaluated interventions Among the included RCTs, most used a placebo, usual care, or sham in the control group, whereas two studies used active controls [52,53]. Regarding the intervention types, (i) 25 studies applied pharmaceutical intervention which comprising 8 studies of sleeping pills (i.e., mela tonin, zolpidem, eszopiclone, L-dopa, L-theanine, and cyproheptadine) and 17 studies of ADHD drugs (i.e., stimulant and non-stimulants); (ii) 16 studies examined non-pharmaceutical interventions (i.e., behavioral sleep [BS] interventions, neurofeedback, cognitive training-combined/engaged physical activity [CPA], light therapy, environmental technique, and slow oscillating transcranial direct cur rent stimulation [so-tDCS]); (iii) 1 study examined the effect of nutrient supplement (i.e., probiotic [54]); and (iv) 1 study tested the efficacy of a combined intervention protocol of BS interventions and a stimulant drug [55]. Most of the included studies tested the intervention effect in a chronic manner (i.e., two weeks to four months), whereas only one study used a single-bout intervention [56]. Among the RCTs incorporating an arm of a training program, the programs lasted for 3–14 weeks, had a frequency of 1–3 times per week, and a session duration of 45 min to 3 h. 3.4. Results of PWMA 3.4.1. Sleep duration Among the parallel-arm RCTs, the reviewed interventions had no effect on the objective-measured TST of participants when compared with those of the control group (post-test outcomes: intervention n = 376 and control n = 295, SMD: 0.00, 95% CI [−0.25, 0.26], poverall = 0.97; I2 = 58%, pheterogeneity = 0.01; psubgroup = 0.34; mean change: intervention n = 384 and control n = 311, SMD: 0.12, 95% CI [−0.14, 0.39], poverall = 0.36; I2 = 62%, pheterogeneity = 0.003; psubgroup = 0.05). Among the crossover-arm RCTs, no significant effect was observed for the TST of intervention participants, when compared with those of the control group (post-test outcomes: intervention n = 276 and control n = 273, SMD: −0.31, 95% CI [−0.72, 0.09], poverall = 0.13; I2 = 80%, pheterogeneity<0.001; psubgroup = 0.09). Based on the self-reported data of other parallel-arm RCTs, no significant effect on subjective sleep dura tion of participants was found in post-test outcomes of the intervention groups in comparison with that of controls (intervention n = 407 and control n = 193, SMD: −0.07, 95% CI [−0.25, 0.11], poverall = 0.45; I2 = 0%, pheterogeneity = 0.87; psubgroup = 0.47). However, a significant small effect was indicated by the mean change comparisons in BS in terventions (intervention n = 124 and control n = 124, SMD: −0.34, 95% CI [−0.59, −0.08], poverall = 0.009; I2 = 0%, pheterogeneity = 0.91). In particular, BS interventions with low risk of bias demonstrated a significant small effect on reducing sleep disturbance in participants of the intervention groups compared to control groups (SMD: −0.43, Figure S1.1-e2). 3.4.5. Latency to persistent sleep LPS data were extracted from parallel-arm RCTs. No significant effect of LPS was observed in the evaluated interventions when they were compared with the controls (post-test outcomes: intervention n = 437 and control n = 225, SMD: 0.01, 95% CI [−0.21, 0.22], poverall = 0.96; I2 = 35%, p = 0.20; psubgroup = 0.28; mean change: intervention n = 437 and control n = 225, SMD: 0.10, 95% CI [−0.06, 0.26], poverall = 0.23; I2 = 0%, pheterogeneity = 0.77; psubgroup = 0.62). 3.4.6. Daytime sleepiness Data on daytime sleepiness were obtained from parallel-arm RCTs that assessed BS interventions. In accordance, a trivial and marginally non-significant effect on reducing daytime sleepiness was revealed in the post-test outcomes of intervention participants, when they were compared with the controls (intervention n = 294 and control n = 289, SMD: −0.17, 95% CI [−0.36, 0.03], p = 0.09; I2 = 22%, p = 0.27). However, a significant small effect was observed by the mean change comparison (intervention n = 294 and control n = 289, SMD: −0.29, 95% CI [−0.51, −0.06], poverall = 0.01; I2 = 40%, pheterogeneity = 0.14). 3.5. Publication bias Publication bias of all outcomes in the PWMA was assessed using funnel plots (Fig. S2), Egger's test, and the trim-and-fill method. As shown in Table S7, no publication bias was found in Egger's test. Nonetheless, the trim-and-fill method inputted missing study(ies) into LPS and daytime sleepiness obtained from parallel-RCTs, and SE calculated based on crossover-RCTs. The estimated SMDs with 95 %CI are shown in Table S7. 3.6. Evidence grading According to the results of GRADE assessment (Table S8), evidence obtained from crossover-RCTs prevalently showed a moderate-to-very low certainty. In contrast, the synthesized evidence emerging from parallel-RCTs exhibited moderate to high certainty. Therefore, PWMA results of this study demonstrated (1) a high certainty that the existing interventions had a significant small effect on reducing the SOL, and (2) a moderate certainty that the existing interventions had a significant small effect on reducing sleep disturbance in children/adolescents with ADHD. However, the current evidence indicates a moderate certainty that existing interventions had no significant effect on sleep duration (both objectively and subjectively measured data), SE, LPS, or daytime sleepiness. 3.7. Results of Bayesian NMA Based on the results of SOL and sleep disturbance, a Bayesian NMA was conducted in 28 parallel-arm RCTs that used a placebo/usual care/ sham control group for comparison. The relative effects (mean differ ence [MD] and 95% credibility interval [CrI]) of reviewed intervention types on SOL showed that sleeping pills had the largest MD than other interventions in comparisons either by post-test outcomes or mean change (Fig. S4–1). Regarding the relative effects on sleep disturbance, BS interventions had the largest MD in comparison by post-test out comes, while it had the second largest MD in comparison by mean change (Fig. S4–2). No significant inconsistencies were observed in the results of the node-splitting analyses (all p > 0.05). Moreover, based on MCMC simulations, SUCRA values also sug gested probable performance ranking results of intervention types and specified interventions on SOL and sleep disturbance, as shown in Fig. 2 and Table S9. To balance the result, the summed SUCRA score of respective comparisons by post-test outcomes and mean change was used to compare. Given the SOL, the ranking of the included interven tion types was sleeping pills, CPA, ADHD drugs, light therapy, BS in terventions, and controls. In terms of sleep disturbance, the ranking of the reviewed intervention types was: BS interventions, a BS-MPH com bined protocol, a probiotic, neurofeedback, ADHD drugs, sleeping pills, CPA, light therapy, and controls. The prior distributions of SOL and SD by intervention types are also presented in Fig. S5. This exhibited a consistent estimation on treatment performance, which may inform future studies and reduce the research bias. 4. Discussion In all, this study suggested that (1) the existing interventions (any type) were unlikely to increase SE or sleep duration, or reduce LPS or daytime sleepiness; however, (2) these interventions (any type) were likely to significantly reduce sleep disturbance at a small level; and (3) the existing interventions (any type) significantly reduced SOL at a small effect. Moreover, among the reviewed intervention types, sleeping pills may be the most effective one to shorten SOL while BS interventions may have the best performance in reducing sleep disturbance. Sleep problems and ADHD may have a bidirectional and complex relationship. In one hand, children and adolescents with ADHD are prevalently affected by sleep problems; in another hand, hyperactivity is significantly associated with short sleep duration with odds ratio (OR) 1.60 among children with ADHD [8]. This may attribute to not only various neurobiological mechanisms including disruptions in circadian rhythms, dopaminergic dysfunction, and increased physiological arousal level, but also negative influence of poor sleep quality on aggravation of ADHD symptoms [19,57]. In particular, methylation processes are implicated in the regulation of circadian rhythms and sleep-wake cycles. Disruptions in methylation pathways can contribute to circadian rhythm sleep disorders (CRSDs) such as delayed sleep phase disorder (DSPD) and advanced sleep phase disorder (ASPD) [58]. Genetic polymorphisms affecting methylation-related genes may influence melatonin synthesis and circadian clock gene expression, impacting sleep timing and quality [59]. Y. Fang et al. Furthermore, dopamine plays a key role in moderating the arousal level and REM/NREM sleep transitions. According to the previous studies [60,61], dopaminergic dysfunction with dopamine transporter (DAT) and receptors (D1/D2), as well as the associated gene expression (e.g., the dopamine transporter gene DAT1) may disturb the arousal regulation, reward sensitivity, and sleep-wake stability. Thus, imbalanced level of dopamine may jeopardize the normality of sleep-wake cycle. Of this, the existing interventions (including pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical types) have been designed to help children and adolescents with ADHD to reduce their malfunctions and rehabilitate towards normalization. may regulate circadian rhythms or moderate brain activity by some particular biomolecular pathways. However, the drugs for treating ADHD, such as stimulant (e.g., MPH), may overly elevate the arousal level in children and adolescents with ADHD and advocate their sleep disturbance. Among the non-pharmaceutical interventions, behavioral sleep hygiene or sleep education (e.g., cognitive-behavioral therapy, CBT) address dysfunctional beliefs about sleep with behavioral in terventions (such as stimulus control and sleep restriction). These techniques focus on modifying maladaptive thoughts and behaviors related to sleep, improving sleep hygiene, and managing arousal and cognitive patterns that interfere with sleep. In particular, for ADHD drugs, neither stimulants nor non-stimulants showed significant improvements in sleep outcomes of the intervention groups in parallel-arm RCTs. The PWMA results of this review are consistent with the literature, that is, sleep problems in children and adolescents with ADHD may be induced/aggregated by the side effects of drugs used for ADHD treatment [32], although these could vary in individual responses [62]. Nonetheless, several studies have indicated that particular formulations of stimulants (e.g., sustained/extended-release MPH) with an optimal dose may decrease the risk of side effects and may not negatively affect sleep in children or adolescents with ADHD [62–66]. Thus, personalized and optimized ADHD medications are warranted for these youth. In terms of sleeping pills, results yielded by post-test outcomes or mean change showed an overall non-significant effect on increasing TST (k = 4, SMD: 0.22 and 0.11) with small heterogeneity, and an overall significant relatively-large effect on decreasing SOL (k = 3, SMD: −0.74 and −0.68) with small-moderate heterogeneity. In particular presented in Table S6, melatonin presented a significant large effect on reducing SOL (k = 2, SMD: −0.98 [67,68]), whereas L-dopa showed a non-significant small effect (k = 1, SMD: −0.21, [69]). Nonetheless, the post-test outcomes showed that L-theanine [70] presented a significant large effect on increasing SE (k = 1, SMD: 2.25) and reducing sleep disturbance (k = 1, SMD: −2.53). L-theanine has shown promising ef fects on stress reduction and mood relaxation, effects relevant to its regulation of brain state modulation via the release or reduction of brain neurotransmitters gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA), dopamine, and serotonin [71]. However, only one included study reported the post-test effects of L-theanine (with no baseline data available, [70]). Thus, more rigorous evaluation of this promising drug is warranted. For other sleeping pills targeting on sleep disturbance, both Z-drugs (k = 3) and antihistamines (k = 1) presented no effect, while melatonin presented a large heterogeneity but a non-significant trivial to small effect. Regarding other interventions (Table S6, Figure S1, and Figure S3), with respect to SOL in particular, BS interventions showed no obvious effect in three studies with low risk of bias, whereas CPA presented a significant moderate effect on reducing SOL. In contrast, BS in terventions exhibited a significant effect on sleep disturbance (i.e., six studies with low risk of bias, SMD: −0.43 by post-test outcomes and −0.41 by mean change, close to moderate effect). This result is in line with that of a previous meta-analysis [9], which reported a moderate certainty of evidence for behavioral interventions to reduce sleep disturbance in children with ADHD to a moderate level (SMD: −0.49). However, the consistent comparison results by post-test outcomes and mean change showed that neurofeedback, CPA, light therapy, an envi ronmental technique, and a nutrient supplement had no effect on sleep disturbance. In line with the results of PWMA, Bayesian NMA results suggested that sleeping pills had the best performance in achieving reduced SOL, whereas BS intervention was assessed to be the most effective one in decreasing sleep disturbance. In particular, with consideration of both post-test outcome and mean change (Table S9), melatonin showed the probable best performance to reduce SOL, and PST (one of BS in terventions) was estimate to be the best in decreasing sleep disturbance. Thus, these interventions may be promising for adjusting the targeted sleep outcomes of children and adolescents with ADHD. Furthermore, in this review, majority of included studies had no specification on exclusion of children and adolescents with ADHD who had comorbid sleep disorders (e.g., RLS, PLMS, OSA). According to the four studies which included participants with primary insomnia only (Fig. S6), CBT intervention presented a small to moderate effect on reducing sleep disturbance (SMD by post-test outcomes: −0.42, p = 0.05; SMD by mean change: −0.50, p = 0.02 [72]), whereas L-dopa [69], Zolpidem [73], and IR-MPH [74] exhibited no significant effect (p > 0.05). This finding is consistent to the study reported by England et al. (2011) [69], i.e., L-dopa exhibited a significant effect on patients with RLS/PLMS rather than those with ADHD-only. This may imply that: (1) the comorbid sleep disorders may largely contribute to the sleep prob lems of children and adolescents with ADHD; (2) the existing inter vention (especially pharmaceutical interventions) may be more effective to treat these comorbidities rather than the primary insomnia; and (3) specific CBT protocols for ADHD-related sleep issues are less established than for other groups with primary insomnia, although CBT (i.e., CBT-I) is widely recognized as the first-line, gold standard treatment for chronic insomnia disorder [75]. This is in line with the findings of a previous review [76], which found inconsistent results of CBT technique and difficulty in long-term maintenance of intervention effect in individuals with neurodevelopmental conditions. However, more evidence is war ranted to examine this inconclusive point. Overall, the current review implied that both pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical interventions may play the important but different roles in reducing sleep problems of children and adolescents with ADHD. Future intervention designs may integrate the effective options into a multi-component strategy. This is possible to achieve a combined or synergetic effect with optimized pharmaceutical dose and intervention regimen, which may concurrently increase the intervention safety and participants’ adherence. Nonetheless, due to the large diverse in indi vidual situation and condition, a tailored or personalized intervention strategy is also highly warranted for children and adolescents with ADHD. This study had some limitations that should be acknowledged. First, results should be interpreted with caution owing to limitations regarding the study design, unbalanced participants' characteristics, intervention design, and reporting bias in the reviewed studies. The acknowledged limitations of the study designs in the included RCTs comprise small sample size, concerns with blinding, adherence issues with objective measures, unbalanced baseline, lack of placebo- or sham- controls, unclear carryover effect in crossover-arm RCT, lack of follow- up, insufficient data or measures, attrition or missing data, and in validity of tools or measures. Regarding participants’ characteristics, homogeneity in age range, sex distribution, comorbidity, and/or recruitment location was attributed to limited generalization and failure of moderator detection. In contrast, diverse ADHD symptoms or medi cation responses, changed medication plans during study (e.g., partici pants took melatonin or self-administered stimulants), as well as inclusion of comorbid sleep disorders (such as RLS, PLMS, or OSA), also contributed to the study limitations. Furthermore, the included studies reported limitations regarding the intervention design, including the timing of the intervention, short intervention duration, inevitable con founders, and the need for a tailored/personalized design. Moreover, parent- or clinician-reported data may have been influenced by expec tations of interventions, resulting in social desirability bias. Finally, the studies selected for review were also limited because only those with specific terms mentioned in the title or abstract were screened for further analysis, and studies published in languages other than English or in conference abstracts, government reports, textbooks, or unpub lished dissertations were excluded. 5. Conclusions By employing PWMA and Bayesian NMA, the current study sys tematically reviewed and analyzed the relevant RCTs to compare the Y. Fang et al. Sleep Medicine Reviews 88 (2026) 102303 9

effects of interventions and controls on sleep among the targeted pop ulation. According to the PWMA results, the existing interventions of any type likely significantly improve the quality of sleep of participants by shortening SOL and reducing sleep disturbance. However, SE, sleep duration, LPS, or daytime sleepiness were unlikely changed by the existing interventions. Moreover, the NMA results suggest that sleeping pills and BS interventions are probably to reduce SOL and sleep distur bance, respectively. More evidence from rigorous assessment of these promising options is warranted to confirm this effect, especially in consideration of those with or without comorbid sleep disorders. Owing to the diversity of sleep issues, a multi-component and tailored/ personalized sleep interventions are crucial for young individuals with ADHD. metadata_title: The influence of existing interventions on sleep of youth with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
pages: Clinical Review The influence of existing interventions on sleep of youth with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials☆ Yuan Fang a,1 , Zixin Wang b,1 , Mengge Zhang c , Fenghua Sun a,* a Department of Health and Physical Education, The Education University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China b Centre for Health Behaviours Research, JC School of Public Health and Primary Care, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China c Department of Educational Psychology, Faculty of Education, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: ADHD Children and adolescents Sleep Interventions Randomized controlled trial Meta-analysis A B S T R A C T Sleep problems are commonly observed among children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorders (ADHD). We completed a literature search by 2025-6-9 on EBSCOhost, PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus to quantify the effects of any existing interventions on sleep outcomes among children/adolescents with ADHD. From a pool of 4081 studies, 40 randomized controlled trials (RCTs; 75% with low-risk-of-bias, 4361 participants and 65.2% attended interventions) were eligible for a pairwise meta-analysis (PWMA). Of these, 28 RCTs were included in a Bayesian network meta-analysis (NMA). Results were yielded from both mean change and post-test measurement of the outcomes if available. In PWMA (moderate-to-high certainty), the examined interventions had small and significant effects on sleep disturbance (standardized mean difference [SMD] by mean change [95% CI]: overall [k = 29]: −0.30 [-0.42, −0.17], p < 0.001; sleeping pills [k = 7]: −0.10 [-0.41, 0.22], p > 0.05; ADHD drugs [k = 6]: −0.25 [-0.52, 0.01], p > 0.05; behavioral sleep [BS] interventions [k = 10]: −0.48 [-0.70, −0.27], p < 0.001) and sleep onset latency (overall [k = 12]: −0.41 [-0.67, −0.14], p < 0.01; sleeping pills [k = 3]: −0.68 [-1.08, −0.27], p < 0.01; ADHD drug [k = 1]: −0.39 [-0.96, 0.18], p > 0.05; BS interventions [k = 5]: −0.36 [-0.88, 0.16], p > 0.05). The examined interventions did not have significant effects on sleep efficacy, sleep duration, latency to persistent sleep or daytime sleepiness. Results of NMA showed that sleeping pills had the best performance in shortening SOL, while BS interventions may be the best choice for reducing sleep disturbance. However, more rigorous evidence is warranted. This review indicates that a multi- component and tailored-designed intervention represents important personalized strategies for improving sleep in youths with ADHD. Introduction Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a commonly diagnosed developmental disorder [1] with a 5.9–7.1 % worldwide prevalence in children and adolescents [2,3]. Besides well-known symptoms such as inattention and/or hyperactivity/impulsiveness [2], sleep problems are also commonly observed in individuals with ADHD. Approximately 70% of children with ADHD present different sleep problems [4,5], and these children have experienced more sleep prob lems than those without this condition [6–8]. These problems [7–9] have been detected using subjectively measured variables such as bedtime resistance, sleep-onset difficulties, night awakening, difficulties in awakening in the morning, sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), and daytime sleepiness, as well as using objectively measured variables (e.g., sleep onset latency [SOL] and latency to persistent sleep [LPS]). Based on the existing evidence, a bidirectional relationship has been established between ADHD symptoms and sleep problems [10,11]. It proposes that sleep problems may be an early predictor of ADHD onset [11,12] and may be negatively associated with poorer child psychoso cial situations [13]. Several associated factors have been identified in the literature. First, children with ADHD were found to have a reduced number of cyclic alternating pattern (CAP) sequences and a lower CAP rate than normal controls, which was due to the low CAP rate during sleep stage 2 non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep [14]. Consistent to this, ADHD population were reported to have a reduction in slow-wave activity across the whole brain, reduced delta power in deep sleep but increased delta/theta activity when they were compared with normal controls [15,16]. These abnormal brain activity during sleep may further aggravate cognitive dysfunction in those with ADHD [15–17]. Second, several neurobiological mechanisms are embedded in sleep problems associated with ADHD, including delayed circadian rhythms [12,18], dopaminergic dysfunction [19], and commencement of mela tonin synthesis [20–22]. Third, sleep disturbances may also correlate with problems in brain morphology and network connectivity in ADHD [23], such as smaller gray matter volumes in the middle and inferior frontal gyri, amygdala, striatum, and insula. Fourth, sleep disorders (such as restless legs syndrome [RLS], periodic limb movements [PLMS], obstructive sleep apnea [OSA]) are observed to associated with ADHD [24–26]. Studies show a high prevalence of PLMS and RLS in individuals with ADHD, with some evidence linking iron deficiency to both ADHD and RLS pathophysiology [27]. As a result, many ADHD symptoms resemble those of sleep deprivation, and children and adolescents with ADHD who experience a lack of sleep may also exhibit hyperactivity and impulsivity [28]. So far, it has been revealed that current drugs for treating ADHD (e. g., stimulant) may cause adverse events such as decreased appetite or even worsening of sleep problems especially if taken later in the day [29]. ADHD medication may interfere the physiological arousal level in those affected by ADHD. Thus, sleep problems in children/adolescents with ADHD can be caused by ADHD drugs [30] or ADHD per se [31,32]. Therefore, the reduction of sleep problems and enhancement of sleep health play important roles in the ADHD management, neuro-development, and well-being of children and adolescents with ADHD. Several types of interventions have been applied to treat sleep problems among children and adolescents with ADHD [9,33], including pharmaceutical treatments (e.g., melatonin, which can regulate circa dian rhythms and inhibit presynaptic dopamine release [34]) and non-pharmaceutical interventions (e.g., behavioral sleep training and sleep hygiene education). Although some sleeping pills [35] and behavioral therapy [9] have been reported to be effective in treating insomnia, a high relapse rate of sleep-onset insomnia when resuming melatonin treatment was also reported in a long-term follow-up study [36]. Thus, the identification of efficient and sustainable strategies is necessary to help children and adolescents with ADHD improve the quality of sleep. Therefore, a comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis of the effects of existing interventions on sleep of children and adolescents with ADHD is warranted; Yet, it is not available. To fill this knowledge gap, the present study aimed to (1) quantify the extent to which the existing interventions influence the sleep of children and adolescents with ADHD, (2) compare the intervention effects on sleep according to various intervention types and subtypes, and (3) calculate the relative effect of existing interventions on participants’ sleep and rank their probable performance. 2. Methods This review was registered in PROSPERO (Ref No.: CRD420251070940). As this review was conducted and analyzed based on published data, internal review board (IRB) approval was not required. Y. 2.1. Search strategy Relevant journal articles were identified by searching PubMed, Web of Science, EBSCOhost, and Scopus databases and platforms covering the published periods of 1966–2025, 1975–2025, 1929–2025, and 1970–2025, respectively; the search was completed on June 9, 2025 (Fig. 1). The Boolean operator was used in the search strategy with “OR” and/or “AND” used to link search terms. The asterisk “*” was used as a wildcard symbol appended at the end of the terms to search for varia tions of those terms. The complete and detailed search strategies for the title, abstract, or topic are presented in Table 1 and Table S1, respectively. 2.2. Inclusion and exclusion criteria Inclusion criteria for the review were studies having to (1) be a true- experiment (i.e., a randomized controlled trial, RCT), (2) be conducted in children or adolescents (age 0-19 years old) diagnosed with ADHD; (3) report the effect of an intervention for children and/or adolescents with ADHD (e.g., the effect of a sleep medicine or a sleep health edu cation program); (4) report the sleep-related continuous variables of children and/or adolescents with ADHD (e.g., mean and standard deviation [SD]); (5) use between-group comparisons to evaluate the effectiveness of the interventions (i.e., comparing the effect between intervention and control group); (6) be published in English, peer- reviewed journals; and (7) have an available full text. Screening process Two authors (YF and ZW) were involved in screening of articles, and a consensus by comparison or discussion was reached between the au thors during the process. As shown in Fig. 1, after initial execution of the search strategy and exclusion using automated tools in each database, the remaining papers were combined and checked for duplicates. After removing duplicates, 4081 articles were screened for relevance by reviewing their titles. Then the abstracts of 1602 articles were reviewed for eligibility, yielding 90 articles for full-text screening. In addition, 22 papers were included after checking the reference lists of 27 previously published systematic reviews in relevant research areas (listed in Table S2). Overall, 112 papers were read in full to determine whether they met the inclusion criteria. Finally, 40 articles were included in the meta-analysis. The inter-rater reliability analyses showed that Cohen's kappa ranged from 0.941 to 0.956 during the article screening process, which indicates almost perfect agreement between two reviewers (see Table S3). These studies provided sufficient data to compare the effect sizes of any primary endpoints, that is, sleep duration (i.e., objectively- measured total sleeping time [TST] and self-reported data), sleeping efficacy (SE), SOL, sleep disturbance, LPS, and daytime sleepiness. Since the majority of included studies provided post-outcome measures (38/ 40) and had a balanced baseline (36/40), the post-test measurements were selected as endpoint outcomes for meta-analysis. 2.4. Assessment for publication quality and risk of bias The risk of bias in the included articles was assessed by risk of bias 2 (RoB 2) in RCTs [37]. The results were categorized as low risk, some concerns, or high risk (Table S4). Each item was assessed by the same authors who had completed the review/screening process, and a consensus was reached through comparison or discussion when necessary. 2.5. Data extraction Relevant information from the included articles was analyzed and summarized using a standardized table with categorized themes of key information (Table S5). This table includes the publication year, coun try, characteristics of participants, intervention content in both the intervention and control groups, and the effectiveness of the designed interventions in terms of the measures utilized and the key results. Two authors (as indicated above) independently completed the review/ screening process and data extraction, with a consensus regarding the final study inclusion, analyses, and summary was achieved via discussion. 2.6. Pairwise meta-analysis RevMan v.5.4.1 (The Cochrane Collaboration, Software Update, Oxford, UK) and Stata v.16 (StataCorp LLC, Texas, US) were used to conduct a pairwise meta-analysis (PWMA). If the mean or SD of an outcome was not provided, it was estimated from the corresponding median, standard error (SE), range, and number of participants in each arm, based on the formula described in the Cochrane handbook [38]. The extracted post-test outcomes (both parallel- and crossover-arm RCTs) and/or mean change of pre-/post-test (for parallel-arm RCTs only, since crossover-arm RCTs had no insufficient data, see Appendix 1) were operationalized as continuous measures for comparison, which may have resulted in a high level of heterogeneity between different studies. Thus, SMD (calculated as Hedge's adjusted g with adjustment for small sample bias [39], Appendix 1) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) was calculated using a random-effects model. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. The SMD (95% CI) was perceived as trivial (0.00–0.19), small (0.20–0.49), medium (0.50–0.79), and large (≥0.80) [40,41]. Subgroup analyses were conducted to detect the potential effect modifiers by using a random-effects model. The potential effect modi fiers were primarily grouped by (1) pharmacological species for sleeping pills (melatonin, Z-drugs, L-Theanine, L-Dopa, and antihistamines) and ADHD drugs (stimulant vs non-stimulant), and (2) intervention content or intensity for non-pharmaceutical interventions (BS vs non-BS, or Hiscock protocol vs other more-intensive-scheduled protocols). For a meta-analysis of a small number of included studies, the Q statistic test, a comprehensive test of the homogeneity of effect sizes and the impact of moderators, was applied [42]. Furthermore, heterogeneity (%) was assessed by the I2 statistic, and the I2 value was interpreted as small (<25%), medium (25-75%), or large (>75%), as per convention [43]. The PWMA results are presented in Table 2 and Table S6. 2.7. Assessment of publication bias The potential publication bias of the selected endpoints was pre sented using funnel plots with SMD on the x-axis and the standard error of SMD on the y-axis. All endpoints were further assessed using Egger's test to detect asymmetry of the funnel plots [44]. Moreover, the trim-and-fill method was used to estimate the true effect sizes, adjusted for potential publication bias and the number of studies needed to bal ance the funnel plot [45]. Significance was set at p < 0.05 for all tests. The results are summarized in Table S7. 2.8. Evidence grading of traditional meta-analytic results For PWMA results, the certainty of evidence was assessed by using the grading of recommendation assessment, development and evalua tion framework (GRADE) [46]. The assessed domains were suggested by the GRADE handbook [47], which includes number of studies, risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias, number of studies, and intervention effects (SMD and 95% CI). Two authors (as indicated above) independently completed the assessment and a consensus was reached by discussion when necessary. The GRADE assessment results are presented in Table S8. 2.9. Network meta-analysis Among the included RCTs, a Bayesian network meta-analysis (NMA) was further applied to 28 parallel-arm, placebo/usual care/sham- controlled RCTs, which allowed the simultaneous comparison of mul tiple arms of the RCTs, including direct and indirect comparisons. Bayesian NMA was conducted using the web-based tool MetaInsight v.6.4.0, which enables users to interactively conduct NMA for both bi nary and continuous outcomes for fixed and random effects models based on R packages and codes [48]. The analyses were applied to each comparison twice as the comparisons were categorized by intervention type or specified intervention. The Bayesian NMA procedures are consistent with the literature with respect to the following steps [49]: First, the network geometry plot consisted of nodes and edges that represented the number of studies that directly examined a treatment and compared two given treatments. Second, a random-effects model based on the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulation method was built to obtain the pooled effect sizes using the Bayesian consistency model. Subsequently, the relative effect Y. Fang et al. Sleep Medicine Reviews 88 (2026) 102303 4

size of each evaluated outcome was calculated using the mean difference (MD) of the continuous variables. The goodness-of-fit of the model was assessed using residual deviance (i.e., deviance information criterion [DIC]). The ranking of the evaluated interventions was completed through MCMC simulations by performing 20,000 sample iterations [50]. The ranking results were obtained using Litmus Rank-O-Gram plots [51]. In these plots, the higher surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) values and cumulative ranking curves near the top left indi cated a probable better performance of the intervention. 3. Results 3.1. Overview of included studies A PRISMA flow diagram describing the search process is shown in Fig. 1. Forty papers published between 1995 and 2025 were included in the meta-analysis. The background information of the included studies is shown in Table S5. A total of 4361 children and/or adolescents with ADHD aged 2–17 years were included in the reviewed RCTs (particu larly, for parallel-RCTs: total n = 3902, intervention n = 2384, control n = 1518; for cross-over RCTs, total n = 459). Apart from four studies with no disclosure of the sex of the participants, 41.7–100% were male. Among the studies with reports of prior status on medication, six studies included drug-naïve participants, two studies included only treatment- naïve participants, and in other studies, 29.0–91.2% of the participants were on prior medication. Furthermore, the reviewed RCTs were con ducted in 13 countries or districts including USA (11 RCTs), Australia (5 RCTs), Canada (4 RCTs), Iran (4 RCTs), the Netherlands (4 RCTs), Brazil (2 RCTs), and 1 RCT was performed in each of the following countries/ districts: Belgium, Egypt, Germany, Hong Kong (China), Spain, Sweden, and Turkey. Moreover, among the 40 included RCTs, 30 were parallel- arm RCTs and 10 were crossover-designed RCTs. 3.2. Risk of bias and study quality Based on the assessment of RoB 2 (Table S4), 75% (30 studies) of the included RCTs showed a low risk of bias, whereas another 10 RCTs were considered to have some concerns. Potential sources of bias included deviations from the intended interventions (e.g., limitations in blind ing), a considerable proportion of missing outcome data, and potential selection bias in reporting the results. 3.3. Design of evaluated interventions Among the included RCTs, most used a placebo, usual care, or sham in the control group, whereas two studies used active controls [52,53]. Regarding the intervention types, (i) 25 studies applied pharmaceutical intervention which comprising 8 studies of sleeping pills (i.e., mela tonin, zolpidem, eszopiclone, L-dopa, L-theanine, and cyproheptadine) and 17 studies of ADHD drugs (i.e., stimulant and non-stimulants); (ii) 16 studies examined non-pharmaceutical interventions (i.e., behavioral sleep [BS] interventions, neurofeedback, cognitive training-combined/engaged physical activity [CPA], light therapy, environmental technique, and slow oscillating transcranial direct cur rent stimulation [so-tDCS]); (iii) 1 study examined the effect of nutrient supplement (i.e., probiotic [54]); and (iv) 1 study tested the efficacy of a combined intervention protocol of BS interventions and a stimulant drug [55]. Most of the included studies tested the intervention effect in a chronic manner (i.e., two weeks to four months), whereas only one study used a single-bout intervention [56]. Among the RCTs incorporating an arm of a training program, the programs lasted for 3–14 weeks, had a frequency of 1–3 times per week, and a session duration of 45 min to 3 h. 3.4.
