Daytime sleepiness Data on daytime sleepiness were obtained from parallel-arm RCTs that assessed BS interventions. In accordance, a trivial and marginally non-significant effect on reducing daytime sleepiness was revealed in the post-test outcomes of intervention participants, when they were compared with the controls (intervention n = 294 and control n = 289, SMD: −0.17, 95% CI [−0.36, 0.03], p = 0.09; I2 = 22%, p = 0.27). However, a significant small effect was observed by the mean change comparison (intervention n = 294 and control n = 289, SMD: −0.29, 95% CI [−0.51, −0.06], poverall = 0.01; I2 = 40%, pheterogeneity = 0.14). 3.5. Publication bias Publication bias of all outcomes in the PWMA was assessed using funnel plots (Fig. S2), Egger's test, and the trim-and-fill method. As shown in Table S7, no publication bias was found in Egger's test. Nonetheless, the trim-and-fill method inputted missing study(ies) into LPS and daytime sleepiness obtained from parallel-RCTs, and SE calculated based on crossover-RCTs. The estimated SMDs with 95 %CI are shown in Table S7. 3.6. Evidence grading According to the results of GRADE assessment (Table S8), evidence obtained from crossover-RCTs prevalently showed a moderate-to-very low certainty. In contrast, the synthesized evidence emerging from parallel-RCTs exhibited moderate to high certainty. Therefore, PWMA results of this study demonstrated (1) a high certainty that the existing interventions had a significant small effect on reducing the SOL, and (2) a moderate certainty that the existing interventions had a significant small effect on reducing sleep disturbance in children/adolescents with ADHD. However, the current evidence indicates a moderate certainty that existing interventions had no significant effect on sleep duration (both objectively and subjectively measured data), SE, LPS, or daytime sleepiness. 3.7. Results of Bayesian NMA Based on the results of SOL and sleep disturbance, a Bayesian NMA was conducted in 28 parallel-arm RCTs that used a placebo/usual care/ sham control group for comparison. The relative effects (mean differ ence [MD] and 95% credibility interval [CrI]) of reviewed intervention types on SOL showed that sleeping pills had the largest MD than other interventions in comparisons either by post-test outcomes or mean change (Fig. S4–1). Regarding the relative effects on sleep disturbance, BS interventions had the largest MD in comparison by post-test out comes, while it had the second largest MD in comparison by mean change (Fig. S4–2). No significant inconsistencies were observed in the results of the node-splitting analyses (all p > 0.05). Moreover, based on MCMC simulations, SUCRA values also sug gested probable performance ranking results of intervention types and specified interventions on SOL and sleep disturbance, as shown in Fig. 2 and Table S9. To balance the result, the summed SUCRA score of respective comparisons by post-test outcomes and mean change was used to compare. Given the SOL, the ranking of the included interven tion types was sleeping pills, CPA, ADHD drugs, light therapy, BS in terventions, and controls. In terms of sleep disturbance, the ranking of the reviewed intervention types was: BS interventions, a BS-MPH com bined protocol, a probiotic, neurofeedback, ADHD drugs, sleeping pills, CPA, light therapy, and controls. The prior distributions of SOL and SD by intervention types are also presented in Fig. S5. This exhibited a consistent estimation on treatment performance, which may inform future studies and reduce the research bias. 4. Discussion In all, this study suggested that (1) the existing interventions (any type) were unlikely to increase SE or sleep duration, or reduce LPS or daytime sleepiness; however, (2) these interventions (any type) were likely to significantly reduce sleep disturbance at a small level; and (3) the existing interventions (any type) significantly reduced SOL at a small effect. Moreover, among the reviewed intervention types, sleeping pills may be the most effective one to shorten SOL while BS interventions may have the best performance in reducing sleep disturbance. Sleep problems and ADHD may have a bidirectional and complex relationship. In one hand, children and adolescents with ADHD are prevalently affected by sleep problems; in another hand, hyperactivity is significantly associated with short sleep duration with odds ratio (OR) 1.60 among children with ADHD [8]. This may attribute to not only various neurobiological mechanisms including disruptions in circadian rhythms, dopaminergic dysfunction, and increased physiological arousal level, but also negative influence of poor sleep quality on aggravation of ADHD symptoms [19,57]. In particular, methylation processes are implicated in the regulation of circadian rhythms and sleep-wake cycles. Disruptions in methylation pathways can contribute to circadian rhythm sleep disorders (CRSDs) such as delayed sleep phase disorder (DSPD) and advanced sleep phase disorder (ASPD) [58]. Genetic polymorphisms affecting methylation-related genes may influence melatonin synthesis and circadian clock gene expression, impacting sleep timing and quality [59]. Y. Fang et al. Furthermore, dopamine plays a key role in moderating the arousal level and REM/NREM sleep transitions. According to the previous studies [60,61], dopaminergic dysfunction with dopamine transporter (DAT) and receptors (D1/D2), as well as the associated gene expression (e.g., the dopamine transporter gene DAT1) may disturb the arousal regulation, reward sensitivity, and sleep-wake stability. Thus, imbalanced level of dopamine may jeopardize the normality of sleep-wake cycle. Of this, the existing interventions (including pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical types) have been designed to help children and adolescents with ADHD to reduce their malfunctions and rehabilitate towards normalization. may regulate circadian rhythms or moderate brain activity by some particular biomolecular pathways. However, the drugs for treating ADHD, such as stimulant (e.g., MPH), may overly elevate the arousal level in children and adolescents with ADHD and advocate their sleep disturbance. Among the non-pharmaceutical interventions, behavioral sleep hygiene or sleep education (e.g., cognitive-behavioral therapy, CBT) address dysfunctional beliefs about sleep with behavioral in terventions (such as stimulus control and sleep restriction). These techniques focus on modifying maladaptive thoughts and behaviors related to sleep, improving sleep hygiene, and managing arousal and cognitive patterns that interfere with sleep. In particular, for ADHD drugs, neither stimulants nor non-stimulants showed significant improvements in sleep outcomes of the intervention groups in parallel-arm RCTs. The PWMA results of this review are consistent with the literature, that is, sleep problems in children and adolescents with ADHD may be induced/aggregated by the side effects of drugs used for ADHD treatment [32], although these could vary in individual responses [62]. Nonetheless, several studies have indicated that particular formulations of stimulants (e.g., sustained/extended-release MPH) with an optimal dose may decrease the risk of side effects and may not negatively affect sleep in children or adolescents with ADHD [62–66]. Thus, personalized and optimized ADHD medications are warranted for these youth. In terms of sleeping pills, results yielded by post-test outcomes or mean change showed an overall non-significant effect on increasing TST (k = 4, SMD: 0.22 and 0.11) with small heterogeneity, and an overall significant relatively-large effect on decreasing SOL (k = 3, SMD: −0.74 and −0.68) with small-moderate heterogeneity. In particular presented in Table S6, melatonin presented a significant large effect on reducing SOL (k = 2, SMD: −0.98 [67,68]), whereas L-dopa showed a non-significant small effect (k = 1, SMD: −0.21, [69]). Nonetheless, the post-test outcomes showed that L-theanine [70] presented a significant large effect on increasing SE (k = 1, SMD: 2.25) and reducing sleep disturbance (k = 1, SMD: −2.53). L-theanine has shown promising ef fects on stress reduction and mood relaxation, effects relevant to its regulation of brain state modulation via the release or reduction of brain neurotransmitters gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA), dopamine, and serotonin [71]. However, only one included study reported the post-test effects of L-theanine (with no baseline data available, [70]). Thus, more rigorous evaluation of this promising drug is warranted. For other sleeping pills targeting on sleep disturbance, both Z-drugs (k = 3) and antihistamines (k = 1) presented no effect, while melatonin presented a large heterogeneity but a non-significant trivial to small effect. Regarding other interventions (Table S6, Figure S1, and Figure S3), with respect to SOL in particular, BS interventions showed no obvious effect in three studies with low risk of bias, whereas CPA presented a significant moderate effect on reducing SOL. In contrast, BS in terventions exhibited a significant effect on sleep disturbance (i.e., six studies with low risk of bias, SMD: −0.43 by post-test outcomes and −0.41 by mean change, close to moderate effect). This result is in line with that of a previous meta-analysis [9], which reported a moderate certainty of evidence for behavioral interventions to reduce sleep disturbance in children with ADHD to a moderate level (SMD: −0.49). However, the consistent comparison results by post-test outcomes and mean change showed that neurofeedback, CPA, light therapy, an envi ronmental technique, and a nutrient supplement had no effect on sleep disturbance. In line with the results of PWMA, Bayesian NMA results suggested that sleeping pills had the best performance in achieving reduced SOL, whereas BS intervention was assessed to be the most effective one in decreasing sleep disturbance. In particular, with consideration of both post-test outcome and mean change (Table S9), melatonin showed the probable best performance to reduce SOL, and PST (one of BS in terventions) was estimate to be the best in decreasing sleep disturbance. Thus, these interventions may be promising for adjusting the targeted sleep outcomes of children and adolescents with ADHD. Furthermore, in this review, majority of included studies had no specification on exclusion of children and adolescents with ADHD who had comorbid sleep disorders (e.g., RLS, PLMS, OSA). According to the four studies which included participants with primary insomnia only (Fig. S6), CBT intervention presented a small to moderate effect on reducing sleep disturbance (SMD by post-test outcomes: −0.42, p = 0.05; SMD by mean change: −0.50, p = 0.02 [72]), whereas L-dopa [69], Zolpidem [73], and IR-MPH [74] exhibited no significant effect (p > 0.05). This finding is consistent to the study reported by England et al. (2011) [69], i.e., L-dopa exhibited a significant effect on patients with RLS/PLMS rather than those with ADHD-only. This may imply that: (1) the comorbid sleep disorders may largely contribute to the sleep prob lems of children and adolescents with ADHD; (2) the existing inter vention (especially pharmaceutical interventions) may be more effective to treat these comorbidities rather than the primary insomnia; and (3) specific CBT protocols for ADHD-related sleep issues are less established than for other groups with primary insomnia, although CBT (i.e., CBT-I) is widely recognized as the first-line, gold standard treatment for chronic insomnia disorder [75]. This is in line with the findings of a previous review [76], which found inconsistent results of CBT technique and difficulty in long-term maintenance of intervention effect in individuals with neurodevelopmental conditions. However, more evidence is war ranted to examine this inconclusive point. Overall, the current review implied that both pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical interventions may play the important but different roles in reducing sleep problems of children and adolescents with ADHD. Future intervention designs may integrate the effective options into a multi-component strategy. This is possible to achieve a combined or synergetic effect with optimized pharmaceutical dose and intervention regimen, which may concurrently increase the intervention safety and participants’ adherence. Nonetheless, due to the large diverse in indi vidual situation and condition, a tailored or personalized intervention strategy is also highly warranted for children and adolescents with ADHD. This study had some limitations that should be acknowledged. First, results should be interpreted with caution owing to limitations regarding the study design, unbalanced participants' characteristics, intervention design, and reporting bias in the reviewed studies. The acknowledged limitations of the study designs in the included RCTs comprise small sample size, concerns with blinding, adherence issues with objective measures, unbalanced baseline, lack of placebo- or sham- controls, unclear carryover effect in crossover-arm RCT, lack of follow- up, insufficient data or measures, attrition or missing data, and in validity of tools or measures. Regarding participants’ characteristics, homogeneity in age range, sex distribution, comorbidity, and/or recruitment location was attributed to limited generalization and failure of moderator detection. In contrast, diverse ADHD symptoms or medi cation responses, changed medication plans during study (e.g., partici pants took melatonin or self-administered stimulants), as well as inclusion of comorbid sleep disorders (such as RLS, PLMS, or OSA), also contributed to the study limitations. Furthermore, the included studies reported limitations regarding the intervention design, including the timing of the intervention, short intervention duration, inevitable con founders, and the need for a tailored/personalized design. Moreover, parent- or clinician-reported data may have been influenced by expec tations of interventions, resulting in social desirability bias. Finally, the studies selected for review were also limited because only those with specific terms mentioned in the title or abstract were screened for further analysis, and studies published in languages other than English or in conference abstracts, government reports, textbooks, or unpub lished dissertations were excluded. 5. Conclusions By employing PWMA and Bayesian NMA, the current study sys tematically reviewed and analyzed the relevant RCTs to compare the Y. Fang et al. Sleep Medicine Reviews 88 (2026) 102303 9

effects of interventions and controls on sleep among the targeted pop ulation. According to the PWMA results, the existing interventions of any type likely significantly improve the quality of sleep of participants by shortening SOL and reducing sleep disturbance. However, SE, sleep duration, LPS, or daytime sleepiness were unlikely changed by the existing interventions. Moreover, the NMA results suggest that sleeping pills and BS interventions are probably to reduce SOL and sleep distur bance, respectively. More evidence from rigorous assessment of these promising options is warranted to confirm this effect, especially in consideration of those with or without comorbid sleep disorders. Owing to the diversity of sleep issues, a multi-component and tailored/ personalized sleep interventions are crucial for young individuals with ADHD. A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Neurodevelopmental disorders Multimodal data integration Deep learning Computer vision Clinical decision support ASD ADHD A B S T R A C T Background: Early and accurate diagnosis of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), including autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), remains a critical challenge in pediatric care. Traditional methods rely on subjective behavioral assessments that are time-intensive and prone to bias. Objective: This systematic review synthesizes biomedical informatics methodologies using deep learning-driven computer vision to enable objective, data-driven diagnostic decision support for pediatric NDDs. Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched Web of Science and Scopus (2020–2024), identifying 43 Q1/Q2 studies. Four informatics-focused research questions were addressed: multimodal feature extraction, deep learning architectures, high-performing strategies, and robust data integration challenges. Methodological quality and bias were assessed using the APPRAISE-AI framework. Results: Multimodal fusion and hybrid informatics pipelines dominated (38% of studies), outperforming uni modal approaches by integrating complementary streams—facial imaging (high specificity), EEG/fMRI (superior sensitivity). Transfer learning and fusion techniques were prevalent, but federated learning and explainable AI were underutilized. APPRAISE-AI revealed strong clinical relevance (72.8%) and reporting quality (66.1%), yet substantial gaps in reproducibility (41.0%) and result robustness (45.1%). Conclusions: AI-driven biomedical informatics holds significant potential to reduce diagnostic delays and costs in NDDs. However, reproducibility, interpretability, and ethical data integration must be improved through standardized, privacy-preserving, and auditable frameworks to enable scalable clinical deployment. ∗Corresponding author at: Department of Information and Computer Sciences, University of Hawaii at Manoa, Honolulu, HI 96822, USA. Introduction The diagnosis of NDDs, such as ASD and ADHD, remains a core chal lenge in biomedical informatics, requiring integration of heterogeneous data for timely, objective clinical decision-making. Traditional work flows rely on subjective behavioral assessments that are labor-intensive, prone to inter-rater variability, and limited by access to standardized data [1–8]. In the United States, 1 in 36 children receives an ASD diagno sis, while ADHD affects 5%–7% of children worldwide [9,10]. Delayed diagnosis incurs lifetime costs exceeding $1.4 million per ASD individ ual, highlighting the need for scalable, reproducible informatics-driven diagnostic support deployable across diverse settings [2,7,9,11–16]. Advances in deep learning and computer vision enable automated ex traction, fusion, and interpretation of multimodal neurobehavioral data [2,8,17–28]. For instance, 3D CNNs (convolutional neural networks) de tect millisecond-level behavioral markers in video with 93% accuracy on the SSBD dataset [29]; transformers identify ASD-specific gait with >92% accuracy [30]. Such pipelines reduce diagnostic delays of 18–24 months in high-income settings—and longer in low-resource areas—by up to 60% via mobile-deployable tools [31,32], promoting equitable early screening. However, unimodal pipelines (e.g., video or eye-tracking) lack gener alizability in comorbid or real-world scenarios [5,33–41]. Ahmed et al. [33] achieved 99.8% accuracy with eye-tracking alone, but performance dropped under variability. Multimodal integration yields 15%–20% ac curacy gains yet increases complexity in data alignment, privacy, and validation [5,36,42–44]. Han et al. [36] reported a 95.56% accurate EEG (electroencephalography)–eye-tracking model requiring impracti cal synchronized acquisition. Key questions include: Can self-supervised pre-training address data scarcity? Do attention-based fusion layers pro vide interpretable rationales? How can pipelines robustly handle noise, bias, and missing modalities in federated networks? This PRISMA-guided review uses the APPRAISE-AI framework to quantify gaps in reproducibility and robustness despite strong clini cal relevance. We address four informatics-centric Research Questions (RQs): • RQ1. How do informatics-driven feature extraction strategies han dle unimodal versus multimodal neurobehavioral data to enhance diagnostic fidelity? • RQ2. How do deep learning architectures leverage computer vision within end-to-end informatics pipelines for pediatric behavioral data analysis? • RQ3. Which learning strategies optimize performance while pre serving reproducibility and interpretability in vision-based diag nostic models? • RQ4. What informatics challenges—data heterogeneity, privacy, bias, and scalability—impede multimodal integration, and which emerging solutions enable robust screening? We synthesize why fusion dominates (complementarity reduces modality bias), benchmark underused strategies (e.g., federated learning), and propose standardized frameworks—XAI (eXplainable Artificial Intelligence) dashboards, ontology-aligned registries, containerized pipelines—for EHR (Electronic Health Records) inte gration. Prioritizing reproducibility, ethical governance, and clinicianin-the-loop validation, we advance AI-augmented decision support to ac celerate diagnosis, lower costs, and serve global populations equitably. 2 . Statement of significance Problem: AI-driven diagnosis of ASD/ADHD lacks rigorous method ological quality assessment, hindering clinical translation of multimodal computer vision approaches. What is Already Known: Existing reviews focus on unimodal data or technical metrics without systematic quality evaluation, missing repro ducibility and bias analysis across modalities. A comparative summary is in Table 1. What this Paper Adds: This review introduces three methodolog ical innovations: using the APPRAISE-AI framework for quality assess ment, feature co-occurrence network analysis for pipeline design, and modality-specific bias evaluation, providing a systematic quantification of reproducibility gaps (41.0%) in NDDs diagnostics. Who would benefit: Biomedical informatics researchers, clinical practitioners, and healthcare organizations implementing scalable, biasaware screening systems for pediatric NDDs. 3 . Methodology This systematic review followed PRISMA guidelines for transparent, reproducible study identification, selection, and synthesis. It comprised four phases: search strategy, eligibility criteria, study selection, and quality assessment. 3.1 . Search strategy We searched Web of Science (WoS) and Scopus (2020–2024) to ensure inclusion of high-impact, peer-reviewed research at the intersec tion of deep learning, computer vision, and NDDs. The query combined four categories using Boolean operators: (1) deep learning techniques, (2) neurodevelopmental conditions (ASD, ADHD), (3) multimodal be havioral data, and (4) feature extraction/fusion methods—additionally ANDed with (“child” OR “pediatr*” OR “adolescen*” OR “minor”). 3.1.1 . Eligibility criteria 3.2.1 . Inclusion (i) Studies using feature engineering + classical machine learn ing (ML) or deep learning (e.g., Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) / Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), transformer, multi modal models) for detection of neurodevelopmental conditions (ASD/ADHD). (ii) Video/image analysis via computer vision. (iii) Q1/Q2 peer-reviewed journal/conference articles (2020–2024), in English, from WoS/Scopus. 3.2.2 . Exclusion (i) Non-deep-learning classification studies. (ii) Reviews, meta-analyses, editorials, book chapters, letters, or abstracts without full text. (iii) Pre-2020 publications. 3.3 . Study selection and screening The PRISMA flow is shown in Fig. 1 and its checklist is provided in Supplementary File S1. WoS yielded 87 records; after applying arti cle/index filters, 56 remained; Q1/Q2 filtering left 30. Scopus returned 35; after deduplication and filtering, 13 remained. Full-text review against the criteria selected 43 out of 122 studies for synthesis. 3.4 . Methodological quality and bias assessment protocol We used APPRAISE-AI [54] to evaluate 43 studies across six domains: Clinical Relevance, Data Quality, Methodological Conduct, Robustness of Results, Reporting Quality, and Reproducibility. Two authors (A.R., F.A.) independently extracted data using a standardized form and scored Fig. 1. Each study was scored item-by-item; domain sums yielded overall quality (0-100): Very High (80-100), High (60-79), Moderate (40-59), Low (20-39), Very Low (019). Item-level scores for all studies are provided in the Supplementary File S2 to ensure standardized, reliable evaluation of clinical applica bility and reproducibility. This review was not prospectively registered. Following the APPRAISE-AI framework, we define: (1) reproducibility as the availability of code, data, and preprocessing details enabling in dependent verification; (2) robustness as consistent model performance across error analysis, bias assessment, and sensitivity testing; and (3) generalizability as external validity across populations, settings, and modalities. 4 . Results Diagnostic informatics pipelines integrate multimodal sources— facial/MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging), EEG/fNIRS signals, and video tracking—via standardized extraction (PCA (Principal Component Analysis), wavelets, or CNNs/RNNs/hybrids). Features undergo ear ly/late fusion to boost accuracy. Transfer learning, attention, and contin ual adaptation enhance generalization across ASD, ADHD, and cognitive profiles (Fig. 2). Study outcomes are synthesized in Table 2, covering data prove nance, feature engineering, architecture, strategies, validation, clinical findings, informatics contributions, and gaps—addressing RQs on de sign, interpretability, reproducibility, and scalability. 4.1 . Quantitative synthesis Feature development analysis (Fig. 3a) shows a dominant preference for fusion and hybrid methods (38%), emphasizing multimodal data integration. Temporal/spatial and statistical/texture-based features are comparably adopted, reflecting their complementary roles in capturing dynamic behaviors and biomarkers. Image-based extraction shows mod erate use, while dimensionality reduction and graph-based methods are underutilized (4 studies), representing missed opportunities for simplify ing high-dimensional neuroimaging data. Diagnostic focus distribution (Fig. 3b) reveals a pronounced emphasis on ASD (47% of studies), com pared to ADHD (19%) and both conditions (16%), highlighting a gap in unified frameworks for shared neurological markers across NDDs. Performance across modalities (Fig. 3c) shows data fusion con sistently outperforming unimodal approaches in accuracy and AUC. These trends derive from narrative synthesis of direct unimodal versus multimodal comparisons; cross-study comparability is limited by het erogeneity in datasets, metrics, and experimental conditions, precluding formal meta-analysis. While facial features achieve high specificity and EEG/fMRI (functional MRI) superior sensitivity, their combination ad dresses individual weaknesses. Learning strategy distribution (Fig. 3d) shows transfer learning dominating (14 papers), followed by fusion (11) and ensembling (10). Advanced methods—federated learning, reinforce ment learning, and chaotic butterfly optimization—are severely under utilized (1 paper each), revealing critical gaps in privacy-preserving collaboration, adaptive learning, and hyperparameter optimization. 4.2 . Feature co-occurrence on multimodal integration To construct the co-occurrence network (Fig. 4), we systematically extracted all modality pairs from the 43 reviewed studies and com puted edge weights as the frequency with which each pair co-occurred in the same pipeline. Only pairs with co-occurrence frequency ≥2 were included to ensure meaningful synergy patterns. This quantitative approach reveals empirically derived synergy patterns guiding standard ized NDDs pipeline design [51,55]. The directed graph identifies EEG as the central hub, with edge weights reflecting co-occurrence frequency driven by complementary diagnostic value and data availability [56]. Synthesis of methodological quality and bias The APPRAISE-AI evaluation of 43 studies reveals critical gaps in translational readiness (Fig. 5). While Clinical Relevance scored highest (72.8% of maximum possible score across all studies), indicating clear diagnostic objectives, and Reporting Quality was adequate (66.1%), fundamental methodological weaknesses prevail. Data Quality (54.5%) and Methodological Conduct (51.0%) were moderate, reflecting in consistent validation and data provenance. Most critically, Robustness of Results (45.1%) and Reproducibility (41.0%) scored lowest, expos ing pervasive deficiencies in error analysis, bias mitigation, and—most severely—the availability of open-source code and datasets that prevent external validation. Analysis of specific reproducibility dimensions re veals that complete source code was available for only 18.6% of studies, data accessible via repository in 37.2%, preprocessing details reported in 72.1%, and only 7.0% provided executable end-to-end replication packages. These findings underscore that reproducibility, not clinical relevance, remains the primary barrier to deploying AI tools in clinical informatics pipelines for NDDs diagnosis. Individual scores are in the Supplementary File S2. Analysis of bias resilience across modalities (Table 3) reveals crit ical vulnerabilities. Facial imaging shows 0% diversity across bias indicators, creating substantial cultural overfitting risks. While fMRI demonstrates better geographic representation (71% multi-country), it lacks low/middle-income cohort inclusion. EEG balances moderate uni versality (44% multi-country) with poor explainability (33% XAI adop tion). Multimodal fusion, while reducing single-modality bias, maintains significant opacity (60% error analysis, 20% XAI). These findings neces sitate standardized, bias-aware informatics pipelines that integrate XAI, federated learning, and ontology-driven governance to ensure equitable diagnostic performance. 5 . Research questions analysis 5.1 . Feature extraction in unimodal vs. multimodal informatics pipelines (RQ1) Computer vision-based feature extraction serves as a foundational component of biomedical informatics pipelines for NDDs diagnosis, con verting heterogeneous inputs into structured, ontology-aligned represen tations for reproducible clinical decision support [51,77–79]. Unimodal approaches offer computational efficiency and targeted biomarker dis covery but suffer from poor generalization across diverse populations [33,55,80]. For instance, facial analysis achieves high specificity in con trolled settings [17,33] but degrades due to cultural biases in expression norms and sensor variability [31,81–83]. Multimodal fusion addresses these limitations by leveraging com plementary data streams—spatial-temporal dynamics from computer vision, electrophysiological signals from EEG/fNIRS, and functional con nectivity from fMRI—to construct robust, bias-mitigated embeddings [36,51,55,61,84]. This integration exploits fundamental modality syn ergy: facial imaging provides high-resolution behavioral phenotyping while EEG captures millisecond-level neural oscillations, collectively re ducing false positives/negatives in heterogeneous NDDs presentations [66]. The success of fusion approaches, demonstrated by 15–20% im provement in ASD detection [61] (derived from narrative synthesis of studies with direct unimodal comparisons; see Section 4.1) and 94.0% comorbidity screening accuracy [66], stems from systematic data har monization including temporal alignment, standardized preprocessing, and clinical ontology mapping [51,67,72,85,86]. However, multimodal pipelines introduce critical informatics bar riers: synchronized data acquisition remains clinically impracti cal, high-dimensional inputs strain computational resources in lowresource settings, and inconsistent feature normalization undermines reproducibility—reflected in the low 41.0% APPRAISE-AI robustness score due to absent data dictionaries and code repositories [55, 56]. Deep learning architectures in end-to-end diagnostic informatics pipelines (RQ2) Deep learning architectures have transformed biomedical informat ics by embedding computer vision for automated, scalable conversion of multimodal pediatric data into standardized diagnostic biomarkers [51,55,88–90]. Unlike traditional machine learning which requires man ual feature engineering [72], modern architectures (CNNs, RNNs, trans formers) learn hierarchical representations directly from raw data, cap turing essential spatiotemporal dynamics for neurobehavioral analysis [29,59]. This addresses the critical informatics challenge of converting heterogeneous behavioral inputs into ontology-aligned, EHR-integrable features [51,56,91]. These architectures succeed through modality-specific optimization and cross-modal alignment [55], demonstrated via three key paradigms: feature extraction as phenotype mapping, where 3D CNNs map be havioral videos to clinical phenotypes (e.g., stereotyped movements) for standardized biomarker registries [51,68]; multimodal fusion via latent space harmonization, where autoencoders project EEG and eyetracking into shared embeddings, improving ASD detection by 12%–18% over unimodal approaches [36,55,61,92–94]; and attention mechanisms for interpretable weighting, where vision transformers highlight di agnostically relevant regions (e.g., reduced face fixation) to produce clinician-readable rationales [73,87,95]. The informatics pipeline ensures reproducibility through systematic governance: preprocessing for interoperability via standardized nor malization enabling federated multi-site training [18,33]; hierarchical representation learning, where CNNs map facial dynamics to clinical severity scores for EHR integration [69]; and temporal modeling using bidirectional LSTMs to capture gaze evolution as prognostic markers of joint attention deficits [59,74,96,97]. Advanced strategies address translational bottlenecks: federated learning preserves privacy while enabling multi-site generalization [18, 23,51]; explainable AI (Grad-CAM) visualizes gaze clusters driving ASD risk scores to bridge AI opacity with clinical intuition [56,70,87,98]; and multiscale connectivity analysis combines CNNs and LSTMs to reveal local activation and network-level disruptions for precision subtyping [59,75,99]. Deep learning thus positions computer vision as a core clinical informatics engine, standardizing data ingestion while ensuring repro ducibility, privacy, and interpretability for scalable NDDs diagnosis [23,51,55,56]. 5.3 . Optimizing performance with reproducible AI strategies (RQ3) Transfer learning, multimodal fusion, and ensemble methods dom inate NDDs diagnosis by addressing core informatics challenges: data scarcity, modality heterogeneity, and model variance [51,55,56]. 1. Transfer Learning: Pre-trained CNNs (VGG, ResNet) overcome pediatric data limitations (<500 samples) by transferring visual hierarchies to NDDs domains, achieving 79.09%–99.29% accu racy while reducing overfitting in resource-constrained settings [18,51,67,73]. 2. Multimodal Fusion: Integrating spatial (vision), temporal (EEG/fNIRS), and connectivity (fMRI) features captures NDDs heterogeneity through modality synergy, achieving 85–99.8% accuracy by combining behavioral phenotyping with neural dynamics [17,33,36,55,71,100,101]. 3. Ensemble Learning: Aggregating diverse learners enhances ro bustness through variance reduction, achieving 0.928 Dice scores and 72.41% classification accuracy, though dependent on model diversity and computationally intensive [54,60,102–104]. Federated learning enables multi-site collaboration without data sharing, achieving 97.5% accuracy while preserving privacy and reducing bias [18,23]. Selfsupervised learning (Simple Contrastive Learning of Representations (SimCLR), Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)) generates synthetic data, reducing annotation needs by 80% while improving generalization [69,109]. XAI integration with Grad-CAM and SHAP provides clini cal rationales, while interactive dashboards support clinician validation [70,87,95]. Edge computing with quantized models enables <2s in ference on wearables, facilitating deployment in low-resource clinics [61,110]. Standardized ontologies through BIDS-compliant repositories with Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) / Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine – Clinical Terms (SNOMED-CT) mapping ensure interoper ability across healthcare systems [60,65]. These solutions form a unified framework that transforms multimodal integration from a technical challenge into a scalable, equitable component of precision pediatric care [18,51,55,56]. 6 . Discussion This systematic review identifies multimodal fusion as a prevalent in formatics paradigm in NDDs diagnosis (38% of studies; Fig. 3a), driven by complementary modality resolution—EEG for temporal fidelity, fMRI for network topology, and computer vision for behavioral quantification [36,51,55,58]. However, a notable translational paradox exists, with APPRAISE-AI revealing critical gaps in reproducibility and robustness despite strong clinical relevance [56], primarily due to absent opensource code, data dictionaries, and external validation. Recent work [111] emphasizes that reproducibility requires empirical verification— including replication attempts, environment capture, dependency pin ning, seed control, and documented compute environments—beyond merely sharing digital artifacts. This reframes reproducibility as an auditable continuum rather than a binary property. Furthermore, en vironmental efficiency aligns with our discussion of computational bottlenecks, suggesting that reproducible pipelines must also be com putationally sustainable for real-world clinical deployment. Federated learning—employed in only one study [18]—emerges as a promising solution, enabling privacy-preserving, multi-site model ag gregation while mitigating data silos and demographic bias [23,51]. Similarly, underutilized XAI methods can generate clinician-auditable rationales through SHAP, Grad-CAM, or attention heatmaps [70,87,95], transforming black-box outputs into FHIR-compliant decision support artifacts essential for regulatory approval [56,112]. The feature co-occurrence network (Fig. 4) provides evidence-based modality selection guidance, indicating EEG-inclusive triplets maximize diagnostic yield. Combined with BIDS-compliant synchronization and HPO-mapped feature registries [60,65], this enables automated pipeline generation across multiple sites. Edge-optimized models further facili tate real-time screening in low-resource settings with minimal accuracy loss [61,110]. Emerging systems demonstrate potential for translation: vision-language models align imaging with clinical reports for differential diagnosis [74,113], while agentic AI reduces workflow time through optimized triage [114,115]. These operate within federated, EHR-integrated ecosystems [18,23,51,65], leveraging FHIR-compliant outputs and privacy-preserving orchestration [56]. Based on these findings, the proposed unified framework (Fig. 6)—integrating federated pre-training, standardized fusion, XAI validation, and edge deployment—directly addresses core informatics challenges in multimodal NDDs screening [18,23,51,55,56,87,116]. It operationalizes key priorities, including data provenance, interop erability, clinical utility, and bias reduction, while enabling equitable deployment through privacy-preserving pipelines. Although the methods in Table 4 show clear methodological advan tages and varying degrees of clinical relevance across modalities, none have been deployed in routine clinical practice or reported for prospec tive patient diagnosis. Reported patient numbers reflect retrospective validation cohorts rather than real-world use. Federated learning [18], edge-optimized lightweight architectures [61,110], and explainable AI [87,95] represent the most promising methodological pathways for clin ical deployment, as they directly address the privacy, computational, and interpretability barriers identified in our APPRAISE-AI analysis. This highlights a persistent deployment gap between high algorithmic performance and clinical adoption. 6.1 . Limitations of our review This review was limited to Q1/Q2 articles from Web of Science and Scopus (2020–2024), excluding other databases and gray literature. This selection prioritized methodologically rigorous, high-impact stud ies with robust peer review, aligning with our focus on reproducible AI pipelines for clinical translation. While ensuring methodological rigor, this approach may have introduced selection bias by underrepresenting innovative pipelines from clinical or open-access venues [56] and omit ting real-world deployment insights from technical reports and federated learning initiatives [18,51]. Additionally, restricting to Q1/Q2 journals in WoS and Scopus—including the Scopus Open Access-only filter— may have excluded relevant studies from subscription-based venues, lower-tier journals, and conferences, potentially overlooking emerg ing methodologies. This restriction may also underrepresent real-world deployment studies and certain modalities (e.g., behavioral sensing) that are more frequently published in clinical or specialized venues outside our search scope. This review was not prospectively regis tered (e.g., PROSPERO), which is acknowledged as a limitation. Despite the availability of deployment-oriented methodologies, such as fed erated learning and lightweight architectures, none of the reviewed frameworks have been integrated into routine clinical practice (Table 5). 6.2 . Future directions Future research must prioritize clinically viable informatics sys tems that extend beyond accuracy metrics. Conclusion Deep learning-driven computer vision is reshaping biomedical in formatics for NDDs diagnosis, shifting from subjective assessment to objective, multimodal decision support. This PRISMA-guided [117] re view of 43 studies confirms that feature fusion and hybrid pipelines (38%; Fig. 3(c)) outperform unimodal approaches by integrating com plementary modalities—EEG for temporal precision, fMRI for network mapping, and eye-tracking for behavioral quantification. However, re producibility (41%) and robustness (45.1%) remain critical barriers to translation. The underuse of federated learning and explainable AI limits privacy-compliant, clinician-trustworthy deployment. By embed ding standardized data harmonization, XAI-driven interpretability, and EHR-integrated validation, these frameworks can accelerate scalable screening—transforming research prototypes into deployable clinical tools. metadata_title: Parent and carer perspectives on behavioural sleep management strategies for children with ADHD
pages: Parent and carer perspectives on behavioural sleep management strategies for children with ADHD Samantha J. Hornsey a,b,c,d,* , Alison Rowsell a , Catherine M. Hill b,e,1, Samuele Cortese f,g,h,i,j,1, Kate Greenwell a,b,2 , Ingrid Muller a,2, On behalf of the DISCA study team3 a Primary Care Research Centre, School of Primary Care, Population Sciences and Medical Education, Faculty of Medicine, University of Southampton, Southampton, UK b Clinical and Experimental Sciences, Faculty of Medicine, University of Southampton, Southampton, UK c Human Development and Health, Faculty of Medicine, University of Southampton, Southampton, UK d Centre for Clinical and Community Applications of Health Psychology, School of Psychology, Faculty of Environmental and Life Sciences, University of Southampton, Southampton, UK e Southampton Children's Hospital, University Hospital Southampton NHS Foundation Trust, Southampton, UK f Developmental EPI (Evidence Synthesis, Prediction, and Implementation) Lab, Centre for Innovation in Mental Health, School of Psychology, Faculty of Environmental and Life Sciences, University of Southampton, Southampton, UK g Clinical and Experimental Sciences (CNS and Psychiatry), Faculty of Medicine, University of Southampton, Southampton, UK h Hampshire and Isle of Wight Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, Southampton, UK i Hassenfeld Children's Hospital at NYU Langone, New York University Child Study Center, New York, NY, USA j DiMePRe-J, Department of Precision and Regenerative Medicine and Ionian Area, University of Bari “Aldo Moro,”, Bari, Italy A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: ADHD Sleep Insomnia Child Parent Behaviour Management A B S T R A C T Objective/background: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is common in children. Many children with ADHD have chronic insomnia, which is associated with negative outcomes for the child and family and can worsen ADHD symptoms. Behavioural sleep interventions can be effective for children with ADHD and are the recommended first-line approach to management. However, many parents/carers may not have access to, or struggle to implement, interventions in practice. This study explored parents/carers views and experiences of: 1) behavioural sleep management strategies, 2) help-seeking for managing sleep problems and 3) perceptions about a potential digital sleep guide for managing sleep problems. Patients/methods: A qualitative study using semi-structured interviews of parents/carers of children with ADHD/ ADHD traits and chronic insomnia symptoms (CIS). Participants were recruited via social media and purposively sampled for diverse characteristics. Interviews were conducted by telephone/videocall, recorded and transcribed verbatim. Data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis. Results: Eighteen parents/carers took part; two themes and six subthemes were developed. Despite valuing behavioural sleep strategies, parents/carers noted many challenges to engaging with them, including perceiving these strategies to be both ineffective for children with ADHD and not easy to implement in the real world. They described that tiredness, exhaustion, ADHD symptoms and challenging behaviour make parent engagement with strategies difficult. Parents/carers welcomed digital support in principle, particularly because they perceived health professional support to be lacking. However, they noted that digital interventions must address their key support needs regarding flexibility, realistic expectations and a pragmatic approach, as well as comradeship, support and testimonials from other parents/carers. * Corresponding author. Conclusion: Tailored but flexible support and reassurance are necessary for parents/carers of children with ADHD and CIS. Digital support must validate parent/carer experiences and include experiences from other parents/ carers. 1. Introduction 1.1. Background Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) affects around 5% of school-aged children worldwide [1]. Characterised by developmen tally inappropriate inattention, hyperactivity/impulsivity or both [2], ADHD can have a major impact on children and families [3]. Around 70% of parents of children with ADHD report that their child experi ences sleep problems and individuals with ADHD have an eight-fold increased risk of a sleep disorder diagnosis (most commonly chronic insomnia), compared to those without ADHD [4]. Chronic insomnia (CI) disorder is defined by the International Clas sification of Sleep Disorders III [5] as difficulty with ini tiating/maintaining sleep or early morning waking, for at least three nights a week and for at least three months. Sleep problems in children can affect cognitive function, emotional regulation and increase risk of obesity [6,7]. They can also worsen ADHD symptoms [8] and impact parental sleep and quality of life [9,10]. Currently, many types of behavioural sleep interventions for CI in children are available [11,12]. These often include parent education, appropriate and consistent bedtime routines and appropriate sleep habits (e.g., improved physical and emotional sleep environment, reduced screen time and reduced caffeine in the evening). More specific sleep interventions include faded bedtime (delaying bedtime in the short term to gradually bring it forward over time), extinction-based strategies (such as camping-out; gradually increasing physical distance between the parent and child at bedtime, to promote independent sleeping) and positive reinforcement (rewards for positive sleep behaviours). Behav ioural sleep interventions are effective for children with ADHD [13] - yet with small to moderate effect sizes and low certainty of evidence - and recommended as the first approach to CI [14]. Parenting interventions for sleep problems in children with ADHD can be effective at improving parent reported ADHD symptoms [15,16], emotional and physical wellbeing and relationships [17] when delivered by practitioners. Whilst the literature suggests that various behavioural sleep in terventions are effective, a qualitative study of 12 parents/carers of children with ADHD, conducted by French et al. [18] aimed to explore experiences of sleep difficulties. The findings highlighted parents usu ally try many types of strategies to improve their child's sleep, using a trial-and-error approach. Rowsell et al. [19], in a qualitative study conducted by the current research team, further found that repeated unsuccessful attempts to address children's sleep issues led to emotional distress and eventual normalisation of the problems. It is therefore important to explore in depth the barriers and facilitators to imple menting specific approaches, to better support parents/carers to persist with appropriate strategies in the future. To date, there are no published studies from the UK exploring this topic. Additionally, many services for children with ADHD, including those provided by the UK national health service (NHS), are overstretched and thus unable to provide timely support [20]. Furthermore, behavioural sleep interventions are resource intensive, and medication is often pre scribed without due adherence to international guidance recommending first-line non-pharmacological interventions [14,21]. It is therefore important to also explore support parents need for their child's sleep problems, to guide the format and delivery of behavioural sleep interventions. Digital interventions specifically designed to address sleep problems in children with ADHD may be low cost, with wide reach and represent an effective solution to current challenges in service provision. Indeed, a digital sleep intervention encompassing CBT for insomnia, aimed at a general population of children with insomnia and their parents, reduced sleep problems and was well accepted by parents [22]. Digital parenting interventions for ADHD, not specific to sleep problems, have also been suggested as acceptable to parents and to increase parenting efficacy and child social performance [23]. We therefore conducted the present study to inform the development of a digital sleep intervention for parents/carers of children with ADHD [24] (https://www.discasleep.org.uk/). 1.2. Study aims and research questions To explore:1) parents'/carers’ (hereafter referred to as “parents”) views and experiences of managing sleep problems in children with ADHD 2) barriers and facilitators to engagement with target behavioural approaches to inform the development of a digital sleep guide. Research questions: what are parents’: 1. Views and experiences of behavioural sleep management strategies? 2. Experiences of seeking information about managing sleep problems? 3. Perceptions about a potential digital sleep guide for managing sleep problems in children with ADHD? We also explored the impact of having a child with ADHD with sleep problems; themes related to this are reported separately [19]. 2. Material and methods This study is reported using the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research [25]. 2.1. Design A qualitative semi-structured interview study. 2.2. Epistemological stance, research team and reflexivity The research team included academics and clinicians with expertise in paediatric sleep medicine, child and adolescent psychiatry, health psychology, qualitative research methods and primary care research. Reflexive notes and diary entries were made throughout the study and data collection/analysis were discussed and developed iteratively within the multidisciplinary team to interpret the data from multiple perspectives. The data was approached with a pragmatic stance, to describe parents’ views/experiences of the techniques and practically inform the future development of an intervention. Personal experiences of being a parent, from both the clinical/academic team members and public contributors, may also have influenced interpretation. 2.3. Sample and recruitment 2.3.1. Eligibility criteria Inclusion criteria were UK parents/carers of children aged 6-12 with both: • Diagnosed ADHD or on a waiting list for an ADHD assessment. • Chronic insomnia symptoms (CIS), i.e., difficulty falling asleep, maintaining sleep or early morning waking, for 3 or more nights a week, for at least 3 months. S.J. Hornsey et al. Sleep Medicine 147 (2026) 109138 2

Parents/carers were excluded if they were unable to understand/ communicate in English or if the child had (1) severe learning difficulty, defined by whether their child had been recommended to attend a school for children with severe learning disabilities, (2) co-morbid mental or physical ill health or disability likely to require specialist supervision or frequent admission to hospital, or (3) other health problems which impacted sleep. 2.3.2. Sample size A priori, it was anticipated that due to specific topic aims and a team consisting of experienced qualitative researchers, 15-25 interviews would provide sufficient information power for interpretation of the data [26]. This was reviewed as data collection and analysis progressed. Furthermore, after 17 interviews with 18 parents, the researchers judged the study had sufficient information power and data collection ended. 2.3.3. Recruitment and sampling strategy The study recruited participants via social media (public posts and targeted advertising for parents with diverse characteristics), a local fostering organisation, word of mouth and snowballing sampling, with adverts directing interested individuals to an online form. The online form checked participant eligibility and asked optional demographics questions to enable the research team to purposively select a maximally diverse sample. These included parent/carer char acteristics (gender, ethnic background, highest level of qualification, relationship to child), child characteristics (age, gender, severity and type of insomnia) and household composition. 2.4. Data collection Semi-structured qualitative interviews were conducted between March-August 2023 via telephone/videocall and lasted between 30 and 60 minutes. Fourteen interviews were conducted by SH (female post doctoral Research Fellow and Psychologist, experienced in qualitative and child sleep research) and three by a master's student, supervised by KG/SH. Neither interviewer knew the participants and both presented themselves as non-clinical and neutral to the participants. A semi-structured topic guide (supplementary information 1), developed based on academic and clinical research team expertise, guided the interview. Open-ended questions asked about 1) experiences of having a child with ADHD and sleep problems, 2) experiences of managing sleep problems, 3) views/experiences about individual behavioural sleep strategies as mentioned below, 4) experiences of seeking information and management support and 5) views about seeking information online and the potential development of a digital sleep guide. Types of behavioural sleep strategies we individually asked about were: • Consistent bedtime routines. • Changing the sleep environment • Encouraging positive sleep habits, including reducing screen us and caffeine, changing the timing of evening meals and increasing physical activity. • Calming activities • Bedtime fading • Extinction-based sleep strategies • Rewards for positive sleep behaviours After the interview, further optional demographics questions asked about parent/carer characteristics (age, sexual orientation, employment status), child characteristics (ethnic background, diagnosed with ADHD or awaiting an assessment, diagnosed with ASD and whether they room share with another household member) and family composition (num ber of children in the household, number of others with ADHD in the household). Participants were given a £20 shopping voucher to thank them for their time. Interviews were audio/video recorded and professionally tran scribed, with transcripts checked by the research team for accuracy. 2.5. Data analysis Data were handled in NVivo software and analysed iteratively based on a thematic analysis using the six steps outlined by Braun and Clarke [27]. This method was chosen due to its descriptive and theoretically flexible nature, to pragmatically inform future development of a digital sleep intervention. The data in this study were analysed on a semantic level, and this analysis was conducted inductively whereby codes and themes were developed from the data collected. The researchers familiarised themselves with the data and SH made summary notes immediately following interviews. AR coded the tran scripts, developed an initial coding framework and themes which were discussed with the wider team (SH, KG, IM, CMH, SC). AR's themes were developed initially for the aims regarding exploring the impact of sleep problems, described in Rowsell et al. [19]. In the context of the current paper, these were developed further by SH to align with the specific research aims of the current paper (regarding 1) parents' views and experiences of managing sleep problems in children with ADHD and 2) barriers and facilitators to engagement with target behavioural ap proaches to inform the development of a digital sleep guide). For this paper, the themes were developed with the inductive and descriptive approach to thematic analysis described above. They were then revised and finalised with KG using summaries/coding frameworks and subse quently the wider team (AR, IM, CMH, SC). Throughout the analysis, data regarding individual sleep strategies, as mentioned in 2.4, fed into the main analysis, whereby common themes across the entire data set (including strategies) are given, and examples of specific strategies are discussed within the themes. To inform content specific to individual strategies in future interventions, more detailed and applied summaries of findings regarding individual strategies are given in the supplementary material. 2.6. Public and patient involvement and engagement Public contributors (parents of children with ADHD) were involved in the design of study materials, ensuring they were relevant and accessible to participants. The topic guide and eligibility check questions were piloted with 2 public contributors prior to data collection, con firming timing, relevance and readability. 2.7. Ethical considerations This study was approved by the University of Southampton Faculty of Medicine ethics committee (ERGO 78034). Participants provided informed consent prior to interview. Transcripts were pseudo- anonymised with participant identification numbers. 3. Results 3.1. Sample characteristics One hundred and eighty-three parents expressed an interest in this study and 107 (58%) were eligible to take part. 18 parents took part in 17 interviews. Parent age ranged from 24 to 48 years (mean 39.1). The children they discussed were aged 6-12 years (mean 8.9). See Table 1/2. 3.2. Themes Two descriptive themes, each with 3 subthemes (Fig. 1), common across techniques, highlighted key influences on engagement with sleep techniques and the support needs of parents. S.J. 3.2.1. The challenges of engaging with sleep techniques 3.2.1.1. Parent/carer belief that behavioural sleep management techniques are ineffective for children with ADHD. Whilst parents were generally in favour of behavioural techniques, this theme describes an overarching parental scepticism about the effectiveness of behavioural techniques for children with ADHD. Participants often reported that they are challenging to implement and not always appropriate or effective for their child. Reasons included child resistance, hyperactivity at bedtime or a strong belief that the parent had tried everything with no success. “... where that [camping out] might work with a child without ADHD and they settle down, that's not how it works with a child with ADHD ... the boundaries just aren't the same with them.” (P22, mother of 9-year-old boy) For example, whilst some parents liked the idea of bedtime fading, common concerns were that their child would not tire and go to sleep, regardless of bedtime delay. “... We've tried just letting him keep going until he crashes, but then we found we never got to that stage where we just wanted to crash, like, we would've just kept going all night long if the opportunity came ... He wasn't able to recognise himself, that he was tired, and the more tired he became, you go into, he almost goes into that overdrive where we're overstimulated and, and just can't get our selves out of that spiral” (P6, mother of 9-year-old boy) Similarly, parents often stated that rewards for positive sleep be haviours would not work for their child for a variety of reasons: the child does not understand what is expected of them, their motivation is different to children without ADHD, or because they would not be able to wait for a reward. Smaller or more immediate rewards or rewards were suggested as something that could help. “that doesn't work for us, and I would say that - I would expect for a lot of ADHD kids it would be the, the same issue, because that route of motivation just isn't the same for us” (P14, mother of 8-year-old boy) “... I think perhaps I, I should have made them smaller goals almost ...” (P25, mother of 11-year-old girl) Most parents commented that increasing physical activity might worsen children's hyperactivity, rather than facilitate sleep. “I've done increasing physical activity before ... it has not worked at all because he, he doesn't get worn out” (P8, mother of 11-year-old boy). To help implementation of bedtime routines, participants often suggested that wind-down activities need to be short, motivating and calming. For example, stories or lego, rather than something that takes longer that their child may easily become bored with. “... it's reading a book for us ... Erm, the other thing that she finds quite calming is story tapes ... when she goes to sleep, just play a story tape and she, she enjoys that and I think that's quite calming. She, she wouldn't entertain yoga or anything because she can't stay focused.” (P25, mother of 11-year-old girl) Participants also often reported that current sleep advice is too vague for children with ADHD. They wanted meaningful advice tailored to their needs without assumption of their situation. Instead, they perceived health professional advice, particularly around bedtime rou tines, to be “like being told to suck eggs”. 3.2.1.2. Challenges of implementing sleep strategies in everyday life for children with ADHD. All participants stated that behavioural strategies, whilst helpful in principle, are difficult to implement in practice. This theme discusses how they described multiple every-day barriers, not directly relating to ADHD, but which make it more difficult for children with ADHD. These include family composition (single versus two-parent households, differing parental roles e.g., more demands in single parent households), sibling room sharing, bedroom/household spaces, working patterns, holidays, visitors, financial constraints and their child having other neurodevelopmental conditions. For example, whilst most acknowledged that screen time in the bedroom can be unhelpful to sleep (supplementary information 2), in some situations they were beneficial and comforting, particularly if the child had ASD or ‘neurodivergent traits’. Some voiced that electronics can be calming/regulating, despite expressing concern that they might be judged by others for this opinion. “like my children have never had the TV or anything in their room, and all but one have never gone to bed with phones. So I think, the majority of people, I think, electronics are bad, but sometimes that, it actually works in the opposite way for a very small minority ... that's the only thing that I k-, that really kind of calms - she's a, a lot more kind of complicated. ... lots of the advice is kind of, demonises the use of technology ... And I do agree in most cases it probably doesn't help, but I think there is some people that it might help with ... it's good advice to try not to have them, but in some cases, that might be the only thing that works, you know.” (P2, mother of 11-year-old girl) Similarly, there were mixed responses about gradually increasing physical distance (camping-out). Some agreed with the principles of this technique, however extinction-based strategies were generally perceived as difficult to implement or inappropriate due to their child's age, co-morbidities or individual/family circumstance (e.g., having an adopted child) and beliefs. “we've tried a million different ways of doing it [extinction-based techniques] and it just doesn't help her ... it doesn't work with the attachment ... you have to work with, see what else the family's situation is” (P13, mother 10-year-old girl). Bedtime fading was sometimes perceived as difficult to implement, due to worry about practical implications such as impact on parent evening routines (disrupting any small amount of time they have for themselves) or on sibling's evening routines. A few participants had not considered this method before but were interested to learn more and with the right information, potentially use it. “... because I've moved homes ... the three of them sleep in one room, it's not possible, 'cause then he's playing downstairs and the other two are, 'Why, why's he downstairs? Why's he downstairs?' Or, they'll deliberately egg each on by making a noise.” (P12, mother of 9-year-old boy) 3.2.1.3. Tiredness, exhaustion, ADHD symptoms and behaviour make parental engagement with strategies difficult. This theme describes that a key barrier to parents' engagement with recommended sleep techniques was parental tiredness/exhaustion and their child's ADHD symptoms/ behaviour impact on this. Alongside feeling they had tried everything with no success, these often seemed to lead parents to ‘give in’. “... you just get to a point of apathy, to be honest, where you just, like, do you know what, I just can't. I just haven't got the energy to, to try and be creative about how we're gonna do these things ... You've got other - you've got your other kid to look after as well. There's only, there's only so much that you can try and follow, like, routines and strategies and whatever” (P15, father of 10-year old girl) For example, participants viewed consistent bedtime routines posi tively but often acknowledged difficulty implementing them consis tently without risking further tiredness and exhaustion. Things that had helped were perseverance, visual timetables, giving the child agency, peer support and setting realistic expectations. “it's sticking to similar routines. I mean, like I say, I - in the holidays, it's not even just for them, it's for me. I have to allow them just to have telly at nighttime to chill sometimes, because I need that bit of respite as well” (P4, mother of 8-year-old boy) “I think just all being on the same page ... everyone kind of knowing what the routine is. And also, with the child, making them know it ... for younger children, visual things are good ... things to get ready in the morning, for instance, and it's, you know, like charts and things of, of what happens when. I know things like that work well”. (P2, mother of 11-year-old girl) Parents often reported a sense of hopelessness around implementing sleep techniques and reported the need for mental and physical health considerations for both parent and child. Some parents also reported their own ADHD diagnosis/symptoms made the situation more chal lenging or made it difficult to engage with techniques. “... I have ADD, so I really struggle at home, erm, with my sleep anyway. So, I am like that person that cannot get out of bed. Whereas he can jump out of bed and he's like, 'Right, let's go there.' ... obvi ously if I'm tired it makes me quite ratty, erm, and then obviously I've Fig. 1.
