Parents are open to trying sleep management interventions that address key support needs 3.2.2.1. Flexibility, realistic expectations and need for a pragmatic approach. All participants emphasised the need for pragmatic ap proaches to sleep techniques incorporating flexibility in choosing/ implementing them and realistic expectations (particularly for strategies they were sceptical about). Although parents were positive about, and used some techniques (e.g., bedtime routines, calming activities, changing the sleep environment, reducing screen time), a pragmatic approach was emphasised as key. “one thing that would be useful would just be, like, more strategies, you know, and different things that you can use, and maybe how you can mix and match ...” (P15, father of 10-year-old girl) “if something doesn't work, try and adapt it ...” (P4, mother of 8- year-old boy) For example, parents often described that consistent bedtime rou tines may not always be possible (e.g., parent/carer working patterns, special occasions or when children live between two households where parents live separately). “... in an ideal world, we'd all love to stick to a routine to, to the T, wouldn't we, but the thing is, is life happens all the time ... now I'm starting a full-time job, so unless I wait, obviously, till I got in a routine, I know roughly what times we'll be back and what times we'll be doing things ... I could, kind of, set up some sort of similar routine. I think the only downfall with that is, like I say, is if they expect something at a certain time and you're not doing it, that could then cause anxiety ... say if you've got to go out somewhere, you know, and it's an accident, or you've got something particular on ... You can't do your routine because that's gonna change it, and then that's gonna make them more anxious. And then they're gonna not want to sleep ...” (P4, mother of 8-year-old boy) 3.2.2.2. Welcoming new digital support. Most participants had searched for information online; including from NHS resources, ADHD websites and social media. However, they often had mixed opinions about them, suggesting they were inaccessible, untrustworthy, or not relevant to their child with ADHD. “... you just want to see what's available out there, what, what support you can get. Like anything, there's always a massive waiting list.” (P13, mother of 10-year-old girl) The parents therefore welcomed development of digital sleep sup port if it accommodated key needs. Important elements to include were holistic and relevant information about ADHD and sleep problems, normal sleep patterns, use of medication (including side effects), tips for children, reassurance that a child with ADHD can have a ‘normal life’, comorbid conditions (for example autism spectrum disorder), accessible and engaging language and signposting. Off-putting features described included use of jargon, content perceived as inauthentic, prescriptive or inflexible. “... if I had more understanding of how ADHD actually affects them, and how, obviously, it can affect their sleep and their appetite, I think if I had more of that information, I'd have more understanding of why they do it.” (P27, mother of 7-year-old boy) “if I've looked at something and then I can find other research then th-, that's, that would make me feel that it's more reliable.” (P22, mother of 9-year-old boy) They suggested that a credible, friendly and trusted digital support guide could fill the online information and health professional access void. Their needs were wider than simply practical advice. They wanted reassurance; that that they are not alone, that sleep can get better and to realistically say ‘try it, if it doesn't work it might not be right for your child’. 3.2.2.3. Comradeship, peer support and stories from other parents. All parents highlighted peer support needs, welcoming experiences and support from other parents of children with ADHD. Many had sought support from family, friends and peers, with mixed experiences, but often described the importance of drawing on experiences of others in similar situations. “Parents always like to hear how other parents get on whether they're good or bad, you know. They don't always want to hear shining stories of, 'Oh, and yes and my daughter slept beautifully after having a weighted blanket on her back for two nights,' you know, they want to hear both success and maybe not so good stories and how, how to overcome them. Or, how, what worked well and what didn't work well.” (P13, mother of 10-year-old girl) Participants described that stories from other parent of children with ADHD would provide examples of individual strategies, but importantly would validate their feelings, reinforce that they are not alone, and promote trust in strategies. Stories would provide hope, acknowledge parents’ needs and encourage them to look after themselves. This was perceived as a contrast to the judgment parents/carers felt from the outside world, including professionals. “some sort of support mechanism-, you know, or signposting to support for parents where they can realise that, you know, there's loads of other people going through similar stuff, and that actually, you're doing a really good job” (P15, father of 10-year-old girl) “it's reassurance for the parents ... this isn't your fault, you are not a failure at being a parent, because I'd be like, well, she just - why won't she go to sleep? I'm doing everything right, everybody's said that this should get her to sleep, and if somebody had just gone, 'It's not you,' that would have been really helpful” (P9, mother of 6-year-old girl) 3.3. Summary of thoughts about individual sleep techniques To pragmatically inform the development of our digital intervention, we also explored parental experiences and views about individual behavioural sleep techniques. Further details for individual techniques and quotes are given in supplementary information 2. 4. Discussion This study provided novel insights into the challenges parents of children with ADHD face when looking for and engaging with behav ioural sleep techniques to improve their child's CIS, a topic that has been previously under-researched. Like previous research [18], parents generally valued behavioural sleep techniques (particularly consistent bedtime routines, regulator s/comforters and limiting things that are unhelpful to or hinder sleep). French et al. [18], similarly, found that some strategies were more valuable than others, albeit with mixed success, and that sometimes they are challenging to implement. These findings are also echoed in more recent qualitative research with 21 child participants with ADHD who highlighted the importance of routines and a calming environment [28]. Although parents in the current study placed less importance on physical S.J. Hornsey et al. Sleep Medicine 147 (2026) 109138 6

activity than the participants in French et al. [18] and Alvstrand et al. [28]. However, the current study also uniquely identified further chal lenges to engaging with sleep techniques; commonly the perception that they are ineffective for children with ADHD. Nonetheless, an umbrella review of meta-analyses of randomised trials exploring the efficacy of sleep interventions for children indicates that sleep techniques are effective for children with ADHD, albeit with small-to-moderate effect sizes and limited certainty of evidence [13]. Given that many parents in the current study also felt advice was not specific enough to children with ADHD, more parental support and the way information is given to parents may influence their motivation and perception of the effec tiveness and appropriateness of these techniques. More reassurance and clarity could be provided to parents about the principles behind the recommended sleep management techniques and why they could help their child with ADHD. For example, whilst the bedtime fading technique may not be appropriate for every child, there were common reservations related to parental worry about the impact of their child going to bed later and the belief that their child would remain active no matter the time of night. Information about how to implement this technique in children with ADHD, which children this would be appropriate for, and reassurance on the long-term benefits may support and empower parents/carers to implement the technique at home. There is evidence from other parenting programmes (sleep and non-sleep-specific) for children with ADHD that parent mediated behaviour change in the child can be ach ieved [15,16,23,29,30]. Another common barrier expressed by parents was a perception that techniques were inflexible and not easy to use in the real world. Parental considerations included 1) increased impulsivity and hyperactivity in their child (therefore resistance to routine, rewards, new behavioural strategies and an inability to switch-off); 2) individual child and family situation and 3) other needs for comorbid disorders, such as ASD. These further demonstrate the importance of tailoring interventions to the child and family's specific needs. An Australian randomised controlled trial tested a practitioner led intervention for managing behavioural sleep problems in children with ADHD; ‘Sleeping Sound with ADHD’. The intervention included sleep education and flexible, but tailored, information and was effective (for reducing parent-reported ADHD symptoms) with samples of <200 children from pediatric practices [16] and <300 children in the community [15]. Other important considerations for engaging with techniques in the real world included parental exhaustion and mental health. As reported in Rowsell et al. [19] parental exhaustion often led to parents giving in to sleep problems. Based on our analysis, this led to giving up on man agement techniques and highlighted the need to encourage persistence and offer reassurance to parents. Furthermore, parents/carers in the current study often reported they themselves have ADHD or other neurodiversity. As ADHD is characterised by high heritability [31], parent-mediated interventions including these sleep techniques must also accommodate the needs of parents who themselves may have inattention and may struggle to self-regulate. Parents/carers further highlighted support needs. In line with pre vious qualitative research of parents' experiences seeking help for young children (not specific to ADHD) [32,33], parents in the current study perceived much current health professional and online advice to be lacking, or to be impersonal or patronising. Parents in the current study often reported a void in information [19] which also often resulted in the use of online resources. As a consequence, they endorsed the development of an evidence-based, relevant and flexible digital resource for the management of their child's sleep problems. 4.1. Implications 4.1.1. Clinical practice and clinical resources Generally, information around behavioural sleep strategies needs to be tailored to families of children with ADHD and diverse family situ ations. Similarly to information included in some available programmes such as the Sleeping Sound with ADHD intervention [15,16], clear and relevant but flexible information from both health professionals and support resources are needed to equip parents with the knowledge and confidence to implement and persist with appropriate strategies effectively. Parents/carers may also benefit hearing from other parents who have been in similar situations. This will validate their feelings, reassure them that they are not alone and help build parental self-efficacy and trust in the strategies they are being advised to try and set realistic expectations. These needs are similarly reported in other studies highlighting the needs of parents of children (not specific to ADHD) [33]. 4.1.2. Future research Parents in this study were supportive of the development of a future digital sleep guide. It should address key challenges highlighted by parents in this study and include the key important elements for parents regarding tailored information and peer support. Notably, tailored in formation and peer support through parent quotes have been used in development of other parent/carer child health interventions such as the management of childhood eczema [34]. Digital intervention should also address challenges with effective and timely implementation of the programmes. Future research with more fathers and parents from ethnic minority backgrounds would also be important to ensure the development of resources sensitive to the needs of diverse parents/carers. Findings in this study were used to inform the development of the DISCA intervention ‘Sleep Buddy’ [35] whereby the intervention in corporates reassurance and support for parents, advice specific for children with ADHD and different family circumstances, and peer support. 4.2. Strengths and limitations This study highlights important considerations for the implementa tion of behavioural sleep strategies for parents of children with ADHD. However, it must be noted that ADHD diagnosis was either self-reported by the parent or to be confirmed. Nonetheless recent UK data from a large child mental health service reported 94% of such children, when assessed, indeed receive an ADHD diagnosis [36]. Whilst it may be possible that not all children would receive a full ADHD diagnosis, this mimics the real-world challenges of families on long waiting-lists and the importance of providing support to these families who reported similar emotional turmoil in managing their child's sleep problems. The families in this sample had a wide range of characteristics, including adoptive parents, same-sex parents, single versus two parent households, perceived sleep problem severity, age and child gender. However, it would have been relevant to include more fathers, families from ethnic minority backgrounds and parents/carers with more varied levels of education. Given the focus of our study on behavioural interventions and the need to limit the number of sampling/demographic questions, we did not gather information on children's medication status. 5. Conclusion Parents of children with ADHD are generally supportive of using behavioural sleep techniques for their child's CIS. However, they often perceive them as ineffective or challenging to implement. Parents require tailored, realistic but flexible and reassuring guidance. They welcome improved evidence-based digital support, while highlighting the importance of embedded validation and experiences from other parents in similar situations. S.J. Hornsey et al. metadata_title: Neurocognitive outcomes of ADHD as a comorbidity in pediatric epilepsy: a systematic review
pages: Neurocognitive outcomes of ADHD as a comorbidity in pediatric epilepsy: a systematic review Laura Zaffari Leal a , In ́acio Kehl a , Nat ́alia Donati Polesello a , Yolanda Aquino de Souza a , Catarina Hauser Schmitz a , Thiago Wendt Viola a,b , Magda Lahorgue Nunes a,b,* a Pontifícal Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul (PUCRS), School of Medicine, Porto Alegre, Brazil b Brain Institute of PUCRS (BraIns/InsCer), Porto Alegre, Brazil A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Epilepsy ADHD Cognition Pediatric Comorbidity A B S T R A C T Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common neuropsychiatric comorbidity in pediatric epi lepsy. Although the cognitive effects of epilepsy are well documented, the impact of ADHD as a comorbidity on neurocognitive outcomes remains unclear. This systematic review evaluates cognitive performance in pediatric patients with both epilepsy and ADHD. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searches were conducted in MED LINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Library and LILACS. Studies were included if they involved patients aged less than or equal to 18 years diagnosed with both epilepsy and ADHD. Fourteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Meth odological quality was assessed using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS), ROBINS-I and NIH/NHLBI tools. Re sults indicated that children with both epilepsy and ADHD exhibited more severe cognitive impairments than those with epilepsy only, ADHD only or healthy controls. These included lower Full-Scale and Verbal IQ scores and more frequent omission and commission errors, as well as increased reaction-time variability in attention tasks. Across studies, domains most affected included perceptual-motor function and executive function, as illustrated in a heat map summarizing the distribution and severity of cognitive impairments. These findings underscore that ADHD comorbidity in pediatric epilepsy is associated with exacerbated neurocognitive deficits, highlighting the need for early identification and tailored interventions to support cognitive development. 1. Introduction The epilepsies comprise a group of disorders defined by an enduring predisposition of the brain to generate epileptic seizures. Based on the 2017 IAE Classification, childhood-onset epilepsy syndromes are divided into three categories: self-limited focal epilepsies, generalized epilepsies, and developmental and/or epileptic encephalopathies. Epi lepsy is the most common pediatric neurological condition, affecting 0.5–1.0 % of children under 16 years of age [1–3]. This disease is associated with numerous neuropsychological comorbidities. Accordingly, cognitive impairment is frequently observed in children with epilepsy and may manifest early in the disease course or even precede the first recognized seizures [3]. Epilepsy often coexists with other neurological conditions, most notably attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), the most common neurobehavioral disorder in childhood. ADHD affects approx imately 8 % of the global pediatric population, and between 22.3 % and 30.7 % of children with epilepsy meet criteria for ADHD. Patients with ADHD exhibit inappropriate levels of inattention, hyperactivity, or impulsivity, which can compromise academic performance, well-being, and social interactions [4–8]. Research indicates that ADHD and epilepsy can have a genetic as sociation, since both are polygenetic disorders, characterized by a combination of common and rare genetic variants playing a role. Moreover, it has been identified that those diseases have associated gene loci and a study suggested a potential genetic basis between ADHD and Genetic Generalized Epilepsy. Notwithstanding, additional studies are needed to explain more about this phenomenon, but these shared ge netic and neurobiological factors might explain the overlapping cogni tive profiles observed in comorbid cases. [9,10]. The fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) classifies ADHD into three presentations: predomi nantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive/impulsive, and com bined. It also defines six key domains of cognitive function: perceptual- * Corresponding author at: Av. Ipiranga 6690, #69- InsCer, room 250.03, 90610-000 Porto Alegre, RS, Brazil. motor function, language, executive function, learning and memory, complex attention, and social cognition. Deficits in executive function, a neurocognitive process that supports goal-directed problem solving, may underline many ADHD symptoms, including impaired response inhibition, working-memory deficits, and broader executive-control weaknesses [11,12]. Epilepsy itself is also associated with cognitive impairment, as epileptic activity can contribute to severe intellectual or behavioral disabilities. A history of seizures and repeated episodes of status epi lepticus may induce progressive alterations in brain connectivity and cognitive decline over time. Moreover, interictal epileptiform discharges can produce transient cognitive impairment [13]. Despite these findings, the combined impact of epilepsy and ADHD on cognitive outcomes in pediatric patients remains unclear due to a paucity of neuropsychological research. This systematic review aims to evaluate cognitive performance in children with both epilepsy and ADHD, thereby informing management and treatment strategies to enhance patient well-being, given the critical role of cognitive function in quality of life, including learning abilities and social interactions. 2. Methods 2.1. Study design This systematic review was registered in PROSPERO (ID: CRD420251012631) and conducted according to the PRISMA 2020 guidelines [14]. The research question was structured using the PICO model (Population, Intervention, Comparator or Control, and Outcome) to ensure clarity and objectivity in defining eligibility criteria and in constructing the literature search strategy. Population (P) was defined as pediatric patients (aged less than or equal to 18 years of age) diagnosed with epilepsy; Intervention (I) as the presence of ADHD as a comor bidity; Comparator or Control (C) as pediatric patients with epilepsy without an ADHD diagnosis; and Outcome (O) as cognitive measures (e. g., performance on neuropsychological tests, IQ, executive functions, memory, attention). Studies not meeting these PICO criteria were excluded. 2.2. Search strategy and selection criteria Four databases (PubMed, Embase, LILACS, and the Cochrane Li brary) were searched for relevant studies published between January 1, 1985, and January 1, 2025, with the last search conducted on January 22, 2025. The search strategy combined descriptors such as “child,” “pediat rics,” “attention deficit disorders,” “ADHD,” “epilepsy,” and “cognitive outcomes,” using Boolean operators (AND/OR). The complete search strategies for each database, including search terms, fields, Boolean operators, filters, dates, and the number of duplicates removed, are available on Supplement. The search strategy was developed with the assistance of a librarian from our institution in collaboration with the review team to ensure transparency and reproducibility. Our inclusion criteria comprised studies including prospective and retrospective clinical studies (obser vational cohorts, cross-sectional and case-control designs), randomized and non-randomized clinical trials, and systematic reviews with meta- analyses. We excluded case reports, conference abstracts, editorials, animal model studies, studies involving participants older than 18 years, other clinical conditions affecting cognitive analysis, studies on epileptic encephalopathies, and studies that did not assess relevant cognitive outcomes. 2.3. Study selection Retrieved records were imported into the Rayyan platform (https://www.rayyan.ai) for screening and duplication. Duplicate studies were removed, and two reviewers (L.Z.L. and I.K.) independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text review. Selection was guided by the PICO framework and the predefined eligibility criteria. The discrepancies were solved by consensus between the reviewers (L.Z. L. and I.K.) followed by consultation with a third reviewer (N.D.P). A stage-by-stage breakdown of the screening and exclusion process, as well as a list of excluded full-text studies with reasons for exclusion, is available in Supplement. 2.4. Data extraction Data extraction from the selected studies was conducted using a spreadsheet on the Google Sheets platform. All extracted data were independently reviewed and verified by consensus between two re viewers (L.Z.L., I.K., C.H.S., Y.A.S.). The extracted information included study details (location, study design), number of participants, type of epilepsy, ADHD diagnostic criteria, ADHD subtypes, methods used for cognitive assessment, results, and conclusions. Only data from the selected studies published in the databases were included. Because pharmacological treatment, particularly with psychostimu lants such as methylphenidate, may significantly influence neuropsy chological outcomes, information regarding medication use was systematically extracted from each study. 2.5. Quality assessment The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using standardized tools according to study design. Cohort and cross- sectional studies were evaluated with the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS). Additionally, cohort and case–control studies were assessed using the ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized studies, whereas cross- sectional studies were evaluated using the NIH/NHLBI Quality Assess ment Tool. Inter-rater reliability for the ROBINS-I and NIH/NHLBI as sessments was calculated using Cohen’s kappa coefficient (κ), indicating moderate agreement between reviewers (κ = 0.50 for ROBINS-I; κ = 0.44 for NIH/NHLBI). To resolve discrepancies and reach a final deci sion, a senior author reviewed the items in question (M.L.N, T.W.V). 2.6. Outcome measures The primary outcomes evaluated in this review were cognitive and executive functions in pediatric patients with epilepsy and comorbid ADHD. Due to the wide range of assessment tools employed across the included studies, no restrictions were imposed on the instruments used. The evaluated domains encompassed cognition, attention, executive functioning, memory, language, behavior, development, emotional regulation, and academic performance. Given the heterogeneity of assessment methods and study designs, a qualitative synthesis of the findings was conducted. 2.7. Procedures for data synthesis To integrate cognitive outcomes across the included studies, a heat map was developed to visually represent the neuropsychological per formance profiles of the different clinical groups. Neuropsychological instruments that directly assessed cognitive performance were first identified, including the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC; WISC-R, WISC-III, WISC-IV), the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Sca le–Fourth Edition (WAIS-IV), and the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence (WASI). These instruments were used in 11 of the 14 studies included in the present review. The six cognitive domains defined by the DSM-5 (complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual–motor function, and social cognition) were mapped onto the corresponding subtests and indices of each instrument. This correspondence was established through structural analysis of each test and conceptual L.Z. Leal et al. Quantitative data (mean ± SD) were extracted for the clinical groups of interest: epilepsy with comorbid ADHD, epilepsy only, ADHD only, and healthy controls, when available. The study by Socanski et al. (2013) [15] was excluded from this step because it did not report quantitative test results. To ensure comparability across studies using different versions of Wechsler instruments, all results were converted into qualitative categories of cognitive performance according to the normative criteria described in the WISC-V Interpretive Report [16]. Subtest scores, expressed as scaled scores (mean = 10, SD = 3), and composite indices, expressed as standard scores (mean = 100, SD = 15), were converted into qualitative levels of cognitive functioning. Extremely low scores (≤4 or ≤69, respectively) were interpreted as indicating severe impairment; scores between 5 and 6 or 70–79 were classified as moderate impairment; scores between 7 and 8 or 80–89 corresponded to mild impairment; and scores equal to or greater than (9 or 90) were considered preserved. The qualitative synthesis design was chosen over meta-analysis due to heterogeneity in assessment tools and outcome reporting. 3. Results 3.1. Selection Out of the 860 articles found through database searches and exclu sion of duplicates, 739 articles were analyzed. The PRISMA 2020 flow diagram is presented in Fig. 1 and The PRISMA 2020 Checklist is available in the supplementary materials. Ultimately, 14 articles were included in this review. Quality assessment was not an exclusion crite rion but rather a variable that was evaluated. 3.2. Study characteristics The publication years ranged from 1999 to 2024. No articles pub lished in 2025 met the inclusion criteria at the time of the search. The studies originated from the United States [17–20], South Korea [21–23], Brazil [24,25], Turkey [26,27], Taiwan [28], and Norway [15]. Addi tionally, one study was a collaborative effort between Switzerland and Germany [29]. All included articles were cross-sectional, case-control, or cohort studies. A total of 2,332 participants aged between 8 and 18 years were analyzed, of whom 405 had a diagnosis of both epilepsy and ADHD. Regarding epilepsy subtypes, six studies did not specify the type of ep ilepsy, four included only one specific subtype, and five included more Fig. 1. PRISMA Flow Diagram of Study Selection. than one subtype. Notably, the study by Sung-Han Kang (2015) [23] was the only one to perform subgroup analyses based on epilepsy type, distinguishing between generalized and focal seizures. Most studies included all ADHD subtypes without conducting sub group analyses. Five studies focused on a single subtype, either the inattentive or the combined type. The studies by Çam Ray (2019) [27] and MacAllister (2012) [19] conducted ADHD subtype analyses specif ically in the results of the Stroop TBAG form. Regarding diagnostic criteria, 12 studies employed DSM, with only one using the third edition (DSM-III) instead of the fourth (DSM-IV). Among the remaining studies, one used the DSM-IV in combination with the SNAP-IV, another used the ADHD Rating Scale along with the ADS, and one relied on a pre-existing clinical diagnosis established prior to the study. The studies used various methods to assess cognitive function. Ex ecutive functions were most commonly evaluated using the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC) or Raven’s Progressive Matrices (RPM). In contrast, attention was assessed using more heterogeneous instruments, with the most frequently used being the Continuous Per formance Test (CPT), the Conners Rating Scale, and the Stroop TBAG form. Table 1 presents the characteristics of the included studies, such as identification, sample, country, Risk of Bias score (RoB), study design, age range, ADHD and Epilepsy subtypes, cognitive evaluation tools used and the main results. A summary of the main cognitive findings for the group of interest, children and adolescents with epilepsy and ADHD, is presented in Table 2. This table summarizes results from the nine studies that assessed DSM-5 cognitive domains using Wechsler-based instruments (WISC, WAIS-IV, or WASI). The certainty of the evidence for each outcome was evaluated using the GRADE approach. This Summary of Findings provides a concise overview of the Wechsler-based results and serves as a framework for the subsequent domain-specific analyses. The types of medications administered, the reported treatment sta tus, whether participants were under active medication at the time of cognitive testing, and whether the studies controlled for these effects in their analyses are summarized in Table 3. This information was used to identify and interpret potential confounding influences on cognitive performance outcomes. The risk of bias assessment for the included non-randomized studies, as evaluated with the ROBINS-I tool is provided on Fig. 2. The cognitive domains defined by the DSM-5 and the corresponding subtests and indices of each instrument were provided in Table 4. 3.3. Association between cognitive outcomes in patients with epilepsy and ADHD Executive function evaluation Although Costa (2015) [24] did not find significant results using Raven’s Progressive Matrices (RPM), in the study by Bechtel (2012) [29], the healthy control group performed significantly better in the 2- back task (p < 0.05) and the 3-back task (p = 0.057) compared to the epilepsy and ADHD group. Lee (2018) [22], Hermann (2007) [20], Hermann (2008) [18], and MacAllister (2012) [19] reported significant findings using the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC), indicating poorer performance among participants with both epilepsy and ADHD compared to other groups. In the Lee (2018) [22] study, patients with epilepsy and ADHD had lower Full-Scale IQ and Verbal IQ scores compared to those with epilepsy only (p = 0.014 and p = 0.011, respectively). Similarly, Mac Allister (2012) [19] found lower performance in IQ, verbal compre hension, intelligence, and reasoning scores in the epilepsy and ADHD group, regardless of ADHD subtype. Hermann (2007) [20] observed significantly lower scores in executive function, motor function, and parent-reported executive function in the epilepsy and ADHD group compared to the epilepsy-only and healthy control groups (all p-values < 0.001). Likewise, in Hermann (2008) [18], similar results were re ported, with significantly worse performance across all cognitive domains in the neurobehavioral comorbidity (ADHD and/or academic problems) group compared to the epilepsy-only and healthy control groups (all p-values < 0.0025), even after adjustment. In contrast, Socanski (2013) [15] did not find any significant differences in execu tive function based on WISC scores. Additionally, MacAllister (2012) [19] reported poorer performance in the epilepsy and ADHD groups on the Digit Span Forward Test compared to those with ADHD only. However, in the Digit Span Back ward Test, subgroup analysis by ADHD subtype revealed no differences between ADHD combined-type groups (p = 0.09). Attention evaluation A variety of scales were used to evaluate the attention domain. The Conners’ Continuous Performance Test (CPT) revealed poorer perfor mance among the epilepsy and ADHD group in the studies by Liu (2011) [28], Hermann (2008) [18], and Lima (2018) [25]. Liu (2011) [28] reported increased variation in reaction time, including slower Hit Re action Time, higher Hit Reaction Time Standard Error, and impaired vigilance based on higher scores in the Hit Reaction Time Inter-Stimulus Interval Change, compared to the epilepsy-only and healthy control groups. Similarly, Lima (2018) [25] found worse performance in CPT reaction time standard error (p = 0.008), CPT variability (p = 0.033), number of perseverations (p = 0.044), and interstimulus reaction time (p = 0.016) in the epilepsy and ADHD group. Differently, Hermann (2008) [18] analyzed group-by-time interaction for CPT omission (inattention) and commission (impulsivity) errors. While the healthy control and epilepsy-only groups showed decreased errors over time, reflecting improved performance, the epilepsy and comorbidity group showed a slight increase in errors (p = 0.03). Another frequently used scale was the Stroop TBAG form. In Çam Ray (2019) [27], the mean Stroop total error + correction (SEC) SEC-1 and SEC-3 scores in the ADHD and epilepsy group were significantly higher than those of the ADHD-only group (SEC-1: p = 0.012; SEC-3: p = 0.004). Among ADHD subtypes within the epilepsy group, the mean ST-3 and SEC-3 scores for the inattentive subtype were significantly higher than those for the combined subtype (p = 0.037 and p = 0.036, respectively). Moreover, mean SEC-1, SEC-2, and SEC-3 scores were higher in the epilepsy and ADHD-combined group compared to the ADHD-combined-only group (p = 0.016; p = 0.041; p = 0.024). Orak (2024) [26] reported similar findings, with significantly longer response times in Stroop 1 (p < 0.001), Stroop 2 (p < 0.001), Stroop 4 (p = 0.042), and total time (p = 0.012) in the epilepsy and ADHD group, suggesting impairments in sustained attention, inhibitory control, and impulsivity. Park (2021) [21] found significantly higher auditory commission error scores in the epilepsy and ADHD group on the Advanced Test of Attention (ATA) compared to the epilepsy-only group (p = 0.026). Significant differences in reaction time and reaction time variability were also observed between both groups and healthy controls (p = 0.008 and p = 0.028). In Lee (2018) [22], the Visual and Auditory ADHD Diagnostic System (ADS) also indicated higher auditory omission error scores in the epilepsy and ADHD group (p = 0.017). Sung-Han Kang (2015) [23] used the Comprehensive Attention Test (CAT) and found lower omission error scores on sustained attention (p = 0.050) and flanker tasks (p = 0.003), as well as lower forward and backward working memory scores in the spatial working memory task (p = 0.025 and p = 0.035, respectively) in patients with generalized seizures and ADHD compared to non-ADHD counterparts. In self limited Childhood Epilepsy with Centrotemporal Spikes (SeLECTs) patients, those with ADHD had higher auditory selection task commission error scores (p = 0.004) and higher omission error scores on sustained attention tasks (p = 0.039) compared to SeLECTs −only patients. In the study by Semrud-Clikeman (1999) [17], which included only patients with focal impaired awareness seizures (FIAS), the Test of Variables of Attention (TOVA) showed significantly poorer performance in all TOVA indices among the epilepsy and ADHD group (p = 0.01). Participants with Idiopathic Generalized Epilepsy (IGE) demonstrated lower scores in overall intellectual functioning (FSIQ = 89.0 ± 17.6) and nonverbal reasoning (PIQ = 88.9 ± 16.3) compared with those with Idiopathic Localization-Related Epilepsy (ILRE) (FSIQ = 96.3 ± 14.8; PIQ = 97.0 ± 16.4). These findings suggest that, even in the absence of ADHD comorbidity, the type of epilepsy itself may influence global cognitive performance. However, for the purpose of standardization in the heat map synthesis, the epilepsy-only group from this study was represented as having preserved domains, as the observed differences were restricted to a single epilepsy subtype, whereas the remaining subtypes assessed in the same study showed preserved values, and the degree of alteration was borderline. This clarification is provided here to ensure transparency and methodolog ical consistency in the interpretation of results. Taken together, this Wechsler-based synthesis provides a standard ized and integrated overview of the cognitive profiles across clinical groups, facilitating the visualization of domain-specific vulnerabilities and highlighting the consistent involvement of attentional and executive processes in pediatric epilepsy with comorbid ADHD. 3.4. Methodological notes and analytical limitations It is important to acknowledge several methodological limitations that may influence the interpretation of the synthesized cognitive findings. First, not all studies administered the Wechsler-based in struments to their entire participant samples, resulting in partial data availability across groups. Second, because each Wechsler scale com prises multiple subtests that capture distinct nuances within the same cognitive domain, occasional discrepancies were observed between subtest outcomes within a single domain. To ensure standardization in the heat map representation, any domain presenting at least one altered subtest was classified as impaired, and the level of alteration (mild, moderate, or severe) was determined by the most pronounced deficit observed. Third, only nine of the fourteen studies included in the sys tematic review were represented in the heat map, as only eleven employed the WISC, WAIS-IV, or WASI. Of these, two could not be standardized: the study by Socanski et al. did not provide numerical results for group comparisons, and Hermann et al. (2008) [18] reported only raw scores, precluding conversion to standardized values. Fourth, data for the epilepsy-only comparator group were available in eight studies, whereas only four studies provided data for the ADHD-only comparator group. These methodological constraints should be taken into account when interpreting the relative distribution and severity of cognitive impairments across the clinical groups represented in the heat map. 4. Discussion This study aimed to evaluate cognitive performance in pediatric patients with epilepsy and comorbid ADHD. Our systematic review indicated that children with both conditions exhibited more severe im pairments than those with epilepsy alone, ADHD alone, or healthy controls. These findings highlight that ADHD comorbidity in pediatric epilepsy is associated with greater neurocognitive deficits. Although the pathophysiological basis for the comorbidity between these two conditions remains unclear, their correlation is well estab lished. Some studies estimate a global prevalence of epilepsy in pediatric patients ranging from 0.5 % to 1 % [30]. For ADHD, an estimated prevalence of 8.0 % is reported among children and adolescents [5]. Among patients with epilepsy, the prevalence of ADHD may range from approximately 30.7 % to 49.2 % [6,23]. A degree of consistency can be observed in the results across studies included in this review. Nearly all articles found a significant cognitive impact in patients with both ADHD and epilepsy, although the severity and specific cognitive domains affected varied. For instance, Park et al. [21] demonstrated negative effects on inhibitory control, aggressive behavior, and parental stress. Orak et al. [26] reported greater impair ments in verbal intelligence and sustained attention. Kang et al. [23] found alterations in selective attention, flanker test results, spatial working memory, sustained attention, and interference, depending on the subtype of epilepsy (generalized vs. focal). These findings under score the importance of analyzing cognitive outcomes in relation to the epilepsy subtype when ADHD is present. Neuroimaging studies support these findings by identifying not only brain alterations associated with epilepsy alone, but also significantly intensified changes in the presence of ADHD. For example, Kim et al. [31] reported anatomical abnormalities in patients with SeLECTs, particularly in regions associated with executive function. Lima et al. [25] further showed that patients with both SeLECTs and ADHD exhibited increased cortical thickness in the left caudal anterior and posterior cingulate gyri, and greater volume in the left pars opercularis gyrus, compared to those without ADHD. These regions, which are functionally connected to the frontal lobe, are involved in executive functions such as working memory, decision-making, the limbic system, selective attention, inhibitory control, and verbal fluency. Collectively, these neuroimaging findings reinforce the notion that ADHD comor bidity exacerbates cognitive deficits in pediatric epilepsy. This review presents several limitations. First, despite an extensive search strategy, only a small number of articles met the inclusion criteria. Randomized clinical trials were not included, primarily due to the lack of eligible studies of this type. Most included studies had small sample sizes, which limited the evaluation of cognitive performance related to ADHD comorbidity across different epilepsy subtypes and may have impacted the robustness of the results. Also, although we did not perform a quantitative meta-analysis due to the heterogeneity of study designs, populations, and outcome measures across the included studies, the possibility of reporting bias cannot be excluded. We acknowledge that small-study effects and selective reporting may have influenced the available evidence, and these factors should be considered when inter preting the findings of this review. Nonetheless, a notable consistency in findings was observed. Most studies demonstrated a significant relationship between cognitive decline and the coexistence of ADHD and epilepsy. Two studies, how ever, did not report a statistically significant association between cognitive performance and the presence of both conditions. Socanski et al. and Costa et al. [15,24], both cross-sectional in design, found no significant differences in IQ among ADHD patients with and without epilepsy. Similarly, Bechtel et al. [29] reported that both the ADHD-only and ADHD + epilepsy groups performed comparably worse than con trols on high cognitive load tasks. A notable finding in this study was the significant improvement observed in both groups with the use of methylphenidate, suggesting that early pharmacological intervention may positively influence cognitive development. Given the substantial cognitive impact of this comorbidity, imple menting systematic screening for ADHD in all children with epilepsy becomes a necessary intervention. Based on expert consensus, screening should be performed for all children with epilepsy starting at age 6, or at the time of diagnosis if older, and repeated annually. The process can be initiated using validated ADHD rating scales administered to parents and teachers. Among the available tools, the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) is supported by Level B evidence for its ability to predict an ADHD diagnosis in this population. Other instruments, such as the Swanson, Nolan, and Pelham-IV (SNAP-IV) questionnaire, have also been used. A positive result on one of these screening tools should then lead to a comprehensive diagnostic evaluation by a qualified healthcare professional with expertise in ADHD, ensuring that children receive a timely and accurate diagnosis, which is the first step toward targeted therapeutic interventions. suggested a bidirectional relationship between ADHD and epilepsy, in which attentional and executive dysfunction may both precede and follow the onset of seizures. In this context, clinical vigilance is war ranted in children diagnosed with ADHD, particularly those with the inattentive subtype who present with paroxysmal events that could indicate seizure activity or who exhibit a poor or atypical response to stimulant medications [33]. This ADHD clinical profile suggests that further neurological evaluation and screening for epilepsy may be appropriate. In conclusion, this review supports a strong correlation between ADHD and epilepsy and suggests that the coexistence of both conditions is directly associated with poorer cognitive outcomes in pediatric pa tients when compared to those with only one of the conditions or healthy controls. Early identification is essential, as it enables timely intervention to support cognitive development and minimize long-term impacts on affected children. This finding raises important questions regarding the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying these cogni tive impairments, whether shared or distinct, and highlights the urgent need for further research to clarify this relationship, develop more effective treatments, and improve long-term outcomes for these patients. metadata_title: Validity of screening tools and risk factors for Co-occurring ADHD in children with epilepsy: a systematic review and meta-analysis
pages: Research Paper Validity of screening tools and risk factors for Co-occurring ADHD in children with epilepsy: a systematic review and meta-analysis Guang Ni , Dong Meng * Department of Neurology, The First Clinical Medical College, Gansu University of Chinese Medicine, Lanzhou, China School of Journalism and Communication, Shanghai Jian Qiao University, Shanghai, China A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: ADHD Epilepsy Children Screening tools Diagnostic accuracy Discriminant validity Risk factors Meta-analysis Antiepileptic drugs Seizure control A B S T R A C T Background: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder(ADHD)is the most common neuropsychiatric comorbidity in children with epilepsy and occurs at prevalence rates 2.5 to 5.5 times higher in children with epilepsy than the general population. To date,the largest comprehensive meta-analysis(46 studies)estimated the pooled ADHD prevalence among children with epilepsy to be almost one-third(30.7%),with a greater proportion of the inat tentive subtype.Children with epilepsy who also have ADHD have poorer seizure outcomes,lower quality of life, academic underachievement,and increased healthcare utilization.Despite being present in so many of them, ADHD frequently remains underdiagnosed in children with epilepsy because of symptom overlap,diagnostic complexity,and the lack of standardized screening protocols. In addition,both the validity of screening in struments and risk factors associated with comorbid ADHD need to be studied to develop ways to diagnose and treat ADHD in this vulnerable population. Objective: To assess the diagnostic accuracy and discriminant validity of ADHD screening tools for children with epilepsy and comorbid ADHD and to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis on the risk factors related to ADHD in children with epilepsy. Methods: We conducted this study according to the PRISMA guidelines(PROSPERO:CRD42018094617).A sys tematic search was performed on PubMed,Embase,PsycINFO,Cochrane Library,and Web of Science from inception until December 2023,based on the developed search strategies.The included studies were appraised for quality using three different approaches according to the three-layer analytical framework,in which diagnostic accuracy of a single instrument(Layer 1)was assessed using QUADAS-2,discriminant validity(Layer 2)was analyzed with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale,and risk factor/prevalence evidence synthesis(Layer 3)was synthe sized narratively.Meta-analyses were carried out using the DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models,and het erogeneity assessment was conducted. Results: Twelve studies met inclusion criteria for qualitative synthesis.Diagnostic accuracy(Layer 1):The SDQ- Hyperactivity subscale had the highest diagnostic accuracy(sensitivity 86.4%,specificity 97.8%,Youden index 0.84,DOR = 285).Discriminant validity(Layer 2):The overall pooled effect size was g = 0.27(95%CI:0.17–0.38) and the externalizing behavior measures showed the highest discriminant validity(g = 0.54).Risk factor evidence was narratively synthesized. In studies which reported extractable association estimates,earlier seizure onset, neurodevelopmental/cognitive vulnerabilities(executive dysfunction,developmental coordination disorder),male sex,medical comorbidities,or higher antiepileptic drug burden were associated with an increased risk of co morbid ADHD. Conclusions: The SDQ-Hyperactivity subscale demonstrates superior diagnostic accuracy for ADHD screening in children with epilepsy,supporting current ILAE recommendations.Externalizing behavior measures,particularly the DBD rating scale(g = 0.60),show the strongest discriminant validity.Children with poorly controlled seizures, early onset epilepsy and those receiving polytherapy warrant heightened screening vigilance.Implementation of systematic ADHD screening targeting high-risk subgroups may substantially improve early identification and intervention outcomes. * Corresponding author at: School of Journalism and Communication, Shanghai Jian Qiao University, China. 1. Introduction 1.1. Epidemiology and clinical significance Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder(ADHD)and epilepsy are among the most common neurodevelopmental disorders in childhood. Studies suggest that ADHD is overrepresented among children with epi lepsy compared with control groups,with prevalence estimates ranging from 12%to 40%according to specific study populations, diagnostic criteria,and methodologies used [1].The pooled prevalence of ADHD in children with epilepsy across all studies was reported by He et al. [2] (n = 46 studies,various populations):30.7%(95%CI:26.4–35.3%)—threefold to fivefold higher than in the general pediatric population,where ADHD affects approximately 5–7%of children.Unlike the general ADHD popu lation,the predominantly inattentive subtype appears to be predominant among children with epilepsy. Not only do we have to consider the impact of each condition separately,but also the combined effect on the child from all points of view:academic,social,emotional,and quality of life [3]. Population- based studies confirm the wide distribution of neurobehavioural comorbidities in epileptic children [4]. Children with epilepsy and ADHD have more severe symptoms than children with one disorder only.Epilepsy in ADHD patients is associated with worse seizure control, higher health-care utilization,higher polypharmacy,and lower compli ance [5]. Comorbid ADHD imposes a high economic burden on children with epilepsy,where both higher direct medical costs(more emergency department visits,hospitalizations,and specialist consultations)and higher indirect costs(more parental work loss,educational support ser vices,and long-term productivity impairment)have been reported for comorbid ADHD in children with epilepsy.Therefore,early identification and appropriate treatment of ADHD should be considered as a clinical priority and a public health consideration,because of the potential cost savings. Comorbid ADHD may be associated with poorer educational out comes(i.e.,lower academic achievement, more grade retention, and greater likelihood of receiving special education services)than children with epilepsy alone.Children with comorbid ADHD have been shown to have worse social functioning(peers'rejection,less friendships,and higher rates of bullying victimization).Parents of children with comor bid ADHD reported worse family functioning(parents'greater stress, depression,and marital conflict).Overall,comorbid ADHD affects all as pects of child functioning,and therefore requires early identification and comprehensive intervention in order to reduce its impact on child and family well-being. However,despite this substantial burden of illness,ADHD remains consistently underdiagnosed in epilepsy populations because of many reasons.The similarity between symptoms of ADHD and epilepsy-related symptoms causes considerable diagnostic confusion,as attention symp toms can be due to different causes(active seizures;postictal state;sub clinical interictal epileptiform discharges;adverse effects of antiepileptic drugs;structural brain abnormalities;and/or independent ADHD) [6]. Health care providers might consider behavior and attention problems as consequences of epilepsy and not recognize them as being associated with a different comorbidity that needs to be addressed separately;this phenomenon,known as diagnostic overshadowing,leads to a missed opportunity to treat a highly treatable disorder,resulting in ongoing disability that would not have been present had the problem been identified earlier and treated. 1.2. Pathophysiological mechanisms Although the pathophysiology for the association between epilepsy and ADHD has yet to be fully understood,there are many possible mechanisms.Uliel-Sibony et al. [7] summarized these into four broad categories:(a)shared genetic vulnerabilities;(b)common neuroanatom ical substrates involving frontal-subcortical circuits;(c)direct effects of seizures on developing attention networks;and(d)neurocognitive effects of antiepileptic medications.The bidirectional relationship is further supported by findings that ADHD symptoms usually precede epilepsy onset,and that children with ADHD have a 2-to 4-fold higher risk of later developing epilepsy than the general population [8]. Neuroanatomical studies with quantitative magnetic resonance im aging have revealed structural abnormalities shared by the two disor ders.Hermann et al.found that children with comorbid epilepsy and ADHD had significantly increased gray matter volume distributed across areas of the frontal lobe,and reduced brainstem volume compared with controls.These results indicate that neurodevelopmental processes of cortical pruning and progressive myelination may be attenuated or static in affected individuals,and persisting morphometric abnormalities occur.Volumetric changes probably reflect anatomical correlates of frontal lobe dysfunction,involved in the executive functions that are characteristically impaired in both conditions. The prefrontal cortex,pre-supplementary motor area,and inferior frontal gyrus play crucial roles in executive functions including inhibi tion control,working memory,and cognitive flexibility.Studies exam ining children with frontal lobe epilepsy have consistently documented prominent executive function deficits,including impaired planning,poor impulse control,and difficulties with motor coordination that appear closely related to behavioral adaptation challenges.Culhane-Shelburne and colleagues demonstrated that children with frontal lobe epilepsy exhibit a distinct neuropsychological profile characterized by intact verbal and nonverbal memory but significant deficits in planning and executive functions,contrasting with the memory impairment pattern observed in temporal lobe epilepsy [9]. The high prevalence of ADHD in patients with frontal lobe epilepsy may reflect direct dysregulation of these frontal lobe networks. Interictal epileptiform discharges(IEDs)represent another important pathophysiological mechanism.IEDs specifically over the frontal lobe have been implicated in the pathophysiology of comorbid ADHD and epilepsy.The most compelling evidence linking IEDs to attention and behavioral dysfunction comes from studies of self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes,where patients with minimal seizure burden and no medication requirement demonstrate cognitive and behavioral im pairments proportional to their nocturnal IED burden.This observation suggests that subclinical epileptiform activity can independently contribute to attention dysfunction beyond the effects of clinical seizures [10]. Genetic epidemiological studies have provided additional evidence for shared etiology.A large Swedish population-based cohort study examining familial aggregation found that individuals with epilepsy had a significantly increased risk of ADHD(OR = 3.47,95%CI:3.33–3.62), with the association extending to relatives,suggesting shared genetic liability [11].Quantitative genetic modeling estimated that approxi mately 40%of the correlation between epilepsy and ADHD could be attributed to shared genetic factors,while the remaining variance was explained by non-shared environmental influences potentially including pregnancy-related complications and preterm birth.Candidate gene studies have identified several potential shared genetic variants,though genome-wide association studies specifically examining the epilepsy- ADHD comorbidity remain limited. Neurotransmitter systems(dopaminergic/noradrenergic pathways) are thought to be involved in both disorders.The catecholamine hy pothesis of ADHD states that ADHD is due to a dysregulation of dopa mine and/or norepinephrine signaling within the prefrontal circuits mediating attention and/or executive function deficits.Intriguingly, epileptogenic processes may also affect the same neurotransmitter sys tems,either directly(through epileptogenic processes),or indirectly G. (resulting from epileptogenic processes;neuronal injury,receptor expression,medication effects).Thus,the overlap in catecholaminergic systems provides an interesting possibility for understanding how both disorders could arise via common mechanisms,and identify new thera peutic targets for each one. 1.3. Risk factors for comorbid ADHD Knowing the risk factors of comorbid ADHD among children with epilepsy is also relevant from a clinical point of view since it can help to better focus screening efforts and develop effective preventive strate gies.Various epilepsy-related,but also non-epilepsy-related,factors have been reported in different epidemiological studies,although not all equally robustly supported by the available literature. Poor seizure control is one of the most consistently identified risk factors.Poor seizure control is a significant risk factor for ADHD, regardless of epilepsy classification or seizure localization,and regard less of whether it is generalized or focal.For example,McCusker et al. found that out of 48 families of children with refractory epilepsy,the children who had the worst behavior problems had the most problems with attention and hyperactivity [12]. A study involving 75 children with epilepsy found that compared to children with less frequent sei zures,children with weekly seizures were seen by their parents as having significantly more hyperactivity symptoms,and this was seen in a dos e–response manner–the more seizures per week,the more severe the ADHD symptoms [13]. This finding has been replicated in studies from different countries,such as China [14]. A younger age of onset of epilepsy can also be seen as another neu rodevelopmental risk factor:seizures occurring during critical periods of brain maturation may disrupt the normal development of attentional networks and executive function pathways;because the infant brain is both more fragile than the adult brain to insults from epileptiform dis charges,and also more plastic,this could result in maladaptive reorga nization of attention-related cerebral networks.However,findings are controversial concerning whether a younger age of seizure onset results in higher rates of ADHD diagnosis,as some studies failed to find asso ciations once adjusting for other epilepsy-related variables.The site of the epileptogenic zone may play a role as well—frontal lobe epilepsy,in some cases,has been linked to less severe ADHD symptoms.One model to explain why people with epilepsy are at higher risk for psychiatric comorbidities is deficient executive control [15]; given the importance of frontal brain areas for attentional and executive functions,several studies have suggested a possible connection between younger age of seizure onset and higher risk of ADHD. For example,children with epilepsy who also have intellectual disability are at higher risk for ADHD;intellectual disability is consid ered a Grade A,evidence-based risk factor for ADHD prevalence among children with epilepsy.Intellectual disability could be considered a compound vulnerability with epilepsy and might indicate that there are common neurodevelopmental etiologies affecting the cognitive and attentional systems.Children with epileptic encephalopathies and developmental epilepsies may be especially at risk because of the severe and early-onset nature of their seizure disorders and high rates of accompanying neurodevelopmental impairment. Family history of ADHD represents a non-epilepsy-related risk factor that should be assessed in clinical evaluation.Given the substantial ge netic component to ADHD susceptibility,children with first-degree rel atives affected by ADHD are at increased risk regardless of their epilepsy status.The combination of familial ADHD risk and epilepsy-related risk factors may result in particularly high vulnerability in some children. Assessment of family psychiatric history should be incorporated into routine evaluation of children with epilepsy. Anti-epileptic drug therapy is an important modifiable risk factor with major clinical consequences.All commonly used anti-epileptic drugs have some impact on cognitive function;this may be consider able,especially when core cognitive functions(attention,learning)are considered [16]. Phenobarbitone is at highest risk of serious cognitive effects that affect attention and memory,and both randomized placebo- controlled and observational studies have shown IQ decline with treat ment and persistent effects on educational performance several years after withdrawal [17]. Topiramate has clear evidence for cognitive impairment affecting attention,memory,and language skills in both adults and children.Lamotrigine has reported evidence of pro-cognitive effects on attention,whereas levetiracetam has been described as being relatively neutral on cognition.Multiple drug therapy is associated with significantly more cognitive impairment compared to monotherapy, irrespective of the specific drugs involved.The ILAE Task Force on Cognition and Epilepsy has highlighted the need to take into account cognitive side effects when deciding on which anti-epileptic to pre scribe,especially in children where there are pre-existing attention difficulties. 1.4. Screening tools and study Objectives Several standardized screening instruments have been developed and validated for ADHD detection in general pediatric populations, though their performance characteristics in children with epilepsy require specific validation given the unique diagnostic challenges in this population.The Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire(SDQ)is a brief 25-item measure widely used internationally to assess child and adolescent mental health problems,including a 5-item hyperactivity- inattention subscale [18]. Japanese validation studies have demon strated its utility for ADHD screening in children with epilepsy [19]. The ILAE Task Force has recommended SDQ as a screening tool for ADHD in children with epilepsy based on Level B evidence [20]. In general pop ulation studies,the SDQ hyperactivity subscale has demonstrated area under the curve values of 0.91–0.95,suggesting excellent discrimination between children with and without ADHD. The Child Behavior Checklist(CBCL)represents another widely used parent-report measure incorporating an Attention Problems scale and DSM-oriented ADHD subscale [21]. Research in general populations indicates the CBCL Attention Problems scale can identify 71–84%of in dividuals with ADHD.Chen and colleagues examined CBCL diagnostic accuracy using receiver-operating characteristic analysis,demonstrating that the Attention Problems scale had the highest discriminating power for ADHD among CBCL subscales [22]. Brazilian studies combining multiple rating scales have shown the value of multi-informant ap proaches [23]. The validity of the CBCL has been specifically examined in children with epilepsy [24]. A Swedish validation study reported 81% sensitivity and 70%specificity for the CBCL ADHD subscale against LEAD diagnoses [25]. The CBCL offers the advantage of comprehensive behavioral assessment across multiple domains but requires more administration time than briefer screening instruments.Additionally,the extensive normative data available for the CBCL across diverse pop ulations supports its use in varied clinical settings. Because ADHD is prevalent among children with epilepsy,it may be clinically important for ADHD to be correctly identified;however,it is unclear whether there are effective screening approaches to do so.We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis with a three-layer analytical framework.In Layer 1 we assessed diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity,specificity,likelihood ratios,diagnostic odds ratios) compared with gold-standard clinical diagnosis.In Layer 2 we evaluated discriminant validity using standardized effect sizes to determine which behavioral constructs and instruments can best discriminate between children with comorbid epilepsy and ADHD and those with epilepsy alone.We also systematically investigated the risk factors associated with comorbid ADHD to facilitate future targeted screening strategies.In Layer 3,risk factor/prevalence evidence was synthesized narratively. 2. Methods 2.1. Protocol and Registration This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accor dance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses(PRISMA)guidelines. The protocol was prospectively registered with PROSPERO(CRD42018094617)prior to initiation of database searches. Any deviations from the registered protocol are documented and justified in this report. 2.2. Search Strategy and study selection We conducted systematic searches of PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science from database inception through December 31, 2023. Search strategies combined controlled vocabulary terms (MeSH, Emtree) and free-text keywords relating to four concep tual domains: (1) epilepsy (epilepsy, seizure, convuls, anticonvulsant, antiepileptic); (2) ADHD (attention deficit, hyperactiv, ADHD, ADD, hyperkinetic); (3) pediatric population (child, pediatric, adolescent, youth, infant*); and (4) screening/diagnostic accuracy (screen*, diag nos, sensitivity, specificity, valid, accuracy, ROC, receiver operating). Boolean operators were used to combine search terms within and be tween domains. No language restrictions were applied. Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were manually searched to identify additional potentially eligible studies. Studies were included if they met all of the following criteria:(1) enrolled children and adolescents aged 4–19 years with a diagnosis of epilepsy confirmed by clinical criteria;(2)evaluated diagnostic accuracy or discriminant validity of at least one standardized ADHD screening instrument;(3)used clinical diagnosis based on DSM or ICD criteria as the reference standard; and(4)reported sufficient data to calculate diagnostic accuracy metrics or standardized effect sizes. Studies were excluded if they enrolled fewer than 10 participants per group, focused exclusively on populations with severe intellectual disability precluding standardized assessment, used screening instruments rather than clin ical diagnosis as the reference standard, or were published only as conference abstracts without full methodology available. Two reviewers(initials blinded)independently screened titles,ab stracts,and full texts using predefined eligibility criteria.Disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus,with a third reviewer consulted when necessary.Inter-rater reliability was calculated using Cohen's kappa statistic.Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers using standardized forms piloted on a subset of studies. Extracted data included study characteristics(design,setting,country, year),participant characteristics(sample size,age,sex distribution,epi lepsy type,ADHD prevalence),screening instrument details(name, version,informant,cutoff values), reference standard details,and outcome data [26] (true positives, false positives, true negatives, false negatives, or group means and standard deviations). 2.3. Quality assessment For Layer 1 diagnostic accuracy studies,we employed QUADAS-2 (Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies,version 2),evalu ating risk of bias across four domains:patient selection(consecutive or random sampling,appropriate exclusions),index test(prespecified cutoff, blinding to reference standard),reference standard(appropriate diag nostic criteria,blinding to index test),and flow and timing(appropriate interval,all patients received reference standard).Applicability concerns were assessed for patient selection,index test,and reference standard domains.Each domain was rated as low,high,or unclear risk of bias based on signaling questions specified in the QUADAS-2 framework. For Layer 2 discriminant validity studies comparing groups with and without comorbid ADHD,we employed the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS),evaluating selection(representativeness,selection of non- exposed,ascertainment of exposure),comparability(control for con founders),and outcome assessment(assessment method,follow-up). Studies scoring ≥7 of 9 stars were considered high quality,5–6 stars moderate quality,and < 5 stars low quality.Two reviewers indepen dently assessed quality for all included studies,with disagreements resolved through discussion.Interrater agreement for quality assessment was substantial(κ = 0.82). 2.4. Statistical analysis We applied a three-layer analytical framework to accommodate heterogeneous outcome reporting across studies.Layer 1 evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of ADHD screening tools against a clinical reference standard(2 × 2 data;sensitivity/specificity and related indices).Layer 2 assessed discriminant validity by pooling standardized effect sizes (Hedges'g)comparing children with epilepsy + ADHD versus epilepsy without ADHD across behavioral measures.Layer 3 synthesized epide miological and clinical risk factor/prevalence evidence narratively when comparable effect estimates were not available for meta-analysis. For Layer 1 diagnostic accuracy analysis,sensitivity,specificity,posi tive likelihood ratio(LR + ),negative likelihood ratio(LR − ),and diag nostic odds ratio(DOR)were calculated for the screening tool at each reported cutoff value.Youden's index(J = sensitivity + specificity − 1) was used as a summary statistic for the discriminatory ability of the screening tool;the larger this number,the better the discrimination. Confidence intervals(95%)were calculated with the exact binomial method.When studies presented more than one cutoff,we included the cutoff with the highest Youden’s index,or the author-recommended cutoff. Layer 2 discriminant validity analysis was performed by calculating standardized mean differences as Hedges'g(small-sample bias correction to Cohen's d),and pooling effect sizes in DerSimonian-Laird random-ef fects models that incorporated both within-study sampling error and between-study heterogeneity.Given anticipated clinical and methodo logical heterogeneity among studies,we chose to use a random-effects approach a priori.Heterogeneity was evaluated with Cochran's Q sta tistic(significance threshold = p < 0.10),and heterogeneity magnitude was gauged via I2statistics(<25%,25–75%,and > 75%corresponding to low,moderate,and high heterogeneity).The between-study variance component(τ2)was estimated using the DerSimonian-Laird method. Subgroup analyses were performed to explore potential sources of heterogeneity by behavioral construct(externalizing behaviors,inter nalizing symptoms,attention problems,sleep disturbances)and screening instrument(CBCL,SDQ,DBD) [27]. We intended to conduct a meta- regression analysis to examine the relationship between effect sizes and continuous moderators,but we did not do so because there were too few studies included.Publication bias was assessed through examination of funnel plot asymmetry,Egger’s regression test,and Begg’s rank correla tion test with significance level set at p < 0.10.The trim-and-fill method was applied as an exploratory analysis.Sensitivity analyses were carried out to determine the impact of one study on the combined results using leave-one-out analysis.All analyses were performed using R version 4.5.1,with meta,mada,and metafor packages. Diagnostic accuracy analysis was performed by constructing 2 × 2 contingency tables using reported numbers or calculating them through provided sensitivity,specificity,and sample size;selecting the cutoff value with the highest Youden's index when several cutoffs were pre sented for one instrument,or choosing the cutoff suggested by the manufacturer;drawing ROC space plots to show the diagnostic efficiency of various screening tools at once,where the best result would be located at the upper-left corner of the graph. Risk of bias was evaluated separately for each analytical layer.For the overall body of evidence,we conducted sensitivity analyses to assess the possible impact of study quality on pooled estimates after removing studies at high risk of bias.Strength of evidence was determined ac cording to the number of studies,sample size,consistency of findings G.
