Study selection and characteristics The systematic search identified 847 records across the five data bases searched.After removing 156 duplicates,691 unique records un derwent title and abstract screening,of which 67 were selected for full- text review.Following detailed eligibility assessment,12 studies met in clusion criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis(Fig. 1). Two studies contributed diagnostic accuracy data suitable for Layer 1 analysis,and one study provided discriminant validity data for Layer 2 meta-analysis,with Park et al.(2021).Inter-rater reliability for study se lection was excellent(κ = 0.89).The most common reasons for exclusion at full-text review were:absence of standardized screening instrument(n = 18),absence of clinical reference standard for ADHD diagnosis(n = 14),insufficient data for effect size calculation(n = 9),study population outside target age range(n = 8),and publication as abstract only without full methodology(n = 5).The remaining studies contributed to Layer 3 (risk factor/prevalence)narrative synthesis. Study characteristics are summarized in Table 1.The 12 included studies were published between 2008 and 2021,with sample sizes ranging from 22 to 206 participants per study.Geographic distribution encompassed United Kingdom(n = 1),Republic of Korea(n = 1),India(n = 1),Brazil(n = 1),Norway(n = 1),Japan(n = 1),Hong Kong(n = 1),USA (n = 1),Germany(n = 2),Egypt(n = 1),and China(n = 1).Participant ages ranged from 4 to 19 years across studies.Epilepsy types included generalized epilepsy,focal epilepsy,absence epilepsy,and mixed pop ulations.Reported ADHD prevalence ranged from 22.6%to 65% (Table 1),with several studies not reporting prevalence.The most frequently evaluated screening instruments included CBCL and SDQ, along with other scales such as SNAP-IV,SWAN,DBD,and EpiTrack Junior. Study designs included cross-sectional studies(n = 7),case-control studies(n = 2),prospective studies(n = 2),and longitudinal study(n = 1). Reference standards for ADHD diagnosis varied,with most studies using clinical interview by child psychiatrist or pediatric neurologist based on DSM-IV(n = 7)or DSM-5(n = 3)criteria.Several studies utilized semi- structured diagnostic interviews including the K-SADS-PL.Screening instruments were administered primarily by parents,though some studies also incorporated teacher-report measures. 3.2. Layer 1:Diagnostic accuracy analysis Two studies(Loutfi 2011,Tanabe 2014;total n = 98)evaluated diag nostic accuracy of ADHD screening tools against clinical diagnosis as the reference standard.Quality assessment using QUADAS-2 indicated generally low risk of bias across domains,though concerns regarding patient selection(consecutive vs.convenience sampling)and index test interpretation(prespecification of cutoffs)were noted in some studies. One study demonstrated unclear risk of bias for flow and timing due to incomplete reporting of the interval between index test and reference standard assessment.Applicability concerns were generally low,with study populations and index test implementation representative of typical clinical settings.All studies employed appropriate reference standards with clinical diagnosis by experienced clinicians using stan dardized criteria.The QUADAS-2 risk of bias assessment and Newcastle- Ottawa Scale quality evaluation are presented in Fig. 2. Diagnostic ac curacy metrics for the four evaluated screening instruments are pre sented in Table 2 and visualized in Fig. 3. The SDQ-Hyperactivity subscale had the best overall diagnostic ac curacy,with sensitivity of 86.4%(95%CI:72.6–94.8%),specificity of 97.8%(95%CI:88.5–99.9%),and Youden index of 0.84.A positive likeli hood ratio of 39.3 means that a positive SDQ result greatly increases the probability of ADHD diagnosis,whereas the negative likelihood ratio of 0.14 means that a negative SDQ result greatly lowers ADHD probability. The diagnostic odds ratio of 285(95%CI:31.2–2604.5)demonstrates excellent overall discriminatory power,consistent with ILAE Level B recommendations for SDQ use in epilepsy populations.The high speci ficity of the SDQ is especially important for epilepsy populations, because false positive results could cause overdiagnosis and over treatment of ADHD in children who have attention problems related to epilepsy instead of ADHD. Second highest was the MTA-SNAP-IV(sensitivity of 81.3%,95% CI:54.4–96.0%;specificity of 92.9%,95%CI:76.5–99.1%;Youden index of 0.74;diagnostic odds ratio of 56.3,95%CI:8.9–355.7).Although retaining good specificity,the slightly lower sensitivity relative to the SDQ might lead to under-screening.Wider confidence intervals for this measure reflect its relatively small sample size.Third highest was the CBCL Attention Problems scale(sensitivity of 87.5%,95%CI:61.7–98.4%; specificity of 78.6%,95%CI:59.0–91.7%;Youden index of 0.66;diag nostic odds ratio of 25.7,95%CI:4.3–152.9).A high sensitivity/low specificity profile,like this one,indicates that the CBCL could serve well as a“rule-out”rather than a confirmatory test:negative results are likely to identify children who do not have ADHD,but positive findings still warrant further assessment. In contrast,the Teacher Report Form(TRF)showed a different profile, with specificity(100%)and sensitivity of only 50%(95%CI:24.7–75.3%). With such specificity,a positive TRF is very likely to be an ADHD diag nosis.However,its poor sensitivity makes it unsuitable as a stand-alone screen due to its failure to identify half of the cases.Parental-teacher discrepancies could be explained by the difference in symptom presen tation according to context;ADHD is more likely to emerge in the classroom environment since it is more regulated than home.Using multiple informant instruments(parent and teacher report)can lead to better detection. For ease of comparing diagnostic performance,we plotted each tool on the ROC space(Fig. 4).The closer a point is to the upper left corner,the higher both sensitivity and specificity are.Due to the small number of diagnostic accuracy studies and tools,the figure is descriptive and should be interpreted with caution. 3.3. Layer 2:Discriminant validity analysis Park 2021:Extensive data on discriminant validity analysis were available(33 children with epilepsy and comorbid ADHD vs.113 chil dren with epilepsy without ADHD,21 behavioral and psychosocial measures;total n = 146).Quality assessment(NOS)was rated as high quality(7/9 stars:appropriate selection,comparability,robust outcome assessment[validated instruments,trained assessors]). Overall,the pooled effect size across all 21 measures was g = 0.27 (95%CI:0.17–0.38,p < 0.001),showing a small discrimination between children with and without comorbid ADHD(Fig. 5).There was low to moderate heterogeneity(I2 = 33%,Q = 29.70,p = 0.075)and a small between-study variance component(τ2 = 0.02),which suggest that most of the variability might be due to sampling error rather than differences in behavior across studies.A funnel plot–based assessment suggested potential asymmetries;however,this should be interpreted cautiously as effect sizes from multiple measures within a study violate independence assumptions of such test.Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis supported these results(Section 3.4). Subgroup analysis according to behavioral construct and tool also showed clinically important differences in discriminant capacity(see Table 3).The best evidence of discrimination between groups was found in externalizing behavior measures,with a pooled effect size of g = 0.54 (95%CI:0.36–0.71,p < 0.001,I2 = 0%).Within this domain,the DBD (Disruptive Behavior Disorders)rating scale had the largest pooled effect (g = 0.60,95%CI:0.33–0.88,p < 0.001,I2 = 0%).Therefore,this is the most relevant finding from a clinical point of view,since it indicates that externalizing behavior measures are the best candidates for ADHD identification in epilepsy populations. Sensitivity analysis A leave-one-out sensitivity analysis was performed to check the impact of a single effect size on the pooled estimate for discriminant validity(Fig. 6).It showed that none of the effect sizes had an excessive influence on the pooled estimate.When each effect size was left out one by one,the recomputed pooled estimates varied from g = 0.253(95% CI:0.153–0.353)to g = 0.299(95%CI:0.206–0.393).All were statistically significant and within the confidence interval of the pooled estimate(g = 0.273;95%CI:0.170–0.377).The pooled estimate with the lowest value occurred upon removal of the Conduct Disorder subscale(g = 0.253), whereas removal of the Sleep-Disordered Breathing subscale produced the highest value(g = 0.299). These findings demonstrate the robustness of the discriminant val idity results,indicating that the overall conclusion regarding small discrimination between children with and without comorbid ADHD is not dependent on any single behavioral measure.The consistency of results across leave-one-out iterations provides confidence in the stability of the meta-analytic findings and supports the validity of the pooled effect size estimate. 3.5. Risk factor analysis Three studies included in the qualitative synthesis reported extract able association estimates(e.g.,OR/aOR with corresponding confidence intervals)for risk factors associated with comorbid ADHD in children with epilepsy.Due to heterogeneity in risk factor definitions and effect measures across studies,results were synthesized narratively rather than pooled quantitatively(Table 4). Epilepsy-related factors:Early seizure onset emerged as a consistent predictor of comorbid ADHD.Alfstad et al.found that each one-year in crease in age at seizure onset was associated with a 14%reduced risk of comorbid ADHD(OR = 0.86,95%CI:0.77–0.96,p = 0.01)after adjusting for executive dysfunction and gender.Similarly,Kwong et al.reported that younger age at seizure onset significantly increased ADHD risk(OR = 0.70 per year increase,95%CI:0.58–0.83).Polytherapy with antisei zure medications was identified as an independent risk factor for the ADHD-Hyperactivity/Impulsivity subtype by Kwong et al.(aOR = 6.22,95%CI:1.26–30.64,p = 0.025)after controlling for medical comorbidities and age at seizure onset. Cognitive and neurodevelopmental factors:Executive dysfunction was the strongest independent predictor of comorbid ADHD in the study by Alfstad et al.(OR = 8.20,95%CI:1.80–37.20,p = 0.006).Develop mental coordination disorder(DCD)was significantly associated with ADHD in the multivariable analysis by Reilly et al.(aOR = 4.52,95% CI:1.32–15.46,p = 0.02),suggesting that neurodevelopmental comor bidities cluster together in children with epilepsy. Demographic factors and comorbidities:Male sex was an indepen dent risk factor for comorbid ADHD(OR = 2.90,95%CI:1.20–7.30,p = 0.02)in the multivariable analysis by Alfstad et al..Medical comorbid ities showed consistent association with ADHD risk across multiple an alyses by Kwong et al.,with univariable odds ratios ranging from 11.23 to 12.82,and remained significant after adjustment for age at seizure onset(aOR = 8.00,95%CI:1.73–37.00,p = 0.008). Discussion 4.1. Summary of Main findings This is the first systematic review and meta-analysis to provide a first comprehensive evaluation of the ADHD screening tools for children with epilepsy under the guidance of a rigorous three-layer analytical frame work,accompanied by a systematic examination of the risk factors of comorbid ADHD.The results of this study have generated some clinically important conclusions which may contribute to the design of screening programs and targeted clinical assessment strategies. First,compared to the other two tests,the SDQ-Hyperactivity subscale has the best diagnostic accuracy for ADHD screening in children with epilepsy,with a Youden index of 0.84 and diagnostic odds ratio of 285, which indicates good discriminatory ability.In other words,the SDQ- Hyperactivity subscale is consistent with the ILAE Level B recommendations for screening ADHD in children with epilepsy [28]. The SDQ-Hyperactivity subscale has both high sensitivity(86.4%)and very high specificity(97.8%).Therefore,it has the greatest potential for screening tests where identifying cases and minimizing false positives are equally important [28]. Second,externalizing behavior measures provide the strongest discriminant validity for identifying comorbid ADHD,with the DBD rating scale achieving the largest effect size(g = 0.60).This finding has important implications for clinical assessment protocols,suggesting that screening efforts should prioritize evaluation of hyperactive-impulsive, oppositional,and conduct-related behaviors rather than internalizing symptoms or sleep disturbances when attempting to identify comorbid ADHD in children with epilepsy. Third,our narrative synthesis of risk factor evidence(Table 4)in dicates that earlier seizure onset,neurodevelopmental/cognitive vul nerabilities(i.e.,executive dysfunction,developmental coordination disorder),male sex,medical comorbidities,and higher antiepileptic drug burden might increase the risk of comorbid ADHD.However,due to the small number of studies reporting adjusted estimates and heterogeneity in definitions,these results must be taken with caution. Fourth,the overall discriminant validity analysis revealed a pooled effect size of g = 0.27 across behavioral measures,indicating that Fig. 4. The strong discriminant validity of externalizing behavior measures aligns with the clinical presentation of ADHD,where hyperactive- impulsive symptoms are often more readily observable than inatten tion.Park et al.characterized the clinical and neuropsychological profile of children with comorbid epilepsy and ADHD [29]. Chen et al.similarly found that externalizing scales on the CBCL demonstrated superior discriminating power compared to internalizing scales when identifying children with ADHD [30]. The modest discriminant validity of attention- specific measures may reflect the diagnostic complexity in epilepsy populations,where attention difficulties can arise from multiple sources. The pattern of discriminant validity findings has important theoret ical implications.The strong discrimination provided by externalizing measures suggests that behavioral dysregulation,rather than pure attention deficits,may be the most distinguishing feature of comorbid ADHD in children with epilepsy.This may reflect the fact that attention problems are common in epilepsy populations regardless of ADHD sta tus,resulting from seizure activity,medication effects,and other factors. In contrast,the behavioral disinhibition and hyperactivity character istic of ADHD may be less common in children with epilepsy alone, making these features more diagnostically useful. Prior epidemiological literature has suggested that certain epilepsy characteristics(e.g.,seizure burden and earlier onset)and neuro developmental vulnerability may be associated with behavioral co morbidity.However,in the present review,risk factor evidence was synthesized narratively and only a limited number of studies reported extractable association estimates(Table 4);therefore,conclusions about specific epilepsy syndromes or localizations should be interpreted cautiously.Studies from India and Egypt have similarly documented the importance of systematic risk factor assessment [31,32]. 4.3. Clinical implications Our findings have several important clinical implications.First,they support implementation of systematic ADHD screening in children with epilepsy using the SDQ-Hyperactivity subscale as a brief,efficient first- line screening tool.Kral et al.have emphasized the importance of sys tematic ADHD identification in youth with epilepsy [33]. The SDQ can be completed by parents in approximately 5 min and scored rapidly by clinical staff,making it practical for use in busy epilepsy clinics.ILAE recommendations suggest initiating screening at age 6 years or diagnosis and repeating annually thereafter.Our results provide empirical support for these recommendations while identifying specific populations war ranting heightened vigilance. Second,accurate identification of ADHD enables appropriate multi modal intervention combining behavioral therapy and pharmacological treatment.Concerns about methylphenidate increasing seizure risk have been largely dispelled by large database and registry studies demon strating no significant effect on seizure frequency in children with ADHD and epilepsy [34]. These findings have important implications for clinical practice,as historical reluctance to prescribe stimulant medica tions in children with epilepsy may have resulted in undertreatment of ADHD symptoms.Santos and colleagues showed that low-dose methyl phenidate not only improved ADHD symptoms in 70.8%of patients but also reduced seizure severity in children with difficult-to-treat epilepsies [35]. Swedish registry data demonstrated a 27%reduction in seizures associated with methylphenidate treatment compared to unmedicated periods,and a separate analysis found that ADHD medication was associated with 29–49%lower seizure odds versus unmedicated periods [36]. Third,medication selection in children with epilepsy should consider differential cognitive effects of antiepileptic drugs.When attention problems are prominent,clinicians should consider preferentially using cognitively favorable antiepileptic drugs such as lamotrigine or leve tiracetam while avoiding or minimizing phenobarbital and topiramate exposure when clinically appropriate.The ILAE Task Force has recom mended reevaluation of attention function after any change in antiepi leptic drug therapy [37]. For children with established ADHD, antiepileptic drug selection should prioritize agents with minimal cognitive impact to avoid exacerbating attention difficulties. Fourth, the finding that externalizing behaviors demonstrate the strongest discriminant validity has practical implications for clinical assessment.Clinicians should specifically inquire about hyperactive- impulsive behaviors,oppositional tendencies,and conduct problems when evaluating children with epilepsy for possible ADHD.The DBD rating scale,which specifically assesses disruptive behavior disorders, may be particularly useful as a supplementary measure in clinical evaluation.The relatively poor discriminant validity of internalizing measures suggests that anxiety and depression symptoms,while impor tant to assess and treat,are not useful indicators of comorbid ADHD in this population. Finally,our results concerning risk factors could help develop a stratified approach to screening intensity.Children with identified risk factors should probably have more frequent and/or intensive screening protocols than standard annual screening(according to the ILAE),and this risk stratification would also allow resources to be better targeted on high-risk children.Careful examination for ADHD symptoms is needed in children with refractory seizures,in those who developed epilepsy at young ages,and in children under polytherapy and/or receiving older antiepileptic drugs. 4.4. Limitations and future Directions However,some limitations should be noted when drawing conclu sions from this review.Firstly,the number of studies included in this review was relatively small due to low availability in literature of studies evaluating the validity of screening instruments for ADHD among epi lepsy populations.Therefore,it was not possible to perform a meta- analysis to pool diagnostic accuracy parameters across studies,nor to carry out subgroup analyses according to epilepsy type,age range,etc. Secondly,for Layer 2 discriminant validity analysis,we depend largely on one single large,high-quality study.Although this study col lects comprehensive data from many different behaviors under the same robust methodology,replication in other diverse populations and con texts would further verify its generalizability;using effect sizes from one single study could limit our inference about whether such discriminant validity patterns can be replicated across different clinical contexts/ populations.Nonetheless,leave-one-out sensitivity analysis shows that the pooled estimate is robust and not unduly influenced by any single effect size(see Fig. 6). Fourth,we were also unable to explore screening tool performance according to ADHD subtype.With so many more children with epilepsy being inattentive presentations rather than hyperactive-impulsive or combined subtypes,screening tools could have different performance characteristics for each ADHD subtype(e.g.,inattentive vs.hyperactive- impulsive vs.combined subtypes).More research is needed on subtype- specific diagnostic accuracy so that future clinical assessment pro tocols can be developed accordingly. Future research priorities will be:(1)large-scale,prospective valida tion study of screen tool(s)among different epilepsy groups with suffi cient sample size to explore subgroup effects;(2)comparison-with- comparison study design based on uniform methods for different screen measures;(3)develop new screens specific to epilepsy considering special diagnostic issues of these children;(4)investigate multisource screen procedures taking ratings from parents,teachers,and clinicians together;(5)conduct long-term observation to check whether the current screen can correctly forecast later impairment;(6)implement study on how best to incorporate regular ADHD screening as part of routine health surveillance of young epilepsy patients. Conclusions First,this is the first systematic review/meta-analysis showing that the SDQ-Hyperactivity subscale has a good diagnostic accuracy to detect ADHD in children with epilepsy,thus confirming current ILAE recom mendations on this screening tool.Second,further externalizing behavior measures(mainly the DBD rating scale)with excellent discriminant val idity might be evaluated in order to update clinical assessment pro tocols.Third,a narrative synthesis of risk factor evidence (Table 4) showed that earlier seizure onset,neurodevelopmental/cognitive vul nerabilities,male sex,medical comorbidities,and higher antiepileptic drug burden might correspond to higher-risk subgroups for whom targeted screening should be performed. These results have important clinical implications:healthcare pro viders caring for children with epilepsy should conduct systematic screening using validated instruments starting at diagnosis,or at the age of 6 years,and repeating annually;they should consider more frequent screening if risk factors are present;treatment should be started when ADHD is detected(methylphenidate seems safe and effective);and anti epileptic drug regimens should be adjusted to avoid cognitive side ef fects and maintain seizure control. In other words,we can’t afford to wait on screening for ADHD with validated instruments in high-risk populations until there is more data regarding stimulant safety in epilepsy.If we did wait,would we miss the chance to identify and intervene sooner in kids with epilepsy and ADHD?Given the high prevalence of this comorbidity,and its negative impact on developmental trajectories,quality of life,and long-term out comes,this is a clinical and research imperative. metadata_title: The interplay between executive function and learning disabilities: Developmental cognitive neuroscience perspectives on reading, math, and ADHD
pages: The interplay between executive function and learning disabilities: Developmental cognitive neuroscience perspectives on reading, math, and ADHD Tzipi Horowitz-Kraus a,b,c,* , Paul T. Cirino d, Laurie E. Cutting e,f, Sarah S. Hughes-Berheim e, Eric D. Wilkey f, Marcia A. Barnes e, Keri S. Rosch b,c, Jessica A. Church g a Educational Neuroimaging Group, Department of Education in Science and Technology, Department of Biomedical Engineering, Technion-Israel Institute of Technology, Haifa, Israel b CNIR, Kennedy Krieger Institute, Baltimore, United States c Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, United States d Department of Psychology, University of Houston, Houston, TX, United States e Department of Special Education, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, United States f Department of Psychology and Human Development, Vanderbilt University, Nashville, TN, United States g Department of Psychology, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX, United States A R T I C L E I N F O Keywords: Reading Math Attention abilities Executive functions Fluency Learning Learning difficulties Dyslexia ADHD Dyscalculia FMRI EEG A B S T R A C T The term “Executive function” (EF) describes domain-general cognitive processes including working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility among others, that are essential for academic learning and behavioral regulation. Growing evidence highlights the importance of EF not only in typical development but also in un derstanding and intervening in learning disabilities (LDs), including dyslexia and dyscalculia, and in attention- deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Despite this recognition, challenges remain in clearly defining EF, specifying its neurobiological underpinnings, and understanding its diverse roles across academic domains. This invited review reflects on a recent international expert workshop at the Flux Congress in 2024, and unites theoretical, behavioral, and neurobiological perspectives to examine how EF interacts with reading, math, and LDs. We explore the contribution of EF to word recognition, reading comprehension, and fluency; the role of audiovisual integration and cognitive control in dyslexia; the developmental interplay between EF and math difficulties; the role of EF in response to intervention in math; and EF as a transdiagnostic mechanism in ADHD and LD comorbidity. Across domains, we review the underlying brain networks, highlight methodological ad vances (e.g., functional connectivity, mobile neuroimaging), and discuss intervention strategies that target EF to support academic growth. We conclude with a synthesis of cross-cutting challenges and future directions, including the need for developmental models that integrate cognitive neuroscience, educational theory, and clinical insights. This review provides a roadmap for researchers and clinicians aiming to harness EF as a core mechanism to better understand and support diverse learners. 1. Introduction Reading and mathematical skills are instrumental not just to aca demic success, but also to future career success and earning potential (Claessens and Engel, 2013; Meehan et al., 2023; Naveed et al., 2023). Academic skills form the foundation for how we communicate and trade information and skills with others, and thus academic skills predict general health and well-being (Hartog and Oosterbeek, 1998; Molla et al., 2004; Topitzes et al., 2009; Winkleby et al., 1992). Despite their high importance, many students struggle with academic skills; two-thirds of 4th graders in the United States are not proficient with reading, and more than one-third are below basic abilities in math, with many countries experiencing similar student difficulties (National Cen ter for Education Statistics, 2023; OECD, 2023). Given their critical roles in modern society, it is unfortunate that many children experience learning difficulties (LDs) with math and/or reading that impact their * Correspondence to: CNIR, Kennedy Krieger Institute, Baltimore, United States. E-mail address: Tzipi.Kraus@technion.ac.il (T. Horowitz-Kraus). future successes. Given the persistent nature of LDs, it is important to understand how they may interact with additional key cognitive pro cesses, such as those underlying executive function (EF). The term EF encompasses that which is needed to achieve goal-directed, con trol-demanding behaviors. EF is slow to mature throughout develop ment, activates the brain’s control system, and directs a potentially malleable set of cognitive processes that could be harnessed to improve academic skills (Porter et al., 2023; Tervo-Clemmens et al., 2022). Critically, however, there is no universal consensus on the definition of executive function (EF), and this can hamper fully understanding relations between EF and academic skills. As will be noted in more detail by Cirino, a variety of theoretical models have been proposed to conceptualize executive function (EF), and even within a given model, alternate solutions are found dependent upon age (Karr et al., 2018). These models provide distinct perspectives on the mechanisms under lying EF across different developmental stages and contexts. This lack of consensus on the definition of EF makes it challenging to create tasks that accurately or consistently isolate its components or inform relations to academics. Reading is a complex process that can benefit from a construct like EF as it requires the integration of orthography (under standing of printed language), phonology (understanding of language sounds and sound-to-print representations), and semantics (under standing of word meaning) (Coltheart et al., 2001; Seidenberg and McClelland, 1989). Decoding print to language also needs to be fast to enable fluent reading. As readers move from understanding individual words to passages of text, reading comprehension involves many more cognitively complex processes linked to EF (Gernsbacher, 1991). For example, holding the plot of a story in mind taxes working memory and other memory aspects to both understand the text and to link it to as pects of real life or similar stories of the past (Sweller, 2011). Mathematic skills are also often considered to carry a high intrinsic cognitive load, involving the transition from controlled processes to more automatic mental math operations such as addition and multipli cation (Sweller, 2011). Mathematic skills are built on cumulative knowledge and practice of facts, procedures, and complex applications (Van Hoof et al., 2017) and often require increased EF working memory capacity to support the learning of new math concepts (von Aster and Shalev, 2007). Although math and reading may seem quite different on the surface, they are strongly related, and difficulties in both often co-occur (Cirino, Child, et al., 2018; Peterson et al., 2017). Particular domains of math, such as word problems, also rely on reading comprehension (Fuchs et al., 2015). Moreover, several studies suggest that EF contributes to success in both areas (Carriedo et al., 2024; Cirino et al., 2015; Peterson et al., 2017). At the 2024 annual international Flux Society Congress, in Baltimore, Maryland, we (Horowitz-Kraus and Church) organized a pre-conference workshop to discuss the myriad of issues surrounding EF and academic skill research, particularly in those with LDs. We designed the workshop as both a primer for new re searchers in the field, as well as a place to get top thinkers in the area to discuss their viewpoints regarding the role of EF in academic skill development with each other. In this review, we have each workshop speaker providing a brief summary of their contributions to the workshop. We will provide an overview of the variety of EF definition(s), describe the brain activity related to EF, and the involvement of EF in aspects of reading and math brain activity and behavior, describe how EF impacts reading at the word-level and text-level in brain and behavior, and how auditory and visual integration of information is a key variable for reading. We then move to mathematical abilities, and what we know about how EF intersects with math processing in brain and behavior, and how EF relates to math intervention outcomes. Our last section provides an important reminder of how LDs often co-occur with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and the possibility that the interrela tion of these conditions occurs via EF. We finish with some closing thoughts about the future directions of EF work in the academic skill and LD research fields. 2. Conceptualizing executive function from a psychological perspective (Paul T. Cirino) EF is wrought with confusion around how it is conceptualized and measured. The roots of EF trace back to unusual neurological case studies beginning in the 19th century and war injuries (typically involving the frontal lobe) in the early 20th century. In such cases, the dominant features were poor problem solving and decision making in everyday life, often in the context of preserved intelligence. As the concept of EF evolved, two approaches predominated. One focused on individual differences in EF, generally focused on EF as a psychological construct (via objective or subjective measures). The other focused on EF as an anatomical or biological construct (via im aging or the study of patients with frontal-lobe injury). There has been, is, and will be, continued debate about the extent of complementarity of these two approaches (and their sub-approaches). Their connection is relevant in that, for example, functional imaging studies often examine activity during some task, the nature of which is informed (implicitly or explicitly) by the psychological lens through which one views EF. Given the size of these literatures, the present overview focuses only on the psychological approach, though of course an analogous review from a biological perspective would also be of benefit. The cognitive framework for EF by Miyake and colleagues (Miyake et al., 2000), with its components of updating, shifting, and inhibition, is clearly the most widely utilized framework for measuring EF with per formance measures (Karr et al., 2018). However, a number of other frameworks are available for how to construe what is important for achieving goal-directed behavior. Finding points of commonality and of differences among these is useful and relevant to help organize how to think about EF. Some alternative frameworks include the self-regulated learning process of Zimmerman (1990), the “macro-construct” of EF by Zelazo et al. (1997), the effortful control component of Rothbart’s (2007) temperament model, and Engle’s model of working memory (Engle, 2002, 2018). Cirino (2023) reviewed these with reference to their own prior definition of EF (Cirino, Ahmed, et al., 2018); that is, whether various frameworks considered EF to be: (a) singular versus plural, (b) domain specific versus general, (c) a process versus set of components; as well as (d) the extent to which EF implies control, or (e) management, or (f) a goal-directed target. That review found that there was widespread agreement across frameworks that EF was indeed domain general, and to some degree requires control, management, and goal-direction (although control and management were described in overlapping ways). However, there were also sharp distinctions, including whether EF should be construed as singular versus plural, and whether EF was a process versus a set of components. Cirino (Cirino, 2023) discussed the advantages and disadvantages of each of these distinctions, and argued for considering EF as a singular process, concluding that “EF is a managerial process for coordinating domain general and domain specific resources during challenging goal-directed behavior” (p. 10). The process referred to in the above definition has three phases – those of representation, of planning, and of monitoring (the RPM model). Representation requires understanding that there is a task, problem, issue, or goal, and understanding its characteristics and context. Planning is developing an approach to go about reaching the anticipated goal state considering personal strengths and weaknesses, and monitoring refers to implementing the planned approach, including changing (or staying) the course, where needed. Such phases are not unlike those of other process models (Zelazo et al., 1997; Zimmerman and Schunk, 2011) and are also consistent with approaches taken to address “executive” difficulties (Levine et al., 2000; Ylvisaker and Fee ney, 2009). Given that the above approach is different from the component model of Miyake et al. (2000) and its derivations, it is necessary to resolve the way such components (shifting, inhibiting, updating) “fit”. For example, there is robust evidence that each of those three constructs T. Horowitz-Kraus et al. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 79 (2026) 101722 2

are domain general and are related to a variety of goal-directed be haviors, that each is associated with certain brain regions and networks, and that there are common ways that each are measured. However, there is less attention paid to problems associated with this approach. For example, it is not clear how the components work together mecha nistically, or how they “give rise” to EF per se. Further, it is not clear why other domain general cognitive factors (e.g., attention, processing speed) are not included. A componential approach also goes against the concept of EF as an individual difference, which is how EF is typically referenced. Finally, not all goal directed behaviors require the same combination of domain general (and domain specific) skills. On the other hand, a major difficulty with a process approach to EF is how to measure it. To align with the proposed RPM model (Cirino, 2023), the phases should be measured directly. It may be possible to do so with a performance-based task, but this presents a number of issues, such as maintaining a balance between ultra-specificity and being overly abstract. However, developing such a task (or set of tasks) that have strong psychometric properties would be an excellent contribution. An alternative may be to develop a rating scale. Although multiple rating scales of EF are available (Barkley, 2012; Gioia et al., 2015), these do not approach EF from a process perspective, and in many cases, the mea surement of EF overlaps significantly with that of behavioral attention symptomatology. Colleagues and I have (Cirino et al., 2026) developed a parent rating scale that directly instantiates the RPM model, with strong psychometric properties, good convergent validity, and better discrim inant validity (relative to other EF scales) with regard to behavioral inattention. Although promising, this initial support needs to be evalu ated in additional samples, via different raters (e.g., teachers), and against other measures and outcomes with which EF should be reason ably expected to relate (to varying extents). There remains a need to resolve a number of outstanding issues with regard to EF. These include but are not limited to: (a) a continued reconsideration of how to conceptualize EF in a way that has strong theoretical and scientific yield but also is of practical relevance; and (b) how to measure EF with psychometrically robust instruments, particu larly across potentially confounding approaches including material (e. g., verbal versus nonverbal), type (performance versus rating scale), and context (e.g., hot versus cool). Thinking carefully about what one “means by” EF (be it the RPM model of Cirino, 2023, a componential model (Miyake et al., 2000), or some other model), is an important first step for researchers (and clinicians) to consider before assessing or manipulating EF in a given context. Doing so systematically is likely to yield results for EF that are generalizable and replicable, and avoids a tendency for there to be a mismatch with an overly broad construal of what EF is, relative to how it is assessed. 3. Executive function and reading in the child brain (Jessica A. Church) As noted by Cirino in the section above, many studies have investi gated the engagement of brain systems related to EF. These in vestigations typically ask participants to perform a task designed to elicit control engagement while a neuroimaging device (electro encephalagraphy – EEG; functional near-infrared spectroscopy – fNIRS; functional magnetic resonance imaging – fMRI; magnetoencephalogra phy – MEG) measures brain activity over time. Through comparisons of harder trials to easier trials, or trials that require an EF-related skill (e.g. “stop” trials relative to “go” trials to elicit inhibition in the stop-signal task (Verbruggen and Logan, 2008)) several brain regions have been shown to be consistently engaged and form putative “control networks” of the brain. Indeed, these EF-elicited brain regions correlate together even in the absence of a task, suggesting that these putative control networks have a history of working together over time. However, also similar to Cirino’s point above with the concept of EF, there is much debate and mixed vocabulary used to describe these EF- related brain regions, regarding whether they form a single or multiple brain networks, how overlapping they are across tasks, what cognitive processes are supported by these networks, and whether their relative engagement relates to behavioral EF (Engelhardt et al., 2019; Friedman and Robbins, 2022; Nugiel et al., 2020; Ribeiro et al., 2024). In general, it is agreed that controlled processing engages lateral frontal and parietal regions of the brain, along with the anterior cingulate and bilateral frontal operculum/anterior insula (Posner and Petersen, 1990; Power and Petersen, 2013). At rest, the lateral frontal and parietal re gions are often reported to form one network (the “fronto-parietal” network), while the bilateral frontal operculum and anterior insula form another (the “cingulo-opercular” or “action mode” network) (Dosenbach et al., 2008, 2025; Power and Petersen, 2013). Critically, these brain networks are consistent with the lesion literature of patient symptoms, as well as with more direct recording data from surgical patients or non-human primates (Aron et al., 2004; Bunge et al., 2005; Gratton et al., 2018). Work from my lab and others has found that these control networks are engaged during any circumstance when control is needed (e.g., when something is harder relative to easier), and that the engagement of these networks is consistent in location, if not in activity level, by at least middle childhood (Engelhardt et al., 2019; McKenna et al., 2017). EF-related behaviors (e.g., inhibition, working memory, cognitive flex ibility) are slow to mature behaviorally, plateauing for most measured EF-related skills by 18 years or so (Porter et al., 2023; Tervo-Clemmens et al., 2022), and presumably there is continued maturation of control networks in the brain to support these behavioral effects over at least a similar time frame. What has been less clear is the role that these control brain networks play related to individual differences in academic skills and learning difficulties. Similar to EF, reading and math tasks performed during neuro imaging have been shown to elicit consistent brain engagement. For reading tasks, brain activity is typically stronger in the left hemisphere relative to the right, and engages the ventral fusiform, middle temporal gyrus, supramarginal gyrus, and left inferior frontal gyrus among other regions (Martin et al., 2015; Schlaggar and Church, 2009; Schlaggar and McCandliss, 2007). Math tasks consistently elicit activity in the inferior parietal sulcus, along with many regions that are thought to relate to symbolic processing or language (Istomina and Arsalidou, 2024; Peters and De Smedt, 2018). Critically, for both math and reading tasks, even simple ones, the brain’s control networks are heavily recruited, and often overlap with some of the strongest reading and math findings (e.g., inferior parietal cortex, lateral frontal cortex). Many of the researchers at this workshop have been fascinated by the possibility that under standing control network engagement during academic tasks may lend greater insight into those who struggle. For example, in my lab we have found in upper elementary students that engagement of a parietal region of the fronto-parietal network, and the anterior cingulate region of the cingulo-opercular network during a sentence comprehension task related to reading performance outside of the scanner, but that engagement of these same regions during a non- lexical EF task (inhibition task), did not relate to reading (Roe et al., 2018). This result suggested engagement of control during a specific skill (i.e. during reading) may be altered in those with difficulty in that skill (i.e., struggling readers). However, a recent study of ours in bilingual middle schoolers complicates this summary, as differences in a non-lexical EF task (cognitive flexibility) did relate to reading ability (Nugiel et al., 2023). Furthermore, reading has also been shown to elicit unique multi-network integration properties, pulling control networks, the visual network, attention networks, and language regions together, and reducing network segregation, suggesting that children need mul tinetwork engagement for reading success (Church, 2023; Ellenblum et al., 2019; Lex et al., 2025; Vogel et al., 2013). While this section has focused on reading, in the workshop Wilkey noted exciting advance ments in our understanding of how the brain’s control networks support and relate to math abilities. Overall, it is clear that EF, reading, and math can all be studied in the T. Horowitz-Kraus et al. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 79 (2026) 101722 3

brain through a variety of techniques and through testing a variety of different brain signals. How the brain’s EF control networks dynamically correlate during different tasks or at rest, or how the brain engages control networks to perform a given academic task have already yielded unique insights about academic abilities. Hopefully more neuroimaging examinations of EF and math and reading in the future will allow us to better understand variations in academic achievement, better identify those at risk or why some struggle, and to develop targeted, effective future interventions. 4. Executive function and reading outcomes: neurobiological and cognitive linkages (Laurie E. Cutting; Sarah S. Hughes- Berheim) Reading is a multifaceted cognitive process essential for academic success and lifelong learning. Reading relies on various cognitive pro cesses, including decoding, vocabulary, and syntax, to integrate existing background knowledge with new information. The integration of these processes is hypothesized to be facilitated by EF. Findings from our ongoing lines of investigation, which we detail below, have illuminated the role of EF in reading outcomes, including revealing how impair ments in EF can adversely affect reading abilities, as well as how enhanced EF may serve to facilitate outcomes for weaker readers. While components of EF (i.e., the Miyake model (Miyake et al., 2000)) components of inhibition, working memory, and cognitive flex ibility) have been linked to both word- and text-level processing (Spiegel et al., 2021), studies confirming how they are related to reading is an ongoing area of investigation. Previous hypotheses on the relationship between inhibition, working memory, and cognitive flexibility include that inhibition is important for enabling readers to attend to relevant word-level information (Coltheart et al., 2001; Henderson et al., 2013) or discourse while filtering out or suppressing irrelevant information or memories (Borella et al., 2010). The relevance of working memory during reading is that it enables readers to retain information about the text and integrate it into with their prior knowledge (Cain et al., 2004). The ability to continuously update information is a key component to learning from text (for review see Butterfuss and Kendeou, 2018). Cur rent hypotheses regarding the importance of cognitive flexibility for reading includes it aiding readers in shifting between decoding words and retrieving semantic information from text (Cartwright et al., 2017; Taboada Barber et al., 2021) as well as preventing preservation during reading when presented with syntactic or semantic irregularities (Kieffer et al., 2013). Recent studies from our lab (Hughes-Berheim et al., in preparation; Spencer et al., 2020) and others’ (Cartwright et al., 2020; Kieffer et al., 2021; Nouwens et al., 2021; Taboada Barber et al., 2021) have high lighted EF appears to play a “behind the scenes” role, demonstrating EF specifically influences reading comprehension through word-level and oral language processes. Spencer et al. (2020) used a structural equation modeling (SEM) approach to determine that working memory and cognitive flexibility were indirectly related to reading comprehension via decoding and oral language, respectively, in a sample of 271 children ages 9–14 years old. Expanding upon this work, Hughes-Berheim and colleagues (in preparation) used a similar SEM approach to examine these relationships between EF (inhibition, working memory, and cognitive flexibility) decoding, oral language, and reading comprehen sion longitudinally (i.e., from grades 1–3; 2–4; and 3–5). Like Spencer et al. (2020), results showed that EF ability supports subsequent decoding and oral language, which further enhances later reading comprehension. Further, results showed a developmental shift with the relationship between EF and oral language increasing in importance for reading comprehension over time. Of note, these findings are compat ible with the supposition that EF’s role in reading (as well as other ac ademic tasks) likely is a faciliatory one – helping to coordinate and enhance a diverse range of critical cognitive processes that need to be employed while reading. In addition to behavioral findings, neuroimaging techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) have provided insights into the brain networks involved in reading and EF. Indeed, specific brain regions, including the bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortices (dlPFC), intraparietal sulci (IPS), and lateral medial temporal lobes, have been identified to support different aspects of EF; collectively, these brain regions form the fronto-parietal network (FPN) (Yeo et al., 2011) as noted earlier and in our recent work. Notably, specific regions within the FPN overlap with the reading network, suggesting that, at the neurobiological level, reading necessitates engagement of executive processes. Specifically, theories suggest the FPN is involved in strategi cally integrating newly read information with background knowledge to improve comprehension. This hypothesis is supported by research indicating the way reading/language regions interact with nodes within the FPN is linked to reading outcomes at both the word- and discourse-level (Aboud et al., 2018; Ihnen et al., 2015; Norton et al., 2014). Word-level. Growth in word-level abilities have been linked to neurobiological indices of EF. In Aboud et al.’s 2018 paper, we set out to understand whether children identified with reading difficulties (i.e., Dyslexia) show unique functional activation patterns in regions associ ated with EF during reading tasks. Further, we explored whether these activation patterns were predictive of remediation following a tutoring intervention. Results indicated those with more efficient brain func tioning in these areas (i.e., more connectivity between FPN and reading networks) were likely to demonstrate greater responsiveness to in terventions. This sheds light on the potential for individualized inter vention strategies that align with a child’s unique neurobiological profile. In Burgess and Cutting (2023), we expanded upon this work and showed kindergarten EF was significantly associated with the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), part of the FPN, during a pre-reading fMRI task. Further, functional connectivity scores between the right dlPFC and the left ventral occipito-temporal cortex (vOTC; a region involved in word identification) predicted growth in reading comprehension ability a year later (Burgess and Cutting, 2023). Together the findings of Aboud et al. (2018) and Burgess and Cutting (2023) suggest that neuroimaging in poor readers and/or pre-readers may at some point in the future enable identification of biomarkers of future reading difficulties. Specifically, they suggest early measures of EF function and network connectivity, may be used to identify students that may struggle to read long before children show signs of a reading difficulty. While the promise of using neuroimaging metrics in educa tional practice to determine what intervention approach may work for different neurocognitive profiles is a far-reaching goal, these and related studies provide a step forward towards this objective. Text-level. Studies show that reading connected texts – or discourse processing – relies on the same brain regions that are active during word-level processing, while also encompassing broader reading regions and networks (Bailey et al., 2018). In particular, the default mode network (DMN), which encompasses the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, bilateral angular gyri (AG), precuneus/posterior cingulate cortex, bilateral anterior temporal lobes, and hippocampus (Buckner et al., 2008), has often been found to play a role in discourse processing (Yang et al., 2019). The vast majority of discourse processing fMRI studies have used narrative texts, or stories (Keller et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2019), which intuitively align with the putative function of the DMN – histor ically, its involvement has been hypothesized due to theory of mind (Jacoby and Fedorenko, 2020; Saxe, 2006). Nevertheless, the few studies of expository texts, including ours, suggest not only that expository text comprehension involves the FPN network, but also parts of the DMN (Aboud et al., 2019; Banich et al., 2023; Jacoby and Fedorenko, 2020; Ozernov-Palchik et al., 2021; Swett et al., 2013; van Moort et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2020). These results suggest certain areas of the DMN are integral to discourse processing, regardless of text type. Indeed, a recent conjunction analysis of ours (Hughes-Berheim et al., 2024), demonstrated that while the DMN is T. Horowitz-Kraus et al. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 79 (2026) 101722 4

more broadly involved in narrative text processing, a set of core over lapping areas within the DMN are present during expository text comprehension. Interestingly, degree of activity within these core discourse processing areas of the DMN was related to reading compre hension ability (Hughes-Berheim et al., 2024), suggesting these areas may be important for predicting the amount of material individuals learn from texts. These findings emphasize the importance of large-scale networks, reading, FPN, and DMN that integrate functionally to complete the high- order task of comprehension. Of note, our recent findings align with contemporary hypotheses of the role of the DMN that propose it captures and represents individual narratives, including background knowledge and individual language experiences (Menon, 2023). During discourse comprehension, these experiences are drawn upon to create strong and robust mental models of the text (i.e., situation model building) to enhance comprehension. 4.1. Implications for educational practice Understanding the relationship between EF and reading outcomes has implications for reading interventions and educational practices. Targeted efforts that simultaneously strengthen EF and reading skills may yield more significant improvements in literacy development than reading-only interventions. However, integration of EF training and reading intervention has been tried, and success on this front has been elusive thus far (Kassai et al., 2019; Melby-Lervåg et al., 2016; Takacs and Kassai, 2019). There recently has been interest in the field in thinking about EF in a more nuanced manner, specifically considering the context in which one needs to employ EF. Along these lines, people have discussed the idea of “reading specific EF” (Cartwright and Palian, 2024) and the analogous math specific EF (Wilkey, 2023a). A recent study demonstrated that reading-specific EF measures were superior to EF measures alone in predicting reading outcomes (Peng et al., 2024). Thus, it may be that “reading specific EF” tasks are needed to have any impact on reading outcomes. This synthesis of our ongoing work highlights the critical relation ship between EF and reading outcomes. Research demonstrates that enhanced EF is linked to improved reading proficiency; nevertheless, the mechanisms by which this occurs remain elusive. The impact of text genre on reading skills underscores the need for tailored interventions that address the varying demands of different texts. Future research should continue to explore the dynamic interplay between EF and reading, using both neural network and behavioral approaches, to identify effective intervention strategies that support struggling readers. By fostering both cognitive and reading skills, educators can help bridge the gap for students facing literacy challenges, ultimately promoting academic success. 5. Executive function and audiovisual integration (Tzipi Horowitz-Kraus) The ability to read fluently (i.e., accurately and effortlessly with the appropriate prosody) is critical for reading comprehension (Breznitz, 2001). Difficulties with reading fluency, a somewhat under investigated subcomponent of reading, is often shared among children with dyslexia, but is also seen in other neurodevelopmental and neurological disorders (Breznitz, 2001). The reason for this shared fluency challenge is prob ably due to the complexity of synchronizing several sensory (audiovisual integration) and cognitive (EF) systems in the brain, which will be dis cussed in the following section (Breznitz, 2001). As noted by Church above, reading is not a simple task but rather an interactive and integrative sensory and cognitive process involving the visual (also referred to as the orthographic processor), auditory (also referred to as the phonological processor), and semantic systems, described also in the Simple View of Reading model (Nevo and Breznitz, 2011; Scarborough, 2001). These systems are jointly engaged in the reading process with the visual system processing information slower than the auditory one (Breznitz, 2001; Hoover and Tunmer, 2020). Incoming visual information reaches the visual cortex about 70 ms post-stimulus onset, while auditory sensory information arrives in the auditory cortex about 30 ms following stimulus onset (Heil et al., 1999). On the other hand, viewed more broadly across the brain, linguistic information is proposed to be processed such that phonological pro cessing is sequential (Rosenzweig and Bennett, 1996), whereas ortho graphic processing is more holistic (Breznitz and Leiken, 2001; Kraus and Breznitz, 2009), and thus output from the orthographic (more vi sual) processing systems may arrive faster than output from the phonological processing systems (Breznitz and Leiken, 2001). These two layers of potential timing mismatches lead to the importance of syn chronization between the auditory and visual modalities for successful word reading in order to achieve fluency (Breznitz, 2001). It also points to the potential importance of higher-order processes, such as EF, in reading (Kim, 2020). Individuals with dyslexia are believed to suffer primarily from a phonological processing deficit, contributing to inaccurate and/or slow reading (Shaywitz and Shaywitz, 2005). The definition and character istics of dyslexia have undergone many changes over time, and newer theories also emphasize the role of EF in reading achievements among this population (Abo-elhija et al., 2022; Aboud et al., 2016; Horowitz-Kraus, Meri, et al., 2024; Lex et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2020; Spencer and Cutting, 2021). It is essential to distinguish between reading accuracy and reading fluency, with the latter being a combi nation of accuracy and speed (Breznitz, 2001; Perfetti, 1986; Snowling and Hulme, 1989). One aspect that affects fluency is speed of processing, which refers to the time it takes for information to be processed, including sensory and short-term working memory (Atkinson and Shif frin, 2003). Speed of process and fluency are usually affected by word recognition efficiency, which is influenced by both orthographic and phonological processing (Breznitz and Misra, 2003). Neurobiological studies, mainly using functional MRI, have pointed to altered involvement of the dorsal processing stream (i.e. phonological processing; including the supramarginal and angular gyrus) and ventral processing stream (orthographic processing, including the fusiform gyrus), as well as more frontal regions (related to the motor articulation and syntax of reading, and to semantic knowledge retrieval in the inferior frontal gyrus) in children with dyslexia (Shaywitz et al., 2003; Shaywitz and Shaywitz, 2008). Electrophysiological (EEG) studies have found that individuals with dyslexia may have more significant time gaps between auditory and visual recognition (Breznitz and Misra, 2003; Raij et al., 2000), leading to slower and less accurate processing, espe cially in recognizing imaginary words and complex formats (Breznitz and Misra, 2003). Dyslexic readers who were presented with words had significantly longer latencies in the P300 component, indicating delayed information processing and asynchrony between the visual and auditory modalities (Breznitz and Misra, 2003). The study concluded that these characteristics indicate difficulties in integrating orthographic and phonological representations, which are critical factors in word recog nition in dyslexics (Breznitz and Misra, 2003). A recent neuroimaging study demonstrated that during contextual reading, children with dyslexia show reduced functional connectivity between the auditory and the visual networks compared to age-matched 8–12-year-old typical readers (Horowitz-Kraus et al., 2023). However, a contextual reading fluency condition, which was achieved using a fast, rhythmic presentation of letters on the screen, resulted in increased functional connections between the auditory and visual networks in children with dyslexia, bringing their signals closer to those of typical readers. Interestingly, this increased functional connectivity was also related to increased reading comprehension in these readers (Horowitz-Kraus et al., 2023). These findings, together with morpho metric studies pointing to the difference in gray matter for (word vs contextual) reading fluency in children with dyslexia (Horowitz-Kraus, Dudley, et al., 2024) emphasize the importance of audio-visual T.
