integration during contextual reading for reading comprehension and raises the question regarding the role of EF in this integrative process among children with dyslexia, as suggested by Zhou et al. (2020). Audio-visual integration (AVI) refers to the process by which the brain combines auditory (sound) and visual (sight) information to form a unified perception enabling the detection of speech in noisy settings, localizing sound sources, and processing synchronized stimuli like lip movements matching spoken words (Driver and Noesselt, 2008; Gao et al., 2023). This integration is crucial for interpreting and responding to complex sensory environments (Shams and Seitz, 2008). Efficient AVI improves how conflicting information from different senses is reconciled (Calvert and Lewis, 2004). Interestingly, speech-related audio-visual integration (AVI) and non-speech AVI demonstrate distinct neural mechanisms, as evidenced by developmental differences observed in previous studies. Speech-related AVI relies on specialized neural pro cessing mechanisms that gradually develop with age and experience, while non-speech AVI is rooted in general sensory integration processes that mature early in childhood (Calvert and Lewis, 2004; Shams and Seitz, 2008). Several models have revealed that AVI is also related to interpretation and expectation processes, which are attributed to addi tional cognitive abilities, such as EF (Zhou et al., 2020). The components involved in the AVI process occur in higher-level brain regions that process complex information. In this model, visual and auditory signals are initially processed separately in their primary sensory areas, the visual and auditory cortices, before being sent to more associative and integrative areas like the superior temporal cortex (STC) and prefrontal cortex (PFC) (responsible for decision-making and higher-order cognitive processing) (Gao et al., 2023; Stanford and Stein, 2007). This model emphasizes the importance of top-down and bottom-up processes in AVI as well as the critical aspect of timing. Top-down processes, including cognitive processes, such as attention, expecta tions, predictability, and prior knowledge, play a critical role in shaping integration. For example, focusing attention on a particular stimulus can enhance its prominence, improving synchronization and perception (Talsma and Woldorff, 2005). Bottom-up processes are stimulus-driven characteristics, such as intensity, timing, and spatial proximity, that influence integration (Talsma and Woldorff, 2005). For instance, stimuli that are closely aligned in time and space are more likely to be perceived as connected (Dixon and Spitz, 1980). Timing also plays a fundamental role in AVI, and is referred to in the AVI model as the time binding window (TBW) (Dixon and Spitz, 1980). TBW is the short time frame within which auditory and visual signals are perceived as synchronous. It allows the brain to merge signals arriving at slightly different times, enabling seamless interpretation of events. This TBW is not fixed; it can expand or contract based on factors like stimulus complexity, attention, and learning experiences. Predictable stimuli, like repeated speech rhythms, or positive emotions, such as happiness, expand the TBW, enabling smoother integration. The TBW changes across the lifespan and differs in individuals with neurodevelopmental and neurological disorders (Woynaroski et al., 2013). Traditionally, the reading literature has focused effort on specific phonological processing interventions for struggling readers (Ahmed et al., 2020). However, my lab and others have recently taken a novel direction, where we focus on training AVI and EF, aiming to improve reading fluency (Cancer et al., 2022). These AVI-based reading in terventions used either rhythm-based auditory (Cancer et al., 2020, 2022) or visually-based stimuli (Horowitz-Kraus et al., 2014a, 2014b; Taran et al., 2023) and were shown to improve reading fluency. The auditory-based rhythmic training investigated the benefits of incorpo rating visual and auditory cues in reading training for Italian children with dyslexia (Cancer et al., 2022). The study found significant im provements in reading fluency abilities under both auditory and visual rhythmic training conditions. Furthermore, the impact of AV synchro nization was examined and showed that while visual cues contributed to engagement, the auditory component remained the primary driver of reading improvement (Cancer et al., 2022). The study findings indicate a significant improvement in reading speed both immediately following the intervention and after three months, suggesting that an auditory-rhythm-based training has lasting effects on reading develop ment (Cancer et al., 2022). In the visual domain, studies examining the effect of a visual- rhythmic training on reading fluency and related neural circuits have demonstrated a similar positive effect. A visual rhythmic reading intervention (VRRT) was achieved by deleting the letters from the screen while presenting text (Taran et al., 2023). The letters were deleted one-by-one from the screen, initially based on the child’s own reading speed, but following several correct responses for the comprehension questions that followed each of the reading trials, the deletion rate increased in 5% increments (and slowed down in the case of erroneous responses). Fast deletion of these letters also engages a number of EF-related skills: the reader has to inhibit themselves from gazing backward (inhibition), they learn to process more letters in a given time (working memory), and speed of processing is potentially improved (Farah et al., 2024; Horowitz-Kraus, 2016; Horowitz-Kraus et al., 2014a, 2014b; Taran et al., 2023). Mechanistically, it was proposed that this manipulation releases the bottleneck of working memory in those with dyslexia and hence AVI occurs more efficiently with a change in strategy of more orthographic reading than decoding attempts (Breznitz and Share, 1992). Training with this program improved reading fluency, accuracy, and comprehension in several studies conducted in children with dyslexia and matched typically-developing Hebrew (Horowitz-Kraus et al., 2014a, 2014b; Horowitz-Kraus and Breznitz, 2014) and English-speaking children (Horowitz-Kraus and Holland, 2015). Not only did reading measures improve, but also EF measures did as well (Horowitz-Kraus and Holland, 2015). Neurobiological measures have the advantage of identifying the neural circuits/pathways underlying changes in performance. After an 8-week training (3 times/week, 20–30 min per session), increased functional connectivity was observed between an EF-related network (cingulo-opercular) and the left fusiform gyrus (Taran et al., 2023), increased functional connectivity within the cingulo-opercular network (Horowitz-Kraus et al., 2015), and increased functional connections between the sensory networks (visual and auditory) and cingulo-opercular and fronto-parietal control networks, and all related to improved word reading fluency (Farah et al., 2024; Horowitz-Kraus et al., 2025). A moderation model demonstrated that changes in EF (specifically inhibition and speed of processing) were related to long-term reading fluency gains (Taran et al., 2022). Taken together, these studies support the role of AVI and EF in reading fluency among children with dyslexia as well as in typical readers and highlight the role of both the sensory system and EF in reading fluency. In conclusion, reading fluency is a complex process relying on several sensory and cognitive processes, including AVI and EF. Targeting these processes hold promise, especially in populations suffering from reading fluency deficits, including dyslexia, but not limited to it. Individuals with low and high ADHD traits (Panagiotidi et al., 2017), those with Autism Spectrum Disorder (Solari et al., 2017), and individuals with epilepsy (Vlooswijk et al., 2010) all suffer from impairments in either AVI, EF, or both, which may contribute to their reading fluency abilities. Additional studies should characterize the similarities and differences in reading fluency and underly mechanisms in these populations and examine the effects of rhythmic interventions on their reading fluency skills. 6. Executive function and math learning difficulties: how we define EF in context and what that means for measurement (Eric D. Wilkey) Individual differences in EF consistently relate to a range of academic skills (Arrington et al., 2014; Draper et al., 2025; Mazzocco and Kover, 2007; Willoughby et al., 2019; Draper et al., 2025). However, EF often T. Horowitz-Kraus et al. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 79 (2026) 101722 6

has a unique relation to mathematics learning based on the cognitive demands of specific math skills such as rational number development (Gilmore et al., 2024) and problem solving (Blair et al., 2008) for a meta-analysis, see Spiegel et al. (2021). Moreover, persistent and severe difficulties learning mathematics (developmental dyscalculia) often co-occur with EF challenges (Agostini et al., 2022). Because EF is “domain-general” (i.e., involved in a variety of goal-directed behaviors, sensory modalities, and stimulus content) we must ask how and why it relates specifically to math. Although knowledge of the neural bases of mathematical cognition and EF is advancing, a clearer account of their mechanisms, and how they interact, is essential for answering questions about the role of domain-general cognition in math learning difficulties. Two recent neuroimaging meta-analyses provide some degree of consensus on the brain regions associated with math learning diffi culties. Martinez-Lincoln et al. (2023) reviewed studies of math and reading difficulties and found over-activation of the right inferior frontal gyrus (IFG)(extending into the insula) and underactivation of the right anterior intraparietal sulcus (IPS) were most consistently associated with math difficulties. Tablante et al. (2023) identified these same re gions and additionally reported underactivation of the ventral occipi totemporal cortex (i.e., fusiform and inferior temporal gyri) in the math difficulties group. There is less consensus about which types of processing drive these neural differences. Tasks contributing to the IPS cluster included math- facts processing, magnitude and ordinality judgments, color compari son, spatial working memory, and transitive reasoning. Tasks contrib uting to the IFG cluster primarily involved ordinality and math facts. Moreover, while the ventral occipitotemporal cortex is known to have a more circumscribed role in symbol-based visual expertise, the frontal and parietal regions identified in these analyses have a wider range of functions. These functions do include magnitude processing (Sokolowski et al., 2017), but they are also frequently associated with attentional allocation (Connolly et al., 2016), visuospatial working memory (Klingberg, 2006; Silk et al., 2010), control of grasping and reaching (Grefkes and Fink, 2005), and task difficulty more generally (Bank ́o et al., 2011; Bokde et al., 2001; Gould et al., 2003). Therefore, although the two meta-analyses identify regions involved in mathematical cognition, regional specification at this level does not answer the fundamental question of which neurocognitive mechanisms drive pro cessing differences in children with math-learning difficulties. Addressing this question, the largest fMRI study of developmental dyscalculia to date tested three theoretical accounts of processing dif ferences to determine which tasks elicited atypical brain activation (Kwok et al., 2023). All children (dyscalculic and control, 8–10 years old, n = 68) completed three tasks: (1) magnitude processing task, (2) arithmetic fluency, and (3) visuo-spatial working memory. Ultimately, Bayesian analyses suggested that there were no consistent differences in any of the tasks with the preregistered fMRI contrasts despite robust behavioral differences in the tasks. The authors proposed that sample heterogeneity may account for the null findings. Group-level analyses, such as mean comparisons, assume that children with dyscalculia differ from typically developing peers in a consistent way across the sample. However, children with math learning difficulties are well-documented to be highly heterogeneous. This vari ability has led researchers to propose multiple subtypes of math diffi culty, involving deficits in working memory, attention, spatial processing, and comorbid learning disorders (Bartelet et al., 2014; Chan and Wong, 2020; Fias et al., 2013; Landerl et al., 2013; Skagerlund and Tr ̈aff, 2016; Sz ̋ucs, 2016). Given this heterogeneity, detecting mean differences in brain activation between groups may not be feasible. Interpreting individual differences in EF adds another layer of complexity. If EFs are defined as higher-order processes that regulate lower-level cognition to achieve a goal (e.g., mathematical reasoning or problem solving), then three elements must be considered: (1) the higher-order EF mechanism, (2) the lower-level cognitive substrate, and (3) their neurobiological interaction. This complexity complicates how we interpret the meta-analytic neuroimaging findings discussed above. Differences in activation could reflect not only processing specific to the target task (e.g., magnitude comparison) but also the EF demands that task imposes, and the dynamic interaction between EF mechanisms and domain-specific cognition. Several studies suggest that interactions between lower-level cogni tive mechanisms and higher-order EFs warrant closer investigation. For example, in a large study of typically developing young adults (n = 546), participants completed multiple EF tasks in the scanner, including an antisaccade task (inhibition), a ‘keep track’ task (working memory), and a number-letter task (switching) (Reineberg et al., 2022). Common activation was observed across EF tasks, consistent with shared domain-general neural resources. However, correlations between brain activation and behavioral performance revealed a different pattern: in dividual differences in performance were associated not with activation in these domain-general EF regions, but with activation in task-specific target regions—the neural substrates upon which EF processes operated. A similar pattern emerges in math-specific contexts. In one study, 3rd- and 4th-grade children completed a magnitude comparison task under two conditions: comparisons of dot quantities with matched vi sual stimuli and comparisons involving misleading visual cues (Wilkey and Price, 2019). In the interference condition, the less numerous set was more visually salient (e.g., larger surface area and greater average dot size) in half of the trials, increasing inhibitory demands. Only indi vidual differences in this interference contrast—not the basic magnitude comparison—predicted math achievement. Importantly, this relation persisted after controlling for brain activity during the Eriksen Flanker task, an interference-suppression task in a non-numerical domain. In other words, it was magnitude processing under conditions of height ened EF demand, rather than magnitude processing alone, that explained variance in math performance. Across these studies, the relation between brain function and behavior could only be interpreted by considering (1) the tasks’ EF de mands, (2) the lower-level cognitive processes involved, and (3) their neurobiological interaction. This highlights a critical recommendation: researchers must carefully consider which aspects of domain-specific processing, domain-general EF processes, and their interaction are being measured, intentionally manipulating each piece of these com ponents (Wilkey, 2023b). Although EFs play a well-established role in the development of academic skills—particularly mathematics—current neuroimaging evidence offers an incomplete picture. Meta-analyses identify candidate neural substrates of atypical processing, yet the cognitive conditions under which these regions function differently remain unclear. Moreover, these conditions likely vary across in dividuals, given the heterogeneity within math-learning difficulties. Processing differences may reflect domain-specific mechanisms, EF mechanisms, or their interplay. Advancing this field will require refined methods for assessing EF and deliberate attention to the construct val idity of tasks intended to measure EF in mathematical contexts. 7. Executive function in the context of mathematics interventions (Marcia A. Barnes) The study of EF has grown rapidly over the past 40 years across many disciplines, including learning disabilities (Müller and Kerns, 2015). The relationship of EF to mathematics development and disability is robust (Peng et al. 2016), and stronger for mathematics compared to reading (e. g., (Morgan et al., 2019; Spiegel et al., 2021). However, because every child neurological, clinical, psychiatric, neurodevelopmental and learning disorder is associated with perturbations in EF, behavioral measures of EF are neither sensitive nor specific to the diagnosis of math disabilities. On the other hand, if EFs are affected by all childhood dis orders perhaps they are important for cognition and learning, leading us to ask whether child EF is useful for understanding effects of in terventions on learning and performance. There are two analytic approaches to answering this broad question. T. Horowitz-Kraus et al. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 79 (2026) 101722 7

Each is associated with different types of questions that can be asked and answered. The first approach is moderation analysis (sometimes called aptitude by treatment interactions (Cronbach and Snow, 1977)), where we ask whether a child’s level of EFs at the start of an intervention af fects intervention response; for example, are intervention effects stron ger for children with relatively lower levels of EF (a compensatory interaction effect), is the effect of the intervention stronger for children entering the intervention with relatively higher levels of EF (a syner gistic interaction), or are treatment effects invariant across levels of EF (a universal effect of the intervention)? The second approach – media tion analysis- is one that allows inferences about causality and mecha nisms of change. The question that is asked in mediation analysis is whether improvements in mathematics are mediated by improvements in EF. Evidence related to each approach in the domain of mathematics disabilities follows. 7.1. Does EF moderate response to intervention in children with or at risk for math disabilities? Consistent with the relatively recent requirements to report moder ator analyses in requests for applications from U.S. federal research agencies (e.g., Institute of Education Sciences), most of the papers reporting moderator effects in U.S.-based studies have been published in the last 10–12 years (Chow and Hampton, 2022; Spybrook et al., 2020). A systematic review conducted by our research group (Barnes, 2023) investigated whether child EF moderated effects of math interventions. Of the studies in the systematic review, the most frequently and consistently tested EF moderator is working memory. Math intervention studies testing working memory as a moderator are largely those addressing math word problem solving with both whole and rational numbers (e.g., (Fuchs et al., 2014, 2016; Swanson et al., 2013; Swanson, Moran, et al., 2014), consistent with the role of working memory in cognitive process models of math word problems (Kintsch and Greeno, 1985), and with meta-analytic findings that working memory is more strongly related to math word problem solving than to some other do mains of mathematics (Peng et al., 2016). Most of these effects were synergistic; that is, children with relatively better developed working memory were more likely to gain more mathematical knowledge from the interventions. One study showed nuanced effects such that a frac tions intervention with a practice component involving fractions computation fluency was most advantageous for students starting rela tively higher in working memory, whereas the same intervention with conceptually based fractions practice (e.g., drawing and explaining fractions) was most advantageous for students starting relatively lower in working memory (Fuchs et al., 2016). Although cognitive strategy instruction is often part of effective intervention practices, Swanson and colleagues (Swanson, Orosco, et al., 2014) found that poorer math outcomes were associated with the attempted application of strategies during learning that exceeded the working memory capacity of students with math disabilities. These findings suggest that one aspect of EF, namely working memory, is implicated in response to math interventions. These findings are important for answering the question of “for whom is this inter vention most beneficial?”. Barnes and Peng (2025) have argued that such findings are also relevant for telling us about the potential for hidden cognitive load in mathematics interventions. The preponderance of synergistic effects means that the content and procedures of several of our generally efficacious interventions produce extraneous load that taxes some children’s cognitive capacity in ways that are not beneficial for learning (Sweller, 2010). Considering EF characteristics of both the learner (i.e., working memory level) and of the intervention (i.e., cognitive load requirements) has the potential to provide information that is important for engineering interventions to produce better learning outcomes for children with math difficulties and disabilities. 7.2. What is the nature of the relationship of EF and learning in children with or at risk for math disabilities? Experimental studies (i.e. intervention studies) provide the level of evidence necessary to determine whether changes in mathematical learning are causally related to growth in EF. There are several meta- analyses of working memory interventions showing a lack of “far transfer” effects on mathematics (e.g., (Melby-Lervåg et al., 2016; Sala and Gobet, 2020), suggesting that increases in working memory do not lead to changes in mathematics learning or performance. The relevance of these meta-analyses for making inferences about students with math disabilities have been critiqued on several grounds (Fuchs et al., 2022). First, few studies had participants with math disabilities. Whether working memory training affects growth in mathematics in such in dividuals is unknown, but typically, interventions have larger effects for those who require intervention. Second, measures of math achievement in these studies are narrow in that they focus on arithmetic to the exclusion of other domains of mathematics that are strongly associated with working memory such as math word problem solving (Peng et al., 2016). Finally, very few studies test whether combined EF and math interventions differentially affect math outcomes compared to math-only or EF-only interventions (for a review of these types of studies see Barnes and Peng, 2025). One study has tested the nature of the relationship of working memory and mathematics in the context of a randomized controlled trial (Fuchs et al., 2022). Second grade children with or at risk for math disabilities received either: a working memory intervention; a schema-based math word problem solving intervention; or the schema-based math word problem solving intervention with 6 min of embedded working memory games using math stimuli. Each of these three active treatment conditions was followed by a 5-minute math calculations and word problem solving practice, which may have pro vided an explicit link between working memory and mathematics for the working memory intervention group. These groups were compared to each other and to a business-as-usual condition. The working memory intervention showed strong effects on working memory and significant, but smaller effects on measures of math word problem solving. The two schema-based math interventions produced large effects on math word problems and significant, but smaller effects on working memory. These findings show that the relationship between working memory and mathematics may be bidirectional (Doebel, 2020; Peng and Kievit, 2020) because a working memory intervention produced positive changes in mathematics, and a mathematics intervention produced positive changes in working memory. Mediation analysis, which tests purported mechanisms of treatment effects showed that: 1) the working memory intervention with a small amount of math practice led to growth in working memory, which, in turn, was related to growth in math word problem solving; and 2) the math interventions led to growth in math word problem solving both directly and also indirectly through (or mediated by) growth in working memory. In conclusion, studying EF in the context of mathematics interven tion reveals several findings of importance. First, moderation analyses show that a child’s level of working memory often affects their response to mathematics intervention. Second, the pattern of moderation effects, namely that interventions were often more effective for children starting somewhat higher in working memory, highlights that there may be extraneous cognitive load in some of our generally effective math in terventions. Third, the relationship of working memory and math word problem solving is bidirectional in that improving working memory improves math word problem solving, and vice versa. Finally, mediation analyses support the idea that the mechanisms behind intervention- related growth in math word problem solving involve both domain specific learning of mathematical content and procedures as well as changes in working memory. These findings are of importance to models of the development of math and EF and serve to underline for T. Horowitz-Kraus et al. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 79 (2026) 101722 8

researchers and practitioners alike, that development of EF may be malleable through engagement with complex academic tasks in children with math learning disabilities. 8. Executive function deficits as a transdiagnostic feature of ADHD and learning disorders: implications for assessment and intervention (Keri S. Rosch) Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is the most com mon neurodevelopmental disorder, with recent prevalence estimates of 10% among school-aged children in the U.S. (Danielson et al., 2022). The defining symptoms of ADHD include developmentally inappropriate levels of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that are present across settings and associated with functional impairment in academic, peer, or family domains (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). In dividuals with ADHD often display deficits in EF, whether defined behaviorally (e.g., parent reports difficulty following multi-step di rections) or measured with a neuropsychological test (e.g., ability to hold and manipulate verbal information in working memory). Academic difficulties are common in individuals with ADHD, often driving the referral for assessment or intervention, with concerns including poor grades, failure to complete schoolwork, difficulty retaining information, inconsistent academic skill demonstration, taking longer than expected to complete work, and feeling overwhelmed by schoolwork. Children with ADHD are more likely to obtain lower school grades and stan dardized test scores and higher rates of educational placement and grade retention (DuPaul and Stoner, 2003). In adolescence, ADHD is associ ated with higher rates of school drop-out and lower rates of college enrollment, which may contribute to lower vocational attainment and less job/financial stability in adulthood (Barkley et al., 2008; Mannuzza, 1993). Improving academic functioning in ADHD is critical to disrupting the negative, long-term trajectories that are characteristic of the disorder. The diagnosis of ADHD is based on the behavioral symptoms listed above and does not include a brain scan or cognitive testing, but the symptoms refer to cognitive functions that affect academic performance (particularly the inattentive symptoms). For example, the symptom “often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes in schoolwork” may be expressed as comprehension errors while reading, spelling/grammar errors while writing, or errors while completing multi-step math problems. Also, the symptom “often avoids, dislikes, or is reluctant to engage in tasks that require sustained mental effort” may apply to schoolwork, resulting in less practice with academic skills, thereby exacerbating weaknesses in these areas for children with ADHD. ADHD frequently co-occurs with learning disorders, with up to 50% of children with one diagnosis meeting the criteria for the other (DuPaul et al., 2013). Given the high rates of comorbidity between ADHD and learning disorders, with poorer outcomes when both disor ders are present, there is a need to better understand the mechanisms contributing to this comorbidity and novel interventions to improve outcomes. The co-occurrence of learning disorders and ADHD is thought to be due, in part, to atypical development of shared neurobiological path ways supporting EF (Denckla, 1989; McGrath et al., 2011). ADHD is a heterogeneous disorder, both in terms of the symptom presentation, associated cognitive/motivational deficits, and clinical course. Multi-process models of ADHD postulate competition between neuro biological circuits involved in executive functions and reward response are thought to underlie the behavioral expression of ADHD symptoms (Sonuga-Barke, 2002, 2005). Among children diagnosed with ADHD, there is significant variability in the extent to which they show cognitive or motivational deficits, or atypical neurobiology. Perhaps for some children with ADHD, the executive circuit is primarily affected which is also implicated in LD, whereas the atypical motivation may be specific to ADHD. Multiple deficit models (MDM) have also been applied to understand the etiology of learning disorders and their comorbidity with ADHD. First proposed by Pennington, MDM is a multi-level framework for un derstanding neurodevelopmental disorders, spanning etiology (genes, environments, and gene-environment interplay), brain mechanisms, neuropsychology, and behavioral symptoms. This model, first applied to understanding developmental disorders by Pennington (2006), accounts for inter-individual variability in profiles by proposing that each risk factor is probabilistically (rather than deterministically) related to neurodevelopmental disorders. Most research has occurred at the neu ropsychological level of analysis. Studies have shown consistent support for the fundamental tenets of the MDM, that multiple probabilistic risk factors are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders and that shared risk factors contribute to comorbidity (McGrath and Stoodley, 2019). The MDM has been tested in a longitudinal twin sample which aimed to identify shared and unique cognitive correlates of learning difficulties and ADHD. Results of this and other studies from the Colo rado Learning Disabilities Research Center group suggest that the shared variance of EF and processing speed explain most of the transdiagnostic risk for ADHD and LD (McGrath et al., 2011, 2020). Following the introduction and research on MDM, researchers believed the field could eventually identify performance patterns across neurocognitive domains that would be diagnostic. However, the dimensional and probabilistic nature of the deficits prevents clear mappings of cognitive profiles to diagnoses. The heterogeneity of neu ropsychological deficits among individuals with the same diagnosis (ADHD or LD) is now well-established, with some individuals showing only a single deficit or even no identifiable deficit. Therefore, diagnosis continues to be based on evaluation of the defining symptoms of the disorder (based on clinical history, observations, and reliable, validated tests) as well as careful attention to functional impairment and possible comorbid conditions. While detailed neurocognitive evaluation may not be necessary for diagnostic decision-making, cognitive profiles might still be helpful for treatment planning and for helping families and ed ucators adapt to the unique cognitive strengths and weaknesses of the child (e.g., accommodations for working memory or processing speed challenges). Given this background, there are several important assessment considerations when there are concerns for ADHD and learning. Among students with learning difficulties, parent and teacher ratings of ADHD symptoms is recommended to determine whether further evaluation of ADHD is necessary (e.g., if symptom ratings exceed a specific clinical threshold). In a similar fashion, classroom performance data (e.g., curriculum-based measurement probes) for reading, math, and writing can be used to determine whether further evaluation of skills deficits is necessary for students with ADHD. Assessment of academic functioning can help identify specific targets for intervention beyond reduction of ADHD symptomatic behaviors. Possible changes in academic func tioning associated with treatment, including medication and behavioral interventions, should be assessed on a regular basis. It is also important to consider the types of learning/academic dif ficulties the child is having and the level at which ADHD symptoms may be contributing to these difficulties. ADHD is associated with weak nesses in multiple levels of each academic domain, raising important questions that may be teased apart with neuropsychological assessment. For example, it is important to understand whether symptoms of ADHD are indirectly influencing advanced skills by undermining the develop ment of foundational skills, or whether ADHD has a direct and unique impact on advanced academic skills, including reading comprehension, writing composition, and mathematical problem-solving. A recent study by Trane and Willcutt (2023) on the Colorado twin sample described above suggests a direct effect of ADHD on advanced academic skills, such that it independently predicted writing composition and reading comprehension after controlling for basic skills. However, individual ized assessment is critical to guiding intervention approaches given the heterogeneity in ADHD and associated learning difficulties. When thinking about intervention, the assessment should help us to T. Horowitz-Kraus et al. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience 79 (2026) 101722 9

understand whether academic functioning is affected by academic skill- deficits, which are LD-related, or performance-deficits, which are ADHD-related. Performance deficits can presumably be addressed by behavioral interventions and/or psychotropic medication as alleviating ADHD symptoms may lead to better academic performance. Academic skill deficits must be addressed directly through empirically supported instruction in the relevant skill area. There are evidence-based behav ioral interventions for youth with ADHD that target EF skills impacting academic performance (DuPaul et al., 2012; DuPaul and Eckert, 1997). These approaches focus on application of EFs to daily activities by teaching behavioral strategies. A behavioral intervention plan is also recommended, which emphasizes the use of clearly defined behavioral targets and expectations followed by frequent feedback and rewards along with facilitating communication between parents and teachers (Iznardo et al., 2020). There has also been a focus on cognitive training interventions in the ADHD literature, designed to directly target and improve EF and processing speed. These include brain training programs such as CogMed, Endeavor Rx, Interactive Metronome, and neurofeed back (Chacko et al., 2014; Enriquez-Geppert et al., 2019; Kollins et al., 2021; Park and Choi, 2017). These are appealing alternatives to the behavioral interventions described above as they are more easily implemented by families, but only seem to show near-transfer, meaning improved performance on that specific skill, but not far-transfer to improving ADHD symptoms or learning difficulties. Further research with randomized controlled trial methodology is needed to determine their effectiveness. There is also value in using intervention as experimentation to clarify the role of EF learning, academic performance, and response to inter vention. For example, we have previously demonstrated that, among children with ADHD, medication effects on classroom performance (math productivity and classroom behavior) were mediated by medi cation effects on certain cognitive functions (inhibition and working memory) (Hawk et al., 2018). This might suggest that children strug gling to complete their classwork who have difficulties with inhibition or working memory may benefit from stimulant medication. Improved understanding of individual cognitive profiles that relate to response to intervention will allow for personalized, targeted interventions and inform our mechanistic understanding of learning/academic difficulties and effective interventions. There is also value in using interventions with EF skill training embedded in the academic skill practice, such as the rhythmic reading training discussed earlier by Horowitz-Kraus, to probe the role of EF in academic performance. We recently published a study (Rosch et al., 2025) of children with reading difficulties with and without ADHD who completed the rhythmic reading training and examined reading and EF skills following the intervention. Results suggest the greatest improve ment in reading comprehension was among children with comorbid ADHD and RD following the intervention. While children with reading difficulties with and without ADHD showed improvement in inhibition, which was normalized relative to the typical readers group, children with reading difficulties and comorbid ADHD showed greater improvement in reading comprehension. We also saw significant change in brain functional connectivity of cognitive control networks (frontoparietal and dorsal attention) in the comorbid group. This is an example of how intervention can be used as experimentation, to test a theory of change or underlying cognitive mechanisms. In conclusion, ADHD and LD frequently co-occur due in part to shared EF and processing speed deficits. Assessment of ADHD and LD should include screening of the other disorder. Intervention across home and school involving behavioral/medication for ADHD and explicit skill instruction for LD is recommended. Finally, development of in terventions targeting shared cognitive deficits or individual cognitive profiles can inform theory and practice. 9. Discussion 9.1. Integrative synthesis and panel insights The workshop held at Flux 2024 in Baltimore, Maryland, brought together a number of exciting and insightful perspectives regarding the interplay between EF, academic skills, and LDs in brain and behavior. Speakers covered a variety of overlapping issues, including issues of how EF is defined and measured (Cirino, Church, Rosch), how EF impacts reading (Church, Horowitz-Kraus, Cutting) and math (Church, Wilkey, Barnes) both behaviorally and with regard to intervention (Barnes, Cirino, Horowitz-Kraus), as well as neurally (Church, Cutting, Wilkey), and reflections on how EF impacts comorbidities with reading and math difficulties like ADHD (Rosch). The consistent theme across the workshop was that we need a better understanding of how all the approaches to defining and studying EF fit together. Some research indicates that there is a common, cross-domain set of EF processes in the brain that are important to consider when studying LD, reading, math, or ADHD. EF, whether assessed by behav ioral task measures, by self/parent/teacher surveys, or by brain mea sures, strongly relates to variation in reading and math abilities. However, the mechanisms by how EF impacts those with LDs and ADHD, and how EF impacts intervention or treatment response remains unclear. It is important that future work consider domain-specific and domain- general EF processes and interactions when trying to understand dif ferences in academic performance across individuals and change in reading or math performance over time. Similarities of EF impact have been observed across reading and math scores, and across those with ADHD and/or LDs, but there have been important observed differences too, as far as the duration, consistency, and specificity of EF effects in a given study. Critically, it remains unclear whether and how including EF aspects in educational interventions is helpful, and under what circumstances. In particular, the context in which EF is incorporated (within the aca demic context or more generally) may affect the duration and impact of EF training. All authors note the need for future work in this area to answer a number of enduring questions about the role of EF in learning interventions. The end of the workshop held a panel with NIH program officers to discuss how EF work in the academic arena could have impact on policy and future research. The work clarifying EF’s role in academic success and individual variation in ability is just beginning, and many exciting directions lie ahead. 9.2. Future directions One thing we learned is that a variety of different neural approaches are used, and the overlap/consistency across them is unclear. A com monality is that EF has been linked to multiple putative control networks in the brain, but especially the fronto-parietal control brain network. As future brain studies work more towards network-level analysis, it will be fascinating to understand how EF abilities are supported by brain net works and to discover which networks show the most plasticity over age and learning change. How EF impacts reading and math processing in the brain may relate to how networks reconfigure, integrate, or segre gate during different tasks. Another thing we learned is that while it is clear that EF (regardless of approach) relates consistently to concurrent reading and math skills, it is unclear how to use that relation to improve educational outcomes over time or intervention. However, as the exciting work described by Barnes shows, EF and academic interventions may be bidirectional, and EF abilities may impact who benefits most from intervention. What is needed now are more studies that push the envelope on how we test those effects. Relatedly, another set of future directions that remains critical with regard to the role of EF in academic success is to understand the impact T. Horowitz-Kraus et al. of subclinical levels of difficulty and the role of comorbidities on the individual. While LDs are often defined based on an individual scoring below a certain percentage of their peers, individuals just above that threshold are likely experiencing similar brain and behavioral effects. Similarly, ADHD symptoms form a spectrum, and the availability of assessment, diagnosis, and treatment is often not equally accessible across all strata of society. The high co-occurrence of ADHD with LDs, of multiple LDs (math and reading) with each other, and of LDs with anxiety and other mental health symptoms remain important directions for future EF research. Large, longitudinal datasets that collect multiple measures of brain and academic skills are critical for clarifying the role of EF in LDs. We need to follow students over time to understand whether and how EF relates to academic skill change over development and within the same individuals. Most studies of academic skills in youth remain cross- sectional or, if longitudinal, are small, reflecting their inherent collec tion difficulty. Collaborative efforts that share and pool neuroimaging and behavioral collections in students across locations and over time could greatly advance our understanding not just of the relationships between EF and academics, but whether and how EF relates to academic skill change over development and within the same individuals. Studying brain and behavioral data across the academic calendar could greatly help us understand the nature of skill change in students at different stages of development. Data sharing will be instrumental in amassing reliable and robust effects. To that end, increased use of more mobile neuroimaging technolo gies like fNIRS (Zhan et al., 2024), or portable EEG (Poulsen et al., 2017) are key technologies for future EF and academic research. They are quiet and cap-based, allowing more freedom of position. Low-field MRI is also an exciting developing technology that could allow more portable MRI collections (Kimberly et al., 2023). Being able to go out of the lab and into the classroom will remove biases inherent in lab-based collections, and allow studies of multiple students at once, or of moments of syn chronization between teacher and learner. As the speakers of the workshop make clear, current studies of EF, reading, and math are highly relevant to educators, parents, and stu dents alike. Understanding more about EF and academics could allow for better and earlier identification of students at risk for future diffi culty, could lead to more effective interventions by incorporating EF instruction in an evidence-based manner, and could suggest ways to tailor treatment to the individual. Much more work is needed, but many exciting research and educational directions lie ahead. 10. Conclusion Understanding the intersection between EF, LD, ADHD, and aca demic abilities is a complex topic that needs interdisciplinary and developmentally sensitive approaches that reach across brain, behavior, and culture. It is somewhat early days for cognitive neuroscience studies of EF and math or EF and reading. We hope this summary, which emerged from the EF workshop at Flux 2024, is helpful for spurring discussion and guiding future research. metadata_title: Pharmacological interventions for ADHD: a systematic review and dose⠍effect network meta-analysis
pages: 485 Articles www.thelancet.com/psychiatry Vol 13 June 2026 Pharmacological interventions for ADHD: a systematic review and dose–effect network meta-analysis Mikail Nourredine, Lucie Jurek, Tasnim Hamza, Andrea Cipriani, Fabien Subtil, Valeria Parlatini, Luis C Farhat, Guilherme Fusetto Veronesi, Orestis Efthimiou, Georgia Salanti, Samuele Cortese Summary Background Optimising the dosage of pharmacological treatments for ADHD is key to maximising their benefits, yet most clinical guidelines provide only limited information on this issue. Dose–effect relationships have not been comprehensively assessed across all ADHD medications and age groups, despite growing concerns about subtherapeutic prescribing. We aimed to estimate dose–effect curves for efficacy and tolerability of ADHD medications (stimulants and non-stimulants) across age groups. Methods We conducted a systematic review and dose–effect network meta-analysis of double-blind randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating oral monotherapy (stimulants and non-stimulants) in individuals aged 5 years and older meeting standardised ADHD criteria. Studies involving genetic syndromes, treatment-resistant populations, or withdrawal-phase designs were excluded. We retrieved eligible studies from the MED-ADHD database, updated on Feb 17, 2025, without language restrictions. We included published and unpublished aggregated-level data. The primary outcome was efficacy (measured using validated clinical scales) and the secondary outcome was tolerability (discontinuation due to adverse events). Within-study bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (version 2). We summarised dose–effect associations using a hierarchical Bayesian model with restricted cubic splines. Separate analyses were conducted for children or adolescents (aged <18 years) and adults (aged ≥18 years). The distribution of key effect modifiers was used to examine transitivity of the network. People with lived experience were involved in the conceptualisation and design of the study, and in the interpretation of the findings. The protocol was pre-registered on OSF. Findings Our 2017 search identified 9948 potential references for inclusion and our Feb 17, 2025 search identified 5148 references. Of these 15 096 references, 8467 were excluded after title and abstract screening, and a further 5862 references were excluded after a full-text read. Of the 767 remaining reports, 164 were included in the systematic review and 113 RCTs (45 in adults and 68 in children and adolescents) were included in the dose–effect network metaanalysis. The 68 RCTs on children and adolescents included 14 138 participants (9981 [70·6%] males and 4157 [29·4%] females) and the 45 RCTs on adults included 11 016 participants (5958 [54·0%] males and 5056 [46·0%] females). Data on ethnicity or race were inconsistently reported across RCTs. We found distinct dose– effect patterns by medication class and age group. In children and adolescents, methylphenidate, amphetamines, and guanfacine showed increasing median efficacy up to 45 mg/day, 25 mg/day and 4 mg/day, respectively, with no evidence of additional benefit at higher doses, although estimates at higher doses were characterised by wide credible intervals. In adults, amphetamines showed a plateau above approximatively 50 mg/day, whereas methylphenidate efficacy increased without evidence of a plateau, possibly due to sparse data. Dose-dependent increases in discontinuation probability due to adverse events were observed for amphetamines (above 25 mg/day for children and 50 mg/day for adults) and methylphenidate (above 50 mg/day for adults, with no clear dose-dependent risk for children). We found no evidence of dose–effect patterns for atomoxetine (in fixed-doses studies) and modafinil. Multiple sensitivity analyses confirmed the robustness of these findings. We found no evidence of intransitivity. Interpretation Our findings challenge both therapeutic inertia—accepting suboptimal response without further dose titration—and uncritical dose escalation beyond licensed limits, when potential harms outweigh expected benefits. Our findings can inform clinical guidelines and should support shared decision making regarding ADHD medication dosage. Funding National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR303122). Articles www.thelancet.com/psychiatry Vol 13 June 2026 486 40–70% of cases, impairing symptoms persist beyond adolescence, with an estimated prevalence in adults of about 3%.4 ADHD is associated, on average, with an elevated risk of adverse outcomes, although trajectories vary across individuals. Although treatment does not fully prevent all negative outcomes, access to evidencebased care remains essential to reduce long-term risks such as suicidal behaviours, substance misuse, or accidental injuries.5,6 Pharmacotherapy is an important component in the multimodal management strategy of ADHD.7 Available medications include stimulants, encompassing methyl phenidate and amphetamines, and non-stimulants, such as atomoxetine, clonidine, guanfacine, and viloxazine. Given the range of therapeutic options, comparative evidence on their efficacy and tolerability is needed to inform clinical decision making. A network meta-analysis of 133 double-blind randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating ADHD pharmacological treatments8 found that, based on clinician-rated ADHD core symptoms at approximately 12 weeks, most medications were superior to placebo in both children and adolescents, and adults. However, amphetamines were also associated with poorer tolerability than placebo in both age groups. Notably, the network meta-analysis did not account for medication dosage, which is a crucial component of treatment effect. In clinical settings, subtherapeutic dosing is not uncommon, especially among children and adolescents,9–12 potentially leading to reduced clinical benefits and adherence.11,13 Most clinical guidelines provide limited guidance on how to dose ADHD medications.14,15 Understanding how efficacy and tolerability vary across doses is therefore essential to inform shared decision making. A dose–effect network meta-analysis builds on standard network meta-analysis methods by modelling the dose–effect relationship across treatments.16,17 This approach enables the identification of the optimal benefit–harm trade-off across dose ranges, thereby enhancing clinical applicability. Four dose–effects meta-analyses on ADHD medications have been published.18–21 Three of them were restricted to children and adolescents19–21 and examine the patterns of dose–outcome associations of stimulants (methylpheni date, amphetamine),19 atomoxetine,20 and viloxazine21 against placebo. Altogether, these papers indicated a pattern of increasing group-level efficacy with increasing doses until a given point, after which further increases in medication dose were associated with diminished gains in average ADHD symptom reduction or increased average risk of treatment discontinuation due to adverse events (eg, 30 mg/day of methylphenidate, 20 mg/day of amphetamine, 1·2 mg/kg per day of atomoxetine, 400 mg/day of viloxazine). However, these analyses relied on only a subset of the evidence (ie, direct evidence from placebo-controlled trials). Ideally, clinical practice should be informed by the entirety of the evidence, comprising both direct and indirect evidence as estimated in network meta-analyses. Research in context Evidence before this study ADHD medications are part of the multimodal approach to ADHD management. Understanding dose–effect for efficacy and safety is essential to maximise their effectiveness and tolerability. To identify existing evidence synthesis on dose–effects, we searched PubMed on July 17, 2025, for dose–effect meta-analyses focusing on ADHD medications, using the following syntax and search terms, with no language restrictions: (“dose-effect” OR “dose-response”) AND (ADHD OR “attention-deficit/ hyperactivity disorder” OR “attention deficit hyperactivity disorder”). We found four dose–effect meta-analyses of stimulant and non-stimulant pharmacological interventions in children and adolescents, and in adults with ADHD. These four meta-analyses focused on specific pairwise comparisons against placebo and did not account for indirect evidence arising from other pairwise comparisons. Therefore, there is a need to assess dose–effects across all ADHD medications (stimulants and nonstimulants) simultaneously and across age groups. Added value of this study We conducted the first dose–effect network meta-analysis of ADHD medications, including both licensed and unlicensed doses, across age groups. We showed that dose–effect patterns vary across medications and age groups. In children and adolescents, methylphenidate, amphetamines, and guanfacine showed increasing median efficacy up to 45 mg/day, 25 mg/day, and 4 mg/day, respectively, with no evidence of additional benefit at higher doses. In adults, amphetamines showed a plateau above approximatively 50 mg/day. Additionally, we found no evidence that escalation beyond licensed maximum doses improves mean efficacy at the patient-group level, and such increases are typically associated with reduced tolerability. Implications of all the available evidence The current dose–effect network meta-analysis presents the most comprehensive evidence to guide dose considerations and inform clinical guidelines at the patient-group level. Overall, our findings indicate that clinicians should avoid suboptimal doses and consider upward titration from minimal doses when symptoms remain insufficiently controlled. Although we found no compelling evidence to support the routine use of doses exceeding FDA-licensed maxima, some individuals with ADHD might require higher-than-licensed doses. In these cases, any potential benefit must be carefully weighed against possible safety concerns identified in longterm observational studies. Articles 487 www.thelancet.com/psychiatry Vol 13 June 2026 We aimed to investigate these important research gaps by conducting the first dose–effect network meta-analysis across available ADHD pharmacological treatments and age groups, considering also dose beyond the FDArecommended maximum dose, estimating dose–effect curves for efficacy and tolerability. Methods Search strategy and selection criteria We conducted a systematic review and dose–effect network meta-analysis of double-blind RCTs evaluating oral monotherapy (stimulants and non-stimulants) in individuals aged 5 years and older meeting standardised ADHD criteria. Studies involving genetic syndromes, treatment-resistant populations, or withdrawal-phase designs were excluded. The protocol was pre-uploaded on OSF and published.22 For the reporting, we followed the PRISMA extensions for network meta-analyses (appendix p 3). Eligible RCTs were identified using the MED-ADHD database, a continuously updated repository of doubleblind RCTs evaluating pharmacological treatments for ADHD. This database was originally developed by the European ADHD Guidelines Group to conduct the network meta-analysis of ADHD medications.8 MED-ADHD includes studies retrieved through compre hensive searches of 12 major bibliographic databases (eg, PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, Web of Science), clinical trial registries, and grey-literature sources (eg, dissertations and trial-registry platforms), without applying language restrictions. The latest update was completed on Feb 17, 2025. The complete search strategy for each database is reported in the appendix (p 5). We included double-blinded RCTs, with a parallel-group or cross-over design, of pharmacological interventions administered as oral monotherapy for at least 1 consecutive week for the treatment of individuals (aged ≥5 years) with a diagnosis of ADHD, established using operationalised diagnostic criteria (DSM-III or later; equivalent ICD criteria for hyperkinetic disorder were also deemed acceptable). We excluded studies in which participants had a co-occurring genetic syndrome. Eligible medications comprised amphetamines (including lisdexamfetamine), atomoxetine, bupropion, clonidine, dexmethylphenidate, extended-release guanfacine, methylphenidate, modafinil, and viloxazine. Trials combining pharmacological treat ment with psychotherapy (other than psychoeducation) were excluded. Fixed-dosing and flexible-dosing schedules were included. Fixed-dosing schedule studies were those in which the maximum targeted dose was specified at baseline, with dose reductions permitted only for safety reasons. Flexible doses were used as sensitivity analyses. To be eligible for inclusion, flexible-dose studies had to clearly specify the maximum intended dose at baseline, with dose adjustments permitted for safety or efficacy reasons. The dose in our analysis should be understood as the maximum intended target dose at baseline, rather than the dose received. This analysis preserves randomisation and avoids issues related to selection bias, but might introduce heterogeneity. Any network meta-analysis assumes transitivity (ie, that all treatment in the network could in principle have been compared in a single RCT, and that effect modifiers are similarly distributed across treatment comparisons). We contacted corresponding authors and manufacturers for additional information and data, included grey literature, and translated papers where necessary. More details are reported in the appendix (p 6). We included summary estimates from each eligible RCT. Two reviewers working in pairs drawn from the author list (LJ, VP, LF, GFV) independently assessed the risk of bias of retained RCTs using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool23 (version 2) in relation to the primary outcome. In case of disagreement between the two reviewers, a third, senior investigator arbitrated (SC). Sensitivity analyses were performed, excluding studies at high risk of bias (appendix pp 337, 350). Data analysis Each step of data collection was conducted independently by pairs drawn from the author list of Cortese and colleagues8 with updated data collection from MN and LJ with discrepancies resolved by a third senior author (SC). The primary outcome was severity of ADHD core symptoms (total combined [ie, inattentive plus hyperactive or impulsive symptoms]), measured as an endpoint score on a standardised scale filled out by parents, teachers, patients, or clinicians. The prioritisation of scales to include used the following order: ADHD Rating Scale (total score), Swanson, Nolan and Pelham (SNAP) ADHD (total score), Conners rating scale (any version, ADHD total score), or other ADHD scales. We selected the assessment closest to 12 weeks. Efficacy of each medication was estimated using standardised mean difference (SMD). For clinical interpretability, we back-transformed SMDs to mean differences using the median observed SD of the ADHD Rating Scale, the most frequently reported scale. The secondary outcome was tolerability of treatment and all-cause discontinuation (see deviation from protocol), defined as the number of patients leaving the study due to any adverse event or any cause, respectively. Both secondary outcomes were estimated as a risk of dropout for each treatment using estimated odds ratio. For the primary analysis, only fixed dosing schedules were planned to be included. Treatments with only one or two different dosages examined across trials were excluded from the analysis. For different formulations of the same medication (eg, immediate and extended release for methylphenidate), we used the conversion doses from Farhat and colleagues,19 converting amphetamine doses as dextroamphetamine-equivalent doses and methylphenidate doses as immediate-release methylphenidate hydrochloride (appendix p 11). If the baseline weights were missing, the trial was excluded from the analysis. Several sensitivity analyses were prespecified including the exclusion of high risk of bias studies. Additional details are reported in the published protocol.22 We conducted a dose–effect network meta-analysis as a three-level hierarchical Bayesian framework, separate for children or adolescents, and adults.24 To evaluate the plausibility of the transitivity assumption, we compared the distributions of the following ad hoc-specified potential effect modifiers across treatment comparisons:25 year of study publication, mean age, sex ratio, trial length, types of rater, and ADHD diagnostic criteria.1,26 To model the dose–effect relationship for each medication, we used a restricted cubic spline function with three knots placed at the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentiles of the observed dose range. We used minimally informative priors for all variance parameters and flat priors for location parameters (appendix p 391). The model was implemented in R (version 4.3.3) using JAGS through the R2Jags package. We used the posterior distributions to obtain estimates of treatment effects and corresponding 95% credible intervals (95% CrI). The robustness of the findings for the primary outcome was evaluated through sensitivity analyses using alternative knot positions and prior distributions for the between-study variance. Full statistical details, including the hierarchical model, prior specifications, sensitivity analyses, and Markov Chain Monte Carlo convergence diagnostics are provided in the published protocol22 and in the appendix (p 393). The R code is freely available. Due to small sample size, we could not conduct separate analyses for each rater type (ie, parents, teachers, patients, or clinicians). We instead did a single analysis, using an ad-hoc rating hierarchy to prioritise which rater type to include when multiple raters were available from the same study. For children and adolescents, we prioritised clinicians, parents, and then teachers, in this order. For adults, we prioritised clinician assessments over selfreports. Small sample size also prevented separate analyses for children (aged ≥5 to <12 years) and adolescents (aged ≥12 to <18 years); this issue led us to analyse them as a single group (aged <18 years). Separate analyses for lisdexamfetamine and amphetamines were not feasible for the adult analysis. Finally, we were unable to conduct the sensitivity analyses or the tolerability analysis using only fixed-dose studies due to high autocorrelation on some parameters (appendix p 10). We did a post-hoc analysis where we added analyses: (1) using mg/kg per day as dose units for children and adolescents; (2) excluding studies sampling only adolescents; (3) estimating dose-curves for all-cause discontinuations; and (4) incorporating study duration as an effect modifier within a dose–effect network meta-regression model to estimates curves for a 6-week duration (appendix p 394). Representatives of ADHD Europe, an association of people with lived experience of ADHD, were involved in the conceptualisation and planning of the study. Details are reported in the appendix (p 395). Role of the funding source The funder of the study had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, writing of the report, or the decision to submit for publication. Of these 15 096 references, 8467 were excluded on the basis of title and abstract suitability. 5862 references were then excluded after a full-text read and of the remaining 767 reports, 164 were included in the systematic review and 113 RCTs (45 in adults and 68 in children and adolescents) were included in the dose-response network meta-analysis (figure 1). The lists of included and excluded RCTs, with reasons for exclusion, are reported in the appendix (pp 13–191). The RCTs included in the analysis recruited a total of 14 138 children or adolescents with a mean age of 11 years (of available data, 9981 [70·6%] were males and 4157 (29·4%) were females) and 11 016 adults with a mean age of 36 years (of available data, 5958 [54·0%] were males and 5056 [46·0%] were females). Data on ethnicity and race were inconsistently reported across RCTs. The characteristics of the included RCTs are presented in the appendix (p 226). The overall risk of bias was classified as high in 20 studies, classified as having some concerns in 43 studies, and classified as low in 50 studies (appendix p 253). Additional data for each analysis, including network plots, dose-distribution plots, and distribution of effect modifiers across comparisons, are available in the appendix (pp 330–394). Interactive tools displaying the estimated efficacy and tolerability of each treatment across doses are available online. The networks are presented in figure 2. Graphical examination of the distribution of key effect modifiers across treatment comparisons suggested that, in both children or adolescents, and adults, the distribution of effect modifiers was broadly balanced, bearing no strong evidence against the transitivity assumption (appendix pp 358–382). The only notable imbalance was related to age in the analyses in children or adolescents, in which the mean age was slightly higher in the amphetamine versus placebo and versus methylphenidate comparisons (appendix p 358). However, dose–effect patterns remained consistent after excluding adolescent-only trials (appendix pp 389–390). The tolerability analysis in adults included 42 RCTs (104 arms, 10 463 adults; appendix p 354). The overall risk of bias was high in 11 studies, with some concerns in 18 studies, and low in 13 studies. This analysis showed that the risk of discontinuation due to adverse events increased with dose across all medications, although the curve for methylphenidate was steeper (figure 6). The risk of discontinuation related to adverse events for both methylphenidate and amphetamines at doses above approximatively 50 mg/day exceeded the risk in placebo, which was estimated at 2·6% (95% CrI 1·8 to 3·6). At the FDA-licensed maximum dose of methylphenidate (ie, 60 mg/day), the estimated absolute risk of discontinuation due to adverse events was 7·3% (95% CrI 4·3 to 12·0), increasing to 10·0% (5·0 to 19·8) at 90 mg/day, while efficacy improved only modestly, from an SMD of −0·38 (95% CrI −0·62 to −0·17) to −0·52 (95% CrI −0·88 to −0·17; flexible-dose analysis). The risk of dropouts due to adverse events with atomoxetine increased with dose, but the association was weaker and more uncertain for doses below 80 mg/day. Regarding all-cause discontinuation, no clear dosedependent risk was observed for any of the medications, but uncertainty was high (appendix p 382). The overall shape of the dose–response curves remained consistent even after excluding high-dose regions where data were limited (appendix p 391). This benefit−risk profile was broadly consistent across age groups, although dose−effect curves for adults were estimated with higher uncertainty, due to fewer data. Conclusions for high-dose methylphenidate in children should be tempered, as our estimates above the licensed maximum dose were informed by a single study,27 which targeted 80 mg/day at the start of week 3, while efficacy was assessed at the end of week 3. This short exposure at the highest dose might partly explain the observed pattern, and the finding should be interpreted with caution. Evidence from real-world studies shows that a substantial proportion of children and adolescents receive low doses of medication without appropriate upward titration.11,13 This is particularly concerning, as timely and adequate dose adjustment has been associated with improved adherence, probably by facilitating earlier symptom improvement and reinforcing engagement with treatment.10 Our findings suggest that, in general, clinicians should not hesitate to titrate upward from minimum doses when symptom control remains insufficient. Some authors have advocated off-label use of higher stimulant doses in patients with a partial response.28 Our study does not support this approach as a general strategy at the patient-group level, given the evidence for a plateau or even decline in efficacy at doses exceeding FDA recommendations. Our results partially align with those of Farhat and colleagues,18,19 who conducted two dose−effect pairwise meta-analyses of methylphenidate and amphetamines in paediatric19 and adult populations.18 In children and adolescents, they observed that gains in efficacy decreased beyond 30 mg of methylphenidate (45 mg in our study) or 20 mg of amphetamines (25 mg in our study). However, their flexible-dose analyses suggested a monotonic improve ment with higher stimulant doses, which our fixed-dose and flexible-doses analysis did not corroborate. In adults, in relation to methylphenidate, they found that doses over FDA-licensed doses were superior in efficacy, although the improvement was described as small.18 Regarding amphetamines, there was no evidence in Farhat and colleagues’ study that non-FDA approved doses of amphetamines led to larger reduction of symptomatology, which was also the case in our study. Notably, our study adds important novel insights to existing evidence. We evaluated the full range of ADHD medications rather than limiting the analysis to stimulants, providing a more comprehensive view of dose−effect patterns, and we assessed licensed and unlicensed doses across age groups. First, only a limited number of doses could be included, particularly in the adult fixed-dose analyses. Second, efficacy was assessed using a heterogeneous set of scales rated by different assessors; however, the distribution of rater types did not appear to differ across comparisons. Third, we could not conduct analyses stratified by sex or ethnicity or race, as subgroup analyses based on these variables were not conducted or reported in most of the included RCTs. Fourth, although we evaluated transitivity across several effect modifiers, others such as impairment severity could not be assessed as they were inconsistently reported across the included RCTs. Fifth, small-study-bias could not be formally assessed. Sixth, our analysis focused on short-term (mean: 7 weeks for adults and 8 weeks for children or adolescents) efficacy and tolerability. Long-term risks must also be considered in clinical decision making. Notably, long-term observational studies have associated high stimulant doses with increased risk of hypertension, particularly for doses in the upper range.29,30 Specific adverse events could not be assessed due to inconsistent reporting across the included trials. Seventh, the generalisability of our findings is limited by reliance on RCTs that enrol selected populations, which might not fully represent patients seen in routine care according to effect modifier distributions.31 Eighth, using the maximum intended target dose at baseline preserved randomisation and avoids issues related to selection bias, but might introduce heterogeneity. Finally, our results are valid at the group level but cannot inform decision making at the individual level. Individual variability in response to medication is well documented,32 and doses higher than the licensed ones might be tolerated and needed to reduce symptom severity in some specific cases. Individuals requiring unusually high doses to achieve symptom relief might also warrant diagnostic reassessment to rule out psychiatric or neurodevelopmental comorbidities (eg, anxiety, mood disorders, sleep problems, autism spectrum disorder). Such comorbidities might influence pharmacological response and mimic ADHD symptoms.28 In addition to diagnostic reassessment, revisiting patients’ expectations regarding treatment outcomes (eg, inappropriate dose escalation following mood-enhancement with stimulants) might also be necessary.33 Notwithstanding these caveats, this dose−network metaanalysis provides the most comprehensive aggregate-level evidence synthesis to inform guidelines and shared decision making on dose selection in clinical practice. We deliberately avoided any firm recommendation on the best specific dose for each treatment and for individuals. Arch Dis Child 2026;111:167–172. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2025-329285 Original research School readiness as a signal of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: a population-based cohort study highlighting structural inequalities Matthew Warburton ‍ ‍ ,1 Blandine French,2 Evie Shore,1,3 Megan Louise Wood ‍ ‍ ,1,3 Mark Mon-Williams1,3 To cite: Warburton M, French B, Shore E, et al. ABSTRACT Objective Assess sociodemographic disparities in attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) diagnoses and determine whether England’s universal assessment of ’school readiness’ could provide a signal for ADHDrelated educational needs. Design Population-based cohort study. Setting Bradford, UK. Method Education and health records were linked using the Connected Bradford database for individuals who completed their first year of compulsory schooling (age 4–5 years) between the 2006/2007 and 2018/2019 academic years (n=1 25 330). School readiness was indexed by the ’good level of development’ threshold within the Early Years Foundation Stage Profile. Primary healthcare records were used to identify individuals with clinical codes recorded that indicate ADHD diagnosis. Regression analyses allowed controlling for covariates, including sex, ethnicity, free school meals receipt and local area deprivation. Results Male and White British heritage individuals were more likely to have received a diagnosis for ADHD than females and those of South Asian heritage or other ethnicities, with the lowest diagnosis rates among South Asian girls. Those who attained a ’good level of development’ were also less likely to have received a diagnosis for ADHD (attained: 1.0%; not attained: 2.6%, OR=0.40, 95% CI (0.35, 0.45)), even after controlling for covariates (OR=0.42, 95% CI (0.37, 0.48)). Conclusions There are structural inequalities in ADHD diagnosis, particularly across sex and ethnicity. Universal school readiness assessments, such as the Early Years Foundation Stage Profile used in England, could act as a signal of ADHD-related educational needs and aid more equitable pathways for ADHD identification and support. INTRODUCTION Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition characterised by inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity with a genetic and environmental aetiology.1 2 ADHD is commonly diagnosed in childhood but often persists into adulthood3 and is associated with a range of negative long-term outcomes including poorer academic attainment, mental and physical health difficulties and reduced quality of life.4 These adverse outcomes are seen especially within those who have symptomatic but undiagnosed ADHD,5 6 suggesting that early identification and timely support are key to improving a child’s longterm prospects. However, there are large disparities in the identification, diagnosis and treatment of ADHD. It has been consistently observed that males are more likely to receive a diagnosis for ADHD than females.7 This may partly reflect true sex differences, given that diagnoses are typically elevated for males even in community and population samples.8 9 However, the greater male-to-female ratio in clinical samples would suggest that there are greater inequalities in receiving a clinical diagnosis for females,9 10 and females tend to be diagnosed later.11 12 This sex disparity is likely to have several causes, including a lack of understanding of ADHD presentation in females and the attribution of ADHD-related behaviours to other conditions.13 There are also notable ethnic disparities in diagnosis, with white individuals more likely to receive a diagnosis than those from minority ethnic backgrounds.14–16 Furthermore, while those from low socioeconomic status families are more likely to receive a diagnosis for ADHD, they are less likely to receive treatment and/or support.17 Importantly, WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC ⇒Clinical diagnoses for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are made less often for females and those from ethnic minorities. ⇒England’s school readiness measures are associated with downstream special educational needs and have the potential to increase the equity of autism identification and support. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS ⇒The ethnic, sex and socioeconomic disparities observed in clinical ADHD diagnoses reflect patterns found in a highly diverse population sample. ⇒School entry assessments can signal ADHDrelated educational needs. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY ⇒School entry assessments could be used to facilitate earlier identification of ADHD need and reduce inequalities in the identification and support of neurodevelopmental conditions.
