Arch Dis Child 2026;111:167–172. doi:10.1136/archdischild-2025-329285 Original research these disparities have remained despite diagnostic rates for ADHD rising in recent years.18 There is a need to identify and support children with ADHD in ways that reduce structural inequalities and allow every child to achieve and thrive within the educational system. One possibility is to make greater use of data generated through education settings, an environment where those with ADHD often struggle. In particular, several countries use ‘school readiness’ measures. For example, state-educated children in England are assessed through the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) Profile during their first year of compulsory education (school Reception year, age 4–5 years). The EYFS comprises a holistic set of ‘early learning goals’ against which teachers assess children’s abilities.19 Several of these early learning goals overlap with typical ADHD symptomology, including ‘listening and attention’ and ‘managing feelings and behaviour’. We therefore hypothesised that performance on the EYFS Profile would be related to ADHD diagnoses. Previous research has demonstrated the utility of the EYFS Profile in identifying children who would benefit from tailored support. For example, research has shown an association between the EYFS Profile and autism diagnoses20 and between the EYFS Profile and downstream special educational needs (SEN) support in school.21 22 The Profile may offer a less biased way of identifying those with neurodevelopmental conditions, given that teachers are well positioned to assess a child’s needs accurately and holistically. In addition, targeted screening for autism based on low Profile scores appears to offer an effective means of increasing equity in the identification of autism.23 In the present work, we sought to assess whether the predictive utility of the EYFS Profile extends to clinical ADHD diagnoses, as identified through primary healthcare records. We also sought to characterise the disparities in clinical diagnosis in a population sample. We used Connected Bradford, a populationscale database collating routinely collected data from individuals across the Bradford district of the UK, to address these topics.24 METHODS Data We identified a cohort of individuals (n=1 25 330) who completed the school Reception year (aged 4–5 years) between the 2006/2007 and 2018/2019 academic years (with each year referred to as a ‘school cohort’ hereafter), where the EYFS profile was assessed and where general practice (GP) medical records were available. The data were obtained from Connected Bradford, a database that links administrative records from the citizens of Bradford, UK.24 The sample excluded those with multiple EYFS records (n=82); who were not assessed or were exempt from the EYFS assessment19 25 (n=266); who did not have complete covariate information including sex, ethnicity, free school meals receipt or a birth year and month available (n=810); or who were diagnosed with ADHD before age 5 years (n=6). We believe these exclusions are unlikely to meaningfully bias the results, given the relatively small proportion of exclusions (~0.9% of the total data) and the similar rates of ADHD among the included (1.4%) and excluded (1.7%) data. Measures School readiness Our binary school readiness measure was whether the individual attained a Good Level of Development (GLD) on the EYFS Profile,26 with data provided by the Department for Education. We included a variable for the version of the EYFS Profile completed, as two distinct versions were conducted between 2006/2007–2011/2012 and between 2012/2013–2018/2019. ADHD diagnosis Individuals diagnosed with ADHD were identified by searching for relevant diagnostic codes across GP records. Specifically, we searched individuals’ records for SNOMED codes27 indicative of a diagnosis of ADHD or a synonymous condition (eg, hyperkinetic conduct disorder). The date of extraction for the GP records was 16 May 2025. Prevalence estimates were made by considering the number of individuals with an ADHD diagnosis versus the total number of individuals in a group, with the group either being defined by the school cohort or by levels of demographic factors. Only 0.9% of those with ADHD were diagnosed before 6 years of age, thus a diagnosis of ADHD preceded the EYFS Profile assessment in most cases. Covariates We controlled for a number of covariates on the basis of research showing differential ADHD diagnoses across sociodemographic factors. In particular, we included sex, ethnicity, having ever received free school meals and whether the individual lived in the most deprived quintile of England (ie, lowest 20%) according to the indices of multiple deprivation (IMD) in Reception year. The school cohort was also included to account for transient changes in ADHD diagnoses over time. We coded Ethnicity as ‘White British’, ‘South Asian’ and ‘Other’ ethnicities as a large proportion of Bradford’s population is made up of White British and South Asian heritage individuals. The demographic information for the sample is shown in table 1. Statistical analyses All analyses were performed using R (V.4.4.1). Statistical significance was assessed by comparing p values against a threshold of α=0.05. ADHD diagnostic rates were first visualised for each school cohort, showing the cumulative percentage of a cohort diagnosed with ADHD across age. We then visualised sex and ethnic disparities in diagnoses for the first and last school cohorts, to track any changes, and also among the whole cohort. We used a likelihood ratio test to check whether an interaction between sex and ethnicity was present by comparing two generalised models with a binomial distribution that either included only the main effects or the main effects and an interaction term. We then assessed whether school readiness was indicative of those who were diagnosed with ADHD. We found that the EYFS Profile version affected the results, so we present analysis on the newer version of the Profile (2012/2013 onwards). We conducted two logistic regressions with ADHD diagnosis as the outcome. The first regression only used GLD attainment as a predictor. The second regression entered GLD and the covariates. Dummy coding was used for binary and categorical variables so: (1) the intercept reflected the log odds of having an ADHD diagnosis at the reference level of all variables and (2) the coefficients reflected the change associated with moving from the reference level to another level of a given variable (reference levels: sex=female; ethnicity=White British; ever received free-school meals=false, IMD quintile=bottom quintile, school cohort=2012/2013). These results were visualised as ORs by taking the exponent of the regression coefficients. For the full model, around 1% of individuals were missing IMD information, so were deleted case wise. RESULTS Trends in ADHD diagnoses We first assessed how the rates of ADHD diagnoses have changed over time. We operationalised this as the cumulative percentage of a given school cohort diagnosed with ADHD by age. We compared these cumulative percentages across school cohorts (figure 1A). We found a stable pattern where ADHD diagnoses generally start being made at around 5–7 years of age. However, it is clear that far more diagnoses were made in more recent school cohorts. To demonstrate this, we extract the cumulative number of individuals diagnosed with ADHD by age 10 years across the different school cohorts (figure 1B). Diagnoses made by age 10 years appear to have risen slowly until 2015, whereafter there has been a rapid rise, with an 8.6 times greater rate for those completing reception year in 2019 compared with those in 2007 (1.41% vs 0.16%, respectively). ADHD diagnoses across demographic factors We next assessed how these trends differ across sex and ethnicity for the first and last school cohorts available. Figure 2A demonstrates that diagnoses are made more frequently for males when compared with females. Inequalities are also evident across ethnicities, with the White British demographic having a higher rate of diagnosis than either South Asians or Other ethnicities. This was true both when the trends in diagnoses with age (figure 2B) or the final percentage of the sample diagnosed at the time of the extract (figure 2C) were considered. These data make it clear that sex and ethnic inequalities do not appear to have appreciably narrowed despite an increase in the overall numbers of diagnoses. However, the low rate of ADHD diagnoses in certain demographics makes their progression over time appear somewhat noisy. To gain a more precise understanding of these inequalities, we pooled data over all the available years (figure 2D). These pooled data show that, across all ethnicities, there is a higher incidence of ADHD diagnoses for males compared with females, and that within both sexes, South Asian and individuals of other ethnicities are diagnosed less frequently than White British individuals. Further, this ethnic inequality is more pronounced for females, demonstrating a double disadvantage (ratio between incidence in White British and South Asian individuals: 5.3× for males, 5.8× for females; ratio between incidence in White British and other ethnicities: 1.9× for males, 3.2× for females). This was supported by a likelihood ratio test that indicated the presence of an interaction between sex and ethnicity (χ2=8.32, p=0.016). Does school readiness signal ADHD diagnoses? We finally assessed whether reaching a GLD on the EYFS Profile, conducted on all state-educated pupils in England, was associated with receiving an ADHD diagnosis. Across the whole sample, those who attained a GLD were less likely to have received an ADHD diagnosis (1.9% vs 0.9%; OR=0.47, 95% CI (0.43, 0.52), p<0.001). However, there was a significant interaction between GLD attainment and the version of the Early Years Foundation Stage profile conducted (OR=0.70, 95% CI (0.57, 0.86), p<0.001), such that achieving a GLD on the pre-2013 version was more weakly associated with an ADHD diagnosis (before 2012/2013: 1.4% vs 0.8%; 2012/2013 onwards: 2.6% vs 1.0%). We therefore present analyses for only those who completed reception year in or after the 2012/2013 academic year (but note that all inferences were consistent for the other version unless highlighted otherwise). For the unadjusted regression, where only GLD attainment was entered, achieving a GLD was associated with significantly lower chances of receiving an ADHD diagnosis (OR=0.40, 95% CI (0.35, 0.45), p<0.001; figure 3). This held even after adjusting for covariates (OR=0.42, 95% CI (0.37, 0.48), p<0.001). Males were more likely to receive a diagnosis, and those from South Asian or other ethnic backgrounds were less likely to receive an ADHD diagnosis. Further, those having ever received free school meals were more likely to receive an ADHD diagnosis (though this was not the case for the pre-2012/2013 sample), as were those completing reception in all years from 2014/2015 to 2018/2019, but living in an area associated with an index of multiple deprivation above the bottom quintile was not significantly associated with ADHD diagnoses. DISCUSSION We have demonstrated—at a population level—that there are large disparities in clinical ADHD diagnoses as a function of sociodemographic factors. These disparities do not appear to have decreased appreciably with time despite an overall increase in diagnostic rates. Further, we have shown that England’s universal assessment of ‘school readiness’ can identify children who are likely to have educational needs related to ADHD. Our use of the Connected Bradford database24 allowed us to investigate the disparities in ADHD diagnoses in a highly diverse population. Our results demonstrated that White British individuals were more likely to have an ADHD diagnosis than either South Asian individuals or individuals from other ethnic backgrounds. This is consistent with a range of prior research showing lower diagnosis rates among ethnic minorities,14–16 though often in the context of the USA. Several reasons have been offered for these ethnic disparities, including cultural differences in the recognition of problem behaviours, fear of stigmatisation, limited knowledge of ADHD and barriers to navigating the referral pathways.28–30 We also found that females were less likely to be diagnosed than males, consistent with prior clinical studies.11 12 Further, the intersection of these two factors meant that female ethnic minorities received the lowest diagnosis rates, aligning with previous work showing intersectionality in ADHD diagnosis.31 Future work could take a qualitative approach to understand the barriers to ADHD diagnoses along different social dimensions, especially in the unique context of Bradford where a traditional minority ethnicity (South Asian) makes up a large proportion of the population. We also demonstrated that attainment of a ‘good level of development’ on England’s universal assessment of school readiness was related to a lower probability of a clinical diagnosis of ADHD. Performance on the EYFS Profile is associated with downstream autism diagnosis and support for SEN,20–22 suggesting school readiness measures may offer a means to aid identification of those who would benefit from support more broadly. Further, the Profile’s association with negative downstream consequences such as poor academic attainment and a ‘Not in Education, Employment or Training’ outcome32 would suggest it captures a broad range of factors important for successful school trajectories. Previous work has shown that targeted autism screening based on EYFS Profile scores can aid the identification of those with autism.23 The current findings suggest the EYFS Profile may also be useful for aiding early and equitable identification and support of ADHD learning needs. It is of note that only a modest percentage of those who failed to attain a GLD went on to receive an ADHD diagnosis (2.6% on the new version). This percentage is likely to rise with systematic screening, but the sensitivity of the measure would likely remain low and would not reflect a cost-effective screening criterion alone. It is possible that a subset of the EYFS assessment might increase sensitivity, given that some of the domains align more strongly with ADHD symptomology than others. However, the EYFS Profile would likely be most effective as a clinical screening tool when combined with other public service measures. These measures could potentially trigger a multi-service assessment of whether the child would benefit from a specialist evaluation. We note that a better approach might be to use the EYFS Profile to identify need and, in the first instance, explore whether that need can be addressed within the educational setting. If the child’s needs cannot be met, then a referral with this information would provide an efficient clinical pathway. There are several limitations to this study. One issue is that the reported data are from the Bradford district, an area with relatively higher diversity than other areas of England which may influence the barriers and pathways to assessment. Further, the current work used clinical diagnoses as the outcome measure, but the study itself shows this outcome is subject to demographic disparities. Thus, the study does not provide any direct evidence as to whether the EYFS can increase equity in diagnoses. Future work could address this issue by taking a similar approach as used previously regarding autism assessments.23 Relatedly, there is evidence that teacher-based assessments are subject to similar disparities across sex and ethnicity,33–35 and factors beyond the individual’s abilities may be used to moderate scores on the assessment.36 37 The extent to which using EYFS Profile scores would introduce different biases to the assessment pathways is therefore unclear. Finally, we were only able to control for a limited set of covariates. Among these, the indicator for having ever received free school meals is likely to underestimate the number of disadvantaged pupils, as more individuals are eligible for free school meals than those who actually apply.38 In conclusion, we have confirmed that large disparities exist in ADHD diagnoses across sex and ethnicity in a highly diverse population sample. We have demonstrated that England’s universal assessment of school readiness is associated with downstream clinical ADHD diagnoses. pages: Workplace adjustments equivalent to reasonable accommodations and workplace maladjustment in a general working population, with a focus on high autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention deficit/ hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) traits Tomoko Suzuki1* , Michiko Nakazato2, Toshiyuki Ohtani3 and Shunya Ikeda1 *Correspondence: tsuzuki2992@gmail.com; taratomo@nifty.com 1Department of Public Health, School of Medicine, International University of Health and Welfare, 4-3 Kozunomori, Narita, Chiba 286-8686, Japan. 2Department of Psychiatry, School of Medicine, International University of Health and Welfare, 4-3 Kozunomori, Narita, Chiba 286-8686, Japan. 3Safety and Health Organization, Chiba University, 1-33 Yayoi-cho, Inage-ku, Chiba-shi, Chiba 263-8522, Japan. Abstract Background: The potential effectiveness of reasonable accommodations for workers with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) has been reported, but quantitative evidence remains limited. It is also unclear whether ASD- or ADHD-equivalent workplace adjustments benefit workers with lower ASD or ADHD trait levels in the general population. This study aimed to quantitatively examine whether individuals with high or non-high levels of ASD or ADHD traits experience greater workplace maladjustment in environments without ASD- or ADHD-equivalent adjustments compared with those where such adjustments are provided. Methods: Participants were 1,000 randomly selected workers from across Japan who completed a self-administered online survey conducted as a cross-sectional study. Workplace adjustments equivalent to reasonable accommodations were identified from 14 examples drawn from two case collections published by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare. ASD traits, ADHD traits, and workplace maladjustment were assessed using the Autism-Spectrum Quotient, the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale, and the Social Adaptation Self-evaluation Scale, respectively. Logistic regression analysis was performed to estimate odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals for workplace maladjustment. Results: Among workers with high ASD or ADHD trait scores, the odds of workplace maladjustment were higher when ASD- or ADHD-equivalent adjustments were not provided than when such adjustments were available; a comparable but less pronounced association was also observed among those with non-high trait scores. Conclusions: These quantitative findings suggest that workplace adjustments equivalent to reasonable accommodations are associated with a lower risk of workplace maladjustment and improved workplace adaptation among employees with high ASD or ADHD trait levels, and may also be beneficial for those with milder traits. Keywords: Attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), Autism spectrum disorder (ASD), Reasonable accommodation, Workplace maladjustment, Worker Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impairments in social communication, social interaction, and the presence of restricted and repetitive behaviors [1]. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a chronic neuropsychiatric disorder with core symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity [2]. These neurodevelopmental conditions often lead to difficulties in various aspects of daily and occupational functioning. Therefore, individuals with high levels of ASD or ADHD traits are generally considered to be socially disadvantaged. For example, high ASD or ADHD traits are more prevalent among workers with low socioeconomic status [3–6]. Additionally, individuals with high levels of ASD or ADHD traits are more likely to have depressive symptoms/depression [7–9]. Indeed, individuals with ASD often experience low and unstable employment [10]. Moreover, ADHD has been associated with underachievement at work [11] and frequent job changes [12]. However, in workplace settings, employees with ASD can thrive when provided with appropriate supports and an enabling environment, contributing a wide range of skills, distinctive perspectives, and high levels of productivity to their organizations [13]. Similarly, employees with ADHD can perform well and thrive when provided with appropriate workplace support [14]. These findings highlight the importance of workplace conditions that actively support neurodivergent employees, particularly through the implementation of reasonable accommodation. Reasonable accommodation is defined by the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) as “necessary and appropriate modification and adjustments not imposing a disproportionate or undue burden, where needed in a particular case, to ensure to persons with disabilities the enjoyment or exercise on an equal basis with others of all human rights and fundamental freedoms” [15]. While the CRPD provides a broad legal definition of reasonable accommodation, empirical research has proposed more operational definitions. In research on autistic employees, Petty et al. defined reasonable accommodations as measures that positively impact their well-being and job performance without adversely affecting non-autistic employees or the organization, and that are low cost and easy to implement [16]. Although several reports have documented examples of reasonable accommodation, including case collections published by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare [17], most existing evidence is derived from case studies or qualitative research, with limited quantitative evaluation. To address this evidence gap, we quantitatively examined workplace adaptation levels and the perceived need for adjustments equivalent to reasonable accommodations for ASD or ADHD in the general population. Most prior research on reasonable accommodation has focused on individuals with diagnosed ASD or ADHD or those with clearly elevated levels of these traits, and it remains unclear whether benefits of ASD- or ADHDequivalent workplace adjustments extend to workers with lower levels of ASD or ADHD traits in the general working population. This perspective is consistent with the concept of universal design in the workplace, which emphasizes creating work environments that accommodate diversity and promote inclusion, thereby benefiting not only individuals with pronounced neurodevelopmental traits but also the broader workforce. Universal design, as defined by the United Nations Development Programme, refers to “the design of products, environments, programmes, and services to be usable by all people, to the greatest extent possible, without the need for adaptation or specialized design” [18]. This study aimed to quantitatively examine whether workers with high or non-high ASD or ADHD trait levels differ in perceived workplace maladjustment according to the presence or absence of workplace adjustments equivalent to reasonable accommodations. We also examined whether they differ in perceived need for such adjustments. Methods Participants Participants comprised Japanese workers who completed a self-administered, Internet-based questionnaire survey conducted as a cross-sectional study in March 2025. The participant flowchart is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1. The sample was drawn from a panel of individuals registered with a Japanese online survey company (Rakuten Insight Inc., Tokyo, Japan), which comprises 279,808 registered members across all Japanese prefectures. A total of 6,624 registered members were randomly selected and invited to participate in the study. Screening was conducted on the basis of the following eligibility criteria: aged 20– 59 years and currently employed. Of these, 2,345 members responded to the screening, and 1,305 met the eligibility criteria and were granted access to the self-administered questionnaire. The survey system was designed to automatically submit responses upon completion, ensuring no missing data as all items had to be answered to finalize the survey. When the survey closed, 1,000 respondents were randomly selected by the survey company, and their responses were provided for analysis. This group of 1,000 participants constituted the final analytic sample. To control for potential bias related to sex and age, the sample was balanced by both attributes: the male-to-female ratio was 1:1, and equal numbers of participants were included in each of the following age groups: 20–29, 30–39, 40–49, and 50–59 years. This equal allocation was adopted to minimize the confounding effects of age and sex on the outcomes. Proportional allocation based on the actual working population would have resulted in underrepresentation of certain age–sex strata, reducing statistical precision and comparability across groups. Workers aged 60 years and older were excluded because the normal retirement age in Japan is 60 or 65 years. Sociodemographic characteristics Sociodemographic characteristics were obtained via a selfadministered questionnaire. These comprised age, sex, marital status (married or unmarried), socioeconomic status (annual household income, educational attainment, job type, and occupational position), and health-related behaviors (smoking status, drinking frequency, and leisure-time physical activity). Annual household was divided income into five groups (<3, 3–5, 5–8, 8–10, and 210 million yen; 150 yen μ 1 USD); educational attainment into three groups (high school or less, postsecondary non-university education, and university degree or higher); smoking status into three groups (current, former, or never smoker); drinking frequency into three groups (rarely, sometimes, or almost every day); and leisure-time physical activity into two groups (“exercise,” defined as light activity 21 time/ week to intense activity 23 times/week, vs. “no exercise”). Job type was categorized into six groups: company employee, professional (e.g., physician, lawyer, accountant), government employee, self-employed, contract/temporary Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine (2026) 31:62 2 of 12

worker, and part-time worker. Among these, employment status was classified into three groups: regular employment (company employee, professional, and government employee), non-regular employment (contract/temporary worker and part-time worker), and self-employed. Occupational position was categorized into four groups: executive/business owner/president, director/executive officer/ department head, section manager/assistant manager, and stafflevel/non-managerial position. Measures Workplace adjustments equivalent to reasonable accommodations for neurodevelopmental disorders were assessed using 14 items derived from two case collections published by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare: one collection on reasonable accommodations for persons with disabilities, including those with neurodevelopmental disorders [17], and another collection focusing specifically on neurodevelopmental disorders [19]. The items were compiled by reviewing multiple publicly available case examples and then consolidating them into 14 representative questions using an iterative process. The final set was judged to capture the main types of workplace adjustments relevant to neurodevelopmental disorders, including communication support, workload adjustment, sensory/environmental accommodation, scheduling flexibility, and supervisory consultation. These items were selected because they represent practical workplace adjustments commonly reported in official Japanese case examples and collectively cover major domains of accommodation relevant to workers with neurodevelopmental disorders. The 14 items are listed in Supplementary Table 1. For this study, workplace adjustments equivalent to reasonable accommodations were defined as adjustments that are equivalent to those required under the reasonable-accommodations framework, regardless of whether an employee has a formally diagnosed neurodevelopmental disorder. Workplace adjustments equivalent to reasonable accommodations were assessed using two sets of items: (1) whether each type of adjustment was implemented and (2) whether the worker perceived it as necessary. For implementation, respondents selected one of four options: ‘implemented,’ ‘partially implemented,’ ‘rarely implemented,’ or ‘not implemented.’ For analysis, the first two categories were combined as ‘implemented’ and the latter two as ‘not implemented.’ For perceived necessity, respondents selected one of five options: ‘strongly necessary,’ ‘necessary,’ ‘depends,’ ‘rarely necessary,’ or ‘not necessary.’ For analysis, the categories were grouped into three levels: ‘strongly necessary,’ ‘necessary,’ and the remaining three categories. The Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ) is a self-report questionnaire that assesses ASD traits in adults of normal intelligence [20]. It consists of 50 items rated on a fourpoint Likert scale (“definitely agree,” “slightly agree,” “slightly disagree,” and “definitely disagree”) across five subscales (10 items each): social skills, attention switching, attention to detail, communication, and imagination. For half the items, responses of “definitely agree” or “slightly agree” are scored as 1, whereas “slightly disagree” or “definitely disagree” are scored as 0; the remaining items are reverse-scored to minimize response bias. Total scores range from 0 to 50, with higher scores indicating greater ASD trait levels. A psychometric evaluation confirmed good test-retest reliability and internal consistency of the AQ. In the original study, test–retest reliability showed a strong correlation (r = 0.70). This study used the Japanese version translated by Wakabayashi et al. [21], which demonstrated similarly high reliability (r = 0.87) and has established validity and reliability. Cutoffscores suggesting likely ASD are 232 (original English version) and 233 (Japanese version). The validity of the cutoff scores has been supported by quantitative indices reported in previous studies. In the original English version, a cutoff of 232 correctly identified 79.3% of individuals with Asperger syndrome and high-functioning autism (AS/HFA; corresponding to ASD in current diagnostic criteria) while misclassifying only 2% of controls, indicating high sensitivity and specificity [20]. In the Japanese version, a cutoff of 233 identified 87.8% of individuals with AS/HFA (now classified under ASD) and misclassified only 3% of controls, demonstrating similarly high discriminative validity [21]. Participants were thus classified into two groups: the high ASD trait group (AQ 2 33) and the non-high group (AQ < 33). The adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) [22] was used to assess participants’ ADHD traits. This study employed the validated Japanese version of the ASRS [23]. The ASRS is an 18-item self-report questionnaire that screens for the 18 DSM-IV [24] symptoms of adult ADHD. The six-item ASRS Screener, a validated short form, was specifically used in this study. Participants rated how often each symptom occurred over the past 6 months. Total scores range from 0 (no symptoms) to 6 (severe symptoms), with scores 24 indicating suspected ADHD. The validity of this cutoffhas been supported by previous studies. The 6-item ASRS Screener has been shown to have high specificity (99.5%) and acceptable sensitivity (68.7%) for identifying adults with ADHD in validation studies, indicating strong discriminative performance [22]. Accordingly, a score of 24 was used to define suspected ADHD in the present study. Participants were therefore classified into two groups: the high ADHD trait group (ASRS 2 4) and the non-high group (ASRS < 4). The Social Adaptation Self-evaluation Scale (SASS) [25] was used to assess participants’ workplace maladjustment. The SASS is a scale developed to evaluate patients’ social motivation and behavior in depression and is widely used to assess social functioning. It consists of 21 items covering different domains of life, including work, leisure, family and non-family relationships, intellectual interests, satisfaction with social roles, and self-perceived ability to manage and control one’s environment. Each item is scored from 0 to 3, with higher scores indicating better social functioning; the total score ranges from 0 to 60. This Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine (2026) 31:62 3 of 12

study used the validated Japanese version of the SASS [26]. A cut-offscore of ̄25 has been suggested as an indication of social impairment [26]. The validity of this cutoffhas been supported by the Japanese validation study, which identified a cutoffof 25/26 as the optimal threshold and reported a sensitivity of 0.93 and a specificity of 0.51 [26]. In this study, workplace maladjustment was defined as having a SASS score of 25 or below. Sample size calculation The sample size was calculated based on the odds ratio (OR) for workplace maladjustment associated with developmental disorders. Because the prevalence of workplace maladjustment in the general working population has not been well established in previous literature, we used the prevalence of depressive symptoms as a proxy, given the strong negative correlation between depressive symptoms and workplace maladjustment (μ = 10.683, p < 0.001) [26]. We referenced a previous study [27] to determine the calculation parameters. The parameters were as follows: : The prevalence of ASD-equivalent individuals (high ASD trait levels, AQ 2 33) was assumed to be 5% of the working population. : The prevalence of depressive symptoms among individuals with non-high ASD trait levels (AQ < 33) was approximately 11%. : The OR for depressive symptoms among individuals with high ASD trait levels ranged from 3 to 16, depending on the type of job stress. To ensure a conservative estimate, we adopted an OR of 3 (the minimum effect size reported), thereby securing sufficient statistical power even under stricter assumptions. With ¡ = 0.05 (two-sided) and 80% power, the required sample size was calculated to be 910 participants using the OR test for two-bin proportions. Statistical analyses Descriptive statistics were performed to summarize participant characteristics and the implementation and perceived necessity of workplace adjustments equivalent to reasonable accommodations. Logistic regression analysis was conducted to estimate the odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for workplace maladjustment. Two logistic regression models were constructed, each using a four-category grouping defined by trait level (high vs. nonhigh) and the presence or absence of reasonable accommodation–equivalent adjustments. In both models, workers with non-high trait scores who received reasonable accommodation–equivalent adjustments served as the reference group. One model examined ASD traits, and the other examined ADHD traits. Univariate analyses were first performed, followed by multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, marital status, annual household income, educational attainment, job type, occupational position, smoking status, drinking frequency, and leisuretime physical activity. Subsequently, we conducted stratified analyses by employment status and by sex. For the stratified analyses by employment status, we excluded self-employed individuals and performed analyses separately for regular and non-regular employees. Using a chi-square test, we compared the perceived necessity of reasonable accommodation–equivalent workplace adjustments between workers with high versus non-high ASD traits and between those with high versus non-high ADHD traits. Regarding perceived necessity, responses were categorized into three groups—strongly necessary, necessary, and other—considering the possibility that some respondents might select “necessary,” even when adjustments were not strictly required, if they perceived potential benefits. “Other” comprised the response options: “casedependent,” “not strongly necessary,” and “not necessary.” Two-tailed p-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. All analyses were conducted using SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 24.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Ethics statement Ethical approval was obtained from the International University of Health and Welfare Ethics Committee (No. 24TA-143). The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the 1964 Declaration of Helsinki and its later amendments. Completion of the anonymous online questionnaire was considered as indicating informed consent, and the requirement for written informed consent was waived by the International University of Health and Welfare Ethics Committee. Supplementary Table 2 shows the stratified analyses of the associations of ASD and ADHD traits with workplace maladjustment by employment status and sex. This table presents the results of stratified analyses of Table 3 by employment status and sex. Stratified analyses by employment status and sex yielded results that were generally consistent with the main analyses. Among regular employees, the associations between ASD traits, ADHD traits, workplace adjustments, and workplace maladjustment showed similar directions and magnitudes to those observed in the overall sample. Table 4 presents the perceived necessity of reasonable accommodation–equivalent workplace adjustments among employees with high versus non-high ASD or ADHD traits. Workers with high ASD trait scores perceived such adjustments as strongly necessary more frequently than those with non-high scores for only 3 of the 14 adjustment types: multiple modes of instruction delivery (non-high ASD: 9.8%, high ASD: 19.2%; p = 0.030), task assignment considering individual strengths (9.9% vs. 19.2%; p = 0.035), and consideration for sensory stimuli (10.7% vs. 19.2%; p = 0.040). By contrast, workers with high ADHD trait scores perceived almost all types of reasonable accommodation–equivalent workplace adjustments as more strongly necessary than those with non-high scores, except for one item (regular meetings with supervisors). Discussion In this study, we examined the associations of ASD or ADHD traits and reasonable accommodation–equivalent workplace adjustments with workplace maladjustment. Even among workers with non-high ASD or ADHD trait scores, the odds of workplace maladjustment were significantly higher in workplaces without reasonable accommodation–equivalent adjustments than in those with such adjustments. Workers with high ASD or ADHD trait scores showed higher odds of workplace maladjustment than those with non-high trait scores, regardless of the presence or absence of reasonable accommodation–equivalent adjustments. Furthermore, among workers with high ASD or ADHD trait scores, the odds of workplace maladjustment were higher in the absence than in the presence of reasonable accommodation–equivalent adjustments. Regarding the perceived necessity of reasonable accommodation– equivalent workplace adjustments, most adjustments were perceived as equally necessary by workers with high and non-high ASD trait scores. By contrast, workers with high ADHD trait scores tended to perceive such adjustments as more strongly necessary than those with non-high ADHD trait scores. Workers with high ASD or ADHD trait scores exhibited higher odds of workplace maladjustment than those with lower trait scores, irrespective of reasonable accommodation–equivalent adjustments. Moreover, among workers with high trait scores, maladjustment odds were substantially elevated in workplaces lacking such adjustments compared with those providing them. Previous case studies have reported the potential effectiveness of reasonable accommodations for workers with ASD and ADHD. The present cross-sectional study provides quantitative evidence suggesting an association between similar adjustments and better job adaptation among workers exhibiting high levels of ASD and ADHD traits. Past reports have identified effective workplace accommodations for autistic employees, including consistent schedules and role clarity, task-organizing tools, reduced unstructured time, clear/direct communication with reminders and reassurance, organizational and coworker support, supportive leadership, advance notice of tasks, opportunities for breaks, appropriate positive feedback, and targeted environmental modifications (e.g., lighting adjustments, headphones, and seating to facilitate interaction) [28, 29]. For employees with ADHD, beneficial measures emphasize quiet or private workspaces, flexible hours, frequent breaks in long meetings, redistribution of tedious tasks, and broad use of assistive tools to support attention, memory, and organization (e.g., to-do lists, electronic planners/calendars, alarms/timers, reminders, notetaking systems, spellcheckers, templates, noise-canceling headphones, fidgets, and key/object finders) [14]. In the present study, the odds of maladjustment were higher among individuals with high levels of ASD traits than among those with high levels of ADHD traits. Previous register-based research has shown that, among young adults with neurodevelopmental disorders, ASDs are associated with the greatest burden of work incapacity, exceeding that observed for ADHD and learning disabilities [30], suggesting that, compared with individuals with ADHD, those with ASD may be particularly vulnerable to workplace maladjustment. Although certain adjustments—for example, considerations for sensory stimuli [28]—are often regarded as particularly relevant to ASD, our findings demonstrate comparable associations among individuals with high levels of ADHD traits. This may indicate that workplaces implementing such adjustments cultivate a generally supportive environment that facilitates adaptation, even when the specific modifications are not directly aligned with an individual’s predominant neurodevelopmental traits. Among workers with lower ASD or ADHD trait scores, those in workplaces lacking reasonable accommodation– equivalent adjustments showed significantly higher odds of workplace maladjustment compared with those in workplaces offering such adjustments. These cross-sectional findings suggest that such adjustments may reduce maladjustment risk even among workers without pronounced ASD or ADHD traits, potentially creating more comfortable and supportive environments for the broader workforce. This aligns with universal design [18] principles, which posit that accommodations for employees with developmental disabilities also benefit those without. Previous studies support this, showing that implementing universal design in facilities enhances human performance, health, wellness, and social participation [31]. The findings from our study empirically support the concept that workplace environments designed with inclusivity principles can enhance well-being and retention across diverse employee groups, reinforcing the value of universal design in organizational health promotion. It remains unclear why workers with lower ASD or ADHD trait scores showed a similar but weaker pattern than those with high trait scores. Therefore, future longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to clarify the underlying mechanisms. These results also suggest that workplace adjustments equivalent to reasonable accommodations may be beneficial not only for employees with pronounced neurodevelopmental traits but also for those with milder or subclinical traits, which supports the broader applicability of inclusive workplace practices. The stratified analyses by employment status and sex supported the robustness of our main findings. Because employment structure and work style differ substantially across regular and non-regular employees in Japan, and because the meaning of workplace adjustments may vary by sex, these factors could potentially confound the associations examined in this study. However, the stratified analyses showed generally consistent associations between ASD and ADHD traits, workplace adjustments, and workplace maladjustment across employment status and between males and females. These findings suggest that the main results were not materially driven by employment structure or sex, although residual confounding cannot be completely ruled out. Regarding the perceived necessity of reasonable accommodation–equivalent workplace adjustments, most adjustments were perceived as equally necessary by workers with high and non-high ASD trait scores, contrary to our hypothesis that workers with high ASD trait scores would perceive a stronger need for each workplace adjustment than those with non-high ASD trait scores. In previous research, participants with ASD had significantly more emotional self-awareness difficulties than those without ASD [32]. Such findings suggest that individuals with high levels of ASD traits may struggle to accurately appraise their emotional strain and workplace difficulties. Therefore, the lack of a stronger perceived need for ASD-related adjustments among workers with high ASD trait scores in our study may indicate limited awareness of their own difficulties and support needs rather than a genuinely lower requirement for such adjustments. These findings thus highlight the importance of awareness and proactive support from colleagues, supervisors, and others in the workplace. Notably, in our study, workers with high ADHD trait scores tended to perceive such adjustments as more strongly necessary than those with non-high ADHD trait scores, because workers with high ADHD traits may be more aware of their need for such adjustments and therefore more likely to initiate requests for support. It should be noted that workplace maladjustment in this study should not be interpreted as an objective risk factor in itself. Rather, it reflects workers’ subjective perceptions of their workplace environment and the extent to which they perceive a need for support or interventions. Therefore, our findings should be understood as indicating how workers with different ASD or ADHD trait levels perceive their work environment and the potential relevance of workplace adjustments, rather than as evidence that workplace maladjustment objectively exists as a workplace characteristic. Limitations This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, because of its cross-sectional design, causal relationships between ASD or ADHD traits, workplace adjustments, and workplace maladjustment cannot be determined. Second, the information about ASD or ADHD traits, workplace adjustments, and perceived necessity was based on self-reported data, which may be subject to reporting bias or inaccuracies. Third, although participants were randomly selected from a nationwide online panel of Japanese workers, generalisability may be limited to populations with limited Internet access or lower digital literacy. Future research should adopt longitudinal or intervention designs to elucidate the causal mechanisms underlying these associations and to assess the long-term effects of workplace adjustments equivalent to reasonable accommodations—those enhancing employees’ workplace adaptation—on well-being and job retention. Fourth, although the SASS has been validated as a reliable indicator of general social functioning, it does not specifically assess workplace-related aspects of adjustment, such as relationships with supervisors, job satisfaction, or work-specific stressors. Therefore, the use of SASS may not fully capture workplace-specific maladjustment. Fifth, because stratified Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine (2026) 31:62 10 of 12

analyses inherently reduce the sample size within each subgroup, the statistical precision was lower than in the main analyses. In particular, the number of non-regular employees was relatively small, and the estimates for this subgroup should be interpreted with caution. Conclusions The present findings from this cross-sectional study quantitatively suggest that workplace adjustments equivalent to reasonable accommodations are associated with a lower risk of workplace maladjustment—and consequently with greater workplace adaptation—among employees with high ASD or ADHD trait levels. This underscores the critical importance of providing such support to promote their adjustment and continued employment. ABSTRACT Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is common and associated with relationship difficulties, which may influence entry into parenthood. Methods We used Finnish population register data to follow 759,430 individuals born in 1982–1993 and examined how ADHD is associated with the likelihood and timing of a first birth. ADHD was identified using healthcare diagnoses and prescription records. We estimated discrete-time event history models and sibling fixed-effects models to account for shared family background. All analyses were conducted separately for women and men. Results In models adjusted for age and birth cohort, ADHD was associated with a lower likelihood of a first birth (ages 18–38) (men OR 0.92; women OR 0.90). After adjusting for partnership characteristics, the association reversed (men OR 1.07; women OR 1.09). All age-stratified analyses showed that ADHD was associated with a higher likelihood of first birth at ages 18–23, but with a lower likelihood at ages 24–30 and 31–38, indicating earlier entry into parenthood among individuals with ADHD. Results from sibling fixed-effects models were broadly similar to the population-level estimates, suggesting limited confounding by shared family background. Conclusions ADHD is associated not only with earlier entry into parenthood but also with a reduced overall probability of having a first child. Accounting for partnership status is important, as it largely explains the negative association observed in age-adjusted models. These findings highlight partnerships as a key pathway linking ADHD to fertility outcomes. INTRODUCTION Investigating how attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is related to adulthood outcomes is societally relevant since ADHD is among the most common neurodevelopmental disorders, affecting an estimated 5%–10% of school-aged children and 2%–5% of adults.1 Neurodevelopmental disorder diagnoses, ADHD in particular, have become increasingly prevalent in recent decades. Prior research on ADHD has focused on various outcomes—such as treatment, life satisfaction, criminality, labour-market and educational attachment2–8—but surprisingly, its links to fertility have not yet been investigated. ADHD diagnoses are more common among boys, who are also diagnosed earlier than girls.9 Symptom presentation differs by gender: boys more often display hyperactivity, impulsivity and other externalising behaviours, whereas girls tend to show internalising symptoms such as anxiety and depression as well as academic underachievement.10 Individuals with ADHD often experience greater difficulties in peer and social relationships, with some studies suggesting stronger impairments among women.11 12 Individuals with ADHD are more likely than their peers to engage in risk behaviours such as smoking, have a lower age at first intercourse and experience teenage pregnancy,8 13 which suggests that ADHD may be related to earlier age at first birth and having a child outside the context of coresidential partnerships. Although ADHD has been linked to various aspects of social functioning, its relationship to childbearing remains largely underexplored. Together, previous research suggests that ADHD may influence not only whether individuals have children but also the timing of first birth. Core ADHD-related challenges—such as difficulties with executive functioning, attention and impulse control—can lead to forgetfulness and disorganisation, which often strain partnerships and increase the risk of separation.14 15 These challenges may also increase the likelihood of remaining unpartnered. Previous studies have examined ADHD in romantic relationships, documenting lower relationship satisfaction, more frequent conflict and higher risks of separation among individuals with ADHD compared with those without.16–20 Couples in which at least one partner has ADHD are also more likely to experience stress and depression than couples without ADHD.21 This WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC ⇒Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is linked to relationship difficulties and early sexual behaviour, but evidence on fertility patterns and timing is limited. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS ⇒Individuals with ADHD are less likely to have children overall, but those who do become parents earlier. Accounting for partnerships reverses the association with first births, highlighting partnership dynamics as a key mechanism. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY ⇒Supporting relationship stability and reproductive health among individuals with ADHD may help reduce inequalities in family formation. In this study, we extend previous research by examining how ADHD is related to the likelihood and timing of a first birth. We also assess the role of partnership status and a partner’s ADHD diagnosis in shaping these associations. To our knowledge, we are the first to examine the link between ADHD and family formation. METHODS Data We use Finnish total population register data for cohorts born between 1982 and 1993 (371,563 women; 387,867 men). The sample is restricted to individuals born in Finland since we have complete linkage of education, healthcare and sociodemographic data throughout the study period for these persons. All methods were carried out in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations. Informed consent is not required for register-based studies in Finland because participants are not contacted. The register-based data cannot be shared due to legal restrictions, but access can be applied for through Statistics Finland and THL. The main explanatory variable is ADHD, and it is measured using both diagnostic information from specialised healthcare registers and data on prescription medication purchases. The ADHD diagnostic information (ICD-10 codes, F90) is derived from the specialised healthcare registers and the medication information (ATC-codes, NO6B) from the prescription register of Social Insurance Institution of Finland. All psychotropic medication is prescribed by clinical doctors, and all persons residing in Finland are entitled to reimbursement for medication expenses by the Social Insurance Institution of Finland, thus increasing the validity of our measure. The partner’s disorders are measured in the same way as the index person’s disorders. In the analysis, ADHD is treated as a time-invariant variable because diagnostic criteria require that symptoms were present already in childhood. The outcome variable is a time-varying indicator of first birth, measured as the occurrence of a first child in a given year between ages 18 and 38. The control variables are year of birth, age, number of partners, own education and current partnership status. All control variables are fully time varying. Year of birth is a categorical variable and varies from 1982 to 1993. Age is a categorical variable and has values from 18 to 38. Own highest (achieved) education was categorised into basic, secondary (including vocational and general tracks) and tertiary education (including those with a bachelor’s degree or higher). The current partnership status was categorised into having a partner without ADHD, having a partner with ADHD and not having a partner. Partnerships are defined as coresidential partnerships, combining both marriages and cohabitations. Number of partners was the highest partner order at each observation point. METHODS We estimated discrete-time event history models of first birth using logistic regression and person-year data, with age as the time scale. Individuals were followed from age 18 until the first birth or censoring. The outcome was a time-varying binary indicator for having a first child in year t, predicted by time-invariant ADHD status. All time-varying covariates were lagged by 1 year (t–1). Education was measured as the highest level completed by the end of year t–1. All analyses were conducted separately for men and women. We estimated both pooled models covering ages 18–38 and agestratified models for ages 18–23, 24–30 and 31–38. To examine potential mechanisms, we fitted stepwise models: model 1 adjusted for age and year of birth; model 2 additionally adjusted for educational attainment; and model 3 further adjusted for current partnership status and number of partners. Results from these models are presented as ORs. To examine age-related heterogeneity in more detail, we additionally estimated interaction models between ADHD and age across ages 18–38. To assess whether the observed associations were driven by shared family background, we additionally estimated sibling fixed-effects discrete-time event history models. These models compared full siblings within the same family and controlled for all time-invariant characteristics shared by siblings, including early-life familial and socioeconomic factors. The sibling fixedeffects analyses include all full siblings from families with two or more children. Identification is based on within-family differences, meaning that only sibships in which siblings differ in ADHD status contribute to the estimation of the ADHD effect. The sibling fixed-effects models were estimated using conditional logistic regression with family-level strata. All analyses were conducted using Stata V.17.0. The main analysis code is available on GitHub. RESULTS The descriptive results are reported at the end of the observation period, that is, in 2020, when individuals were aged 27–38. Young adults with ADHD were less likely to have children, had lower levels of education and were less often in partnerships (table 1). ADHD was associated with a roughly 10 percentagepoint higher prevalence of childlessness among both men and women, and with an age at first birth approximately 2 years younger compared with individuals without ADHD. Models 1–2 capture the overall association between ADHD and first birth, including pathways operating through partnership formation and stability (table 2). Model 3, which conditions on current partnership status and number of prior partners, can be interpreted as estimating the association under a hypothetical scenario in which individuals with and without ADHD have similar partnership trajectories. Across ages 18–38, ADHD is associated with lower first-birth odds in models that adjust only for age and cohort (men M1 OR=0.918, 95% CI 0.895 to 0.942; women M1 OR=0.900, 95% CI 0.873 to 0.928). Adding education explains part of this negative association (men M2 OR=0.941; women M2 OR=0.921). After additionally accounting for current partnership status and number of prior partners, the association reverses and becomes positive overall (men M3 OR=1.071, 95% CI 1.044 to 1.098; women M3 OR=1.089, 95% CI 1.059 to 1.120). This reversal indicates that conditional on similar partnership histories, individuals with ADHD would have a higher likelihood of entering parenthood. These findings suggest that ADHD is associated with lower rates of partnership formation and stability, contributing to a lower overall probability of first birth. Next, we estimated models stratified by age group. At ages 18–23, ADHD is linked to higher first-birth odds in all models (men M3 OR=1.324, 95% CI 1.243 to 1.411; women M3 OR=1.369, 95% CI 1.308 to 1.433). At ages 24–30, the association is negative in all models for women (M3 OR=0.928, 95% CI 0.882 to 0.976), whereas for men it changes from negative in M1 and M2 (OR=0.82–0.85) to slightly positive (but not statistically significant) in M3 (OR=1.023, 95% CI 0.976 Protected by copyright, including for uses related to text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies. . We also conducted a robustness analysis by examining whether the results remained similar when ADHD was measured for all individuals by age 27. The results were largely unchanged, with only a slight strengthening of the association (online supplemental appendix table A2 and figure A2). To explore how partner characteristics are associated with entry into parenthood, we further estimated age-stratified models including interactions between own ADHD status and current partnership status (no partner, partner without ADHD, partner with ADHD). This approach was motivated by the possibility that the association between ADHD and first birth may be amplified when both partners have ADHD (c.f. previous findings on mental health disorders).22 23 However, analyses stratified by partner ADHD status did not indicate meaningful effect modification (online supplemental appendix figure A3). DISCUSSION This study examined how ADHD is associated with the likelihood and timing of first births among young adults using Finnish total population register data. The results show that young adults with ADHD are less likely to have a first birth between ages 18 and 38 but controlling for partnership status reverses this association. These findings are consistent with previous studies showing that ADHD is associated with interpersonal difficulties and relationship instability17 18 and underscores the role of partnerships as a key mechanism connecting ADHD to family formation outcomes. Furthermore, although individuals with ADHD were less likely to have a first birth overall, those who became parents did so at younger ages, suggesting less postponement and potentially a greater role of less planned childbearing, including births outside stable partnerships. Some support for this interpretation comes from our additional analyses, which indicate that individuals with ADHD may in some cases have a higher likelihood of having children outside coresidential partnerships. This pattern is consistent with research linking ADHD to impulsivity, earlier sexual debut and an increased likelihood of teenage pregnancy.8 13 Sibling fixed-effects analyses further showed that these associations were broadly similar when comparing full siblings within the same family, suggesting that shared family background Figure 1 Average marginal effects (AMEs) of own ADHD on the probability of a first birth by age (interaction between own ADHD and age). This strengthens the interpretation that individual-level life-course processes, rather than unobserved family-level factors, play a central role in shaping fertility outcomes among individuals with ADHD. Robustness analyses confirmed the stability of our findings. Restricting ADHD measurement to diagnoses made by age 27 produced nearly identical results. In addition, the consistency between population-level and sibling fixed-effects estimates supports the robustness of the results to confounding by shared family background. Together, these analyses strengthen the conclusion that partnership formation and stability are key pathways in the relationship between ADHD and first births. The strengths of this study include the use of comprehensive nationwide register data, measurement of ADHD based on healthcare diagnoses and medication records, and the ability to link individual and partner characteristics. Nonetheless, several limitations should be acknowledged. ADHD prevalence in these cohorts reflects the diagnostic practices of the time. However, our additional analyses comparing early and late cohorts did not indicate systematic attenuation of associations (available from author). ADHD is measured as a binary variable in our data, and we were, therefore, unable to examine variation in severity even though ADHD represents a continuous spectrum of symptoms and functional impairment. In addition, while partnership status and number of partners were included, information on partnership quality or informal relationships such as living-aparttogether unions was not available. Finally, our analyses capture fertility outcomes only up to ages 27–38 and, therefore, do not reflect completed fertility, as follow-up ends at age 38 at the latest and earlier for younger cohorts. As the age at first birth has increased across cohorts, measures focusing on early adulthood increasingly reflect differences in the timing of childbearing rather than completed fertility. Future research should examine whether the associations observed here persist across the full reproductive life course once these cohorts reach older ages, particularly given that ADHD has become increasingly common in more recent cohorts. Overall, this study highlights partnership dynamics as a central mechanism through which ADHD influences family formation. The results show that young adults with ADHD are less likely to have children overall, but those who become parents do so at a younger age than their peers without ADHD. By showing that these patterns persist after accounting for shared family background, the findings underscore the importance of relationship trajectories and life-course timing in understanding fertility outcomes among individuals with ADHD. Supporting stable relationships and reproductive health among individuals with ADHD may help reduce fertility disparities. Understanding these dynamics is particularly relevant in light of the rising prevalence of ADHD. Contributors SKB designed the study, conducted the analyses and drafted the manuscript. ATTENTION AND HYPERACTIVITY A Meta-Analysis of the Prevalence of ADHD in Youth Across Racial and Ethnic Groups Andrea L. Glenna, Shelby Hunterb, and Olivia K. Thompsona aCenter for Youth Development and Intervention, Department of Psychology, The University of Alabama; bDepartment of Psychology, Patton State Hospital ABSTRACT Objective: To compare the prevalence of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) among Asian, Black, Latino, and White children and adolescents across studies while considering method of diagnosis. Method: Studies were included if they reported the prevalence of ADHD among at least two different racial/ethnic groups in an unselected population. Studies were grouped based on the method of diagnosis; studies involving juvenile offenders were analyzed separately. A total of 9,019 articles were retrieved and 371 articles were evaluated. After excluding studies with overlapping datasets, 28 studies were included in the population-based meta-analysis, and five studies were included in the meta-analysis involving juvenile offenders. Results: For studies asking caregivers if the child had received a diagnosis of ADHD (k = 23), the pooled prevalence of ADHD was lower for Latino (6.1%) and Asian (2.6%) youth than White youth (10.5%); the prevalence in Black youth (9.4%) was not significantly different from White youth. Among juvenile offenders (k = 5), the prevalence of ADHD was significantly lower in Black (19.1%) and Latino (17.0%) youth than in White youth (31.9%). Conclusions: The present study finds some racial/ethnic differences in prevalence rates of ADHD. The study demonstrates that the type of sample and method for assessing ADHD diagnosis are important to consider. Introduction ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with a range of negative long-term outcomes, including problems with academic performance, strained relation ships with caregivers, peers, and teachers, poor health outcomes, and increased risk for criminal justice invol vement (Egbert et al., 2018; Lifford et al., 2008; Rogers et al., 2015; Scholtens et al., 2013; von Polier et al., 2012). Several forms of treatment have been found to be effec tive in reducing ADHD symptoms (Coghill et al., 2023), including medication, behavioral interventions, and educational services (Wolraich et al., 2019). However, receipt of these treatments requires that children are appropriately identified and diagnosed. Several studies have documented disparities in ADHD diagnosis and treatment across racial and ethnic groups with White children being more likely to receive a diagnosis (Davis et al., 2021; Hall et al., 2023; Morgan et al., 2013). Other studies, including a recent meta-analysis (Cénat et al., 2024) have found little evidence of racial and ethnic differences in ADHD prevalence in youth (Danielson et al., 2024). Understanding whether there are racial and ethnic disparities in ADHD diagnosis rates is important for several reasons. Disparities in prevalence may indicate inequities in sequence of steps necessary to obtain a diagnosis. This includes identifying children in need of assessment, which often depends on teacher and/or parent knowledge, access to resources for obtaining a diagnosis, and the receipt of comprehensive, evidence- based, unbiased assessments of ADHD. Identifying potential racial differences in prevalence may also high light areas where targeted interventions and policy changes may be needed. Awareness of prevalence differ ences may also spur the development of culturally sen sitive approaches to improving ADHD awareness and knowledge in families, and in reducing the stigma asso ciated with an ADHD diagnosis (Slobodin & Masalha, 2020). This may ultimately improve outcomes for underserved groups. When evaluating whether racial or ethnic dispari ties in ADHD diagnosis rates exist, it is important to consider how different studies determine the ADHD diagnosis of the study participants. caregivers are asked whether their child has ever received a diagnosis of ADHD from a physician or mental health professional. This provides information about which children are receiving diagnoses within the context of existing educational and medical sys tems. However, it is unclear from this method whether differences in diagnosis rates between demo graphic groups are because of true differences in symptom levels, or because of differences in the iden tification of ADHD symptoms by caregivers and tea chers, and/or differences in access to mental health services needed to obtain an assessment and diagno sis. For example, studies have found that caregivers from minoritized groups have less familiarity with or knowledge about ADHD and related treatments (Bussing et al., 2012; Coker et al., 2009), which may make these caregivers less likely to seek a diagnosis for their child. Additional issues such as potential bias in teachers’ perceptions of children’s behavior, cultural differences in perceptions of behavior, mis trust of institutions, and financial considerations may also differentially affect diagnosis rates across differ ent racial and ethnic groups (Moody, 2016; Nasol et al., 2019). To determine whether there are actual differences in ADHD symptoms levels between racial and ethnic groups, some studies have assessed ADHD symptoms within the context of the study to determine diagnosis rates. By screening every child in a classroom, for exam ple, this method eliminates reliance on proper identifi cation and access to ADHD assessments and may be more likely to accurately assess whether there are true differences in diagnosis rates between demographic groups. One study used both methods for determining ADHD prevalence. Coker et al. (2016) assessed ADHD prevalence in a sample of 10th graders in two ways. First, they asked parents to rate their child’s symptoms of ADHD and used this data to determine whether the child would meet criteria for ADHD or not. Then, parents were asked if a physician or health professional had ever told them that their child had ADHD. They found that 9% of White children meet criteria for ADHD based on parent-reported symptoms, but 19% reported having received a diagnosis from a professional. The opposite pattern was true for Black children, in which 13% met criteria for ADHD based on parent-reported symptoms, but only 10% reported hav ing received a diagnosis. These results suggest that there may be true racial differences in actual ADHD symp toms levels (9% in White children compared to 13% in Black children), but there also may be differences in the ability to obtain a diagnosis of ADHD (19% of White children had received a diagnosis versus 10% of Black children). The present study is novel because it uses meta- analysis to test whether these findings by Coker et al. (2016) hold true across a wide range of studies. We conducted separate meta-analyses for studies that con ducted a diagnostic assessment of ADHD as part of the study and studies that relied on receipt of a diagnosis from a physician or mental-health professional. Receiving a diagnosis would require that a child pre viously be identified and then tested, which would necessarily require resources from the school and/or caregiver. In contrast, screening all youth for ADHD symptoms may provide a more objective measure of the true prevalence of ADHD in different racial and ethnic groups. We hypothesized that potential racial disparities in ADHD diagnosis would be larger in studies using caregiver reports of receiving a diagnosis, which rely on appropriate identification and diagnosis, compared to studies that directly assess ADHD symptoms in youth. The present study expands on a recently published meta-analysis by Cénat et al. (2024) that examined racial and ethnic differences in ADHD prevalence. Cénat et al. (2024) did not find differences in prevalence between ethnic groups, or between Black and White children. They did find that the prevalence rate for Asian children was marginally lower than the prevalence rates for Black and White children. Because this study combined stu dies that used different methods for determining ADHD diagnoses, it is unclear how these results may change when examining studies with different methodologies separately. In addition, the meta-analysis by Cénat et al. (2024) included several studies that involved special or clinical populations such as youth with autism spectrum disorder or youth in the juvenile justice system, which are likely not representative of youth generally (for additional detail, see Supplementary Table S1). The present study includes only studies with population- based samples, and separates studies based on method of ADHD diagnosis. A separate analysis is also con ducted for studies of children in the juvenile justice system. Methods Identification and Selection of Studies In the present study, we used the reporting guidelines from the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA; Moher et al., 2009). A literature search was conducted using the major search engines PsycINFO, Medline, PubMed, and Web of Science. The electronic search was 674 A. L. GLENN ET AL.

completed in May 2025. Search terms are available in the Supplementary Materials. Following the search and retrieval process, identi fied articles were reviewed to determine whether they met the inclusion criteria described below (Figure 1). The initial search yielded a total of 9,019 articles. After removing duplicates, the first and third authors independently assessed the titles and abstracts of 3,584 articles. If one or both raters indicated that an article should be retained for full- text evaluation, the article was included in the next step. The 23 studies already identified in the meta- analysis by Cénat et al. (2024) were directly consid ered for inclusion. Inclusions and Exclusion Criteria Journal articles were included if they met the following criteria: (1) the article was peer reviewed; (2) the study reported empirical data on the prevalence of ADHD separately for at least two of the following racial/ethnic groups (Black, White, Latino, and Asian); (3) the study was conducted in countries where Black people live in a minority context and White people of European *Coker et al.
