ancestry live in a majority context (United States, Canada, European and Eastern European countries, Russia, Australia, New Zealand); (4) participants in the study were 0–18 years of age, (5) the study was pub lished in English. We excluded studies that examined special populations such as youth with autism or other significant psychological disorders. We also excluded studies in which youth were pre-screened and selected for higher levels of ADHD symptoms, which would affect prevalence rates. We included studies involving juvenile offenders, but these studies were analyzed in a separate analysis. We limited studies to those pub lished after 1994 aligning with the publication of DSM- IV. Regarding ADHD diagnosis, we included studies that reported an ADHD diagnosis as a category (yes/no) and excluded studies that only reported mean levels of ADHD symptoms, as prevalence rates could not be determined from these studies. Within the studies that utilized a categorical ADHD diagnosis, we divided them into two groups. The first group consisted of studies that conducted a diagnostic assessment or in which researchers evaluated symptom levels to approximate diagnoses (e.g., parents reported on the child’s ADHD symptoms); the second group consisted of studies that relied on parent- or self-reporting that the child had received a diagnosis from a physician or mental-health professional. Coding The two raters (first and third authors) identified 371 articles to be retained for full-text evaluation. Both raters independently reviewed the full text of these arti cles and coded them based on the inclusion and exclu sion criteria. Each article that was excluded was coded based on the reason for exclusion (Figure 1). Each included article was categorized into one of four groups: (1) studies assessing ADHD symptoms to determine a diagnosis, (2) studies assessing receipt of diagnosis from a physician or mental health professional at any point in the child’s lifetime, (3) studies assessing a current diagnosis from a physician or mental health professional, and (4) studies involving juvenile offen ders. The first and third authors met to discuss discre pancies in the coding for inclusion/exclusion criteria, re-reviewed the articles, and came to a consensus about each article. From the 371 full-text articles, 39 met the inclusion criteria for the main meta-analysis, and five met criteria for the meta-analysis involving juvenile offenders. One of the five studies involving juvenile offenders included an age range from 10 to 21 (Harzke et al., 2012); due to the small number of studies involving juvenile offenders, we decided to include this study. Data in the Harzke et al. (2012) study were from youth committed to juvenile facilities, and 71.3% were 16 or younger at the time of commitment. Of the 39 studies meeting inclusion criteria for the main meta- analysis, many included data from the same overarching study or dataset (Supplementary Table S2). When mul tiple studies were identified from the same overarching study, studies were selected to maximize the number of participants included and to avoid overlapping data. Eleven studies were excluded due to overlapping data, resulting in a total of 28 studies included in the meta- analysis reflecting the general population of youth (Supplementary Table S2). Of these, six studies assessed ADHD symptoms in youth, and were therefore ana lyzed separately. The remaining 23 assessed lifetime or current ADHD diagnoses. No studies involving juvenile offenders utilized overlapping data. All of the included studies were conducted in the United States. Table 1 depicts the characteristics of the included studies in the population-based meta-analysis. The table is organized based on whether the ADHD diag nosis was based on report of a diagnosis received or based on a threshold of reported symptoms. Table 1 also lists studies included in the meta-analysis of studies involving juvenile offenders. Meta-Analysis Analyses were performed on Comprehensive Meta Analysis Version 4. A random effects model was utilized to estimate overall pooled prevalence to account for expected variance across samples. For subgroup analyses, a mixed effects analysis was utilized. Heterogeneity was assessed in each meta-analysis using the I2 statistic, Q, and prediction intervals (PIs). The I2 statistic reflects the proportion of total variation in summary estimates across studies that is due to true heterogeneity rather than sampling error. PIs provide an estimate of the range within the true prevalence is expected to fall in compar able populations, reflecting the dispersion of estimates across studies. Sensitivity analyses were conducted in each meta-analysis to assess the potential for publication bias and robustness of summary estimates. These included the calculation of Egger’s regression intercept, visual inspection of funnel plots, and a leave-one-out (one-study-removed) analysis to determine whether any one study had a disproportionate influence on the sum mary estimate. Given the use of a random-effects model, which tends to give relatively more weight to smaller studies (Borenstein et al., 2021), it was anticipated that smaller studies might disproportionately impact the sum mary estimate. The study consisted of three separate meta-analyses. The first analysis included studies that used ADHD symptom ratings in which researchers evaluated symp tom levels to approximate diagnoses (k = 6). The second analysis included studies that used lifetime or current diagnosis of ADHD in which the caregiver was asked whether the child had ever received or currently had a diagnosis of ADHD from a mental health professional (k = 25). Separate sub-analyses for lifetime (k = 19) and current diagnoses (k = 7) can be found in the Supplementary Materials. The third analysis included studies that included juvenile offenders (k = 5). Overall estimates of ADHD prevalence are provided for each group of studies, along with prevalence estimates for each race/ethnicity within that group. Subgroup ana lyses were conducted to test the effect of race/ethnicity on the overall prevalence estimate for each group of studies. For groups with an adequate number of studies, meta-regression analyses using Method of Moments (also known as the DerSimonian and Laird method; Borenstein et al., 2021) were conducted to assess the unique impact of each racial/ethnic group on ADHD prevalence. Meta-regression analyses were conducted when at least 10 studies were available for a given mod erator, consistent with commonly cited guidance aimed at ensuring sufficient power and stable estimates, though it is acknowledged that no universally agreed- upon cutoff exists (Borenstein et al., 2021; Higgins et al., 2024). This threshold was established a priori. In one subgroup (juvenile offenders), fewer than 10 studies were available (k = 5); however, an exploratory meta- regression was conducted post hoc to examine potential sources of heterogeneity within this unique sample population. Across these studies, the overall mean prevalence of ADHD was 14.0% (95% CI [9.3, 20.4]). However, there was a wide dispersion of effects, suggest ing the prevalence in any true population could range from about 3% to 47% (PI [2.9, 47.0]). Despite this influence, the McConaughy et al. study was retained in the meta-analysis for several reasons. First, under a random-effects model, smaller studies may have greater influence on the summary estimate due to the way study weights are calculated. McConaughy et al. had a relatively small sample size compared to other studies using symptom rating scales. However, there was no evidence that this study introduced systematic bias; its methodology appeared sound and offered a reasonably unbiased estimate of ADHD prevalence. We considered it important to retain all methodologi cally reliable studies to ensure the summary estimate reflects the full range of available data and remains generalizable. Nonetheless, readers are encouraged to interpret not only the summary estimate but also the prediction intervals, which reflect the expected range of ADHD prevalence in a true population and help con textualize variability across studies. The pooled prevalence rate of ADHD among Black participants was 19.1% (95% CI [14.3, 25.2] PI [7.8, 40.0]), whereas it was 31.9% among White participants (95% CI [24.7, 39.9] PI [14.3, 56.8]), and 17.0% among Latino/as (95% CI [12.2, 23.3] PI [6.7, 36.9]). Meta-regression indicated Black and Hispanic/Latino/a groups were statistically significantly associated with lower estimates of ADHD prevalence (Z = −2.68, p < .01; Z = −3.0, p < .01, respectively; Table 2). The over all model testing the effect of race/ethnicity explained some but not all the variation in true effects (Q = 1337.42, df = 17, p < .001, R2 = 0.35). Of note, while the model accounted for a proportion of the between-study variance, the relatively small number of studies included ( < 10) may limit the stability and generalizability of the findings. As such, results should be interpreted with caution and considered exploratory. For the 25 studies in which caregivers were asked if their child had been diagnosed with ADHD by a physician or mental health professional (currently or ever), we found that Latino (6.1%) and Asian (2.6%) children had lower rates of diagnosis than White children (10.5%). These results contrast those of the recent meta-analysis by Cénat et al. (2024) who did not find lower prevalence of ADHD in Latino youth and found that the prevalence in Asian youth was only marginally lower. The differences in findings may be due to the types of populations included in the Cénat et al. (2024) meta-analysis (e.g., youth with autism, juvenile justice involved youth), or because of the inclusion of studies that involve different methods for determining ADHD diagnosis. The present study also included several additional studies that were not included in Cénat et al. (2024) such as the more recent large-scale study by Hall et al. (2023). The find ings of the current study are consistent with recently published results from the 2022 National Survey of Children’s Health (Danielson et al., 2024) which indi cated that Hispanic/Latino children had a lower preva lence than non-Hispanic/Latino children, and that Asian children had a lower prevalence than White children. These results suggest that it is important to investi gate the reasons why rates of diagnosis may be lower in Latino and Asian communities. Several factors may contribute, including cultural differences in the percep tion of ADHD-like behaviors, language barriers, reduced access to mental health services generally, as well as a lack of access to and availability of culturally sensitive and linguistically appropriate mental health care services (Kapke et al., 2019; Feng et al., 2024). Haack et al. (2018) found that Latino families may be more likely to underestimate ADHD symptoms. Parental acculturation to the United States mainstream culture, stigmatized mental health attitudes, and beliefs that children’s problems should be managed within the family unit also influence help-seeking in the Latino community (Kapke et al., 2019). In Asian families, Feng et al. (2024) outline several factors that may contribute to lower rates of ADHD diagnosis. First, they note that the inattentive presenta tion of ADHD may be more common in Asian samples, which may be less likely to be identified as ADHD- related than the hyperactivity symptoms. Additional factors include mental health stigma in Asian American communities; parent perception of ADHD as misbehavior rather than a neurodevelopmental disorder; and parent support for children’s academic activities that may mask impair ment. Culturally sensitive interventions with families and communities that focus on building relationships, address gaps in knowledge about ADHD symptoms, and providing information about opportunities for treatment may help to reduce the disparities in diagno sis rates in Latino and Asian communities. Consistent with the findings of Cénat et al. (2024), for children with who had received a diagnosis of ADHD, we did not find differences in the prevalence rates for White (10.5%) and Black (9.4%) children. This is also consistent with the 2022 National Survey of Children’s Health (Danielson et al., 2024), which did not show differences between prevalence rates in Black and White children. These findings suggest that previous concerns about the underdiagnosis of ADHD in Black children (Coker et al., 2016; Morgan et al., 2013) may no longer be present. However, our findings from studies using symptom ratings of ADHD suggest that under diagnosis may still be an issue. In the present study we distinguished between stu dies that asked caregivers about whether their child had received a diagnosis from studies that used symptom ratings of ADHD to assess prevalence. Whereas receiv ing a formal diagnosis requires that the child be identi fied as in need of assessment and that a caregiver is willing and able to seek the diagnosis, symptom ratings may be more objective indicators of prevalence. Only six studies used symptom ratings, so results should be interpreted with caution. However, we did find that the prevalence of ADHD was higher when using symp tom ratings (14.0% when assessing symptoms versus 9.2% when asking about receipt of a diagnosis). This was true for each racial and ethnic group (17.5% com pared to 9.4% in Black children, 12.6% compared to 10.5% in White children, 11.2% compared to 6.1% for Latino children (no studies reported symptom ratings in Asian youth)). These higher estimates when using symptom ratings may indicate that some children are being missed for diagnosis when universal screening of ADHD symptoms is not conducted. The differences appear to be particularly pronounced for Black and Latino children. Of note, for studies using symptom ratings, there was a wide dispersion of effects, suggesting the true preva lence in any population could range from about 3% to 47% (PI [2.9, 47.0]). In contrast, the dispersion among studies using lifetime or current ADHD diagnosis was relatively smaller (PI [3.4, 22.5]). Greater dispersion may reflect methodological differences among studies using symptom ratings for ADHD identification (e.g., use of different rating scales), as well as variability in study-level characteristics such as sample size. Future research may assess how estimates of ADHD prevalence are influenced by these methodological factors. Nonetheless, the current results suggest the use of rating scales may improve ADHD detection. Underdiagnosis and thus a lack of treatment for ADHD may result in a wide range of negative outcomes, including poor aca demic performance, difficulties in social relationships, and increased likelihood of criminal justice involvement (Arnold et al., 2020; Retz et al., 2021). Various methods for improving the process of diagnosis and treatment have been proposed, including two-stage screening methods (Coghill et al., 2022), universally eliciting par ental concerns about child behavior in primary care, and providing mental health education through com munity resources (Coker et al., 2016). Only five studies involving juvenile offenders were identified, so results should be interpreted with caution. The rates of ADHD in juvenile offenders were much higher (25.5%) than in the general population of youth (9.2%), suggesting that these populations should be examined separately in meta-analyses. Further, across these five studies, we found that Black and Latino/ Hispanic youth involved in the juvenile justice system had lower rates of ADHD than White youth (19.1% for Black youth, 17.0% for Latino youth, 31.9% for White youth; Asian samples were not included in the available studies). ADHD is associated with many factors that may increase risk for antisocial behavior, including def icits in executive functioning (e.g., impulsivity, poor self-control, altered reward processing, impaired emo tion regulation), academic failure, and negative relation ships with caregivers, teachers, and peers (Tamm et al., 2021). When undiagnosed and untreated, these factors are likely to increase risk for school suspensions and expulsions and involvement in the criminal justice sys tem (Lettieri & Lewis, 2022). Underdiagnosis of ADHD in Black and Latino youth may contribute to the racial disparities present in the juvenile justice system. In the study by Baglivio et al. (2017), Black and Latino juvenile offenders were diagnosed with ADHD less often but were more likely to be diagnosed with conduct disorder than White juvenile offenders, even when controlling for trauma, behavioral indicators, and criminal offending. One possibility is that among youth with more severe antisocial behavior, such as those in the juvenile justice system, clinicians may be more likely to overlook the ADHD diagnosis among Black and JOURNAL OF CLINICAL CHILD & ADOLESCENT PSYCHOLOGY 683

Latino youth and focus on the conduct disorder diag nosis. Concerns have been raised that unconscious biases may affect the way clinicians judge and interpret behaviors based on race or ethnicity (Fadus et al., 2020). Addressing these potential biases is essential to ensure that vulnerable youth receive fair and objective evalua tions and appropriate treatment. The present study has several limitations. First, although race and ethnicity are separate constructs, based on the data reported in the studies, we were not able to include this distinction. Second, limited data was available for other racial and groups, including Asian, Middle Eastern, or Indigenous communities. Third, for the analyses involving lifetime and current diagnoses, the effect of race/ethnicity explained none of the var iance in true effects. The reduced ability of the model’s ability to account for a meaningful amount of variance in the overall effect may be related to a) lack of precision (i.e., high amount of variability) in the overall and between group estimates, b) relatively small number of studies in some subgroups, or some combination thereof. For these reasons, it is possible that the groups with smaller number of studies (e.g., juvenile offender groups) overestimate the true impact of race/ethnicity on ADHD prevalence in the available studies. Thus, results from these subgroups should be interpreted cau tiously, and should be replicated when more studies are available to compare these groups with more precision and confidence. An additional consideration when interpreting this study’s findings is the significant degree of between study variability in ADHD prevalence, both in general and across racial/ethnic groups. The degree of variabil ity can be assessed by focusing on the prediction inter vals, which provides an indication of the extent of dispersion of the effect in any given population. For instance, when focusing on the group of studies using lifetime ADHD diagnosis, ADHD prevalence among White individuals could range from 4% to 24% in any given population. This suggests that the true rates of ADHD vary, and while the results of this study suggest that race/ethnicity may explain some of this variability, a significant amount of variability remains unexplained. Even within the context of this study’s limitations, the results provide evidence that race/ethnicity is sta tistically and clinically related to estimates of ADHD prevalence. In particular, Asian and Hispanic/Latino/ a populations are consistently associated with lower rates of ADHD compared to White and Black popu lations. While Asian populations were not repre sented in the studies comprised of juvenile offenders, lower rates were observed among both Hispanic/Latino/a and Black youth compared to White youth. The present study improved on the previous meta-analysis of racial differences in the prevalence of ADHD by examining a more homoge neous population-based sample (e.g., excluding stu dies with comorbid autism spectrum disorder, and analyzing ADHD in juvenile offenders separately) as well as by considering the method of ADHD diagno sis assessment. Research Article Disability and Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology 2026, VOL. 21, NO. 6, 2818–2838 A multi‐stakeholder preliminary needs assessment to inform the co‐design of a digital telerehabilitation tool for children and adolescents with ADHD Marina Rivas-Garcíaa,b , Carmen Vidal-Ramíreza , Marta Mora-Traversoc , Abel Toledano-Gonzálezd , María del Carmen Rodríguez-Martíneze , Esther Molina-Torresf , José-Antonio Marín-Maríng , José-Matías Triviño-Juárezh , Miguel Gea-Mejíasi and Dulce Romero-Ayusoj,k,l aFaculty of Medicine, University of Granada, Granada, Spain; bHospital Universitario San Cecilio, Granada, Spain; cUniversity of Zaragoza, Zaragoza, Spain; dDepartment of Psychology, University of Castilla-La Mancha, Ciudad Real, Spain; eDepartament of Physical Therapy, Occupational Therapy Division, Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Malaga, Málaga, Spain; fSpecialized Educational Guidance Team of Granada, Department of Educational Development and Vocational Training, Andalusian Government, Granada, Spain; gDepartment of Didactics and School Organization, Faculty of Science Education, University of Granada, Granada, Spain; hDepartment of Radiology and Physical Medicine, Faculty of Medicine, University of Granada, Granada, Spain; iDepartment of Computer Languages and Systems, School of Computer and Telecommunications Engineering, University of Granada, Granada, Spain; jDepartment of Physical Therapy, Occupational Therapy Division, Faculty of Health Sciences, University of Granada, Granada, Spain; kBrain, Mind and Behaviour Research Center (CIMCYC), University of Granada, Granada, Spain; lInstituto de Investigación Biosanitaria de Granada, IBS, Granada, Spain ABSTRACT Purpose: This study presents a preliminary multi‐stakeholder needs assessment to inform the subsequent co‐design of a digital telerehabilitation tool aimed at supporting organisation, planning, and prospective memory in children and adolescents with ADHD. The primary outcome was to identify functional challenges, environmental determinants, and user‐reported priorities across stakeholder groups. The secondary outcome was to translate these needs into preliminary design requirements and guiding principles for future co‐design phases. Methods: A qualitative study was conducted using focus groups guided by the CFIR framework, involving 49 participants: children and adolescents with ADHD, caregivers, occupational therapists, and educational professionals. Data were analysed through deductive thematic coding and inductive grounded‐theory synthesis. Matrix mappings and Sankey diagrams were used to visualise convergence and divergence across stakeholder perspectives. Results: Three cross‐cutting priority areas emerged: (1) emotional self‐regulation, (2) autonomy in daily routines through customisable reminders and supports, and (3) psychoeducation for families and educators. Children emphasised reminders, prospective‐memory support, privacy control, and motivational feedback. Educators highlighted the need for training and classroom‐based co‐regulation strategies. Occupational therapists emphasised ecological, participation‐oriented interventions. Caregivers reported emotional burden, concerns about independence, and a need for accessible psychoeducational resources. Conclusions: This needs assessment provides a structured, replicable foundation for the co‐design of a digital telerehabilitation tool for ADHD, integrating emotional, functional, and educational dimensions. Future research should evaluate the feasibility, usability, and the impact of the resulting prototype on autonomy, participation, and family dynamics. hIMPLICATIONS FOR REHABILITATION • The study proposes a reproducible, collaborative model for designing digital telerehabilitation that address three key priorities: emotional self-regulation, independence in daily routines, and psychoeducation for families and educators. • Children and adolescents emphasised the need for customisable reminders, privacy controls, and motivational feedback. © 2026 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group CONTACT Dulce Romero-Ayuso dulceromero@ugr.es Facultad de Ciencias de la Salud, Universidad de Granada, Avda. de la Ilustración n° 60, Granada, 18600, Spain Supplemental data for this article is available online at https://doi.org/10.1080/17483107.2026.2648864 https://doi.org/10.1080/17483107.2026.2648864 ARTICLE HISTORY Received 22 September 2025 Accepted 16 March 2026 KEYWORDS Attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity; self-regulation; telerehabilitation; user-centred design; executive function

A MULTI‐STAKEHOLDER PRELIMINARY NEEDS ASSESSMENT 2819 • The results highlight the systemic impact of ADHD and the importance of family-centred support in digital health solutions for their rehabilitation. • Professionals underscored the importance of ecological interventions and the development of self-regulation skills. Introduction Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is one of the most prevalent neurodevelopmental disor ders in childhood and adolescence, affecting ~5–7% of the school population [1]. This disorder is char acterised by persistent patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that significantly interfere with academic, social, and family functioning. Executive dysfunction in ADHD has been widely docu mented as a contributing factor to difficulty in behavioural and emotional self-regulation, as well as in the execution of complex tasks that require sequential planning and inhibitory control [2]. People with ADHD often experience difficulties in perceiving time, initiating tasks, and maintaining focus on future goals, which can lead to feelings of overwhelm and low self-esteem [3]. Although pharmacological treatments, particularly stimulants, are currently the first therapeutic choice, their impact on executive functions (EF) has proven to be limited [4,5]. In addition, many non-pharmacological tools used in assessment and intervention lack ecological validity and have limited applicability in everyday contexts. A large part of neurorehabilitation programs has focused on decon textualised cognitive functions, without adequately considering the user’s functional environment or daily experience. In response to these limitations, the concept of functional cognition has gained relevance in both applied neuropsychology and occupational therapy (OT). This approach integrates cognitive functions with the effective execution of meaningful tasks in real environments and allows assessing how a person applies skills such as prospective memory (PM) or organisation in their daily lives. PM, understood as the ability to remember future intentions at the right time [6], is crucial in activities that require temporal coordination or reactions to specific events, such as turning in homework, taking medication, or going to an appointment. Their deterioration can lead to disorganised functioning and over-reliance on adult figures. Studies have shown the effectiveness of various interventions and support systems in helping children and adolescents with ADHD develop better organisational and time management skills [7,8]. Implementing specific strategies, such as breaking tasks down into smaller components, using visual supports, and establishing clear prioritisation systems, is especially beneficial for this population [9]. In addition, multi modal approaches that combine various interventions, such as parent training programs and social skills training, have shown positive results in improving both emotional symptoms and daily time manage ment skills [8]. These approaches, when combined with appropriate goal-setting techniques and consis tent routines, contribute to creating a favourable environment for successful task completion and better self-regulation [4,5]. A meta-analysis on organisational skills training (OST) for children and adolescents with ADHD revealed moderate to large improvements in organisational skills, as assessed by teachers and parents, as well as moderate improvements in inattentive symptoms and academic performance [4]. Taken together, organisational skills interventions appear to be an effective approach to addressing ADHD-related impairments in academic and daily functioning. OT plays a key role in addressing these challenges by focusing on improving children’s functional participation and independence in meaningful contexts, helping them to develop an appropriate sense of competence. However, access to them may be limited by economic, logistical, or geographical barriers, especially in rural areas or in low-income families [10]. Faced with this situation, the potential of emerg ing technologies such as virtual reality (VR) and personalised tele-rehabilitation platforms has begun to be explored. These tools allow EF to be evaluated and trained in controlled environments with high representation of real life, favouring transfer to everyday contexts [11,12], and offer an accessible alter native to traditional limitations on access to specialised services. In this context, digital technologies have emerged as a promising alternative to complement traditional treatments, offering opportunities to per sonalise, scale, contextualise, and monitor the results of interventions in real time [13,14]. Digital

2820 M. RIVAS-GARCÍA ET AL. interventions can be developed through mobile phones, tablets, or web platforms providing interven tions that are more accessible, better integrated into multiple settings (e.g., home, school, and health services), and enable individuals (and families) to take care of themselves [15]. Digital therapies have the potential to be implemented anytime, anywhere, which could ease the burden on caregivers when organising interventions for their children with ADHD. In turn, this can improve patient adherence to the intervention and generate long-lasting therapeutic effects [15]. Likewise, the use of digital games is an effective strategy to increase adherence to interventions in the child population. By offering an interac tive and engaging environment, these resources can enhance children’s motivation to continue treat ment, while allowing for appropriate feedback during their development [16]. On the other hand, these interventions can be easily adapted to the specific needs of each user, promoting participation, motiva tion, and personalisation based on different levels of development and individual preferences, depending on the areas in which they present deficits [17,18]. The rise of therapeutic and gamified digital interventions for ADHD has shown that technological platforms can modulate attentional processes and certain executive dimensions, although evidence spe cifically oriented to organisation and planning in child and adolescent populations remains incipient and fragmented [13]. For example, some gamified platforms are highly effective in improving cognitive and behavioural skills, encouraging participation in structured activities in playful environments that reinforce positive behaviours [19,20]. However, these studies have relevant methodological limitations, such as small sample sizes, scarce information on the implementation context, and a limited description of the specific functionalities of digital tools. This underscores the need to develop more robust research that not only evaluates the efficacy of these interventions but also actively integrates end-user perspectives into their design and validation. In this sense, co-creation and co-design, as participatory approaches in the development of health technologies, make it possible to involve children and adolescents with ADHD, their families, occupational therapists, educators, and technology developers in a collaborative process that favours the relevance, usability, and acceptance of digital solutions [14,21,22]. Within the ADHD literature, difficulties in organisation and planning are understood as core compo nents of executive functioning and functional cognition [5,23]. These skills depend on processes such as working memory, prospective memory, inhibitory control, and self‐regulation, which together support the ability to initiate, sequence, monitor, and complete daily activities [6]. In children and adolescents with ADHD, impairments in these domains often translate into challenges in managing routines, com pleting school tasks, and maintaining autonomy in daily life [24,25]. For this reason, the present study focuses specifically on organisation and planning skills as the primary functional targets for a future digital telerehabilitation tool, while acknowledging the broader executive processes that underpin them. Given this convergence of clinical needs, technological opportunities, and user-centered design prin ciples, this paper presents a preliminary needs assessment to inform the co-design of a digital telereha bilitation tool for children and adolescents with ADHD, with a particular focus on organisation and planning skills. Specifically, the study aims to: (a) identify and prioritise functional needs and daily chal lenges as perceived by key stakeholders; (b) describe the participatory qualitative methodology used to elicit these perspectives; and (c) translate stakeholder input into user-informed design requirements and guiding principles. By systematically integrating the perspectives of children and adolescents, families, educators, and clinicians, this study provides a robust empirical foundation for the development of meaningful, feasible, and user-centered digital interventions for ADHD. Methodology Study design This qualitative study was conducted within a user-centered design framework and used focus groups to engage four key stakeholder groups: children and adolescents with ADHD, their primary caregivers, occu pational therapists, and educational professionals with experience and direct contact with these children and adolescents. The CFIR was used to guide the development of the discussion guide, as it conceptu alises barriers and facilitators as implementation-relevant determinants, providing a structured framework to prospectively explore contextual, organisational, and individual factors that may influence the future

This structure provided a theoreti cally grounded rationale for selecting and organising the domains explored in the focus group questions. CFIR served as the determinant-based structure for the discussion guide, organising questions around the domains of Intervention Characteristics (adaptability, complexity, perceived advantage), Individual Needs and Resources, Outer Setting, and Process. This structure ensured that all stakeholder groups were systematically asked about barriers, facilitators, contextual factors, and implementation needs relevant to the future implementation of the digital intervention. A detailed mapping of the discussion questions to CFIR domains and thematic blocks is now provided in Supplementary Table S1. Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of the Research Centre of Granada (CEI-GRANADA), and written informed consent was provided by all participants. The study complied with the Declaration of Helsinki and Spanish Law 14/2007 on Biomedical Research. Focus groups and preparatory meetings were held at the Faculty of Health Sciences of Granada, Spain, in accessible ground-floor laboratories designed to offer a comfortable and familiar environment. A total of 49 participants were included in eight focus groups conducted in May and June 2024: two with chil dren and adolescents with ADHD (n = 8), two with caregivers (n = 11), two with occupational therapists (n = 20), and two with educational professionals (n = 10, whom 8 were teachers and 2 were school coun sellors). Although formal data saturation was not evaluated, the number of groups aligns with estab lished guidelines, indicating that 80–90% of key themes typically emerge within 2–6 focus groups. Participant recruitment Purposive sampling was employed to ensure representation from all stakeholder categories. Children and adolescents and their primary caregivers were recruited through the Specialised Educational Guidance Team for Severe Behavioural Disorders of Granada (Ministry of Educational Development and Vocational Training, Regional Government of Andalusia), which distributed invitations through school guidance staff. Additional recruitment was supported by neuropediatricians from the Virgen de las Nieves Hospital, pae diatricians from the Zaidín Sur health centre, and families involved in a previous AMPA-linked project. Educational professionals were also recruited through the Educational Administration, specifically via the same Specialised Educational Guidance Team. Occupational therapists were contacted through the Spanish Council of Occupational Therapy Colleges, the Spanish Scientific Society of Occupational Therapy for Children and Adolescents (TOPES), and institutional mailing lists. Some professionals were contacted directly based on known experience with neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) populations. Recruitment followed a three-step process: (1) Initial contact via email or phone, providing study infor mation and confirming voluntary participation. (2) Up to three in-person meetings at the university to clarify objectives, resolve doubts, and obtain written informed consent (and assent in the case of chil dren and adolescents). (3) Assignment to one of eight scheduled focus groups, ensuring balanced composition. A total of 72 formal invitations were extended across the four participant categories. Sessions were strategically scheduled on different dates and at varying times to accommodate participants’ personal and professional commitments. Each stakeholder group (children and adolescents, caregivers, occupa tional therapists, and educational professionals) were invited to participate in two specific sessions, allow ing for greater flexibility and facilitating participation. This staggered and targeted scheduling approach enhanced attendance and ensured a balanced representation across all stakeholder groups. Although not all invitees attended, this multi-date strategy optimised participation and group diver sity. The final sample comprised 49 participants: 8 children and adolescents, 11 caregivers, 20 occupa tional therapists, and 10 educational professionals (8 teachers and 2 school counsellors). Inclusion and exclusion criteria Children and adolescents were eligible to participate if they were between 9 and 17 years old, fluent in Spanish (spoken and written), had an educational or clinic diagnosis ADHD, an intelligence quotient (IQ) above 69, and scored equal to or above 65 on both the Cognitive Regulation Index and the Behavioural

The selection of the 9–17 age range was grounded in developmental and functional considerations. This interval was selected because it encompasses a developmental period in which executive functions (e.g., planning, working memory, inhibitory control, and self‐regulation) undergo substantial maturation and show considerable interindividual variability [27,28]. From approximately age 9 onward, students encounter increased academic complexity, heightened organisational expectations, and a progressive need for autonomous task man agement; these demands intensify during adolescence and directly influence daily functioning in individ uals with ADHD [31]. Therefore, the 9–17 range aligns with the evolving contextual challenges that this population faces in school, home, and community settings [30]. In addition, children aged 9 years and older generally demonstrate sufficient digital competence to participate meaningfully in user‐centered design activities and needs‐assessment procedures, while adolescents up to 17 years typically report extensive exposure to digital technologies, enabling them to provide detailed and relevant feedback regarding usability, acceptability, and functional requirements—key components in the early stages of tele‐rehabilitation development. Finally, the selected age span captures a developmental window in which needs related to time management, planning, task initiation, emotion regulation, and autonomy change substantially; including this period facilitates the identification of both age‐dependent and age‐invariant needs to inform subsequent phases of tool refinement and evaluation [27,28]. Exclusion criteria for this population were the presence of sensory or motor limitations that preclude the use of electronic devices (e.g., tablets, computers, or smartphones), documented photosensitive epi lepsy, or uncontrolled aggressive behaviour. Importantly, children presenting visual hypersensitivity or visual‐seeking behaviours were not excluded based on these sensory characteristics alone, as such pro files are common in ADHD [32,33] and directly relevant to the co‐design and preliminary needs assess ment of a visually delivered telerehabilitation tool. Uncontrolled aggressive behaviour was assessed through caregiver reports of incidents occurring within the previous three months (e.g., episodes result ing in injury or property damage, emergency intervention, or school suspension) and, when applicable, clinician input. Exclusion due to photosensitive epilepsy was determined based on medical records or caregiver/participant reports of prior seizures triggered by visual stimuli, clinical advice to avoid screen exposure, or a positive response to a pre‐session screening item indicating seizures, migraine with visual aura, or discomfort induced by flicker or visual patterns. For sensory or motor limitations, verification relied primarily on clinical documentation available at referral, and this information was subsequently confirmed with caregivers during the enrolment visit before consent. Caregivers were eligible if they were legal guardians, fluent in Spanish (spoken and written), co-resided with the child/adolescent at least 50% of the time in cases of shared custody, expressed a clear willing ness to participate, and signed a written informed consent form. All caregivers who participated in the study were the primary caregivers of the children and adolescents included in the child/adolescent focus groups. No caregivers whose children did not participate were recruited. Each child/adolescent had a corresponding caregiver who attended the caregiver focus group, ensuring complete dyadic representa tion across stakeholder sessions. Professionals (occupational therapists and professional educators) were included if they had a mini mum of five years of experience working with children or/and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD, were currently employed in educational or clinical settings, were fluent in Spanish (spoken and written and provided written informed consent). Discussion guide The development of the focus group questions followed established qualitative research guidelines ensuring an open, flexible script suitable for diverse participants. We first identified cross‐cutting themes relevant across stakeholder groups primarily experiences with technology and digital therapeutic tools [34] to ensure conceptual coherence and facilitate comparison across stakeholder perspectives. Guided by these initial themes, the research team developed a core set of questions addressing: • Daily life challenges and support needs • Desired design and usability features • Preferences for content organisation (levels, themes, activity types) • Feedback and progress‐tracking expectations

RIVAS-GARCÍA ET AL. • Motivational systems • Privacy and data protection expectations The structure and wording of the questions were refined through five iterative team meetings held between January and June 2024. To standardise phrasing and ensure systematic alignment with imple mentation constructs, we incorporated the CFIR Interview Guide Tool (https://cfirguide.org/guide/app/ index.html), which supported script refinement and ensured comprehensive coverage of the following domains: Intervention Characteristics, Individual Needs and Resources, Outer Setting, Inner Setting, and Process. Building on this framework, group‐specific questions were developed for children/adolescents, care givers, teachers, and therapists. Children and adolescents, as well as caregivers, were asked prompts such as: “What would you like the app to include?”, “How could it help you in your daily life?”, and “Would seeing your progress after each session be useful?”. Professionals were additionally asked about the potential integration in practice, priority content areas, appropriate automated features (e.g., reminders), and strategies for delivering meaningful feedback. They were also invited to identify outcome domains relevant to future clinical trials, including clinical, behavioural, usability, autonomy, and daily functioning metrics. Given the exploratory nature of this study, caregiver burden was not included as an independent theme. However, issues related to time demands, feasibility, and routine organisation emerged naturally within several CFIR domains and were explored through moderator‐led probes as participants raised them. Moderators used targeted probes to elicit practical strategies to minimise potential caregiving burden, including preferred session scheduling and frequency, coordination with school/family routines, division of responsibilities, reminders/automation, and acceptable time‐on‐task and reporting require ments. A detailed mapping of questions to CFIR domains and thematic blocks is provided in Supplementary Table S1. Each focus group lasted ~90–120 min. All sessions were audio‐recorded and transcribed verbatim. In the first phase, a deductive thematic analysis was conducted, guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). This framework provided a struc tured lens for the initial coding process, allowing the research team to categorise data according to established domains and constructs relevant to implementation science [26,34]. In the second phase, an inductive analytic process informed by grounded theory principles was employed to synthesise individual codes into higher-order themes, allowing novel and context-specific patterns to emerge beyond the predefined CFIR categories. Following this synthesis, the resulting higher-order themes were subsequently situated within the WHO International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF/ICF-CY), with particular empha sis on Environmental Factors (e1 products and technology; e2 natural environment; e3 support and relationships; e4 attitudes; e5 services, systems and policies), to foreground environmental determinants of participation [35]. In parallel, these higher-order themes were cross-walked to the family of Participation-Related Constructs (fPRC)—including attendance, involvement, activity competence, sense of self, preferences, and environment—to enhance interpretive depth regarding participation processes and outcomes [35]. To enhance the credibility and trustworthiness of the findings, the coding process was carried out independently by three researchers with expertise in qualitative methods. Regular meetings were held to discuss discrepancies, refine coding categories, and reach consensus, thereby minimising individual bias and promoting inter-coder reliability. All qualitative data were systematically managed and organ ised using ATLAS.ti software (version 9.1), which facilitated the coding process, supported the retrieval of coded segments, and enabled the transparent documentation of analytic decisions throughout the study. In addition to coder triangulation, several integrative procedures were implemented to synthesise per spectives across stakeholder groups. Analyst triangulation was carried out among researchers from reha bilitation medicine, occupational therapy, neuropsychology, and education, ensuring multidisciplinary interpretation of the data. To systematically compare viewpoints, we developed matrix mappings of themes by stakeholder group (youth, caregivers, teachers, and therapists), which enabled the identifica tion of convergent, divergent, and complementary needs. A series of consensus sessions was then con ducted to consolidate these themes into higher‐order categories aligned with the CFIR domains. Subsequently, integration sessions were held to merge convergent priorities into shared design principles (e.g., usability, flexibility, personalisation, ecological validity). Finally, a model‐building phase synthesised these insights into a preliminary conceptual model of the digital intervention, ensuring that the needs assessment process resulted in a coherent and theoretically grounded framework. The analysis followed a hybrid approach: CFIR domains were used to identify implementation determinants (barriers and facil itators), while the fPRC and ICF frameworks categorised the functional needs and participation factors related to organisation and planning. Following the synthesis of individual codes into higher-order themes, a brief analytic memo was used to guide the interpretive mapping of these themes to ICF Environmental Factors (e1–e5) and to fPRC constructs. Empirical literature on environmental determi nants of participation in ADHD (e.g., PEM-CY–based studies across home, school, and community) was used as a sensitising corpus to support the interpretation and labelling of barriers and facilitators (e.g., cognitive demands, sensory qualities, teacher/peer support, organisational and policy-related features) [36]. A cross-walk of higher-order themes to ICF domains (including Environmental Factors e1–e5) and fPRC constructs is provided in Supplementary Figure S2. Positionality The research team comprises ten members from two Spanish public universities with experience in the field of neurodevelopmental disorders. Six members identify as women and four as men. The women include a physiatrist (MR‐G); three occupational therapists (CVR, MMT, MCRM); a teacher and educational psychologist (EMT); and an occupational therapist and neuropsychologist (DRA). The men include a teacher and pedagogue (JAMM); an occupational therapist (ATG); a primary care physician specialised in

All members have back grounds in research and practice across clinical and/or educational settings. The team acknowledges that its training and practice contexts (e.g., occupational therapy, medicine— rehabilitation, primary care, preventive and public health, psychology/neuropsychology, education, and computer science) shape interpretive lenses and may influence how questions are framed, how experi ences are interpreted, and which needs are prioritised. Working within Spanish public health and educa tion systems may heighten attention to organisational feasibility, integration with public services, equity of access, and acceptability among families and professionals. Clinical and educational profiles may also orient discussions towards functional and participation outcomes, as well as usability and real‐world applicability. To mitigate potential bias arising from this positionality, the team implemented explicit safeguards in the design and facilitation of focus groups: (a) a CFIR‐informed discussion guide with open, comparable questions across stakeholder groups; (b) reflexive moderation with predefined probes to surface diver gent perspectives, caregiving burden, and burden‐reducing strategies; (c) analyst triangulation across dis ciplines; and (d) internal auditability of analytic decisions via consensus meetings, memos, and coding matrices. Positionality is approached as both a resource and a responsibility, making the team’s lenses transparent so readers can assess the scope and boundaries of the interpretations. Results The coding analysis carried out on the qualitative corpus allowed us to identify the distribution of relevant topics, from their experiences and needs to the conceptualisation of a digital tool for children and ado lescents with ADHD in relation to the main actors involved: children and adolescents, teachers, occupa tional therapists, and mothers/fathers/caregivers. These descriptive patterns also reflected the CFIR‐informed struc ture of the discussion guide, with codes aligning with domains such as Intervention Characteristics, Outer Setting, Characteristics of Individuals, and Process, as detailed in Supplementary Figure S1. The resulting higher-order themes and their illustrative examples were subsequently interpreted within the WHO ICF/ICF-CY and the family of Participation-Related Constructs (fPRC) frameworks, as detailed in Supplementary Figure S2. Overall, the results show that the design of the tool and intervention should contemplate: 1) Emotional components, including the emotional regulation of the child and family, self-esteem and sense of com petence in the daily life of the child/adolescent; 2) Cognitive training: attentional, in EF and prospective memory (planning, organisation, reminders); 3) An educational dimension (psychoeducation, understand ing of the child/adolescent) aimed at both parents and educators. In addition, it must be customisable and adaptable to different user profiles, integrating the perspectives of all the actors involved in the rehabilitation process. From identified priorities to design features Across stakeholder groups, the three cross‐cutting priorities—emotional self‐regulation, independence in daily routines, and psychoeducation—were consistently associated with concrete expectations about how a digital tool should function in everyday contexts. These expectations emerged spontaneously in participants’ narratives and reflected patterns aligned with CFIR domains and fPRC constructs. For emotional self‐regulation, children, caregivers, teachers, and therapists described the need for fea tures that help identify, express, and modulate emotions in real time. Participants proposed emotion‐la belling interfaces, short, guided strategies (e.g., breathing, movement breaks), and prompts that support self‐awareness. These expectations corresponded to CFIR Intervention Characteristics (adaptability, per ceived advantage) and Individual Needs and Resources and mapped onto fPRC constructs related to participation—particularly involvement and sense of self—as children emphasised the importance of feeling understood, supported, and autonomous. For independence in daily routines, participants described highly specific supports for planning, organ isation, and prospective memory. Children repeatedly mentioned customisable alarms, visual planners, and step‐by‐step task sequences to scaffold homework, self‐care, and daily responsibilities. Parents and therapists reinforced the need for tools that enhance activity competence and reduce family burden, reflecting CFIR Outer Setting determinants (family needs and resources) and Process elements related to monitoring and feedback. These expectations aligned with fPRC constructs of activity competence, pref erences, and attendance, as children expressed a desire for tools that were motivating, personalised, and responsive to their routines. For psychoeducation, all groups—especially parents and educators—highlighted the need for accessi ble, evidence‐based information to better understand ADHD, executive functioning, emotional regulation, and effective support strategies. Participants requested short videos, demonstrations, curated resources, and guidance tailored to different user profiles. These expectations reflected CFIR Intervention Characteristics (complexity, design quality) and Outer Setting needs for coordinated support across home and school. Finally, from an fPRC perspective, these needs related to the environment dimension—particularly the desire for supports that were acceptable, accessible, accommodating, affordable, and available for fami lies and professionals Discussion This study delimits, based on the experience of children and adolescents with ADHD, their families, edu cational professionals, and occupational therapists, the contents and principles of design of a digital tool aimed at organisation, planning, and prospective memory. Three major priorities were identified: emo tional self-regulation, customisable supports for daily autonomy (routines and reminders with privacy controls), and practical psychoeducation for school and family, with significant feedback. These perspec tives were collected through focus groups guided by a semi-structured script, chosen for its flexibility

RIVAS-GARCÍA ET AL. and adaptation to the context, to facilitate the generation and exchange of ideas around the central theme, in line with previous approaches in health technology design [37]. Collaboration between devel opers, clinicians, educators, and families, along with the active participation of children and adolescents, is essential to create useful, adaptable, and motivating digital health solutions, focused on users’ real needs, which can translate into improvements in daily functioning, social skills, participation, and quality of life [36]. The findings of this qualitative study reveal a complex but manageable set of needs, which serves as a guide for the design of a comprehensive digital intervention (emotional, functional, educational, and family) that goes beyond simple digitalisation. In this context, the focus groups made it possible to identify key issues related to content organisation, usability, motivation, reward systems, and personali sation [38]. In particular, the contributions of children and adolescents underline the centrality of executive func tions as the core of their daily difficulties. The repeated need for personalised reminder systems, supports for daily planning, positive feedback, and tools that favour emotional and behavioural self-regulation is consistent with the literature that points to deficits in prospective memory, organisation, and emotional regulation in ADHD [12,39]. The mention of control and privacy mechanisms over reminders also indi cates an explicit desire for autonomy and self-management, which reinforces the importance of avoiding paternalistic designs in digital interventions [40]. This type of technology has significant potential to offer immersive and motivating experiences, where children and adolescents can practice social skills and reduce anxiety in simulated social situations, favouring the generalisation of skills to real contexts [41]. Likewise, gamification—through rewards such as points, badges, or levels—has proven to be an effective strategy to capture and maintain attention, motivating children and adolescents to continue using these digital platforms and contributing to the learning of multiple skills [42]. Other authors have pointed out that digital interventions should include content about health care and self-management and be acces sible to people with different care capacities. Components such as symptom monitoring, wearable devices, and SMS messaging can increase engagement [43]. It’s important to do more research into practical tools, such as medication reminders and interactive assistants. Co-producing future solutions with stakeholders and adapting them to underserved populations will be key to moving towards more inclusive digital care for young people with ADHD [43]. Professionals involved in clinical and educational settings have shown interest in solutions that are easy to use, that allow the progress of children and adolescents to be monetised in real time, and that can be adapted to the different stages of development, promoting more effective and personalised interventions [44]. However, the perception and expectations regarding the usefulness of these technologies vary depending on previous experience, training, and willingness to incorporate digital solutions into their daily practices [45]. In the case of educational professionals, needs emerge that transcend direct help to students and point to a structural lack of specific training in emotional regulation strategies, academic planning, and classroom methodologies adapted to attentional difficulties. These findings coincide with studies that identify a training deficit in teachers regarding ADHD and a feeling of overflow due to the lack of specific resources [46]. The demand for evidence-based training resources, such as podcasts and up-to-date articles, reinforces the need to turn the digital tool into a platform not only for the student but for the entire educational community. Interventions using technologies such as robots, virtual reality, and interactive games create personalised and engaging experiences, as reported by educators and par ents [44]. Also, when education professionals are involved in the intervention, they are more aware of their role in assisting students with special needs in school, and it is very important and effective for teachers, parents, educational psychologists, and other professionals to work together to provide a learn ing environment that is conducive to students with special needs rather than working separately [47]. For their part, occupational therapists emphasised a comprehensive approach, encompassing not only self-regulation but also activities of daily living and the transfer of functional learning to the home envi ronment. This perspective, aimed at promoting the autonomy and motivation of children and adoles cents, coincides with the growing evidence that advocates ecological and transversal interventions in real contexts [8]. The proposal to use technology as a motivational vehicle, while avoiding the abuse of the screen, underlines a key challenge in the design of digital interventions: maximising adherence without increasing technological dependence [48,49].

A MULTI‐STAKEHOLDER PRELIMINARY NEEDS ASSESSMENT 2833 The analysis of the group of families clearly exposes the systemic impact of ADHD, especially in terms of parental overload, stress associated with daily supervision, and lack of understanding of the specific needs of their children. These concerns have been widely described in the literature, showing how ADHD not only affects the child, but family dynamics [50–52]. The explicit demand for psychoeducation content, both in audiovisual format and in self-help systems, points to a relevant opportunity for the digital tool as a space for family accompaniment [53], facilitating the improvement of parental self-efficacy and pro moting healthier dynamics [54]. Parents may experience difficulties when trying to understand how devices work, generating the need for additional technical support [55]. In response, the incorporation of visual support materials—such as graphic or video tutorials—is recommended, as well as the availability of personalised technical assistance, especially for those users interested in integrating mHealth tools into behaviour-oriented interventions. In addition, consistent with other studies, concerns related to aspects such as usability, accessibility, privacy protection, and integration with traditional interventions also arose in the group of parents [56]. The implementation and design of these technologies must consider the particularities of each group, as well as the possible risks of excessive or misdirected use. User acceptance, ease of use, and integration of reward systems into everyday contexts are crucial elements to ensure the long-term sustainability and effectiveness of these digital interventions [57]. It is also advisable to antici pate difficulties associated with the use of devices—distraction, overuse of screens, digital divide, learning curve, or privacy issues—and address them by design through accessibility criteria and privacy principles. Interpreting the findings through the WHO International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF/ICF-CY) and the family of Participation-Related Constructs (fPRC) provided a coherent frame work to situate stakeholder-identified needs within everyday participation contexts. Rather than focusing solely on individual impairments or skills, this perspective highlighted how participation challenges in children and adolescents with ADHD emerge from the dynamic interaction between functional abilities and environmental conditions across home, school, and community settings. The identified themes mapped primarily onto ICF Environmental Factors, including products and tech nology, support and relationships, attitudes, and services and systems, underscoring the central role of contextual determinants in shaping participation. Framing the results using the fPRC further allowed differentiation between attendance and involvement, while incorporating related constructs such as activity competence, sense of self, and preferences. This integrative perspective supports a shift from symptom-focused approaches towards participation-oriented, context-responsive digital interventions. In addition, the interpretation of the findings was informed by empirical literature on environmental determinants of participation, particularly studies using the Participation and Environment Measure for Children and Youth (PEM-CY) across home, school, and community contexts. This body of evidence pro vided a sensitising lens to support the labelling and interpretation of barriers and facilitators identified in the qualitative data. Across stakeholder groups, recurrent factors such as cognitive demands of tasks, sensory qualities of environments, availability of teacher and peer support, and organisational or policy-related features emerged as central determinants shaping participation for children and adoles cents with ADHD. Situating these findings within established empirical frameworks strengthens their interpretive coherence and underscores the relevance of addressing contextual and environmental con ditions when designing participation-oriented digital interventions. The integration of perspectives across stakeholder groups revealed a coherent conceptual structure that informs future co-design processes by clarifying shared priorities, design considerations, and contex tual requirements. Although each group emphasised different priorities—children focusing on reminders, autonomy, and emotional cues; parents highlighting family burden, psychoeducation, and communica tion; teachers emphasising classroom strategies and institutional constraints; and occupational therapists underscoring functional autonomy and motivation—these viewpoints converged around shared imple mentation determinants. When interpreted through CFIR domains (Intervention Characteristics, Individual Needs and Resources, Outer Setting, and Process) and fPRC constructs related to participation (atten dance, involvement, activity competence, sense of self, preferences, and environmental fit), these diverse contributions aligned into a unified conceptual model. This model positions emotional regulation, rou tine‐building supports, and psychoeducational resources as interdependent components embedded within an adaptable, context‐responsive digital tool. The resulting framework reflects the environmental and relational dynamics that shape participation across home, school, and therapeutic settings and

Strengths and limitations This study provides ecological value by integrating, through co-design, the perspectives of four key groups (children and adolescents, families, educational professionals, and occupational therapists), using a thematic guide anchored in the CFIR and a dual (deductive–inductive) analytic approach conducted by at least three independent researchers, which reinforces the credibility and traceability of the findings [34]. However, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the sample was drawn from a single geo graphic region, which may limit the generalisability and transferability of the findings to other cultural or educational contexts. Second, the use of convenience and purposive sampling, while appropriate for qualitative research, may have introduced selection bias, as participants who were more motivated or had greater access to resources may be overrepresented. Third, although the number of focus groups aligns with established guidelines, formal assessment of data saturation was not conducted, which may mean that some relevant themes or minority perspectives were not fully captured. Additionally, the study relied on self-reported data and group discussions, which may be influenced by social desirability bias or group dynamics, potentially limiting the depth or authenticity of some responses. The absence of longitudinal follow-up also precludes assessment of how stakeholder perspec tives might evolve over time or after exposure to the digital intervention. Furthermore, while the inclu sion of multiple stakeholder groups is a strength, the relatively small number of children and adolescents may have limited the diversity of experiences represented within this key group. Finally, the findings are based on the early stages of needs assessment and do not include co-designing of the digital tool, which needs to be developed in future research, evaluating the impact and sustain ability of the intervention in real-life contexts. Conclusion Together, the findings consolidate three functional blocks already described—(1) emotional/self-regulation, (2) functional (autonomy, planning, time management, and prospective memory), and (3) educational (understanding ADHD, stigma reduction, and evidence-based practices)—as axes of a user-centered design. Integrating these blocks into a customisable and modular platform aligns with current recommendations Figure 5. Integration of multi-stakeholder needs into a preliminary intervention model for ADHD.

Finally, it is worth highlighting the coherence of the results with theoretical frameworks such as the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) [34,37], showing that any digital tool must consider not only the needs of the individual (user characteristics), but also family dynamics (characteristics of the environment), the perceptions of professionals (characteristics of the intervention) and structural barriers in the educational and clinical context (characteristics of the system). The results allow us to propose future lines of development, highlighting the importance of co-designed, reiterated, and evidence-based strategies, as well as the evaluation of not only clinical results, but also daily function ality, quality of life, and satisfaction of the users involved [62]. metadata_title: Regional Variation in ADHD Treatment and Diagnosis Among Children and Adolescents in Denmark
pages: 1 of 8 Basic & Clinical Pharmacology & Toxicology, 2026; 139:e70298 https://doi.org/10.1111/bcpt.70298 WILEYlogo Basic & Clinical Pharmacology & Toxicology ORIGINAL ARTICLE OPEN ACCESS Regional Variation in ADHD Treatment and Diagnosis Among Children and Adolescents in Denmark Heidi Sonne1 | Anton Pottegård1 | Anna Sofie Kjærgaard Hansen2,3 | Mickael Bech4 | Helene Kildegaard1,5 1Clinical Pharmacology, Pharmacy and Environmental Medicine, Department of Public Health, University of Southern Denmark, Odense, Denmark | 2Psychiatry, North Denmark Region, Aalborg University Hospital, Aalborg, Denmark | 3Department of Clinical Medicine, Aalborg University, Aalborg, Denmark | 4Department of Political Science and Public Management, University of Southern Denmark, Odense, Denmark | 5Mary Elizabeth's Hospital, University Hospital Copenhagen, Rigshospitalet, Denmark Correspondence: Helene Kildegaard (hckildegaard@health.sdu.dk) Received: 11 May 2026 | Revised: 17 August 2026 | Accepted: 18 August 2026 Keywords: adolescent psychiatry | attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity | child psychiatry | Denmark | geographic variation ABSTRACT Geographic variation in ADHD treatment and diagnosis among children and adolescents is well documented, yet the systemlevel factors driving such differences remain poorly understood. We examined nationwide patterns of ADHD medication use and diagnoses in Denmark in 2024 and assessed whether municipal socioeconomy, regional hospital waiting times or private child psychiatrist capacity contributed to geographic variation. In this register-based cross-sectional study, we included all Danish res idents aged 4–17 years using data from national registers. Pharmacological treatment was defined as at least one redeemed pre scription for ADHD drugs, and diagnosis was defined as at least one hospital contact with ICD-10 codes F90.x/F98.8. Prevalence was calculated overall and stratified by sex and age, with associations explored using Spearman's rank correlations and regression analyses. ADHD medication prevalence varied sixfold across municipalities (9.6–58 per 1000), with parallel variation in diagno ses (15–74 per 1000) and the largest differences observed among adolescents. Municipal socioeconomic status was weakly and inversely correlated with medication use (ρ = −0.20, p = 0.049), but not diagnoses. Neither waiting times nor specialist capacity was significantly associated with either outcome. Marked geographic variation in ADHD medication use and diagnoses persists in Denmark despite a uniform healthcare framework, and appears largely unexplained by the system-level factors examined. 1 | Introduction The prevalence of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) diagnoses has increased substantially over recent de cades [1]. International studies have documented marked regional variation in both the diagnosis and treatment of ADHD, includ ing evidence from Norway, Sweden and the United States [2–4]. These differences are only partly explained by underlying patient needs [2] and may also reflect supply- and demand-side factors, including access to services and local medical practices [5, 6]. Geographic variation in healthcare utilisation has been well doc umented for decades, often referred to as ‘small area variation’ [5]. Such differences are typically regarded as unwarranted when they cannot be attributed to evidence-based guidelines or population health needs [7]. Similar concerns apply to ADHD, where local practices and system-level factors may drive differ ential access to diagnostic and treatment services. In Denmark, approximately 9% of children receive an ADHD diagnosis before age 18 [1]. Earlier Danish research has found substantial regional variation in incidence, with lower rates in the Region of Southern Denmark, particularly on Funen, and higher rates in the Zealand Region [8]. These findings point to unwarranted variation in care delivery and highlight potential inequalities in access to diagnosis and treatment.
