2 of 8 Basic & Clinical Pharmacology & Toxicology, 2026 This study provides updated nationwide estimates of geographic variation in ADHD treatment in Denmark in 2024. We further examine system-level factors that may drive these differences, to assess whether regional variation reflects true population needs or unwarranted variation in care. By doing so, we aim to gener ate evidence that can inform strategies to promote more equita ble access to ADHD treatment across the country. 2 | Methods We conducted a nationwide register-based study to estimate the prevalence of ADHD diagnosis and medication use among Danish children and adolescents, and to examine selected re gional and municipal indicators potentially associated with variation. Data were obtained from the Danish National Patient Register [9], the Danish National Prescription Registry [10], the Danish Civil Registration System [11], the Ministry of the Interior and Health [12] and the Danish Health Data Authority [13–15]. 2.1 | Setting Denmark has a universal, tax-funded healthcare system in which all residents are entitled to publicly financed healthcare. Access to diagnostic assessments, consultations and hospitalbased services is provided free of charge, while a fixed percent age copayment applies to outpatient prescription drugs [16]. The system is organised into five regions responsible for managing hospital services, general practitioners and private specialist care [17]: The Capital Region of Denmark, Region Zealand, the Region of Southern Denmark, the Central Denmark Region and the North Denmark Region [16, 18], which are shown in Figure S1. These regions are subdivided into 98 municipalities, most of which have at least 20 000 inhabitants [18]. Child and adolescent psychiatry in Denmark is organised as a specialised regional service [17]. Access requires referral from a general practitioner, the municipality or another authorised healthcare professional, after which referrals are assessed by the regional child and adolescent psychiatry services [19, 20]. Once a referral is accepted, the patient undergoes a standardised diagnostic assessment, followed by a treatment plan that may include pharmacological treatment. Depending on symptom severity, complexity and waiting time, patients may be referred to private practicing child and adolescent psychiatry clinics working under agreements with the public health insurance system [21]. In 2023, approximately 5000 patients were treated by private child and adolescent psychiatrists working under the public reimbursement system, compared with about 48 700 pa tients in hospital-based child and adolescent psychiatry [21]. An unknown number of private child and adolescent psychiatrists work outside the public reimbursement system, requiring full out-of-pocket payment by families [21]. Diagnostic information from private practices is not systemati cally reported to the Danish National Patient Register, while all prescriptions redeemed at pharmacies are mandatorily recorded in the Danish National Prescription Registry [10], enabling more complete monitoring of medication use compared with diagnos tic data. 2.2 | Study Population The study population consisted of all individuals aged 4–17 years residing in Denmark between 1 January and 31 December 2024. The population was obtained from the Danish Civil Registration System along with key demographic information, including date of birth, sex and residential region and municipality. The age range was chosen from 4 years, as ADHD symptoms can be dif ficult to distinguish from normative behaviour before this age [22], and diagnosis before age 4 is rare [23]. 2.3 | Analyses Prevalence estimates were calculated overall and stratified by sex, age groups (4–6, 7–12 and 13–17 years), region and mu nicipality. Age groups were chosen to align with key stages in the Danish educational system: kindergarten and preschool (4–6 years), primary and middle school (7–12 years) and secondary school to early upper secondary education (13– 17 years). For analyses stratified by municipality, residence as of 31 December 2024, was used to assign individuals. The de nominator was estimated as the number of individuals within the age range in each region and municipality alive on 1 July 2024 (Table S1). Users of ADHD medication were defined as individuals who re deemed at least one prescription for methylphenidate (Anatomic Therapeutic Chemical [ATC] code: N06BA04, 62% of all defined daily doses filled in 2024 for age 0–17) [24], lisdexamphetamine (N06BA12; 29%), atomoxetine (N06BA09; 6.7%), dexamphet amine (N06BA02; 1.4%), or guanfacine (C02AC02; 1.1%) be tween 1 January and 31 December 2024, identified using the Danish National Prescription Registry [10]. The prevalence of ADHD diagnoses was defined as the propor tion of individuals in the study population who had received a diagnosis before 31 December 2024, using all available look back. An ADHD diagnosis was defined as at least one hospital contact, either inpatient or outpatient, recorded in the Danish National Patient Register with a diagnosis according to the Plain Language Summary We examined how often children and adolescents in Denmark were diagnosed with ADHD or received ADHD medication across municipalities in 2024. Despite a taxfunded healthcare system with equal access, we found large geographic differences. Some municipalities had more than six times as many children receiving ADHD medication as others, with the largest differences seen among adolescents. Municipal socioeconomic indicators were only weakly associated with these patterns, and differences could not be explained by waiting times or specialist availability. The findings suggest that factors beyond medical need may influence access to ADHD di agnosis and treatment in Denmark. 17427843, 2026, 4, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/bcpt.70298 by Stony Brook University Libraries, Wiley Online Library on [21/10/2026]. 3 of 8 Basic & Clinical Pharmacology & Toxicology, 2026 International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision (ICD-10), codes F90.x or F98.8 [9, 25]. To explore potential drivers of geographic variation, we in cluded three types of regional and municipality-level indi cators, capturing both demand- (1) and supply-side factors (2 + 3): (1) The municipal socioeconomic index, obtained from the Ministry of the Interior and Health, which estimates each municipality's relative expenditure needs based on a range of indicators, including the proportion of adults not in employ ment and the number of residents with psychiatric conditions [12]. Values above 1 indicate higher-than-average expenditure needs, while values below 1 indicate lower-than-average needs [12]. (2) Waiting time in the hospital sector, obtained from the Danish Health Data Authority. We examined two waiting time indicators: (a) the time from referral to completed diagnostic assessment, defined as the number of calendar days from re ferral to completed assessment [15] and (b) the time from the completed diagnostic assessment to treatment initiation, or, if workup occurred outside the hospital system, from the re ceipt of referral to treatment start [13]. For both indicators, quarterly regional estimates for the third and fourth quarters of 2024 were averaged. (3) The number of private practicing child and adolescent psychiatrists working under the pub lic reimbursement system, obtained from the Danish Health Data Authority and expressed as full-time equivalent capaci ties (FTEs) per 100 000 inhabitants, where a full-time practice counted as one FTE and part-time practices typically counted as one-third FTE [14]. Associations between municipal and regional indicators and the prevalence of ADHD diagnoses and medication use were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation coefficients (ρ). For the municipal socioeconomic index, we additionally fitted population-weighted linear regression models with prevalence proportion as the outcome. For the regional indicators (waiting time and psychiatrist capacity), associations were further exam ined using simple linear regressions based on regional preva lence estimates. All analyses were performed using R version 4.4.3 and validated internally by a data manager not otherwise involved in the study. The study was conducted in accordance with the Basic & Clinical Pharmacology & Toxicology policy for experimental and clinical studies [26]. 3 | Results In 2024, the prevalence of ADHD medication use among Danish children aged 4–17 years varied substantially across munic ipalities, ranging from 9.6 to 17 per 1000 in municipalities on Funen in the Region of Southern Denmark to 30 to 58 per 1000 in municipalities in the North Denmark Region and the Central Denmark Region (Figure 1A; Table S2). ADHD diagnoses fol lowed a similar pattern, with the lowest prevalence (15–26 per 1000) in municipalities on Funen in the Region of Southern Denmark and the highest (32–74 per 1000) in municipalities in the North Denmark Region and the Central Denmark Region (Figure 1B). When stratified by age, variation in medication use was lowest among children aged 4–6 years (1.2–4.7 per 1000 across mu nicipalities with reportable numbers), higher among children aged 7–12 years (8.9–62 per 1000) and highest among adoles cents aged 13–17 years (12–94 per 1000) (Figure S2; Table S3). ADHD diagnoses showed the same age-dependent pattern, with the widest geographic variation among adolescents (22–113 per 1000), somewhat narrower variation in children aged 7–12 years (15–74 per 1000) and low rates in children aged 4–6 years (3.1–10 per 1000) (Figure S3; Table S4). When stratified by sex, ADHD medication use was consistently higher among boys than girls. For girls, municipal prevalence ranged from 7.6 to 46 per 1000, while the range for boys was 10–73 per 1000 (Figure S4; Table S5). Diagnostic prevalence showed a similar sex difference, ranging from 9.3 to 48 per 1000 among girls and 21–100 per 1000 among boys (Figure S5; Table S6). Socioeconomic index values varied across municipalities with no clear regional pattern (Figure 1C; Table S7). ADHD med ication use was slightly higher in municipalities with lower relative expenditure needs (ρ = −0.20, p = 0.049), whereas no significant association was found for ADHD diagnoses (ρ = −0.042, p = 0.68) (Table S3). In sex-stratified analyses, the inverse correlation between socioeconomic index and ADHD medication use was numerically stronger in girls (ρ = −0.29, p = 0.005) than in boys (ρ = −0.15, p = 0.15). Weighted linear regression yielded similar findings, showing a statistically sig nificant inverse association between socioeconomic index and ADHD medication use (β = −0.013, p = 0.027), but no associa tion with ADHD diagnoses (β = −0.0041, p = 0.52) (Table S9). However, there was no evidence that the association between socioeconomic index and either ADHD medication use or ADHD diagnoses differed by sex (interaction p = 0.86 and p = 0.85, respectively) (Table S10). Regional waiting times varied considerably. The average waiting time from referral to completed diagnostic assessment ranged from 108 days in the Capital Region of Denmark to 223.5 days in the North Denmark Region, while the average waiting time from completed diagnostic assessment to treatment initiation ranged from 27.5 to 54 days (Figure 1E, Figure 1F; Table S3). However, neither waiting time measure was significantly associated with ADHD medication use or ADHD diagnoses (Table S8; Table S9). Capacity in private child and adolescent psychiatry working under the public reimbursement system ranged from 1.9 per 100 000 in the Central Denmark Region to 3.5 per 100 000 in the North Denmark Region, but was likewise not significantly asso ciated with medication use (ρ = 0.40, p = 0.50) or ADHD diagno ses (ρ = 0.30, p = 0.62) (Figure 1D; Table S8). 4 | Discussion Our nationwide register-based study found marked geographic variation in ADHD diagnoses and medication use among Danish children in 2024, with prevalence proportions differing more than sixfold across municipalities. Municipal socioeconomic status, private specialist capacity and public hospital waiting times explained very little of these differences. 5 of 8 Basic & Clinical Pharmacology & Toxicology, 2026 such variation should not be interpreted as low prevalence being inherently preferable or high prevalence being undesirable. Rather, the concern is that the observed magnitude of variation appears too great given the uniform health system and lack of clear explanatory factors in our data. Similar variations in ADHD diagnoses have been reported previously in Denmark, with high diagnostic rates in Region Zealand and low rates in the Region of Southern Denmark, especially on Funen [8]. Comparable findings have been ob served in Norway, where geographic differences in diagnostic rates greatly exceeded variation in underlying ADHD symptom levels, indicating that morbidity alone cannot account for geo graphic patterns [3]. Likewise, regional variability in ADHD within a universal health system has been documented in Spain [27], suggesting that structural uniformity does not eliminate local-level differences. In our study, ADHD diagnoses and medication use showed broadly similar geographic patterns, even though they reflect different observation windows: cumulative diagnosed preva lence for diagnoses and one-year treatment prevalence for med ication use. Although previous studies have reported higher ADHD preva lence in disadvantaged areas [28, 29], and more consistent phar macotherapy among children from wealthier families [30], we observed no clear socioeconomic gradient in ADHD diagnoses. Medication use, however, showed a weak negative correlation with the socioeconomic index, suggesting slightly higher use in municipalities with lower relative expenditure needs. Earlier Danish studies also point in different directions: one study found considerable geographic clustering of ADHD incidence and medication use, but no significant associations with socio economic or municipal-level factors [31], while another study showed that regional prescribing differences were particularly pronounced among children facing social adversity, reflecting strong social gradients in some regions but not in others [32]. Norwegian data show that socioeconomic indicators are more strongly associated with service contact rates than with ADHD prevalence once children access mental health services [2]. They suggest that inequalities act mainly at the access stage, not at the diagnostic stage. Conceptual frameworks of healthcare ac cess further highlight that such differences may occur at multi ple stages of the care pathway, from the perception of needs to health care seeking, reaching and engagement, and not only at the point of diagnosis [33]. Specialist availability and waiting times may also contribute to geographic variation in access to child and adolescent psy chiatry and thereby prevalence of ADHD. However, we found no statistically significant associations between either special ist capacity or regional waiting times and the prevalence of ADHD medication use or diagnoses. Results from the United States show that higher numbers of relevant physicians are as sociated with greater ADHD diagnosis and medication rates [34]. This suggests that supply-sensitive care may be a partial driver: higher availability of specialist services may increase detection and diagnosis, even when demand is constant [7]. The absence of clear associations in our study may reflect that these regional indicators do not fully capture local differences in access to care, or the limited statistical power of analyses based on five regions. Additional drivers such as parental de mand, municipal referral pathways or local diagnostic culture may play an important role. Research from Norway has shown inter-clinician variation in diagnostic thresholds [35], and a similar factor could plausibly influence Danish practice de spite uniform national guidelines. Evidence from Denmark further indicates that specialist physicians differ considerably in their prescribing behaviour across hospitals, and that such variation directly affects the probability that children receive pharmacological treatment [36]. Such preference-sensitive care, driven by differing professional judgements, remains a likely contributor [7]. Educational system incentives may also play a role. In some municipalities, access to special educational support requires a formal diagnosis, which can create incentives for parents, schools and professionals to seek diagnostic assessments. A re cent qualitative study highlights how ADHD diagnoses are used institutionally in some Danish primary schools as a prerequisite for categorising children with emotional and behavioural dif ficulties and for allocating support services [37]. 6 of 8 Basic & Clinical Pharmacology & Toxicology, 2026 reliance on diagnostic categorisation varies across local school systems. Community-level dynamics may further shape ADHD preva lence. In autism, proximity to diagnosed children increases the likelihood of receiving a diagnosis, likely through heightened awareness and parent-to-parent information exchange [38]. Similar processes may influence ADHD patterns. 4.1 | Future Research Beyond the factors examined in this study, other demand- and supply-side mechanisms could also influence regional varia tion in ADHD treatment. On the demand side, parental healthseeking behaviour, school-level incentives and local awareness networks may shape both referral patterns and treatment up take. On the supply side, differences in municipal Educational Psychological Counselling Services (PPR), which often consti tute the first step in the referral pathway to child and adolescent psychiatry, as well as distance to care, the distribution of private practising and public hospital-based child and adolescent psy chiatrists, regional prioritisation of resources and varying pro fessional norms, including potential differences between private and hospital-based diagnostic practices, could contribute. Future research should therefore combine register data with qualitative and survey-based approaches to capture these dimensions and assess how such mechanisms interact with structural factors to generate the observed variation. 4.2 | Strengths and Limitations Key strengths include the use of nationwide registry data, en suring complete population coverage and eliminating selection bias. Prescription data include all community pharmacy dispen sations, regardless of prescriber or sector. Several limitations should be noted. Diagnoses made by private practising child psychiatrists are not captured in the Danish National Patient Registry, which leads to underestimation and potentially biases geographic comparisons. However, in 2024, 91% of capturable ADHD diagnoses made by child and adoles cent psychiatrists were recorded in the hospital sector and are therefore present in our data [39]. Second, prevalence was de fined as at least one prescription in 2024, which may overesti mate active treatment rates, though relative geographic patterns are unlikely to change. Waiting time was available only for hospital-based child and ad olescent psychiatry. Current expected waiting times reported by private practising psychiatrists working under the public reim bursement system can be obtained [40], but historical data are lacking. Specialist capacity data were available only for private practis ing psychiatrists working under the public reimbursement sys tem. Information on public hospital-based capacity is available in the Health Workforce Mobility Register [41], which was not obtained for this study, and publicly accessible data on hospital capacity divided by region extend only until 2023 [42]. Statistical associations at the regional level were strongly limited by the small number of regions (n = 5), which reduced power and increased uncertainty around effect estimates. Furthermore, the outcome measures were assessed at municipal level (n = 98), whereas the supply-side indicators (waiting times and psychia trist capacity) were only available at regional level (n = 5), a res olution mismatch that may partly explain the null associations observed for these factors. Given the number of correlation and regression analyses per formed across municipal, regional and sex-stratified indicators, the borderline association between socioeconomic index and medication use (ρ = −0.20, p = 0.049) should be interpreted cau tiously, as we did not correct for multiple comparisons. Additionally, the organisation of child and adolescent mental health services varies geographically, with some areas served by multiple units and others by only one. In the latter case, a single department can account for a large proportion of diagnoses in the region, potentially amplifying local practice effects. However, information on hospital catchment areas was not consistently available across all Danish regions, limiting our ability to exam ine whether variation clustered around individual departments. Geographic attribution was based on municipality of residence in 2024, although ADHD diagnoses or treatment may have orig inated elsewhere following residential migration. Finally, we lacked data on symptom severity, parental demand, local clinical practice norms and individual-level socioeconomic background, all of which may be important explanatory factors. 5 | Conclusion In conclusion, large geographic differences in ADHD diagno ses and medication use persist in Denmark despite a uniform healthcare framework. These differences appear only weakly related to specialist capacity, waiting times and socioeconomic context, suggesting that variation might be driven by other factors. Reducing inequities will likely require a multifaceted approach that addresses both resource distribution and local practice variation, ensuring equitable and consistent pathways to diagnosis and treatment. pages: 1 of 10 Child: Care, Health and Development, 2026; 52:e70219 https://doi.org/10.1111/cch.70219 Child: Care, Health and Development REVIEW ARTICLE OPEN ACCESS Parenting Practices in Families of Children With Comorbid ADHD and Anxiety Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Isabelle Denis1,2,3 | Laurie Côté1 | Stéphane Turcotte2 | Guillaume Foldes-Busque1,2,4 1School of Psychology, Laval University, Quebec, Canada | 2Research Centre of the Centre intégré de santé et de services sociaux de Chaudière-Appalaches, Quebec, Canada | 3University Research Center on Youth and Families, Quebec, Canada | 4Research Centre of the Quebec Heart and Lung Institute, Quebec, Canada Correspondence: Isabelle Denis (isabelle.denis@psy.ulaval.ca) Received: 10 June 2025 | Revised: 24 November 2025 | Accepted: 1 December 2025 Keywords: anxiety disorders | attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder | children | parenting practices ABSTRACT Background: Comorbid anxiety disorders affect up to 28% of children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). While coercive parenting is often linked to ADHD and overprotectiveness to anxiety disorders (ADs), little is known about parenting practices in children with both disorders (ADHD+ADs). This systematic review and meta-analysis examined parenting practices in children aged 5–12 years with ADHD+ADs. Methods: Studies were identified through PsycINFO (Ovid), Medline (Ovid), EMBASE, and Web of Science from inception date to January 23, 2025. Of the 1838 records screened, four studies were included in the review, and three were included in the meta-analysis. Results: Compared to parents of children with ADHD alone, those of children with ADHD+ADs reported greater use of anxietyrelated parenting practices (k = 3, g = 0.32, 95% CI = 0.11, 0.53, p = 0.002) and fewer positive parenting practices (k = 3, g = −0.35, 95% CI = −0.55, −0.14, p = 0.001). No significant differences were found in ADHD-related parenting practices (k = 2, g = 0.27, 95% CI = −0.16, 0.70, p = 0.26). Conclusion: These findings suggest that families of children with ADHD+ADs may be characterized by increased anxietyrelated parenting practices and reduced positive parenting compared to families of children with ADHD alone. Further research is needed to inform the development of targeted interventions. 1 | Introduction Approximately 28% of children diagnosed with attentiondeficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) also meet criteria for a comorbid anxiety disorder (Shroff and Sanchez-Lacay 2018). This co-occurrence is associated with more severe consequences than either disorder alone (Bowen et al. 2008; Mikami et al. 2011; Shroff and Sanchez-Lacay 2018; Souza et al. 2005). For instance, children with comorbid ADHD and anxiety disorders (ADHD+ADs) exhibit greater school-related worries, higher rates of absenteeism (Sciberras et al. 2014) and an elevated risk of academic failure (Jensen et al. 2001) compared to those with only one of these disorders. They also present more significant deficits in social skills and are more vulnerable to peer rejection and isolation (Mikami et al. 2011; Nadeau et al. 2018). Furthermore, children with ADHD+AD have lower self-esteem, reduced quality of life and a greater risk of suicidal ideation than children with either ADHD or anxiety disorders (Choi et al. 2017; Sciberras et al. 2014; Tannock 2000; Tannock 2009). At the family level, this comorbidity is linked This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs License, which permits use and distribution in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited, the use is non-commercial and no modifications or adaptations are made. © 2025 The Author(s). 2 of 10 Child: Care, Health and Development, 2026 to increased relational strain (Chan et al. 2022; Tannock et al. 1995) and poorer parental mental health (Eun et al. 2018; Mulraney et al. 2018; Pfiffner and McBurnett 2006; Sciberras et al. 2014; Shroff and Sanchez-Lacay 2018). Parenting practices play a central role in the maintenance and exacerbation of both ADHD and anxiety disorders in children (Chronis-Tuscano et al. 2008; Claussen et al. 2024; Vasey et al. 2014). For instance, coercive and aggressive parenting is more commonly associated with ADHD (Chronis et al. 2004; Chronis-Tuscano et al. 2008; Cussen et al. 2012; Gair et al. 2021; Keown and Woodward 2002; Pfiffner et al. 2005; Woodward et al. 1998), whereas overprotectiveness, excessive control and reinforcement of avoidance behaviours are more specifically linked to anxiety disorders (Drake and Ginsburg 2012; Laurin et al. 2015; McLeod et al. 2007; Murray et al. 2009; Negreiros and Miller 2014; van der Bruggen et al. 2008; Vasey et al. 2014). The literature suggests parenting practices typically associated with each disorder are overrepresented in families of children with ADHD+ADs (Kepley and Ostrander 2007; Pfiffner and McBurnett 2006; Yap and Jorm 2015). Furthermore, this comorbidity has also been linked to a reduction in positive parenting practices (e.g., warmth, communication, involvement, positive discipline; Gair et al. 2021; Kepley and Ostrander 2007; Pfiffner and McBurnett 2006, Yap and Jorm 2015), which otherwise serve as protective factors (Clayborne et al. 2021; Haack et al. 2016; McRae et al. 2020). Despite the well-established clinical and theoretical relevance of parenting practices in the course of ADHD and anxiety disorders (Claussen et al. 2024; Coates et al. 2015; Turgeon et al. 2023; Zwi et al. 2011), few studies have specifically examined their association with ADHD+ADs. To our knowledge, no systematic review or meta-analysis has been conducted on this topic. Advancing our understanding of parenting practices associated with ADHD+ADs is essential to inform the development of more effective psychosocial interventions. Indeed, parent training is a core component of ADHD management (Wolraich et al. 2019), and family-based interventions are increasingly recognized as effective in treating childhood anxiety disorders (Byrne et al. 2023; Schwartz et al. 2019), especially in the presence of comorbidity such as ADHD (van Steensel et al. 2024). 2 | Objectives This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to identify parenting practices associated with ADHD+ADs in children aged 5–12 years, and, when possible, to compare them with those observed in children with either condition alone. 3 | Method This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (Page et al. 2021). The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD42021219479). 3.1 | Search Strategy Search strategies were developed in collaboration with an information specialist and adapted for each database (see Supplementary Table 1). Studies were identified through PsycINFO (Ovid), Medline (Ovid), EMBASE and Web of Science from inception date to January 23, 2025. The ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global database was also consulted to identify unpublished literature. Additionally, reference lists of included studies were manually screened. 3.2 | Eligibility Criteria Studies were eligible if they (1) included children aged 5–12 years diagnosed with ADHD+ADs, (2) assessed parenting practices and (3) were published in English or French. Studies were excluded if the sample comprised children with autism spectrum disorder or psychotic disorders. 3.3 | Study Selection Two independent reviewers screened studies using the Covidence Systematic Review Software (Veritas Health Innovation 2020). Discrepancies were resolved through discussion, and when consensus could not be reached, a third reviewer (ID) was consulted. A total of 2656 studies were identified, and after removing the 371 duplicates, 26 full-text articles were assessed. Four studies met the inclusion criteria, including one identified through reference lists. See the PRISMA flow diagram in Figure 1 for details. 3.4 | Data Extraction and Risk of Bias Assessment Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were independently conducted by two reviewers. Any discrepancies Summary • This systematic review identified only four studies examining parenting practices in children with ADHD+ADs. • Families of children with ADHD+ADs exhibit more anxiety-related parenting practices and lower levels of positive parenting practices compared to families of children with ADHD alone. • The knowledge gap regarding parenting practices in these families is concerning given their importance in evidence-based interventions for both ADHD and anxiety disorders. • These findings highlight the potential clinical value of targeting disorder-specific parenting behaviours while enhancing positive parenting practices to improve outcomes for children with ADHD+ADs and their families. 13652214, 2026, 1, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/cch.70219 by Stony Brook University Libraries, Wiley Online Library on [21/10/2026]. Extracted data included participant characteristics, study design, diagnostic procedures, parenting measures and results (including effect sizes when available). Authors of three studies were contacted to obtain missing data; one study was excluded from the meta-analysis due to unavailable effect size data (McGee 2007). Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Appraisal Checklist—Quantitative Intervention Studies (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence [NICE], 2012). 4 of 10 Child: Care, Health and Development, 2026 3.5 | Data Analysis Parenting practices were categorized as follows, based on the literature: (1) parenting practices typically associated with ADHD (e.g., coercive and aggressive discipline; Chronis et al. 2004; Chronis-Tuscano et al. 2008; Cussen et al. 2012; Keown and Woodward 2002; Pfiffner et al. 2005; Woodward et al. 1998), (2) those linked with anxiety disorders (Drake and Ginsburg 2012; Laurin et al. 2015; McLeod et al. 2007; Murray et al. 2009; Negreiros and Miller 2014; van der Bruggen et al. 2008; Vasey et al. 2014) and (3) positive parenting practices (see Table 1 for details). Effect sizes were estimated using Hedge's g, as it provides greater accuracy than Cohen's d in small samples (Borenstein et al. 2009). A random-effects model was applied to account for methodological heterogeneity across studies (Borenstein et al. 2009). When multiple parenting practices within a category were assessed in a single study, their mean effect size was computed to represent that category. Heterogeneity was examined using the Q statistic; if statistically significant (p < 0.05), the proportion of variance attributable to heterogeneity was calculated using the I2 statistic (Higgins and Thompson 2002) and interpreted as follows: 25% = low, 50% = moderate and 75% = high (Borenstein et al. 2009; Card 2015). Subgroup analyses were planned to explore heterogeneity when I2 reached 40% or more (Deeks et al. 2024) and to examine the influence of study characteristics on findings. However, these analyses could not be conducted due to the small number of eligible studies. All analyses were performed using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis Software (Biostat Inc., Version 3). Quantitative analyses were complemented by a descriptive synthesis of individual study results. 4 | Results 4.1 | Characteristics of the Studies The four studies included in this review were published between 2006 and 2013. Two were peer-reviewed journal articles and two were doctoral dissertations. Three studies used cross-sectional designs (Kepley and Ostrander 2007; McGee 2007; Pfiffner and McBurnett 2006) and one used a longitudinal design (CurchackLichtin 2013). In the latter study, only the assessment conducted at age 6 provided data on ADHD, anxiety disorders and parenting practices; this time point was therefore included in the metaanalysis. One study provided effect size data exclusively for statistically significant results (Pfiffner and McBurnett 2006), and another did not provide sufficient data for effect size calculation (McGee 2007). A total of 122 children with ADHD+ADs and 278 with ADHD only were included in the four selected studies. None of the studies included a comparison group of children with anxiety disorders only. All participants were between 5 and 12 years of age and resided in the United States. Demographic data indicated that the samples were predominantly composed of Caucasian children (73.18%, n = 221/302, 3 studies) and boys (75.17%, n = 227/302, 3 studies). The mean age, reported in two studies, was 8.36 years (SD = 1.75). One study described the children as being school age (Kepley and Ostrander 2007). 6 of 10 Child: Care, Health and Development, 2026 criteria and participant recruitment procedures was frequently incomplete, limiting the ability to fully evaluate methodological rigour across studies. 4.3 | Main Findings 4.3.1 | Parenting Practices Typically Associated With ADHD The meta-analysis revealed a small and non-significant difference between ADHD+ADs and ADHD-only groups in the use of parenting practices typically associated with ADHD (k = 2, g = 0.27, 95% CI = [−0.16, 0.70], Z = 1.24, p = 0.26). There was no significant heterogeneity in effect sizes between samples (Q(1) = 0.16, p = 0.69). See Figure 2. Kepley and Ostrander (2007) found no differences between groups in conflict scores, whereas Curchack-Lichtin (2013) reported no differences in punitive parenting, inconsistent parenting and parent negative affect. Pfiffner and McBurnett (2006) also reported no significant differences in inconsistent discipline, poor monitoring/supervision and power assertion. Finally, McGee (2007) found that poor monitoring/supervision, inconsistent discipline and corporal punishment were not associated with the presence of comorbid anxiety disorders in children with ADHD. However, negative parenting significantly predicted child anxiety symptoms, accounting for up to 6% of the variance. 4.3.2 | Parenting Practices Typically Associated With Anxiety Disorders The meta-analysis revealed a small to moderate increase in parenting practices typically associated with anxiety disorders among parents of children with ADHD+ADs compared to those of children with ADHD alone (k = 3, g = 0.32, 95% CI = [0.11, 0.53], Z = 3.03, p = 0.002). No significant heterogeneity was observed across studies (Q(2) = 0.18, p = 0.91). See Figure 3. Pfiffner and McBurnett (2006) reported that possessiveness was significantly higher among parents of children with ADHD+ADs compared to those with ADHD alone. Similarly, Kepley and Ostrander (2007) found that independence scores were significantly lower in the ADHD+ADs group. However, in this study, no significant differences were observed between groups on parental control, organisation or achievement orientation. In line with these findings, Curchack-Lichtin (2013) reported that parental control did not vary between groups. 4.3.3 | Positive Parenting Practices Results of the meta-analysis indicated that parents of children with ADHD+ADs reported fewer positive parenting practices compared to those of children with ADHD alone (k = 3, g = −0.35, 95% CI = [−0.55, −0.14], Z = −3.30, p = 0.001). The combined effect size was small to moderate, and no significant heterogeneity was found across studies (Q(2) = 0.41, p = 0.81). See Figure 4. 7 of 10 Child: Care, Health and Development, 2026 According to Pfiffner and McBurnett (2006), parents of children with ADHD+ADs reported using positive parenting practices less frequently than those of children with ADHD alone. However, no significant differences were found in parental involvement or warmth scores in that study. Kepley and Ostrander (2007) observed lower active-recreational orientation scores in the ADHD+ADs group compared to the ADHD-only group, but no significant differences in communication/involvement. Curchack-Lichtin (2013) did not report any between-group differences in positive parenting practices. Finally, McGee (2007) found that positive parenting practices were not significantly associated with the presence of ADHD+ADs. 5 | Discussion This systematic review synthesizes evidence on parenting practices in families of school-age children with ADHD+ADs compared to those with either disorder alone. Although no significant differences were found in ADHD-related parenting practices, small to moderate differences were observed in anxiety-related parenting practices and in the use of positive parenting between the ADHD+AD group and the ADHDonly group. These findings suggest that differences in how parents interact with children with ADHD+ADs may be reflected less in FIGURE 2 | Parenting practices typically associated with ADHD: results of the meta-analysis. 8 of 10 Child: Care, Health and Development, 2026 ADHD-related practices and more in reduced positive interactions combined with increased control or overprotection. This observation is consistent with previous research highlighting the role of these anxiety-related parenting practices in the development and maintenance of anxiety disorders in children (Drake and Ginsburg 2012; Laurin et al. 2015; McLeod et al. 2007; Murray et al. 2009; Negreiros and Miller 2014; van der Bruggen et al. 2008; Vasey et al. 2014). Such practices notably encourage children to avoid confronting their fears and, consequently, contribute to the maintenance or exacerbation of anxiety (Affrunti and Ginsburg 2012; van der Bruggen et al. 2008; Van der Sluis et al. 2015). Although the effect size of anxiety-related practices was small to moderate, it is likely to be clinically meaningful, considering that the comparison group also faced the parenting challenges associated with ADHD. The small to moderate reduction in positive parenting practices among parents of children with ADHD+ADs compared to those of children with ADHD alone is also consistent with previous research (Yap and Jorm 2015). This reduction may reflect the increased burden experienced by these families, which, in turn, can disrupt family functioning (Bowen et al. 2008; Mikami et al. 2011; Shroff and SanchezLacay 2018; Souza et al. 2005; Tannock et al. 1995). Moreover, lower levels of positive parenting practices in children with ADHD at ages 3 and 5 have been prospectively associated with a higher likelihood of an anxiety disorder diagnosis at age 8 (Curchack-Lichtin 2013). Taken together, these findings suggest that low levels of positive parenting practices may constitute a risk marker for anxiety disorders in children already vulnerable due to ADHD (Gair et al. 2021; Shroff and SanchezLacay 2018). This hypothesis is further supported by evidence demonstrating the protective effect of positive parenting on the development of internalizing and externalizing symptoms in children (Clayborne et al. 2021; Haack et al. 2016; McRae et al. 2020). Overall, this systematic review and meta-analysis identified a parenting profile marked by increased use of anxiety-related parenting practices and reduced use of positive parenting practices in families of children with ADHD+ADs, compared to families of children with ADHD only. This study also highlights the lack of research on this topic, limiting conclusions regarding the specific parenting practices associated with ADHD+ADs, and how they differ from those observed in families of children with either condition alone. In fact, no study with an anxiety disorder comparison group were identified in this systematic review. An additional priority for future research is to identify parental characteristics associated with these practices. Such data are essential to advance our understanding of parenting in the context of ADHD+ADs and to guide the development of targeted psychosocial interventions for this highly vulnerable population. In the meantime, the current findings combined with previous studies (van Steensel et al. 2024) suggest that clinicians should consider systematically assessing and addressing these parenting practices as part of a comprehensive care approach for children with ADHD+ADs. 6 | Limitations of the Study Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of this study. First, the search strategy was limited to publications in French or English, which may have excluded relevant studies published in other languages. Second, the small number of eligible studies prevented the assessment of publication bias and limited the examination of how potential sources of bias may have influenced the results. Third, reporting of participant selection and recruitment procedures was frequently incomplete, and the sample were predominantly composed of Caucasian boys from the United States, thereby limiting the generalizability of the findings. Moreover, parenting practices were assessed primarily by mothers, limiting conclusions regarding fathers' parental practices. Finally, one study reported only statistically significant results, raising concerns about the possibility of an overestimation of group differences in anxiety-related and positive parenting practices. 7 | Conclusion This systematic review and meta-analysis suggest a parenting profile characterized by increased use of anxiety-related parenting practices and reduced use of positive parenting practices in families of children with ADHD+ADs. This review also underscores the limited research on this topic and emphasizes the need to clarify the specific nature and implications of parenting practices in families of children with ADHD+ADs. Advancing knowledge in this area is essential to inform clinical decisionmaking and improve the efficacy of psychosocial interventions for children with ADHD+ADs. metadata_title: Barriers to and Enablers of the Transition From Child to Adult Mental Health Services for Autistic Young People and/or Those With Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Scoping Review
pages: 1 of 12 Child: Care, Health and Development, 2025; 52:e70201 https://doi.org/10.1111/cch.70201 Child: Care, Health and Development REVIEW ARTICLE Barriers to and Enablers of the Transition From Child to Adult Mental Health Services for Autistic Young People and/or Those With Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Scoping Review Kim Tang1 | Craig Thompson1,2 | Elizabeth Hill1,2 | Elizabeth Pellicano3 | Phoebe Wan1 | Bronwyn Myers2,4,5 1Curtin School of Allied Health, Faculty of Health Sciences, Curtin University, Perth, Western Australia, Australia | 2Curtin enAble Institute, Faculty of Health Sciences, Curtin University, Perth, Western Australia, Australia | 3Department of Clinical, Educational and Health Psychology, University College London, London, UK | 4Mental Health, Alcohol, Substance Use and Tobacco Research Unit, South African Medical Research Council, Tygerberg, South Africa | 5Department of Psychiatry and Mental Health, University of Cape Town, Cape Town, South Africa Correspondence: Kim Tang (kim.n.tang@postgrad.curtin.edu.au) Received: 18 September 2024 | Revised: 7 August 2025 | Accepted: 29 October 2025 Keywords: adolescent | attention deficit hyperactivity disorder | autism spectrum disorder | mental health | transition to adult care ABSTRACT Background: Many autistic young people and/or those with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) have co-occurring mental health conditions. These individuals can experience significant challenges when transitioning from child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) to adult mental health services (AMHS). However, barriers and enablers to the transition from CAMHS to AMHS are poorly understood for this population. This scoping review sought to synthesise the available evidence on barriers and enablers to the transition from CAMHS to AMHS for autistic young people and/or those with ADHD. Methods: Arksey and O'Malley's six-step framework for scoping reviews was used to map out the evidence available and report the findings with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines (PRISMA-ScR). Electronic databases of Medline, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Scopus and ProQuest Central were searched for relevant studies published in English with no date limitations. The review included studies that focused on young people with a primary diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and/or ADHD (population) and their care transition barriers and/or enablers (concept) from CAMHS to AMHS (context). A socioecological framework informed data extraction and narrative synthesis of data on barriers and enablers to transition. Results: This review identified 1677 studies, of which 66 proceeded to full-text screening, and 10 were included. Most studies focused on institutional-level transition barriers, including poor communication between CAMHS and AMHS and lack of clarity about their role in the transition process. Involvement of the neurodivergent young person in decision-making processes about their mental health care and clinicians who tailored their approaches to the needs of the neurodivergent young person emerged as key enablers of a positive transition experience. Studies largely failed to examine community and policy-related barriers to mental health care transitions. Most studies examined the perspectives of providers or carers, with only five representing the perspectives of neurodivergent people. Conclusion: Young people who are autistic and/or have ADHD experience many barriers to their transition from CAMHS to AMHS; however, few studies have examined barriers and enablers to the service transition process. © 2025 John Wiley & Sons Ltd.

2 of 12 Child: Care, Health and Development, 2025 1 | Introduction Global changes over the past two decades have contributed to the significant increase in mental health conditions among young people between the ages of 12 and 25 (McGorry et al. 2024). For approximately 70% of this population, these mental health conditions will persist into adulthood, requiring continued support from mental health services (Cleverley et al. 2020; World Health Organization 2024). Mental health conditions are the leading cause of disability accounting for 45% of all disability adjusted life years among this age group and impacting on young people's potential to engage with their environment socially and economically (McGorry et al. 2024). Critically, neurodivergent young people are at elevated risk of mental health difficulties (Barber 2021). ‘Neurodivergent’ is an umbrella term used to describe a broad range of differences in neurocognitive functioning outside of societal norms. The term emphasises neurological variation as part of human diversity rather than pathology (Pellicano and Houting 2022). For autistic young people, and those with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), the risk of experiencing mental health difficulties, including anxiety and depression, is approximately three times higher than their neurotypical peers (Barber 2021; Pellicano and Houting 2022; Accardo et al. 2022). Consequently, neurodivergent young people are likely to be overrepresented in the population who need access to child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) (World Health Organization 2024; Accardo et al. 2022). Neurodivergent young people are more likely to require ongoing support from mental health services into adulthood due to persisting challenges to independently navigate all of life's changes during this period (World Health Organization 2024; Accardo et al. 2022). These transitions can include leaving school, starting a job or tertiary education or reductions in social supports (World Health Organization 2024; Accardo et al. 2022). Many young people experience difficulties with the transition from CAMHS to adult mental health services (AMHS). The transition from CAMHS to AMHS typically occurs at 18 years of age, at which point the young person no longer meet the CAMHS eligibility requirements (Cleverley et al. 2020). CAMHS and AMHS differ in their expectations of young people and caregiver involvement in mental health care. As young people transition to AMHS, there is an expectation that they will assume greater autonomy for their mental health care and there will be less involvement from caregivers (Cleverley et al. 2020; Barber 2021). This service transition appears particularly challenging for neurodivergent youth who experience higher rates of care disruption and disengagement compared with their neurotypical peers (Cleverley et al. 2020; Barber 2021; Mulvale et al. 2019; Dunn 2017; Roughan et al. 2019; Cheak-Zamora and Teti 2015; McNicholas et al. 2015; Crane et al. 2019). Given the greater difficulties that neurodivergent youth experience with care transition, it is crucial that these barriers are understood from their perspective to help guide interventions to facilitate the transition from CAMHS to AMHS so they can continue to engage in the care they need (Cheak-Zamora and Teti 2015). At a time when the neurodivergent young person is often experiencing multiple simultaneous life transitions, disruption to service access to AMHS can increase vulnerability to mental health crises and increase difficulty in managing activities of daily living (Appleton et al. 2022). Previous reviews have sought to explore the factors that influence care transitions for young adults with ADHD (Price et al. 2019; Rudgley 2013; Scarpellini and Bonati 2023; Swift et al. 2014), highlighting the limited availability of adult ADHD services, the young person's readiness for this service transition and (Price et al. 2019) and provider-related factors as barriers to the transition process (Rudgley 2013; Scarpellini and Bonati 2023). While these reviews provide important insight into care transition barriers, they all focus on ADHD. It is unclear whether these findings are also applicable to autistic young people. Although there are often overlapping features between ADHD and autism diagnoses, such as difficulties with executive function, behaviour and social skills, the nature and presentation of these features can differ (Mayes et al. 2012). One notable difference is that children with ADHD often have difficulty sustaining their focus, while autistic children can become hyperattentive to topics of interest to them (Mayes et al. 2012). Therefore, not all recommendations made for young people with ADHD will support the behavioural, social or cognitive needs of autistic young people (Coghill et al. 2023; Whitehouse et al. 2020). This scoping review aimed to identify and synthesise the literature on barriers and enablers to the transition from CAMHS to AMHS for autistic young people and/or those with ADHD in order to inform intervention to facilitate care transition. This scoping review focused on autism and ADHD, the two most common forms of neurodivergence. To systematically identify gaps in the evidence base, we used Bronfenbrenner's socioecological model (SEM) as a conceptual framework (Bronfenbrenner 1976; Bronfenbrenner 1977; Kilanowski 2017). The SEM views mental health service use as being influenced by a range of interrelated factors relevant to the individual (e.g., beliefs), their interpersonal relationships (e.g., immediate social supports), their community (e.g., extended social supports), the health service organisations they engage with (e.g., their service policies and procedures) and broader mental health policies (Bronfenbrenner 1976; Bronfenbrenner 1977; Kilanowski 2017). The SEM is widely used to understand the barriers to a broad range of mental health interventions across different populations and settings (Thum et al. 2023; Wold and Mittelmark 2018; Jenkins et al. 2023; Tanhan and Francisco 2019; Scharpf et al. 2021). Summary • There are few studies reflecting the perspectives of autistic young people and/or those with ADHD on barriers and enablers to mental health care transition. Future research should prioritise eliciting their lived experience to enhance understanding of how to support these care transitions. • Studies focused on institutional barriers and enablers to mental health service transition, largely neglecting community and policy-level barriers. To ensure a comprehensive understanding of mental health service transition barriers and enablers, future research should examine barriers at these levels. 13652214, 2026, 1, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/cch.70201 by Stony Brook University Libraries, Wiley Online Library on [21/10/2026]. 3 of 12 Child: Care, Health and Development, 2025 2 | Methods This review was informed by Arksey and O′Malley's framework for scoping reviews (Arksey and O'Malley 2005) and reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) Checklist (Tricco et al. 2018). The protocol was registered with the Open Science Foundation (OSF) on 18/09/2023 (doi:/10.17605/OSF.IO/BZPQF) and published (Tang et al. 2024). 2.1 | Identifying the Research Question We used the population, concept and context (PCC) framework to define the research question for this review. For this scoping review, the i. population of interest were young people with a primary diagnosis of autism and/or ADHD; ii. concept was barriers and enablers to the transition from CAMHS to AMHS; iii. context was mental health services that provide psychotherapy support rather than medication only management. More specifically, this review aimed to address the following research question: What are the barriers and enablers to the transition from CAMHS to AMHS for autistic young people and/or those with ADHD? 2.2 | Identifying Relevant Studies We used a three-step approach to identify relevant studies. First, we developed an initial search strategy with the aid of a health sciences librarian that included search terms related to the PCC framework used for this scoping review. To ensure relevance, we sought feedback from a lived experience advisory group comprising members with lived experience of mental health services and who identified as being autistic and/or having ADHD. Members were not health practitioners. This advisory group provided input into terms to include in the initial search strategy such as previous neurodivergent diagnostic names, for example, Aspergers, pervasive development disorder and ADD. This search strategy was piloted in Medline before being revised to include key words related to the PCC framework used to define the research question for this review as outlined in Section 2.1, as well as MeSH terms to yield more accurate results. In the second step, one reviewer (K.T.) used the revised search strategy to conduct the database search. Medline (Ovid), CINAHL (EBSCO), PsycINFO (Ovid), ProQuest and Scopus Central electronic databases were searched for relevant studies on September 2023. See sample search in Table 1. Medline, CINAHL and PsychINFO databases were the three main data bases searched first, before searching for any additional relevant studies on ProQuest and Scopus Central databases. 4 of 12 Child: Care, Health and Development, 2025 In the third step, the reference lists of all included studies were checked for additional studies not captured by the searches. SpiderCite (https://​sr-​accel​erator.​com/#/​spide​rcite​) was used to conduct forward and backward citation checks of included studies to identify any additional studies missed by the database searches. An updated search was conducted in August 2024 to identify relevant studies published between October 2023 and August 2024, with no additional relevant studies found. 2.3 | Study Selection Study selection occurred in two stages between September and October 2023. After identifying articles from all five databases, articles were exported into Endnote and duplicates were removed. The list of deduplicated articles was extracted into an Excel spreadsheet and stored on a password protected drive through Curtin University in preparation for selection. During first stage screening, two reviewers (K.T. and P.W.) independently screened the titles and abstracts of all identified sources, using the Excel spreadsheet to record whether to include the article or exclude it from full-text review because the study focused on the incorrect population, context or concept. Articles that appeared relevant or where there was insufficient information about the population, context or concept to make an informed decision were progressed to full-text review for second stage screening. The same reviewers then assessed the articles that progressed to full-text review against predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria, recording their responses and reasons for exclusion on an Excel spreadsheet. Studies were eligible for inclusion if they looked at adolescents and/or young people (aged 18–24) with a primary diagnosis of autism and/or ADHD, who had experience with the transition process from CAMHS to AMHS. Studies were excluded if they mentioned other forms of neurodivergence that were not autism or ADHD (wrong population), did not explore the transition process from CAMHS to AMHS (wrong concept), only described the transition process for ongoing ADHD medication management (wrong context), did not report on individual study data, were not peer-reviewed, not written in English or could not be accessed. Reviewer discrepancies were discussed with the rest of the research team for both the title and abstract and full-text screening stages and resolved by consensus. Intercoder agreement for title and abstract screening was almost perfect (Cohen's kappa = 0.94) and substantial (Cohen's kappa = 0.80) for full-text screening (Landis and Koch 1977). Studies that met the inclusion criteria in the full-text review were included for data extraction. 2.4 | Charting the Data A data charting sheet was developed and piloted to ensure it captured all relevant information. Two research team members then used this tool to independently chart all relevant study information from each included article between February and March 2024 (K.T. charted data from all 10 included articles, BM charted data from four articles, C.T. and E.H. both charted data from three articles). More specifically, these reviewers charted data on (1) study characteristics (authors, publication year, country, study setting, study design and sample size), (2) the population (age, gender, ethnicity and type of neurodivergence) and (3) reported barriers and enablers to the transition from CAMHS to AMHS. Any disagreements were resolved by discussion with all four team members until a consensus was reached. 2.5 | Collating, Summarising and Reporting Results The SEM was used as a framework for guiding the narrative synthesis and reporting of these findings (Kilanowski 2017). We had initially proposed using Bronfenbrenner's SEM (Bronfenbrenner 1976) in conjunction with the Social-Ecological Model of Adolescent and Young Adult Readiness for Transition (SMART) framework (Schwartz et al. 2011). During data charting, we found that few elements of the SMART framework were represented in the charted data and those that were represented overlapped with the SEM. We therefore decided to only use the SEM (Thum et al. 2023) as a conceptual framework. As none of the included studies explicitly referenced or applied the SEM, the research team met to categorise each charted barrier or enabler as an intrapersonal, interpersonal, community, institutional or policy-related factor in line with the components of the SEM (Kilanowski 2017). The definitions we used to categorise these barriers against the SEM levels are presented in Table 2. The quality of the included studies was assessed using the Standard Quality Assessment Criteria for Evaluating Primary Research Papers from a Variety of Fields (hereafter referred to as the Standard Quality Assessment) (Kmet et al. 2004). Once the 843 duplicates were removed, 834 titles and abstracts were screened and 72 progressed for full-text review. The barriers and enablers are reported below according to the relevant SEM level. See Table 4. 4 | Discussion This scoping review found a paucity of literature describing barriers and enablers to mental health service transition for neurodivergent youth, with only 10 studies meeting the inclusion criteria for this review. This small evidence base is a cause for concern given the urgent need to inform interventions that support ongoing access to mental health care as neurodivergent young people age out of CAMHS (Crane et al. 2019; Hall et al. 2013, 2015; Merrick et al. 2020; Newlove-Delgado et al. 2018; Price et al. 2022; Reale et al. 2015; Reis et al. 2021; Roberti et al. 2023; Swift et al. 2013). This is particularly important given that this service transition is likely to occur at a time when neurodivergent young people are also experiencing developmental and social transitions that can impact their mental well-being (World Health Organization 2024; Accardo et al. 2022). The limited evidence base and the variable quality of available evidence, as highlighted by this review, underscores the need for more research on this topic so that tailored and person-centred, community and institutional-level strategies can be developed to facilitate the transition from CAMHS to AMHS for neurodivergent young people. 4.1 | Key Findings of Barriers and Enablers to the Transition Process Despite these concerns, this review nevertheless identified key intrapersonal, interpersonal, community and institutional barriers that need to be addressed to facilitate the transition process. Barriers identified included a lack of individual knowledge information provided to all key stakeholders about the young person's transition process, professional support on how to provide mental health support to autistic young people and/or those with ADHD and joint planning between all key stakeholders (Crane et al. 2019; Hall et al. 2013, 2015; Merrick et al. 2020; Newlove-Delgado et al. 2018; Price et al. 2022; Reale et al. 2015; Reis et al. 2021; Roberti et al. 2023; Swift et al. 2013). Conversely, enablers of the transition process also exist at the same levels and include strong client–therapist relationships advocating for the individual, clear communication on why the transition was necessary and transition process expectations to help prepare the individual discharge from CAMHS and access AMHS and caregiver involvement to help advocate for the young person where they were unable to communicate their needs (Crane et al. 2019; Hall et al. 2013, 2015; Merrick et al. 2020; NewloveDelgado et al. 2018; Price et al. 2022; Reale et al. 2015; Reis et al. 2021; Roberti et al. 2023; Swift et al. 2013). Interestingly, these barriers are similar to those reported by studies examining care transitions for young people with chronic health conditions or disabilities (Terry 2023; Kennedy et al. 2022). 4.2 | Gaps in the Literature Identified by This Review In addition, this review highlighted three important gaps in the literature that would benefit from further research. First, despite the recognition of positioning the neurodivergent young person at the centre of the service design and delivery to enhance service outcomes (Marshall-Lee et al. 2020), young people's perspectives have not been extensively explored in the existing literature. Where five of the studies reported on the lived experiences of the young person, it was a small sample size (7–130 participants) (Crane et al. 2019; Merrick et al. 2020; NewloveDelgado et al. 2018; Reis et al. 2021; Swift et al. 2013). Efforts have been made to improve outcomes for young people leaving CAMHS through a co-produced transition preparation programme with young people, health professionals and researchers, with the aim to collaboratively work together to produce original material rather than just commenting on existing policy and practice guidelines (Dunn 2017). Although existing transition guidelines exist for autism and ADHD, respectively, such as NICE (National Institute for Health and Care Excellence 2024), no studies have sought to include the lived experiences of autistic young people and/or those with ADHD in the development of a transition framework. Furthermore, previous studies have not sought to compare the perceived barriers and enablers of the transition process between neurodivergent young people compared with neurotypical youth. Therefore, it is uncertain how similar or different the transition process experience is and how well already available resources cater to the needs of neurodivergent young people or what neurodivergent specific supports need to be developed to support them to continue engaging in their mental health care (Crane et al. 2019; Swift et al. 2013). A second limitation of the existing literature is that none of the included studies explicitly sought to explore barriers and enablers to the transition process across the entire treatment ecosystem. Studies often only examined the perspective of a single group of stakeholders within the service system (e.g., providers or young people), with none exploring the perspectives of policymakers or other health system leaders. Unsurprisingly, studies identified few barriers and enablers at the community and policy level as the opinions of community services and those involved with the policy-making process were not consulted. Community factors such as access to community resources, positive relationships and social connections have generally been identified as critical predictors of successful transition in mental health literature (Eriksson et al. 2018). However, comparable findings within this body of literature are limited, therefore restricting the knowledge of how similar or different the community level barriers to the transition process are for young people who are autistic and/or have ADHD. While no studies included in this review explicitly highlighted policy-level factors, we identified one policy enabler, namely, the active involvement of mental health professionals who are knowledgeable and have direct experience working with the community in advocating, drafting and shaping legislation to meet the needs of marginalised communities (Gondek et al. 2017). 10 of 12 Child: Care, Health and Development, 2025 system is complex and multifaceted (Bronfenbrenner 1976), suggesting that it requires stakeholder collaboration to effectively meet the neurodivergent young person's needs. As none of the included studies specifically sought to elicit the perspectives of all key stakeholders and integrate these data, it is difficult to implement a sustainable change at a policy level within mental health systems, to support the transition process for autistic and/ or ADHD young people. A third limitation of the existing literature is that it is limited to European mental health systems. Most studies were conducted in the context of the UK National Health System (NHS), two in Italy and one based in Belgium. Both the United Kingdom and Italy have adopted an NHS model that is publicly funded, making it more accessible to their residents, in comparison with Belgium, which is a regulated market system (RMS) where they are ‘mostly for-profit (outpatient doctors) or not-for-profit publicly funded private providers’ (Nicaise et al. 2020, 27). Enablers of an NHS model may include more continuity of care and better chronic care delivery rather than private or mixed health systems; however, RMS may allow their providers to have better management autonomy, making it easier to change and implement institutional policies and procedures (Nicaise et al. 2020). As a result, findings from these studies should be generalised with caution as not all countries will have the resources or be equipped to implement the enablers highlighted or reduce the barriers at each SEM level identified to support the transition process from CAMHS to AMHS for neurodivergent young people. While acknowledging the limited evidence available, this scoping review has identified some key barriers and enablers to the mental health service transition process for autistic and/or ADHD young people. This can enable mental health services to address these key barriers identified in this review by (1) exploring how their existing policies impact neurodivergent populations; (2) allocating their resources to support the needs of neurodivergent young people, for example, staff training on the differences of neurodivergence and to ensure health professionals can adapt their communication styles when working with neurodivergent young people; and (3) providing open communication channels to actively invite feedback from neurodivergent young people to share their experiences in mental health services and making necessary adjustments to ensure safety and well-being, to encourage ongoing involvement in their mental health care (Hudson et al. 2019). 4.3 | Limitations This review has several limitations. First, we excluded studies within the grey literature, which could have provided more breadth to the review findings regarding what is known and available in research. The decision to exclude these studies was related to difficulties in (1) searching systematically and transparently due to web search limitations to accommodate full search strategies and (2) ensuring quality control, as the grey literature produced by organisations or individuals may lack detailed descriptions of the methodological approaches used or can have biases if it is an area of interest, which could impact the credibility of the results (Mahood et al. 2014). Second, while recognising the range of forms of neurodivergence, this scoping review only looked at studies that were specific to autism and/or ADHD due to their prevalence in the general population (Stenning and Bertilsdotter-Rosqvist 2021; Doyle 2020). Therefore, recommendations may not be generalised to other forms of neurodivergence. Third, studies were excluded if they were not in English or could not be accessed. As a result, the studies included in this review were limited in geographical location which may not accurately represent what has been researched in other parts of the world. Additionally, of the studies that included the gender or ethnicities of their sample, it was predominantly Caucasian male participants thus findings of this review may not accurately reflect the lived experiences of neurodivergent young people with diverse gender and ethnic identities. 5 | Future Directions More high-quality research is clearly needed to represent the diversity of mental health in neurodivergent young people. The existing literature provides a restricted and incomplete picture of the factors influencing service transition from CAMHS to AMHS for neurodivergent young people. Future studies should examine the perspectives of policymakers related to CAMHS to AMHS service transition to understand how state or national policies influence the allocation of resources and accessibility to mental health services, which in turn affects how the service provides treatment to the young person in their care. While recognising that no two people are the same, no two health systems are the same either. Therefore, to better understand the similarities or differences between health systems and implement neurodiverse tailored recommendations, further research is needed within other countries. 6 | Conclusion This scoping review only included 10 studies, demonstrating the limited available literature regarding the transition process for autistic young people and/or those with ADHD. Findings suggest that neurodivergent young people experience many institutional barriers to their transition to AMHS. However, the extent to which community and policy-level factors influence care transition for autistic young people and/or those with ADHD remains poorly understood. Efforts to identify the full breadth of barriers and enablers to care transition are critical to designing and implementing targeted interventions to promote optimal service transitions and facilitate continued mental health care for this population. Hill3,7 | on behalf of the DISCA team 1NTU Psychology, School of Social Sciences, Nottingham Trent University, Nottingham, UK | 2Centre for Innovation in Mental Health (CIMH), School of Psychology, Faculty of Environmental and Life Sciences, University of Southampton, Southampton, UK | 3School of Clinical and Experimental Sciences (Paediatric Neuroscience), Faculty of Medicine, University of Southampton, Southampton, UK | 4Hampshire and Isle of Wight Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, Southampton, UK | 5New York University Child Study Center, Hassenfeld Children's Hospital at NYU Langone, New York City, New York, USA | 6DiMePRe-J—Department of Precision and Rigenerative Medicine-Jonic Area, University of Bari ‘Aldo Moro’, Bari, Italy | 7Paediatric Sleep Medicine, Southampton Children's Hospital, Southampton, UK Correspondence: Lucy Smith (lucy.smith@ntu.ac.uk) Received: 18 June 2025 | Revised: 5 January 2026 | Accepted: 7 January 2026 Keywords: attention deficit hyperactivity disorder | clinicians | developing digital interventions | sleep difficulties ABSTRACT Background: This study aims to explore for the first time the knowledge, understanding and management of sleep problems in children with ADHD among clinicians who specialise in sleep and ADHD. The aim was to inform the development of digital sleep awareness training for clinicians. Method: Fifteen clinicians who work with children with ADHD and sleep difficulties in the United Kingdom participated in semistructured qualitative interviews. Data were analysed using a reflexive thematic analysis approach to generate and guide the content of digital sleep awareness training. Results: Four core themes were developed: ‘It's a Problem’ highlighted the extent to which children with ADHD were reported to struggle with sleep difficulties and the impact this has on the child and family. Clinicians also discussed the difficulty they had in finding evidence-based information they could share with caregivers. With little to no formal training, most of the advice they gave came from ‘learning on the job’. When discussing ADHD specific sleep difficulties and disorders, clinicians reflected on their own ‘insight into limitations of knowledge’. ‘Learning for practice’ highlighted the divergence in the methods of learning preferred by clinicians, despite convergence of learning content needed. Conclusions: Sleep problems in children with ADHD are common, and clinicians often struggle to support these due to lack of formal training. There is a need for accessible, authoritative training for UK practitioners who work with children with ADHD. 1 | Introduction Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by inattention and/ or hyperactivity and impulsivity that is persistent and causes substantial impairment in functioning (Koutsoklenis and Honkasilta 2023). The global prevalence of ADHD varies, but most rigorous estimates report a prevalence of about 5% in children (Cortese et al. 2023). Symptoms of ADHD often begin in early childhood, at critical developmental time periods (SonugaBarke and Halperin 2010), and are one of the most common reasons children are referred to mental health services (Hansen et al. 2021). Indeed, within the United Kingdom, the demand for care is significantly outstripping the capacity of services (French et al. 2023). Within the United Kingdom, ADHD service configuration and delivery vary widely, including community paediatrics, child and adolescent mental health services, CAMHS and occasionally local government.
