For the association between neurodevelopmental conditions and ADHD persistence, the moderating effect of the tracking period (into adolescence or adulthood) (QM = 10.60, p < .05) was significant. However, we found that neurodevelopmental conditions did not significantly correlate with ADHD persistence in studies tracking participants into adolescence (d = 0.28, p = .06) or into adulthood (d = 0.15, p = .16). The method of assessing childhood comorbidities, sex, participant age at the start of the study, and reporter for adult ADHD did not significantly influence estimated associations between the persistence of ADHD and the presence of comorbidities. Sensitivity analysis As we adopted the most conservative approach to estimate unreported p values in the adjusted results, a sensitivity analysis was conducted to explore whether the reduction in effect sizes in the adjusted results was attributable to studies lacking specific data. Consequently, we excluded the seven studies without specific p values (Biederman et al., 1996, 2011; Elkins et al., 2020; Mick et al., 2011; Miranda et al., 2015; Murray et al., 2022; Tandon, Si, & Luby, 2011) and re-ran the meta-analysis (see Figure S7). The adjusted results continued to indicate smaller Cohen’s d (dadj = 0.16, CI = 0.06, 0.26) than that of unadjusted results (d = 0.31, CI = 0.19, 0.43) for the association between externalizing conditions and ADHD persistence, consistent with the findings that included all studies. There were not enough studies to conduct the sensitivity analysis for internalizing conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. There were also four studies that used different criteria to define ‘persistent ADHD’ (Biederman et al., 1996, 2011, 2012; McAuley et al., 2017). We excluded these four studies and re-ran the meta-analysis (see Figures S8a,b and S9a,b). Smaller Cohen’s d values were observed in the models that included adjusted internalizing (dadj = 0.11, CI = 0.09, 0.31) and externalizing (dadj = 0.09, CI = 0.03, 0.14) problems, compared to the models that included unadjusted internalizing (d = 0.18, CI = 0.04, 0.31) and externalizing (d = 0.32, CI = 0.19, 0.45) problems. These results were consistent with our main analysis, indicating that removing these studies did not affect the interpretation of the findings. Quality of studies and publication bias The results of our quality assessment are shown in Table 1. All studies were rated as ‘good’ (30.8%) or ‘fair’ (69.2%). However, the results still indicated potential publication bias in Egger’s test in the models for the internalizing (t = 4.28, p < .05), externalizing (t = 5.32, p < .05) and neurodevelopmental (t = 2.49, p < .05) problems/conditions. We were unable to use the trim-and-fill method typically used to correct for potential small study bias in models (Duval & Tweedie, 2000); as it is not suitable for multilevel models. Funnel plots (see Figures S10–S13) indicated positive publication bias, with more points falling to the right of the reference line. Upon further examination of these studies, we found that the publication bias was primarily driven by studies that included teacher-reported or self-reported information. Among the studies that used only parent-reported information (see Figures S14a,b and S15), we still found a significant unadjusted association between internalizing conditions, externalizing conditions, and ADHD persistence, with pooled Cohen’s d values of 0.18 (0.03, 0.32) and 0.48 (0.26, 0.70), respectively. After controlling for confounding variables, the association between externalizing conditions and ADHD persistence was no longer significant, with a pooled Cohen’s d value of 0.23 (0.20, 0.67) based on the only three available results from two remaining studies (Murray et al., 2022; Tandon et al., 2011). However, there were not enough studies to test for publication bias in the models of internalizing conditions or neurodevelopmental conditions and ADHD persistence that included only parent-reported information. Discussion We conducted a series of comprehensive meta-analyses to examine the associations between childhood internalizing, externalizing, neurodevelopmental conditions, and the persistence of ADHD. The unadjusted results indicated that childhood comorbid internalizing and externalizing conditions were significantly correlated with ADHD persistence. We did not find significant associations between neurodevelopmental conditions and ADHD persistence. In the meta-analysis of studies including adjusted results, the association between externalizing conditions and ADHD persistence diminished, and the association between internalizing conditions and ADHD persistence was no longer significant. Therefore, accounting for possible confounders (e.g., sex, age, and other comorbidities) can reduce the association between childhood comorbidities and ADHD persistence.  2025 The Author(s). The association between comorbid internalizing, externalizing, or neurodevelopmental conditions and ADHD persistence The association between internalizing conditions and ADHD persistence diminished when only including studies that reported adjusted results. Children with more internalizing conditions were more likely to persist with their ADHD symptoms into later developmental stages (e.g., Hurtig et al., 2007; Mick et al., 2011; Musser et al., 2016). However, the effect size of the association between internalizing conditions and ADHD persistence is relatively low. As a result, although adding the moderating variables did not significantly change estimated associations, it did widen confidence intervals, meaning associations became nonsignificant. Therefore, future papers on the prediction of ADHD persistence by internalizing conditions should publish both adjusted and unadjusted results. Additionally, the role of internalizing conditions on ADHD persistence might be worth exploring again after more studies have been published, particularly those that report adjusted results. Externalizing conditions were significantly associated with ADHD persistence both before and after controlling for covariates. Children with more externalizing conditions were more likely to continue experiencing ADHD symptoms. This may be due to symptomatic overlaps or shared physiological mechanisms between externalizing conditions and ADHD. The symptoms of externalizing conditions have high overlap with ADHD symptoms, such as impulsive behavior, having difficulties following rules, and emotional dysregulation (Janssens et al., 2015; Martel, Levinson, Lee, & Smith, 2017; Shader & Beauchaine, 2020). Children with ADHD and comorbid externalizing conditions typically exhibit more severe ADHD symptoms (Armstrong, Lycett, Hiscock, Care, & Sciberras, 2015; Lapalme, Dery, Dube, & Lemieux, 2018), also making it more likely for them to meet ADHD diagnostic criteria later on. Therefore, children who typically have more externalizing conditions are also more likely to meet additional diagnostic criteria for ADHD, making it more difficult for them to achieve clinical remission or symptom reduction at later developmental stages. Beyond the overlap in symptoms, previous research has identified shared physiological mechanisms and genetic influences between ADHD and externalizing conditions. For example, research on neural mechanisms suggests that ADHD, along with externalizing behavior problems such as CD and ODD, is associated with sensitivity to reward and a ‘disinhibitory’ deficit (Sergeant, Geurts, Huijbregts, Scheres, & Oosterlaan, 2003). Neurobiological studies have shown functional abnormalities in regions such as the prefrontal cortex, amygdala, and striatum across these conditions (e.g., Ghosh, Ray, & Basu, 2017; Halperin & Schulz, 2006; Noordermeer, Luman, & Oosterlaan, 2016; Van Dessel et al., 2019). Additionally, a meta-analysis of genetic studies indicated that the genetic correlation between ADHD and externalizing conditions was 0.49 (Andersson et al., 2020). This overlap in symptoms, neural mechanisms, and genetic characteristics may contribute to the persistence of externalizing behavior problems in childhood ADHD. Besides identifying the association between externalizing conditions and ADHD persistence, another notable finding is that we observed a reduction in the effect size, albeit nonsignificant, of externalizing conditions on ADHD persistence after controlling for covariates. As such, the association between externalizing conditions and ADHD persistence may not be a strong direct effect, but rather the relationship may be (at least partially) explained by confounding factors. Neurodevelopmental conditions were not significantly associated with ADHD persistence, which aligns with previous studies. We found that most research examining the neurodevelopmental conditions and ADHD persistence has not found significant associations (Biederman et al., 1996; Chang et al., 2020; Rinsky, 2012; Willcutt et al., 2007; Chang et al., 2020). This may be due to the changing symptoms and changing genetic impact of ADHD across development. Although ADHD is often classified as a neurodevelopmental disorder and has high comorbidity and high genetic overlap with other neurodevelopmental conditions such as learning disabilities and autism (Andersson et al., 2020; Antshel & Russo, 2019; Crisci, Caviola, Cardillo, & Mammarella, 2021). Previous research suggests that the risk genes influencing early-onset ADHD (e.g., genes related to the dopamine system) may differ from those influencing later-stage ADHD or persistent ADHD (Palladino, McNeill, Reif, & KittelSchneider, 2019). This could result in neurodevelopmental conditions having high comorbidity and genetic overlap with early-onset ADHD (Daucourt, Erbeli, Little, Haughbrook, & Hart, 2020; Ronald, Simonoff, Kuntsi, Asherson, & Plomin, 2008), but these disorders may not necessarily be associated with the risk of ADHD later in development. Additionally, regarding the impact of specific types of comorbidities on ADHD persistence, we found that childhood ODD and CD were both associated with ADHD persistence. Similarly, in line with the overall analysis of neurodevelopmental disorders’ impact on ADHD persistence, childhood learning disabilities were not related to ADHD persistence. However, when it comes to specific internalizing problems, results indicate that childhood anxiety, as an internalizing condition, significantly predicted ADHD persistence, whereas childhood depression did not. These findings suggest a differential role of anxiety and depression in predicting ADHD persistence. However, the difference in effect sizes between anxiety and  2025 The Author(s). These findings have important practical implications. For instance, regular follow-ups may be especially relevant for children with ADHD and comorbid conditions. Many externalizing conditions are observed less frequently in school settings, which may lead to teachers’ reports not fully capturing the child’s behavior (King et al., 2018). However, the issue of common informant bias should also be considered. In many studies where childhood symptoms were reported by teachers, ADHD symptoms in later stages were assessed through parent or self-reports (e.g., Agnew-Blais et al., 2016; Cheung et al., 2015). In contrast, studies where childhood symptoms were reported by parents often continued to rely on parent reports in later stages (e.g., Biederman et al., 2011; Lecendreux, Konofal, Cortese, & Faraone, 2015; Murray et al., 2022). Therefore, the observed influence of parent-reported childhood externalizing symptoms on ADHD persistence may partly stem from common informant bias. In future research, findings should be interpreted in the context of who reported the symptoms, as our research suggests that this may influence associations. Publication bias The Egger’s test indicated the possibility of publication bias in studies where childhood symptoms were reported by teachers. Our analysis suggested that studies with significant results were more likely to be published. This could lead to an inflated overall effect size. After removing studies based on teacher reports, the predictive effect of childhood externalizing behaviors on ADHD persistence remained only in the unadjusted results but not in the adjusted results. However, as there are only three studies presenting adjusted results (August et al., 1998; Manfro et al., 2019; Musser et al., 2016), caution is required in interpreting this. More research investigating the effect of externalizing problems on ADHD persistence after adjusting for covariates is needed. In addition, due to the limited number of studies, we were unable to test the impact of publication bias in the studies, including other comorbid conditions. As more studies in this field are published in the future, an updated meta-analysis should examine the influence of reporter-related publication bias on research outcomes. Strengths and weaknesses Our study extended a previous meta-analysis (Caye et al., 2016) to examine the association between three types of ADHD comorbidities—internalizing, externalizing, and neurodevelopmental disorders— and ADHD persistence. We extended previous research by exploring the role of covariates (assessment method, sex, age at start, tracking period, reporters for childhood symptoms, reporters for adulthood symptoms) in this association. Since the original meta-analysis was published, the number of eligible studies for each comorbidity type has increased. As a result, certain associations that were not significant in Caye’s research, such as the predictive effect of ODD on ADHD persistence, reached statistical significance in our analysis. On the other hand, we found that MDD, which was a significant predictor of ADHD persistence in Caye’s study, was no longer significant in our metaanalysis. This may be due to the inclusion of a larger number of studies in our analysis, which increased the heterogeneity of results and widened the confidence interval, leading to a loss of significance. Additionally, our definition of depression includes major depression, depressive symptoms, mood disorders, and affective disorders. These definitions are broader than the one used in Caye’s study, which only included major depression. differences between Caye’s study and the current study suggest that different types of emotional problems may vary in their predictive power for ADHD persistence. Our results should be interpreted in light of some limitations. Firstly, we did not specify a particular time range for ADHD persistence from childhood; we only required ADHD measurements at two time points. In the future, when more studies become available, meta-analyses could be conducted to examine ADHD persistence from childhood to adolescence and from childhood to adulthood, as well as exploring which comorbidities may affect these transitions. Second, we still faced the issue of a limited number of studies when conducting meta-analyses on categorized and specific conditions. Particularly after adding covariates, some groups had insufficient sample sizes, which could potentially affect the assessment of the moderation effects of covariates. Thirdly, the assessment of the covariate ‘childhood reporter’ might be influenced by shared informant bias, since the ADHD symptoms at the second time point were most often reported by parents or the participants, and rarely by teachers. Childhood comorbid symptoms reported by parents are more likely to be associated with the persistence of parent-reported ADHD compared to those reported by teachers. Lastly, we observed that publication bias is more likely to arise for studies that include other reporters (e.g., teachers rather than parent or self-report). This requires further investigation as more studies become available. Conclusion This study focused on the association between childhood comorbidities and ADHD persistence, and it was found that internalizing and externalizing conditions were significantly associated with the persistence of childhood ADHD in analyses unadjusted for confounding. However, this association decreased or disappeared after controlling for covariates. The association between ADHD persistence and internalizing or externalizing conditions may be entirely or partly due to confounding by covariates. Comorbid neurodevelopmental conditions were not associated with ADHD persistence. Further examination of the moderating effects of possible covariates revealed that the reporter of childhood symptoms moderated the association between childhood externalizing conditions and ADHD persistence. Specifically, the association between ADHD persistence and externalizing conditions was found only in studies with parent-reported data. This study explored the relationship between various comorbidities and ADHD persistence, which has important clinical implications for the intervention and management of ADHD and its comorbid conditions. What’s new? • We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis including 26 studies to investigate the extent to which specific childhood comorbidities predict the persistence of childhood ADHD into later developmental stages. What’s relevant? • Childhood comorbid externalizing and, to a lesser extent, internalizing conditions were associated with the persistence of ADHD, but this association may be partially due to confounders. • Our results have implications for education professionals, who may need to recognize that children with ADHD and comorbid conditions might require more long-term support. metadata_title: Editorial: ADHD persistence – the interplay of genes, socioeconomic context, and symptom domains over development
pages: Editorial: ADHD persistence – the interplay of genes, socioeconomic context, and symptom domains over development ADHD persistence as a developmental question The persistence of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms into adulthood is common, associated with adverse outcomes in multiple domains including education, occupation, and comorbid mental health disorders (Caye et al., 2016; Faraone et al., 2024). A binary label of persistence, however, obscures the reality that for many individuals ADHD symptoms vary considerably across time (Sibley et al., 2022). Inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity show different developmental trajectories and are differentially associated with long-term outcomes (Faraone et al., 2024; Pingault et al., 2015; Sonuga-Barke et al., 2023). For example, hyperactivity/impulsivity typically declines from childhood into adulthood and is more strongly linked to externalizing and risk-taking outcomes, whereas inattention is relatively more stable and more strongly associated with persistent academic and occupational impairment (Garner et al., 2013). Current evidence recognizes that genetic contributions to ADHD symptoms vary by age and symptom domain (Pingault et al., 2015), but the importance of environmental factors such as socioeconomic context for symptom persistence remains underexamined (Rakesh, Lee, Gaikwad, & McLaughlin, 2025). We present evidence supporting a unified framework for conceptualizing ADHD symptom persistence as a dynamic developmental process shaped by three components: (1) stable genetic liability, (2) time-varying gene–environment interplay, and (3) independent environmental effects by symptom domain. We focus on socioeconomic status (SES) as a case study, to guide future research applying genetic and environmental data to predict risk for ADHD symptom persistence over the long term. Conceptual foundations: Heritability and environmental context ADHD is a highly heritable condition, with twin studies reporting mean heritability estimates of around 70–80% (Faraone et al., 2024). Genome-wide genetic risk for ADHD, reflected in polygenic risk scores, is also consistently associated with ADHD diagnosis. However, such polygenic scores do not necessarily differ between those with remitted versus persistent ADHD in the long term (Agnew-Blais et al., 2021). This suggests that genetic liability may be a stronger predictor of stable, early-emerging symptom levels than of developmental change (Pingault et al., 2015). There are two possible nonmutually exclusive explanations for this. First, different genes and genetic mechanisms may relate to baseline symptom levels and changes over time, which are not well-captured by current polygenic risk scores derived from case–control genome-wide association studies, predominantly conducted in cross-sectional adult samples. Without genome-wide studies explicitly modelling symptom changes, the distinction between stable versus changing genetic influences remains difficult to test (Pingault et al., 2022). Addressing this may require either large, pooled datasets spanning multiple age groups or – more ambitiously – large-scale longitudinal genetic studies. Second, while genetics may be the predominant influence on childhood ADHD presence, environmental factors may exert a unique and strong influence on its developmental trajectory. For example, SES represents one of most important contextual influences associated with ADHD, linked to both higher rates of prevalence (Rowland et al., 2018) and persistence (Kim, King, & Jennings, 2019). Multiple mechanisms may link environmental factors and ADHD, including (1) gene–environment correlation with genetic factors influencing both SES and ADHD (Sonuga-Barke et al., 2023), (2) gene–environment interaction where SES moderates genetic liability (e.g., through differential exposure to stress), or (3) independent SES effects on longitudinal brain and cognitive development (Rakesh et al., 2025). Thus, symptom changes may reflect a reweighting of contributions over time from genetic liability, environmental effects, and environmental modulation of genetic liability, which have somewhat distinct impacts on inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity domains. Below, we briefly introduce evidence and hypotheses for these ideas. Conflict of interest statement: No conflicts declared. ADHD symptom persistence as a dynamic developmental process shaped by three components: (1) stable genetic liability, (2) time-varying gene– environment interplay, and (3) independent environmental effects by symptom domain.  2026 Association for Child and Adolescent Mental Health. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry 67:5 (2026), pp 605–608 doi:10.1111/jcpp.70150

Process I. Genetic liability Progress in unravelling the genetic architecture of ADHD through cross-sectional studies has been well-described (Sonuga-Barke et al., 2023). Studies examining genetic contributions to longitudinal changes in inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms are limited but find that genetic factors contribute differentially to changes in symptom dimensions over time. For example, a study by Pingault et al. (2015) comparing identical and nonidentical twins found that the genetic influences on childhood ADHD severity are largely distinct from those driving symptom changes over time, although some genetic influences are shared. They also observed that genetics explained more variance in changes in hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms (81%) relative to inattention (54%). However, classical twin studies do not allow us to pinpoint the roles of specific genes relating to baseline levels versus change over time. ADHD, like many conditions, is highly polygenic. However, many of the key genes associated with ADHD diagnosis are enriched in the early pre/ postnatal period (e.g., neurite outgrowth) or are active in later-maturing processes (e.g., maturation of dopaminergic/noradrenergic circuits). One possibility is that the genes relating to hyperactivity– impulsivity symptom change are linked to broad regulatory and developmental processes (e.g., maturation of cortico-striatal networks in adolescence), explaining the decline in these symptoms for many individuals over time. In contrast, baseline inattention symptoms may be more strongly related to genes linked to synaptogenesis and circuit refinement expressed in the early postnatal or childhood period, which have a relatively reduced impact on rate of change later in development. Thus, some genes may anchor early ADHD symptom levels, while other variants may be more instrumental in its later progression, particularly for hyperactivity/impulsivity. These hypotheses remain to be tested but provide a biologically informed framework for understanding differential developmental trajectories across symptom domains. Process II. Effects of socioeconomic context In parallel to genetic impacts on biological development, some environmental factors such as SES – which reflects access to material and nonmaterial resources – contribute independent variance to symptom trajectories. SES, often measured using indicators including income, educational attainment, and neighborhood quality, has a profound influence on development (Rakesh et al., 2025). Although isolating these effects is challenging due to confounding and gene–environment correlations, evidence supports their contribution to ADHD occurrence and progression (Faraone et al., 2024). This warrants consideration of SES and other environmental factors as predictors rather than confounds. For example, effects of family income are more relevant for ADHD prevalence in those without high genetic liability for ADHD (Rowland et al., 2018). This suggests that environmental influences such as low income – through, for example, increased stress or reduced support/ cognitive stimulation – may play a greater role in ADHD when genetic risk is lower. Extending this logic across symptom domains, evidence showing that genetic contributions are greater for hyperactivity/impulsivity than inattention symptoms (Pingault et al., 2015) raises the possibility that change in inattention may be better explained by stress or support from environmental sources. Process III. Environmental calibration of liability Alongside independent influences of environmental factors, low SES may also moderate genetic influences on ADHD outcomes (Badini et al., 2024). Aligned with this idea, findings show that ADHD-associated genetic variants are often found in noncoding regulatory regions, which are more sensitive to environmental influences (Faraone et al., 2024). For hyperactivity/impulsivity, factors such as low stress and nutrition may promote gene expression for timely biological maturation of frontal brain regions beneficial for symptom decline. Meanwhile, reduced inattention may rely on genes linked to cognitive reserve or working memory capacity, and sufficient sleep, which can facilitate the development and refinement of compensatory mechanisms over time. Though speculative, these ideas can be examined in future work to establish how household or neighborhood environments may amplify or buffer liability resulting in symptom changes (with careful modelling considerations; Pingault et al., 2022). Although we focus on SES as an illustrative example, it is important to note that many environmental factors – such as childhood maltreatment, trauma, and institutionalization – contribute to ADHD symptomatology and potentially interact with genetic liability. Developmental transitions as amplification windows Development is also marked by significant transitions – including school transitions and puberty – where the balance of effects of genetics, environment, and their interaction on ADHD symptoms may be reweighted. For example, puberty involves developmentally triggered gene expression, which could appear in twin studies as new genetic effects (i.e., genetic innovation). It is also a time of increasing independence and mobility, resulting in greater exposure to neighborhood factors (e.g., safety)  2026 Association for Child and Adolescent Mental Health. 606 Phoebe Thomson, and Divyangana Rakesh J Child Psychol Psychiatr 2026; 67(5): 605–8 14697610, 2026, 5, Downloaded from https://acamh.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jcpp.70150 by Stony Brook University Libraries, Wiley Online Library on [21/10/2026]. (Rakesh et al., 2025). These periods also coincide with rises in symptoms of other mental health conditions, increasing persistence risk (Caye et al., 2016). Careful study of these developmental transitions may reveal key genetic and environmental innovation effects linked to symptom changes. In addition, changes in symptom levels do not necessarily map onto changes in ADHD-related functional impairment (Sibley et al., 2022), and these periods of divergence represent a valuable opportunity to examine their potentially distinct associations with long-term outcomes. Synthesis and future steps It is undeniable that genetics have a strong influence over ADHD development, which warrants considerable empirical effort to unravel. Equally, environmental liability is the result of additive effects over multiple environmental factors, requiring substantial effort to unpack. Environmental effects have often been overlooked in prior longitudinal literature due to the high heritability of ADHD, and limited variance in twin studies associated with shared environmental effects (e.g., household and neighborhood factors) (Pingault et al., 2015). However, these effects require further research for several reasons. First, unlike underlying genetic liability, environmental factors can shift over time – some discretely (e.g., parental job loss, or trauma) or fluctuating (e.g., housing instability) – which have different impacts on symptom progression and cannot be captured by studies with relatively large intervals between time points (e.g., 2–4 years). Second, studies often assume a common average symptom trajectory across people, but 17%–64% of children with ADHD have a fluctuating symptom pattern over development potentially due to sensitivity to environmental variation (Norman et al., 2023; Sibley et al., 2022). Third, the environment is partly correlated with genetics through passive transmission of both genes and environments from parents, the way a child’s genetic traits evoke responses from others, and children’s active selection of compatible environments. Fourth, environmental effects most strongly linked to persistence risk have the potential to be mitigated through intervention. As one example, inclusive education settings increase odds of ADHD remission specifically in low SES contexts, providing one way forward to reducing disparities (Kim et al., 2019). Environmental factors, including both risk (low SES, trauma) and protective factors that may promote resilience (peer support, positive parenting), are a critical, yet underexplored, dimension that longitudinal research of ADHD symptoms has yet to fully address. Synthesizing the ideas above, we endorse a framework that considers the effects of genetic factors, environmental factors, and their interplay in shaping inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity symptom trajectories with the aim of mapping persistence pathways, while accounting for their shifting contributions over time. Methods such as latent growth curve and dynamic structural equation modelling, when paired with high-quality longitudinal data, can capture how specific genetic and environmental effects differentially influence symptoms over time. Such a framework would allow the testing of several hypotheses. For example, changes in hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms may be more closely explained by genes linked to maturation of the cortex (e.g., fronto-striatal circuits) over adolescence and into adulthood, as well as interactions with environmental factors. By contrast, inattention symptoms may be more sensitive to conditions in the environment such as changes in stress or support. In addition, building on prior clustering studies, approaches such as latent class growth analysis or mixed effects modelling can be used to identify subgroups with distinct developmental trajectories and to characterize the genetic and environmental factors underlying these differences. Summary ADHD persistence represents more than a static continuation of early ADHD severity and genetic liability. It is the result of contributions from genes, environmental context, and their interaction over development, with specific testable mechanisms linked to hyperactivity/impulsivity versus inattention persistence. Applying unified models that dynamically partition variance from these different sources may improve both mechanistic insight and prediction. Further work aimed at identifying interventions and environmental supports that reduce the impact of genetic or environmental liability on ADHD persistence rates can reduce disparities and promote positive outcomes in the long term. Do Children and Adolescents with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder Use Screens More? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Paulo Gonçalves Júniora, Italo Emmanoel Silva e Silvab, Marcela Baraúna Magnoc,d, Lucianne Cople Maiac, Matheus Melo Pithonc, and Raildo da Silva Coqueiroa aPost-Graduate Program in Physical Education, Universidade Estadual do Sudoeste da Bahia (UESB), Jequié, Brazil; bPost-Graduate Program in Nursing and Health, UESB, Jequié, Brazil; cDepartment of Pediatric Dentistry and Orthodontics, School of Dentistry, Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; dPost- Graduation Program in Dentistry, Universidade Veiga de Almeida, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil ABSTRACT Background: Our aim in conducting this review was to investigate whether children and adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) exhibit differences in screen time when compared to children and adolescents with typical development. Method: The study protocol was registered in the PROSPERO data base. Databases and gray literature were screened. Studies that com pared screen time between children and adolescents with ADHD and those with typical development were included and critically evaluated with the Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Meta-analyses were performed considering screen time ≥2 hours/day or its mean (hours/day). The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach was applied for evaluating the certainty of the evidence. Twenty-two studies were included. Results: In total, 235 283 children and adolescents of both sexes were evaluated. ADHD was diagnosed clinically or based on care giver reporting, and different screen types were reported. With a low and very low certainty of evidence, children and adolescents with ADHD were more likely to spend ≥2 hours/day during the week with computers and screens in general and had a higher mean screen time (p < .05). ADHD medication did not seem to influence these results. Conclusions: Children and adolescents with ADHD spent more time during weekdays using screens and were therefore more likely to exhibit excessive screen and computer use. ARTICLE HISTORY Received 25 February 2025 Accepted 27 February 2026 KEYWORDS ADHD; children; adolescents; sedentary behavior; screen time; typical development Introduction Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition that typically emerges in childhood and persist into adulthood (American Psychiatric Association, 2014). Its presentation may vary significantly across individuals and contexts, and diagnostic criteria continue to evolve. Additionally, the manifestation of symptoms can differ notably between males and females, with hyperactivity CONTACT Raildo da Silva Coqueiro rscoqueiro@uesb.edu.br Department of Health 1, Universidade Estadual do Sudoeste da Bahia, Rua José Moreira Sobrinho, S/N, Jequiezinho, Jequié, Bahia 45210-506, Brazil. sometimes presenting as cognitive restlessness rather than overt physical behavior (Musálek et al., 2020). While challenges related to attention and impulsivity are often highlighted, it is important to acknowledge that individuals with ADHD may also exhibit strengths such as creativity, hyperfocus, and innovative thinking (American Psychiatric Association, 2014). ADHD is associated with developmental differences that may impact personal, social, academic, and/or occupational functioning (Arango-Tobón et al., 2023; Ayano et al., 2023; Dona et al., 2023). However, estimating its true prevalence remains challenging due to variability in diagnostic criteria and methodologies across studies. Global prevalence estimates in children and adolescents range from 3,4% a 13,9%, with a predominance in males (Ayano et al., 2023). This gender difference may, in part, be attributed to diagnostic biases and the underrecognition of symptoms in females, who often present with less overt forms of inattention or internalizing behaviors. Moreover, diagnostic delays are common, particularly when symptoms are mild, masked by coping strategies, or occur in environments that do not pose significant demands on attention and behavioral regulation (Ayano et al., 2023). In recent decades, rapid changes in humanity’s daily habits, related to environ mental, physical, economic, and social factors, have occurred (Fujiwara et al., 2022). One issue that has drawn attention and concerned health agencies is the increase in time spent in sedentary behavior among school-aged youth (Mahumud et al., 2021). Such behavior is recognized as a major risk factor for various adverse physical and mental health outcomes in children and adolescents, such as obesity, sleep distur bances, anxiety, and lower academic performance (Saunders & Vallance, 2017). Sedentary behavior is also associated with morbidity and mortality in adults and older adults (Katzmarzyk et al., 2019). In children and adolescents, most of the time spent in sedentary behavior involves screen use as part of activities such as watching television, playing video games, and using a computer, tablet, or smartphone, among others (Saunders & Vallance, 2017). Over the last two decades, screen time has increased substantially in this population, due to greater access to mobile technologies, streaming services, and digital plat forms in daily life (Saunders & Vallance, 2017). Given this context, most of the literature on sedentary behavior in children and adolescents is based on the assess ment of screen time (Kim et al., 2011). Some evidence suggests that screen time has a greater negative impact on indi viduals with ADHD than on people with typical development. These impacts may involve both physical and mental health domains, such as increased risk of sleep problems, anxiety symptoms, and difficulties with self-regulation (Merrill et al., 2021; Verma et al., 2022). However, many studies have focused on the potential adverse effects rather than on the amount of time spent on screens (Merrill et al., 2021; Verma et al., 2022). There is still no consensus in the literature on whether screen time duration differs between children and adolescents with ADHD and those with typical development (Ebenegger et al., 2012; Párraga et al., 2019). Therefore, our aim in undertaking this systematic review was to answer the following question: do children and adolescents with ADHD exhibit differences in screen time when compared to children and adolescents with typical development? 96 P. Materials and methods Protocol and registration The study protocol was registered in the PROSPERO database under the number CRD42022327389 and is accessible at the following direct link: https://www.crd.york.ac. uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42022327389. Following protocol registration, minor methodological adjustments were required based on the characteristics of the eligible studies. The original protocol was designed to evaluate sedentary behavior broadly (i.e., time spent sitting or reclining with energy expenditure ≤ 1.5 MET), including outcomes such as screen time, electronic media use, and reading time. However, after applying the inclusion criteria, we found that most eligible studies assessed screen time specifically. Therefore, the Population, Exposure, Comparison, and Outcome (PECO) framework was refined to adopt screen time—rather than sedentary behavior in its broader definition—as the primary outcome (Morgan et al., 2018). The PRISMA statement recommendations for systematic review reporting were followed (Ardern et al., 2021). Eligibility criteria The eligibility criteria were based on the PECO strategy (Morgan et al., 2018), considering children and adolescents (P) with ADHD diagnosis, as defined by the original studies, including diagnoses based on clinical assessment or parent report (E), compared to their peers with typical development (C), in relation to screen time (O). Observational studies that addressed all components of the PECO framework were considered eligible. Editorials, letters to the editor, literature reviews, case reports, and case series were excluded, as these designs do not provide empirical comparative data required for this type of review. Observational studies that did not include a comparison group (children and adolescents with typical development) or that assessed exposure and outcome in an adult population were also excluded. Literature search strategy The articles were identified through a systematic search of the following electronic data bases: MedLine via PubMed, Cochrane Library, EMBASE, EBSCO (CINAHL Database/ SPORTDiscus), ProQuest, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of Science, Lilacs, and the gray litera ture from Google Scholar and Open Grey. The search strategies defined for the databases described above are listed in Table 1. Two authors (PGJ and IESS) performed the search independently. Subject-matter experts were also consulted to assist in the systematic search. Searches were performed including studies published up to December 2022, with updates given via alerts in the respective databases. The terms that guided the search were: ‘‘sedentary behavior,” “lifestyle,” ‘‘screen time,” ‘‘lack of physical activity,” “lifestyle,” “lifestyles,” ‘‘video games,” ‘‘computer games,” ‘‘tele vision viewing,” ‘‘digital media,” ‘‘sitting position,” ‘‘bed rest,” “rest,” ‘“bedrest,” “bedrests,” ‘‘attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity,” ‘‘attention deficit hyperactivity disorder,” and ‘‘attention deficit and disruptive behavioral disorders,” along with their synonyms and COMPREHENSIVE CHILD AND ADOLESCENT NURSING 97

The evaluations were independently performed by two authors (PGJ and IESS) and used to make the final decision. A third author (RSC) was consulted in cases of disagreement between the two authors’ evaluations. Data collection process Two authors (PGJ and IESS) extracted the required information from the included articles independently. The following data were extracted: study characteristics (authors, year of publication, country, study design, number of participants included in the study, and age of participants in years), population characteristics (sex, medication use, and number of participants diagnosed or not diagnosed with ADHD), exposure characteristics (type of diagnosis and comorbidities), screen time assessment instrument, type of screen, and measurement (unit) of screen time. Disagreements between authors were resolved by discussion with a third author (RSC) or by consensus. The authors of the included studies were contacted for further details when relevant data were not reported, or for additional information. Meta-analysis Data from the studies were analyzed using RevMan software (Review Manager v. 5.3, The Cochrane Collaboration; Copenhagen, Denmark) to assess the association between screen time and ADHD. Two types of analyses were performed: ●Screen time ≥ 2 hours: The odds ratio (OR), log OR, and standard error (SE), or the number of children and adolescents who used screens for ≥2 hours/day (events) and the total number of children and adolescents assessed with (exposure) and without (comparator) ADHD were included in the software to calculate the OR and 95% confidence interval (95%CI). The adjusted OR was used whenever provided by the study; otherwise, the unadjusted OR was calculated and included in the analysis. When necessary, the effect estimates (ORs) were calculated and converted using the RevMan® software tools. Values of p < .05 were considered significant. ●Mean screen time: The mean and standard deviation of time (in hours) using screens per day and the number of children and adolescents assessed in each group (with and without ADHD) were extracted from the studies, and the mean difference (MD) and 95%CI were calculated. When possible, individual or subgroup analyses considering screen type, the inclusion of medicated or unmedicated children, and weekly time were performed. A random-effects model was used, and heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic. Assessment of the certainty of evidence The certainty of the evidence (certainty in the effect estimates) was determined for each combined outcome in the meta-analysis using the Grading of Recommendations 100 P. Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. With the GRADE approach, observational studies begin with low evidence; however, this can decrease to very low if serious or very serious issues related to the risk of bias, imprecision, incon sistency, indirect validity, and publication bias are present. The magnitude of the effect and dose-response are not applicable and were judged so as not to alter the certainty of the evidence. The influence of possible confounding factors was judged and may increase the certainty of the evidence (Ryan & Hill, 2016). The presence of age groups including children (zero to 10 years) and adolescents (11 to 19 years) was considered to assess indirect validity. The presence of a “large effect” was considered for OR > 4 or <1 due to the risk of 0.5 being equivalent to a probability of 1; thus, the corresponding OR was measured by the formula OR = RR/(1 − RR) (Schünemann et al., 2019). Thus, the quality of the evidence can range from very low to high. Meta-analysis and GRADE Five studies were not included in the meta-analysis because they did not provide sufficient data (Basay et al., 2020; Hong et al., 2021; Masi et al., 2021; Merrill et al., 2021; Verma et al., 2022), and one because the sample consisted of children under 5 years of age (Khalil et al., 2022). • Two hours or more of screen time: The studies had sufficient data only for the analyses considering screen time during the weekdays. Seven studies and eight groups (8,513 children and adolescents with ADHD and 11,961 without ADHD) were included. The results of the meta-analysis of the seven included studies showed a higher likelihood of screen use for ≥2 hours/day on weekdays among children and adolescents with ADHD, with very low certainty of evidence [OR 1.38 (1.07, 1.77); p = .001; I2 = 66%), compared to their peers with typical development. Subgroup analysis indicated that, in studies evaluating screen time overall, the odds were similar between groups [OR 1.14 (0.94, 1.38); p = .17; I2 = 46%]. However, when only computer use was considered, children and adolescents with ADHD were found to be more likely to use this type of screen for ≥2 hours/day on weekdays [OR 2.61 (1.37, 4.99); p = .004; I2 = 0%] (Figure 2 and Table 4). Regarding the use or not of medication, children and adolescents with ADHD on medication [OR 1.01 (0.84, 1.21); p = .93; I2 = 29%] showed similar odds of engaging in ≥2 hours/day of screen use compared to their typically developing peers, and children and adolescents off medication [OR 1.06 (0.85, 1.33); p = .61; I2 = 44%] also presented similar odds of ≥2 hours/day of screen use. However, in studies that did not specify medication use in their inclusion criteria or outcomes, a higher like lihood of screen use was observed among children and adolescents with ADHD [OR 1.81 (1.06, 3.09); p = .03; I2 = 65%] (Figure 3). According to the GRADE framework, the certainty of the evidence was considered low in the analyses involving children and adolescents on or off medication, and very low in studies that did not specify medication use (Table 4). • Daily mean screen time: The analyses are presented below according to the type of screen evaluated. For overall screen use, three studies were included. On weekdays, children and adolescents with ADHD (n = 222) had higher mean screen time than those without ADHD (n = 201) [MD = 0.49 (0.18, 0.80); p = .002; I2 = 54%]. However, during weekends, mean screen time was similar between children and adolescents with ADHD (n = 113) and controls (n = 316) [MD = 0.37 (−0.01, 0.75); p = .06; I2 = 7%] (Figure 4). Discussion The evidence available in the literature raises questions about whether children and adolescents with ADHD are more or less exposed to screen-based sedentary behavior than their typically developing peers (Ebenegger et al., 2012; Párraga et al., 2019). This systematic review and meta-analysis suggests that children and adolescents with ADHD spend more time during weekdays using screens and are more exposed to excessive screen time (i.e., ≥2 hours/day) overall and in relation to computer use. These results do not seem to be influenced by medication use in ADHD patients. A positive association was observed between a screen time of ≥2 hours/day on the computer and ADHD (subgroup analysis). However, this difference was not observed for the analysis with continuous data, where children and adolescents with and without ADHD had similar mean computer use time. The conflict in the results may be associated with the difficulty of eliminating individual factors that may interfere with the results, such as age, gender, social context, and relationship with parents, among others. In the dichotomous analyses, adjusted OR data were entered into the analyses whenever they were available in the included studies. However, only two studies (Kim et al., 2011; Tandon et al., 2019), presented adjusted data, indicating the need for further research that considers confound ing factors to confirm or ratify this result. When considering screen types individually, the mean time spent using computers, television, and video games was similar among children and adolescents with and without ADHD. It should be noted that, in most analyses, the daily mean usage exceeded 1 hour for each medium. Although these may be considered low values, several types of media are usually used by children during the day (Bourchtein et al., 2019; Párraga et al., 2019), suggesting that the sum of screen time on different media may reach values considered excessive. Most of the studies included in this review were conducted in high-income countries, which may be associated with the higher media use in this population, as there is a significant global digital divide in Internet access, which is substantially higher in high- income nations compared to low-middle income countries (International Telecommunication Union [ITU], 2023). Only one included study (Khalil et al., 2022) was conducted with a sample of children younger than 5 years old and demonstrated an association between screen use and ADHD. This result should be interpreted with caution, as ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition and not caused by screen time. Although excessive screen time may negatively impact attention and self-regulation, this is distinct from a clinical diagnosis of ADHD. Guidance should be provided to parents, educators, healthcare professionals, and the community at large about the harmful physiological and psychological health-related effects of excessive electronic media use on children and adolescents. Recommendations, educational campaigns, and public policies to reduce screen use among children and adolescents may be a way forward, as exemplified by the Common Sense organization, promoter of the Digital Detox Figure 7. campaign, which guides families on the healthy and safe use of technology and encourages children and adolescents to spend more time on offline activities (Syvertsen, 2020). Medication is an important element of therapeutic strategies for ADHD; in this scenario, the specific medication, daily dosage, and duration of use may act as moderating factors in this association. However, this is a complex topic that involves variability in medication types, dosing strategies, and individual responses. Due to its breadth, it was not possible to explore these factors in depth in the present review. It is reported that adverse effects related to ADHD medication use are less evident in youth when it is taken for longer periods (Becker & Lienesch, 2018). This factor may be related to the chance of using screens for ≥2 hours/day being similar in the analyses that included the studies with both medicated and unmedicated patients; however, children and adolescents with ADHD were more likely to use screens in the studies that did not specify medication use. Future studies evaluating the influence of different medications, as well as their dosages and duration of use, on sleep, media use, and sedentary behavior may shed more light on this issue. In addition, considering the broad developmental and technological changes in child hood and adolescence, it may be difficult to isolate ADHD as a primary contributing factor to screen time patterns. This challenge highlights the potential value of qualitative research to explore individual experiences, motivations, and contexts that influence screen use behaviors among this population. It is also essential to acknowledge the potential positive uses of screen-based technologies for children and adolescents with ADHD. Screens are not exclusively a source of sedentary behavior or distraction; they can be powerful tools for learning, cognitive training, and self- regulation. For instance, certain educational apps and structured digital platforms can leverage immediate feedback, novelty, and interactive elements to improve executive func tions and attention skills in ways that traditional methods may not (Löchner et al., 2025). Furthermore, video communication and online communities can facilitate crucial social engagement and belonging, particularly for individuals who may struggle with face-to-face social cues due to their condition (Radesky & Christakis, 2016). Thus, the focus should not solely be on minimizing time, but also on promoting high-quality, active, and productive screen engagement (Kollins et al., 2020). It should be kept in mind that the digital age is a reality and digital game-based therapies may have the potential to treat ADHD, as computer use can improve attention in some children and adolescents by addressing neurocognitive domains with mild side effects (Pandian et al., 2021). However, there is an urgent need to develop measurement approaches regarding children’s media use in a non-educational and non-therapeutic manner. Physical activities have several benefits for children with ADHD and may reduce their ADHD symptoms; thus, such activities should be encouraged in this population (Vysniauske et al., 2020). Exergames (i.e., video games that require physical exertion or movement from the player) can also be a tool in this context, merging media and physical activity (Benzing & Schmidt, 2019). A higher chance of excessive computer use among children and adolescents with ADHD was observed compared to the control group. No study included in the meta- analysis evaluated screen time durations of ≥2 hours/day on weekends. According to Sigmundová and Sigmund (2021), weekends are characterized by more recreational screen time for all family members (parents and children) relative to weekdays. 114 P. GONÇALVES JÚNIOR ET AL.

Studies that evaluate screen use for ≥2 hours/day during weekends are needed to elucidate this issue. It is important to highlight that the outcomes assessed in this systematic review were classified with low or very low evidence certainty, indicating that the confidence in the estimated effect found in the meta-analysis is limited and that the true effect may be substantially different from the estimated effect, reinforcing the need for new studies on the subject with appropriate methodological designs. Although this review included 22 studies, the evidence from these, in compilation, still does not prove robust. A limitation is that screen time was assessed in the studies through questionnaires answered by parents, caregivers, and teachers, which may have resulted in response bias. In some studies, ADHD diagnosis was also based on parent report rather than clinical confirmation, which may introduce additional misclassification bias. Objective methods for assessing screen time, such as direct observation, the use of cameras/filming, and electronic applications should be considered in future studies. Another limitation is that several studies did not clearly specify whether screen time included use during school hours or only out-of-school exposure, which may affect comparability across age groups and week days. Finally, the search strategy covered studies published up to 2022, and more recent evidence may therefore not be captured in this review. In conclusion, this systematic review and meta-analysis suggests with low or very low evidence certainty that compared to their typically developing peers, children and adoles cents with ADHD (i) spend more time during weekdays on screen use and (ii) are more likely to have an excessive screen and computer time in general. (iii) Medication use in ADHD patients does not seem to influence these findings. These results should be inter preted with caution, and further studies are needed. REVIEW ARTICLE Do Wechsler intelligence scales predict academic achievement in children with ADHD or autism? A systematic review and meta-analysis Maria Marinopouloua,b , Jakob Åsberg Johnelsa,c,d, Carl-Gustaf Bornehage,f , Maria Unenge Hallerb€acke,g, and Eva Billstedta,c aGillberg Neuropsychiatry Centre, Institute of Neuroscience and Physiology, Sahlgrenska Academy, University of Gothenburg, Gothenburg, Sweden; bChild and Adolescent Habilitation, Region V€armland, Karlstad, Sweden; cChild Neuropsychiatric Clinic, Queen Silvia’s Childrens Hospital, Sahlgrenska University Hospital, Gothenburg, Sweden; dSpeech and language pathology unit, Institute of Neuroscience and Physiology, Sahlgrenska Academy, University of Gothenburg, Gothenburg, Sweden; eDepartment of Health Sciences, Karlstad University, Karlstad, Sweden; fIcahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY, USA; gSchool of Medical Sciences, Faculty of Medicine and Health, €Orebro University, €Orebro, Sweden ABSTRACT Intelligence tests predict academic achievement in typically developed children, however if this is the case also in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and/or autism spec trum disorder (ASD) is not clear. This systematic review and meta-analysis examined if Wechsler intelligence scales predict academic achievement and/or grades in children, ages 6-16 years, with ADHD and/or ASD. We searched the databases PubMed, PsycINFO and Education Research Complete for studies published between 2000 and 2023. We used the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale to assess risk of bias. Narrative synthesis and meta-analysis were performed. Twelve studies (ADHD n 1⁄4 1,834, ASD n 1⁄4 176) were included in the review, and six samples (ADHD n 1⁄4 1,112) of those were included in the meta-analyses. The results of the meta-analyses showed moderate overall weighted correlations between IQ and word reading, written language, and mathematics respect ively. Similarly, the overall weighted correlations between processing speed and the aforemen tioned domains of academic achievement were moderate. Meta-analysis with additional Wechsler scales composite scores could not be conducted. In the narrative synthesis, Full Scale IQ was asso ciated with academic achievement in both ADHD and ASD, and grades in ADHD. The limited num ber of ASD participants and the heterogeneity of the samples need to be considered when interpreting results. Generally, the results indicate that Wechsler scales are valuable in predicting academic achievement in children with ADHD or ASD. Motivation and other factors related with academic achievement need to be further explored in these groups. KEYWORDS Intelligence; academic achievement; Wechsler scales; ADHD; autism Introduction Rationale Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are both considered neurodevelop mental disorders (NDDs), often identified and diagnosed in childhood, affecting the individual’s development and behavior. Though more prevalent in males, ADHD and ASD affect both males and females, are heterogeneous in their clinical presenta tion and etiology, and frequently coexist (Leitner, 2014). Individual outcomes vary, but in many cases symptoms and impairment continue into adulthood (Thapar et al., 2017). ADHD, which is the most common NDD, is character ized by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that inter fere with a person’s functioning (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Findings of slightly lower mean FSIQ scores compared to controls have been reported in groups with ADHD (Agnew-Blais et al., 2020; Frazier et al., 2004), but others have suggested that lower FSIQ scores occur only in certain subgroups (Bridgett & Walker, 2006). FSIQ at an individual level in ADHD varies widely (Cadenas et al., 2020; Lindblad et al., 2013). Other cognitive deficits are related to executive function, including poor inhibitory con trol and poor working memory (Pievsky & McGrath, 2018; Ramos et al., 2020), and to processing speed (Cook et al., 2018). Furthermore, ADHD has been associated with unfavorable academic outcomes measured with achievement tests, grade point average, grade retention, school dropout rates, and years of education (Arnold et al., 2020; Fleming et al., 2017; Klein et al., 2012). their peers (Lawrence et al., 2021), and a systematic review has shown a negative association between ADHD and math ematical ability, stronger for inattentive symptoms (Tosto et al., 2015). Furthermore, better cognitive performance in memory, inhibitory control, and processing speed has been reported to be associated with better mathematic performance in children with ADHD (Kanevski et al., 2022). Working memory is consistently correlated with several aspects of liter acy, whereas smaller correlations have been found between processing speed and literacy (McDougal et al., 2022). Distinguished features of ASD are deficits in social com munication and social interaction, combined with restrictive, repetitive behaviors and interests (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). ASD is, similar to ADHD, a highly het erogeneous disorder that occurs at all levels of intellectual functioning (Wolff et al., 2022). Intelligence and intellectual disability (ID) in ASD have been studied extensively. Initially considered highly prevalent in ASD, the rates of concurrent ID in ASD have during the last five decades diminished from about 70% to 30% (Wolff et al., 2022), and a recent meta- analysis reported rates of about 23% (Mutluer et al., 2022). Similar to intellectual functioning, function in other cognitive domains varies widely among individuals with ASD. Apart from social cognitive deficits (Braconnier & Siper, 2021), executive function deficits, including in flexibility and work ing memory (Lai et al., 2017), are common in ASD. Deficits in processing speed have also been reported (Mayes & Calhoun, 2008). Regular school environment poses challenges for children with ASD (Ashburner et al., 2010), and there is a need for educational interventions and accommodations (Hyman et al., 2020). Academic outcomes in ASD are vari able and factors associated with favorable academic outcome are higher IQ, no working memory problems, less behavior problems, and better social skills (Keen et al., 2016). The Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC) is an individually administered standardized test to assess general intellectual functioning in children aged 6 to 16 years. The Wechsler scales are often the first choice by school psycholo gists and by clinical neuropsychologists, not only in North America and Europe, but globally (Oakland et al., 2016; Rabin et al., 2016). WISC is used for different purposes including for neuropsychological assessment in ADHD (Thaler et al., 2013) and ASD (Braconnier & Siper, 2021). The first edition was introduced in the 1940s (Wechsler, 1949) and updated versions have been published since, WISC-V (Wechsler, 2014) being the most recent. Besides scores of Verbal IQ (VIQ), Performance IQ (PIQ), and Full Scale IQ (FSIQ) featured in WISC, WISC-III (Wechsler, 1991) also included scores for four factor-analytically derived indexes called Verbal Comprehension Index (VCI), Perceptual Organization Index (POI), Freedom from Distractibility Index (FDI), and Processing Speed Index (PSI). FDI comprised the Arithmetic and Digit Span subtests, and was replaced in the subsequent WISC version, the WISC-IV (Wechsler, 2003a), with Working Memory Index (WMI), that comprised Digit Span and Letter-Number Sequencing to min imize the impact of mathematics (Kaufman et al., 2006). Similar to WISC-III, WISC-IV has also a four-factor structure reflected in the indexes VCI, Perceptual Reasoning Index (PRI), WMI, and PSI. In both WISC-III and WISC-IV, PSI is based on the Coding and the Symbol Search subtests, while WMI in WISC-V comprises Digit Span and a new, visual, working memory subtest (Picture Span). The correlation between FSIQ in WISC-III and in WISC-IV is strong (Wechsler, 2003b). The latest edition of WISC, the WISC-V (Wechsler, 2014), has a five factor-structure including the indexes VCI, Visual Spatial Index, Fluid Reasoning Index, WMI and PSI. Adolescents from 16 years and adults can be assessed with the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS; Wechsler, 2008). In addition to the aforementioned tests, the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence (WASI; Wechsler, 1999) and its subsequent version WASI-II (Wechsler, 2011) are both abbreviated measures for estimation of intellectual functioning to be used when comprehensive assessment is not possible or needed, or for screening purposes to deter mine if further assessment is required. Intelligence (defined as IQ) is a robust predictor of aca demic achievement in the general population (Deary et al., 2007; Neisser et al., 1996; Plomin & von Stumm, 2018). Intelligence tests predict academic achievement (Deary et al., 2007) and school grades (Roth et al., 2015). Furthermore, contemporary research has proposed that the relationship between intelligence and academic achievement might be bidirectional rather than unidirectional, i.e., that intelligence and achievement influence each other during development. This also applies to working memory and academic achieve ment. These relationships seem stronger during certain developmental periods, and schooling, particularly in the primary and secondary years, may facilitate this bidirection ality (Peng & Kievit, 2020). However, these relationships might be weaker or absent among children with learning disabilities (Ferrer et al., 2010; Quinn et al., 2020). Studies examining the association between WISC- or WASI-results and academic achievement in ADHD and ASD, point out intelligence as a predictor of academic achievement (Alloway & Stein, 2014; Mayes & Calhoun, 2008). In clinical settings, there is a notion that children with NDD and normal or higher IQ would do better in school than children with NDD and lower IQ, which is plausible and maybe true for some individuals. However, despite correlations between IQ and academic achievement in ASD (Mayes & Calhoun, 2008) and ADHD (Mayes & Calhoun, 2007), discrepancy between IQ and academic achievement is relatively common in ASD (Jones et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2018; Mayes et al., 2020), and ADHD (Mayes et al., 2020), encompassing mostly underachieve ment. Furthermore, IQ and adaptive functioning are posi tively correlated in the general population, but this relationship is less clear in children and adolescents with IQ > 70 and ADHD, ASD or other NDDs, as higher IQ in these groups is not consistently associated with improved adaptive functioning (Alvares et al., 2020; Åsberg Johnels et al., 2021). These findings together highlight the need for clarifying the role of IQ in academic achievement. Wechsler scales are related to academic achievement in chil dren with ADHD and/or ASD. Objectives The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to examine if Wechsler intelligence scales predict academic achievement and/or grades in children with ADHD and/ or ASD. Methods Protocol and registration The systematic review has been registered in PROSPERO (International prospective register of systematic reviews, registration number CRD42022338617). The PRISMA (the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta- Analysis) guidelines (Page et al., 2021) were followed in this review. Eligibility criteria Studies were considered eligible if they were observational (case-control, cross-sectional, longitudinal), included original data, were published in peer-reviewed publications between 01-01-2000 and 24-02-2023, and were written in English. The eligible participants were children attending school, clinically assessed at ages 6-16 years and diagnosed with ADHD or/and ASD. Studies including children aged 0- 5 years, adolescents from 17 years and older, and adults were considered ineligible. Furthermore, studies were eligible if they reported quantitative measures of intellectual function ing; more specifically Wechsler scales (WISC, WASI). Academic achievement and/or grades were the outcomes of interest, and, thus, studies reporting quantitative measures of those were considered eligible. Studies on children with intellectual disability (ID) alone or as comorbidity, and stud ies where data from children with ID could not be excluded from correlation and/or regression analyses were also con sidered ineligible. If ADHD and/or ASD diagnosis was based only on parental ratings of symptoms, the studies were con sidered ineligible. Information sources PubMed, PsycINFO and Education Research Complete were searched for studies. Search strategy The search was first conducted on the 14th of June 2022 and updated on the 24th of February 2023. The search strategy included a combination of 3 key elements: i) intellectual functioning or Wechsler scales, ii) academic achievement, and iii) diagnosis (ADHD, ASD). The search terms for each database are presented in supplementary Table S1. Study selection Two reviewers (MM, EB) independently screened the retrieved studies, based on their title and abstract to deter mine if inclusion or exclusion criteria were met. The reviewers were blind to each other’s decisions during this process and resolved disagreements afterwards. Full-text was retrieved for studies identified as potentially eligible, and for studies where decision was not possible based on title and/or abstract. The two reviewers (MM, EB) independently reviewed all full-text for eligibility and resolved disagreements by discussion. Figure 1 presents the study selection process. Data collection process The following information was extracted: general information about the study (author, year, country), study design, sample size, participant demographics (sex, age at test, age at assess ment of academic achievement/grade), diagnosis (ADHD and/ or ASD), comorbidity, test, test result, measure of academic achievement/grades, outcome (result of academic achievement/ grades). Data were extracted by two reviewers (MM, EB). Risk of bias assessment Risk of bias assessment was conducted independently by two reviewers (MM, EB) and any disagreements were resolved by discussion. The Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS; Wells et al., 2009), that is designed for assessing the quality of non- randomized studies, was used in this review. NOS has been developed for assessing case-control and cohort studies but has also been adapted for assessing the quality of cross-sectional studies. Since the objective of the review was to study associ ation between WISC/WASI scores and achievement, compari sons of test scores between ADHD, ASD, and other clinical groups or typically developing controls were not included in the review. For this reason, case-control studies were evaluated as cross-sectional in the risk of bias assessment, if they did not explicitly compare the strength of correlations or associations between groups. We used the NOS adaptation for cross-sec tional studies provided by Stewart et al. (2017), assessing the included studies based on the selection of study groups, com parability of the groups, and outcome. We tailored the ques tions in the comparability section to include school support and socioeconomic status as confounding factors, since they are relevant for the present review. In accordance with (Kanevski et al., 2022), a score of 5 to 9 stars/points indi cated low risk of bias, 3-4 stars medium risk of bias, and <3 stars high risk of bias. Synthesis methods The extracted data were tabulated in two tables, one for ADHD studies and one for ASD studies. Data from other diagnostic groups or typically developing controls in the studies were not included in the synthesis. A narrative syn thesis of the included studies was conducted. We decided a priori that meta-analysis examining correlations between 94 M. MARINOPOULOU ET AL.

FSIQ (or other Wechsler scales indexes) and academic achievement or grades required at least four studies or sam ples to be performed. The meta-analyses were conducted with the tool Meta-Essentials (Suurmond et al., 2017), using a random effects model due to expected heterogeneity across studies. The I2 statistic was used to assess heterogeneity. Publication bias was assessed with funnel plots including the results of a trim-and-fill procedure (Duval & Tweedie, 2000a; 2000b) provided by the Meta-Essentials software. Results Study selection Details of the screening and exclusion processes are presented in the PRISMA flowchart (Figure 1). The search rendered 2,431 results. After de-duplication, titles and abstracts of 1,849 records were screened by MM and EB, and 1,807 records were excluded. This resulted in 42 studies for full text screen ing. Of those, 12 were included in the systematic review. Study characteristics Table 1 and 2 present the main characteristics of the included studies. Three studies (Assouline et al., 2012; Mayes & Calhoun, 2003; 2008) included samples with ASD with a total of 176 participants. The rest of the studies (Alloway & Stein, 2014; Calub et al., 2019; Carrasco et al., 2022; Ek et al., 2011; Krane & Tannock, 2001; Mayes & Calhoun, 2007; Tallberg et al., 2021; Thaler et al., 2013; Zendarski et al., 2017) included samples with ADHD with a total of 1,834 partici pants. Zendarski et al. (2017) reports ASD as comorbidity in 33% of the ADHD sample, but results for this group are not separated from subjects with ADHD without ASD. Alloway and Stein (2014), Carrasco et al. (2022), Krane and Tannock (2001), and Tallberg et al. (2021) reported that ADHD medication in the samples was discontinued 24h prior to assessment in, while Mayes and Calhoun (2007) reported that participants did not take their morning dose of ADHD medication before assessment. Several versions of WISC were used in the studies, except for two studies (Alloway & Stein, 2014; Zendarski et al., 2017) that used WASI. As regards outcomes, two studies used school grades; overall after grade 9 (Ek et al., 2011) or school grades 3-4years after initial cognitive assessment (Tallberg et al., 2021). The rest of the studies used instruments to assess aca demic achievement. The Wechsler Individual Achievement Test (WIAT; Wechsler, 1992, 2002, 2009) was used as outcome Figure 1. In general, the assessment of outcome in the studies was of high quality and the included samples were considered representative for the children with the disorder of interest. However, controlling for confounding factors was often missed. Narrative synthesis of included studies Overall findings of ADHD studies In all, the included ADHD studies highlight FSIQ/IQ as a predictor of academic achievement (Carrasco et al., 2022; Ek et al., 2011; Mayes & Calhoun, 2007; Zendarski et al., 2017). Working memory (Calub et al., 2019; Carrasco et al., 2022; Krane & Tannock, 2001; Mayes & Calhoun, 2007), vocabu lary, verbal comprehension and verbal reasoning (Calub et al., 2019; Carrasco et al., 2022; Mayes & Calhoun, 2007) are implicated in academic achievement and emerge as pre dictors, but one study did not find correlations between working memory and achievement (Zendarski et al., 2017). The impact of processing speed is less clear, and this ability might contribute to achievement to a lower degree than other abilities (Carrasco et al., 2022; Mayes & Calhoun, 2007).
