Longitudinal studies examining WISC-results and academic achievement and grades are few (Ek et al., 2011; Tallberg et al., 2021). Specific results of ADHD studies As regards the findings of the included studies, Calub et al. (2019) found that WMI and VCI (WISC-IV) combined accounted for 50% of the relation between ADHD and aca demic achievement, of which 30% was contribution of WMI and 20% of VCI. Also, Mayes and Calhoun (2007) focused on academic achievement in a large sample of children with IQ >80. They reported significant correlations between FSIQ and all WIAT scales (p 1⁄4 .0001) for both the WISC– III and WISC–IV. FSIQ accounted for 22% to 58% of the variance in achievement scores and was the best overall sin gle predictor of achievement. Entering the four index scores in a multivariate analysis the explained variance (30% − 59%) was somewhat higher than for FSIQ alone. FDI/WMI and VCI were more correlated with reading, math, and writ ten expression than POI/PRI and PSI. Furthermore, Alloway and Stein (2014) found that WASI Vocabulary and Matrix correlated significantly with arithmetic and spelling from WIAT-II. In the regression analysis, Vocabulary accounted for 38.3% of the variance in spelling and 34.2% of the vari ance in arithmetic. Carrasco et al. (2022) found significant correlations between estimated IQ and word reading, spell ing, and math computation domains in four samples with ADHD. The results of regression analyses showed that esti mated IQ was a significant predictor of variance in academic achievement, except for spelling in the sample with larger proportions of boys and ADHD combined type. Semantic language, measured with the WISC subtest Vocabulary, was a predictor of word reading across samples, and predicted spelling in three samples, and math computation in one. Age and verbal working memory were also predictors of academic achievement, while the influence of the severity of ADHD symptoms on academic achievement was limited. Likewise, the contribution of processing speed was restricted. Explanatory hierarchical regression analyses showed that processing speed only explained additional vari ance in spelling in two samples and math computation in one sample. It did not explain additional variance in word reading. Moreover, Zendarski et al. (2017) showed that IQ explained the greatest proportion of variance in NAPLAN scores with strongest effects for grammar and punctuation scores and weakest effects for persuasive writing and spell ing. Higher IQ was associated with higher numeracy and reading scores. Working memory measured with WISC-IV Digit Span was not independently related to any of NAPLAN domains. In addition, Krane and Tannock (2001) reported correlations between WISC-III FDI and a reading composite comprised of the average score from WRAT-3 Reading, WRMT-R Word Attack and WRMT-R Word Identification subtest, and between FDI and WRAT Arithmetic. Last, Thaler et al. (2013) found a five-cluster solution through a hierarchical cluster analysis. The clusters “Reduced Processing Speed Index” and “Below Average Working Memory Index/Processing Speed Index” performed poorer than the clusters “High Average” and “Superior Verbal Comprehension Index” on the reading fluency. On math fluency, they found that the cluster “Reduced Processing Speed Index” and the cluster “Below Average Working Memory Index/Processing Speed Index” also per formed poorer than did the “High Average” cluster. As regards studies using grades as outcome, Ek et al. (2011) and Tallberg et al. (2021) examined the association between WISC-results and grades. Ek et al. (2011) found significant correlations between FSIQ, VIQ, VCI at school grade 4 and overall grade at school grade 9. Tallberg et al. (2021) included WISC-indexes and found that baseline VCI significantly predicted having a majority of passing grades at follow-up. The explanatory effect of the model was 36%. Furthermore, they also found an association between VCI scores obtained at follow-up and the likelihood of passing grades at follow-up. Overall findings of ASD studies In all, the number of studies examining the relationship between WISC scores and academic achievement in ASD is limited, and none of those has used grades as achievement outcome and none included a longitudinal design. FSIQ (Mayes & Calhoun, 2008), WMI, and PSI (Assouline et al., 2012; Mayes & Calhoun, 2008) emerge as significant concur rent predictors of academic achievement in ASD, while VCI and PRI (Assouline et al., 2012; Mayes & Calhoun, 2008) are also implicated in achievement but the limited number of studies does not allow conclusions to be drawn on their contribution. Specific results of ASD studies As regards the findings of the included studies, Assouline et al. (2012) reported in a group of intellectually gifted stu dents with ASD that WISC-IV WMI and PSI correlated with written language, reading, and mathematics assessed with WJ-III ACH. In contrast, PRI only correlated with oral language, while VCI did not correlate with any academic achievement scores. In the regression analyses, WMI and PSI explained 61% of the variance in reading, while WMI predicted 25% of the variance in written language. In add ition, PSI, fine-motor coordination, and participation in tal ented and gifted programs together predicted 60% of the variance in mathematics. PRI predicted 22% of the variance in oral language. Additionally, Mayes and Calhoun (2008) have reported correlations between WISC-IV FSIQ and WIAT-II achievement (r 1⁄4 0.64 −0.80) accounting for 41 - 64% of the variance. FSIQ was the best overall single pre dictor of reading, math, and writing achievement. On index level, they found an association between PRI and achieve ment, similar with FSIQ, in the younger cohort (age 6– 7 years). However, for the older half of the study group PRI had the lowest overall correlation with achievement, and FSIQ the highest. Finally, dividing a sample in a subgroup with IQ <80 and a subgroup with IQ 80 (measured with APPLIED NEUROPSYCHOLOGY: CHILD 99

WISC-III), Mayes and Calhoun (2003) found that, in the IQ < 80 group, WIAT reading decoding significantly exceeded IQ, whereas math and spelling scores were in line with IQ. For children in the IQ  80 group, achievement scores did not differ from IQ, except for written expression scores that were significantly lower than IQ, and lower than reading decoding, reading comprehension, math, and spelling scores. Meta-analysis Meta-analysis was possible to conduct in ADHD samples for FSIQ and academic achievement, and for PSI and academic achievement. FSIQ, estimated IQ, and PSI from WISC-III and WISC-IV were used in the analysis. Corrected correl ation coefficients for WISC-III FSIQ and WISC-IV FSIQ (r 1⁄4 .89), and for WISC-III PSI and WISC-IV PSI (r 1⁄4 .81) are high (Wechsler, 2003b), enabling these measures to be used in the meta-analysis to measure FSIQ and processing speed, respectively. Academic achievement in the included samples was measured with editions of WIAT or WRAT. The editions of WIAT correlate well with each other (Burns, 2010; Johnson, 2011), many of the WRAT-3 items are also included in WRAT-4 (Dell et al., 2008), and both instru ments are well-established tests of academic achievement. In addition, these instruments use the same type of scaled scores. Achievement scores, irrespective of instrument, were, thus, included in the analysis in the respective domain of academic achievement. Meta-analysis with grades could not be conducted, as grades were only used in two samples. Full Scale IQ and academic achievement As regards ADHD, a total of two studies (Carrasco et al., 2022; Mayes & Calhoun, 2007), which in turn included in total six samples (n 1⁄4 1,112), were entered in meta-analyses focusing on the FSIQ. Three sets of outcome measures were possible to group for the meta-analysis, math (K 1⁄4 6), word reading (K 1⁄4 6), and written language (K 1⁄4 6), see Figure 2. Regarding mathematics, the overall weighted correlation was .48 (95% CI: .21-.68). The heterogeneity value I2 was 92%, indicating large heterogeneity. We note that the correlations reported by Mayes and Calhoun (2007) were larger than those of Carrasco et al. (2022). As regards word reading, the overall weighted correlation was .43 (95% CI: .27-.57). The heterogeneity value I2 was 75%, indicating large heterogen eity. Again, the correlations reported by Mayes and Calhoun (2007) were larger than those of Carrasco et al. (2022). Regarding written language, the overall weighted correlation was .38 (95% CI: .24-.50). The heterogeneity value I2 was 65%, indicating large heterogeneity. Due to the small num ber of samples, we did not perform a formal moderating analysis of the results presented above. There were too few studies on ASD to conduct a meta-analysis on this subgroup. Figure 2. Forest plots of correlations between intellectual functioning and domains of achievement. Processing speed and academic achievement As regards ADHD, the same two studies as above (Carrasco et al., 2022; Mayes & Calhoun, 2007) including six samples (n 1⁄4 1,112) were entered in meta-analyses focusing on PSI. Three sets of outcome measures were possible to group for the meta-analysis, math (K 1⁄4 6), word reading (K 1⁄4 6), and written language (K 1⁄4 6), see Figure 3. Regarding mathemat ics, the overall weighted correlation was .40 (95% CI: .33- .46). The heterogeneity value I2 was 4%, not indicating het erogeneity. As regards word reading, the overall weighted correlation was .29 (95% CI: .14-.42). The heterogeneity value I2 was 60%, indicating heterogeneity. The correlations reported by Carrasco et al. (2022) were in the small range, whereas those of Mayes and Calhoun (2007) were moder ately sized. Regarding written language, the overall weighted correlation with processing speed was .35 (95% CI: .26-.43). The heterogeneity value I2 was 32%. Again, there were too few studies on ASD to conduct a meta-analysis on this subgroup. Publication bias Due to the small number of samples included in the meta- analysis and presence of large heterogeneity in part of the analyses, considerable caution is required when interpreting results from analysis on publication bias. For transparency, funnel plots including results of trim-and-fill procedure were generated for the studies included in the meta-analyses and are provided in the supplementary material together with results of the trim-and-fill procedure (S2-S7). Discussion This systematic review included 12 studies that examined the associations between Wechsler scales and academic achievement and/or grades in children with ADHD or ASD. A total of six samples with ADHD from two of those studies were included in a meta-analysis. Of the 12 studies, three had low risk of bias and nine had medium risk of bias, sug gesting that the results might be liable to bias, however, probably not enough to invalidate the results. The main finding of the systematic review is that FSIQ is associated with achievement in ADHD and ASD, and influences all studied domains (reading, written language, and mathemat ics). The abilities measured with WISC indexes (verbal rea soning and conceptualization, perceptual reasoning, working memory and processing speed) are all implicated in achieve ment, but the magnitude of impact of WISC indexes vary among studies. The number of studies examining WISC results and grades in ADHD is limited, and none of the included studies examined this relationship in ASD. In ADHD, higher VCI seems to increase the likelihood of pass ing grades. In the meta-analyses, FSIQ and PSI predicted academic achievement in reading, written language, and mathematics to moderate degree in ADHD. The included ADHD studies demonstrated correlations between IQ/FSIQ and academic achievement (Carrasco et al., 2022; Mayes & Calhoun, 2007; Zendarski et al., 2017), and that FSIQ/IQ was, in relation to the other WISC indexes, the strongest predictor of academic achievement (Mayes & Calhoun, 2007; Zendarski et al., 2017). (Krane & Tannock, 2001) focused exclusively on working memory (WISC-III FDI) and found correlations between FDI with reading and with mathematics. The impact of working memory on achievement has also been highlighted in other studies (Calub et al., 2019; Carrasco et al., 2022; Mayes & Calhoun, 2007), and working memory was found to mediate academic achievement deficits in ADHD (Calub et al., 2019). However, Zendarski et al. (2017) did not find working memory to be independently associated with achievement (NAPLAN scores) when other explanatory vari ables (such as FSIQ, parent education, inattention, conduct problems) were included in the regression model. Instead, they found that FSIQ explained the greatest proportion of variance in NAPLAN scores. The authors discussed that this could be either due to working memory measure not being sensitive enough to capture working memory deficits or due to different academic achievement tests involving different aspects of working memory. As regards other indexes, VCI was also implicated in aca demic achievement (Calub et al., 2019). Vocabulary subtest was a predictor of the variance in reading (Carrasco et al., 2022), spelling (Alloway & Stein, 2014; Carrasco et al., 2022), and arithmetic (Alloway & Stein, 2014). In addition, PRI correlated with scores of achievement (Alloway & Stein, 2014; Mayes & Calhoun, 2007), but did not make a signifi cant contribution in regression analysis including other index scores. The contribution of PSI in academic achieve ment was limited in Carrasco et al. (2022), and both VCI and WMI correlated higher with achievement than PSI in Mayes and Calhoun (2007). Furthermore, children with ADHD and below average scores in WMI/PSI, had lower scores in reading fluency and math fluency compared to children with ADHD and high average WISC-IV scores (Thaler et al., 2013). In sum, it seems that working memory, which is associated with academic achievement in typically developing children (Caemmerer et al., 2018; Cortes Pascual et al., 2019), is also associated with academic achievement in ADHD. This result is consistent with findings of recent sys tematic reviews on cognition and literacy in ADHD (McDougal et al., 2022), and cognition and mathematics (Kanevski et al., 2022). As expected from current literature (Caemmerer et al., 2018), verbal comprehension abilities including vocabulary are important for academic achieve ment in ADHD. Lower processing speed has been associated with academic difficulties (Cook et al., 2018), which is evi dent in some of the included studies, but the magnitude of the impact of processing speed is less clear in the narrative review. Though numerous studies have examined IQ, WISC pro files, and academic achievement in ASD, only a few have focused on the relationship between Wechsler intelligence scales and academic achievement. In the Mayes and Calhoun (2003) groups academic achievement scores were consistent with IQ in most domains, and FSIQ was the best overall single predictor of reading, math, and writing achievement in Mayes and Calhoun (2008). All WISC indexes correlated with achievement and the highest correla tions on the index level were WMI for reading, PRI for math, and PSI for written expression. Furthermore, in an intellectually gifted ASD group, Assouline et al. (2012) found that both WMI and PSI correlated significantly with academic achievement and predicted a significant proportion of the variance in reading. WMI predicted variance in writ ten language, and PSI together with other factors predicted a significant proportion of the variance in mathematics. Notably, VCI did not predict any scores of academic achievement, and PRI only predicted oral language. Generally, FSIQ, WMI, and PSI emerge as significant predic tors of academic achievement in ASD, which is in line with the knowledge on IQ, working memory, processing speed, and academic achievement in other groups (Neisser et al., 1996; Titz & Karbach, 2014; Wechsler, 2003a). In addition, PRI correlated with math, reading, and writing achievement in Mayes and Calhoun (2008), but only with oral language in Assouline et al. (2012). This shows that perceptual rea soning is clearly implicated in academic achievement, but due to the limited number of studies, it is unclear if the dif ferences between studies are related to the level of intellec tual functioning of the participants, use of different instruments or other factors. As regards the studies including grades as outcome, Ek et al. (2011) found moderate correlations between FSIQ, VIQ, VCI and PSI, and overall grade at grade 9 in ADHD. Tallberg et al. (2021) found that higher VCI at baseline was associated with having a majority of passing grades at fol low-up. Lower VCI is implicated in poor academic out comes in ADHD. The study did not examine the relationship between FSIQ and grades. Taken together, the studies underline the importance of verbal reasoning, com prehension, and conceptualization, general intellectual func tioning and processing speed, for school grades. The findings are in line with the well-established predictive importance of intellectual functioning for grades (Roth et al., 2015). Future longitudinal studies could further exam ine the relationship between IQ and academic achievement in NDDs through exploring possible bidirectionality in these relations. In the meta-analysis, including six ADHD samples, the overall weighted correlations between FSIQ and the three aspects of academic achievement (reading, written language, and mathematics) were moderate in size. Similarly, the over all weighted correlations between PSI and written language, and PSI and math, were moderate, and the correlation between PSI and reading was almost moderate. Notably, the correlations reported by Mayes and Calhoun (2007) are in some cases larger than those of Carrasco et al. (2022). This could be due to differences in sample characteristics such as mean FSIQ, which was slightly higher in Mayes and Calhoun (2007), comorbidities, and ADHD symptom sever ity. These factors are also mentioned by Carrasco et al. (2022) as regards differences between the samples included in their study. Furthermore, the overall weighted correla tions found in the meta-analysis are lower than the correla tions between WISC-IV and WIAT-II reported in the WISC-IV technical manual from a general population sam ple (Wechsler, 2003b). This also the case for the correlations 102 M. MARINOPOULOU ET AL.

reported in Carrasco et al. (2022), while the correlations reported in Mayes and Calhoun (2007) are more in line with those reported in the manual, except for the correla tions between FSIQ and written language, and between PSI and written language that are lower in Mayes and Calhoun (2007). These findings suggest that other characteristics related to ADHD or comorbidities may affect the strength of the relationship between intellectual functioning and aca demic achievement in ADHD. The included samples dif fered in terms of comorbidity, ADHD subtypes, and mean FSIQ, which reflects the heterogeneous nature of ADHD and ASD. Furthermore, as reflected in the magnitude of correlations between cognitive domains and achievement, other factors, though not as strong as IQ, also need to be considered when studying and improving academic achievement in ADHD and/or ASD. Motivation, for example, also plays a significant role in academic achievement (Lavrijsen et al., 2022; Smith et al., 2020). Besides working memory, other executive functions (inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility) are related to academic achievement (Zelazo & Carlson, 2020). Executive function deficits affect academic achieve ment in ADHD (Biederman et al., 2004) and ASD (St. John et al., 2018), and cognitive training may improve academic outcomes (Veloso et al., 2019). In addition, ordinary class room environment normally includes a variety of sensory stimuli and distractions, and poses demands on flexibility and other executive functions, which may be challenging for many children with ADHD and/or ASD (Ashburner et al., 2010; Kos et al., 2006). This stresses the importance of edu cational accommodations and interventions, such as close family-school partnership, behavioral classroom interven tions, and individualized instructional supports that are rec ommended in ADHD (Wolraich et al., 2019), and visual supports and self-monitoring strategies that have been found effective in ASD (Watkins et al., 2019). The evidence presented in this review has several limita tions. Though the academic achievement instruments used in the studies are well established, there is some variation in selected versions and measures, limiting the number of sam ples included in the meta-analysis, which is a clear limita tion. Another limitation for making general conclusions relates to the limited number of studies with participants with ASD and the relatively small – albeit not uncommon in clinical research- samples, requiring some caution when generalizing results, particularly on specific WISC indexes and domains of academic achievement. Lastly, factors such as socioeconomic status and school supports were not always reported in the studies. Conclusion Wechsler intelligence scales are frequently used for assessing intellectual functioning in ADHD (Thaler et al., 2013) and ASD (Linnenbank et al., 2022). The results of the present meta-analysis, which was also supported in the narrative synthesis, show that WISC FSIQ and PSI have bearing in predicting academic achievement in reading, written language, and mathematics to moderate degree in ADHD. This association is less studied in ASD, but results of exist ing studies provide support for association between WISC scores and academic achievement. Wechsler scales are, thus, valuable in predicting academic achievement in ADHD and ASD, but other factors also should be considered when pre dicting academic achievement in these groups. pages: 1 of 13 Early Intervention in Psychiatry, 2026; 20:e70123 https://doi.org/10.1111/eip.70123 Early Intervention in Psychiatry REVIEW Neurodevelopmental, Pharmacological and Substance Use Factors in the Association Between ADHD and First-Episode Non-Affective Psychosis: A Systematic Review Valerio Ricci1 | Marialuigia Barresi1 | Gabriele Di Salvo2 | Giuseppe Maina1,2 1San Luigi Gonzaga Hospital, University of Turin, Orbassano (TO), Italy | 2Department of Neurosciences “Rita Levi Montalcini”, University of Turin, Torino (TO), Italy Correspondence: Valerio Ricci (v.ricci@sanluigi.piemonte.it) Received: 14 March 2025 | Revised: 19 September 2025 | Accepted: 22 December 2025 Keywords: ADHD | first-episode psychosis | methylphenidate | neurodevelopment | substance use ABSTRACT Objective: This systematic review investigates the complex relationship between attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and first-episode non-affective psychosis (FEP), focusing on neurodevelopmental, pharmacological and substance use factors that may influence this association. Methods: Following PRISMA guidelines, we conducted a comprehensive literature search across PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and PsycINFO databases for studies published between January 2001 and June 2024. We included experimental and observational studies examining ADHD and FEP in participants aged ≥ 16 years. Quality assessment was performed using standardised tools specific to each study design. Results: From 1243 initially identified records, 13 studies met inclusion criteria. Five studies addressing neurodevelopmental factors revealed shared neurobiological vulnerabilities between ADHD and psychosis, including impaired cortical inhibition, neurophysiological markers and cognitive deficits. Five pharmacological studies demonstrated that whilst stimulant-induced psychosis can occur, the absolute risk appears low, with amphetamines carrying a 1.65-fold higher risk than methylphenidate. Three studies on substance use patterns showed that ADHD patients with FEP had significantly higher rates of substance use disorders, particularly cannabis use, which was associated with earlier psychosis onset and poorer outcomes. Conclusions: Individuals with ADHD, particularly those with persistent symptoms from childhood and neurocognitive deficits, may have an elevated risk of developing FEP. Substance use appears to be an important mediating factor in this relationship. Regarding pharmacological treatment, recent epidemiological evidence provides a more nuanced perspective on stimulant safety, though the evidence remains mixed and requires further investigation. These findings highlight the importance of comprehensive assessment, substance use prevention and individualised risk stratification when managing ADHD patients at risk for psychosis. 1 | Introduction The association between attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and psychosis has received increasing attention in psychiatric and neurodevelopmental research. ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder classified within major international diagnostic systems, including the DSM-5-TR and ICD-10. Although commonly diagnosed in childhood, ADHD frequently persists into adulthood, affecting approximately 3%–7% of school-aged children (Polanczyk et al. 2015). The disorder is © 2026 John Wiley & Sons Australia, Ltd.

2 of 13 Early Intervention in Psychiatry, 2026 primarily defined by deficits across three core domains: inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity, typically organised into two main symptom clusters. According to the DSM-5-TR, the disorder manifests in different clinical presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive–impulsive and combined presentation. Whilst ADHD as a disorder tends to persist over time, the specific manifestation of symptoms evolves during development. Notably, hyperactive–impulsive behaviours generally diminish with age, whereas inattentive symptoms are more likely to persist into adulthood (Carter et al. 2024; Murray et al. 2021; Wang et al. 2024). This developmental trajectory is observed in both male and female patients. ADHD is thought to result from underlying neurobiological dysfunctions, leading to chronic issues with attention, restlessness and impulsivity, which substantially impair daily functioning (Henning et al. 2024; Murray et al. 2018). Adult ADHD prevalence is estimated to be between 4% and 6%. Recent epidemiological data indicate that the maleto-female ratio varies significantly by developmental stage and has narrowed over time due to improved recognition in females. In childhood, clinical samples show ratios of approximately 4:1, whilst community-based studies suggest ratios closer to 2:1 (Martin 2024). In adulthood, this ratio further narrows to approximately 2:1 or approaches 1:1 in community-based epidemiological studies, reflecting the historical underdiagnosis of females during childhood (Martin 2024; Stibbe et al. 2020). The conceptualisation of schizophrenia as a neurodevelopmental disorder – characterised by early developmental abnormalities that manifest progressively from childhood through adolescence – reveals significant overlap with ADHD in terms of timing, cognitive profile and underlying neurobiological mechanisms (Gogtay and Thompson 2010). Whilst our review focuses specifically on first-episode non-affective psychosis (FEP), we acknowledge that schizophrenia represents a primary example within this diagnostic category. Shared features between the two conditions are evident in childhood, particularly in the form of cognitive alterations that emerge during school age. These cognitive dysfunctions include deficits in sustained attention, executive functions (planning, response inhibition, cognitive flexibility), working memory and information processing speed. In vulnerable individuals, there may be a gradual worsening of subthreshold symptoms that can eventually culminate in full-blown psychosis (Cornblatt et al. 2003). From a clinical perspective, both ADHD and schizophrenia present specific overlapping characteristics that distinguish their relationship from other psychiatric comorbidities. These include shared deficits in executive functioning domains (working memory, cognitive flexibility, inhibitory control), similar patterns of attention and information processing abnormalities, comparable impairments in social cognition and theory of mind, and overlapping neurobiological dysfunction in dopaminergic and frontostriatal circuits (Hasan et al. 2013). Additionally, both disorders frequently show abnormalities in impulsivity and inhibitory control domains, which may contribute to maladaptive behaviours and functional difficulties (Lim et al. 2018; Vande Voort et al. 2014). The relationship between ADHD and psychosis is complex, with growing evidence indicating shared neurobiological pathways, genetic susceptibilities and environmental risk factors (Mahrous et al. 2024; Pingault et al. 2015; Zheng et al. 2020). Specifically, schizophrenia shares numerous genetic and environmental risk factors with ADHD, including genetic variants involved in dopaminergic neurotransmission and pre- and perinatal complications (Lim et al. 2018). Both disorders exhibit common clinical characteristics, including a male predominance, high comorbidity with substance abuse, and challenges in emotional regulation and social relationships. Furthermore, individuals with ADHD are at increased risk of developing comorbid conditions, such as substance use disorders (SUDs), which may further contribute to the progression toward psychosis (Katz et al. 2009; Zucker et al. 2002). Recent studies have also highlighted that patients with FEP and a history of ADHD (FEP-ADHD+) may represent a distinct subgroup with a worse prognosis, characterised by earlier onset of psychosis, more pronounced negative symptoms and greater cognitive deficits (Sanchez-Gistau et al. 2020). The study by Hollis et al. (2019) published in Lancet Psychiatry further emphasised the importance of this association, demonstrating a significantly increased risk of developing psychotic disorders in patients with ADHD. This systematic review aims to investigate the complex connection between ADHD and the onset of FEP, focusing on identifying the key factors involved in the development of psychotic symptoms, including the role of pharmacological treatment. Amongst the specific objectives, we intend to analyse which psychopathological factors may predict the development of psychosis in ADHD patients, examine the evidence regarding risks associated with pharmacological treatments for ADHD (including methylphenidate and amphetamines), and evaluate the clinical implications for managing patients with comorbidity. Through an extensive review of the literature, including experimental studies, observational studies, case reports and case series, this study seeks to provide a comprehensive analysis of the current evidence, emphasising shared neurodevelopmental disruptions and potential pathogenic mechanisms linking ADHD and psychosis. 2 | Methods Following the methodology proposed by Moher et al. (2009) and adhering to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, we conducted a systematic review to thoroughly examine the relationship between ADHD and first-episode psychosis. This process involved defining precise research objectives, implementing a comprehensive search strategy, applying rigorous study selection criteria, conducting thorough data extraction, assessing the quality of included studies and synthesising the findings in a structured narrative format. This methodical approach ensured transparency and reproducibility whilst allowing for a comprehensive analysis of the current evidence base. 17517893, 2026, 1, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/eip.70123 by Stony Brook University Libraries, Wiley Online Library on [21/10/2026]. 3 of 13 Early Intervention in Psychiatry, 2026 2.1 | Research Questions and Conceptual Framework Prior to conducting the literature search, we developed a comprehensive conceptual framework based on existing evidence that suggested three key domains relevant to the relationship between ADHD and first-episode psychosis: neurodevelopmental factors, pharmacological impacts (particularly stimulant medications) and substance use patterns. Our primary research aims were to identify the neurodevelopmental factors in ADHD individuals associated with increased risk of developing first-episode psychosis, to evaluate the impact of pharmacological treatments for ADHD (particularly methylphenidate) on psychosis risk, and to examine how substance use mediates the relationship between ADHD and the development of first-episode psychosis. These research objectives guided our systematic approach to literature identification and evidence synthesis. 2.2 | Development of Conceptual Framework and Identification of Thematic Areas At the beginning of our review process, we conducted a preliminary literature consultation and meetings with clinical experts to identify the main thematic areas connecting ADHD to first-episode psychosis. This systematic process led to the identification of three primary domains: neurodevelopmental factors, pharmacological impacts and substance use patterns. These thematic areas were not arbitrarily determined but emerged from: (i) a preliminary literature search that identified these themes as predominant; (ii) consultations with clinical experts in the field of neurodevelopment and FEP; (iii) analysis of existing theoretical models linking ADHD to psychosis. This thematic structure guided our search strategy and the organisation of findings, ensuring a systematic and evidencebased approach. 2.3 | Search Strategy and Information Sources A structured literature search was conducted using multiple electronic databases: PubMed (via MEDLINE), Scopus, Web of Science and PsycINFO on 21 June 2024, covering the period from January 2001 onwards. Additionally, we reviewed reference lists of included articles for potentially relevant studies not captured in the database searches. The search strategy was designed to identify literature at the intersection of ADHD and first-episode psychosis, whilst also capturing studies related to our three predetermined focus areas. The primary search string included: (‘first episode non-affective psychosis’ OR ‘first episode psychosis’ OR ‘FEP’ OR ‘first episode schizophrenia’ OR ‘schizophrenia prodromal phase’ OR ‘schizophrenia prodromal symptoms’ OR ‘psychosis’). AND (‘ADHD’ OR ‘attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder’ OR ‘attention-deficit spectrum disorder’ OR ‘hyperkinetic disorder’). This primary search string was then combined with additional search terms for each focus area: • For neurodevelopmental factors: AND (‘neurodevelopment’ OR ‘cognitive deficit*’ OR ‘executive function*’ OR ‘intellectual disability’ OR ‘autism’ OR ‘developmental delay*’ OR ‘7mmerik7logy*’ OR ‘brain development’). • For pharmacological impacts: AND (‘methylphenidate’ OR ‘stimulant*’ OR ‘amphetamine*’ OR ‘psychostimulant*’ OR ‘ADHD medication*’ OR ‘drug-induced psychosis’ OR ‘atomoxetine’ OR ‘pharmacotherapy’ OR ‘drug safety’). • For substance use: AND (‘substance use’ OR ‘substance abuse’ OR ‘addiction’ OR ‘cannabis’ OR ‘marijuana’ OR ‘alcohol’ OR ‘tobacco’ OR ‘cocaine’ OR ‘stimulant abuse’ OR ‘comorbidity’ OR ‘dual diagnosis’). 2.4 | Eligibility Criteria Studies were considered eligible if they met the following inclusion criteria: included patients aged 16 and older; applied diagnostic criteria for ADHD in accordance with DSM-IV, DSM-5 or ICD-10/11 guidelines; applied diagnostic criteria for FEP (excluding bipolar disorder, schizoaffective disorder and psychotic depression) in accordance with standardised diagnostic systems; addressed at least one of our three focus areas: neurodevelopmental factors, pharmacological impacts or substance use patterns; original research articles (experimental, observational, post-marketing surveillance reports, case reports and case series); full-text articles available in English. Studies were excluded if they met any of the following criteria: involved patients with pre-existing diagnoses of schizophrenia or other disorders within the schizophrenia spectrum prior to study initiation; involved patients with personality disorders or neurocognitive impairments such as dementia as primary diagnoses; involved patients with neurological or infectious conditions as primary diagnoses; non-original research (e.g., reviews, commentaries, editorials, book chapters and letters to the editor); non-full-text articles (e.g., meeting abstracts); articles not in English; research incorporating animal or in vitro experiments only. 4 of 13 Early Intervention in Psychiatry, 2026 we recognised their methodological limitations compared to observational and experimental studies. Consequently, we adopted a more nuanced strategy, treating case reports as supplementary rather than primary evidence. In our analysis, we carefully distinguished between conclusions derived from case reports and those supported by more robust study designs. We explicitly acknowledged the limitations of case reports in establishing causal relationships, instead utilising them primarily to illustrate potential mechanisms or rare effects that merit further investigation through more rigorous methodologies. This reassessment has led to a clearer hierarchy of evidence in our analysis, with priority given to observational and experimental studies. 2.5 | Study Selection Process The study selection process followed a two-stage approach. In the first stage, three investigators (V.R., M.B. and G.D.S.) independently screened titles and abstracts against the eligibility criteria. In the second stage, the full texts of potentially eligible studies were retrieved and independently assessed by two investigators (V.R. and M.B.). Any disagreements were resolved through discussion with a third investigator (G.M.) serving as arbiter. The literature search and selection process were conducted by three investigators under the guidance of two supervisors. This involved a two-stage independent review by the investigators, followed by a collaborative cross-check to ensure consistency and thoroughness. 2.6 | Data Extraction and Categorisation The following parameters were extracted from each eligible article: first author, publication year, country, study design, sample size, participant demographics, diagnostic methods used, measurements/outcomes and key findings related to our three focus areas. The primary outcome was to identify which psychopathological factors are associated with the development of first-episode psychosis in individuals with ADHD. Data extraction specifically focused on evidence related to: (i) neurodevelopmental factors (including cognitive deficits, neurophysiological markers and comorbid neurodevelopmental disorders); (ii) pharmacological impacts (particularly methylphenidate and other stimulant medications); (iii) substance use patterns (with special attention to cannabis and other substances known to potentially trigger psychosis). 2.7 | Quality Assessment We conducted a formal quality assessment for all included studies using standardised tools specific to each study design: (i) for observational studies: Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS); (ii) for randomised controlled trials: Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 2.0; (iii) for case series: Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Case Series; (iv) for case reports: Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Case Reports. Detailed quality assessment scores for individual items are provided in Tables S1–S6. Two reviewers independently assessed each study, with a third reviewer resolving any disagreements. Quality scores were categorised as high, moderate or low, and these levels of evidence were explicitly considered in the synthesis of evidence and conclusions drawn. Studies with higher levels of evidence received greater weight in the overall analysis. A complete table of quality scores is included in Tables S1–S6. 2.8 | Ethical Considerations This review article is based exclusively on previously published data and studies and did not involve the collection of any primary data from human or animal subjects. Therefore, ethical approval was not required for this work. 3 | Results A total of 1243 articles were identified across all databases (538 from PubMed, 412 from Scopus, 175 from Web of Science and 118 from PsycINFO). After removing 243 duplicates, 1000 titles and abstracts were screened, resulting in 82 articles for fulltext review. Of these, 13 were ultimately selected based on our predefined criteria. Exclusion of the other 69 articles was due to irrelevance to our specific research questions (42) or noncompliance with selection criteria, including reviews, letters to the editor, commentaries, book chapters and non-English papers (27 articles). The detailed selection process is presented in Figure 1, following the PRISMA flow diagram format. The relatively small number of included studies reflects the highly specific focus of our review on the intersection between ADHD and first-episode psychosis, which represents an emerging research area with limited dedicated literature. This specificity was intentional to ensure direct relevance to our research questions, though it highlights an important gap warranting future investigation. These 13 studies selected comprise: five studies on neurodevelopmental factors (one cross-sectional study, three case–control studies and one retrospective cohort study), five studies on pharmacological effects (one RCT, one retrospective cohort study, one retrospective case–control study, one case series and one case report) and three studies on substance use (two prospective cohort studies and one cross-sectional study). 3.1 | Neurodevelopmental Factors A growing body of literature investigates the intersection between neurodevelopmental disorders such as ADHD and the onset of FEP. Amongst the primary neurodevelopmental factors identified are cognitive delays and other disorders like autism and intellectual disability. Strålin and Hetta (2019) provide significant insights into this area by demonstrating how comorbidity between ADHD, autism and intellectual disability influences the clinical course of FEP. Specifically, they found that patients with autism or intellectual disability, when coupled with psychosis, require longer treatment durations and higher doses of antipsychotic medication compared to other FEP patients. 17517893, 2026, 1, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/eip.70123 by Stony Brook University Libraries, Wiley Online Library on [21/10/2026]. 5 of 13 Early Intervention in Psychiatry, 2026 Conversely, those with ADHD are at a higher risk for SUDs and self-harm, both before and after the first psychosis hospitalisation (Strålin and Hetta 2019). Rydkjær et al. (2017) advance this area of research by investigating neurophysiological markers, specifically mismatch negativity (MMN) and P3a amplitude, in adolescents with FEP and ADHD. Their findings indicate that adolescents with FEP demonstrate significant pre-attentive deficits, reflected in reduced MMN amplitudes, when compared to healthy controls. The ADHD group showed intermediate deficits, with MMN amplitudes falling between those of the FEP group and healthy controls, although not significantly different from either. These results suggest a potential overlap in neurodevelopmental abnormalities between ADHD and FEP, possibly pointing to shared neurobiological vulnerabilities (Rydkjær et al. 2017). Similarly, Sanchez-Gistau et al. (2023) compared cognitive biases in 121 first-episode psychosis patients with and without ADHD versus healthy controls. Results showed FEP patients with childhood ADHD (FEP-ADHD+) had significantly more cognitive biases than those without ADHD (FEP-ADHD−) and healthy controls, particularly in ‘Intentionalising’ (attributing intentions to others) and ‘Emotional Reasoning’ (using emotions as facts). Cognitive biases correlated with positive psychotic symptoms in both FEP groups, but with depression only in FEP-ADHD− and with poor functioning only in FEPADHD+. The findings suggest FEP patients with comorbid ADHD represent a particularly vulnerable subgroup requiring targeted metacognitive interventions to address their heightened tendency toward biased interpretation of social information. Peralta et al. (2011) examined the relationship between childhood ADHD symptoms and first-episode schizophrenia-spectrum psychosis, providing support for a neurodevelopmental model. Their findings showed that the severity of childhood ADHD symptoms was significantly related to obstetric complications and neurodevelopmental delays. This indicates that ADHD symptoms in individuals with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders may be part of a broader neurodevelopmental dysfunction, rather than independently contributing to the clinical expression of psychosis. These results highlight shared neurodevelopmental risk factors between ADHD and schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, supporting the hypothesis that ADHD may represent an early manifestation of the underlying neurodevelopmental abnormalities that predispose individuals to psychosis (Peralta et al. 2011). 6 of 13 Early Intervention in Psychiatry, 2026 Adding to this body of evidence, Hasan et al. (2013) investigated cortical excitability in FEP and ADHD patients using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to explore whether there are shared neurophysiological pathways between the two disorders. Their findings revealed a similar pattern of impaired cortical inhibition and hemispheric imbalance of excitability in both FEP and ADHD patients, suggesting that these two disorders may share common pathophysiological mechanisms, particularly related to GABAergic and dopaminergic transmission. These results highlight potential neurobiological overlaps between ADHD and psychosis, further supporting the neurodevelopmental hypothesis of comorbidity between these conditions. The main findings related to neurodevelopmental factors are summarised in Table 1. 3.2 | Methylphenidate Therapy Another critical aspect of the ADHD-FEP relationship concerns the use of stimulant medications like methylphenidate in ADHD treatment, which may trigger psychosis in some patients. Moran et al. (2019) explored the differential risk of psychosis onset between methylphenidate and amphetamine in ADHD patients. Their findings revealed that amphetamine use was associated with a significantly higher risk of inducing psychosis compared to methylphenidate, with approximately 1 in 660 patients experiencing psychosis. The risk was 1.65 times higher for amphetamine users compared to those on methylphenidate, a finding that may be explained by amphetamine's more potent release of dopamine, which closely mimics the dopaminergic dysfunction seen in primary psychotic disorders (PPDs) (Moran et al. 2019). The study by Takahashi et al. (2014) was a randomised, doubleblind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial conducted at 39 sites in Japan. It evaluated the efficacy and safety of osmoticcontrolled release oral delivery system (OROS) methylphenidate (MPH) in adults with ADHD. A total of 284 adults were randomised to receive either OROS MPH or placebo. During a 4-week titration period, patients were started on 18 mg/day of OROS MPH, with weekly increments of 18 mg to reach an individualised dose, up to a maximum of 72 mg/day. The primary endpoint was assessed after a subsequent 4-week efficacy assessment period. In this study, one patient in the OROS MPH group developed a psychotic disorder, which was classified as a serious treatment-emergent adverse event (TEAE). The investigators determined that the psychotic episode was probably related to the methylphenidate treatment. This highlights the importance of monitoring patients closely during stimulant treatment, especially those with potential predispositions to psychosis (Takahashi et al. 2014). Three cases were reported in which patients, aged 29, 38 and 45, with no prior history of psychotic symptoms, developed such symptoms after taking standard doses of methylphenidate. Once methylphenidate was discontinued and antipsychotic treatment was initiated, their psychotic symptoms resolved within 2–21 days (Kraemer et al. 2010). Auger et al. (2005) conducted a retrospective case–control study at a sleep centre, involving 116 patients with narcolepsy or idiopathic hypersomnia. They compared a high-dose stimulant group (≥ 120% of the maximum recommended stimulant dose) to a standard-dose group. The high-dose group showed a significantly higher prevalence of psychosis (24% vs. 5% in the standard-dose group), with an odds ratio of 12.0. Notably, six patients in the high-dose group developed psychosis on methylphenidate at a median dose of 170 mg/day (range 120–500 mg), and their symptoms improved with dose reduction to a median of 80 mg/day (Auger et al. 2005). Additionally, Ghadrdan et al. (2018) reported a rare case of methylphenidate-induced psychosis in a 65-year-old female with ADHD. The patient, who was consuming three to four methylphenidate tablets daily, developed psychotic symptoms which resolved after discontinuation of the stimulant and initiation of antipsychotic medication. This case highlights that psychosis induced by methylphenidate, whilst uncommon, can occur in both young and elderly populations and that dose mismanagement may play a role in precipitating psychotic episodes (Ghadrdan et al. 2018). Sanchez-Gistau et al. (2020) examined 133 FEP patients, with approximately 25% presenting childhood ADHD (c-ADHD). Results showed that the FEPADHD+ group had significantly worse cognitive performance, particularly in attention, processing speed and executive function compared to FEP-ADHD− and healthy controls. Clinically, the FEP-ADHD+ group had fewer years of education, higher rates of tobacco and cannabis use, and required higher antipsychotic doses to achieve clinical response. Whilst the two FEP groups did not differ in psychopathology severity, there was a gradient of cognitive severity increasing from healthy controls to FEP-ADHD− to FEP-ADHD+. The study concludes that FEP-ADHD+ represents a subgroup with worse prognosis than FEP-ADHD. In a prospective observational study involving 179 first-episode psychosis (FEP) patients, with 15% having a history of childhood ADHD, it was found that FEP patients with ADHD had poorer premorbid functioning, lower educational achievement and an earlier onset of psychosis compared to those without ADHD. Additionally, the FEP-ADHD group demonstrated worse clinical outcomes, with more severe positive and negative symptoms, as well as poorer social and occupational functioning over time. Notably, the FEP-ADHD group had a higher prevalence of SUDs (75% vs. 56%), particularly involving tobacco and cannabis, which likely contributed to their increased risk of psychosis and poorer treatment response (Rho et al. 2015). Cassidy et al. (2011), in a prospective observational study, explore the relationship between childhood ADHD symptoms and subsequent cannabis use in 75 patients with FEP. The findings revealed that early life symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity significantly predicted lifetime cannabis use disorder and an inability to maintain abstinence from cannabis during treatment. Specifically, the inattention symptom alone was a stronger predictor of ongoing cannabis use, even after controlling for other factors like conduct disorder (CD) and oppositional defiant disorder (ODD). The study highlights that inattention–hyperactivity in childhood may play a crucial role in predisposing individuals to cannabis use in the context of psychosis, which could, in turn, exacerbate psychotic symptoms (Cassidy et al. 2011). Overall, the association between ADHD and substance use in FEP patients is clear, with cannabis use being a particularly prominent issue. These findings highlight the importance of early identification and management of substance use in ADHD patients with psychosis to improve clinical outcomes and prevent further complications. The main findings related to substance use and its influence on psychosis risk are summarised in Table 3. 3.4 | Quality Assessment Results The quality assessment revealed generally good methodological rigour across included studies. Of the 13 studies, 8 (61.5%) were rated as high quality, 3 (23.1%) as moderate quality and 2 (15.4%) as low quality. The single RCT demonstrated low risk of bias across all assessed domains. Cohort and case–control studies scored well on the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (median score 7/9), with good representativeness and adequate follow-up. Case studies, whilst methodologically limited by design, provided valuable clinical insights with adequate reporting quality. Higher quality studies were given greater weight in evidence synthesis, particularly the large epidemiological studies (Hollis et al. 2019; Moran et al. 2019) which informed our primary conclusions regarding pharmacological safety. 4 | Discussion Based on the data obtained thus far, we have identified three key areas concerning the onset of non-affective psychosis in individuals with ADHD. Our findings suggest that the first episode of psychosis appears to occur more frequently in ADHD patients with neurocognitive deficits or delays, particularly those with persistent ADHD symptoms from childhood (referred to as childhood-onset ADHD that continues into adolescence and adulthood). Furthermore, ADHD patients with a history of substance use appear to have an increased susceptibility to psychotic episodes. The relationship between pharmacological treatment of ADHD and psychosis risk requires nuanced interpretation. ADHD, as a neurodevelopmental disorder, may serve as a risk factor for developing psychosis in adulthood. This risk may be mediated by several factors observed in both conditions, including genetic variants affecting dopaminergic pathways, neurodevelopmental abnormalities, impaired executive functioning and structural brain alterations. Additionally, comorbid conditions such as CD and intellectual disability may contribute to this risk, suggesting that ADHD may impact neurodevelopment in ways that potentially increase vulnerability to psychosis (Dennis et al. 2004; Kousha et al. 2012). Recent broader studies beyond our review have also identified shared genetic risk loci between ADHD and schizophrenia, particularly in genes involved in dopamine regulation and neurodevelopment (Demontis et al. 2019; Faraone and Larsson 2019). These genetic overlaps provide additional support for neurodevelopmental connections between these conditions. Supporting these theories, schizophrenia is increasingly conceptualised as a neurodevelopmental disorder, with brain abnormalities and prodromal symptoms manifesting during childhood and adolescence, well before the onset of psychosis. Risk factors that may be shared with ADHD include obstetric complications, early neurodevelopmental disruptions, alterations in dopamine system functioning, genetic predisposition and early life adversities. These factors may interact with environmental stressors, potentially influencing neurodevelopment and the transition to psychosis. Additionally, inattention has been associated with the development of psychosis during late adolescence and adulthood in some studies (Kraemer et al. 2010). The extensive discussion of SUDs in our review is warranted by evidence indicating that SUD may represent an important mediating factor in the relationship between ADHD and psychosis. Adolescents with SUD appear to have higher rates of ADHD compared to the general population (Colaizzi et al. 2023; Frodl 2010; Muhammad et al. 2023; van Emmerikvan Oortmerssen et al. 2012). For instance, an NIH study found ADHD in 38% of adolescents with cannabis use disorder (Dennis et al. 2004), whilst a meta-analysis by van Emmerikvan Oortmerssen et al. reported ADHD in 23% of young adults seeking treatment for substance abuse (van Emmerik-van Oortmerssen et al. 2012). The International ADHD in Substance Use Disorders Prevalence (IASP) study, involving 3558 participants from 10 countries, reported a 40% prevalence of ADHD (van de Glind et al. 2013). Research suggests that children with ADHD may be at increased risk of developing SUD, with potentially higher risk if they have comorbid CD (Ercan et al. 2003). A meta-analysis by Charach et al. found ADHD youth were 2.4 times more likely to smoke and 1.5 times more likely to develop SUD (Charach et al. 2011; Lee 2011; Margherio et al. 2024), with Groenman et al. reporting similar findings in a 4-year follow-up (Groenman et al. 2013). Some studies indicate that ADHD youth may develop SUD earlier and progress more rapidly (King et al. 1999; Kousha et al. 2012; Riggs 1998; Riggs et al. 2004), particularly with comorbid CD (González et al. 2020; Mustonen et al. 2023). 10 of 13 Early Intervention in Psychiatry, 2026 Research indicates that approximately 50% of individuals with mental disorders, particularly schizophrenia, have a cooccurring SUD (Ricci, Ceci, et al. 2021), higher than rates observed in the general population. Substance-induced psychosis (SIP) has been reported in 7%–25% of first-episode psychosis cases. A study in Scandinavia found the annual incidence of SIP was 6.5 per 100 000, compared to 9.7 amongst those with a PPD and SUD, and 24.1 in PPD alone (Ricci et al. 2023; Ricci, Martinotti, et al. 2021). Studies suggest ADHD patients with SUD may face an increased risk of psychosis, possibly because both conditions involve dopaminergic system alterations, and early substance use, especially cannabis and tobacco, has been associated with psychosis in some individuals (Ghadrdan et al. 2018; Rho et al. 2015; Sanchez-Gistau et al. 2020). Regarding pharmacological treatment of ADHD, the evidence warrants careful interpretation. The well-designed study by Hollis et al. (2019) challenges concerns about methylphenidate and psychosis risk. Their data showed ‘no evidence of an increase in the immediate risk of psychotic events when comparing the 12-week periods before and after initiation of methylphenidate treatment, neither for those with or without a history of psychosis’. More notably, 1 year after starting methylphenidate treatment, they observed ‘a 36% reduction in the incidence of psychotic events in those with a history of psychosis and an 18% reduction in incidence in those without a history of psychosis relative to the period immediately before initiation of methylphenidate treatment’. These findings contribute important evidence that challenges concern about methylphenidate use in individuals with or without a history of psychosis. This perspective is further supported by larger meta-analyses not included in our primary review. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Cortese et al. (2018) examining 10 randomised controlled trials in adults found no significant increase in serious adverse events with methylphenidate compared to placebo. Similarly, a comprehensive review by Storebø et al. (2018) of 185 randomised trials concluded that whilst methylphenidate may increase the risk of non-serious adverse events, there was no statistically significant increase in serious adverse events compared to placebo or no intervention. However, as most RCTs are of short duration, these findings may not fully capture the risk of psychosis with long-term treatment, a limitation acknowledged in these reviews. Methylphenidate, a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant, is frequently prescribed for the treatment of ADHD in both children and adults. It is available in immediate-release and extended-release forms, which differ in terms of half-life and duration of action. Although generally considered safe and effective, methylphenidate is associated with common side effects such as insomnia, headaches, loss of appetite and gastrointestinal issues (Storebø et al. 2018). The drug also carries a risk of misuse, particularly amongst adolescents, due to the euphoric effects that can occur at high doses, whether taken orally, intranasally or intravenously (Heal et al. 2013; Shram et al. 2022). A critical distinction that emerges from our review is between the short-term and long-term effects of stimulant medications on psychosis risk. Most randomised controlled trials, including Takahashi et al. (2014), examined relatively short treatment durations (typically 8–12 weeks), which may not capture delayed onset psychotic symptoms or cumulative risk over years of treatment. Conversely, the epidemiological study by Hollis et al. (2019) provided valuable 1-year follow-up data, finding no evidence of increased psychosis risk and observing lower rates of psychotic events in the post-treatment period compared to pre-treatment, though the authors did not conclude that methylphenidate has protective effects. These apparently contradictory findings highlight the possibility of different risk profiles over different time frames: acute adverse events may occur shortly after treatment initiation or dose increases, whilst longer-term dopamine stabilisation might potentially reduce psychosis risk in certain populations. This temporal dimension of risk is particularly important for clinicians to consider, as it suggests the need for closer monitoring during treatment initiation and dose adjustments, whilst possibly offering reassurance about long-term treatment in stable patients. Future research should specifically address this temporal aspect of psychosis risk with stimulant treatment through extended longitudinal studies. Based on available evidence, including literature beyond our primary review, methylphenidate appears to play a significant role in managing ADHD symptoms, with well-established short-term efficacy. Regarding psychotic symptoms, when they do occur in patients taking stimulant medications, case reports and pharmacovigilance data suggest they may often resolve following discontinuation of the stimulant, though the exact proportion requires further investigation through more robust study designs. Current guidelines for ADHD management suggest that cautious reintroduction of stimulants after an episode of stimulant-induced psychosis may be considered in some cases (Cortese et al. 2023), though this approach requires individualised risk assessment. The comparative study by Moran et al. suggests that methylphenidate may have a lower risk profile than amphetamines regarding psychosis, though the absolute risk of psychotic events appears to be relatively small for both medications (Moran et al. 2019). This finding is consistent with a recent large-scale pharmacoepidemiological study by Solmi et al. (2022) that found amphetamines were associated with a higher risk of psychotic events compared to methylphenidate. Nevertheless, further research is required to explore the outcomes of stimulant rechallenge in individuals with a history of psychotic symptoms. It remains prudent to assess any pre-existing vulnerability to psychosis, as well as the concomitant use of psychostimulant substances before prescribing methylphenidate. 4.1 | Methodological Limitations We acknowledge several limitations in our methodological approach. Despite the expansion of our search strategy, some relevant studies may have been omitted. In particular, we recognise that the RCT by Takahashi et al. (2014) represents only one of many trials examining stimulant medications, and a more comprehensive approach would involve citing meta-analyses that thoroughly investigate stimulant-related adverse effects, including psychosis. The heterogeneity of included studies limits the possibility of quantitative syntheses. The lack of high-quality longitudinal studies in some thematic areas restricts our ability to establish causal relationships, particularly regarding long-term effects of stimulant medications. The small number of included studies (n = 13) reflects our specific focus on ADHD and first-episode psychosis but may limit the generalisability of our conclusions. Certain conclusions in our original manuscript were based on limited evidence, such as case reports, which we now recognise as a significant limitation. Another important limitation concerns the significant heterogeneity in sample sizes across included studies. Our review encompasses a wide range of sample sizes, from individual case reports to large-scale epidemiological studies involving over 300 000 participants (Moran et al. 2019). Whilst our quality assessment process took sample size into consideration, we acknowledge the inherent challenge in balancing evidence from studies with vastly different statistical power. We attempted to address this by giving greater weight to larger, more robust studies in our synthesis and conclusions, particularly when formulating clinical implications. For instance, the large cohort study by Moran et al. (2019) comparing psychosis risk between methylphenidate and amphetamine users was given more weight in our conclusions regarding pharmacological risk than individual case reports, despite the latter providing valuable insights into clinical presentations and potential mechanisms. We must also acknowledge the potential for publication bias in our review. This is particularly relevant for case reports and small clinical studies, which are more likely to be published when they describe unusual, severe or novel outcomes. This publication bias may lead to an overestimation of adverse events such as psychosis in relation to stimulant treatment. Case reports of psychosis associated with standard doses of stimulants, for example, may be more likely to be published than uneventful clinical courses. Similarly, studies finding no association between ADHD and psychosis risk may be less likely to be published than those identifying significant associations. Whilst we attempted to mitigate this by including larger epidemiological studies and emphasising their findings, the potential for publication bias remains a limitation of the available literature in this field and should be considered when interpreting our conclusions. 5 | Conclusion This systematic review examined the relationship between ADHD and FEP. Evidence suggests individuals with ADHD, particularly those with neurocognitive deficits or persistent childhood symptoms, may have elevated psychosis risk. Substance use, especially cannabis use, appears to mediate this relationship. Regarding pharmacological treatment, recent epidemiological studies provide a more detailed perspective on methylphenidate safety, with large-scale studies finding no evidence of increased psychosis risk in the immediate period following treatment initiation, though the evidence remains mixed and requires further investigation. When psychotic symptoms occur during stimulant treatment, they often resolve upon discontinuation. Clinicians should consider individual risk profiles, particularly psychosis vulnerability and substance use patterns, when managing ADHD. Further longitudinal research is needed to elucidate these complex relationships. Funding The authors have nothing to report. Ethics Statement The authors have nothing to report. pages: 1 of 13 Family Process, 2026; 65:e70179 https://doi.org/10.1111/famp.70179 Family Process REVIEW ARTICLE OPEN ACCESS Parenting Research The Stigmatization of Caregivers of Children With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Systematic Review Samuel Guerin1 | Jeffrey McCrossin2 | Romuald Blanc3 | Émilie Cappe1,4 1Laboratory of Psychopathology and Health Processes, Université Paris Cité, Boulogne-Billancourt, France | 2École de psychoéducation, Université de Montréal, Montreal, Canada | 3INSERM, Imaging Brain & Neuropsychiatry iBraiN, Université de Tours, Tours, France | 4Institut Universitaire de France (IUF), Paris, France Correspondence: Émilie Cappe (emilie.cappe@u-pariscite.fr) Received: 10 December 2024 | Revised: 1 March 2026 | Accepted: 7 April 2026 Keywords: affiliate stigma | courtesy stigma | neurodevelopmental disorders | parent–child relations | parenting | psychological distress ABSTRACT Research on Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)-related stigma has centered on individuals with the diagnosis. Evidence concerning caregivers exists but has not been brought together in a way that clarifies its scope, correlates, and implica tions, despite caregivers' central role in navigating services, supporting daily functioning, and treatment engagement. The pres ent study therefore to systematically review the empirical literature on the stigmatization of caregivers of children with ADHD. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched PubMed and PsycINFO for studies between 2013 and 2024. Of the 4136 articles, 15 studies examining affiliate and courtesy stigma met criteria. Across studies, affiliate stigma was consistently linked to higher levels of caregiver depression, anxiety, and distress, as well as coping strategies and parenting styles. Higher education levels among caregivers were associated with lower affiliate stigma. The severity of the child's ADHD symptoms and internalizing/ex ternalizing problems significantly associated with the level of stigma experienced by caregivers. Courtesy stigma was associated with several factors, including negative attitudes (e.g., anger or blame directed at children with ADHD) among members of the general public. These findings highlight the multifaceted associations of stigma on caregivers. The association between affiliate stigma and caregiver psychological distress underscores the need for targeted interventions, however only one intervention study met inclusion criteria for this review. The association between negative attitudes and courtesy stigma indicates the importance of addressing public perceptions. Future research should focus on developing and testing interventions that aim to reduce stigma and improve the well-being of caregivers and their families. Trial Registration: Prospero registration number: CRD42024527305 1 | Introduction Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurode velopmental disorder characterized by patterns of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity that interfere significantly with functioning and development (American Psychiatric Association 2022). These symptoms typically manifest in multiple settings (e.g., at home and school) and can lead to significant impairments in academic or social functioning (Cortese et al. 2023). Worldwide prevalence rates of ADHD are estimated at about 5.9% of children, making it the second most common psychological disorder among young people (Faraone et al. 2021). Stigma may interfere with family dynamics and the effective ness of family-based interventions. Recent research suggests that ADHD is linked to increased parental stress, harsher or inconsistent parenting practices, and a decline in the quality of the parent–child relationship (Babinski and Sibley 2022). Family therapy has shown promise in improving parenting behaviors, reducing criticism and expressed emotion, and fostering more cooperative behavior in children (Daley et al. 2018; Hornstra et al. 2023). Yet, stigma may hinder caregivers' engagement in these therapeutic approaches. Investigating how stigma affects caregivers' emotional resources, parenting, and participation in behavioral treatments may thus be crucial for optimizing family therapy practices. Several types of stigma affect families of individuals with ADHD. Public stigma targets individuals through bias and discrimina tion in schools, workplaces, and clinics, resulting in hurtful communication, exclusion, and denial of opportunities (Mueller et al. 2012). Courtesy stigma affects those associated with indi viduals with ADHD, like family members and caregivers, often blaming them for the condition (Birenbaum 1970). Internalized stigma, or self-stigma, involves individuals with ADHD adopt ing negative beliefs about themselves, which are associated with low self-esteem and isolation. Similarly, affiliate stigma is ob served among families and caregivers who internalize negative societal perceptions (Papadopoulos et al. 2022). Together, these distinctions provide a conceptual framework for understanding stigma across individuals and their social environments, while highlighting forms of stigma that may also be experienced by caregivers, which are examined more specifically in the present review. Public stigma has been particularly well-documented within the ADHD literature. This type of stigma relates to societal stereotypes, attitudes, and discrimination toward stigmatized individuals (Corrigan and Kleinlein 2005). Such stigma can be enacted by peers, teachers, or healthcare professionals (Greenway et al. 2023; Metzger and Hamilton 2021; TatlowGolden et al. 2016). Public stigma varies across these groups. For instance, healthcare professionals' stigma often involves questioning the validity of ADHD, despite its recognition in international classifications and its initial clinical descrip tions dating back to the 18th century (American Psychiatric Association 2022; Van Kernebeek and Crunelle 2024; World Health Organization 2022). Teacher stigma typically results in the exclusion or underestimation of academic abilities of students with ADHD (Metzger and Hamilton 2021; Toye et al. 2019). Peers often exhibit stigma by falsely attributing socially undesirable traits to youth with ADHD, such as being “more violent” and requiring greater social distance (Walker et al. 2008). These factors are associated with poorer social relationships (Pelham and Fabiano 2008), as higher levels of anxiety, depression, and low self-esteem (Becker et al. 2017) in individuals with ADHD. The difficulties associated with ADHD symptoms often ex tend to caregivers who may experience courtesy and affiliate stigma due to their close relationship with the child. Caregivers of children with ADHD report lower self-efficacy, self-liking, physical health, psychological health, and poorer social rela tionships compared to caregivers of children without ADHD (Ahmed et al. 2022). Alongside these notable challenges, there is a significant burden of stigma borne by families, who are often blamed for their child's disorders and receive little social support (Ching'oma et al. 2022; Leitch et al. 2019). Qualitative studies illustrate how stigmatizing experiences manifest for caregivers of children with ADHD. For example, in the study by Leitch et al. (2019), one caregiver described being labeled as lazy and having faced guilt-inducing comments regarding the pharmacological treatment given to their child (e.g., “If you learned to control your kids there wouldn't be a problem”). Other caregivers reported experiencing social isolation and expressed high levels of frustration due to the lack of social support. The internalization of stigma has also been qualita tively documented, with caregivers reporting that they delib erately avoid busy public places or religious services in order to prevent “people looking at us in a certain way,” (Schoeman and Voges 2022, 5) reflecting an anticipation of judgment consistent with affiliate stigma. These findings suggest that stigma affects not only the individual child but also extends to the family system as a whole. It is crucial to expand our focus from the individual child and dedicate our attention to fully understanding and addressing how stigma is linked to caregivers. Both courtesy stigma and affiliate stigma are significantly linked to the mental and emotional well-being of caregivers. Furthermore, affiliate stigma has been found to mediate the negative relationship between general mental health disor der label avoidance and care seeking (Kosyluk et al. 2022). Several studies have indicated that education and knowledge about ADHD are associated with lower levels of public stigma (Ching et al. 2023; Lebowitz 2016; Speerforck et al. 2021). Although public stigma primarily targets individuals with ADHD, it also shapes the broader social climate in which families evolve. These findings therefore underscore the importance of developing a deeper understanding of stigma processes among caregivers in order to better address family needs and to identify the mechanisms that sustain stigma in the general population. Two previous reviews of ADHD and stigma provide in sight into the stigma experienced by caregivers. Lebowitz et al. (2016) found that adults often fail to recognize ADHD as a mental health disorder, resulting in less support and more stigmatizing attitudes toward individuals with ADHD. This stigma extends to the treatments for ADHD, particularly med ications, which are often viewed negatively. Parents often face blame for their child's ADHD, which is associated with social isolation and emotional distress. Mueller et al. (2012) found that caregivers experience courtesy stigma, where family members and close associates of individuals with ADHD face social rejection and judgment. Caregivers also internalize this stigma, which is linked to their mental health and quality of life. Widespread misconceptions about ADHD, such as beliefs that it results from poor parenting or lifestyle choices, exacer bate the stigma faced by caregivers.
