While these reviews highlight the associations of stigma with caregivers, an up-to-date systematic review dedicated to care giver stigmatization is needed to provide a clearer overview of how these experiences are described in the literature, par ticularly in the context of caregivers supporting a child with ADHD, and to identify current challenges and directions for support and intervention. The aim of this article is to systematically review recent scien tific literature on the stigmatization of caregivers of children with ADHD. More specifically, the following objectives will be addressed: • Objective 1: Report descriptive characteristics of the exist ing literature on the stigmatization of caregivers of children with ADHD. • Objective 2: Synthesize knowledge regarding the associa tions between stigmatization of these caregivers and other relevant outcomes. 2 | Method This systematic review was conducted according to the PRISMA guidelines (Page et al. 2021). The review protocol was registered with the Prospero database. 2.1 | Eligibility Criteria Our inclusion criteria encompassed quantitative research, including cross-sectional studies; case–control studies that compared stigmatizing attitudes and experiences between caregivers of children with and without ADHD; prospective cohort studies that followed caregivers over time to examine associations between stigma and various outcomes; and ret rospective cohort studies. Similarly, in the case of courtesy stigma, when a hypothetical situation was discussed (e.g., clinical vignette), the concept of ADHD had to be explicitly mentioned and not limited to child characteristics of impul sivity or inattention. Studies were included if ADHD was diag nosed as the primary disorder. Studies including participants with ADHD and comorbidities (e.g., oppositional defiant dis order, anxiety disorders) were not excluded to accurately re flect common complex presentations of the condition (Ottosen et al. 2019). Moreover, to be included in the review, the study had to focus on a homogeneous group of caregivers of chil dren with ADHD. Studies that included participants who were caregivers of children with other neurodevelopmental disorders without intragroup distinctions, for example, were excluded. 2.2 | Information Sources An electronic search was undertaken with the support of an ex pert librarian in February 2024 using PubMed and PsycINFO databases, accessed via the National Center for Biotechnology Information, EBSCOhost, and PubPsych platforms. These databases were chosen because they are prominent global sources for psychology and psychiatry research. To refine the search, several criteria were set: the articles had to be (a) in a peerreviewed journal, (b) published between 2013 and 2024, given the most recent review was conducted in 2013 (Lebowitz 2016), and (c) available in English or French. The search terms focused on ADHD and issues of stigmatization, employing Boolean logic: ((stigma* OR self-stigma* OR stereotyp* OR attitude* OR discrimin*) AND (ADHD OR “attention deficit” OR hyperac tiv*)). The query utilized the term truncations like “attention deficit*” and the abbreviation “ADHD,” as defined in the DSM-5 (American Psychiatric Association 2022), to capture a wide array of literature related to attention deficit hyperactivity disor der. Consistent with Corrigan and Kleinlein's (2005) definition of public stigma, which includes the dimensions of discrimi nation, stereotypes, and attitudes, we have incorporated these terms into our algorithms using truncations to gather as many articles as possible. 2.3 | Selection Process The initial screening of the database findings was performed by the first two authors using the Rayyan online systematic review software (Ouzzani et al. 2016). Duplicate articles were identified and removed prior to title and abstract screening for relevance based on the predetermined inclusion and ex clusion criteria. A random sample of 60 articles was selected for independent title and abstract screening by both authors to ensure consistent application of study selection criteria. The two researchers largely agreed on the articles selected for in clusion, with a 98.9% agreement rate resolving any differences through discussion. Articles that passed the initial screen ing were included for full-text review by the first and second authors. Following the selection process, they also reviewed the references within the chosen articles to uncover any addi tional pertinent studies related to stigmatization of caregivers of children with ADHD. 2.4 | Data Collection Process 1 2 2.5 | Quality and Risk of Bias Assessment Evaluation Criteria We used the Quality Assessment Tool for Observational Cohort and Cross-Sectional Studies (National Institutes of Health 2014) to evaluate the quality and potential biases of the articles. Consequently, studies were rated as “good” (minimal risk of bias, yielding valid results), “fair” (presence of some bias, yet not significant enough to undermine the results), or “poor” (substan tial risk of bias). This evaluation was independently conducted by the first two authors, achieving an inter-rater agreement of 82.4%. Additionally, in the study by Chou et al. (2020), caregivers were invited to identify the etiological and causal factors of ADHD. They found that affiliate stigma was positively associated with the causal attribution of several factors such as caregivers' failure to discipline, teachers' failure to discipline, poor diet, poor living environment, an excessive focus on academic success, and attributing causes to supernat ural beings or reasons based on divination. The most frequently cited cause was brain dysfunction (84.8%), followed by inade quate caregiver discipline (44.0%); an unhealthy diet, such as high sugar intake (40.8%); a poor living environment (38.8%); children mimicking inappropriate behaviors from peers (37.3%); insufficient discipline by school staff (29.0%); and the education system's strong focus on academic performance (27.3%). These findings demonstrate that extrabiological factors and those in herent to educational factors are often understood by the public as having a causal value in the explanation of ADHD. 4.1.6 | Intervention The study by Nissley-Tsiopinis et al. (2023) showed that a foursession group intervention designed to prepare parents as in formed consumers to engage in multimodal evidence-based treatment for ADHD had no effect on reducing affiliate stigma, both immediately after the intervention and 6 weeks later. However, a large proportion of participants expressed little to no concern about affiliate stigma at baseline, indicating essentially no concern about stigma prior to receiving the intervention. 4.2 | Courtesy Stigma The emotions expressed by and toward children with ADHD are linked to the courtesy stigma experienced by their caregiv ers. Research by Sheeper and Vaughn (2021) and Wiley and Vaughn (2020) demonstrated that when individuals from the gen eral public observed a child with ADHD displaying positive emo tions in a vignette, they were less likely to blame the mother for the child's condition. Conversely, higher levels of anger directed at the child were associated with increased blame toward the mother. Furthermore, the blame and responsibility the public places on mothers for the child's ADHD are likely linked to their attitudes toward these families. For example, Wiley and Vaughn (2020) further demonstrated that the extent to which respondents be lieved the mother was responsible for the child's ADHD was as sociated with the relationship between the perceived likability of the mother and the willingness to offer her personal assistance. In the study by Sheeper and Vaughn (2021), among the six condi tions evaluated (ADHD, anxiety, depression, juvenile delinquency, obesity, and fetal alcohol syndrome), stigmatization (responsibility and blame of parents) as well as associations of anger toward the mother were the lowest for ADHD. In the study by Wadian et al. (2019), the general public rated perceived causes of children's disorders, including ADHD, on a six-point scale. Parental responsibility was rated 2.87 for the onset and 3.29 for the perpetuation of ADHD. These ratings were lower for the children themselves (onset = 2.3; perpetua tion = 2.54), whereas biological explanations were rated higher (onset = 4.86; perpetuation = 4.74). 5 | Discussion This systematic review investigated the stigmatization of care givers of children with ADHD, incorporating 15 quantitative studies published between 2015 and 2023. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review to focus exclusively on the stigmatization of caregivers of children with ADHD. The first objective of this review was to report descriptive characteristics of the existing literature. The majority of the articles used sam ples from either Taiwan or the USA (n = 13). The most common type of caregiver stigmatization evaluated was affiliate stigma (n = 12). Two studies focused solely on female caregivers, and the samples across all studies were predominantly female (80.9%). Among the included articles, almost all were published since 2019, indicating growing interest in the topic. The second objective of the review was to synthesize knowledge regarding the associations between stigmatization of these care givers and relevant outcome variables. Our review highlights several key associations between caregiver stigmatization and caregiver sociodemographic variables, the clinical presentation of ADHD in the child, as well as caregiver coping and parenting styles. Furthermore, the findings related to courtesy stigma sug gest that emotions evoked by stories of children with ADHD are linked to both how the public feels about mothers of children with ADHD and the extent to which they blame or hold mothers responsible for their child's condition. Increased caregiver education was found to be inversely related to affiliate stigma, which in turn was associated with nega tive attitudes toward ADHD treatments (Chang et al. 2020). However, none of the studies in our review shed light on how parental education and knowledge regarding ADHD are specif ically linked to affiliate stigma. Previous studies demonstrated that higher levels of knowledge about ADHD are associated with lower levels of public stigmatization and negative attitudes (Barnett et al. 2012; Kosyluk et al. 2016). While a plethora of parenting interventions for caregivers of children with ADHD exist (Rimestad et al. 2019), we are not aware of any studies that have examined the impact of such programs on affiliate stigma. This may be a particularly interesting approach to ad dressing affiliate stigma since it is linked to various maladap tive coping strategies and parenting styles, parental negativity and relational difficulties (Chang et al. 2021a; Lin et al. 2023; Mikami et al. 2015) that parenting interventions tend to target (Barkley 2013). 15455300, 2026, 3, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/famp.70179 by Stony Brook University Libraries, Wiley Online Library on [21/10/2026]. 9 of 13 Family Process, 2026 Affiliate stigma is associated with the severity of the child's ADHD symptoms and with internalizing (e.g., anxiety, depres sion, somatic complaints) and externalizing problems (e.g., rulebreaking, aggressive behavior; Charbonnier et al. 2019; Mikami et al. 2015; Özaslan and Yıldırım 2021). The relationships be tween these variables seem to be bidirectional since Mikami et al. (2015) showed that parental negativity mediates the asso ciation between affiliate stigma and child social skills, indicat ing that affiliate stigma could play a role in generating parental negativity and unfavorable outcomes for children. Our review revealed associations between affiliate stigma and both child and parent gender. Affiliate stigma is more pro nounced for parents of girls with ADHD (Chang et al. 2020). This finding could potentially be explained by the higher prevalence of ADHD among boys (Ayano et al. 2020; Pastor et al. 2015) and poorer social acceptability of ADHD diagnoses in girls (Kok et al. 2016). Parents of girls with ADHD may experience greater stigma because the female presentation of the disorder is not normalized in the same way as that of their male counterparts. Furthermore, a meta-analysis demonstrated that parents of girls with ADHD may experience lower levels of stress, suggesting that gender differences in ADHD may be linked to parental experiences through other mechanisms than the symptoms of the disorder themselves (Theule et al. 2013). Although Özaslan and Yıldırım (2021) found no differences in affiliate stigma be tween genders of parents, mothers and fathers of children with ADHD tend to exhibit differences in parenting styles (El-Deen et al. 2021), which one study in our review indicated is asso ciated with affiliate stigma (Chang et al. 2021a). This suggests that even though direct parent gender-based differences in af filiate stigma might not be evident, differences in parenting approaches may influence how affiliate stigma is experienced. Further to this, positive emotions toward a child with ADHD are associated with lower maternal blame and increased supportive behaviors (Sheeper and Vaughn 2021; Wiley and Vaughn 2020). These findings highlight the systemic interactions of affiliate stigma, showing how public attitudes toward children influence maternal experiences. Shifting public attitudes from blaming mothers to acknowledging their responsibility for their children may encourage supportive behaviors. Together, these findings highlight the need to account for both child and parent sex and gender in future research on affiliate stigma. To deepen our understanding of these findings, it is useful to consider how some of the included studies drew on theoretical models to frame their methods or interpret their results. Several theoretical models were used to conceptualize the mechanisms underlying caregiver stigmatization. Ecological Systems Theory (Bronfenbrenner 1979) was the most frequently cited model, used to describe the influence of multilevel contextual factors on affiliate stigma. At the mesosystem level, Chang et al. (2021b) found that higher levels of social support are associated with lower affiliate stigma in caregivers, suggesting that interactions between immediate environments (e.g., family and clinical sys tems) may shape stigma experiences. Chen et al. (2021) also reported that family support and caregiver self-esteem are asso ciated with lower levels of depression in the presence of affiliate stigma, while internalizing symptoms and ADHD severity in the child are associated with higher levels. These associations could be interpreted within the ecological framework as evidence that stigma-related processes unfold at the intersection of individual and relational contexts. Chou et al. (2020) referred to the mac rosystem to account for caregivers' preference for complemen tary and alternative interventions over conventional treatments. This behavioral pattern could reflect an adaptive response to in ternalized stigma, whereby socially sanctioned alternatives are perceived as more acceptable. Lin et al. (2023) conceptualized affiliate stigma as embedded in exosystemic and macrosystemic forces, reporting that the association between inattention symp toms and caregiver hopelessness is stronger among caregivers reporting higher stigma. This interaction may illustrate the in fluence of societal norms and expectations on individual psy chological outcomes. The self-stigma model by Corrigan and Watson (2002) served as a theoretical basis for several studies. This model proposes that caregivers may internalize public stigma, which could in turn impact psychological functioning. Charbonnier et al. (2019) drew on this framework to examine the mediating role of af filiate stigma in the association between child ADHD symp toms and maternal depressive symptoms. Mikami et al. (2015) aligned their conceptualization of affiliate stigma with the af fective (shame), cognitive (guilt), and behavioral (avoidance) dimensions described by Mak and Cheung (2008). The authors also discussed a limitation of their measure, noting that it does not distinguish between the stages proposed by Corrigan and Rao (2012), such as stereotype awareness, agreement, and selfapplication. This methodological reflection could encourage the development of more theoretically aligned measurement tools that differentiate perceived stigma from internalized self-devaluation. Attributional theory (Weiner et al. 1988) was used in studies focusing on courtesy stigma and public attitudes toward par ents. Sheeper and Vaughn (2021) found that lower perceived parental responsibility is associated with increased liking and willingness to help, while higher blame is associated with anger and reduced support. These effects were mediated by emotions such as pity and anger, which play a central role in attributional models of social judgment. This pattern could be interpreted as evidence that emotional responses to perceived responsi bility shape behavioral intentions toward caregivers. Wadian et al. (2019) reported that when responsibility for ADHD onset was attributed to the child, participants expressed more nega tive attitudes. Attributions to parents or biological causes were not significantly associated with attitudes. This finding was specific to perceptions of symptom onset, which may suggest that beliefs about the origin of a condition carry more weight in stigma formation than beliefs about its maintenance. Wiley and Vaughn (2020) similarly found that greater parental blame is associated with lower liking of the parents themselves, which in turn is associated with lower willingness to help. 5.1 | Study Limitations Several limitations should be noted in this review. First, the exclusion of qualitative studies limited findings related to con textual insights and reports of lived experience of caregiver stigmatization. Second, the vast majority of studies included in the review were either from the USA or Taiwan, of which 15455300, 2026, 3, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/famp.70179 by Stony Brook University Libraries, Wiley Online Library on [21/10/2026]. Fourth, several studies used unvalidated measures of stigma (Charbonnier et al. 2019; Özaslan and Yıldırım 2021; Sheeper and Vaughn 2021; Wiley and Vaughn 2020). The use of unvalidated instruments is prob lematic because it undermines the reliability and validity of the data collected, potentially introducing measurement error and limiting the comparability of results across studies and contexts (Boateng et al. 2018). These factors may limit the generalizability of the findings and could introduce a cultural bias. For example, the availability and use of pharmacological treatments for ADHD vary across countries, shaped by legislation, healthcare infrastructure, and cultural norms (Chappuy et al. 2020; Massuti et al. 2021). These factors not only influence treatment access but also shape the meanings ascribed to ADHD and its medical management, which can affect the degree and form of stigma experienced. As such, generalizing findings of associations between severity of ADHD symptoms and stigma across contexts requires caution (Cortese 2012; Storebø et al. 2015). For example, one study from Taiwan in our review indicated an association between affili ate stigma and unfavorable attitudes toward treatment (Chang et al. 2020). Similarly, a recent study from Saudi Arabia reported that more than half of parents (54%) hesitated or discontin ued ADHD pharmacological treatment due to concerns about others' judgments and societal views on medication (Alsubaie et al. 2024). While such findings suggest that stigma can be a barrier to treatment, cross-national differences may limit the extent to which these results can be generalized. Further re search is needed that specifically takes sociopolitical contexts into account. Most studies included in this review relied on self-report ques tionnaires, which do not distinguish between objective exposure to stigmatizing attitudes and subjective emotional responses. This conflation may limit interpretability, as high stigma scores could reflect either actual negative experiences or caregivers' internalization and emotional reactivity. To address this limita tion, future research should also assess stigma as it is expressed in the general population, not only as it is perceived or internal ized by caregivers. This dual approach would allow for a more accurate understanding of how societal attitudes contribute to caregiver burden, as illustrated in studies on courtesy stigma (Sheeper and Vaughn 2021; Wadian et al. 2019; Wiley and Vaughn 2020). 5.2 | Clinical Recommendations and Implications for Future Research This review has highlighted numerous associations between af filiate stigma and variables both in caregivers (levels of depres sion, anxiety, hopelessness, self-esteem, parenting styles, life satisfaction, coping strategies, parental distress, parent–child dysfunctional interactions, unfavorable attitudes toward diag nosis, etc.) and children (severity of ADHD symptomatology, internalizing and externalizing problems, social withdrawal, social skills, etc.). These findings demonstrate the impor tance of assessing affiliate stigma in caregivers and proposing psychoeducation methods that could help reduce it. Only one study in this review explored the impact of an intervention on affiliate stigma (Nissley-Tsiopinis et al. 2023), highlighting a significant gap in the literature. We have seen that higher levels of education are associated with lower levels of affiliate stigma (Chang et al. 2020); however, further studies are still needed to determine the effectiveness of targeted parent educational pro grams related to ADHD on reducing affiliate stigma. Implicit stigma refers to involuntary, unconscious, and auto matic attitudes, behaviors, and emotions directed toward a targeted population (Dovidio et al. 2002). Several studies show that children with ADHD experience implicit stigmatization by their peers, notably through verbal labels such as “dangerous; scary; guilty; weak” (O'Driscoll et al. 2012). However, none of the studies in our review reported on implicit stigmatization among caregivers (Dovidio et al. 2002). This is a significant gap in the literature that should be explored to understand the extent to which this hidden stigma impacts caregivers and how it may be addressed. The findings from the present review may inform future adap tations of family-based interventions for children with ADHD. While existing programs already aim to improve parenting prac tices and overall family functioning (Babinski and Sibley 2022; Daley et al. 2018; Hornstra et al. 2023), our review suggests that caregiver stigma—through its associations with less adaptive coping strategies, dysfunctional parenting styles, heightened depressive and anxiety symptoms, and reduced parental selfesteem—may represent an additional target for clinical atten tion. Stigma-related burden may not only increase parental distress but also reduce treatment engagement, undermine the implementation of parenting strategies, and ultimately limit in tervention efficacy. While correlational, these findings suggest that integrating psychoeducational or supportive components focused on stigma reduction and caregiver emotional well-being into family-based programs may be valuable. Further research is needed to evaluate the feasibility and clinical benefits of such enhancements. 6 | Conclusion This systematic review underscores the significant challenges faced by caregivers of children with ADHD, highlighting the pervasive effects of affiliate and courtesy stigma. These stigmas are linked to caregivers' mental health and social functioning but also predict their interactions and coping strategies. It is hy pothesized that education and knowledge about ADHD could be crucial factors in reducing stigma, suggesting the need for targeted interventions to improve caregiver well-being. Despite the review's limitations, the literature remains clear: address ing caregiver stigmatization is essential for enhancing the over all well-being of caregivers of children with ADHD and their families. pages: International Journal of Methods in Psychiatric Research - ORIGINAL ARTICLE OPEN ACCESS Psychometric Assessment of the Arabic Translation of the Adult ADHD Self‐Report Scale Version 1.1 6‐Question Screener Melyssa Assaf1 | Nelly Kheir1 | Rabih Hallit2,3,4 | Diana Malaeb5 | Kamel Jebreen6 | Fouad Sakr7 | Mariam Dabbous7 | Sahar Obeid8 | Feten Fekih‐Romdhane9,10 | Souheil Hallit2,11 1Faculty of Medicine, Paris‐Saclay University, Le Kremlin‐Bicêtre, France | 2School of Medicine and Medical Sciences, Holy Spirit University of Kaslik, Jounieh, Lebanon | 3Department of Infectious Disease, Bellevue Medical Center, Mansourieh, Lebanon | 4Department of Infectious Disease, Notre Dame des Secours University Hospital, Byblos, Lebanon | 5College of Pharmacy, Gulf Medical University, Ajman, UAE | 6Department of Computational Sciences, Palestine Technical University – Kadoorie, Hebron, Palestine | 7School of Pharmacy, Lebanese International University, Beirut, Lebanon | 8Social and Education Sciences Department, School of Arts and Sciences, Lebanese American University, Jbeil, Lebanon | 9Department of Psychiatry “Ibn Omrane”, The Tunisian Center of Early Intervention in Psychosis, Razi Hospital, Manouba, Tunisia | 10Faculty of Medicine of Tunis, Tunis El Manar University, Tunis, Tunisia | 11Applied Science Research Center, Applied Science Private University, Amman, Jordan Correspondence: Souheil Hallit (souheilhallit@usek.edu.lb) | Feten Fekih‐Romdhane (feten.fekih@gmail.com) Received: 27 January 2026 | Revised: 3 May 2026 | Accepted: 18 May 2026 Keywords: adult ADHD | Arabic | ASRS | Lebanon | psychometric validation | screener ABSTRACT Background: In the Middle East and North Africa, there is a dearth of research on Adult Attention‐Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). Offering a brief, publicly available, and psychometrically valid screening instrument for adult ADHD that can be easily used in large‐scale surveys among Arabic‐speaking populations could encourage research and facilitate case detection. The purpose of this study was to translate the Adult ADHD Self‐Report Scale v1.1 6‐Question Screener (ASRS‐6) into Arabic and assess its psychometric properties among a sample of Lebanese adults from the general population. Methods: A cross‐sectional study was conducted between April and May 2025 using an online survey distributed via a mixed convenience and snowball sampling. A total of 1059 Lebanese adults participated (mean age = 28.52 ± 11.41 years; 66.0% fe males). The questionnaire included the Arabic ASRS‐6, the validated Arabic versions of the Stress Numerical Rating Scale‐11, the Patient Health Questionnaire, and the World Health Organization‐Five Well‐Being Index. The total sample was randomly divided into two split‐half subsamples, one for the exploratory (EFA) and the second for the confirmatory (CFA) factor analysis. Results: The EFA and CFA supported the one factor structure, which showed acceptable fit indices. A correlation was added between residuals of items 5 and 6, which improved the model fit and was consequently used in the analysis. A Cronbach's alpha of 0.68 indicated acceptable internal consistency. A significantly higher ASRS‐6 mean scores was found in females versus males (10.85 ± 3.98 vs 10.22 ± 4.09; t (1057) = −2.41, p = 0.009, Cohen's d = 0.157). A significantly higher ASRS‐6 mean score was found in single participants compared to married ones (10.84 ± 3.95 vs 10.19 ± 4.16; t (1057) = 2.46, p = 0.014, Cohen's d = 0.163). However, no significant difference was found between participants with a secondary level of education or less compared to those with a university education level in terms of ASRS‐6 scores (10.20 ± 4.32 vs 10.73 ± 3.95; t (1057) = −1.68, p = 0.094, Cohen's d = 0.131). Higher ASRS‐6 scores were significantly associated with higher depression (r = 0.33; p < 0.001), anxiety (r = 0.33; p < 0.001), stress (r = 0.30; p < 0.001), and lower well‐being scores (r = −0.38; p < 0.001). Conclusion: The results provide initial support for applying the Arabic version of the ASRS‐6 screener in community epide miological surveys, clinical outreach, and case‐finding initiatives. However, additional work is needed to approve its validity and expand its use in different Arab nations. 1 | Introduction Attention‐Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) characterized by disruptive symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity‐ impulsivity, is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with a multifactorial etiology involving genetic and environmental factors (Assaf et al. 2024). It is typically identified in early school years and one of the most prevalent childhood disorders, but it may also endure into adolescence and adulthood. The global prevalence of ADHD in children is estimated at 5%, while persistent adult ADHD (with a childhood onset) is around 2.58%, and symptomatic adult ADHD (regardless of its onset during childhood) is 6.76%, signifying important public health burden (Song et al. 2021). Depending on the predominant symptoms, ADHD is divided into three presentations: predom inantly inattentive (ADHD‐I), predominantly hyperactive‐ impulsive (ADHD‐HI), and combined (ADHD‐C) (Magnus et al. 2025). The clinical presentation of ADHD changes over time; compared to children with the condition, adults are less likely to be hyperactive‐impulsive and more likely to experience inattention. As overt hyperactive‐impulsive symptoms abate with time, the remaining inattentive symptoms can be masked by compensatory strategies, making ADHD symptoms less noticeable in adults and contributing to missed or delayed diagnosis (Rivas‐Vazquez et al. 2023). Notably, of the three ADHD subtypes, the predominantly inattentive subtype is the most common among adults (Ayano et al. 2023). Furthermore, while the existence of ADHD symptoms before the age of 12 is required to establish a diagnosis as per the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (DSM‐5) (Magnus et al. 2025), observations in which some adults met the criteria for ADHD with no childhood history of the disorder suggest that there may be a variant of adult ADHD that is not a continuance of a childhood ADHD, challenging the theory of a merely neurodevelopmental origin (Caye et al. 2016; Moffitt et al. 2015). However, the validity of late‐onset or adult (first)‐ onset ADHD remains highly debated (Hutt Vater et al. 2024; Waltereit et al. 2023). Adults with ADHD often face educational and career under achievement. Their symptoms may also strain relationships with work colleagues, family members, friends, and partners. Moreover, ADHD is linked to higher rates of delinquency, imprisonment, and substance use disorder. Patients are also prone to driving‐related dangers, such as collisions, speeding, and traffic violations. Overall, ADHD can interfere with almost every facet of adult life, particularly if it remains undiagnosed, untreated, or ineffectively managed (Ginsberg et al. 2014). Adult ADHD remains under‐detected, despite the high prevalence, particular clinical presentation, and potential negative conse quences leaving these individuals susceptible to impairments in many aspects of their lives and at risk for poor mental health outcomes, including stress, anxiety, and depression (Garcia‐ Argibay et al. 2024; Ogrodnik et al. 2023; Rivas‐Vazquez et al. 2023). In the absence of confirmed biomarkers, the diagnosis of ADHD is established clinically through a multi‐step process that may include a detailed clinical interview considering personal and family history, self‐report behavior rating scales identifying the presence of characteristic symptoms, observer reports from family and employers, and continuous performance tests eval uating impairments in attention and impulse control (Cabral et al. 2020). While these tools collectively provide comprehen sive information for an ADHD diagnosis, the process is time‐ intensive and resource‐demanding. A screening tool is easy to administer, quicker, and less expensive than a full diagnostic assessment and thus can be offered to a wide population. While it cannot establish a definitive diagnosis of a condition, it can be considered a form of triage that helps flag individuals who are more likely to have a condition and require referral to in‐depth evaluation (Newlove‐Delgado and Ford 2020). To provide a screening tool for ADHD in adults in the general population, the World Health Organization (WHO) developed the Adult ADHD Self‐ Report Scale version 1.1 (ASRS) based on DSM‐IV criteria (Kessler et al. 2005). There are two versions for the ASRS: a full version with 18 questions divided into two main symptom domains—9 assessing inattention, 9 assessing hyperactivity‐ impulsivity, and a shorter 6‐question version (ASRS‐6) (Kess ler et al. 2005). The ASRS‐6 proved superior sensitivity (68.7%v.56.3%), specificity (99.5%v.98.3%), total classification accuracy (97.9% v.96.2%), and Cohen's kappa (0.76 v.0.58) than the full version (Kessler et al. 2005). After being translated and validated in several languages (including Spanish, Turkish, Hungarian, and Swedish) in clinical and non‐clinical samples, the ASRS‐6 proved to be a psychometrically reliable and valid measure for adult ADHD screening (Daigre et al. 2009; Evren et al. 2016; Farcas et al. 2018; von Wallenberg Pachaly et al. 2024). The 6‐item version encompasses four items retrieved from the inattention domain of the full ASRS and two items from the hyperactivity‐impulsivity domain (Kessler et al. 2005). Validation studies of the ASRS‐6 have reported heterogeneous findings regarding its dimensionality, with some supporting a unidimensional structure (Green et al. 2018; Kessler et al. 2007; von Wallenberg Pachaly et al. 2024) and others favoring a two‐ factor model reflecting inattention and hyperactivity‐impulsivity (Carlucci et al. 2017; Daigre et al. 2009; Farcas et al. 2018; Hesse 2013; Panagiotidi et al. 2023), depending on the popula tion and context. Several studies across diverse samples have supported a two‐factor structure. For example, in an adult 2 of 11 International Journal of Methods in Psychiatric Research, 2026 15570657, 2026, 2, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mpr.70083 by Stony Brook University Libraries, Wiley Online Library on [21/10/2026]. Hungarian general community sample (N = 567), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported a two‐factor model with acceptable internal consistency (Total α = 0.72; inattention α = 0.77; hyperactivity α = 0.54) (Farcas et al. 2018). Similarly, among Spanish outpatients with substance use disorders (N = 80), exploratory factor analysis with Varimax rotation identified two factors explaining 67.7% of the variance, with Cronbach's α of 0.82 for inattention and 0.52 for hyperactivity (Daigre et al. 2009). In a Turkish inpatient sample with alcohol use disorder (N = 190), principal component analysis (PCA) revealed two components accounting for 38.64% and 18.08% of the variance (Evren et al. 2016). Likewise, in a Canadian clinical sample of adults with eating disorders (N = 500), exploratory factor analysis followed by CFA confirmed a two‐factor solution, with factor 1 (inattention) explaining 49.51% of the variance and factor 2 (hyperactivity‐impulsivity) 19.98%, and internal con sistency estimates of α = 0.83 (inattention), α = 0.63 (hyperac tivity), and α = 0.78 (total) (Carlucci et al. 2017). In contrast, other studies have supported a unidimensional structure. In a large U.S. adolescent community sample (N = 2472), one‐factor CFA demonstrated good fit and internal consistency (α = 0.80), with invariance across gender (Green et al. 2018). Similarly, in a Swedish psychiatric sample of young adults with ADHD and/or borderline personality disorder and/or bipolar disorder (N = 151), CFA supported a one‐factor model with acceptable internal consistency (α = 0.74) (von Wallenberg Pachaly et al. 2024). The variability in factorial validity and reliability across cultural and clinical contexts, underscores the impor tance of conducting context‐specific psychometric evaluations when adapting screening tools such as the ASRS‐6 for use in new linguistic and cultural settings. Despite being used in a few studies involving Arabic‐speaking populations such as Egypt (Abd El‐Hay and El Sawy 2011; Khalil et al. 2016), Iraq (Ashor 2012), and Lebanon (Farchakh et al. 2022), to the best of our knowledge, neither the factor structure of the Arabic version of the ASRS‐6 screener had not been tested, nor its psychometric properties have not been evaluated. The very few studies focusing on the topic showed that adult ADHD is prevalent in the Arab World, is highly co morbid with other mental health problems, and associated with significant impairment (Abd El‐Hay and El Sawy 2011; Ashor 2012; Farchakh et al. 2022; Hayek et al. 2019; Khalil et al. 2016). Yet, it continues to be largely under‐researched and undertreated throughout the Middle East and North Africa (Hayek et al. 2019). Providing a practical and psychometrically valid screening instrument for detecting potential adult ADHD cases from the general Arabic‐speaking populations could pro mote research in this area, assist healthcare professionals in guiding referrals, and facilitate detection, which can reduce the burden of untreated ADHD‐related impairments and improve quality of life. Furthermore, normalizing ADHD assessment in the general population could help reduce stigma and encour ages people to seek help (Younes et al. 2024). To address the absence of a validated tool for ADHD screening in Arabic‐ speaking populations, this study aimed to: (1) examine the factor structure of the Arabic ASRS‐6 using exploratory factor analysis followed by confirmatory factor analysis in a sample of Lebanese adults from the general population, and (2) assess the internal consistency, sex invariance, and concurrent validity of the screener. We hypothesized that the ASRS‐6 would demonstrate acceptable reliability and validity, and invariance across gender. 2 | Methods 2.1 | Data Collection and Sampling Procedure This cross‐sectional study recruited 1059 participants between April and May 2025 using a mixed convenience and snowball sampling approach. The mean age of the participants was 28.52 years and 66.0% were females. Other descriptive statistics of the sample can be found in Table 1. Participants were recruited through a Google Forms survey distributed via social media platforms. The research team first shared the survey link with possible respondents, who were then encouraged to for ward it within their networks to other eligible individuals. Prior to filling the questionnaire, the participants provided digitally their consent. Inclusion criteria included Lebanese nationality, age ≥18 years, ability to read Arabic, access to the internet, and willingness to participate. Individuals reporting a prior psychi atric diagnosis by a psychiatrist were excluded. The participa tion in the study was voluntary and unremunerated. 2.2 | Ethic Statement The Lebanese International University's School of Pharmacy ethics committee granted this study ethics permission (2025ERC‐013‐LIUSOP). A written informed consent was ob tained from each participant when completing the online form. All methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations (in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki). 2.3 | Minimal Sample Size Calculation A minimum of 60 and 120 participants was required to conduct the exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses respectively, as per the recommendation of using 10 and 20 times (Comrey and Lee 2013) the number of scale variables to calculate the sample size for factor analysis, and considering the 6‐question ASRS screener. 2.4 | Instruments The questionnaire was prepared in Arabic, Lebanon's official language. It included socio‐demographic data, the Adult ADHD Self‐Report Scale Version 1.1 6‐Question Screener, and three additional scales to assess concurrent validity. It commenced with an introduction describing the study's purpose and comprised an online consent form to secure voluntary partici pation and ensure confidentiality and anonymity. The socio‐ demographic segment retrieved information regarding age, sex, marital status, and education level. The four self‐ administered scales are described as follows: Adult ADHD Self‐Report Scale Version 1.1 6‐Question Screener (ASRS‐6) (Kessler et al. 2005): It is a subset of the WHO's 18‐ question Adult ADHD Self‐Report Scale v1.1 based on DSM‐ IV criteria. It evaluates how often symptoms have arisen over the past 6 months on a 0–4 scale: never (0), rarely (1), some times (2), often (3), and very often (4). The total score, obtained by summing the points, ranges from 0 to 24, with a cut point of International Journal of Methods in Psychiatric Research, 2026 3 of 11 15570657, 2026, 2, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mpr.70083 by Stony Brook University Libraries, Wiley Online Library on [21/10/2026]. 14 or higher indicating a positive ADHD screening. Scores are categorized into four‐stratum: low negative (0–9), high negative (10–13), low positive (14–17), and high positive (18–24) (Har vard Department of Health Care Policy 2024). The 6‐question screener has been translated into a number of languages, including Arabic, using the standard WHO translation and back‐translation protocol through an unrestricted educational grant from the Eli Lilly Company (HARVARD MEDICAL SCHOOL DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH CARE POLICY). The translations are available on the official website from which the Arabic version used in this study was retrieved (https://www. hcp.med.harvard.edu/ncs/asrs.php). The Cronbach's alpha in this study was 0.68. Stress Numerical Rating Scale‐11 (SNRS‐11) (Karvounides et al. 2016): Validated in Arabic (Obeid, Hallit, et al. 2024a), the SNRS‐11 is a single‐item scale that asks participants to respond to the question, “On a scale of 0–10, with 0 being no stress and 10 being worst stress possible, what number best describes your level of stress right now?”. Responses are classified as follows: no stress (0), mild stress (1–3), moderate stress (4–7), and severe stress (8–10). Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ‐4) (Kroenke et al. 2009): Validated in Arabic (Obeid, Hemade, et al. 2024b), the PHQ‐4 is an ultra‐brief four‐item scale designed to assess symptoms of anxiety and depression experienced over the past 2 weeks. Each of its two subscales (anxiety and depression) possesses two items. Answers are rated on a four‐point scale: 0 (“Not at all”), 1 (“Several days”), 2 (“More than half the days”), and 3 (“Nearly every day”). Each subscale yields a score ranging from 0 to 6. Scores of ≥3 on the respective subscales indicate relevant symptoms of anxiety or depression. The Cronbach's alpha in this study was 0.75. The World Health Organization‐Five Well‐Being Index (WHO‐5) (World Health Organization 2024): Validated across six Arab countries (Fekih‐Romdhane et al. 2023), the WHO‐5 assesses subjective psychological well‐being through five positively phrased items. Each item is rated on a five‐point Likert scale ranging from 0 (At no time) to 5 (All of the time), based on how the respondent felt during the past 2‐week period. The total score ranges from 0 to 25 and can be multiplied by 4 to yield a percentage score ranging from 0 (worst possible mental well‐ being) to 100 (best possible mental well‐being). A percentage score below 50 (or a raw score below 13) has been suggested as a cut‐off for poor mental well‐being (Topp et al. 2015; World Health Organization (WHO) 2024). The Cronbach's alpha in this study was 0.90. 2.5 | Analytic Strategy The total sample was randomly divided into two split‐half subsamples using the SPSS option. The first split‐half sample was analyzed using principal‐axis exploratory factor analysis (EFA) within R software (The R Core Team 2026). Following the recommendations of (Hair et al. 2009), the suitability of the data for factor analysis was evaluated using the Kaiser‐Meyer‐ Olkin (KMO) index of sampling adequacy and Bartlett's sphe ricity (expected to be significant). Principal‐axis factoring was selected because it provides results comparable to maximum likelihood estimation while not requiring multivariate normality (Goretzko et al. 2021). Given the hypothesized pres ence of a single orthogonal factor, quartimax rotation was employed (Pedhazur and Schmelkin 2013). We conducted a CFA via the lavaan (Rosseel 2012), semTools (Jorgensen et al. 2018) with R software on the second subsam ple. Multiple fit indices were calculated: root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) (≤0.08), standardized root mean square residual (SRMR) (≤0.05), Tucker‐Lewis Index (TLI) and Comparative Fit Index (CFI) (≥0.90 for both) (Hu and Ben tler 1999). Additionally, the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) were calculated for model comparisons. A difference < 2 between AIC and BIC values indicated that both models were acceptable, whereas a difference > 10 favored the model with the lower value (Burnham and Anderson 2004). Multivariate normality was not verified as shown by the Mardia skewness (167.59; p < 0.001) and kurtosis (8.67; p < 0.001) values, so parameter estimates TABLE 1 | Sociodemographic characteristics of the sample (N = 1059). were obtained using the robust maximum likelihood method. A multi‐group CFA was conducted to examine measurement invariance of the ASRS‐6 screener scores between sexes (Chen 2007) at the configural, metric, and scalar levels (Van denberg and Lance 2000). ΔCFI ≤0.010 and ΔRMSEA ≤0.015 or ΔSRMR ≤0.010 supported the evidence of invariance (Swami et al. 2022). Comparison of ASRS‐6 scores between sexes was done using the independent samples t test. Internal consistency was assessed using McDonald's ω and Cronbach's α, with values greater than 0.70 reflecting adequate internal consistency (Dunn et al. 2014). The association between the ASRS‐6 scores and other scores was evaluated using the Pearson correlation test. 3 | Results In total, 1059 individuals participated in this study, with a mean age of 28.52 years and 66.0% females. Other descriptive statistics of the sample can be found in Table 1. The categorical distributions of ADHD screening and psycho logical measures, along with the corresponding mean scores, are presented in Table 2. Among the participants, 229 (21.6%) par ticipants screened positive for ADHD. Moreover, 575 (54.3%) and 279 (26.3%) had moderate and severe stress, 488 (46.1%) had anxiety symptoms, 501 (47.3%) had depressive symptoms, and 381 (36.0%) had poor mental well‐being. 3.1 | Exploratory Factor Analysis Data from the first split‐half subsample (n = 528) were subjected to principal‐axis exploratory factor analysis. The Kaiser‐Meyer‐ Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy was acceptable (KMO = 0.76), and Bartlett's test of sphericity was significant (χ2 (15) = 418.23, p < 0.001), indicating that the data were suitable for factor analysis. Inspection of the scree plot (Figure 1) and results from parallel analysis suggested a two‐factor solution. However, the second factor accounted for only a small proportion of vari ance (4%) and did not demonstrate a meaningful pattern of loadings, with most items loading primarily on the first factor. Therefore, the two‐factor solution lacked interpretability. Given that a one‐factor solution was retained, rotation was not necessary as it does not affect single‐factor models. All items demonstrated sampling adequacy (MSA > 0.70), supporting their retention. Consequently, in line with theoretical expectations, a one‐factor solution was retained. This model showed acceptable model fit χ2 (9) = 30.29, p < 0.001; χ2/df = 3.37; RMSEA = 0.067, 90%CI [0.042, 0.094]; TLI 0.91; RMSR = 0.040. Factor loadings ranged from 0.35 to 0.64, with all items exceeding the recommended threshold of 0.33. Communalities ranged from 0.12 to 0.41, indicating moderate item representation by the latent factor. Overall, the results supported a unidimensional structure of the screener. A CFA was conducted on the second split‐half subsample (n = 531) to test the one‐factor model identified in the EFA. The initial one‐factor model showed an acceptable but not optimal fit to the data (χ2 (9) = 58.22, p < 0.001; CFI 0.928; TLI = 0.881; RMSEA = 0.102, 90% CI [0.08, 0.13]; SRMR = 0.051). All stan dardized factor loadings were statistically significant (p < 0.001), supporting the contribution of each item to the latent construct (Table 3). Inspection of modification indices suggested a meaningful correlated residual between ADHD5 and ADHD6 (modification index = 17.48), indicating shared variance between these two items beyond the common latent factor. Given the conceptual similarity between these items, this covariance was added to the model. The revised one‐factor CFA model including the residual covariance between items 5 and 6 demonstrated improved model fit and was retained as the final model (χ2 (8) = 31.56; CFI = 0.966; TLI = 0.936; RMSEA = 0.075, 90% CI [0.048, 0.103]; SRMR = 0.037). All standardized factor loadings remained statistically significant (p < 0.001) and ranged from 0.32 to 0.71. The standardized residual covariance between items 5 and 6 was significant (r = 0.21, p < 0.001). These findings supported the retention of the six‐item one‐factor model with a correlated residual between ADHD5 and ADHD6 as the final factorial structure of the scale. In the EFA performed on the first subsample (n = 528), the five‐ item model showed slightly poorer factorial adequacy compared to the original six‐item model. The Kaiser‐Meyer‐Olkin value decreased from 0.76 to 0.74, and Bartlett's test of sphericity was significant (χ2(10) = 367.35, p < 0.001), indicating that the data were suitable for factor analysis. Inspection of the scree plot and parallel analysis again suggested a two‐factor solution; however, the first factor was clearly dominant and the second factor lacked theoretical interpretability. Therefore, a one‐factor solu tion was retained. The one‐factor model showed slightly poorer fit compared to the original six‐item model (χ2(5) = 25.47, p < 0.001; χ2/df = 5.09; TLI = 0.89; RMSEA = 0.088, 90% CI [0.056, 0.123]; SRMR = 0.05; BIC = −5.88). Factor loadings ranged from 0.49 to 0.65, with all items exceeding the recommended threshold of 0.33. Overall, although all remaining items loaded adequately, the factorial structure was less satisfactory than that observed for the six‐item model. A CFA was subsequently conducted on the second split‐half subsample (n = 531) to test the one‐factor five‐item model. The model showed slightly improved fit indices compared to the initial six‐item CFA model (χ2(5) = 28.78, p < 0.001; CFI = 0.96; TLI = 0.92; RMSEA = 0.095, 90% CI [0.063, 0.130]; SRMR = 0.041). All standardized factor loadings were statisti cally significant (p < 0.001) (Table 4). Internal consistency remained borderline, with Cronbach's alpha = 0.68 and McDonald's Omega = 0.68. In contrast, the poorer EFA fit and reduced conceptual coverage argued against removing item 6. The six‐item model also demonstrated a lower BIC value compared to the five‐item model, further supporting the retention of the original facto rial structure. Therefore, item 6 was retained to preserve the factorial integrity and conceptual completeness of the scale. Overall, the six‐item one‐factor model with a correlated residual between ADHD5 and ADHD6 was retained as the final and most theoretically appropriate structure of the scale. 3.3 | Sex Invariance Full configural and metric invariances were supported in the one‐factor model, with fit indices falling within the acceptable ranges (Table 5). However, full scalar invariance was not sup ported, as indicated by substantial declines in model fit (ΔCFI = 0.113 and ΔRMSEA = 0.066). To try to achieve some level of scalar invariance, partial invariance was evaluated by allowing the intercepts of non‐invariant items to vary while constraining the rest. Acceptable model‐fit indices were then achieved (ΔCFI = 0.057 and ΔRMSEA = 0.034), confirming partial scalar invariance and indicating that comparisons of mean scores across sexes would be acceptable using this in strument. A significantly higher ASRS‐6 mean scores was found in females versus males (10.85 ± 3.98 vs 10.22 ± 4.09; t (1057) = −2.41, p = 0.009, Cohen's d = 0.157). In terms of percentages, no significant difference was found between the females who screened positive for ADHD compared to males (n = 163 (23.3%) versus n = 66 (18.3%), X2 = 3.49, p = 0.070, Effect size = 0.062). Moreover, a significantly higher ASRS‐6 mean score was found in single participants compared to mar ried ones (10.84 ± 3.95 vs 10.19 ± 4.16; t (1057) = 2.46, p = 0.014, Cohen's d = 0.163). However, no significant differ ence was found between participants with a secondary level of education or less compared to those with a university education level in terms of ASRS‐6 scores (10.20 ± 4.32 vs 10.73 ± 3.95; t (1057) = −1.68, p = 0.094, Cohen's d = 0.131). 3.4 | Concurrent Validity Higher ASRS‐6 scores were significantly associated with higher depression (r = 0.33; p < 0.001), anxiety (r = 0.33; p < 0.001), stress (r = 0.30; p < 0.001), and lower well‐being scores (r = −0.38; p < 0.001) (Table 6). 4 | Discussion This study aimed to assess the factor structure and other psy chometric properties of the Arabic translation of the Adult ADHD Self‐Report Scale v1.1 6‐Question screener among Arabic‐speaking adults from the general population of Lebanon. The results may suggest a one factorial structure based on EFA and CFA, with adequate internal consistency, partial sex invariance, and evidence supporting its concurrent validity. Overall, the findings could provide initial evidence in favor of utilizing the Arabic version of this instrument for adult ADHD screening. Of the 1059 participants, 229 (21.6%) screened positive for ADHD using the ASRS‐6. Comparisons are not possible because, as far as we are, no prior epidemiological studies in Lebanon have estimated the prevalence of adult ADHD (Assaf et al. 2024). However, a positive result does not confirm ADHD despite the screener strong concordance with clinician di agnoses (Kessler et al. 2007). Individuals screened positive should undergo a psychiatric evaluation; it is essential to emphasize that a screening instrument only serves as a guiding tool and cannot substitute a comprehensive clinical assessment to establish a diagnosis. In terms of factor structure, the EFA results supported a uni factorial structure for the screener which was confirmed by CFA. Similar to our findings, some studies reported a unidi mensional structure, including a study on a sample of sub scribers to a large health plan in the US (Kessler et al. 2007), a study on a US adolescent community sample (Green et al. 2018), and another on a Swedish patient sample with ADHD and/or borderline personality disorder, and/or bipolar disorder (von Wallenberg Pachaly et al. 2024). Kessler et al. explained that the absence of a second factor in the ASRS‐6 could be a joint function of the limited number of items and the strong in tercorrelations between inattention and hyperactivity‐ impulsivity symptoms; even though the symptoms of ADHD are known to be two‐dimensional, they can be captured by a single underlying dimension whereas ADHD as a disorder in cludes both types of symptoms (Kessler et al. 2007). conducted with various populations, including Hungarian adults from the general community (Farcas et al. 2018), Spanish patients with substance use disorders (SUD) (Daigre et al. 2009), a Danish sample of university students, and another sample of patients with SUD (Hesse 2013), a Turkish sample of inpatients with alcohol use disorder (Evren et al. 2016), and a Canadian clinical sample with eating disorders (Carlucci et al. 2017). The two‐factor model aligns with the theoretical and diagnostic frameworks of ADHD, which conceptualize the disorder as two dimensions of inattention and hyperactivity‐impulsivity symp toms that are used to define its three subtypes: ADHD‐I, ADHD‐ HI, and ADHD‐C (Administration and Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services 2016). These discrepancies in factor structures may be partly explained by differences in sample characteristics and study settings. Studies supporting a two‐ factor structure have often been conducted in clinical pop ulations e.g., substance use or eating disorder samples (Carlucci et al. 2017; Daigre et al. 2009; Evren et al. 2016; Hesse 2013), where symptom differentiation may be more pronounced. In contrast, unidimensional solutions are more frequently observed in large community‐based samples (Green et al. 2018; Kessler et al. 2007), where symptom severity is lower and di mensions may be less distinct (Niina et al. 2022). The internal consistency of the ASRS‐6 was adequate for the total score (ω = 0.68, α = 0.68) supporting its reliability as a unidimensional screening measure. This estimate is comparable to those reported in previous studies (e.g., α = 0.72 in (Farcas et al. 2018); α = 0.78 in (Carlucci et al. 2017).), and is in line with expectations for brief scales, as reliability coefficients are sen sitive to the number of items (Tavakol and Dennick 2011). Sex invariance examines whether an instrument is interpreted equivalently by males and females. For both models of the ASRS‐6, full configural and metric invariance were established. However, partial invariance was established at the scalar level, suggesting that although some items function differently across genders, the overall latent construct remains comparable, allowing comparisons of latent mean differences (Putnick and Bornstein 2016). In the current study, ADHD positive screening rates were comparable between males and females. In a review by Faheem et al. (2022) on sex‐based differences in the preva lence of ADHD in adults, 8 out of 20 studies reported an equal prevalence among males and females, with one study indicating a higher prevalence in females (male‐to‐female ratio 2:3). In contrast, the remaining 11 studies found a higher prevalence in males, with male‐to‐female ratios ranging from 1.5:1 to 3:1 (Faheem et al. 2022). Despite increasing research on sex dif ferences in ADHD, little is known about differences in its prevalence by sex in adults, and there remains a dearth of re views limiting the ability to draw firm conclusions. Regarding the assessment of concurrent validity, it was sup ported by significant positive correlations between ASRS‐6 scores and measures of depression, anxiety, and stress, as well as negative correlations with mental well‐being scores. These findings showed the expected patterns of correlations between ASRS‐6 scores and the study variables and are, therefore, consistent with existing literature. Within the internalizing domain, anxiety disorders are the most commonly comorbid with ADHD and are associated with worse clinical presentation (e.g., lower level of education, suicidal attempt, higher rate of hospitalization) (Quenneville et al. 2022; Ryan et al. 2023). Anxiety may arise as a consequence of ADHD due to appre hension stemming from past failures. Additionally, ADHD and anxiety disorders share common neurobiological dysfunctions (D'Agati et al. 2019; Ryan et al. 2023). ADHD symptoms could elicit stressful environments, such as failures in work and re lationships, which in turn increase the risk of depression (Knouse et al. 2013; Panevska et al. 2015). Shared genetic factors can also account for the co‐occurrence of ADHD and depression (Powell et al. 2021; Riglin et al. 2021). 4.1 | Limitations We advise interpreting the results cautiously, taking into thought the following limitations, until these results are repli cated. First, a non‐random sample may have occurred due to the snowball sampling technique, which may have limited the sample's representativeness to the wider Lebanese adult popu lation. Second, while self‐report measures speed up data collection, they are vulnerable to interpretation and response bias. Third, the analysis was limited to finding correlations be tween the measured variables because this study was conducted at a single time, restricting its ability to establish causal re lationships. Additionally, our study did not employ clinical as sessments to confirm the presence of adult ADHD, given that it was an online, anonymous, cross‐sectional survey. While it would have been ideal, conducting clinician assessments in a large community sample would have been costly. Nevertheless, we recognize the importance of validating the Arabic version of the ASRS‐6 against a gold‐standard ADHD diagnosis for future research contributions. In addition, other aspects of validity were not assessed in this study. Convergent validity with ADHD‐specific instruments, known‐groups validity, and diag nostic accuracy (e.g., ROC analysis and optimal cut‐off deter mination) could not be evaluated as the collected data in this study did not include appropriate comparator measures and clinical diagnostic data required for such analyses. Furthermore, test–retest reliability was not examined. Future research should address these limitations to strengthen the psychometric eval uation of the ASRS‐6 and enhance confidence in its temporal stability. Finally, the validation of the Arabic version was limited to a sample of Lebanese adults, which may not represent the entire Arab world, necessitating further studies to confirm its validity across various Arab countries. 4.2 | Practical Implications Despite these limitations and the need for further research, this study may provide initial evidence for the reliability and validity of the Arabic version of the ASRS‐6. Such a screener, by facili tating data collection on adult ADHD prevalence and correlates, could increase epidemiological research within Arabic‐speaking nations. Moreover, it represents a valuable tool for clinical outreach and case‐finding initiatives in academic settings, workplaces, and primary care due to its ease of self‐ administration and speed (in less than 2 minutes) (Kessler et al. 2007). Widespread screening may facilitate the detection of ADHD cases, enabling timely interventions that reduce un treated ADHD‐related impairments, ultimately enhancing pro ductivity and quality of life. contribute to raised awareness and lesson misconceptions about ADHD, particularly within Arabic‐speaking communities where mental health issues are often stigmatized (Younes et al. 2024). Such efforts may foster a more informed and accepting perspective on ADHD, encouraging individuals to seek profes sional assistance. 5 | Conclusion According to the preliminary findings, the Arabic version of the ASRS‐6 seems valid for screening adult ADHD in the general population. However, to confirm its validity, assess additional psychometric properties, and validate it across other Arab na tions to improve its applicability, further research is needed. The availability of such a brief, free, and easy‐to‐administer screener is a significant step toward advancing ADHD epidemiological research and case‐finding initiatives in Arabic‐speaking pop ulations. A comprehensive clinical evaluation should be per formed on those who screen positive for ADHD with this tool in order to confirm the diagnosis and rule out comorbid conditions. metadata_title: Gut Microbiome and ADHD: A Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence and Practice Implications
pages: Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics INVITED REVIEW Gut Microbiome and ADHD: A Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence and Practice Implications Kinga Sadowska | Kathryn Hart University of Surrey, Guildford, UK Correspondence: Kathryn Hart (k.hart@surrey.ac.uk) Received: 28 December 2025 | Revised: 18 July 2026 | Accepted: 22 July 2026 Keywords: ADHD | adjunctive therapy | gut microbiome | gut‐brain axis | probiotics | synbiotics ABSTRACT Objective: This narrative review evaluates the current evidence on the efficacy of probiotic interventions for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) symptoms in both medicated and drug‐naïve paediatric and adult populations and assesses the implications for clinical dietetic practice. Design: A narrative review synthesizing randomized controlled trials and observational microbiome studies in paediatric and adult populations, specifically distinguishing between probiotic monotherapy and adjunctive protocols. Results: Observational data confirm gut microbiome alterations in ADHD populations, although specific bacterial signatures vary across studies. Evidence from treatment trials demonstrates that the efficacy of probiotics as monotherapy for core ADHD symptoms remains inconclusive. However, specific adjunctive trials combining probiotics with conventional medication have reported preliminary positive findings on symptom reduction, though results remain heterogeneous. Adult evidence is sparse but indicates potential benefits for emotional dysregulation in specific contexts. Conclusions: This review concludes that current data do not support universal probiotic supplementation or routine clinical recommendation. However, when families inquire about complementary approaches, the existing literature enables evidence informed guidance within a shared decision‐making framework that acknowledges the preliminary nature of current findings and sets realistic expectations. 1 | Introduction Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental condition affecting populations across the lifespan. The disorder is characterized by persistent patterns of inattention and hyperactivity‐impulsivity that directly impact academic, occupational, and social functioning [1]. Approxi mately 8% of children and adolescents and 3%–7% of adults worldwide meet diagnostic criteria for ADHD [2–4], with in dividuals experiencing significant functional impairment across multiple life domains [1]. Current management relies primarily on stimulant medications targeting dopaminergic neurotransmission [5]. While approxi mately 60% of patients demonstrate moderate‐to‐marked symptom improvement [5], concerns regarding side effects, treatment acceptability, and access disparities persist [6]. These limitations have prompted growing interest in complementary therapeutic strategies, with families increasingly seeking nutritional and life style interventions to support standard care. Recent research has investigated the gut microbiome as a potential therapeutic target through the microbiota‐gut‐brain axis. The theoretical rationale builds on bidirectional commu nication between the gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system through neural, endocrine, immune, and metabolic pathways [7–9]. Specifically, gut microbial production of neu rotransmitter precursors, short‐chain fatty acids, and bioactive metabolites may influence the dopaminergic and inflammatory This is an open access article under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License, which permits use, distribution and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited. © 2026 The Author(s). dysregulation characteristic of ADHD pathophysiology [10–13]. Foundational studies demonstrate that specific probiotic strains can modulate central neurotransmitter receptor expression [14], with evidence showing beneficial effects on anxiety and stress‐ related outcomes [15]. Given the growing research interest in the microbiota‐gut‐ brain axis and the increasing number of families inquiring about complementary approaches, critical evaluation of the clinical evidence is warranted. This narrative review syn thesizes findings from randomized controlled trials in pae diatric and adult populations alongside observational microbiome evidence. This review distinguishes between monotherapy and adjunctive use to examine whether current data can inform dietetic practice when families seek guidance on probiotic interventions. 2 | Methods This narrative review was conducted following the SANRA (Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles) guidelines to enhance methodological transparency and quality [16]. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and Google Scholar were searched between January 2000 and October 2025, combining terms related to ADHD (“attention deficit hyperactivity disorder” OR “ADHD”), microbiome interventions (“probiotic*” OR “synbiotic*” OR “micro biome” OR “gut microbiota”). Searches were limited to peer‐ reviewed English‐language articles. Reference lists of included systematic reviews and meta‐analyses were hand‐ searched to identify additional studies. Included study designs comprised randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta‐analyses, and observational studies documenting microbiome alterations in ADHD populations. Studies were excluded if they focused solely on other neurodevelopmental conditions or involved only non‐ human subjects. To capture theoretical context for evalu ating intervention rationale, foundational studies on gut‐ brain axis mechanisms were included [7, 8] and compre hensive reviews on gut microbiota in neurodevelopmental disorders [9, 11], identified through targeted citation searching. 3 | Observational Evidence Before evaluating whether probiotics help, we need to ask: do people with ADHD actually have different gut microbiomes? If not, there would be little reason to expect microbiome‐targeted interventions to work. The evidence suggests yes, though findings are inconsistent. Evidence comes from cross‐sectional case‐control studies, lon gitudinal birth cohorts, and systematic reviews. Pediatric studies yield mixed findings. Investigations have re ported decreased [17], increased [18], or no significant differ ences [19] in gut bacterial diversity between children with ADHD and healthy controls. One study of 14 boys with ADHD found reduced bacterial variety compared to 17 controls [17]. Another, with 30 children, found higher diversity in the ADHD group [18]. A third, comparing 41 children with ADHD to 39 controls, found no differences [19]. These inconsistencies persist despite similar sequencing meth ods (16S rRNA), suggesting other factors play a role: age, sample size, diet, medication status, and geography. Never theless, several bacterial genera appear repeatedly as altered in ADHD, including Faecalibacterium [20, 21], Bifidobacterium [20, 22], Ruminococcus [23, 24], and Bacteroides [18, 21]. Longitudinal birth cohort studies offer stronger evidence by tracking children over time. The WHEALS cohort (n = 314) collected stool samples at 1 and 6 months and assessed ADHD at age 10 [25]. Of these children, 59 (18.8%) developed ADHD. At 6 months, bacterial diversity was significantly higher in children who later developed ADHD (p = 0.017), and bacterial composition differed between groups (p = 0.006). Notably, children who developed ADHD showed relative depletion of lactic acid bacteria, with 14 taxa from the order Lactobacillales underrepresented. Fungal microbiota also differed between groups at both time points. A Swedish cohort tracking 16,440 children found similar pat terns, identifying early microbiome signatures among bio markers predicting neurodevelopmental disorders [26]. These prospective studies provide the strongest observational support for a potential causal link. Adult studies show similar patterns. A meta‐analysis of four case‐control studies (312 adults with ADHD, 305 controls) found consistent alterations in gut microbiome composition, including increased Ruminococcus torques and decreased Eu bacterium xylanophilum [23]. Systematic reviews note that some taxa replicate across studies, particularly decreased Faecali bacterium prausnitzii, but methodological variation prevents definitive conclusions [20, 21, 27, 28]. Some findings point in opposite directions. Bifidobacterium appears elevated in some populations but reduced in others. Dialister is decreased in unmedicated patients but increased after treatment [28]. The studies above establish that the ADHD microbiome differs from controls, but correlation alone says nothing about how these Key Points • Current evidence does not support the use of pro biotics as a standalone treatment for core ADHD symptoms; therefore, they should not replace stan dard pharmacological care. • Preliminary findings suggest that specific probiotic strains may offer symptomatic benefits when used adjunctively with medication, though results vary by strain and individual. • Clinicians should utilize a shared decision‐making framework to help families interpret emerging evi dence, ensuring that any complementary use is safe and that expectations are realistic. 2 of 10 Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics, 2026 1365277x, 2026, 4, Downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jhn.70327 by Stony Brook University Libraries, Wiley Online Library on [21/10/2026]. differences could shape behaviour. The plausibility of microbiome‐ targeted intervention rests on the routes through which gut microbes can influence the brain. Three principal pathways are most relevant to ADHD and are described below, although they overlap rather than act independently (Figure 1) [29]. The first pathway is neural. The vagus nerve and enteric ner vous system provide direct bidirectional communication between gut and brain, and microbes can signal through this route via the production of neurotransmitters and their pre cursors to alter central neurotransmission. Several of the genera altered in ADHD contribute here. For example, Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium synthesise gamma‐aminobutyric acid (GABA) and influence the availability of tryptophan for sero tonin synthesis. Lactic‐acid‐producing genera are depleted in several paediatric cohorts [20, 25], whereas the direction for Bifidobacterium is inconsistent, with reductions in some infant cohorts but increases in adolescent and adult ADHD [28]. Most relevant to ADHD, the microbiota can also act on dopaminergic and wider catecholaminergic neurotransmission, the systems central to the disorder [9, 20, 30]; for instance, the increased Bifidobacterium abundance reported in ADHD has been asso ciated with greater microbial capacity for synthesis of a dopa mine precursor [28]. In a preclinical model, a Lactobacillus strain modified central GABA‐receptor expression and beha viour, and the effect was abolished by vagotomy [14]. The second pathway is immune. Microbial alterations and increased intestinal permeability may allow products such as lipopolysaccharide to enter the circulation, promoting low‐ grade inflammation and cytokine signalling that can act on the brain [8]. Frequently reported, though not consistently repli cated across cohorts, is the depletion of the butyrate‐producing Faecalibacterium prausnitzii [20, 21], which normally supports gut‐barrier integrity and exerts anti‐inflammatory effects, alongside enrichment of taxa such as Ruminococcus that have been linked to inflammation [23, 24]. Elevated pro‐ inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL‐6, TNF‐ ) have been proposed to impair the blood‐brain barrier (BBB) and act on the pre frontal and striatal circuits implicated in ADHD [30]. In ADHD this cascade remains proposed rather than established, but it aligns with evidence implicating inflammation in the dis order [13]. The last pathway is metabolic. Bacterial fermentation produces short‐chain fatty acids (SCFAs), principally butyrate, propio nate, and acetate, which signal along the axis and influence microglia, the blood‐brain barrier, and neurotransmission [10]. Beyond crossing the blood‐brain barrier, SCFAs activate free fatty acid receptors on enteroendocrine cells, modulating gut‐ hormone release and hypothalamic‐pituitary‐adrenal (HPA) axis activity [31]. Notably, lower faecal SCFA concentrations have been reported in psychostimulant‐medicated than in un medicated children with ADHD [32], linking this pathway to the medication‐status differences discussed later. The micro biota also shapes tryptophan metabolism, shifting it toward either the serotonin or the kynurenine route [33]. Both systems are implicated in ADHD [9]. These three pathways do not operate in isolation but form an interconnected network. For example, SCFA deficiency simul taneously compromises BBB integrity (metabolite pathway), reduces anti‐inflammatory signaling (immune pathway), and alters vagal afferent signaling (neural pathway). Similarly, dysbiosis‐driven inflammation can impair vagal tone, which in turn worsens gut barrier function [29, 30]. It is important to FIGURE 1 | Three principal pathways of the microbiota‐gut‐brain axis implicated in ADHD. Neural: vagus nerve and enteric nervous system signalling modulates central GABA, serotonin, and dopaminergic systems [9, 14]. Immune: increased intestinal permeability and microbial products (e.g., lipopolysaccharide) drive low‐grade inflammation and cytokine signalling [8, 13]. Metabolic: bacterial short‐chain fatty acids and microbially shaped tryptophan metabolism influence microglia, the blood‐brain barrier, and neurotransmission [10, 33]. The pathways overlap rather than act independently [29].
