7 of 9 Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, 2026 previous studies showing that MVPA was positively related to sleep among adolescents with ADHD [40] and more than 60 min per PA intervention significantly improved sleep in children and adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders [35], our results strengthen earlier findings that PA programs with MVPA inten sity may have beneficial effects on improving sleep problems in children with ADHD [18]. Among our participants, 68.8% met the WHO-recommended 60 min of MVPA guidelines. Children with ADHD who attain the MVPA guideline show better sleep quality than those who do not meet the MVPA guideline, exhib iting shorter sleep latency and WASO, higher sleep efficiency, and longer total sleep time. These findings highlight the impor tance of promoting sleep quality in children with ADHD. Overall, we found that children with ADHD engaged in an aver age of 75.35 min of MVPA per day in the current study. It was noted that previous findings on accelerometer-measured MVPA on chil dren with ADHD are mixed in different regions, such as Taiwan (51.75 min/day) [15], Germany (38.47 min/day) [11], the USA (23.5 mins/day) [41], and Mainland China (79.06 mins/day) [14]. Thus, disparities in MVPA among children with ADHD warrant fur ther investigation concerning potential sample characteristics or cultural factors. The 2020 WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviors recommended that MVPA can improve impaired cognition, including attention, executive function, and social disorders in children with ADHD [20]. Longitudinal stud ies identifying the daily MVPA threshold are much needed for children with ADHD to uphold healthy behaviors. The key finding of this study was that MVPA at 8 h before bed time was negatively related to sleep latency and WASO and pos itively associated with sleep efficiency. Consistent with a recent randomized controlled trial (RCT), a 12-week morning jogging intervention significantly improved sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency, and WASO in children with ADHD [19]. Furthermore, an experimental study showed that 30 min exercising at 11:00 AM daily with sun exposure significantly improved sleep quality [42]. The possible explanation is that daylight entering the retina during morning exercise triggers signals to the brain's suprachi asmatic nucleus (SCN), which functions as the body's master clock. The SCN coordinates various physiological processes, in cluding regulating the sleep–wake cycle. In response to daylight exposure, the SCN directs the pineal gland to decrease melatonin secretion. Reduced melatonin levels during the day contribute to maintaining alertness and wakefulness. Morning exercise and exposure to natural light help synchronize the body's internal clock with the external environment, strengthening the circadian rhythm. This synchronization ensures that melatonin production increases in the evening as daylight diminishes, facilitating sleep onset [43, 44]. However, the latest meta-analysis showed that morning PA intervention showed nonsignificant effects on sleep in children and adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders [35]. Due to the limited studies included in the analysis (n = 3), further evidence is required to elucidate the relationship between morning exercise and sleep in children with ADHD. The novel findings of this study showed that MVPA at 3 h be fore bedtime was positively correlated with WASO and nega tively related to sleep efficiency. Previous meta-analyses showed that acute evening exercise within 4 h of bedtime did not disrupt nighttime sleep in healthy young and middle-aged adults [28, 29]. This may be because exercising too close to bedtime can lead to physiological arousal, negatively impacting sleep. This arousal can manifest as a sustained increase in core body temperature, elevated heart rate, and heightened sympathetic nervous system activation. These physiological changes can interfere with falling asleep and a potential change in circadian rhythms [27, 45, 46]. For individuals with ADHD, these effects may be more pro nounced due to existing challenges in regulating autonomic functioning [47]. ADHD is often comorbid with other conditions, including sleep disorders, and disturbances in autonomic arousal can exacerbate these issues [48]. Evening exercise might further complicate the regulation of autonomic functions in individuals with ADHD, potentially leading to increased sleep difficulties. PA plays a crucial role in maintaining a healthy sleep–wake cycle and improving sleep quality, thereby promoting more restorative rest [49]. Exercise helps regulate endogenous circadian rhythms and has been shown to boost melatonin levels, particularly in children with neurodevelopmental disorders, including ADHD [35]. Melatonin deficiency is linked to sleep problems, including delayed sleep onset and early waking. Evidence suggests that tar geted PA interventions can effectively modulate melatonin secre tion in this group, thereby improving sleep quality by increasing melatonin production [50]. Therefore, it may be beneficial for in dividuals, particularly children with ADHD, to schedule exercise earlier in the day to minimize its impact on sleep. This approach can help ensure that the body has adequate time to return to a state conducive to restful sleep. To the best of our knowledge, this study was the first to explore the timing of MVPA and adherence to the MVPA guideline on sleep in children with ADHD. A primary strength of this study was using actigraphy to objectively and prospectively measure physical activity and sleep in children with ADHD in their natu ralistic environment, which was not fully considered or adopted in previous research. Nonetheless, this study had some limitations. First, we used a cross-sectional design, which limits the possibil ity of exploring the causal relationships between the timing of ex ercise and sleep in children with ADHD. Further research with an experimental design is needed to determine the best timing of exercise for improving sleep in children with ADHD. Also, a longi tudinal study design is recommended as it would enable tracking changes over time and offer stronger evidence regarding whether MVPA timing influences sleep patterns or vice versa. Second, we did not perform a clinical interview to ascertain presence of sleep disorder in the recruited participants. Further studies should consider using objective and reliable measures of sleep (e.g., poly somnography) to understand the effects of sleep in children with ADHD comprehensively. Third, controls without ADHD were not recruited for the current study. Fourthly, our study did not spe cifically examine vigorous-intensity activities in children with ADHD. Further research is recommended to investigate the dose– response relationship between daily vigorous-intensity activities and sleep, as well as other health indicators for children with ADHD [51]. Fifthly, we recognize that the compositional nature of 24-h activity data, where time allocated to sleep, physical activ ity, and sedentary behavior (screen time) sums to a fixed total, is a limitation of our study as the fixed-sum constraint can influence associations between sleep duration and MVPA. Further studies should consider exploring the relationships between 24-h activity and other health-related outcomes in children with ADHD. We employed wrist-specific cut-points developed for children with typical development, which may overestimate MVPA and potentially lead to a higher propor tion of participants being classified as meeting the guidelines. Future studies should also evaluate the impact of the chosen accel erometer cut-off points on MVPA estimation. As such, it is recommended that regular participation in MVPA, especially in the morning time slots, is beneficial for improving sleep in children with ADHD. Additionally, school-based PA in terventions during the daytime are encouraged for children with ADHD, which can help researchers explore the mechanisms un derlying exercise-induced sleep improvements and determine the optimal timing for performing MVPA to enhance sleep in children with ADHD and those with sleep disturbances. 5 | Perspective The current study provides evidence that children with ADHD who have achieved the MVPA guideline have better sleep qual ity than those who have not. Attainment of the MVPA guideline and MVPA at 8 h before bedtime are associated with improved sleep. MVPA close to bedtime is related to decreased sleep effi ciency and increased WASO. Although our study did not deter mine the direction of the causal relationship between exercise timing and sleep, the observed association emphasizes the po tential importance of MVPA at 8 h before bedtime as a key factor in improving sleep among children with ADHD. Future longi tudinal and interventional studies are needed to identify the op timal timing of exercise for sleep improvement in children with ADHD and other clinical groups, such as children with autism spectrum disorder who also face sleep disturbances. This study aimed to establish preliminary therapeutic reference ranges for methylphenidate (MPH), damphetamine (d-AMP), atomoxetine (ATX), and guanfacine (GFC), based on a systematic review of the existing relevant literature. Methods Therapeutic reference ranges were calculated based on blood concentrations measured in responder children and adolescents with ADHD. Therapeutic ranges were determined both as mean values plus one standard deviation (SD) and using the 25th/75th IQRs. The results provide preliminary recommendations that can serve as reference values for therapeutic drug monitoring in children and adolescents treated with MPH, AMP, ATX, and GFC. Review Thieme Introduction According to international guidelines [1, 2], pharmacotherapy is a key component in the treatment of attention deficit-/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in childhood and adolescence, particularly when psychoeducational or behavioural therapy interventions are ineffective or inaccessible. Available ADHD drugs include psychostimulants, such as methylphenidate (MPH) and amphetamine (AMP), and non-psychostimulant drugs, including atomoxetine (ATX), clonidine, and guanfacine (GFC). Both MPH and AMP increase intrasynaptic concentrations of dopamine and noradrenaline by inhibiting their reuptake in presynaptic neurons [3, 4]. ATX is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, [5] whereas clonidine and GFC are selective α2-adrenoceptor agonists [6]. The MPH molecule has two asymmetric C-atoms and occurs as four different stereoisomers with differing pharmacological effects. Only the racemates of d-threo-MPH (d-MPH) and l-threo-MPH (lMPH) are included in currently available MPH formulations as a 50:50 mixture [7–9]. However, the d-MPH-isomer alone is responsible for the pharmacodynamic and therapeutic effects of MPH [10]. Using enantioselective assay procedures showed that the mean maximum concentration (Cmax) of d-MPH in plasma was approximately sixfold greater than that of l-MPH [11]. MPH is available as immediate release (IR) and slow-release formulations, such as osmotic pressure-based release by osmotic controlled release delivery systems (OROS) or bi-modal release by spheroidal drug absorption systems (SODAS) (see ▶Table 1 for the pharmacokinetic (PK) properties of MPH) [12]. The AMP molecule has one asymmetric C-atom and therefore occurs as two stereoisomers with differing pharmacological effects, i. e., (R)-AMP (synonym dextro- or d-AMP) and (S)-AMP (synonym levo- or l-AMP). AMP products for the treatment of ADHD are either a 3:1 enantiomeric mixture of d- and l-AMP or d-AMP alone [13]. Clinical trials comparing d- and l-AMP in treating ADHD children have shown that l-AMP is very effective, but less so than the pharmacologically more potent d-isomer [14]. Preclinical studies have shown that d-AMP has ten times the AMP potency of the corresponding l-isomer [15]. AMP is available as immediate- and slowrelease formulations as well as the long-acting oral prodrug formulation lisdexamphetamine (see ▶Table 1 for the pharmacokinetic [PK] properties of AMP). Lisdexamphetamine, which comprises the naturally occurring amino acid l -lysine, is covalently bound to dAMP via an amide-linking group. After absorption into the bloodstream, it is metabolized by red blood cells to yield the active agent, d-AMP and l-lysine by rate-limited, enzymatic hydrolysis [16]. The time to reach peak concentrations (tmax) of psychostimulants can vary significantly among the different galenic formulations. It is usually longer in extended-release formulations and shorter in rapid-release formulations -- with the latter achieving a slightly higher Cmax -- and also varies between fasting and fed conditions. Ingestion of instant-release formulations of MPH and AMP with food, particularly a high-fat meal, can delay tmax compared to administration on an empty stomach. This delay may lead to a slightly slower onset of action. The presence of food in the stomach appears to have a lesser impact on the tmax of extended-release formulations than on instant-release formulations; however, the degree of impact varies across different formulations. ATX is metabolized through the CYP2D6 (Cytochrome P450) enzyme pathway, which is known to be genetically polymorphic in humans (poor and extensive metabolizers). This leads to high interindividual variations in plasma concentrations of ATX [17]. A study by Michelson et al. When taking similar doses of ATX, poor metabolizers experienced greater efficacy and some differences in tolerability in comparison to CYP2D6 extensive metabolizers [17]. ATX PK were similar in paediatric patients and adult subjects after adjusting for body weight [18]. Important PK properties of ATX are described in ▶Table 1. GFC and clonidine are both α2-adrenergic agonists. Though not as commonly prescribed as stimulant medications, these drugs provide an alternative, particularly in cases where stimulants are ineffective or poorly tolerated. Important PK characteristics of GFC are outlined in ▶Table 1. GFC is generally regarded as a second-line treatment for ADHD, while clonidine is used infrequently, primarily as an adjunct therapy. No significant studies on plasma levels of clonidine in children and adolescents have been identified. Consequently, this review focuses on the four most clinically relevant substances, MPH, AMP, ATX, and GFC, which are more commonly prescribed and supported by stronger evidence. Dose adjustment of ADHD medications is primarily based on clinical assessment, ideally objectified by using psychometric scales. Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM) is generally not recommended for these substances [19]. However, when clinical response to ADHD drugs with recommended doses is insufficient or in case of tolerability problems, TDM will clarify if drug concentrations in blood are as expected for the given dose. We also point out that the costs associated with TDM are relatively low, especially when compared to the potential impact on patient well-being and treatment outcomes. TDM is a well-established tool for optimizing psychopharmacotherapy by quantifying and interpreting drug concentrations in blood samples. It considers the inter-individual variability of PK and thus enables personalized pharmacotherapy. In addition, it is a measure to control drug adherence (compliance), a challenge in the pharmacotherapy of ADHD that jeopardizes the effectiveness of the pharmacological treatment. In terms of drug safety, TDM in patients with ADHD can reveal whether high drug concentrations contribute to adverse effects and inform decisions on dose reduction. Given the variability in drug metabolism, response, and tolerance among patients with ADHD, TDM can help identify individual differences in drug concentrations due to individual PK factors and guide personalized dose adjustments. If a drug does not reach therapeutic levels in the blood, dose adjustment or switching to an alternative drug should be considered for non-responders. TDM guided neuropsychopharmacotherapy mostly relies on therapeutic ranges based on minimal drug concentrations (Cmin: trough level) at steady-state [19]. Steady-state is reached under constant doses after at least four to six elimination half-lives. However, for psychostimulant drugs used in the treatment of patients with ADHD, blood has to be drawn at tmax, the time of maximum drug concentration Cmax, because most of these drugs have a short elimination half-life and clinical effects correlate with Cmax ▶Table 1. Although ADHD medications are among the most commonly prescribed pharmacological treatments for children and adolescents, blood concentrations for establishing therapeutic reference ranges have not been systematically studied to date. This systematic review focused on determining preliminary therapeutic reference ranges for MPH, AMP, ATX, and GFC in children and adolescents with ADHD [20]. Methods The protocol for systematic reviews to identify therapeutic reference ranges from Hart et al. (2021) was followed [21]. Information sources and study selection process The database MEDLINE was screened via the PubMed interface, last updated April 20th, 2023, using the following search terms: “Plasma”, “Serum”, “Pharmacokinetic”, “Methylphenidate”, “Amphetamine”, “Atomoxetine”, “Guanfacine”, and “ADHD” without applying pre-set database search filters. Two independent reviewers screened the literature according to PRISMA guidelines. After removing duplicates, manual literature screening was performed. The titles and abstracts were read, reviewed, and evaluated to select publications that corresponded to the inclusion criteria. The reference lists of the selected articles were manually reviewed to identify complementary publications. In cases where a final decision on inclusion could not be made based on the abstract alone, the full article was reviewed. To complete the research, the same keywords were applied in Google Scholar, which allowed the identification of additional publications. Inclusion and exclusion criteria No restrictions were placed regarding the publication date or study design, and both observational and interventional studies were included. The indications were limited to the treatment of paediatric patients under 18 years of age with confirmed ADHD, diagnosed according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM) or the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) criteria. Children had to be treated with therapeutic doses of the drug (see ▶Table 1). Animal or in vitro studies were excluded. Studies in which patients received concomitant psychotropic medication leading to drug-drug interactions were excluded from this review. Serum or plasma concentrations of the specific drug or enantiomer had to be measured after the intake of the respective drug dose prescribed by a specific and defined protocol. The scientific method to measure blood levels could be radioimmunoassay, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) or liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Selection of studies to evaluate therapeutic ranges To statistically define therapeutic reference ranges, studies fulfilling the inclusion and exclusion criteria described above were selected. In these studies, children or adolescents were defined as responders based on appropriate psychometric test results, such as the Conners Teaching Rating Scale, the 10-item Action-Based Cognitive Therapy Rating Scale, laboratory classroom procedures, paired associate learning, M-Mat testing, or the Swanson, Kothin, Agler, M-Flynn, and Pelham Scale (SKAMP). In addition, patients who had previously been treated with the drug in question were defined as responders under the assumption that a change in treatment would have occurred if the precedent response/control of symptoms was insufficient. Due to the high instability of methylphenidate, only studies that placed the blood samples on ice immediately after withdrawal were included in the analysis. To define a therapeutic reference range, plasma or serum levels of children and adolescents responding to the drugs were used. Qualitative and quantitative synthesis The following information was extracted from each study: lead author and publication year, responder defined yes/no, number and age of the patients, fasted/fed conditions, mean dose of drug ± SD, half-life ± SD, tmax ± SD, mean blood concentration ± SD as well as main outcomes, summarized in tables for each of the included drugs. All studies meeting the inclusion criteria are listed in the tables. However, only those studies that met the selection criteria were used to calculate therapeutic reference ranges. Statistical analysis A combined analysis was performed using Microsoft Excel to determine the therapeutic reference range of each drug. The I2 statistic was used to evaluate heterogeneity. Ninety-five percent confidence intervals were defined from mean Cmax or Cmax,ss, SD, and number of patients. Forest plots were constructed using Microsoft Excel, following the process described by Suurmond et al. (2017) [22]. We presented our results using different statistical methods: interquartile ranges (IQRs) and mean with SD, as well as 95 % confidence intervals [23]. Parametric computation methods, such as mean ± SD ranges, introduced by the AGNP Consensus Guidelines [19], assume a Gaussian distribution of drug concentrations. Consequently, IQRs of drug concentrations in the blood of responders represent effective working ranges for psychotropic drugs. This makes IQRs a more reliable measure for establishing preliminary therapeutic reference ranges, as it reflects the typical response of most patients and eliminates the influence of outliers. For studies where blood concentrations were not given in ng/ mL but sufficient data were available, we manually converted the concentrations to other units for comparison. Therapeutic reference ranges of methylphenidate A total of 27 studies measuring MPH plasma or serum levels in children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD after MPH administration were identified. The detailed results of each study are presented in ▶Table 2 [25–51]. Out of these studies, 10 [27, 37–39, 43, 45, 46, 49–51] met all selection criteria to calculate a therapeutic reference range. The reference ranges given refer to studies in which concentrations were determined using non-enantioselective methods. ▶Fig. 3A shows a forest plot and 95 % confidence intervals of MPH blood concentrations from each study, as well as the combined 95 % blood concentration interval for MPH. The latter could suggest Cmax blood levels, which should be reached after MPH administration for optimal use of the drug. With a 95 % confidence interval of 8.5–9.2 ng/ mL (Q = 522.12, P < .01, I2 = 93.49 %, τ2 = 14.49, τ = 3.81), a mean ± SD MPH concentration of 8.8 ± 7.7 ng/mL, the first reference range for MPH calculated is 1.1–16.6 ng/mL. When using the 25th and 75th IQR-method, this results in a median MPH concentration of 7.2 ng/mL and an interval of 7.2–11.3 ng/mL. Particularly noteworthy is the study by Stevens et al. (2010) [43], in which patients were treated with doses higher than the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved doses of OROS-MPH; these were generally well tolerated. No patient had a Cmax of more than 50 ng/mL or showed clinical signs of toxicity. The patients were also taking other drugs, such as lithium, bupropion, or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), but no major drug interference was observed. No associations were observed between MPH and other co-medications, and there were no serious adverse effects or cardiovascular outcomes. Therapeutic reference ranges of d-amphetamine Of the 322 studies screened for AMP, nine measured the plasma or serum levels of the drug. Key information for each study is presented in ▶Table 4 [52–60]. Of these, five studies were included to determine a therapeutic reference range for AMP [54–58]. Weighted mean Cmax concentration of d-AMP was 31.9 ng/mL with 95 % confidence interval of 30.8–32.9 ng/mL (Q = 1570.38, P < .01, I2 = 99.04 %, τ2 = 496.69, τ = 22.29) and a mean ± SD of 31.9 ± 15.2 and range of 16.6–47.1 ng/mL, as shown in ▶Fig. 3B. Using the median d-AMP concentration of 28.4 ng/mL and the 25th/75th IQR method, a reference range of 18.4–32.5 ng/mL was obtained. Therapeutic reference ranges of atomoxetine A total of 124 studies on ATX were identified. After the review, only seven met our inclusion criteria. Important information from these studies are presented in ▶Table 4 [18, 61–66]. Two studies [18, 61] were used to define the therapeutic reference range for ATX (see ▶Fig. 3C). The combined mean blood Cmax,ss concentration of ATX of these studies was 589.7 ng/mL with a 95 % confidence interval of 331.0– 848.3 ng/mL (Q = 2.06, P = 0.36, I2 = 2.93 %, τ2 = 426.00, τ = 20.64). When applying the mean ± SD method (589.7 ± 656.3), this resulted in a range of 0.0–1245.9 ng/mL. The combined median ATX concentration was 537.0 ng/mL with a 25th/75th interval of 537.0– 635.5 ng/mL. Sugimoto et al. (2021) [64] measured the trough plasma levels of ATX in children diagnosed with ADHD according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual, 5th edition (DSM-V) and the ADHD rating scale using HPLC. The measured concentration was 83.3 ± 32.3 ng/mL in seven responders (which was significantly higher than 29.5 ± 23.9 ng/mL for the non-responders). Their results suggest that a minimum effective plasma concentration of ATX is necessary to achieve sufficient clinical efficacy. However, this likely only applies to the responder group, because even when the plasma concentration was increased in the unqualified non-responder group, this did not lead to symptom improvement. Therapeutic drug monitoring of guanfacine After literature screening, only three of the 58 studies were eligible. The main characteristics of these three studies are listed in ▶Table 5 [67–69]. Only one study on GFC was conducted in responder children [69], therefore, a forest plot could not be calculated. The results of this study yielded a Cmax,ss blood concentration of 7.5 ng/mL. This concentration offers an initial reference for expected blood levels when utilizing TDM following GFC administration. Measuring GFC concentrations and comparing them with reference values may provide clinical utility in cases of unclear clinical presentations, such as confirming a diagnosis of intoxication, particularly in instances of unobserved exposure [70]. In a PK study, children showed higher plasma drug and PK parameter-related GFC concentrations compared with adolescents [67]. Another population PK study showed a decrease of 2.3 % (2.1– 2.7 %) in heart rate for every 1 ng/mL of GFC in paediatric patients [71]. Furthermore, an exposure-dependent reduction in the ADHD Rating Scale IV total score was found in Japanese paediatric ADHD patients, even for low plasma exposure levels when compared with the placebo group [68]. Discussion This systematic review investigated the TDM of four drugs used in the treatment of children and adolescents with ADHD. Preliminary therapeutic reference ranges were calculated for MPH, AMP, and ATX, which may be useful when guiding TDM in the treatment of ADHD in children and adolescents. The analysis of heterogeneity reveals considerable variability and significant heterogeneity in the presented results for MPH, AMP, and ATX, underscoring the need for careful interpretation of these findings. This high level of heterogeneity may reflect differences in study designs, patient populations, dosages, or methods used to assess clinical outcomes, highlighting the complexity of generalizing findings of drug efficacy in treating ADHD. As the scientific database for GFC is not sufficient enough to calculate a therapeutic reference range, we suggest that the mean concentration of GFC (7.5 ng/mL) measured in a single responder study be used as a preliminary reference value for TDM. However, we would also consider a preliminary therapeutic reference range for GFC of 1–17 ng/mL based on a study by Boellner et al. (2007) [67]. A study by Tsuda et al. Fourth, the validity of the analytical method used to determine drug concentrations in serum or plasma may have been limited. An analytical method is considered valid if it can measure the concentration of a substance accurately, precisely, selectively, sensitively, reproducibly, and stably. Generally, chromatographic methods, such as HPLC and LC-MS, are selective and sensitive. In two studies on AMP [52, 53], a radioimmunoassay was also used. In addition, measurements were not always performed by two independent individuals or by methods that did not exclude measurement errors. Fifth, the blood collection schemes of the included studies, which should ideally be precise and transparent, differed between studies. Additionally, blood samples containing methylphenidate should be placed on ice immediately after withdrawal due to its inherent instability. This instability presents a challenge in accurately measuring plasma concentrations in everyday clinical settings. Sixth, there was no standardized scale to define a child as being a responder. Clinical outcome measures varied, with unclear cutoffs, and some studies assessed only blood levels in responders without clinical outcomes. Additionally, differences between objective performance-based tests (laboratory math tests) and subjective behavioral assessments (Conners Rating Scale) may further impact response comparability. Seventh, the reference ranges proposed for ATX don’t differentiate between poor and extensive metabolizers, because there are not enough studies available yet. Eighth, two studies on MPH and AMP were included, even though the administered doses were higher than recommended. Stevens et al. (2010) [43] treated children with higher than FDAapproved doses (up to 170 mg) of MPH. No signs of toxicity were observed, and all plasma levels measured were under 50 ng/mL. They observed that adolescents who weighed less than 75 kg exhibited a significant beneficial response at lower doses of MAS extended-release (20–30 mg/day), while heavier adolescents required higher doses of MAS extended-release (50–60 mg/day) to achieve significant ADHD symptom control. Ninth, a significant limitation in TDM of psychostimulants, particularly racemates, is that blood concentrations reflect the total racemate without distinguishing the proportion that is pharmacologically active. The therapeutically active isomer, such as d-MPH, is often the critical component, yet the racemic mixture is typically measured. Furthermore, isomer-specific differences in metabolism can complicate the interpretation of TDM results. Tenth, for ATX, we propose a statistical therapeutic reference range with the SD method of 0.0–1245.9 ng/mL, acknowledging the significant variability in the data and the high SD. This indicates that this method may not accurately reflect the true therapeutic reference range for ATX, as the presence of values such as 0.0 ng/ mL in therapy responders raises concerns about the relevance of these measurements in relation to the medication's effectiveness. Conclusion The results of this review reveal an enormous lack of information in this field. This explains why 95 % confidence intervals are quite large. The number and quality of the studies were limited, and the overall sample size was small. We emphasize that this review is the first attempt to make ADHD drugs accessible for TDM. More research should be conducted in this field to further investigate the many co-factors that may influence our results, as mentioned in the limitations section. Nevertheless, this approach is valuable as an initial guide, and the results seem to correlate with our clinical experience. Although TDM of MPH, AMP, ATX and GFC is not a common practice, we recommend that TDM of these drugs may be helpful in cases of uncertain adherence to medication, lack of clinical improvement and adverse effects under recommended doses, abnormally high or low body weight, and problems occurring after switching from an immediate-release formulation to a long-acting formulation, vice versa, or between long-acting formulations [19]. Hopefully, more TDM studies of high quality and with larger sample sizes will be conducted in pediatric patients in the near future to adapt or confirm the preliminary therapeutic reference ranges suggested in this review. Gill 1 , 3 , †, Matthew Jerram 2 , Setari Parsa 1 , * 1Department of Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA 02215, USA 2Department of Psychology, Suffolk University, Boston, MA 02108, USA 3Department of Clinical Psychology, William James College, Newton, MA, 02459, USA *Corresponding author at: Department of Psychiatry, Neuropsychological Assessment Center, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, 185 Pilgrim Rd., Boston, MA 02215, USA. Tel.: (617) 632-0908. Email address: sparsa@bidmc.harvard.edu (S. Parsa). †Sydney Burton, Gabriela Castro and Alyssa G. Gill contributed equally to this work. ABSTRACT Objective: This cross-sectional study investigated the prevalence of adult Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) evaluations in an outpatient neuropsychology clinic and the sensitivity and specificity of neuropsychological assessments in differentiating ADHD with comorbid psychiatric conditions from psychiatric-related cognitive deficits. Method: Logistic regression analyses were run on neuropsychological testing results extracted from medical records to evaluate each test’s ability to predict ADHD diagnosis. Receiver Operating Characteristic curves were plotted, and an Area Under the Curve (AUC) >0.7 was considered acceptable. Results: Sixty-seven of 252 reviewed charts were included (n = 30 with ADHD, n = 37 without ADHD). Overall, 54% of individuals presenting to the clinic were referred for ADHD, and 58% of those diagnosed with ADHD had a comorbid psychiatric disorder. No cognitive testing was predictive of ADHD diagnosis (AUC range: 0.503–0.636). The Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 was the strongest predictive scale of ADHD (AUC = 0.800; χ 2 (28) = 8.216, p = .004, Nagelkerke R 2 = 0.333). Adults who endorsed higher levels of anxiety were 28% more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD (OR = 1.28, 95%CI [0.05, 0.45]). Subtests of ADHD scales performed worse, but still within the adequate range (AUC range: 0.703–0.751). Sample demographics were notable for over- representation of women (n = 46, 69%), and they skewed White (n = 43, 64%) and highly educated (M years of education = 15.79, SD = 1.94), which may limit generalizability. Conclusions: Cognitive testing profiles and screeners of current inattention and hyperactivity were indis- criminate between individuals with ADHD and comorbid psychiatric conditions versus psychiatric conditions alone. Current anxiety was the strongest predictor of adult ADHD diagnosis. Keywords: Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), anxiety, depression, executive functions, assessment Introduction Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neu- rodevelopmental disorder marked by persistent and func- tionally impairing symptoms of inattention and/or hyper- activity and impulsivity ( American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2022). Inattentive symptoms may include forgetful- ness in daily activities, such as while running errands or in keeping appointments, avoidance of tasks requiring sustained attention, and difficulty with organization ( American Psychi- atric Association [APA], 2022). Hyperactive symptoms may include fidgeting, difficulty engaging in quiet leisure, and talking excessively ( American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2022). Inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity are consid- ered deficits in executive functions, as they are directly related Downloaded from academic.oup.com/acn/article/41/6/acag057/8748595 by Richard Bronson user on 21 October 2026

2 • Archives of Clinical Neuropsychology, 2026, Vol. 41, Issue 6 to cognitive processes such as working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility, which regulate attention, behavior, and impulse control ( Barkley, 1997; Nigg, 2005). Although ADHD symptoms must be present prior to age 12 to meet Diagnostic Statistical Manual-5-Text Revised (DSM-5- TR) criteria for diagnosis, many individuals with ADHD may not be diagnosed until adulthood ( Rivas-Vazquez et al., 2023). While estimates of ADHD prevalence rates in adulthood range from 2.5% to 4.4% ( American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2022), a meta-analysis found that among epidemiological research on ADHD, very little research exists using samples of adults >25 years old ( Willcutt, 2012). Thus, existing studies on ADHD prevalence may not generalize across the lifespan. Moreover, despite worldwide prevalence rates falling below 5%, a recent meta-analysis found that as many as 26.7% of adults presenting to outpatient psychiatric clinics were diagnosed with ADHD ( Adamis et al., 2022). This finding highlights the high prevalence of ADHD presentations within psychiatric settings and underscores the importance of accu- rate assessment and differential diagnosis in adulthood. ADHD in adulthood is highly comorbid with psychiatric disorders. A World Health Organization survey of 15,991 first year college students found an ADHD prevalence of 15.9%, of which 58.4% had psychiatric comorbidities ( Mak et al., 2022). Internalizing disorders were most common (36.0%), followed by bipolar disorder (11.3%), and exter- nalizing disorders (9.8%; Mak et al., 2022). Gerhand and Saville’s (2022) systematic review of research published in adult samples concluded that ADHD may be underdiagnosed in a psychiatric population. Their review found prevalence rates ranging from 6.9 to 38.75%, significantly higher than the estimated 2.8% ADHD prevalence in the general adult population. ADHD diagnosis in adulthood poses certain challenges to appropriately identifying the disorder. Retrospective stud- ies of childhood ADHD symptom recall have demonstrated recall bias ( Katzman et al., 2017; Taylor et al., 2022; Von Wirth et al., 2021). Vitola et al. (2017) found that DSM- 5-TR criteria were more likely to yield an ADHD diagnosis among adult samples compared to DSM-IV criteria, attributing this effect to the higher relevance of inattentive phenotypes in adult populations. It is important to note, however, that the DSM-5-TR criteria were developed to better address the underdiagnosis of ADHD in adulthood ( Rivas-Vazquez et al., 2023). Nonetheless, an important diagnostic criterion is that inattentive/hyperactive symptoms are not better explained by another mental disorder ( American Psychiatric Associa- tion [APA], 2022). The high prevalence of comorbid psychi- atric conditions with ADHD in adulthood can further muddle the clinical picture, as many psychiatric diagnoses, such as depression ( Keller et al., 2019), bipolar disorder ( Camelo et al., 2013), and anxiety disorders ( Volel et al., 2018), present with impairments in executive functioning. An additional challenge in adult ADHD assessment involves the potential influence of symptom exaggeration, secondary gain, or noncredible self-reporting, particularly in contexts where diagnosis may provide access to stimulant medication, academic accommodations, or occupational support services ( Becke et al., 2021; Sadek, 2022). Prior literature has demon- strated rates as high as 36.6% of symptom validity test (SVT) and 49.3% of performance validity test (PVT) failure among adults referred for ADHD evaluations ( Hirsch et al., 2022). Although meta-analyses have found low rates of PVT failure among individuals with psychiatric diagnoses such as depression and anxiety ( Legemaat et al., 2023; McWhirter et al., 2020), less research exists on SVTs failure rates in psychiatric populations. However, one study investigating SVT failure rate in Veterans with combat exposure found that 78% of individuals who failed an SVT had at least one psychiatric diagnosis, compared to 46% without ( Ord et al., 2021). In the context of ADHD, Woloszyn et al. (2026) found that perceived stress was associated with increases in ADHD symptom reporting, and that removing individuals with failed SVTs from their analysis resulted in depression and anxiety symptoms no longer being associated with ADHD symptoms reported in childhood. This suggests that ADHD comorbidity with psychiatric disorders could amplify risk of PVT or SVT failure. In all, these findings emphasize the importance of incorporating validity assessment procedures into diagnostic formulations, particularly among individuals with ADHD and comorbid psychiatric conditions. At the same time, clinicians must balance consideration of symptom validity with the recognition that psychiatric dis- tress, executive dysfunction, and developmental histories may legitimately contribute to attentional complaints. Moreover, delayed recognition of ADHD symptoms in adulthood may be associated with poorer long-term psychiatric and functional outcomes ( Holden & Kobayashi-Wood, 2025; Katzman et al., 2017; Long & Coats, 2022). Persistent attentional and exec- utive functioning difficulties may contribute to impairments across academic, occupational, interpersonal, and emotional domains, while delayed identification may limit access to appropriate interventions and supports. Importantly, qualita- tive analyses have demonstrated that identification of ADHD has important implications on quality of life, such as increased self-efficacy via feelings of relief at seeking appropriate and targeted treatment and no longer viewing one’s life as an “unnecessary struggle” ( Long & Coats, 2022). Present study Although adult diagnosis of ADHD has been gaining more attention in recent years ( Rivas-Vazquez et al., 2023), lit- tle research is available in this population ( Willcutt, 2012). Psychiatric clinics experience a high rate of adults present- ing with concerns for ADHD ( Adamis et al., 2022). Similar symptoms to ADHD are present across a myriad of psychiatric disorders, which can make differential diagnosis difficult. Given the difficulty of assessing ADHD in adulthood due to the high prevalence and confounding influences of psychi- atric comorbidities ( Waltereit et al., 2023), it is important for researchers to investigate the clinical utility of existing standard-of-care neuropsychological assessments used in the diagnosis of ADHD. While studies have investigated the utility of neuropsychological tests in differentiating individuals with ADHD from healthy and clinical controls (for a review, see Pettersson et al., 2018), to our knowledge, no study has specifically compared individuals with ADHD and comorbid Downloaded from academic.oup.com/acn/article/41/6/acag057/8748595 by Richard Bronson user on 21 October 2026

Archives of Clinical Neuropsychology, 2026, Vol. 41, Issue 6 • 3 psychiatric conditions to individuals with psychiatric condi- tions alone. There are important treatment implications for correctly differentiating ADHD from cognitive sequelae secondary to psychiatric diagnoses alone. Adults diagnosed with ADHD are more likely to be treated using stimulants than individuals diagnosed in childhood ( Young & Goodman, 2016). While stimulants may help treat ADHD symptoms, they may be ineffective for executive functioning deficits associated with psychiatric etiologies. For example, while they may provide initial relief in the treatment of depression, these effects have been found to be short-lived, pointing to a potentially differ- ent biomechanism underlying attention deficits in depression ( Malhi et al., 2016). On the other hand, underdiagnosing ADHD may contribute to worse long-term psychiatric trajec- tories ( Katzman et al., 2017). The present study aims to address gaps in the knowledge of how ADHD and comorbid psychiatric conditions may affect cognition, as well as identify the utility of standard- of-care assessments in differentiating individuals diagnosed with ADHD from those diagnosed with other psychiatric disorders. With the use of available medical records, the aims of the study are as follows: (a) to present demographic and neuropsychological data of individuals presenting for an ADHD evaluation to an adult outpatient neuropsychology clinic within the psychiatry department of an urban academic medical center, (b) to describe characteristics of individuals diagnosed with comorbid ADHD and psychiatric disorders versus those not diagnosed with ADHD, and (c) to evaluate the sensitivity and specificity of standard-of-care neuropsycho- logical assessments in differentiating ADHD comorbid with psychiatric diagnoses versus psychiatric related cognitive deficits alone. Method Setting Neuropsychological assessment records were reviewed of all individuals presenting to the clinic from July 1, 2024 through May 31, 2025. The outpatient clinic was situated in an aca- demic medical center in a populous city in the Northeastern United States. The clinic has two neuropsychologists on staff. Assessments are completed by trainees (practicum students enrolled in PhD and PsyD clinical psychology programs, American Psychological Association accredited program interns, and postdoctoral students) under the supervision of staff neuropsychologists. Each neuropsychologist sees two to five cases per week, with one patient slot per provider being reserved for ADHD evaluations. The clinic requires referrals for evaluation by a medical provider and accepts private and public medical insurance, including state and federal plans. Evaluations involve 2–4 hours of in-person cognitive testing using a variety of modalities, such as hands-on tasks, auditory tasks, visual tasks, and pencil and paper tasks. Domains mea- sured include executive functions (processing speed, atten- tion span, working memory, problem-solving approaches), verbal abilities (verbal reasoning and fluency, confrontation naming), visuospatial and visuomotor abilities (visual and spatial reasoning, hands-on assembly, fine motor dexterity), and memory (word-lists, stories, and visual). Self-reported surveys on child and current behavioral functioning and current psychological functioning are additionally completed. Testing batteries are created on a case-by-case basis, depend- ing on each patient’s unique presenting concerns and differen- tial diagnoses. The order of tests administered is additionally varied per patient. Trainees have been instructed not to administer tasks that could interfere with memory encoding and retrieval during delays between memory test trials. For example, a visuospatial task would not be administered during the delay of a visual memory task. Participants Individuals included in the study were those who presented to the clinic with a differential diagnosis question of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder versus psychiatric related cog- nitive deficits. Certain individuals were excluded to ensure that the sample reflected the study’s goal of examining the utility of common neuropsychological assessments in differ- ential diagnosis. Exclusion criteria were as follows: referral reason other than ADHD; absence of a primary or comorbid psychiatric diagnosis; Intelligence Quotient (IQ) ≤ 70 in order to minimize confounding effects of global intelligence; age restrictions (<18 or ≥65) were applied to maintain con- sistency with the adult population and to minimize effects of aging; participants with untreated sleep apnea, epilep- sy/seizures, traumatic brain injury within three years, or suspected neurodegenerative conditions due to the potential for such medical conditions to cause cognitive deficits that mimic/obscure ADHD symptoms; current stimulant treatment at the time of testing in order to avoid medication-related enhancements on testing; invalid test results based on embed- ded and stand-alone PVTs; or absence of a data summary attached to the neuropsychological testing report. Standard practice in the clinic from which data were collected is to not report raw data from tests in which individuals failed SVTs— thus, data from these measures was not included by the nature of the scores available in chart review. However, neuropsy- chological data was still included, as research suggests that SVT and PVT failure are not strongly concordant ( Benowitz et al., 2025; Ovsiew et al., 2023). Individuals with ADHD and no comorbid psychiatric diag- nosis were excluded from the sample, as the primary research question was to investigate whether standard of care neu- ropsychological tests are specifically sensitive and specific to ADHD psychiatric comorbidity. Sensitivity and specificity analyses are well-documented in other studies on adults with ADHD ( Rosso et al., 2023; Wasserman & Wasserman, 2012), but less is known about how tests perform in individuals with both ADHD and a comorbid psychiatric diagnosis. Existing studies have combined individuals with ADHD with and without psychiatric comorbidity into one diagnostic group, with the resulting samples having less psychological burden than their respective clinical control groups ( Guo et al., 2021; Onandia-Hinchado et al., 2021; Pettersson et al., 2018). Data collection The present study was conducted via retrospective chart review. Available medical records of all individuals present- ing for neuropsychological assessment to an adult outpa- tient clinic within an urban academic medical center were Downloaded from academic.oup.com/acn/article/41/6/acag057/8748595 by Richard Bronson user on 21 October 2026

4 • Archives of Clinical Neuropsychology, 2026, Vol. 41, Issue 6 reviewed from May 1, 2025 through June 10, 2025. Due to a shift to a new electronic medical record system, records were only available starting July 1, 2024. All study activities were approved by the local Institutional Review Board (IRB). This study met criteria for exempt research, and the IRB thus approved a waiver of informed consent. The study was conducted in compliance with the IRB. All charts were evaluated for inclusion and exclusion cri- teria. The number of charts meeting exclusion criteria were recorded. Data were entered from charts meeting inclusion criteria using solely the neuropsychological testing report, which detailed a narrative clinical history, including demo- graphics, provided a data summary of neuropsychological test scores (raw and normed), and assigned a diagnosis based on a combination of clinical interview and testing outcomes. All variables included were determined a priori to reduce potential for bias. The following demographic variables were recorded: age at testing, birth sex, gender identity, race and ethnicity, handedness, and years of education. The following covariates were selected for exploratory analyses due to their potential confounding effects on cognition and/or the testing environment: provider seen for the evaluation, presence of vascular risk factors (defined as an elevated A1C of 6.5 or higher ( Sola et al., 2024), high blood pressure ( Hughes et al., 2020), high cholesterol ( Zhao et al., 2024), smoking ( Anstey et al., 2007), or obesity ( Phirom et al., 2025), self-reported poor sleep quality (defined as disrupted sleep, snoring, feeling poorly rested, and self-reported hyper or hypo somnolence; Qin et al., 2023), prior substance use disorder (SUD) and/or SUD at the time of testing, SUD duration ( Ramey & Regier, 2019), marijuana use at time of testing and how long the patient abstained from marijuana prior to testing ( Scott et al., 2018), history of migraines ( Gu et al., 2022), whether or not English was the patient’s dominant language, whether or not an interpreter was used for testing ( Casas et al., 2012), history of childhood trauma or neglect ( Kavanaugh et al., 2017), presence of pain during testing and level of pain reported (0– 10, 10 = the worst; Zhang et al., 2021), mood rating at time of testing (1–10, 10 = the best; Rock et al., 2014)), anxiety rating at time of testing (1–10, 10 = the most; Nguyen et al., 2025), and hours of sleep achieved prior to testing ( Lo et al., 2012). Each neuropsychological evaluation report provided a descriptive estimate of each patient’s premorbid cognitive abilities based on performance on word reading and verbal and/or visual reasoning, depending on the patient’s reported history, together with reported educational and vocational background. Descriptive estimates followed the following percentile estimates, which were converted to z-scores based on a normal distribution: exceptionally low (<3%ile; z = − 2), below average (3%ile–8%ile; z = − 1.5), low average (9%ile– 10%ile; z = − 1), low average to average (21%ile–32%ile; z = − 0.5), average (33%ile–50%ile; z = 0), average to high average (51%ile–75%ile, z = 0.5), high average (76%ile– 85%ile; z = 1), high average to above average (85%ile– 91%ile; z = 1.25), above average (92%ile–97%ile; z = 1.5), and exceptionally high (>97%ile, z = 2). These estimates served as a reference point for interpretation of each individual’s neuropsychological testing results. Raw and normed scores of each neuropsychological test administered and reported were recorded for analysis. Each normed score was converted to a z score. The premorbid estimate scores were subtracted from normed neuropsychological testing scores to create a deviation score for each neuropsychological testing variable. Positive numbers indicate where individuals performed better on a given test than their premorbid estimate, while negative numbers indicate worse than expected performance. The following outcome variables were reported: whether or not ADHD was diagnosed, ADHD type that was diagnosed, whether or not another neurodevelopmental disorder was diagnosed, and which psychiatric comorbidities were diag- nosed. Psychiatric conditions were sorted into the follow- ing categories: mood disorders, anxiety-spectrum disorders, both mood and anxiety disorders, and others. Conditions such as major depressive disorder, unspecified depressive disorder, and bipolar disorder, were coded as mood disor- ders. Disorders such as generalized anxiety disorder, post- traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive compulsive disorder, were coded as anxiety-spectrum disorders. Examples of other disorders include substance use disorders and adjustment disorders. Neuropsychological and psychiatric measures The following neuropsychological and psychiatric measures were utilized: Advanced Clinical Solutions (ACS): Test of Premorbid Functioning (TOPF; Pearson Clinical, 2009; Wech- sler, 2011), Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale–Fourth Edition (WAIS-IV; Wechsler, 2008), Conners Continuous Performance Test–3rd Edition (CPT-3; Conners, 2014), Boston Naming Test–Second Edition (BNT; Heaton et al., 2004; Kaplan et al., 2001), Neuropsychological Assessment Battery (NAB) Naming Test ( Stern & White, 2003), Controlled Oral Word Associa- tion Test (FAS/Animals; Benton et al., 2017; Heaton et al., 2004; Tombaugh, 1999), Delis-Kaplan Executive Function Scale (DKEFS)–Verbal Fluency ( Delis et al., 2001), Trail Mak- ing Test (TMT) A and B ( Army Individual Test Battery, 1944; Heaton et al., 2004; Tombaugh, 2004), California Verbal Learning Test–Second Edition (CVLT-II; Delis et al., 2000), Wechsler Memory Scale–Fourth Edition (WMS-IV; Wechsler, 2008), Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure Test (RCFT; Meyers & Meyers, 1995; Osterrieth, 1944; Rey, 1941; Somerville et al., 2000), Brief Visual Memory Test–Revised (BVMT-R; Bene- dict, 1997), Tower of London–Drexel University, 2nd Edition (TOLDX; Culbertson & Zillmer, 2005), Barkley Adult ADHD Rating Scale–IV (BAARS-IV; Barkley, 2011) symptom counts, Conners’ Adult ADHD Rating Scales–Self Report: Long Version (CAARS; Conners et al., 1999), Beck Depression Inventory– Second Edition (BDI-II; Beck, 1996), Generalized Anxiety Disorder–7 (GAD-7; Spitzer et al., 2006), and Personality Assessment Inventory (PAI; Morey, 1991). Data from individ- uals failing SVTs on the PAI and the CAARS were not reported in neuropsychological reports and were therefore implicitly excluded. Finally, an SVT cut off of ≥36 on the BDI-II ( Kent et al., 2025) was applied to the present sample, and BDI-II data from individuals scoring above this threshold were excluded from analyses. They were separated by cohort: individuals diagnosed with ADHD and a comorbid psychiatric diagnosis, and individuals not diagnosed with ADHD. Means (M ) and standard deviations (SD) were reported for continuous variables, while frequencies and percentages were reported for categorical variables. The data were evaluated to ensure assumptions for respective statistical methods were met. Independent samples t-tests were conducted to evaluate for statistically significant differences between cohorts for continuous variables, and Cohen’s d was computed to evaluate effect size. Chi-square analysis was conducted on categorical variables. Fisher’s exact test was conducted on variables containing <5 items in a cell. Statistical significance was set at α = 0.05. Effect sizes greater than d = 0.6 would be discussed, as well as means that reflected clinical significance (i.e., neuropsychological deviation scores (z) ≤ − 1.5 standard deviations from an individual’s premorbid estimate and survey scores meeting clinical thresholds). Logistic regressions were conducted for the deviation score of each neuropsychological test to determine whether the test predicted cohort membership. A Receiver Operating Char- acteristic (ROC) curve was plotted, and the Area Under the Curve (AUC) was used to determine the clinical utility of tests, with measures above 0.7 being considered acceptable ( Hosmer et al., 2013). Depending on total available sample size, statistically significant covariates were to be included in the logistic regression. All variables included in logistic regression were assessed for normality via computing skew- ness and kurtosis. Corrections for family wise error were not completed, as the primary outcomes were sensitivity and specificity analyses not reliant on p-values. Variables were considered normally distributed with a skewness between − 2 and 2 and kurtosis between − 7 and 7. Statistical analysis was performed in JASP 0.18.3 and figures were created in https:// BioRender.com and Python 3× ( Python Software Foundation, n.d.). Results Aim 1: ADHD evaluation clinic summary Two hundred and fifty-two individuals presented for neu- ropsychological evaluation from July 1, 2024 to May 31, 2025. Fifty-four percent (n = 137) of individuals seen at the clinic were referred for an ADHD evaluation. Of these, 16.1% (n = 22) were not diagnosed with a comorbid psychiatric disorder and were thus excluded from the study. Twenty-four percent (n = 28) were older than 65 years old. Other rates of meeting exclusion criteria are presented in Fig. 1. The final sample included 67 participants, of which 44.8% (n = 30) were diagnosed with ADHD and a comorbid psy- chiatric disorder, while 55.2% (n = 37) were diagnosed with a psychiatric disorder alone. Overall, 57.7% of individu- als with ADHD met criteria for another DSM-5 psychiatric disorder. Of those diagnosed with ADHD, 33.3% (n = 10) were diagnosed with ADHD inattentive presentation, 3.3% (n = 1) were diagnosed with ADHD hyperactive presentation, 33.3% (n = 10) were diagnosed with ADHD combined type, and 30% (n = 9) were diagnosed with an unspecified ADHD presentation. Demographics for each cohort are presented in Table 1. Demographics were not statistically significantly different between groups. Forty-nine percent of individuals (n = 33) were diagnosed with both mood and anxiety disorders, 28.4% (n = 19) were diagnosed with an anxiety disorder only, and 19.4% (n = 13) were diagnosed with a mood disorder only. Two participants were classified under other disorders (alcohol use disorder and adjustment disorder). Among those with ADHD, 20% (n = 6) were diagnosed with a mood disorder, 26.67% (n = 8) were diagnosed with an anxiety disorder, and 50% (n = 15) were diagnosed with both. Anxiety disorders included generalized anxiety disorder, unspecified anxiety disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, unspecified obsessive-compulsive and related disorder, social anxiety disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder, unspecified trauma- and-stressor-related disorder, and somatic symptom disorder. Mood disorders included persistent depressive disorder, major depressive disorder, major depressive disorder with seasonal pattern, recurrent depressive disorder, unspecified mood disorder, unspecified depressive disorder with anxiety, major depressive disorder with anxious distress, unspecified bipolar and related disorder, and bipolar II disorder. Other diagnoses included cannabis use disorder, unspecified binge eating disorder, excoriation disorder, trichotillomania, and insomnia disorder. Sensitivity and specificity analyses As there were no statistically significant differences in demographic characteristics and covariates, no variables other than each test being evaluated were included in the logistic regression models. Logistic regressions revealed that no cognitive measures were predictive of ADHD diagnosis ( Supplementary Table 4). The Generalized Anxiety Disorder- 7 was the strongest predictive scale of ADHD diagno- sis (AUC = 0.800; χ 2 (28) = 8.216, p = .004, Nagelkerke R 2 = 0.333; Fig. 3) and correctly predicted 76% of cases. Adults who endorsed higher levels of anxiety were 28% more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD (OR = 1.28, 95%CI [1.05, 1.57]). ADHD scales were less predictive of diagnosis. The most predictive clinical scale of the ADHD surveys was CAARS Self-Concept, (AUC = 0.750; χ 2 (27) = 5.436, p = .020, Nagelkerke R 2 = 0.236; Fig. 3), which correctly predicted 75% of cases. Nonetheless, individuals who scored higher on this clinical scale were only 7% more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD (OR = 1.07, 95%CI [1.00–1.13]). Additional clinical scales that predicted ADHD diagnosis, in order of highest sensitivity and specificity to lowest, include the following: Childhood Hyperactivity symptom counts on the BAARS-IV (AUC = 0.712; χ 2 (53) = 6.682, p = .010, Nagelkerke R 2 = 0.156), which correctly predicted 65% of cases and in which individuals who endorsed more childhood hyperactivity symptoms were 36% more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD (OR = 1.36, 95%CI [1.06– 1.75]); the ADHD Index on the CAARS (AUC = 0.708, χ 2 (27) = 5.169, p = .023, Nagelkerke R 2 = 0.225), which predicted 61% of cases and in which individuals with a greater ADHD Index were 8% more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD, and Childhood Inattention symptoms counts on the BAARS-IV (AUC = 0.706; χ 2 (53) = 7.527, p = .006, Nagelkerke R 2 = 0.175), which predicted 69% of cases and in which individuals who endorsed more childhood inattentive symptoms were 33% more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD (OR = 1.33, 95%CI [1.07–1.66]; Fig. 3). DSM-IV Hyperactive Symptoms on the CAARS had an AUC of 0.700, but the model overall was not statistically significant ( χ 2 (27) = 3.615, p = .057, Nagelkerke R 2 = 0.162). No PAI clinical scales were predictive of ADHD diagnosis ( Supplementary Table 4). Discussion This study examined adults referred for ADHD evaluation within an outpatient psychiatric neuropsychological setting, where there was substantial overlap between individuals diag- nosed with ADHD and other psychiatric conditions. Aim 1: ADHD evaluation clinic summary A large proportion of the referrals to the clinic were for ADHD evaluations, suggesting that concerns about attention and executive functioning are a major reason adults seek neuropsychological assessment. For many years, ADHD was viewed as a childhood condition. It is now recognized that symptoms continue into adulthood, which means that many adults who struggled earlier in life were never evaluated. National data revealed that a large portion of adults with ADHD were diagnosed after age 18, suggesting that many cases were missed rather than newly developed ( Staley et al., 2024). Modern life, including workplaces and daily routines, now demands high levels of sustained attention, organization, multitasking, and self-management, which can expose weak- nesses that previously went unnoticed. Even people with- out ADHD may feel stressed, which leads some to wonder whether ADHD is the explanation. Additionally, symptoms like poor concentration, forgetfulness, and mental fatigue also are common in anxiety and mood disorders, so many adults experiencing emotional distress may wonder if ADHD explains their difficulties. Emotional distress can make attentional problems feel similar to ADHD, prompting evaluations. Finally, a concrete ADHD presentation (i.e., inattentive, hyperactive, or combined) was not identified in almost a third of individuals diagnosed with ADHD in the present sample. This could reflect difficulty with retrospective report of childhood ADHD symptoms, which are required for a DSM- 5-TR diagnosis, and difficulty parsing out the relative impact of ADHD symptoms versus comorbid psychopathology on daily functioning. For example, a clinician may have been reluctant to specify a specific ADHD presentation if there was significant discordance between childhood and adult symptom report, or if there were unclear patterns of symptoms depending on setting (i.e., inattentive symptoms isolated to work settings but hyperactive symptoms present across work, home, and social settings), particularly in light of psychiatric comorbidity. Aim 2: Covariates and cognitive and psychological profiles The ADHD and non-ADHD groups were well matched on many background variables, reducing the likelihood that differences in the clinical outcomes were driven by demographic factors or evaluator bias. Both providers also appeared consistent in diagnostic decision-making, supporting the reliability of clini- cal evaluations across clinicians. Notably, both groups showed high rates of substance use histories and current marijuana use, which reflects real-world psychiatric populations but may complicate interpretation of cognitive performance. Average abstinence from marijuana was 10 days prior to testing; however, long-term effects on cognition cannot be fully ruled out. Half of the participants identified English as their primary language, which introduces potential cultural and linguis- tic influences on testing and symptom reporting. Childhood trauma and/or neglect were common in both groups. This is clinically meaningful because trauma history can produce attentional problems, emotional dysregulation, and execu- tive difficulties that overlap with ADHD symptoms, making diagnostic differentiation more challenging. Literature sug- gests that trauma exposure may increase the likelihood of anxiety and functional impairment in adults presenting with ADHD symptoms ( Peleikis et al., 2022). The most striking finding was that cognitive testing did not clearly differentiate adults with ADHD from those without ADHD who had psychiatric conditions. This notably includes the CPT-3, which is one of the most frequently recommended tests for ADHD ( Fuermaier et al., 2019), although an increas- ing number of studies have been published demonstrating its weak predictive utility ( Callan et al., 2024). Both those with and without ADHD showed similar cognitive patterns, and both demonstrated mild difficulties on tasks involving visual scanning speed, organization, and incidental memory. Addi- tionally, both groups reported similar psychological distress on the PAI, with clinically elevated scales relating to thought dysfunction, impulsivity, risk-taking, anxiety, and depression. This merely highlights that disorders such as anxiety, depres- sion, or chronic stress may produce cognitive inefficiencies similar to those of ADHD. In other words, cognitive challenges seen during testing may reflect general psychiatric burden rather than ADHD-specific deficits. The effect sizes and cognitive findings in the present study are lower than those reported in prior meta-analyses and systematic reviews on adult-ADHD neurocognitive profiles ( Hervey et al., 2004; Onandia-Hinchado et al., 2021). Notably, however, these studies compared those with ADHD to normal healthy controls, rather than psychiatrically matched con- trols, as the present study did. Existing studies comparing cognitive profiles of those with ADHD to psychiatric controls differ from the present study in that their ADHD groups included those with ADHD alone in addition to individuals with ADHD who meet diagnostic criteria for another DSM psychiatric diagnosis ( Rosso et al., 2023). Thus, the ADHD groups in these studies contain less psychiatric burden than the present sample and cannot necessarily be directly com- pared to the current studies. Nonetheless, Rosso et al.’s (2023) narrative systematic review confirms that the results from these studies are largely aligned with those of the present study, in that, apart from continuous performance tests, they have provided minimal evidence for differences in neuropsy- chological testing in ADHD when psychiatric controls serve as the comparison group. For example, the effect sizes comparing ADHD to psychiatric controls reported in Guo et al.’s (2021) study ranged from 0.004 to 0.20, and Pettersson et al.’s (2018) effect sizes ranged from 0.001 to 0.104 when controlling for age and IQ, compared to the present study’s effect sizes rang- ing from 0.009 to 0.445. More research is needed to compare individuals with ADHD-psychiatric-comorbidity to psychiatri- cally matched controls to better understand whether cognitive deficits in ADHD are unique to the condition or instead reflect psychiatric comorbidity. Although cognitive scales were not different among those with and without ADHD, self-report ADHD scales provided clearer differentiation. Individuals diagnosed with ADHD described more childhood attention and hyperactivity problems and greater concerns about self-concept, consistent with clinical models proposing that long-standing attentional difficulties can negatively influence self-esteem over time. Importantly, current inattentive symptoms were elevated across both ADHD and non-ADHD groups. This finding has strong clinical implications, such as that adults with anxiety, depression, or other psychiatric difficulties may report significant attention problems even in the absence of ADHD. This reinforces the need to interpret symptom questionnaires within a developmental and emotional context rather than in isolation. The pattern of stronger self-concept concerns in the ADHD group may reflect the cumulative impact of lifelong functional struggles, repeated experiences of underachievement, or chronic frustration associated with executive functioning difficulties. Aim 3: Sensitivity and specificity Anxiety symptoms emerged as the strongest indicator associated with receiving an ADHD diagnosis, even more than cognitive measures or many ADHD-specific questionnaires. This finding highlights the close relationship between anxiety and adult ADHD presentation. ADHD and anxiety frequently co-occur in adulthood, with comorbidity rates indicating that anxiety symptoms are a clinically meaningful feature of ADHD presentations in adulthood ( Kessler et al., 2006; Sobanski, 2006). Several interpretations are possible. Anxiety may develop secondary to chronic attentional and executive functioning difficulties, reflecting years of coping challenges and functional concerns. Moreover, anxiety may be closely linked to the subjective experience of attentional difficulties and executive dysfunction, increasing symptom endorsement during the evaluation. Alternatively, anxiety itself can intensify perceptions of inattention and cognitive inefficiency, leading individuals to seek an ADHD assessment. The overlap likely reflects bidirectional influences rather than a simple causal relationship. Emotional symptoms, specifically anxiety, play a role in adult ADHD presentations clinically and may strongly influence both referral and diagnostic outcomes. Notably, an additional interpretation is that anxiety could reflect broader psychological distress rather than ADHD-specific pathology. Generalized distress may increase endorsement of symptoms across multiple domains and influence referral patterns. There is consistent evidence that general symptom measures can be predictive of a diagnosis as well as disorder-specific instruments ( Arbisi et al., 2012). Additionally, dimensional models of psychopathology emphasize a general “p” factor underlying internalizing and eternalizing psychiatric symptoms ( Caspi et al., 2014). Together, these findings suggest that anxiety may play a role in adult ADHD assessment, potentially reflecting both comorbidity and nonspecific distress that influence diag- nostic outcomes, supporting prior findings suggesting that psychological symptom questionnaires may lack diagnostic specificity ( Arbisi et al., 2012). Although individual neuropsychological tests may not accurately identify ADHD among psychiatric samples, increasing evidence shows that the apparent heterogeneity in adult ADHD assessment outcomes often observed may reflect underlying distinct neurocognitive phenotypes ( Cerny et al., 2025; Leib et al., 2021; McGuigan et al., 2025). These neurocognitive phenotypes in turn may be associated with comorbid psychopathology, although the evidence is mixed. For example, Leib et al.’s (2021) latent profile analysis (LPA) in a cohort of individuals with ADHD completing the WAIS- IV identified four classes of neuropsychological performance: low general cognitive performance, average performance, high working memory, and high processing speed. The high working memory group self-reported significantly fewer symptoms of depression and anxiety than the other groups. However, Cerny et al.’s (2025) LPA of individuals diagnosed with ADHD found similar rates of elevated comorbid psychopathology across neurocognitive classes. Individuals in the “inattentive” class, marked by worse performance on WAIS-IV Coding, TMT-A, and certain subscales on the CPT- 3, self-reported significantly more symptoms of depression than individuals in the “Low Learning/Memory” class and more symptoms of anxiety than the “High Average” class, although these effect sizes were small. This finding mirrors the present results, which found that individuals with ADHD and psychiatric conditions performed below expectation on TMT-A—although the results in the present study were not unique to ADHD and could reflect psychopathology instead.
