12 • Archives of Clinical Neuropsychology, 2026, Vol. 41, Issue 6 McGuigan et al.’s (2025) study is perhaps most compa- rable to the present study, as their LPA included individu- als with and without ADHD who presented for neurocogni- tive evaluations in a clinical setting. Their identified “Neu- ropsychiatrically Distressed” class most closely resembles our study’s cohort, which included individuals both with and without ADHD with elevated inattentive, hyperactive, and mood scores and overall worse cognitive performance relative to other classes. Interestingly, this class was less likely to be diagnosed with ADHD than other classes. The present study addresses the clinical question of how individuals within this class can be accurately classified as having or not having ADHD based on neuropsychological testing. It is possible that the present sample is comprised of individuals within one of the aforementioned neurocognitive phenotypes, as perhaps driven by psychopathology. Alterna- tively, the present sample may contain a number of distinct neurocognitive phenotypes that cannot be segmented due to limits on statistical power, which could account for the lack of observed differences between individuals with and without ADHD in the present clinical sample. Future studies should expand upon existing LPA studies to investigate whether observed profiles in ADHD that are associated with comor- bid psychopathology are also present in non-ADHD clinical samples, and whether the presence of ADHD differentiates cognitive functioning among these groups specifically. Limitations The present study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings. First, the final sample size following eligibility confirmation was relatively small (n = 67), which may limit the generalizability of results. Because all participants were evaluated at an academic med- ical center rather than in private practice or community settings outside the Boston area, the sample may not fully represent the broader population of adults assessed for ADHD. Second, there is the potential for misclassification bias, such that some participants may have been inaccurately catego- rized based on self-report measures or subtle clinician bias during the diagnostic interview. Third, unmeasured confound- ing variables, including behavioral observations, psychosocial factors, and aspects of clinical history not captured in the dataset, may have influenced diagnostic outcomes. Fourth, parental psychiatric/psychological conditions and outcomes among adults aged 65 years and older were not examined, as these factors were beyond the scope of the study. Future research should investigate their potential role in ADHD- related outcomes across the lifespan. Finally, there may have been bias in the results as driven by the types of assessments that each clinician chose for each individual, and which results, such as failed SVTs, each clinician chose not to include in the report, rendering these raw data to be unavailable. The use of real-world archival data was a strength of this study, as it adds to a body of literature of present- day neuropsychological practices in adult ADHD evaluations. Nonetheless, the nature of this study lends itself to constraints on generality. For one, given the study’s archival nature, we were unable to test less-frequently used materials in ADHD diagnosis that could have performed better in differentiating ADHD from psychiatric cognitive deficits. Given this study’s findings, future studies should augment clinical neuropsycho- logical assessments with different diagnostic scales and vali- date the present study’s findings in an intentionally recruited more socio-demographically diverse sample. The participants on whom the present assumptions are based could be a reflection of socio-demographic factors in adult ADHD referrals rather than the actual nature of ADHD in adulthood across a diverse set of individuals. Included par- ticipants were predominantly White women with at least some college level education and with an average estimated IQ (based on word-reading) falling in the 75th percentile. Given that all individuals presenting to our clinic were screened, these demographics reflect the demographics of patients most commonly referred for ADHD who are also diagnosed with comorbid psychiatric disorders. The demographics in the present study align with those presented in systematic reviews on adult ADHD presentations ( Adamis et al., 2022; Faheem et al., 2022). For example, although ADHD has been demon- strated to be more prevalent among males ( Faheem et al., 2022), other studies of adult ADHD outpatient clinic referrals have similarly found an increased rate of female referrals ( Adamis et al., 2022). This may be because girls are under- diagnosed in childhood ( Tapia et al., 2024), and symptoms may become more impactful in adulthood due to increased psychological comorbidity ( Faheem et al., 2022). Similarly, the high level of education and IQ could account for missed diagnoses in childhood. Alternatively, relative privilege and bias within our hos- pital network may be reflected in our sample. While the clinic from which data were collected accepts both public and private insurance, it is unlikely that individuals without insur- ance coverage and substantial financial means were included in the study. Additionally, the clinic does not accept self- referrals, meaning that physician bias may have played a role in who was referred for an assessment in the first place. Other epidemiological studies have found that racially and ethni- cally minoritized adults are less likely to have documented medical visits related to ADHD ( Adams et al., 2024), perhaps reflecting either cultural differences in symptom perception and engagement with the medical system to address symp- toms, or physician bias in taking patient complaints seriously. In fact, studies have found that primary care providers refer Black patients disproportionally less to specialists than White counterparts ( Landon et al., 2021). Additionally, racial bias may account for more Black individuals being diagnosed with ADHD in childhood, while White individuals have been found to be disproportionally diagnosed as adults ( Shalaby et al., 2024). Finally, ADHD is underdiagnosed in girls, leading to increases in adult diagnoses in women coupled with psycho- logical sequelae ( Attoe & Climie, 2023). Given the above, reflexivity is important when interpreting our study’s findings. Rather than using our results to reinforce ADHD diagnostic stereotypes, it is important to evaluate them within the specific socio-demographic context in which the data were collected. It may not be the case that edu- cated White women are more likely to have concerns about ADHD in adulthood over and above individuals with other demographics, but rather that on average, this demographic group is more likely to be referred to and have the means Downloaded from academic.oup.com/acn/article/41/6/acag057/8748595 by Richard Bronson user on 21 October 2026

Thus, the study findings may only apply to a population with presumed relative racial and economic privilege. Clinical implications and future directions The study findings have significant clinical implications for assessment of ADHD in outpatient psychiatric settings. The overlap of cognitive performance between individuals diagnosed with ADHD and those with other psychiatric conditions suggests that neuropsychological test results alone have limited specificity in complex clinical samples. Shared weaknesses in attention and incidental memory appear to reflect transdiagnostic inefficiencies rather than disorder-specific deficits. In contrast, developmental history, particularly evidence of childhood ADHD symptoms, and current emotional functioning were more informative in distinguishing diagnostic outcomes. This highlights the importance of conceptualizing ADHD as a neurodevelop- mental condition that requires evaluation of longitudinal symptom course, cross-situational impairment, and functional impact over time. Collectively, these findings support a comprehensive, multimethod assessment approach that prioritizes clinical interview, developmental history, and psychological context, with cognitive testing serving as an adjunctive tool for characterization and treatment planning rather than a standalone diagnostic determinant. Future research using longitudinal designs is recommended to better understand additional factors that may contribute to ADHD symptoms, including sleep quality and collateral developmental histories. Although the present study did not identify differences in associated covariates among the ADHD and non-ADHD cohort, such approaches may help clarify the directionality between factors that may affect cognition, such as sleep quality and ADHD-related symptoms, as well as the extent to which sleep-related cognitive difficulties and other modifiable factors may improve with appropriate treatment. Along these lines, neurobiological mechanisms may be an emerging area of research looking at sleep quality and ADHD symptomology, specifically longitudinal methodologies in a larger sample. More general future studies may also focus on generating broad treatment recommendations based on shared cognitive deficit patterns in individuals with ADHD and comorbid psychiatric conditions, as well as developing more sensitive tools to distinguish diagnoses. Technol. 2026, 60, 21465−21479 Read Online ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations * sı Supporting Information ABSTRACT: Although neurotoxic, prenatal exposure to organophosphate esters (OPEs) and phthalic acid esters (PAEs) and their effects on preschoolers’ autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) cotrajectories and underlying metabolic mechanisms remain unclear, we aimed to elucidate these links. Maternal urinary OPEs/PAEs were measured in 3040 dyads from the Ma’anshan Birth Cohort across three trimesters. Child ADHD/ASD symptom scale scores were assessed at ages 3, 5, and 6, and cotrajectories were identified using groupbased multitrajectory modeling. Single-pollutant models revealed that bis(2-ethylhexyl) phosphate (BEHP) across pregnancy was positively associated with high-score trajectories (HST) (OR = 1.20, 95% CI: 1.06, 1.37), whereas bis(2-butoxyethyl) phosphate (BBOEP) exhibited U-shaped associations. Second-trimester diphenyl phosphate (DPHP) (OR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.01, 1.26), BEHP (OR = 1.14, 95% CI: 1.04, 1.24), and monobutyl phthalate (OR = 1.15, 95% CI: 1.00, 1.32) were positively associated with HST. First-trimester DPHP exhibited a positive correlation with moderate-score trajectories and HST in girls, while bis(1-chloro-2propyl) phosphate across pregnancy was inversely associated with HST in boys (psex‐int < 0.05). No mixed effects were detected. BBOEP across pregnancy was negatively associated with ADHD symptoms, whereas BEHP was positively associated. BEHP, monomethyl phthalate, and mono-(2-ethyl-5-oxohexyl) phthalate were positively associated with ASD symptoms, whereas dibutyl phosphate and monoethyl phthalate were negatively associated (p < 0.05). Cord blood metabolomics identified pyrimidine, biotin, lysine, cysteine, and methionine metabolism as key mediators of OPE-induced cotrajectories, and purine metabolism mediated PAEs’ effects (p < 0.05). This study highlights OPE/PAE neurotoxicity and reveals novel cord metabolomic insights. INTRODUCTION Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are common neurodevelopmental disorders in children, and their prevalence is increasing;1−3 symptoms and functional impairments often persist into adulthood.4 Despite differences in clinical manifestations, overlapping symptoms and heritability have been reported, suggesting shared developmental pathways.5 In one study, 13% adolescents with ADHD were diagnosed with comorbid ASD.6 Other studies have reported that approximately one in eight adolescents with ADHD has ASD.7 ADHD is also among the most common comorbid conditions in patients with ASD, with a comorbidity rate ranging from 40% to 70%.8 Co-occurring disorders not only complicate diagnosis and rehabilitation but also affect prognosis.9 The high co-occurrence rate between ADHD and ASD stems from potential shared pathophysiological mechanisms, as both can influence brain neurodevelopment through similar genetic, immune, gut microbiota, and environmental pathways.10 Notably, individuals who present with partial disease symptoms or subclinical functional deficits (e.g., ADHD and ASD symptoms) are far more Received: January 26, 2026 Revised: July 16, 2026 Accepted: July 17, 2026 Published: July 30, 2026 Article pubs.acs.org/est © 2026 American Chemical Society 21465 https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.6c01402 Environ. The etiology of ADHD and ASD remains unclear, and organophosphate esters (OPEs) and phthalic acid esters (PAEs) are two standard classes of emerging environmental chemicals with increasingly recognized neurotoxicity. widely used, halogen-free flame retardants in industrial and consumer goods (e.g., furniture, electronics).12,13 PAEs are synthetic endocrine-disrupting plasticizers added to polymers (e.g., in food packaging and medical devices) to enhance flexibility and durability.14 Owing to weak interactions between OPEs and PAEs, and between these materials and other materials during production (van der Waals forces), they readily migrate from polymers into the environment.14,15 The prenatal period is a phase of rapid fetal development, during which the fetus is susceptible to damage from exogenous stimuli. Current research has detected OPEs in placental tissues at the maternal−fetal interface, including the chorion and decidua.16,17 Similarly, PAEs have been identified in amniotic fluid and cord serum.18 OPEs and PAEs share numerous similarities in terms of their exposure pathways and health effects.14 When humans are simultaneously exposed to both substances, the combined effects may be more complex and pronounced.19 Therefore, combined exposure to OPEs and PAEs warrants serious attention, particularly during critical periods of fetal neurodevelopment in utero. Cunha et al. systematically reviewed 8 cohort studies on prenatal PAE and ASD: 4 reported a positive association, and 4 reported no significant association.20 A Chinese study indicated that prenatal exposure to metals and PAEs may increase the risk of ASD at age four by 2.11-fold.21 A cohort study reported that diphenyl phosphate (DPHP) and bis(1,3dichloro-2-propyl) phosphate (BDCIPP) in the second trimester were associated with increased ADHD risk in children, with girls more susceptible to DPHP.22 Hall et al. reported that prenatal exposure to di-n-butyl phosphate and BDCIPP may increase the risk of ADHD in offspring. And bis(2-butoxyethyl) phosphate (BBOEP) exhibited a sexspecific, risk increased with high exposure in boys, whereas it decreased in girls.23 A U.S. birth cohort study demonstrated significant positive correlations between maternal DPHP and BDCIPP and hyperactivity-impulsivity, attention problems, and externalizing behavior problems in 3-year-old children, and that girls’ cognitive and behavioral development is more susceptible to BDCIPP exposure.24 These studies suggest that prenatal exposure to OPEs/PAEs may affect offspring neurodevelopment, with potential sex-and trimester-specific effects. Nevertheless, few studies have examined the role of cord blood metabolomics in the association between prenatal chemical exposure and offspring neurodevelopmental disorders.25−27 Cord blood metabolomics closely mirrors fetal metabolic status and is widely used to characterize biological perturbations.27 Previous studies have linked alterations in cord blood metabolomics to ADHD/ASD. For instance, linolenic acid in cord serum is negatively associated with ASD, whereas perfluorooctanoic acid shows the strongest positive association.28 A prospective birth cohort study demonstrated that elevated levels of branched-chain amino acids in cord plasma are associated with an increased risk of ADHD.29 Additionally, research has revealed that cord blood plasma-chained 5-methoxytryptophol is negatively correlated with the risk of both ASD and ADHD, and that tryptophan and other metabolites were associated with subsequent ADHD risk.30 Prenatal OPEs and PAEs have also been shown to alter the profile of neonatal metabolites, particularly in the tyrosine and tryptophan pathways, which are associated with infant neurobehavioral outcomes.15,25,27 By identifying metabolites related to environmental exposure and disease, metabolomicswide association studies (MWASs)especially when combined with the “meet-in-the-middle” (MITM) approachoffer a promising strategy for uncovering key molecular mechanisms linked to health effects.27 Based on the Ma’anshan Birth Cohort (MABC), with multiple time-point repeated measurements of maternal urinary exposure and childhood assessments of ADHD and ASD symptoms. This study aims to (1) investigate the relationship between individual and combined exposure to OPEs and PAEs and the cotrajectory of ADHD-ASD symptoms; (2) identify sensitive exposure windows and sexspecific disparities in prenatal exposure to OPEs and PAEs; and (3) explore potential cord blood metabolic pathways linking coexposure to OPEs and PAEs to the cotrajectory by integrating the MWAS and MITM methods. The overall study design is shown in Figure 1. 2. METHODS 2.1. Study Population We used data from the MABC,31 involving 3226 pregnant women who provided at least one urine sample during the three trimesters. We further excluded 186 individuals whose ASD and ADHD symptom questionnaires were completed fewer than once. Ultimately, our study included 3040 mother−child dyads, with cord blood samples available for 1992 individuals, who underwent metabolomics analysis (Figure S1). The number of individuals in the first, second, and third trimesters was 2909, 2939, and 2834, respectively. The study was approved by the Ethics and Research Committees of Anhui Medical University (No. 20131195), and all participants provided written informed consent before enrollment and follow-up. 2.2. Measurement of Urine OPEs and PAEs Maternal morning urine samples collected during each trimester were aliquoted into 50 mL polypropylene urine cups, transferred to 5 mL polypropylene cryovials, and stored at −80 °C until measurement. On the basis of the initial exploration of OPE detection methods and a literature review, we selected an OPE [tris(2-chloroethyl) phosphate (TCEP)] and five OPE metabolitesDPHP, bis(1-chloro2-propyl) phosphate (BCIPP), BBOEP, bis(2-ethylhexyl) phosphate (BEHP), and dibutyl phosphate (DBP)for urine testing during pregnancy. These metabolites are relatively common and have relatively high detection rates.32 The six OPEs were detected in urine samples using solvent-induced phase change extraction (SIPTE) and ultraperformance liquid chromatography−tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC−MS/MS) (Xevo TQ−SLC−MS, Waters Corporation, 34 Maple Street, Milford, MA, USA) with an isotope internal standard assay.32 UPLC was performed on an ACQUITY C18 BEH column (50 mm × 2.1 mm × 1.7 μm) from Waters Corporation (Milford, MA, USA). Several quality assurance and control (QA/QC) measures were followed to ensure accurate quantification. Additional details of the urine OPE measurements and QA/QC procedures are available in Text S1 and Tables S1−S2. The detailed experimental method for the OPEs has been previously described.13,32 The limits of detection (LODs) for OPEs are listed in Table S2. Similarly, six target PAEsmonomethyl phthalate (MMP), monoethyl phthalate (MEP), monobutyl phthalate (MBP), mono-2ethylhexyl phthalate (MEHP), mono-(2-ethyl-5-hydroxyhexyl) phthalate (MEHHP), and mono-(2-ethyl-5-oxohexyl) phthalate (MEOHP)were measured using previously published methods.33 The concentrations of PAEs in the urine samples were quantified using an isotopic internal standard method, namely, solid-phase extraction and high-performance liquid chromatography−tandem mass spectrometry (6410 LC−MS, Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA).14,15,33 QA/QC measures were implemented to ensure accurate quantification of PAEs. Detailed information on urine PAE measurements and QA/QC procedures is provided in Text S2 and Tables S3−S4. The LODs for the PAEs are listed in Table S4. To account for individual urine dilution, a commercial assay kit (Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, Nanjing, China) was used to measure urinary creatinine (CR) concentrations via the picric acid method, followed by creatinine correction for OPE and PAE concentrations in urine, according to the formula detailed in our previous study.32 2.3. Cord Blood Metabolome Profiling Untargeted metabolomic profiling of cord blood serum was performed using a liquid chromatography−high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC−HRMS) system comprising a Waters ACQUITY UPLC I-Class Plus ultraperformance liquid chromatography system and a Thermo QE HF high-resolution mass spectrometer, operating in both positive and negative ion modes. Detailed methods, including sample extraction, quality control procedures, UPLC MS/MS settings, and data annotation workflows, are provided in Text S3. 2.4. Assessment of ADHD and ASD Symptoms The Chinese version of the Conners Abbreviated Symptom Questionnaire (C-ASQ) was used to assess ADHD symptoms in children aged 3, 5, and 6 years. The C-ASQ included 10 items, with responses ranging from “none” (1) to “a lot” (4). Parents completed the C-ASQ for each age group; a total score ≥15 indicated ADHD symptoms. The C-ASQ is adapted from the Revised Conners Parent Rating Scale.34,35 As previously reported, its sensitivity, accuracy, and specificity are 76.0%, 82.1%, and 92.9%, respectively.34 The internal consistency coefficients (Cronbach’s α) at ages 3, 5, and 6 were 0.871, 0.845, and 0.878, respectively. The number of ADHD symptom questionnaires at ages 3, 5, and 6 was 2884, 1836, and 2136, respectively. The Clancy Autism Behavior Scale (C-ABS) is the most widely used tool for assessing ASD symptoms. The C-ABS includes 14 items completed by parents or guardians. In 1983, researchers in China revised it and adopted a three-point scoring system, replacing the options “yes” and “no” with “never,” “occasionally,” and “often,” assigning scores of 0, 1, and 2, respectively. A total score ≥14 indicated suspected ASD symptoms. In Chinese children, the sensitivity, specificity, and positive predictive value are 58%, 84%, and 65%.33 Cronbach’s α was 0.802, 0.798, and 0.853 at ages 3, 5, and 6 years, respectively. The number for the ASD symptom questionnaire at ages 3, 5, and 6 was 2892, 1838, and 2125, respectively. 2.5. Covariates and Other Information In our study, trained on-site staff collected basic information using the self-designed Maternal and Infant Health Record Form during women’s prenatal checkups. Moreover, pregnancy complications, mode of delivery, fetal birth outcomes, and fetal sex were obtained from the hospital’s electronic medical record system. The intelligence quotient (IQ) of pregnant women was assessed by trained research staff using the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-IV subtest.13 On the basis of previous studies13,25,34 and the use of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to identify potential covariates, the final covariates were as follows: maternal age, prepregnancy body mass index (BMI), gestational weight gain, per capita monthly family income, maternal educational level, delivery mode, parity, maternal IQ, infant sex, and feeding mode, as detailed in Figure S2. 2.6. Statistical Analysis We present quantitative data as the mean ± standard deviation and qualitative data as frequency and composition ratios. The concentrations of OPEs and PAEs below the LOD were estimated as LOD/ √2.36 Intragroup correlation coefficients (ICCs) for OPEs and PAEs before and after CR-adjustment were used to assess reproducibility, which revealed that all OPEs and PAEs exhibited high temporal variability (ICCs ≤0.25; see Table S6) across the three trimesters. As a result, geometric mean values for the three trimesters were calculated to better reflect the average exposure level during pregnancy. Since the concentrations of OPEs and PAEs were generally skewed, their distributions were described using the geometric mean and the 25th−75th percentiles (P25−P75). Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was employed to assess pairwise correlations between OPEs and PAEs. Owing to the skewed distribution, concentrations after CR-adjustment were transformed using the natural logarithm (ln) to approximate normality and were used in subsequent analyses, thereby reducing the influence of extreme values. Missing covariate data were imputed using the random forest method. Differences between groups were analyzed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) for three groups, independent t tests for two groups, and chi-square tests for categorical variables. We used group-based multitrajectory modeling (GBMTM) to analyze the bivariate trajectories of ASD and ADHD symptom scale scores in preschool children at ages 3, 5, and 6. GBMTM enabled the use of a detailed longitudinal data method that employs maximumlikelihood estimation to impute missing data and group individuals with similar patterns of outcomes measured over time.34 To determine the optimal number of stable trajectories for the multitrajectory model and verify the statistical hypotheses, we initially estimated each dimension with TRAJ in Stata. Model selection should take into account field knowledge to ensure the practical usefulness of the findings.37 It should also consider the following: (1) the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), where a value closer to zero indicates a better fit; (2) higher entropy, which indicates more apparent separation between trajectory groups; (3) the average posterior probability (AvePP), which should exceed 0.7; and (4) each trajectory group containing more than 5% of participants.38 Primary analysis employed a four-step approach. First, restricted cubic splines (RCSs) were used to examine whether a nonlinear relationship existed between prenatal OPEs and PAEs with children’s ASD and ADHD symptoms cotrajectory. Second, we conducted stratified multivariate logistic regression analyses by trimester and sex. Third, we used generalized estimating equations (GEEs) to thoroughly assess longitudinal relationships among OPEs/PAEs between ASD/ADHD symptoms. Fourth, we used Bayesian kernel machine regression (BKMR) and quantile-based g-computation (QGC) models to evaluate the association between combined prenatal OPE and PAE exposures and the cotrajectory. To minimize the false-positive rate (Type I error) across multiple comparisons, the false discovery rate (FDR) was used to adjust p-values via the Benjamini−Hochberg method, yielding q-values. In the metabolomics analysis, the metabolite data were log2transformed to achieve normality. Owing to the observed sex disparity, we performed MWAS, combined with the MITM method, separately for boys, girls, and all children. First, a multivariate linear regression model was used to identify metabolites associated with exposure, and a multivariate logistic regression model was used to analyze metabolites related to the cotrajectory, adjusting for relevant covariates. Although an FDR threshold of <0.05 was initially applied, fewer associations remained after correction because of the high dimensionality and limited statistical power of the data. To detect potential subtle associations, nominal p-values (<0.05) were used for exploratory metabolite identification.26 The MITM analysis involved two steps: first, enriched pathways related to exposure and cotrajectory were identified, and second, shared metabolites involved in both associations were identified. Next, the “mediation” package in R was used to further analyze the mediating role of these shared metabolites in the relationship between exposure and cotrajectory. Metabolites showing significant mediation effects were subjected to additional enrichment analysis. Data analysis was conducted using SPSS 23.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL), Stata 14.0 (StataCorp, TX, USA), and R (4.1.2). Graphs were created with GraphPad Prism 9.0 (GraphPad Inc., California, USA), and pathway enrichment analysis was performed using the “MetaboAnalyst 6.0” online platform. The significance level was set at 0.05. 2.7. Sensitivity Analysis To evaluate the robustness of the main results, several sensitivity analyses were conducted. Participant Characteristics Among the 3040 mother−child dyads included in our study, the mean maternal age was 26.66 years, and most mothers (68.9%) had a prepregnancy BMI within the normal range. The majority of mothers (80.5%) had completed high school or higher, and most were primiparous (88.7%). The study group included 1556 boys and 1484 girls. Significant differences (p < 0.05) in prepregnancy BMI, educational level, parity, and IQ scores were detected between the included (n = 3040) and excluded (n = 434) mother−child dyads, as shown in Table S5. 3.2. Maternal OPE Concentration and Variability As shown in Table S6, the detection rates for OPE metabolites ranged from 73.7% to 95.5%, with DPHP achieving the highest rate. The PAE detection rates exceeded 98% for all the compounds, with MEHP showing the lowest rate. For both uncorrected and CR-adjusted concentrations, the ICC for all OPE and PAE metabolites was ≤0.25, indicating poor reproducibility and high variability over time. Associations between OPE and PAE Exposure with Cotrajectory 3.4.1. Individual OPE and PAE Exposure. 3.4.1.1. Nonlinear Associations Between Average OPEs and PAEs with Cotrajectory. Using RCS analysis (Figures S4−S5), we further explored the dose−response relationship between the two substances throughout pregnancy and their cotrajectory after adjusting for covariates. For OPEs, we found a nonlinear relationship between BBOEP (pnonlinear = 0.047) and DBP (pnonlinear = 0.007) with the HST. The results for PAEs revealed a nonlinear relationship between MEHP and the HST (pnonlinear = 0.027); however, no statistically significant nonlinear relationship was observed for the other metabolites (pnonlinear > 0.05). 3.4.1.2. Associations between Average OPEs and PAEs with Cotrajectory Are Shown. The relationships between the average concentrations of OPE and PAE metabolites across pregnancy and cotrajectories are shown in Figure 3A−B and Table S13. Among OPEs, higher DPHP concentrations were associated with an increased risk of being in the HST (OR = 1.20, 95% CI: 1.03, 1.40). However, this association was no longer significant after adjusting for covariates. BBOEP was associated with decreased odds of the MST and HST (q < 0.05), both before and after covariate adjustment. BEHP was associated with an increased risk of HST [OR (95% CI): before, 1.16 (1.02, 1.31); after, 1.20 (1.06, 1.37), q < 0.05], with significance maintained after adjustment for multiple comparisons (Figure 3A). No statistically significant associations were observed for PAEs (Figure 3B). 3.4.1.3. Sex Stratification Analysis of Average OPEs and PAEs with Cotrajectories. The logistic regression model, after adjusting for covariates, revealed that in boys, BBOEP exposure throughout pregnancy was negatively associated with MST (OR = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.73, 0.93) and HST (OR = 0.79, 95% CI: 0.68, 0.92; q < 0.05); BCIPP was also negatively associated with HST among boys (psex‐int < 0.05). However, among girls, only BEHP was associated with an increased risk of HST (OR = 1.27, 95% CI: 1.03, 1.56). For detailed information, please refer to Figure 3A and Table S14. 3.4.1.4. Trimester Stratification Analysis of OPEs and PAEs with Cotrajectories. After adjusting for covariates, compared with the LST, BBOEP in the first trimester was negatively associated with the MST (OR = 0.93, 95% CI: 0.87, 0.99) and HST (OR = 0.87, 95% CI: 0.80, 0.96), and BCIPP was negatively associated with the HST (OR = 0.83, 95% CI: 0.72, 0.96); second-trimester DPHP (OR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.01, 1.26), BEHP (OR = 1.14, 95% CI: 1.04, 1.24), and MBP (OR = 1.15, 95% CI: 1.00, 1.32) were positively linked to the HST, and third-trimester DBP was positively related to the MST (p < 0.05), while TCEP was negatively associated (p < 0.05) (Figure 3C and Table S15). We also observed sex- and trimester-specific disparities (Figure 3C and Table S16). After adjusting for covariates, in boys, BBOEP in the first and third trimesters was negatively associated with MST and HST compared with LST, and DBP in the first trimester was negatively associated with MST. In the second trimester, BCIPP was negatively linked to HST (p < 0.05). In girls, first-trimester DPHP was positively associated with MST and HST (psex‐int < 0.05); in the second trimester, BEHP was positively associated with MST and HST (q < 0.05), whereas TCEP was negatively associated with HST in the second and third trimesters. 3.4.2. Exposure to OPEs and PAEs Mixtures. After adjusting for covariates, the BKMR model indicated that mixed exposure to OPE and PAE metabolites across pregnancy and during the three trimesters was not significantly associated with cotrajectory (Figure S6). We further analyzed exposure by sex across pregnancy and found no mixture effect. However, an interesting pattern emerged: a negative association was observed among boys (Figure 4A−B), whereas the opposite was observed among girls (Figure 4C−D). Additionally, among girls, when the combined concentration exceeded the P75, the risk of HST might increase, and this association was statistically significant (Figure 4D). The QGC model results aligned with those of the BKMR model (Figure 4A−D). 3.5. 3.7. Overlapping Enriched Pathways Associated with Both OPE and PAE Exposure and Cotrajectories The results of the pathway analysis are shown in Figure 5C−D and Table S22. Across all children, metabolites associated with OPEs were primarily enriched in 12 metabolic pathways. In contrast, PAEs were enriched in 7 pathways, with two overlapping pathways (cysteine and methionine metabolism and glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism). For HST, 5 pathways were enriched, four of which were amino acid metabolic pathways. Four pathways were enriched for both exposure and outcome, which were primarily represented by amino acid metabolic pathways (Figure 5C−D and Table S22). In boys, metabolites related to OPEs were enriched mainly in 16 metabolic pathways, whereas those related to PAEs were enriched in 15 pathways, with 7 pathways overlapping. With respect to HST, 7 pathways were enriched, all of which involved amino acid metabolism pathways; regarding MST, 6 pathways were enriched. Five pathways were enriched for both exposure and outcome, which were represented primarily by amino acid metabolic pathways (Figure 5C−D and Table S22). In girls, metabolites related to OPEs were enriched in 8 metabolic pathways, whereas those related to PAEs were enriched in 8 pathways, with only one pathway overlapping (valine, leucine, and isoleucine biosynthesis). For HST, 5 pathways were enriched, and for MST, 2 pathways were enriched. Five pathways were enriched for both exposure and outcome, which were represented primarily by amino acid metabolic pathways (Figure 5C−D and Table S22). In all the children, BBOEP, MMP, MBP, MEHP, MEOHP, and MEHHP all had overlapping pathways with HST. In boys, BBOEP, BEHP, MMP, MEP, MBP, MEHP, and MEHHP all had overlapping pathways with HST, whereas DPHP, MEHP, and MEOHP had overlapping pathways with MST. In girls, only MEHP and MEOHP had overlapping pathways with HST, whereas DBP and MEHP had overlapping pathways with MST (Figures 5C and Table S22). From the above finding, we can see an apparent sex disparity, and OPEs and PAEs may cause neurodevelopmental disorders in offspring via the same metabolic pathways. 3.8. Overlapping Metabolites Associated with Both OPE and PAE Exposure and Cotrajectories The results of the exploratory MITM analysis revealed that the number of cross-metabolites related to OPEs and MST in all children, boys, and girls were 105, 139, and 74, respectively; the numbers of OPEs and HST were 159, 193, and 96, respectively; the numbers of PAEs and MST were 197, 233, and 121, respectively; and the numbers of PAEs and HST were 207, 220, and 211, respectively (Figure 5A and Table S23). After these metabolites were classified, the top three rankings were the same across all the children and, for sex stratification, consisted of lipids and lipid-like molecules, organic acids and derivatives, and organoheterocyclic compounds (Figure 5B). A total of 129 metabolites showed significant mediation in the analysis of all children (105 in the mediation analysis of boys, and 93 in the mediation analysis of girls; Tables S24−S26). We further required that both the total and the mediation effects be significant; only 6 metabolites were significant in all children, 9 in boys, and 6 in girls (Figure 5E). Pathway enrichment analysis of these biomarkers revealed that pyrimidine metabolism mediated exposure to OPEs and the cotrajectory of all children, whereas biotin metabolism and lysine degradation mediated exposure to OPEs and the cotrajectory of boys (Table S27). Cysteine and methionine metabolism mediated exposure to OPEs, whereas purine metabolism mediated exposure to PAEs and the cotrajectory of girls (Table S27). 3.9. Sensitivity Analyses We replaced data < LOD with LOD/2, and using the missingindicator method for OPEs with a detection rate below 85%, the results remained unchanged (Table S28). Further excluded preterm infants, and even after controlling for smoking, alcohol consumption during pregnancy, and folic acid supplementation, the results remained robust (Table S29). Both ADHD and ASD symptom scale scores ultimately follow three trajectories (Table S10 and Figure S9). Some differences were detected between the results for the separate trajectory and the cotrajectories: the effects of prenatal OPE and PAE exposure on the common trajectory were more pronounced (Table S30). 4. DISCUSSION On the basis of 3040 mother-child dyads in the MABC, increased BEHP exposure across pregnancy was associated with a higher risk of HST among preschoolers. BBOEP exhibited significant nonlinear and U-shaped associated HST. Sex-specific disparities were identified. The first-to-second trimester may emerge as a sensitive window. No mixed effects were observed. Prenatal exposure to OPEs and PAEs may be further linked to offspring neurodevelopment through the disruption of cord blood metabolomics. Overall, the concentrations of OPEs detected in pregnant women in our study were comparable to those reported in other Chinese provinces but lower than those reported in Canada and the United States. For a detailed summary, please refer to the previous literature.32 The PAE concentrations in this study also align with those in the most recent Chinese research but differ from those reported in other countries. In summary, the detection rates and patterns for both OPEs and PAEs vary across nations, indicating regional-specific exposure scenarios in which disparities may influence national policies, dietary habits, lifestyles, detection methods, and sampling times. For detailed information, please refer to the cited literature.33 The detection rates of ADHD symptoms at ages 3, 5, and 6 were 6.4%, 2.5%, and 3.2%, respectively. These rates are lower than the global prevalence of 7.2% reported in a metaanalysis.40 North America had the highest prevalence (6.2%), followed by Europe (4.7%), whereas the Middle East had the lowest prevalence (2.3%).41 In Italy, the prevalence among 5 to 17-year-olds ranged from 1.1% to 3.1%, with boys’ prevalence higher than girls’, consistent with our findings.42 ASD symptom detection rates (9.3%, 5.1%, 4.3%) are higher than the global meta-analytic estimate of 1.19%.43 Recent research has also indicated that the highest estimated prevalence occurs in high-income super-regions, with an estimated value of approximately 1090.2 per 100000 people.3 Our higher prevalence reflects screening-based assessment rather than clinical diagnosisa trade-off enhancing efficiency in largescale epidemiology.32,34 Age also drives these variations: ASD emerges with early signs (e.g., language and social delays) at ages 2−3, yielding higher rates in children under 5. manifests with early signssuch as language delays and social withdrawalthat usually become apparent between ages 2 and 3, leading to higher diagnostic rates among children under 5,45 in contrast, inattention/hyperactivity is often missed in children under 5, where behavioral expectations are lower.11 However, entering school, increased academic and behavioral demands make these symptoms more apparent, leading to higher diagnosis rates.46 This phenomenon explains our higher detection rate of ASD than ADHD. Moreover, we reported that ASD detection rates declined with age, aligning with prior reports.45 Because reliance on parental reports may inevitably be influenced by parents’ educational and cultural backgrounds, necessitating cautious interpretation. Our reliance on questionnaire-based scales limits the ability to draw definitive conclusions, underscoring the need for future validation using clinical diagnostics. Due to the questionnaire and the age group, the rate of detected ASD symptoms was high, which may further affect the generalizability of the results. One study reported that maternal exposure to DPHP in the third trimester was associated with an increased risk of ADHD in children.22 Moreover, BBOEP showed no association, with the effect being more pronounced in girls.22 Another study indicated that maternal exposure to di-n-butyl phosphate and bis (1,3-dichloro-2-propyl) phosphate in the first trimester was positively correlated with ADHD among preschool children. As BBOEP exposure increased, the risk decreased among girls but increased among boys.23 A study revealed that maternal di (2-ethylhexyl) phthalate exposure in the third trimester increased the odds ratio for ASD among 2-year-olds.47 Prenatal MEHHP exposure was also associated with increased ADHD symptoms in children aged 2.5 and 11 years (OR = 2.98) in both sexes.48 Kim et al. further demonstrated a positive association between MEHHP and ASD traits in 4-year-old children, with stronger correlations observed in boys.49 Prenatal exposure to mixed PAEs was also positively correlated with behavioral disorders such as ADHD.50 Concurrently, our prior research indicated that prenatal exposure to PAEs increases offspring risk for ASD symptoms, with notable sex disparities.33 We observed a negative correlation between BBOEP and the cotrajectories. This phenomenon may be due to the nonlinear effect of BBOEP suggested by the Maternal And Developmental Risks from Environmental and Social Stressors study.51 Our RCS analysis revealed that, in the highscore trajectory, significant nonlinear and U-shaped patterns emerged during maternal BBOEP exposure. This finding explains why some compounds are positively correlated while others are negatively correlated. Future explanations of how exposure influences health outcomes should consider differences in dose and chemical potency. Few studies have combined OPE and PAE exposure. Our prior work confirmed that combined prenatal exposure to OPEs and PAEs impairs offspring cognition.13 Although no overall population combined effect was observed, girls exposed above the 75th percentile showed an increased risk of HST. The underlying mechanisms of OPE/PAE that affect children’s neurodevelopment remain unclear. Animal studies link environmental OPE/PAE exposures to altered early behavioral development via multiple pathways (inflammation, neurotransmitter systems, oxidative stress, endocrine disruption).51 A study found that OPEs reduced glutamate and dopamine, triggering inflammation and disrupting myelin formation.52 The placenta mediates OPE neurotoxicity, with greater accumulation in male placentas driving reduced prefrontal serotonin, inflammation, and endocrine disruption.51 OPE/PAE metabolites may disrupt fetal neurodevelopment by interfering with maternal thyroid hormone levels.13,33,34 PAE exhibit complex sex hormone interactions (estrogenic/androgenic effects), likely driving the observed sex-specific responses, and vary with exposure timing. For example, early exposure to endocrine-disrupting compounds is strongly associated with greater male behavioral deficits, while females may be more susceptible to stress encountered in later life.53 Sex-specific trajectories underscore the need for sexstratified analyses to avoid misclassifying risk and to inform targeted public health interventions. Our results showed that different chemicals present different effects and patterns. These inconsistencies may be attributed to various factors, such as misclassification of exposure, critical exposure windows, sexspecific effects, and the influence of other mixtures.53 Our findings demonstrate that prenatal OPE/PAE exposures disrupt cord blood lipid metabolism and accumulation, corroborating prior research on their established effects on offspring’s physical development.32,54 Pathway analysis linked both OPEs and PAEs predominantly to amino acid metabolism, notably cysteine and methionine metabolism/ glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism, with enhanced convergence observed specifically in male offspring. Exposure− outcome pathway overlaps revealed histidine metabolism/ glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism/lysine degradation/ pantothenate and CoA biosynthesis. Mediation analysis revealed that pyrimidine metabolism mediated the effects of OPEs across all children. Sex-specific pathways included biotin metabolism and lysine degradation (boys, OPEs) and cysteine/methionine and purine metabolism (girls, OPEs/PAEs). These mediation pathways are biologically coherent. Purine and pyrimidine metabolism are fundamental to brain development, where nucleotide imbalances disrupt phospholipid synthesis and membrane integrity, linking OPEs/PAEs to neurodevelopmental risk.54−57 Biotin is an essential cofactor for neurodevelopment, supporting neuronal energy metabolism and gene regulation via histone biotinylation;58−61 its role aligns with our prior finding that prenatal vitamin supplementation mitigates environmental neurotoxicity.13,33,34 Lysine degradation provides acetyl-CoA for myelin and cholesterol synthesis, while cysteine/methionine metabolism maintains glutathione-dependent antioxidant defenses critical for protecting the lipid-rich developing brain.62−65 Together, these pathways suggest that prenatal OPEs and PAEs exert neurotoxic effects primarily by disrupting metabolic homeostasis rather than through direct neurotoxicity, consistent with prior research findings.15,25−27 Our study has several strengths, including a prospective birth cohort design and a comprehensive collection of gestational data. An integrated metabolomics framework was employed to identify overlapping pathways and metabolites involved in the association between maternal urinary OPEs and PAEs and the cotrajectory of preschoolers’ ADHD-ASD symptoms. This approach enabled a holistic evaluation of all metabolites detected within pathways to assess potential mediating pathways. Furthermore, our study included multiple outcome assessments and conducted cotrajectory analyses, offering novel insights for future research. The relatively large sample size of our study also enhances the robustness of the outcome findings. Our study has several limitations. First, residual confounding factorssuch as exposure to OPEs and PAEs during Environmental Science & Technology pubs.acs.org/est Article https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.6c01402 Environ. Sci. childhood, physical activity, and sleep patternsmay remain in observational studies and could affect the observed associations. Second, two scales were used to evaluate ADHD and ASD symptoms in children. However, while these scales are suitable for large-scale epidemiological surveys, their sensitivity and specificity are limited. Additionally, among the 3040 mother−child dyads included in our study, 94.9%, 60.4%, and 70.3% of the children underwent follow-up for ADHD symptoms at ages of 3, 5, and 6 years, respectively, while 95.1%, 60.5%, and 69.9% underwent follow-up for ASD symptoms at these ages. More than 30% of the children lacked available scores, which could introduce bias when interpreting the model results stratified by age. Therefore, comparisons across age-stratified models should be approached with caution. Third, in this observational exploratory study, the use of an uncorrected significance threshold in metabolomics analysis may increase the Type I error rate, but this was a necessary compromise to balance the likelihood of missed discoveries and the risk of false discoveries.26 These results should still be considered preliminary and exploratory, and they should be interpreted with caution. Fourth, the metabolite detection method employed in this study utilized a nontargeted metabolomics strategy. Fifth, we employed the ACQUITY UPL CHSST3 column for metabolite separation, which exhibited poor retention of both nonpolar and polar compounds, potentially resulting in fewer metabolites being detected.66,67 Finally, owing to variations in geographic location, lifestyle habits, and regional levels of control over environmental pollutants, exposure levels to OPEs/PAEs differ among populations. Overall, the results of this study support the current mechanistic understanding of how prenatal exposure to OPEs and PAEs may be linked to neonatal metabolomics and how these biological disruptions could influence neurobehavioral outcomes. Further research is needed to assess the generalizability of these findings, examine differences across populations, incorporate additional coexposures, and explore the potential of these metabolic responses for detection, treatment, and prevention strategies in public health and clinical settings. ■ASSOCIATED CONTENT Data Availability Statement Data from all participants in this study were anonymized and accessible only to authorized members of the study team. * sı Supporting Information The Supporting Information is available free of charge at https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.est.6c01402. metadata_title: The Effect of Methylphenidate Treatment on Oxidative Stress Levels in Children Diagnosed with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: An Observational Study
pages: The Effect of Methylphenidate Treatment on Oxidative Stress Levels in Children Diagnosed with Attention-Deficit/ Hyperactivity Disorder: An Observational Study Enes Faruk Altunkılıc, MD,1 Alper Alnak, MD,2 Gul Karacetın, MD,2 Hacer Eroglu Iclı, MD,2 Binay Kayan Ocakoglu, MD,2 and Ipek Ege Gurel Fıcıcıoglu, MD2 Abstract Background: Oxidative stress (OS) has been implicated in the pathophysiology of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), yet findings—particularly regarding treatment-related changes—remain inconsistent. This study evaluated short-term differences in circulating oxidant/antioxidant markers after methylphenidate (MPH) treatment and explored whether baseline biomarkers predict clinically significant symptom improvement. Methods: In this single-center, prospective observational cohort study, medication-naïve children aged 6–11 years diagnosed with DSM-5-TR ADHD were assessed at enrollment and after 3 months of conventional MPH treatment. Clinical severity was measured using the Conners’ Parent Rating Scale–Revised: Short Form (CPRS-R:S) and Conners’ Teacher Rating Scale–Revised: Short Form (CTRS-R:S). Serum biomarkers included total oxidant status (TOS), total antioxidant status (TAS), superoxide dismutase (SOD), malondialdehyde (MDA), oxidized LDL (Ox-LDL), and the OS index (OSI = TOS/TAS). Changes were tested with paired analyses; correlations were examined between percent changes in scale scores and biomarkers; and ROC analyses evaluated baseline biomarkers’ ability to identify a >50% reduction in CPRS-R:S and CTRS-R:S total scores. Results: Thirty-nine participants completed both assessments (SOD analyses: n = 37). Significant reductions were observed in CPRS-R: S and CTRS-R:S total and subscale scores (all p < .001). TOS, TAS, SOD, MDA, and Ox-LDL decreased significantly over 3 months, while OSI showed a nonsignificant downward trend (p = 0.066). No significant correlations emerged between percent symptom change and percent biomarker change. In ROC analyses, baseline MDA, Ox-LDL, and TOS significantly discriminated >50% CPRS-R:S improvement (AUC  0.71–0.74), whereas for >50% CTRS-R:S improvement, several biomarkers demonstrated good discrimination (AUC  0.82–0.85). Conclusions: Three months of MPH treatment was associated with robust clinical improvement and parallel reductions in multiple oxidant and antioxidant biomarkers. Baseline OS markers may help identify children most likely to show marked symptom reduction, though findings should be interpreted cautiously, given the sample size. Keywords: attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), oxidative stress, methylphenidate, observational study, prepubertal Introduction A ttention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a multifaceted neurodevelopmental disorder with childhood onset, distinguished by hyperactivity, inattention, and impulsivity, and it can negatively affect an individual’s academic and social functioning across the lifespan (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). Globally, its prevalence among children and adolescents is estimated to range from approximately 7.2% to 8.0%, and it is observed about twice as often in boys as in girls (Ayano et al., 2023; Elia et al., 2008; Faraone et al., 2021). Recent studies suggest that oxidative stress (OS) and neuroinflammation may play a critical role in the ADHD pathogenesis (Corona, 2020; Visternicu et al., 2024). Brain tissue is particularly susceptible to oxidative damage due to its high oxygen consumption, abundant lipid content, and relatively limited antioxidant defense mechanisms compared with other organs (Ceylan et al., 2012; Visternicu et al., 2024). OS, defined as a disruption in the balance between antioxidant and oxidant systems, can trigger neurological damage by facilitating lipid peroxidation in cell membranes, inducing DNA damage, and impairing neurotransmitter receptor function (Lopresti, 2015; Visternicu et al., 2024). Findings about the relationship between OS and ADHD remain inconsistent in the current literature; while some studies report increased OS and reduced antioxidant capacity in individuals with ADHD, others have found no significant differences (Bas ̧ay et al., 2025; Guney et al., 2015; Miniksar et al., 2023; Oztop et al., 2012; Visternicu et al., 2024). Specifically, antioxidant response has a complex nature. Some studies highlight that, in response to an increased oxidant burden, the body may upregulate antioxidant levels (e.g., total antioxidant status [TAS]) through compensatory mechanisms (Guney et al., 2015; Selek et al., 2012). This may indicate that, once oxidant levels return to normal, the body may, as an adaptive response, downregulate its defense mechanisms (Aydın et al., 2024; Bas ̧ay et al., 2025). Although most clinical studies suggest that methylphenidate (MPH) restores redox balance by strengthening antioxidant defenses, experimental models also provide evidence that stimulants may paradoxically induce oxidative damage; therefore, findings regarding the effects of MPH are inconsistent (Foschiera et al., 2022; Garre-Morata et al., 2024; Martins et al., 2006; Sanches et al., 2025). First-line pharmacological agents for ADHD, such as the psychostimulant MPH, improve symptoms by blocking norepinephrine and dopamine transporters (Shier et al., 2013; Spencer et al., 2005). However, the effects of MPH on oxidative mechanisms in human plasma and the neuroadaptive consequences of long-term use remain controversial. Some recent studies report that MPH treatment may restore disrupted redox balance by enhancing antioxidant defense mechanisms and, in parallel with symptomatic improvement, may reduce serum OS (Foschiera et al., 2022; Garre-Morata et al., 2024; Novo et al., 2023; Visternicu et al., 2024). This study aims to fill a gap in the literature by analyzing the potential effects of MPH treatment on plasma oxidant/antioxidant parameters in treatment-naive children aged 6–11 years with ADHD and also by examining the relations between these parameters and clinical rating scales. Methods Study design and setting This single-center, prospective cohort (observational) study investigated changes in oxidant/antioxidant parameters in children diagnosed with ADHD according to DSM-5-TR criteria by comparing pretreatment values with those obtained at the third month of MPH treatment. The study was conducted at the Child Psychiatry Outpatient Clinic of Bakirkoy Prof. Dr. Mazhar Osman Training and Research Hospital for Psychiatry and Neurological Diseases, Istanbul, T€urkiye. Participants were recruited between August 2024 and January 2025 and followed for 3 months. Participants and eligibility criteria Children aged 6–11 years presenting to the outpatient clinic with a previous or new ADHD diagnosis and for whom MPH initiation was planned were enrolled. This prepubertal age range was selected to reduce developmental (puberty-related) variability in OS-related processes and thereby improve interpretability of biomarker changes. Families received study information, and the legal guardian provided a written consent; written assent was obtained from literate children, and verbal assent from nonliterate children following verbal information. Exclusion criteria were autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, or having other neurodevelopmental disorders; hereditary/metabolic disorders, structural brain abnormalities, or progressive neurological disease; active infection, allergic disease, or any chronic medical condition; alcohol or psychoactive substance use; current use of any psychotropic or nonpsychotropic medication; and any prior use of psychotropic medication for any reason, including ADHD medication. Eligibility criteria were shared with experienced child psychiatrists providing active clinical care; potentially eligible cases were referred and reevaluated by the principal investigator. Diagnoses and comorbidities were assessed using the Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age Children—Present and Lifetime Version, DSM-5 Turkish Adaptation (K-SADS-PLDSM-5-T) (Kaufman et al., 1997; Unal et al., 2019). Families were informed that participation would not affect routine clinical care. Clinical follow-up and treatment As an observational study, treatment followed routine practice and clinical indications. Only MPH-containing preparations were used. Formulation (immediate-release, intermediate-release, and long-acting [OROS]) and dosing were determined by the treating physician based on weight, clinical status, and adverse effects, and were titrated during follow-up. Routine visits were scheduled every 4 weeks, with earlier visits when needed (e.g., adverse effects or family concerns). The researcher’s contact information was provided for adverse or unexpected events. Blood sampling and sample processing Participants attended between 09:00 and 12:00 following 10– 12 hours of fasting. Sociodemographic and clinical data were recorded, and ‡5 mL venous blood was collected into a yellow-top gel serum separator tube. Samples were rested at room temperature for 10–20 minutes and centrifuged at approximately 1000 · g for 20 minutes, and the serum was separated into Eppendorf tubes and stored at -80C until analysis. The serum samples were transferred from -80C to a +4C environment 15 hours before the scheduled analysis. After 15 hours at +4C, the samples were removed and analyzed. After blood collection, MPH treatment was prescribed by the treating physician at an appropriate dose and formulation. Participant flow The study was planned to conclude once 39 participants completed both baseline and month-3 assessments; withdrawals were replaced by new participants. Overall, 53 participants provided written informed consent and entered the study; 14 withdrew for various reasons, and recruitment continued until 39 completers were reached. Analyses were conducted in participants with complete baseline and measurements at the third month. OXIDATIVE STRESS MARKERS AFTER MPH IN ADHD 201

Serum assays Frozen serum samples stored at -80C were transferred to +4C and kept for 15 hours before analysis. The five biomarkers (TAS, total oxidant status [TOS], malondialdehyde [MDA], superoxide dismutase [SOD], and oxidized LDL [Ox-LDL]) were measured simultaneously using ELISA kits from Bioassay Technology Laboratory: TAS (Cat. No. E4350Hu; Shanghai, China), TOS (Cat. No. E1599Hu; Shanghai, China), MDA (Cat. No. E1371Hu; Shanghai, China), SOD (Cat. No. E0918; Shanghai, China), and Ox-LDL (Cat. No. E1521Hu; Shanghai, China). Assays were performed in the Medical Biochemistry Laboratories of Bakirkoy Dr. Sadi Konuk Training and Research Hospital by a biochemistry specialist according to manufacturers’ ELISA protocols. Plate washing and reading were conducted using an Allsheng Microplate Washer APW-200 and an Allsheng Microplate Reader AMR-100T (Hangzhou, China). OS index (OSI) was calculated as TOS/TAS. In brief, standards and samples were loaded (40 lL serum), specific antibody (10 lL) was added, plates were incubated at 37C for 60 minutes, washed five times, substrate solutions A and B (50 lL each) were added, plates were incubated for 10 minutes at 37C in the dark, and stop solution (50 lL) was added before reading at 450 nm within 10 minutes (see Images 1 and 2). Data collection instruments Informed consent for voluntary participation: Legal guardians were informed about study aims, procedures, potential risks, and voluntariness; written informed consent was obtained (signed by the legal guardian and the researcher). For pediatric participants, assent procedures followed the “Turkish Medicines and Medical Devices Agency” guideline on “Ethical Approaches in Clinical Research Conducted in the Pediatric Population”; written assent was obtained from literate children and verbal assent from nonliterate children. Sociodemographic and clinical data form: A researcher-developed form recorded sociodemographic characteristics (e.g., age, sex, educational status, family income level) and clinical data, including height, weight, and body mass index (BMI). Diagnostic assessment: To confirm ADHD and assess comorbidities, the K-SADS-PL-DSM-5-T was administered by the researcher (Kaufman et al., 1997; Unal et al., 2019). ADHD symptom severity scales Parents completed the Conners’ Parent Rating Scale–Revised: Short Form (CPRS-R:S) and teachers completed the Conners’ Teacher Rating Scale–Revised: Short Form (CTRS-R:S) (Conners, 1997; Kaner et al., 2013a; Kaner et al., 2013b). Items are rated 0–3, with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity. Scales were administered at baseline and repeated at month 3. Control of confounding factors To reduce confounding, we included only 6- to 11-year-old children with confirmed ADHD, no significant psychiatric comorbidity, and no prior psychotropic exposure (including ADHD pharmacotherapy). Blood sampling was postponed in cases of active infection or acute transient illness until recovery, and children with chronic medical conditions were excluded. Seasonal and subclinical influences on OS markers could not be entirely eliminated and may have modestly affected results. Sample size calculation Sample size was based on a similar study examining the preand posttreatment change in the ARES serum biomarker after MPH (Guney et al., 2015). Using ARES values from that study and assuming r = 0.50 between paired measurements, an a priori power analysis was conducted in G*Power 3.1 for a pairedsamples t-test (means: difference between two dependent means, matched pairs) (Faul et al., 2007, 2009). With two-tailed alpha = 0.05 and power (1 - beta) = 0.80, the estimated effect size was Cohen’s d_z = 0.56, yielding a minimum required sample size of n = 27. To increase power, we targeted 39 completers. Statistical analysis Analyses were conducted using Jamovi (Jamovi project, 2025; R Core Team, 2025) (retrieved from https://www.jamovi.org). Descriptive statistics (mean, standard deviation, median, and percentages) were summarized in tables or bar charts. Normality was assessed using Shapiro–Wilk tests (Ghasemi and Zahediasl, 2012; Mohd Razali and Bee Wah, 2011). For paired comparisons, paired-samples t-tests were used when difference scores were normally distributed; otherwise, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were applied. Effect sizes were reported as Cohen’s d for paired t-tests and rank-biserial correlation for Wilcoxon tests (Cohen, 2013; Pallant, 2020). Correlations between percentage changes in total Conners’ scores (CPRS-R:S and CTRS-R:S) (Percent change = [Baseline - Month 3]/Baseline · 100) and percentage changes in OS biomarkers were examined using Pearson correlations for normally distributed variables and Spearman’s rho when appropriate. Exploratory (hypothesis-generating) ROC curve analyses evaluated whether baseline biomarkers discriminated participants achieving a ‡50% reduction in total CPRS-R:S and CTRS-R:S scores at month 3 (Coghill et al., 2020; Pelsser et al., 2009). For ROC analyses, AUC, 95% confidence interval (CI), p values, and optimal cutoffs (Youden index) with sensitivity/specificity were reported (Robin et al., 2010). Given the small sample size, CIs are reported, and ROC findings should be interpreted as exploratory. Two-tailed p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR-BH) correction was applied for multiple comparisons; this is indicated in the relevant tables/text. Recruitment continued until 39 completers were reached, and analyses included participants with complete baseline and month-3 measurements. For SOD, two samples showed no reaction (no color change) and could not be read; thus, SOD analyses were based on n = 37. Results Participant flow diagram A total of 53 participants were enrolled, 14 were lost to followup, and 39 completed the study. Reasons for withdrawal/exclusion (n = 14) were nonattendance and unreachable by phone (n = 5), children’s refusal to take medication (n = 2), parental refusal due to stigma concerns (n = 2), parental concerns about potential adverse effects (n = 2), request for a second specialist opinion (n = 2), and dizziness at treatment initiation (n = 1). Participants who withdrew were replaced with additional eligible participants during the study period (Fig. 1). No enrolled participant (including those who later withdrew) reported rare or very rare adverse effects, and no serious medically significant adverse events occurred. 202 ALTUNKILIC ET AL.

Sociodemographic and clinical characteristics The mean age was 8.38 – 1.11 years, and 67.7% were male. School grades ranged from preschool to seventh grade, with the majority of patients being in second grade (25.0%) and first grade (20.0%). Most parents were married (82.1%), and a first-degree family history of psychiatric disorders was reported in 23.1%. Academic achievement was classified as low (42.1%), moderate (36.8%), or high (21.1%); the preschool participant was excluded from this analysis (Table 1). Changes in rating scale scores and serum parameters with treatment Over 3 months of MPH treatment, symptom severity decreased substantially on both parent- and teacher-rated Conners’ scales. Total CPRS-R:S and CTRS-R:S scores both showed significant improvement from baseline to month 3 (both p < 0.001), and improvements were observed across all subscales (all p < 0.001) (Table 2). Serum OS parameters also changed over the treatment period (Table 3). TOS, TAS, SOD, MDA, and Ox-LDL decreased significantly from baseline to month 3 (p £ 0.021 for all), whereas OSI showed a small, nonsignificant change (p = 0.066). After applying the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction for multiple comparisons, the significance status of the parameters did not change (Table 3). Correlations between percentage changes in Conners’ total scores (CPRS-R:S and CTRS-R:S) and percentage changes in OS biomarkers were not statistically significant (Table 4). Exploratory ROC analyses examined whether baseline OS biomarkers discriminated participants achieving a ‡50% reduction in Conners’ total scores at month 3. For CPRS-R:S responders (n = 33), baseline MDA, Ox-LDL, and TOS demonstrated significant discrimination with moderate performance (Fig. 2A; Supplementary Data). For CTRS-R:S responders (n = 31), discrimination was significant for multiple biomarkers and was generally stronger for teacher-rated outcomes (Fig. 2B; Supplementary Data). Detailed ROC parameters (cutoffs, sensitivity, specificity, and CIs) are provided in the Supplementary Data. Discussion In this prospective, observational, single-center cohort study, OS and clinical change after 3 months of MPH monotherapy in 6to 11-year-old children with ADHD diagnosed according to DSM5-TR were evaluated. Clinically, CPRS-R:S and CTRS-R:S total and subscale scores decreased significantly at the third month, consistent with current evidence supporting MPH efficacy in ADHD. Biochemically, significant decreases were observed in TOS, MDA, and Ox-LDL, alongside reductions in TAS and SOD. OSI (TOS/TAS) showed a downward trend, but it was not statistically significant. Previous studies primarily examine the relationship between OS and ADHD cross-sectionally and include ADHD and control groups. These studies generally report higher oxidant parameters in ADHD, whereas findings for antioxidant parameters are less consistent, although they are often lower (Corona, 2020; Joseph et al., 2015; Sezen et al., 2016). A meta-analysis likewise found higher oxidant biomarkers in ADHD but no difference in antioxidant biomarkers compared with controls; heterogeneity was particularly influenced by age, with larger effect sizes in children than in adults, leading the authors to recommend greater focus on pediatric samples (Joseph et al., 2015). Overall, studies on children and adolescents, particularly those targeting the preadolescent period, remain limited. As puberty involves substantial biological changes that may influence OS, we focused on a preadolescent sample to reduce potential confounders and to address this gap in the literature. In studies assessing TOS, TAS, and OSI, oxidant markers such as TOS and OSI have generally been reported to be higher in patients with ADHD than in controls, whereas TAS has typically been lower (Koç et al., 2023). Similar patterns have been seen in several cross-sectional case-control studies (Kul et al., 2015; Sezen et al., 2016). In a 2015 study, TOS and OSI were higher in ADHD, while TAS did not differ between groups, and the authors attributed this to compensatory mechanisms (Guney et al., 2015). Findings have also been inconsistent across adulthood; one study reported no group differences in TOS or TAS (Aksoy et al., 2020), whereas another found higher TOS, OSI, and TAS in adults with ADHD, attributing elevated TAS as a compensatory response (Selek et al., 2012). MDA is a metabolite of chain reactions that result from the oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids. Therefore, it serves as a marker of OS and has been linked to various neuropsychiatric disorders. In several studies conducted on ADHD, higher MDA levels have been reported in patients with ADHD compared with control groups (Bulut et al., 2013; Ceylan et al., 2010; Elhady et al., 2019). For SOD, an antioxidant enzyme, the literature is inconsistent, similar to other antioxidant measures. Some studies have reported lower SOD levels in patients with ADHD (Ceylan et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2022). There are also studies reporting no significant difference in SOD levels between the ADHD and control groups (Ceylan et al., 2012; Russo, 2010). MPH on OS have resulted in highly inconsistent findings, and several explanations have been proposed. Acute, supratherapeutic exposure of MPH may induce OS in young rats due to insufficient antioxidant defenses, whereas chronic therapeutic exposure has been suggested to increase antioxidant enzyme activity and also adaptive mechanisms, thereby not enhancing OS in the brain (Sanches et al., 2023; Schmitz et al., 2012; Witt et al., 2010). Observational studies on treatment-related oxidative changes in humans remain limited. In the second phase of a 2015 study involving children aged 6–18 years, MPH was associated with increased antioxidant levels and reduced OSI (Guney et al., 2015). Similarly, another study in children and adolescents reported reductions in oxidant biomarkers alongside increases in antioxidant biomarkers during MPH treatment (Garre-Morata et al., 2024). In this study, decreases in both oxidant and antioxidant levels after MPH treatment in children with ADHD were consistent with some reports but differed from others. Notably, our findings align with studies that emphasize compensatory mechanisms and interpret results within this framework. The literature recognizes that the oxidant and antioxidant systems operate in a complementary balance and influence one another. Recent evidence also suggests that low-dose chronic OS can enhance adaptive responses and thereby increase antioxidant activity (Wan et al., 2024; Wang and Wang, 2025). Antioxidants neutralize the body’s oxidant burden. Therefore, for many antioxidant systems, oxidants that exert toxic effects serve as the substrates they act upon (Ji and Yeo, 2021). As the oxidant burden increases, it is predictable that antioxidant system activity may also increase. Indeed, when the aforementioned ADHD studies are taken into account, the observation that inconsistent findings predominantly involve antioxidant biomarkers suggests that antioxidant measures may vary in accordance with oxidant levels (Altun et al., 2018; Davinelli et al., 2025). Within this framework, our results suggest that the magnitude of change in oxidant biomarkers after MPH treatment was greater than that observed for antioxidant biomarkers. In other words, antioxidant measures showed a smaller decrease than oxidant measures. This pattern is consistent with a compensatory perspective. We interpret these findings as follows: When ADHD is treated with MPH, the oxidant burden decreases, and, as a result, there is less need for antioxidant defenses to detoxify it, leading to a secondary decline in antioxidant levels.
