Bioscience Reports (2026) 46 BSR20254061 https://doi.org/10.1042/BSR20254061 Causal inference Beyond quantifying genetic correlations, GWAS enable the assessment of whether observed relationships arise from vertical pleiotropy (i.e., due to causal effects) or horizontal pleiotropy, in which shared genetic influences without direct causality play a role [350]. For instance, Mendelian randomization (MR) studies have provided evidence supporting a causal relationship between ADHD liability and an increased likelihood of tobacco smoking initiation, smoking heaviness, and cannabis initiation as well as a decreased likelihood of tobacco smoking cessation. Conversely, the genetic liability to substance use does not appear to cause ADHD, suggesting that associations in this direction are likely attributable to horizontal pleiotropy [386]. Moreover, the most comprehensive MR study to date expanded these findings by evaluating causal relationships between ADHD liability and 124 traits spanning anthropometry measures, cognitive function, early-life exposures, education attainment, college completion, employment, lifestyle and environment, longevity, and psychiatric and mental health [387]. The present study provided evidence for a causal effect of ADHD genetic liability on decreasing average total household income and increasing the lifetime number of sexual partners. It also identified positive effects of anthropometric traits, such as predicted arm mass and weight, and time spent watching television on ADHD liability. Furthermore, the results revealed bidirectional negative effects between ADHD and educational outcomes, including years of schooling and the age of completing full-time education. Similar bidirectional effects were observed between ADHD liability and age at first sexual intercourse, as well as past tobacco smoking in non-heavy smokers. These findings underscore the complex interplay between genetic and environmental factors—many of which are themselves genetically influenced—that contribute to ADHD and its broader impact on life outcomes. Other ‘omics’ Several studies have investigated ADHD using other ‘omics’ approaches in both human samples and animal models. While these studies are typically smaller in scale than GWAS, they still provide insights into environmental and molecular mechanisms contributing to the disorder. They encompass the epigenome, reflecting environmentally driven modifications; the transcriptome and proteome, which capture tissue- and cell-specific molecular signatures; and the metagenome, which examines the influence of the gut microbiome. Epigenomic research in ADHD has primarily focused on 5-methylcytosine levels, assessed either at birth or during childhood, often in longitudinal cohorts. Early studies identified specific genes with differential methylation patterns, though replication has been inconsistent, likely due to methodological differences [388–391]. Nevertheless, two specific gene findings are worth mentioning: VIPR2 (vasoactive intestinal polypeptide receptor 2) replicated between studies [389,391] and associated with brain functioning and ST3GAL3, previously linked to intellectual disability [392] and associated with ADHD through GWAS [54] and animal models [393]. Large meta-analyses have shown enrichment for genes related to brain development and function at birth but not in later childhood [394]. In adults, findings instead implicated immune- and neuron-related genes, as well as loci linked to autoimmune disease, cancer, and neuroticism [395,396]. More recent work highlights the dynamic nature of the methylome, showing that epigenome-wide association studies (EWAS) findings at one developmental stage may not generalize to others [397]. Global methylation levels (GMe) were also explored in ADHD patients, being lower than in controls, as well as in women [398]. In addition, a polygenic risk score (PRS) for ADHD was negatively correlated with GMe, showing the intersection between ADHD genomics and the epigenome [398]. Taken together, these studies underscore the need for caution when interpreting epigenomic signals, particularly given sex-specific effects and developmental timing. Transcriptomic research has aimed to clarify the functional roles of ADHD risk genes identified by GWAS. Early studies of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) in persistent ADHD implicated the ubiquitin-proteasome system [399], while later analyses reported differentially expressed genes overlapping with other psychiatric and comorbid conditions [400]. MicroRNA studies have revealed disrupted myo-inositol signaling [401] and immune-related pathways [402]. More recently, a comprehensive multi-step study in PBMCs identified seven modules of co-expressed genes enriched for genetic and epigenetic risk signatures, implicating pathways related to gene regulation, epigenetics, and immune function [403]. These findings highlighted candidate genes and pathways, underscoring the potential of blood-based expression studies and the value of multi-omics integration for advancing our understanding of ADHD biology. Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) integrating expression quantitative trait loci with GWAS signals [53] demonstrated enrichment for genes expressed in fetal astrocytes, neurons, and microglia/macrophages [404]. A follow-up TWAS leveraging the gene-based ADHD GWAS showed enrichment for genes expressed in the brain, particularly in the cortex [54]. Proteomic studies in ADHD remain scarce. Animal models include WKY rats, SHR rats, Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats, and thyroid hormone-responsive protein-overexpressing (THRSP-OE) mice. Striatal protein profiling in WKY, SHR, and SD rats found no significant changes following maternal separation [406]. In contrast, THRSP-OE mice showed hippocampal Wnt signaling dysregulation linked to impaired attention, memory deficits, and altered neural stem cell activity [407], as well as striatal Snap25 overexpression, suggesting SNARE (Soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor Attachment protein REceptor) complex dysfunction and neurotransmitter dysregulation [408]. Only one study has investigated the impact of ADHD treatment on the proteome, showing that methylphenidate altered cortical protein expression in WKY rats, with enriched effects on components of synaptic transmission (e.g., SNARE) that were also observed in clinical samples [409,410]. Microbiome and metagenome studies support a role for gut microbiota in ADHD pathophysiology via the gut–brain axis. Microbiota assessed via 16s measurements have shown differences between ADHD cases and typical development controls in diversity levels [411–413] and specific taxa [411–417]. However, meta-analysis results only support differences in the Shannon index of alpha diversity and the increase in the Blautia genus in ADHD patients [418]. On the other hand, case–control studies exploring shotgun metagenomics report reduced abundance of beneficial taxa such as Faecalibacterium and Veillonellaceae and increased levels of Odoribacter and Enterococcus, with functional pathway analysis implicating neurotransmitter metabolism, including serotonin and dopamine [419]. Larger cohorts confirmed significant differences in microbial diversity and identified potential microbial biomarkers of ADHD spanning nine representative species that best explain the differences [420]. Integrative metagenomics-metabolomics approaches further revealed disruptions in nicotinamide metabolism, while fecal microbiota transplantation from ADHD patients into rats induced hyperactivity-like behaviors, suggesting a potential causal contribution of the microbiome in ADHD-related traits [421]. Nonetheless, the causal direction between microbiome variability and ADHD symptoms remains unclear. It is also important to note that the studies cited here have several limitations, including small sample sizes and substantial heterogeneity in diversity metrics and taxonomic classification, which increase the risk of false-positive associations [422]. Overall, this is an evolving field that would benefit from more standardized guidelines and evaluation criteria. Environmental contributions Environmental factors play a key role in ADHD, particularly through non-shared influences that uniquely affect individuals, as demonstrated in twin studies [352,423]. While psychosocial adversities—such as poverty and negative parenting—may not directly cause ADHD, they can shape its course and prognosis, especially in Western contexts where most studies have been conducted [8,424]. Early developmental periods are especially sensitive to environmental factors, including low birth weight, prematurity, maternal stress, and prenatal exposure to substances such as tobacco and alcohol [425–429]. Environmental pollution has also emerged as a factor of growing interest in neurodevelopmental research [430–432]. Recent meta-analyses report associations between exposure to lead and traffic-related pollutants, particularly fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and increased likelihood of ADHD diagnosis or greater symptom burden, although effect sizes are typically modest and findings vary across studies depending on exposure window, assessment strategy, and control for socioeconomic and contextual factors [430,431,433]. Importantly, the current body of evidence does not support the view that environmental pollution acts as a deterministic cause of ADHD [430,431]. Rather, it is more consistent with a multifactorial liability model in which environmental exposures may contribute to risk magnitude or symptom expression, particularly among individuals with pre-existing neurobiological or genetic vulnerability. How these exposures become biologically embedded is therefore a central question. Some of these environmental effects may be mediated by epigenetic mechanisms, such as DNA hypo- or hypermethylation, which influence gene expression and have been linked to ADHD status and symptom variability [395,397,398,434]. Additionally, somatic mutations occurring during early embryonic development may lead to brain mosaicism and help explain why monozygotic twins can differ phenotypically [435,436]. Bioscience Reports (2026) 46 BSR20254061 https://doi.org/10.1042/BSR20254061 An additional dimension involves gene-environment correlation (rGE), whereby genetic factors shape the environments individuals are exposed to. This can occur passively (e.g., disorganized households reflecting inherited traits), evocatively (e.g., impulsive children eliciting negative parental responses), or actively (e.g., selecting peer groups or environments aligned with genetically influenced tendencies) [439–442]. Recognizing the role of rGE is essential not only for informing clinical strategies, such as psychoeducation and family-based interventions, but also for interpreting associations between ADHD and environmental exposures correctly. These interpretative challenges are evident in studies of environmental risk factors potentially involved in ADHD. Paracetamol use during pregnancy is a relevant example, as it is one of the few environmental exposures classified as having Class I evidence for ADHD risk [428]. A study investigating ADHD and pain-related traits found that, although the strong genetic correlation between ADHD and chronic pain argues against a purely causal environmental effect, follow-up gene-drug enrichment analyses indicated that paracetamol may also modulate the expression of neurodevelopmentally relevant genes [377]. This suggests that genetic predisposition and xenobiotic influences are not mutually exclusive. Instead, they may operate in parallel, with both complex genetic effects and direct environmental mechanisms contributing to risk. While this interpretation is consistent with preclinical evidence showing that paracetamol can disrupt neurodevelopmental processes [443], it also helps explain why epidemiological studies have yielded mixed results regarding the association between prenatal paracetamol exposure and ADHD [444,445]. Recent syntheses reach differing conclusions [446–448], largely reflecting recurring methodological challenges, including uncertainty in exposure measurement (over-the-counter use, dose, duration, and timing), confounding by indication (e.g., pain, fever, and infection), and shared familial, genetic, and environmental factors. Applying a different evaluative strategy, a 2025 assessment using the Navigation Guide framework [446] concluded that the overall body of evidence is consistent with an association between prenatal paracetamol exposure and increased probability of neurodevelopmental disorders, despite substantial heterogeneity across study designs and definitions. In contrast, a meta-analysis published the same year [447], incorporating explicit bias analyses, estimated a small increase in ADHD risk (odds ratio ≈1.17) and did not find clear evidence for autism, emphasizing the potential impact of residual confounding and exposure misclassification. Furthermore, a recent umbrella review [448] rated confidence in many existing reviews as low or critically low, noted extensive overlap among primary studies, and concluded that the available evidence does not establish a clear link between prenatal paracetamol exposure and ADHD or autism. Importantly, associations observed in whole-cohort analyses frequently did not persist in sibling-comparison designs, supporting a relevant contribution of shared familial, genetic, or environmental influences. This interpretation is reinforced by a large national population study [444] including approximately 2.5 million children, which detected modest associations in conventional models but found no significant association in analyses comparing differentially exposed siblings. Such designs substantially reduce confounding from familial liability and are widely interpreted as indicating that signals detected in traditional cohort analyses may not reflect direct causal effects of the medication. Importantly, even if interpreted causally, effect sizes of this magnitude imply a small absolute difference. Assuming a baseline ADHD prevalence of ∼5%, an odds ratio of 1.17 would translate into an estimated risk of approximately 5.9% among exposed offspring—roughly one additional case per 100 pregnancies. Thus, the vast majority of exposed children would not develop ADHD, underscoring the importance of contextualizing relative risks within clinical and public-health perspectives. Taken together, the literature calls for caution. If a causal effect exists, it is likely small and highly sensitive to confounding and exposure uncertainty. Part of this confounding may itself reflect rGE, whereby familial liability associated with ADHD risk can also influence patterns of medication use during pregnancy. Clinical decisions are therefore framed within risk-benefit reasoning, balancing hypothetical medication-related risks against the known consequences of untreated maternal conditions. Distinct from rGE, gene-environment interactions (G×E) occur when genetic factors modify how individuals respond to environmental exposures—a concept highly relevant to ADHD [449]. Classical epidemiological models suggest that genetic and environmental influences may act independently or synergistically. However, such models often assume independence between genes and environment, a condition rarely met in practice, as many exposures—such as trauma or socioeconomic status—are themselves influenced by genetics [363,450]. As mentioned above, even prenatal paracetamol exposure may reflect shared genetic liability, given overlaps between ADHD and chronic pain [377]. The polygenic architecture of ADHD, involving thousands of common variants of small effect [53], poses challenges for detecting robust G×E effects. Candidate gene studies have yielded few replicable results [451], but genome-wide interaction studies hold promise, although none have yet been published for ADHD. A study of over 33,000 individuals found that ADHD-PRS and psychosocial risk factors independently contributed to ADHD risk, with no significant interaction [452]. Similarly, a Danish population study showed only limited interaction between ADHD-PRS and psychosocial adversities or birth-related risks [453]. In U.S. preadolescents, ADHD-PRS predicted suicidal ideation independently of early life stress [454], while in adolescent cohorts, additive—but not interactive—effects of PRS and family conflict were observed [455]. Several studies instead support rGE over GxE interactions. For instance, genetically influenced ADHD traits predicted lower parental involvement and inconsistent discipline [456], and individuals with higher ADHD genetic liability were more likely to experience maltreatment during childhood [457]. This bidirectional relationship—where maltreatment also increased ADHD risk—was further supported in a Brazilian birth cohort. In the present study, higher ADHD symptoms mediated the link between genetic risk and adversity exposure [442]. Nonetheless, evidence for genuine G×E interaction is emerging. In another Brazilian sample, ADHD-PRS significantly interacted with environmental stress, amplifying ADHD risk without evidence of rGE or similar effects for depression and anxiety [458]. Another study in Norway found that the influence of ADHD traits and PRS on academic performance varied across schools, with higher-performing environments buffering genetic risk [459]. Finally, spatial analyses in the United Kingdom revealed that the association between PRS and ADHD traits varies geographically, suggesting regional environments may shape genetic expression [460]. Consistent with this, recent work has shown that rGEs can extend beyond the family level to broader geographic and socioeconomic structures, influencing GWAS signals and heritability estimates [461]. Collectively, these findings highlight the multifaceted nature of gene-environment dynamics in ADHD, with evidence for additive effects, rGEs, and G×E interactions depending on the population, context, and outcome studied. Future research must continue integrating genetic and environmental data across developmental, social, and geographic domains to clarify ADHD etiology and improve clinical prediction. Translational and clinical implications From biology to ADHD risk prediction Despite extensive research into the biological underpinnings of ADHD—spanning neurochemistry, neuroimaging, genomics, other omics, and more recently their integration—validated biomarkers for clinical use are still lacking [3,10]. This reflects the complexity of ADHD, a highly polygenic and multifactorial condition in which individual risk factors exert only very small effects. Consequently, there is no single ‘ADHD gene,’ in contrast with autism, where approximately 30% of cases can be traced to monogenic or oligogenic variants [462]. Given this landscape, a promising strategy for identifying clinically useful biomarkers in ADHD is the development of composite biological scores. For instance, no single neuroimaging finding has shown an effect size large enough to reliably distinguish individuals with ADHD from those without it. However, neuroimaging-based scores, or brain scores, could combine multiple small effects into a single metric. Large meta-analyses of neuroimaging studies provide the association coefficients that can be aggregated into such scores, allowing individuals to be placed along a risk distribution [463]. A recent study showed that an ADHD brain score for cortical surface area was higher in individuals with ADHD compared with controls [464]. However, this score was not associated with the number of ADHD symptoms or with clinical trajectories over time. While this approach is promising, current brain scores account for only a small fraction of the phenotypic variance [463]. Their performance relies heavily on the quality and statistical power of the meta-analyses used to derive effect sizes, which remain underpowered to capture the full spectrum of associations relevant to ADHD. In this sense, their current picture represents a tool that is relevant to study the relationship between neuroimaging features of a given phenotype (ADHD) and other traits. An important innovation comes from circuit-based scores. For example, in depression and anxiety, functional brain circuit scores have been shown to identify clinically distinct biotypes that differ in symptoms, cognition, and treatment response [465]. This raises the possibility that future approaches in ADHD could leverage brain circuit scores as well as the integration of structural and functional features to enhance the predictive performance of composite biological scores. Similarly, PRSs aim to capture the cumulative effect of numerous genetic variants of very small effects associated with a trait or disorder. They are derived from large GWAS—or from EWAS in the case of methylation risk scores—by summing the number of risk alleles carried by an individual, each weighted by its estimated effect size [350]. No single genetic variant has an effect size large enough to reliably distinguish individuals with ADHD, but PRSs provide a way to combine these small effects into a single quantitative measure. 22 © 2026 The Author(s). Bioscience Reports (2026) 46 BSR20254061 https://doi.org/10.1042/BSR20254061 In ADHD, PRSs have been associated not only with case–control status across independent samples but also with clinically relevant traits such as comorbidities, cognitive performance, executive function, and attentional measures, reflecting the disorder’s clinical profile [466]. As with brain scores, however, current PRSs explain only a modest proportion of phenotypic variance—about 5.5% in ADHD—limiting their predictive power [53]. Even under a highly hypothetical scenario where a genetic score captured the entire heritability of ADHD, only the extreme end of the distribution would be clinically decisive: for example, in the top 1% of the PRS distribution, ADHD would be expected in 92% of individuals (Figure 5). In fact, the strongest genetic information currently available still comes from family history [353]. As shown in Figure 3, individuals with two first-degree relatives with ADHD have almost a 50% risk of developing the disorder. Therefore, PRSs, like brain scores, are not suitable as stand-alone diagnostic tools but may ultimately contribute as one component of a multimodal framework, complementing family history (e.g., parental diagnosis) and standardized clinical assessments and serving as an additional pillar in the diagnostic process. Diversity as a source of innovation Although GWAS (and other omics studies) have been pivotal in understanding complex behavioral conditions such as ADHD, they suffer from a strong Eurocentric bias [469–474]. Over the past five years, 85% of the samples included in major psychiatric GWAS meta-analyses were from individuals of European ancestry residing in high-income countries. For ADHD specifically, this percentage is almost 100%, underscoring a major gap in representativeness [473]. This perspective builds on recent work highlighting ancestral diversity as a critical determinant of gene discovery, biological interpretation, and the equitable translation of ADHD genomics [475]. Genomic diversity in ancestral and admixed populations is increasingly recognized as a source of underexplored genetic variation that can uncover biological mechanisms that would remain invisible in more homogeneous datasets [476]. A notable example is the discovery of loss-of-function mutations in PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) among African Americans, which were associated with lower cholesterol levels and reduced cardiovascular risk [477]. These mutations had a combined frequency of 2% in African Americans but were rare in European Americans (<0.1%). This discovery led to the development of PCSK9 inhibitors, such as alirocumab and evolocumab [478,479]. Similar patterns have emerged in other loci identified through the study of diverse populations. For instance, risk variants in APOL1, largely restricted to individuals of African ancestry, have revealed a trade-off between protection against trypanosomal infection [480] and increased susceptibility to kidney disease [481,482], reshaping our understanding of renal pathophysiology and informing ongoing therapeutic development [483]. Although these examples are not specific to psychiatry, they illustrate how diversity can generate findings with major translational impact—something needed in psychiatry and ADHD research. Beyond limiting mechanistic discovery, Eurocentric bias in psychiatric genomics also contributes to the amplification of health disparities [473]. A clear example is the reduced portability of PRSs, whose predictive performance declines substantially as the genetic distance between the discovery and target populations increases [350,484]. This reduction in accuracy arises from differences in allele frequencies, linkage disequilibrium patterns, and environmental contexts across populations, leading to systematically poorer risk prediction in individuals of underrepresented ancestries. As a result, these groups, including individuals with ADHD, are less likely to benefit from advances driven by GWAS, such as risk stratification, early detection, and the development of precision medicine approaches. Expanding ancestral diversity in genomic studies is therefore essential from both ethical and public health perspectives, particularly in countries characterized by high levels of admixture and environmental heterogeneity [473,475]. Increasing diversity in genomic studies in psychiatry is a challenging but essential endeavor that demands substantial investments in human resources, equipment, and supplies. Moreover, long-standing analytical obstacles must be addressed. Historically, GWAS pipelines for data quality control and analysis often excluded individuals of non-European ancestry to form more homogeneous groups, thereby reducing the risk of false positives caused by population stratification [485–487]. Population stratification arises when systematic differences in allele frequencies exist between subgroups within a population due to ancestry [488]. For example, an allele with a higher frequency in individuals of African descent and a lower frequency in Europeans might appear to be associated with a trait if there is an imbalance in genetic ancestry between cases and controls. In such situations, genome-wide analyses of millions of genetic variants can yield hundreds of significant findings driven by ancestry differences rather than genuine biological effects linked to the trait under investigation [475]. This is particularly concerning for highly polygenic phenotypes like ADHD, where subtle effects spread across the genome can be easily confounded by ancestry-related artifacts if they are not handled properly. © 2026 The Author(s). A groundbreaking study in psychiatry recently applied this approach, conducting the largest meta-analysis of major depression to date, which included over 5 million individuals, more than 1 million of whom were of diverse ancestry [357]. This trans-ancestry GWAS identified 697 variants and 308 genes associated with depression, implicating postsynaptic density, neuronal dysregulation, and amygdala involvement. Notably, half of these loci are novel, with 100 identified solely due to the inclusion of diverse samples. The findings are enriched for potential antidepressant targets and highlight opportunities for drug repurposing. Similarly, a multi-ancestry GWAS of bipolar disorder, including 158,036 cases and 2.8 million controls, identified 298 genome-wide significant loci, with evidence that some signals were ancestry-specific and that multi-ancestry data improved fine-mapping resolution and polygenic prediction [490]. Together, these studies show that incorporating ancestral diversity is not merely a matter of representation but a strategy that can expand locus discovery, refine biological inference, and improve translational potential. These examples highlight how diversity-aware analytic frameworks can generate discoveries that would probably remain undetected in exclusively European datasets, reinforcing their relevance for future ADHD genomics. Further innovations, such as advances in local ancestry inference (LAI) methods, are transforming the inclusion of admixed samples in GWAS. Local ancestry refers to the ancestral origin of specific genome regions in an admixed individual. LAI methods estimate the ancestry of each haplotype—a physical grouping of genetic variants within the genome—by comparing individual genetic data with reference population panels derived from dense DNA sequencing data [491]. These algorithms have become integral to some GWAS pipelines. Admixture mapping, for example, serves as a powerful approach to identifying genetic variants associated with diseases or traits that exhibit ancestry-specific risk patterns [492,493]. Recent tools like the Tractor pipeline further enhance the ability to model admixture in genomic studies. Tractor systematically analyzes admixed populations and has shown promising performance in both simulated and real datasets [494]. This advancement enables researchers to conduct GWAS on ancestral tracts within a single cohort, reflecting the population from which the study sample was recruited. By generating ancestry-specific effect size estimates, Tractor enhances the detection of genetic associations, especially when gene effects vary across ancestries. In ADHD, the potential of these methods remains vastly underutilized. While recent GWAS meta-analyses have begun to unravel the biological underpinnings of the disorder, nearly all of them rely on data from European populations. Diversity is the missing ingredient with the potential to unlock unprecedented advancements in the field and make precision psychiatry a reality worldwide. However, ADHD genomics still lags behind. To date, only one study has applied new approaches, such as Tractor, to ADHD research. The present study analyzed a sample of just over 500 Colombian and Mexican individuals [495]. Although it marked a significant milestone—as the first GWAS of admixed individuals with ADHD—its small sample size limited statistical power, precluding the identification of genome-wide significant variants. Expanding such efforts is essential to ensure that ADHD research reflects the global population it aims to serve. Only by incorporating diversity in genomics will we be able to fully uncover the clinical and biological complexity of ADHD, improve diagnostic tools across populations, and develop equitable, targeted interventions. Conclusions Methodological considerations and strength of evidence Over the past decades, the biological investigation of ADHD has progressed from small, conceptually pioneering studies to large-scale collaborative science. This transition has profoundly reshaped how evidence is weighed, interpreted, and integrated across levels of analysis. Findings from early neuroimaging and experimental investigations remain essential for their historical and hypothesis-generating value. However, contemporary inference regarding robustness, reproducibility, and generalizability increasingly depends on meta-analytic efforts and international consortia, including initiatives such as ENIGMA-ADHD, which provide the statistical power required to detect the modest effects expected for a highly heterogeneous and polygenic condition. The same evolution characterizes psychiatric genetics. Initial efforts centered on candidate-gene hypotheses inspired by prevailing neurobiological models. As data accumulated, it became evident that ADHD liability is far more polygenic and widely distributed across the genome than originally assumed. This realization drove the adoption of hypothesis-free genome-wide approaches and underscored the need for global collaborative frameworks capable of achieving the sample sizes required for reliable discovery, as exemplified by the pioneering work of large international consortia. © 2026 The Author(s). Treat models as platforms to interrogate specific dimensions rather than as replicas of the disorder; align tasks with homologous human cognitive constructs; incorporate human genetic liability into experimental strategies; promote multi-laboratory replication; and develop cross-species and developmental frameworks. Neuroimaging Robust group-level differences but extensive overlap at the individual level; small effect sizes; diagnostic heterogeneity; medication and environmental confounding; predominance of cross-sectional contrasts; limited clinical translation [499]. Increase scale through harmonized consortia; prioritize longitudinal within-subject trajectories; invest in deep phenotyping; integrate imaging with behavioral and computational models; embed biomarkers in treatment studies; adopt preregistration, transparent pipelines, and external validation. Genetics/Genomics Individual loci account for small fractions of risk, persistent Eurocentric sampling, reduced portability of polygenic estimates, and difficulty moving from association to specific mechanisms (non-shared mechanisms) [350,473,475,500]. Increase recruitment in underrepresented and admixed populations; implement ancestry-aware designs and local ancestry inference; leverage diverse LD patterns for fine-mapping; integrate common and rare variation with functional annotation; strengthen equitable global collaborations. Epigenomics/Transcriptomics Strong tissue and developmental specificity; modest sample sizes; limited replication; challenges in separating cause from consequence [501]. Establish longitudinal cohorts beginning early in life; harmonize laboratory and computational pipelines; jointly model genetic liability and environmental exposures; prioritize replication across tissues and populations. Microbiome/metagenomics High heterogeneity in sampling and analytics; small cohorts; inconsistent microbial signatures; major influence of diet, medication, and shared environment; typically small variance explained; frequent causal overinterpretation [422]. Move toward large, standardized, and collaborative frameworks; incorporate family-based and longitudinal designs; predefine hypotheses and report effect sizes; integrate host genomics and metabolomics; apply formal causal inference strategies before translational claims. Yet, despite rapid progress in gene discovery, clinical heterogeneity remains one of the field’s most formidable challenges. ADHD encompasses diverse developmental trajectories, symptom profiles, and patterns of comorbidity. Disentangling what is specific to ADHD from what reflects broader, shared psychopathological mechanisms is only now becoming feasible and will depend critically on coordinated investments in deep phenotyping, longitudinal designs, and harmonized integration of biological, clinical, and environmental data. Importantly, effect sizes observed in psychiatric case–control contrasts are typically small. Differences in the range of d ≈0.2–0.3, such as those discussed in the neuroimaging subsection, imply substantial overlap between individuals with and without ADHD, emphasizing that these results illuminate population-level mechanisms rather than serving as diagnostic signatures. Recognizing this statistical reality is fundamental for a balanced and mature interpretation of biological findings. Future directions Progress in ADHD biology will depend less on isolated discoveries and more on coordinated advances in scale, design, and integration across levels of analysis (Table 1). The polygenic architecture of the disorder requires increasingly large and collaborative efforts to refine risk loci, improve fine-mapping resolution, and connect association signals to biological function. At the same time, overcoming the historical Eurocentric composition of samples is essential both for scientific validity and for ensuring that emerging tools are broadly applicable across populations [475]. Beyond genomic discovery, the field faces a shared challenge across experimental systems. Effect sizes are typically small, heterogeneity is substantial, and findings that are robust at the group level often show limited utility for individual prediction. Addressing these constraints will require harmonization of methods, deeper phenotyping, longitudinal designs, and explicit modeling of environmental and treatment-related influences. Importantly, progress will also depend on strengthening bridges between domains. Genetic discoveries must increasingly inform experimental models; neuroimaging findings need integration with computational and behavioral frameworks; and emerging omics layers such as epigenomics and the microbiome require larger, standardized, and replicable infrastructures before causal or translational claims can be sustained. Furthermore, artificial intelligence may accelerate this transition by enabling multimodal integration at a scale previously unattainable. In this context, predictive modeling may help identify probabilistic risk profiles, stratify patients, and refine hypotheses about treatment response, contributing to more precise and biologically informed psychiatry. Finally, after more than 50 years in which the concept of endophenotypes has remained largely a ‘future perspective’ in psychiatry—since Gottesman first proposed it in 1973 [496]—we now face a more concrete possibility of identifying them and applying them to diagnosis and treatment. Recent conceptual advances have reframed endophenotypes as genetically influenced phenotypes linked not only to disease liability but also to treatment-related characteristics and their associated biological events [497]. The increasing resolution of omics technologies, combined with advances in cellular and molecular neuroscience, now enables a more precise characterization of biological pathways and mechanisms relevant to neurodevelopment. This evolving framework strengthens the search for ADHD endophenotypes and may help move the field beyond theoretical aspirations toward biologically informed markers capable of linking genetic liability to clinical expression and treatment response. metadata_title: School-Based Social Skills Interventions for Youth With ADHD: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
pages: https://doi.org/10.1177/10870547251364578 Journal of Attention Disorders 2026, Vol. 30(4) 427–448 © The Author(s) 2025 Article reuse guidelines: sagepub.com/journals-permissions DOI: 10.1177/10870547251364578 journals.sagepub.com/home/jad Article Introduction ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity (American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2013). Approximately 8.7% of children between the ages of 3 and 17 years old are diagnosed with ADHD (Bozinovic et al., 2021). Students with ADHD often experience difficulties in academic, behavioral, and social domains, which can negatively impact their overall quality of life (DuPaul & Langberg, 2015). Social skills deficits are a strong predictor of overall functioning, both in the short and long term, underscoring the importance of addressing these challenges (Al-Yagon et al., 2020; Bagwell et al., 2001; Fabiano et al., 2018; Rutherford et al., 2008). Behaviors demonstrated by students with ADHD are frequently incompatible with social competence, especially in academic settings. As such, they often experience social skills deficits (i.e., behaviors and abilities necessary for successful interactions with others; Hoza, 2007). Nonetheless, evidence has suggested that this is not always due to knowledge of social skills, but instead performance (Aduen et al., 2018). Specifically, individuals with ADHD tend to interrupt, not follow directions, be forgetful in daily activities, and demonstrate behavioral dysregulation when strong emotions are present (Zoromski et al., 2015). As such, individuals with ADHD are more likely than their peers without ADHD to be socially rejected (Strine et al., 2006). Consider the student with ADHD assigned to a group project. The student may struggle to stay on task, talking excessively, and interrupting others (Hoza, 2007; Wehmeier et al., 2010). The student is likely to become distracted, distract the group, and less likely to complete the task on time. These behaviors interfere with interpersonal relationships and academic progress. In this study, we refer to social skills deficits as both acquisition and performance of social skills. In addition to the immediate effects of social skills deficits, the associated peer dislike and rejection can lead to 1364578 JADXXX10.1177/10870547251364578Journal of Attention DisordersBussanich et al. research-article2025 1Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ, USA 2University of Oklahoma, Norman, USA Corresponding Author: Judith R. Harrison, Graduate School of Education, Rutgers University, 10 Seminary Place, New Brunswick, NJ 08901, USA. Email: judith.harrison@gse.rutgers.edu School-Based Social Skills Interventions for Youth With ADHD: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Gabriella Bussanich1, Judith R. Harrison1 , Corey Peltier2, Aayushi Patel1, Paulomi Mehta1, and Kashees Patel1 Abstract Objective: Children and adolescents frequently struggle with social skills performance in academic settings, which can negatively impact quality of life. As such, social skills training is frequently recommended; however, the effectiveness of school-based social skills training has not been synthesized. As such, the purpose of the current study was to evaluate the empirical evidence pertaining to both stand-alone and multimodal school-based social skills programs for students with ADHD, and to assess the effects of potential moderating variables. Method: A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted of studies between the years of 1975 and 2023 following the recommendations of the Cochrane Foundation and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA). Results: Seventeen studies, single-case, within group, and between-group designs met the established inclusion criteria, with 10 included in the meta-analysis. The findings revealed small to large effects; however, the overall meta-analytic effect size was negligible (ES = 0.09). The differences in social skills approaches, intensity, parent involvement, and setting did not moderate the effects.Conclusion: These findings underscore the necessity for ongoing exploration and refinement of social skills interventions tailored for youth with ADHD. (J. of Att. Dis. 2026; 30(4) 427-448) Keywords ADHD, social skills, training, programs Correction (September 2025): The article has been updated with the minor data correction in the Table 1.

For example, a correlation has been found between parent-reported (Karustis et al., 2000; Mikami et al., 2011; Mulraney et al., 2018; Sciberras et al., 2014), and child-and teacher reported (Karustis et al., 2000; Mikami et al. 2011) anxiety and peer rejection. These studies provide evidence that adolescents who have ADHD and struggle with social skills are more likely to be diagnosed with comorbid conditions that require additional support. Although 16.5% of youth have at least one mental health disorder that is likely to interfere with social functioning, only 49.4% receive services (Whitney & Peterson, 2019). This is especially true for youth from underserved communities, including those of color and low-income families (Slobodin & Masalha, 2020). One means of increasing supports and services is to provide them in school (Kappi et al., 2022). However, researchers and practitioners have noted that the low ratio of counselors to students in schools might interfere with implementation (Donohue et al., 2022). Fortunately, social skills training (SST) can be implemented by teachers in classrooms along with school counselors (Bauminger, 2002). Furthermore, collaborating across professions (e.g., different teachers, counselors, occupational therapists) increases the potential to generalize skills taught in a classroom or small group setting (Powell & Sable, 2001). School-Based Social Skills Training Programs and Interventions SST programs are designed as stand-alone interventions that focus on specific skill-building or multimodal interventions that integrate interventions across areas of impairment (e.g., academic, social, and behavioral; Evans et al., 2011; Willis et al., 2019). However, the differential effectiveness is not known. Although not focused on school-based services in the last 5 years, three systematic reviews and meta-analyses have synthesized the literature on the effects of training aimed at improving the social skills of children and adolescents with ADHD. Overall, SST resulted in inconsistent findings across study design and outcome measures, with observed effects ranging from null to moderate. Randomized controlled trials (RCT) tended to result in no to low effects, whereas within-subject designs demonstrated small to moderate effects. Furthermore, parent ratings were more likely to demonstrate positive effects than teacher ratings. Willis et al. (2019) summarized the findings of a systematic review with 16 group design studies as individual study authors “reported at least initial evidence to support the efficacy of stand-alone SST aimed at reducing social impairment” (p. 355) and noted inconsistent findings across studies with variations in reports from parents, teachers, and peers. Morris et al. (2021) calculated an overall effect across four RCTs and four betweengroup studies. They reported that the RCTs found no differences in social functioning between treatment and control groups as reported by parents (ES = −0.08). Nonrandomized studies demonstrated improvements in social functioning from baseline to postintervention by parent report with a moderate effect (ES = 0.57) and no effect by teacher report (ES = 0.04). Powell et al. (2022) calculated the overall effect with eight RCTs (with comparison groups of treatment as usual only) and found a small effect for teacher (ES = 0.32) and parent (ES = 0.39) ratings. Thirty-two unique studies were included across all reviews, with only 10 conducted in schools or analogous settings (e.g., Summer Treatment Programs, After School Programs). Willis et al. (2019) focused on stand-alone SST in clinical settings, and Powell et al. (2022) focused on stand-alone and multimodal interventions with a focus on the psychoeducational components in clinical settings (six of eight studies). Morris et al. (2021) focused on nonpharmacological multimodal interventions in various settings, including schools. Furthermore, none of the three reviews included single case design studies, a typical design used in school-based research (Parker et al., 2006). Additionally, although differences were noted between RCT and withingroup studies and parent and teacher ratings, none of the prior studies evaluated moderator effects. As such, our goal was to review the school-based intervention studies, synthesize the literature, and calculate the effectiveness of stand-alone and multimodal SST programs implemented in schools, and evaluate potential moderators. Reviews and meta-analyses of clinic-based SST interventions have demonstrated positive outcomes; however, they also highlight a gap in research synthesis regarding the effectiveness of SST implemented in school settings. The current literature does not provide researchers or practitioners with information about the effects of SST implemented in schools. Examining school-based SST is essential for several reasons. First, the generalization of skills from clinical environments to school contexts is often limited, as the structure and routines of clinics are different than school settings. In contrast, when SST is implemented in schools, instruction and practice occur in authentic settings, such as classrooms, recess, and cafeterias, where students are more likely to use the skills and reinforcement from peers and adults is more likely to occur. This setting also enables educators to provide immediate feedback, which is likely to enhance skill acquisition and performance (Ajogbeje, 2023). As such, intervention effects may be different in school settings compared to clinics.

Bussanich et al. 429 Additionally, delivering SST in schools helps address systemic barriers to access, including transportation difficulties, limited availability of services, and high clinical care costs (Eiraldi et al., 2015). By embedding interventions in the school day, educators can reach students who might otherwise be unable to receive services, thereby promoting educational equity. Finally, the natural interplay between learning and behavior in school settings reinforces the relevance of SST. When social skills instruction is integrated into daily academic and social routines, it is likely to support classroom engagement, peer and adults relationships, behavioral regulation, and academic success. Potential Moderators Although not analyzed in prior meta-analyses, potential moderators emerged from findings and discussion within the literature. Several prior meta-analyses (e.g., Morris et al., 2021; Powell et al., 2022; Ros & Graziano, 2018) mentioned challenges with assessment. First, differences were found between parent and teacher ratings of social skills. Powell et al. (2022) noted that parent ratings were more likely to demonstrate a significant positive effect than teacher ratings. It is noteworthy that each intervention reviewed by Powell and colleagues included some form of parent training, suggesting that parents were invested in the outcomes and that blinding raters to the intervention was not possible. Morris et al. (2021) noted that the results of RCTs were similar regardless of rater. However, the results of non-randomized studies indicated that parents rated improved social functioning while teachers and students did not. As such, in conjunction with the exploration of SST outcomes, it is essential that we explore the impact of the reporters of skill when rating scales are the prime measure. Second, some have questioned (e.g., Ros & Graziano, 2018) potential differences between findings when dependent measures were distal or broadband scales (e.g., BASC, SSIS). Specifically, questions regarding outcomes evaluated by tools that measure distal multiple dimensions (Raiker et al., 2017) versus proximal or narrowband, which measure just one proximal dimension (e.g., ADHD-specific rating scales; J. Pelham et al., 2005) have been questioned. For example, if a social skills program is used to teach problem-solving (e.g., Webster-Stratton & Reid, 2008), then direct observation or a single or multiple-item scale directly related to the use of problem-solving skills (i.e., narrowband) might be more sensitive to change in behavior associated with the intervention than a broadband scale. The third was the type of control group (i.e., passive, active). The purpose of a control group is to account for influences on outcomes that are not directly associated with the intervention being tested. If the control group is active, some researchers argue that the potential for placebo effects is minimized, as the key is participant expectation (i.e., to improve based on the intervention). As such, comparing the effects of an intervention to the effects of a passive or notreatment control group could potentially introduce confounding effects caused by differences in participant expectations (Boot et al., 2013), suggesting that effect sizes from studies with passive controls would result in larger effect sizes. For example, Noble et al. (2019) found that the effect of shared reading on language development was moderated by type of control group with negligible effect for studies with active control groups and larger for studies with passive controls. As such, using an active control group that receives support, or intervention will likely lead to lower effect size estimates than using a business-as-usual group that continues to receive services provided in the context without intervention. The fourth was the type of intervention (i.e., stand-alone, multimodal). Stand-alone interventions target one outcome (e.g., social competence) through one intervention (e.g., social skills training groups). Alternatively, multimodal interventions target multiple outcomes (e.g., academic, behavioral, social) across numerous domains through various interventions (e.g., homework assistance, token economy, social skills training groups). Morris et al. (2021) mentioned that among the various interventions included in their meta-analysis, only one intervention focused only on the social domain, with others also targeting vocational, organizational, or others. Researchers suggest that multimodal interventions designed to target different areas of impairment (e.g., organization, academic functioning) have the potential to secondarily impact social skills due to the influence on protective factors, such as peer acceptance (Mrug et al., 2007). This introduces variability in the calculation of overall effects that quantify the extent to which the observed improvements in social functioning can be attributed to the intervention. As such, the type of intervention may moderate the overall effects. Finally, the age and/or grade level of the students in the study have the potential to impact effectiveness. It is possible that age impacts the outcomes of SST, as maturity might affect how students engage with and benefit from social skills instruction. Social functioning becomes increasingly important as children move into adolescence, as peer relationships gain significance (Gresham et al., 2001). Furthermore, SST programs often require mature cognitive functioning, such as the ability to reflect on one’s behavior, infer others’ emotions or intentions, and apply learned strategies across settings (Merrell & Gimpel, 2014). As such, results of studies with younger children may result in smaller effects than those with older children or adolescents.

430 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(4) Need for Current Review and Meta-Analysis As such, the purpose of the current study was to systematically evaluate the empirical evidence for school-based stand-alone and multimodal interventions that include SST for students with ADHD and evaluate potential moderators. Specifically, this systematic literature review and metaanalysis addressed the following research questions: RQ1: What was the overall effect of social skills training implemented in schools on outcomes for students with ADHD? What was the heterogeneity in effects within and across studies? RQ2: What was the scientific quality of studies of social skills training implemented in schools? RQ3: To what extent did study characteristics (i.e., rater, measures, type of control group, type of intervention, age/grade level of participants) moderate the effect of social skills training? Method This systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted following the recommended procedures of the Cochrane Foundation (Henderson et al., 2010) and two methodological guidance papers (Alexander, 2020; Pigott & Polanin, 2020). Additionally, we consulted the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Standards (Page et al., 2021) to provide transparent and clear reporting of our methodology and results. The study was conducted in three phases: (a) systematic search and study selection, (b) data coding, and (c) data analysis. The following sections are organized accordingly. Phase 1: Study Selection and Systematic Search In the following sections, we outline the criteria for including source studies in this meta-analysis and describe our search procedures. Inclusion Criteria. Studies were included that were (a) conducted between 1975 and 2023; (b) published in English; (c) published in peer reviewed journals; (d) used group or single case design; (e) included participants with a diagnosis of ADHD, at risk for ADHD, or with ADHD and comorbid condition; (f) included participants and setting in primary and secondary schools (K-12), or analogous settings (e.g., a summer treatment program, after school program) designed to align with typical classrooms; (g) examined the effects of a social skills intervention (i.e., designed to increase social competence, prosocial skills, interpersonal skills, and/or decrease social impairment, disruptive, or offensive behaviors in social settings; Gresham et al., 2004) as indicated by the authors, (h) included an outcome measure of social skills /social competence with scores disaggregated from other outcomes; and (i) was not a study of the effects of medication alone or as a comparison group. We included studies that were only implemented in schools or analogous settings. As such, studies that included both clinic and school components were excluded from inclusion. We defined outcome measures of social skills as those designated to measure social skills (e.g., Social Skills Improvement Rating Scales; Gresham & Elliot, 2008) per the authors, with scores of social impairment included and disaggregated by the author (e.g., Impairment Rating Scale [IRS] Fabiano et al., 2006) or determined to be a social skill measure by the authors of the current paper. Specifically, when outcomes were not clearly defined as social outcomes, two authors reviewed the definition provided by source study authors and determined whether we agreed that the measure was an assessment of social skills. For example, Sibley et al. (2011) measured “inappropriate behavior during business meetings.” As a team, we agreed that in this study inappropriate behavior was a social behavior due to the author definition, as “any verbal or nonverbal social interaction that would typically annoy others in the group or decrease the popularity of the adolescent.” (p. 582). Villodas et al. (2013) included social development grades as an outcome. The authors reported that “the participating school district utilizes a standardsbased report card system that requires teachers to rate students on grade-specific expectations for social development, such as “Respects self and others,” “Resolves conflicts,” and “Follows directions.” In another example, Evans et al. (2004) disaggregated scores on the CIS that we agreed met the definition of social skills (i.e., relationships with playmates, sibling, parents, family). For the meta-analysis, we further restricted the inclusion criteria. We restricted the study type parameter to only include group design studies with a minimum of two groups comparing different conditions. We excluded pre-post designs with only one group due to limitations in inferring causal relations and the inability to report a standardized effect size that was comparable to the included betweengroup studies. We excluded single-case designs because we identified only two studies, and one of these studies did not meet the requirements for using an analogous effect size metric (i.e., between-case standardized mean difference; see Hedges et al., 2013) in between-group design studies. Search Procedures. Following procedures of the Cochrane Foundation (Henderson et al., 2010) and referring to methodological guidance (Alexander, 2020), an electronic database search was conducted. Additionally, we repeated the search, including the years 2022 and 2023. We initiated our search process by selecting databases that would be likely to include journals that publish articles fitting our inclusion

Bussanich et al. 431 criteria: (1) Education and Resource Information Center (ERIC), (2) Academic Search Premier, and (3) PsycINFO. We searched each database using the following Boolean string: (“social skills training” OR “social skills instruction” OR “social skills intervention” OR “peer problems” OR “social relationships” OR “friendships” OR “social competence” OR “social cognition” OR “problem solving” OR “problem-solving” OR “multimodal”) AND (“school” OR “school-based”) AND (“attention deficit hyperactivity disorder” OR “ADHD”). After our initial search, we conducted an ancestral review of the citations of the included studies and added two studies recommended by reviewers. Our search was conducted in June 2023. Phase 2: Coding Each study was coded based on the following categories: (1) study characteristics, (2) program or intervention characteristics, (3) Council for Exceptional Children (CEC, 2014) quality indicators, and (4) study outcomes, measures, and means of result reporting. Study characteristics included: (a) author; (b) year; (c) diagnosis; (d) setting; (e) name of intervention; (d) number of participants, (e) grade level; (f) age; (g) gender, and (f) implementer. Program and intervention characteristics included the content addressed in the interventions (e.g., peer relationships, communication) and the specific components implemented (e.g., parent training, role-play). The Council for Exceptional Children Standards for Evidence-Based Practices in Special Education (CEC, 2014) were used to evaluate the study quality of both group and single-case designs. For group design studies, 24 characteristics categorized across eight indicators were coded. Each indicator was coded dichotomously with response options indicating whether the criterion was met or not. For single-case design studies, 22 characteristics categorized across eight indicators were coded. Each indicator was coded dichotomously with response options indicating whether the criterion was met or not. If a study met all eight indicators it was coded as meeting standards, and if a study met fewer than eight indicators it was coded as not meeting standards. Study outcomes, for both group designs and single-case designs, were coded as academic, social, behavior, symptomology (ADHD, other), and/or executive functioning (e.g., self-management, organization, planning). Measurement tools were coded directly from study author reports (e.g., observation, SSIS, IRS) in a textual format. Regarding statistical reporting for group designs, we extracted means, standard deviations, and sample sizes for each group, across all measures, at pretest and posttest. If means and standard deviations were not provided, other information was extracted (e.g., F-statistic, p-value) to estimate an effect size index. For single-case design studies, a screenshot of the time-series graph was uploaded to a graph digitizer with demonstrated evidence of reliable and valid estimates of raw data values (Rohtagi, 2022). The x-axis and y-axis value were estimated for each data point and coded for condition (e.g., baseline, intervention, maintenance). Training and Inter-Rater Agreement on Coding Activities. Prior to independent coding, the second author (doctoral level with extensive experience) trained the members on all coding manuals. Specifically, the author reviewed the codes with coauthors, explained the codes in detail, modeled coding procedures, and conducted exercises in which raters identified one example and non-example of each coded variable. If codes were unclear, the team deliberated until a consensus was reached. The members of the team who coded articles were three Ph.D. level researchers, one Ph.D. candidate, and three doctoral students. During training the team reviewed five studies together to define and clarify codes as needed. Initial training was conducted on four separate occasions (one training per criterion) for an hour each. This was followed by four practice sessions. Prior to the practice sessions, each member of the research team, independently coded five articles. Each article was independently coded by three raters simultaneously for discussion and clarification of codes when questions arose. During the meetings, the entire team reviewed and discussed disagreements. No disagreements were found for study characteristics and outcomes. As such, simple agreement was 100%. Disagreements were found within the CEC criteria; specifically, when the term “sufficient” was used in the description of the indicators (e.g., sufficient description of . . . ). When disagreement occurred, raters discussed until 100% consensus was reached. If consensus was not reached, the second author made the final decision. Finally, two study authors independently coded 62% of all studies. Simple agreement was 96%. Phase 3: Data Analysis The data analysis process involved four phases. The first phase was a descriptive evaluation of included studies (k = 17). The second phase was restricted to the single-case design studies (k = 2). We conducted visual analysis and reported effect size indices for these studies (see below). The third phase was restricted to one group, pre-posttest design studies (k = 9). We computed standardized mean difference effect sizes comparing changes in scores from prepost using Cohen’s d. The fourth phase was the meta-analytic model (see below), which was restricted to the studies meeting inclusion criteria defined above (k = 9). Descriptive Evaluation. First, we reported the coded variables for each study. Next, to evaluate the sample of studies included in our review across variables, we reported

432 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(4) descriptive data (i.e., frequency, percent) at the variable level for all coded variables. Then, we coded the scientific quality of each study using the Council for Exceptional Children Standards for Evidence-Based Practice in Special Education (CEC, 2014). Visual Analysis and Quantitative Analysis of Single-Case Design Studies. For the single-case design studies (k = 2), we conducted visual analysis to evaluate the existence of a functional relationship between the independent and dependent variable(s). Our visual analysis process was informed by the What Works Clearinghouse (WWC) protocol (Kratochwill et al., 2010) with guidance from Lane and Gast (2014). Specifically, we analyzed data by visually inspecting the: (a) level, variability, and trend of baseline data; (b) level, variability, and trend of intervention data; (c) and changes in level or trend between baseline and intervention, number of overlapping data points between baseline and intervention, immediacy of effect, and consistency across similar phases. We identified the number of basic effects observed (i.e., individual AB) and calculated the ratio of positive to negative or null effects. For the single-case design studies, we reported a nonoverlap metric (i.e., Tau-U; Parker et al., 2011) and the between-case standardized mean difference for the one study that fit criteria (Hedges et al., 2013). Quantitative Analysis of One Group Pre-Post Designs. For the one group pre-post test designs we reported Cohen’s d as presented by the source study authors or calculated it using the reported means and standard deviations, Meta-Analysis. We included quasi-experimental and RCTs, if they included a minimum of two groups of students assigned to different conditions (k = 9, effect sizes = 81). The standardized mean difference effect size was used as the effect size metric (see Lipsey & Wilson, 2001). This involved the mean difference between the posttest scores from the target experimental condition versus the target comparison condition divided by the pooled standard deviation of the treatment and comparison groups’ posttest scores. We corrected for small sample sizes by converting Cohen’s d to Hedges’ g. In cases where the means and standard deviations were not provided by authors, we estimated the effect size estimate using the information provided (see Wilson, n.d.). Multiple studies used more than one social outcome measure, resulting in multiple effect size estimates per study. Similarly, some studies included multiple subgroups (e.g., boys in treatment A versus boys in treatment B; girls in treatment A versus girls in treatment B), which led to multiple effect size estimates per study. An issue arises if each effect size is treated as independent; effect sizes from the same study are likely to be more correlated than they are to effect sizes from other studies. If ignored, this dependency can lead to bias estimates in treatment effects. Thus, we provide two models for readers to interpret. In our first model, we built a random effects meta-analyses model that used the inverse variance weighted mean at the study level. However, this model loses valuable pieces of information, specifically, the heterogeneity of effect sizes at the study level. Thus, the final model built for interpretation was a multilevel, multivariate model with robust variance estimate (see Hedges et al., 2013). Although the average effect may be of interest, a key strength of meta-analysis is to investigate how effects vary across studies and to investigate the nature of this variation, or heterogeneity. To investigate this heterogeneity, we started by creating a forest plot of effect sizes from each included study. Next, we computed the standard deviation of the true effects (τ) and the variance in true effects (τ2). Third, we computed a prediction interval, which is the range of the true effects if a new study were added in the future (IntHout et al., 2016). Fourth, we used empirical Bayes estimates to generate a distribution of effect sizes that uses the estimates generated from the studies included in the metaanalysis and the average effect size across studies. Last, we conducted moderator analyses on five specific variables of focus: (a) age/grade of participants, (b) active versus business-as-usual comparison group, (c) the role of the person providing ratings for outcome measure, (d) intervention type (i.e., multimodal vs. stand-alone), and (e) broad versus narrow band outcome measures. Publication Bias. Publication bias occurs when the published literature is systematically similar across specific variables from the entire population of literature on the phenomenon of interest. The most general case discussed related to this phenomenon is that published literature is more likely to include interventions demonstrating statistically significant effects compared to the entire population of literature on the topic. In systematic reviews and meta-analysis this can lead to overestimates of intervention effectiveness. To investigate publication bias, we started by generating two funnel plots, which plot the standard error (y-axis) versus the effect size estimate (x-axis). The first funnel plot included all 81 effect size estimates (see Supplemental Figure 1), and the second funnel (see Supplemental Figure 2) plot included the weighted mean effect of the nine included studies. We then used Egger’s regression test as a quantitative approach to supplement our visual analysis. To further explore the potential nature of publication bias we analyzed the distribution of effect sizes across different p-value buckets (<.025; 0.025 to 0.50; and 0.50–1.0) along with the estimated effect size estimate at each bucket.

Study Identification and Characteristics Results of the search can be found in the PRISMA Flow Diagram (see Figure 1). A total of 1,713 records were identified for the systematic review, including 1,694 from database searches and 19 from other sources. After removing 15 duplicate records and 683 records flagged as ineligible by automation tools, 1,015 records remained for title and abstract screening. Of these, 365 records were excluded, and 650 reports were sought for full-text retrieval. Thirty-seven reports could not be retrieved, leaving 613 reports assessed for eligibility. A total of 596 reports were excluded for the following reasons: not published between 1975 and 2023 (k = 58), not in English (k = 24), not peerreviewed (k = 144), not focused on social skills interventions (e.g., medication-only, assessment, or review articles; k = 290), no disaggregated or relevant social outcome measures (k = 3), not conducted in a school setting (k = 44), incorrect use of single-case design (k = 1), and other analytic or methodological limitations (k = 32). Seventeen studies met all inclusion criteria and were included in the final review. The studies included a total of 2,195 participants with 1,288 in treatment groups and 907 in nine control groups. Of the 2,195 participants, 1,452 (66.2%) were male and 743 (33.8%) were females. Within those instruments, outcomes were measured as: (a) social problems; (b) social skills; (c) social functioning (e.g., relations with peers, social impairment); (d) social behavior (negative, positive, inappropriate, appropriate); (e) relationships or interpersonal behavior (i.e., with children, peers, parents, teachers, siblings, playmates); (f) peer nominations/ratings (i.e., positive/negative nominations, reciprocated friendships, peer sociometric ratings; peer interactions; message from peers); (g) specific social skills (i.e., communication, cooperation, assertion, responsibility, empathy, engagement, self-control); (g) isolated play; (h) social development grades; (i) student report of parent support; and (j) student report of teacher support. Studies were conducted in schools (k = 9) and analogous settings (k = 7; i.e., summer treatment programs [STP], after-school programs), and both (k = 1; i.e., school and analogous settings; see Table 1). Several studies were conducted with students across schools, including elementary (k = 7), elementary/middle school (k = 1), middle school (k = 6), middle/high (k = 1), and high school (k = 2). Scientific Quality. Of the 17 studies, 10 met all eight CEC quality criteria (see Table 2). Four met seven out of eight criteria, one met six criteria, and two met five out of eight criteria. Four studies (Barney et al., 2022; Evans et al., 2004, 2005; Schultz et al., 2017) did not report fidelity (i.e., adherence, integrity) to procedures. Three studies (Barney et al., 2022; Evans et al., 2005, 2011) did not document attrition and one single-case design study did not document three opportunities to demonstrate an effect at three different points in time (Sibley et al., 2011). Two studies (i.e.., Barney et al., 2022; Evans et al., 2005) did not provide sufficient details of interventionists’ training for replication. One study (Evans et al., 2004) did not report reliability of the measurement. Interventions. Three stand-alone interventions and variations of three multimodal interventions were evaluated in the 17 studies. In the following sections, we describe the interventions, including the content, components, and summary of evidence within the categories of stand-alone and multimodal interventions. Stand-Alone. Stand-alone social skills training programs are defined as training programs aimed only at improving and measuring social skills. Social Skills Training Program. Colton and Sheridan (1998) investigated the effectiveness of a social skills training program. The intervention involved child training and conjoint behavioral consultation (CBC) with parents and teachers to support the child in demonstrating cooperative peer interactions. Procedures involved: (a) a problem identification interview with the child’s mother and teacher; (b) problem analysis conversation between the consultant and the teacher and parent, identify target behaviors, and planning skills to be taught in the program. Child skills training involved: (a) coaching and role-play; (b) self-monitoring; (c) home-school communication; and (d) positive reinforcement. Working Together: Building Children’s Social Skills Through Folk Literature. Corkum et al. (2010) explored the effectiveness of a SST manualized program, Working Together: Building Children’s Social Skills through Folk Literature. The intervention was a program conducted in group sessions that involved the presentation of a folktale and its relationship to a specific social skill. The procedures involved discussion, practice, activities, feedback, contingency management, and role-play. MOSAIC. Mikami et al. (2013, 2022) evaluated the effectiveness of the social skills program, Making Socially Accepting Inclusive Classrooms (MOSAIC). Mikami et al. (2022) compared MOSAIC to business as usual. MOSAIC is a program conducted in group sessions and involved two components: (a) teacher modeling of warm positive relationships with children and highlighting child strengths in front of peers to encourage peer acceptance, (b) classroom behavior management strategies (token economy, points for social skill demonstration), and (c) brief daily social skills lessons. The procedures for the social skills training included a class discussion of a specific skill, role-play of the skills, and reinforcement throughout the day for demonstrating the skill. Multimodal. Multimodal programs are defined as those designed to improve multiple skills, such as organization, study skills, homework completion, academic performance, and social skills. Challenging Horizons Program (CHP). Seven studies investigate effects of the Challenging Horizons Program (Evans et al., 2004, 2005, 2007, 2011, 2016, 2023; Schultz et al., 2017), designed for middle and high school students
