Bussanich et al. 437 with ADHD. Various versions of the CHP were investigated including an after-school and a teacher consultant model. The CHP includes individual and group education groups, recreation time, interpersonal skills group/training (ISG), contingency management, and parent consultation/training. Social competencies were the focus of ISG and are generalized throughout the program and recreation activities. Specifically, ISG was developed to help youth with ADHD understand the connection between their behavior and the reactions of others and the impressions individuals have of them. Procedures for the intervention involved: (a) instruction in problem solving steps and vocabulary related to ISG; (b) the development of “IDEAL self-goals,” or goals for how they want others to perceive them; and (c) games and activities during, in which students and teacher rate the student’s behavior to their IDEAL self-goals. Collaborative Life Skills Program (CLS). Four studies investigated the effects of the CLS program (Pfiffner et al., 2011, 2016, 2023; Villodas et al., 2013), a program designed for students with ADHD in elementary schools. CLS includes a teacher component, parent component, and child skills component with a focus on collaboration across settings. The teacher component consists of behavior modification consultation, a school-home daily report, a homework-plan, and classroom accommodations. The parent component consisted of parent training modules focused on elements, such as improving homework routines, organization, peer interactions, stress management, use of praise, commands, rewards, discipline, and home-based token economy. The child component consisted of social skills modules (i.e., being a good sport, accepting consequences, assertion, dealing with teasing, problem solving, self-control, friendship making) and independence (homework skills, chores/tasks, and routines). Procedures for skills training included: (a) didactic instruction, (b) behavior rehearsal, and (c) in vivo practice with feedback and reinforcement). Additionally, Pfiffner et al. (2023) described the development and testing of a remote adaptation of CLS (CLS-R). The CLS-R adapted the program by shifting the delivery of training and support for school mental health providers to a web-based format. Coaching and resources were provided remotely, and progress monitoring was conducted through an online system. Summer Treatment Program (STP). Two studies investigated summer treatment programs (Barney et al., 2022; Sibley et al., 2011), which was originally designed by W. E. Pelham et al. (2005). The STP includes contingency management (token/point system, praise, effective commands, time out, daily report card) across academic and recreation settings, parent training, group problem solving, and SST (Fabiano et al., 2014). SST involves instruction in specific skills including communication, participation, validation, and cooperation and reinforcement of use of the skills throughout the day. Procedures for the group sessions include: (a) instruction, (b) modeling, (c) role-playing; and (d) practice. Additionally, during peer-focused activities, such as sports activities, in vivo teaching and reinforcement are used to increase generalization of the skills taught. Similarities and Differences. When comparing overall components, the programs are very similar (see Figure 2). Across all programs, interventions included child/adolescent social skills training, in vivo practice, and reinforcement. Five programs included behavior management strategies, such as token economies, and teacher training or consultation. Four programs included parent training or consultation. The primary difference lies in the inclusion of skills other than social competence, including academic and organizational skills, in the three multimodal programs and not the stand-alone programs. Additional differences can be found in implementation setting and methods of intervention design and implementation. CLS is implemented in schools during the academic day, CHP is implemented in an after-school program or as a consultation model during the academic day, and STP is implemented in a summer treatment program. All but CHP are designed for elementary school students. Differences are evident in the social skills approach. Specifically, social skills are taught through direct instruction in explicit modules in CLS, through self-awareness and social goal setting including IDEAL self-goals in CHP, and daily training in STP. Both CHP and STP include in-vivo instruction and reinforcement of social skills through recreation time periods. Differences can also be found in parent training, with structured weekly sessions in CLS, periodic sessions (e.g., monthly) in CHP, and intensive weekly sessions in STP. Additionally, differences can be found in behavior management strategies used. Both CLS and CHP rely on systems developed in schools when the program was implemented during the school day. CHP, when implemented in an afterschool setting, and STP include intensive behavioral systems. Differences can be found in the interventionists. School mental health staff implement CLS; teachers, counselors, and researchers implement CHP; and training clinicians and paraprofessionals implement STP. Finally, the intensity of the programs varies from approximately 12 weeks (CLS) to semester of yearlong (CHP) to daily for 6 to 8 weeks (STP). Outcomes Overall, the studies were single-case design (k = 2), one group, pre-post test design (k = 6), and between subjects (k = 9). There were 108 effect sizes, with 42 indicating no effect, 34 small effects, 20 moderate effects, and 12 large effects on social outcomes.

438 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(4) Effects at Study Level Single-Case Design Studies. Single-case design studies (k = 2; Colton & Sheridan, 1998; Sibley et al., 2011) included four participants (ages 8–9 years old) and reported six outcomes all measured through direct observation (see Table 3). One study was implemented in analogous classroom setting (Sibley et al., 2011; STP) and one in an elementary school (Colton & Sheridan, 1998). We analyzed the data through visual analysis (see Ledford et al., 2018; Vannest et al., 2016), Tau-U (Parker et al., 2011), and between-case standardized mean difference (BC-SMD; Pustejovsky et al., 2014) for one study that met the requirements (Colton & Sheridan, 1998). Results indicated that social skills training produced small to large effects. Using visual analysis, only one study (Colton & Sheridan, 1998) used a design with sufficient experimental control. Colton and Sheridan (1998) established a functional relation between a conjoint behavioral consultation treatment package and positive social interactions and playing in isolation with moderate effects. No functional relation was established for negative social interactions as baseline data indicated very minimal negative interaction. One Group Pretest/Posttest Design Studies. Within-group studies (k = 5; Corkum et al., 2010; Evans et al., 2004, 2005; Pfiffner et al., 2011; Villodas et al., 2013) included 117 participants and measured outcomes through five tools (CIS, IRS, SRSS/SSIS, ACES, and report cards). We calculated Cohen’s d (see Table 4) and qualified effects as no effect (<0.20), small (0.21–0.49), moderate (0.50–0.79), or large (≥0.80; Cohen, 1988). We caution the reader to interpret the qualifications cautiously as Cohen (1988) suggested that effect sizes be interpreted within context. Results indicated that across all measures (SRSS/SSIS, CIS, IRS, and report card), parents and teachers rated small (k = 9) to moderate (k = 9) effects of social skills training on broadband and narrowband ratings of social skills with one study finding no effect on one rating (i.e., math teacher ratings of social functioning with peers, Evans et al., 2005). Meta-Analysis Outcomes. We included nine studies in the meta-analysis, which included 81 effect sizes and 1,340 total participants. The first model built was a random effects meta-analytic model that used the inverse variance weighted mean at the study level. The base model provided an estimated effect of g = 0.0585 (SE = 0.09; 95% CI [−0.14, 0.26]). The model indicated large heterogeneity in effect size estimates. The I2 index was 60.18% and the Q-statistic was significant (df = 8; Q = 18.385; p = .0185). The standard deviation of effect sizes at the study level was large (τ = .19) and the variance of effect size estimates (τ2) was.0365. We evaluated publication bias in two steps. First, we investigated two funnel plots; the first included all 81 effect size estimates (see Supplemental Figure 1), and the second included the weighted average of the nine studies (see Supplemental Figure 2). Our visual inspections of the plots led us to believe there is potential asymmetry in the effect sizes estimates. Second, we conducted an Egger’s regression test that aligned with our visual analysis in suggesting asymmetry in the funnel plots (z = 2.46, p = .01; b0 = −0.003; 95% CI [−0.013, 0.07]). Discussion This is the first systematic literature review and meta-analysis to explore the effects of school-based social skills interventions on the social outcomes of youth with ADHD. We included single-case design studies, within-group, and between-group studies. Although the meta-analytic effect for the nine between-group effects was negligible (g = 0.09), we found a large range of effect sizes from no effect to large effects. Our findings related to school-based social skills programs contribute to the knowledge base that previously included clinic-based (Powell et al., 2022; d = 0.32) and clinic and school-based group design studies (Morris et al., 2021; d = 0.57). Across studies and 108 measured outcomes, effects were heterogenous, with 12 large effects, 20 moderate effects, 34 small effects, and 42 negligible or no effect. This suggests that it is possible that certain interventions and/or conditions may result in substantial improvements in specific contexts or with particular measures (Morris et al., 2021; Powell et al., 2022). Due to the likely influence of the small number of studies, none of the moderating variables we tested statistically significantly influenced the model. Nonetheless, to offer Figure 3. 442 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(4) some perspective, we discuss several of the moderators we examined. First, the identity of the individual who rated child behavior seemed to differentiate outcomes with selfratings indicating the largest effects, followed by teacher ratings, and then parent ratings. This pattern contradicts findings from Morris et al. (2021), who reported that parents perceived greater improvements than other raters. In addition to the small number of studies, the explanation for this discrepancy may be the context in which the interventions were delivered. For instance, Pfiffner et al. (2016) suggested that parent-reported improvements may be influenced when parents are aware of the intervention, a situation less likely to occur in schools than when interventions are delivered in clinical settings. Furthermore, because all interventions in this review were school based, it is likely that teachers had greater knowledge of the intervention content and implementation. Nonetheless, this pattern did not hold across all studies. For example, Pfiffner et al. (2023) found that parent ratings reflected greater effects than teacher ratings. The authors proposed that teachers may be less able to observe social interactions in unstructured settings such as lunch and recess, limiting their capacity to detect change. The implications of these rater discrepancies remain unclear. It is possible that the difference could be contributed to the rating scales themselves. Evans et al. (2023) emphasized the importance of developing and using social outcome measures that are sensitive enough to detect intervention effects. Furthermore, regarding self-ratings, only one study contributed data (five effect sizes), so this finding should be interpreted with caution. Additionally, in the current review outcomes were greater in elementary schools compared to middle or high schools. This finding contradicts previous research. For example, Evans et al. (2023) suggested that high school students with ADHD were more likely than middle school students to respond positively to social skills taught in CHP. They proposed that social skills interventions may be better suited for older adolescents. Given that social functioning often improves with maturity, it would be reasonable to expect stronger effects among high school students. This expectation may be particularly relevant when interventions require mature cognitive functioning, such as the IDEAL self-goals emphasized in CHP. However, this was not the case in the current review. It is possible that the age-related effects observed may be influenced by specific components of the intervention and/or characteristics of students, warranting further investigation. Although the limited number of studies and insufficient information precluded an analysis of gender as a moderator, Mikami et al. (2013) disaggregated findings by participant gender and program (i.e., MOSAIC, COMET). Their results revealed that only boys (not girls) benefited from the Mosaic program relative to COMET. As the study relied on peer ratings, the authors hypothesized that girls with ADHD may be perceived as more deviant than boys with ADHD in general, as students are likely to be more exposed to boys with ADHD due to prevalence. As such, ratings of girls would be lower than those of boys. Consequently, peer perceptions of girls may have been more resistant to change, even when teachers modeled acceptance. Additional research should explore the moderating effect of differences in programs. Although many similarities across programs were found, differences in social skill approaches, intensity, parent involvement, and settings were found. For example, interventions that provide opportunities to practice strategies learned in natural settings were more likely to show promising outcomes than those that did not. For example, Barney et al. (2022) found that the 360 hr of intervention, combined with scaffolded social activities, provided adolescents with ample opportunities to practice social skills and build reciprocal friendships. This type of in situ instruction, as was included in studies evaluated in this meta-analysis, where skills are practiced in authentic contexts, might be more effective than traditional, isolated instruction. Adolescents with ADHD often possess social knowledge, but struggle to apply it in everyday situations, making context-based practice essential for longterm improvement (de Boo & Prins, 2007). These findings emphasize the importance of providing opportunities for authentic practice in interventions, highlighting the broader factors that can influence the success of school-based social skills programs for students with ADHD. Unfortunately, the sample in this review was too small to make those comparisons. As more studies are conducted, it will be possible to explore specific differences in programs. Additionally, with time, as research continues to explore the interventions discussed in the current study, and others that might be developed, it is important that this review be replicated exploring the impact of duration and intensity on student outcomes. Future studies should examine how length of the intervention and time required influence the effectiveness of social skills interventions for youth with ADHD. Understanding these relationships will help guide practitioners in selecting and implementing interventions that are both developmentally appropriate and contextually feasible. Finally, differences in the effectiveness of social skills training may be attributed to individual child characteristics. Children with ADHD represent a heterogeneous population, and specific characteristics likely impact their response to intervention. For example, the severity of core ADHD symptoms may influence a child's ability to acquire and generalize social skills. Comorbid conditions, such as oppositional defiant disorder or anxiety may further complicate social functioning and lessen intervention effects. Additionally, cognitive abilities, including verbal skills, working memory, and emotion regulation, likely facilitate

Bussanich et al. 443 the acquisition and application of new social behaviors. A child's awareness of their own social challenges may also play a role, with greater insight potentially leading to increases in engagement and receptivity to intervention. Finally, intrinsic motivation to improve peer relationships may enhance the impact of social skills training. Together, these factors underscore the importance of considering individualized approaches to social skills interventions. An important finding in this review is the limited availability of school-based interventions specifically targeting social skills challenges among students with ADHD. Although only a small number of such interventions met inclusion criteria, it is encouraging that several have been evaluated across multiple studies and adapted in various formats. For example, multimodal interventions like the Summer Treatment Program (STP; Barney et al., 2022; W. E. Pelham et al., 2005; Sibley et al., 2011), Challenging Horizons Program (CHP; Evans et al., 2004, 2005, 2007, 2011, 2016, 2023; Schultz et al., 2016), and Collaborative Life Skills (CLS; Pfiffner et al., 2011, 2016, 2023; Villodas et al., 2013) have been tested across diverse settings and delivery models. The repeated evaluation of these interventions highlights their potential for scalability, adaptability, and sustained implementation in real-world school environments. However, it is also evident that the field remains largely dominated by these three multimodal programs, all of which have scholarly or conceptual ties to the original Summer Treatment Program (W. E. Pelham et al., 2005). However, we encourage researchers to consider findings across studies and potential moderators to continue expanding on these interventions and considering alternative approaches to supporting the social development of students with ADHD. Although only a small number of school-based interventions for social skills challenges of students with ADHD were included, it was encouraging that several have been evaluated in multiple studies with varying versions. For instance, multimodal interventions, such as the Summer Treatment Program (STP), Challenging Horizons Program (CHP), and Collaborative Life Skills (CLS) have been tested across different settings and formats. The repeated evaluation of these interventions underscores their potential for scalability and adaptation. The field appears to be dominated by these three multimodal interventions (STP; CHP; and CLS) that share similar overlapping theoretical orientations (i.e., cognitive behavioral) and practices. Nonetheless, they include different content and were developed separate from each other, limiting what can be concluded when comparing the results of each. Future research, following a design-based research model could evaluate the effects of including specific components based on ongoing assessment of student needs and responsiveness to intervention (e.g., Anderson & Shattuck, 2012). Consider the student with ADHD who demonstrates strengths in verbal reasoning but struggles with emotional regulation; the intervention could be tailored to capitalize on their verbal abilities through discussion-based strategies while simultaneously incorporating explicit instruction and practice in emotional regulation skills. Similarly, a student with strong motivation to form peer relationships but pronounced impulsivity may benefit from interventions emphasizing self-monitoring and reinforcement for behavioral inhibition. By embedding flexibility and responsiveness into intervention frameworks, researchers and practitioners may better address the heterogeneity of ADHD presentations and improve the effectiveness of social skills training efforts. Limitations Several limitations should be noted in this meta-analysis that may have affected the interpretation and generalizability of the findings. First, the limited number of studies specifically focused on school-based social skills interventions reduces the robustness of the conclusions drawn. Although we identified 17 studies, only 9 group design studies met the criteria for the meta-analysis. This limited sample size might diminish the statistical power or increase the likelihood that the effect sizes may not fully capture the variability of school-based social skills interventions across different educational settings and student populations. Another limitation is the variability in outcome measures across the included studies. Although we examined the effects of both broad and narrow measures of social functioning, the inconsistency in measurement tools and the reliance on self, peer, parent, and teacher ratings present challenges. Another limitation was that the studies reviewed varied significantly in the intensity, duration, and fidelity of intervention implementation, which may have contributed to the heterogeneity in the results. Some interventions were implemented over several weeks or months, while others spanned an entire academic year or summer program, making it difficult to assess the impact of the intervention application on outcomes. Additionally, not all studies reported fidelity checks or adherence to the intervention protocols, further complicating the ability to assess the actual effectiveness of the interventions. Future research should prioritize detailed reporting on implementation fidelity and focus on developing measurement tools to improve the consistency and comparability of outcomes within school settings. Finally, we did not include the prior terms used to describe ADHD, such as ADD, Hyperkinetic Reaction of Childhood, or AD/HD in our Boolean string. As such, some earlier studies might not have been included. Nonetheless, we conducted an exploratory brief search and did not find any additional studies.

444 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(4) Conclusion This systematic literature review and meta-analysis offers a comprehensive evaluation of the available data on the effectiveness of school-based social skills interventions (SST) for students with ADHD, addressing a crucial gap in the literature. Although the overall effect of these interventions are modest, specific programs, particularly multimodal ones, show significant promise by incorporating practice in educational settings (Barney et al., 2022; Evans et al., 2004; Pfiffner et al., 2016). Established interventions like the Summer Treatment Program (STP), Challenging Horizons Program (CHP), and Collaborative Life Skills (CLS) have been widely studied, providing valuable insights into how these programs can be effectively implemented in school settings to address the social skills deficits faced by students with ADHD (Evans et al., 2016; Pfiffner et al., 2011; Schultz et al., 2016). However, this study also highlights important challenges. Additionally, variability in outcome measures across studies complicates direct comparisons of effectiveness. Moving forward, improving the rigor of methodologies through detailed reporting on implementation fidelity and the development of standardized measurement tools will enhance the consistency and comparability of results. Addressing these gaps will provide educators, administrators, and policymakers with more precise guidance on designing, implementing, and evaluating social skills interventions that promote long-term social and academic success for students with ADHD, ultimately contributing to more supportive and inclusive school environments. She holds a Master’s degree in Developmental Psychology from Columbia University and a Bachelor’s degree in Psychology from Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey. Her research centers on ADHD, social abilities, and school-based interventions. Judith R Harrison, Ph.D, is an associate professor of Educational Psychology, Special Education Programs, at Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey. Her research interests are the effectiveness of accommodations and feasible and acceptable interventions for youth with ADHD. Corey Peltier is an associate professor of special education at the University of Oklahoma. His primary research interests are around effective assessment and intervention practices to enhance the math outcomes of children at-risk or identified with a disability. His secondary research interests are on the use of single case experimental designs and systematic reviews and meta-analysis to inform evidence-aligned practice Aayushi Patel is a Health Science Specialist at the Department of Veterans Affairs, with a primary focus on evaluating the effects of military environmental exposures and trust levels in veterans. She holds a Bachelor’s degree in Psychology and Sociology from Rutgers University, where she assisted in research for schoolbased interventions in students with ADHD. Paulomi Mehta is a psychotherapist at Gaya Therapy in New York City. She works primarily with individuals with an AEDP and EFT informed lens. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in Psychology from Rutgers University, where she worked in her role as research coordinator for school based interventions for students with ADHD. She also holds a Masters of Education in Counseling and Mental Health Services, and a Masters of Philosophy in Professional Counseling from the University of Pennsylvania. Kashees Patel is an Anti-Violence Advocate at Sakhi for South Asian Survivors, where she supports survivors of domestic violence through trauma-informed crisis intervention and safety planning. She earned her B.A. in Psychology and Health and Society from Rutgers University, where she contributed to research on school-based interventions for students with ADHD.

Epub 2025 Jan 3. http://doi.org/10.47626/2237‐6089‐2024‐0797 Are parents with bipolar disorder at higher risk of having offspring with ADHD? A systematic review Leandro L. Ferreira,1 Antonio E. Nardi,1 Laiana A. Quagliato1 Abstract Objective: The offspring of parents with bipolar disorder (BD) and with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) have a higher risk of having the same condition. Both disorders also share psychopathological symptoms; however, little is known about their genetic overlap. To examine whether the offspring of parents with BD have a greater chance of being affected by ADHD, we conducted a systematic review. Methods: From inception to August 12, 2024, we searched the PubMed, SciELO, PsycInfo and Cochrane databases. We included studies if they investigated the association of parental bipolar disorder with offspring outcomes and made a proper investigation of disorders using validated instruments based on the Diagnostic Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) or the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) criteria. Studies were excluded if: parents were under 18 years old or over 70; did not report original data; systematic reviews; in vitro studies; with an animal model; offspring older than 17 years of age or with any comorbid diagnosis with ADHD. To assess risk of bias, two authors independently used the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale quality assessment tool. Results: 23 articles met the inclusion criteria. The majority of the studies reported that the offspring of parents with BD were at higher risk for ADHD. Particularly, in all case-control studies, the risk of ADHD was higher in the case group than the control group. Conclusion: The current studies are yet heterogeneous and literature did not uncover the biological correlation of these disorders regarding genetic, biochemical, neuroimaging and neuropsychological aspects. Keywords: Bipolar, attention, hereditary, offspring, intergenerational. Introduction Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a highly hereditary, neurodevelopmental disorder that is associated with the risk of other mental disorders later in life, such as anxiety, substance use and depressive disorders.1‐3 Bipolar disorder (BD) is a mood disorder that is frequently associated with mental comorbidities but is rarely diagnosed in childhood.4 Various studies have already shown that bipolar disorder is also highly hereditary5,6; some have reported a seemingly higher chance of individuals with ADHD being diagnosed with BD later in life,7 but few have focused on the risk of mental disorders other than BD, especially neurodevelopmental disorders, among the offspring of parents with BD. Both BD and ADHD present some psychopathology similarities, such as mood lability, psychomotor agitation and distractibility.8 The neurobiology and neural circuitry deficiencies associated with bipolar disorder onset are not yet fully known, but the common symptomatology could indicate that these two disorders

Parents with bipolar disorder and ADHD offspring - Ferreira et al. 2 – Trends Psychiatry Psychother. 2026;48:e20240797 have some neurobiological correlation. Furthermore, evidence from genome-wide association studies have already identified significant single nucleotide polymorphism-based genetic correlation between these disorders and risk loci with shared effects on the two of them consistent with the existence of genetic overlap between BD and ADHD. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first review intended to investigate whether parents with bipolar disorder may have a greater chance of having offspring with ADHD. Positive findings may reinforce perspectives that suggest ADHD symptoms might be an initial phase of a longitudinal development of bipolar disorder.7,8 Methods This systematic review was reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidelines9 and was conducted following an a priori established protocol on PROSPERO10 (CRD42023431438). Database selection and search strategy From inception to August 12, 2024, PubMed database was searched using the following terms: “bipolar disorder,” “offspring,” “progeny,” “inheritance,” “family history,” “familial history,” “attention deficit hyperactivity disorder” and “ADHD.” SciELO, PsycInfo and Cochrane databases were also searched using these terms: “bipolar disorder,” “manic depression,” “bipolar affective disorder,” “children” “descendants,” “parents,” “genetic,” “family background, “family history,” “familial history,” “attention deficit hyperactivity disorder,” “hyperactivity disorder,” “attention deficit disorder” and “ADHD.” To avoid publication bias, non-English language studies and grey literature (for example, conference abstracts) were included. A structured search strategy based on the PICOS framework was used.11 Studies were included if they met the following criteria: a) enrolled adult parents with bipolar disorder and their offspring; b) investigated the association of parental bipolar disorder with offspring outcomes; c) conducted a proper investigation of bipolar disorder among parents made by a psychiatrist or using validated instruments based on the Diagnostic Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV, DSM-IV TR, DSM-5) or the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-9 and ICD-10) criteria; d) conducted a proper investigation of ADHD among the offspring of parents with BD made by a psychiatrist or using validated instruments based on DSM-IV, DSMIV TR, DSM V, ICD-9 or ICD-10 criteria; e) used any study design; f) a comparison group was preferable, but not mandatory. When reported in the study, both parents and offspring should have the control group. Studies were excluded if: enrolled parents who were adolescents under 18 years of age and elderly people (over 70); systematic reviews; studies that did not report original data; studies with an animal model; in vitro studies; enrolled offspring who were not under 18 years of age or had any comorbid diagnosis with ADHD. The systematic search protocol and full search terms for each database are detailed in Supplementary Materials S1 and S2. Two reviewers working independently considered the potential eligibility of each of the abstracts retrieved via the search strategy. Full-text articles were obtained unless both reviewers decided that an abstract was ineligible, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. The overall interobserver agreement of abstract selection was K = 0.70, which is deemed good to excellent agreement. Each full-text report was assessed independently by two reviewers for final study inclusion, and the agreement for final texts inclusions was K = 0.90. Data abstraction and risk of bias assessment Data on study-, parent-, and offspring-related characteristics were abstracted using a standardized form, and conducted independently by 2 researchers, with disagreements resolved by a third researcher. The following variables were extracted from all studies: authors, year of publication and subject characteristics of the parent and offspring groups. The risk of bias assessment of the individual studies was conducted independently by two authors (LLF and LAQ) using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale quality assessment tool.12 The overall interobserver agreement of methodological quality assessment was K = 0.64, which is deemed good to excellent agreement. Any disagreements were settled following discussion with a third reviewer (AEN). The details of the quality assessment are reported in Supplementary Table S1. Results 366 studies were found using the previously described strategy. Four duplicate records were removed. 424 records were screened, and after reading the abstracts, 94 systematic reviews and 261 reports which did not meet the inclusion criteria of enrolling adult parents with BD and/or their offspring were excluded. 69 studies were then assessed for full reading, and 46 of them were disqualified based on this article’s inclusion and exclusion criteria. Finally, a total of 23

Parent results The age of the parents ranged from 24 to 47 years old among the total sample. Thirteen studies identified the sex of the parents. In two of them, only female patients were included. All of the others identified the sex from a randomized sample selection, and noted the mother as being the most affected parent. Six studies identified substance use disorder as a comorbidity among parents, and five of them provided the percentage, which varied from 8% to approximately 85% among the investigated parents. Other comorbidities were also found, with one study pointing out that all parents had an associated Axis I disorder in addition to BD.26 In two studies, 21.8%7 and 20%29 of the parents were also diagnosed with ADHD. Nine studies reported the most common school grade among the offspring: in five of them, the majority of the participants were of school age; in three of them, they were of preschool age; one study showed high school as the most common school grade, while another identified the majority of participants as having already graduated. The majority of the studies found that parents with bipolar disorder had a higher risk of having offspring who developed ADHD. In three of these studies, this correlation was highly positive (OR = 2.67),14 (OR = 1.51),15 (OR = 2.88).19 Three other studies also confirmed that there was an association between bipolar disorder in parents and a higher prevalence of ADHD in offspring (OR = 0.19),13 (OR = 2.6),18 (OR = 1.63).20 Seven case-control studies compared the prevalence of comorbidities among parents with bipolar disorder and healthy controls, also reporting that the offspring of parents with bipolar disorder were more affected by ADHD than the offspring of control parents.7,21,22,24‐26,34 In one of these studies, this correlation even reached 39% of the sample.22 In the study conducted by HirshfeldBecker DR et al., the control group was formed by patients with panic disorder and major depressive disorder (MDD), which had a prevalence of occurrence of ADHD of 8.4% among the offspring meanwhile offspring of parents with BD had 23.5%.34 Two longitudinal studies also identified a significant prevalence of ADHD among parents with bipolar disorder of 28% and 40%, respectively.29,30 Specifically, maternal bipolar disorder was linked to a higher risk of ADHD in offspring in two studies.31,33 In the study conducted by Chen MH et al., women who developed bipolar disorder after giving birth and their children were followed for investigation and among those patients the prevalence of having offspring with ADHD in the follow-up was significant (OR = 4.18).33 A study comparing the frequency of ADHD, conduct disorder (CD) and emotional disorders among children of parents with BD, drug dependence and control found that the prevalence of ADHD among the offspring of parents with BD was higher than control. However, it was equivalent to the group of parents with drug dependence, suggesting that ADHD may be more frequent among parents with psychiatric disorders in general than control (OR = 0.2).32 Two studies found a meaningful correlation only before controlling for comorbid parental diagnoses and demographic variables.17,23 In the study conducted by Goetz et al. to investigate quality of life (QoL) in offspring of a parent with BD using the self-report questionnaire KIDSCREEN, between-group differences in parental and self-assessment were controlled for cooccurring conditions (DSM-5 disorders) with the use of logistic regression. Cross-informant (parent–child) agreement in the assessment of symptoms of mood and anxiety disorders was calculated as Kendall’s rank correlation coefficient (tau) and concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) for an ordinal rating and Cohen’s kappa for a dichotomous rating. To compare the KIDSCREEN (QoL) between groups, the raw scores were converted to the T scores (The KIDSCREEN Group Europe 2006) and unpaired t-tests were conducted followed by Cohen’s d calculation and least-square multiple regression to control for between-group differences for current psychopathology and family status.17 Sparks et al. used Odds ratios (ORs) to estimate the risk of disruptive mood dysregulation disorder based on status as offspring of bipolar parents or community control parents were calculated using generalized linear mixed models with family of origin used as a random effect variable. The model was initially constructed as a univariate model. Subsequently, demographic variables (age, gender, race, SES, and offspring living with both biological parents) and proband parent non-BD lifetime diagnoses (ADHD, depressive disorder, anxiety disorder, ODD/CD, and substance use disorder) were entered as potential covariates. Models were constructed with backward model selection procedures, removing demographic variables and parental diagnoses with p > 0.10 iteratively in order of magnitude until all variables remaining in the model were significant.23 One study did not find a higher prevalence of ADHD among the offspring of parents with bipolar disorder in comparison to control parents. In this study, this correlation was definitely negative.28 A study evaluating psychopathology in offspring of both parents with bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder (MDD) reported ADHD as being no more likely among the offspring of parents with bipolar disorder than among those of parents with MDD.25 In a 2021 case–control study comparing the most prevalent mental disorders among the offspring of parents with bipolar disorder, parents with ADHD and control parents, it was found that ADHD was more prevalent among offspring of parents with bipolar disorder than among offspring of control parents; however, it was not more prevalent among offspring of parents with ADHD.16 Discussion This systematic review shows that many studies in the literature point to a higher risk for parents with bipolar disorder of having offspring predisposed

The majority of the investigated studies reported that, in comparison to control parents, parents with bipolar disorder had a higher prevalence of having children being affected by ADHD. The follow-up of the longitudinal studies that investigated only the offspring of parents with bipolar disorder indicated a high risk of ADHD among their children as well. It is well known that a family history of bipolar disorder is associated with a higher risk for the condition.5 In addition, ADHD symptoms in childhood are commonly discussed as possible prodromes for adult bipolar disorder,7,8 conduct disorders35 and substance use disorders.36 Identifying epidemiological findings that suggest that ADHD could also be a significant outcome for the offspring of parents with BD may help to improve knowledge about the chances of children to have ADHD being in fact higher if their parents have BD. Some studies have already demonstrated that ADHD shares a positive genetic correlation with major depressive disorder, insomnia and depressive symptoms in general,37 which are not uncommon among BD patients. A meta-analysis of family genetic studies examining the comorbidity between ADHD and BD type I found a significantly higher prevalence of ADHD among relatives of bipolar I probands and a significantly higher prevalence of bipolar I disorder among relatives of ADHD probands.38 An analysis of shared heritability in common disorders of the central nervous system searching to understand the joint effect exerted by a pool of several small effect genomic variants which are in turn used to estimate the heritability that seems to be shared in between disorders pointed out that a common variant risk for psychiatric disorders was shown to correlate significantly especially among attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder and schizophrenia.39 Moreover, genomewide association studies (GWAS) have already found overlapping genes among the two disorders. In a crosstrait meta-analysis of GWAS on schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and depression, the SORCS3 gene was highlighted due to the fact that it was involved in all the five conditions of study.40 In an analysis of genomewide single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) data from the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium for the same five disorders, SNPs at four loci – regions on chromosomes 3p21 and 10q24, and SNPs in two L-type voltage-gated calcium-channel subunits, CACNA1C and CACNB2 – exceeded the cutoff for genome-wide significance (p < 5×10(-8)) in the primary analysis.41 Besides the genetic evidence, according to the current DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for ADHD, it also shares a psychopathology overlap with BD, such as talkativeness, hyperactivity and distractibility presented as manic episodes, in addition to emotional features seen in mood instability and irritability, which are also common in both disorders. The common overlap of psychopathology alterations between BD and ADHD could be related to shared neurocircuitry alterations.42 Another similar neurobiological alteration between these disorders was found in a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) monoamine metabolite concentrations analysis of ADHD and BD patients, which identified that both disorders were associated with higher CSF homovanillic acid (HVA) concentration in that sample.43 These previous findings suggest that these two mental disorders are somewhat correlated despite the present lack of robust information about the neurobiological mechanisms of BD. Regardless, clinical and epidemiological studies have shown rates of BD in subjects with ADHD are proportionally more elevated than other psychiatric conditions, and previous results from family studies show increased incidence of ADHD in offspring of probands with BD.8 Given that several staging models of bipolar disorder have been proposed over time, including an initial prodromal phase where mild symptoms of mood disorder similar to ADHD such as overactivity and impulsivity could happen before culminating in a first threshold episode of illness, it is possible that many ADHD symptoms that correlate with BD psychopathology may be involved in the first stage of a longitudinal development of bipolar disorder.44 The present review had a number of limitations. Performing a meta-analysis was not possible due to the heterogeneity of the results. Given that only a few studies were not originally from America, the crosscultural validity and applicability of the findings of this review to the global youth population is limited. It is worth noting that since ADHD is the most prevalent psychiatric disorder in children, it could also be that the results which show a higher prevalence of this disorder among the offspring of parents with bipolar disorder only represent the well-known higher prevalence of disorders in general among offspring of individuals with psychiatric disorders. Eight studies have indicated that parents with bipolar disorder also have comorbidities such as anxiety disorders, MDD or ADHD, which might represent confounders. Despite these limitations, our analysis of the evidence showed a methodologically robust corpus of studies. While it is well established that BD and ADHD might have a neurobiological and genetic linkage, the current studies are yet heterogeneous and literature did not uncover the biological correlation of these disorders regarding gene expression, biochemical pathways,

STRENGTHS AND LIMITATIONS OF THIS STUDY ⇒ ⇒This systematic review protocol is guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) to ensure methodological transparency and structured reporting. ⇒ ⇒A comprehensive search strategy will be employed across multiple electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus and the Cochrane Library, to ensure a thorough identification of relevant qualitative literature. ⇒ ⇒The restriction to peer-reviewed studies published in English from 2010 onwards may introduce language and publication bias, potentially excluding relevant studies from other languages or earlier periods. ⇒ ⇒The synthesis of findings is inherently dependent on the methodological quality and reporting standards of the primary qualitative studies, which may vary across research contexts. Abstract Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a widely recognised mental health condition that frequently persists into adulthood, significantly impacting emotional wellbeing, interpersonal relationships, education and employment. Adults with ADHD often report substantial psychosocial challenges, including stigma, emotional dysregulation and occupational impairment. However, current literature has primarily concentrated on clinical diagnosis, comorbidities and treatment outcomes with a disproportionate emphasis on quantitative symptom-based metrics. Consequently, there is a lack of synthesised evidence regarding the subjective psychosocial experiences of this population. This study aims to systematically synthesise qualitative evidence to develop a comprehensive understanding of how adults with ADHD navigate these psychosocial challenges. The findings will provide evidence-based information to inform the development of holistic clinical assessments and targeted psychosocial interventions that better address the lived realities of adults with ADHD. Methods and analysis A systematic search will be conducted across three electronic databases: PubMed, Scopus and the Cochrane Library. Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and keywords will be adapted according to the search syntax of each database. The Population–Exposure–Outcome framework will guide the definition of inclusion and exclusion criteria. Inclusion will be restricted to empirical, peer-reviewed qualitative studies published in English between 1 January 2010 and 31 December 2025 that explore the psychosocial experiences of adults (defined as ≥16 years) with a confirmed diagnosis of ADHD. Two reviewers will independently conduct study selection, data extraction and quality appraisal, with disagreements resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Methodological quality will be assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research. Data will be synthesised using Thomas and Harden’s thematic synthesis approach. Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval is not required as this review uses publicly available data from previously published studies. The findings will be disseminated through publication in a peer-reviewed journal and presentations at academic conferences. PROSPERO registration number CRD420251159182 Introduction Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADH D) is a commonly recognised mental health disorder that is characterised by difficulties with attention, increased levels of restlessness and impulsivity, typically beginning in childhood.1 However, for a substantial proportion of affected children, ADHD symptoms do not fully resolve with age and may persist into adulthood.2 According to the World Federation of ADHD International Consensus Statement,3 ADHD is no longer viewed solely as a childhood condition.3 4 Evidence also suggests that up to 40% of individuals diagnosed with ADHD in childhood continue to experience symptoms into adulthood.4 Although the prevalence of both persistent and symptomatic adult ADHD is observed to decline with advancing age,5 it remains a condition of significant public health importance. Consequently, adults who are diagnosed with ADHD face myriad psychosocial experiences in their daily life functioning. ADHD is increasingly understood as a complex condition arising from the combined influence of multiple genetic, environmental and psychosocial factors, rather than from a single cause.3 Prior research suggests that ADHD is associated with challenges and distress across psychological and working life.7–9 These challenges often extend beyond clinical symptoms to include difficulties in personal functioning and economic outcomes, particularly in relation to employment and job stability.7 10 Longitudinal studies tracking individuals from childhood into adulthood, as well as cross-sectional investigations of adult populations, indicate that ADHD is associated with an elevated risk of unemployment.11–13 Moreover, in workplace settings, individuals with ADHD are more likely to experience poorer job performance, frequent job changes, voluntary job leaving and dismissal compared with individuals without ADHD.14 Despite growing evidence on adult ADHD burden, adults’ psychosocial experiences of living with ADHD in everyday life remain insufficiently understood in a focused, experiencecentred synthesis. Prior qualitative evidence, such as interviews with 20 adults diagnosed with ADHD aged between 20 and 64 years, Oscarsson et al reported a range of social challenges linked to both ADHD symptoms and workplace demands.8 Participants described common difficulties, such as inattention, forgetfulness and impulsivity, as well as less frequently recognised challenges, particularly problems related to emotional regulation.8 In addition, adults diagnosed with ADHD often face psychological factors such as mood swings, depression, stress, sleep disturbance and anxiety.2 However, these are often treated as comorbidities, which may complicate recognition and management.2 Similarly, another study from Alghamdi et al among university students showed that, among university populations, ADHD sufferers have been linked with depressive and anxiety symptoms and poorer academic performance.9 Further findings from a qualitative case study involving Indonesian elementary school teachers indicated that insufficient understanding of ADHD contributes to students’ academic, social and behavioural problems, alongside stigma and negative labelling, underscoring the importance of teacher education and supportive school policies.15 In a qualitative phenomenological study of parents of children with ADHD, Mesfin and Habtamu revealed pervasive psychosocial challenges, including stigma, emotional distress, financial pressure and marital strain, alongside the use of both inward and outward coping strategies to manage caregiving demands.16 Furthermore, Chen et al stated that beyond symptoms, ADHD can affect functional outcomes such as employment participation; comorbid stress-related and mood conditions may increase vulnerability.17 ADHD has also been linked to a higher risk of road traffic accidents, substance use disorders, suicidality and chronic physical illnesses. Over time, these factors may contribute to lower earning potential among individuals living with ADHD.3 18–21 Furthermore, particularly in adulthood, ADHD is linked to substantial psychosocial difficulties, many of which are compounded by late diagnosis. Katzman et al,22 in a narrative clinical review of adult ADHD, reported that ADHD is highly comorbid with mood, anxiety, substance use and personality disorders, and that overlapping symptomatology substantially complicates diagnosis and management.22 Through thematic analysis of interviews with adult-diagnosed women, Morgan demonstrated that late ADHD diagnosis is associated with cumulative psychosocial harm, including trauma, internalised ableism and unmet psychological care needs, despite diagnosis being perceived as validating.23 Therefore, adults diagnosed with ADHD go through strong emotional reactions before accepting the diagnosis, suggesting that psychological support is essential during and after diagnosis.24 Additionally, several quantitative pieces of evidence also indicate adults’ experiences, including a large questionnaire-based study (N=414), which illustrated that early recognition and stimulant treatment of ADHD, especially during childhood, was the strongest independent predictor of occupational participation in adulthood, regardless of psychiatric comorbidity or current treatment status.13 A comparative survey study in Japan demonstrated that adults with ADHD show markedly greater psychosocial and occupational impairment, including comorbid mental health conditions, reduced work productivity and adverse effects on relationships and self-esteem, compared with non-ADHD adults.25 Furthermore, a field study of 171 employees26 found that adults with ADHD experienced higher levels of job burnout compared with non-ADHD employees, and that this relationship was significantly mediated by executive function deficits.26 ADHD and psychological factors such as depression and stress have a significant relationship.11 12 27 Studies27 suggest that adults with ADHD are at an increased risk of depressive disorders. Much of the research on adult ADHD has focused primarily on clinical diagnosis, psychiatric comorbidity and treatment outcomes, with a strong emphasis on quantitative measurement and symptom-based assessment. Although individual qualitative studies have provided important insights, these findings remain scattered across diverse settings and topics and have not yet been systematically synthesised in a focused, experience-centred manner. This fragmentation results in a limited integrated understanding of adults’ lived psychosocial experiences of ADHD, creating a critical gap in the evidence base required for comprehensive clinical management. While quantitative data are effective in measuring impairment, they often fail to capture the subjective, nuanced ways in which adults perceive, navigate, and cope with the challenges of ADHD in their personal, social and occupational lives. Addressing this evidence gap is therefore imperative for multiple audiences, most notably for clinical practice. For clinicians and mental health professionals, a robust synthesis of adults’ lived psychosocial experiences can facilitate a move beyond traditional, symptom-based diagnostic frameworks towards more holistic and accurate person-centred assessments. Specifically, such an evidence synthesis can inform the development and refinement of targeted psychosocial interventions that address the daily functional and emotional challenges, including workplace difficulties, relationship strain and internalised stigma, which are frequently overlooked in standard clinical care. For researchers, this review will help to identify critical dimensions of the adult ADHD experience that are insufficiently captured by existing comorbidity profiles alone, thereby highlighting priorities for future investigation. Therefore, the purpose of this qualitative evidence synthesis is to synthesise research on the psychosocial and everyday life experiences of adults with ADHD, with the explicit goal of generating actionable insights to inform future research, clinical practice and person-centred approaches to support and care. Study aim 1. To systematically identify and synthesise qualitative evidence on the psychosocial experiences of adults living with ADHD. 2. To develop a comprehensive understanding of how adults with ADHD experience and navigate psychosocial challenges in everyday life, including social, emotional and occupational contexts. Methods Protocol and registration The protocol is registered in the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420251159182).29 The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P) guideline has been maintained to structure the protocol (online supplemental file PRISMA-P Checklist).30 The systematic review will be conducted within a predefined timeframe, commencing in June 2026 and anticipated to conclude in December 2026, in accordance with established systematic review procedures. Design A qualitative narrative synthesis design will be used for this systematic review. Eligibility criteria Inclusion and exclusion criteria Types of participants This review will include studies with participants who have a confirmed diagnosis of ADHD. Participants will be selected based on the recognised diagnostic criteria, including Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5)/ Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR), Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition (DSM-IV), Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-IV-TR), International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10)/ International Classification of Diseases, Eleventh Revision (ICD-11) definitions, or clinician-confirmed medical record diagnosis. Studies wherein the diagnosis was confirmed through a clinician’s assessment of medical records or via structured/semistructured diagnostic interviews such as Diagnostic Interview for ADHD in Adults, Fifth Edition (DIVA-5), Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview (MINI), Structured Clinical Interview for DSM Disorders (SCID), Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age Children (K-SADS), will also be eligible for inclusion (K-SADS) will also be considered eligible. The eligible participant age range will be defined as 16 years and older to capture the psychosocial experiences of both young and established adults. While studies focused solely on paediatric populations will be excluded, those reporting on mixed-age samples will be included if the data for participants aged 16 and above can be distinctly analysed or if this age group constitutes the majority of the sample. Children, infants and older adults (aged over 65) will be excluded to ensure a focused synthesis on the core adult life-course and to maintain methodological homogeneity. Qualitative studies include, but are not limited to, study designs such as phenomenology, grounded theory, ethnography and action research. Mixed-method studies will be deemed eligible if their qualitative components and associated findings can be clearly and independently extracted for synthesis. Literature based on quantitative data, particularly observational studies such as cross-sectional, case–control, cohort, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, scoping reviews, commentaries, conference abstracts, editorials and opinion pieces will be excluded from the review. We will also exclude all clinical trials, randomised controlled trials (RCTs), cluster-RCTs and quasi-RCTs, as this study area includes public health research. The search will be restricted to studies published between 2010 and 2025 to capture contemporary literature reflecting the evolving recognition of ADHD as a lifespan condition, particularly following the transition towards DSM-5 diagnostic conceptualisations. In addition, recent decades have seen increasing qualitative attention to the psychosocial and lived experiences of adults with ADHD within changing social and technological contexts. Preliminary scoping searches also indicated that the majority of relevant qualitative studies were published after 2010, supporting the appropriateness of this time frame. Types of phenomena of interest The central phenomenon of interest for this review encompasses the psychosocial experiences of adults diagnosed with ADHD. Outcome measures Primary outcome Primary outcomes will be to identify the key themes in the psychosocial and lived experiences of adults living with ADHD, including experiences in social life, education and work and how they cope with daily challenges and social difficulties. For this protocol, ‘psychosocial experiences’ is defined as a broad, multidimensional construct that includes the interplay between an individual’s psychological processes, such as self-perception, emotional regulation, coping mechanisms, etc, and their social-contextual factors, including interpersonal relationships, occupational functioning, educational attainment, etc. Rather than predefining specific factors, this review will employ an inductive approach, consistent with qualitative narrative synthesis, where the key themes and constituent factors of the psychosocial experience will be systematically derived directly from the narratives and interpretations reported in the included primary studies. Secondary outcome The secondary outcome of this review is to deliberate on the implications of the review findings for future research, clinical practice and policy related to adult ADHD. Search strategy A preliminary search of the PROSPERO international prospective register of systematic reviews was conducted to ensure the novelty of the review topic and to avoid duplication of existing research. As the review team has already ensured that, we then developed our search strategy and the selection of electronic databases. Every team member was associated with the strategic plan. A comprehensive search of several international bibliographic databases will be conducted to identify all relevant published literature. The criteria for including and excluding articles will be set before identifying those relevant articles that match the review’s objective. A useful way to clarify objectives, pinpoint key terms and create set inclusion and exclusion criteria is the Population, Exposure and Outcome (PEO) framework.31 The PEO framework31 will be used to identify search terms using Boolean operators (AND/OR/NOT). A detailed PEO-based search term is in table 1. A comprehensive search of three core electronic bibliographic databases, PubMed, Scopus and Cochrane Library, will be conducted. These databases have been selected for their extensive and authoritative coverage of international biomedical health and psychological literature, ensuring a robust foundation for identifying relevant studies. The search will be restricted to studies published on or before 31 December 2025. In addition, different search strategies will be used for each database, where we will use a combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and keywords, depending on the search methods of the databases. To further enhance the comprehensiveness of our search and mitigate potential publication bias, the primary database search will be supplemented by a thorough review of the reference lists of all included studies (snowballing) and by conducting forward citation searches on key included articles. An example of a search strategy for the PubMed database is added in table 2. Study selection Following the comprehensive database search, all retrieved records will be collated and imported into Zotero bibliographic software (V.8.0) to facilitate the identification and removal of duplicate entries. Following the removal of duplicates, the remaining unique records will undergo a three-stage screening process, which will be conducted independently by two reviewers (AHMF and SAU). In the initial stage, titles will be screened against the predefined eligibility criteria. In the second stage, the abstracts of all retained records will be reviewed to determine their relevance and suitability for full-text assessment. The final stage will consist of a detailed examination of the full texts of all potentially eligible studies to confirm their final inclusion. Risk of bias (Quality) assessment The methodological quality of the included studies will be assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research.32 33 This tool is specifically designed to evaluate the methodological rigour, credibility, and relevance of qualitative studies based on empirical data. The checklist consists of 10 items that assess key methodological domains, including the congruity between the research methodology and the research question, the adequacy of data collection methods, the appropriateness of data analysis, the representation of participants’ voices, and the coherence between data, analysis and interpretation. Each included study will be independently appraised by two reviewers (AHMF and SAU). For each item, studies will be rated as ‘yes’, ‘no’, ‘unclear’ or ‘not applicable’, in accordance with JBI guidance. Any discrepancies between reviewers will be resolved through discussion, and if consensus cannot be reached, a third reviewer (NMRAC) will be consulted to make the final decision. This process will help to ensure transparency and consistency in the quality appraisal. The results of the quality assessment will be used to inform the interpretation of the review findings, but will not be used as a basis for excluding studies. Additional information will not be sought from study authors if methodological details are unclear or missing in the published reports, and assessments will be based solely on the information available in the studies included. Data extraction For the included studies, a structured data extraction form will be developed. Data will be extracted using the JBI Qualitative Assessment and Review Instrument, which is a standardised tool recommended for the organisation and synthesis of qualitative evidence.34 Two reviewers (AHMF and SAU) will independently extract data from each included study, and the extracted information will be cross-checked for accuracy. Any conflict will be resolved through discussion, with the involvement of a third reviewer (NMRAC) where necessary. The data extraction form will capture key study characteristics, including the research methodology, phenomena of interest, study setting, geographical and cultural context, participant characteristics, data analysis methods and main findings. Additional bibliographic and descriptive information will also be recorded, such as author details, publication year, journal name, study objectives, study design, sample size and other relevant contextual information necessary for the synthesis. Data synthesis The synthesis of qualitative data will be conducted following the three-stage thematic synthesis approach as described by Thomas and Harden.35 The synthesis process will involve several structured and iterative steps to ensure rigour and depth of analysis. In the initial stage, all relevant findings from the included studies will be examined through line-by-line coding. This process will involve careful reading of the findings sections of each study to identify meaningful units of text related to the review objectives. Initial codes will be generated inductively to reflect participants’ experiences, perceptions and interpretations. Coding will be iterative, and data segments may be assigned more than one code where appropriate to capture the complexity of the data. In the second stage, related codes will be compared and grouped to form descriptive themes. These themes will summarise patterns across studies and provide an organised description of the key psychosocial experiences reported by adults living with ADHD. During this stage, the themes will be refined through repeated comparison with the original data to ensure that they accurately represent the underlying findings. In the final stage, analytical themes will be developed by interpreting the descriptive themes in relation to the review questions. This stage will move beyond description to generate higher-level explanations and insights into how adults experience, understand and cope with ADHD in their daily lives. NVivo V.14 software will be used to support data management, coding and theme development throughout the analysis process, helping to organise the data systematically and enhance transparency. Patient and public involvement None. Discussion Adults living with ADHD frequently encounter significant challenges that adversely affect their emotional well-being, interpersonal relationships, education and employment. The literature indicates that experiences of stigma, difficulties with emotional regulation and impairments in occupational functioning are commonly reported. ADHD exerts a marked influence on occupational functioning in adulthood.36 The core symptoms of the disorder, such as impaired concentration and difficulties with executive functions like organisation and time management, can directly undermine work performance and productivity. Consequently, adults with ADHD often report feeling persistently overwhelmed by routine responsibilities, which may lead to strained professional relationships and frequent job changes. As a result, frequent job changes are common among adults who are diagnosed with ADHD.13 Transitions to new roles typically involve heightened expectations for self-discipline, organisational skills and emotional regulation.25 Over time, these sustained demands can increase vulnerability to Protected by copyright, including for uses related to text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies. . This risk is compounded not only by the intrinsic features of ADHD but also by the high prevalence of coexisting mental health conditions.13 25 26 37 The findings may inform more person-centred clinical practice and service planning. A better understanding of lived experiences may support the development of interventions that address psychosocial needs alongside clinical management. The review may also identify gaps in current research and highlight priorities for future qualitative inquiry. To our knowledge, this will be the first systematic review to synthesise qualitative evidence on the psychosocial experiences of adults diagnosed with ADHD. Existing research related to ADHD has mainly focused on its symptoms, prevalence, comorbidities and treatment outcomes. There remains a limited synthesis of qualitative findings that reflect how adults experience ADHD in everyday life, and this review aims to address this gap. This review has potential limitations. Only peer-reviewed studies published in English from 2010 onwards will be included, which may introduce language and publication bias. Although a comprehensive search strategy will be applied, some relevant studies may not be identified. The conclusions will depend on the methodological quality of the included studies. Despite these limitations, this review will provide a transparent synthesis of qualitative evidence and contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of adult ADHD. Study status This review protocol was prospectively registered with PROSPERO before the commencement of the systematic review process. At the time of protocol submission, the review was in its preliminary stages, with only the development of the search strategy and initial screening procedures underway. No data extraction, quality appraisal or data synthesis had been conducted. The protocol remains open to refinement, and any amendments arising from peer review will be transparently documented and justified in the final review. The study is projected to be completed by the end of 2026. Amendments Any modifications to this protocol will be explicitly documented, with a clear description of the changes and the rationale for each amendment. The revised version will also be updated and recorded in the PROSPERO register to ensure transparency, including details of the previous version of the systematic review protocol. Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval is not required for this review because it is based on a retrospective analysis of publicly available data and involves the secondary use of previously published studies. The findings will be disseminated through publication in a peer-reviewed journal and presented at relevant conferences and academic meetings. Existing continuous performance tests are unimodal and lack validity. Objective: This study aimed to conduct an initial evaluation of the diagnostic discrimination of BOKE STARS (Sustained Task and Attention Response Screening), a culturally adapted bimodal continuous performance test, for distinguishing children with ADHD from typically developing children in a Chinese clinical setting. Methods: In this prospective, single-center diagnostic accuracy study with a case-control design, 100 children aged 6 to 12 years (n=50 with ADHD and n=50 controls) were recruited at Xinhua Hospital between January and May 2024. Parents completed the Swanson, Nolan, and Pelham Rating Scale–fourth version (SNAP-IV), and children completed the BOKE STARS assessment on a tablet device under standardized conditions. Group comparisons were conducted using independentsample 2-tailed t tests or Mann-Whitney U tests, as appropriate. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed in the full case-control sample to assess diagnostic discrimination. Sensitivity and specificity were reported descriptively across ROC-derived cutoffs; these cutoffs were not interpreted as clinically validated diagnostic thresholds. Secondary exploratory analyses included comparisons among ADHD subtypes and correlations between BOKE STARS indices and parent-reported SNAP-IV symptom severity scores. Results: Compared with controls, children with ADHD performed significantly worse on all major BOKE STARS indices, including errors of omission, errors of commission, reaction time, reaction time variability (RTV), discrimination prime, and total score. In the full case-control sample, the total score showed the strongest diagnostic discrimination (area under the ROC curve [AUC] 0.962, 95% CI 0.931-0.992), followed by RTV (AUC 0.919, 95% CI 0.867-0.971), errors of omission (AUC 0.884, 95% CI 0.818-0.950), and discrimination prime (AUC 0.819, 95% CI 0.737-0.900). Errors of commission (AUC 0.689, 95% CI 0.585-0.792) and reaction time (AUC 0.634, 95% CI 0.524-0.743) showed comparatively weaker discrimination.
