A valid linkage required an exact match of mother and child identification numbers and delivery date. We excluded pregnancies with missing linkage or incomplete key information (eg, infant sex, last menstrual period [LMP]), followed by miscarriages, perinatal death, and multifetal pregnancies, creating a singleton live birth cohort. To strengthen association, we used a triangulation of approaches.30Theprimaryanalysisusedasibling-matcheddesign. From the singleton live birth cohort, we identified all maternalsiblings(ie,childrensharingthesamebiologicalmother) and constructed a cohort of families with discordant prenatal paracetamol exposure (ie, at least 1 sibling exposed and another unexposed) (eFigure 1 in Supplement 1).31 We also conducted a conventional cohort analysis and negative control exposure analysis (prepregnancy and postpregnancy) in the full population.32,33 Prenatal Paracetamol Exposure The pregnancy period was defined as from the LMP to delivery, with LMP derived by subtracting clinically determined gestational age (based on first-trimester ultrasonography imaging) from the delivery date. Trimesters were defined as first (0-12 weeks), second (13-27 weeks), and third (28 weeks to delivery). Prenatal paracetamol exposure was ascertained from prescription records in the public health care system; over-thecounter (OTC) purchases and private prescriptions were not captured. Prescription records provided detailed, preprescription information, including drug name, formulation, strength (mg), prescribed number of tablets per administration, administration frequency (times/d), and start and end dates. Paracetamol was identified using the British National Formulary (BNF), section 4.7.1. Data completeness for key fields was high (99.98%), enabling robust derivation of exposure timing, pattern, and dosage. Theprimaryexposurewasanyparacetamoluseduringpregnancy. To assess critical developmental windows (timing) and exposure patterns,34 we created mutually exclusive categories: unexposed, sporadic (use in 1 trimester only), intermittent (use in any 2 trimesters), and persistent (use in all 3 trimesters). To assess for a biological gradient, we calculated mean daily dose (mg/d) as strength × dosage per administration × frequency, then categorized use as: none; low (<27.5mg/d;<25thpercentile);medium(27.5to<75.2mg/d;25th to 75th percentile); and high (≥75.3 mg/d; >75th percentile). Outcomes and Follow-Up Primary outcomes were clinically diagnosed ASD, per ICD9-CM code 299; or ADHD per code 314 or a filled prescription for an ADHD-specific medication licensed in Hong Kong (ie, methylphenidate,atomoxetine,orlisdexamfetamine;BNF,section 4.4.26,35 Children were included in the ASD analyses only if they had 2 or more years of follow-up, and in ADHD analyses only if they had 5 or more years of follow-up. Follow-up began at delivery and continued until the first occurrence of outcome, death, or December 31, 2023 (eFigure 2 in Supplement 1). Covariates We adjusted for a comprehensive set of covariates selected a priori based on literature and clinical expertise including maternalcharacteristicsatdelivery,medicalconditionsandmedication use before or during pregnancy, and child characteristics at birth (eTable 1 in Supplement 1). Statistical Analysis Sibling-Matched Analysis We used stratified Cox proportional hazards regression (stratified by family) with cluster-robust standard errors to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) for the association between prenatal paracetamol exposure and ASD or ADHD. A 2-sided P < .05 was considered statistically significant. Data analysis was conducted from October 2, 2025, to March 24, 2026. Subgroup Analysis Using the exposure metrics defined previously, we estimated risks by exposure patterns (sporadic, intermittent, and persistent), dose-response (categorized mean daily dose). Given the established male predominance in neurodevelopmental disorders (approximately 3:1 for ASD and 2:1 for ADHD),36,37 we stratified by child sex. To account for temporal changes in diagnostic criteria and prescribing practices, we stratified by birth era (2001-2010 vs 2011 onwards). We also evaluated maternal age (≥35 years) as a potential modifier. Sensitivity Analysis We evaluated the robustness of our findings to alternative exposure definitions: (1) sustained use (≥1 prescription of ≥7 consecutive days); and (2) cumulative use (total supply ≥7 days for all prescriptions).38 Then, to mitigate potential confounding by indication, we excluded from the unexposed group those mothers who were prescribed alternative analgesics (oral opioids or nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs [NSAIDs]) during pregnancy.39 Full Cohort Analysis As part of our triangulation strategy, we reestimated the association in the full cohort using propensity score (PS) matching (1:1, calliper width = 0.05), and inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), achieving covariate balance (standardized mean differences [SMD] < 0.10).40,41 In addition, we conducted negative control exposure analyses using maternal paracetamol use in the year preceding pregnancy (prepregnancy) and in the year after delivery (postpregnancy). For ASD analysis, the cohort comprised 124 333 children (mean [SD] age, 9.3 [4.7] years; 61 775 females [49.7%] and 62 558 males [50.3%]) with discordant prenatal paracetamol exposure. Median (IQR) follow-up was 10.2 (6.8-14.1) years, during which 3445 children were diagnosed with ASD (2.8%). For ADHD analysis, the cohort comprised 97 285 children (mean [SD] age, 7.6 [4.2] years; 48 455 females [49.8%] and 48 830 males [50.2%]) with discordant prenatal paracetamol exposure. Prenatal Paracetamol Exposure and ASD or ADHD in Offspring Primary and Subgroup Analyses (Sibling-Matched Cohort) In the primary sibling-matched analysis, prenatal paracetamol exposure was not associated with ASD (adjusted HR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.91-1.11) or ADHD (adjusted HR, 1.01; 95% CI, 0.93 to 1.08). There was no evidence of a critical exposure window by trimester nor meaningful variation in risk by exposure patterns (sporadic, intermittent, persistent) or categorized mean daily dose, with no dose-response relationship for either outcome (Figure 2 and Figure 3). This included when exposure was redefined based on sustained use (≥7 consecutive days) or cumulative use (total supply ≥7 days), and when the unexposed comparator was restricted to women not dispensed alternative analgesics (opioids or NSAIDs) (eTable 3 in Supplement 1). Discussion This study triangulated evidence using a sibling-matched design, a conventional cohort analysis, and a negative control exposure analysis in the full cohort. Our primary siblingmatched analysis, which accounted for unmeasured familial confounding, found no association between prenatal paracetamol exposure and the risk of ASD or ADHD in offspring. This null finding was robust across exposure timing, patterns,anddoses.Incontrast,theconventionalcohortanalysis, despite extensive adjustment for measured confounders, replicatedthepositiveassociationsfrequentlyreportedinprior literature.6ThepersistenceofpositiveassociationsafterPSand IPTW adjustment suggests that unmeasured familial factors, particularlygeneticpredispositionandhealthliteracy,arelikely the primary source of residual confounding. These factors are inherently accounted for in the sibling design but cannot be fully captured by conventional administrative data. Most critically, the negative control analyses also yielded positive associationswithbothprepregnancyandpostpregnancyexposure— periods when an associated effect of paracetamol on fetal neurodevelopment is biologically implausible. Collectively, these findings suggest that the positive signal observed in both conventional and negative control analyses reflect residual familial confounding, rather than a true pharmacologic effect of prenatal paracetamol exposure.44,45 Together, these study findings—positive associations in conventional cohort analyses but null results in siblingmatchedanalyses—reconciletheconflictingliterature.Theconsistency of null findings from robust sibling-matched designs across different populations,11-13 now provides strong evidence against a causal link. The collective evidence supports current regulatory guidance on the safety of indicated antenatal paracetamol use. Paracetamol remains a safe and essential analgesic and antipyretic during pregnancy, whereas alternatives such as NSAIDs and opioids carry welldocumented risks, including teratogenicity, oligohydramnios, neonatal abstinence syndrome, and kidney damage.46-48 Unwarranted reluctance to use paracetamol could lead to undertreatment of pain and fever, or the use of more harmful alternatives, both posing risks to the pregnancy and developing fetus.49 Clinicians should reassure patients that paracetamol is safe when used as clinically indicated, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary duration. Strengths and Limitations A key strength of our study is the application of complementary analytical designs to address pervasive unmeasured confounding, including confounding by indication and shared familial factors. Given the strong familial aggregation of ASD and ADHD,15,16 our sibling-matched design inherently controlled for stable genetic and environmental factors shared within families. Our null results align with sibling-matched studies from Norway, Sweden, and Japan, which also found attenuated associations after controlling for familial factors.6,12,17,18 This convergence across diverse populations strengthens the evidence against a causal effect. Moreover, this study extends the existing literature in several ways. First, extended follow-up (up to 23 years) provides stable estimates with sufficient statistical power, as reflected in the narrow confidence intervals of our null findings. Second, using prospectively recorded electronic prescriptions records, we moved beyond binary ever-use assessment that characterized most prior sibling-matched studies.12,17 This objective data source enabled granular analyses of exposure timing, patterns of use, and doseresponse relationships.12,18 Third, these detailed analyses offer timely evidence to address specific clinical concerns regarding paracetamol used during pregnancy. Several limitations warrant consideration. First, while the sibling-matched design controls for shared familial confounders,ithasinherentlimitations.31Althoughweadjustedformeasured nonshared factors (eg, age, birth order), residual nonshared confounding may persist and could even be amplified in sibling comparisons.50 The design generally assumes an Table 2. First, our quantitative bias analysis indicated that such misclassification is unlikely to fully explain the null findings. Second, within a sibling-matched design, maternal behavior regarding uncaptured medication use is likely consistent across pregnancies, reducing bias in withinfamily comparisons. Lee, PhD; Viktor H. Ahlqvist, PhD In September 2025, the US administration held a press conference stating that its ongoing investigation into the causes of autism had identified maternal use of acetaminophen ( p a r a c e t a m o l ) d u r i n g pregnancy as a potential causal factor. This was concerning given that acetaminophen is among the most used medications in pregnancy for the management of pain and fever, in part because alternative options are limited or contraindicated (eg, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications and opioids). Assessing pregnancy medication safety with regard to long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes is challenging. This research requires large sample sizes, long-term follow-up into childhood, and is highly susceptible to confounding. The causes of neurodevelopmental conditions are multifactorial and often strongly correlated with maternal health, behaviors, and genetic predisposition.1 Addressing these sources of bias is necessary before any inference that acetaminophen causes neurodevelopmental outcomes can be made. One approach to attempt to eliminate this confounding is the sibling comparison design, in which exposed and unexposed siblings are compared directly. By leveraging within-family comparisons, this design accounts for all confounding factors shared by siblings, including maternal genetics and stable environmental influences.2 In the context of acetaminophen and neurodevelopmental outcomes, 4 prior studies, conducted in Japan, Norway, Sweden, and Taiwan, have applied sibling comparison designs and consistently found no increased risk when comparing siblings.3,4 However, the Japanese and Norwegian studies were relatively small, and although the Swedish and Taiwanese studies were larger, they warrant replication in independent populations before definitive conclusions can be drawn.3-5 In this issue of JAMA Internal Medicine, Luo et al6 extend the literature by reporting findings from a large-scale study conducted in Hong Kong. Evidence Against a Causal Association Using comprehensive health records from the Hong Kong Hospital Authority and a mother-child linkage, Luo et al6 identified 597 937 and 516 928 liveborn singleton children for analyses of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/ hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), respectively, after excluding thosewithinsufficientfollow-upormissingcovariatedata.Approximately 43.3% of these pregnancies involved dispensed acetaminophen. Inanalysesofthefullpopulationcohort,adjustingformeasured confounders, prenatal acetaminophen exposure was associated with increased risks of autism (hazard ratio [HR], 1.17; 95% CI, 1.13-1.20) and ADHD (HR, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.20-1.27), findings consistent with those of prior studies. Interestingly, maternal acetaminophen use in the year prior to pregnancy was associated with a similar increase in risk, suggesting that these associations reflect residual confounding rather than a causal effect, given that prepregnancy exposure would not be expected to affect offspring neurodevelopment (ie, a negative control exposure). Within this cohort, the authors further identified 124 333 and 97 285 exposure-discordant sibling pairs for analyses of ASD and ADHD, respectively. In sibling comparison analyses, the associations attenuated to the null (ASD: HR, 1.00 [95% CI, 0.91-1.11]; ADHD: HR, 1.01 [95% CI, 0.93-1.08]), consistent with confounding observed in the negative control analysis. Taken together, the modest associations observed in the full cohort, the comparable estimates for prepregnancy exposure (negative control), and the attenuation to the null in sibling comparisons provide converging evidence against an associated causal relationship between prenatal acetaminophen exposure and ASD or ADHD. Changes in Genetic Contributions to ASD and ADHD by Year of Diagnosis Sonja LaBianca, MD, PhD; Mette Lise Lousdal, PhD; Morten Dybdahl Krebs, MD, PhD; Ole Sahlholdt Hansen, MSc; Kajsa-Lotta Georgii Hellberg, BSc; Mischa Lundberg, PhD; Johanne Østerby Sørensen, MD; Jesper R. Gådin, PhD; Henrik Ohlsson, PhD; Jakob Grove, PhD; Anders Børglum, PhD; Esben Agerbo, PhD; Thomas Werge, PhD; Clara Albiñana, PhD; Bjarni J. Vilhjálmsson, PhD; Kenneth S. Kendler, MD; Oleguer Plana-Ripoll, PhD; Andrew J. Schork, PhD; for the iPSYCH Study Consortium and Autism Spectrum Disorder Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium IMPORTANCE The incidences of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) have increased markedly over recent decades, raising concerns about the emergence of new risk factors. Current literature typically attributes increased rates to changes in diagnostic practice, stigmatization, and awareness, but critically few studies have explored changes in underlying risk factors. OBJECTIVE To assess changes in the genetic risk profile of individuals diagnosed with ASD or ADHD by year of incident diagnosis and explore results in comparison with those expected under simulated scenarios. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS This cohort study used data from the Lundbeck Foundation Initiative for Integrative Psychiatric Research (iPSYCH2015) study, a population-based case-cohort in Denmark among individuals with incident diagnoses for ASD and ADHD made from 1994 to 2016. Data were analyzed from January 2024 until September 2025. EXPOSURE Year of incident diagnosis. Regression models tested changes in the mean genetic risk profile of individuals diagnosed in each consecutive year (1994-2016), adjusting for age, sex, and ancestry. MAIN OUTCOMES Polygenic scores for psychiatric (ADHD, ASD, depression, bipolar, and schizophrenia) and cognitive-behavioral (addiction, educational attainment, IQ, neuroticism, and risk-taking) outcomes were used to capture genetic risk profiles of diagnosed individuals. Empirical trends were compared with those expected under different simulated drivers of increasing rates. RESULTS A total of 17 071 individuals with incident diagnoses for ASD (4196 female [24.6%]; mean [SD] age at diagnosis, 9.7 [4.6] years) and 20 111 with diagnoses for ADHD (5960 female [29.6%]; mean [SD] age at diagnosis, 11.0 ([4.7] years) were analyzed. A more recent ADHD diagnosis was associated with decreased genetic risk for ADHD as shown by difference in mean polygenic score (β estimate per 10-year increase, −0.06 SDs; 95% CI, −0.09 to −0.03 SDs; P = .001) and other disorders, including ASD, bipolar, and schizophrenia (eg, ASD: β per 10-year increase, −0.07 SDs; 95% CI, −0.10 to −0.03 SDs; P < .001). Similarly, a more recent ASD diagnosis was associated with decreased genetic risk for ASD (β per 10-year increase, −0.07 SDs; 95% CI, −0.10 to −0.04 SDs; P < .001) and other disorders and traits, including bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and educational attainment (eg, bipolar disorder: β per 10-year increase, −0.05 SDs; 95% CI, −0.08 to −0.02 SDs; P = .001). CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE By analyzing multiple polygenic scores together with simulated expectations, this study could disambiguate among competing hypotheses about scenarios that may be associated with increased rates of ADHD and ASD diagnoses. Findings support broadening diagnostic criteria as an explanation for increasing rates, with implications for understanding changes in risk factors and clinical practice. O ver recent decades, rates of attention-deficit/ hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) diagnoses have increased remarkably, with reports of 4- to 10-fold increases across multiple populations.1-4 This has sparked debates regarding the emergence of novel environmental risk factors and contributions of changing clinical practice or societal awareness.5 The nosology of ASD and ADHD has evolved significantly over the last 40 years.6-8 Initially conceived as distinct, narrowly defined childhood disorders, they are now considered lifelong conditions with a spectrum of manifestations and high rates of cooccurring mental health difficulties.9,10 Additionally, there has been increased clinical and public awareness, driven in part by concerns of underdiagnosis.9,11 Undiagnosed ADHD, for example, is associated with negative outcomes, such as unemployment, criminality, and premature mortality.11,12 Conversely, sharp increases in diagnostic rates have brought about concerns of overdiagnosis,13-17 which can lead to unnecessary treatments and adverse effects of interventions18 or can be a consequence of social services requiring a diagnosis to allocate support.15,17 Furthermore, changes in the environmenthavebeenproposedintermsofnovelexposures(eg,perinatal acetaminophen exposure19 or screen time20) and societal changes (eg, school environment21). Finally, the increased emphasis on diagnosis in females, adolescents, and adults,2,3 where clinical manifestations differ from previously predominant childhood, male presentations,10,22-24 further complicates discussions. Although increasing diagnostic rates are often attributed to the interplay of these changes,9,11 few studies have evaluated whether underlying risk factors are also changing. ADHD and ASD are highly heritable disorders (heritability estimates of approximately 0.8),25,26 indicating a large etiological contribution from genes. Environmental exposures, clinical guidelines, and societal factors evolve continuously or may change abruptly. However, an individual’s inherited genetic risk remains fixed throughout their lifespan, and population levels are constant over recent decades.27 This creates a unique opportunity to study the association between time-varying diagnostic trends and time-invariant genetic factors to explore whether diagnoses have evolved to capture different constellations of risk. To our knowledge, only 2 studies, both among twins, have examined this association for ASD28 and ADHD29 using indirect measures of genetics and could not detect evidence of changing genetic or environmental risk contributions. Our 2025 study27 was the first to use polygenic score (PRS), an emerging tool for directly indexing the inherited genetic risk carried by an individual that offers promise in clinical and etiological studies.30 We showed that individuals diagnosed with any of multiple psychiatric disorders, including ASD and ADHD, carried a lower PRS if born and diagnosed more recently.27 However, PRSs in that study were restricted to those of the index disorder, and the study did not explore how the association with PRSs for other disorders or traits changed over time. Taken together, the limited studies and current relevance of changing rates of ADHD and ASD necessitate deeper, targeted investigations, and emerging studies31 suggest that more powerful applications of PRS (ie, using multiple scores to disambiguate among explanations) could add clarity. Inthisstudy,wetookanovelapproach,usingmultiplePRSs toexamineanddisambiguateamongpotentialexplanationsfor increasing diagnostic rates: (1) a lowering threshold, consistent with less severe or more heterogeneous symptomatology or emerging environmental risk factors; (2) shifting diagnostic boundaries allowing for different clinical manifestations previouslyassignedtootherdiagnoses;or(3)betterdetection,which implicates catching up on previously undiagnosed individuals. We use the Lundbeck Foundation Initiative for Integrative Psychiatric Research (iPSYCH2015) case-cohort study,32 the largest geneticresearchcohortofADHDandASD,withdiagnosesspanning more than 2 decades. We analyzed multiple PRSs for psychiatric, cognitive, and behavioral traits (genetic risk profile) to test how each was associated with year of diagnosis. In simulations, we addressed temporal changes to the genetic risk profile under potential explanations for increased rates and used this framework to interpret our results. Methods Study Population This cohort study used data from iPSYCH2015,32,33 a Danish case-cohort study using national biobanks and registers. The source population consists of all 1 657 449 singleton births May 1, 1981, to December 31, 2008, with the individual alive and residing in Denmark at age 1 year. The sample of 143 265 individuals selected all 93 608 incident diagnoses of major psychiatric disorders through 2015 and a random population cohort of 50 615 individuals. Over the entire study period, only the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) was implemented in Denmark. We included 29 668 individuals with a registered diagnosis of ADHD (ICD-10 code F90.0) and 24 975 individualswithASD(ICD-10codesF84.0,F84.1,F84.5,F84.8, or F84.9) in the Danish Psychiatric Central Research Register34 between January 1, 1994, and December 31, 2015 (individuals could have both diagnoses). Findings In this cohort study among 17 071 individuals with incident diagnosis of ASD and 20 111 individuals with incident diagnosis of ADHD, genetic contributions to ASD and ADHD diagnoses weakened over the past 2 decades. Meaning These results suggest that recent increases in ASD and ADHD diagnoses coincided with a broadening of diagnostic criteria. Genotyping and Quality Controls DNA was extracted and amplified from dried blood spots at the Danish Neonatal Screening Biobank35 and genotyped using the Illumina Global Screening or the Infinium PsychChip v1.0 Array. Data quality control is described elsewhere.32,33 Imputation followed the Rapid Imputation for Consortias Pipeline (RICOPILI) pipeline36 using the Haplotype Reference Consortium panel.37 Ancestry principal component analysis was conducted to create the largest homogenous group for analysis, a sample of broadly northern European genetic ancestry, and retain 10 principal components as analytical covariates. Genetic Risk Profiles Genetic risk profiles included 10 PRSs constructed using results from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) in public repositories. GWAS included 5 psychiatric disorders (ADHD,38 ASD,39 bipolar disorder,40 major depressive disorder,41 and schizophrenia42) and 5 cognitive or behavioral traits (educational attainment,43 IQ,44 risk-taking,45 neuroticism,46 and addiction47) (eTable 1 in Supplement 1). For psychiatric disorders, we used the meta-PRS method48 to construct PRSs that were weighted combinations of PRSs trained using published GWAS independent of iPSYCH (external PRS;eTable 1 in Supplement 1) and PRSs trained by crossvalidation within iPSYCH (internal PRS; eTable 1 in Supplement 1). Briefly, for each iteration of cross-validation, singlenucleotide variation weights were estimated by GWAS with BOLT-LMM in 80% of iPSYCH and used to train a PRS in the held-out 20%, with sample size weights used to combine internal and external PRSs. For cognitive and behavioral traits, where phenotypes were not available in iPSYCH, PRSs were computed with LDpred249 based on external GWAS only (eTable 1 in Supplement 1). Results Diagnostic Rates of ADHD and ASD in Denmark, 1994-2015 Previous reports have shown an increasing diagnostic rate of ASD and ADHD.3 We depict these trends in our specific analysis samples. From the iPSYCH case-cohort study, we included 20 111 individuals (5960 female [29.6%]; mean [SD] age at diagnosis, 11.0 ([4.7] years) first diagnosed with ADHD between January 1, 1994, and December 31, 2015 (Figure 1A; eTable 2 in Supplement 1) and 17 071 individuals (4196 female [24.6%]; mean [SD] age at diagnosis, 9.7 [4.6] years) first diagnosed with ASD in the same period (Figure 1B; eTable 3 in Supplement 1). For both disorders, there was an appreciable increase in the numberofdiagnosesatagivenagewithincreasingyear,asseen in the increasing brightness from left to right in Figure 1. Simulation of Estimated Changes to Genetic Risk Profiles We conducted simulations to explore trends in genetic risk profiles that were estimated to coincide with increases in diagnostic rates associated with different hypothetical scenarios (Figure 2; eNote 2 in Supplement 2). Our model posits that new cases were diagnosed from 1 of 3 undiagnosed segments of populations: (1) individuals from the general population with milder forms of the index disorder (referred to as lowering threshold), (2) individuals with a set of symptoms consistent with or previously referred to as a second disorder (referred to as shifting boundaries), and (3) individuals with a set of symptoms consistent with the index disorder but who were not previously diagnosed (referred to as better detection). Under a lowering threshold scenario, the index PRS was reduced. The secondary-disorder PRS changes according to the genetic correlation between disorders; in this scenario, it will be reduced due to positive genetic correlation. Discussion In this cohort study, we found a decreasing genetic risk by year of diagnosis of ASD and ADHD over a period in which the diagnostic rate increased more than 4-fold. We interpret these results as consistent with prior studies suggesting a broadening of diagnostic criteria is the most plausible driver of increasing rates of both diagnoses. Our approach is informative for differentiating among certain higher-level hypotheses, but we are limited in our ability to draw strong conclusions as to why a lowering threshold appears most consistent with our data. For example, the genetic risk profile can be reduced by misdiagnosis or overdiagnosis.13,15-17 In this study, individuals without ADHD or ASD (and thus with low genetic risk) or milder and more heterogeneous presentations (assuming severity and genetic Figure 4. An equivalent framing is that a lowering thresholdisoccurringbecausepreviouslyonlyindividualswith the most extreme genetic liability were diagnosed; this is because although the profile decreased, PRS levels in new cases with a lower mean genetic liability remained significantly higher than observed in the general population. Likewise, an increased burden of environmental causes could be consistent with a lowering threshold given that our study can inform only on the genetic threshold. For example, increased exposure to screens and social media20 or changes to early education environments21 have been proposed as risk factors, although evidence is neither consistently reported nor required to explain current trends. It is difficult to disambiguate among these hypotheses retrospectively; however, intervention studies, prospective longitudinal cohorts, and the extraction of detailed measures from, for example, clinical notes could help. Evolving nosology and changing clinical practice around adult diagnosis and recognition in females is reflected in time trends of the diagnosed population.3 As such, we adjusted for age in our models and tested for sex interaction. While we did notobservesexdifferencesinthegeneticriskprofileovertime, PRS associations for age revealed a transition with increasing age toward less neurodevelopmental and more internalizing and substance use genetic risk but no changes in the index disorderPRS,consistentwithourpreviousresultsforADHD.32This preliminary finding suggests that genetic associations with other clinical features change with age, which could be explored in future studies. Thisstudysignificantlyextendsthelimitedbodyofworkassociating genetic risk with diagnostic time trends (ie, year) in ADHD and ASD. Our results draw different conclusions than 2 previous studies using Swedish twin registers, which suggestedthatgeneticandenvironmentalcontributionstoADHD29 andASD28havenotchangedmarkedlyovertime.Webelievethat direct measures of genetics (eg, PRS) provide a more powerful index, and this difference in design may be critical. This study adds significantly to our previous work,27 in which we observed a decreased index PRS for ADHD and ASD diagnosed in individuals from more recent birth cohorts. We confirm initial support of lowering threshold with consistent evidence from multiple PRS and reveal unique associations with age. Our results have important implications for the design, interpretation, and application of large-scale genetic epidemiological and gene-mapping studies. Few studies27-29 have consideredtheyearoffirstdiagnosisasacontributortodifferences among cohorts. Our results in this study and previously reported changes3 over time in epidemiological or clinical characteristics (eg, prevalence, age, and sex ratio) suggest that time trendscouldcontributetocross-cohortheterogeneity.Thismay be especially true when considering age of onset or first diagnosis given that there are well-described time trends across all disorders3 and given that age (ie, age at diagnosis) can be confounded with period (ie, year of diagnosis) and cohort (ie, birth year) in ways that are difficult to disambiguate.50 Such differences could impact GWAS, which map different polygenes, if cases of ADHD or ASD were sampled using diagnoses made in different year windows, for example. Speculatively, diagnostic time trends could also have implications for the design and results of studies that involve downstream applications of GWAS (eg, PRS associations with other outcomes, GWAS revealing different patterns of genetic correlations, or different pathways being enriched for polygenic burden). As metaanalyses become broader and more inclusive and aggregate across longer times, understanding how time trends may impact our inferences into etiology and estimative ability is important. Limitations Our study has several limitations. First, data from Danish registers do not include diagnoses made in primary care or by psychiatristsinspecializedcareoutsidehospitalinpatientandoutpatient facilities. Second, birth year truncation is embedded in the iPSYCH case-cohort design, which should be considered when generalizing findings. However, we note that our previous work27 included restrictions to limit this and that results are consistent. Third, the iPSYCH case-cohort is relatively young (ie, few patients older than 35 years), which limits our ability to study a full life-course and earlier birth cohorts. However, the recent introduction of ADHD and ASD and the typically early age at diagnosis for these conditions are reassuring for our design. Fourth, published GWAS will have ascertained cases from earlier periods and therefore may better resemble earlier-diagnosed cases in our cohort. This increased similarity could result in PRSs trained on external GWAS associating more strongly with earlier-diagnosed cases in our study. There was consistency in associations observed when using meta-PRS, which includes cross-validated training GWAS data from iPSYCH, where most cases were diagnosed in recent periods, and when using PRS trained using these external GWAS data, where cases are likely diagnosed from earlier periods. We believe this consistency suggests that our results were not driven by spurious time-dependent ascertainment. Fifth, the association of year of ADHD diagnosis with ADHD PRS was driven by internal (iPSYCH) training samples, which are 55% to 70% of cases in recent ADHD GWAS. Furtherreplicationwithlargerexternaltrainingsamples,when they become available, could contextualize generalizability of our results to other cohorts. Sixth, our analysis was limited to Denmark using individuals of broadly Northern European ancestry.Giventheinterestinthistopic,replicationtootherpopulations, countries, societies, racial and ethnic groups, and health care settings is important. Conclusions This cohort study offers a new perspective for ongoing debates about increasing diagnostic rates of ASD and ADHD. By analyzing genetic risk profiles across 2 decades of diagnoses in a large population-based case cohort, we demonstrated that individuals diagnosed more recently had systematically lower genetic risk. These findings suggest that clinical practice and diagnostic criteria have changed over time to include a broader phenotypic manifestation of ASD and ADHD. Mapping ADHD Heterogeneity and Biotypes by Topological Deviations in Morphometric Similarity Networks Nanfang Pan, MD; Yajing Long, MD; Kun Qin, PhD, MD; Isaac Z. Pope, BSc; Qiuxing Chen, MD; Ziyu Zhu, MD; Ying Cao, BSc; Lei Li, PhD, MD; Manpreet K. Singh, MD; Robert K. McNamara, MD; Melissa P. DelBello, MD; Ying Chen, PhD, MD; Alex Fornito, PhD; Qiyong Gong, PhD, MD IMPORTANCE Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is characterized by considerable clinical heterogeneity, and existing classification frameworks constrain the development of neurobiologically informed subtyping approaches. OBJECTIVE To investigate whether normative modeling of topological properties derived from brain morphometry similarity networks can provide robust stratification markers for children with ADHD. DESIGN, SETTINGS, AND PARTICIPANTS This case-control study leveraged multisite cross-sectional neurodevelopmental datasets with a longitudinal follow-up cognitive assessment for a subset. Morphometric similarity networks were constructed and normative models were developed for 3 topological metrics: degree centrality, nodal efficiency, and participation coefficient. Through semisupervised clustering, putative biotypes were delineated and their clinical profiles were examined. Brain profiles of these biotypes were further contextualized in terms of their neurochemical and functional correlates using large-scale databases, and model generalizability was assessed with external validation performed in an independent transdiagnostic cohort. Study data were analyzed from November 2023 to January 2025. EXPOSURES Normative modeling of topological properties derived from brain morphometry. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES Topological deviations in morphometric similarity networks derived from brain structural image. RESULTS The discovery cohort comprised 446 children with ADHD (mean [SD] age, 11.5 [2.6] years; 339 male [76.0%]) and 708 controls (mean [SD] age, 11.0 [2.3] years; 429 male [60.6%]), whereas the validation cohort included 554 children with ADHD (mean [SD] age, 10.1 [2.8]; 372 male [67.1%]) and 123 controls (mean [SD] age, 10.1 [3.0]; 70 male [56.9%]). ADHD exhibited atypical hub organization across all 3 topological metrics, with significant case-control differences primarily localized to a covarying multimetric component in the orbitofrontal cortex. Three biotypes emerged: severe-combined with emotional dysregulation (widespread medial prefrontal cortex-pallidum alterations, n = 142), predominantly hyperactive/impulsive (anterior cingulate cortex-pallidum circuit alterations, n = 177), and predominantly inattentive (superior frontal gyrus alterations, n = 127), each characterized by distinct clinical profiles and longitudinal trajectories. These neural profiles of each biotype showed distinct neurochemical and functional correlates. Critically, the core findings were replicated in the validation cohort, demonstrating robust generalizability. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE Results of this case-control study reveal that the integration of normative modeling with semisupervised clustering provided both dimensional and categorical insights into ADHD heterogeneity, identifying 3 distinct ADHD biotypes with unique clinical-neural profiles that advance the understanding of ADHD’s neurobiological complexity and lay the groundwork for personalized management. A ttention-deficit/hyperactivitydisorder(ADHD)isacommon neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by considerable clinical heterogeneity that extends beyond the DSM-5 diagnostic framework.1 Although its symptoms are partitioned into inattentive and hyperactive/ impulsive domains, this binary behavioral classification inadequatelycapturesthecomplexityofADHDpresentations.2 Clinical observations reveal diverse patterns across DSMdefined domains,3 but these consensus-based distinctions within DSM may oversimplify the diverse neurobiological mechanisms underlying ADHD, precluding more informative andneurobiologicallyhomogeneoussubtyping.Supervisedapproaches that define subtypes using checklist thresholds typically generate only severity-based cognitive subgroups.4,5 In contrast, data-driven clustering may offer a superior solution by leveraging phenotypic data that best informs the delineation of disorder subtypes. There have been multiple attempts to identify ADHD subtypesbyanalyzingvaryingsymptomcombinations,6butmany fail to distinguish normative from atypical variations in phenotypic measures.7 Normative modeling incorporating neuroimaging metrics offers a powerful framework for overcoming this limitation and understanding atypical features,8 compared with case-control comparisons that rely on group contrasts and ignore individual heterogeneity. The approach is analogous to pediatric growth charts, allowing one to quantify centiles of normative variation in a given phenotype that can be used to evaluate the extent to which a given individual deviates from population expectations.9 Nevertheless, identifying reproducible patterns within this dimensional framework through data-driven clustering may reveal subgroups that can be used for clinical decision-making.10 Previous normative modeling studies in ADHD have primarily examined regional morphology,2 including gray matter volume,11 cortical thickness,12 and white matter volume.13 However, regional variations are often coupled across disparate brain systems, and the network-level coupling of deviations from normative regional morphometry remains poorly understood. Morphometric similarity networks (MSNs) can be used to characterize the covariance patterns of brain regional features, offering an individualized modeling approach with high robustness and reproducibility for identifying accessible and cost-effective magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)– derived biomarkers.14 Variations within MSNs can arise from a combination of interregional structural connections through axonal pathways, similarities in cytoarchitecture, and shared patterns of gene expression.15 These networks often exhibit hubs—specific regions that are considered particularly influential in brain networks by virtue of their coupling patterns.14 Multiple measures exist for characterizing the hubness of a node within MSNs, indicating that an approach that integrates various information may be particularly fruitful.16 Such approaches provide a promising framework for understanding brain network alterations in neurodevelopment with robust sensitivity17 and may also serve as neurobiological markers for ADHD.18 We therefore hypothesized that (1) normative modeling of MSN hubness would reveal heterogeneity in children with ADHD, (2) data-driven clustering of these multimetric hubness deviations would identify distinct neurobiological biotypes with unique clinical-biological profiles, and (3) these biotypes could be contextualized with respect to distinct neurotransmitter density maps and functional correlates. Methods Our discovery project analyzed multisite data from West China Hospital of Sichuan University (WCH), University of Cincinnati (UC), Kennedy Krieger Institute, New York University Langone Medical Center, Oregon Health & Science University, and Peking University Institute of Mental Health. The WCH and UC datasets received ethics approval from their respective research ethics committees. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants and their parents. This study followedtheStrengtheningtheReportingofObservationalStudies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guidelines. Data Collection and Morphometric Similarity Network Construction Inclusion and exclusion criteria across sites are available in eTable 1 in Supplement 1. We also included control samples from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE) initiative that matched the protocols of the corresponding ADHD200 sites. To reconcile sample and cross-site heterogeneity, we excluded left-handed children and those younger than 6 years or older than 18 years. Data from a transdiagnostic database, the Healthy Brain Network initiative, were obtained as validation samples.19 ADHD symptom subscales were rescaled to a range of 0 to 1.0 to facilitate cross-site individual predictions.20,21 The majority of samples did not disclose race and ethnicity information; therefore, these data were not included in our study. We generated individual gray matter volume maps derived from anatomic T1-weighted images by using the Computational Anatomy Toolbox (CAT) CAT12 pipeline (Christian Key Points Question Can normative modeling of topological properties derived from brain morphometric similarity networks yield robust stratification biomarkers for pediatric populations with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)? Three distinct biotypes emerged, each exhibiting unique clinical-neural profiles with characteristic neurochemical and functional correlates, validated in an independent transdiagnostic cohort of 554 ADHD cases. Statistical Analysis Normative Modeling and Multimodal Fusion Framework Normative models for each nodal topological phenotype were implemented using the warped bayesian linear regression framework from PCNtoolkit,8 which estimates normative ranges for topological metrics with respect to demographic covariates (age and sex) in the training dataset (Figure 1D), using B-spline basis expansion for age and likelihood warping to accommodate non-Gaussian nonlinear effects (settings in the eMethods in Supplement 1).24-26 Individual ADHD deviations were quantified as z scores relative to normative centiles derived from typically developing control (TDC) training data. To assess potential site-related artifacts, we performed 2-fold linearsupportvectormachineclassificationtodeterminewhether scanning site could be predicted.27 Given subtle brain alterations characterized in ADHD,27 we identified extreme deviations in topological patterns using a threshold of |z| ≥2.028,29 and calculated the proportion of children exhibiting atypical patterns at each node. ADHD deviation maps were then subtracted from those of TDCs to obtain maps of case-control differences in extreme deviations. To assess the statistical significance of these differences, we performed both group-based and spatial permutation tests to generate null distributions of case-control differences (details in the eMethods in Supplement 1). We identified nodes with statistically significant differences using thresholds of uncorrected P <.05 and false-discovery rate (FDR) P <.05. To identify joint independent components that robustly encompassed covarying multimetric patterns and summarize nodal findings, topological phenotypes were subjected to a data-driven model—multiset canonical correlation analysis plus joint independent component analysis (multimodal canonical correlation analysis [mCCA] + joint independent component analysis [jICA]) (Figure 1E) using the Fusion ICA Toolbox30,31 (details in the eMethods in Supplement 1). Biotype Identification Heterogeneity through discriminative analysis (HYDRA), a semisupervised algorithm, was implemented to analyze individual deviations in 3 hubness measures to identify putative ADHD biotypes.32 It leverages support vector machines to create multiple hyperplanes that separate controls from cases to form a convex polytope, with each facet representing a distinct biotype (Figure 1F). To capture the heterogeneity of brain topological properties, we trained HYDRA models utilizing a 10-fold nested cross-validation protocol to determine the optimal k-dimensional space. The clustering stability was quantifiedthroughtheadjustedRandindices.Therobustnessofthe identified ADHD biotypes was validated via 3 reproducibility analyses:permutationtesting,sex-specificvalidation,andsplithalf cross-validation (analytical details in the eMethods in Supplement 1). To investigate the corresponding clinical profiles of the ADHD biotypes, Kruskal-Wallis analysis was used to examine their differences in symptom severity.33 To quantify differencesinatypicaltopologicalpatternsamongbiotypes,wecomputed the frequency of extreme deviations within each node and used χ2 analyses to assess statistical differences across biotypes (uncorrected P <.05 and FDR P <.05). Biotype-specific extreme deviation maps were depicted using the same procedures described above. To examine longitudinal changes in ADHD symptoms across biotypes, we analyzed follow-up data from the Child BehaviorChecklist34collectedannuallyover4yearsattheWCH site (exclusively beginning with medication-naive participants) using linear mixed-effect modeling to examine the interaction effects of time and biotype.35 Additionally, we monitored the development of mood disorders (eg, anxiety and depression) among ADHD participants during follow-up. Biological Correlates of Biotype Profiles To elucidate molecular signatures underlying our topologyderived ADHD biotypes, we characterized their correspondencetothespatialdistributionsofneurotransmitterreceptors (Figure 1G).36 The neurotransmitter receptor maps encompass density distributions of 19 distinct receptors derived from positron emission tomography imaging studies (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 and analytical procedures in the eMethods in Supplement 1).37 To comprehensively characterize brain networkorganizationofADHD,weaggregatedcase-controldifference maps in extreme deviations across 3 topological metrics (termed as fused topological deviations)38 and then used Spearman correlation to quantify the spatial correspondence with neurotransmitter receptor distributions with spin tests (ie, spatial permutation tests) assessing statistical significance (5000 surrogates).39 We used the Neurosynth-based meta-analytic task activation maps to contextualize our findings beyond the available clinical measures and to explore associations with a broader spectrum of psychological processes.40 Neurosynth Compose,41 an automated neuroimaging meta-analytic platform with 30 578 functional MRI studies was used to derive meta-analytic task activation maps. We selected activation maps corresponding to 123 cognitive terms based on the Cognitive Atlas framework.42 Partial least-squares regression analysis was used to examine the spatial relationship between fused topological deviation maps and cognitive terms across biotypes (eMethods in Supplement 1). Results Clinical Characteristics of Included Data We included 446 children diagnosed with ADHD (mean [SD] age, 11.5 [2.7] years; 107 female [24%]; 339 male [76.0%]) and 708 TDCs (mean [SD] age, 11.0 [2.3] years; 279 female [39.4%]; 429 male [60.6%]) in the discovery cohort. We included 554 children with ADHD (mean [SD] age, 10.1 [2.8]; 182 female [32.9%]; 372 male [67.1%]) and 123 TDCs (mean [SD] age, 10.1 [3.0]; 53 female [43.1%]; 70 male [56.9%]) in the validation cohort (selection process detailed in eFigures 1 and 2 in Supplement 1). Demographic and phenotypical characteristics across sites, along with scan parameters, are provided in eTables 3 and 4 in Supplement 1, respectively. The study workflow is depicted in Figure 1A. Individual Deviations in Topological Properties A multimetric approach that incorporated 3 topological metrics was used to assess each region’s MSN hubness.38,44 Fitting performance of our normative models was illustrated in eFigure 3 in Supplement 1 with examination of site effects presented in eTable 5 in Supplement 1. Among children with ADHD, 95.1% (424 of 446), 96.4% (430 of 446), and 71.8% (320 of 446) exhibited at least 1 extreme deviation in degree centrality, nodal efficiency, and participation coefficient, respectively, from the normative range. Compared with TDCs, childrenwithADHDshowedsignificantlymoreextremedeviations per individual in degree centrality (mean [SD], 4.54 [2.96] vs 4.19 [2.82]; t = 2.05, Cohen d = 0.12; P = .04) and participation coefficient (mean [SD], 3.27 [4.22] vs 2.63 [3.53]; t = 2.78, Cohen d = 0.17; P < .001), but not nodal efficiency (mean [SD], 4.45 [2.79] vs 4.36 [2.69]; t = 0.57, Cohen d = 0.04; P = .57) (eFigure 4 in Supplement 1). The proportion of children with suprathreshold positive or negative deviations at each topological node revealed distinct patterns across topological metrics (Figure 2A). Case-control comparison at the level of extreme deviation overlap (Figure 2B and C and eTable 6 in Supplement 1) revealed notable degree centrality differences in the caudate and hippocampus (observed difference = 7.79% and 6.33%; Cohen h = 0.30 and 0.24, respectively; FDR P <.001), and participation coefficient differences were primarily identified in the inferior frontal gyrus and orbitofrontal cortex (5.50% and 4.52%; Cohen h = 0.24 and 0.20, respectively; FDR P ≤.045). For nodal efficiency, significant spatial overlap patterns emerged in the hippocampus and pallidum (4.31% and 4.24%; Cohen h = 0.17 and 0.15, respectively; both FDR P <.001 in spatial permutation testing). Covarying Multimodal Signatures Having established individual deviation patterns across topological metrics, we applied mCCA + jICA to validate our multimetricapproachandsummarizetopologicalfindings.Theoptimal selection of 8 components preserved a substantial proportion of the explained variance across metrics (80.7%, 83.2%, and 82.9% for degree centrality, nodal efficiency, and participation coefficient, respectively). Notably, the fusion model yielded a joint component that demonstrated significant case-control differences in mixing coefficients across topologicalmetrics(t = −2.49,Cohend = −0.15;P = .01;t = −2.24, Cohen d = −0.14; P = .03; and t = 2.19, Cohen d = 0.13; P = .03, respectively) (Figure 3A). Within this group-differentiating component, covarying patterns were predominantly localized to the orbitofrontal cortex and were significant across topological metrics (z = −2.11, −3.15, and 2.31, respectively) (Figure 3B and eTable 7 in Supplement 1). ADHD Biotypes Corresponding to Clinical Profiles The 3-biotype solution best captured the heterogeneity of topological deviations with high robustness and reliability according to 4 criteria: the highest adjusted Rand indices (0.21 for k = 3, 0.18 for k = 2, and 0.17 for k = 4); alternative adjusted Rand indices (k = 3) were significantly higher than null expectations;neuraldeviationpatternsexcludingfemaleswere similar compared with the full-sample model; k = 3 emerged as the optimal solution in split-half cross-validation based on adjusted Rand indices with the clustering scheme demonstrating replicability in neural patterns (eFigures 5-8 in Supplement 1). Cluster-wise margin distance and assignment entropy are available in eTable 8 in Supplement 1. Discussion Phenotypic heterogeneity poses a major challenge in the diagnosis and treatment of ADHD,5 as the current diagnostic framework assigns a single diagnostic label to what is fundamentally a heterogeneous syndrome that likely arises from diverse neural mechanisms.33 Our study advances the understanding of ADHD heterogeneity through a novel huboriented fusion framework that integrates multimodal topological deviations in morphometric similarity networks. The replication of our findings across 2 cohorts suggests that our approach may offer a feasible framework for stratifying ADHD cases. Overall, our integrated approach adheres to the recommended workflows for investigating ADHD heterogeneity.4,45 Brain-First Approach for ADHD Subtyping Thisbrain-firstapproachprovidesbiologicalvalidationofidentified subtypes through completely data-driven clustering. Although DSM classifications exclusively rely on consensusderived symptoms, our neuroimaging-derived clusters converged with clinical phenotypes without using any clinical features. This convergence provides compelling evidence that these presentations reflect genuine neurobiological entities, biologically validating these long-observed clinical distinctions. Although partial overlap emerges in the distributions of topologically deviated hubs between biotypes, our multimetrictopologicalapproachenablescomprehensivecharacterization of subtle network-level deviations that may be obscured by single-metric or symptom-based analyses.4 Robust classification boundaries could be identified within multivariate neuroimaging landscape for subgroup differentiation, remaining clinically valuable for adjudicating distinct management strategies.2 These circuit-specific mechanisms may provide potential targets for stratified interventions tailored tobiotype’suniquenetworkdysfunctionprofile.Critically,biotype 1, marked by the most widespread deviation patterns, reveals a clinically valuable subgroup with distinct developmental trajectories requiring early interventions, providing neurobiological markers of vulnerability.46,47 Topological Deviations of ADHD From Normative Centiles Our finding that children diagnosed with ADHD exhibit prominent degree centrality and nodal efficiency deviations in subcortical hubs, particularly the striatum, suggests a weakened functionality consistent with Enhancing Neuroimaging Genetics through Meta-analysis (ENIGMA)–ADHD consortium findings of reduced subcortical gray matter volume.48 Given the altered participation coefficient patterns, the roles of inferiorfrontalgyrusandorbitofrontalcortexmayshiftfromprovincial hubs to connector hubs in ADHD,49 representing compensatory adaptation to reduced processing capacity in other nodes, manifesting as early increases.50 The classical ADHD modelofpathophysiologysuggestsdelayedbrainmaturation,51 particularly in frontal cortex and frontostriatal connections.52 Prefrontal areas, particularly the inferior frontal gyrus,53 and their associated networks could act as a brake for inhibitory control and decision-making optimization, and striatal inhibitory projections that modulate dopaminergic neuron activity may drive impulsivity.54-56 Characterizations of Distinct Biotypes Our multimodal fusion analysis identified the orbitofrontal cortex as a common covarying component across topological metrics, suggesting it may serve as a fundamental network anchor point in ADHD pathophysiology that transcends biotype boundaries. This finding aligns with the orbitofrontal cortex’sroleoforchestratingthetransitionbetweenimpulsiveand reflective behaviors engaged with goal-directed actions.57,58 Building on this shared foundation, biotype-specific deviations emerge in distinct neural circuits: widespread medial prefrontal cortex-pallidum alterations in biotype 1 (severecombined with emotional dysregulation) could indicate dysregulationinfrontostriatalcircuitry59;anteriorcingulatecortexpallidum circuit alterations in biotype 2 (predominantly hyperactive-impulsive) may preferentially drive hyperactive/ impulsive behaviors through dysregulated action-mode networks60; and superior frontal gyrus alterations in biotype 3 (predominantly inattentive) may selectively impair sustained attention through default mode network interference2 (a discussion about parallel and distinct neural dysfunctions is available in the eDiscussion in Supplement 1). This hierarchical model, in which orbitofrontal cortex dysfunction represents a common substrate while region-specific deviations shape individual-specific symptomatic profiles, may explain why certain neural signatures appear consistently in casecontrol comparisons, whereas others emerge only through biotype stratification. This correspondence to a large-scale database validates our ADHD biotype classification system derived from topological deviations.Further,theapplicationofapretrainedmodelinthevalidation cohort substantially externally replicated the clustering patterns observed in the discovery datasets. Specifically, the validation cohort exhibited consistent hyperactive/ impulsive patterns across biotypes, although inattention profiles could not be fully reproduced, likely due to confounding factors including younger participant age, different recruitment strategies, and cross-cultural variations. Limitations Several limitations should be considered. First, our samples of participants were not medication naive. Although psychostimulant use does not significantly influence brain morphometricfindingsinADHDmega-analysis,48,70wecannotrule out their potential confounding effects. Our exclusion criteria for comorbid conditions may limit our generalizability to real-world clinical settings where comorbidities are prevalent. Second, the overlap in topological deviations between ADHD and TDCs underscores the subtle and complex nature of ADHD-related brain alterations. This complexity may reflect the inherent challenges in identifying discrete neurobiological markers.27 As morphology-derived correlation matrices,networkconfigurationsofMSNsrequirecautiousmechanistic interpretation.71-73 Third, our putative biotypes may represent salient points along underlying dimensional continua rather than qualitatively distinct diagnostic entities. Future directions for clinical translation were discussed in the eDiscussion in Supplement 1. Conclusions In this case-control study, we have identified 3 distinct topology-derived biotypes, each characterized by unique clinicalneural profiles, longitudinal trajectories, and spatial molecular signatures, with rigorous validation through cognitive profiles from large-scale databases and independent cohorts. Ourcomprehensiveapproach,fromfeatureextractionthrough data-driven clustering to external validation, offers a promising framework for parsing the inherent ADHD heterogeneity in a clinically valuable way, which may ultimately create a path toward developing personalized therapeutic strategies. Age at First Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Diagnosis and Educational Outcomes Lotta Volotinen, MSc; Hanna Remes, PhD; Pekka Martikainen, PhD; Niina Metsä-Simola, PhD IMPORTANCE Early diagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is often recommended, but it is unknown whether age at diagnosis is associated with educational outcomes. OBJECTIVE To estimate whether age at ADHD diagnosis is associated with school performance, completed degrees, educational enrollment, and school dropout. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS This population-based cohort study used national registry data for individuals born in Finland between January 1, 1990, and December 31, 1999, followed up until age 20 years. Individuals were born without a diagnosis of intellectual disability (International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision [ICD-10] codes F70-F79). Analyses were conducted from May 2024 to December 2025. EXPOSURES Age at ADHD diagnosis, identified by the first clinical diagnosis (International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision code 314; ICD-10 code F90; or medication purchase). MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES Grade point average (GPA; range, 4 [failing] to 10 [excellent]) at the end of compulsory education (approximately 16 years of age), completed degrees in upper secondary education (vocational or academic), enrollment in tertiary education, and school dropout at age 20 years. RESULTS The study sample included 580 132 individuals (51.2% male). Of these, 12 208 males (2.1%) and 3753 females (0.7%) had a first ADHD diagnosis between ages 4 and 20 years: mean (SD) age for males was 11.3 (4.1) years and for females was 14.4 (4.6) years. ADHD diagnosis at any age was associated with worse educational outcomes and greater likelihood of vocational than academic upper secondary education. After adjusting for sociodemographic covariates, if a diagnosis was received by age 16 years, younger age was associated with higher GPA for males (range, 7.12 [95% CI, 6.99-7.26] at age 4 years to 6.52 [95% CI, 6.46-6.58] at age 16 years) and females (range, 7.64 [95% CI, 7.49-7.78] at age 6 years to 6.95 [95% CI, 6.82-7.07]) at age 12 years, higher probability of completing an academic upper secondary degree for males (range, 20.77% [95% CI, 15.41%-26.12%] at age 4 years to 5.29% [3.78%-6.80%] at age 15 years) and females (range, 31.04% [95% CI, 15.60%-46.47%] at age 4 years to 12.01% [95% CI, 7.80%-16.21%] at age 14 years), and lower probability of school dropout for males (range, 9.16% [95% CI, 4.89%-13.42%] at age 4 years to 29.52% [95% CI, 25.85%-33.19%] at age 16 years) and females (range, 9.57% [95% CI, 4.49%-14.65%] at age 6 years to 27.16% [95% CI, 19.75%-34.57%] at age 13 years). However, after educational track choices (ages 17-20 years), older age at diagnosis was associated with higher and more academic education. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE In this cohort study, earlier age at ADHD diagnosis was associated with better school performance, more academic education, and lower school dropout rates than diagnoses closer to age 16 years. The findings suggest that individuals who are diagnosed closer to age 16 years could benefit from targeted support to prevent school dropout. A ttention-deficit/hyperactivitydisorder(ADHD)isacommon neurodevelopmental disorder affecting individuals at all life stages.1,2 ADHD has been associated with poorer school performance, lower attendance in higher education, and an increased likelihood of vocational than academic education.3-11Somestudiescomparingindividualswhodidand didnotreceivetreatmentforADHDhavesuggestedthateducational outcomes could be improved with treatment3-5,12; thus, anearlydiagnosisisoftenrecommended.3-5Toourknowledge, no studies have empirically examined the association of age at first ADHD diagnosis and different educational outcomes. ADHD is most often diagnosed during early to mid-childhood.13-19 Receiving a diagnosis in childhood requires that symptoms, including inattention with or without hyperactive-impulsive behavior, negatively affect academic or socialfunctioning.1,2Still,onsetofADHDmayoccurearlierthan the receipt of the diagnosis; according to the current diagnostic criteria, a later diagnosis is feasible if the symptoms were present before age 12 years.1,2 For some, a diagnosis may be delayed until adolescence due to more externally perceivable ADHD symptoms occurring only after the onset of puberty.20 Alaterdiagnosismayalsobepromptedbyhinderedschoolperformance and attendance21 that may, to some degree, be explained by the increasing demands at higher levels of education and changes in social surroundings due to school transitions.Adelayeddiagnosisisparticularlycommonamong females,whotendtohavebetterschoolperformanceandfewer externally perceived symptoms than males.13-16,20-23 In this study, we used data from Finnish national registers on individuals born in between January 1, 1990, and December 31, 1999, as the universal education and health care systems in Finland provide an ideal setting to study the associations between age at diagnosis and educational outcomes. ADHD is commonlydiagnosedinpublichealthcare,withregularscreening of children’s health and development and statutory health checkupswithphysiciansaroundages4,7,11,and14years,24and teachersandparentsareaskedtopre-evaluatethestudent’slearningandbehavior(eg,participation,attendance,andtakingcare of belongings and assignments).25 These questions are likely to capturesomesymptomsofADHD.Educationisfreeatalllevels in Finland, with nearly all children completing compulsory basiceducation(aroundage16years)andmostadvancingtoupper secondary education.26,27 Furthermore, academic and vocational education diverge only after completing compulsory education,26,28 avoiding the complication that early tracking mightaffectthelikelihoodofreceivingadiagnosis.Thecurrent studyexamined(1)theincidenceofADHDdiagnosisbyageand (2)whetherageatdiagnosiswasassociatedwithgradepointaverage (GPA) at age 16 years, vocational or academic upper secondary degree completion, tertiary education enrollment, and school dropout at age 20 years. Methods Data and Sample This cohort study used data based on individual-level observations of the Finnish total population from national registers. To form the sample, we used information from the Medical Birth Register on all live-born individuals in Finland between 1990 and 1999, with follow-up until age 20 years. We identified age at first ADHD diagnosis with health care data from the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare and ADHD medication purchases from the Social Insurance Institution of Finland. Datasets provided by Statistics Finland enabled the linkage of demographic and educational information as well as information on parental and family characteristics. Use of the pseudonymized data was approved by the ethical committeesofStatisticsFinlandandFindata.InFinland,informedconsent is not required from study participants when register data are used for scientific research carried out in public interest. This study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guideline.29,30 We excluded individuals with any diagnosis of intellectual disability(InternationalStatisticalClassificationofDiseasesand Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes F70F79),thosewhoemigratedordiedbeforeage20years,andthose without knowledge of their biological mother or without region of residence. We also excluded individuals who had received a diagnosis of ADHD before age 4 years, as they are more prone to misdiagnosis,1 as well as those diagnosed after age 20 years. The final sample was followed up for their first ADHD diagnosis between ages 4 and 20 years. Educational Outcomes In Finland, preprimary education typically begins at age 6 years, primary education (International Standard Classification of Education [ISCED] level 1) at age 7 years, lower secondary education (ISCED level 2) at age 13 years, and upper secondary education (ISCED levels 3 and 4) at age 16 years.28 For those born between 1990 and 1999, primary and lower secondary education were mandatory (hereafter referred to as compulsory education), and this compulsory schooling usually ended at age 16 years.27 After compulsory education, individuals could apply to vocational or academic upper secondaryeducationlasting2to4years.Tertiaryeducation(ISCED levels ≥6), universities of applied sciences or academic universities, is usually applied for after the completion of an upper secondary degree.26,28 Key Points Questions Is age at first attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) diagnosis associated with educational outcomes? Findings In this cohort study of 580 132 individuals, earlier age at ADHD diagnosis was associated with better grade point average at age 16 years, higher probability of academic than vocational studies, and lower probability of school dropout at age 20 years compared with diagnosis during the last years of compulsory basic education. Meaning The findings suggest that earlier ADHD diagnosis is associated with better educational outcomes, while individuals first diagnosed toward the end of compulsory education may be at high risk of school dropout. GPA School performance was measured by final grades at the end of compulsory education and was retrieved from the first applications to upper secondary education submitted from 2004 to 2019. We calculated GPA (range, 4 [failing] to 10 [excellent]) of compulsory theoretical subjects (languages, biology, mathematics, physics, chemistry, geography, history, social studies,andhealtheducation).GPAwasonlyavailableforthose who had applied to upper secondary education. Completed Upper Secondary Degrees, Enrollment in Education, and School Dropout We measured the other educational outcomes at age 20 years, when most individuals have completed upper secondary education. We identified outcomes from educational registers, including completed upper secondary degrees in vocational (no or yes) or academic education (no or yes) and current enrollment in upper secondary vocational (no or yes) or academic education (no or yes) or tertiary education (no or yes). Additionally, we measured school dropout (no or yes) as not having completed any upper secondary degrees and not being enrolled in upper secondary or tertiary education at age 20 years. Age at ADHD Diagnosis As in a previous study,13 we identified ADHD diagnoses from data on public-sector specialized and primary health care and purchases of ADHD medication (data availability are given in Figure 1 and specific registers and codes in eTable 1 in Supplement 1). Age at diagnosis refers to the calendar year of the first recorded clinical diagnosis or medication purchase. Statistical Analysis Analyses were conducted from May 2024 to December 2025. We used linear regression with a robust variance estimator to observe whether age at diagnosis (4-16 years for GPA and 4-20 years for other outcomes) was associated with GPA at age 16 years and logistic regression to estimate completed vocational or academic upper secondary degrees and enrollment in vocational or academic upper secondary education or tertiary education at age 20 years. Results from logistic regression models are presented as estimated probabilities that were derived using marginal standardization, which sums estimated probabilities to a weighted mean of the confounder distribution in the overall population.31 All models included the interaction of age at diagnosis and sex (male and female) assigned at birth. The models were adjusted for birth year (1990-1999) and region of residence (19 regions) to control for temporal changes and area-level differences in both ADHD diagnostics and educational outcomes.26,32-34 Since the association of age at diagnosis and educational outcomes may be confounded by sociodemographic factors,22,35,36 we further adjusted the model with the following family characteristics: maternal age at birth (<25, 25-29, 30-34, and ≥35 years), birth order (1, 2, and ≥3), number of children living in the child’s household (1, 2, ≥3, and other or unknown), and living arrangements (with 2 biological parents, with 1 biological and 1 social parent, with a single parent, and other or unknown). The full model was also adjusted for the highest achieved educational level (basic, secondary, and tertiary) of biological parents and household disposable income in annual quintiles (other or unknown; 1 [lowest income] to 5 [highest income]). The number of children living in the household, living arrangements, parental educational level, and household income were measured at the beginningoftheyearoftheindividual’sfourthbirthday(thestudy design is given in Figure 1). The final sample included 580 132 individuals followed up for their first ADHD diagnosis between ages 4 and 20 years (48.8% female; 51.2% male). Of these individuals, we identified 12 208 males (2.1%) and 3753 females (0.7%) born from 1990 to 1999 without a diagnosis of intellectual disability who were diagnosed with ADHD between ages 4 to 20 years: mean (SD) age for males was 11.3 (4.1) years and for females was 14.4 (4.6) years (Table). Among females, ADHD diagnoses were less common at age 8 years (incidence, 0.07%; 95% CI, 0.06%-0.08%), but incidence increased between ages 14 years (0.07%; 95% CI, 0.06%-0.08%) and 20 years (0.16%; 95% CI, 0.15%-0.18%). The cumulative incidence of ADHD was 4.11% (95% CI, 4.04-4.18) among males and 1.33% (95% CI, 1.28-1.37) among females (Table and eTable 3 in Supplement 1). Discussion To our knowledge, our study is the first to report the associations of age at ADHD diagnosis and educational outcomes. The results showed that although individuals with an ADHD diagnosis had poorer educational outcomes and chose academic studies less often than those without a diagnosis,3-11 the outcomes differed by the age at diagnosis. Individuals diagnosed with ADHD at the beginning of compulsory education had better school performance, were more likely to continue theirstudiesinuppersecondaryortertiaryeducation,andwere less likely to drop out of school than those diagnosed toward the end of compulsory education. These associations were independent of covariates relating to family characteristics and socioeconomic position. The findings support the idea that an early diagnosis could be beneficial for later educational outcomes.3-5 Anearlierdiagnosismaybeassociatedwithimprovededucational outcomes through multiple pathways. First, an ADHD diagnosis is usually required to access pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic treatment, which may improve educational outcomes of the individuals with an ADHD diagnosis; however, more studies are needed on the longer-lasting effects.3-5,12 Second, support measures in schools may become Figure 4.
