Institutional review boards at each participating site approved the program, and all participants provided written informed consent. The present analysis used deidentified data available through the All of Us Researcher Workbench. This study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guideline for cross-sectional studies. We analyzed data from participants in the All of Us (Controlled Tier Dataset version 8 [C2024Q3R5]) who completed the Personal and Family Health History questionnaire (N = 298 091). The survey responses included in this analysis were collected between June 2017 and September 2023. Outcomes Participants were classified as having ADHD based on affirmative responses to the question “Are you still seeing a doctor or health care provider for ADHD?” from the Personal and Family Health History questionnaire. To further categorize individuals based on age of ADHD diagnosis, we used their responses to the question “About how old were you when you were first told you had ADHD?” Participants answering a child (0-11 years) or adolescent (12-17 years) were classified as youthdiagnosed ADHD, while those answering an adult (18-64 years), older adult (65-74 years), or older adult (75 years) were classified as adult-diagnosed ADHD. Individuals missing the age at diagnosis were excluded. Psychiatric conditions were ascertained from the same survey using questions following an identical wording pattern “Are you still seeing a doctor or health care provider for [condition]?” Conditions assessed included anxiety reaction or panic disorder, social phobia, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, depression, eating disorder, personality disorder, posttraumatic stress disorder, schizophrenia, alcohol use disorder, and drug use disorder. For this study, anxiety reaction or panic disorder and social phobia were grouped together under anxiety disorder, and alcohol use disorder and drug use disorder were grouped as substance use disorder. Somatic conditions were also ascertained from the Personal and Family Health History questionnaire and comprised 9 categories of conditions: bone, joint, and muscle; brain and nervous system; cancer; digestive; hearing and eye; heart and blood; hormone and endocrine; kidney; and lung. A category was coded present when the respondent endorsed seeing a clinician for at least 1 condition within that category. Description of conditions within categories is provided in eTable 1 in Supplement 1. Impairment was measured using self-reported ratings of general health and daily functioning, including general health, physical health, mental health, quality of life, satisfaction with social activities, ability to perform physical and social roles, fatigue, and emotional distress. Further details are provided in the eMethods in Supplement 1. Covariates Demographic and socioeconomic variables were self-reported from the All of Us survey The Basics. Sex at birth was reported as female, male, or neither (included intersex, none of these, prefer not to answer, and skip). Self-reported race and ethnicity were assessed to more fully characterize the cohort and coded as Hispanic, non-Hispanic Black or African American, non-Hispanic White, other (included American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, Middle Eastern or North African, and more than 1 race or ethnicity), or not reported (included none of these, prefer not to answer, and skip). Educational achievement was categorized as less than high school, high school graduate or General Educational Development, some college, college graduate, advanced degree, or not reported. Annual household income was analyzed in ordered categories with an additional not-reported level. Propensity Score Matching For each ADHD group (youth-diagnosed and adult-diagnosed), we constructed an independent control cohort using 1:2 nearest-neighbor propensity score matching without replacement.11 The propensity score was estimated using logistic regression as the predicted probability of ADHD conditional on age at survey, sex, race and ethnicity, educational achievement, and household income. “Not reported” levels were retained as categories where applicable. Eligible controls were participants who reported no lifetime ADHD. Matching was implemented separately within each group, with complete-case inclusion for the matching covariates. Covariate balance was evaluated by standardized mean differences, with absolute values less than 0.10 considered acceptable. In a sensitivity analysis, we repeated the 1:2 nearest-neighbor matching to construct independent clinical control cohorts (matched clinical controls), restricting eligible controls to participants who reported seeing a clinician for at least 1 somatic condition. Propensity scores were re-estimated using the same covariates. These analyses evaluated whether the main findings were robust when using a clinically ascertained control sample. PRS ADHD-PRSs were calculated from All of Us Controlled Tier array genotypes12 using PRSice, version 2.3.5,13 and summary statistics from the most recent ADHD genome-wide association study.14 After standard sample- and variant-level quality control,15 PRSs were computed across 11 genome-wide association study P value thresholds, and the first principal component across thresholds was used as the ADHD-PRS measure.16 Additional details are provided in the eMethods in Supplement 1. Statistical Analysis For adult- vs youth-diagnosed ADHD, we fit multivariable logistic regression models for each psychiatric condition, somatic category, and impairment outcome, adjusting for age and sex. In exploratory analyses, we separated the youth-diagnosed group into child-diagnosed (0-11 years of age) and adolescentdiagnosed (12-17 years of age) groups and repeated pairwise comparisons among adult-, adolescent-, and child-diagnosed ADHD. Sex moderation was examined by including an interaction term between diagnosis timing and sex. We report predicted probabilities and odds ratios (ORs) with 95% CIs. As sensitivity analyses, we repeated these comparisons with additional adjustment for educational achievement, and separately with additional adjustment for income. Educational achievement and income were examined in separate sensitivity models to reduce collinearity concerns and preserve model interpretability. Each ADHD group was also compared with its own propensity score–matched control cohort using logistic regression without additional covariates. For genetic analyses, ADHD-PRSs were regressed on age, sex, and the first 10 genetic ancestry principal components in the full genetic subsample. Standardized residuals from this model were used in all PRS analyses. Group differences in PRSs were estimated with linear regression and summarized as mean differences with 95% CIs and the Cohen d with 95% CIs. In addition, we performed quintile analyses of the residualized ADHD-PRS. Global cut points were defined in the pooled analytic sample using the 20th, 40th, 60th, and 80th percentiles of the standardized residuals, ensuring identical thresholds across contrasts. Logistic regression models estimated ORs and 95% CIs for quintiles 2 through 5 compared with 1 (reference). All tests were 2-sided. The false discovery rate (FDR) was controlled at .05 across outcomes using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, and P < .05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were conducted between July and December 2025 in R, version 4.4.0 (R Project for Statistical Computing), within All of Us Researcher Workbench. In sex-moderation analyses, a significant interaction was observed for autism spectrum disorder. Adult-diagnosed ADHD was associated with lower adjusted probabilities of autism compared with youth-diagnosed ADHD in both sexes, but this difference was stronger among males (interaction OR, 0.55 [95% CI, 0.38-0.80]; FDR-adjusted P = .02) (eTable 12 in Supplement 1). In exploratory analyses separating youth-diagnosed ADHD into child- and adolescentdiagnosed groups, adult-diagnosed ADHD showed lower adjusted probabilities of most psychiatric comorbidities, somatic comorbidities, and impairment outcomes compared with both child- and adolescent-diagnosed ADHD. Differences between child- and adolescent-diagnosed ADHD were less consistent; adolescent-diagnosed ADHD was associated with lower adjusted probabilities for 3 of 9 psychiatric comorbidities and 1 of 9 somatic comorbidities, with no statistically significant differences in impairment outcomes (eTables 13-15 in Supplement 1). Compared with their matched control participants without ADHD (eTable 2 and eTable 3 in Supplement 1), both the youth- and adult-diagnosed ADHD groups exhibited a markedly higher burden of all comorbid psychiatric conditions (eg, depression: probability difference, 39.33 [95% CI, 38.19-40.48] pp for adult-diagnosed ADHD and 36.92 [95% CI, 35.05-38.83] pp for youthdiagnosed ADHD) and somatic conditions (eg, brain and nervous system conditions: probability difference, 21.86 [95% CI, 20.64-22.93] pp for adult-diagnosed ADHD and 22.84 [95% CI, 21.0524.83] pp for youth-diagnosed ADHD), except for cancer (probability difference, −0.42 [95% CI, −1.07 to 0.22] pp for adult-diagnosed ADHD and 0.05 [95% CI, −0.71 to 0.82] pp for youth-diagnosed ADHD) (Table 3; eTables 6-8 in Supplement 1). Individuals with adult-diagnosed ADHD had lower adjusted ADHD-PRSs than those with youthdiagnosed ADHD (Cohen d, −0.17 [95% CI, −0.21 to −0.12]), and both groups had higher PRSs than their respective matched controls (adult-diagnosed ADHD vs matched controls mean difference Cohen d, 0.12 [95% CI, 0.09-0.15]; youth-diagnosed ADHD vs matched controls Cohen d, 0.21 [95% CI, 0.16-0.26]) (eTable 17 in Supplement 1). Across ADHD-PRS quintiles, higher quintiles were associated with lower odds of adult vs youth diagnosis (Figure 2A). For both youth- and adultdiagnosed groups, higher quintiles showed a stepwise increase in the odds of ADHD relative to matched controls (Figure 2B and C). Compared with matched clinical controls (eTable 4 and eTable 5 in Supplement 1), similar results were observed (eTables 9-11, eTable 18, and the eFigure in Supplement 1). Discussion In this large All of Us sample, the following main conclusions were reached: (1) individuals first diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood had a milder clinical profile than individuals diagnosed in childhood or adolescence, represented by fewer psychiatric and somatic co-occurring conditions that are commonly observed in ADHD17; (2) adult-diagnosed individuals reported less impairment in overall health and daily activities than youth-diagnosed individuals; (3) relative to youth-diagnosed individuals, adult-diagnosed individuals had lower ADHD-PRSs, supporting an attenuated genetic profile of ADHD; (4) compared with matched controls without ADHD, both ADHD groups showed JAMA Network Open | Psychiatry Age at Diagnosis and Clinical and Genetic Profiles Among Adults With ADHD JAMA Network Open. 2026;9(9):e2634125. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.34125 (Reprinted) September 16, 2026 8/16 Downloaded from jamanetwork.​com by SUNY Stony Brook user on 10/​22/​2026

clinical and genetic profiles highly consistent with ADHD; and (5) compared with matched controls, both ADHD groups reported significant impairments in overall health and daily activities, indicating both as important subgroups warranting assessment and clinical management. Similar findings were observed using matched controls selected from a clinical sample. Taken together, our findings are most consistent with a severity continuum, rather than qualitatively distinct ADHD subtypes, defined by age at first diagnosis, with adult-diagnosed ADHD representing a comparatively milder expression of ADHD-like clinical and genetic profiles. Our results showed lower rates of most psychiatric disorders in adult-diagnosed ADHD compared with youth-diagnosed ADHD, with depressive disorder as the only exception among the comorbidities assessed. results.8,9 In one review of medical records at a university hospital, investigators compared 50 adults diagnosed with ADHD in childhood and 58 adults diagnosed in adulthood and found a higher total number of comorbidities in the childhood-diagnosed group.8 A second study of 134 adults referred to an adult ADHD clinic, with age at diagnosis verified in electronic medical records, found no statistically significant differences between groups in prior exposure to antianxiety, mood stabilizer, or antipsychotic medications and no differences in quality of life assessed via structured questionnaires.9 In a much larger and more diverse sample, our findings support higher rates of psychiatric comorbidities in youth-diagnosed ADHD relative to adult-diagnosed ADHD. Given that greater symptom severity and psychiatric comorbidity have been associated with persistence of ADHD into adulthood in longitudinal studies,18 adults with youth-diagnosed ADHD who remain in clinical care may be expected to show greater psychiatric burden. Importantly, both ADHD groups had higher rates of every psychiatric comorbidity examined compared with their matched controls, consistent with prior literature showing elevated psychiatric burden in adults with ADHD.19 Our findings indicate that individuals with adult-diagnosed ADHD have lower rates of somatic comorbidities than those diagnosed with ADHD in youth. Both ADHD groups showed higher rates of somatic comorbidities than their matched controls, with cancer conditions as the only exception. This pattern aligns with prior work showing substantial somatic morbidity in ADHD populations, likely influenced by shared genetic vulnerability and overlapping risk factors.20-22 In our data, the largest probability differences between ADHD groups and their matched controls were observed for neurological, respiratory, and musculoskeletal conditions, with differences of approximately 13 to 23 pp across comparisons, consistent with large epidemiological studies.21 Prior studies also suggest that somatic comorbidities are more common with more severe ADHD presentations.23,24 Taken together, these observations point to a higher somatic burden in youth-diagnosed ADHD compared with adult-diagnosed ADHD. Regarding self-reported impairment, analyses adjusted for age and sex initially suggested lower impairment among adult-diagnosed than youth-diagnosed adults. After further adjustment for educational achievement or income, these differences were substantially attenuated and were not significant, indicating that socioeconomic status strongly influences the reported impairments. This is not surprising, given that socioeconomic factors are well-established determinants of overall health.25 Moreover, higher educational achievement and income among adult-diagnosed individuals may partly reflect their older age and greater time to complete education and accumulate income. Both ADHD groups reported worse overall health and overall functional impairment in daily activities compared with their matched controls, in line with prior literature demonstrating functional Figure 2. impairment in ADHD.26,27 Thus, despite fewer comorbidities, individuals diagnosed with ADHD as adults report a similar level of functional impairment once socioeconomic status is accounted for, underscoring the importance of recognizing and treating ADHD even when diagnosis occurs in adulthood. We observed that individuals in the adult-diagnosed ADHD group had lower ADHD-PRSs than those in the youth-diagnosed ADHD group. Consistent with our findings, LaBianca et al28 observed higher ADHD-PRSs among individuals first diagnosed in childhood than among those first diagnosed in adulthood. In contrast, Rajagopal et al29 found no statistically significant differences after correction for multiple comparisons, with only nominal differences between individuals diagnosed in childhood and adulthood vs those diagnosed only in adulthood. Notably, both studies showed clear ADHD-PRS elevations in adult-diagnosed cases relative to controls without ADHD.28,29 This finding aligns with our results, in which both ADHD groups had higher ADHD-PRSs than their matched controls. The effect sizes for ADHD-PRS vs controls in our study are at the lower end of those reported in the literature,30-32 which may reflect the use of self-reported ADHD diagnosis, introducing misclassification that can attenuate genetic findings. Overall, ADHD-PRS patterns are consistent with adult-diagnosed ADHD representing a less severe expression of ADHD liability. Most individuals with ADHD in our sample were women in both the adult- and youth-diagnosed groups. This contrasts with the broader literature, in which ADHD is more prevalent among boys in childhood and roughly comparable by sex in adulthood.33 Our definition of ADHD required currently seeing a clinician, which may bias toward female participants, as women are more likely to seek professional help for mental health concerns.34 Although women have been reported to seek an ADHD evaluation in adulthood more often than men,35 we did not observe a higher proportion of women in the adult-diagnosed group compared with the youth-diagnosed group. This may reflect the high prevalence of women in both groups, which could dilute between-group differences. Exploratory moderation analyses did not suggest broad sex differences in the associations between adult- vs youth-diagnosed ADHD. Autism spectrum disorder was the only outcome with a statistically significant interaction after correction for multiple comparisons, with adult-diagnosed ADHD showing lower probability of autism spectrum disorder in both sexes but a larger difference among males. This may reflect sex differences in neurodevelopmental diagnostic recognition, whereby co-occurring autism spectrum disorder may facilitate earlier ADHD identification more strongly among males than females. Exploratory analyses separating child- and adolescent-diagnosed ADHD were broadly consistent with a graded pattern in which earlier diagnosis is associated with greater genetic and clinical burden, particularly psychiatric comorbidity. However, this pattern was not uniform across clinical domains and may have been blurred by retrospective misclassification of childhood vs adolescent diagnosis timing. Notably, this study did not evaluate the late-onset ADHD hypothesis.36 That is, we were unable to determine absence of childhood symptoms, which would be required to substantiate late-onset ADHD, since childhood symptom data were unavailable. Our goal was conceptually different and focused on characterizing the growing number of individuals receiving a first ADHD diagnosis in adulthood, irrespective of childhood symptom history. Our findings should not be interpreted as evidence for or against late-onset ADHD. Limitations Findings from this study should be interpreted with consideration of the following limitations. First, this study relied on self-reported ADHD diagnoses, including age at first diagnosis, and on selfreported co-occurring conditions, which may be subject to misclassification or recall bias. Importantly, the ADHD-PRSs showed patterns across groups that were consistent with the clinical results, supporting the overall validity of the classification. Second, despite propensity score matching, residual confounding is possible, including differences in access to care, regional practice patterns, and screening intensity. limit generalizability. The All of Us research Program deliberately prioritizes groups historically underrepresented in biomedical research10 but is not a probability-based sample of the US population. In the present analysis, 4.5% of the assessed sample met our ADHD definition. This estimate should not be interpreted as population prevalence, but it is broadly compatible with recent nationally representative Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data showing that 6.0% of US adults reported current ADHD.2 However, the sociodemographic composition of our ADHD analytic sample differed from nationally representative estimates of adults with current ADHD, including a higher proportion of female participants, a lower proportion of non-Hispanic Black participants, and substantially higher educational attainment.2 Together, these differences suggest that the present results should be interpreted as comparisons among All of Us participants meeting the study definitions rather than as nationally representative estimates of ADHD frequency, comorbidity, or impairment. Fourth, our ADHD definition required participants to report currently seeing a clinician for ADHD, which limits generalizability. Adults with greater health care access or health-seeking behavior may be more likely to obtain a diagnosis, and those with more severe symptoms may be more likely to remain in care. Fifth, our aim was to compare adults with current ADHD by age at diagnosis; thus, individuals diagnosed in youth who are not in clinical care as adults (and are more likely to be remitted) were outside our scope. Sixth, controls without ADHD included individuals who reported no lifetime ADHD diagnosis; however, some individuals with undiagnosed ADHD may have been included in this group. Conclusions In this cross-sectional study of adults with ADHD, adults first diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood showed a milder clinical and genetic profile than individuals first diagnosed in childhood or adolescence, which may have contributed to later recognition. However, both groups had clinical profiles typical of individuals with ADHD relative to individuals without ADHD, with substantial burden. These findings support the premise that adult-diagnosed ADHD is a clinically important subgroup that warrants recognition and treatment. ARTICLE INFORMATION Accepted for Publication: July 22, 2026. It is usually diagnosed in childhood, though it may persist into adolescence and adulthood. ADHD is diagnosed clinically in accordance with the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual for Mental Disorders-5 (DSM-5; Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, 2016). Email: bryan.leow@mohh.com.sg Association between Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder and Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Bryan Hao Wei Leow1, Claire Jing-Wen Tan1 , Brian Sheng Yep Yeo2, Noelle Na En Ng2, Seraphina Cheng Yong Low2, Adele Chin Wei Ng1,3,4, Oon Hoe Teoh3,5,4, Song Tar Toh1,3,4, and Ellen Ghim Hoon Tay4,5 Abstract Background: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) are two relatively common conditions in the pediatric population, with multiple studies demonstrating a strong association between the two. Hypoxia and sleep fragmentation caused by OSA has been shown to exacerbate ADHD symptoms, while treatment for OSA, such as with continuous positive airway pressure or adenotonsillectomy, may improve ADHD symptoms. We aim to provide an updated systematic review and meta-analysis on the complex relationship between OSA and ADHD in children. Methods: PubMed, Embase, and SCOPUS were searched from inception to 1 December 2024 for longitudinal studies investigating the association between OSA and ADHD in children. Two independent authors selected relevant articles, extracted data, assessed bias using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale and evaluated quality of evidence following the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations framework. Random-effects meta-analysis was performed to synthesize pooled prevalence, while descriptive reviews were performed for all other outcomes. Results: This systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies and 903 children formally diagnosed with OSA or ADHD found that the pooled prevalence of OSA in children with ADHD was 44% ( 95% CI [2%, 56%]). Descriptive analysis found that adenotonsillectomy for OSA consistently led to significant improvements in both OSA and ADHD symptoms, suggesting its potential in complementing existing pharmacological therapy in improving ADHD symptoms. Conclusion: OSA and ADHD are closely related comorbid conditions. Physicians should be cognizant of this association and consider concurrent evaluation for OSA in children with ADHD symptoms, which can effectively guide treatment strategies and potentially reduce the need for long-term pharmacological treatment. Leow et al. 823 partial or complete obstruction of the upper airway during sleep, leading to intermittent cessation of airflow and sleep arousal. The underlying causes of OSA in children can be multifactorial, with major risk factors being adenotonsillar hypertrophy and obesity, and other risk factors being prematurity, asthma, allergic rhinitis, craniofacial abnormalities, neuromuscular disorders and a family history of OSA (Hasuneh et al., 2024). Clinically, OSA severity is categorized by the Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI). It can be challenging to diagnose OSA in children as presentation may be distinct from that in adults. Children with OSA usually present with snoring, night awakenings, unusual sleep positions and sometimes nocturnal enuresis. In children, the sleep disruption may also lead to behavioral issues including hyperactivity, irritability, and even aggression. Adenotonsillectomy is the most common treatment for pediatric OSA (American Academy of Pediatrics. Section on Pediatric Pulmonology, Subcommittee on Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome, 2002). Several studies have shown that OSA and ADHD in children may be closely linked. Chronic sleep disruption caused by OSA can exacerbate the core symptoms of ADHD, leading to a cycle of worsening sleep disturbances and behavioral difficulties. Conversely, the hyperactive and impulsive behaviors commonly associated with ADHD may mask the presence of OSA in affected children, and lead to complications such as developmental delays, behavioral issues, cardiovascular problems, and impaired cognitive function (Youssef et al., 2011). Of note, a previous systematic review and meta-analysis by Urbano et al. found that adenotonsillectomy in children with OSA was effective in the short-term treatment of ADHD symptoms. However, the success of other treatment options including Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) therapy was not established (Urbano et al., 2021). Another meta-analysis by Sedky et al. demonstrated that ADHD symptoms are related to OSA and improve after adenotonsillectomy, reducing the need for reliance on pharmacological intervention for control of ADHD. As such, it would be worthwhile to examine the association between these two comorbid conditions to guide clinical management (Sedky et al., 2014). We aim to perform an updated systematic review and meta-analysis to summarize the latest literature and provide deeper insights on the relationship between OSA and ADHD in children. Materials and Methods According to a pre-registered protocol on PROSPERO (CRD42025645881), this systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) recommendations (Page et al., 2021). The PRISMA checklist can be found in Supplemental Table S1. Search Strategy PubMed, Embase and Cochrane Library were searched from inception to 1 December 2024, using search terms pertaining to OSA and ADHD, treatment methods and their relevant synonyms. Study Selection The selection of eligible articles by titles and abstracts, followed by full texts, was performed by three independent authors (CJWT, NNEN, SCYL), with disagreements resolved through the consensus of another independent author (BHWL). Based on the Population, Intervention, Comparators, Outcomes (PICO) framework, we selected studies that met the following inclusion criteria: randomized controlled trials or observational studies (cohort, cross-sectional) published as full-length articles in peer-reviewed journals studying the associations between OSA and ADHD in children. We included peer-reviewed observational studies that were published as full-length articles in English and utilized formal methods of diagnosis of OSA and ADHD. We utilized an AHI cut-off of ≥1 event per hour for the diagnosis of pediatric OSA, in accordance with the American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines (Marcus et al., 2012). We excluded studies that did not meet the inclusion criteria, duplicate studies, case reports, case series, reviews, meta-analyses, letters, conference abstracts, and studies with incomplete data. Data Extraction We extracted data from each included article into a standardized extraction template. The data extraction process was performed by two independent authors (CJWT, BHWL). We extracted the following information: first author, year of publication, study design, country, follow-up duration, total number of participants, age, gender, prevalence of OSA in ADHD patients and vice versa, severity of OSA by AHI, intervention for OSA and ADHD respectively, subjective and objective outcomes following treatment, covariates, statistical methods and key findings. Risk of Bias Assessment The risk of bias of observational studies was appraised by four independent authors (CJWT, BHWL, NC, SL) using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS; Wells et al., 2014) acknowledged by the Cochrane Collaboration (Higgins et al., 2017), for interventional and observational studies respectively. The NOS is a nine-point grading system derived from an eight-item checklist, designed to evaluate the extent of selection, information, and confounding biases, in determining the risk of bias in non-randomized studies. As per the NOS grading in past reviews, we graded the studies as having a high (<5 stars), moderate (5–7 stars)

824 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(6) or low risk of bias (≥8 stars; Wells et al., 2014). Risk of bias assessment via the Newcastle-Ottawa scale is demonstrated in Supplemental Table S2. Statistical Analysis We conducted all statistical analyses on RevMan (version 5.4), in accordance with statistical approaches laid out by the Cochrane handbook (Higgins et al., 2017). Unless otherwise specified, a p-value of ≤.05 was considered statistically significant. When two or more studies were available, we proceeded with our planned meta-analyzes. Using a random-effects model, maximally covariate-adjusted ratios were pooled from each study. We assessed for between-study heterogeneity using Thompson’s I2 values and the Cochran Q Test, where an I2 value of 25%, 50% and 75% represented low, moderate, and high degree of heterogeneity respectively and a τ2 p-value of ≤.10 was considered significant for heterogeneity. To assess for publication bias, we qualitatively examined funnel plots for asymmetry and imputed potentially missing studies using the trim-and-fill method. For all other outcomes in which there were insufficient data for a meta-analysis, descriptive analysis was performed. Results The PRISMA flowchart demonstrating the study selection process is presented in Figure 1. Literature search of the 4 databases (PubMed, Embase, Scopus and Cochrane Library) retrieved 825 results. 292 duplicates were removed. Title and abstract screening further excluded 498 articles. Full text screening excluded 24 articles. 11 articles were included in the final analysis (Chin et al., 2018; Dillon et al., 2007; Galland et al., 2011; Goraya et al., 2009; Huang et al., 2004, 2007; Li et al., 2006; Nguyen-Ngoc-Quynh et al., 2022; Pagel et al., 2004; Tsai et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2023). Study Characteristics Baseline study characteristics of the included studies are summarized in Table 1. Briefly, of the 11 included studies, eight cohort studies, two case-control studies and one crosssectional study. The proportion of males in the included studies ranged from 51.9% to 90%, while mean age ranged from 7.8 to 10.7 years. Six studies had low risk of bias while five studies had moderate risk of bias as per the NewcastleOttawa Scale in Supplemental Table S2. Meta-Analysis Four studies reported the prevalence of OSA in ADHD patients (Goraya et al., 2009; Huang et al., 2004; Pagel et al., 2004; Tsai et al., 2012). The pooled prevalence of OSA in children with ADHD was 44% ( 95% CI [32%, 56%], I2 = 72.2%; Figure 2). Systematic Review Association Between OSA and ADHD. Two studies investigated the prevalence of ADHD in children with OSA. Nguyen et al. found that the prevalence of ADHD in children with OSA is 43.1% (25 events out of 58 subjects), while Dillon et al. found that the same prevalence is 27.8% (22 events out of 79 subjects; Dillon et al., 2007; NguyenNgoc-Quynh et al., 2022). Three studies investigated the association between AHI and ADHD. Wu et al. demonstrated that attention deficit and hyperactive impulsivity scores graded by an 18-item ADHD rating scale were independently associated with the obstructive AHI (p < .001; Wu et al., 2023). Similarly, Chin et al. found that children with ADHD had significantly higher AHI (p = .002), hypopnea counts (p = .003) and lower slow-wave sleep percentages (p = .006) on polysomnography (Chin et al., 2018). Conversely, categorical analyses performed by Galland et al. in a small study population did not show any significant difference in AHI between children with and without ADHD (Galland et al., 2011). Adenotonsillectomy ADHD Parameters. Dillon et al. demonstrated that following adenotonsillectomy for the clinical indication of obstructed breathing while awake, obstructed breathing while asleep and recurrent tonsillitis, the overall prevalence of ADHD declined modestly from 27.8% to 20.5%. Among the 22 children diagnosed with ADHD at baseline, 50% remitted and no longer fulfilled DSM-IV criteria for ADHD, while the remaining 50% continued to have ADHD. The follow up prevalence remained high at 20.5% despite the 50% remission of ADHD because five children were newly diagnosed with ADHD at follow up (Dillon et al., 2007). Two studies examined changes after adenotonsillectomy on the Disruptive Behavior Disorder Rating cale (DBDRS). Dillon et al. found that among the children whose ADHD remitted after adenotonsillectomy, rating changes on DBDRS corresponding to preoperative diagnosis changed by an average of 51.1%, with a mean decrease in DBDRS inattentive, hyperactivity and combined scores by 8.4, 6.0 and 18.0 respectively (Dillon et al., 2007). (2007) also demonstrated statistically significant changes in the overall DBDRS scores and hyperactivity/impulsivity sub scores post-adenotonsillectomy (p = .007 and p = .002 respectively; Huang et al., 2007). (2007) showed demonstrated a statistically significant change only in inattention sub scores (p < .01), but not for hyperactive sub scores or total score on the ADHD-RS after 6 months of methylphenidate use. However, there were no statistically significant changes in any of the eight subscales on the CBCL with methylphenidate use over the same time period (Huang et al., 2007). Separately, Chin et al. found that there was a statistically significant change in both inattention and hyperactive sub scores and total scores on the ADHD-RS after 6 months of methylphenidate use in children with ADHD (p < .05). Findings on the CBCL were dissimilar as only externalizing behavior, anxiety, obsession/compulsion and aggression subscales showed statistically significant change with methylphenidate use (p < .05) while the rest of the subscales had no significant change with methylphenidate use (Chin et al., 2018). In children with OSA, Huang et al. demonstrated a nonsignificant change in AHI from 2.24 ± 1.44 to 2.50 ± 2.95 with methylphenidate use after 6 months. In children who were not on methylphenidate, there was a change in AHI from 2.56 ± 1.46 to 2.31 ± 2.19 over the same duration. There was also no statistically significant change in other sleep parameters measured in the PSG, especially for snoring index, arousal index and total sleep time which showed significant changes post-adenotonsillectomy in the same study. Similarly, there was no significant change in OSA-18 QOL scoring for methylphenidate use, in comparison to adenotonsillectomy (Huang et al., 2007). Similarly, Galland et al. showed that in case-matched paired analysis done between 28 pairs of ADHD children and controls, only total sleep time showed statistically significant change on the medication night in children with ADHD (p < .01),and showed that methylphenidate use had no significant effect on AHI, desaturation events or snoring percentage (Galland et al., 2011). Chin et al. found a statistically significant increase in AHI from a mean of 1.20 ± 1.22 from 1.98 ± 2.78 (p = .012) following treatment with methylphenidate for 6 months. However, polysomnography findings showed significantly increased total sleep time and reduced periodic limb movement index, while the pediatric sleep questionnaire findings showed significant reduction in snoring. This suggests that while methylphenidate treatment may improve certain nonrespiratory aspects of sleep in children with ADHD, it does not have a positive effect on sleep disordered breathing (Chin et al., 2018). Discussion Our systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies and found that close to half of children with ADHD have concomitant OSA, suggestive of a strong association between the two conditions. Descriptive analysis demonstrated that adenotonsillectomy consistently leads to improvement in both OSA and ADHD symptoms, and may be considered as an option before methylphenidate or as a complement to Figure 2. 828 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(6) existing pharmacological therapy in improving ADHD symptoms in children with both conditions. In establishing the relationship between OSA and ADHD, it has been hypothesized that OSA is one of the five sleep phenotypes associated with ADHD, with the other phenotypes comprising delayed sleep onset insomnia, restless legs syndrome, narcoleptic and sleep EEG epileptiform discharges (Miano et al., 2019). With regards to biochemical changes, a previous study found that the systemic inflammatory response caused by OSA led to increased levels of inflammatory mediators like C-reactive protein and interleukin-6, which correlate with sleep disruption and hypoxia (Tauman et al., 2004). Children with OSA also demonstrated evidence of decreased arterial blood oxygen saturation and brain hypoxemia (Kim et al., 2018). Such a phenomenon then limits the restorative benefits of sleep, disrupting cellular and chemical balances, eventually leading to prefrontal cortical dysfunction which may manifest as features of overactivity and impulsivity (Beebe & Gozal, 2002). Furthermore, sleep deprivation and fragmented sleep due to OSA can result in exacerbation of ADHD symptoms. This may explain why OSA and ADHD are strongly linked and may present concurrently in childhood. Nonetheless, we acknowledge that there exists heterogeneity in our analysis of the prevalence rates of ADHD in children with OSA. Notably, Nguyen et al. reported a high prevalence of 43.1% of ADHD in children with OSA. Current epidemiological literature suggests a prevalence of 20% to 30% of ADHD in children with OSA (NguyenNgoc-Quynh et al., 2022; Urbano et al., 2021), which is similar to figures provided by Dillon et al. This may be attributed the fact that Nguyen et al. recruited subjects who were all diagnosed with asthma, regardless of whether they had OSA. A previous systematic review and meta-analysis by Kaas et al. demonstrated a positive association between asthma and ADHD after adjusting for relevant confounders (Kaas et al., 2021). A large-scale genome-wide cross-trait analysis by Zhu et al. also found a significant genetic correlation between ADHD and asthma with seven jointly associated loci (Zhu et al., 2019). Since children with asthma are more likely to have ADHD, this could have led to significant confounding and hence a higher prevalence of ADHD among the children with OSA in this study. Adenotonsillectomy may improve ADHD symptoms in children by improving overall sleep architecture and providing better quality of sleep which is critical in promoting optimal neurocognitive development in early adolescence, in areas including attention, reward, emotional processing and regulation, memory, and executive control (Brooks et al., 2022). In fact, children with habitual snoring but without clinically significant hypoxia as measured by pulse oximetry have been shown to have poorer academic performance than those who do not snore (Brockmann et al., 2015). A prospective, nonrandomized study by Wei et al. showed that in 117 children with sleep disordered breathing who underwent adenotonsillectomy, correlations between sleep and behavior scores were statistically significant before and after surgery. Not only did both behavior and sleep improve independently before and after adenotonsillectomy for sleep disordered breathing in this group of patients, they also improved in correlation with each other (Wei et al., 2007). As such, the associations between poor sleep and neurocognitive, behavioral issues in children are evident, and adenotonsillectomy aims to restore proper sleep quality. Our findings are consistent with the Childhood Adenotonsillectomy Trial (CHAT) in 2013. The CHAT trial was a multicenter, single-blind, randomized study investigating the on neurocognitive and behavioral outcomes in children aged 5 to 9 years old with OSA who were subjected to early adenotonsillectomy versus watchful waiting. The study demonstrated significantly greater behavioral improvements post-surgery, as reported by caregivers and teachers using the Conners’ Rating Scale. In addition, modest improvement for the adenotonsillectomy group was noted compared to the watchful waiting group in the attention and executive-function score on the Developmental Neuropsychological Assessment (p = .06; Redline et al., 2011). For the purposes of our study, the CHAT trial was excluded as participants did not have a formal diagnosis of ADHD; instead, general cognitive and behavioral outcomes were analyzed. Furthermore, several studies examining children with sleep-disordered breathing and ADHD have similarly shown substantial improvement in ADHD symptoms following adenotonsillectomy. Ahmadi et al. demonstrated that in 59 children with ADHD, adenotonsillectomy led to statistically significant change in ADHD rating scale score in both domains, in 1 month and 3 months follow-up period (p = .001; Ahmadi et al., 2016). Another study by Amiri et al. showed similar findings with adenotonsillectomy leading to significant reduction in the severity of ADHD symptoms (oppositional behavior, cognitive disorders, inattention, hyperactivity and ADHD index) at 3- and 6-month postoperative intervals (Amiri et al., 2015). These studies were not included in our current systematic review and meta-analysis as children did not have a formal diagnosis of pediatric OSA. Nonetheless, it is evident from current literature that adenotonsillectomy improves sleep quality which leads to enhanced cognitive function, reduced hyperactive behaviors and improved attention consistent across different rating scales. It is interesting to note that adenotonsillectomy may potentially give rise to greater improvement in ADHD symptoms than methylphenidate. While both interventions can ameliorate inattentiveness, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, they target distinct underlying mechanisms: methylphenidate addresses neurochemical dysregulation within dopaminergic

Leow et al. 829 and noradrenergic pathways and modulates attention networks, whereas adenotonsillectomy alleviates airway obstruction during sleep, a potentially reversible cause of neurobehavioral dysfunction. It is known that OSA can cause ADHD-like symptoms or worsen ADHD symptoms (Youssef et al., 2011). This overlap in behavioral manifestations between OSA-related sleep fragmentation and ADHD often leads to diagnostic ambiguity. The symptoms of children initially identified to have ADHD may be secondary to underlying OSA, which could explain the substantial improvement in ADHD symptoms following adenotonsillectomy. As such, physicians should consider sleep evaluation concurrently with ADHD work-up in this group, especially in the presence of other supporting symptoms, which can help to reduce unnecessary long-term stimulant use and yield more sustained cognitive and behavioral benefits. Future studies providing a direct, head-to-head comparison between the two therapeutic modalities would be valuable and help to pave the way in formulating individualized, pathophysiologydriven treatment approaches for ADHD symptoms. While our study has found that adenotonsillectomy improves ADHD symptoms, it would be worthwhile to evaluate if the degree of adenotonsillar hypertrophy affects subsequent outcomes. In Huang et al. 56% of study participants who underwent adenotonsillectomy had grade 1 or 2 tonsils, and 20% did not have adenoid enlargement as evaluated on naso endoscopy and lateral neck radiographs. All other studies did not report data on the degree of adenotonsillar hypertrophy and did not conduct any subgroup analysis to adjust for the above. The strong association between the two conditions in the pediatric population should prompt physicians to assess and evaluate for OSA in ADHD, which can then guide subsequent treatment strategies. Both OSA and ADHD in children are associated with long-term health consequences, including metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular morbidity, neurocognitive deficits and depression in OSA, (Blechner & Williamson, 2016) as well poor somatic and psychiatric outcomes in ADHD (French et al., 2024). While central nervous system stimulants are typically considered to be first line treatment of ADHD, it is meaningful to appreciate that adenotonsillectomy may improve ADHD symptoms when co-diagnosed with OSA together. Moreover, it is widely known that methylphenidate can be associated with sideeffects including insomnia, irritability and anxiety, reduced appetite, hypertension, tachycardia, tics, growth retardation and even suicidal ideation (Verghese et al., 2024). As such, the potential of adenotonsillectomy in improving ADHD symptoms may shape the future of ADHD treatment for children with co-occurring OSA. Strengths and Limitations To our knowledge, this study is the first systematic review and meta-analysis that describes the bidirectional relationship of PSG-diagnosed OSA and ADHD diagnosed in the same setting in a pediatric population. While a previous systematic review by Urbano et. al similarly studied the association between sleep-disordered breathing and ADHD, our study differs in evaluating the bidirectional relationship of pediatric OSA and ADHD specifically with objective clinical diagnosis via polysomnography and DSM criteria respectively. It is widely known that children with sleep disturbances often display behavioral patterns that resemble some features of ADHD, (Horiuchi et al., 2014) but may not fulfill its full criteria, limiting the strength of conclusions drawn from previous review papers. Another strength of our study includes the use of a rigorous protocol and structured methodology to systematically search and grade the included studies based on international guidelines. All included studies were of good quality and had a sizeable sample size, and the longitudinal studies had sufficient follow-up duration. Additionally, none of our included studies had high risk of bias. Moreover, we adopted a well-defined scope of analysis and only included studies which utilized gold standard, validated means of objective diagnosis for OSA and ADHD. We intentionally excluded papers examining general sleep-disordered breathing disorders, which may encompass central sleep apnea, complex sleep apnea and hypoventilation syndromes with different underlying pathophysiology, as well as primary snoring disorders. As such, our study presents a focused and precise analysis on the complex relationship of OSA and ADHD while avoiding confounding factors. Nonetheless, our study must be interpreted in the context of known and potential limitations. Firstly, there were relatively few studies investigating pediatric OSA and ADHD. Only a handful of studies used formal polysomnography to diagnose pediatric OSA, likely due to its time-consuming and cost ineffective nature, as well as difficulty in administering the test on young children. Instead, majority of studies relied on parent questionnaires or screening tools for OSA symptoms alone, such as use of the Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire, which can be subjective. Owing to limited number of studies, we were unable to adjust for confounders including obesity, allergic rhinitis, asthma, depression, learning disabilities, all of which can affect both OSA and ADHD in children (Nguyen-Ngoc-Quynh et al., 2022; Prajsuchanai et al., 2022). Furthermore, there was heterogeneity among studies related to baseline demographic characteristics of participants and clinical subtype of ADHD (inattentive vs. hyperactive vs. combined). Different studies also used various clinical checklists and rating scales for assessment of ADHD. Inclusion of a greater number of studies would allow us to perform additional analyses to adjust for these confounders and draw more robust conclusions on the relationship and optimal treatment approaches for both OSA and ADHD. Moreover, while majority of studies have demonstrated clear short-term benefits of adenotonsillectomy on ADHD

830 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(6) symptoms in pediatric OSA patients, few have evaluated the long-term benefits of adenotonsillectomy. As OSA has been known to recur in some children post-adenotonsillectomy, it would be useful to determine the long-term behavioral changes in this group of children. Future Studies Future studies should focus on addressing current gaps in understanding causality, mechanisms, and treatment outcomes. Longitudinal cohort studies with longer follow-up durations would be helpful in determining whether early identification and treatment of OSA can reduce the onset or severity of ADHD symptoms over time. Neuroimaging and biomarker-based research may help uncover shared neurobiological pathways, such as dysregulation in dopamine or inflammatory markers. This can lead to development of novel pharmacological therapies. For example, Meliante et al. previously studied the potential role of antioxidant therapy with vitamin C or N-acetylcysteine in reducing oxidative stress produced during episodes of intermittent hypoxia in OSA (Meliante et al., 2023). It would also be interesting to explore how different ADHD subtypes can possibly relate to specific patterns of sleep disruption such as arousals or rapid eye movement (REM) suppression. This is especially in light of promising developments in wearable sleep technology in the consumer market today, allowing for convenient yet accurate means for diagnosis. Lastly, future studies should investigate if other OSA treatment including CPAP therapy and orthodontic devices can improve ADHD symptoms in children. Hobzova et al. found that in the adult population, CPAP therapy demonstrated significant improvement in attention, working memory, and depressive symptoms in OSA patients, (Hobzova et al., 2017) while Escobar et al. previously hypothesized the use of oral appliance therapy for OSA treatment may reduce the symptoms of ADHD (Escobar et al., 2021). Conclusion OSA and ADHD are closely related conditions of childhood with overlapping symptomatology. Adenotonsillectomy consistently leads to statistically significant improvement in both ADHD and OSA symptoms and may be considered as an option before or as complementary therapy to methylphenidate in improving symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity in children with both conditions. Moreover, children with ADHD symptoms would benefit from sleep evaluation concurrent with ADHD work-up. A greater number of largescale, robust studies are required to further evaluate the treatment outcomes between OSA and ADHD. Rooted in the family systems theory, FQoL recognizes families as intricate social entities where members mutually influence each other’s behaviors (Kerr, 1981). This interconnectedness means that one family member’s experiences ripple through the entire family system, impacting the well-being of others (Samuel et al., 2011). In the disability field, the presence of special educational needs in children and their families’ reactions takes on particular significance as they can profoundly affect their FQoL (Wang et al., 2004; Wang & Kober, 2011). The current study aims to shed light on the complex relationship between special educational needs diagnoses and FQoL, with a specific focus on the roles of the child’s executive functions (EF) and family socioeconomic status (SES), especially among children with Specific Learning Disabilities (SpLD), Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), and their co-occurrence. The Impact of SpLD, ADHD, and Their CoOccurrence on FQoL Children are diagnosed with ADHD through a combination of behavioral assessments, clinical interviews, and standardized rating scales that evaluate symptoms such as inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. According to Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed.; DSM-5; American Psychiatric Association, 2013) criteria, these symptoms must be present in multiple settings and must significantly impair functioning (Harris, 2024). Email: yyum@eduhk.hk The Family Quality of Life of Children With Specific Learning Disabilities, Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, and Their Co-Occurrence: A Cross-Sectional Study Di Chao Liang, MEd1 , Kean Poon, PhD1,2, and Yen Na Yum, PhD1 Abstract Research on Family Quality of Life (FQoL) has increasingly focused on the impact of learning disabilities on families. However, there is a lack of comprehensive understanding of how Specific Learning Disabilities (SpLD) or Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity/Disorder (ADHD) affect executive function (EF) deficits in children and FQoL across different household income levels. The current study compared the FQoL ratings from caregivers of three groups of Hong Kong Chinese children with learning disabilities (SpLD n = 107; ADHD n = 43; SpLD & ADHD n = 67, no typically developing control group was included). Results revealed that group classification of learning disabilities was related to two domains of FQoL (family interaction and parenting) through the child’s EF. Children with co-occurring SpLD and ADHD exhibit relatively stable EF deficits across income levels, maintaining higher EF deficits than those with SpLD alone and showing less variation than those with ADHD, who demonstrate a significant decrease in EF deficits at higher household income. Executive function deficits were associated with lower family interaction and parenting ratings across group and income levels. The findings enhance our understanding of FQoL among children with SpLD, ADHD, and their co-occurrence, highlighting the need for additional support for these families. Keywords ADHD, caretaker, comorbidity, executive function, family quality of life, socioeconomic status, SpLD

On the contrary, Specific Learning Disabilities (SpLD) are characterized by unexpected but significant difficulties in specific learning areas, such as reading and mathematics, and are diagnosed using standardized assessments and clinical evaluations. SpLD affects up to 12.6% of elementary and secondary students in Hong Kong (D. Chan et al., 2007). Caregivers of children with learning disabilities like ADHD or SpLD often face psychological, social, and managerial challenges, which can have profound implications for FQoL (e.g., Dizdarevic et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2009). Previous research consistently reveals a negative correlation between FQoL and the severity of behavioral problems in children with ADHD, a pattern observed both in Western contexts and in Hong Kong (e.g., Armstrong et al., 2014; Cussen et al., 2012; Romaniuk et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2009). Parents of children with ADHD, particularly those of children with the inattention and combined subtypes, often experience depression and anxiety due to the child’s ADHD symptoms and their own ineffective coping strategies, which can lower FQoL and family functioning (Cussen et al., 2012; Kashdan et al., 2004; Smit et al., 2021). Despite the high prevalence of SpLD among school-age children, only recently has a single study examined its impact on FQoL (Xu et al., 2025). The findings from this study revealed that the challenges associated with SpLD, including academic struggles and emotional and behavioral difficulties, had a significant impact on parental stress and a negative effect on the child’s self-esteem and overall FQoL (Xu et al., 2025). However, given that this is a single study, the existing body of research on the FQoL in children with learning disabilities remains limited, particularly in Chinese contexts. In addition, there is a distinct lack of research on the FQoL of children with comorbid ADHD and SpLD. Comorbidity refers to the presence of multiple special educational needs diagnoses. In Hong Kong, around 25% of families recruited from primary schools reported comorbid developmental disabilities in their children (R. C. H. Chan et al., 2020). Studies have estimated that up to 30% of individuals with ADHD also present with dyslexia (Hendren et al., 2018; Nelson & Gregg, 2012). Children with comorbid ADHD and SpLD may exhibit more pronounced difficulties across various domains of functioning, placing greater demands on caregivers (Hendren et al., 2018; Karande & Venkataraman, 2013; Taurines et al., 2010; Willcutt et al., 2001). Severe psychosocial difficulties in the child are likely to elicit strict parenting in response, resulting in tension in family relationships (R. C. H. Chan et al., 2020). Given the high comorbidity rate between ADHD and SpLD, studying these conditions together, rather than in isolation, is imperative. The Role of Executive Function and SES Families caring for children with SpLD or ADHD frequently confront challenges linked to deficits in the child’s EF (Frazier et al., 2022; Rapport et al., 2013). EF is a sophisticated cognitive process that coordinates thoughts, emotions, and actions, and it includes components such as working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility (Elliott, 2003). These EF components are crucial for goal-directed behaviors and highly correlated with daily functions and academic success (Dajani et al., 2016). Deficits in EFs in children with ADHD or SpLD significantly impact their social, emotional, and academic functioning. Research indicates that children with ADHD exhibit impairments in EFs which correlate with difficulties in social interactions and emotional regulation, leading to increased behavioral issues and peer rejection (Chiang & Gau, 2014). Similarly, children with SpLD often face challenges in EFs that manifest in academic tasks such as reading and writing, which can exacerbate feelings of frustration and low self-esteem (Zuppardo et al., 2023). Moreover, severe executive dysfunction is linked with a range of challenging behaviors, including property destruction, selfinjury, or aggression (Allen et al., 2017; Frazier et al., 2022; Takacs & Kassai, 2019), potentially increasing the family’s financial burden due to costs associated with damages or therapeutic interventions. These dysfunctions can significantly impact overall family dynamics and the caregivers’ personal well-being. In summary, deficits in EFs can affect various aspects of FQoL, such as family interaction and emotional well-being, which can tax the family’s coping mechanisms by inducing additional stress and potential disruptions to their daily life (Frazier et al., 2022). While comorbid SpLD and ADHD may result in unique combinations of executive dysfunctions, they do not necessarily indicate more profound deficits compared with single diagnoses due to their shared symptoms (Fernández-Andrés et al., 2019; Moura et al., 2016). To clarify this point, recent studies have shown that comorbid SpLD and ADHD may result in unique combinations of executive dysfunctions (Bental & Tirosh, 2007; Poon & Ho, 2014; Willcutt et al., 2005), which may suggest a compounded effect on FQoL when multiple learning disabilities are present. However, this connection still requires empirical research to substantiate. The close relationships between learning disabilities and EF, and between EF and behavioral difficulties in children, hint at potential connections between these variables. The nature of these connections, whether causal or correlational, remains largely unexplored and warrants further investigation. Furthermore, the influence of family SES on these dynamics between EF and FQoL is critical but not yet comprehensively understood. Socioeconomic status encompasses

Liang et al. 121 factors such as parents’ education levels, occupations, and household income. It can be related to physical well-being, one aspect of FQoL measuring the subjective availability of resources to support the family’s daily needs. High-SES families may have a higher rate of marital harmony and employ less coercive discipline than low-SES families (Hartley et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2004). In particular, household income plays a critical role in child development, as poverty has been associated with long-term stress and deficits in EF due to factors such as lack of nutrition and unsafe home environment (Blair, 2010; Duncan et al., 2017). These suggest moderating effects of financial income on children’s EF and family wellbeing. Low-income families of children with ADHD or SpLD may have fewer available resources to support their children’s education, intensifying their vulnerabilities (Guajardo et al., 2009). Conversely, investing financial resources into supporting the children’s diverse educational needs may diminish the family’s overall material resources. For instance, parents of children with learning disabilities may choose to forego full-time work to spend more time with their children, thus reducing the household income. Although high-income families tend to possess more resources and access to information to address challenges associated with learning disabilities, how this interacts with executive dysfunctions observed in children with ADHD or SpLD remains inadequately explored. Understanding these intricate relationships is pivotal for informed interventions and policy support. Study Aims Given these research gaps, our study aimed to understand the FQoL among families in Hong Kong with children diagnosed with ADHD, SpLD, or both. Specifically, the study sought to compare the FQoL of these families with that of the general population and explored how these conditions, in conjunction with SES, affect a child’s EF and overall FQoL. We anticipated that children with any of these conditions would have a lower FQoL than the general population, and those with both SpLD and ADHD would have an even lower FQoL due to their greater difficulties with EF (e.g., Karande & Venkataraman, 2013; Taurines et al., 2010). Thus, we hypothesized that EF would mediate the relationship between a child’s SpLD/ADHD status and FQoL (Frazier et al., 2022; Poon & Ho, 2014), potentially revealing the mechanisms through which learning disabilities affect family well-being. In addition, we examined the moderating role of household income in the relationships between a child’s SpLD/ADHD status, EF, and FQoL, expecting that it might influence various aspects of this mediation and offer critical insights for tailored interventions. We also hypothesized that children with both SpLD and ADHD from lower-income families might demonstrate disproportionately lower EF (Blair, 2010; Duncan et al., 2017), resulting in cumulative reductions in FQoL. Method Design and Participants In this cross-sectional study, participants were adult caregivers of a child with SpLD, ADHD, or both SpLD and ADHD. Participants were recruited from ordinary primary schools in Hong Kong. The authors obtained the children’s diagnostic information from the schoolteachers after the parents or caregivers consented. Children with ADHD or SpLD diagnoses were identified based on comprehensive psychological reports conducted by clinical or educational psychologists or psychiatrists and included multiple sources of information. These reports included results from standardized psychological assessments on students’ abilities in reading and writing, such as The Hong Kong Test of Specific Learning Difficulties in Reading and Writing for Primary Students—Third Edition (HKT-P(III); Ho et al., 2016). ADHD-specific symptoms were assessed using tools like the Conners Continuous Performance Test (Conners et al., 2018), alongside other clinical evaluations and behavioral checklists, such as the Conners Parent and Teacher Rating Scales. Full-scale IQ was also evaluated. Participants were then grouped based on their child’s special educational needs conditions (ADHD, SpLD, or Co-occurrence), regardless of other comorbidities. All participants gave written informed consent before responding to the survey. Of the initial 325 responses, 217 were valid for analysis. Excluded responses were due to incomplete data or withdrawal of consent from participants. Data were analyzed from caregivers of three groups of Hong Kong Chinese children with learning disabilities based on certified special educational needs diagnoses (SpLD n = 107; ADHD n = 43; SpLD & ADHD n = 67; no typically developing control group was included). We conducted a power analysis of a three-group one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) using GPower with input parameters of effect size (η2) of 0.25, an alpha level of .05, and a power of .9, which yielded a sample size of 210. Therefore, we inferred that our data had sufficient power to detect the intended effects. Measures Demographic Questions. The questionnaire included demographic information including age, sex, relationship with the child, and parental education level. The child’s special educational needs types were indicated on a list, including SpLD, ADHD, autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disabilities, developmental language disorder, social communication disorder, sensory impairments,

122 Journal of Learning Disabilities 59(2) emotional disorders, or other conditions. Monthly household income was scored on a scale of 1 to 12 from “$10,000 or below” to “$50,001 or above” in Hong Kong dollars and was used as a proxy measure of SES. Family Quality of Life. Participants reported their FQoL using The Beach Center Family Quality of Life Scale (BC-FQoL; Hoffman et al., 2006). This scale contains 25 items in five subscales: Family Interaction (e.g., My family solves problems together), Parenting (e.g., Family members teach the child how to get along with others), Emotional Well-being (e.g., My family has the support we need to relieve stress), Physical/Material Well-being (e.g., My family gets dental care when needed), and Disability-Related Support (e.g., My family member with special needs has support to make friends). Each item was rated on a Likert-type scale from 1 to 5 (very dissatisfied to very satisfied), with higher scores indicating greater FQoL. Based on previous literature (Xiang et al., 2009) and available local statistics, we included only the first four subscales (21 items) to understand the caregivers’ satisfaction with their FQoL. The internal consistencies for the subscales were acceptable, with Cronbach’s alpha ranging from .724 to .891 and McDonald’s omega from .769 to .894. Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function. An abbreviated 24-item version of the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF) for children ages 5 to 18 was used to assess EF of children in the context of their home environments (LeJeune et al., 2010). The response categories were 1 = never, 2 = sometimes, and 3 = often, with total scores ranging from 24 to 72. The raw scores were converted to T-scores, with scores of 60 or above indicating elevated executive dysfunction. The Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s omega for this scale were both .905. Procedure Participants completed the questionnaire either on paper or electronically on the Qualtrics platform. Data were collected between May 2021 and February 2022. This study was reviewed and approved by the research ethics committee of the first author’s institution. Data Analysis Household income and BRIEF T-scores were standardized into z-scores in the statistical models. We used one-way ANOVAs to test the hypothesis that parenting children with co-occurring SpLD and ADHD is associated with lower FQoL levels than parenting children with SpLD or ADHD alone. Significant group effects were followed up using Tukey’s post hoc multiple comparison tests to identify pairwise differences. To examine the mediating effect of EF and the moderating effect of household income, we ran a conditional process model using Model 7 of the SPSS Macro Program PROCESS (version 2.13) in SPSS (Hayes, 2013). The predictor variable was group classification (SpLD, ADHD, or Co-occurrence), and dummy variable coding was used as there were three groups. The Co-occurrence group was set as the reference level, such that the mediation and moderation effects showed comparisons of the single diagnosis groups (SpLD or ADHD) relative to their co-occurrence. The child’s EF was tested as a mediator between group classification and FQoL using bias-corrected 95% confidence interval (parametric bootstrapping of 5,000 samples), with household income as the moderating variable on the mediations (see Figure 1A). In the moderated mediation models, unstandardized β of the conditional indirect effects were presented. An absence of zero within the confidence intervals or p values of .05 or below were taken as significant effects for hypothesis testing. Results Descriptive Statistics Demographic information for the three groups is shown in Table 1. There were no significant differences in demographic variables between the three groups, except for the number of other co-occurring special educational needs. Post hoc comparisons showed that the ADHD group reported more comorbid special educational needs than the SpLD group (0.7 and 0.3, respectively, p = .014). Table 2 shows the bivariate correlations of the continuous variables in the study. In line with previous reports, subscales of FQoL were negatively related to the child’s executive dysfunctions (rs = −.322 to −.145), while all subscales of FQoL except for Parenting are positively related to household income (rs = .137 to .167). Group Differences The mean BC-FQoL scores were below 3 out of 5 and the mean BRIEF T-scores were above 60 for all three groups (see Figure 2), suggesting that the participants were generally dissatisfied with their FQoL and reported elevated executive dysfunction in their children with learning disabilities. Higher FQoL scores represent more positive outcomes, which is opposite to the directionality of EF scores, where higher scores indicate more dysfunction. Results of the one-way ANOVAs showed small to medium group differences in EF scores and two FQoL domains, namely, family interaction and parenting. Post hoc analyses showed that the SpLD group displayed better EF, that is, lower T-scores

Discussion The current study investigated the FQoL of 217 families with children with ADHD, SpLD, or their co-occurrence in Hong Kong. Specifically, we compared the FQoL of these families with that of the general population and explored how these conditions, in conjunction with household income affects a child’s EF and overall FQoL. In contrast, reference surveys by the Hong Kong Family Welfare Society (HKFWS) in 2017 and 2018 found significantly higher BC-FQoL mean scores of 3.69 to 4.08 among the general population (n = 1,033 and 1,003, respectively; HKFWS, 2017, 2018). Differences in social environments, particularly family SES—a variable known to positively correlate with FQoL (Wang et al., 2004)—likely contributed to these discrepancies. While more than half of the HKFWS participants reported a monthly income exceeding HK$30,000, less than 25% of our sample fell into this income bracket. Therefore, our findings should be considered in light of the sample’s demographic characteristics. Beyond sample differences, the stark disparity in the reported FQoL between our sample and the community average may be due to the unique circumstances associated with caring for children with special educational needs. Existing studies have reported a negative correlation between FQoL and children with ADHD, SpLD, and other special educational needs (e.g., Romaniuk et al., 2022; Xiang et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2025). It is equally important to recognize the mutual influence of family members on overall family well-being. Families may respond to children’s learning disabilities with great efforts and financial investments in behavioral, emotional, and social management, potentially resulting in diminished FQoL (Dizdarevic et al., 2022; Ginieri-Coccossis et al., 2013; Xiang et al., 2009). While corroborating results from Xu et al. (2025), this study found relatively low FQoL among families with children diagnosed with SpLD compared with community averages. This could be due to parental distress related to academic concerns or the social stigma surrounding SpLD and lower academic performance in the competitive educational atmosphere in Asia (R. C. H. Chan et al., 2020; Deater-Deckard et al., 2012). It is noteworthy that the lowest FQoL scores were reported for families with children in the ADHD and co-occurrence groups, suggesting that the additional challenges associated with ADHD, such as behavioral issues and attentional difficulties, may further exacerbate family stress and reduce quality of life. This finding expands on the existing research on FQoL in children with developmental disabilities by highlighting the varying impacts of different conditions. The Mediation Effect of Executive Dysfunction A central aim of the current study is to examine whether and how the child’s EF may mediate the relationship between their learning disabilities status and FQoL.
