Our study partially aligns with these findings, with group comparisons revealing that children with co-occurring SpLD and ADHD exhibited elevated executive dysfunction compared with those with SpLD alone. Notably, however, when family income was not taken into account, the executive dysfunction levels observed in children with co-occurring SpLD and ADHD did not significantly differ from those with ADHD alone. One possible explanation was that the number of co-occurring special educational needs was higher on average in the ADHD group compared with the SpLD group (0.7 and 0.3, respectively). As many different special educational needs, such as autism spectrum disorder, may influence EF, polymorbidity in diagnostic background may be correlated with greater reported executive dysfunction. However, this pattern was also consistent with prior studies suggesting that comorbidity does not necessarily lead to more severe executive dysfunction compared with single diagnoses of SpLD or ADHD (Fernández-Andrés et al., 2019; Moura et al., 2016). Instead, learning disabilities such as SpLD or ADHD may be associated with distinct profiles of EF, which may relate to FQoL in different ways. For instance, more pronounced executive dysfunction could exacerbate some children’s behavioral issues, for example, noncompliance or social problems, leading to stricter parental discipline and impacting family interactions (DeaterDeckard et al., 2012). Executive dysfunction in ADHD may also present as the child’s difficulties initiating or persisting in tasks, requiring more parenting efforts (R. C. H. Chan et al., 2020). A crucial finding of this study was that the child’s executive dysfunction slightly impaired specific domains of FQoL in the family interaction and parenting domains. The Moderation Effect of Household Income Our study also identified a moderating effect of family income on the relationship between group status (ADHD vs. co-occurrence) and executive dysfunction. Although the overall EF levels were similar between ADHD and cooccurrence groups, for children with ADHD alone, higher family income appeared to offer a protective buffer against the adverse effects of executive dysfunction on family wellbeing. This result highlighted the role of household income in mitigating the impact of ADHD, as suggested by previous research (Guajardo et al., 2009). Contrary to our expectations, however, the impact of co-occurring learning disabilities on EF did not vary significantly across different household income levels. Meanwhile, the SpLD group demonstrated lower levels of executive dysfunction compared with the co-occurrence group, also regardless of household income levels. This overall pattern aligned with previous research suggesting that comorbid SpLD and ADHD can result in distinct patterns of executive dysfunction compared with SpLD alone (Bental & Tirosh, 2007; Poon & Ho, 2014; Willcutt et al., 2005). The co-occurrence group may exhibit a broader range of executive dysfunctions which might reduce the protective benefits typically associated with higher household income. However, as our sample primarily consisted of families from lower SES backgrounds, this may have influenced the observed effects (Blair, 2010; Duncan et al., 2017). Future research should explore this relationship further, taking into account the complexity of EF in children with both SpLD and ADHD. The significance of SES is underscored by the broader context of income inequality in Hong Kong. In Hong Kong, approximately 20% of the population is estimated to be living in poverty (Choi et al., 2022). In situations where children from low-SES families have more complex needs, such as co-occurring special educational needs, these families often lack sufficient social or financial support, leading to increased parenting stress (Duncan et al., 2017; Guajardo et al., 2009). Moreover, it is important to consider the timing of our study, which was conducted during the pandemic—a period when the effects of SES were likely intensified. The pandemic caused the unemployment rate in Hong Kong to peak at 6.5% by the end of 2020 and further exacerbated poverty levels (Choi et al., 2022). As a result, many children struggled to adapt to sudden disruptions in their daily lives and confinement at home, which could have led to increased anxiety or depression (Fogel et al., 2022). This context may have placed an even greater strain on families caring for children with SpLD or ADHD, particularly in terms of family health and resources (Dhiman et al., 2020). Implications This study represents the first comprehensive exploration of FQoL among children with SpLD, ADHD, and their cooccurrence in Hong Kong, paving the way for future research. Our findings revealed a reliable connection between a child’s EF and their FQoL, which has practical implications for service providers and policymakers aiming to cater to the unique needs of these families. Given our findings that EF plays a role in the FQoL for this population, clinicians should consider understanding children’s EF at an early stage. This might involve early identification and support, alongside caregiver guidance, to potentially enhance family relationship and child adaptation in home, school, and community settings. Policymakers could consider implementing comprehensive support measures for families with children with co-occurring SpLD and ADHD, as these families face ongoing challenges related to managing behavioral, emotional, and attentional difficulties, which persist across SES levels. By providing these families with a range of resources, such as educational programs, counseling services, and community support, the FQoL of

128 Journal of Learning Disabilities 59(2) these families may show a corresponding increase. Furthermore, our research underscores the importance of adopting a family-centered model in education and rehabilitation services. This model could include parental education that involves strategies to improve the quality of family interactions and parenting skills, and timely services and relevant support to alleviate parental and caregiver stress, ultimately enhancing the FQoL of these families. Limitations and Future Directions Several limitations in this study warrant consideration. First, it is essential to consider the timing of this study, which coincided with the COVID-19 pandemic and led to restrictions on the data collection process. For instance, the study mainly relied on caregiver self-reports on the child’s overall EF performance, which may introduce the possibility of respondent bias. Future studies should include task-based EF performance data for more comprehensive assessments that can separate components of EF, such as working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility. Second, this study employed a cross-sectional survey, limiting the ability to draw causal inferences. Third, despite our best efforts, the group sizes and cooccurring special educational needs numbers were not matched for the three groups of participants. Finally, although surveys conducted by HKFWS reported the FQoL scores of the general population in 2017 and 2018, the lack of control group data from families with similar demographic backgrounds makes direct comparisons challenging. Future research could employ longitudinal or experimental designs to investigate these variables’ causal relationships thoroughly. Conclusion This study significantly enhances our understanding of FQoL among children with SpLD, ADHD, and their cooccurrence in Hong Kong. It highlights how executive dysfunction may affect family interaction and parenting within these groups. In addition, the study shows that family income plays a crucial role in moderating the child’s executive function in the ADHD group, relative to the co-occurrence group. These findings emphasize the need for future interventions and family-based support systems to improve the overall well-being of these families. Longitudinal associations among autism and ADHD traits, social maladjustment, and mental health in school-aged children Eriko Hashimoto1 , Hiroyuki Ito2, Megumi Hamada3, Takahiro Nakajima4, Nobuya Takayanagi5, Mitsunori Myogan3, Yasuo Murayama6 and Masatsugu Tsujii7 1Graduate School of Humanities and Sciences, Ochanomizu University; 2Faculty of Core Research, Ochanomizu University; 3School of Psychology, Chukyo University; 4School of Human Care Studies, Nagoya University of Arts and Sciences; 5Department of Psychology, Aichi University of Education; 6College of Human and Social Sciences, Kanazawa University and 7School of Contemporary Sociology, Chukyo University Abstract Background. Neurodevelopmental disorder traits are associated with a range of psychosocial difficulties, yet the longitudinal processes linking these traits to mental health remain insufficiently explored. This study examined developmental associations among autism spectrum disorder (ASD) traits, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) traits, social maladjustment, and mental health from childhood through adolescence. Methods. Longitudinal data were drawn from 9,619 students across 11 grade cohorts in mainstream classrooms. Cross-lagged structural equation modeling was used to estimate independent longitudinal associations among ASD traits, ADHD traits, social maladjustment, and mental health, while controlling for confounding factors. ASD and ADHD traits were modeled simultaneously to clarify their unique developmental patterns. Results. ASD traits were consistently associated with later internalizing problems and peer difficulties. ADHD traits were associated with later internalizing and externalizing problems, as well as academic challenges and strained teacher–parent relationships. These associations differed by trait type, suggesting distinct developmental pathways. Several bidirectional associations also emerged: poorer mental health was associated with subsequent social maladjustment, which was subsequently linked to persistent developmental difficulties. Conclusions. The findings indicate that social maladjustment is involved in the longitudinal associations between developmental disorder traits and mental health and may shape developmental trajectories. These results highlight the need for comprehensive support approaches that consider peer relationships, learning environments, and family–school relationships. Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are neurodevelopmental disorders that exhibit high comorbidity rates with psychiatric disorders (Hossain et al., 2020; Larson, Russ, Kahn, & Halfon, 2011; Simonoff et al., 2008). Such comorbidities have also been observed in mild cases that do not meet the full diagnostic criteria of these disorders (Kim et al., 2009; Lundström et al., 2011; Rai et al., 2018), indicating that children with subthreshold symptoms often exhibit equivalent clinical support needs (Balázs & Keresztény, 2014; Kamio et al., 2013). As mental-health–related problems during school age have long-term effects on educational, occupational, and social functioning in adulthood (Copeland, Wolke, Shanahan, & Costello, 2015), early intervention is a critical public health priority. However, the specific temporal pathways linking neurodevelopmental disorder traits to secondary mental health problems and the mechanisms for this association remain poorly understood. Moreover, minimal research has been conducted on children with subthreshold symptoms, and their support systems remain underdeveloped. This study addresses this gap by using large-scale longitudinal data from Japanese elementary and middle-school students to examine longitudinal associations between ASD and ADHD traits, social adjustment, and mental health outcomes from childhood through adolescence. By treating neurodevelopmental characteristics as continuous spectra and examining their effects in a nonclinical population, this study aims to inform early intervention strategies and preventive support practices beyond traditional diagnostic frameworks. whereas 40% had two or more comorbid conditions, with anxiety disorders and oppositional defiant disorder being particularly prevalent (Simonoff et al., 2008). Similarly, a large-scale epidemiological study in the United States examining children aged 6–17 years revealed that only 33.1% of children who had been diagnosed with ADHDpresentedwithoutcomorbidities or complications, with most exhibiting co-occurring conditions such as conduct disorder, anxiety disorders, and depression (Larson et al., 2011). Comparable patterns have been observed for subthreshold ASD and ADHD traits, which are associated with elevated risks of anxiety, depressive symptoms, and externalizing problems (Kim et al., 2009; Lewinsohn, Shankman, Gau, & Klein, 2004; Lundström et al., 2011; Moriwaki & Kamio, 2013; Noda et al., 2013; Rai et al., 2018). These findings highlight the importance of examining mental health among children who present with elevated traits but do not meet diagnostic thresholds. Processes linking ASD/ADHD traits and mental health Although elevated ASD and ADHD traits are associated with increased mental health difficulties, the pathways underlying these associations remain unclear. One possible explanation for this link is that neurodevelopmental traits and psychiatric symptoms share biological underpinnings. For example, family and twin studies suggest genetic overlap between ADHD tendencies and emotional problems (Chen et al., 2016; Cole et al., 2009). However, genetic explanations alone may not fully account for the heterogeneity and high co-occurrence of symptoms, and evidence for shared biological mechanisms remains inconclusive. Another possibility is that neurodevelopmental traits impede social adaptation, resulting in secondary mental health problems. For example, children with elevated ASD traits often experience challenges in peer interactions (Kasari, Locke, Gulsrud, & RotheramFuller, 2011; Whitehouse, Durkin, Jaquet, & Ziatas, 2009). Similarly, children with elevated ADHD traits are prone to academic underachievement and interpersonal difficulties owing to concentration problems and impulsivity (Herman, Lambert, Ialongo, & Ostrander, 2007; Humphreys et al., 2013; Powell et al., 2020). Such adaptive difficulties may lead to decreased self-esteem, social isolation, and chronic stress, potentially resulting in secondary emotional problems. Nonetheless, causal pathways cannot be presumed on the basis of these associations alone, and alternative explanations, including moderation by contextual factors, remain plausible. Social domains relevant to adjustment Considering the practical importance of identifying school-based targets for support, this study focuses on three domains of social adjustment that have been consistently linked with ASD/ADHD traits and mental health outcomes. Peer relationships Children with ASD tend to have fewer friendships and lower friendship quality and often occupy peripheral positions in classroom social networks (Kasari et al., 2011; Whitehouse et al., 2009). Furthermore, population-based studies indicate that elevated ASD traits are linked with difficulties in maintaining friendships and increased risks of bullying victimization (Hsiao, Tseng, Huang, & Gau, 2013; Nakajima et al., 2021; Tanaka et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2015). Similarly, children with ADHD face heightened risks of peer rejection and bullying. Impulsivity and aggression contribute to exclusion, interpersonal conflict, and social isolation, with a substantial proportion of children with ADHD experiencing victimization regularly (Bagwell, Molina, Pelham, & Hoza, 2001; Becker, Mehari, Langberg, & Evans, 2017). Relationships with teachers and parents Children with ADHD are often reprimanded for impulsivity and noncompliance, which can strain parent–teacher relationships. These patterns are linked to increased parenting stress and harsher disciplinary practices, which may impair emotional regulation and increase internalization and externalization problems (Matsuoka et al., 2011; Rogers & Tannock, 2018). Conversely, children with ASD often show reduced attention to social cues and fewer attachment behaviors, making connections with supportive adults more difficult (Grzadzinski, Luyster, Spencer, & Lord, 2014; Jones, Carr, & Klin, 2008). Other research has highlighted that adult and peer support act as protective factors against depression, bullying, and school refusal (Jackson & Warren, 2000; Murayama et al., 2016; Williams, Connolly, Pepler, & Craig, 2005). Academic problems Children with ADHD often struggle with core academic skills such as reading, writing, and mathematics (Barkley, Anastopoulos, Guevremont, & Fletcher, 1991), with higher trait severity linked with poorer performance (DuPaul & Stoner, 2003; Kawabata, Tseng, & Gau, 2012). Classroom studies show greater off-task behavior and shorter attention spans among children with ADHD compared to their peers (Kofler, Rapport, & Alderson, 2008; Rapport et al., 2009). Moreover, large-scale research has confirmed higher rates of absenteeism, dropout, and poor outcomes among children with ADHD (Fleming et al., 2017). These findings highlight the broad academic impact of ADHD traits. Meanwhile, children with ASD may face difficulties in comprehension, limited interest in tasks, or avoidance of new content due to anxiety (Uno, 2020). Although some studies have reported discrepancies between intellectual ability and actual achievement in individuals with ASD without intellectual disability (Estes et al., 2011), evidence on the link between ASD traits and academic problems remains limited. Study aim While many previous studies have examined the associations between neurodevelopmental disorders and psychosocial problems, few have explored the specific social domains that may help explain how ASD and ADHD traits are associated with mental health outcomes. In particular, few studies have simultaneously modeled ASD and ADHD traits while longitudinally examining multiple domains of social adjustment (peer relationships, academic performance, and relationships with teachers and parents). To address this gap, this study analyzes six-wave longitudinal data from children in grades 4–9 to examine whether ASD and ADHD traits show longitudinal associations with internalizing (depression and anxiety) and externalizing problems (anger and aggression), and how these associations relate to difficulties in peer, academic, and adult–child relationship domains. The study does not test causal mediation but instead investigates temporal associations among these constructs. Hypotheses Social difficulties have been widely discussed as potential pathways linking neurodevelopmental traits and mental health. Therefore, the following hypothesis was proposed: Hypothesis 1: ASD traits are longitudinally associated with internalizing problems (depression and anxiety), and these associations are related to difficulties in peer relationships. Academic challenges are particularly salient for ADHD. Children with elevated ADHD traits often experience persistent learning difficulties, which are associated with later emotional problems (Powell et al., 2020). Therefore, the following hypothesis was proposed: Hypothesis 2: ADHD traits are longitudinally associated with internalizing problems (depression and anxiety), and these associations are related to academic difficulties. ADHDtraits have also beenlinked withexternalizing problemsin the context of interpersonal and environmental interactions.Reviews suggest that difficulties in emotion regulation contribute to aggression and oppositional behavior (Kraft, Ebner, Leo, & Lindenberg, 2023). Moreover, stressful or conflictual relationships with adults may exacerbate behavioral problems (Mak et al., 2020). These findings highlight the importance of relational contexts. Thus, the following hypothesis was proposed: Hypothesis 3: ADHD traits are longitudinally associated with externalizing problems (anger and aggression), and these associations are related to difficulties in relationships with parents and teachers. Methods Participants and procedures This study was conducted as part of an ongoing longitudinal cohort project. It aimed to elucidate the mechanisms underlying development and adaptation in children and adolescents through a comprehensive population-based survey encompassing all public elementary and junior high schools in a medium-sized city in Chubu, Japan. The surveyed municipality is located within commuting distance of a major metropolitan area while maintaining robust industrial and agricultural sectors. Consequently, it encompasses households with diverse socioeconomic backgrounds, including families with members employed in urban centers and those engaged in locally based occupations. With a population of approximately 90,000, the municipality is nearly equivalent tothe nationalaverage for cities and wards (approximately 100,000), excluding government-designated cities and Tokyo’s 23 special wards. Data were analyzed from longitudinal surveys conducted from FY2012 to FY2023. Information was collected from all enrolled students, their parents, and their homeroom teachers. To ensure the validity of the longitudinal analysis, students who participated in only one wave or none were excluded. The final sample included 9,619 students from an initial 11,549 enrolled students (participation rate: 83.3%). Detailsofcohortcomposition andgradeprogressionare provided in Supplementary Table S1. The data in this study comprise both complete longitudinal data from participants who continued across multiple waves and incomplete longitudinal data from those who participated in only some waves. Given the nature of school-based surveys, not all students could participate in every wave because of absences, school transfers, family circumstances, and other factors, leading to incomplete longitudinal data. Comparisons of sex, student grade, and mean values of key variables showed no significant differences between the included and excluded students. All standardized mean differences were d < .20, suggesting that selection bias was limited. The average missing rate per wave was 11.6%, primarily due to absences and school transfers. This pattern is typical of school-based surveys, and the missingness was judged unlikely to violate the missing-atrandom (MAR) assumption. To address the mixed presence of complete and incomplete longitudinal data, missing values were handled using full information maximum likelihood (FIML), using all available information for estimation. Before data collection, informed consent was obtained from the students and parents via explanatory documents stating that participation was voluntary and that no disadvantages would result from nonparticipation. This study was reviewed and approved by our institution’s Ethics Committee. Survey content Developmental characteristics ASD and ADHD tendencies were measured using parent-report measures: the shortened Japanese versions of the Autism Spectrum Screening Questionnaire (ASSQ; Ito, Matsumoto, et al., 2014a; Ito, Tanaka, et al., 2014b) and the ADHD Rating Scale-IV (DuPaul, Power, Anastopoulos, & Reid, 1998; Ichikawa & Tanaka, 2008; Tanaka et al., 2015). The ASSQ primarily captures Asperger-like social and behavioral characteristics, which represent a narrower subset of the broader ASD phenotype described in DSM-5 and ICD-11. Both scales are suitable for assessing dimensional variation in neurodevelopmental traits within nonclinical school populations. Social maladjustment Social maladjustment was measured using the Social Maladjustment Scale for Elementary and Junior High School Students (Ito, Matsumoto, et al., 2014a; Ito, Tanaka, et al., 2014b), a self-report questionnaire that captures children’s subjective sense of maladjustment. The scale evaluates difficulties in three domains: academic problems (e.g. ‘Has difficulty keeping up with classwork’), problems with teachers (e.g. ‘Often conflicts with teachers’), and family problems (e.g. ‘Frequent arguments with parents’). Peer problems were assessed using the five-item ‘peer relationships’ subscale from the Japanese version of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ; Harada et al., 2014). The ratings obtained from students, teachers, and parents were z-standardized and then combined into a composite variable (α = .898). The multi-informant SDQ approach reduces rater bias and captures peer difficulties across home and school contexts. The SDQ Peer Problems subscale is internationally validated and complements aspects of social functioning not fully represented in the Social Maladjustment Scale. Mental health Depression was measured using the shortened Japanese Birleson Depression Self-Rating Scale for Children (DSRS-C; Murata, Shimizu, Mori, & Oshima, 1996; Namikawa et al., 2011). Aggression was assessed using the shortened Hostility-Aggression Questionnaire for Children (HAQ-C; Sakai et al., 2000). Teacher and parent SDQ ratings of emotional symptoms and conduct problems were integrated with DSRS-C and HAQ-C to form composite variables for internalizing (α = .861) and externalizing problems (α = .895). Statistical analysis We used structural equation modeling (SEM) to estimate crosslagged panel models across six waves. A conceptual diagram of the longitudinal associations examined in this study is presented in Supplementary Figure S1. Analyses were conducted using JASP (Version 0.18.3; JASP Team, 2024). Parameters were estimated with robust maximum likelihood (MLR), which provides standard errors and test statistics that are robust to non-normality. Missing data were handled using FIML, incorporating all available data under the MAR assumption. The cross-lagged panel model included autoregressive paths for each construct across adjacent waves; cross-lagged paths among ASD and ADHD traits; social maladjustment variables (peer, academic, teacher, and family problems); internalizing and externalizing problems; and within-wave correlations among all variables. All primary variables were z-standardized to facilitate comparison of standardized coefficients. Because the model was saturated (df = 0), fit indices were not informative and therefore were not reported. To reduce potential confounding, sex and school grade were included as time-invariant covariates in all models. Results Descriptive statistics and correlation coefficients Summary statistics, distributional characteristics, reliability coefficients, and correlations for all major variables are provided in Supplementary Tables S2–S4 and Supplementary Figure S2. Overall, the variables showed right-skewed distributions with most participants scoring in the lower range. Tables 1–3 present descriptive statistics and correlation coefficients for each fourth- and ninth-grade variable. ASD traits showed a slight decrease from fourth to ninth grade, whereas ADHD traits demonstrated a more pronounced decline. In contrast, academic problems and depressive symptoms increased across development. ASD and ADHD traits were moderately correlated at both time points, and ASD traits showed strong associations with peer problems. Peer problems were also strongly associated with internalizing symptoms. Cross-lagged effects Cross-lagged structural equation models were used to examine longitudinal associations among variables. Regression coefficients were interpreted using Orth et al.’s (2024) guidelines (~.03 = small, .07 = medium, .12 = large). All effects reported below reflect temporal associations rather than causal influence. The major cross-lagged effects are shown in Figure 1, and the full set of cross-lagged coefficients is summarized in Table 4. Internalizing problems ASD traits showed small-to-medium longitudinal associations with later internalizing problems (β = .068–.097). Associations were relatively stronger from fourth to fifth grade (β = .093) and seventh to eighth grade (β = .097). Peer problems also showed small-to-large associations with later internalizing problems (β = .046–.121), with the largest association observed from fifth to sixth grade (β = .121). Academic problems during elementary school showed small associations with later internalizing problems (β = .055–.090). Discussion This study examined longitudinal associations among ASD traits, ADHD traits, social adjustment, and mental health outcomes in a large cohort of Japanese children and adolescents. The findings highlight distinct patterns of association for ASD and ADHD traits across multiple social domains and underscore the importance of considering dynamic, bidirectional processes rather than unidirectional causal pathways. Association between ASD traits and internalizing problems The results showed that ASD traits were associated with peer relationship difficulties over time. Moreover, peer relationship difficulties were subsequently associated with increases in internalizing symptoms, supporting Hypothesis 1. However, these associations do not establish mediation or causal direction. This pattern aligns with prior research reporting that peer problems are related to emotional difficulties among youth with elevated ASD traits (Rai et al., 2018). These associations were particularly pronounced during the upper elementary years, a developmental period characterized by increasing importance of peer group belonging and social competence. Difficulties in social communication and peer interactions associated with ASDtraitsmayplacechildrenatheightenedriskforemotionaldistress, especially as peer relationships become more central to daily life. These findings emphasize the importance of school-based support systems that strengthen peer relationships, such as structured social skills programs and peer-mediated interventions, which may help reduce emotional distress during this sensitive developmental stage. Association between ADHD traits and internalization Although ADHD traits were significantly associated with internalizing problemsatseveralgradeintervals,themagnitudeoftheseassociations was generally small, suggesting limited direct links. Instead, ADHD traits were more consistently associated with academic difficulties, which themselves were associated with later internalizing symptoms. This pattern is consistent with prior work showing that inattention and impulsivity are linked with academic challenges (Barkley et al., 1991; DuPaul & Stoner, 2003; Kawabata et al., 2012). The results provide partial support for Hypothesis 2: academic difficulties may represent one pathway through which ADHD traits relate to internalizing symptoms. However, these associations were not consistent across all developmental periods and do not indicate formal mediation. These findings suggest that academic support – such as individualized instruction, organizational skills training, and self-efficacy enhancement – may help reduce emotional distress among children with elevated ADHD traits. Association between ADHD traits and externalizing problems ADHD traits showed strong and consistent longitudinal associations with externalizing problems, particularly during elementary school. This pattern is consistent with the core behavioral characteristics of ADHD, including impulsivity and difficulties with behavioral regulation, which are often linked with oppositional and aggressive behaviors. Difficulties in relationships with teachers and parents were also associated with externalizing problems, although these associations Figure 1. These findings highlight the importance of earlybehavioral interventions targetingself-regulation, combined with collaborative support between families and schools, to help reduce the escalation of behavioral difficulties. Bidirectional associations between social maladjustment and mental health A key contribution of this study is the identification of bidirectional associations between social adjustment and mental health. Peer difficulties and internalizing problems showed mutual associations, as did teacher–student and parent–child relationship problems with externalizing behaviors. These findings suggest that social difficulties and mental health symptoms may reinforce one another over time, forming dynamic cycles rather than simple one-way pathways. For example, peer isolation may be associated with increases in depressive symptoms, while emotional distress may, in turn, be associated with further withdrawal or victimization. Similarly, strained relationships with teachers or parents may be associated with increases in oppositional behavior, which may contribute to additional relational conflict. These patterns underscore the importance of school-based mental health services, including counseling and early identification systems, to interrupt these cycles and provide continuous support throughout adolescence. Interaction between developmental traits and social environment The findings also indicate that ASD and ADHD traits are not static characteristics; rather, their subsequent levels may be associated with ongoing interactions with social environments. Peer difficulties were associated with later increases in ASD traits, and externalizing problems were associated with later increases in ADHD traits, suggesting reciprocal associations between traits and social experiences. These results align with the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) framework, which conceptualizes functioning as an interaction between individual characteristics and environmental contexts. This perspective is also consistent with Bronfenbrenner’s (1979) ecological systems theory, in which peer relationships, teacher– student interactions, and academic contexts represent key microsystems that shape developmental outcomes. Understanding ASD and ADHD traits within these dynamic systems highlights the importance of interventions that address both individual needs and environmental supports, including classroom accommodations, teacher training, and family–school collaboration. Limitations Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, clinical diagnostic information, including ASD, ADHD, and internalizing/externalizing disorders, was unavailable, and the study relied on dimensional trait measures. Given the size of the sample, it is likely that some children with clinical diagnoses were included, which may have influenced the distribution or variability of the measured constructs. However, because the analyses focused on dimensional traits rather than diagnostic groups, the inclusion of clinically diagnosed cases does not undermine the validity of the dimensional approach. Second, although six waves of data were analyzed, the follow-up intervals varied and the design did not constitute a fully closed cohort, which limits causal interpretation despite the prospective ordering of variables. Third, the high correlations observed among some constructs, particularly between ASD traits and internalizing problems, may reflect item overlap, shared method variance, or rater biases. Future studies should incorporate multiple measurement approaches, including observational methods and performance-based assessments, to reduce shared-method dependencies. Fourth, the distribution of ASD traits deviated from normality, showing the positively skewed pattern typically observed in general-population samples. This non-normality may have influenced parameter estimates, including regression coefficients and variance estimation. Fifth, formal tests of longitudinal measurement invariance across waves could not be conducted because identical item-level data were not available across all waves. This raises the possibility that changes in psychometric properties may have affected longitudinal estimates. Sixth, some variables were assessed through selfreport, which may be influenced by subjective perceptions and response styles. In addition, the composite variables used in the analyses required integrating information across informants; although the construction procedures were described in detail, the weighting scheme may still introduce measurement heterogeneity. Seventh, although this study examined prospective associations, it did not formally test mediation or indirect effects. The social adaptation indicators included in the model were treated as correlates rather than mediators, and the study did not evaluate whether these variables moderated the associations between developmental traits and mental health outcomes. Thus, the possibility that social contexts may buffer or amplify these associations remains an important direction for future research. Eighth, assumptions related to missing data were based on the MAR framework, but MAR could not be empirically verified. Similarly, although standardized mean differences for attrition analyses were generally below 0.20, indicating limited selection bias, these thresholds should be interpreted cautiously. Finally, the sample was drawn from mainstream classrooms in a single region of Japan, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other cultural or educational contexts. Conclusions This study examined longitudinal associations among ASD traits, ADHD traits, social adjustment, and mental health outcomes using large-scale cohort data. The findings showed that social environmental maladjustment was not a simple mediating mechanism but was a part of a broader set of temporal associations linking developmental traits and mental health. In particular, bidirectional associations between social adjustment and mental health suggest that these processes unfold dynamically over time rather than through a single, unidirectional pathway. Furthermore, the results indicate that social contexts, such as peer relationships, academic environments, and interactions with teachers and parents, play a meaningful role in shaping developmental trajectories. These contexts were associated with both later mental health outcomes and subsequent levels of ASD and ADHD traits, underscoring the importance of understanding developmental characteristics within their environmental settings. Overall, these findings highlight the need for comprehensive, context-sensitive support strategies that address both individual characteristics and the social environments in which children develop. Interventions that strengthen peer relationships, enhance academic support, and improve family–school collaboration may help promote healthier developmental pathways. By emphasizing dynamic interactions between traits and environments, this study provides a conceptual foundation for developing integrated support systems that respond to both social and individual needs. metadata_title: Maternal ADHD Diagnoses Before and After Childbirth: A Danish Population-Based Cohort Study
pages: https://doi.org/10.1177/10870547251372730 Journal of Attention Disorders 2026, Vol. 30(3) 283–291 © The Author(s) 2025 Article reuse guidelines: sagepub.com/journals-permissions DOI: 10.1177/10870547251372730 journals.sagepub.com/home/jad Research Brief Introduction ADHD diagnoses have increased significantly among women of reproductive age in recent years, possibly driven by heightened awareness, recognition of the disorder’s persistence into adulthood, improved diagnostic practices, and evolving societal perceptions (Anderson et al., 2018; Kooij et al., 2019; Scoten et al., 2024; Zetterqvist et al., 2013). Many women with ADHD, however, experience delayed diagnosis (Skoglund et al., 2024), often due to difficulties with recognizing ADHD symptoms in girls and women, which are frequently masked by compensatory behaviors or misinterpreted as mood or anxiety disorders (Attoe & Climie, 2023; Madsen et al., 2018). The increased attention to females with ADHD and their common diagnostic delay emphasize the existing gap in understanding how life events unique to this population, such as childbirth and the perinatal period, affect symptomatology, help-seeking behaviors and the timing of ADHD diagnosis. Giving birth represents a profound physiological and psychological transition. Cognitive impairment and decreased executive functioning, key symptoms of ADHD, are more common during pregnancy than in non-pregnant states (Davies et al., 2018). Hormonal fluctuations during pregnancy and the postpartum period may contribute to neurobiological alterations that exacerbate ADHD symptoms, 1372730 JADXXX10.1177/10870547251372730Journal of Attention DisordersMadsen et al. research-article2025 Maternal ADHD Diagnoses Before and After Childbirth: A Danish Population-Based Cohort Study Kathrine Bang Madsen1,2 , Mette Winther3 , Amalie Thea Jensen1, Katrine Marcussen1 , Trine Munk-Olsen1,2 , Rikke Wesselhoeft1,4,5, and Sarah Kittel-Schneider6,7,8 Abstract Objective: The rates of women of reproductive age diagnosed with ADHD have increased significantly. However, little is known about how pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period influence ADHD related problems, helpseeking behaviors or the timing of ADHD diagnosis. This study aimed to investigate incident ADHD diagnoses among women from 5 years before to 5 years after childbirth. Method: The population-based cohort study utilized Danish nationwide registers to identify mothers of all childbirths between 2010 and 2018. ADHD diagnoses, defined as ICD-10 codes (F90 or F98.8) or redemption of ADHD medication prescriptions, were recorded during 1994 to 2023. Women who received an ADHD diagnosis prior to the five-year pre-birth period were excluded. We estimated calendar-year adjusted incidence of first-time maternal ADHD diagnoses using Poisson regression, and compared incidence across pre-pregnancy, pregnancy, postpartum up to 2 years, and 2 to 5 years postpartum, reporting adjusted incidence rate ratios (IRRs). Analyses included psychiatric comorbidities and non-ADHD psychotropic medication use prior to an ADHD diagnosis, for women diagnosed with ADHD postpartum. Results: The study included 363,904 mothers with a total of 524,936 childbirths. ADHD incidence rates decreased significantly during pregnancy (IRR = 0.28, 95% CI [0.22, 0.37]), remained lower than the pre-pregnancy period 2 years postpartum (IRR 0.82, 95% CI [0.74, 0.92]), and increased significantly above pre-pregnancy levels 2 to 5 years postpartum (IRR = 1.24, 95% CI [1.13, 1.35]). Among mothers diagnosed with ADHD postpartum, 53.9% had an in- or outpatient contact to psychiatric services or redeemed non-ADHD psychotropic medication prescriptions, in the period from childbirth until ADHD diagnosis. Conclusion: Incident ADHD diagnoses among women giving birth increased postpartum above pre-pregnancy levels, with peak rates observed between 2 and 5 years after childbirth. These findings highlight the postpartum period as a potential critical window of ADHD symptom worsening, underscoring the need for targeted mental health screenings and support for women during the years after childbirth. (J. of Att. Dis. 2026; 30(3) 283-291) Keywords ADHD, pregnancy, childbirth, postpartum psychiatric disorders, incidence

284 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(3) including changes in brain structure and function (Hoekzema et al., 2017; Rehbein et al., 2021). These changes, combined with the heightened demands of pregnancy and early parenthood, may amplify distractibility and cognitive fatigue, posing additional challenges for women with ADHD. Eddy et al. (2019) found that inattentive symptoms were significant predictors of professional life impairment, daily life impairment, and relationship impairment, while impulsivity uniquely predicted variability in professional life and relationship impairment in pregnant women with ADHD. The postpartum period may further exacerbate these challenges. New or worsened cognitive impairments, disruptions to previously effective daily strategies, and the demands of caring for a newborn may increase ADHD symptoms and functional impairments, possibly prompting help-seeking behaviors. Evidence suggests that parents with ADHD and their partners experience greater parenting distress in the first year of their child’s life than parents without ADHD (Joseph et al., 2022). Also, postpartum depression, a common condition for mothers with ADHD (Andersson et al., 2023), may also act as a trigger for ADHD diagnosis, as its overlapping symptoms, such as emotional dysregulation and executive dysfunction, may prompt clinical attention to previously unrecognized ADHD. This study investigates whether the transition into parenthood, including pregnancy, childbirth, potential postpartum psychiatric comorbidity, and the demands of caring for a young child, drives maternal help-seeking, as reflected by the timing of first-time ADHD diagnoses. We hypothesize that this transition will amplify previously unrecognized ADHD symptoms and thereby prompt women to seek evaluation and care. Consequently, we expect a rise in incident first-time maternal ADHD diagnoses during the postpartum years exceeding pre-pregnancy levels. Methods Study Design and Population This descriptive population-based cohort study utilized data from Danish nationwide registers. All childbirths occurring from 2010 to 2018 were identified through the Danish Medical Birth Registry (Bliddal et al., 2018). After excluding 8,991 childbirths due to missing or unlikely gestational ages (<154 or >315 days) and 3,326 childbirths by mothers with a preexisting record of ADHD diagnosis before the 5-year pre-birth period, the final cohort included 363,904 mothers to 524,936 liveborn children. Incidence of ADHD Before and After Childbirth First-time records of ADHD were considered each month, starting at 5 years before until 5 years after childbirth, with 1 month defined as 30.44 days. To ensure only incident diagnoses were included, we excluded women with an ADHD diagnosis recorded between 1994 and 2005 or before the 5-year pre-birth period leaving enough time to exclude women who had received a diagnosis in childhood or adolescence. The 5-year pre-childbirth window provides sufficient time to establish a stable baseline for ADHD incidence, while extending follow-up to 5 years postpartum accounts for the possibility of delayed diagnoses between initial symptom recognition and formal diagnostic recording. An incident diagnosis of ADHD was defined as an ICD-10 F90 or F98.8 diagnosis identified in the Danish National Patient Register (Lynge et al., 2011) or a first time use of ADHD medication using the following Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification codes for stimulant treatment: N06BA04 “Methylphenidate,” N06BA01 “Amphetamine,” N06BA02 “Dexamfetamine,” N06BA12 “Lisdexamfetamine,” and other treatment: N06BA07 “Modafinil,” and N06BA09 “Atomoxetine” in the Danish National Prescription Register (Kildemoes et al., 2011). In Denmark, citizens have the right to consult privately practicing specialists free of charge if waiting times at public hospital services exceed 1 month. However, private psychiatrists are not required to report diagnoses to national registries. Therefore, we used redeemed ADHD medication prescriptions as a proxy for ADHD diagnoses, since only psychiatrists are authorized to prescribe these medications following a comprehensive clinical assessment confirming ADHD. Recorded ADHD diagnoses in the Danish registers are deemed valid and reliable (Mohr-Jensen et al., 2016). Madsen et al. 285 with the ICD-10 diagnostic codes F10 to F19 “Mental and behavioral disorders due to psychoactive substance use,” F30 to F39 “Mood disorders,” and F40 to F48 “Neurotic, stress-related, and somatoform disorders” and non-ADHD psychotropic medication prescription fills; antidepressants (ATC N06A), anxiolytics (ATC N05B), and drugs used in alcohol dependence (ATC N07BB) in the period from childbirth until ADHD diagnosis. Statistical Analyses Women were followed from 5 years pre-childbirth until an ADHD diagnosis, 5 years after childbirth, or December 2023, whichever occurred first. The incidence was based on the first-ever ADHD diagnosis within the period from 5 years before through 5 years after birth; meaning that incident cases could not have had earlier records of ADHD treatment. To estimate the incidence of first-time maternal ADHD diagnosis across different time periods surrounding childbirth adjusting for calendar year of diagnosis, we fitted Poisson regression models with robust standard errors. The dependent variable was the count of ADHD diagnoses in each quarter from 5 years before to 5 years after childbirth. The offset term was the natural logarithm of person-years observed in each quarter, allowing us to model incidence rates with 95% CI. We defined four exposure periods relative to childbirth: pre-pregnancy (5 years to 9 months before childbirth), pregnancy (9 months before to childbirth), postpartum 0 to 2 years, and postpartum 2 to 5 years to compare incidence rates in these periods. The Poisson model included the period variable as a categorical predictor and adjusted for calendar year to account for secular trends in ADHD diagnosis. Adjusted incidence rate ratios (IRRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using the IRR option in Stata. Marginal incidence rates (per 1,000 personyears) for each period were estimated using the margins command. Also, we determined the proportion diagnosed with other psychiatric disorders or filling prescriptions for non-ADHD psychotropics among mothers who received an ADHD diagnosis in the 5-year postpartum period. We restricted this comorbidity analysis to the interval between childbirth and the mother’s first ADHD diagnosis postpartum, because this window provides a uniform, diagnosisanchored frame, whereas an equivalent pre-pregnancy interval would be arbitrary and capture temporally distant disorders that are not directly comparable to the time period between childbirth and initial ADHD diagnosis. Finally, we conducted a sensitivity analysis including a random sample of one childbirth per mother to take into account the possible counting of the same mother multiple times across different childbirths. Analyses were conducted using Stata (version 18 StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). Results Between 2010 and 2018, our study included 363,904 mothers who gave birth to 524,936 children. During the 10-year period surrounding childbirth (5 years before and 5 years after), 7,940 childbirths were associated with a maternal ADHD diagnosis, corresponding to 7,077 unique mothers. Of these, 2,974 mothers received their diagnosis within the 5 years before childbirth, and 4,103 within the 5 years after childbirth. Maternal mean age at first childbirth was significantly lower for Figure 1. 286 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(3) mothers who received an ADHD diagnosis in the period from 5 years pre-birth to 5 years postpartum (mean age 26.9 years [SD = 5.3]) compared to mothers who did not (mean age 29.3 years [SD = 4.8]; t-test, p < .001). Calendar year–adjusted incidence rates with 95% CI of first-time maternal ADHD diagnosis are presented quarterly across the study period in Figure 1 and for the first quarter each year in Table 1. The adjusted incidence rate 5 years before childbirth was 1.59 per 1,000 person-years (95% CI [1.35, 1.83]) and increased to 2.18 (95% CI [1.82, 2.57]) 5 years after childbirth, which can be interpreted as one new ADHD diagnosis for every 630 and 460 women, respectively. As presented in Table 2, compared with the pre-pregnancy period (defined as 5 years to 9 months before childbirth), the incidence was significantly lower during pregnancy (IRR = 0.28, 95% CI [0.22, 0.37]). In the first 2 years postpartum, the adjusted incidence was slightly but significantly lower compared to the pre-pregnancy period (IRR = 0.82, 95% CI [0.74, 0.92]). A significant increase was observed in the period from 2 to 5 years postpartum, peaking at 4 to 5 years postpartum, where the adjusted incidence was significantly higher than in the pre-pregnancy period (IRR = 1.24, 95% CI [1.13, 1.35]). Of the 4,597 childbirths where mothers received an ADHD diagnosis within 5 years postpartum, 2,476 (53.9%) involved mothers who were diagnosed with depression, anxiety, or substance use disorder or redeemed prescriptions for antidepressants, anxiolytics, or alcohol dependence medication before their initial ADHD diagnosis (Table 3). The same pattern was observed in the sensitivity analysis restricting to one random childbirth per mother (Figure 2, Tables 4–6). Discussion This study demonstrated that ADHD diagnosis incidence decreased during pregnancy but increased significantly in the postpartum period, reaching pre-pregnancy levels between 1 and 2 years postpartum and continuing to rise, peaking at about 4 years postpartum. Additionally, a majority of mothers were diagnosed with depression, anxiety, or substance use disorder or redeemed prescriptions for nonADHD psychotropics in the period from childbirth until receiving their ADHD diagnosis postpartum. The significant decline in ADHD incidence during pregnancy may reflect multiple factors, including symptom reduction or masking due to hormonal changes (Eng et al., 2024), lower likelihood of help-seeking during this period, or hesitancy among healthcare providers to diagnose ADHD or initiate treatment during pregnancy (Hinshaw et al., 2022). This may lead to unmet needs that resurface postpartum where ADHD incidence increased above pre-birth levels. Table 2. Madsen et al. 287 Also, the challenges associated with parenting, combined with the cumulative cognitive and emotional demands of the postpartum period, may highlight previously unrecognized ADHD symptoms. The caregiving task itself, usually including deprived sleep and emotional outbursts or demands of the infant or preschooler, might amplify ADHD core symptoms, and impairment may initially present as depression or anxiety, which, in our data, often preceded the ADHD diagnosis (Joseph et al., 2022). We observed a peak in ADHD incidence 4 to 5 years after childbirth, which could be due to the documented delay between women’s first recognition of ADHD-related difficulties and their action upon them (Agnew-Blais, 2024; Skoglund et al., 2024). Women with ADHD, and their relatives, may initially attribute inattentiveness, disorganization, and emotional lability to regular postpartum exhaustion or parenting stress. It is possible that formal evaluation is not requested until these problems have persisted for years. Strikingly more than half of mothers diagnosed with ADHD postpartum had other psychopathology (defined as in- or outpatient contacts for depression, anxiety, or substance use disorders, or redeemed prescriptions for nonADHD psychotropic medications) before receiving their ADHD diagnosis. 288 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(3) may cause physicians to overlook the diagnosis of ADHD (Young et al., 2020) contributing to diagnostic delays or even misdiagnosis (Quinn & Madhoo, 2014). Conversely, postpartum depression symptoms, such as concentration difficulties (inattention) and psychomotor agitation (hyperactivity/ impulsivity), may exaggerate ADHD symptoms, increasing the risk of temporarily pushing those with elevated but still normative levels of ADHD symptoms into the clinical range. We found a significantly lower maternal mean age at first childbirth for mothers with ADHD compared to mothers without in line with previous research (Amikam et al., 2024; Skoglund et al., 2019). A recent study found a fourtimes higher rate of unplanned pregnancies in young women with ADHD compared to non-ADHD controls (Owens & Hinshaw, 2020). Such unintended, and often early pregnancies, are consistently associated with adverse obstetric and perinatal outcomes (Skoglund et al., 2019) that are also linked to postpartum psychiatric disorders (Meltzer-Brody et al., 2017). Our findings emphasize the need for heightened clinical awareness of ADHD in women during the perinatal period. Although limited research has examined the consequences of delayed ADHD diagnosis in women, existing evidence highlights its profound and far-reaching effects. Late diagnosis is associated with diminished self-esteem, significant mental health challenges, disruptions in personal identity, and reduced life opportunities (Attoe & Climie, 2023; Skoglund et al., 2024; Young et al., 2020). These impacts often lead to increased psychosocial burdens and adverse outcomes, including strained relationships and impaired caregiving capacity (Morgan, 2024). To address this, perinatal care providers should be trained to recognize the overlapping symptoms of ADHD, depression, and anxiety, and always consider ADHD as differential diagnosis in women presenting with executive dysfunction or emotional dysregulation. Integrating mental health screenings into routine perinatal care could facilitate earlier identification and treatment, reducing the long-term burden of undiagnosed ADHD for both mother and child. Strengths and Limitations The use of a nationwide cohort with comprehensive data on ADHD diagnoses, medication prescriptions, and psychiatric comorbidities is a major strength of this study, allowing us to capture population-wide trends and minimize selection bias. Additionally, the longitudinal design enabled us to examine diagnostic patterns over a 10-year window, providing a nuanced understanding of ADHD incidence relative to childbirth. However, limitations should be acknowledged. First, ADHD diagnoses were based on clinical records and medication prescriptions, which may underestimate true incidence, particularly for women with mild symptoms, and the absence of data on subjective experiences or self-reported symptoms limits our ability to fully understand the psychosocial factors driving help-seeking behaviors. Second, we deliberately capped follow-up at 5 years postpartum to minimize referral bias from mothers who seek evaluation only after their child is assessed (Chatwin et al., 2025). This restriction, however, prevents us from determining whether the rising diagnostic trend after childbirth plateaus, continues, or declines into child school age. Third, we interpreted a first-time ADHD diagnosis in the registers as a proxy for maternal help-seeking; however, because registry data lack information on the motivations and pathways that lead women to initiate evaluation, this proxy cannot fully capture the complexity of help-seeking behavior. Future research should move beyond describing the postpartum rise in diagnoses to clarifying the mechanisms that drive it. One plausible pathway is that the heightened executive and emotional demands of early parenthood exacerbate previously unrecognized ADHD symptoms, prompting women to seek help and, ultimately, receive a diagnosis, but this hypothesis remains untested. Likewise, although the striking rates of postpartum depression and anxiety in newly diagnosed mothers raise the possibility that mood symptoms are, in part, downstream consequences of undetected ADHD, the temporal and causal links are still unknown. Conclusion This study highlights distinct patterns in ADHD diagnosis incidence among women before and after childbirth. While ADHD diagnoses decreased significantly during pregnancy, incidence rates returned to pre-pregnancy levels by 2 years postpartum and peaked at 4 to 5 years postpartum. A significant proportion of mothers diagnosed with ADHD postpartum had prior contacts to hospital care for depression, anxiety, or substance use disorders or redeemed non-ADHD psychotropic medications before receiving their ADHD diagnosis. This highlights both the overlap of psychiatric symptoms and the possibility that unrecognized ADHD may contribute to the development of these comorbidities, potentially delaying accurate ADHD diagnosis. These findings emphasize the postpartum period as a critical window for ADHD detection, highlighting the importance of integrating mental health screenings into routine perinatal care to facilitate timely diagnosis and intervention. Early identification of ADHD in mothers could improve outcomes not only for the women themselves but also for their children, reducing the intergenerational burden of untreated ADHD. Across the lifespan, ADHD is associated with a plethora of negative psychosocial and health outcomes, such as low quality of life, academic underachievement, unemployment, teenage pregnancies, relationship problems, sleep problems, addiction, and delinquency (Faraone et al., 2021). Historically, most research has focused on boys and men leading to several knowledge gaps regarding how biological sex differences, fluctuating sex hormones, and the use of hormonal contraceptives influence ADHD symptoms and comorbid conditions (Martin, 2024; Young et al., 2020). 1427555 JADXXX10.1177/10870547261427555Journal of Attention DisordersMcTaggart et al. research-article2026 1Danderyd Hospital, Stockholm, Sweden 2Karolinska Institutet, Stockholm, Sweden 3Smart Psykiatri AB, Stockholm, Sweden 4Uppsala University, Sweden 5Dalarna University, Falun, Sweden Corresponding Author: Julia McTaggart, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Danderyd Hospital, 182 88 Danderyd, Stockholm, Sweden. Email: julia.mctaggart@ki.se “Controlled by Female Hormones”: A Qualitative Interview Study of Swedish Women’s Experiences of Gender-Specific Aspects of Life With ADHD Julia McTaggart1,2 , Lisa B Thorell2 , Charlotte Borg Skoglund3,4, Niklas Envall2,5 , and Helena Kopp Kallner1,2 Abstract Objective: There is limited knowledge about how female specific factors such as fluctuating sex hormones influence symptom display and health-related conditions that are unique to, or more prevalent in females with ADHD. This study aims to investigate how women of reproductive age with ADHD experience their ADHD symptoms and well-being in relation to hormonal fluctuations, and secondly, how they perceive hormonal and reproductive counseling in healthcare. Method: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 14 women with ADHD and analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. Results: Three main themes emerged from the analysis; (1) Controlled by female hormones, (2) Frustration with lack of knowledge/understanding, and (3) Living with ADHD and comorbidities. Many women have experienced challenges and fluctuations related to hormonal changes during their menstrual cycles and in different stages of life. Using hormones to stabilize mood and impulsivity and adjusting stimulant doses were suggested as potential solutions. Participants expressed frustration about the lack of knowledge, interest, and understanding from healthcare professionals regarding ADHD and how hormones influenced symptoms of ADHD and comorbidities in women. Conclusion: This qualitative study highlights the impact of cyclical hormonal fluctuations on daily functioning across the menstrual cycle. Specifically, participants reported cyclic patterns of high energy and productivity related to ovulation followed by low energy and difficulty managing tasks in the premenstrual week. This aligns with clinical experience, anecdotal evidence, and limited literature that suggest that women with ADHD may be particularly vulnerable to hormonal fluctuations. Our findings suggest that especially the premenstrual phase is a challenging time for women with ADHD. Our results emphasize the need for healthcare professionals to improve their understanding of the role sex hormones and the menstrual cycle play in female ADHD. The potential effect of adjusting ADHD medication dosage and introducing hormonal treatment for premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) in women with ADHD should be further explored. (J. of Att. 796 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(6) Previous research demonstrated that females are diagnosed with ADHD approximately 4 years later than males (Skoglund et al., 2024). As a result, boys often receive earlier intervention during critical developmental periods. Females tend to present with more severe impairment at diagnosis, report higher healthcare utilization, and are more frequently prescribed pharmacotherapy for comorbid conditions (Skoglund et al., 2024). The limited understanding of female ADHD, especially the role of sex-specific factors, may contribute to delayed diagnosis and increased psychiatric and somatic comorbidity and healthcare utilization in girls and women with ADHD. Emerging evidence indicates that many psychiatric symptoms in women may be exacerbated during specific phases of the menstrual cycle, particularly the premenstrual phase and the first days of menstruation (Handy et al., 2022). Disorders, often comorbid with ADHD, such as eating disorders, have also been associated with hormonal fluctuations across the menstrual cycle (Edler et al., 2007; Klump et al., 2013). The menstrual cycle starts with the onset of menstruation. This is the beginning of the follicular phase, which lasts until the first day of ovulation and is characterized by gradually increasing estrogen levels. The luteal phase begins at ovulation and lasts until the first day of menstruation. It is typically around 14 days long and characterized by rapidly increasing progesterone and moderately increasing estrogen levels (Diczfalusy & Landren, 1977; Reed & Carr, 2000). The term premenstrual phase, used in this paper, is not a physiologically distinct phase but a descriptive term for the last part of the luteal phase (i.e., the last few days before menstruation). This is the phase when premenstrual symptoms (PMS) most commonly occur. Of all women of reproductive age, approximately half experience PMS (A et al., 2014), with 3% to 8% meeting the criteria for premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) (Halbreich et al., 2003; Hantsoo & Epperson, 2015). PMDD is characterized by emotional symptoms such as affective lability, irritability, or anxiety during the luteal phase when progesterone and progesterone metabolites are present. These symptoms are often accompanied by cognitive difficulties such as poor concentration or feeling overwhelmed. Behavioral and somatic changes may also be present, including fatigue, overeating, sleep disturbances, and decreased interest in activities (Reilly et al., 2024). Small studies have shown that more than 40% of women with ADHD exhibit symptoms indicative of PMDD (Dorani et al., 2021). ADHD has historically been presented as a disorder of externalizing behavior. However, growing awareness of female-specific challenges, has started to shift attention toward the overlap with comorbid conditions and internalization of symptoms, which are more common among females (Young et al., 2020). Females with ADHD and comorbid emotional dysregulation exhibit higher rates of suicidal ideation and attempts, as well as disordered eating and bulimia nervosa (BN) compared to those without ADHD or PMDD (Nobles et al., 2016; Prasad et al., 2021). Mood and emotional dysregulation, although not part of the formal ADHD diagnostic criteria, are widely recognized as central and impairing features in females with ADHD, affecting their everyday life (Bodalski et al., 2023). Thus, PMDD symptoms of executive dysfunction and emotional dysregulation resemble and overlap with characteristics of ADHD. This study aims to explore the lived experiences of women of reproductive age with ADHD, focusing on gender-specific challenges. Specifically, we aim to investigate how women with ADHD: (a) experience their symptoms and well-being in relation to hormonal fluctuations during the menstrual cycle and contraceptive use, and (b) perceive hormonal and reproductive counseling within the healthcare system. Methods A qualitative design and analysis method was chosen as it allows for in-depth exploration of the personal experiences of women with ADHD (Braun & Clarke, 2014), enabling a more nuanced understanding of the impact of hormonal fluctuations on daily functioning. Qualitative interviews are an important addition to epidemiological studies and randomized control trials, giving women the possibility to express their feelings and experiences in their own words. The findings are reported following the Standards for Reporting Qualitative Research (SRQR) guidelines (O’Brien et al., 2014). The study was conducted in accordance with “Good research practice” guidelines and the principles of the Helsinki declaration. The study was approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (No: 2023-00645-01). Informed written consent was collected from all participants prior to participating in the study. Selection and Description of Participants Based on the study’s objective, a sample size of 10 to 20 participants was considered sufficient to ensure information power (Malterud et al., 2016). To recruit women diagnosed with ADHD, a purposive sampling strategy was employed. Information about the study was shared through the researchers’ social media channels, inviting women to participate. Additionally, advertisements were placed in both inpatient and outpatient healthcare settings, including psychiatric, maternal health, youth, and sexual health clinics across four healthcare regions in Sweden (Uppsala, Stockholm, Gävleborg, and Västra Götaland). Purposive sampling, which involves selecting participants who are rich in information, enables a thorough examination of their experiences (Patton, 2014). The inclusion criteria were: (1) identifying as a woman, (2) having a formal diagnosis of ADHD, and (3) being a biological woman aged 15 years and above of reproductive age.

McTaggart et al. 797 Women who expressed interest in participating were invited consecutively. No formal exclusion criteria were applied, other than being able to participate in Swedish, in order to capture a broad range of experiences. After having performed 14 interviews, which were all found to be rich in data (Braun & Clarke, 2021), no more interviews were performed guided by the “informationpower” concept. Data Collection and Measurements A semi-structured interview guide based on Creswell and Creswell (2017) was developed through an iterative process within the research group. The guide consisted of openended questions designed to encourage the women to share and elaborate on their current and previous experiences. After a few background questions, the interview focused on the following three main questions: (1) Have you experienced any problems related to menstruation, the menstrual cycle, or hormonal contraceptives? (2) Have you experienced any variations in daily life functioning (e.g., emotions, cognition, social relations, routines, exercise, sleep, food, and addictive behaviors) during the menstrual cycle? (3) What are your thoughts about the knowledge of professionals within the healthcare system regarding female ADHD (e.g., menstruation, the menstrual cycle, and hormones)? Probing questions were also used to get the women to elaborate on the main themes (e.g., are there any other ways in which you feel variations in your functioning across the menstrual cycle?) Two pilot interviews were conducted, after which minor adjustments were made to the interview guide, including question order and probing question formulation. The pilot interviews were found to be rich in data and were therefore included in the data analysis. The study was conducted from November 2023 to February 2024. All interviews were performed by authors Julia McTaggart (JM) and Niklas Envall (NE), one-onone, online via Zoom using end-to-end encryption to ensure confidentiality. The interviews lasted for an average of 64 min, ranging from 30 to 137 min (median: 50.5 min). Transcribed interviews were stored electronically in a password protected research drive at the investigating university. Analysis Data were retrieved from the interview transcripts and analyzed using inductive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2006). Each transcript was read by three members of the research team to identify patterns and recurring elements in the open-ended responses. These patterns were then categorized into themes and synthesized into key themes related to the research questions of this study The qualitative analysis consisted of six phases of thematic data analysis as described by Braun and Clarke (2006): (1) Familiarization with the data, (2) Generating initial codes, (3) Searching for themes, (4) Reviewing the themes, (5) Defining and naming the themes, and (6) Producing the report. Researcher Characteristics and Reflexivity Charlotte Borg Skoglund (CBS), Helena Kopp Kallner (HKK), and Lisa Thorell (LT) designed the study and its protocol. CBS and HKK are experienced senior consultants in psychiatry and gynecology respectively, CBS is associate professor (MD, PhD), and HKK is MD and professor in gynecology. They have extensive experience with the patient group and the healthcare system. LT is professor of psychology. NE created the interview guide with input from CBS and JM. NE is a registered nurse midwife, PhD, and senior lecturer with experience from a sexual health clinic. JM is a doctoral student, MD, and a resident in gynecology and obstetrics with experience in clinical work and contraceptive counseling. NE and JM conducted the interviews, and the data analysis was performed by JM, CS, NE, and HKK. The research group includes a member with an ADHD diagnosis, as well as members with lived experience through close relatives with the condition. In addition, we had an ongoing co-creation process with women with ADHD prior to designing our studies. However, patient representatives were not involved in coding or interpreting the data in the present study. As researchers with backgrounds in gynecology, midwifery, and psychiatry/psychology, including expertise in ADHD and sexual and reproductive health, we were mindful of our own potential biases throughout the study. To minimize the risk of unintentionally influencing the interview process, interviews were conducted by members of the research team with the least specialized knowledge of ADHD. JM and NE kept a journal to document their thoughts and assumptions during data collection and analysis, ensuring their interpretations were based on the participants’ perspectives. The research team reviewed the transcriptions individually and discussed them multiple times to ensure the data’s authenticity. JM and NE also considered how cultural, social, and institutional factors influenced the interactions and data collected. By being reflective, we aimed to maintain transparency and rigor in the research. This approach not only improved the study’s trustworthiness but also provided a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics involved. Results A total of 14 interviews with women diagnosed with ADHD were included in the study. The women were aged 22 to 47 years and had been diagnosed with ADHD at ages 15 to 46 years. See Table 1.

798 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(6) Eight participants were in a stable relationship, defined as either married or in a long-term partnership. Twelve participants reported one or more additional psychiatric diagnoses besides ADHD, with anxiety being the most common comorbid condition (n = 8; 57%), followed by depression (n = 6; 43%) and eating disorders (n = 4; 29%). Nine participants had tried two or more different contraceptive methods, three participants had tried one, and one participant had never tried any contraceptives. Ten participants were currently using ADHD medication. The qualitative analysis yielded three key themes: 1. Controlled by female hormones 2. Frustration with lack of knowledge/understanding 3. Living with ADHD and comorbidities. Key themes and subthemes are displayed in Figure 1. Illustrative and supportive quotes from the interviews are presented under their related themes below. Theme 1: Controlled by Female Hormones To be controlled by female hormones was a recurring feeling expressed by the participants, who shared a desire to better understand how hormonal fluctuations throughout their menstrual cycles, and in response to contraceptive methods, affect them. This theme includes subthemes related to the participants perceptions of how female hormones influence their emotions, overall wellbeing, and relationships. Need to See Hormonal Patterns. The respondents described feelings of confusion and frustration about not knowing whether their emotions are linked to their menstrual cycle, a consequence of their ADHD symptoms, or part of who they are. Others shared that, over the years, they had gained a deeper understanding of how their cyclical hormones may impact their mood, body image, ADHD symptoms, relationships, daily functioning, feeling of self-worth, and overall quality of life. P11: To feel down and sad and stuff, and so difficult when you don’t know if it’s part of the cycle or just as it is. P6: I can feel fat before I get my period and after my period, I feel thin, so it’s a big difference in how I see myself in the different phases of the menstrual cycle. P9: In this chaos as a teenager. If I just had understood more then. There was so much that happened then, that I couldn’t navigate through. It’s been 15 years and it’s first now that I’m starting to understand what is happening in my body and how it affects my ADHD symptoms. P5: It has also been very difficult with friends. When I have my menstruation perhaps I become too “all over the place” and a bit too impulsive, so I have had difficulties establishing good relationships. And that has affected me socially. And now that I am older I feel that when I have my menstruation or the week before I become a little . . . like I have no energy to meet people and prefer to be close to those who know me or are close to me. For some participants, it is the use of period-tracking apps that have helped them notice patterns in their physical and mental well-being related to their menstrual cycle. These encounters often led to a frustrated and defensive attitude and a growing distrust of healthcare resources.
