Potential mechanisms Several biological mechanisms have been proposed to explain the association between C-section and altered neurodevelopmental outcomes. Among the most studied are dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, impaired oxytocin signaling, and disruptions to the early establishment of gut microbiota. Vaginal delivery induces mechanical and hormonal stimuli that activate specific brain regions, such as the piriform cortex and caudate nucleus, promoting early-life stress responses and the functional maturation of the HPA axis (Kenkel et al., 2019). In contrast, cesarean-born neonates exhibit significantly lower levels of glucocorticoids at birth, which may hinder the development of stress-adaptive systems. Animal studies have demonstrated that inadequate glucocorticoid signaling can inhibit neurogenesis and synaptogenesis, particularly in the hippocampus, a critical region for learning and memory (Kenkel et al., 2019). Cesarean-delivered mice also show lower corticosterone levels at birth and later display cognitive deficits during adolescence (Huang et al., 2019). In human neonates, cortisol levels are highest following vaginal delivery, intermediate in emergency C-sections, and lowest in elective C-sections (Miller et al., 2005), suggesting a gradient of early stress exposure with potential implications for neurodevelopment. In parallel, the oxytocin system—crucial for regulating social behavior, emotional bonding, and stress reactivity—is also influenced by delivery mode. Neonates born via vaginal delivery have been shown to exhibit higher circulating oxytocin levels compared to those delivered by C-section (Kuwabara et al., 1987; Kenkel et al., 2019; Green et al., 2021). Experimental studies further reveal that early oxytocin administration in cesarean-born mice not only improves social and anxiety-like behaviors but also enhances immune function (Morais et al., 2021; Morais et al., 2020), indicating a modulatory role of oxytocin in postnatal brain development. Another plausible pathway involves the gut-brain axis. C-section significantly alters the initial colonization of the infant gut microbiota by interrupting vertical transmission of maternal microbial strains, thereby affecting the composition and function of the neonatal gut microbiome (Sherwin et al., 2019). These changes have been associated with long-term effects on cognition, emotional regulation, and social interaction (Neumann & Slattery, 2016; Wei et al., 2009; Codagnone et al., 2019; Dinan & Cryan, 2017; Yang et al., 2016). Moreover, psychological stress experienced during early development can further modify gut microbial communities, reinforcing the bidirectional relationship between gut health and brain function (Morais et al., 2021; Morais et al., 2020; Wampach et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2020a; Xu et al., 2020b). Intriguingly, oxytocin treatment in animal models not only modulated behavior but also partially restored gut microbial diversity in cesarean-born mice (Dangoor et al., 2021). Collectively, these findings suggest a complex interplay between hormonal, neuroendocrine, and microbial systems in shaping neurodevelopmental trajectories following C-section. However, the precise causal pathways remain to be fully elucidated and warrant further investigation in longitudinal and mechanistic studies. Wei et al. (2026), PeerJ, DOI 10.7717/peerj.20603 13/22

Implications for neurodevelopmental disorders Our findings align with previous research suggesting that C-section may confer increased risk for a broader spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders. Prior meta-analyses have reported a 10–30% elevated risk of conditions such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and ADHD among cesarean-born individuals (Curran et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2024). However, earlier studies often grouped neurodevelopmental outcomes together, lacking disorder-specific granularity. A 2020 meta-analysis focusing solely on ADHD concluded that the observed associations might have been overstated, in part due to limited population diversity and methodological inconsistencies (Xu et al., 2020a; Xu et al., 2020b). In addition to ADHD, recent large-scale cohort studies have elucidated further links between C-section and early neurodevelopmental impairments. A study based on the Japan Environment and Children’s Study (JECS) reported that C-section was associated with an increased risk of neurodevelopmental disorders at age three, including motor delays, intellectual disabilities, and ASD. Interestingly, the strength of these associations varied by sex, underscoring the potential for sex-specific vulnerability to cesarean-associated neurodevelopmental disruption (Yoshida et al., 2023). Similarly, a prospective cohort study conducted in a Shanghai Jiao Tong University-affiliated hospital found a significant association between C-section and sensory integration dysfunction in preschool children— a neurodevelopmental condition affecting motor coordination, attention, and sensory processing (Zhao et al., 2021). These findings collectively suggest that C-section may influence multiple domains of early brain development, though the exact biological mechanisms remain to be fully elucidated. Taken together, the evidence suggests that reducing unnecessary elective cesarean deliveries may contribute to lowering the population burden of ADHD and potentially other neurodevelopmental disorders. Strengths and limitations This study has several strengths, including a comprehensive literature search across multiple databases, inclusion of both case-control and cohort designs, and representation of diverse populations across Western and Asian countries. Subgroup analyses by delivery type further enriched the interpretation. Nevertheless, certain limitations must be acknowledged. First, as an observational metaanalysis, residual confounding cannot be fully excluded. Second, substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies, stemming from variability in sample sizes, ethnic backgrounds, diagnostic criteria, and covariate adjustment strategies. Third, the number of eligible studies remains limited, potentially affecting the robustness and generalizability of the findings. Additionally, outcomes were not stratified according to specific medical indications for cesarean delivery, but rather based solely on whether the procedure was elective or emergency; such a distinction may hinder the ability to isolate independent effects. Finally, differences in outcome assessment and follow-up periods may introduce bias and limit cross-study comparability. Wei et al. (2026), PeerJ, DOI 10.7717/peerj.20603 14/22

CONCLUSIONS This meta-analysis provides evidence that C-section is associated with an increased risk of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children. The observed associations were consistent across both elective and emergency C-section. Although the underlying mechanisms may differ, the comparable effect sizes suggest that both types of C-section warrant attention in public health and clinical decision-making. From a preventive perspective, reducing the rate of non-medically indicated elective C-sections and optimizing the clinical criteria for emergency surgical interventions may contribute to lowering the population burden of ADHD. Further prospective and mechanistic studies are needed to clarify causal pathways and inform early intervention strategies. metadata_title: Maternal Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder and Perinatal Depression: A Systematic Review
pages: https://doi.org/10.1177/10870547251383430 Journal of Attention Disorders 2026, Vol. 30(3) 300–314 © The Author(s) 2025 Article reuse guidelines: sagepub.com/journals-permissions DOI: 10.1177/10870547251383430 journals.sagepub.com/home/jad Article Introduction Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder with an estimated prevalence of 5.9% to 7.1% in youth populations (Willcutt, 2012) and 2.5% of adults (Simon et al., 2009). Core symptoms include inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Once considered a childhood condition, there is now increasing recognition that symptoms persist into adulthood with significant costs at both an individual and societal level. Adults with ADHD have been shown to under-achieve in terms of education and employment compared to their intellectual abilities (Kaiser et al., 2008). They also report more impairment in interpersonal relationships relative to adults without ADHD (Safren et al., 2010). The economic burden of ADHD is estimated to be between $US356 million to 20.27 billion for national estimates (Chhibber et al., 2021). Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is commonly comorbid with other mental disorders, including depression, anxiety and substance use disorders (Choi et al., 2022). Depression, in particular, has a strong association with ADHD both in childhood and as an adult (Chang et al., 2016; Meinzer et al., 2013, 2014). It has been estimated that 44% of individuals with ADHD experience a depressive episode before age 30 compared to 25% of 1383430 JADXXX10.1177/10870547251383430Journal of Attention DisordersPierotti and Jayakody research-article2025 1Bendigo Health, Bendigo, VIC, Australia 2Faculty of Medicine Nursing and Health Sciences, School of Rural Health, Monash University, Burwood, VIC, Australia 3Institute for Mental and Physical Health and Clinical Translation (IMPACT), School of Medicine, Deakin University, VIC, Australia Corresponding Author: Natalie Pierotti, Bendigo Health, Level 2, 100, Barnard Street, VIC 3551, Australia. Email: npierotti@bendigohealth.org.au Maternal Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder and Perinatal Depression: A Systematic Review Natalie Pierotti1 and Kaushadh Jayakody1,2,3 Abstract Background: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is well-established as a disorder that persists into adulthood and is commonly comorbid with other mental health conditions. Despite increasing numbers of women entering reproductive years with this diagnosis, there is limited research on it in the perinatal period. Objective: To critically appraise the available literature and examine the association between maternal ADHD and depression in the perinatal period. Methods: A systematic review was conducted by searching EMBASE, PsycINFO, MEDLINE and Google Scholar up to August 2024. The available literature was evaluated in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines (PRISMA). The quality assessment was performed using the Joanna Briggs Institute framework, and a narrative synthesis was completed. Results: Ten studies were identified as meeting the inclusion criteria. The majority were of medium quality, with issues identified in sample size, study design and validity of the self-report scale used. Our review found a prevalence of 16.76% to 57.6% of perinatal depression in women with ADHD. An increased risk of developing perinatal depression was also identified in women with ADHD (OR 1.8–2.63) compared to those without the disorder. Finally, our review also found a positive association between ADHD symptoms and depressive symptoms in perinatal women. Conclusion: Our findings suggest a much greater vulnerability to perinatal depression among women with ADHD, and an association between ADHD symptoms and depressive symptoms in the perinatal period. There is, however, a clear need for more high-quality studies to replicate and further explore these findings. (J. of Att. Dis. 2026; 30(3) 300-314) Keywords ADHD, depression, perinatal, antenatal, postnatal

Pierotti and Jayakody 301 individuals without ADHD (Meinzer et al., 2013). Importantly, women with ADHD tend to have more prolonged episodes of depression and are at greater risk of suicide (Biederman et al., 2008). Twin studies suggest that the association between ADHD and depression co-occurrence is explained principally by shared genetic factors (Faraone & Larsson, 2019). However, it has also been proposed that ADHD causes depression through exposure to increased psychosocial stressors such as discordant relationships and poor academic attainment, which in turn increases the risk of depression (Riglin et al., 2021). Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder has historically been under-recognised in women due to a different symptom profile, with less so-called disruptive behaviours. Masking and internalisation of symptoms may delay receiving a diagnosis and appropriate treatment (Fraticelli et al., 2022). This, in turn, leads to lower levels of self-esteem and self-efficacy (Rucklidge & Kaplan, 1997). Despite increasing numbers of women entering reproductive years with a diagnosis of ADHD, there is a paucity of research on the subject, particularly in the perinatal period, with most studies to date focused on the impact of medication in pregnancy and breastfeeding (Anderson et al., 2020; Bang Madsen et al., 2023; Källén et al., 2013; Li et al., 2020; Nörby et al., 2017). The perinatal period, encompassing both the antenatal and postnatal periods, is defined in Australian clinical practice by the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists as being from conception to 12 months postpartum (RANZCP, 2021). Other definitions vary (WHO, 1977); however, all agree it is a uniquely vulnerable time for the mother, infant, and the wider family. It is a time of increased stress, both physiological and psychosocially, and is likely to represent a high-risk time for women with ADHD, as with other chronic mental health conditions (Wesseloo et al., 2016). ADHD is known to be associated with an increased risk of unplanned pregnancy (Owens & Hinshaw, 2020) and pregnancy at an earlier age (Lehti et al., 2012), as well as obstetric complications such as preterm birth, preeclampsia and hyperemesis (Walsh et al., 2022). Perinatal depression, encompassing both antenatal and postpartum phases, is well recognised. The prevalence of antenatal depression is estimated to be between 7% and 20% in high-income countries, and for postpartum depression between 7% and 30% across low, middle and high-income countries (Biaggi et al., 2016). Depression in the perinatal period is associated with significantly increased morbidity and mortality, including adverse birth outcomes such as preterm birth, low birth weight and stillbirth (Simonovich et al., 2021). Perinatal depression is also associated with disrupted attachment and adversely impacts the infant’s emotional, social, motor, cognitive and behavioural development (Slomian et al., 2019). Significantly, suicide remains one of the most frequent causes of death in women in the postnatal period (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2023). Recent research has highlighted the role of hormones in ADHD (Dorani et al., 2021; Eng et al., 2024; Martel et al., 2009). It appears that rather than being perinatal in origin, females may have multiple critical developmental periods corresponding with reproductive life events. Symptom severity may also fluctuate across the menstrual cycle, corresponding to changes in oestrogen (Eng et al., 2024). It has been hypothesised that reproductive hormones also play a role in the pathophysiology of perinatal depression through the regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and the production of neurotransmitters (Meltzer-Brody, 2011). It is, therefore, possible that the hormonal changes that occur in the postpartum period may play a causal role in the development of both perinatal depression and ADHD. To the best of our knowledge, there are no systematic reviews examining the association between ADHD and depression in the perinatal period. Kittel-Schneider et al.’s (2021) systematic review examined the association between ADHD and adverse pregnancy and birth outcomes but did not address depression. Antoniou et al.’s (2022) literature review examines the association between maternal ADHD and parental distress more widely. Despite growing recognition of adult ADHD, its interplay with perinatal depression remains an underexplored area. Our review intends to address this deficit. Our aim is to examine the association between maternal ADHD and depression in the perinatal period. Our objectives were to identify: 1. The rates or prevalence of perinatal depression in women with ADHD 2. If women with ADHD are at risk for developing perinatal depression 3. If there is a relationship/correlation between ADHD symptoms and depressive symptoms Methodology Search Strategy and Selection Criteria To achieve these objectives, a systematic review was conducted after applying inclusion and exclusion criteria. Available literature was reviewed per the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses criteria (PRISMA) (Page et al., 2021) across four databases: EMBASE, PsycINFO, MEDLINE and Google Scholar. EMBASE, PsycINFO and MEDLINE were searched from inception to August 2024, using a search strategy. For a detailed search strategy, see Supplementary Material S1. Google Scholar was searched using a modified search string ‘Maternal ADHD and perinatal depression’ and the first 20 pages of results were included. Studies were limited to peer-reviewed published articles written in English. Results were supplemented by searches of reference lists, citations and author searches.

302 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(3) Inclusion Criteria •• Any study based on original empirical data published in a peer-reviewed journal, in the English language, all years, with full-text availability. •• Where the timeframe of the study was within the perinatal period, defined as from conception to the end of the first year of life in keeping with Australian clinical standards (RANZCP, 2021). •• Where the study assessed maternal ADHD (including attention deficit disorder). This included studies in which participants were identified as having ADHD symptoms via a self-report scale, who were diagnosed with ADHD following a formal assessment, or who had a relevant Diagnostic Statistical Manual (DSM) or International Classification of Diseases (ICD) code assigned to them in their records. •• Where the study assessed depressive symptoms. This included studies in which participants were diagnosed with clinical depression, such as major depressive disorder or dysthymia, following DSM or Structured Clinical Interview for DSM Disorders (SCID) assessments, or who had a relevant DSM or ICD code assigned to them in their records. Studies that assessed depressive symptoms using self-report tools were also included. Exclusion Criteria •• Qualitative studies, case reports, and systematic reviews •• Studies looking at the relationship between ADHD and depression outside of the perinatal period •• Studies examining the relationship between ADHD and other diagnoses during perinatal period Outcome Measures The outcome measures used were prevalence or prevalence ratio (PR) of perinatal depression in women with ADHD. The main measures used for the risk of developing perinatal depression were odds ratio (OR) and or relative ratio (RR), depending on the availability of data. Measures of association between ADHD and depressive symptoms were assessed using correlation coefficient and regression models. Data Extraction and Qualitative Assessment Search results were imported into Covidence software (Veritas Health Innovation, n.d.). All screening stages were completed on this platform. The lead author performed title and abstract screening to exclude studies that did not meet the inclusion criteria, engaging in discussions with the other author to address any uncertainties. For studies that did, the full article was sourced and assessed for relevance. The second author conducted a cross-check by independently reviewing 50% of the quality-screened papers to ensure they met criteria. Data was extracted from the articles and combined into tables where appropriate. Quality appraisal of the included papers was conducted using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tool (Moola et al., 2017) for the relevant study type. For further details, see Supplementary Material S2. Papers were assigned a rating of good, medium or poor quality based on a consensus decision between the two authors. The outcome was reflective of the information included in the critical appraisal tool. Given the limited number of papers found and the considerable variability in study design, statistical methods, quality and reporting, a full meta-analysis was not possible. Therefore, the results are presented as a systematic narrative review. Results Search Results An initial search of the electronic databases returned 2,634 references. A total of 844 were excluded as duplicates by the Covidence software. 49 were assessed for eligibility at full text, and ten studies were included in the final review (see Figure 1). Included in the final review (see Tables 1–3) are three cohort studies: one prospective (Baker et al., 2022), two retrospective (Andersson et al., 2023; Walsh et al., 2022) and seven cross-sectional studies (Dorani et al., 2021; Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al., 2018; Jones, Eddy, Rabinovitch, et al., 2018; Ninowski et al., 2007; Semple et al., 2011; Watkins & Mash, 2009). Of these 10 included studies, five (Baker et al., 2022; Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al., 2018; Jones, Eddy, Rabinovitch, et al., 2018; Ninowski et al., 2007; Walsh et al., 2022) examined the antenatal period, and four (Andersson et al., 2023; Dorani et al., 2021; Semple et al., 2011; Watkins & Mash, 2009) examined the postpartum period. One study (Walsh et al., 2022) appears to have examined both; however, the timeframes are ambiguous. Most of the studies came from the USA or Canada, with two (Andersson et al., 2023; Dorani et al., 2021) from Europe and one (Murray et al., 2022) looking at eight low and middle-income countries. Two studies (Andersson et al., 2023; Dorani et al., 2021) reported the prevalence of depression in those with ADHD, two studies (Baker et al., 2022; Walsh et al., 2022) looked at the risk of developing depressive symptoms in women with ADHD and six studies (Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al.,

Pierotti and Jayakody 303 2018; Jones, Eddy, Rabinovitch, et al., 2018; Murray et al., 2022; Ninowski et al., 2007; Semple et al., 2011; Watkins & Mash, 2009) looked at the association between ADHD and depressive symptoms. Methodological Quality of Reviewed Studies Half of the included studies were rated medium based on JBI checklist criteria (see Supplementary Material S2), with only one study (Andersson et al., 2023) obtaining a good rating. Two studies (Baker et al., 2022; Semple et al., 2011) were downgraded to poor as a result of having very low numbers included. Significantly, nine studies (Baker et al., 2022; Dorani et al., 2021; Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al., 2018; Jones, Eddy, Rabinovitch, et al., 2018; Murray et al., 2022; Ninowski et al., 2007; Semple et al., 2011; Walsh et al., 2022; Watkins & Mash, 2009) did not adequately control for confounding variables. Six studies (Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al., 2018; Jones, Eddy, Rabinovitch, et al., 2018; Murray et al., 2022; Ninowski et al., 2007; Semple et al., 2011; Watkins & Mash, 2009) were scored lower based on the validity or reliability of the self-report scale used; for example, the use of unvalidated scales, scales with limited data to support its use, or with low sensitivity in the perinatal population. Measurements Used in ADHD Two retrospective cohort studies (Andersson et al., 2023; Walsh et al., 2022) used the inclusion of an ICD code specific to ADHD to define ADHD diagnosis. Two studies (Baker et al., 2022; Dorani et al., 2021) completed structured clinical interviews for DSM5 diagnostic criteria for ADHD. Murray et al. (2022) used a non-validated self-report scale consisting of a 5-item questionnaire measuring current ADHD symptoms. This was reported as an attempt to create a more sensitive tool to pick up ADHD in women but was found to have low internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha 0.59). Semple et al. (2011) used the ADHD Quick Screen to inform recruitment but relied on the ADHD Behaviour Checklist for Adults (ABCA) in analysis. This scale measures childhood and current symptoms. The remaining four studies (Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al., 2018; Jones, Eddy, Rabinovitch, et al., 2018; Ninowski et al., 2007; Watkins & Mash, 2009) used the Conner’s Adult ADHD Rating Scale – Self Report, Short form (CAARS). This scale measures current symptoms via selfreport and informant report. Measurements Used for Depression/Depressive Symptoms The two retrospective cohort studies (Andersson et al., 2023; Walsh et al., 2022) used an ICD code as evidence of a diagnosis of clinical depression. All other included studies used self-report scales rather than clinical interviews. Two studies (Baker et al., 2022; Dorani et al., 2021) used the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPNDS). This is the most widely used screening tool for postnatal depression (Park & Kim, 2023). Three studies (Ninowski et al., 2007; Semple et al., 2011; Watkins & Mash, 2009) used the Brief Symptom Inventory (BSI-18). It includes three subscales: depression, anxiety and somatisation, as well as a Global Severity Index score (Hamidia et al., 2022). The depression subscales were used for the purpose of our review. Murray et al. (2022) used the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). The PHQ-9 is the most widely used depression measure globally. Its nine questions correspond to the DSM criteria for depression (Wang et al., 2021). Finally, two studies (Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al., 2018; Jones, Eddy, Rabinovitch, et al., 2018) used the Patient Health Questionnaire -2 (PHQ-2). The PHQ-2 is an abbreviated version of the PHQ-9, containing only two questions that assess the frequency of depressed mood and anhedonia. (Gigantesco et al., 2021). Primary Outcomes Prevalence of Perinatal Depression in Women with ADHD. Two studies (Andersson et al., 2023; Dorani et al., 2021) examined the prevalence of perinatal depression in women with ADHD. The combined sample size was 773,132. Both studies reported on the postnatal period. Andersson et al. (2023) completed a retrospective cohort study (N = 773,047) using Swedish registry data. The study reported a prevalence of depression of 16.76% in women with ADHD compared to 3.29% in women without ADHD. This equated to a prevalence ratio (PR) of 5.09. This can be compared to existing estimates of the prevalence of postnatal depression, of 7% -30% in the general population with variation in results noted depending on the country and measure used (Biaggi et al., 2016). The result, however, is subject to possible surveillance bias as women with ADHD are more likely to be seen in psychiatric clinics and, therefore, have a diagnosis of depression made. Interestingly, the study had overall statistically low levels of ADHD compared to the general population (approximately 0.5%), which may represent the fact that ADHD is underdiagnosed in adult females. A study by Polyzoi et al. (2018) reported the estimated prevalence of ADHD in adulthood in Sweden of 0.58% in 2006, increasing to 3.55% in 2011, with a corresponding increase in the proportion of females with the diagnosis from 37.5% to 44.8%. Dorani et al. (2021) examined the prevalence of hormone-related mood disorders in women with ADHD. Results from this study (N = 85) showed a prevalence of 57.6% of women with ADHD meeting the criteria for postpartum depression after the birth of their first child. This is substantially higher than the general population estimates of between 7% and 30% across low, middle and highincome countries (Biaggi et al., 2016). The overall study followed 209 women with ADHD, however, only 85 were mothers and were therefore included in their analysis. This may have led to selection bias, as the study was also assessing other hormone-related mood disorders. Depression was also assessed retrospectively, making the results likely susceptible to recall bias. Risk of Developing Depression. Two studies (Baker et al., 2022; Walsh et al., 2022) with a combined sample size of 85,860 investigated the risk of developing perinatal depression in women with ADHD. Baker et al. (2022) stratified the risk of developing depression in the antenatal period based on patterns of ADHD medication use. This was a prospective cohort study (N = 28) where the cohorts were defined based on patterns of medication use: discontinuers, maintainers, and a group who changed their regime with the aim of reducing use. The

Pierotti and Jayakody 307 study showed significant differences between those who discontinued medication versus those changing medication (p < .0001) and discontinuers versus maintainers (p = .0009). This suggests that women who discontinued psychostimulant treatment during pregnancy had a clinically significant increase in EPNDS scores. Although not explicitly stated, the overall average EPNDS score was low across all three groups, and participants would not have met the threshold for suspected depression. This may be why the Montgomery– Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) results were not statistically significant. This was also a low-powered study (N = 28) and included high levels of education and full-time work within the study population, which may not be representative of the wider population of women with ADHD. Lower socioeconomic status and low levels of education are independent risk factors for developing perinatal depression (Yang et al., 2022). Walsh et al. (2022) examined the risk of developing obstetric complications in women with ADHD. This study was a retrospective cohort study utilising the TriNetX database, which sources information from insurance claims and electronic hospital records. They looked at two cohorts of 42,919 women with and without ADHD matched based on age, race and ethnicity. The study found that 2.1% of women with an ADHD diagnosis also had a postpartum depression diagnosis versus 1.2% in those without ADHD (p = .001 OR 1.8). Furthermore, 15.7% of women with an ADHD diagnosis also had a depression diagnosis, versus 6.6% in those without ADHD (p = .001 OR 2.63). This could be compared to a study by Kiewa et al. (2022) which reported the most significant individual comorbidity among women with perinatal depression was ADHD (p = .009 OR 2.3). The study also completed sub-analyses based on the type of medication prescribed. Compared to the cohort without any medications, women on stimulant medications had statistically lower rates of depression OR 0.733 (CI [0.66, 0.813], p = .001) and postpartum depression OR 0.727 (CI [0.605, 0.874], p = .001). This is consistent with previous studies that show that being prescribed ADHD medication was associated with a reduced risk for subsequent and concurrent depression (Chang et al., 2016). Concerns have been raised about the safety of ADHD medications in pregnancy, however, recent systematic reviews have shown that the overall risk is low (Bang Madsen et al., 2023; Li et al., 2020), and opinions are starting to reflect this (Scoten et al., 2024). Women on non-stimulant medications did not have statistically significant results for either depression or postpartum depression. The study concedes that this may be because several of the medications, including bupropion and atomoxetine, are also used to treat depression. Walsh et al. (2022) have reported postpartum depression separately from depression, presumably to allow cases of antenatal depression to be included; however, as it did not clarify if a woman could obtain both diagnoses, the results are unable to be combined. It also seems probable that, given the significantly higher rates of depression, at least some cases of depression occurring postnatally have been coded as depression. Association Between ADHD and Depressive Symptoms. Six studies (Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al., 2018; Jones, Eddy, Rabinovitch, et al., 2018; Murray et al., 2022; Ninowski et al., 2007; Semple et al., 2011; Watkins & Mash, 2009) investigated the association between ADHD symptoms and depressive symptoms assessed via self-report screening measures. They had a combined sample size of 1,743. Two studies (Semple et al., 2011; Watkins & Mash, 2009) were postnatal, four studies (Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al., 2018; Jones, Eddy, Rabinovitch, et al., 2018; Murray et al., 2022; Ninowski et al., 2007) were antenatal, and all reported on cross-sectional data. Murray et al. (2022) reported on an exploratory multicentre study encompassing eight low and middle-income countries (N = 1,204). Results from all sites were pooled, so there is no site-specific data. They found that ADHD symptoms are associated with higher levels of depressive symptoms on the PHQ-9 (p < .001) during pregnancy, even after correcting for multiple comparisons. Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al. (2018) included 116 black pregnant women as part of a larger study of prenatal behaviours, maternal psychopathology, and quality of life (QoL). ADHD and depression risk were strongly positively correlated (p < .001). In addition, increased depression risk corresponded to decreased QoL; however, they were unable to draw conclusions as to the nature of this relationship. Three studies (Jones, Eddy, Rabinovitch, et al., 2018; Ninowski et al., 2007; Watkins & Mash, 2009) reported a positive correlation between depression and all the CAARS subscales. Ninowski et al. (2007) also performed a partial correctional analysis and found that depression remained significantly positively correlated with the CAARS ADHD Index (p < .05) when controlling for the other subscales on the BSI-18. The positive association found is consistent with existing research supporting an association between ADHD and depression both in children and adults (Biederman et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2016; Meinzer et al., 2014; Riglin et al., 2021). The only negative study was Semple et al. (2011) which found maternal ADHD symptoms were positively correlated with the BSI-18 anxiety subscale (p < .05) but not with scores on the depression subscales (N = 40). However, Semple et al. (2011) included only a small sample size of 40 women with low overall levels of ADHD; only five mothers scored above the clinical cut-off. Two of the studies (Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al., 2018; Murray et al., 2022) included depression as a primary outcome, while the remaining four studies (Jones, Eddy,

308 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(3) Rabinovitch, et al., 2018; Ninowski et al., 2007; Semple et al., 2011; Watkins & Mash, 2009) included it as a confounding factor to be controlled for while exploring other aspects of parenting, such as maternal-child attachment. While this still provides valuable evidence, it should be interpreted with caution, as relevant confounding factors for depression were not included. Discussion Summary of Findings Our systematic review was undertaken to explore the links between maternal ADHD and perinatal depression. Ten studies were found and included in our review. Two studies looked at the prevalence of perinatal depression in women with ADHD, two studies examined whether women with ADHD are at risk of developing perinatal depression, and six studies looked at the association between ADHD and depressive symptoms in the perinatal period. We found an increased prevalence (16.7%–57.6%) of perinatal depression in women with ADHD compared to the general population (Biaggi et al., 2016). An increased risk of developing perinatal depression was also identified in women with ADHD (OR 1.8–2.63) compared to those without. Our review also found a positive association between ADHD symptoms and depressive symptoms in perinatal women. Discussion In examining the relationship between ADHD and perinatal depression the studies included in this review are not able to make any causative statements. They do however suggest some potential contributing factors. Baker et al. (2022) suggested that women with ADHD who discontinued psychostimulant treatment during pregnancy had significant impairments in family functioning. Specifically, that they are more likely to experience conflict within the family, have a harder time having fun as a family, rate parenting as more difficult, and describe being more isolated from their family. Murray et al. (2022) also found that ADHD symptoms in the third trimester of pregnancy were associated with lower social support from family, friends and significant others. Ninowski et al. (2007) found that ADHD symptoms were significantly negatively correlated with prenatal expectations about what the baby will be like, enjoyment of motherhood, life as a mother, and abilities as a mother. ADHD symptoms significantly predicted negative reports of maternal self-efficacy. Watkins and Mash (2009) also found that ADHD symptoms significantly predicted parenting satisfaction after controlling for co-occurring symptoms of psychological distress. Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al. (2018) found moderate to large negative correlations between maternal ADHD symptoms, depression risk and quality of life; defined as life outlook, productivity and relationships. Women high on ADHD symptoms were also less likely to report that they wanted to get pregnant at the time they became pregnant. ADHD symptoms were also negatively related to feelings of happiness when participants found out they were pregnant according to Ninowski et al. (2007). Murray et al. (2022) also found an increased likelihood of an unwanted pregnancy. ADHD symptoms were significantly negatively correlated with attendance at recommended prenatal checkups according to Ninowski et al. (2007) while Jones, Eddy, Rabinovitch, et al. (2018) showed that ADHD was positively associated with many of the prenatal health behaviours including poor eating and increased physical strain. Finally, Walsh et al. (2022) demonstrated higher rates of negative pregnancy outcomes in women with ADHD such as hyperemesis, eclampsia, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, gestational diabetes and early pregnancy haemorrhage. This constellation of decreased support, lower levels of self-efficacy and parenting satisfaction, higher levels of stress and negative birth outcomes will likely contribute to an increased risk for depression in women with ADHD. The broader evidence base supports also this hypothesis, that depression arises in women with ADHD as a result of being exposed to higher levels of psychosocial stressors (Riglin et al., 2021). Outside of the perinatal period women with ADHD have already been demonstrated to experience lower levels of educational achievement (Fredriksen et al., 2014), and higher levels of discordant relationships (Barkley et al., 2007; Faraone & Biederman, 1997) which will predispose them to developing depression. Additional risk factors within the perinatal period includes the fact that women with ADHD are more likely to have an unplanned or unwanted pregnancy (Owens & Hinshaw, 2020), and pregnancy at a younger age (Lehti et al., 2012), likely due to higher levels of disorganisation and impulsive behaviours. Finally, it is important to recognise that the perinatal period is a time of increased stress, and women with ADHD may find the adjustment more challenging due to the increased requirements to be organised and manage time efficiently. These executive functioning difficulties, when combined with difficulties in emotional regulation, selfesteem and sensory processing will create challenges when becoming a parent. The current literature also suggests a biological basis for the relationship between ADHD and depression. This is supported by the results of Andersson et al. (2023) which found higher levels of teen pregnancies/younger age of mother, decreased cohabitation levels, lower levels of education and higher levels of co-morbid psychiatric

Pierotti and Jayakody 309 conditions in keeping with previous results. However, even after adjusting for these factors, estimates showed an independent association between ADHD, depression, and anxiety disorders postpartum. Early family studies suggest that the co-occurrence of ADHD and depression is influenced by shared familial factors (Cole et al., 2009). More recent twin studies suggest that ADHD and depression co-occurrence is primarily explained by shared genetic factors (Cole et al., 2009; Faraone & Larsson, 2019). While a Genome-Wide Association Study of ADHD reported significant genetic correlation with various psychiatric disorders, the strongest of which was with depression (Demontis et al., 2019). Riglin et al. (2021) used two different designs, a longitudinal population cohort design and Mendelian randomisation to investigate a possible causal relationship between ADHD and depression. Their findings suggest that ADHD does increase the risk of depression later in life and are consistent with a causal effect of ADHD genetic liability on subsequent major depression. In addition to this genetic association, several recent papers have examined the possible contributions of sex hormones in the development, and symptom expression of both ADHD (Dorani et al., 2021; Eng et al., 2024; Martel et al., 2009) and depression in women (Meltzer-Brody, 2011). Current theories suggest that hormones such as oestrogen and progesterone have both organisational and activational effects on neurotransmitters including dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline. Dopamine is recognised as a key neurotransmitter implicated in ADHD pathology (Martel et al., 2009). As well as modulating neurotransmitters, sex hormones play a prominent role in regulation of stress and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis including at the hypothalamic corticotropin releasing hormone gene and multiple interactions between the estrogen and glucocorticoid receptors. As such they are also implicated in the development of post-partum depression. During third trimester of pregnancy, levels of oestrogen and progesterone rise dramatically, accompanied by activation of the HPA axis and increased levels of cortisol. After parturition the levels rapidly drop and the HPA axis must quickly compensate (Patterson et al., 2024). Eng et al. (2024) proposes a similar theory of activation effects of cyclical circulating ovarian hormones on ADHD with increasing risk at times of rapid declines in oestrogen. While the evidence remains limited at this time, a recent systematic review concluded that a relationship between sex hormones and ADHD symptoms in females is likely, specifically in puberty and across the menstrual cycle (Osianlis et al., 2025). Quality and Sources of Bias There was substantial variability in the quality of the included studies; although the majority were of medium quality, several areas were consistently identified as potential sources of bias, including study design, sample size, lack of control for confounding factors and use of selfreport scales. Seven studies (Dorani et al., 2021; Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al., 2018; Jones, Eddy, Rabinovitch, et al., 2018; Murray et al., 2022; Ninowski et al., 2007; Semple et al., 2011; Watkins & Mash, 2009) included in our review were cross-sectional studies, many of which either included multiple outcomes or did not look at depression as a primary outcome. All, with the exception of Baker et al. (2022), used a single point of assessment and were therefore unable to investigate changes in symptoms across the perinatal period. This will significantly limit the ability to draw conclusions about the direction of causality in the relationship or to determine periods of higher risk. Longitudinal studies would be required to elicit this information. Importantly, Andersson et al. (2023) was the only study to attempt to control for relevant confounding factors. While many of the studies reported on comorbid psychiatric conditions, they did not include it in the analysis. This limits the validity of the results, given that many of these factors are independent risk factors for the development of perinatal depression (Yang et al., 2022). Five out of six of the association studies had low or subthreshold levels of ADHD symptoms within their study populations based on self-report. This will limit the ability to detect a true effect. The exception was Jones, Eddy, Bourchtein, et al. (2018), in which 19.9% of the study population reported clinically significant symptoms of ADHD. It was, however, unclear how they obtained this. A variety of measures were used to identify symptoms, and the lack of consistency across studies posed a challenge for comparing findings. Specific concerns should also be considered with the use of self-report scales. While most of the scales used have demonstrated acceptable sensitivity and specificity, screening tools are not meant to be utilised in isolation but are designed to be an adjunct to the gold standard structured clinical interview (Levis et al., 2019; Mulraney et al., 2022). Even for those studies utilising structured clinical interviews, no additional information was provided on how these were undertaken. All the self-report scales utilise a Likert scale, which asks patients to assess how ‘often’ they manifest a symptom (Taylor et al., 2011). This is challenging to standardise as it is by nature subjective. Individuals with ADHD may have difficulty not only with accurately recalling their childhood symptoms, which would be subject to recall bias, but also with reporting their current symptoms. This may be due to limited self-awareness of behaviours that have been present since childhood, particularly externally manifested symptoms (Taylor et al., 2011). There is also an observed discrepancy between self and informer reports of symptoms, in particular inattentive symptoms (Zucker et al., 2002), which

310 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(3) affects reliability. Finally, Dunlop et al. (2018) noted that ADHD screening tools might have lower sensitivity and specificity in patients with major depressive disorder. In depressed patients, a negative screen strongly suggests the absence of ADHD, but a positive screen ‘requires careful evaluation to determine whether self-reported ADHD symptoms simply emerge from depression or whether comorbid ADHD is present’ (Dunlop et al., 2018). Given these issues, good quality ADHD scales should have both informant and self-rated versions for assessment of both adult and childhood symptoms (Barkley et al., 2002). Only one study, Ninowski et al. (2007), used partner reports of symptoms in addition to a self-report scale, and none of the studies provided data on childhood symptoms or age at which the diagnosis was made. In terms of depression, the BSI-18 has very limited evidence for its use in the perinatal population. The PHQ-2 has also been shown to have low sensitivity in the perinatal population at the cut-off >3 (Gigantesco et al., 2021). This may be due to the fact that it is unable to account for those with mild depression, particularly in a low-prevalence population. Consideration should also be given to the cut-off scores used to determine depression. In studies utilising the EPNDS, the cut-off point for depression was set as 10/30, which indicates ‘possible depression’. Gibson et al. (2009) suggested that a cut-off of 12 or 13 was likely to be more sensitive for a diagnosis of depression. They also suggested a higher cut-off for the antenatal population. This highlights the challenge of measuring symptoms in a diverse population across the perinatal period. Strengths and Limitations To the author’s knowledge, this is the first systematic review to explore the association between maternal ADHD and the development of perinatal depression and, as such, fills an important gap in the clinical literature. Our study has included both antenatal and postnatal populations; however, a limitation identified was the low number of studies able to be included. It is possible that additional papers may have been identified through grey literature searching or by directly contacting authors. Our review has, therefore, been unable to make any distinction between the various time periods or identify periods of particularly high risk. Our review was also unable to combine results in a metaanalysis due to low numbers and lack of standardisation in population, diagnosis and measurements. Despite these issues, our review highlights the association between ADHD and depression, which has previously been wellestablished in a non-perinatal population. Additional limitations include the fact that research has been mainly conducted in high-income countries, in community samples with no data provided from mother-baby units or similar inpatient units. Clinical Implications Our review has important implications for mental health clinicians and psychiatrists as well as midwives, obstetricians, maternal child health nurses, and GPs, all of whom are involved in the care of women during their childbearing journey. Depression is already routinely screened for in clinical practice. The Centre of Perinatal Excellence (COPE, 2023) recommends that the EPNDS is completed at least once antenatally and once postnatally, generally at 6 weeks postpartum. In the future, women with ADHD would benefit from early and more frequent screening for depression during the perinatal period to pick up on symptoms of concern. Additional psychoeducation and support for the woman and her family would also be beneficial to optimise their mental health in the perinatal period. ‘This includes education about the signs and symptoms of deteriorating mental health and strategies for supporting mental wellness’ (Scoten et al., 2024). For women scoring positive for depression, a brief screen for ADHD could be incorporated into clinical practice. If scoring positive on this, referral to a perinatal or adult mental health service for further evaluation would be indicated to allow for appropriate assessment and management. To facilitate these outcomes, education for health professionals on ADHD and its presentation in women, the links with depression, and appropriate pathways and treatments in the perinatal period would be indicated. Future Directions Our review has demonstrated that for women with ADHD, perinatal depression is an important consideration. Despite the limitations in terms of quantity and quality of data, our review should be used to inform future research on the topic. Further large studies using gold standard measurements such as a self-rating scale (encompassing self and informer ratings) followed by a clinical interview and controlling for relevant confounding factors are required. This would allow for a future meta-analysis on the topic. Longitudinal studies with assessments at various time points across the antenatal and postnatal period would also be beneficial to investigate trends and high-risk times. Conclusion Our systematic review found an increased prevalence (16.7%–57.6%) of perinatal depression in women with ADHD compared to the general population (Biaggi et al., 2016). An increased risk of developing perinatal depression was also identified in women with ADHD (OR 1.8–2.63) compared to those without. Our review also found a positive

Pierotti and Jayakody 311 association between ADHD symptoms and depressive symptoms in perinatal women. There is, however, a clear need for more high-quality studies to replicate and further explore these findings. With the growing recognition of adult ADHD, this review has important implications for clinical practice, as well as policy and service development for this vulnerable population. Our review highlights the importance of regular screening for depression in women with ADHD, as well as ensuring they have appropriate support to navigate the perinatal period successfully. Observational Study 1 Medicine ® Quality assessment of ADHD-related short videos on Chinese social media A cross-sectional study Pinfang Zou, MMeda , Si Chen, MDa, Junlu Xiang, MMeda, Wenzhi Zhou, MBa, Xiaorong Yang, MMeda,* Abstract Short videos on health information related to Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) on mainstream platforms in China are increasing; however, the quality of relevant content has not been systematically evaluated. A search was conducted on Douyin, Bilibili, and Xiaohongshu from August 18 to 22, 2025, using the keywords ‘Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder ‘, ‘ Hyperactivity Disorder ‘, and ‘ADHD’. The top 100 videos under each keyword were collected. Two researchers independently evaluated them using GQS, mDISCERN, PEMAT-A, PEMAT-U and JAMA benchmark criteria. A total of 228 eligible videos were analyzed. Most of the videos focused on disease-related knowledge (n = 124, 54.4%) and were published by medical professionals (n = 89, 39.0%). Senior professionals had the highest content quality score (GQS median: 3). The median of mDISCERN: 2)The scores of Bilibili videos on GQS, mDISCERN and PEMAT-U were significantly higher than those of Douyin and Xiaohongshu (all P < .05). However, the overall information reliability (mDISCERN median: 1) and operability (PEMAT-A median: 25%) were low. It is worth noting that there was no significant positive correlation between user engagement indicators (likes, comments, sharing) and any quality score (all | r |<0.2), indicating weak associations with limited practical importance, while video duration was significantly but weakly positively correlated with PEMAT-A score (R = 0.187, P < .001, suggesting limited practical value). In short, although ADHDrelated videos are widely prevalent on mainstream short video platforms in China, their popularity cannot fully reflect scientific validity. Overall video quality and reliability remain to be enhanced. In the future, relevant parties may consider optimizing platform algorithms, standardizing content publishers” obligations and enhancing public media literacy, to facilitate sound development of ADHD-related public health communication. Keywords: attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), health information, quality assessment, short videos, social media, user engagement 1. Introduction Attention-Deficit/ Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neuro developmental disorder that commonly occurs in childhood and is characterized by persistent inattention, impulsivity and hyperactivity.[1,2] Even in adulthood, these symptoms may con tinue to be observed, which brings many problems to patients in learning, work, life and so on.[3] At the same time, the patient ‘s family will also suffer great mental and economic pressure.[4] Therefore, it is critical to improve the prognosis of patients by accurately identifying the early symptoms of the disease and taking correct interventions. With the rapid development of digital new media, shortvideo platforms have gained tremendous popularity and become the main way for the public to obtain health infor mation. Benefiting from massive active user groups and pre cise algorithmic dissemination mechanisms, an increasing number of users and medical practitioners share diseaserelated experience and popular science knowledge on Douyin, Bilibili, Xiaohongshu and other mainstream domestic shortvideo platforms.[5,6] Nevertheless, a large number of unregu lated self-published contents exist on these platforms, and misleading medical information will bring hidden risks to The authors have no funding and conflicts of interest to declare. Accordingly, research results obtained from foreign plat forms cannot be directly applied to domestic situations. Most existing studies evaluate ADHD-related content using single or limited assessment tools, each of which only reflects a single dimension of content quality.[13–15] Comprehensive evaluation of ADHD information therefore requires the combined use of mul tiple instruments. At present, there is still a lack of systematic empirical research evaluating the information quality of ADHDrelated content on mainstream domestic short-video platforms. In summary, the quality of ADHD-related short-videos on mainstream Chinese short video platforms needs to be system atically evaluated. The primary objectives of this study is to con duct a cross-sectional quality analysis of ADHD short videos across 3 major platforms: Douyin, Bilibili, and Xiaohongshu and to analyze the correlation of engagement metrics and video quality. A set of well-established assessment tools was employed to comprehensively evaluate the content characteristics and sci entific rigor of the videos. These included the Global Quality Scale (GQS), the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) benchmark criteria, the modified DISCERN instrument (mDISCERN), and the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Actionability (PEMAT-A) and Understandability (PEMAT-U). The videos will be assessed across multiple dimen sions, such as overall quality, source credibility, reliability, understandability, and actionability. The findings of this study not only provide evidence-based reference for clinicians and families of ADHD patients, but also have reference value for public health advocates and platform regulators to optimize information governance and help promote the construction of high-quality ADHD health information ecology. 2. Methods 2.1. Ethics approval This study analyzed only publicly available short video con tent posted on open social media platforms (Douyin, Bilibili, and Xiaohongshu). No personal identifying information, user private data, or protected health information was accessed, col lected, or processed in the course of this research. All content included in the analysis is freely accessible to the general public, and no human subjects were enrolled or interacted with. Given the nature of the data source and the absence of personal pri vacy concerns, ethical approval for this study was not required in accordance with relevant ethical review guidelines. 2.2. Data source and search strategy The search was conducted on Douyin, Bilibili, and Xiaohongshu from August 18, 2025 to August 22, 2025. To minimize bias from personalized algorithms, we created brand-new accounts, cleared all browsing history and cache, and performed all searches on the same device under fixed network and geographic conditions to standardize settings and reduce IP‐related varia tion. Three Chinese keywords were used: “注意缺陷多动障碍, ” “多动症, ” and “ADHD.” Previous studies have shown that most users only browse the top-ranked search results.[20] Therefore, we selected the top 100 videos per keyword per platform to reflect typical user exposure and represent the content most fre quently accessed by the public.[21] This approach may introduce sampling bias because the sample is limited to high-ranking vid eos rather than a fully random selection. Although we used new accounts and standardized search conditions, residual algorith mic bias may still exist due to inherent platform recommenda tion mechanisms. 2.3. Video screening and data extraction Videos were included only if they met all of the following criteria: (1) Content contained information related to ADHD; (2) Its language was Chinese; (3) Its duration did not exceed 5 minutes (consistent with the standard definition of a short video); (4) The video was publicly available and open access; (5) The video could be viewed in its entirety during the data collection period. Exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Non-Chinese videos; (2) Duplicate videos (identified by unique video ID or identi cal content); (3) Purely commercial ads; (4) Videos lacking an audio track; (5) Videos exceeding 5 minutes in duration; (6) Videos with content irrelevant to ADHD. For each eligible video, the following metadata were extracted: video URL, unique video ID, title, uploader’s user name, duration (measured in seconds), upload date, and engage ment metrics, including the number of likes, collections, shares, comments, and the uploader’s follower count. The video publisher types were divided into 2 main groups: medical sources group (including junior-, intermediate-, and senior-level medical professionals) and nonmedical sources group (including parents, patients themselves, individual science communicators, and nonprofit organizations, etc). The video content is independently coded by 2 trained researchers into the following 5 categories.: disease-related knowledge, clinical/outpatient scenarios, parenting experience, illness experience, and news reports. 2.4. Video quality assessment This study used 4 validated assessment tools to comprehensively evaluate the content and quality of the videos. The GQS is a 5-point scale and was used to evaluate the overall quality and informational fluency of videos.[21,22] The JAMA benchmark cri teria are a widely used, reliable tool for the evaluation of health information sources and include 4 dimensions: authorship, attribution, disclosure and currency.[23,24] The mDISCERN is a well-established tool for evaluating the reliability and quality of online information and consists of 5 items.[24,25] Additionally, the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT) was used to evaluate the actionability (PEMAT-A) and under standability (PEMAT-U) of the audiovisual materials.[26] The detailed scoring criteria for each assessment tool are available in Supplementary Tables S1–S4, Supplemental Digital Content 1. All videos were rated independently by 2 physicians (S C and Jl X) with specialized clinical expertise in ADHD. Prior to

All video materials were randomly ordered and distributed to the raters for independent evaluation. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), which was calculated based on a two-way random-effects model for absolute agreement. The reliability levels were defined as follows: poor (ICC<0.50), moderate (ICC = 0.50–0.75), good (ICC = 0.75–0.90) and excellent (ICC ≥ 0.90).[27] For items with initial rating discrepancies, both raters reviewed and discussed them. If they could not reach an agreement, a third senior clin ical researcher (Wz Z) arbitrated to determine the final score. The agreement between the 2 raters was good for all assess ment tools. JAMA benchmark score: ICC = 0.831 (95% CI: 0.787–0.868); GQS score: ICC = 0.902 (95% CI: 0.874–0.924); mDISCERN score: ICC = 0.871 (95% CI: 0.836–0.899); PEMAT-A score: ICC = 0.905 (95%CI: 0.879–0.926); and PEMAT-U score: ICC = 0.935 (95%CI: 0.913–0.952). All ICC values were statistically significant (P <. 001). 2.5. Statistical analysis Data reduction was performed using Microsoft 365 Excel (Microsoft, Redmond). Data analysis was performed using SPSS (Version 23.0, IBM Corp) and OriginPro (Version 2024, OriginLab Corporation). As the data were not nor mally distributed, descriptive statistics were presented as medians (interquartile ranges) and categorical variables were presented as frequencies (percentages). Group compar isons were conducted using the Mann–Whitney U test for 2 groups or the Kruskal–Wallis test for 3 or more groups. Post hoc pairwise comparisons were performed using Dunn’s test, adjusted by the Bonferroni correction. Spearman’s rank correlation analysis was used to assess correlations between variables. A two-sided P value of<.05 was considered statis tically significant. 3. Results 3.1. The general characteristics and engagement metrics As shown in Figure 1, after applying the exclusion criteria, a total of 228 ADHD videos were included for analysis, with 141 videos (61.8%) sourced from Douyin, 26 videos (11.4%) from Bilibili, and 61 videos (26.8%) from Xiaohongshu. As presented in Table 1, videos from Douyin and Bilibili exhibited significantly higher interaction metrics: including likes, shares, comments, collections: and higher creator follower counts com pared to videos from Xiaohongshu (all P<.05). No statistical difference in video duration was observed among the 3 plat forms (P>.05). 3.2. Distribution of video publisher types and content across platforms As shown in Figure 2, medical professionals were the main pub lishers of the videos (89/228; 39.0%), most of whom held senior professional positions (78/89; 87.6%). The proportion of vid eos published by senior medical professionals was the highest on Douyin (58/141, 41.1%). Among nonmedical sources, the largest subgroup was parents of patients (62/139, 44.6%), fol lowed by individual science communicators (37/139, 26.6%) and patients themselves (36/139, 25.9%). The proportion of individual science communicators was the highest on Bilibili (11/26, 42.3%). In terms of video content, the most prevalent topic was disease knowledge (124/228, 54.4%), followed by parenting experience (55/228, 24.1%) and clinical/outpatient scenarios (29/228, 12.7%). Disease knowledge was the dominant theme on both Bilibili (20/26, 76.9%) and Xiaohongshu (43/61, 70.5%), whereas a substantial proportion of videos on Douyin focused on parenting experience (52/141, 36.9%). 3.3. Video quality across platforms The quality of ADHD videos varied significantly across the 3 social media platforms (Fig. 3). The Kruskal–Wallis test revealed significant differences in the GQS, mDISCERN, PEMAT-U, and JAMA scores between Douyin, Bilibili, and Xiaohongshu (all P < .05), but no significant difference was observed in the PEMAT-A score (P=.116). Post hoc Dunn tests showed that videos on Bilibili had significantly higher GQS scores than those on Douyin (adjusted P < .001) and Xiaohongshu (adjusted P = .010). Similarly, videos on Bilibili had significantly higher mDISCERN, PEMAT-U, and JAMA scores than those on the other 2 platforms in pairwise compar isons (all adjusted P < .05). 3.4. Video quality by publisher type and content A substantial variation in video quality was identified among diverse publisher categories (Fig. 4) and content themes (Fig. 5) (all P < .05). Publisher type: In general, videos from medical sources achieved significantly higher scores in the GQS, mDISCERN, and PEMAT-U assessments than those from nonmedical sources (P < .001). Among medical sources, videos produced by profes sionals in senior positions received the highest median scores in terms of overall quality (GQS score: 3), reliability (mDISCERN score: 2), and understandability (PEMAT-U score: 64%), thus demonstrating superiority over other subgroups (all P < .001). Nonprofit organizations also obtained notably high scores on several metrics (e.g., mDISCERN score: 2.5). Conversely, videos from nonmedical publishers (e.g., parents, patients, individual communicators) exhibited lower performance across these core quality indicators. Video content: Disease knowledge received the highest median scores in core quality metrics (GQS score: 3; PEMAT-U score: 64%). News report achieved the highest scores in the JAMA benchmark (median score: 2.5) while having lower reliability scores (mDISCERN score: 2). Significant variations were iden tified in the GQS, mDISCERN, PEMAT-U, and JAMA scores across different content themes (P < .01). Video popularity and dissemination Previous studies have shown that the number of likes, comments, collections, and shares are core indicators that reflect the popu larity of video.[30,31] This study found that some ADHD-related videos have received hundreds of thousands of likes and tens of thousands of collections and shares, which reflects a lot of public attention to ADHD. These results show that there are cognitive differences in the choice of video publishing platform among different pub lisher types.[32] In contrast, the high proportion of “individual science communicators” on Bilibili (42.31%) aligns with the platform’s community culture, in which users actively seek sys tematic, knowledge-based content. The driving factors behind the spread of different content themes need to be understood in combination with the specific characteristics of the disease. This study found that ‘parenting experience ‘ videos accounted for a relatively high proportion (36.88%) in Douyin. These vid eos have a high degree of participation, which is mainly related to their ability to meet the needs of ADHD caregivers (mainly parents) for medical knowledge, emotional resonance, sense of community belonging, and practical strategies to deal with daily challenges.[2] Research indicates that families of children with ADHD have faced various challenges that are underestimated by society for a long time, including education system pressure, parenting pressure, children ‘s social dilemma, psychological burden, etc[33,34] Therefore, the behavior of parents sharing ‘ par enting experience ‘ on short video platforms essentially creates a convenient and accessible online peer support network, provid ing an outlet for emotional expression and a medium for shar ing experiences for originally isolated families. However, such experiential content may lack sufficient scientific evidence and could inadvertently spread non–evidence-based information, which warrants public caution.[13,35] 4.3. Video quality This study further clarifies the factors related to video quality. Firstly, uploader identity is a key factor affecting video qual ity. The quality-related indicators of videos produced by senior medical professionals (P<.001) were significantly better than those of nonprofessionals, which was consistent with inter national findings that the content produced by medical ser vice providers is usually more professional and accurate.[14,36] Secondly, platform attributes are also a key factor affecting the quality of video content. Specifically, this study found that Bilibili was significantly better than Douyin and Xiaohongshu in many quality indicators, which may be due to its commu nity ecology that encourages in-depth and systematic content creation. Therefore, for ADHD, which requires long-term management and professional guidance, Bilibili may be more conducive to the effective communication of such health knowledge. This finding is also consistent with the conclusions of short video studies on other health issues, such as gastro intestinal tumors.[17,30] Noticeably, evident quality disparities also exist among videos of different themes: videos focusing on standardized disease knowledge obtain higher quality scores than those centered on personal experience sharing. Such experiential content lacks sufficient scientific rigor, and blind credence in relevant personal narratives may easily mislead patients and their families, a hidden risk also mentioned in overseas studies on ADHD online health content.[13–15] In addi tion, research shows that platform format constraints such as video duration are important factors restricting information operability. This study confirmed a significant positive correla tion between video duration and PEMAT-A scores (R = 0.187, P < .001, suggesting limited practical value), which is consis tent with other health communication research.[14,32] The short duration of most videos (half of the videos included in this study were under 1 minute) makes it extremely difficult to include specific, step-by-step behavioral guidance or detailed healthcare navigation advice for complex conditions such as ADHD. Therefore, low “actionability” is a common challenge of the short-video format for disseminating complex health information. 4.4. Correlation of engagement metrics and video quality The correlation analysis in this study revealed a critical and cautionary finding: there was no significant positive correla tion between video popularity metrics (such as likes, comments, shares, and collections) and any of the scientific quality indi cators (|r|<0.2). This result challenges the common assumption that “high engagement equates to high informational value,” suggesting that in the context of ADHD, the logic underlying the widespread dissemination of content is distinct from that ensuring scientific rigour. This finding is consistent with a number of recent research conclusions, that is, emotional resonance or misleading infor mation is more likely to obtain algorithm recommendations and user interaction.[13,35–37] This phenomenon may be attributed to the algorithmic orientation of mainstream platforms with user interaction as the core. The design goal of such algorithms is mainly to extend the user ‘s stay time and improve interactive indicators such as likes, comments, and sharing, rather than evaluating the scientific quality of the content. Therefore, some content with insufficient scientific basis but strong narrative and prominent emotional impact can often obtain exposure opportunities far beyond its actual scientific value.[13,30] This phenomenon has a profound impact on public health. Studies have confirmed that exposure to ADHD-related misinformation on social media weakens the public’s accurate understanding of the disease and increases the risk of self-diagnosis or inap propriate medical behavior. The potential link to the DunningKruger effect remains interpretive and lacks direct empirical support in this study, so it is not further emphasized.[38] In addition, long-term exposure to such content may also distort the public’s perception of the true prevalence of the disease, forming an information ‘ echo chamber ‘, thereby exacerbating the solidification and dissemination of misconceptions.[13,39] It is worth noting that the Bilibili platform showed significantly better video quality in this evaluation. This means that algo rithm design may take into account the long-term value of user immediate feedback and content. The above findings have some Figure 6. Recommendations These findings have clear and actionable public health implica tions. First, healthcare professionals should play a more active role in producing and disseminating evidence-based ADHD content to improve the overall quality of online information. Second, structured digital health literacy programs are needed to help the public critically evaluate online health information and avoid overreliance on engagement metrics. Third, platforms may consider implementing appropriate content verification strategies for health-related topics, such as creator credential verification and clear labeling of experiential content, and fur ther optimize medical content recommendation mechanisms to increase exposure of high-quality professional popular science content. Given the high professional threshold of ADHD-related popular science knowledge, such professional content is hard to fit the entertaining expression style of mainstream short vid eos, restricting its wide public dissemination. In this context, both professional creators and ordinary experience sharers are suggested to enrich videos with specific and operable practical guidance. Experience-sharing creators should clearly distin guish personal perceptions from formal medical facts, and add explicit reminders to consult professional clinicians. For the general public, it is essential to remain cautious toward emo tional parenting and disease experience videos, verify creators’ professional qualifications rationally, and treat relevant online content merely as auxiliary reference rather than the basis for clinical medical decisions. 4.6. Limitations There are some limitations in this study. First of all, the video data came from China’s Douyin, Bilibili and Xiaohongshu, and social media platforms with other language or cultural back grounds might not be able to directly use the results of this study. Second, the number of video samples of the 3 platforms was unevenly distributed, and the sample size of Bilibili was rel atively small, which might affect the stability and representative ness of some statistical results. Thirdly, although several widely used assessment tools were selected in this study, and the consis tency assessment of the independent assessment scores of the 2 raters was conducted, it was undeniable that these assessments were still subjective. Fourth, this study adopted a cross-sectional design that only captured data at a single time point, which can only reflect associations rather than causal relationships; thus, causal inference between video exposure and audience cognition or behavior is limited. Finally, in order to reduce the interference of personalized recommendations, although this study used new accounts, the inherent recommendation mechanism of the plat form was still difficult to eliminate. Specifically, platform algo rithms may still prioritize trending or high-engagement content rather than scientifically rigorous information; the search-based sample in this study may not fully represent the personalized feeds that individual users normally view; and regional or tem poral variations in content ecology and algorithm rules may also reduce the representativeness of the sampling, which might affect the representativeness of the final sample. 5. Conclusion Although ADHD-related short videos are widely popular on mainstream Chinese social media platforms, their scien tific value cannot be accurately judged by user engagement alone, and overall quality and reliability require improve ment. Findings suggest the need for improved content qual ity and reliability of ADHD-related health information on these platforms. Future research and platform collaboration may help address these gaps by optimizing recommendation algorithms, clarifying content creator responsibilities, and enhancing public digital health literacy, thereby supporting sound development of ADHD public health communication. This cross‐platform analysis demonstrates that videos were primarily posted by medical professionals (especially seniorlevel providers), with disease knowledge as the dominant theme. Nevertheless, overall quality varied widely, and action ability scores were consistently low. While experiential content such as parenting experience was widely disseminated, it may carry potential risks of inaccuracy. Our findings further con firm that high video popularity does not equate to stronger scientific reliability. The public should remain cautious when viewing ADHD-related online content and prioritize informa tion from verified professional sources. Platforms and creators are encouraged to work together to improve the accuracy and practical value of health information. Biomedically, ADHD is conceptualised as a neurodevelopmental condition, comprising challenges with hyperactive and impulsive behaviours and/or maintaining attention relative to norms (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). Yet alternatives to this perspective are emerging in the literature, which consider ADHD as a difference associated with strengths as well as challenges, rather than a disorder (Bölte et al., 2021; Sonuga-Barke et al., 2023). With recent clinical guidelines calling for strengths-based methods in ADHD assessment and support (ADHD Guideline Development Group [AGDG], 2022), it is timely to further consider strengths in relation to the phenomenology of ADHD. Historically, ADHD has been conceptualised and studied through a deficit-based lens (Champ et al., 2021; Chaulagain et al., 2023).
