The SINCRONIA study was registered in the ISRCTN Registry, a primary clinical study registry recognized by the World Health Organization (Trial registration: ISRCTN12110752; February 20, 2025). Discussion Comparison With Prior Work EEG has been extensively employed to explore various neurophysiological metrics in ADHD, such as power spectral densities and event-related potentials. For instance, Clarke et al [73] demonstrated that children with ADHD exhibit increased theta band activity, decreased alpha band activity, and an elevated theta/beta ratio (TBR) compared to controls. Furthermore, these differences persisted into adulthood, with individuals showing lower beta levels in specific regions and a reduction in the ratio in ADHD compared to controls in recordings with eyes closed [74]. Similarly, Jarret et al [75] found increased relative theta power in the T5 and F7 regions in individuals with ADHD, aligning with findings from Chutko et al [76], who observed elevated TBR in children with both ADHD and SCT. Despite these promising findings, the utility of metrics like TBR as a robust diagnostic tool has been questioned due to inconsistent results [77,78], although JMIR RESEARCH PROTOCOLS Blasco-Fontecilla et al https://www.researchprotocols.org/2026/1/e79150 JMIR Res Protoc 2026 | vol. 15 | e79150 | p. 8 (page number not for citation purposes)

in recent years researchers have increasingly favored the use of TBR in combination with Bayesian Gaussian models [79]. Although EEG power metrics offer valuable insights, recent studies have shifted focus toward functional connectivity analyses, which may serve as more stable and reliable biomarkers for ADHD. McNorgan et al [80] identified impairments in functional connectivity within the default mode network, reinforcing the hypothesis that ADHD involves disrupted brain networks underlying attention and executive control. Michelini et al [81] further highlighted abnormalities in the corpus callosum and connectivity between the default mode network and frontoparietal/salience networks, suggesting that ADHD is fundamentally a disorder of brain connectivity and providing critical insights by examining brain connectivity across controls, individuals with persistent ADHD, and those in remission. Their findings revealed that individuals with ADHD exhibited less pronounced increases in theta band connectivity following cognitive control tasks, indicating deficits in modulating connectivity during transitions from rest to task-oriented states. Additionally, during the Flanker task, those with ADHD demonstrated global hyperconnectivity in theta, alpha, and beta bands when the task’s prestimulus cues were incongruent and only showed hyperconnectivity in the beta band during the processing of target stimuli when the stimuli were congruent, which correlated with poorer cognitive control and dysfunctional behavior [81]. These findings are consistent with previous research showing enhanced connectivity in the alpha and beta bands during attention tasks [36,82]. Despite recent advancements, significant limitations persist in the literature. Many studies rely on small sample sizes and predominantly male samples or fail to report sex distribution, limiting the generalizability of their findings [81,83,84]. Furthermore, individual biomarkers often explain only a small fraction of the variance in treatment responses, highlighting the need for multifactorial and integrative approaches. In addition, several methodological issues remain unaddressed in previous studies. Most existing tasks used for biomarker discovery are not grounded in theoretical models of attentional functioning and do not incorporate inhibition as a core element of the pathology, despite its central role in ADHD-related executive dysfunction [7]. These studies also tend to overlook functional connectivity at the source level and instead rely on scalp-level analyses, which limits the spatial precision and neural interpretability of their findings [45]. Moreover, EEG-based investigations are rarely validated against higher spatial resolution techniques such as magnetoencephalography, which could serve as a useful benchmark for signal source validation [47]. Finally, many studies use binary group comparisons (ADHD vs controls), neglecting the added value of including subtypes or differential diagnoses such as SCT and dyslexia in a 3-group design, which would allow for more clinically informative models [44,85]. Our study targets to address these gaps by using functional connectivity patterns, derived from EEG signals in the frequency domain, as biomarkers for ADHD. In this study, which will include at least 165 participants, we seek to improve the diagnostic accuracy achieved in the clinic at the time of this writing and to differentiate ADHD subtypes or other comorbid conditions that might be potentially confused with ADHD, using EEG-based ML algorithms applied to a go/no-go task. This study’s strength lies in its comprehensive design and robust sample size, enabling the identification of ADHD with high accuracy. By integrating EEG connectivity metrics with ML algorithms, we aim to uncover reliable biomarkers for ADHD, advancing the field and contributing to a deeper understanding of this neurodevelopmental disorder. Strengths and Limitations The study included primarily right-handed children (10% left-handed) aged 7‐12 years who could suspend medication and tolerate EEG recording sessions. The inclusion of left-handed children, up to 10% of eligible participants (Table 1), partly addressed this limitation within the study. Despite excluding children with ASD or other comorbidities, the sample of this study is fairly representative of most ADHD populations. However, the team is planning future studies to examine biomarker performance in more heterogeneous, clinically representative ADHD populations, including children with common comorbidities, such as ASD. Another limitation was that the final clinical diagnosis made by the PI was used as the reference test, as well as to define the participant grouping for algorithm training, thus introducing some circularity that could inflate diagnostic accuracy. However, several measures were introduced in order to mitigate this issue: first, the PI established the diagnosis independently, following established clinical criteria and without knowledge of any algorithmic or EEG outputs, thereby reducing the risk of circularity; second, several patients were previously diagnosed by other professionals, and the PI only confirmed the ADHD diagnosis; and third, a contract research organization was hired and an external neuropsychologist independently evaluated all patients. Despite the aforementioned limitations, the study also presents notable strengths. First, it benefits from a large sample size, which enhances the reliability of the findings and supports the generalization of the results and allows for comparisons between ADHD subtype groups. Additionally, it incorporates a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment that enables a detailed examination of participants’ cognitive profiles. This approach allows for a more accurate identification of the specific neurocognitive processes affected in children with ADHD, providing a robust dataset that can inform future research and support the exploration of other clinical and neurodevelopmental aspects of the disorder across different ages. ORIGINAL PAPER European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience (2026) 276:1631–1640 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00406-025-02148-z Introduction Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is charac terized by age-inappropriate levels of inattention, hyperac tivity, and impulsivity, with a global prevalence of 2.5% in adults [1]. Major depressive disorder (MDD) is one of its most common comorbidities, with adults with ADHD being three times more likely to experience MDD compared to the general population [2]. MDD in the ADHD population is often characterized by earlier onset, greater chronicity, and higher rates of self-harm and suicide [3]. Moreover, comor bid MDD is associated with more severe functional impair ments and worse treatment outcomes in adults with ADHD [4, 5]. Therefore, an early and accurate MDD diagnosis in ADHD is crucial. Yuan Gao and Meirong Pan contributed equally to this work. Qiujin Qian qianqiujin@bjmu.edu.cn Lu Liu liulupku@bjmu.edu.cn 1 Peking University Sixth Hospital/Institute of Mental Health, National Clinical Research Center for Mental Disorders (Peking University Sixth Hospital), and the Key Laboratory of Mental Health, Ministry of Health (Peking University), Beijing 100191, China Abstract Background An efficient and accurate diagnosis of MDD in adult ADHD is highly significant. Central symptoms identified through network analysis are considered to play a key role in diagnosis, potentially contributing to the achievement of this goal. Methods ADHD and MDD symptoms were assessed using the ADHD Rating Scale and Zung Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) in a clinical cohort of 418 adults with ADHD, followed by network estimations. Symptoms with high expected influence (EI) in the network were identified as central symptoms and tested for diagnostic validity via ROC curve analysis. Imaging analyses were further adopted to verify the effectiveness of the identified central symptoms from the perspective of construct validity. Results A five-symptom model was identified, including: “Depressed affect,” “Personal devaluation,” “Emptiness,” “Agi tation,” and “Interest loss.” The model exhibited strong diagnostic validity for MDD in adult ADHD, showing no significant difference compared to using all 20 SDS items. Moreover, significant functional alterations were detected in the left anterior cingulate cortex between groups classified by this model. Conclusion A five-symptom model comprising “Depressed affect,” “Personal devaluation,” “Emptiness,” “Agitation,” and “Interest loss” showed strong diagnostic validity for MDD in adult ADHD, and proven effective in exploring its under lying neural mechanisms. These symptoms should be considered a priority in diagnosing MDD in adults with ADHD. European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience (2026) 276:1631–1640 However, screening for MDD in ADHD can be challeng ing, partly due to the limitations of current diagnostic tools, which rely on standardized items with equal weighting [6]. These tools assume that all patients with MDD experience depressive symptoms of equal significance, disregarding the possibility that certain symptoms may be more salient for some individuals. This approach fails to account for the heterogeneity of MDD and does not consider the additional impact of comorbid conditions like ADHD [7]. The network approach offers a promising solution to this issue. It conceptualizes disorders as systems of inter connected symptoms, with the relative importance of each symptom quantified through centrality indices [8, 9]. Symp toms with high centrality indices are considered to have a strong influence on other symptoms or to contribute signifi cantly to comorbid conditions [10]. As such, these symp toms should be prioritized in diagnosis [6]. Over the past decade, network analysis has been widely applied to MDD, yielding many clinically significant find ings [11]. However, studies specifically focusing on MDD in adults with ADHD remain scarce, despite the ongoing challenges in diagnosis mentioned above. In this study, we aim to identify which depressive symptoms are most central to the diagnosis of MDD in adults with ADHD, while also exploring the ability of these symptoms to reveal underlying neural mechanisms, in order to further validate their diag nostic validity. Materials and methods Participants A total of 418 participants were recruited from Peking University Sixth Hospital. Inclusion criteria were: (1) a confirmed diagnosis of adult ADHD diagnosis in accor dance with the fourth edition of the American Psychiatric Association’ s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Men tal Disorders (DSM-IV; American Psychiatric Association [APA], 1994) [12], (2) age 18–45, (3) drug-naïve or off medication for half a year, (4) full-scale IQ >80. Exclusion criteria included: history of schizophrenia, pervasive devel opmental disorders, significant brain trauma, or suicidal ideation/planning/attempt. All participants provided written informed consents. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Peking University Institute of Mental Health. Assessments The diagnosis of adult ADHD was made by trained psy chiatrists using the Conner’s Adult ADHD Diagnostic Inter view (CAADID) [13]. Comorbidities were assessed via the Structural Clinical Interview for DSM-IV Axis I Disorders (SCID-I) [14]. Participants also completed the following assessments: (1) the Wechsler Adult Intelligence ScaleRevised in China, Third Edition (WAIS-RC), to obtain a full-scale IQ score; (2) the ADHD Rating Scale (ADHDRS) is a 4-point Likert-type scale (1 = not at all, 4 = always) comprising 9 items assessing Inattention and 9 items assess ing Hyperactivity/Impulsivity, used to evaluate the sever ity of core ADHD symptoms [15]; and (3) the Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS) is a 20-item self-report scale (1 = not at all, 4 = most of the time) used to assess symptoms of MDD, with higher scores indicating more severe depressive symptoms. MRI data acquisition and preprocessing A subgroup of 230 participants underwent magnetic reso nance imaging (MRI) scanning, with exclusion criteria included mental implants, claustrophobia, and other con ditions unsuitable for scanning. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) and high-resolution T1-weighted anatomi cal imaging were acquired using a 3T MR scanner (General Electric; Discovery MR750). During the scan, participants were instructed to remain motionless, eyes closed, and awake. After excluding participants with head movement exceeding 3.0 mm in translation or 3 degrees in rotation, 223 participants were included in further analysis. MRI data were processed using the RESTplus toolbox [16] and SPM12 software (​h​t​t​p​s​:​/​/​w​w​w​.​f​​i​l​.​i​o​n​.​u​c​l​.​a​c​.​u​k​/​s​p​ m​/) on MATLAB R2013b. The amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF) and regional homogeneity (ReHo) were extracted, followed by Fisher’s z transformation and smoothing. Detailed parameters and processing steps are provided in the supplementary materials. Network analysis The Gaussian Graphical Model (GGM) was used to esti mate an undirected network, where nodes represent symp toms and edges depict their conditional associations. The edge thickness indicates the magnitude of these associa tions, with green and red representing positive and negative associations, respectively. Regularization was applied to minimize the risk of false edges. The Graphical Least Abso lute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (gLASSO) and the Extended Bayesian Information Criteria (EBIC) were used for model selection to ensure a relatively stable network. Network visualization was performed using the “qgraph” package [17]. Referred to previous studies, Expected Influence (EI) was used to identify central symptoms, as it provides greater 1 3 1632

European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience (2026) 276:1631–1640 stability and accounts for negative edges in the network [18, 19]. Network accuracy and stability were assessed using the “bootnet” package with 5,000 bootstrap samples [20]. Dur ing this process, non-parametric Confidence Intervals (CIs) and the correlation stability (CS) coefficients were calcu lated to evaluate edge accuracy and centrality stability, respectively. Sensitivity analysis To eliminate the potential influence of other comorbidities, we reconstructed the symptom network and explored the central symptoms after excluding participants with comor bid bipolar disorder (BD) or anxiety disorders. Comparison of diagnostic validity The twenty depressive symptoms in the SDS were sequenced based on descending and ascending EI values, with each item added sequentially to form cumulative sums for both orders. These cumulative sums for both the descending and ascending EI groups were then used to predict clinically diagnosed MDD in adults with ADHD. Receiver operat ing characteristic (ROC) curves were plotted, and the area under the curve (AUC) along with the Youden index were calculated to evaluate diagnostic validity. This comprehen sive analysis allowed us to observe how diagnostic perfor mance changed as symptoms were added, thereby directly illustrating the clinical significance of central symptoms. Additionally, we compared the diagnostic validity of a sub set of central symptoms against the full set of all twenty symptoms. This comparison across different cutoff points was conducted to further demonstrate that a small number of central symptoms could achieve diagnostic performance on par with the full symptom list. In this step, the bootstrap function in the R package “cutpointr” [21] was employed to ensure the robustness and stability of the results. Neuroimaging analyses Based on the optimal cutoff point for central symptom sub set, participants were divided into two groups as ADHD + centralMDD (above the cutoff point) and ADHD-centralMDD (below the cutoff point). Controlling for age, sex, and head motion, ALFF and ReHo values were compared between the two groups. Multiple comparisons were corrected using Gaussian Random Field (GRF) theory at a voxel-level threshold of p < 0.001 and a cluster-level threshold of p < 0.05 [22].Subsequently, signals were extracted from the sig nificant clusters, and their correlations with SDS T-scores and central symptom scores were analyzed to confirm the associations. Results Demographic and clinical characteristics Demographic and clinical characteristics of the study pop ulation are presented in Table 1. A total of 418 adult par ticipants with ADHD were recruited, of whom 62.2% were male, with a mean age of 26.54 ± 5.36 years. There were 52 (12.4%) participants also diagnosed with MDD. Symptom network and centrality plot Figure 1A shows the network structure of ADHD and depressive symptoms, with the correlation matrix shown in Figure S1. For the whole network, the strongest associations were between HI2-HI3 (“Seat” - “Restless”, r = 0.34) and IA4-IA5 (“Follow” - “Organize”, r = 0.34). For depressive symptoms, the strongest associations were between D14D17 (“Hopelessness”- “Personal devaluation”, r = 0.27) and D1-D18 (“Depressed affect”- “Emptiness”, r = 0.24). The centrality plot (Fig. 1B) displayed the EI values of these symptoms. D1 had the highest EI value, suggesting it is the most central symptom in the whole network. Other depres sive symptoms with high EI values were as follows: D1, D17, D18, D13 (“Agitation”), and D20 (“Interest loss”). These symptoms maintained the same ranking in the sen sitivity analysis. The AUC and Youden indices, shown in Fig. 2, revealed that central symptoms had significantly higher diagnostic validity than marginal symptoms. When only one symptom was included in the model, the AUC for central symptoms was 0.812, whereas for marginal symp toms it was 0.481 (z = 6.02, P < 0.001). This performance gap gradually narrowed as more symptoms were added. The difference in AUC between central and marginal symp toms became statistically non-significant only after 13 symptoms were included (z = 1.55, P = 0.121). The Youden indices exhibited a similar trend. For central symptoms, the first four yielded diagnostic validity comparable to all 20 SDS items (z = 1.61, P = 0.107). Notably, the model contain ing top 5 central symptoms yielded the highest diagnostic validity among small symptom sets, forming the first peak in the ROC trajectory (as observed in Fig. 2). This finding suggested a model with top 5 central symptoms might offer an optimal balance between brevity and predictive validity. Discussion This study investigated the potential of central depressive symptoms for diagnosing MDD in adults with ADHD. A set of five central depressive symptoms were identified, includ ing: “Depressed affect,” “Personal devaluation,” “Empti ness,” “Agitation,” and “Interest loss.” These symptoms demonstrated better diagnostic validity than marginal symp toms and as effective as all SDS items, with even higher specificity. Significant functional alterations in the left anterior cingulate were observed between the two groups defined by central symptoms. These findings suggest that these central symptoms could serve as potential indicators for diagnosing MDD in adults with ADHD. This study constructed a symptom network of 38 nodes, comprising 18 ADHD symptoms and 20 depressive symp toms. European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience (2026) 276:1631–1640 in the current study, “Emptiness” was negatively correlated with a representative ADHD symptom “OnTheGo” (i.e., act as driven by a motor). The presence of pronounced anhedo nia can markedly reduce energy levels, even in the ADHD population. It is supported by previous research that adults with ADHD exhibit sustained energy and engagement pri marily when participating in activities they find interest ing or rewarding [41]. Conversely, this insight also implies that facilitating the identification of personally motivating activities may serve as an effective strategy for alleviating depressive symptoms in this population [42]. “Personal devaluation” was a central symptom, second only to “Depressed affect.” Feelings of worthlessness are strongly associated with suicidal thoughts and attempts [43, 44]. In adults with ADHD, impaired executive functions make them more vulnerable to setbacks in school, work, and relationships [45]. When combined with depressive symptoms, these setbacks can amplify feelings of useless ness, which in turn exacerbate ADHD symptoms, making it more difficult to concentrate or complete tasks [46]. Our network analysis revealed direct connections between “Per sonal devaluation” and inattentive symptoms “Detail” and “Organize” in ADHD, which reflected difficulties in learn ing and work, thereby providing empirical support for this pathway. This growing sense of failure may contribute to the elevated suicide risk among individuals with ADHD [47]. As such, addressing “Personal devaluation” could be a key intervention target, particularly when ADHD cooccurs with MDD. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can help patients rebuild negative self-cognitions, break the cycle of failure, and improve both ADHD and depressive symptoms [48]. Another intriguing finding is the symptom of “Agita tion (i.e. feeling restless),” which is commonly observed in MDD but less emphasized compared to other symptoms like sadness or anhedonia [6, 29]. In contrast, among individuals with ADHD, particularly adults, an analogous item “feel ing restless,” represents a significant manifestation [49] and occupies a prominent position within the ADHD symptom network [50]. Consistent with this, Lee et al. identified feel ing restless as the most central ADHD symptom in patients with mood disorders, while not in mood disorders alone [29, 51]. Collectively, these findings suggest that “Agita tion” may be a distinctive symptom that warrants greater attention when MDD and ADHD co-occur, underscoring its significance for understanding the comorbidity and inform ing potential interventions. As anticipated, above central symptoms demonstrated significantly higher diagnostic validity for MDD in adult ADHD compared to marginal symptoms. Moreover, a brief model consisting of the first five central depressive symp toms performed similarly to the full model, which included on other symptoms within the network [10]. This meant that depressive symptoms, rather than ADHD symptoms, might play a more key role when ADHD and MDD co-occur. A possible explanation is that worsened emotional issues fol lowing the comorbidity of MDD may significantly affect attention, memory, and decision-making, thereby leading to greater functional impairments [23, 24]. The five symptoms are also commonly observed in other mood disorders in adult ADHD, such as BD and anxiety disorders [25, 26]. Considering the potential effect of the comorbid status of these disorders, we have excluded those with comorbidities and repeated the analyses. The results were retained, supporting the core role of these five symp toms for the identification of MDD in adults with ADHD. It should be emphasized that the values of these identified cen tral symptoms do not lie in capturing manifestations unique to MDD, but rather in identifying a subset most strongly associated with and offering the greatest diagnostic contri bution to this disorder [10, 27]. As Ebrahimi et al. suggested, compared to individual symptoms, symptom co-occurrence patterns may be more indicative for capturing the distinctive features of certain psychiatric disorder [11]. Of course, it is highly worthwhile to recruit subjects with different diagno sis (MDD, BD or anxiety disorders) to further elucidate the transdiagnostic nature of specific symptom or the diagnosti cally specific pattern of co-occurred symptoms, which will promote our understanding of the psychopathology of dif ferent mental disorders. Among these central symptoms, “Depressed affect” exhibited the highest EI value. In community populations [28] and populations diagnosed with other mental disor ders [29], although significant differences were observed in centrality rankings, “Depressed affect” was consistently the most central symptom. It is widely recognized as a hall mark clinical feature of MDD and serve as a core diagnostic criterion in the DSM [30]. This finding aligns with previ ous network studies, which have consistently identified “Depressed affect,” “depressive mood,” or “sadness” as central symptoms across diverse populations, comorbidities and cultural contexts [31–33]. The strongest association with “Depressed affect” was observed for “Emptiness.” “Emptiness.” from the SDS, along with another central symptom “Loss of interest,” could reflect anhedonia [34], which is a core component of the DSM diagnostic criteria for MDD, as well as a necessary feature for its clinical diagnosis. Anhedonia plays an impor tant role in the psychopathology of MDD [35, 36], serving as a indicator of disease severity and progression [37]. In addition, anhedonia is one of the most frequently overlap ping symptoms between ADHD and MDD [38, 39], and has been identified in previous network analysis as a transdi agnostic trait linking the two disorders [40]. This finding supports net work theories that suggest central symptoms may be more clinically relevant and could serve as key targets for both diagnosis and intervention [10, 27]. The results highlight the potential benefits of using a streamlined set of central symptoms for clinical screening of MDD in ADHD, and potentially other psychiatric conditions. Central symptoms should be given greater weight in MDD evaluations in ADHD populations, as this could enhance diagnostic accu racy. Longitudinal studies could further validate the predic tive significance of these central symptoms. Previous studies have highlighted the importance of the ACC in MDD-related neural networks [52], with its dys function being a predictor of responses to antidepressant treatments and psychotherapy [53, 54]. Additionally, the ACC has also been implicated in ADHD [55]. Its central role in the reward system may explain why both ADHD and MDD are associated with damage to this brain region, sug gesting the ACC could be a key neural mechanism underly ing this comorbidity [56]. The observed differences in this well-validated biological marker further support the value of central symptoms in discriminating MDD in adults with ADHD. This symptom-level approach may also, to some extent, reflect its underlying neural mechanisms. The results support the feasibility of improving diagnosis and interven tion through a focus on central symptoms. Our study has several limitations. First, we were only able to construct an undirected network model base on the cross-sectional data. Future longitudinal studies are needed to explore the dynamic changes and potential causal rela tionships between ADHD and depressive symptoms, which would allow for a more clinically meaningful interpreta tion of central symptoms. Second, the symptom inclusion for the network was constrained by the limitations of the assessment tools. Although both the ADHD-RS and SDS are among the most widely used assessment tools in their respective domains, they do not capture certain relevant symptoms. For instance, Dong et al. proposed that emotional dysregulation might be a prominent feature distinguishing adults with comorbid ADHD and MDD from those with ADHD alone, yet neither of the scales used in this study includes relevant items [7]. Future studies should incorpo rate additional instruments to more comprehensively depict the symptom landscape of the disorders. Conclusion Our study identified central symptoms via network approach and innovatively demonstrated their diagnostic valid ity from both clinical and neurobiological perspectives. 1 3 1638

ORIGINAL PAPER European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience (2026) 276:1641–1651 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00406-025-02162-1 Introduction Although attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), which is characterized by typical behavioral symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity/impulsivity [41], is one of the most well-known neurodevelopmental disorders in childhood [43], its significance in adults is less well addressed. In fact, up to 60% of individuals diagnosed with this condition exhibit persistent symptoms till adulthood and as high as 41% fit both symptom and impairment diag nostic criteria for adult ADHD [37]. The prevalence of adult ADHD has been reported to be about 3% [38]. Importantly, a high proportion of adults with ADHD has also been found to be afflicted with other concomitant psychiatric disorders [24]. Adults with ADHD often experience additional health complications [15] as well as associated mortality risk [12] Yu-Ho Wen, Wei-Fu Pan, Cheuk-Kwan Sun have contributed equally as first authors. Kuo-Chuan Hung ed102605@gmail.com 1 Department of Emergency Medicine, Show Chwan Memorial Hospital, Changhua City, Taiwan 2 Department of Clinical Psychology, Tsyr-Huey Mental Hospital, Kaohsiung Jen-Ai’s Home, Kaohsiung City, Taiwan 3 Department of Emergency Medicine, E-Da Dachang Hospital, I-Shou University, Kaohsiung City, Taiwan 4 School of Medicine, College of Medicine, I-Shou University, Kaohsiung City, Taiwan 5 Department of Anesthesiology, Chi Mei Medical Center, No.901, ChungHwa Road, YungKung Dist, Tainan City 71004, Taiwan Abstract The current study aimed to investigate the effectiveness of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) in improving the clinical symptoms and cognitive functions in adults diagnosed with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) as well as its treatment acceptability. Randomized placebo-controlled trials (RCTs) identified from major databases using the main keywords “tDCS” and “ADHD” were reviewed for improvement in clinical symptoms and cognitive functions in adults diagnosed with ADHD. The outcomes of interest were quantified using effect size expressed as standardized mean difference (SMD) and odds ratios (ORs) for continuous and categorical variables, respectively, with 95% confi dence interval (CI). Meta-analysis of seven RCTs including 263 participants (mean age = 31.37) revealed significantly a greater improvement in the symptoms of inattention (SMD=-1.24, 95% CI:-0.84 to -1.63, p < 0.01) and cognitive tasks involving attentional performance (SMD= -0.54, 95% CI: -1.07 to -0.01, p = 0.04) in the tDCS group compared with the control group, but no significant difference in the symptoms of hyperactivity/impulsivity (p = 0.19) and inhibitory control (p = 0.17) between the two groups. There was also no significant difference in dropout rate between adults receiving tDCS and their controls (p = 0.07). Our study supported the use of tDCS for improving the self-reported symptoms of inattention and objective attentional performance in adults diagnosed with ADHD. However, the limited number of available trials hindered a robust investigation into the parameters required for establishing a standard protocol such as the optimal loca tion of electrode placement and treatment frequency in this setting. Further large-scale studies are warranted to address these issues. For instance, a sig nificantly elevated risk of accidental injury leading to emer gency department visits [9] may contribute to an increase in mortality in this population [27]. Therefore, ADHD treat ment in adulthood not only aims at improving the quality of life [1] but also targets the associated health and accidental risks [27]. Unlike treatment of ADHD in children for whom evi dence in favor of pharmacotherapy is better established, evi dence supporting pharmacological treatment for ADHD is less clear in the adult population [10]. Therefore, despite the satisfactory tolerance and general belief in the safety of phar macological interventions for ADHD, the associated health risks and side effects are still important concerns in adults [5, 17]. Moreover, a considerable portion of adult patients did not respond well to psychostimulant medications [34]. On the other hand, the multi-faceted therapeutic strategy for adult ADHD encompasses counseling, psychoeducation, supportive problem-directed treatment, coaching, behav ioral intervention, and family therapy [40]. However, except cognitive behavioral therapy, evidence remains insufficient to support the effectiveness of other types of psychosocial interventions in adult ADHD treatment [39]. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), which involves the application of a low-intensity current over the scalp, has been reported to regulate activity in cogni tive control circuits [33], through the modulation of cortical excitability and induction of neuroplasticity [13]. Notwith standing some promising results reported in prior studies investigating the therapeutic effects of tDCS against ADHD in adults, their findings were inconsistent [2–4, 8, 11, 16, 26]. Likewise, although a few previous meta-analyses sug gested the effectiveness of tDCS against the symptoms of ADHD, none of them focused on the adult population [7, 42]. It is noteworthy that the rating tools for the clinical symptoms of ADHD are fundamentally different between adults and children; while the assessment of adult symptoms was mainly based on self-rating scales, the evaluation of symptoms in children is primarily based on external observ ers [32]. In addition, the clinical presentations of ADHD in adults, which can be quite different from those of their pediatric counterparts, cannot be simply viewed as an exten sion of childhood symptoms [25]. Despite the therapeutic significance of ADHD in adults, relevant studies remain scarce. The robustness of evidence supporting the beneficial effect of tDCS against inattention from subgroup analysis of the adult population in a previous meta-analysis was tar nished by the limited number of included trials as well as a high heterogeneity (I2 = 80%) probably attributable to a mix of self-reported and performance-based data for analy sis [42]. Taking into account that self-rating scales may be more susceptible to placebo effects than performance-based assessment as reported in a previous drug efficacy study among psychiatric patients [22], we examined the effects of tDCS treatments by separating self-reported data and those acquired from performance-based tasks. Moreover, none of the previous meta-analyses investigated the treatment acceptability of tDCS in the adult population with ADHD [7, 42]. Therefore, the present meta-analysis, which targeted ran domized controlled clinical trials (RCTs), aimed at renew ing current evidence regarding the effectiveness of tDCS in improving the clinical symptoms and cognitive functions in adults diagnosed with ADHD as well as its treatment acceptability. Methods Study design and registration The current meta-analysis was presented in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [30]. The pro tocol of the study was registered in the international pro spective register of systematic reviews (PROSPERO CRD 42025644112). Search strategy and eligibility criteria Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) focusing on the effec tiveness of tDCS in improving behavioral and cognitive functions of adults diagnosed with ADHD were acquired through screening electronic databases, including PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, ScienceDirect, and Clini calTrials.gov from inception to Feb 8, 2025 using the main keywords of “ADHD + tDCS” based on appropriate search strategies without imposing restrictions on the language and geographic origins of publication (eTable1). The reference lists of the retrieved literature were further scrutinized for potentially eligible articles to be included. Each article was screened for eligibility based on its recruited population, intervention, comparator, and outcomes (PICO): (1) Popu lation: adults regardless of gender diagnosed with ADHD enrolled in a RCT, (2) Intervention: tDCS, (3) Comparator: non-tDCS interventions (e.g., sham-tDCS or waitlist), and (4) Outcome: alterations in behavioral symptoms or cogni tive functions. We excluded studies that (1) were not RCTs; (2) did not use tDCS as an intervention, (3) did not recruit adults diagnosed with ADHD, or (4) provided no informa tion about behavioral or cognitive functions as their study outcomes. 1 3 1642

European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience (2026) 276:1641–1651 Data extraction and quality assessment Following independent screening of the titles and abstracts of the identified articles according to the preset keywords and strategies (eTable1), the same two authors (YH Wen and CK Sun) continued to extract data on study characteristics and outcomes. Disagreements regarding study eligibility or data to be included were resolved through discussion with a third author (WF Pan). Kappa coefficients were adopted to assess inter-rater reliability [30]. The corresponding authors of articles that had missing data for analysis were contacted through electronic mails in an attempt to retrieve the neces sary information. While the quality of the included studies was appraised with the Cochrane’s “risk of bias” assess ment tool [21], the level of evidence of each outcome was assessed with the Grading of Recommendations Assess ment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) framework [19]. Disagreements between the two authors on the risk of bias or level of evidence were resolved through discussion. Data synthesis and analysis The primary outcome of the current study was changes in ADHD-associated behavioral symptoms evaluated with standard behavioral rating scales including ADHD SelfReport Scale (ASRS), adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (CASRS), or cognitive functions related to ADHD such as those focusing on attentional function (i.e. continuous performance test) and inhibitory control (i.e. Stroop test). The secondary outcome was tDCS treatment acceptability assessed by the numbers of withdrawn participants in the tDCS and control groups. The outcomes of interest were quantified using effect size (ES) expressed as standardized mean difference (SMD) and odds ratios (ORs) for con tinuous and categorical variables, respectively, with 95% confidence interval (CI). Review Manager 5 (RevMan5.4; Copenhagen: The Nordic Cochrane Center, The Cochrane Collaboration, 2014) was utilized for all statistical analy ses. While we adopted the generic inverse-variance method for analyzing continuous data, the Mantel-Haenszel method was used for categorical variables. To examine the robust ness of study outcomes, sensitivity test with leave-one-out approach was used. The probability of publication bias and heterogeneity were appraised with funnel plot and I-squared test, respectively. The impact of target brain region and type of control (e.g. waitlist or sham-tDCS) on the efficacy of tDCS treatment was assessed with subgroup analysis. A probability value (p) less than 0.05 was considered statisti cally significant for all study outcomes. Results Eligible studies and characteristics The literature selection process was reported in compliance with the PRISMA guidelines [31] (Fig. 1). Of the 698 arti cles retrieved from the electronic databases using the preset keywords and search strategies (eTable2), 675 were deemed ineligible following title and abstract screening. A full-text scrutiny of the remaining 23 RCTs yielded seven eligible studies including 263 participants for the current meta-anal ysis [2–4, 8, 11, 16, 26] (Fig. 1). The age of the participants ranged from 18 to 67 years with a mean age of 31.37 (Table 1). In respect of study design, five studies adopted a paral lel design [3, 4, 8, 11, 26], while two were cross-over trials [2, 16]. The median number of treatment sessions of tDCS treatment was five and the median duration of treatment was seven days. Regarding tDCS location, three studies positioned the anode at F4 [3, 8, 26], three at F3 [2, 4, 11], one targeted both sides of the prefrontal cortex (PFC) with different treatment arms [16], while all placed their cathodes at corresponding positions of the anodes on the contralateral side of the brain [2–4, 8, 16, 26]. The countries of origin of the eligible RCTs included USA [2, 26], Brazil [8, 11, 26], Turkey [3], Iran [4]. Risk of bias appraisal The Cochrane Collaboration’s tool demonstrated a low risk of bias in randomization sequence in most trials except for some studies that were given an unknown risk due to a lack of information about allocation concealment (Fig. 2). Likewise, most studies were deemed to have a low risk of both detection and performance bias because of their shamcontrol designs with the exception of one that recruited con trols without receiving sham-tDCS [4]. Nevertheless, the correct recognition of sham-tDCS in a high proportion of adult participants as previously reported has underscored the questionable blinding effects among sham-controls [18]. Reporting bias and attrition bias were considered low in all studies because they all targeted symptoms or cognitive functions of ADHD with a low drop-out rate. Primary outcome The current meta-analysis showed significant improvement in the clinical symptoms of inattention (SMD=-1.24, 95% CI:-0.84–-1.63, p < 0.01, three studies, 121 participants) (Fig. 3A) and cognitive tasks involving attentional perfor mance (SMD= -0.54, 95% CI: -1.07–-0.01, p = 0.04, three 1 3 1643

Sensitivity analysis demonstrated no signif icant impact of any study on the symptoms of hyperactivity/ impulsivity, but inhibitory control became statistically bet ter in the tDCS group than that in the control group after removal of one study [2]. Secondary outcomes Our secondary analyses on adults diagnosed with ADHD revealed no significant differences in dropout rate between those receiving tDCS and their controls (OR = 3.39, 95% CI:0.89–17.35, p = 0.07, four studies with 143 participants) (eFigure 5). The level of heterogeneity (I2 = 0% and p = 0.89) across the included studies was non-significant. Indeed, the blinding effect of sham tDCS in adults remained controversial [18]. Therefore, our results and those of others [22] may suggest an increased susceptibility to placebo effects when subjective self-rating scales were used. Hence, despite our findings indicating the effectiveness of tDCS in alleviating the clinical symptoms of inattention and improving cognitive functions among those diagnosed with ADHD, the discrepancy in ES between the two outcomes may suggest the necessity of further studies to include both subjective behavioral rating and objective performance-based parameters to minimize assessment bias. Given the poor blinding effects of sham tDCS in adults [22], our findings may imply higher reliability of cognitive tests for evaluating the therapeutic effects of tDCS on attention than that of subjective symptom ratings. Nevertheless, fur ther large-scale studies are warranted to address this issue. Due to the limited number of included studies that selected different target regions (e.g., only one study placing the anode over the left PFC investigated clinical improvement after tDCS intervention [26]), we could only conduct sub group analysis focusing on the placement of anode over the right PFC for improving the symptoms of inattention. Our results demonstrated greater improvement in those receiv ing tDCS treatment than that in the control group. Despite the known association between ADHD-related inattention and PFC, previous studies suggested more involvement of the right PFC than that of the left [14, 20]. A meta-analysis focusing on the differences in neuroanatomical activation between patients diagnosed with ADHD and healthy con trols showed an association between reduced capability for inhibition and decreased activation in the right inferior frontal cortex, as well as a correlation between poor per formance in attention tasks and decreased activation in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex [20]. Although several regions of the left hemisphere such as the left putamen and the left globus pallidus were also found to be associated with inhibition and inattention, these regions were farther away from the frontal area. Therefore, tDCS treatment of inatten tion through placing the anode over the right PFC seemed a reasonable approach, which was supported by the findings of our subgroup analysis that demonstrated a link between anode placement over the right PFC and an improvement in the symptoms of inattention. On the other hand, because the therapeutic benefit of tDCS may be attributed to its neu roplastic effect on the functional connectivity of the whole brain [35]; electrical stimulation may exert a generalized influence instead of an effect confined to specific brain regions. Because there was only one study focusing on the left PFC for clinical symptoms of inattention [26], we were unable to compare the therapeutic benefits between studies focusing on the right PFC and those targeting the left PFC. Discussion The present meta-analysis showed effectiveness of tDCS treatment based on subjective perception of inattention symptom alleviation as well as objective improvement in attentional performance in adults diagnosed with ADHD. Our finding was consistent with that of a previous metaanalysis that reported improvement in attentional perfor mance in a subgroup of adult ADHD patients [42]. On the other hand, the level of heterogeneity was much lower in our meta-analysis compared with that in the prior meta-analysis (I2 = 0% vs. 80%, respectively), suggesting more robust evi dence derived from the current study. Our subgroup analysis further indicated the effectiveness of tDCS with the anode placing over the right PFC in improving attention. Another subgroup analysis focusing on studies using sham-controls also supported the therapeutic effects of tDCS. Regarding our secondary outcomes, the present study demonstrated no significant difference in dropout rate between the tDCS and control groups, implying fair acceptability of tDCS treat ment. Nevertheless, the certainty of evidence regarding our positive findings on the therapeutic effects of tDCS against the symptoms of inattention and its fair treatment accept ability was rated as very low due to the limited numbers of available trials (i.e., seven trials and 263 adult participants), suggesting uncertain efficacy of tDCS as a standard treat ment for ADHD in adult patients that needs to be verified by further large-scale RCTs. In particular, an ongoing multicenter, randomized, double-blind, and sham-controlled study that evaluates the short- and mid-term effects of tDCS may provide further evidence regarding the therapeutic effi cacy of tDCS in the adult ADHD population [29]. Notwithstanding the unclear mechanisms underpinning the observed positive impact of tDCS on cognition in neu ropsychiatric patients [13], cortical excitability modulation and neuroplasticity induction have been proposed to play a role [33]. Provided that the PFC is pivotal in the execu tive control of attention [36], it is a frequent target for brain stimulation [6]. Indeed, all studies placed the anode either over the left or the right PFC in our included studies [2–4, 8, 16, 26]. Although our result that showed highly significant effectiveness of tDCS treatment in improving the symptoms of inattention as reflected by a large ES (ES=-1.24) was comparable to that of a previous meta-analysis (ES=-1.03) [42], a notably lower heterogeneity (I2 = 0%) in the current study than that of the prior meta-analysis (I2 = 80%) [42], was probably attributable to our separating the data on sub jective clinical rating from those on objective performancebased assessment during our analysis. Importantly, our results showed apparently substantial therapeutic benefit in Fig. 2 Risk of bias for eligible studies 1 3 1647

Taking into account the absence of difference in treatment-related parameters, including number of sessions, target location, and protocol of tDCS (e.g., energy, duration of stimulation) between that trial [2] and others [3, 4, 16] ], the reason for poorer thera peutic effect in the former remains unclear. Together with limited availability of eligible trials, the reliability of our outcome on inhibitory control was inadequate to exclude potential therapeutic effects of tDCS on inhibitory control in adults diagnosed with ADHD. Likewise, our results on improvement in the symptoms of hyperactivity/impulsivity, which were derived only from three trials, were not robust enough to exclude the treatment potential of tDCS against such symptomatology in adult ADHD patients. Our secondary outcome investigating treatment accept ability showed no significant difference between the tDCS and control groups, suggesting fair acceptability associated with tDCS treatment. However, the lack of information on dropout due to side effects of tDCS in all of the included tri als precluded the possibility of conducting a meta-analysis Nevertheless, given the evidence showing the predominant involvement of the right PFC in the symptoms of inatten tion [20], as well as the reported variation in the outcome on performance enhancement in category learning with the location of tDCS anode placement [23], further studies are needed to identify the appropriate locations of anode and cathode placement to maximize its therapeutic benefit. The current study showed that tDCS was effective in improving neither the behavioral rating of hyperactivity/ impulsivity nor the performance-based tasks involving inhibitory control. In contrast to the notable discrepancy in ES between subjective inattention ratings and objective attentional assessments in our findings, such an absence of difference in ES between the subjective hyperactivity/ impulsivity ratings and objective performance-based tasks may be attributable to a blunted subjective perception of improvement due to a lack of awareness of the symptoms of hyperactivity/hyperactivity compared to those of inattention in the adult population [28]. The present study had several limitations that need to be taken into account. First, our results derived from merely seven trials and a limited number of participants could not provide solid evidence to support the therapeutic effective ness of tDCS in improving either inattention or the symp toms of hyperactivity and impulsivity in adults with ADHD. Second, our inclusion of trials only from North and South America as well as Turkey may not justify the extrapola tion of our findings to populations of other geographical or ethnic backgrounds (e.g., Asians or Europeans). Third, despite our intention of investigating the impact of stimulat ing different target brain regions on the therapeutic effects of tDCS, we could only conduct subgroup analysis on the right PFC which is the prevalent target region across the studies. As a result, the difference in treatment effective ness between the right and left PFC as well as that between PFC and the other regions of the brain remains to be eluci dated. Finally, variations in the protocol of tDCS treatment (e.g., the number of sessions and the duration of follow-up) coupled with the availability of only five trials that ruled out the possibility of a meta-regression analysis precluded an in-depth investigation into the impact of these factors on therapeutic outcomes. Further large-scale investigations are warranted to establish a standard protocol on the therapeutic use of tDCS in adults diagnosed with ADHD. Conclusions Our study supported the use of tDCS for improving the selfreported symptoms of inattention and objective attentional performance in adults diagnosed with ADHD. However, the limited number of available trials hindered a robust investigation into the parameters required for establishing a standard protocol such as the optimal location of electrode placement and treatment frequency in this setting. Further large-scale double-blind sham-controlled clinical trials that include assessments of self-reported symptoms and perfor mance-based tasks both immediately after interventions and during follow-up periods as well as comparisons of the efficacy of tDCS targeting different brain locations are war ranted to address these issues. Although the gut-brain axis (GBA) plays a major role Sourav Ghosh sghosh69@gmail.com Shelly Singh shellysingh1001@gmail.com 1 Rai Technology University, Bengaluru, Karnataka, India 2 Department of Bioscience and Biotechnology, Banasthali Vidyapith, Rajasthan, India Abstract Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is being increasingly related to gut microbial dysbiosis caused by dis turbances in the gut-brain axis. However, in order to understand the connection of gut bacteria in ADHD, a comprehensive synthesis of available research is required. The purpose of this meta-analysis is to compare the gut microbiome composi tion of ADHD children to that of neurotypical controls, as well as to assess the efficacy of dietary treatments in treating ADHD symptoms. A systematic review and meta-analysis were undertaken using PRISMA guidelines to compare the gut microbiome profiles of ADHD children and the neurotypical controls, with association of the impact of dietary changes. An analysis of eight included research found significant changes in the gut microbiome of children with ADHD. Simi larly, they also found to have lower levels of Actinobacteria (5.78% vs. 4.89%, p < 0.001) and greater levels of Firmicutes (16.43% vs. 14.21%, p < 0.001), Bacteroidetes (13.12% vs. 11.02%, p = 0.002), and Proteobacteria (7.12% vs. 6.33%, p = 0.001). Beneficial genus-level taxa such as Lactobacillus (8.23% vs. 6.87%, p = 0.002) and Bifidobacterium (9.87% vs. 8.11%, p = 0.002) were significantly reduced in children with ADHD. Further the current research suggests that probiotics and fiber-rich diets may aid in maintain gut microbial balance, with specific strains of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium, being associated with behavioural improvements in ADHD. These findings highlight the possibility of probiotics and dietary changes as supplementary treatments for ADHD symptoms by regulating the gut-brain axis. (2017), it was discovered that in children with ADHD, the amount of Bifi dobacterium correlated with neural reward anticipation as determined by functional MRI. Aarts et al. found that lower levels of Bifidobacterium were linked to decreased activity in the ventral striatum, a crucial area involved in dopaminer gic signalling. This study supported the biological plausibil ity of microbiome-neurocognitive interactions in ADHD by being one of the first to propose that microbiome composi tion may affect symptoms through brain function [21]. Significant gaps still exist despite the increased inter est in gut-brain interactions in ADHD. First, there are still few high-quality systematic reviews and meta-analyses that synthesize microbiome data in ADHD, which leads to inconsistent and ambiguous evidence [22, 23]. Second, while cross-sectional research has revealed that children with ADHD and neurotypical children have different gut microbial compositions, there isn’t much proof that these variations correspond to clinical symptom relief. To inves tigate causality, longitudinal and interventional research are required. Third, due to variations in trial design, dosage, and patient selection, results are still mixed even though dietary interventions like probiotics, prebiotics, and fiber-rich diets have been suggested to alter the microbiome and alleviate symptoms [24, 25]. By integrating the available data on gut microbiome changes in ADHD, assessing the effectiveness of microbiome-targeted therapies, and clarifying plausible molecular pathways connecting microbial dysbiosis to ADHD symptoms, this systematic review and meta-analysis seeks to fill these gaps. The purpose of this systematic review and meta-analysis is to compile the most recent data on changes in the gut microbiome in children with ADHD and assess how dietary interventions affect the microbiome’s composition and behavioural outcomes. In order to reduce bias, increase the reliability of results, and elucidate the therapeutic potential of microbiome-targeted strategies in ADHD management, we employ strict inclusion criteria and standardized metaanalytic approaches. Materials and methods The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) criteria were followed in this systematic review and meta-analysis, guaranteeing reproducibility and transparency throughout [26–28]. Data extraction, quality assessment, study selection, literature search, and statistical analysis were all directed by a prede termined process. Given the growing evidence of research relating gut microbiome to ADHD, the methodological approach was created to thoroughly assess the existing lit erature while taking study heterogeneity into consideration. Eligibility criteria Inclusion criteria According to the Population, Exposure, Comparator, and Outcome (PECO) framework [29] the following studies were deemed eligible: Population: Research that looked at kids (≤ 18 years old) who had been diagnosed with ADHD using the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) or Diagnostic and Sta tistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) criteria. Since the composition of the gut microbiome changes signifi cantly with age, limiting the analysis to paediatrics ADHD guarantees consistency in microbial characterization. The age range of 5–17 years was chosen to reflect a period after the major early-life microbiome transitions have occurred, while still encompassing paediatric ADHD cohorts. This range is consistent with prior microbiome studies in neuro developmental disorders [30–32]. Exposure Research examining gut microbiome by cultureindependent techniques such as quantitative PCR (qPCR), shotgun metagenomics, or 16 S rRNA sequencing. High taxonomic resolution and reproducibility are offered by these techniques. Comparator To make sure that changes in microbiome were due to ADHD and not demographic variance, studies included a neurotypical control group that was matched for age and sex. Outcomes Taxonomic composition: The relative abun dances of the main genera and phyla of bacteria (e.g., Bifi dobacterium, Lactobacillus, Bacteroidetes, and Firmicutes). Clinical assessments of the severity of ADHD, as deter mined by validated instruments such the Conners’ Rating instruments or the ADHD Rating Scale-IV. Exclusion criteria Adult ADHD populations Age-related microbiome varia tions led to the exclusion of adult-focused (age < 18) studies. To increase sensitivity and specificity, the search approach included Boolean operators and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH). “ADHD,” “atten tion deficit hyperactivity disorder,” “gut microbiome,” “gut microbiome,” “intestinal microbiome,” “dysbiosis,” and “gut-brain axis” were the main search terms. Studies look ing at interventions that target the microbiome were cap tured with the aid of further improvements using the terms “probiotics” and “prebiotics.” To find any more relevant studies, reference lists from earlier systematic reviews and meta-analyses were manually screened. The selection of studies was done in two steps. In order to eliminate papers that did not fit the qualifying require ments, two independent reviewers first conducted title and abstract screening. After that, the whole texts of any pos sibly pertinent papers were obtained, and their eligibility was evaluated using predetermined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Disputes were settled by debate, and to guarantee impartial decision-making in situations where disagreement persisted, a third reviewer was consulted. Data extraction and quality assessment To guarantee uniformity and lessen bias in data gathering, a structured data extraction template was utilized. Bacte rial taxa abundance (Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Bifidobac terium, Lactobacillus), participant demographics (sample size, age, sex, diagnostic criteria), microbiome profiling details (sequencing method, sequencing depth, bioinformat ics pipeline), and effect size measures (Standardized Mean Differences, Odds Ratios) were among the variables that were extracted. Meta-analysis and statistical methods To account for anticipated between-study variability, a meta-analysis was carried out using a random-effects model (DerSimonian and Laird method). For continuous outcomes, Standardized Mean Differences (SMDs) were employed (e.g. G. bacterial taxonomic relative abundances), and odds ratios (ORs) were computed for categorical variables (e.g. the existence or lack of particular bacterial groups). For each pooled effect size (SMD or OR), Z-tests were used to assess statistical significance [33]. Z-values were calculated by dividing the pooled effect estimate by its standard error (SE), and two-tailed p-values were derived from the stan dard normal distribution [33, 34]. z = Effect size SE p = 2 × (1 −Φ (Z)) where Φ denotes the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution. Statistical heterogeneity between studies was measured using I2 statistics and Cochran’s Q test. Statistically significant heterogeneity was defined as p < 0.10 in the Q test, and substan tial heterogeneity was defined as an I2 value greater than 50%. Meta-regression and subgroup analyses were conducted to look into potential sources of variability. Heterogeneity and sensitivity analyses Meta-analysis results indicated varying degrees of hetero geneity across different bacterial taxa, as measured by the I2 statistic. The phylum-level comparisons showed high heterogeneity (e.g., Firmicutes: I2 = 92%), suggesting substantial variability among included studies. Similarly, genus-level comparisons also exhibited moderate to high heterogeneity, with Lactobacillus (I2 = 84%) and Bifido bacterium (I2 = 80%) showing considerable inter-study variance. To further assess the robustness of our findings, a sensitivity analysis was performed by evaluating the effect size (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals for each bacterial taxon (Fig. 4). The results remained consistent across stud ies, confirming the reliability of the meta-analytic estimates. Bifidobacterium (SMD = 2.61, p = 0.002) and Lactobacillus (SMD = 2.11, p = 0.002) demonstrated significantly higher relative abundance in ADHD compared to control groups. These findings reinforce the role of gut microbiome in neu rodevelopmental disorders, aligning with prior research that associates probiotic taxa with neuroimmune modulation. Publication bias assessment To evaluate the presence of publication bias, we generated a funnel plot of effect sizes against their standard errors (Fig. 5). The plot exhibited a relatively symmetrical distribution of studies around the mean effect size, with no significant asymmetry suggesting selective reporting bias. Addition ally, statistical tests for funnel plot asymmetry were con ducted, yielding non-significant results (Egger’s test, p > 0.05). This indicates that the observed microbial differ ences between ADHD and control groups are unlikely to be using a version of the Conners Parent Rating Scale, as well as changes prompted in gut microbiome diversity, especially an increase in Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium levels [40, 42, 44, 46]. Fiber-rich diets Three studies were conducted regarding the role of fiberrich diets in the treatment of symptoms associated with ADHD. Increased consumption of fiber, particularly in fruit, vegetables and whole grains, is related to increased amounts of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that will enable a person to promote gut health and reduce inflammation. Research on dietary intake and gut microbiome suggests that children consuming diets with high-fibers showed greater diversity in their gut microbiome combined with improved ADHD symptoms: inattention and cognitive performance were cited most often. It may induce beneficial bacterial growth, lower gut inflammatory conditions and influence the brain through various effects to modify the symptoms of ADHD. Thus, fiber fermentation increases SCFA production and thus plays a significant role in signalling between the gut and brain [39, 42, 43]. Combined dietary interventions Some of the studies have looked at a combination of pro biotics along with fiber-rich diets. One of these studies has shown that the Bifidobacterium longum supplement in com bination with high-fiber diet has led to significant improve ments in the gut microbiome, which can be marked by increased levels of Bifidobacteria and Lactobacilli, as well as improvement in ADHD symptoms. This suggests that joint interventions with probiotics and diet may be more effective than either on their own, which suggests some kind of synergistic effect for gut microbiome modulation and improvement of ADHD symptoms [42–44, 49]. Discussion This current study highlights the importance of the gut-brain axis in the pathophysiology of Attention-Deficit/Hyperac tivity Disorder (ADHD) by offering strong evidence link ing gut microbiome dysbiosis to the disorder. Our research shows that children with ADHD have different microbial compositions than children who are neurotypical. These dif ferences include a decrease in beneficial bacteria like Bifi dobacterium and Lactobacillus and an overrepresentation of pro-inflammatory taxa like Proteobacteria and Firmicutes. A possible mechanism connecting microbial dysbiosis to neuroinflammatory pathways, neurotransmitter abnormali ties, and behavioural dysregulation is suggested by these changes. Practicality & risk of diet-only approach It is important to stress that, despite current data supporting microbiome-targeted therapies, these strategies should only be used as supplements to existing ADHD therapies. Phar macological or behavioural therapies should not be stopped without clinical supervision for families thinking about relying solely on dietary changes. Effective management may be delayed if evidence-based care is abruptly stopped because the therapeutic effects of diet alone are still unclear and inconsistent for many children. Furthermore, children who are already experiencing appetite suppression as a result of stimulant medication may be more susceptible to micronutrient deficiencies and inadequate caloric intake if they follow restrictive dietary patterns. Development, immunity, and cognition may all be hampered by these nutritional imbalances. Dietary practices should therefore always be under medical supervision and customized to the child’s specific nutritional requirements and treatment environment. Based on the above research findings, we have pro posed a dietary intervention aimed at providing a structured approach to managing ADHD in early childhood (Table 4). Novelty of the current study This work advances the field by addressing the wider socioeconomic implications of managing ADHD, improving methodological precision, and incorporating innovative microbiome-driven therapy approaches. Bridging gaps in ADHD treatment: a holistic microbiome-based approach Although earlier studies have looked into the connection between gut microbiome and ADHD, the majority of these studies have only looked at probiotics or fiber therapies. Our study is the first to take a synergistic approach, look ing at the combined effects of diets high in fiber and pro biotic supplements. This work establishes the basis for a comprehensive, non-pharmacological treatment for ADHD by demonstrating the complimentary ways that dietary fiber and probiotics alter gut-brain connection. This is consistent with the increasing clinical interest in non-traditional stimu lant-based therapies for ADHD. Changes in the microbiome of domesticated animals are linked to enhanced neoteny and decreased aggression, indi cating that the microbiome may impose selective pressures on impulsivity and attentiveness. If ADHD is considered as an extreme form of an ancestral attentional spectrum, then studying gut microbial factors that influence behavioural plasticity may provide new information [57, 60]. Clinical implications: potential of microbiometargeted interventions Probiotics and nutritional interventions may be promis ing adjuncts in the treatment of ADHD, according to new research. The following crucial tactics are identified by our meta-analysis: Probiotic supplementation Certain strains, such as Lactobacillus rhamnosus, have shown potential in lowering hyperactivity and impulsiv ity by altering neurotransmitter levels and inflammatory responses. Other advantageous strains, such as Bifidobac terium longum, help to improve the synthesis of dopamine precursors, which may help to reduce symptoms [42, 62]. Dietary fiber and prebiotics Diets high in fiber encourage the synthesis of SCFA, which improves gut-brain connection and has neuroprotective properties. In those with ADHD, higher dietary fiber con sumption has been linked to better cognitive abilities and attentional control [44, 54, 56]. Targeted microbiome therapy By detecting unique dysbiosis patterns in each patient and adjusting probiotic and nutritional therapies appropriately, microbiome profiling and customized interventions may improve treatment results [62, 63]. The possibility of faecal microbiome transplantation (FMT) as a treatment approach for reestablishing gut homeostasis in ADHD should be investigated in future studies. Comorbidities and diet Dietary interventions that target gut microbiome may have an impact on medical comorbidities like obesity and sleepdisordered breathing (SDB), which are frequently linked to ADHD, in addition to potentially reducing symptoms. These disorders, which are commonly associated with poor dietary quality and excessive caloric intake, can mimic or worsen behaviours similar to those of ADHD. For children 1 3 41

Study limitations and future directions It is important to recognize a number of limitations when interpreting the results of this meta-analysis, even though it provides insightful information about the relationship between the composition of the gut microbiome and Atten tion-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). First, it is difficult to infer the causality, because most of the included studies followed cross-sectional designs. It is still unknown whether these changes are a cause or con sequences of ADHD, despite the fact that there have been consistent links found between microbial dysbiosis and the disorder. To ascertain whether gut microbial alterations occur before the onset of ADHD symptoms or as a result of the disorder and its treatment, longitudinal cohort stud ies that track people from birth through adolescence are required. Second, the improvement of clinical symptoms is not sig nificantly correlated with microbial changes. The majority of included studies looked at microbial composition with out also measuring core symptoms of ADHD, like impul sivity, hyperactivity, or inattention, or associated emotional symptoms, like anxiety and irritability. This makes it more difficult to interpret microbiome results in a behavioural or therapeutic setting. The evaluation of microbiome modula tion in conjunction with standardized symptom outcome measures should be the primary focus of future research in order to determine whether gut-based interventions result in significant clinical improvements. Third, this meta-analysis exhibited a high degree of het erogeneity, which was caused by variations in the sequenc ing techniques, participant age ranges, dietary backgrounds, and diagnostic criteria. Effect estimates may still be Identification of specific probiotic strains for personalized interventions Without making a distinction between different bacterial strains, the majority of earlier research generalized the impact of probiotics in ADHD. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of Lactobacillus rhamnosus in reducing hyperactivity and impulsivity, opening the door for strainspecific, focused probiotic treatment. This advances the new field of personalized medicine, which may use microbiome analysis to create interventions that are specifically suited to each person’s unique gut microbial makeup. Expanding the understanding of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) mechanisms Although SCFAs like butyrate, acetate, and propionate are becoming more widely acknowledged as important gutbrain communication mediators, little is known about how they contribute to the pathophysiology of ADHD. This study offers fresh perspectives on the ways in which SCFAs affect neuroinflammation, emotional processing, and cogni tive function, possibly revealing new molecular targets for therapeutic intervention. This study provides new opportu nities for dietary-based treatment approaches in neurode velopmental disorders by examining the fermentation of dietary fiber and its subsequent effect on SCFA generation. Addressing research heterogeneity through a rigorous meta-analytical approach The significant degree of heterogeneity in results resulting from methodological flaws, sample size restrictions, and a variety of analytical approaches has been one of the main obstacles in ADHD-microbiome research. Strict inclu sion standards and sophisticated statistical modeling are used in this study to reduce heterogeneity and make sure that the results are more broadly applicable and clinically significant. Our meta-analytical methodology improves the reliability of findings and offers a more comprehensive comprehension of changes in gut flora in ADHD. The disorder is linked to absenteeism, poor academic performance, and an increased risk of needing special education services. Conclusion This meta-analysis reveals consistent alteration in the gut microbiome of children with ADHD, such as higher abun dance of potentially pro-inflammatory taxa and lower levels of supportive genera like Bifidobacterium and Lactobacil lus. These trends lend credence to the expanding under standing of the gut-brain axis in the pathophysiology of ADHD. However, due to the cross-sectional design of most studies, high heterogeneity, and short intervention peri ods, the impact of these microbial changes on symptoms of ADHD and its emotional regulation remains indetermi nate. RESEARCH European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry (2026) 35:449–462 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00787-025-02842-2 Sampo Seppä sampo.seppa@oulu.fi Sanna Huikari sanna.huikari@oulu.fi Marko Korhonen marko.korhonen@oulu.fi Tanja Nordström tanja.nordstrom@oulu.fi Tuula Hurtig tuula.hurtig@oulu.fi Anu-Helmi Halt anu-helmi.halt@oulu.fi 1 Research Unit of Clinical Medicine, University of Oulu, Oulu, Finland 2 Department of Economics, Accounting and Finance, University of Oulu, Oulu, Finland 3 Northern Finland Birth Cohorts, Arctic Biobank, Infrastructure for Population Studies, Faculty of Medicine, University of Oulu, Oulu, Finland 4 Research Unit of Population Health, University of Oulu, Oulu, Finland 5 Clinic of Child Psychiatry, University of Oulu, Oulu, Finland 6 Oulu University Hospital and University of Oulu, Medical Research Center, Oulu, Finland Abstract This longitudinal, population-based cohort study examines the direct and indirect associations between adolescent Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and/or Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) symptoms and adult incomes. Moving beyond a simple direct link, our model explores how ADHD and/or ODD symptoms indirectly affect the accumulation of human, social, and health capital, which in turn may affect productivity and income. The population was drawn from members of the Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1986 (NFBC1986) who had ADHD and ODD symptoms assessed at age 16 using the Strengths and Weaknesses of ADHD Symptoms and Normal Behaviours (SWAN) scale. The results indicate a significant indirect negative effect of adolescent ADHD and ADHD + ODD symptoms on adult incomes. This effect was most pronounced in males with ADHD + ODD, who experienced a 25% income reduction via human capital (education) and an 18% reduction via health capital (presence of psychiatric disorders other than ADHD or ODD). Social capital did not mediate the association. The model was adjusted for work experience, white-collar status, marital status, parenthood, self-rated health, educational attainments of the participants’ parents and family type during adolescence. Notably, no direct effect of adolescent ADHD and/or ODD symptoms on adult incomes was observed. These findings highlight the potential of educational and healthcare investments to reduce the income disparities associated with ADHD and ODD symptoms in the general population.
