European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry (2026) 35:449–462 Introduction Longitudinal studies have indicated that symptoms of AttentionDeficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) are associated with an increased risk of unemployment [1], and that employees with ADHD tend to perform less effectively than those without this condition [2]. Both individual and socioeconomic concerns arise due to the negative impact of ADHD on one’s ability to cope in the workplace, and income disparities between such individuals and the general population can stem from ADHD-specific symptoms, comorbid conditions, educational difficulties, or various social factors correlated with ADHD. One of the most robust predictors of the consequences in terms of adult incomes is education [3]. Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) may also affect various socioeconomic indicators, such as educational level, occupational status, and income, so that some studies have found that symptoms of ODD are associated with a lower annual income than for controls [4, 5], while others have not found any such association [6, 7]. Given the somewhat limited previous research, it has been hypothesized that edu cation may also mediate these effects [8]. Although ADHD and ODD are classified as distinct disorders, they frequently co-occur, with comorbidity rates estimated at 50–60% in population-based samples [9, 10]. Prior research has shown that individuals with comorbid ADHD and ODD experience more severe and persistent functional impairments than those with either disorder alone [11]. Accordingly, this study examines both the independent and combined effects of ADHD and ODD symptoms on adult income to assess their additive and interactive impacts. Given the well-documented sex differences in the expression, prevalence, and functional outcomes associated with both ADHD and ODD [12, 13], analyses were stratified by sex to allow for the detection of potentially divergent patterns between males and females. Although ADHD and ODD symptoms are associated with reduced income, the factors mediating these challenges are not well understood. To move beyond a simple association between adolescent ADHD/ODD symptoms and adult income, and to gain a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying this relationship, we employ mediation analysis. The motivation for estimating the indirect effects stems from the idea that ADHD/ODD symptoms may influence an individual’s developmental trajectory and life-course outcomes. These effects may manifest through early-life factors such as educational attainment and social relationships, as well as later-life factors including employment stability and health-related challenges. These life-course pathways are linked to the accumulation of human, social, and health capital, which in turn are known to shape adult income [14–16]. Empirical evidence supports this conceptual framework. Adolescents with ADHD/ODD exhibit lower educational attainment [4, 17], strained interpersonal relationships and diminished trust [18, 19], and higher rates of additional psychiatric conditions [20, 21], all of which correspond to deficits in the three capital domains that underpin long-term socioeconomic well-being [14, 16, 22]. We hypothesize that the impact of adolescent ADHD/ ODD symptoms on income are partially mediated through these capital constructs. Although mediation analysis is relatively straightforward statistically, it is appropriate for exploring potential mechanisms through which ADHD/ODD symptoms may affect income, i.e., through the mediating role of human, social, and health capital. The validity of this approach depends on several assumptions, most notably the assumption that ADHD and ODD symptoms are exogenous to the outcome (income) and to the mediators, conditional on observed covariates. We rely on the developmental stability and early-onset nature of ADHD and ODD, typically diagnosed in childhood and known to persist over time, as justification for treating these variables as plausibly exogenous for mediation purposes [23, 24]. Thus, mediation analysis provides a theoretically grounded and statistically appropriate method to identify potential indirect pathways through which adolescent ADHD and ODD symptoms may impact income outcomes later in life. Understanding the long-term socioeconomic consequences of adolescent ADHD and ODD symptoms—and the path ways through which they operate—is essential for informing early intervention and public policy. By identifying the edu cational, social, and health-related mechanisms that mediate income disparities, our findings may inform targeted strate gies to support occupational success among individuals with early-onset behavioral and neurodevelopmental conditions. METHODS Sample description The data were obtained from the Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1986 (NFBC1986), a comprehensive, ongoing follow-up study that initially included 9,432 live-born children with expected birth dates between July 1, 1985, and June 30, 1986. The cohort represents 99% of all children born alive in Finland’s two northernmost provinces during that period [25, 26]. In the follow-up at the age of 16 years, questionnaires based on the Strengths and Weaknesses of ADHD-Symptoms and Normal-Behaviours (SWAN) scale [27] were sent to the parents of 9,215 adolescents whose addresses were known. A total of 6,985 parents (75.8%) returned the completed 1 3 450

European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry (2026) 35:449–462 questionnaires along with a statement of informed consent. The Ethical Committee of the Northern Ostrobothnia Hospital District approved the study (Cohort 1986: Northern Ostrobothnia Hospital District Ethical Committee 108/2017 (15.1.2018)). The SWAN scale, a revision of the SNAP-IV scale [27], was initially used to assess ADHD and ODD symptoms based on items directly linked to DSM-IV-TR [28] criteria. These items evaluated attention, hyperactivity/impulsivity, and disruptive behaviour on a seven-point scale, ranging from “Far Below Average” to “Far Above Average,” with “Average” as the midpoint. This approach allowed for a normally distributed assessment of behavioural traits. Exposure Variables: Symptoms of ADHD and ODD ADHD symptoms identified across the Inattentive, Hyperactive-Impulsive, and Combined scales were assessed using 18 items, ranging from “Gives close attention to detail and avoids careless mistakes” to “Enters into conversations and games (controls interrupting/intruding)”. Additionally, ODD symptoms were assessed using eight items ranging from “Controls temper” to “Controls spitefulness and vindictiveness”. One missing item was allowed in each subscale and replaced with the mean of that subscale for the adolescent concerned. Following the scale developer’s recommendation [29] and in alignment with previous research [30], the 95th percentile of the distribution was taken as the cut-off point for identifying symptoms. Participants were categorized into four groups based on their symptom profiles: (1) those with only ADHD symptoms, (2) those with only ODD symptoms, (3) those exhibiting both ADHD and ODD symptoms and (4) controls, who exhibited neither ADHD nor ODD symptoms. The 95th percentile cutoff for ADHD and ODD symptoms was determined based on the distribution of the total sample rather than sex-specific distributions. This approach was chosen to maintain a consistent threshold across sexes, reflecting population-level clinical risk as would be applied using standardized norms in diagnostic settings. The SWAN scale has proved reliable and valid in previous studies, and thus offers a solid foundation for assessing behavioural problems in adolescents [31, 32]. Outcome Variable: Income The outcome variable was individual gross income in 2016, when participants were 30 years old. Participants with zero income were excluded from the analyses to avoid distortion in the log-transformation and to ensure interpretability of percentage-based estimates. Following recent methodological guidance [33], income was modelled as a continuous variable using a natural logarithmic transformation to reduce skewness and improve interpretability. This approach allows effect estimates to be expressed as percentage differences and aligns with best practices for income modelling in population-based studies. Income data were obtained from the Finnish Tax Administration (https://www.vero.fi/en). Mediators This study draws on a theoretical framework combining human, social, and health capital models to examine how adolescent ADHD and/or ODD symptoms may influence adult income. To reduce model complexity and minimize multicollinearity, one proxy variable was selected a priori for each capital domain: educational attainment for human capital, interpersonal trust for social capital, and the presence of psychiatric disorders other than ADHD or ODD for health capital (Table 1). These choices were guided by both theoretical frameworks and prior empirical research linking these domains to income and labour market functioning [34, 35]. Tertiary education was used as the primary proxy for human capital, given its strong and consistent association with long-term earnings and productivity [36]. This variable was selected a priori due to its well-established theoretical and empirical relevance in life-course and economic research [37, 38]. Educational attainment remains the most widely accepted indicator of human capital, as it reflects an individual’s accumulated skills and economic potential [39, 40]. In our previous study using the same cohort [41], we showed that adolescent symptoms of ADHD, ODD, and particularly their co-occurrence, were associated with lower educational attainment in adulthood. While tertiary education served as our main proxy, additional indicators of human capital—work experience and occupational status—were also included to complement the analysis (Table 1). Occupational status was classified using a white-collar framework: upper white-collar included managerial, professional, and higherlevel administrative roles; lower white-collar referred to clerical and lower-level administrative positions. All other categories including manual workers, students, pensioners, and others were coded as 0. Interpersonal trust was used as the primary proxy for social capital, based on its strong conceptual and empirical grounding in the literature. Trust plays a foundational role in the development of social networks that enable access to information and opportunities [15, 42, 43]. Among various indicators, trust has consistently emerged to be a robust and least prone to endogeneity concerns, particularly in relation to economic outcomes [34, 35, 44]. While variables such as 1 3 451

European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry (2026) 35:449–462 marital status [45] and parenthood [46] have been linked to aspects of social capital, the empirical support for trust as a core indicator of social capital is stronger [34, 35]. Marital status and parenthood by age 30 were included as additional indicators of social capital in this study (Table 1). Health capital was proxied by the presence of psychiatric disorders other than ADHD or ODD, given their consistent association with reduced earnings, particularly when onset occurs during adolescence [47–49]. Psychiatric comorbidity with ADHD is more the rule than the exception, and previous studies suggest that disorders such as anxiety, depression, and bipolar disorder alongside ADHD tend to further worsen occupational outcomes [50, 51]. This supports the role of co-occurring psychiatric conditions as a meaningful indicator of compromised health capital in early adulthood. Diagnoses were obtained from the Care Register for Health Care maintained by the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare, covering specialized inpatient care (through 2016) and outpatient care (1998–2016), and primary care outpatient treatments (2011–2016). If participants had only ADHD or ODD in the health notifications, they were not considered in connection with this variable: 314.0B and 314.1 A were used as diagnostic criteria for ADHD and 313.8 A for ODD in ICD9, while F90.0 was used as a diagnostic criterion for ADHD and F91.3 for ODD in ICD10. Participants were classified as having a psychiatric disorder if at least one diagnosis other than ADHD or ODD was recorded (Table 1). Self-reported health, while often used as a measure of perceived physical well-being and shown to correlate with objective health indicators [52, 53], was not used as a primary health capital measure in this study due to its subjectivity and early measurement at age 16. Covariates Numerous factors influencing occupational outcomes and income have been identified in prior research, many of which are also associated with ADHD and ODD [7, 54, 55]. To better isolate the associations between adolescent ADHD and ODD symptoms and adult income, we adjusted the multiple mediation model for several covariates. Parental education and family type during adolescence were included to account for early socioeconomic background (Table 1). Parental education, reported via questionnaire when participants were 16 years old, was coded as 1 for tertiary education (i.e., a university or university of applied sciences degree) and 0 for all other educational levels. Family structure was based on adolescent questionnaire data and coded as 1 if the participant lived with both biological parents, and 0 for all other family arrangements. Within a regression framework, the population parameters representing the direct and indirect effects are estimated with a set of two individual regression models [58]. We conducted the mediation analyses as recommended by Iacobucci (2012) [59], using the “products of coefficients” approach [60]. First, we computed the mediated effects of ADHD and/or ODD symptoms for each mediator individually, and then we expanded the simple mediation tests by performing a multiple mediation analysis using one proxy variable for each form of capital: educational attainment for human capital, interpersonal trust for social capital, and the presence of psychiatric disorders other than ADHD or ODD for health capital. This approach was chosen to reduce model complexity and minimize potential multicollinearity among variables. All the analyses were conducted separately by sex, and the indirect effects of adolescent ADHD and ODD symptoms on adult incomes were presumed to be mediated through constructs that we refer to as human, social, and health capital (Fig. 2). The independence of the means in the contingency tables was assessed using the Pearson χ2 test for categorical variables and an analysis of variance (ANOVA), with the Welch test applied where necessary, for continuous variables. Post hoc tests were performed using the Tukey test and the Games-Howell test, as appropriate. Income was modelled in natural logarithmic form in the mediation analyses, thus allowing the results to be expressed We also include the remaining variables used in the simple mediation analyses as covariates in the full model, as they are associated with both income and the selected mediator variables (see Supplementary Tables S1 and S2 for correlations between variables). Given that the correlation coefficients between the mediators and covariates range from 0.596 to − 0.151 for males and from 0.410 to − 0.169 for females, there is no indication of problematic multicollinearity that would substantially bias model estimation or prediction [56, 57]. Statistical methods We used mediation analyses to explore how ADHD and ODD symptoms in adolescence affect adult incomes. The direct effect is shown by the income difference between individuals with and without these symptoms, while the indirect effect is concerned with how these symptoms influence life choices, such as education, career, social interactions, and health, which in turn affect incomes. At a general level, mediation processes can be expressed in terms of mediator variables operating between an independent variable and an outcome variable, i.e. a mediator variable is thought of as transmitting the effect of the independent variable to the outcome variable [58]. The total effect of the independent variable on the outcome variable, c, can thus be partitioned into a combination of a direct effect, c’, and an indirect effect transmitted through the mediator variable, a*b (Fig. 1). All the statistical analyses were performed using Stata 16.0 (StataCorp LLC), and all the tests were two-tailed, with p-values below 0.05 considered statistically significant. A Bonferroni correction [63, 64] was applied to account for six statistical tests per group in the multiple mediation analysis: three specific indirect effects (one per mediator), the total indirect effect, the direct effect, and the total effect. Finland’s high standard of living and powerful social safety nets for single-parent and lowincome families may have contributed to this outcome. Interpersonal relationships are crucial to the psychosocial development of adolescents, and a lack of friendships can result in poor social skills and eventual withdrawal from the community ́s social networks. Although low levels of trust are linked to loneliness [70], some adolescents may compensate for their social deficits by channelling their efforts into academic and occupational achievements in order to maintain a positive self-image. Alternatively, traits such as risk-taking and entrepreneurial tendencies could reduce reliance on traditional social interactions in one ́s career pathways. The fact that we found no direct or indirect effect of ODD symptoms on incomes for either males or females may be related to the stronger impact of disruptive behaviour on academic achievement during the earlier stages of life, such as adolescence and early adulthood, i.e. the effects of ODD symptoms may diminish as individuals mature and age. Previous research into the association between ODD symptoms and income has yielded inconsistent results. The Columbia County Longitudinal Study, for example, showed that aggressive behaviour in childhood or adolescence negatively affected educational status in early adulthood, which in turn predicted a poorer occupational status in middle adulthood [8]. Likewise, the Jyväskylä Longitudinal Study of Personality and Social Development reported that teacher-rated aggression at age eight predicted school maladjustment at age 14, which in turn was both directly and indirectly related to longterm unemployment (via problem drinking and a lack of occupational alternatives at age 27) [71]. Strengths and limitations The principal strength of this study lies in its large, population-based sample and longitudinal prospective design, which together provide robust insights through comprehensive statistical analyses. The NFBC1986 cohort has maintained high participation rates throughout its follow-ups, with 76% of the parents and 80% of the included in the 16-year follow-up. Also, the sample data are linked to accurate Finnish national registers, providing reliable information on participants’ incomes and other variables. This linkage will enhance the reliability of the data and minimize attrition bias. Another notable strength of the study is the use of symptom-based groupings rather than formal diagnoses, enabling the identification of individuals with high symptom levels in a populationbased setting. Although we used a 95th percentile cutoff, outcomes, though the findings are mixed. A longitudinal, register-based study performed in Sweden [54], for instance, demonstrated that while educational attainment partially explained the connection between ADHD and occupational outcomes, disparities between individuals with and without ADHD persisted over time regardless of the level of education. One genetically sensitive study found that education played a minor role in occupational outcomes among siblings with differing ADHD symptoms [65], while another found that it significantly mediated the relationship between a polygenic ADHD score and income [66]. Our findings are in line with the above, suggesting a significant indirect association via education between adolescent ADHD symptoms and adult incomes. Measuring health capital via self-rated health and the presence of psychiatric disorders other than ADHD or ODD, we found in our multiple mediation analyses that co-occurring psychiatric disorders mediated the relationship between adolescent ADHD symptoms and adult incomes for both males and females. This is consistent with previous suggestions that psychiatric comorbidities in addition to ADHD itself play a substantial role in occupational outcomes. One European study, for instance, reported a link between psychiatric comorbidities and higher unemployment rates among adults with ADHD [67]. In addition, research has shown that employment rates are comparable between individuals with ADHD and a clinical control group with other psychiatric conditions but without an ADHD diagnosis [68]. It is significant, however, that the Swedish study excluded ADHD-related psychiatric comorbidities, such as depression, from their analyses, citing concerns about potential moderating effects. They argued that these comorbidities could be influenced by both ADHD and occupational outcomes, such as income, thereby complicating the relationship between ADHD and career success [54]. In contrast, our study included psychiatric comorbidities but found no evidence of a moderating effect. ADHD and/or ODD symptoms were not associated with social capital variables such as marital status, parenthood, or trust when compared to controls in the present instance, although there was a statistical trend (p = 0.051) in the oneway ANOVA, suggesting that trust was more prevalent among the controls than in the symptomatic groups. As a result, social capital (trust) did not mediate the relationship between these symptomatic groups and adult incomes. These findings are somewhat unexpected in the light of previous research. For instance, it has been reported from Norway that the relationship between ADHD symptoms and occupational outcomes was entirely mediated by social and role-emotional functioning [69]. Despite this, tertiary education remains a widely accepted indicator of human capital, reflecting skill acquisition and long-term economic potential. Interpersonal trust—measured as having a close friend at age 16—was used as the primary proxy for social capital. While this measure is conceptually grounded and supported by prior research, it is not exhaustive and exhibited limited variability, with over 80% of participants reporting at least one close friend. Combined with its early measurement, this may reduce its ability to meaningfully differentiate between individuals and limit its relevance for adult social functioning. Alternative indicators, including marital status and parenthood at age 30, were explored in sensitivity analyses. However, these variables may reflect broader structural or socioeconomic factors rather than core dimensions of social capital, and their conceptual fit may be considered outdated in contemporary social research. Nonetheless, within the NFBC1986—where early family formation remains relatively common and socially normative—these indicators may retain some contextual relevance, though this naturally limits generalizability. Health capital was proxied by the presence of psychiatric disorders other than ADHD or ODD, due to their established association with reduced earnings. Although self-reported health was available, it was not used as a primary proxy due to its subjectivity and early measurement at age 16. While proxies were selected a priori based on theoretical and empirical relevance, future research should consider more sensitive, multidimensional, and temporally appropriate measures to better capture the roles of human, social, and health capital. Conclusions It was found here that both ADHD and combined ADHD + ODD symptoms experienced in adolescence could indirectly affect adult incomes, the impact being mediated through human capital (education) and health capital (co-occurring psychiatric disorders). Social capital (trust) did not mediate this association, and contrary to previous research, we observed no direct effect of adolescent ADHD or ODD symptoms on adult incomes. Our mediation analyses highlighted the fact that it is not the ADHD symptoms themselves that reduce incomes, but rather their influence through educational attainments and health. These findings have significant socio-economic implications. Enhanced student counselling and early screening for psychiatric symptoms could help narrow the income gap between individuals with ADHD or ODD symptoms and the general population. Future research should focus on gaining a deeper understanding of how ADHD and ODD symptoms this approach retains a dimensional perspective and captures individuals who may not meet diagnostic criteria but still face functional challenges. Some limitations should be acknowledged. Our approach relies on the assumption that ADHD/ODD symptoms are exogenous to both income and the mediators, conditional on observed covariates. Symptoms were measured in adolescence and income was assessed in adulthood, thereby establishing a clear temporal ordering. This timing supports the plausibility of treating the symptoms as exogenous to income, although the possibility of unmeasured confounding remains. Unmeasured confounding may bias estimates if factors such as personality traits or time preferences affect both mediators and income [72, 73]. Some mediators were measured at age 16, potentially overlapping symptom assessment. This raises temporal concerns, especially given the theoretical role of mediators as downstream mechanisms. Likewise, income was measured at age 30, providing only a snapshot of early adulthood earnings, which may not capture long-term economic trajectories. In addition, excluding participants with zero income— necessary for log-transforming the income variable—may slightly limit generalizability to those fully detached from the labor market or facing severe economic hardship. However, this improves the robustness and interpretability of the estimates and likely has minimal impact, as these cases represent a small share of the sample. Furthermore, ADHD and ODD symptoms were assessed at age 16, a developmental stage at which puberty-related changes may amplify the expression of symptoms, potentially introducing an element of bias [74]. Group definitions were based on a pooled (non-sexspecific) 95th percentile cutoff, which may underrepresent symptom severity in females due to known sex differences in symptom distribution and expression. This may affect crosssex comparability and should be interpreted accordingly. Fewer findings were observed for the ODD-only group, which may reflect true attenuation of effects over time as noted in the discussion. However, the small group size likely limited statistical power to detect effects and must also be considered when interpreting null findings. Furthermore, the study is drawn from two provinces in Finland and the cohort is ethnically and socioeconomically homogenous. While this minimizes cultural variability, it limits generalizability to more diverse populations and contexts. Using a single proxy for each capital domain may oversimplify complex constructs. Our alternative indicators of human capital—work experience and occupational status—were less appropriate given the relatively young age of participants (30 years), which limits accumulated work experience. Specifically, during middle childhood IC shows rapid improvements as the prefrontal cortex matures [4]. In adolescence, IC may reach near-adult levels but remains sensitive to emotional and social influences by imbalance between emotion-related neural systems and still-developing cognitive control network, rendering IC less stable [5]. Psychosocially, there is a relationship between greater IC and better classroom self-regulation, improved peer relationships, and fewer behavioral problems [6]. Edu cationally, IC is positively associated with classroom learn ing, sustained attention, and academic performance [2, 7]. Conversely, deficits in IC could lead to learning difficulties, poor academic performance, and emotional problems. These deficits are more pronounced in children and adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) due to its key characteristics such as inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity [2, 8]. As a key component of cognitive and socioemotional develop ment [1], IC supports self-regulation, including emotional control, impulse inhibition, and adherence to social norms [2]. Developmentally, IC is fundamental to brain maturation and cognitive growth during childhood and adolescence, reflecting protracted development of the prefrontal cortex Yiwei Min minyiwei@tamu.edu 1 Department of Kinesiology and Sport Management, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX 77843, USA 2 Qiaokou District Government Agency Kindergarten, Wuhan City, Hubei Province 430000, China Abstract This meta-analysis aims to identify intervention parameters (e.g., intensity, session time, frequency, and intervention dura tion) of targeted physical activity (PA) to improve inhibition control (IC) in children and adolescents with ADHD. The sys tematic search was conducted across PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library. In this meta-analysis we assessed the overall effect of PA interventions and then conducted subgroup meta-analyses and meta-regression to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. Finally, we checked publication biases and performed sensitivity analyses. Sixteen stud ies (591 participants aged 7–17 years) were included. The result showed that targeted PA interventions improved IC with high heterogeneity (SMD = 0.71, 95% CI [0.30, 1.11], I2 = 83.11%). Long-term interventions improved IC (SMD = 0.84, 95% CI [0.36, 1.31], p < 0.01), whereas acute interventions did not. Although no statistically significant group difference in long-term interventions was found (p > 0.05), examination of individual studies suggested greater improvements with session time around 60 min (SMD = 1.43), 2–3 times/week (SMD = 1.04), and intervention duration of at least 8 weeks (≥8 weeks: SMD = 0.49; ≥12 weeks: SMD = 1.19). Meta-regression revealed an inverted U-shaped relationship between frequency and intervention effects (βfrequency = 2.15; βfrequency*frequency = -0.57). Targeted PA interventions could improve IC in children and adolescents with ADHD, particularly designed with a moderate frequency. Although session time and intervention duration in long-term interventions showed no statistical significance in this meta-analysis, examination of individual studies revealed their promising results. Further investigations are therefore recommended. Current treatments of IC deficits rely on pharmacological approaches [10]. These approaches, however, target primar ily core symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity rather than improving IC [11, 12]. Also, the benefits of medica tions are not sustainable in the absence of prescriptions. What’s worse, long-term use of medication therapies (e.g., amphetamines or atomoxetine/stimulant) may elicit or exac erbate psychotic symptoms in children and adolescents with ADHD [13]. Concerns about pharmacological treatments’ side effects, long-term reliance, and limited improvement in IC have spurred interests in alternative or complementary methods [11]. Physical activity as an alternative treatment In response to limitations of pharmacological treatments, physical activity (PA), particularly targeted PA, has emerged as a non-medical and cost-effective intervention for improving IC in children and adolescents with ADHD [14]. In this review, targeted PA refers to physical activities that are intentionally designed to improve executive func tion. Engaging in targeted PA (e.g., aerobic activities, ball games) may enhance the function of frontal brain, contribut ing to the improvement of IC [15]. These cognitive benefits are mainly associated with sufficient nerve stimuli through release of brain derived neurotrophic factors (BDNF), and an increased level of cerebral blood flow [16]. When engag ing in PA, children and adolescents with ADHD are required to show coordination, sustained effort, and motor planning, which help them maintain focus, practice self-control, and channel hyperactivity in proper physical movements [17]. Activities, such as soccer, may enhance IC by activating the prefrontal cortex through repeated demands for participa tion and response inhibition in dynamic and unpredictable environments [18]. To examine the effect of PA on IC in children and ado lescents with ADHD, researchers have compared different PA types (e.g., open-skill vs. close-skill, aerobic activity vs. cognitively engaging activity) [14, 19–21]. In this text, open-skill activities involve movements in unpredictable and dynamic environments (e.g., table tennis), and closedskill activities are performed in a relatively stable and pre dictable environment (e.g., running) [19]. Aerobic activities refer to sustainable, rhythmic, and continuous exercises (e.g., swimming) that elevate the heart rate and breathing by mainly engaging large muscle groups [22]. Cognitively engaging activities (e.g., exergaming) are goal-directed and characterized with cognitive demands such as atten tion flexibility, inhibition control, planning [23]. However, meta-analysis studies focusing on children and adolescents with ADHD revealed that, regardless of types, targeted PA interventions generally yielded moderate improvements in executive function, including IC, and the effectiveness did not significantly differ across activity types [14, 21, 24]. For example, Song and his collogues found both open-skill and close-skill PA improved IC but no significant differences between the two groups [14]. Likewise, Liang reported there was no group difference between aerobic activity and cogni tively engaging activity [21]. These results post a challenge for scholars and practitioners to pinpoint “best practices” to improve IC in children and adolescents with ADHD. Thus, it may be more meaningful to examine common interven tion parameters that underline all types of physical activity, such as intensity, session time, frequency, and intervention duration. Physical activity intervention parameters Regarding the four intervention parameters, intensity refers to the level of physiological load achieved by participants during PA, usually expressed as a percentage of maximum heart rate (HRmax). Session time is defined as the average duration of PA for each session, measured in minutes (min). Frequency is the number of times by which a participant engages in PA per week. Intervention duration is the length of time from the beginning to the end of the entire interven tion, usually in weeks. Among these parameters, intensity has received most attention in research. From a neurocognitive perspective, researchers found moderate-intensity PA improved IC by promoting dopamine release and prefrontal cortex activa tion without depleting attentional resources [12]. This effect can be seen in meta-analysis studies that show moderateto-vigorous intensity PA yielded optimal results for IC in ADHD participants [25, 26]. Researchers, however, found excessive intensity may cause cognitive fatigue and there fore limit IC improvement [27]. These findings indicate that optimal IC task performance occurred during PA at a mod erate intensity level [28]. Moreover, emerging neurophysio logical evidence suggests that excessively high intensity PA may lead to downregulation of prefrontal cortex activation and induce negative affective responses (e.g., discomfort and frustration), which can consequently impair execu tive functioning [29]. Interestingly, PA with low intensity, such as Yoga and Tai Chi, also showed positive effects on IC, likely due to their high cognitive demands rather than physical exertion [30, 31]. Despite the growing body of lit erature focusing on intensity, other intervention parameters including session time, frequency, and duration, have often been overlooked. Therefore, this meta-analysis will not only examine the effect of intensity based on previous studies, 1 3 728

European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry (2026) 35:727–747 but also explore the dose-response relationship between these parameters and the effectiveness of PA interventions. Session time and frequency determine the balance between stimulation and recovery. A 60-min per session is considered as the effective setting to balance the neural stimulation and fatigue [23, 32]. Shorter session times (e.g., < 30 min) may not yield meaningful improvement in IC, while extended session times (e.g., >90 min) may result in diminishing cognitive benefits due to mental fatigue [27, 33]. For frequency, 1–3 sessions per week appear to be most effective due to neuroplastic adaption cycles [2, 34, 35]. Although researchers reported cognitive benefits might be associated with higher frequencies [36], these benefits could be offset when combining with high intensity or lon ger session time, largely due to the reduction in compliance and cognitive resource exhaustion [33]. Thus, a moderate frequency combined with proper intensity and optimal ses sion time may provide a sustainable improvement on IC in children and adolescents with ADHD. For intervention duration, a growing body of stud ies suggest that long-term interventions were effective in accumulating cognitive benefits and sustaining measurable improvement [37–40]. Concerning time efficiency, research ers also explored the effectiveness of PA with a minimum duration. Some studies asserted that acute interventions (i.e., a single session of PA without repeated engagement over time) could enhance IC via short neuroplastic adap tions and behavioral improvement [12, 15, 41]. Other stud ies, however, argued that acute interventions might not yield significant effects or sustained improvement on IC [21, 42]. These conflicting findings highlight the need of identifying effective parameters within PA interventions to improve IC in children and adolescents with ADHD [43]. While the benefits of PA for behavior and cognition in children and adolescents with ADHD have been described in the literature, there are still gaps. First, although many stud ies assessed how intensity moderated the effectiveness of PA on IC, few have explored the effect of time parameters, i.e., session time, frequency, and duration. Concurrently, schol ars examining children and adolescents with ADHD found that heterogeneity in intervention outcomes might be due to intervention parameters rather than PA types [21]. Mean while, WHO guidelines and scholars also emphasized the research gap in dose-response studies regarding the effect of intervention parameters in improving IC in children and adolescents with ADHD [2, 35, 44]. This lack of analysis on how intervention parameters bring improvement in IC may limit the development of effective and targeted intervention designs. These gaps, hence, necessitate the need of a sys tematic meta-analysis to synthesize existing evidence and identify dose-response relationships, translating fragmented findings into an optimal PA intervention design. The present study Given the aforementioned reasons, it is necessary to identify how these parameters affect the outcomes of PA interven tions [43]. With this purpose, this meta-analysis will focus on two research questions: (1) Do targeted PA interventions lead to measurable improvements in IC among children and adolescents with ADHD? (2) How do frequency, intensity, session time, and intervention duration moderate the effec tiveness of PA programs on IC respectively? By conducting the present study, we hope to provide a unique perspective about how each of the intervention parameters affects the overall effectiveness of an intervention. The results can be further used by researchers and practitioners to design effec tive PA interventions for improving IC in children and ado lescents with ADHD. Method Search strategy This meta-analysis was registered in the Prospective System atic Evaluation Registry (PROSPERO, CRD42024597006) and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guide lines [45]. Search strategy was performed across four data bases, including PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and Cochrane Library, that focus on biomedical research and healthcare interventions. The initial search was conducted from October 16th to November 9th, 2024, and was last updated on January 13th, 2025. Figure 1 presents the proce dure of the search. We searched titles, abstracts, and subject headings by using medical terms (MeSH) and relevant tree words, such as physical activity, executive function, children, adoles cent, and ADHD. The Boolean Operators (AND, OR) for keywords combination are presented in Appendix Table 5. We also used a handsearching method to ensure a complete capture of the literature. We reviewed previous relevant meta-analysis studies and cross-checked references that may meet the inclusion criteria. Screening and study eligibility The inclusion criteria based on the PICOS principle (P: Population or Patient; I: Intervention; C: Comparison; O: Outcome; S: Study design) included: (1) Participants were children and adolescents with ADHD of any sub types aged > 5 years and < 18 years. Referred to previous systematic review and meta-analy sis studies, an acute intervention was defined as a one-time, single-session intervention with no ongoing cycles [55], and a long-term intervention lasts at least four weeks [56–58]. To be noted, in the present study, all included acute inter ventions were single-session designs, while all long-term intervention lasted four weeks or longer. Particularly in this study, acute and long-term interventions differ fundamen tally in how the four intervention parameters are included. An acute intervention contains a single session and therefore only includes two parameters: intensity and session time [15]. In contrast, long-term interventions are often repeated over multiple weeks, involving all four intervention param eters [57, 58]. Then, based on the characteristics of included studies and other experimental studies, the intervention duration was firstly coded as acute intervention and longterm intervention separately, and the long-term intervention was then categorized as ≥ 4 weeks [59], ≥ 8 weeks [34], and ≥ 12 weeks [55]. Accordingly, if heterogeneity exists, subgroup analysis for acute intervention was focused on the effect of intensity and session time on IC, and for long-term intervention we assessed the effect of all four parameters— intensity, session time, frequency, and intervention duration. Assessment of the methodological quality of included studies Quality of methodology of included articles was assessed using the Physiotherapy Evidence Database Quality Scale (PEDro scale). The PEDro scale assesses the clarity of par ticipants eligibility, method of random allocation, blind ing of subjects, assessors, and therapists, compliance rate, intention-to-treatment analysis, between-group statistical comparisons, as well as point estimates and variances. It includes 11 scales in four categories: “poor” (scores 0–4), “fair” (4–5), “good” (6–8), and “excellent” (9–10) [60]. Studies with a PEDro score < 4 were excluded, as such scores indicate a poor methodological quality and high risk of bias [46, 47]. The assessment was conducted by the first two authors. Disagreements were discussed until a consen sus was reached. Data analysis Focusing on the research questions, we first used Stata 18.0 software to assess the overall effect of PA interventions on IC in children and adolescents with ADHD. All effect sizes were calculated using unadjusted means and standard using Covidence. Two authors (Min and Chen) indepen dently screened the title and abstract of the remaining studies according to the inclusion and exclusion criteria. During this stage, reviews, meta-analyses, and irrelevant studies—such as those not mentioned key terms related to PA, ADHD, or IC—were excluded. Full texts of potential eligible studies were then retrieved and assessed for eligi bility. The final decision was made after screening the full text of included studies. In case of disagreement, there was a joint discussion and a consensus reached between the two authors (Min and Chen). After screening the full text and assessing quality, the data were extracted, including information about: (1) first author, year of publication, and study area, (2) study design, (3) subject information (sample size, sex ratio, age), (4) physical activity intervention (type of intervention, exercise intensity, time of one session, frequency of physical activ ity, and total duration of intervention), (5) inhibition control measures and outcomes, including mean and standard devi ations (SDs) of pre-test data and post-test data. If the study reported standard errors (SE) only, we converted SEs to SDs by using an established formula [49, 50]. Studies that did not report these values (e.g., mean, SD or SE, and sample size) were excluded. If multiple publications reported over lapping data from a same database, only the most recently published study was included. If there were two or more IC measurements, only the data with the most commonly used assessment was extracted. The study selection and data extraction process is presented in Fig. 1. Extracted outcome data (means, SDs, and sample sizes) were subsequently used to compute standardized mean differences (Hedges’ g) with 95% confidence intervals, as detailed in the Data Analysis section. Data coding and management Intensity was coded using heart rate maximum (HRmax) categories, with reported and evaluated intensity < 60% HRmax considered low intensity activity (LPA), 60–75% HRmax as moderate intensity activity (MPA), >75% HRmax as vigorous intensity activity (VPA), and ≥ 60% HRmax as moderate-to-vigorous intensity activity (MVPA) [51]. When studies reported MVPA as a combined intensity cat egory or reported a heart rate range (e.g., 70–80% HRmax) overlapping moderate and vigorous zones, the intensity was classified as MVPA. This coding strategy follows the PA guidelines used in previous meta-analysis studies [21, 35, 52]. Session time was coded into five categories: 30 min or less, [30 min, 45 min), [45 min, 60 min), [60 min, 90 min) and 90 min or longer [34, 44, 53]. Results Search results A total of 639 articles were retrieved from four electronic databases: Web of Science (n = 295), Cochrane Library (n = 150), PubMed (n = 135), and Embase (n = 59). After remov ing duplicates (n = 165) and automatically excluded reviews (n = 189), 285 records remained for title and abstract screen ing. Of these, 120 records were excluded for not meeting the inclusion criteria (e.g., meta-analysis, participants with autism and/or medical treatment). The remaining 165 arti cles were eligible for full-text screening. During full-text screening, 58 articles were excluded due to inaccessibility of the full text [72, 73], 25 for ineligible populations (e.g., participant with Autism Spectrum Disorder) [74–77], 27 for irrelevant outcomes (e.g., motor function) [78, 79], 24 for unsuitable study designs (e.g., not RCT) [80, 81], 13 for missing data [82, 83], and 2 for non-English languages (e.g., Spanish) [84, 85]. The remaining studies passed the method ological quality threshold (PEDro >4), and no studies were excluded at this stage. Finally, 16 articles were included in the meta-analysis [39–42, 59, 86–96] (see Fig. 1). Description of studies The total 16 studies included 591 participants (75.13% male) aged 7–17 years. Among them, four studies were con ducted in China, three in Iran, two in Tunisia, two in the United Kingdom, two in the United States, and one each in Italy, Korea, and Turkey. The characteristics of the studies are presented in Appendix Table 6,7,8,9. For the intervention parameters, eight studies reported moderate to vigorous intensities at an average of 50% to 80% maximum heart rate (HRmax). Specifically, three interventions employed MPA, four applied MVPA, and nine did not report PA intensity. Each session for included deviations reported in the studies (or converted from SEs) to ensure consistency across studies. We used the standardized mean difference (SMD, Hedges’ g) to represent the effect size of the intervention, and reported 95% confidence inter vals (CI) to assess the confidence of effect sizes [61]. The effect size was calculated using a random-effects model due to the nature of experimental studies [62–64]. SMD values < 0.2, from 0.2 to 0.5, from 0.5 to 0.8, ≥ 0.8 were considered as fair, small, moderate, and large effect sizes, respectively [61]. The Forest plot was used to present the result of metaanalysis. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2. When I2 ≤ 25%, it means low heterogeneity among studies, 25% < I2≤ 50% means moderate heterogeneity, 50%< I2 ≤ 75% means substantial heterogeneity, and I2 >75% means high hetero geneity [65]. The Galbraith plot was used to illustrate the heterogeneity results. Then, we conducted subgroup meta-analyses and metaregression analyses to investigate potential moderators of intervention effects. These analyses were planned as part of the research aim to explore intervention parameters but were statistically conducted only when heterogeneity exceeded I2 >50%. This practice is in line with best practices for metaanalytic methodology [50, 66]. If I2 was larger than 50%, we conducted subgroup meta-analyses stratified by intervention durations (acute vs. long-term), as explained previously. Between-group heterogeneity was tested using Qb, with p < 0.05 indicating statistically significant subgroup differ ences [64]. If significant between-group heterogeneity was detected, further subgroup meta-analyses were performed based on key intervention parameters [21, 50]. Specifi cally, for long-term interventions, subgroup analyses were conducted according to intensity, session time, frequency, and intervention duration. For acute interventions, intensity and session time were examined. A p-value less than 0.05 in these computations indicated a statistically significant mod erating effect of the corresponding intervention parameter on IC. Although intervention intensity was pre-specified as a moderator of interest, subgroup meta-analysis or metaregression for intensity was not conducted due to the lim ited number of studies reporting clearly defined intensity. Instead, we did a descriptive summary of effect sizes across studies categorized by intervention intensity (e.g., LPA, MPA, or MVPA) to explore its potential impacts on IC. Next, we used R software with the metafor package to examine potential dose-response relationships through meta-regression using SMDs as the dependent variable and session time, frequency, and intervention duration as contin uous predictors. European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry (2026) 35:727–747 Discussion This meta-analysis aimed to explore the effect of targeted PA interventions and the impact of intervention parameters on IC in children and adolescents with ADHD. The results showed that targeted PA interventions could improve IC in this population. Specifically, long-term interventions brought about a significant improvement in IC, but acute interventions did not. For intervention parameters, although subgroup meta-analyses of long-term interventions did not yield statistically significant between-group differences, examination of individual studies in each subgroup iden tified a moderate effect. Using meta-regression, we found an inverted U-shaped relationship between the intervention effect and PA frequency, with an estimated maximum effect occur at approximately 2 times/week. These findings sup port the effectiveness of targeted PA interventions and pro vide evidence for designing effective interventions. From the perspective of neurocog nitive mechanisms, MVPA can activate the function of the prefrontal cortex and stimulate the release of dopamine, norepinephrine, and BDNF to promote neuroplasticity [15, 16, 100, 101]. Excessive stimuli, on the other hand, may cause physical fatigue and deplete cognitive resources for IC [33, 103]. LPA (e.g., Yoga, Tai Chi) also showed a mea surable improvement in IC [30, 31], and this effect may be explained by sensorimotor integration and cognitive pro cesses. Both of them emphasize cognitive challenges rather than demanding high levels of intensity [33]. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to the nature of descriptive summary that limits the strength of causal inference. Time parameters This meta-analysis explored the doseresponse relationship between PA intervention parameters and IC in children and adolescents with ADHD. While group differences for session time, frequency, and interven tion duration were not statistically significant, examination of individual studies in each subgroup allowed us to observe a moderate effect. Specifically, interventions with session time around 60 min, ≤ 3 times/week, and duration more than 8 weeks seemed to be more effective to improve IC than other categories. Meta-regression analyses showed that an inverted U-shaped relationship between PA frequency and intervention effect size. For session time, individual studies with interventions around 60 min per session showed a large effect. This is aligned with the recommended exercise time per day by the WHO guidelines [35]. Likewise, Tomporowski and collogues found that around an hour of PA allowed chil dren and adolescents with ADHD to raise the arousal level that was conducive to cognitive improvement without overstimulation [37]. From a neurocognitive viewpoint, moderate session time (e.g., around 60 min) is sufficient to bring nerve stimulation (e.g., increased cerebral blood flow) while avoiding attention exhaustion [32]. In this study, shorter sessions seemed unable to provide sufficient stimulus for the improvement of cognitive functioning, and longer sessions led to fatigue that could diminish the effectiveness of PA [27, 33]. Meanwhile, based on the dualtask load theory, since executive function is an advanced cognitive function, the effect of PA will be affected by the allocation of limited cognitive and attentional resources [103]. If the cognitive load of the task (e.g., higher inten sity activity, complex motor skill, or longer time per ses sion) is too high, it may lead to the depletion of cognitive signaling, particularly in the prefrontal cortex associated with attention regulation and executive function [2, 101]. Regular participation in MVPA has been shown to upreg ulate BDNF expression, which may help enhance neural connectivity and cognitive flexibility [96]. Also, PA is known to increase the release of neurotransmitters such as dopamine and norepinephrine, both of which are essential in executive functioning and are dysregulated in individu als with ADHD [102]. Moreover, PA interventions could enhance cerebral blood flow that carries oxygen and nutri ents to the brain, improving metabolic resources needed to support higher-level cognitive processing like IC in chil dren and adolescents with ADHD [32]. Interpretations of heterogeneity The overall meta-analysis revealed high heterogeneity (I2 = 83.11%), suggesting significant variability in the intervention effects across studies. To better understand this variability, we firstly examined the acute and longterm intervention groups separately. The acute interven tion group showed no heterogeneity (I2 = 0%), indicating consistent effects across one-time interventions, and this result made further moderation analysis unnecessary. On the contrary, analysis of the long-term intervention group revealed high heterogeneity (I2 = 84.96%), warranting further exploration of moderators. Subsequent subgroup meta-analyses based on session time, frequency, and inter vention duration, however, did not yield statistically sig nificant between-group difference (p >0.05), possibly due to the limited number of studies within subgroups. How ever, examination of individual studies in each subgroup resulted in statistical significance, indicating the interven tion delivered 2–3 times per week, lasting around 60 min, and with intervention duration of ≥ 8 weeks were better than other categories. In addition, meta-regression analy sis found an inverted-U relationship between frequency and intervention effect, suggesting that PA interventions at moderate frequencies may be more beneficial for cogni tive outcomes, while those at very low or high frequen cies might be less effective. Although this finding is in line with neurocognitive theories on arousal and cognitive load [68], it should be interpreted with caution due to the lim ited number of studies in each frequency category. Moreover, IC is complex executive function involving sustained attention, cognitive flexibility, and inhibition, requiring repeated activation and strengthening of relevant neural pathways to observe change [2]. The prefrontal cortex, critical for IC, under goes slow and experience-dependent plasticity, which is less likely to be shaped by short-term interventions [23]. In contrast, long-term interventions provide sufficient time and repeated practice for children and adolescents with ADHD, contributing to neural adaptations and consolidate the improvement in IC [40]. Through repeated and sus tained PA interventions, the increase in the activation level of the prefrontal cortex in children with ADHD directly contributes to IC improvement and neuroplasticity [16, 58, 100]. Another explanation may lie in the limited num ber of eligible acute intervention studies (k = 3) that has restricted statistical power. Moreover, all included acute interventions had a relatively small sample size, inflat ing the risk of imprecise estimates and wide confidence intervals. Therefore, while acute interventions may hold some promise in empirical studies, current meta-analytic evidence is insufficient to draw a firm conclusion. Future research with large sample can continue to explore the effect of different intervention design in children and ado lescents with ADHD. The findings of this meta-analysis are consistent with those of previous studies, demonstrating that PA interven tions could improve executive function, particularly IC, in children and adolescents with ADHD [24, 58, 99, 106]. Several meta-analysis studies found that targeted PA inter ventions, such as cognitively engaging PA or structured programs, were associated with improvement of executive function [24, 38, 110]. Compared to these reviews, the pres ent study focused on IC as a specific executive function and investigated how intervention parameters, particularly for session time, frequency, intervention duration, may moder ate intervention effectiveness. While most previous reviews examined general effect of PA or compared types of PA, few studies explored how specific intervention parameters influ ence outcomes. Specifically, researchers highlighted the potential of MVPA but did not quantify the dose-response relationship between intervention parameters and cognitive outcomes [26, 111]. Our study adds new findings by identi fying an inverted U-shaped relationship between frequency and intervention effect, suggesting that PA with moderate frequencies may be more beneficial than that with higher resources and then hinder the improvement of executive functioning [104]. For frequency, meta-regression results revealed an inverted U-shaped relationship, with optimal intervention effects observed around 2 times per week. This finding indicates that the frequency of 1–3 sessions/week was most effective for the improvement of IC, which aligns with neurocognitive models suggesting that moderate fre quencies may yield cognitive benefits by balancing neu ral stimulation with adequate recovery [2, 17]. Although daily PA may theoretically improve executive function, practical factors, such as fatigue and adherence, may have a negative impact on the effectiveness of PA [105]. With 1–3 session per week, the intervention could provide suf ficient time for children and adolescents with ADHD to recover from mental and physical fatigue and maintain engagement over time. A higher frequency, however, may lead to overstimulation and inadequate recovery and therefore diminish the intervention’s cognitive ben efits [12, 27, 33]. The U-shaped relationship between frequency and intervention effects, however, should be interpreted with caution. Because the number of studies within each frequency category was limited and unequal, the statistical power to detect robust moderator effects was constrained. This relationship may be also influenced by unmeasured confounding factors. For instance, partici pant characteristics (e.g., age, gender, ADHD severity, or baseline executive function) are known to moderate inter vention effects but were not consistently reported across included studies [106]. In addition, variation in the types of PA may require different optimal frequencies to achieve cognitive benefits [14, 38]. Due to limited reporting in included studies, we were unable to examine the inter action between frequency and these potential moderators in the present study. Future research might use muti-arm randomized designs to explore these potential interactive relationships. Regarding intervention duration, while acute interven tions appeared to have no significant impacts on IC in chil dren and adolescents with ADHD, long-term interventions brought about a moderate to large improvement. While some studies claimed that acute interventions (e.g., acute aerobic exercise with 30 min) could temporarily improve IC [17, 41, 107], this meta-analysis did not find a signifi cant effect, which could be explained by the temporarily increase in neurotransmitter levels [108]. Fourth, this study only focused on four inter vention parameters but did not explore other moderating factors such as age or gender. This is because most stud ies did not report data for different age or gender groups separately. Therefore, we were unable to extract suffi cient data for these variables. Meanwhile, small number of available studies further limited the feasibility of sub group analyses. Future research can examine how these variables interact with each other. Finally, this study did not account for different ADHD subtypes or severity lev els, again due to the limited number of studies reporting ADHD subtypes, which may have moderated the effective ness of interventions. Further studies may take the ADHD subtype or severity into consideration to establish effective PA intervention protocols. Nevertheless, this meta-analy sis provides new insights into and evidence for interven tion design to improve IC in children and adolescents with ADHD. These studies would facilitate the development of more precise and personalized PA intervention protocols for youth with ADHD, and assist practitioners to design intervention therapies for and enhance executive function in children and adolescents with ADHD. Conclusion This meta-analysis found targeted PA interventions were associated with improvements in IC in children and ado lescents with ADHD. Long-term interventions appeared to be more beneficial than acute interventions. Although group differences for session time, frequency and inter vention duration in long-term interventions did not yield statistical significance, examination of individual empiri cal studies suggested that moderate frequencies, session time around 60 min, and longer intervention duration may be associated with more favorable outcomes. Addi tionally, meta-regression indicated a potential inverted U-shape relationship between frequency and intervention effect, which may need further investigation. Finally, we hope this meta-analysis may provide preliminary insight to motivate future researchers invest more effort in this area. Meanwhile, the results may assist practitioners in design ing PA-based intervention programs for children and ado lescents with ADHD. or lower frequencies. In addition, examination of individual studies in subgroup meta-analyses suggested that interven tions with session time around 60 min and intervention duration of at least 8 weeks may bring cognitive benefits, which offers preliminary evidence and indicates potential directions for future research. Limitations and implications While providing valuable insights into how PA interven tions and parameters affect IC in children and adolescents with ADHD, this study has certain limitations. First, a relatively large number of full-text articles were inacces sible and therefore excluded, which may have introduced selection bias and limited the comprehensiveness of our synthesis. Second, the small number of studies included in subgroup meta-analyses, particularly those reporting intensity, limited the statistical power to detect modera tor effects. Also, due to the limited and unequal numbers within each category, we were unable to conduct subgroup meta-analysis or meta-regression analysis on PA intensity. Future research may include more studies with reported intervention parameters to further investigate doseresponse relationships. Detailed reporting of exercise char acteristics, such as objective intensity measures (e.g., heart rate, RPE), would allow for more accurate dose-response estimations. Future studies are also recommended to adopt multi-arm randomized controlled trials comparing specific intervention parameters (e.g., different frequency, ses sion time, or intensity level. Third, as stated in the intro duction, we did not include PA types as a moderator in this study, because previous meta-analysis studies have already examined but did not find any moderation effect of PA on IC [14]. Also, the total number of empirical studies included in the present meta-analysis is relatively small. The types of PA employed in these studies are even few and far between. Therefore, dividing these studies based on PA types would make the number in the subcategories unbalanced and negligible. Consequently, continuing with subgroup- or meta-regression analyses would compromise statistical power and may yield misleading results. RESEARCH European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry (2026) 35:1133–1149 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00787-025-02906-3 Yongzhe Hou tedyong@163.com Yanping Shu syp_8053@163.com Qin Zhang 1402974053@qq.com Jiaoying Liu liujiaoying0418@163.com Qiang He GZ_HeQiang@163.com 1 Department of Psychiatry of Women and Children, The Second People’s Hospital of Guizhou Province, No. 206 South Section of Xintian Avenue, Yunyan District, Guiyang, Guizhou Province 550000, China 2 Department of Radiology, The Second People’s Hospital of Guizhou Province, Guiyang, China Abstract Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder that often persists from child hood into adolescence and adulthood. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) provides valuable insights into the intrinsic neural activity associated with ADHD. However, despite increasing neuroimaging research, the developmental specificity of spontaneous alterations in brain activity in children and adolescents with ADHD remains poorly understood. A comprehensive activation likelihood estimation (ALE) meta-analysis was performed on rs-fMRI data to investigate alterations in spontaneous brain activity in children and adolescents with ADHD compared with healthy controls (HCs). A contrast analysis was conducted to assess potential overlap in altered brain regions between the child and adolescent ADHD groups. The robustness of the findings was evaluated using a jackknife sensitivity analysis. A sys tematic review of the literature identified 28 rs-fMRI studies (1019 ADHD patients and 943 HCs). In children with ADHD, ALE revealed decreased spontaneous neural activity in the left middle frontal gyrus, superior frontal gyrus, medial frontal gyrus, precentral gyrus, and subgyral region, with no regions showing increased activity. In adolescents with ADHD, increased activity was observed in the bilateral paracentral lobule, left postcentral gyrus, and medial frontal gyrus, whereas decreased activity was found in the cerebellar tonsil, uvula, declive, anterior lobe, and superior/medial frontal gyrus. No significant clusters were identified in the contrast analyses. The jackknife sensitivity analysis demonstrated robustness in 9 of 17 iterations for children and 4 of 5 iterations for adolescent-specific cerebellar findings. Spontaneous alterations in brain activity in children and adolescents with ADHD reflect developmentally distinct neural mechanisms and may guide future age-specific neuroimaging research. European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry (2026) 35:1133–1149 Introduction Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a highly prevalent and heterogeneous neurodevelopmental disorder that is driven primarily by polygenic genetic influences and characterized by structural and functional abnormalities within corticostriatal circuits. These neural alterations are closely linked to deficits in attention, impulse control, and executive function [1]. ADHD commonly manifests during early childhood and often continues into adolescence and adulthood, with a global prevalence estimated at approxi mately 6–7% in pediatric populations and 4–5% among adults [2]. Despite recent advances in the delineation of the roles of large-scale brain networks and neuroanatomical mechanisms in the pathophysiology of ADHD [3, 4], further investigation into age-specific neurofunctional alterations remains essential to elucidate its developmental trajectory and heterogeneity. Researchers have hypothesized that neurodevelopmental abnormalities in patients with ADHD reflect a delay in brain maturation, which contributes to impairments in late-devel oping cognitive functions [5, 6]. Neuroimaging evidence has repeatedly shown atypical development across largescale brain systems in patients with ADHD, with consistent disruptions observed in the prefrontal cortex, basal ganglia, and cerebellum [7]. These abnormalities are reflected in compromised white matter integrity and altered patterns of functional connectivity, underscoring widespread structural and functional dysregulation in patients with the disorder. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rsfMRI) is considered more suitable than task-based fMRI for pediatric populations because it allows the assessment of intrinsic brain activity under natural, task-free conditions [8]. A range of voxel-level indices, including amplitudes of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), dynamic ALFF (dALFF), fractional ALFF (fALFF), and regional homoge neity (ReHo), are routinely applied in neuroimaging studies to capture intrinsic fluctuations in resting-state brain activity [9]. ALFF and fALFF capture the strength of slow oscilla tory activity linked to local neuronal excitability, whereas dALFF extends this framework by quantifying temporal variability in ALFF signals, thereby reflecting dynamic fluctuations in regional activity over time. Moreover, ReHo assesses the local synchronization of blood oxygen leveldependent (BOLD) signal time series among neighboring voxels, offering a measure of regional functional coherence [10]. Rs-fMRI has become an essential modality for inves tigating intrinsic brain activity in individuals with ADHD. Previous studies using ALFF, fALFF, dALFF, and ReHo have reported aberrant spontaneous activity across multiple brain regions, including the prefrontal cortex, sensorimotor areas, parietal lobe, basal ganglia, and cerebellum [11–38]. These alterations are believed to reflect the neurophysi ological basis of core ADHD symptoms such as inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity. However, although many studies have reported resting-state functional abnormalities in both children and adolescents with ADHD, the findings have been inconsistent and remain a subject of debate. Given the heterogeneity of previous findings, a quantita tive meta-analytic framework is warranted to identify con sistent and replicable patterns of altered spontaneous brain activity in individuals with ADHD. Activation likelihood estimation (ALE) offers a robust coordinate-based approach to synthesize voxel-level neuroimaging results across inde pendent studies, thereby increasing statistical power and mitigating interstudy variability [39]. ALE provides a rigor ous quantitative framework that synthesizes findings across independent studies, allowing the identification of spatially convergent brain regions and yielding more reliable infer ences about functional alterations under specific conditions. Nevertheless, Samea et al. reported no significant conver gence across structural and functional alterations in indi viduals with ADHD, possibly because of the inclusion of heterogeneous imaging modalities and the lack of restric tion to rs-fMRI data alone [40]. Lukito et al. utilized seedbased mapping (SDM) to examine structural alterations and observed reduced gray matter volume in the ventromedial orbitofrontal cortex of ADHD patients; however, their study did not investigate alterations in spontaneous brain activity during the resting state [41]. Chen et al. identified overlap ping and modality-specific abnormalities in the orbitofrontal cortex and other regions without age stratification and using SDM rather than ALE [42]. Sutcubasi et al. conducted a seed-based resting-state meta-analysis and reported default mode network (DMN) dysconnectivity in ADHD patients but did not assess spontaneous activity using ALE [43], and Cortese et al. did not observe a consistent connectivity con vergence in an ALE meta-analysis [44]. We addressed these gaps by conducting an ALE metaanalysis to examine alterations in spontaneous brain activity in children and adolescents with ADHD. We hypothesized that, compared with healthy controls (HCs), children and adolescents with ADHD would exhibit distinct, age-specific patterns of spontaneous neural activity. Additionally, con trast analyses were conducted to examine shared versus dis tinct regional abnormalities across age groups. The findings of this meta-analysis may provide novel insights into the age-dependent neurofunctional mechanisms of ADHD and a foundation for more developmentally informed diagnostic and intervention strategies. 1 3 1134

European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry (2026) 35:1133–1149 Materials and methods We preregistered the study protocol on PROSPERO on April 12, 2024 (CRD42024531049) to promote transparency and minimize the risk of bias. A summary of any deviations in the protocol is provided in the Supplementary Table 7. Literature search Following the PRISMA guidelines [45], we systematically searched four major electronic databases, namely, PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and CNKI, for studies published up to December 19, 2024. The search strategy included the following keywords: (“attention deficit hyperactivity dis order” OR “ADHD”) AND (“adolescent” OR “child” OR “children” OR “teenager” OR “youth” OR “pediatric”) AND (“resting-state functional magnetic resonance imag ing” OR “rs-fMRI” OR “functional MRI” OR “fMRI”) AND (“amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations” OR “ALFF” OR “low frequency fluctuation” OR “regional homogene ity” OR “ReHo” OR “homogeneity” OR “brain activity”). We screened the reference lists of relevant studies to iden tify potentially missed studies and minimize omissions. Inclusion and exclusion criteria Studies were considered eligible for inclusion if they met the following criteria: (1) ADHD was diagnosed according to the DSM-IV or DSM-5; (2) rs-fMRI studies of ADHD patients using ReHo, ALFF, fALFF, or dALFF; (3) a case‒ control design was employed to assess differences in rest ing-state neural activity between ADHD patients and HCs; and (4) whole-brain analysis results were reported in stan dardized stereotaxic space (Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) or Talairach). Studies were excluded if they (1) utilized functional connectivity, independent component analysis, or degree centrality; (2) utilized task-based fMRI (t-fMRI) studies on ADHD patients or cerebral perfusion assessments; (3) were literature reviews, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, case reports, letters, conference abstracts, or editorials; (4) did not report complete stereotactic coordinates (x, y, z); or (5) lacked an HC group. In cases of overlapping datasets, the publication with the largest sample size and most rigor ous methodological detail was prioritized to preserve data independence. Data extraction Two authors (SYP and HYZ) separately performed data extraction based on a standardized protocol and predefined data collection form. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus. The extracted variables included key study characteristics, such as the first author, publica tion year, number of participants, sample size, mean age, sex distribution, intelligence quotient (IQ), ADHD sub type, diagnostic criteria, and medication status. Details of the rs-fMRI data included the scanning equipment, applied methods, the number of differentially altered brain regions between ADHD patients and healthy controls, corrective methods, and standard coordinate systems used for report ing the results. All coordinates were extracted indepen dently based on the methodological requirements of an ALE meta-analysis. Consistent with previous studies [46], we applied an age threshold of 12 years to distinguish adolescents from children. We categorized the populations in the studies into child (< 12 years) and adolescent (≥ 12 years) groups based primarily on the reported mean ± standard deviation (SD) of participant age to explore developmental differences. If the mean ± SD clearly placed the sample in one group, the study was classified accordingly, regardless of whether the age range spanned both groups. When the mean ± SD was not available, classification was based on the minimum age reported. If neither criterion allowed clear categorization and if the age range spanned both groups (e.g., Yang et al., 2011), the study was excluded from the age-specific sub group analyses. This approach enabled a more developmen tally informed analysis of age-specific neural alterations in ADHD patients. Quality and risk of bias assessments To evaluate methodological rigor, The Newcastle–Ottawa Quality Assessment Scale (NOS), which is a standardized instrument for evaluating nonrandomized studies, was used to evaluate methodological rigor [47]. Based on total scores, the risk of bias was categorized as low (7–9), moderate (4–6), or high (< 4) [48]. Additionally, we referenced the domains outlined in the Risk of Bias 2.0 (ROB 2.0) tool developed by the Cochrane Collaboration, including participant selection, deviations from the intended interventions, missing data, outcome measurements, and selection of reported results. Each domain was rated as “low risk”, “some concerns”, or “high risk”, and an overall risk judgment was assigned accord ingly. Quality assessments were independently performed by two authors (SYP and HYZ), with any discrepancies resolved through discussion with additional team members. 1 3 1135
