Conclusion The present study contributes to the understanding of how the COVID-19 pandemic and parental anxiety influenced the development and persistence of internalizing problems in children and adolescents with ADHD. The study revealed that as the impact of COVID-19 increased, child and adolescent internalizing symptoms also increased, and this relationship was longitudinally moderated by low levels of parental anxiety. This research provides evidence of the significant and negative impact that the COVID-19 pandemic had, and continues to have, on the mental health of young individuals with ADHD. These findings emphasize the need for public health measures to prioritize stability in daily routines and to ensure access to mental health care during and after major national/global events, such as the COVID-19 pandemic. The results also highlight the need to equip parents and children with appropriate mental health resources and strategies to navigate the emotional challenges that arise from a novel global crisis. Summary The COVID-19 pandemic was a trying time, with children and adolescents with ADHD showing heightened vulnerability to pandemic-related changes and internalizing problems. Pandemic studies have shown elevated anxiety and depression symptoms in children and adolescents with ADHD to be related to their parents worsening of anxiety. Although the intersection of COVID-19, child internalizing problems, and parental anxiety has been explored in neurotypical populations, it had yet to be explored in children with ADHD, nor in a post-pandemic setting. Therefore, the current longitudinal study assessed whether child internalizing problems were linked to the impact of COVID-19 and whether parental anxiety moderated this relationship during (Time 1–Spring 2021) and after (Time 2–Fall/Winter 2022) the pandemic in a Canadian sample. At Time 1, 278 parents and their child with a formal ADHD diagnosis, participated, and 89 of the same parents and their same child participated at Time 2. At both timepoints, parents filled out measures about the impact of COVID-19 on their child, their child’s internalizing problems, and their own anxiety. A series of linear regressions and simple moderations were run. Results revealed that the impact of COVID-19 uniquely predicted child internalizing problems during the pandemic, but not after. Experiencing a high impact of the pandemic on one’s life was found to be related to worse internalizing problems a year later, but only among children and adolescents who had a parent with low anxiety. These findings demonstrate the potent role that COVID-19 and parental anxiety played on the mood of children and adolescents with ADHD during the pandemic, and even after it was over. Evidently, it is imperative that continued mental health support and education be given to these young people with ADHD as well as their parents. These findings inform future research and on the lasting effects of the pandemic on vulnerable youth. Research on Child and Adolescent Psychopathology (2026) 54:103 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10802-026-01488-1 Berkan Sahin berkan.sahin@giresun.edu.tr; mail.berkan@gmail.com 1 Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, Faculty of Medicine, Giresun University, Giresun 28200, Turkey Abstract Off-time pubertal development defined as pubertal onset or progression deviating meaningfully from age- and sex-matched normative expectations confers heightened risk for internalizing and externalizing psychopathology during adolescence. Children and adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), including autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), carry pre-existing impairments in theory of mind (ToM) the capacity to represent and respond to the mental states of others that substantially compromise their capacity to navigate the increas ingly complex social demands that puberty introduces. Evidence indicates that ASD is associated with elevated rates of precocious puberty and altered pubertal tempo, and that ADHD in females is linked to earlier pubertal onset with consequent internalizing symptom exacerbation; yet the mechanisms connecting pubertal timing, ToM impairment, and psychopathological risk in these populations have not been systematically reviewed. This scoping review, guided by the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), synthesises evidence from 19 studies (2016–2026) examining pubertal timing in ASD and ADHD, the neurobiological mechanisms linking puberty to social cognition, and the clinical and psychopathological consequences of their convergence. We identify three mechanisms through which off-time puberty and pre-existing ToM impairment interact: (1) demand-capacity mismatch amplification, (2) masking and camouflag ing under elevated social load, and (3) physical-cognitive developmental asynchrony. No primary studies have directly examined the moderating role of ToM on the puberty-psychopathology relationship in NDD populations, representing a critical research gap. We propose a dual-vulnerability framework and outline research priorities for future longitudinal and intervention studies in this underserved population. These effects are multiply determined, encompassing psychosocial stressors related to maturational deviance, neurobiological changes in limbic-prefrontal circuitry, and hormonal modulation of mood regulation and social salience systems (Goddings et al., 2012; Morningstar & Burns, 2025). A critical and systematically overlooked feature of this literature is its near-exclusive focus on neurotypically devel oping populations. Children and adolescents with autism Introduction The onset of puberty represents one of the most consequen tial biological transitions of the lifespan. Beyond well-docu mented physical changes, puberty initiates cascading effects on brain development, social cognition, and peer relation ship complexity that fundamentally reshape adolescent mental health vulnerability (Pfeifer & Allen, 2021). Pubertal

1 3 103 Page 2 of 11 Research on Child and Adolescent Psychopathology (2026) 54:103 spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) represent a substantial proportion of the youth population with ASD affecting approximately 1 in 36 children (Maenner et al., 2023) and ADHD approximately 7.2% globally (Polanczyk et al., 2014). Both conditions are characterised by pre-existing impairments in theory of mind (ToM): the capacity to represent and respond to the mental states of others. In ASD, both cognitive and affective ToM are affected; in ADHD, deficits concentrate in affective ToM and social perspective-taking under attentional load, while cognitive ToM is largely preserved (Bolte, 2025; Capuozzo et al., 2024; Haza et al., 2024). ToM underpins the social navigation skills reading social hierarchies, interpreting peer feedback, managing romantic interest, and maintaining friendships that become critically important during adoles cence. When puberty arrives off-time for a child whose ToM is already substantially impaired, the developmental conse quences are not simply additive: an accelerating social envi ronment meets a social-cognitive system that was already operating below normative capacity. Despite the theoretical and clinical significance of this intersection, no scoping review has systematically exam ined the evidence for altered pubertal timing in ASD and ADHD, the neurobiological mechanisms linking puberty to social cognition, and the consequences of their conver gence for psychopathological outcomes. The present scop ing review addresses this gap, with the following objectives: (1) to synthesise evidence on pubertal timing in ASD and ADHD relative to typically developing peers; (2) to exam ine the neurobiological mechanisms through which pubertal hormonal changes modulate social-cognitive development in these populations; (3) to map the psychopathological consequences of the convergence of off-time pubertal tim ing and pre-existing ToM impairment; and (4) to identify research and clinical priorities arising from this synthesis. Method Design and Protocol This review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR; Tricco et al., 2018) and the methodological framework for scoping reviews proposed by Arksey and O’Malley (2005) as refined by Levac et al. (2010). A protocol was not pre-registered, consistent with the exploratory nature of the review. Search Strategy Systematic searches were conducted in PubMed/MED LINE, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and Scopus in May 2026. The search strategy combined three conceptual domains using Boolean operators: (1) pubertal tim ing: (“pubertal timing” OR “off-time puberty” OR “early puberty” OR “precocious puberty” OR “late puberty” OR “delayed puberty” OR “pubertal tempo” OR “adrenarche” OR “menarche” OR “Tanner stage”); (2) neurodevelopmen tal disorders: (“autism spectrum disorder” OR “ASD” OR “autistic” OR “attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder” OR “ADHD” OR “attention deficit”); (3) outcomes: (“theory of mind” OR “social cognition” OR “mentalizing” OR “psy chopathology” OR “internalizing” OR “externalizing” OR “anxiety” OR “depression” OR “camouflaging” OR “mask ing”). Searches were limited to English-language publica tions from January 2010 to April 2026. Reference lists of included articles and relevant systematic reviews were hand-searched for additional eligible studies. Eligibility Criteria Studies were eligible for inclusion if they: (1) examined pubertal timing, pubertal tempo, or hormonal correlates of puberty in children or adolescents with ASD or ADHD; OR examined the relationship between pubertal develop ment and social cognition, ToM, or social-cognitive brain development in ASD, ADHD, or typically developing youth relevant to NDD populations; OR examined masking/cam ouflaging and mental health outcomes during adolescence in ASD or ADHD; (2) included participants aged 8–18 years; (3) were published in peer-reviewed journals. Studies were excluded if they: (1) focused exclusively on adult popula tions; (2) examined puberty only in the context of medica tion side effects without examining pubertal timing per se; (3) did not include a clinical or population sample with ASD or ADHD (for primary studies); or (4) were case reports. Data Extraction and Quality Assessment Methodological quality of included primary studies was assessed using the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Prev alence Studies and the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Systematic Reviews, adapted to the study designs included (Moola et al., 2020). Each study was rated on eight criteria relevant to its design: (1) sampling representativeness; (2) validity and reliability of puberty measurement; (3) pres ence of a comparison group; (4) control for key confound ers (age, sex, IQ, ethnicity); (5) sex-stratified analyses; (6) appropriate statistical methods; (7) adequate follow-up (for longitudinal studies); and (8) transparency of reporting. Studies were rated as high (≥ 7/8), moderate-high (5–6/8), or moderate (3–4/8) quality. Narrative synthesis was used to integrate findings, given the heterogeneity in study designs, populations, and outcome measures.

1 3 Page 3 of 11 103 Research on Child and Adolescent Psychopathology (2026) 54:103 Results Search Results and Study Characteristics The initial database searches identified 847 records (PubMed: 312, PsycINFO: 218, Web of Science: 196, Sco pus: 121). After removal of duplicates (n = 203), 644 records were screened by title and abstract. Following application of eligibility criteria, 54 full-text articles were assessed, of which 19 met inclusion criteria (see Fig. 1 for PRISMAScR flow diagram). Of the 19 included studies, 9 examined pubertal timing directly in ASD or ADHD populations (7 ASD; 4 ADHD; 2 overlapping), 3 examined hormonal mech anisms linking puberty to social-cognitive development, 3 examined masking and camouflaging at pubertal transition, and 4 examined ToM development across adolescence (1 in ASD, 1 in ADHD, 2 in typically developing samples pro viding normative context). Methodological quality ranged from moderate to high across included studies (Table 1). The most significant methodological limitation across the literature was the absence of any primary study that directly examined the moderating role of ToM capacity on the asso ciation between pubertal timing and psychopathological outcomes in ASD or ADHD populations. Methodological quality ratings for all included primary studies are presented in Table 1. Pubertal Timing in ASD Primary Studies: Physical Examination-Based Evidence Six primary studies examined pubertal timing in ASD using direct physical assessment (Tanner staging) or biomarkers, yielding a consistent pattern of altered pubertal develop ment relative to typically developing (TD) peers. Corbett and colleagues conducted the most methodologically rig orous longitudinal programme of research in this area. In a cross-sectional study of 239 youth (137 ASD, 102 TD) aged 10 to 13 years, females with ASD showed significantly earlier menarche (t = − 2.56, p = .018) and advanced Tan ner staging relative to TD females, while no significant timing differences were observed in males (Corbett et al., 2020). A subsequent three-wave longitudinal study of 244 youth confirmed earlier pubertal onset in both sexes with ASD and demonstrated faster pubertal tempo in males, with ASD males showing a significantly accelerated progression through Tanner stages relative to TD males (Corbett et al., 2022). The same longitudinal cohort was further character ised hormonally: ASD youth showed significantly elevated morning salivary testosterone concentrations relative to TD peers, with a significant age-by-sex interaction reveal ing distinct developmental slopes (Muscatello et al., 2022). Most recently, a four-wave longitudinal analysis spanning ages 10 to 17 years demonstrated that testosterone and cor tisol followed a coupled developmental trajectory in ASD males, with hormone levels mediating the relationship between diagnostic status and behavioural outcomes across puberty (Corbett et al., 2025). Population-Level Epidemiological Evidence Two large-scale epidemiological studies provide important complementary evidence using clinical diagnoses of preco cious puberty (PP) rather than Tanner staging, permitting examination of risk at the population level. Geier and Geier (2021), using Florida Medicaid data (N = 101,736), found that the incidence of PP was 3.15 times higher in ASD youth relative to undiagnosed peers, with a Cox proportional haz ard ratio of 4.64 (95% CI: 3.11–6.93). Tsai and colleagues (2024), using Taiwan’s National Health Insurance Research Database (N = 22,208), reported that ASD was an indepen dent risk factor for PP regardless of comorbid intellectual disability, with a hazard ratio of 6.48 for autistic females (95% CI: 4.11–10.22). The first systematic review and meta-analysis of this literature, conducted by Tian and Gao (2026) across 12 studies including over 42,000 ASD youth, confirmed a pooled hazard ratio of 3.64 for PP in ASD (95% CI: 1.42–9.34). These findings establish that ASD is asso ciated with a substantially elevated population-level risk of precocious puberty, particularly in females, with effect sizes that are large and consistent across health systems and countries. Neurobiological Mechanisms The neurobiological mechanisms underlying atypical puber tal timing in ASD are not fully elucidated but converge on two primary pathways: adrenarche alterations and hypotha lamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis dysregulation. Szakal and Crespi (2025) conducted a series of systematic reviews examining the hypothesis that alterations in adrenarche defined as the prepubertal phase involving onset of dehy droepiandrosterone (DHEA) and DHEAS secretion, typi cally beginning between ages 7 and 10 may be implicated in both the developmental expression of autistic traits and the timing of subsequent gonadarche. Adrenarche represents a neurologically significant hormonal transition linked to the development of complex ToM and social competencies dur ing middle childhood; premature adrenarche (PA) has been associated with anxiety, depression, and emotional dysregu lation in typically developing populations. Read and colleagues (2024), reviewing the overlap between disorders of puberty and neurodevelopmental conditions, documented shared brain circuitry between the neuroendocrine systems controlling puberty onset and the social brain networks underlying ASD-associated features. The review reported that rates of central precocious puberty were highest in patients with ASD (16%), psychomotor delay (48%), and epilepsy (20%), suggesting a significant genetic and neurobiological component to the ASD-puberty association that may involve shared vulnerability in hypo thalamic-limbic circuits governing both GnRH secretion and social motivation. These findings converge with evi dence from genetic studies indicating shared polygenic architecture between autistic traits and earlier pubertal tim ing in females (Warrier et al., 2020, 2024). Pubertal Timing in ADHD Evidence regarding pubertal timing in ADHD, while less extensive than that for ASD, points to a pattern of earlier pubertal onset particularly in females, with evidence for sex-differentiated hormonal modulation of ADHD symp tom expression across puberty. Ostojic and Miller (2016) reported a significant association between earlier selfreported menarche and greater ADHD severity in a sample of female university students (r = .21, p < .01), providing preliminary evidence for a female-specific puberty-ADHD relationship. Rosenthal and Hinshaw (2024), in an allfemale longitudinal sample, confirmed earlier pubertal tim ing in ADHD relative to TD females using Tanner staging and menarche age, and demonstrated that earlier timing was associated with elevated internalizing symptoms including anxiety and depression at adolescent follow-up. In a large prospective cohort analysis using the ECHO consortium (Mlodnicka et al., 2024), pubertal timing as indexed by age at peak height velocity moderated the relationship between childhood ADHD symptoms and later psychopathology differentially by sex: earlier APHV in ADHD females pre dicted elevated conduct disorder symptoms, while later APHV in ADHD males was associated with depression and aggression at follow-up. Osianlis and colleagues (2025), in a systematic review spanning studies from 1980 to January 2025 (11 studies included), synthesised evidence that sex hormone fluctuations particularly estrogen decline modulate ADHD symptom severity in females through dopaminergic and noradrenergic pathways, with puberty representing the first major hormonal inflection point at which this sensitiv ity becomes clinically apparent. The review highlighted that ADHD in females is systematically underdiagnosed during childhood and adolescence, with the diagnostic gap widen ing precisely during puberty when hormone-driven symp tom fluctuations may be misattributed to mood disorder or adjustment difficulties. Masking, Camouflaging, and Psychopathological Risk at Pubertal Transition Three included studies examined the mental health conse quences of masking and camouflaging the deliberate sup pression of autistic behaviours and effortful performance of social scripts at the pubertal transition in ASD and ADHD populations. McKinney and colleagues (2024), using par ticipatory methods with neurodivergent girls (ASD, ADHD, and developmental coordination disorder) at the transi tion to adolescence, found that camouflaging predicted anxiety and depression symptoms, with the mental health gap between neurodivergent and neurotypical girls widen ing during the pubertal period. Bernardin and colleagues (2021), in a sample of 140 adolescents aged 13 to 18 years (62 non-autistic controls), demonstrated that camouflaging predicted internalizing symptoms (β = 0.31, p < .001) and externalizing symptoms after controlling for age, sex, and IQ, with internalizing symptoms mediating the camouflag ing-externalizing relationship. Khudiakova and colleagues (2025), in a comprehensive systematic review of the cam ouflaging-mental health literature, noted that the association between camouflaging and mental health is inconsistent across cross-sectional studies and that no longitudinal stud ies have been published, highlighting a significant gap in understanding the developmental trajectory of camouflag ing and its mental health consequences across the pubertal transition specifically. Theory of Mind Development Across Adolescence: Normative and NDD-Specific Evidence Three included studies examined ToM development across adolescence or its neurobiological correlates, providing nor mative context for understanding how ToM impairment in ASD and ADHD may interact with pubertal development. Discussion The evidence synthesised in this review supports a view of off-time puberty in ASD and ADHD as a developmentally amplifying risk factor rather than an additive one. The con sistency of the ASD-early puberty association across physi cal examination-based longitudinal studies, large population cohorts, and meta-analytic synthesis (pooled HR = 3.64 for precocious puberty) establishes altered pubertal timing in ASD as a replicable and clinically significant finding. The ADHD-puberty relationship, while less well-characterised, is supported by converging evidence from longitudinal studies and systematic review, with a clear sex-differenti ated profile: earlier puberty in females, with hormonal mod ulation of symptom expression through estrogen-dopamine pathways. Neither of these literatures, however, has been examined in conjunction with the social-cognitive pro file of affected youth specifically, with the ToM capacity that determines how effectively the child can navigate the increasingly complex social demands that pubertal develop ment introduces. Drawing on the convergent evidence reviewed, we pro pose a dual-vulnerability framework with three specific mechanisms. The first, demand-capacity mismatch ampli fication, posits that off-time puberty particularly early pubertal timing accelerates the rate at which social demands escalate, producing a wider and faster-growing gap between the social-cognitive demands of the peer environment and the child’s mentalising capacity. An early-maturing autistic girl faces the social demands of mid-adolescence with the mentalising resources of a child whose social cognition is both impaired and developing more slowly than TD peers. Puberty substantially increases the social load under which masking must be sustained: the social envi ronment becomes more complex precisely when hormonal changes are simultaneously increasing emotional reactivity. Earlier pubertal timing compresses the developmental win dow during which masking strategies can be consolidated, potentially increasing their fragility under elevated social load. The third mechanism, physical-cognitive develop mental asynchrony, identifies a vulnerability unique to NDD populations: physical maturation outpaces social-cognitive developmental level, generating social expectations from peers and adults that substantially exceed the child’s actual mentalising capacity creating specific vulnerability to social exploitation, peer victimisation, and social isolation. Critically, the review identifies a significant primary evidence gap: no published study has directly examined whether baseline ToM capacity moderates the associa tion between pubertal timing and psychopathological out comes in ASD or ADHD populations. This represents the most important research priority arising from the synthe sis. Future longitudinal studies should: (1) assess baseline ToM using performance-based measures (false belief tasks, Faux Pas Recognition, CANTAB ERT) at puberty onset and examine whether ToM profile predicts steeper mental health deterioration in off-time developers; (2) include assessment of puberty using gold-standard physical examination-based Tanner staging alongside hormonal biomarkers rather than parent or self-report alone; (3) include adequate representa tion of female participants across ASD and ADHD, given the sex-differentiated nature of both the puberty effects and the masking mechanisms; and (4) follow participants lon gitudinally from pre-puberty through mid-adolescence to capture the temporal dynamics of the puberty-ToM-psycho pathology relationship. Clinically, the framework argues for several adjustments to practice. First, assessment protocols for NDD youth aged 8 to 12 years should systematically document pubertal stage and timing, identifying off-time developers as a priority subgroup for enhanced mental health monitoring. Second, social cognition and social skills intervention content for NDD youth should be calibrated to pubertal stage as well as chronological age: an autistic girl who is experiencing early puberty at age 10 faces social demands analogous to those faced by a TD 13-year-old. Third, diagnostic re-evaluation is warranted for ADHD females presenting in early adoles cence with internalising symptom escalation coinciding with pubertal onset, as this pattern may reflect hormone-mod ulated ADHD rather than primary mood disorder. Fourth, family and educator psychoeducation should address the physical-cognitive developmental asynchrony in ASD and ADHD, helping caregivers calibrate social expectations to cognitive rather than physical developmental level. Limitations Several limitations of this review should be noted. First, the scoping methodology does not permit meta-analytic pooling of primary studies; effect size estimates reported are derived from individual studies rather than synthesised. Second, the evidence base for ADHD is substantially smaller and less methodologically rigorous than that for ASD, with no Tanner staging-based longitudinal study in an ADHD-diag nosed sample identified for females. Third, the literature on DLD and ID was excluded to permit depth of synthesis in the populations with the strongest evidence base; this lim its generalisability to the broader NDD spectrum. Fourth, the overwhelming majority of the reviewed literature comes from high-income English-speaking countries, limiting gen eralisability to other cultural and socioeconomic contexts. Fifth, no primary study directly testing the key hypothesis of this review that ToM moderates the puberty-psychopa thology relationship in NDD populations was identified, rendering the dual-vulnerability framework necessarily theoretical at this stage. Conclusion Off-time pubertal development and pre-existing ToM impairment represent two well-documented but separately studied risk factors for adolescent psychopathology in ASD and ADHD. This scoping review is the first to systemati cally map the evidence at their intersection, identifying a substantial and consistent literature on altered pubertal timing in ASD, emerging evidence in ADHD with a clear sex-differentiated profile, and converging neurobiological mechanisms linking puberty to social-cognitive brain devel opment. The absence of any primary study directly exam ining ToM as a moderator of the puberty-psychopathology relationship in NDD populations represents the most criti cal gap in this literature. The dual-vulnerability framework proposed here integrating demand-capacity mismatch amplification, masking under social load, and physical-cog nitive developmental asynchrony as specific mechanisms is intended to provide the theoretical scaffolding for the next generation of longitudinal and intervention research in this clinically important and underserved population. Recent shifts in ADHD research, highlighted in the Annual Research Review (Hinshaw et al., 2022), are now increasingly directed towards studying ADHD in women. There is also a growing recognition that girls and women may camouflage their ADHD symptoms, a phenomenon previously identified in autism research, particularly in autistic females, and now considered relevant for ADHD (Agnew-Blais & Michelini, 2023; Hinshaw et al., 2022; Schuck et al., 2019; Tubío-Fungueiriño et al., 2021). Our study seeks to address the gap in understanding ADHD in women by focusing on social camouflaging that can be defined as the behaviors and strategies that individuals with ADHD use to hide, mask, or compensate for their ADHD symptoms in social situations (Hull et al., 2017, 2019; Mylett, 2022; van der Putten et al., 2024). This process is aimed at conforming to neurotypical expecta tions and may involve using strategies to minimize the visibility of symptoms of neurodevelopmental condition Introduction The underrepresentation of females in Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) research has resulted in a significant gap in understanding this condition’s unique aspects in women, including their specific manifesta tions, developmental trajectories, and the most effective assessment and treatment strategies (Attoe & Climie, 2023; Chronis-Tuscano, 2022). This oversight has left many girls and women with ADHD undiagnosed and untreated, as most research and clinical practices have Małgorzata Gambin mgambin@psych.uw.edu.pl Fryderyka Wicherkiewicz fryderykawicher@gmail.com 1 Faculty of Psychology, University of Warsaw, ul. Stawki 5/7, Warsaw 00-183, Poland Abstract Background: This study investigated the relationship between social camouflaging, life satisfaction, and depression symp toms in Polish women with ADHD. It aimed to fill a research gap in understanding ADHD manifestations in women, particularly focusing on social camouflaging—a concept known in autism, referring to strategies used to mask symptoms in social interactions. Methods: A total of 329 women with ADHD took part in an online survey. The survey measured ADHD symptoms using the ADHD Self Report Scale (ASRS-vI.I), life satisfaction with the Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS), and depressive symptoms using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Additionally, a novel set of ques tions, inspired by the Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire (CAT-Q) but tailored for ADHD, was utilized to assess social camouflaging. Results: Results indicated a significant negative association between social camouflaging and life satisfaction and a positive correlation with depressive symptoms, even after controlling for demographic variables. Addi tionally, factors like being in a relationship and having a positive subjective financial situation correlated with higher wellbeing. Limitations: Reliance on self-report measures, the cross-sectional design, and participants’ self-reported ADHD diagnosis are the main limitations of the study. Conclusion: The research underscores the importance of social camouflag ing in understanding ADHD in women, suggesting that efforts to mask symptoms and meet societal expectations may link to lower life satisfaction and increased depressive symptoms. These findings advocate for continued research into these dynamics to develop more effective support for women with ADHD. and conform to societal expectations (Hull et al., 2017, 2019; Mylett, 2022; van der Putten et al., 2024). Previ ous studies have identified complex relations between social camouflaging and mental health difficulties in autistic individuals suggesting that the act of camouflag ing, while serving as a coping mechanism for navigating social interactions, can paradoxically exacerbate mental health difficulties (Field et al., 2024). Although camou flaging has been previously examined mostly in the con text of autism, this phenomenon is highly pertinent to ADHD (Mylett, 2022; van der Putten et al., 2024), espe cially considering the associated psychosocial pressures and stigma that affect not only adults but individuals at all ages (Lebowitz, 2016). These pressures include reluc tance to socially interact with individuals diagnosed with ADHD, often stemming from misconceptions that they are unreliable, less trustworthy, or careless (Fuermaier et al., 2012). Furthermore, stigma manifests in various forms, such as the belief that adult ADHD is not a legiti mate disorder, with some suggesting that symptoms are simulated or that the condition is fabricated by pharma ceutical companies (Masuch et al., 2019). Consequently, individuals with ADHD may employ social camouflag ing techniques to avoid encountering these stereotypes and mitigate negative social repercussions. Van der Putten and colleagues’ comparative analysis (2024) has revealed that adults with ADHD, like those with autism, engage in camouflaging behaviors, however to a lesser extent. Their work underscores the necessity for nuanced measures to accurately capture camouflaging behaviors across neurodevelopmental conditions. In the current study, we investigate the relationship between social camouflaging, depressive symptoms, and life satisfaction in Polish women with ADHD, in light of the high comorbidity with internalizing disorders such as depression and anxiety. Our research, conducted with Polish women, aligns with the increasing call for more inclusive and diverse ADHD studies, emphasizing the importance of research across various countries and cultures (Chronis-Tuscano, 2022; Hinshaw et al., 2022). The focus on this population is informed by the authors’ backgrounds and a notable deficiency in research on ADHD within the Polish context, where neurodevelop mental disorders, including ADHD and ASD, are often misunderstood and underdiagnosed (Lenart & Pasternak, 2023; Szaniawska, 2010). Recent discussions in Poland highlight significant challenges in the diagnosis and treatment of ADHD (Pankowski & Wytrychiewicz-Pan kowska, 2024). Medications are frequently inaccessible and reimbursable only for individuals under 18 years, despite the growing acknowledgment of adult ADHD in Poland. Furthermore, the visibility of the topic of ADHD through social media is increasing, significantly influencing public perception and awareness (Karteczka, 2012). This increased awareness sharply contrasts with ongoing healthcare challenges, underscoring the gap between public engagement and actual support for indi viduals with ADHD. Additionally, there is a discrepancy between government claims of ADHD overdiagnosis and what research indicates to be a persistent underdiagnosis and a lack of adequate treatment options (Buźniak et al., 2022; Pankowski & Wytrychiewicz-Pankowska, 2024). This context underscores the need to better understand the predictors of well-being for individuals with ADHD living in such complex sociocultural environments. Building on previous research, our study extends the findings of van der Putten and colleagues (2024), who investigated camouflaging behaviours using the Camou flaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire (CAT-Q; Hull et al., 2019), initially designed for autistic individuals. We have developed the Social Camouflaging of ADHD Symptoms Scale, a 10-item questionnaire adapted from the Camou flaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire (CAT-Q; Hull et al., 2019) and tailored for ADHD. We hypothesize that social camouflaging will be positively associated with depres sive symptoms and inversely related to life satisfaction in women with ADHD, controlling for the intensity of ADHD symptoms and various demographic and diagno sis-related variables. The demographic questions, as well as those regarding ADHD diagnosis and comorbid condi tions, were chosen due to their potential impact on the well-being of women with ADHD. Our aim in controlling for these variables was to distinguish the unique associa tion between social camouflaging and depressive symp toms and life satisfaction beyond other variables like age, education, and mental health status. Methods Participants and Procedure The data were collected from 28 March 2023 to 6 Sep tember 2023 via an online survey posted on two Polish Facebook groups for people with ADHD. These groups consisted of individuals with ADHD and their family members and significant others. Given the substantial size of these groups, which collectively include up to 50,000 users, it is reasonable to assume a diverse range of ages, educational backgrounds, and socioeconomic statuses among the members. The recruitment mes sages were designed to be clear and accessible to ensure understanding across various educational levels. How ever, despite these efforts to include participants from 1 3 Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2026) 56:2875–2883 2876

diverse backgrounds, the majority of the participants were women with a higher education degree and from big cities. When the survey link was posted it was specified that the only people with an ADHD diagnosis who are over the age of 18 are invited to participate in the study. Informed consent was provided by participants through the survey platform. Prior to initiating the survey, par ticipants were presented with detailed information that described the purpose, content, and estimated duration of the survey. This introduction also emphasized that partic ipation was entirely voluntary and that participants could withdraw from the study at any time without any reper cussions. This information ensured that participants were fully aware of the study details and their rights before they proceeded. We assessed ADHD symptoms through the ADHD Self Report Scale (ASRS-vI.I) to make sure that the recipients actually met the screening criteria for an ADHD diagnosis. The final analysis included 329 Pol ish women (mean age of 30.82 and standard deviation of 8.02) who reported having a psychiatric diagnosis of ADHD and scores on the ASRS scale above a cut-off indicative of ADHD (Kessler et al., 2005). Demograph ics of the sample are presented in Table 1. Measures ADHD Self Report Scale (ASRS-vI.I) The ADHD Self Report Scale (ASRS-vI.I; Kessler et al., 2005) is an 18-item instrument designed to measure ADHD symptoms experienced over the previous six months. Participants provide ratings of symptoms’ fre quency that contribute to an overall score (α = 0.73 in the current study), which can be further analyzed through two nine-item subscales for Inattention (INA; α = 0.63) and Hyperactivity-Impulsivity (HI; α = 0.68). A specific cutoff point, derived from the ASRS, identifies scores indicative of ADHD, facilitating diagnostic screening. Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS) The Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS; Pavot & Die ner, 2008) employs a 5-item questionnaire to assess an individual’s overall satisfaction with their life score (α = 0.87 in the current study). Participants respond using a 7-point Likert scale, with aggregated item scores form ing a composite measure of life satisfaction. This scale offers a global assessment of subjective well-being. Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) The Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9; Kroenke et al., 2001) is a nine-item self-report inventory used to assess the presence and severity of depressive symptoms within the last two weeks (α = 83 in the current study). Responses are scored on a scale ranging from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day), allowing for a quantitative evaluation of depression severity. Social Camouflaging of ADHD Symptoms Scale To assess social camouflaging in individuals with ADHD, we developed a novel 10-item questionnaire inspired by the Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire (CAT-Q; Hull et al., 2019) and existing literature on camouflaging in ADHD (Mylett, 2022). Results Descriptive statistics and correlation between analyzed variables can be found in Table 2. Hierarchical regression, which was conducted, explains 29% of variances for life satisfaction (R2 = 0.29, F = 10.87, p < 0.01) and 36% of variances for depressive symptoms (R2 = 0.36, F = 15.33, p < 0.01). Detailed findings are presented in Tables 3 and 4. Our analysis shows that in the final step of hierarchi cal regression analysis, symptoms of inattention (β = − 0.14, p < 0.01), and social camouflaging (β = − 0.14, p < 0.01) were significantly negatively related to life sat isfaction. Furthermore, being in a relationship (β = 0.10, p < 0.05) and having a subjectively good financial situa tion (β = 0.37, p < 0.01) positively predicted life satisfac tion. Regarding depressive symptoms, our research has shown that social camouflaging (β = 0.18, p < 0.01), hav ing diagnosed depression (β = 0.14, p < 0.01) or anxiety disorder (β = 0.11, p < 0.01) and hyperactivity-impulsiv ity (β = 0.32, p < 0.01) or inattention symptoms (β = 0.23, p < 0.01) were significant positive predictors of depres sive symptoms. The items were consulted with two clinicians who are also researchers specializing in clinical psychology, with experience in the clinical work with individuals with ADHD. Before conducting this research we ran a pilot survey to assess the understandability of the questions of the Social Cam ouflaging scale. This scale uses a 7-point Likert scale for responses, with higher scores indicating greater engage ment in camouflaging behaviors. This instrument demon strates a one-factor structure (Table S1 in supplementary material) and high reliability (α = 0.91). Additionally, we have calculated the mean and standard deviation for each item (shown in Table S2 in supplementary material) to verify that the items effectively differentiate among participants, ensuring that the scale accurately measures varying levels of camouflaging behaviors. Data Analysis We conducted the analyses using SPSS version 29. The hierarchical regression was conducted with life satis faction as a dependent variable, followed by depressive symptoms as a dependent variable. In the first step of our hierarchical regression, we incorporated key demo graphic factors and clinical diagnoses to establish a base line model of factors that may affect the well-being of individuals with ADHD. This included participant’s age, age of diagnosis, diagnosed ASD, diagnosis of depres sion, anxiety disorders or personality disorders, lack of psycho- and pharmacotherapy, subjective evaluation of the financial situation, and being in a relationship. In the next step, we added ADHD-specific symptoms of hyperactivity-impulsivity and inattention to isolate their unique effects beyond those of the demographic and diag nosis-related factors. This differentiation highlights the nuanced impact of differ ent ADHD symptom dimensions on mental well-being. Moreover, in line with previous research (Medgyesi & Zólyomi, 2016) the subjective evaluation of one’s finan cial situation was positively related to life satisfaction. Our results also show that being in a relationship can have a positive effect both on life satisfaction and the prevention of depressive symptoms in women with diag nosed ADHD. These findings support previous research showing that being in a relationship can mitigate depres sive symptoms (Whitton et al., 2013) and increase life satisfaction partly due to the sense of social support and love it provides (Facio & Resett, 2014; Yalçin, 2011). Limitations Our study’s findings are limited by its reliance on selfreport measures, the cross-sectional design, and partici pants’ self-reported ADHD diagnosis, which may affect the generalizability and interpretability of the results. The majority of the survey’s recipients were women with a higher education degree and from big cities. Conse quently, the results can not be generalized for the whole Polish female population. It is needed to conduct fur ther studies with a more diverse sample, also including women from smaller towns and with lower education lev els. Additionally, the predominance of highly educated women from big cities in the study may reflect greater access to diagnosis and a better understanding of ADHD and its symptoms in these areas. Our new scale for mea suring social camouflaging in ADHD, still in its early validation stages, might not yet fully grasp the complex nature of social camouflaging in individuals with ADHD e.g. it does not distinguish various dimensions of social camouflaging (compensation, masking, and assimilation) that were found in autism research. Moreover, it primar ily focuses on the masking of hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms, with less emphasis on the camouflaging of inattention symptoms. These shortcomings may impact the reliability and validity of our findings and suggest a need for further refinement of the measure to better represent the diverse experiences of social camouflag ing in ADHD. To address these gaps, future research should expand the validation process of the scale across varied populations and settings to ensure its robust ness and applicability. Additionally, integrating qualita tive research methods could significantly enhance our understanding of social camouflaging. Detailed, qualita tive accounts of how women with ADHD manage their symptoms in different social situations would enrich the Discussion Our research shows that social camouflaging is negatively related to life satisfaction and positively to depression symptoms in women with ADHD even after adjusting for other demographic variables. This aligns with find ings in the literature on autistic individuals (Field et al., 2024; Hull et al., 2021; Bradley et al., 2021), suggest ing that social camouflaging serves similar psychological functions across these groups. From the perspective of Gender Schema Theory (Bem, 1981; Salciunas, 2021), societal norms about ‘appropriate’ female behavior may pressure women to camouflage ADHD symptoms. These gendered expectations, deeply internalized from a young age, often emphasize traits such as compliance, good behavior, calmness, and submissiveness in girls, which conflicts with ADHD symptoms, leading women to feel a need to mask these traits to fit societal expectations. In addition, consistent with Goffman’s seminal work on stigma and the ‘spoiled identity’ (1963; Bos et al., 2013), women with ADHD may use social camouflaging as a strategy to mitigate the psychosocial challenges and stigma and avoid social exclusion. Awareness of public stigma often leads to self-stigma, where negative ste reotypes are internalized and have a negative impact on self-esteem and well-being (Bos et al., 2013). In effect, the act of camouflaging to ‘pass’ as normal within soci etal norms underscores the perpetual struggle between concealing one’s stigmatized identity and the ongoing threat of being discredited. This tension may introduce significant psychological stress, particularly in scenarios where disclosure might lead to increased social rejection (Bos et al., 2013). Social camouflaging may not only be threatening, exhausting and cognitively demanding but can also make one feel as if they are hiding their true self (Field, 2024; Mylett, 2022). In effect, it may lead to feel ings of inauthenticity and identity conflict. According to self-determination theory (SDT), acting authentically is crucial for well-being (Ryan et al., 2019). Social camou flaging may undermine this authenticity by impacting all three basic psychological needs posited by SDT: auton omy, competence, and relatedness. By masking their true selves, individuals may compromise their autonomy, perceive themselves as less competent, and struggle to form genuine connections, all of which are essential for psychological health. Consequently, the failure to meet these basic needs can lead to increased anxiety, stress, and depression. Consistent with previous research (Ogg et al., 2016), our study found that inattention symptoms were asso ciated with both lower life satisfaction and higher depressive symptoms. Clinical Implications Social camouflaging may significantly impact mental health and complicate the clinical presentation of ADHD symptoms, leading to delayed diagnoses. Our data indi cate that most women were diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood, likely due to long-term camouflaging behav iors and cultural factors prevalent in Poland, where neu rodevelopmental disorders are often misunderstood and underdiagnosed. These findings emphasize the need for clinicians to assess both ADHD symptoms and camou flaging behaviors. The refinement of the Social Cam ouflaging ADHD Scale is crucial to accurately measure these behaviors, enhancing diagnostic precision and enabling tailored treatment strategies. Clinicians require specific training to detect social camouflaging effectively. Additionally, educational support systems must adapt to better accommodate neurodiverse students and minimize the need for camouflaging ADHD symptoms. Public health policies should focus on reducing ADHD stigma and increasing awareness of neurodiversity, particularly among women. Effective social support systems, includ ing online and in-person support groups, can provide essential networks for women with ADHD, promoting social inclusion and mitigating the psychological burden of camouflaging. Finally, the development and evaluation of therapeutic and preventive interventions specifically designed for women with ADHD are essential. These interventions should address social camouflaging and support individuals at risk. Conclusions Our research contributes to an enhanced understanding of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in women, examining the interaction between social cam ouflaging, demographic variables, and mental well-being. The findings indicate that women with ADHD may expe rience a psychological cost due to their efforts to mask symptoms and conform to societal norms. This study highlights the importance of recognizing social camou flaging as an important factor that may affect the mental health of women with ADHD We advocate for further research across diverse age groups, genders, and cultural settings, emphasizing the need for longitudinal studies and mixed-methods research to deepen our understanding of camouflaging behaviors. metadata_title: Sleep Problems in Children with ADHD: Associations with Internalizing Symptoms and Physical Activity
pages: Vol.:(0123456789) Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2026) 56:1163–1172 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10803-024-06623-9 S.I. :SLEEP IN AUTISM AND DEVELOPMENTAL DISORDERS Sleep Problems in Children with ADHD: Associations with Internalizing Symptoms and Physical Activity Xiao Liang1,2 · Mengping Zhao3 · Li Su3 · Justin A. Haegele4 · Richard H. Xu1 · Jiayue Li5 · Jinxian Guo5 · Andy Choi‐Yeung Tse6 · Shirley X. Li7,8 · David H. K. Shum1,2 Accepted: 20 October 2024 / Published online: 1 November 2024 © The Author(s) 2024 Abstract Children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) experience high rates of sleep problems and are at increased risk for developing internalizing problems. This study aimed to examine the association of sleep problems and physical activity with internalizing symptoms in children with ADHD. This cross-sectional study included 188 children with ADHD (M age = 8.60 ± 1.38, 78.7% boys). Self-reported questionnaires were used to assess sleep problems (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index [PSQI]) and internalizing symptoms (Depression Anxiety Stress Scale 21 [DASS 21]). The presence of sleep problems was defined as a PSQI score > 5. Physical activity was recorded by an ActiGraph GT9X Link accelerometer for 7 consecutive days. In total, 111 children with ADHD presented with sleep problems (59%). Compared with their counterparts without sleep problems, children with sleep problems spent less time in daily moderator-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA) (F = 15.35, η2 = .079), had a lower proportion of meeting the WHO-recommended 60 min of daily MVPA guideline (F = 9.57, η2 = .050), and showed more internalizing symptoms: depression (F = 10.09, η2 = .053), anxiety (F = 15.84, η2 = .081), and stress (F = 6.98, η2 = .037). BMI, daytime dysfunction of PSQI, and MVPA guideline attainment were significantly associated with internalizing symptoms in children with ADHD. Daytime dysfunction of PSQI is associated with more severe internalizing symptoms, and MVPA guideline attainment may reduce the likelihood of developing depression and anxiety in children with ADHD. Future studies are needed to examine the long-term effects of sleep on internalizing symptoms and the effects of PA-based interventions on sleep and internalizing symptoms in children with ADHD, respectively. Keywords ADHD · Sleep · Physical activity · Internalizing symptoms · Children Introduction Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a pervasive childhood psychiatric disorder characterised by a persistent condition of age-inappropriate levels of inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), affecting approximately 5–6% of school-aged children (Sayal et al., 2018). Individuals with ADHD may experience significant comorbidities beyond the core symptoms of ADHD, including those related to psychological difficulties, such as internalizing symptoms (i.e., depression, anxiety, and social withdrawal) and externalizing symptoms (i.e., aggression, conduct problems and being oppositional), sleep disturbances and physical inactivity (Gillberg, 2010). * Xiao Liang shawn.liang@polyu.edu.hk 1 Department of Rehabilitation Sciences, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hung Hom, Kowloon, Hong Kong SAR, China 2 The Research Institute for Sports Science and Technology, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong SAR, China 3 School of Public Health, Lanzhou University, Lanzhou, China 4 Department of Human Movement Sciences, Old Dominion University, Norfolk, VA, USA 5 Centre for Early Child Development, Gansu Maternity and Child Health Care Hospital, Lanzhou, China 6 Department of Health and Physical Education, The Education University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China 7 Department of Psychology, University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China 8 The State Key Laboratory of Brain and Cognitive Sciences, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong SAR, China

1164 Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2026) 56:1163–1172 Together, all these symptoms can cause substantial deficits in the daily routine of these children (Becker, 2020). Sleep is essential for the overall health of children (Matricciani et al., 2019), yet sleep problems are common in children with ADHD (Becker, 2020). Increasing evidence suggests that behavioural sleep problems are significantly more common in children with ADHD than in children without ADHD, with estimated prevalence rates ranging from 25 to 50% (Becker, 2020). The most common subjective sleep complaints in children with ADHD include sleep latency delay, bedtime resistance, nocturnal awakenings, and daytime sleepiness (Cortese et al., 2009). A recent meta-analysis concluded that compared with peers without ADHD, children and adolescents with ADHD show a longer sleep latency and decreased sleep efficiency, as measured by actigraphy (Liang et al., 2023a). Indeed, there is evidence to suggest that sleep problems may exacerbate existing ADHD symptoms, academic problems, and adverse effects on health-related quality of life for children with ADHD and their families (Hvolby, 2015; Langberg et al., 2013). Furthermore, a number of studies have demonstrated that behavioural sleep problems are related to a range of internalizing and externalizing symptoms in children with ADHD, resulting in reduced quality of life (QoL) and academic underachievement (Becker et al., 2019; Dimakos et al., 2021). Despite the high prevalence of sleep problems, the evidence of how sleep problems may influence daytime functioning in children with ADHD is limited (Hansen et al., 2014). Recent reviews summarized that externalizing and internalizing problems contribute to dysfunction in youth with ADHD and can be amplified by behavioural sleep disturbances (Bondopadhyay et al., 2022; Dimakos et al., 2021). Specifically, there is a significantly positive association between reported sleep problems and both internalizing and externalizing in youth with ADHD ranging from preschool to adolescence (Dimakos et al., 2021). However, while the causal associations between sleep disturbances and externalizing symptoms (e.g., oppositional behaviours, inattention, and behavioural disorders) were consistently found in youth with ADHD, the relationships between sleep problems and internalizing problems (e.g., depression and anxiety) were equivocal (Dimakos et al., 2021). In addition, a previous study of 239 children with ADHD found that those with ADHD with moderate-to-severe sleep problems showed more severe ADHD symptoms than children with no or mild sleep problems (Sung et al., 2008). In another cross-sectional study of 63 children with ADHD, those with insomnia symptoms showed more severe ADHD symptoms and poorer cognitive function performance compared with children with ADHD without insomnia and healthy controls (Li et al., 2022). Despite these findings, very limited research has been developed to identify predictors of internalizing symptoms in children with ADHD, which is critical to designing tailored intervention programs (Becker et al., 2015). While the impact of behavioural sleep problems on internalizing symptoms is emerging in youth with ADHD, the mechanisms associated with sleep problems in children with ADHD appear multi-factorial, including biological (e.g., genetic factors, circadian rhythm alterations), neurological (overlap in disrupted brain circuitry), psychological (conduct problems) (Dong et al., 2024), and environmental (e.g., night media use) (Becker, 2020; Bondopadhyay et al., 2022; Lycett et al., 2015). Given the risks posed by internalizing symptoms and the fact that behavioural sleep disturbances can lead to an increased risk of internalizing symptoms in children with ADHD (Dimakos et al., 2021), sleep problems have emerged as a pivotal risk factor for internalizing symptoms in youth with ADHD. However, there is still a poor understanding of the behavioural mechanisms by which sleep problems exert effects on internalizing symptoms in children with ADHD. PA has consistently been reported to have beneficial effects on improving sleep problems (e.g., decreased sleep latency) (Liang et al., 2022a, 2022b), as well as reducing depression (Gawrilow et al., 2016; Liang et al., 2023b) and stress (Liang et al., 2023b) in children with ADHD. Sleep problems and physical inactivity are significantly more common in children with ADHD (Becker, 2020). Growing evidence shows an association between ADHD and decreased PA, with subjective reports indicating that children with ADHD tend not to meet the World Health Organization’s (WHO’s) minimum guidelines of 60 min per day of moderate-to-vigorous PA (MVPA) (Tandon et al., 2019). For example, one recent study found that MVPA guideline attainment and sleep duration significantly predicted locomotor skills development in children with ADHD. Moreover, significantly lower accelerometer-measured MVPA was observed in children with ADHD compared to those without ADHD (Liang et al., 2023c). In addition, one recent pilot study reported beneficial training effects of a 12-week PA intervention on psychological resilience and internalizing symptoms (e.g., anxiety/depressed, withdrawn/depressed, and somatic complaints) and externalizing symptoms (e.g., rule-breaking behaviour and aggressive behaviour) in children with ADHD (Liang et al., 2024). However, few studies have considered how PA may affect the associations between sleep and internalizing symptoms in children with ADHD. Therefore, the current study aimed to (a) compare internalizing symptoms and PA between children with ADHD and sleep problems with children with ADHD but without sleep problems; and (b) determine the association among sleep problems, PA and internalizing symptoms among children with ADHD. Overall, we hypothesized that (a) children with ADHD and behavioural sleep problems would have more severe internalizing symptoms and

1165 Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2026) 56:1163–1172 lower PA levels as compared with children with ADHD but without behavioural sleep problems; (b) there would be a significant association of sleep problems and physical activity with internalizing symptoms. Methods Study Design and Participants This cross-sectional study recruited 188 children with ADHD (M age = 8.60 ± 1.38, 78.7% boys) (with or without behavioural sleep disturbances) aged between 6 and 12, who were outpatients attending a children’s hospital in Lanzhou, China. The clinical diagnosis of ADHD (any subtypes) was confirmed by expert child psychologists based on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders-Fifth version (DSM-5) (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). All the recruited children met the following study criteria: (1) IQ of at least 75 on Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, 4th Edition (WISC-IV) (Zhang, 2009) as assessed by a clinical psychologist; (2) absence of prominent medical conditions that limited PA capability (e.g., asthma, cardiac disease) was also checked by pediatricians; (3) absence of neuropsychiatric disorders (e.g., bipolar disorder, autism spectrum disorder, substance abuse) (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). All recruitment and participant screening was carried out by pediatricians following the standard protocol at the hospital. Procedure This study’s design followed the Declaration of Helsinki’s ethical standards and was approved by the Institutional Review Board for Human Subjects (Clinical), The Hong Kong Polytechnic University (Reference No: HSEARS20230314005). Informed consent was obtained from the participants’ parents or guardians. Participants individually visited the consulting room with their parents/ guardians. Weight and height were measured by clinicians, and body mass index (BMI) was calculated by dividing body mass (kg) by height squared (m2). All participants individually completed the two questionnaires (i.e., PSQI and DASS 21) with the assistance of trained research assistants. Then, each participant was asked to wear an Actigraphy on the non-dominant wrist, and a logbook was also provided for his/her parents to record put-on/take-off time and reasons. After seven days of wearing it, the participant’s parents/ guardians brought or mailed the Actigraphy back to the hospital. Measures Behavioural Sleep Disturbances Sleep disturbances were measured by the self-reported Chinese version of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) questionnaire (Liang et al., 2022a, 2022b). This measure consists of 18 questions and forms seven-component scores ranging from 0 to 3 (i.e., sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, sleep medication and daytime dysfunction). The sum of each component is the total score, which ranges between 0 and 21, where a higher score describes poorer sleep quality. A total PSQI score greater than 5 has been validated as being highly sensitive and specific in distinguishing good from poor sleepers in children and adolescents with ADHD (Liang et al., 2023a). The cut-off score of 5 was used to determine the differences between children with ADHD and behavioural sleep disturbances and children with ADHD but without sleep disturbances. Specifically, an overall score of 5 or higher indicates ADHD children with behavioural sleep disturbances, while an overall score of less than 5 indicates ADHD children without sleep disturbances (Zitser et al., 2022). The internal consistency was acceptable in the present study (α = 0.784). Internalizing Symptoms Internalizing symptoms were measured using the Chinese version of the Depression Anxiety Stress Scale 21 (DASS 21) (K. Wang et al., 2016). The DASS 21 is comprised of 21 items and designed to assess three dimensions of a 1-week state of negative affect (7 items in each of the depression, anxiety, and stress subscales). DASS 21 is rated using a four-point Likert scale from (0) never to (3) almost always. Higher scores indicate a more severe level of depression, anxiety, or stress. The Chinese version of the DASS 21 has been applied to Chinese children with ADHD and has been shown to be useful for this particular population (Liang et al., 2023b). The internal consistency of each subscale was reported to be acceptable in this study (depression: α = 0.77; anxiety: α = 0.73; stress: α = 0.75). Physical Activity Physical activity data used for analysis were time spent in MVPA, which was assessed by ActiGraph GT9X Link (ActiGraph, Pensacola, Florida, USA). All participants were asked to wear the actigraph around their non-dominant wrist for seven consecutive days (five weekdays and two weekend days) and were instructed to follow their typical daily routines and only take off the actigraph when they were taking baths or swimming. Participants were excluded if they had

1166 Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2026) 56:1163–1172 less than four valid days of wearing time (a minimum of three weekdays and one weekend day). MVPA values were calculated by averaging MVPA metrics for each participant's valid days. The Actigraph has been used extensively to measure physical activity and is well-validated in MVPA records in children with ADHD (Liang et al., 2023b, 2023c). Engaging an average MVPA for ≥ 60 min/day in valid days was considered to meet the WHO-recommended MVPA guideline (Liang et al., 2023c). Data Analysis All statistical analyses were performed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS, version 29.0). Participants were divided into two groups: poor sleepers (PS) (PSQI ≥ 5) and good sleepers (GS) (PSQI < 5). Independent t-tests or chi-square tests were used to compare the differences in background information (e.g., age, sex, IQ, height, weight, BMI, ADHD subtype, comorbidity, and medication) between the two groups. Then, a multivariate analysis of covariance controlling for age, sex, IQ, BMI, comorbidity, medication, and ADHD subtypes was carried out to compare the group differences in internalizing symptoms, physical activity and sleep characteristics. Bivariate correlations were calculated among our variables of interest: PSQI (i.e., sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, sleep medication and daytime dysfunction), MVPA, MVPA guideline attainment, and internalizing symptoms (i.e., depression, anxiety, and stress). Lastly, hierarchical regression models were used to predict internalizing symptoms (i.e., depression, anxiety, and stress). For all analyses, statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. Results Characteristics of the Participants Table 1 shows the characteristics of the participants. Of the initially recruited 191 children with ADHD, 3 participants dropped out of the study due to their poor compliance with wearing the actigraphy and were excluded from data analyses, resulting in a final dataset of 188 children with ADHD. All participants had valid accelerometer data for at least four days, including three weekdays and one weekend day. Among the 188 ADHD participants in this study, 148 (78.7%) were boys, while 40 (21.3%) were girls. The average age of the participants was 8.6 ± 1.38 years old. The mean IQ of the participants was 92.88 ± 10.92. Regarding the ADHD subtype, the majority of the participants were diagnosed with ADHD Inattentive subtype (ADHD-I) (n = 105, 55.9%), followed by ADHD Combined subtype (ADHDC) (n = 61, 32.4%) and the ADHD Hyperactive-Impulsive subtype (ADHD-H) (n = 22, 11.7%). Additionally, 10.6% of the participants reported regular use of medication for ADHD management. Based on a PSQI cutoff score of 5, the Good Sleeper (GS) group consisted of 77 ADHD children (41%) (Mage = 8.74, 80.5% boys) and the Poor Sleeper (PS) group consisted of 111 ADHD children (59%) (Mage = 8.51, 77.5% boys). There were no significant differences in age, sex, IQ, BMI, ADHD subtype, comorbidity, and medication between the good and poor sleep groups. Comparisons of Sleep Characteristics, Internalizing Symptoms and Physical Activity Level Between Good Sleepers and Poor Sleepers Table 2 presents the GS/PS group comparison of all outcome variables. Compared to the GS group, the PS spent significantly less time in MVPA (F = 15.35, η2 = 0.079, p < 0.001) and had a lower proportion of meeting the MVPA guidelines (72.7% Vs 55.9%, F = 9.57, η2 = 0.050, p = 0.002). The PS group had significantly higher scores in depression (F = 10.09, η2 = 0.053, p = 0.002), anxiety (F = 15.84, η2 = 0.081, p < 0.001) and stress (F = 6.98, η2 = 0.037, p = 0.009), indicating more severe internalizing symptoms, compared to those without sleep disturbances. There were significant group differences in PSQI general scores (F = 257.98, η2 = 0.589, p < 0.001). Specifically, the PS group reported lower general sleep quality (F = 72.69, η2 = 0.288, p < 0.001), longer sleep latency (F = 57.50, η2 = 0.242, p < 0.001), less sleep duration (F = 8.69, η2 = 0.046, p = 0.004), lower sleep efficiency (F = 9.81, η2 = 0.052, p = 0.002), more sleep disturbances (F = 4.27, η2 = 0.023, p = 0.040), having more sleep medicine (F = 17.67, η2 = 0.089, p < 0.001), and more severe daytime dysfunction (F = 81.86, η2 = 0.313, p < 0.001) than in the GS group. In addition, the PS group had significantly later bedtimes than the GS group (F = 6.36, η2 = 0.034, p = 0.013). MVPA guideline attainment was negatively associated with depression and anxiety. Association of Sleep Problems and Physical Activity with Depression, Anxiety and Stress A three-step hierarchical regression analysis was carried out to identify significant factors associated with internalizing symptoms such as depression, anxiety, and stress. The independent variables were entered as follows: Step 1 included covariates such as IQ, age, BMI, sex, ADHD subtype, comorbidity and medication use; Step 2 included the behavioural sleep problems variable such as sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, sleep medication and daytime dysfunction, and Step 3 included the PA variables, including daily MVPA and MVPA guideline attainment. The results of the regression analysis related to the variables associated with internalizing symptoms are depicted in Table 4. Regarding depression, we found that daytime dysfunction (β = 0.319, p < 0.001) and MVPA guideline attainment (β = -0.302, p = 0.005) made a significant contribution and accounted for 25.7% of the variance of the depressive symptoms. Regarding anxiety, we found that BMI (β = 0.150, p = 0.041), sleep disturbance (β = 0.162, p = 0.032), daytime dysfunction (β = 0.402, p < 0.001), and MVPA guideline attainment (β = -0.218, p = 0.038) significantly contributed to the model. Regarding stress, BMI (β = 0.185, p = 0.017) and daytime dysfunction (β = 0.325, p < 0.001) significantly contributed to predicting the stress symptoms. Discussion This study aimed to compare the differences in internalizing symptoms and physical activity between children with ADHD and sleep problems and children with ADHD but without sleep problems and to determine the factors associated with internalizing symptoms in children with ADHD. The most important and novel finding was that 59% of children with ADHD were found to experience sleep problems. This result is in line with previous findings reporting the high prevalence rates of sleep problems ranging from 25 to 71% (Li et al., 2022; Sung et al., 2008) in children with ADHD. As expected, we found significant differences in internalizing symptoms and PA in children with ADHD and sleep problems and children with ADHD but without sleep problems. Thus, our results strengthened the point that children with ADHD and sleep disturbances had more severe internalizing symptoms than those without sleep problems. Additionally, our results showed that compared to children with ADHD but without sleep problems, children with ADHD and sleep disturbances engaged less time in MVPA daily (78.11 min/day Vs 66.70 min/day) and had a lower proportion to meet the MVPA guidelines (72.7% Vs 55.9%). Consistent with previous studies, youth with insufficient sleep duration (≤ 9 h/ night) had significantly lower daily MVPA than youth sleeping longer than 10 h (Ortega et al., 2011). These novel findings strengthen the view that poor sleep may decrease children’s PA levels (Tambalis et al., 2018). Therefore, our study suggests that children with ADHD and co-occurring sleep problems present with a more severe clinical presentation of internalizing symptoms and physical inactivity. Previous studies suggested that both ADHD and sleep difficulties reflect a common physiological mechanism (e.g., irregular arousal) (Ball et al., 1997), causing them to be particularly vulnerable in specific domains (Bar et al., 2016), such as executive dysfunction, co-occurring psychiatric problems, and academic underachievement (Becker, 2020). Given the high comorbidity rates between ADHD and sleep, further studies should examine the interplay of sleep and other health behaviours among individuals with ADHD (Becker, 2020). In the current study, MVPA guideline attainment negatively affects depressive and anxiety symptoms in children with ADHD. In line with a recent study, MVPA was negatively associated with depression and stress in children with ADHD (Liang et al., 2023b). 1170 Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2026) 56:1163–1172 with ADHD who had higher-than-usual PA showed less depressed affect in the evening compared with those with lower-than-usual PA (Gawrilow et al., 2016), and better scores in health-related QoL were correlated with increased frequency of PA in children with ADHD (Gallego-Méndez et al., 2020). Consistent with children without disabilities, previous studies also reported that increased PA in childhood is related to a lower incidence of internalizing symptoms in adolescence and young adulthood (Wu et al., 2018) and higher MVPA at baseline was associated with lower symptoms of both depression and anxiety at follow-up (Buchan et al., 2021). In contrast, previous studies reported no prospective association between MVPA guideline adherence and depressive symptoms in youth (Patte et al., 2020) and that meeting the MVPA guideline was not related to flourishing, school engagement and BMI in children with ADHD (W. Wang et al., 2022). It is worth noting that previous findings were based on the proxy report, which may be prone to reporting bias. The current study utilized actigraph to objectively measure PA levels, confirming the associations between objectively assessed MVPA and mental health benefits in children with ADHD. In addition, we found that BMI was a significant predictor for developing anxiety and stress symptoms in children with ADHD. Consistent with previous studies, internalizing symptoms (e.g., distress and anxiety) are associated with increases in BMI in children (Ames et al., 2015; Gibson-Smith et al., 2020), and BMI and internalizing symptoms were reciprocally associated with each other for children 7–11 years old (Zhou et al., 2022). In children with ADHD specifically, there have been significant associations between ADHD and obesity/overweight (Cortese et al., 2016). The possible explanation is that children with ADHD and higher BMI are more likely to experience sleep disturbances, bullying and social exclusion and have low PA levels and a disrupted diet; thus, they may have a higher risk for the development of internalizing symptoms (Zhou et al., 2022). The key finding of this study was that sleep-related daytime dysfunction (as measured by PSQI) was significantly associated with internalizing symptoms (i.e., depression, anxiety, and stress) in children with ADHD. Consistent with previous studies, sleep problems in children with ADHD predicted internalizing symptoms (i.e., depression) one year later after controlling for baseline symptoms (Becker et al., 2015); sleep problems at baseline predicted internalizing symptoms (i.e., emotional problems) at 6 months (Mulraney et al., 2016); and daytime sleepiness in children with anxiety disorders predicted internalizing problems (Hansen et al., 2014). Recent evidence has suggested that sleep problems may contribute to the development of internalizing and externalizing problems in children with ADHD and the relationship between sleep and internalizing and externalizing problems is bidirectional (Becker et al., 2015; Mulraney et al., 2016).It is possible that specific sleep problems, such as sleep disturbances or night awaking, may cause daytime sleepiness at school, and emotional and behavioural problems and poor academic performance at school may be criticised by teachers or parents, causing internalizing problems in children with ADHD over time (Lucas et al., 2019). Our findings were well-aligned with those of previous studies showing that poor sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep disturbance and daytime dysfunction are positively correlated with internalizing symptoms (depression, anxiety, and stress) in children with ADHD (Lycett et al., 2015; Mayes et al., 2009). The novel findings of this study showed that meeting the WHO-recommended 60 min of MVPA guideline was negatively related to anxiety and stress in children with ADHD. In line with previous studies among the general population, children with ADHD who accumulated high PA levels experienced fewer mental health problems than those who had medium- and low-level PA (Ganjeh et al., 2021). As such, it is recommended that children with ADHD should do at least an average of 60 min per day of MVPA to improve impaired cognition, physical function, and mental health (World Health Organization, 2020). This study is one of the very few that explored the effects of sleep on internalizing symptoms and physical activity in children with ADHD. A primary strength of this study was the use of actigraphy to objectively measure physical activity levels, which were not fully considered or adopted in previous research. Nonetheless, this study has some limitations. First, we used a cross-sectional design, which limits the possibility of making causal conclusions about sleep problems, internalizing symptoms, and PA. There is a need for longitudinal research to examine the causal mechanisms supporting our observations. Second, as the current findings on sleep quality and internalizing symptoms are based on child reports, our results may be prone to reporting biases. Further studies should be designed to use objective and reliable measures of sleep (e.g., polysomnography) and internalizing disorders biomarkers (e.g., cortisol) to gain a more nuanced understanding of sleep's effect on health-related outcomes in children with ADHD. Last, healthy controls were not recruited in the current study to have a comparison with the ADHD groups. Conclusion The current study provides evidence that children with ADHD and sleep problems are less active and present with more severe internalizing symptoms than ADHD children without sleep problems. BMI, daytime dysfunction and MVPA guideline attainment predict the internalizing symptoms. Given the high rates of children with ADHD who experience sleep problems and children with ADHD
