Social difficulties are a transdiagnostic feature for children with ADHD and autism and are central to both disorders (Leitner, 2014), although their difficulties may vary in nature (Mikami et al., 2019). Regarding youth with ADHD, it has been suggested that attention problems may limit their opportunities to notice social cues and demonstrate appro priate social skills (Mikami et al., 2019). Impulsive and hyperactive children may be considered intrusive by peers, which may lead to rejection by the group (Hoza, 2007; Ros & Graziano, 2018). Overall, research has shown that youth with ADHD are more likely to have problems socially, are liked less compared with peers without ADHD, and have Dagmar Kr. Hannesdottir dkh@hi.is 1 Department of Psychology, University of Iceland, Saemundargata 12, Reykjavik 102, Iceland 2 Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, LandspitaliThe National University Hospital of Iceland, Reykjavík, Iceland 3 Department of Business and Economics, Reykjavik University, Reykjavik, Iceland 4 Department of Psychology, Reykjavik University, Reykjavik, Iceland 5 Children ́s Mental Health Center for the Primary Health Care of the Capital Area (Gedheilsumistod Barna Heilsugaeslu Hofudborgarsvaedisins), Reykjavik, Iceland Abstract Children with neurodevelopmental disorders tend to have more social difficulties than typically developing children. The aim of the current study was to examine parent and teacher-reported effects of age and gender on social functioning in a large clinical sample of children and adolescents with ADHD, autism, or co-occurring ADHD and autism using a crosssectional study design. This nationwide clinical sample included 2132 Icelandic children and adolescents (35% girls, 65% boys) aged 5–18 years referred for a neurodevelopmental diagnostic assessment (ADHD and/or autism) in Iceland. Social functioning was measured using the Prosocial behavior and Peer problem subscales on the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ) completed by parents and teachers. Results revealed that autistic youth and youth with co-occurring ADHD and autism experienced more peer problems and showed less prosocial behavior than youth with ADHD only. According to parents and teachers, girls were found to experience more social difficulties compared to boys. Interaction for age and gender, although only significant for teacher reports, indicated that younger girls with neurodevelopmental disorders experience more peer problems and show less prosocial behavior than older girls. In contrast, boys with neuro developmental disorders experience similar issues at all ages. The results suggest different patterns of social difficulties for boys and girls with neurodevelopmental disorders. Future research should examine different developmental pathways of social challenges for boys and girls. Implications for developing and providing clinical interventions appropriate devel opmental stages are discussed. Gender differences have also emerged in studies on social functioning among children with ADHD. Boys with ADHD tend to show more noncompliance than boys without ADHD but show no difference in the frequency of prosocial behavior, such as taking initiative socially, showing leader ship, resolving conflicts, and setting social norms (Erhardt & Hinshaw, 1994). However, ADHD has been suggested to be somewhat more impairing for girls than boys. Hyperac tivity and impulsivity symptoms may be considered more inappropriate in girl groups, causing girls to experience peer rejection, long-lasting social problems, and increased rates of co-occurring psychiatric disorders (Mikami et al., 2013; Mikami & Lorenzi, 2011; Ragnarsdottir et al., 2018; Tung et al., 2016). In contrast to the social difficulties experienced by chil dren with ADHD, limited prosocial behavior and social motivation may partly be driving the social difficulties experienced by autistic children in terms of making friends and maintaining friendships (Mikami et al., 2019). It has been suggested that diminished social interest in early child hood may reduce social input and chances to learn for autis tic youth, which may, in turn, contribute to their difficulties in social communication. Autistic children have been found to engage in fewer verbal interactions and less social play than typically developing children (Corbett et al., 2014). It has been hypothesized that a low sense of reward experi enced from social interaction diminishes the motivation to initiate and sustain social behavior, potentially resulting in a reluctance to perform prosocial behaviors (Chevallier et al., 2012). Research has also shown that autistic youth are more likely to be isolated across all grade levels and that they become more isolated in later grades (Rotheram-Fuller et al., 2010), indicating that older autistic children may face more social difficulties than younger children. However, not all autistic children lack social motivation. Some seek out social interactions with peers but may struggle to demon strate appropriate social behaviors (Scheeren et al., 2012). Some gender differences have been noted in studies on social interactions among autistic youth. Studies have shown that autistic boys are more likely to be excluded socially by peers. Autistic girls are, on the other hand, neither accepted nor rejected but seem to be ignored or overlooked (Dean et al., 2014). It has been suggested that autistic girls may blend in more efficiently, while boys are more prone to isolation (Hiller et al., 2014). According to the camouflage hypothesis (Lai et al., 2011), autistic females may use com pensatory behaviors to mask their social challenges and use social opportunities to watch the interactions of other girls to mimic them. This imitation of appropriate social behavior may help them blend in with peers (Attwood, 2008; Cook et al., 2021; Dean et al., 2017). It is important to note that camouflaging seems easier for those with better executive functioning skills, irrespective of gender (Fletcher-Watson & Happé, 2019; Hull et al., 2021). Research on social behavior and functioning among children diagnosed with co-occurring ADHD and autism has shown mixed results. However, some studies indicate greater impairment in social and emotional cognitive pro cesses when children are diagnosed with both disorders (e.g., Antshel et al., 2016; Rosello et al., 2022). It has been sug gested that if social behavior patterns switch between aloof ness (e.g., in autism) and intrusiveness (e.g., in ADHD), the unpredictability in response might cause increased prob lems in social situations (Mikami et al., 2019). Some stud ies have shown that children with co-occurring ADHD and autism face more social challenges than children diagnosed only with autism (Factor et al., 2017; Rao & Landa, 2014; Sikora et al., 2012). Other studies have, however, shown no differences in peer problems when comparing boys with cooccurring ADHD and autism to boys with either ADHD or autism. Boys with the combined diagnoses have been found to show less prosocial behavior than boys with ADHD only. However, no difference emerged for boys with the com bined diagnosis and boys with autism (e.g., Yamawaki et al., 2020). Similarly, a recent study found comparable social difficulties for autistic children compared with children who have co-occurring ADHD and autism (Harkins et al., 2022). Unfortunately, almost no studies have been conducted on the social functioning of girls with co-occurring ADHD and autism (Mikami et al., 2019). Therefore, information is lack ing on how girls with ADHD and autism fare socially and whether it is necessary to provide different clinical interven tions based on age and gender for this group of youth with co-occurring neurodevelopmental disorders. Additionally, most previous studies on social functioning have relied on parent reports, but very few studies have pro vided teacher reports of social behaviors among youth with ADHD and/or autism (Mikami et al., 2019). The field lacks information on how youth with co-occurring ADHD and autism are viewed socially in the school environment. While obtaining information on social behaviors from parents and teachers is informative, discrepancies between these two types of informants frequently occur (De Los Reyes et al., 2023). Discrepancies in multi-informant information can however provide valuable and relevant information on how behavior presents in a certain context, have high internal consistency, correlate with the perspectives informants have on the children they are assessing and relate to varia tions in the context where the informants are observing the children (De Los Reyes, 2011). Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2026) 56:1808–1819 this group should add meaningfully to the current literature. Since social functioning is a central part of both ADHD and autism, providing more comprehensive research on this cru cial aspect of children ́s lives is essential and valuable for the field of clinical child psychology. The purpose of the current study was to examine par ent and teacher-reported effects of age and gender on social functioning in a large clinical sample of children and ado lescents with ADHD, autism, or co-occurring ADHD. In a previous study (Ragnarsdottir et al., 2018) we examined the interaction effects of gender and age differences on peer problems and prosocial behavior among younger children with ADHD only. The focus of the current study includes a much larger clinical group aged 5 to 18 of autistic children and adolescents and youth with co-occurring ADHD and autism, a group that has been underrepresented in clinical research. Based on previous findings (e.g., Mikami et al., 2019; Yamawaki et al., 2020), it is expected that the group with ADHD will experience the most severe peer problems compared with the other groups. The autism-only group is expected to show less prosocial behavior, according to both parents and teachers, compared with the ADHD group and co-occurring ADHD and autism group. It is also expected that the group with co-occurring ADHD and autism will show the most significant impairment and have more peer problems and less prosocial behavior in comparison to the groups diagnosed only with autism or ADHD since earlier research has indicated more impairment for this group over all (Factor et al., 2017; Rao & Landa, 2014; Sikora et al., 2012; Rosello et al., 2022). It is also expected that girls will experience more social difficulties overall, as previous studies on girls with ADHD have suggested (e.g., Mikami et al., 2013; Mikami & Lorenzi, 2011). A significant interaction effect of age and gender is also expected to emerge for peer problems and prosocial behavior, as earlier research on youth with ADHD has shown (Ragnarsdottir et al., 2018). Whether similar interaction effects of age and gender will emerge for the groups of autistic youth and youth with co-occurring ADHD and autism will also be examined. Method Participants Medical records of children and adolescents who were referred from all over Iceland for a neurodevelopmental assessment of ADHD and/or autism at the Center for Child Development and Behavior (CCDB) in Iceland (currently the Children’s Mental Health Center for the Primary Health Care of the Capital Area) were examined. Referrals came from professionals within the healthcare system, school psy chologists, or social services, in collaboration with parents. Still, parents were not allowed to self-refer their children to the CCDB for a neurodevelopmental assessment. The refer ral and evaluation process was free of charge and thus acces sible to all families independent of socioeconomic status. In Iceland, the primary health care system monitors children’s developmental levels and well-being systematically from birth to six years of age. Additionally, they see a school nurse for a standardized health assessment at six, nine, and twelve upon entering elementary school. Children ́s devel opmental levels are also monitored by school services in kindergarten and elementary school. Approximately 86% of children in Iceland attend kindergarten (Hagstofa Íslands, 2024) and all children in Iceland attend elementary school since homeschooling is not allowed. Inclusion criteria for the current study were the follow ing: (i) meeting diagnostic criteria for ADHD, autism, or both disorders, (ii) being between the ages of 5 and 18 years, (iii) having a full-scale intelligence quotient (IQ) score of 70 or higher (or a verbal comprehension score of 70 if the fullscale score was not available) on the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-IV (WISC-IV) or the Wechsler Preschool Primary Scale of Intelligence (WPPSI-R) and (iv) having the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ; Good man, 1997) completed by at least one parent or teacher. If the children had been assessed at a younger age, only the most recent assessment was included in the current study. The final sample included 2132 children and adolescents (35% girls, 65% boys; mean age = 10.07 years; SD = 2.98), where 223 children were diagnosed with autism (5–11-year-olds n = 118; 12–18-year-olds n = 105), and 359 children were diagnosed with co-occurring ADHD and autism (5–11-yearolds n = 234; 12–18-year-olds n = 125). For children diag nosed with ADHD (n = 1550) (5–11-year-olds n = 1209; 12–18-year-olds n = 341), 1078 (69%) were diagnosed with the combined presentation, 448 were diagnosed with the predominantly inattentive presentation (29%), and 24 were diagnosed with the predominantly hyperactive/impulsive presentation (2%). Children in the sample had an average IQ total score of m (SD) = 95.9 (14.9). Further participant characteristics are presented in Table 1. As part of the diagnostic process, par ents of all youth undergoing a neurodevelopmental assess ment were administered a diagnostic interview to assess and rule out co-occurring disorders. The Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS; Kaufman et al., 1997; Kaufman et al., 2016) and/or the Anxiety Disor ders Interview Schedule (ADIS-C/P; Silverman & Albano, 1996) were administered to all parents and the youth them selves if they were over ten years of age. The Icelandic ver sion of K-SADS-PL DSM-5 has recently been shown to have good psychometric properties, such as inter-rater reli ability (Hannesson et al., 2023). Children who were diag nosed with an autism spectrum disorder were administered the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule Test-Second Edition (ADOS-2; Lord et al., 2012) during the assessment process. Additionally, the parents were interviewed exten sively about the child ́s developmental history using the Autism Diagnostic Interview (ADI-R; Lord et al., 1994) and/or the Social Communication Questionnaire (Berument et al., 1999; Rutter et al., 2003) All diagnoses were final ized according to ICD-10 diagnostic criteria (World Health Organization, 2016) during a consensus meeting with a psychologist and pediatrician/child psychiatrist. The child’s overall functioning was rated using the Children ́s Global Assessment Scale (C-GAS; Shaffer et al., 1983). The study is a part of the NICE project: Characteristics of neurodiverse youth in Iceland, an extensive research series of children with neurodevelopmental disorders. The study was approved by the National Bioethics Committee in Ice land (VSNb2022010022/03.01) and the Ethical Committee of the Primary Health Care of the Capital Area. behavior. In the present study, only the Prosocial behavior and Peer problems subscales scores were used to assess children’s social functioning and behavior. Higher scores on the Prosocial behavior subscale and lower scores on the Peer problems subscale indicate better social skills and functioning. The scale has been translated into Icelandic, normed, and has good psychometric properties (Hrafnsdóttir, 2005; Skar phéðinsson & Magnússon, 2008). Gender and age-specific normative t-scores were used in this study. A t-score of 65 or higher is considered above the clinical cutoff for Peer prob lems, and a t-score of 35 or lower is the clinical cutoff score for Prosocial behavior. The Children‘s Global Assessment Scale (C-GAS; Shaffer, 1983) C-GAS is a numeric scale clinicians use to rate the gen eral function of children aged 18 and younger. Values range from 1 to 100, where lower scores indicate more functional impairment and higher scores indicate a better function in the last month (Shaffer, 1983). The reliability of the C-GAS score is moderate (Hanssen-Bauer et al., 2007; Rey et al., 1995). Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2026) 56:1808–1819 Discussion This study aimed to examine peer problems and proso cial behavior from parents’ and teachers’ perspectives in a large clinical nationwide sample of youth with ADHD and/ or autism. It was expected that children with co-occurring ADHD and autism would have the greatest impairment in social functioning when compared to youth with only ADHD or only autism, as some previous studies have indi cated (e.g., Factor et al., 2017; Rosello et al., 2022). The results only partly supported this hypothesis. Parents rated the group with co-occurring ADHD and autism to have sig nificantly more peer problems compared with youth with ADHD only or autism only. However, teachers reported similar levels of peer problems for autistic youth and youth were performed for comparison on the four dependent variables (parent and teacher reports of Peer problems and Prosocial behavior) for a separate dataset of youth referred to the CCDB for an ADHD or an autism assessment pro cess but who did not meet diagnostic criteria for ADHD or autism (n = 320; 38% girls, 62% boys; mean age = 9.53 years; SD = 2.44). The four models — each using age, gen der, and an age-by-gender interaction as predictors — were all found to be non-significant, indicating that this pattern of results only emerged for children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD, autism or both. The same interac tion effect was seen for prosocial behavior, where teachers reported that younger girls showed less prosocial behavior than older girls. These results suggest that girls with neu rodevelopmental disorders struggle to a greater extent with social functioning compared to boys, especially younger girls. It has been suggested that girls with neurodevelopmental difficulties, like ADHD and/or autism, may seem to stand out as more deviant in a group of girls. At the same time, there may be more variability in groups of boys, so boys with neurodevelopmental disorders may blend in more easily (Mikami et al., 2013; Mikami & Lorenzi, 2011). It is unclear why younger girls had greater difficulties than older girls in this particular study. Research has shown that higher-functioning girls with autism may be identified later than boys and that the average time between initial concern and a diagnosis of autism may be longer for girls than boys (Begeer et al., 2013). Perhaps older girls have gotten better at using compensatory behaviors to mask their social chal lenges, as other research has suggested (Attwood, 2008; Cook et al., 2021; Dean et al., 2017). It is also possible that the older girls have found common ground with others regarding their unique interests and are now part of a peer group that shares their interests, thus experiencing fewer peer problems and showing increased prosocial behavior. Since this is a cross-sectional study, this issue remains unan swered, and longitudinal data would be necessary to answer these questions. Strengths and Limitations The current study has many strengths. First, the results are based on a large, nationwide sample of boys and girls who completed an extensive and interdisciplinary in-person assessment protocol for their ADHD and/or autism diag noses. Results for these youth with neurodevelopmental disorders are based on synchronized standard assessment protocols and not just on questionnaire reports for symp toms of ADHD and/or autism, as in some previous studies (e.g., Factor et al., 2017). Second, the sample consisted of youth referred for various neurodevelopmental difficulties, that is, either ADHD symptoms, autism, or both. In similar studies, the clinical samples have been referred mainly for an autism evaluation (e.g., Harkins et al., 2022), thus miss ing out on essential comparisons with a more basic clinical group of youth with only ADHD. Fourth, this is one of the few clinical samples where 35% of the youth with neuro developmental disorders are females. Few such studies are available on girls with co-occurring ADHD and autism, and with co-occurring ADHD and autism, while the ADHDonly group had significantly fewer peer problems. Never theless, results for the prosocial behavior subscale were in line with other previous studies (e.g., Harkins et al., 2022; Yamawaki et al., 2020). Both parents and teachers reported significantly more prosocial behavior for the ADHD group compared to the autistic group and the group with cooccurring ADHD and autism. These results suggest that children with ADHD have fewer peer problems and demon strate to a greater extent prosocial behavior when compared with autistic youth or youth with co-occurring ADHD and autism. The results also indicate that overall, social difficul ties of youth with autism are rated greater by parents and teachers, independent of whether they have co-occurring ADHD or not. Interestingly, the interaction of age and gender was only significant according to teacher reports of peer problems and prosocial behavior and not by parent reports. These results are unsurprising since informant discrepancies are usually the rule rather than the exception in clinical child research (De Los Reyes, 2011). Often, informant discrepancies arise between teachers and parents because they see children in different circumstances. Different situations call for differ ent behavior demands, and raters from various settings have been found to have a lower agreement than raters from the same setting (Achenbach, 2006; De Los Reyes et al., 2023). This may be especially true for ratings of social behavior and peer interactions since parents usually see the child at home playing with one child or in a small group. In contrast, the teachers see children interacting in a large group setting. Previous studies in different countries on the SDQ have shown that parent and teacher agreement on the Peer prob lems and Prosocial behavior subscales tends to be low to moderate (Cheng et al., 2018). It has been argued that parent and teacher discrepancies reflect more than a measurement error but can provide valuable insights into how children behave differently depending on who they are interacting with within different settings. Such information can be used to improve treatment effects (De Los Reyes, 2011). In terms of gender differences, the results showed that girls had greater peer problems than boys, according to both teachers and parents, and girls showed less prosocial behavior. The hypothesis that girls would have more social difficulties than boys was supported and in line with previ ous studies (e.g., Mikami et al., 2013; Ragnarsdottir et al., 2018). However, significant interaction effects of age and gender were only found for teacher reports of peer problems and prosocial behavior. While it could be assumed before hand that youth being referred for a neurodevelopmental assessment at a younger age would likely be more impaired than those being referred during adolescence, this pattern of results only emerged for girls and not for boys. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2026) 56:1808–1819 to the sparse literature on characteristics of youth with cooccurring ADHD and autism. The study is clinically rele vant since it adds insights into how treatment for girls and boys might be developed differently to address their social difficulties at different developmental stages. The results also highlight that autistic youth struggle more with social difficulties compared with youth with ADHD only and that younger girls have more social difficulties compared with older girls. In the future, longitudinal research of peer problems and prosocial behavior would help establish the developmental trajectories of those social difficulties of youth with ADHD and/or autism, as well as shed light on gender and age dif ferences of those difficulties across different developmen tal stages. The current study does, however, indicate that it might be important to support youth with neurodevel opmental disorders, especially younger girls, in the school setting. These findings could help clinicians develop appro priate social interventions that might benefit groups of chil dren with neurodevelopmental disorders at a certain age, for example, during the first years of elementary school. Such intervention programs, if successful in minimizing peer problems and increasing prosocial behaviors, could, in turn, impact youth with neurodevelopmental disorders develop ing further problems. Since various co-occurring disorders, such as anxiety and depression, are more common among youth with neurodevelopmental disorders (e.g., GordonLipkin et al., 2018; Tung et al., 2016), it is important to consider whether appropriate social interventions at the appropriate developmental stage could reduce the chances of developing such co-occurring disorders. Finally, while many previous studies have focused mainly on parent-reported social functioning (Mikami et al., 2019), the current study provides valuable insight into how teachers view these children’s social functioning. Missing information from teachers was minimal since over 90% of teachers for the current sample completed the SDQ for these youth with neurodevelopmental disorders. Knowing that young girls with co-occurring ADHD and autism are strug gling socially in the school environment adds meaningfully to our understanding of gender differences in children with these disorders. Identifying how behavior appears in differ ent situations provides valuable insights into where more support is needed and at what developmental stage appro priate interventions should be a priority. The current study also has some limitations. First, only one questionnaire was administered to assess social func tioning and behavior. Additional information from direct observations would have been valuable for this study. Sec ond, social functioning evaluated in terms of peer problems and prosocial behaviors reported only by parents and teach ers tells us very little about how the children view their social difficulties or how their peers evaluate them. It also tells us very little about the number and quality of friend ships youth with neurodevelopmental disorders may have, which are essential areas of research (e.g., Petrina et al., 2014; Spender et al., 2023), especially for developing effec tive interventions. Third, although the predictive models are significant, they explain a relatively low proportion of the variance. Adding additional variables into our data col lection and models would have been beneficial since other factors such as low SES (Becker et al., 2015), maternal education, parents psychological well-being and being in a reconstituted family (McMunn et al., 2001), having fewer adaptive skills and more severe autism symptoms (Hastings et al., 2022) have all been associated with worse outcomes on the SDQ questionnaire. Finally, the clinical group con sisted only of youth with no intellectual impairment. While this makes it easier to generalize the results to similar groups of youth, further research is needed to examine whether the same patterns of social functioning emerge for youth with neurodevelopmental disorders and intellectual impairment. Longitudinal studies would be valuable in exploring how social difficulties develop differently between boys and girls throughout various developmental stages. Pharmacists have established expertise in medicines optimisation and, in some settings, are authorised to prescribe. Aim This scoping review aims to map the existing empirical evidence on pharmacist involvement in ADHD services, synthesise reported roles and impacts, and identify key evidence gaps to inform future research and service development. Method A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the Arksey and O’Malley framework and reported using PRISMA-ScR guidance. Six databases (PubMed, PsycINFO, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, and Web of Science) were searched from inception to December 2025. Empirical studies evaluating implemented pharmacist involvement in ADHD services were included, irrespective of study design. Data were charted and synthesised narratively across domains relating to clinical care, service delivery, economic outcomes, and barriers to implementation. Results Thirteen studies were included, published between 2008 and 2025, primarily from the United States and the United Kingdom. Most were service evaluations or pre-post studies, with one randomised trial. Pharmacists were involved in a broad range of activities, including medication initiation, titration, monitoring, follow-up, patient education, and service governance, often as independent prescribers or within collaborative multidisciplinary models. Reported impacts included improved adherence to recommended monitoring standards, increased service capacity, reduced waiting times, and more efficient workforce utilisation, with some evidence of potential cost savings. However, outcome measures varied widely, and patient-reported outcomes, comparative effectiveness, and implementation processes were inconsistently examined. Conclusion This review identifies a small but expanding evidence base indicating potential roles for pharmacists in ADHD services, particularly in medicines management and service delivery. However, the absence of clearly defined service models and limited comparative and implementation-focused evidence constrain wider adoption across health systems. Further research is needed to inform scalable and sustainable approaches to pharmacist integration in ADHD care. It demonstrates that pharmacists can contribute effectively to medication initiation, titration, monitoring, and service delivery, with potential benefits for access to care and adherence to recommended monitoring standards. • Findings suggest that integrating pharmacists into ADHD care pathways may improve service capacity and workforce efficiency, particularly in health systems experiencing workforce shortages and long waiting times. Introduction Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition affecting approximately 8% of children globally [1] and 2.6% of adults [2]. In the United Kingdom (UK), prevalence estimates suggest ADHD affects around 5% of children and 3–4% of adults [3]. ADHD is characterised by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity and is associated with impaired educational attainment, increased psychiatric comorbidity, and long-term socioeconomic disadvantage [4]. Pharmacological treatment, alongside psychosocial interventions, remains a cornerstone of ADHD management for many individuals, with stimulant and non-stimulant medications requiring ongoing clinical review and monitoring [3]. Despite the availability of effective treatments, access to ADHD services remains a significant challenge internationally. Rising demand, workforce shortages, and increasing complexity of care have placed sustained pressure on specialist services [5–7]. In the UK, waiting times for assessment and treatment initiation are frequently prolonged. The NHS England ADHD Taskforce reported waits of up to four years for children and eight years for adults [8], contributing to delayed treatment, inconsistent medication monitoring, and variable patient experience [9]. The requirement for regular physical monitoring further increases service burden and exacerbates inequalities in access [10]. Pharmacists are a highly skilled but underutilised workforce in mental health and neurodevelopmental care [11]. Particularly, specialist and clinically trained pharmacists possess expertise in medicines optimisation, safety monitoring, and patient education, positioning them to support ADHD services. Evidence from broader mental health settings suggests pharmacist involvement can improve medication management and service efficiency [11]. In ADHD care, pharmacists may contribute to medication initiation and titration, routine monitoring, adherence support, and coordination across care settings. However, the scope, implementation, and impact of these roles remain poorly characterised. Emerging empirical studies, predominantly from the United States (US) and the UK, have evaluated pharmacist-led or pharmacist-supported ADHD services across a range of settings [12–14]. However, this literature varies widely by study design, populations, pharmacists’ role, service model, and the evidence base remains fragmented. It is also unclear to what extent existing studies have examined patient-reported outcomes, clinician perspectives, or implementation challenges relevant to the sustainability and scalability of pharmacist involvement in ADHD services. Existing narrative reviews and book chapters describe potential pharmacist contributions but do not synthesise empirical evaluations of service delivery or outcomes [15–17]. To date, no review has comprehensively mapped the empirical evidence on pharmacist involvement in ADHD services. Aim This scoping review aims to map the existing empirical evidence on pharmacist involvement in ADHD services, synthesise reported roles and impacts, and identify key evidence gaps to inform future research and service development. Method This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the framework proposed by Arksey and O’Malley [18] and informed by subsequent methodological guidance [19] and reported in line with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) [20]. Although a formal protocol for this scoping review was not registered or published, a structured approach informed by the methodological guidance outlined above was followed in conducting the five stages of the review: (1) identifying the research question, (2) identifying relevant studies, (3) study selection, (4) charting the data, and (5) collating, summarising, and reporting the results. Stage 1: identifying the research question The review was guided by the following research question: What is the current evidence on the roles and impacts of pharmacists in ADHD services, and what gaps exist to inform future service development? This broad question was selected to enable mapping of the range, nature, and extent of empirical evidence relating to pharmacist involvement across different ADHD care settings, populations, and service models. Stage 2: identification of relevant studies A comprehensive search strategy was developed and applied across six electronic databases: PubMed, PsycINFO, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, and Web of Science. Searches

1814 International Journal of Clinical Pharmacy (2026) 48:1812–1826 were limited to studies published from inception to December 2025 to capture the evolution of pharmacist involvement beyond traditional dispensing roles. Only English-language publications were included. The search strategy combined terms related to ADHD (e.g. attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, ADHD) with terms describing pharmacists and pharmacy professionals (e.g. pharmacist, clinical pharmacist, specialist pharmacist, independent prescriber) and terms relating to services, roles, and care delivery (e.g. prescribing, titration, monitoring, intervention). Database-specific subject headings (e.g. MeSH terms) and Boolean operators were used to optimise sensitivity and relevance. A sample search strategy is provided in Appendix 1. In addition to database searching, reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were hand-searched to identify further eligible articles. Conference proceedings were also screened to capture emerging evidence not yet published in full. Stage 3: study selection Study selection was conducted in two stages. First, titles and abstracts of all identified records were independently screened by two reviewers (MUK & AN) to assess potential eligibility. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus. Second, full-text screening was undertaken by one reviewer (MUK) and cross-checked by a second reviewer (AN). Studies were included if they reported on the involvement of a pharmacist in an ADHD service and evaluated the impact of pharmacist activities on patient care, clinical processes, or service delivery. For the purpose of this review, evaluation of impact was interpreted broadly and included both quantitative outcomes (e.g. monitoring rates, waiting times, or prescribing outcomes) and descriptive or service-level evaluations reporting changes in practice, service delivery, or implementation. Studies were excluded if ADHD was not the primary focus, if pharmacist involvement was limited to theoretical or conceptual descriptions without service implementation, or if no evaluation of impact was reported. Conference abstracts were included where sufficient methodological detail and outcome data were available to inform the review. The study selection process was documented using a PRISMA-ScR flow diagram. Stage 4: charting the data Data were charted using a data extraction form and piloted by the review team. Extraction was undertaken primarily by one reviewer (MUK), with all extracted data checked by a second reviewer for accuracy and completeness (AN). Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus. Extracted data included study characteristics (author, year, country), study design and duration, care setting, target population, sample size, and pharmacist role (e.g. independent prescriber, specialist pharmacist, collaborative model). Information on service models, additional training, and the number of pharmacists involved was also collected where reported. Outcome data were extracted verbatim and included clinical and medication management outcomes, service delivery and access outcomes, economic or resource-related outcomes, and system-level or professional contributions. Where reported, information on implementation barriers and facilitators was also charted. Consistent with scoping review methodology, no formal assessment of study quality or risk of bias was undertaken, as the aim was to map the extent, nature, and characteristics of the evidence rather than to evaluate effectiveness [18]. All data were managed using Microsoft Excel. Stage 5: collating, summarising, and reporting the results Extracted data were collated and synthesised using a narrative descriptive approach. Study characteristics were summarised in tabular form, while findings were organised into several domains reflecting the objectives of the review. These domains included clinical and medication management outcomes, service delivery, efficiency, and access to care, economic and resource outcomes, professional contribution and system-level functions, and barriers to implementation and sustainability of pharmacist-led ADHD services. Given the diversity of study designs, settings, and outcome measures, quantitative data were summarised descriptively, and qualitative findings were synthesised narratively. Results are presented in accordance with PRISMA-ScR guidance (Appendix 2). Results The database searches identified 1618 records, with an additional six records identified through other sources (conference proceedings). After the removal of 947 duplicates, 671 records were screened by title and abstract. Of these, 578 records were excluded, and 93 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Eighty-two full-text articles were excluded for not meeting the inclusion criteria, resulting in 11 studies included from database searches. Of the six records identified from other sources, four were excluded due to duplication or ineligibility, and two were included. In total, 13 studies were included in the final analysis (Fig. 1).

Clinical and medication management outcomes Across studies, pharmacists were involved in medication initiation, titration, monitoring, and follow-up, operating as independent prescribers [13, 14, 28, 29] in some settings and under collaborative or delegated prescribing models in others [12, 21–27, 30]. Improvements in adherence to physical health monitoring were reported in several studies. In a pre–post college health centre study, pharmacist-led care achieved higher rates of blood pressure (77% vs 11%) and heart rate monitoring (75% vs 6%) than psychiatrist-led care [12]. In a cluster randomised controlled trial, children managed by pharmacists were more likely to meet height and weight monitoring standards compared with paediatrician-led care (88.6% vs 66.1%), with comparable parental ratings of care quality [21]. Furthermore, Shah et al. reported that pharmacist contributions, including monitoring of physical parameters, were positively received by families and multidisciplinary team members [13], while Watthanathiraphapwong et al., reported reduced stimulant prescribing errors and enhanced parental satisfaction in ADHD care management [30]. Discussion Summary of key findings This scoping review mapped the existing empirical evidence on pharmacist involvement in ADHD services and identified a small but growing body of literature published predominantly in the last decade. The evidence base is concentrated in the United States and the United Kingdom and is characterised largely by service evaluations, pre-post studies, and post-implementation reports, with relatively few comparative or experimental designs. Across diverse settings and populations, pharmacists contributed to a wide range of ADHD-related activities, spanning clinical and medication management, service delivery and access to care, medicines-related education and governance, and broader system-level functions. Overall, the findings suggest that pharmacist involvement in ADHD care is feasible across multiple care settings, but the nature, scope, and reported impacts of these roles vary considerably. Nature and scope of pharmacist roles in ADHD services Pharmacist involvement in ADHD services predominantly occurred through prescribing and advanced clinical roles embedded within multidisciplinary teams, reflecting the extent to which pharmacists are clinically integrated within local service structures. The balance between prescribing and non-prescribing activities appears less indicative of role capability than of how pharmacists are positioned within care pathways, with variation largely shaped by regulatory permissions and scope-of-practice arrangements across health systems, particularly between the United States (US) and the United Kingdom (UK). In the US, pharmacist prescribing authority is governed at the state level and implemented through a range of models, including patient-specific and population-specific Collaborative Practice Agreements, statewide protocols, and class-specific prescribing [31]. This regulatory complexity contributes to substantial heterogeneity in pharmacist autonomy and responsibility within ADHD services, shaped by state legislation, institutional policies, and local service agreements. In contrast, the UK operates under a nationally regulated framework for pharmacist independent prescribing, established in 2006, which permits pharmacists to prescribe any medicine within their area of competence [32]. Despite this enabling framework and the increasing number of pharmacist Fig. 2 Role of pharmacist in ADHD care

1823 International Journal of Clinical Pharmacy (2026) 48:1812–1826 independent prescribers, including reforms whereby all newly registered pharmacists will qualify from 2026 [33], evidence from this review suggests that pharmacist involvement in ADHD services remains limited, with few empirical studies and no standardised models of practice. Where implemented, pharmacists often worked with a high degree of autonomy in medication titration and monitoring, but these roles appeared locally developed rather than systematically embedded within national care pathways. This gap between regulatory permission and service-level implementation highlights the need for stronger empirical evidence and more consistent models to support workforce expansion and reduce regional variation in access to ADHD care [4]. Interpretation of reported outcomes The outcomes used to evaluate pharmacist involvement varied according to local service priorities. Studies embedded within service redesign initiatives focused primarily on operational outcomes such as appointment capacity, waiting times, and workflow efficiency, whereas clinically oriented evaluations emphasised monitoring adherence, medication stabilisation, and follow-up frequency. This pattern suggests that outcome selection was often driven by organisational pressures rather than a shared evaluative framework, resulting in stronger evidence for feasibility and service performance than for patient-centred or clinical effectiveness outcomes. Comparative evidence was limited; however, where evaluated, pharmacist-led care achieved comparable clinical outcomes to other prescribing models, consistent with broader evidence from chronic disease and mental health care [11, 15, 34]. These findings likely reflect pharmacists’ expertise in medicines management and structured monitoring. However, the small number of comparative studies and the predominance of single-site evaluations constrain generalisability. Economic outcomes were primarily reported in retrospective evaluations and long-term service reviews, with cost savings largely attributed to workforce reconfiguration rather than changes in medication use or care intensity. In these models, pharmacists assumed responsibility for routine medication management, enabling specialist clinicians to focus on diagnostic assessment and complex cases. This suggests that economic benefits are mediated through role substitution and redistribution of workload rather than direct patient-level effects [27]. While indicative of potential value, further cost-effectiveness analyses are needed to robustly establish these findings. Furthermore, patient-reported outcomes, such as symptom control, quality of life and treatment experience, were less prioritised. Where patient satisfaction or perceived quality of care was assessed, it was typically secondary to service efficiency outcomes and reported descriptively. This contrasts with the broader ADHD literature, which emphasises patient experience, shared decision-making, and continuity of care, particularly for long-term medication management [35]. Although evidence from other contexts suggests that patient experiences of pharmacist prescribing are generally positive [36], there remains a clear need for ADHD-specific evidence. However, it is important to note that these findings should be interpreted in the context of the underlying study designs. The predominance of descriptive and non-comparative studies limits the ability to draw causal inferences regarding effectiveness, and reported benefits should therefore be interpreted cautiously. Child and adult service contexts Differences were observed between paediatric and adult services. Particularly in the UK context, most studies identified in this review were conducted within children’s services, particularly CAMHS. This likely reflects the historical conceptualisation of ADHD as a childhood condition and the earlier development and relative maturity of paediatric ADHD pathways. Although ADHD is now recognised as a lifelong condition for many individuals, adult services have developed more recently and remain unevenly commissioned and variably accessible [37]. Rapid growth in adult ADHD diagnoses over the past decade has placed significant pressure on services that were not designed to accommodate current demand [38]. Adult ADHD care in the UK is characterised by fragmented pathways, limited specialist provision, and prolonged waiting times, often exceeding those seen in children’s services [8]. These structural differences may partly explain why pharmacist roles have been more frequently evaluated in paediatric settings, where pathways are more established and monitoring requirements are clearly defined. At the same time, this highlights a notable evidence gap in adult ADHD care and during transition from child to adult services, a period associated with increased risk of treatment discontinuity [39]. Barriers and implications for service development Reported barriers to pharmacist-led ADHD services included regulatory constraints, limited prescribing authority, inadequate funding or reimbursement mechanisms, and time pressures. These challenges are consistent with the broader mental health pharmacy literature [11]. However, ADHD-specific implementation barriers, particularly those relating to competencies required for safe titration and monitoring, remain underexplored. Addressing these challenges will require clearer role definitions, ADHD-specific training supported by supervised practice, and commissioning models that enable sustainable pharmacist integration. Future research should generate robust evidence on clinical,

1824 International Journal of Clinical Pharmacy (2026) 48:1812–1826 service, and economic outcomes to support the development of effective and scalable pharmacist-led ADHD services. These findings also highlight the importance of broader implementation considerations when integrating pharmacist roles into ADHD services. Factors such as training requirements, clinical governance structures, prescribing supervision, and commissioning arrangements (e.g., funding, service planning) may influence the scalability and sustainability of these models but were inconsistently reported across studies. Future research should adopt an implementation science perspective to more systematically examine these contextual determinants and inform the development of scalable service models. Strengths and limitations This review is timely, addressing pharmacist involvement in ADHD care at a point when services are under increasing pressure, and there are growing calls to strengthen and expand provision. By focusing specifically on pharmacist roles, it provides a targeted synthesis with direct relevance to workforce development and service innovation. Methodologically, the review followed established scoping review frameworks, incorporated comprehensive database and conference searches, and included independent verification of data extraction. However, several limitations warrant consideration. The review was restricted to English-language publications, potentially excluding relevant international evidence. Included studies were heterogeneous in design, setting, and outcomes, and were predominantly service evaluations, pre–post studies, or uncontrolled designs, limiting the strength of conclusions that can be drawn regarding effectiveness and causal inference. Similarly, economic findings should be interpreted cautiously, as reported cost savings were largely derived from retrospective service evaluations without formal economic evaluation methods, and therefore do not represent robust cost-effectiveness analyses. Consistent with scoping review methodology, no formal quality appraisal was undertaken. Finally, unpublished service evaluations and local reports may not have been captured, potentially underestimating the extent of pharmacist involvement in ADHD care. Conclusion This scoping review identified a small but growing body of empirical evidence on pharmacist involvement in ADHD services, primarily from the US and the UK. Pharmacists were engaged in a broad range of activities, including medication initiation, titration, monitoring, and patient education, with potential benefits for service efficiency and adherence to monitoring guidelines. However, the evidence base remains limited by heterogeneity in study design, outcomes, roles, and settings, with few comparative studies and limited reporting of patient-reported outcomes or long-term clinical impact. The findings highlight an emerging role for pharmacists in ADHD care but also indicate that more detailed investigation is needed to clarify the most effective models of integration, the competencies required for ADHD-specific practice, and the contextual factors influencing implementation. Future research should prioritise robust evaluation of clinical, service, and economic outcomes to inform evidence-based service development and workforce planning. metadata_title: Peripheral Inflammation In Adult ADHD: Sex Differences And Hematological Markers
pages: Vol.:(0123456789) Psychiatric Quarterly (2026) 97:865–878 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11126-025-10185-z ORIGINAL PAPER Peripheral Inflammation In Adult ADHD: Sex Differences And Hematological Markers Pınar Kızılay Çankaya1,2 Accepted: 29 June 2025 / Published online: 10 July 2025 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025 Abstract Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impairments that persist into adulthood. Despite advancements in our understanding of ADHD, the factors influencing its course remain unclear. The inflammatory hypothesis suggests that immune dysregulation may contribute to ADHD pathophysiology. However, research examining inflammation in adult ADHD is limited. This crosssectional study aimed to compare complete blood count (CBC) parameters and derived inflammatory indices between adult patients with ADHD and healthy controls, with particular attention to sex differences. The study included 72 drug-free adults with ADHD (aged 18–38 years) diagnosed according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) and 72 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. CBC parameters and inflammatory indices, including neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR), basophil-tolymphocyte ratio (BLR), mean platelet volume (MPV), platelet distribution width (PDW), systemic immune-inflammatory index (SII), and pan-immune inflammatory value (PIV), were compared between the groups. Monocyte counts were significantly higher in the ADHD group than in the control group (p = 0.019). Sex-specific analysis revealed no significant differences in inflammatory parameters among females. However, male patients with ADHD showed significantly elevated leukocyte, neutrophil, and monocyte counts compared to male controls (p = 0.031, p = 0.049, and p = 0.038, respectively). These findings suggest that elevated monocyte levels, indicative of chronic inflammation, may have diagnostic implications in adult ADHD, particularly among males. These findings underscore the necessity to incorporate sex-specific biological mechanisms when investigating and developing therapeutic strategies for ADHD. Keywords ADHD · Inflammation · Monocytes · Sex differences · Immune dysregulation · Hematological markers * Pınar Kızılay Çankaya pkizilay@gmail.com 1 Private Practice, Psychiatry, Ankara, Türkiye 2 Institute of Health Sciences, Department of Medical Pharmacology, Gazi University, Ankara, Türkiye

866 Psychiatric Quarterly (2026) 97:865–878 Introduction Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common and multifaceted neurodevelopmental condition that manifests as patterns of inattention, excessive activity, and reduced impulse control, substantially impairing academic, social, and professional functioning [1, 2]. Beyond its core symptoms, ADHD commonly presents alongside other psychiatric conditions, including depressive disorders, anxiety, and substance use disorders, further exacerbating functional impairments and diminishing quality of life [1, 3]. Although historically conceptualized as a childhood disorder, longitudinal studies have confirmed its persistence into adulthood in 50–70% of cases [4, 5]. As ADHD symptoms evolve throughout life, the complex interplay between genetic and environmental factors is believed to contribute to the persistence of the disorder [4]. The mechanisms underlying sex differences in various developmental processes in ADHD patients remain poorly understood [6]. Despite extensive research, the precise etiology of ADHD remains elusive, involving complex interactions between genetic, neurobiological, and environmental factors [4, 7–11]. However, emerging evidence suggests that immune system dysregulation and lowgrade chronic inflammation may significantly contribute to pathophysiology [12–16]. This hypothesis aligns with broader findings implicating neuroinflammatory processes in other neuropsychiatric disorders, including depression, schizophrenia, and autism spectrum disorder [17–19]. In recent years, research has increasingly focused on investigating how systemic inflammation and immune dysregulation contribute to ADHD [20, 21]. Studies have indicated that conditions with inflammatory components, such as eczema, asthma, rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, and hypothyroidism, are more common in individuals with ADHD [22, 23]. It remains unclear whether inflammation plays a causal role in the persistence of ADHD symptoms into adulthood or whether immune activation occurs as a secondary consequence of ADHD-related stressors and comorbidities [11]. Sex-based differences in immune responses represent an important yet underexplored area in ADHD research that might help explain these sex differences. This connection is particularly relevant because most autoimmune diseases are more prevalent in women, and the incidence and clinical presentation of other immune-related conditions vary between sexes [24]. These variations can be attributed to the crucial role of sex hormones in regulating immune responses, with testosterone generally having immunosuppressive effects and estrogen typically enhancing immune activity [25]. Consistent with this pattern, adult females of many species mount more robust antibody responses to immune challenges than males [26]. Throughout childhood and adolescence, the immune system changes, partly due to fluctuating levels of steroids and sex hormones during these developmental stages [27, 28]. This makes it challenging to compare the immune signatures from childhood or puberty to those of adult patients. Sex hormones, particularly estrogen, progesterone, and androgens, play crucial roles in modulating immune cell function and responses [26, 29, 30]. Environmental factors such as chronic stress, dietary habits, and physical activity also influence immune responses and may interact with sex-related hormonal mechanisms [20]. The question of sex-based differences in the immune response in ADHD remains underexplored, despite well-documented differences in both clinical presentation and immune regulation between males and females [31, 32]. Blood-based inflammatory markers derived from complete blood count (CBC) provide a cost-effective and accessible method for assessing systemic inflammation [33, 34].

867 Psychiatric Quarterly (2026) 97:865–878 Several ratios and indices calculated from CBC parameters, including the neutrophil-tolymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR), basophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (BLR), mean platelet volume (MPV), and platelet distribution width (PDW), have been used to evaluate inflammation in various neuropsychiatric disorders [35–38]. The Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index (SII) offers a more integrated representation of immune system activity [39]. The Pan-Immune Inflammation Value (PIV) is elevated in adults with obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) and children with ADHD [40, 41]. Studies examining the role of inflammation in ADHD have yielded conflicting results, largely due to small sample sizes, heterogeneous study populations, and variations in the inflammatory markers examined [42–48]. Understanding this relationship holds promise in elucidating the etiology of this disorder and identifying novel therapeutic targets. Despite the increasing recognition of adult ADHD, only one study to date has investigated peripheral inflammation indicators in adult patients, finding no significant differences compared to controls and no association with treatment or clinical symptoms [47, 49]. Notably, to the best of our knowledge, no studies have evaluated peripheral inflammation indicators concerning sex differences in adult patients with ADHD. The present study addresses this gap by comparing CBC-derived inflammatory markers, including NLR, PLR, MLR, BLR, MPV, PDW, SII, and PIV, between drug-free adult patients with ADHD and healthy controls. We also investigated the sex-based differences in these parameters. Clarifying the role of peripheral inflammation and sex-specific immune responses may support the development of targeted and individualized treatment strategies for adult ADHD. Methods Ethical Approval Ethical approval was obtained from the Ethics Committee of Koru Ankara Hospital on. September 12, 2023 (approval number: 3201). Sample We recruited 144 participants from the psychiatric outpatient clinic of Koru Ankara Hospital between April 2022 and April 2023. The sample comprised 72 drug-free adults (aged 18–38 years) diagnosed with ADHD according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) criteria and 72 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. The control participants were aviation personnel who had undergone health examinations at the Koru Hospital Aeromedical Center and were certified to be in optimal health. A power analysis using G*Power (version 3.1.9.7) indicated that a minimum of 34 participants per group would achieve 80% power to detect a large effect size (0.70) at a significance level of α = 0.050 using a two-sided two-sample equal-variance t-test. Data were collected retrospectively through a medical record review by the author affiliated with the outpatient clinic. This cross-sectional study initially enrolled 125 patients with ADHD; however, after applying the exclusion criteria, the final sample consisted of 72 adult patients with ADHD and 72 healthy controls, all of whom had CBC values within the normal reference ranges.

868 Psychiatric Quarterly (2026) 97:865–878 Participants with abnormal hematological values, including anemia, polycythemia, lymphopenia, lymphocytosis, neutropenia, neutrophilia, thrombocytopenia, or thrombocytosis, were excluded. Sociodemographic data of all participants were retrospectively obtained from their medical records. The exclusion criteria for the ADHD group included psychiatric comorbidities, current medication use, or any medical conditions potentially influencing inflammatory parameters. Specifically, we excluded individuals with inflammatory or autoimmune diseases, hematological disorders, liver or renal failure, clinical evidence of active infections, obesity, heavy smoking (defined as smoking > 15 cigarettes per day), or use of anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive medications. Additionally, individuals whose ADHD diagnosis was revised during follow-up or whose medical records contained incomplete or conflicting data were excluded. All laboratory analyses were conducted at the Koru Ankara Hospital Medical Biochemistry and Medical Microbiology Laboratory using an automated hematological analyzer (Sysmex 1800i). Blood samples were collected as part of the participants’routine laboratory evaluation during their clinical visit, typically between 8:00 and 10:00 a.m. However, the exact time of day for blood collection was not standardized across participants, as the data were collected retrospectively. The study adhered to the standard reference intervals for hematological parameters as follows: leukocytes (4.8–10.8 × 103/mm3), neutrophils (2.06–7.02 × 103/mm3), lymphocytes (1.3–3.5 × 103/mm3), platelets (150–450 × 103/ mm3), monocytes (0.3–0.8 × 103/mm3), eosinophils (< 0.42 × 103/mm3), and basophils (< 0.2 × 103/mm3). An automated hematology analyzer was used to measure the PDW and MPV. SII was calculated using the following formula: SII = (platelet count × neutrophil count)/lymphocyte count. PIV was calculated using the following formula: PIV = (platelet count × neutrophil count × monocyte count)/lymphocyte count. NLR, PLR, MLR, and BLR were calculated by dividing the absolute counts of the relevant cells. Statistical Analysis Statistical analyses were performed using IBM Statistical Package for Social Sciences (SPSS) version 22. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages. Continuous variable normality was evaluated through visual assessment (histograms and probability plots) and analytical methods (Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Shapiro–Wilk tests). For descriptive statistics, normally distributed variables were presented as means with standard deviations, while non-normally distributed variables were expressed as medians with interquartile ranges (1st and 3rd quartiles). Between-group comparisons of continuous variables were performed using Student’s t-test or the Mann–Whitney U test according to the distribution characteristics. Chi-square analyses were performed for categorical variables, applying either Pearson’s chi-square or Fisher’s exact test, as methodologically appropriate. Statistical significance was established at p < 0.05 for all analyses. Results This study included 72 participants diagnosed with ADHD and 72 healthy controls. The ADHD group consisted of 36 females (50%) and 36 males (50%), while the control group included 39 females (54.2%) and 33 males (45.8%). The median age was 19 years (range:

869 Psychiatric Quarterly (2026) 97:865–878 18–21 years) in the ADHD group and 20 years (range: 19–23 years) in the control group. Statistical analysis revealed no significant differences between the groups in terms of age (p = 0.090) or sex distribution (p = 0.617) (Table 1). Table 1 presents a comparison of hematological parameters between the ADHD and control groups. No statistically significant differences were observed in NLR, PLR, MLR, BLR, SII, or PIV (p > 0.05). Similarly, platelet indices, including mean platelet volume (MPV) and platelet distribution width (PDW), did not differ significantly between the groups (p > 0.05). However, analysis of the CBC results revealed significantly higher monocyte counts in the ADHD group than in the control group (z = −2.347, p = 0.019) (Table 1). The effect size for the group difference in monocyte counts was large, with Cohen’s d of 1.66. The rank-biserial correlation for this comparison was –0.76, indicating a strong association between ADHD diagnosis and elevated monocyte levels. Sex-stratified analyses revealed different patterns between males and females. Among female participants, no statistically significant differences were observed in any hematological parameters between the ADHD and control groups (p > 0.05) (Table 2). In contrast, the male participants showed significant differences in several parameters. Males with ADHD demonstrated higher leukocyte counts (t = −2.200, p = 0.031) and significantly elevated neutrophil counts (t = −2.006, p = 0.049) than the male controls. Additionally, monocyte counts were significantly higher in males with ADHD than in male controls (z = −2.079, p = 0.038) (Table 3).
