A total of 141 preschool children (4.90 ± 0.52 years) with ADHD were included, comprising 119 males (84.4%) and 22 females (15.6%). Correlation analyses were performed to examine any potential associations among demographic vari ables (Fig. 1). For SNAP-IV-AD, scores showed posi tive correlations with BRIEF-P-Working memory (r =.59, p <.001) and BRIEF-P-ISCI (r =.37, p <.001). For SNAP-IV-hyperactivity/impulsivity, scores were posi tively correlated with the BRIEF-P-GEC (r =.55, p <.001), BRIEF-P-FI (r =.36, p <.001), BRIEF-P-Plan/Organize (r =.51, p <.01), and Communication Interests (r =.25, p <.05); and were negatively correlated with PEOPSSSelf-management (r = −.35, p <.001). For SNAP-IVoppositional defiant symptoms, scores demonstrated positive correlations with BRIEF-P-ISCI (r =.61, p <.001) and BRIEF-P-Inhibit (r =.50, p <.001), and a negative correlation with PEOPSS-Self-management (r = −.39, p <.001). Multiple linear regression analysis of SNAP-IV We conducted a stepwise linear regression analysis on the AD, hyperactivity/impulsivity, and oppositional defi ant symptoms scores of SNAP-IV using clinical scale indicators (Table 2). BRIEF-P-Working memory (β = 0.62, p <.001), PEOPSS-Pioneership (β = 0.35, p <.001), and PEOPSS-Expressiveness (β = − 0.20, p <.05) significantly predicted AD score (F(3,137) = 32.24, p <.001); BRIEFP-GEC(β = 0.78, p <.001), PEOPSS-Self-management(β = − 0.21, p <.05), PEOPSS-Pioneership(β = 0.19, p <.05), BRIEF-P-FI(β = − 0.33, p <.05), Age(β = 0.15, p <.05), and Communication interests(β = 0.14, p <.05) sig nificantly predicted hyperactivity/impulsivity score (F(6,134) = 17.20, p <.001); BRIEF-P-ISCI(β = 0.99, p <.001), PEOPSS-Self-management(β = − 0.22, p <.05), BRIEF-P-Inhibit(β = − 0.46, p <.05), and Communication interests(β = − 0.14, p <.05) significantly predicted oppo sitional defiant symptoms score (F(4,136) = 29.50, p <.05). Identification AD, hyperactivity/impulsivity and oppositional defiant symptoms of SNAP-IV in ADHD in preschoolers by EF We used stepwise logistic regression to construct the models and then assessed the ability of the EF indicators to identify group membership of SNAP-IV (AD/hyper activity/impulsivity/oppositional defiant symptoms, i.e., average score > 1 or not). For identification of SNAPIV-AD, BRIEF-P-Working Memory yielded an AUC of 0.854 (85.1% sensitivity, 70.4% specificity), while BRIEFP-ISCI yielded an AUC of 0.591 (42.1% sensitivity, 74.1% specificity). For identification of SNAP-IV-hyperactivity/ impulsivity, BRIEF-P-Plan/Organize achieved an AUC of 0.719 (63.9% sensitivity, 68.2% specificity). For identifica tion of SNAP-IV-oppositional defiant symptoms, BRIEFP-ISCI showed an AUC of 0.852 (66.2% sensitivity, 86.3% specificity). Complete results are presented in Table 3; Fig. 2. Findings from this study showed that the BRIEF-P Working mem ory and ISCI subscales were associated with the attention deficit subscale of SNAP-IV, the BRIEF-P Plan/Organize subscale was significantly associated with the hyperac tivity/impulsivity subscale of SNAP-IV, and the BRIEF-P ISCI subscale was significantly associated with the oppo sitional defiant symptom subscale of SNAP-IV. Further more, poorer developmental coordination was strongly associated with inattention, while deficits in social skills and communication interests were also linked to ADHD symptomatology. BMC Pediatrics (2026) 26:112 Working memory and ISCI in the identification of attention deficit We found that the BRIEF-P Working memory and ISCI (comprising Inhibit and Emotional control) subscales differentiated preschoolers on the SNAP-IV attention deficit subscale, with Working memory demonstrat ing superior discriminative validity (Table 3; Fig. 2). Although the behavioral expression of ADHD may be influenced by cultural norms, growing neurocognitive evidence indicates that its core cognitive deficits - par ticularly working memory dysfunction - demonstrate remarkable consistency across diverse cultural contexts [16]. Working memory, a system for the temporary stor age and processing of information during cognitive tasks, guides behavior via the mid-lateral prefrontal cortex. Studies have revealed that 89% of children with ADHD exhibit impairment in at least one executive function, and those with working memory deficits show more severe inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity symp toms [32]. Longitudinal evidence indicates that superior working memory predicts better long-term ADHD out comes. Furthermore, research specifically links working memory deficits to inattentive symptoms and subsequent functional impairment, but not to hyperactive/impul sive symptoms [33, 34]. One study with up to 13 years of follow-up found that preschool working memory and reaction time variability predicted future inattention and were linked to later academic performance [17]. Thus, impairment in working memory is likely to be directly manifested as significant inattentive symptoms, regard less of cultural background. Inhibitory control – defined as the capacity to sup press prepotent responses and filter irrelevant stimuli – constitutes a core component of EF, that regulates con text-appropriate behavioral. Compared to typically devel oping children, those with ADHD exhibit significant deficits in response inhibition, working memory, and response variability. Crucially, longitudinal data sug gest that while most EF differences diminish by adoles cence, response inhibition deficits persist into puberty, highlighting their enduring neurodevelopmental impact [35]. Furthermore, one study demonstrated that simple inhibition and selective attention at age 5 independently predict complex inhibition and working memory at age 6. The results also showed that, even in young children, EF components primarily predicted symptoms of inat tention rather than hyperactivity/impulsivity [36]. Thus, inhibitory control appears to be a developmental precur sor to later development and more complex EF deficits in children with ADHD and is primarily associated with inattention. Prior research indicats that approximately half of chil dren with ADHD experience emotion regulation difficul ties, which in turn lead to greater distress and impairment than ADHD symptoms alone [37, 38]. A significant and robust association exists between ADHD and emo tional reactivity, meaning that adolescents with ADHD are more likely to experience intense emotions (both negative and positive) and exhibit stronger reactions to stressful and/or frustrating situations [38]. Bunford et al. reported that emotional dysregulation in adolescents is associated with ADHD and does not differ by subtype [39]. Furthermore, three measures of emotional func tioning—anger regulation, anger recognition, and the regulation of happiness/exuberance—significantly dis criminate children with ADHD from typically developing Table 3 Results of differentiating symptoms of ADHD in preschoolers by EF Identification group Identification criteria Sensitivity (%) Specificity (%) AUC [95%CI] AD BRIEF-P-Working memory 85.1 70.4 0.854[0.783,0.925] BRIEF-P-ISCI 42.1 74.1 0.591[0.474,0.709] hyperactivity/impulsivity BRIEF-P-Plan/Organize 63.9 68.2 0.719[0.603,0.835] oppositional defiant symptoms BRIEF-ISCI 66.2 86.3 0.852[0.791,0.913] AD Attention deficit, BRIEF-P Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function -Preschool version, ISCI Inhibitory Self-Control Index, AUC Area under the curve, CI Confidence interval Fig. 2 ROC analysis of ADHD symptoms

Page 7 of 10 Gao et al. BMC Pediatrics (2026) 26:112 peers, with emotion regulation showing independent effects on ADHD identification [40]. Notably, one study found that the regulation of happiness/exuberance was significantly related to inattention, suggesting that emo tion regulation deficits constitute an important aspect of ADHD [17]. Another study supports this, showing that preschool ADHD symptoms are associated not only with pronounced and often occurring negative emotions, but also specifically with the regulation of negative and posi tive emotions. Importantly, the significant independent effects of emotion regulation on ADHD symptoms out weigh those of cognitive and motivation-based regulation [41]. However, research on the synergistic effects of inhi bition and emotion regulation on inattentive symptoms remains lacking. Plan/organize in the identification of hyperactivity/ impulsivity Our study demonstrated that the BRIEF-P Plan/Orga nize subscale differentiate the hyperactivity/impulsivity subscale of the SNAP-IV (Table 3; Fig. 2). This finding extends the current literature by establishing the dis criminative validity of planning and organization skills for early ADHD identification. Plan/Organize involves the ability to anticipate future events, set goals, and plan out steps to accomplish tasks. However, these skills are challenging to assess in preschoolers due to their lim ited cognitive maturity. Behavioral observation protocols (e.g., the Tower of London) may have higher sensitivity in capturing ​planning and ​organization skills compared with parent-report questionnaires, though further refine ment of scoring criteria and ecological validity in natural istic settings remains necessary. ISCI in the identification of oppositional defiant symptoms As shown in Tables 2 and 3; Fig. 2, the BRIEF-P ISCI sub scale is strongly associated with the oppositional defiant symptoms subscale of SNAP-IV in preschool children. EF, particularly inhibitory control, is associated with externalizing behaviors from the preschool period. Metaanalyses confirm this link and reveal differential associa tions across EF domains: working memory and cognitive flexibility show small effect sizes, whereas inhibition demonstrates a medium effect size [42]. Consistent with prior evidence, our results indicate that impaired inhibi tory control predicts elevated problematic behaviors. Moreover, previous studies suggest that inhibitory defi cits underlie the development of externalizing problem behaviors and exacerbate core ADHD symptoms [43]. In a cohort comparing irritable/emotionally dysregu lated ADHD children (n = 105) to non-irritable ADHD peers (n = 395), the former group showed a higher risk of oppositional defiant symptoms [44]. Therefore, both inhibitory control and emotion control are involved in the emergence and development of oppositional defiant symptoms. Associations between socio-functional competences and ADHD symptoms According to Table 2, some indicators from PEOPSS and Early Childhood Communication Interest Questionnaire are associated with symptoms of ADHD. Attention defi cit was related to Pioneership and Expressiveness, hyper activity/impulsivity was linked to Self-management, Pioneership and communication interests, while opposi tional defiant symptoms were associated with Self-man agement and communication interests. Previous research indicated significant differences in EF between Chinese and American preschoolers [45]. EF profiles may vary across cultures due to several interre lated factors. Cultural values shape parenting practices and educational goals, which in turn prioritize and rein force different cognitive and behavioral skills. Further more, culturally specific experiences and skills trained from an early age can lead to differential strengths in neural circuits supporting distinct aspects of EF. There fore, the assessment of EF and its manifestation in ADHD cannot be divorced from the cultural context in which a child develops. The PEOPSS tailored to the Chi nese social and cultural context, provides a scientific and effective measurement tool for the comprehensive assessment of young children’s social skills. The internal consistency reliability of the questionnaire and each fac tor ranged from 0.85 to 0.93, the retest reliability ranged from 0.70 to 0.77 over a four-week period, and the cor relation with the validity scale ranged from 0.31 to 0.54. Pioneership operationalizes a preschoolers’ capacity for prospective thinking–anticipating future scenarios and initiating preparatory actions. Expressiveness reflects the child’s active communication of emotions and thoughts. Self-management refers to the child’s ability to exert con trol over their own emotions and behaviors. During the preschool years, the focus of social skill development revolves around sharing and communicating, interacting with peers in a positive way, cooperating, and regulat ing emotions. Communication interests in early child hood are examined in terms of young children’s primitive declarative pointing to things with their fingers, eye-toeye gaze, and pretend play skills. These skills are associ ated with the differentiation of ADHD symptoms and future development. Figure 1 demonstrates significant associations between attention deficits and Fine motor, Motor coordination, and the total score on the DCDQ-C. Previous studies showed that a considerable proportion of preschool ers with ADHD also have motor deficits that manifest as difficulties with fine and gross motor movements and motor control. These deficits negatively impact activities

Page 8 of 10 Gao et al. BMC Pediatrics (2026) 26:112 of daily living—such as writing, using utensils, and tying shoelaces—often causing children to lag behind their peers [46, 47]. In particular, research found that chil dren with ADHD exhibit poorer performance on all fine motor coordination tasks. Notably, lower performance was associated with symptoms of inattention rather than hyperactivity/impulsivity [48]. The context of the COVID-19 pandemic that was pres ent during the period of data collection must be consid ered when interpreting these findings. The heightened levels of family stress, limited social interactions and potential alterations in healthcare-seeking and refer ral patterns, may have exacerbated children’s behavioral symptoms and influenced parental reporting. Although the core neurocognitive relationships we investigated are considered fundamental and enduring, the generalizabil ity of our specific findings to more stable periods merits future investigation. Limitations and future directions Several limitations are important to note. First, given the considerable challenges in validly assessing EF in pre schoolers, our data were derived from caregiver reports of children’s observable behaviors, rather than from child performance-based tasks. While individuals, including children, can report on their own experiences in unique ways, preschool children have limited language compre hension and self-insight, making their survey responses less reliable than those of adults. However, this singleinformant approach may introduce potential measure ment bias. Future studies should incorporate objective standardized neuropsychological tests, longitudinal designs, and multiple informants to obtain a more accu rate and context-sensitive understanding of children’s functioning [24]. Second, the sample’s sex imbalance may limit generalizability to female populations. Our sample included a significantly higher number of male partici pants. This may be attributed to the greater prevalence in boys of hyperactive behaviors, which are often read ily observable and potentially disruptive. However, since previous research indicates that EF deficits are compa rable between girls and boys with ADHD [49, 50], the imbalance is unlikely to have substantially biased the observed relationships within our sample. Nonetheless, future research should recruit more balanced cohorts to ensure findings are generalizable across genders. Third, we did not systematically assess parental stress or men tal health, which are potential confounders. Distressed parents may rate their children’s behaviors more nega tively, potentially inflating the observed associations. As a standardized measure, the BRIEF-P incorporates qual ity control procedures specifically designed to reduce such bias, including the calculation of an Inconsistency score and a Negativity score from the original ratings. Future research should incorporate standardized assess ments of parental psychological status to better disen tangle children’s inherent behavioral characteristics from state-dependent biases in parent reports, thereby yielding more robust conclusions. Finally, our participant recruit ment was confined to a single urban hospital in Zhejiang province. The findings may not be fully generalizable to children from rural areas, different socioeconomic back grounds, or non-clinical settings, which should be con sidered when interpreting the results. Conclusion In summary, ADHD symptoms in preschoolers are asso ciated with deficits in EF, motor coordination, social skills, and communication interests. Our findings under score the strong discriminative validity of EF measures for identifying ADHD symptoms within the Chinese pre school population. Early detection of EF deficits contrib utes to a comprehensive assessment of ADHD symptoms and optimizes personalized intervention efficacy. BMC Pediatrics (2026) 26:329 https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-026-06646-4 BMC Pediatrics †Dandan Bai and Qi Gu contributed equally to this work. *Correspondence: Jin Cai 174749@qq.com Youjia Wu francis_nt@163.com 1Department of Pediatrics, Affiliated Hospital of Nantong University, No. 20 Xisi Road, Nantong, Jiangsu Province, China 2Department of Pediatrics, Pingchao Center Health Center, Tongzhou District, Nantong, Jiangsu Province, China 3Department of Pediatrics, Zigong Fourth People’s Hospital, Zigong, Sichuan Province, China Abstract Background This study aimed to investigate the environmental factors associated with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in Chinese children and adolescents with adiposity (obesity or overweight). Methods A total of 130 children and adolescents with adiposity and 130 age- and sex-matched controls with normal weight were enrolled in this cross-sectional study. Children with ADHD were identified based on International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) codes. The severity for psychiatric and behavioral problems, ADHD symptoms, and oppositional defiant disorder was compared between the groups. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with the comorbidity of ADHD in children and adolescents with adiposity. Results The detection rate of ADHD was significantly higher in the adiposity group compared to control group (15.4% vs. 6.2%; p = 0.016). Children and adolescents with adiposity exhibiting higher scores in learning problems, impulsivity/hyperactivity, anxiety, and hyperactivity indices. Exploratory analyses indicated a positive correlation was found between BMI percentile (BMI-P) and inattention symptoms scores in individuals with ADHD (r = 0.512, p = 0.005). Logistic regression results showed that factors associated with ADHD in children and adolescents with adiposity included prolonged adiposity duration (> 3 years) (OR = 5.61, 95% CI: 1.79–17.59, p = 0.003) and excessive screen time (> 3 h/day) (OR = 6.45, 95% CI: 1.59–26.11, p = 0.009). Conclusions Prolonged adiposity duration and excessive daily screen time were found to be associated with ADHD among children and adolescents with adiposity. BMC Pediatrics (2026) 26:329 Introduction Over the past decades, the prevalence of childhood adi posity (obesity or overweight) has increased drastically worldwide, raising substantial public health concerns [1]. In China, the rates of overweight and obesity among children aged 6–15 years have reached 19.1% and 12.4%, respectively [2]. Beyond the elevated risk of metabolic and cardiovascular complications, children and ado lescents with adiposity display a higher prevalence of psychiatric comorbidities, including attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety, and depression [3]. ADHD is recognized as one of the most prevalent neu rodevelopmental disorder in pediatric populations, typi fied by persistent patterns of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, which impair academic, social, and fam ily functioning [4]. A meta-analysis, encompassing 67 studies, estimated the prevalence of ADHD to be approx imately 6.2% in Chinese children and adolescents, with the inattention presentation being the most common [5]. More recently, a national survey reported that the over all prevalence of ADHD to be 6.4% [6]. Existing evidence suggests a complex interplay between obesity and ADHD [7, 8]. Meta-analytic findings indicate that youth with ADHD have a 30% higher risk of developing obesity later in life compared to their non-ADHD counterparts [8]. Conversely, the prevalence of ADHD is also elevated in children and adolescents with obesity compared to their normal-weight peers [9, 10], reaching as high as 28.6% among severe obese adolescents [9]. Furthermore, early ADHD symptoms may predict subsequent weight gain or obesity, while overweight status may, in turn, exacerbate ADHD symptoms severity [11]. A comprehensive understanding of the co-occurrence mechanisms underlying ADHD and obesity necessitates considering the inherently complex etiology of ADHD itself. ADHD is recognized as a highly heritable disor der, with heritability estimates reaching 76% [12]. How ever, genetic predisposition is not solely deterministic; its phenotypic expression is significantly modulated by environmental factors, demonstrating the concept of “gene-environment interaction“ [7, 13]. Within this inte grated framework, acquired factors such as dietary pat terns, physical activity, lifestyle habits, and psychosocial stress are not merely direct drivers of weight gain. They may also function as environmental risk factors, interact ing with an individual’s genetic background, and conse quently influencing the onset and progression of ADHD [14]. Currently, research concerning ADHD in Chinese chil dren primarily focuses on the genetic aspects, with com paratively limited exploration of environmental factors. Chinese society exhibits high academic expectations and significant competitive pressure. This context can lead to children experiencing prolonged sedentary study peri ods, insufficient physical activity, and can even trigger stress-induced eating behaviors [15, 16]. Furthermore, concurrent with rapid economic development, Chinese household dietary patterns are undergoing a “nutrition transition,” marked by a sharp increase in the consump tion of high-calorie, high-fat, and high-sugar fast food and processed foods [17]. The pervasive social stigma and inadequate public understanding surrounding men tal health issues like ADHD can result in delayed diagno sis or misinterpretation of symptoms. Collectively, these culturally specific elements likely shape the distinct man ifestations and developmental trajectories of ADHD and obesity in Chinese children and adolescents. Therefore, this study aims to investigate the occurrence of ADHD among children and adolescents with adipos ity in our center. Furthermore, it seeks to analyze the association between obesity status and ADHD symptom presentation, and to identify potential environmental fac tors linked to ADHD. The findings will provide objective evidence developing more targeted obesity management strategies, contributing to the improved physical and mental well-being of Chinese children and adolescents. Methods Study design and participants This was a retrospective cross-sectional study conducted using data from the Affiliated Hospital of Nantong Uni versity between October 2021 and November 2022. The study population was derived from a retrospective screening of electronic medical records (EMR) for chil dren and adolescents diagnosed with overweight or obe sity. Inclusion Criteria: (1) Age between 6 and 14 years; (2) Normal intellectual development; (3) Overweight (85th ≤ BMI-P < 95th percentile) or obesity (BMI-P ≥ 95th percentile) [18]. Exclusion Criteria: (1) Secondary obesity caused by drugs, endocrine or metabolic dis eases, and central nervous system lesions; (2) Chronic diseases such as asthma, nephropathy, or thyroid dys function; (3) Neurodevelopmental or psychiatric disor ders include epilepsy, autism, depression, mania, cerebral palsy, or dementia. The absence of these conditions was determined by a review of the patient’s medical history and the lack of a formal ICD-10 diagnosis; (4) Inability to cooperate, poor compliance, or incomplete data. Ultimately, 130 overweight or obese children (adipos ity group) meeting the specified criteria were included. A Control Group (n = 130) of age- and sex-matched children with a BMI-P in the normal range (5th ≤ BMIP < 85th percentile) was then selected from the same pop ulation covering the same time period.

BMC Pediatrics (2026) 26:329 Diagnosis of ADHD Children diagnosed with ADHD were identified retro spectively from the standardized medical record system based on International Classification of Diseases (ICD10) codes. All diagnoses were made by board-certified pediatricians and psychiatrists based on a comprehen sive clinical evaluation. Raw data from their assessments were retrieved, including family factor questionnaires, the Swanson, Nolan, and Pelham IV (SNAP-IV) Parent 26-Item Rating Scale, and the Conners Parent Symptom Questionnaire (PSQ). Assessment tools Parent Symptom Questionnaire (PSQ) The PSQ is an internationally recognized and reliable behavioral assessment scale widely used for evaluat ing ADHD symptoms [19]. This 48-item questionnaire includes five subscales: Conduct Problems, Learning Problems, Psychosomatic Problems, Impulsivity-Hyper activity, and Anxiety. The psychometric properties of the Chinese version of the PSQ have been validated in prior research, demonstrating test-retest reliability ranging from 0.15 to 0.63, a Cronbach’s α of 0.92, and item-total consistency between 0.49–0.85 [20].Swanson, Nolan, and Pelham IV (SNAP-IV) Parent 26-Item Rating Scale. The SNAP-IV scale is structured according to the cri teria outlined in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV). It comprises three sub scales: Inattention (items 1–9), Hyperactivity/Impulsivity (items 10–18), and Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD; items 19–26). Based on the scores from the ADHD sub scales, individuals are categorized into three presenta tions: Inattentive, Hyperactive/Impulsive, and Combined Presentation. The Chinese version of the SNAP-IV has demonstrated good internal reliability (Cronbach’s α = 0.88–0.90) and satisfactory test-retest reliability (intra class correlation = 0.59–0.72) [21]. Individual and family factors questionnaire The individual and family factor questionnaires consisted of eleven individual factors related items and four family factors related items. Sleep disorder data were based on guardian-reported physician diagnoses. For initial screen exposure age, daily screen time, and duration of adipos ity, specific values were reported by parents or older chil dren and subsequently categorized into two groups. Daily screen time was defined as total daily time spent on elec tronic devices for both educational and recreational pur poses, without distinguishing weekdays from weekends. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were performed using R (version 4.4.2). Continuous variables were tested for normality. Normally distributed data are presented as mean ± SD, independent samples t-tests were used to compare dif ferences between two groups; Non-normally distributed data are presented as median (interquartile range, IQR) and compared using the Mann–Whitney U test. Categor ical variables were presented as n(%) and compared using the chi-square test. Pearson correlation coefficients were used to assess correlation between continuous variables. Logistic regression was conducted to identify factors associated with the comorbidity of ADHD in population with adiposity. Variables found to be significantly associ ated with ADHD in the univariate analysis (p < 0.05) were selected for inclusion in the multivariable logistic regres sion analysis to identify independent factors. A two-sided P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Ethical approval and consent Written informed consent was obtained from guardians of all participants. The study was approved and super vised by the hospital Ethics Committee (approval num ber: 2022-K017). Results In the adiposity group, 67.7% were male and 32.3% were female, with a mean age of 9.72 ± 1.90 years. In the con trol group, 59.2% were male and 40.8% were female, with a mean age of 9.56 ± 1.97 years. There were no significant differences in sex distribution or age between the two groups (p = 0.160) (Table 1). ADHD was present in 15.4% (20/130) of the adipos ity group and 6.2% (8/130) of the control group, with a significant difference between two groups (p = 0.016) (Table 1). Among ADHD-diagnosed participants, there was no statistical difference in the distribution of ADHD presentations between those with obesity (n = 20) and those with normal weight (n = 8) (Table 2). BMC Pediatrics (2026) 26:329 Severity of psychiatric and behavioral problems, ADHD symptoms and ODD The severity of psychiatric symptoms was further ana lyzed among children with ADHD. The results suggested that children with adiposity had higher scores for learn ing problems, impulsivity/hyperactivity, anxiety, and hyperactivity indices compared to their normal-weight peers (p < 0.05) (Table S1). They also showed higher ADHD symptoms scores and ODD scores (p < 0.05) (Table S2). Furthermore, an exploratory correlation anal ysis indicated a positive correlation between BMI-P and inattention scores (r = 0.512, p = 0.005) (Table S3). Con sidering the modest sample sizes (adiposity, n = 20; nor mal weight, n = 8), the findings from these exploratory analyses should be regarded as preliminary and inter preted with appropriate caution. Environmental factors of ADHD Univariate analysis was conducted to examine individual and family environmental factors associated with ADHD within the adiposity group. The results demonstrated that BMI-P, daily screen time, and adiposity duration were significantly higher in the adiposity with ADHD group than in the adiposity without ADHD group (p < 0.05). (Table 3). Logistic regression was performed to identify fac tors independently associated with ADHD in individu als with adiposity. The analysis revealed that adiposity duration ≥ 3 years (OR = 5.609, 95%CI: 1.79–17.59) and daily screen time ≥ 3 h (OR = 6.451, 95%CI: 1.59–26.11) were both significantly associated with ADHD (p < 0.05). BMI-P did not associate with ADHD (OR = 1.01, 95%CI: 0.81–1.25, p = 0.955) (Table 4). Hosmer-Lemeshow test indicated an adequate model fit (χ2 = 12.04, p = 0.15), and multicollinearity was not observed among the predictors. Discussion This cross-sectional study offers key insights into the comorbidity of adiposity and ADHD in Chinese youth. Our primary finding is that prolonged adiposity dura tion (≥ 3 years) and excessive daily screen time (≥ 3 h) are significantly associated with the presence of ADHD in children and adolescents with adiposity. These results underscore the importance of considering long-term weight status and lifestyle habits in this population. Fur thermore, the overall detection rate of ADHD was higher in the adiposity group compared to the control group (15.4% vs. 6.2%). The result aligns with previous study and meta-analysis [9, 10], highlighting the strong clinical association between these two conditions. Our findings reveal that individuals with adiposity and ADHD exhibited more pronounced learning difficulties, impulsivity, hyperactivity, and anxiety compared to their normal-weight peers with ADHD (p < 0.05). Additionally, the ADHD and ODD symptoms appeared more severe in participants with adiposity (p < 0.05). This observa tion is consistent with the work of Sönmez et al. [22] who reported an association between obesity in children and increased behavioral problems and ADHD symptoms. However, our results should be interpreted with caution due to the small sample size. Nevertheless, these results suggest a potential relationship between adiposity and the severity of psychiatric and behavioral health. Such a relationship could be partially mediated by neurobio logical factors. Existing study [23] suggests that excessive weight may be associated with gray matter loss in key brain areas, which could be related to atypical psycho social development, though the precise mechanisms and directionality require further dedicated investigation. Our exploratory analysis also suggested a positive cor relation between BMI-P and inattention scores in chil dren with ADHD. This preliminary observation contrasts with Hughes et al. [24], who reported no significant asso ciation between BMI and ADHD symptoms in a large sample of eight-year-olds. One proposed explanation from that study was the greater impact of family factors on mental health at that age [24]. It has been hypothe sized that Inattention is linked to impairments in impulse control and planning [25], which in turn may be associ ated with dysregulated eating and other lifestyle habits (regular physical activity, healthy dietary choices) [26]. Substantial further research with larger cohorts is essen tial to validate this potential correlation and determine its clinical significance. A significant finding from our study was that among children and adolescents with adiposity, those who reported three or more hours of daily screen-related activities had 6.45 times the odds of having an ADHD diagnosis (OR = 6.45, 95% CI: 1.59–26.11, p = 0.009) compared to their peers with lower screen exposure. This result is consistent with previous studies. Lee et al. [27] observed a positive relationship between screen time, BMI, and waist circumference. Lingineni et al. [28] also found that children with ADHD symptoms spent sig nificantly more time on screens than their peers. Fur thermore, a meta-analysis [29] showed an association between media use and ADHD symptoms. The potential mechanisms underlying this observed association are multifaceted. Excessive screen time is often associated with reduced physical activity. In China, where intense academic competition and the pervasive availability of high-quality online educational content are prominent, children’s “educational” screen time has surged. Concurrently, the widespread appeal of social media and Tik-Tok has drastically reduced their engage ment in sports and outdoor activities. This reduction in physical activity is particularly concerning, as evidence [30, 31] indicates that insufficient physical activity is

Secondly, beyond mere duration, some stud ies suggest that exposure to age-inappropriate media content may be associated with poorer psychosocial out comes [32, 33]. Repeated exposure to highly stimulating or rapidly paced media content may be linked to change in children’s arousal thresholds, which could be related to aggressive behaviors, inattention, and hyperactivity [33]. Page 6 of 7 Bai et al. BMC Pediatrics (2026) 26:329 Furthermore, the relationship between screen exposure and ADHD symptoms may be bidirectional. Screen time could also be a correlation or even an outcome of preexisting attentional challenges [32]. Our study observed an association between sustained adiposity and the presence of ADHD symptoms, par ticularly when adiposity persisted for three years or more. While multiple studies have explored the com plex and interactive association between adiposity and ADHD, limited research has examined the influence of adiposity duration. For instance, Khalife et al.‘s longitudi nal cohort study [31] discussed the trajectory of weight changes across ages. Cortese et al.‘s meta-analysis [8] addressed obesity persistence at various developmental stages. However, neither explicitly investigated the rela tionship between the adiposity duration and ADHD. We propose that persistent adiposity during critical devel opmental periods, especially exceeding three years, may be linked to more adverse behavioral, neurodevelop mental, or lifestyle outcomes associated with ADHD. Such circumstances could be associated with challenges in children’s neurocognitive and social development. It remains unclear whether adiposity duration is inde pendently associated with ADHD development or acts through mediating factors. Further longitudinal studies are required to clarify these relationships. The associations observed in our study suggest that for children with adiposity, addressing lifestyle factors like screen time and physical activity may be an important component of a comprehensive management plan. Pedia tricians, during routine physical examinations and weight management consultations, could consider preliminary inquiry or observation for ADHD-related presentations, especially in children with prolonged adiposity. This ini tial attention can facilitate earlier identification of chil dren who might require further evaluation. Such early detection provides an opportunity for potential diagnosis and intervention. This study examines the factors associated with the co-occurrence of adiposity and ADHD in Chinese chil dren and adolescents, an understudied population. How ever, there are limitations to consider. As a single-center study with limited participant, the generalizability of our findings is restricted, requiring cautious interpreta tion. Recalling bias and uncontrolled residual confound ing factors (such as genetic susceptibility) may affect the study results. In addition, the study was cross-sectional in nature, and odd radio reflects the relative prevalence of the disease in the two groups, not a strict representa tion of risk incidence or causal effect. Longitudinal stud ies integrating neurocognitive and lifestyle measures are therefore needed to clarify the bidirectional relationship between ADHD and adiposity and to establish causality. Conclusion This cross-sectional study reveals that the detection rate of ADHD among obese children and adolescents in Nantong, China, is significantly higher than that in their normal-weight peers. Within the obese population, a lon ger duration of adiposity (≥ 3 years) and excessive daily screen time (≥ 3 h) are significantly associated with the presence of ADHD. To view a copy of this licence, visit ​h​t​t​p​:​/​/​c​r​e​a​t​i​ v​e​c​o​m​m​o​n​s​.​o​r​g​/​l​i​c​e​n​s​e​s​/​b​y​-​n​c​-​n​d​/​4​.​0​/​.​ Abstract Background Physical activity (PA) has gained attention as a potential behavioral marker for ADHD, yet findings remain inconsistent. Most research focuses on school-aged children, leaving a critical gap in understanding PA patterns in preschoolers with ADHD symptoms. Aim The study aims to investigate the association of physical activity level and ADHD symptoms and focus on characterizing physical activity profiles of preschool children with ADHD symptoms. Methods Totally 18 children with ADHD symptoms and 66 typically developing children were enrolled in this study. Physical activity was objectively assessed using actigraphy over five school days. Two-sample Wilcoxon rank-sum test was used to assess differences between groups. Multivariate regression models were further employed to control potential confounding variables. Results Preschool children with ADHD symptoms had less time in most of the daily physical activities. Especially, ADHD groups had lower light (24.11 min vs. 27.25 min, P = 0.023), moderate (16.56 min vs. 20.43 min, P = 0.009) and moderate-to-vigorous physical activities (MVPA, 23.26 min vs. 29.20 min, P = 0.018) than control group. Potential interactive effects among light, moderate, MVPA and routine afterschool physical activities were further investigated using multivariate regression analysis. Conclusions The observed pattern of reduced PA in preschool children with ADHD symptoms may reflect behavioral characteristics associated with early ADHD manifestations. However, further longitudinal research is needed to determine whether activity differences could serve as potential early markers for ADHD. BMC Pediatrics (2026) 26:709 ​Introduction Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), a clinically significant neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent inattention, hyperactiv ity, and impulsivity [1], affects approximately 7.6% (95% CI: 6.1–9.4) of children aged 3–12 years and 5.6% (95% CI: 4.8–7.0) of adolescents aged 12–18 years globally [2]. Although clinical diagnosis typically occurs dur ing school years, accumulating evidence indicates that 70–80% of preschool children exhibiting ADHD symp toms maintain clinically relevant symptomatology into middle childhood [3, 4], highlighting the importance of early identification. However, the inherent behavioral variability characteristic of typical preschool develop ment complicates reliable diagnosis at this critical stage [5], underscoring the need for objective behavioral mark ers to facilitate early screening. Physical activity (PA) represents a promising behav ioral domain for both early identification and interven tion of ADHD [6, 7]. As a quantifiable manifestation of behavior, PA may reflect core ADHD-related character istics, including executive dysfunction. Indeed, existing research has identified distinct PA profiles in children with ADHD, including greater overall PA volume [8], increased movement variability [9], higher activity lev els [10]and reduced sedentary time [11] compared to typically developing peers. However, current evidence regarding PA patterns in ADHD presents apparent para dox. While some studies report elevated activity levels, others demonstrate reduced PA engagement or no sig nificant differences. A critical synthesis of these studies suggests that these discrepancies are not arbitrary but may be attributed to several key factors. First, method ological heterogeneity plays a crucial role. Observational studies often rely on parent or teacher reports, which tend to capture macro-level, perceptible hyperactivity and may be biased by recall or situational specificity, fre quently indicating reduced structured PA participation [12, 13]. In contrast, device-based accelerometry objec tively quantifies micro-level movement patterns across the entire intensity spectrum, often revealing greater total volume and more variable movement in children with ADHD [8]. Second, environmental context exerts a regulatory influence. Structured environments (e.g., kin dergarten settings) with adult supervision may suppress hyperactive behaviors compared to less-controlled envi ronments (e.g., home settings), leading to context-depen dent PA profiles. Third, and critically, the developmental stage of the sample is a likely pivotal variable. The major ity of existing evidence is derived from school-aged chil dren with established ADHD diagnoses. The preschool period represents a distinct neurodevelopmental stage characterized by rapid maturation of motor control and executive functions. The expression of ADHD-related motor signatures in this early period may differ qualita tively and quantitatively from later childhood of symp toms [14], yet it remains systematically understudied. Consequently, the central question evolves from merely whether PA differs in ADHD to under what conditions, how, and at which developmental stage these differ ences emerge. The present study addresses this question directly by focusing on the understudied preschool popu lation, employing objective accelerometry, and observing within the semi-structured kindergarten environment. This design allows us to characterize early, contextspecific PA profiles associated with ADHD symptoms, thereby contributing data from a critical developmental window to help resolve the broader scientific debate. Methods Study design This study is part of the prospective cohort of physical exercise intervention for preschoolers with ADHD symp toms. The clinical trial was registered with ​h​t​t​p​:​/​/​w​w​w​.​c​h​ i​c​t​r​.​o​r​g​.​c​n​, ChiCTR2400083571. Participants From March to June 2025, a total of 84 children (18 with ADHD symptoms and 66 typical developing controls) from a public kindergarten in Shanghai were enrolled in this study. Eligible children with ADHD symptoms met the following criteria: 1) elevated ADHD symptoms (Factor IV or Factor VI scores ≥ inline-eq-IEq1+1SD) on Conners Parental Symptom Questionnaire; 2) ADHD symptoms confirmed by a qualified and experienced pediatrician using DSM-5 diagnostic criteria; 3) aged between 3 and 6 years at recruitment, and 4) parents or legal guardians were willing to participate. Exclusion criteria included: 1) meeting criteria for autism spectrum disorder; 2) mental illness (primary mental illness, such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder), 3) neurological disorders. In addition, a total of 66 neurotypical children were recruited from the same kindergarten. The inclusion criteria of the neuro typical group were age and sex matched with the ADHD group, but without any mental, neurological, or meta bolic disease. Measures Conners parental symptom questionnaire The Conners Parental Symptom Questionnaire (CPSQ) is a common tool used for screening ADHD symptoms. There are 48 items in the questionnaire, and the fourlevel scoring method (0, 1, 2, 3) could be summarized into six factors, including conduct problem (Factor I), learning problem (Factor II), somatic complaints (Fac tor III), hyperactivity (Factor IV), anxiety (Factor V), and Conners Index of hyperactivity (CIH, Factor VI). CPSQ has been introduced in China since 1980 s and has good

Physical activity Physical activity was measured using the Actigraph w3GTX-BT accelerometer (ActiGraph Corp, Pensacola, FL, USA). The devices were secured on the right hip at 8:30 AM upon children’s arrival at kindergarten and maintained continuous wear until 4:30 PM retrieval for five consecutive school days. Raw accelerometer data were collected at 30 Hz with 10 s epoch intervals [16]. Using Actilife (version 6.13.3) software to download and process raw accelerometer data, the Choi (2011) algo rithm was employed to identify periods when children were not wearing the accelerometer [17]. Valid data is defined as a single day of valid wearing time ≥ 180 min and valid data days ≥ 3 days, which were included for further analysis. The Pate cutoff rule is used to classify physical activity as time spent in sedentary (0–799 counts per minute), light PA (800–1679 counts per minute), moderate PA (1680–3367 counts per minute), vigorous PA(≥ 3368 counts per minute) and moderate to vigorous PA (MVPA, ≥ 1680 counts per minute) for preschoolers. Data collection We used online surveys as methodology to collect demo graphic and questionnaire data via the WeChat network. Demographic data including age, sex, the only child, main caregiver, parental education level, and parental occupation were collected by self-administered question naire. Additionally, information on outside of kinder garten physical exercise (including type, frequency per week, and duration of each session) was simultaneously collected. Regular extracurricular physical exercise (EPE) was defined as structured sports activities occurring: 1) outside of kindergarten hours; 2) more than once a week; and 3) ≥ 30 min per session. Ethical approval The study was conducted according to the guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the institu tional ethics committee of Minhang Hospital, Fudan Uni versity (2025–030-01 K). Procedure We used a two-step screening protocol to identify the early ADHD symptoms among preschoolers. Conners Parental Symptom Questionnaire was used for pre liminary screening, where children who test positive undergo clinical evaluation. Clinical interviews were conducted in kindergarten by an experienced pediat ric team, including interviews with parents, teachers, and patients. ADHD symptoms were assessed based on DSM-5 criteria. Formal diagnosis was not required given the well-documented challenges in establishing clinical ADHD diagnoses in preschool-aged populations [18, 19]. Discussion To our knowledge, this study provides the first objective evidence characterizing PA patterns in preschool chil dren with ADHD symptoms. Our accelerometer data suggests that preschoolers with ADHD symptoms may exhibit significantly lower engagement in light (LPA), moderate (MPA), and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA). This aligns with studies reporting reduced PA partici pation in older ADHD populations [13, 20], suggesting that PA deficits may emerge early in development. Notably, our results contrast with studies reporting higher overall PA volume or reduced sedentary time in school-aged children with ADHD [9–11]. This discrep ancy may be explained by these factors highlighted in our introduction. First, methodological differences in accel erometer use may play a role. While our study focused on kindergarten hours, previous 24-h/7-day monitoring studies captured total daily movement [8], potentially masking context-dependent PA variations. Second, envi ronmental influences are especially important in early childhood. Preschool settings typically enforce stricter behavioral rules than home environments. This may suppress spontaneous movement. Finally, developmen tal differences are key. Older children with ADHD often express hyperactivity through frequent movement [21]. In contrast, preschoolers with ADHD symptoms may lack sufficient motor skills or behavioral control for con sistent PA participation. These findings underscore the importance of age-specific PA interventions tailored to early ADHD symptoms. Our findings extend previous work by revealing PA reductions are detectable even in preschool ADHD symptoms. ADHD children tend to engage in less PA [22], which may be associated with executive dysfunc tion (e.g., impaired planning and inhibitory control) [23, 24]. Some evidence suggests a potential bidirectional relationship, where executive function deficits could limit PA participation, while low PA exacerbates EF impairments (e.g., Tower of London task performance: adjusted R2 = 0.28, P < 0.05) [25]. Besides, ADHD fre quently co-occurs with comorbidities that compound PA reduction. Insufficient PA mediates the longitudinal link between childhood ADHD symptoms and adoles cent obesity (OR = 1.91, 95%CI: 1.10–3.33) [26]. These findings raise the possibility of a cyclical pattern: ADHDreduced PA-weight gain-further activity decline [27]. From a neurobiological perspective, these patterns could be linked to dopamine dysfunction [30]. The dopamine system plays key roles in cognitive control and motivation. In ADHD, this sys tem’s dysregulation may lead to reduced motivation for effortful activities. Specifically, individuals with ADHD may show decreased engagement in exercise, particularly when rewards are delayed [31]. Supporting this, MAOA genotype variations influence ventral striatum activation patterns (reward circuitry) [32], suggesting genetic mod ulation of activity-related behaviors. Extracurricular physical exercise (EPE) and in-kinder garten physical activities are both important components of movement behaviors in preschool children [33]. In our study, we found no significant interaction between EPE and group differences in kindergarten PA levels (P > 0.05). This suggests that lower PA levels in preschool ers with ADHD symptoms were not significantly linked to their overall daily activity patterns. The reduced PA likely reflects kindergarten-specific challenges, including structured participation deficits [20] and impaired social interactions [34]. These findings support tailored edu cational strategies to promote PA independent of their baseline activity levels. This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, the most notable limitation is the modest sample size, particularly of the group with ADHD symptoms (n = 18), which necessitates cautious interpretation of the findings. This sample size, however, reflects two fundamental challenges in preschool ADHD research:1) The epidemiological context: The popula tion prevalence of clinically significant ADHD symptoms in preschoolers is estimated to be low (approximately 1.9–3.3%) [35, 36]. 2) The rigor of ascertainment: Our two-step screening procedure was employed to enhance diagnostic precision and reduce false positives, a critical concern in preschool populations where normative high activity overlaps with pathology. The main implication of this sample size is reduced statistical power, increas ing the risk of unstable estimates. Nevertheless, confi dence in the primary between-group findings is bolstered by key methodological strengths: the use of objective, high-resolution accelerometry; the well-characterized control group drawn from the same environment; and the consistency of the observed effect directions with larger-scale studies in older children with ADHD. There fore, while the findings regarding global PA reductions in children with ADHD symptoms appear reliable within this context, they should be viewed as robust preliminary evidence that necessitates replication in larger, multisite cohorts. Second, the participants were recruited only from public kindergartens in Shanghai, potentially limiting the representativeness of the results for other preschool-aged children, particularly those from diverse socioeconomic or cultural backgrounds. Third, while accelerometers provide objective measures of physi cal activity, they cannot capture contextual factors (e.g., structured vs. unstructured activities) that may influ ence movement patterns in children with ADHD symp toms. Our study did not conduct subtype clas sification of preschool ADHD symptoms. We could not assess whether specific symptom domains differentially relate to PA engagement. Future investigations with larger samples and dimensional symptom assessments are warranted. Fifth, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference regarding the direction of the observed relationship. Future multi-center longitudinal studies with larger, diverse samples are essential to establish cau sality and to examine whether reduced PA is a precursor, correlate, or consequence of emerging ADHD symptom atology in early childhood. In conclusion, this study reveals that preschool chil dren with ADHD symptoms exhibit significantly lower PA. These findings highlight the importance of early identification and targeted PA interventions to promote their overall health. Future research should further clarify the causal relationship between these factors and explore potential intervention strategies in this population. Although more common in children, ~ 2.5% of adults worldwide have ADHD. In this cross-sectional observational study, we estimated the annual socioeconomic burden of adults with ADHD in Japan (societal perspective). Methods We used retrospective data from the JMDC claims database, a prospective web-based survey of adults with self-reported ADHD, adult family members living with an adult with ADHD, and adults without ADHD who had an Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale score < 4 (control population), and Japanese government agency websites to estimate medical costs (outpatient costs and drug costs), social welfare costs (disability pensions and employment support services), and productivity losses due to unemployment, low income, absenteeism, and presenteeism. In addition to the base-case analysis, we conducted scenario and sensitivity analyses to examine the effects of changing estimation and matching methods on costs, as well as a subgroup analysis of costs stratified by the number of psychiatric comorbidities. Results Cost estimates were based on 30,730 adults with an ADHD diagnosis in the JMDC database and, from the web-based survey, 309 adults with self-reported ADHD, 309 adult family members of adults with ADHD, and 927 adults in the control population. Using an estimated 260,120 adults with ADHD in Japan, the base-case analysis estimated annual medical costs at 74.0 billion Japanese yen (JPY), social welfare costs at 389.6 billion JPY, and productivity losses at 571.1 billion JPY. Productivity losses in family members were estimated at 542.2 billion JPY. Total socioeconomic burden was estimated at 1.58 trillion JPY (~ US$10.9 billion) (~ 4 million JPY [~ US$29,000] per adult with ADHD). Social welfare costs and productivity losses increased with the number of comorbidities. In the scenario analyses, cost estimates varied from − 68.9% to + 96.1% relative to the base case and were most strongly affected by the method used to estimate the total number of adults with ADHD. BMC Psychiatry (2026) 26:378 Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by inatten tion and hyperactivity/impulsivity at levels that negatively affect social, academic, and occupational functioning [1–3]. The worldwide prevalence of ADHD has been estimated to be about 7.2% in children and adolescents [4] and about 2.5% in adults [5], although estimates vary widely depending on criteria used [6, 7]. In Japan, the prevalence of ADHD has been reported to be 5.8–7.7% in children and adolescents [8, 9] and 1.65% in adults [10]. However, these estimates were based on communitylevel surveys, and no nationwide prevalence estimates are available for adult ADHD in Japan. Because the inci dence of newly diagnosed ADHD among Japanese adults increased steadily between 2010 and 2019 [11], the cur rent prevalence may be higher than previously suggested. ADHD is often diagnosed in childhood, and although not all patients continue to meet the full diagnostic criteria for ADHD in adulthood, functional disabilities or sub threshold symptoms persist at a high rate into adulthood [12, 13]. In addition, patients with ADHD frequently have psychiatric comorbidities [14], which place an additional burden on patients. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Dis orders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision states that ADHD in adults is associated with poorer occupational perfor mance, attainment, and attendance, and a higher prob ability of unemployment [1]. Reduced work productivity (absenteeism and presenteeism) in adult patients with ADHD has been reported in various countries, including Japan [15–17]. Productivity is likely reduced by the core symptoms of ADHD, which can adversely affect time management, organization, and interpersonal relation ships [18, 19]. Moreover, poor understanding of ADHD by society may lead to stigma [20] and reduce the oppor tunity for adults with ADHD to obtain and hold a job [21]. Under such circumstances, some people may be reluctant to visit a psychiatrist because they fear being diagnosed with ADHD, resulting in a lack of or a delay in receiving appropriate diagnosis, treatment, or welfare. In Japan, people with ADHD are eligible to receive medical treatment as well as work support, including social skills training, self-reliance support systems, and/ or a disability pension in severe cases [22]. However, it is unclear whether current employment support services are effective enough to help adults with ADHD who are willing to work. In addition, problems associated with caregiving may impose a considerable burden on family members of adults with ADHD [23]. Recently, employers have started to include people with neurodevelopmental disorders in their workplaces under the concept of neuro diversity, which recognizes the competitive advantages of a neurodiverse workforce in rapidly changing and highly specialized work environments [24, 25]. Thus, discus sions regarding appropriate work support for adults with ADHD and family members who are willing to work, and its socioeconomic impact, would be very meaningful. In this context, the estimation of the socioeconomic bur den of ADHD would provide useful data for policy dis cussions. Multiple analyses of the socioeconomic burden of pediatric and/or adult ADHD have been conducted, primarily in the USA and Europe [26–28]. However, to the best of our knowledge, there have been no reports estimating the socioeconomic burden of adult ADHD in Japan or in Asia more broadly. We conducted a cross-sectional observational study to estimate the annual socioeconomic burden of adult patients with ADHD in Japan from a societal perspective by combining a retrospective claims database analysis with a web-based survey and statistics from the Japanese government. We estimated medical costs (ADHD drugs and outpatient healthcare) and costs due to productivity losses and social welfare expenses. In addition, as work productivity and employment of adult family members of adults with ADHD can be impaired [23], we also esti mated productivity losses in family members. Methods Study design This was a nationwide cross-sectional observational study using retrospective data from the JMDC claimsbased database, prospective data from a web-based survey, and publicly available data from the Japanese government. JMDC (JMDC Inc., Tokyo, Japan) is a nationwide database of receipts and medical examina tion data from multiple health insurance societies in Japan, which started in 2005. As of February 2022, JMDC included data from approximately 14 million registered Conclusion This study, the first estimate of the annual socioeconomic burden of adult ADHD in Japan, underscores the necessity of more appropriate support for adult patients with ADHD and their families to reduce productivity losses. Trial registration University hospital Medical Information Network Center (UMIN000051654; registered July 20, 2023). Keywords Attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity, Cost of illness, Direct medical costs, Family members, Health care costs, Productivity losses, Social welfare costs, Socioeconomic burden, Unemployment, Work performance

The web-based survey, conducted between July 26, 2023, and August 9, 2023, was completed by participants from panels managed by Macromill, Inc. (Tokyo, Japan). Participants were recruited from a general panel and a panel of patients with ADHD and family members, and participants were located throughout Japan. Data col lection in the general panel was allocated by sex and age category according to the composition of the adult popu lation in Japan. An additional survey, conducted between July 26, 2023, and August 2, 2023, recruited participants from an adult ADHD population who visited Nihon Chouzai pharmacies in the Kanto area (Nihon Chouzai Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan) with a prescription for ADHDspecific medication. These participants were considered more likely to have a diagnosis of ADHD compared with participants in the Macromill panels who self-reported ADHD, and survey results were used for validation of the Macromill panel results. Survey participants in the Macromill panels received points equivalent to 60 Japa nese yen (JPY) and those from Nihon Chouzai received an Amazon gift card equivalent to 500 JPY as compensa tion. Survey participants provided informed consent on the web screen before starting the survey and were deidentified by Macromill and Nihon Chouzai prior to pro viding data to the researchers. Data on the Japanese population, outpatient and drug costs, public employment support services, unemploy ment, income, and working hours were derived from the most recent data available from the websites of govern ment agencies, including the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW), the Statistics Bureau of Japan, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, and the National Tax Agency JAPAN. The study was conducted in compliance with ethical principles based on the Ethical Guidelines for Life Sci ence, Medical and Health Research Involving Human Subjects. The study protocol was approved by the Non-Profit Organization MINS Institutional Review Board (ID: 230222) and registered at the University hospital Medical Information Network Center (UMIN000051654) on July 20, 2023. Study population JMDC claims database Adults (aged ≥ 18 and < 65 years at April 1, 2022) reg istered in the JMDC database who had a diagnosis of ADHD, based on the International Statistical Classifica tion of Diseases and Related Health Problems 10th Revi sion code F90, during the Japanese financial year 2022 (April 2022 to March 2023) were eligible for inclusion. Web-based survey Male or female adults (aged ≥ 18 and < 65 years at informed consent) who were living in Japan were eligible for inclusion if they met the following criteria for each group: • Adults with ADHD: self-reported diagnosis of ADHD. • Adult family members of adults with ADHD: no diagnosis of ADHD; currently living with a family member aged ≥ 18 years who is diagnosed with ADHD. • Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) negative non-ADHD adults (control population): no diagnosis of ADHD; no family member aged ≥ 18 years who is diagnosed with ADHD; ASRS score < 4. The ASRS is an 18-item self-administered test used to screen for adult ADHD, which has been validated in Japanese [29]. In the 6-item screening version used here, which is widely used as a screener in Japanese clinical practice [30], the result is considered positive if at least four of six questions in Part A of the test are answered positively [29, 31, 32]. An adult ASRS-positive nonADHD population was also identified for exploratory analyses not reported herein. The target sample size for adults with ADHD was set at 300, based on a previous study by the Nomura Research Institute, which recruited more than 300 adults with ADHD from Macromill panels [33]. To provide a similar sample size, the target number of adult family members of adults with ADHD was also set at 300. The target sam ple size for adult ASRS-negative non-ADHD adults was set at 900 (i.e. three times the size of the ADHD and fam ily member samples) to allow for matching. Base-case analysis The analysis methods used to estimate the socioeco nomic burden of ADHD in Japan are summarized below; details are shown in Additional file 1 (Supple mentary Methods and Fig. S1). The number of adult patients with ADHD in Japan, defined as the number of adult patients with ADHD who received outpatient care from April 2022 to March 2023, was calculated based on data from JMDC and Japanese population data from the Statistics Bureau of Japan. The formula used was as below: The number of adult patients with ADHD = 64 ∑ i=18 ( nadhd,male,i,jmdc × Nmale,i,japan nmale,i,jmdc +nadhd,female,i,jmdc × Nfemale,i,japan nfemale,i,jmdc )

Medical costs, defined as the total costs of medical care (outpatient costs and drug costs) for adult patients with ADHD from April 2022 to March 2023, were calculated by multiplying average medical costs per person derived from JMDC data by the number of patients. Drugs for ADHD (in-hospital and pharmacy) were identified based on the World Health Organization’s Anatomical Thera peutic Chemical codes N06BA04 (methylphenidate), N06BA09 (atomoxetine), and C02AC02 (guanfacine). Social welfare expenses, defined as the total annual expenses incurred for adult patients with ADHD as social welfare services provided by the government, were calculated by summing disability pensions and public employment support services. Data for disability pen sions were derived from the web-based survey. Data for public employment support services were derived from the web-based survey and from MHLW websites [34, 35]. Productivity losses were defined as the total of losses due to unemployment, low income, absenteeism, and presenteeism. The web-based survey included questions from the Work Productivity and Activity Impairment questionnaire [36], which asked how many hours were missed from work (absenteeism) and to what extent their work productivity was impaired (presenteeism) because of health problems during the previous 7 days. For adult family members, the absenteeism and presenteeism questions referred both to problems due to ADHD in the adult with ADHD and to their health problems. Produc tivity losses were calculated for the adult ADHD popula tion and for adult family members of adults with ADHD. The number of adult family members was estimated by multiplying the proportion of family members in the web-based survey relative to the total number screened for the survey by the number of adults in the Japanese population using data from the Statistics Bureau of Japan [37]. Prior to analysis, exact matching was performed between each population (adults with ADHD; family members) and ASRS-negative non-ADHD adults based on age, sex, and place of residence (region of Japan) data collected in the web-based survey. Losses due to unem ployment and losses due to low income were calculated by taking the difference between the mean values in the Japanese population derived from the websites of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications [38, 39] and the National Tax Agency JAPAN [40], and the mean values in adults with ADHD derived from the survey. Losses due to absenteeism and losses due to presentee ism were calculated by taking the difference between the mean values in adults with ADHD and ASRS-negative adults without ADHD using data from the web-based survey and the MHLW [41]. The total socioeconomic burden (primary endpoint) was the sum of medical costs (adults with ADHD), social welfare expenses (adults with ADHD), and productivity losses (adults with ADHD and adult family members). Additional analyses Subgroup analysis based on number of comorbidities Social welfare expenses and productivity losses were calculated as above with minor modifications (see Addi tional file 1 [Supplementary Methods]) in adults with ADHD stratified by the number of self-reported psychi atric comorbidities (0, 1, 2, or ≥ 3) provided by partici pants in the web-based survey. Scenario analysis To evaluate the effect of changes in the estimation meth ods on costs, we conducted a total of 40 scenario (sen sitivity) analyses (10 scenarios for medical costs × four scenarios for productivity losses). Variations in meth odology were as follows (method used in the base-case analysis underlined): • Estimation of number of adults with ADHD and medical costs: top-down approach based on MHLW statistics or bottom-up approach based on webbased survey versus bottom-up approach based on JMDC. • Definition of ADHD: ADHD as main diagnosis only versus ADHD as main diagnosis and subdisease. • Definition of the drugs: ADHD medications plus medications for associated mental disorders versus ADHD medications only. • Estimation of unemployment rate in non-ADHD adults: based on the result of web-based survey versus statistics from the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications. • Estimation of average annual income in non-ADHD adults: based on the result of web-based survey versus statistics from the National Tax Agency JAPAN.

Sensitivity analysis As an additional sensitivity analysis, productivity losses in adult patients with ADHD and adult family members of adult patients with ADHD were also estimated after matching with ASRS-negative non-ADHD adults by sex, age, place of residence, educational background, and occupation, and without any matching. Comparison of Macromill and Nihon Chouzai survey participants To assess the validity of the web-based survey data, we compared the results from the combined Macromill panels (Macromill general panel and Macromill ADHD patient panel) with those from Nihon Chouzai. Prior to analysis, exact matching was performed between adult patients with ADHD from the Macromill panel and those from Nihon Chouzai based on sex, age, place of resi dence, educational background, and occupation. All costs are reported in JPY; during 2022, the average exchange rate was approximately 137.4 JPY to 1 US$. All statistical analyses were conducted using R, Version 4.2.0 or later (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). We also identi fied 927 adults without ADHD who were ASRS negative and were used for matching analyses, as well as 309 adults without ADHD who were ASRS positive (used for explor atory analyses not reported herein). Based on an estimated 260,120 adult patients with ADHD in Japan (Additional file 1 [Table S3]), the total medical costs for adult patients with ADHD in Japan were estimated to be approximately 74.0 billion JPY, including approximately 14.3 billion JPY for outpatient costs and approximately 59.7 billion JPY for ADHD drug costs (Table 2). Social welfare expenses for adult patients with ADHD In the web-based survey, after matching, 48.7% of patients with ADHD received a disability pension (Addi tional file 1 [Table S1]), at an average amount of 752,329 JPY per person (Additional file 1 [Table S3]). The total cost of disability pensions for Japanese adults with ADHD was estimated to be approximately 95.2 billion JPY (Table 2). Transition support for employment, continued employment support type A, and continued employment support type B was received by 27.3%, 20.0%, and 18.7% of patients with ADHD, respectively (Additional file 1 [Table S1 and Table S3]). BMC Psychiatry (2026) 26:378 Discussion This is the first report to estimate the socioeconomic burden of adult ADHD in Japan from a societal perspec tive and the first in any Asian country. Our analysis not only included medical costs, but also social support wel fare expenses and productivity losses associated with adults who have ADHD and their adult family members. The total annual costs attributable to adult ADHD in Japan were estimated to exceed 1.5 trillion JPY (approxi mately US$10.9 billion), with costs of nearly 4 million JPY (approximately US$29,112) per adult with ADHD. More than half (55%) of the total socioeconomic bur den for adults with ADHD was due to work-related productivity losses, while social welfare expenses and medical costs accounted for approximately 38% and 7% of overall costs, respectively. The large contribution of productivity losses is generally consistent with socio economic studies of adult ADHD conducted in the USA and Europe, although the specific costs vary depending on the social and medical environments in each country and the estimation methods used [27, 42, 43]. In one US analysis, 71–83% of costs were due to productivity losses (including disability services and worker’s compensa tion, which we categorized as social welfare expenses) and income losses, with medical costs contributing 15–26% [27].
