Page 7 of 10 Baxmann et al. BMC Oral Health (2026) 26:275 routines. Impulsivity and hyperactivity can also increase the likelihood of removing, misplacing, or damaging appliances during daytime activities, further undermin ing retention protocols and potentially increasing the risk of post-treatment relapse. Although relapse outcomes were not systematically tracked across studies, the behavioral profiles commonly associated with ADHD—characterized by forgetfulness, reduced routine adherence, and diminished task persis tence—suggest a potential for lower compliance during the retention phase [8, 27]. This concern was particularly evident in reports involving removable appliances, where issues such as device loss, inconsistent wear, or caregiverreported noncompliance were described [29]. Taken together, these observations support the need for closer monitoring of retention-phase adherence in patients with ADHD and justify future research to evaluate long-term treatment stability in this population. Treatment success and duration Across the included studies, treatment success in patients with ADHD was most often reflected through providerreported impressions of clinical progress, behavioral cooperation, and completion of treatment phases rather than standardized outcome metrics. Several studies noted that children with ADHD required more frequent reminders, extended chairside interaction, or additional behavioral support to complete procedures, suggesting a higher clinical burden that may affect efficiency [8, 19]. Individual case studies described positive outcomes when tailored behavioral strategies were implemented, includ ing the use of structured appointments and positive reinforcement to complete active treatment phases such as functional appliance therapy [33]. These reports illus trate how adapting clinical routines to match attentional and behavioral needs can support treatment progress in ADHD-affected individuals. While treatment dura tion and success were not consistently quantified across studies, observed patterns suggest that ADHD-related behavioral traits may influence the pace and structure of orthodontic care. These findings reinforce the impor tance of individualized management strategies to support clinical completion and suggest that treatment planning for patients with ADHD should anticipate a potentially greater need for time, reinforcement, and flexibility. Oral habits and orthodontic outcomes Parafunctional oral habits—including bruxism, tongue thrusting, nail biting, pacifier use, and mouth breath ing—were consistently reported at higher rates among individuals with ADHD. Across both caregiver-reported and clinical assessments, bruxism emerged as a particu larly prevalent finding, often linked to stimulant medica tion use, though not always stratified by pharmacologic status [10, 20]. Habits such as tongue thrusting and nail biting were also frequently observed, with several stud ies noting their potential to disrupt appliance stability or contribute to occlusal complications [16, 17]. Large population-based and cross-sectional investigations rein forced these associations, linking ADHD symptoms to elevated rates of bruxism, snoring, and mouth breath ing—patterns that may further complicate orthodontic care by impacting appliance retention, airway develop ment, or compliance [21, 24, 25]. Hyperactivity traits in particular were associated with increased malocclusion and parafunctional habits, suggesting that symptom dimensions may influence oral development and behav ior during treatment [26, 30]. Evidence from children with ADHD and co-occurring sleep-disordered breathing also pointed to more severe obstructive symptoms and poorer oxygen saturation, reinforcing the complex inter play between neurobehavioral traits, airway health, and orthodontic outcomes [32]. These behavioral patterns were further reflected in early childhood habits. Prolonged pacifier use and bot tle feeding were significantly more common in ADHD populations, contributing to occlusal development con cerns in both high- and moderate-quality studies [19, 22, 31]. While most studies did not directly measure the orthodontic consequences of these behaviors, the consis tency of findings highlights the importance of behavioral screening and habit management as part of orthodontic treatment planning. In addition, anatomical differences such as reduced airway volume and altered craniofa cial dimensions in adolescents with ADHD may further contribute to treatment complexity, particularly in cases involving functional appliances or airway-related con cerns [23]. Missed appointments and follow-up adherence Inconsistent follow-up and missed appointments were frequently reported as clinical challenges in manag ing orthodontic care for patients with ADHD. Providers described a higher incidence of scheduling disruptions, late arrivals, and missed visits among these patients, which often required additional effort to maintain treat ment continuity and contributed to overall therapeutic difficulty [8, 27]. These behaviors were commonly men tioned alongside cooperation issues and were identified as complicating factors in case progression and appliance management. Individual case studies provided further insight, not ing that impulsivity, distractibility, and reduced task persistence contributed to difficulty maintaining multiphase treatment schedules and regular follow-up [29]. Although visit attendance was not consistently measured as a standalone outcome, the recurrence of these pat terns across clinical reports highlights the relevance of

Page 8 of 10 Baxmann et al. BMC Oral Health (2026) 26:275 behavioral traits in shaping treatment consistency. These findings suggest that close monitoring and proactive scheduling strategies may be especially important in sup porting adherence to follow-up protocols among ADHDaffected patients. ADHD medication and orthodontic outcomes Among the included studies, ADHD medication—par ticularly stimulant use—was associated with behavioral traits relevant to orthodontic care. In one case-control study, children receiving stimulant medication exhibited higher rates of bruxism and dental attrition compared to both non-medicated ADHD peers and neurotypical controls, suggesting a potential pharmacologic contri bution to parafunctional activity [10]. In a large adoles cent cohort, persistent behavioral and neurophysiologic disruptions were observed in individuals with ADHD, even when medicated participants were excluded from analysis, indicating that medication may influence—but does not fully account for—clinical traits relevant to orthodontic management [28]. While most studies refer enced medication status descriptively, observed patterns highlight the importance of considering pharmacologic context when assessing cooperation, oral habits, and treatment behavior in ADHD-affected patients. Fixed vs. removable appliances in ADHD populations Several studies referenced appliance type when dis cussing behavioral management in orthodontic care for patients with ADHD. Removable appliances were described in case studies as offering flexibility during behavioral episodes, though challenges with consistent wear and increased need for caregiver oversight were noted [29, 33]. In a descriptive study, removable devices were associated with more variable cooperation among children with behavioral concerns, highlighting the importance of parental involvement in treatment adher ence [8]. In contrast, fixed appliances were discussed in relation to hygiene maintenance and appointment adherence but were less frequently linked to behavioral outcomes. These observations suggest that appliance selection may interact with behavioral characteristics in ADHD populations, particularly in terms of supervision requirements and wear consistency. Differences in treatment success across ADHD subtypes Studies describing orthodontic behavior in ADHDaffected populations revealed distinct patterns that align with known symptom profiles, suggesting that specific traits may influence treatment engagement differently. Inattentive symptoms were associated with missed appointments, poor follow-through on instructions, and reduced adherence as reported by caregivers and clini cians [8]. Hyperactivity and impulsivity, on the other hand, were more frequently linked to appliance misuse, disruptive behavior during appointments, and increased need for behavioral management [27]. Observations of appliance breakage and higher treatment complex ity in patients exhibiting restlessness or distractibility further underscore the relevance of behavioral presen tation in shaping orthodontic care experiences [19, 29]. These patterns highlight the value of tailoring treatment approaches to the attentional and behavioral characteris tics most prominent in each patient. Behavioral and educational interventions to improve compliance A range of behavioral and educational strategies was described across studies as integral to managing orth odontic treatment challenges in children with ADHD. Clinicians emphasized the importance of simplified instructions, visual aids, shorter or more frequent appointments, and structured routines designed to match the child’s attentional and behavioral profile [8, 27]. These strategies were associated with reductions in disruptive behavior and improved cooperation during appliance placement and follow-up care. Case studies illustrated the practical implementation of these tech niques, including the use of 10-minute activity intervals, positive reinforcement, and predictable visit structures, which supported successful appliance wear and phase completion [29, 33]. Across both descriptive and obser vational sources, increased caregiver involvement—par ticularly in monitoring appliance use and reinforcing routines—was frequently cited as a factor associated with better adherence, especially among younger children or those exhibiting inattentive traits. One quasi-experimen tal study evaluating Myobrace therapy in children with ADHD also reported improved cooperation and oral function, potentially reflecting the benefits of structured therapeutic routines embedded within appliance-based interventions [18]. Although formal evaluations of intervention effective ness were limited, the consistent use of these strategies across multiple contexts underscores their clinical rel evance. Orthodontists who adapted their communica tion style, engaged families in behavioral reinforcement, and modified environmental factors such as appointment length or task sequencing reported fewer behavior man agement concerns during treatment [8, 27]. Increased caregiver involvement—particularly in monitoring appli ance use, supporting behavioral routines, and encourag ing treatment follow-through—was frequently cited as a factor associated with better adherence, especially among younger children or those exhibiting inattentive traits [29, 33]. These findings suggest that integrating individualized behavioral approaches into treatment planning may off set core challenges associated with ADHD, particularly in

Page 9 of 10 Baxmann et al. BMC Oral Health (2026) 26:275 settings where pharmacologic management is absent or insufficient. Taken together, the evidence supports a mul timodal approach to improving compliance, rooted in behavioral tailoring and sustained caregiver engagement. Limitations Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. The overall certainty of the evidence was low. Of the 18 non-randomized studies assessed with ROB INS-I, three were judged to have a low overall risk of bias, while 15 were rated as having a moderate or serious risk of bias. Bias due to confounding and outcome measurement was particularly frequent. ADHD was defined using het erogeneous methods across studies, including DSM-based clinical diagnoses, various parent- or teacher-completed questionnaires, and, in some cases, chart documentation without standardized reassessment, which complicates comparison of populations. Adjustment for potential con founders such as socioeconomic status, comorbid behav ioral or neurodevelopmental conditions, and caregiver involvement was limited or absent in most analyses. Key outcomes, especially cooperation, adherence, and appli ance-related complications, relied heavily on clinician impressions or non-validated rating scales rather than objective or standardized orthodontic indices. Beyond risk of bias, there was substantial clinical and methodologi cal heterogeneity. Participant age ranges were broad and often not stratified; follow-up duration and the timing of outcome assessment varied considerably and were not always clearly reported, making direct comparison of suc cess rates, adverse events, or relapse difficult. Most designs were cross-sectional or retrospective, restricting causal inference and precluding robust evaluation of temporal relationships or response to specific interventions. Taken together, these limitations indicate that the findings of this review should be interpreted with caution and regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive. Future research directions Future research should prioritize the use of standardized, objective measures—such as electronic attendance logs, appliance wear sensors, and validated treatment outcome indices—to improve the accuracy and comparability of orthodontic adherence data in ADHD populations. Pro spective cohort studies and intervention trials are needed to evaluate the effectiveness of behavioral, educational, and pharmacologic strategies, particularly when outcomes are stratified by ADHD subtype, medication status, and appli ance modality. Subgroup analyses could clarify whether specific presentations, such as inattentive or hyperac tive-impulsive profiles, are differentially associated with treatment response or compliance. To support generaliz ability and causal inference, studies should incorporate suf ficient sample sizes and multivariate modeling to account for confounders such as age, sex, socioeconomic status, comorbidities, and caregiver involvement. Collaborative research involving both orthodontic and mental health professionals may also enhance the ecological validity of future findings and support the development of tailored, evidence-based care models for patients with ADHD. Conclusion This systematic review suggests that individuals with ADHD may be at increased risk of lower orthodontic treat ment adherence, more frequent parafunctional oral habits, and greater behavioral management demands compared with neurotypical peers. However, the magnitude and clinical implications of these differences remain uncer tain because the evidence is derived predominantly from observational studies with considerable heterogeneity in design, populations, and outcome definitions. Of the 18 non-randomized studies included, 15 were judged to have a moderate or serious overall risk of bias according to the ROBINS-I assessment, and outcomes were often assessed using non-standardized or subjective measures with lim ited control for key confounders such as age, follow-up duration, and timing of outcome assessment. Within these limitations, the available data do not suggest that ADHD should fundamentally alter the core principles or objec tives of orthodontic treatment planning. Rather, an ADHD diagnosis should heighten clinical awareness and prompt additional support: orthodontists may need to adapt time management in the clinical setting, modify communication strategies, and structure follow-up more proactively, in col laboration with caregivers and, where appropriate, mental health professionals. Tailored behavioral approaches and active caregiver involvement appear pragmatically associ ated with improved cooperation and may help mitigate some of the practical difficulties encountered when treat ing orthodontic patients with ADHD. metadata_title: Dietary inflammatory index (DII) and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a cross-sectional study in US children and adolescents and Mendelian randomization study
pages: Hu et al. European Journal of Medical Research (2026) 31:7 https://doi.org/10.1186/s40001-025-03711-z RESEARCH Dietary inflammatory index (DII) and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a cross‐sectional study in US children and adolescents and Mendelian randomization study Jue Hu1†, Jing‐ying Ma2†, Fa‐dan Tang2†, Jie‐yi Wang3, Jia‐ye Xu1, Bo‐han Wang1, Yu‐lu Pan1, Ying Wang1, Xiao‐bo Xuan4* and Jian Chen1* Abstract Background Diet may impact the risk of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) via altering inflammation. However, no investigations have been conducted to evaluate the relationship between ADHD and the diet’s inflam‐ matory potential. The study sought to investigate the relationship between ADHD and the dietary inflammatory index (DII). Methods We used data from the cross-sectional National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2001–2004 to investigate the relationship between DII and ADHD in 6481 children and adolescents aged 6–19 years. The relation‐ ship between ADHD and DII was investigated using weighted logistic regression and restricted cubic spline (RCS). We also explored the potential causal associations between ADHD and 187 types of food preferences using Mendelian randomization (MR). Results Despite thorough multivariate correction, a significant association between lower DII scores and an elevated probability of ADHD persisted (OR = 0.91, 95% CI 0.82–0.99). Nevertheless, when stratifying the DII into quartiles (T1–T4) for analysis, no statistically significant correlation was seen between DII and ADHD (P > 0.05). RCS analysis indicated a U-shaped correlation between DII and ADHD, with an inflection point at approximately 2.9. Media‐ tion analysis indicated that the Frailty Index partly mediated the association between DII and ADHD, representing about 5.49% of the overall impact. The findings from the univariate MR analysis revealed that fruit liking is significantly linked to a reduced risk of ADHD. Conversely, a liking for red meat, such as lamb, as well as a fondness for flavorings like onions, is significantly associated with an increased risk of ADHD. Reverse two-sample MR analyses revealed that genetic predisposition to ADHD significantly altered 37 food preferences (FDR < 0.05). Open Access © The Author(s) 2025. European Journal of Medical Research (2026) 31:7 Introduction Over the last two decades, there has been a substantial rise in pediatric neuropsychiatric disorders [1], resulting in severe implications for the afflicted children, their families, and the public health system. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is the most prevalent neuropsychiatric illness that begins in childhood, with an estimated global incidence of about 5% among school-aged children [2], and boys exhibit more symptoms than girls [3]. Prior studies have shown a substantial correlation between ADHD and inflammation, with inflammation perhaps contributing to the genesis of ADHD [4]. A meta-analysis of 10 studies revealed that persons with ADHD had increased levels of IL-6 and markedly decreased levels of TNF-α [5]. Although prior studies have not reached a consensus on the changes in inflammatory markers among individuals with ADHD, they generally support the notion that immune system dysregulation is present in this population [6, 7]. Inflammation is a fundamental biological process that facilitates the connection between an organism and its environment, including dietary factors. Numerous dietary elements linked to child neurodevelopment are recognized for their pro-inflammatory properties (e.g., fatty products) and anti-inflammatory properties (e.g., fermented goods) [8]. The Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII) is an epidemiological tool designed to estimate the overall inflammatory potential of an individual’s diet based on the association between dietary components and levels of specific inflammatory biomarkers reported in the literature [9–11]. It provides a composite measure that facilitates the assessment of diet as a whole in relation to inflammation [12]. Furthermore, emerging research into mechanisms such as the microbiota-gut-brain axis suggests that diet may influence neurodevelopment and behavior, potentially through modulation of systemic inflammation and gut microbiota [13]. Observational studies have linked various dietary patterns (e.g., high intake of fruits and vegetables vs. high intake of processed snacks) to differences in ADHD symptoms or related behavioral profiles [14– 16]. However, the overall inflammatory potential of the diet, as an integrative measure, has not been thoroughly investigated in relation to ADHD diagnosis. Conclusions We observed a U-shaped association between the DII and ADHD risk. The Frailty Index may partially mediate (5.49%) the association between DII and ADHD. However, the cross-sectional design precludes causal infer‐ ence. Fruit liking lowered ADHD risk, while red meat/onion liking increased risk. ADHD was associated with a general‐ ized reduction in liking for a wide range of foods. Future studies should investigate the role of a moderate-inflamma‐ tory diet in ADHD prevention. Key points 1. U-Shaped Association: A non-linear, U-shaped association was observed between the Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII) and ADHD risk in children and adolescents, indicating that both highly pro-inflammatory and antiinflammatory diets may be associated with increased risk. 2. Potential Mediation: The Frailty Index partially mediated (5.49%) the association between DII and ADHD, suggest‐ ing that the diet-ADHD link may be partly explained by diet’s impact on overall health status. 3. Specific Food Preferences: Mendelian randomization analysis suggested that genetic predisposition for liking fruit is associated with lower ADHD risk, while liking for red meat and onions is associated with higher risk. ADHD genetics also broadly influenced food preferences. 4. Clinical Implication: Promoting a balanced, anti-inflammatory diet (e.g., increasing fruit intake) could be a valu‐ able component of preventive strategies and clinical management for ADHD in the pediatric population. European Journal of Medical Research (2026) 31:7 Although there are possible links between food, inflammation, and ADHD, the precise impact of dietary inflammation (assessed by DII) on ADHD is still ambiguous. This research seeks to investigate the relationship between diet-induced inflammation, measured by the DII, and ADHD using data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES). Additionally, we conducted a multi-omics Mendelian randomization (MR) study to investigate the effects of various food preferences on ADHD. Through the examination of this connection, we aim to provide significant insights into the diet-ADHD relationship, which could inform future research on potential dietary strategies for ADHD management. Materials and methods Study participants The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) conducts the NHANES, a population-based, cross-sectional survey that evaluates the nutritional status and overall health of the civilian, noninstitutionalized population in the United States. The data used in this analysis were taken from this survey. A sophisticated, stratified multistage probability sample design is used to choose the sample, which oversamples certain subpopulations to reflect the U.S. population across all age groups. A home interview was used to gather data about the study participants. In a mobile examination facility, a standardized physical examination was performed, which included a few medical and laboratory procedures. The NCHS institutional review board authorized the study’s operations; minor children (those under the age of 17) gave written agreement to participate, and children who gave their consent in front of the interviewer and their parent or guardian [17]. Publicly accessible data for children and adolescents aged 6–19 who took part in two consecutive NHANES cycles (2001–2002 and 2003–2004) were utilized in this research. A random subsample of subjects aged ≥ 6 was subjected to DII exposure measurements. Based on the availability of exposure, outcome, and important covariate data, we chose study cycles and age range. First, we included 21,161 subjects from two cycles. Second, we excluded 13,962 participants who were younger than 6 years old or older than 19 years old. Then, we further excluded 699 participants with missing dietary data. Finally, we excluded 19 participants whose ADHD data were categorized as "unknown," "refused to answer," or "missing." After screening, the final study comprised 6481 eligible subjects in total (Fig. 1). The procedures were approved by the NCHS’s ethical review board, and participants completed informed consent documents. Study variables Measurement of diagnosed ADHD Consistent with the primary outcome variable in prior NHANES studies [18, 19], we assessed ADHD diagnoses among children and adolescents using information derived from the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) Computerized Diagnostic Interview Schedule for Children, Version IV (C-DISC IV) framework. The questions in the diagnostic interview were structured according to the diagnostic criteria of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition (DSM-IV) and the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10). In the NHANES cycles from 2001 to 2004, ADHD diagnosis was obtained solely through the parent informant/self-report interview (DISC-P). It is important to clarify that although the questions were aligned with the C‐DISC IV framework, the actual assessment in NHANES was based on parentreported clinician diagnosis rather than a direct structured clinical interview. Specifically, parents were asked: “Has a doctor or health professional ever told [child] that he/she has attention deficit disorder?” [20]. DII exposure assessment We used the Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII) to assess the overall inflammatory potential of participants’ diets. The DII was developed by Shivappa et al. as a scoring system based on the effects of dietary components on six inflammatory biomarkers (IL-1β, IL-4, IL-6, IL-10, TNFα, and CRP), originally comprising 45 dietary parameters (Table S1-1). As stated by Shivappa et al., the DII score remains valid and retains its predictive value for dietrelated inflammation even when fewer than 30 parameters are used [11]. In this study, dietary intake data were obtained from 24-h recall interviews conducted in the Mobile Examination Center (MEC) as part of the NHANES project. We excluded supplements and medications, and used the average of two reliable 24-h recalls to estimate usual nutrient intake. Due to the limited variety of dietary components available in the NHANES database, we used 26 available components from the original 45 parameters for calculation. For components present in the original DII but missing from NHANES (i.e., the 19 unused parameters), we followed the methodological recommendations of the developers by treating them as having a "null" effect, meaning their intake was assumed to be equivalent to the standard global average intake. This approach does not compromise the validity of the final DII score [11]. The DII calculation was standardized based on global intake reference values. First, the Z-score for each dietary component was calculated for each participant as

Page 4 of 17 Hu et al. European Journal of Medical Research (2026) 31:7 the difference between their daily intake and the global daily intake mean, divided by the global standard deviation (Z-score = [individual daily intake—global mean intake]/global SD). This Z-score was then converted to a percentile and further transformed to a score ranging from −1 to + 1 (Z-score’ = percentile × 2−1). Finally, this score was multiplied by the respective component’s inflammatory effect score (derived from the literature) to obtain the component-specific DII score. The overall DII score for an individual was the sum of all component scores. A positive total DII score indicates a pro-inflammatory dietary potential, while a negative score indicates an anti-inflammatory potential; the theoretical range of DII is from −8.87 (maximum anti-inflammatory potential) to + 7.89 (maximum pro-inflammatory potential). The DII was not energyadjusted per 1000 kcal in this study, in accordance with the original DII calculation method and to facilitate comparison with other studies [11] (Table S1-2). Measurement of indicators of Frailty Index (FI) Frailty is increasingly recognized as a meaningful concept in pediatric populations, transcending mere physical vulnerability to encompass psychosocial and developmental dimensions. This broader understanding now informs clinical approaches for children with chronic conditions, disabilities, or complex healthcare requirements [21–23]. 49 health questions covering multiple systems make up the Frailty Index. These include one question about cognition, 15 questions about daily living activities, seven questions about mental health and depressive symptoms based on the patient’s health questionnaire-9 questionnaire [24], 13 questions about chronic diseases, 5 questions about self-rated health, two anthropometric indicators, and six laboratory measurements (Table S2). On a scale of 0–1, each of these health issues has a score. According to Blodgett et al. [25], the information gathered from individuals who answered 30 or more items in a thorough health evaluation is considered enough to Fig. 1 Flow chart of sample selection from the NHANES 2001–2004

The ratio of the total number of health issues to the sum of the scores for those problems is the frailty score. Participants with greater frailty scores had a worse prognosis. Drawing on prior research, we established the cut-off point for the Frailty Index at 0.25. The FI was constructed following the established deficit-accumulation approach to serve as a composite indicator of overall health burden, consistent with its growing application in pediatric health research. Individuals with an FI score below 0.1 were classified as nonfrailty, those with an FI score between 0.1 and 0.25 were categorized as pre-frailty, and those with an FI score of 0.25 or higher were classified as frailty [26]. Assessment of other variables To gather information on demographics, lifestyle, selfreported health status, anthropometric measures, and biochemical markers, the CDC used a computer-assisted personal interview (CAPI) system. Demographic factors in this research were health insurance status, age, sex, and race/ethnicity. The socioeconomic situation of participants was represented by the poverty income ratio (PIR), which was the ratio of family income to the poverty criteria suitable for household size. Categories for the PIR were < 1.00, 1.00–1.84, 1.85–3.00, and > 3.00 [27]. Aggregate Index of Systemic Inflammation (AISI) [28] = (Platelet count × Neutrophil count × Monocyte count)/Lymphocyte count. A self-reported history of hypertension, self-reported use of antihypertensive drugs, or an average systolic or diastolic blood pressure that is higher than the 90th percentile for age, sex, and height were all considered indicators of elevated blood pressure (EBP). EBP was taken into consideration for children 13 years of age and older if their systolic or diastolic blood pressures were more than 120 mmHg or 80 mmHg, respectively [29]. Platelet count, neutrophil count, and lymphocyte count are combined to create the Systemic immunological-Inflammation Index (SII), an indication obtained from standard blood testing that evaluates the body’s inflammatory and immunological condition. The following is the calculating formula: SII is equal to (neutrophil count × platelet count)/lymphocyte count [30]. Mendelian randomization Data sources MR analyses utilized publicly accessible genetic data. The GWAS summary statistics for food liking were derived from a cohort of 161,625 UK Biobank participants. Participants rated their preference for individual food items on a 9-point Likert scale ranging from "Extremely dislike" to "Extremely like." These preferences were further grouped into three categories: "Highly-palatable," "Acquired," and "Low-caloric" [31]. The data were collected via questionnaire, with full details available at: https://​bioba​nk.​ndph.​ox.​ac.​uk/​showc​ase/​showc​ase/​docs/​ foodp​ref.​pdf. Basic characteristics of the 187 dietary factors included as exposures or outcomes in the Mendelian randomization analysis are provided in Table S10. ADHD GWAS data were obtained from the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium (https://​pgc.​unc.​edu/), wherein cases comprised individuals diagnosed by psychiatrists using ICD-10 criteria (F90.0, F90.1, F98.8) or those receiving pharmacotherapy for ADHD symptoms [32]. Instrumental variable (IV) selection Independent single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) serving as IVs for the food preferences were selected. Genome-wide significant SNPs (p < 5 × 10−8) were clumped for linkage disequilibrium (LD) using a reference panel (r2 threshold < 0.001 within 1 Mb genomic windows). Two-sample MR analyses were subsequently conducted using these IVs and the ADHD GWAS summary statistics. For each of food preferences, SNPs serving as genetic instruments were rigorously screened. To ensure the robustness of genetic instruments, we excluded palindromic SNPs (i.e., those with A/T or G/C alleles) from the analysis to avoid potential strand ambiguity and misalignment between exposure and outcome datasets. Additionally, we aligned all SNPs to the forward strand based on the reference genome prior to harmonization. Statistical analysis Cross‐sectional study Sample weights were used in all analyses because of the NHANES’ intricate survey methodology. We utilized combined data from NHANES 2001–2004, applying the 4-year interview weight (WTINT4YR) for overall analyses. For analyses involving dietary data (e.g., DII calculation), the average of two-day dietary recall weights ([WTDRD1 + WTDRD2]/2) was used to improve accuracy in estimating dietary exposures and outcomes. In R (v4.4.0), the survey package (v4.4–0) was employed to define the survey design, specifying: strata = SDMVSTRA, primary sampling units (PSUs) = SDMVPSU, and weights = WTINT4YR (overall analysis) or the average dietary weight (diet-related analysis). All regression models, including weighted logistic regression and restricted cubic spline (RCS) models, were fitted using the svyglm() function to ensure parameter estimation and hypothesis testing accounted for the complex survey design. In RCS analyses, svyglm() combined with rms::rcs() was used, with knot locations determined based on the weighted data distribution to ensure the spline fitting also

Continuous variables were described using the median and interquartile range (IQR), while categorical variables were represented using the unweighted frequency and weighted percentage. DII scores were divided into interquartiles for analytical reasons (T1: < 0.92, T2: 0.92–2.16, T3: 2.16–3.11, T4: > 3.11). With higher DII scores suggesting a larger inflammatory potential of the diet, the highest quartile (T4) reflects the most pro-inflammatory diet. On the other hand, the lowest quartile (T1), which has lower DII values, indicates a stronger anti-inflammatory diet. The Kruskal– Wallis H test or weighted chi-square was employed to ascertain differences between groups. Weighted logistic regression models were used to examine the relationship between DII scores and ADHD. For each DII score, odds ratios (ORs) and 95% CIs were calculated, using the lowest quartile as the reference. Using a restricted cubic spline (RCS), the likely non-linear relationship between ADHD and DII was shown. A total of three models were employed throughout the analysis. Model 2 adjusts for age, sex, race/ethnicity, household reference person’s education level. Model 3 continues to adjust health insurance and PIR. Additionally, we conducted subgroup analyses and tested for interaction effects among the subgroup results (These analyses are interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating, since they report subgroup-specific p-values without multiple-testing correction). To explore the potential non-linear relationship between DII and ADHD, we fitted restricted cubic splines (RCS). The knots were placed at the following percentiles of the DII distribution: the 5th (−1.30), 35th (1.46), 65th (2.72), and 95th (3.92) percentiles, resulting in 3 degrees of freedom. The model formula was: logit (ADHD) = rcs(DII, 3) + covariates. The median DII value (2.16) was used as the reference for the unadjusted model. For the multivariable-adjusted model (adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, household reference person’s education level, PIR, and health insurance status), the median DII value (2.15) was used as the reference. All RCS analyses incorporated the NHANES complex survey weights to ensure the representativeness of the estimates for the US child and adolescent population. To further quantify the inflection point of the non-linear association, we performed a piecewise linear regression analysis to identify a potential threshold effect. Using the segmented package in R, the breakpoint was identified through an iterative process that maximizes the model’s likelihood function. The optimal breakpoint was identified at approximately DII 2.9. We then used a likelihood ratio test (LRT) to compare the goodness-of-fit between the two-piecewise linear model (with the breakpoint) and the simple linear model. The LRT chi-square statistic indicated that the two-piecewise model provided a significantly better fit to the data than the linear model (P = 0.001), confirming the presence of a threshold effect. To explore the potential mediating role of the FI in the association between the Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII) and ADHD, we conducted a mediation analysis. The analysis was based on the counterfactual framework and proceeded in three steps: (1) fitting a linear regression model (svyglm with family = "gaussian") of DII on the mediator (FI); (2) fitting a logistic regression model (svyglm with family = "quasibinomial") of DII on the outcome (ADHD); and (3) fitting a logistic regression model of both DII and FI on ADHD. Formal mediation analysis was performed using the mediation package in R. To quantify the uncertainty of the mediation effect, we computed 95% confidence intervals (CIs) using the QuasiBayesian method based on 50 simulations. We first tested for the potential exposure-mediator interaction (DII × FI) by including an interaction term in the outcome model; as it was not statistically significant (P > 0.05), it was omitted from the final model. The proportion mediated (PM) and its 95% CI were estimated accordingly. For variables with missing values, the zstats platform (www.​zstats.​net) performs multiple imputation with 5 imputations (m = 5), using predictive mean matching (PMM) for continuous variables and logistic regression imputation for categorical variables. All variables included in the analytical model are automatically incorporated into the imputation model. The imputation process convergence is ensured by the platform’s internal algorithms, and the final results are pooled following Rubin’s rules. All analyses were conducted bilaterally, with the statistical significance level for alpha established at 0.05. Data processing and analysis were conducted using R version 4.4.0 (2024–04–24) and Zstats 1.0 (www.​ zstats.​net). Mendelian randomization MR leverages genetic variants as instrumental variables to infer causal relationships between exposures (food preferences) and outcomes (ADHD), contingent upon satisfying three core assumptions. We employed inversevariance weighted (MR-IVW) analysis with a randomeffects model as the primary analytical method to derive causal estimates for each exposure, which combines Wald ratio estimates from individual SNPs through meta-analysis. Comprehensive sensitivity analyses were conducted to validate MR assumptions, including MR-Egger regression (assessing directional pleiotropy), weighted median estimation (providing robustness against invalid instruments), and heterogeneity testing via Cochran’s Q statistic. Crucially, the UK Biobank sample was explicitly excluded from this ADHD GWAS meta-analysis [31].

Results Cross‐sectional study Features of the research population A total of 6481 participants were included in this study, of whom 488 had ADHD, accounting for 7.53%, and 5993 were non-ADHD participants, accounting for 92.47%. Significant differences were observed between the two groups in terms of age, sex, race/ethnicity, SII, segmented neutrophil count, white blood cell count, AISI, Frailty Index, EBP, health insurance status, and DII levels (P < 0.05). No significant variations were seen in the education level of the household reference person and the PIR (P > 0.05). It is apparent that, in comparison to non-ADHD participants, those with ADHD were more often male, Non-Hispanic White, and had health insurance. Moreover, the higher Frailty Index values among ADHD participants may indicate a greater accumulation of health deficits or a higher risk of health issues, such as metabolic syndrome, functional impairments, developmental problems, and psychological and behavioral health concerns (Table 1). It is noteworthy that the significant negative correlations between ADHD and several indices closely related to inflammation and immune system activation—DII, SII, segmented neutrophil count, white blood cell count, and AISI, which further highlight the potential link between ADHD and systemic inflammation or immune dysregulation. Association between DII and ADHD We conducted a multivariate logistic regression analysis to examine the association between DII and ADHD. In the unadjusted model, the DII exhibited a significant inverse association with ADHD, such that each oneunit increment in DII corresponded to an 11% reduction in the odds of ADHD (OR = 0.89; 95% CI 0.82–0.96; P = 0.008). Subsequently, in Model 2 and Model 3, after adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, health insurance status, PIR and household reference person’s education level, the relationship between DII and ADHD remained significant and negatively associated (OR = 0.91; 95%CI 0.82–0.99; P < 0.05) (Table 2). When DII was stratified into quartiles (T1–T4) for analysis, we constructed three weighted logistic regression models to examine the association between DII and ADHD. The Model 1 (T3) and Model 2 (T3) demonstrated statistically significant associations between DII and ADHD (P < 0.05) (Table S3). Figure 2 RCS demonstrates a U-shaped association between the DII and ADHD, providing empirical evidence for this nonlinear relationship (P for nonlinearity < 0.01). We consequently employed a piecewise logistic regression model to quantify the DII-ADHD association. Threshold effect analysis using a two-segment logistic regression model (Table 3) identified an optimal DII inflection point at approximately 2.9 (loglikelihood ratio test P = 0.001, confirming superior model fit compared to linear regression). Below this threshold, each unit increase in DII was associated with a 13% reduction in ADHD risk (OR = 0.87, 95% CI 0.81–0.94). Conversely, above the inflection point, each DII unit increment corresponded to a significant 161% elevation in ADHD prevalence (OR = 1.61, 95% CI 1.03–2.54), revealing differentiated dose–response patterns across DII ranges. Subgroup analysis Subgroup analyses were performed to explore potential effect modification. Importantly, all interaction terms were non-significant (interaction P-value > 0.05; Fig. 3), indicating no statistically robust evidence that the association between DII and ADHD differed across the subgroups examined. However, within specific strata, exploratory observations showed nominally significant negative correlations (P < 0.05) in participants with/ without health insurance, among Other Hispanic individuals, and in those with low neutrophil counts, low SII/ AISI scores, or pre-frailty/frailty status, both before and after adjusting for age, household education, and PIR (Table S4). Given the lack of significant interaction, these stratum-specific observations should be interpreted with caution and considered hypothesis-generating for future research, rather than as evidence of true subgroup differences. Our observations indicated that the Frailty Index serves a partial mediating function between DII and ADHD in the analysis. The mediation model and the pathways are depicted in Fig. 4. The study results demonstrate a significant correlation between DII and the Frailty Index (β = 0.002, P = 0.01), as well as a significant positive correlation between the Frailty Index and ADHD (β = 2.88, P < 0.001). MR-PRESSO detected no outliers (P > 0.05), and Steiger directionality tests supported the correct causal direction (P < 0.05). Heterogeneity was low (Cochran’s Q P > 0.05). Instrument strength was sufficient across analyses (F-statistics 41–604), minimizing weak instrument bias. Together, these results support the robustness of the causal inferences (Table S6-7). To investigate whether ADHD might influence the association between DII and ADHD observed in the cross-sectional study by altering dietary preferences, we further performed reverse two-sample MR analyses using ADHD as the exposure and 187 food preferences as outcomes. Our analysis revealed that genetic predisposition to ADHD significantly altered 37 food preferences (FDR < 0.05). Delving into the pattern uncovered an intriguing phenomenon: ADHD was associated with a generalized reduction in liking for a wide range of foods (accounting for 81.08% of the significant associations). Specifically, ADHD was associated with an increased liking for the following 8 food items or derived factors: BBQ/grilled meat, cherry, F-savour/caloric food liking, apple juice, F-seafood liking, sardines, aubergine, and salty pretzels. Discussion This study reports for the first time, using NHANES data, a U-shaped association between DII and ADHD risk: When DII < 2.9, an increase in DII was associated with a reduced ADHD risk (OR = 0.87); whereas when DII ≥ 2.9, each 1-unit increase in DII significantly elevated ADHD risk by 61% (OR = 1.61). This nonlinear pattern suggests that both extremely anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory diets may be associated with ADHD risk, implying that the inflammatory potential of diet, at both extremes, might be a relevant factor to consider in future investigations into ADHD etiology. This U-shaped association remained significant after adjusting for all covariates (sex, race/ethnicity, education, PIR, age, health insurance) (P for nonlinearity = 0.01, log-likelihood ratio test P = 0.001), with an inflection point at approximately 2.9 (Fig. 2). Notably, analysis using DII quartile groups (T1–T4), which imposes linearity, likely diluted the nonlinear trend when adjusting for all covariates, resulting in no significant differences between groups; the Cochran-Armitage trend test further confirmed a nonlinear change in ADHD risk across DII quartiles (trend test P = 0.139) (Table S3). RCS analysis is capable of characterizing the true relationship between exposure and outcome without presuming a predefined functional form. Therefore, our key finding—that a diet with moderate inflammatory potential is associated with the lowest risk of ADHD, whereas both extreme anti-inflammatory and pro-inflammatory diets may increase the risk—is primarily informed by the results of the RCS analysis. This observation underscores the importance of employing nonlinear modeling approaches when investigating complex exposures such as diet. Research on dietary patterns and ADHD has grown substantially in recent years [16, 33]. As a key environmental factor, diet may influence ADHD onset and development through multiple mechanisms [34, 35]. Inflammation is a feature in some, but not all, ADHD patients and may be influenced by ADHD medication and lifestyle factors including diet, smoking, and stress [7]. To elucidate potential causal links between dietary liking and ADHD, we performed MR analyses on 187 dietary likings. Results revealed that a genetic predisposition for fruit liking significantly lowered ADHD risk (OR = 0.659, 95%CI 0.521–0.833, P = 5.007 × 10−4). Studies report that fruits are rich in antioxidants (e.g., flavonoids, vitamin C) and fiber. Deficiencies in vitamins B, C, and E may increase vulnerability to oxidative stress abnormalities, as these antioxidants protect neuronal cell membranes from free radical damage [36]. Dietary fiber promotes probiotic proliferation, while pectin in fruits can bind neurotoxic heavy metals like lead and cadmium. Conversely, preferences for red meat (e.g., Lamb: OR = 1.408, 95%CI 1.157–1.714, P = 6.467 × 10−4) and condiments (e.g., Onion: OR = 1.345, 95%CI 1.128–1.605, P = 9.753 × 10−4) significantly increased ADHD risk. Diets high in red meat, processed foods, and refined carbohydrates are associated with elevated plasma inflammatory markers [37]. Red meat consumption (especially lamb, beef) is linked to risks of various psychiatric disorders (e.g., depression, schizophrenia) [38], potentially related to high levels of trans-unsaturated fatty acids in red meat. High saturated fat intake is also closely associated with reduced BDNF [39]. However, in multivariable MR analyses adjusting for correlated dietary traits, the association for lamb liking was attenuated and became non-significant, suggesting that its effect may be confounded by other dietary factors (such as a Western dietary pattern or processed food intake). This highlights the complexity of dietary exposures and the necessity of accounting for the co-varying structure of diet in causal inference. Studies show a significant association between a Western dietary pattern (high in takeaway foods, fast food, and red meat) and elevated CBCL scores in children, reflecting both internalizing and externalizing behaviors. In contrast, a healthy dietary pattern featuring nuts and low-energy-dense foods is associated with improved behavioral scores [40]. The association between genetically predicted cheesecake liking and lower ADHD risk was unexpected and contrasts with most observational data. This finding requires replication and should be interpreted with extreme caution; it may reflect unmeasured confounding or shared genetic influences rather than a protective effect of cheesecake per se. Recent MR studies suggest causal associations between seven inflammatory cytokines (CD40, IL-18, MMP10, bNGF, MCSF, FGF19, AXIN1) and ADHD. For instance, mast cells may induce neuronal damage via CD40, while Roseburia spp. increase ADHD risk indirectly by elevating MCSF (mediation effect 3.7%) [4, 41]. Diet can induce functional changes beyond the gastrointestinal tract (including the brain) by modulating interactions between microbiota and local immune cells, altering cytokine release into systemic circulation, or regulating immune cell distribution [42]. Dietary preferences can modulate gut microbiota, transmitting inflammatory signals to the brain via the vagus nerve. Imbalances from antibiotics, poor diet, or other factors can lead to dysbiosis, elevating levels of cytokines like TNF, IL-6, and IFN-β, causing inflammation that increases intestinal permeability

Page 13 of 17 Hu et al. European Journal of Medical Research (2026) 31:7 ("leaky gut" syndrome) [43, 44]. These findings suggest dietary changes may impact ADHD risk, but this effect is likely modulated by multiple factors, including genetic background, lifestyle, and environmental factors. Future research will involve deeper mechanistic studies, such as using neuroimaging (e.g., PET scans) to detect CNS inflammatory marker expression or analyzing cerebrospinal fluid samples to directly measure CNS inflammatory markers. Additionally, animal models can simulate dietinduced inflammation effects on the CNS, with histological and molecular biology methods used to observe CNS inflammation changes, further validating the impact of diet and CNS inflammation on ADHD risk. Mediation analysis indicated that the Frailty Index may partially mediate the association between the DII and ADHD, accounting for 5.49% of the total effect. Nevertheless, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inferences or delineation of temporal precedence; consequently, these findings should be regarded as a preliminary hypothesis to be tested in future longitudinal investigations. Moreover, although the Frailty Index was constructed with a standardized protocol, its interpretation in a predominantly healthy pediatric cohort warrants caution, and subsequent studies should validate this metric against long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes [23, 25]. Although the 5.49% effect size is statistically significant, suggesting FI is a potential pathway, other unmeasured mechanisms (e.g., neuroinflammation, gutbrain axis regulation) likely play important roles [4, 45]. To validate this pathway, future studies should employ prospective cohorts to track temporal changes in DII, FI, and ADHD symptoms; use animal models to investigate molecular mechanisms of DII regulating FI (e.g., effects of inflammatory cytokines IL-6/TNF-α on neurodevelopment); and integrate multi-omics technologies (epigenetic/metabolomic) to dissect the DII-FI-ADHD biological pathway. Baseline analysis showed children with ADHD had significantly lower levels of inflammatory markers including white blood cells, neutrophils, AISI, and SII (P < 0.05). At first glance, lower levels seem counter to a simple proinflammatory hypothesis. However, existing literature on inflammatory markers in ADHD is inconsistent [46, 47], suggesting immune dysregulation may not manifest as uniform elevation across all markers or individuals. Our finding of an association between lower DII scores and ADHD diagnosis in baseline comparisons can be understood in this context of complexity. This phenomenon may partly stem from limitations of linear modeling. RCS analysis revealed a significant U-shaped association (P for nonlinearity < 0.01): the negative association at the low DII end (DII < 2.9) and the positive association at the high DII end (DII ≥ 2.9) together form the complete nonlinear pattern. This negative association might also reflect ADHD-diagnosed children adhering to higher quality diets. Furthermore, using the average of two 24-h recalls for DII calculation introduces potential bias due to representativeness issues of transient diet. Residual confounding (e.g., family dietary environment, exercise habits) may persist despite adjusting for multiple covariates. We also evaluated the possibility of reverse causation—where an ADHD diagnosis might influence dietary behavior—using reverse MR analysis. The results indicated that genetic predisposition to ADHD was significantly associated with alterations in 37 food preferences, manifesting as a generalized reduction in preference for both pro-inflammatory foods (e.g., lamb, sausages) and anti-inflammatory foods (e.g., fruit, avocado). This pattern suggests that genetic liability to ADHD may influence appetite or food preferences through biological pathways (e.g., reward system dysfunction). The causal effect of ADHD genetic liability on food preferences, as suggested by reverse MR, provides a plausible biological mechanism that could partly explain the observed cross-sectional association between ADHD diagnosis and lower DII scores. However, this does not preclude other interpretations. Interestingly, this finding parallels a birth cohort study [48] which found higher maternal DII was associated with significantly reduced risks of inattention (OR = 0.86; 95% CI = 0.77–0.96), hyperactivity (OR = 0.82; 95% CI = 0.72–0.92), and overall ADHD risk (OR = 0.82; 95% CI = 0.72–0.93) in boys, suggesting a sex-specific negative association. However, other studies found prenatal pro-inflammatory diets (e.g., Western pattern) significantly increased offspring ADHD risk: three large mother–child cohorts confirmed associations with ADHD/autism, and metabolomic analysis identified 15 mediating metabolites during pregnancy that improved ADHD prediction [49]. Researchers also found that higher prenatal unhealthy diet scores were associated with methylation of the insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2) gene at birth in children diagnosed with ADHD or conduct disorder. They concluded that higher IGF2 methylation predicted ADHD symptoms and suggested preventing unhealthy diets during pregnancy could reduce childhood ADHD prevalence [50]. While reports of U-shaped associations between extremely low maternal DII and offspring ADHD are scarce, substantial evidence indicates that severe deficiencies of key nutrients during pregnancy (e.g., iron, iodine, folate, vitamin D, Omega-3 DHA) significantly increase risks of neurodevelopmental delays and cognitive/behavioral problems (including ADHD-like symptoms) [51]. Extreme restrictive diets causing nutritional inadequacy can alter maternal immunity, milk, and serum metabolomic profiles, and induce widespread changes in fetal brain transcriptomics

Page 14 of 17 Hu et al. European Journal of Medical Research (2026) 31:7 and metabolomics, including subsets of microbiomedependent metabolites. Such diets are recognized as potentially increasing adverse pregnancy outcomes, and their long-term effects on offspring neurodevelopment warrant attention [51]. This highlights the need for balanced and adequate prenatal nutrition: avoiding highly pro-inflammatory diets while ensuring all essential nutrients are obtained for fetal neurodevelopment. Future research should explore the dose–response relationship between prenatal DII and offspring neurodevelopment more meticulously, particularly investigating whether risks increase at the low DII end due to nutritional insufficiency. Furthermore, baseline analysis showed elevated blood pressure was significantly positively associated with ADHD, potentially linked to ADHD medication use and increased cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk [52]. Although most studies have relatively short follow-up periods, limiting assessment of long-term associations, some suggest no direct link, or a time-varying link, between ADHD and elevated blood pressure in children and adolescents [53]. Notably, the U-shaped relationship (Fig. 2) might underlie the lack of significance in some subgroup analyses. ADHD risk increases at both extremely low DII (strong anti-inflammatory) and high DII (strong pro-inflammatory) values. In subgroups like race/insurance, differences in the range of DII distribution may mask the nonlinear effect of the continuous variable. For instance, the median DII (2.218) in the "Other Hispanic" group is closer to the U-curve trough (inflection point ≈ 2.9), making the protective association easier to detect. Regarding healthcare access, children with ADHD were more likely to have health insurance. However, the negative association between DII and ADHD remained significant after adjusting for insurance status, and subgroup analyses showed consistent effects in both insured and uninsured groups (interaction P > 0.05), indicating that this association is unlikely to be entirely driven by differences in healthcare accessibility. Nevertheless, residual confounding (e.g., by family health awareness) cannot be fully ruled out. This study has several notable strengths. First, all participants were directly sourced from the NHANES database, greatly enhancing sample representativeness and the generalizability of our conclusions. Second, we adhered to NHANES analysis standards, performing all analyses using appropriate sampling weights. Employing a stratified multistage probability sampling design, our results are generalizable to the US national population of children and adolescents. Third, while DII associations with other disorders exist, this is the first study to report a U-shaped association between DII and adolescent ADHD (inflection point ≈ 2.9). However, limitations must be acknowledged. First, the cross-sectional design precludes establishing a causal relationship between DII and ADHD risk. Second, all dietary information was self-reported (based on the average of two 24-h recalls), potentially introducing reporting bias, and the lack of long-term dietary data limits our ability to capture habitual dietary patterns. Differences in medical accessibility may introduce selection bias. Third, despite controlling for confounders via multivariable adjustment and sensitivity analyses, residual confounding (e.g., family dietary environment, exercise habits) may persist. Fourth, the inflammatory markers measured (e.g., WBC, neutrophils, AISI) reflect peripheral inflammation and cannot be directly equated to central nervous system (CNS) inflammation; future studies require validation via CSF analysis or neuroimaging (e.g., PET). Fifth, as NHANES primarily reflects the US population, subgroups with unique dietary patterns or health issues may be underrepresented, potentially limiting the generalizability of our findings to more diverse or international populations. Sixth, the use of a non-energy-adjusted DII, while consistent with the original index design and facilitating comparison with much of the literature, may introduce some confounding when comparing individuals with substantially different total energy intakes. Future studies could consider using the energy-adjusted DII (E-DII) to further verify the robustness of these findings. Furthermore, this analysis reveals a causal association between genetically predisposed "liking tendencies" and ADHD risk. This relationship may be partially mediated by actual dietary behaviors but could also reflect shared neurobiological pathways, such as those involving the reward system. Therefore, the results should be interpreted with caution. Their primary value lies in providing genetic-level support for a causal link between diet and ADHD, generating hypotheses for further investigation. To address these limitations and rigorously test the hypothesis that ’moderate dietary interventions may help prevent ADHD’, we propose a multi-level research agenda. First, there is a need to establish large-scale prospective birth cohorts with repeated dietary assessments from pregnancy through adolescence to confirm the U-shaped relationship and delineate critical exposure windows. Second, the ’gold standard’ for establishing causality would be randomized controlled trials evaluating the efficacy of anti-inflammatory dietary patterns (e.g., a modified Mediterranean diet) in preventing ADHD onset or mitigating its symptom severity, particularly in highrisk populations. Finally, future research should integrate multi-omics approaches—including detailed measurements of inflammatory biomarkers, gut microbiota, and neuroimaging—to elucidate the precise biological mechanisms underpinning the DII-ADHD association, such as

Such mechanistic insights are crucial for developing targeted and effective nutritional strategies for ADHD prevention and management. Furthermore, although our mediation analysis indicates that the FI partially mediates the association between the DII and ADHD, it is important to note that the FI is a multidimensional construct encompassing cognitive, physical, psychological, and metabolic domains, comprising a total of 49 health deficits. Our analysis did not evaluate which specific components of frailty—such as impaired cognitive function, depressive symptoms, or limitations in daily activities—exhibit the strongest association with ADHD risk. Future studies with larger sample sizes and longitudinal designs could develop mediation models based on specific deficit clusters or distinct dimensional pathways to identify the most critical mechanistic routes—for instance, neurocognitive deficits or immunometabolic dysregulation—through which diet-related inflammation may influence the development of ADHD. Such findings would help inform more targeted interventions for at-risk pediatric populations. Additionally, the generalisability of adult-derived genetic variants underlying food preferences to paediatric populations and to diverse dietary-cultural contexts—particularly the United States—remains equivocal, as large-scale genome-wide association studies of food preferences have yet to be conducted in children. Although the present study employed the best-available data, future investigations leveraging child-specific genetic repositories are imperative to corroborate the putative causal pathways. Conclusion In US children and adolescents, we observed a U-shaped association (inflection point ≈ 2.9) between the DII and ADHD risk: moderate DII is protective, while extremely low or high DII may increase risk. The Frailty Index may partially mediate (5.49%) the association between DII and ADHD. Fruit liking lowered ADHD risk, while red meat/ onion liking increased risk. However, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. Future research should validate the preventive potential of dietary interventions through birth cohorts or randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Contributions to the literature First large-scale evidence: This is the first nationally representative study (using NHANES data) to investigate the relationship between DII and ADHD diagnosis in US children and adolescents; Reveals complex relationship: It uncovers a novel U-shaped association between DII and ADHD risk, indicating that both highly anti-inflammatory and highly pro-inflammatory diets are linked to increased ADHD probability, challenging simple linear assumptions; Identifies a new pathway: The study provides initial evidence that the Frailty Index (a measure of accumulated health deficits) partly explains (mediates) the link between dietary inflammation and ADHD, suggesting a potential biological mechanism; The findings from the MR analysis revealed that fruit liking is significantly linked to a reduced risk of ADHD. Conversely, a liking for red meat, such as lamb, as well as a fondness for flavorings like onions, is significantly associated with an increased risk of ADHD. ADHD was associated with a generalized reduction in liking for a wide range of foods (accounting for 81.08% of the significant associations). Informs prevention: These findings highlight the potential importance of moderate dietary interventions targeting inflammation for ADHD prevention strategies in children. Mudasser Shah mudasser.shah35@gmail.com Fatimah Sayer Alharbi fsaalharbi@pnu.edu.sa 1Institute of Developmental Psychology, Beijing Normal University, Beijing, China 2Self-Development Skills Department of Common First Year Deanship, King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia 3Department of Health Sciences, College of Health and Rehabilitation Sciences, Princess Nourah Bint Abdulrahman University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia Abstract Background Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) often coexists with Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD), exacerbating impairment. The distinct neurological and biological patterns that differentiate this comorbidity from ADHD alone remain unclear. Method We conducted systematic review of multi model correlates differentiating ODD+ADHD from ADHD alone following PRISMA 2020 with databases like MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO and Web of Sciences until August 2025. 144 full texts were reviewed and 26 studies were selected for final inclusion after 1457 records with 37 other sources. Designs included cross-sectional case-control studies, longitudinal studies, and imaging based on the ABCD framework, while measures covered structural and functional MRI, diffusion MRI, resting and task fNIRS, EEG and ERP, HPA-axis and immune-metabolic biomarkers, and executive and cognitive indices. The evaluation of bias employed RoB 2, ROBINS-I, and JBI, while synthesis utilised Braun-Clarke thematic analysis. Results Oppositionality involved limbic–striatal and cerebello-cortical differences, with ODD+ADHD showing greater executive and emotion-processing deficits than ADHD alone. ODD was linked to lower cortisol and reduced sympathetic reactivity, while ADHD showed higher cortisol and tryptophan–kynurenine shifts, with cytokines decreasing after methylphenidate. Conclusion ODD along with ADHD showed a distinct neurobiological and physiological pattern from ADHD alone. Such pattern is marked by greater executive and emotional regulation deficits with unique stress-response patterns, highlighting the need for tailored assessments and intervention approaches. BMC Psychology (2026) 14:882 Introduction Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) fre quently coexists with Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD) in children and adolescents. Approximately 60% of individuals with ADHD were concurrently diagnosed with ODD [1]. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) delineates ADHD as marked by inattention and/or hyperactivity/impulsivity, while ODD is characterized by irritable and angry disposi tions alongside defiant and disobedient behaviors. The presence of comorbid ODD in individuals with ADHD is associated with increased functional impairment and a poorer long-term prognosis [2–5]. Contemporary nosol ogy defines ODD by a persistent angry or irritable mood, argumentative or defiant behavior, and vindictiveness lasting for a minimum of six months. This phenotype overlaps with, yet is not limited to, conduct disorder and often complicates ADHD presentations [6, 7]. It has been widely reported that ODD is associated with increased emotional lability and delinquency in children with ADHD [4, 8]. Cognitive inhibition and visuospatial episodic memory are associated with ADHD-symptoms, whereas cognitive flexibility is related to ODD-symptoms [9]. Neuroimaging studies demonstrate structural and functional brain changes in ADHD and ODD [10, 11]. ADHD with ODD reveals cortical thickening [12], cere bellum [13], and volume decreases in multiple brain areas [14]. Lower FA in left lateral frontotemporal white matter is associated with antisocial behavior [15], although the results are inconsistent [16], suggesting neural correlates of irritable and aggressive behaviors. The accumulation of multimodal evidence suggests dysfunctions in fronto-striatal and fronto-limbic circuits across the spectra of disruptive behavior and ADHD. However, it remains uncertain whether children with ODD+ADHD exhibit additive, synergistic, or distinct neural signatures compared to “pure” ADHD or ODD/ CD groups—an essential gap this review aims to address [17–19]. Large-scale consortia analyses yield substantial findings: an ENIGMA-ASB coordinated analysis encom passing 15 cohorts revealed significant reductions in cor tical surface area and alterations in subcortical structures among youth with conduct disorder, highlighting effects relevant to externalizing liability in the context of ODD comorbidity [17]. In contrast, ENIGMA-ADHD identi fied diminished volumes in the amygdala, accumbens, and hippocampus, indicative of delayed subcortical maturation unaccounted for by medication [18]. Work at the network level adds to these regional findings: Dys connectivity in the default mode network (DMN) and interference with task-positive systems are consistently observed in ADHD, likely contributing to executive con trol failures and social dysfunction, which may be exacer bated in individuals with both ODD and ADHD [20–22]. Meta-analytic task-fMRI evidence demonstrates that emotion-regulation demands recruit amygdala–pre frontal coupling and that irritability, a central feature of ODD, is associated with disrupted amygdala con nectivity with regulatory prefrontal regions implicat ing a “hot EF” mechanism that is likely to exacerbate ADHD-related “cool EF” deficits [23–25]. Based on metaanalyses of inhibitory control, the deficiency in ODD/ CD was partially ADHD-related and thus emphasiz ing comorbidity-stratified designs [19]. Stress-immune markers suggest decreased baseline levels and morning cortisol and abnormalities in cytokines among pediatric ADHD, being influenced by externalizing characteristics and adversity availabilities prevalent in ODD [26–28]. Early MRS and EEG results indicate the neurochemis try of DMN-node and abnormal indices associated with ADHD, thus there is a need for ODD+ADHD specific ity (Vidor et al. 2024). Data from genomic and cohort studies indicate that co-occurrence of ODD results from increased polygenic load for externalizing behavior and gene–environment interaction [29–31]. Despite these advances, the literature seldom empha sizes ODD+ADHD as a primary analytical focus; numer ous reviews conflate ODD with conduct disorder or examine ADHD without distinguishing ODD, thereby limiting mechanistic specificity and minimizing whether the identified neural, stress-axis, or immune signals are specific to comorbidity, additive, or influenced by symp tom dimensions [1, 26, 32]. Furthermore, variability in tasks, preprocessing, comorbidity management, and covariate control, coupled with insufficient consider ation of development, sex, medication, and adversity, compromises the comparability and generalizability of studies [32–34]. Dimensional research indicates that the irritable and defiant/vindictive aspects of ODD demon strate distinct correlations with internalizing and exter nalizing trajectories, implying that comorbidity-specific biomarkers may align with symptom dimensions rather than syndromic classifications [35–37]. Developmental and familial-context studies reveal bi-directional coer cive cycles between parents and children, likely affecting stress-related immune physiology and neural regulatory systems. This highlights the need to incorporate multi level moderators in ODD+ADHD analyses [38, 39]. These gaps necessitate a systematic review focused on children and adolescents with ODD comorbid with ADHD, incor porating multimodal MRI (structural, task-based, and resting-state connectivity), electrophysiology, HPA-axis assessments, inflammatory biomarkers, and genetic find ings. It makes a clear distinction between ODD+ADHD and groups with only ADHD or ODD/CD. It also looks at moderators (age, sex, medication, adversity) and dimen sional mappings (irritability vs. defiance; cool vs. hot EF) to move away from the idea of comorbidity and toward
