Although ADHD has undergone many behavioral and cognitive studies, relatively fewer studies have addressed the neurobiological differences of comorbid ODD. This research gap is of significance since ODD is commonly co-occurring with an ADHD affecting 30–60% of chil dren diagnosed with ADHD. Their combine association is linked to higher functional impairment, poorer psycho social outcomes and enhanced risk of antisocial behavior compared with an ADHD alone [41–43]. Neurobiologi cal studies suggest that the main features of ADHD are dysfunctions in fronto-striatal and fronto-cerebellar neural circuits, which are responsible for executive func tioning, attention regulation, and inhibitory control [44, 45]. In contrast, disruptive behavior disorders like ODD and CD have been associated with abnormalities in emo tios’ processing and regulation, especially those involv ing the amygdala and prefrontal cortex [1, 46]. However, relatively few studies have compared directly the neural mechanisms underlying an individual with an ADD alone and ADD with comorbid ODD. Understanding these dis tinctions is important because the presence of ODD has important and significant implications for developmen tal trajectories and treatment response in ADHD among these populations [47]. The objective is to identify neurological and biologi cal correlates that are shared, unique, or synergistic in ODD+ADHD compared to single-diagnosis counter parts, while assessing their developmental and contextual influence. The goals are fourfold: to describe structural, functional, and network-level brain changes that set ODD+ADHD apart from ADHD-only, ODD/CD-only, and typically developing groups; to combine electrophys iological and stress-immune biomarkers in ODD+ADHD and measure moderators like age, sex, adversity, and medication; to look at how irritability and defiance map onto certain neural circuits (like amygdala–mPFC coupling and DMN–frontoparietal interactions) and stress-immune indices; and to suggest methodological standards for future research (like comorbidity-stratified analyses, harmonized tasks and preprocessing, and pre registration) that can help clarify mechanistic inference and lead to targeted, mechanism-informed interven tions like emotion-regulation training and stress-axis or inflammation-modulating adjuncts. Methodology Design and reporting framework This systematic literature review (SLR) was planned and documented in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guide lines [48]. A PICO framework organized the inquiry, eli gibility standards, and data documentation [49]. Due to the variability in designs and outcome metrics, the find ings were integrated narratively through an inductive, reflexive thematic analysis utilizing Braun and Clarke’s six-phase method [50]. Risk of bias (RoB) was evaluated using design-appropriate instruments (refer to “Risk of Bias Assessment”), and RoB determinations were incor porated into the synthesis weighting [51]. Though, meta-analysis is strong quantitative synthesis approach, this is not suitable in studies where heteroge neity in methodologies, population, sample and outcome measures. Here, statistical pooling can have misleading results, and instead, a qualitative or narrative synthesis should be used [14]. Thus, these circumstances led us to qualitative synthesis approach. Review question and PICO Population (P). Children and adolescents (generally aged 5–18 years) diagnosed with ADHD, with or without con current ODD. Research that included both children and adolescents was acceptable if outcomes were presented for the overall youth cohort or categorized by age group. Intervention/Exposure (I). The presence of ODD comorbidity in adolescents with ADHD and/or ADHDrelated interventions, where ODD status was assessed (e.g., stimulant exposure) and biological or neurological correlates were evaluated as outcomes. Comparator ADHD absent ODD, typically develop ing controls, or intra-subject pre–post comparisons for intervention studies. Results (O). The main outcomes were biological and neurological links between ADHD and ODD, both with and without ODD. Biological correlates encompassed neuroendocrine function (e.g., hair/salivary cortisol), immune/inflammatory markers (e.g., interleukins; tryp tophan–kynurenine metabolites), and additional periph eral biomarkers. Neurological correlates encompassed brain structure (e.g., cortical/subcortical volumes; cer ebellar metrics), brain function and connectivity (restingstate/task fMRI, DTI, fNIRS/fNIRS-hyperscanning), and electrophysiology (e.g., ERP/RewP). Neurocognitive indi ces intimately associated with neural systems (cool/hot executive functions, affective decision-making, temporal processing) were incorporated as secondary correlates in the analysis of biological and neurological outcomes. The review question was: How does comorbid ODD relate to biological and neurological correlates in chil dren and adolescents with ADHD? The broad scope of populations was managed through transparent study selection following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and by conducting risk-of-bias assessments for all included studies to ensure balanced interpretation of the evidence [48].

Search strings integrated controlled vocabulary and keywords per taining to ADHD, ODD, youth terminology (child*, adolescen*, youth), and outcome domains (cortisol, inter leukin*, cytokine*, kynuren*, fMRI, DTI, rs-fMRI, fNIRS, ERP, executive function*, working memory, reward, irri tab*, emotional lability). There were no plans for grey literature, to maintain methodological rigor by focusing only on peer-reviewed empirical studies, ensuring higher quality and reliability of the evidence synthesis [48]. In addition to database searches, we also used backward and forward citation chasing and manually checking ref erence lists, conducted using Google Scholar and other citation tools by two independent reviewers, applying the same predefined inclusion criteria to ensure a com prehensive and unbiased literature search. The PRISMA diagram shows the yield for the review: We found 1,457 records in databases: MEDLINE (302), EMBASE (311), CINAHL (223), PsycINFO (287), Web of Science (198), and Scopus (136)0.37 more records from citation chasing or manual sources as shown in Fig. 1. Eligibility criteria Inclusion: (a) peer-reviewed empirical studies; (b) par ticipants were children/adolescents with ADHD; (c) ODD was measured or samples were stratified by ODD status, or ODD symptoms were modeled; (d) at least one biological or neurological correlate (as defined above) was an outcome; and (e) observational (cross-sectional, case–control, cohort) or experimental/quasi-experimen tal designs. Exclusion: Samples restricted to adults; lacking focus on ADHD/ODD or insufficient data on ADHD/ODD; non-empirical works (reviews, editorials, protocols with out results); not subjected to peer review; case reports/ series with n < 10; conference abstracts; studies devoid of biological/neurological outcomes. Study selection and screening Rayyan was used to import references for deduplica tion and dual-reviewer screening [52], conducted title, abstract and full-text screening inter-rater reliability Cohens’ Kappa (k = 0.85), showing strong agreement and ensuring consistency in selection process. After get ting rid of duplicates, there were 1,109 unique records left. Two reviewers looked at the titles and abstracts separately. If there were any disagreements, they talked about them and a third reviewer stepped in if necessary. Fig. 1 PRISMA diagram

Two reviewers looked at the full texts of 144 records to see if they met the criteria. 118 were excluded for the following reasons: incorrect population (n = 57), lack of ADHD/ODD focus or insufficient data (n = 31), absence of peer review (n = 18), and failure to be observational/experimental (n = 12). The final qualitative synthesis comprised 26 peer-reviewed studies examin ing biological and/or neurological correlates in child and adolescent ADHD, both with and without ODD. Data were synthesized qualitatively because of the heterogeneous nature of included studies i.e., with dif ferent research methods, including fMRI, vMorphom etry (VBM), resting-state functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS ALFF), serum tryptophan-kynuren ine profiles, cytokine panels, and executive function (EF) profiling. We chose this in order to provide a compre hensive overview of the available evidence regardless the differences in designs, sampling populations and mea surement methods. It is worth mentioning that qualita tive synthesis provides a lower level of evidence than a quantitative strategy, such as meta-analyses, would, in which studies with the same methodology and results would need to be used. Hence, it creates the need to do careful in interpretation of the findings as exploratory but not conclusive. Data extraction A pilot extraction template recorded: Study design; coun try/setting; sample characteristics (age range, sex distri bution, diagnostic instruments, medication status); ODD definition (diagnosis vs. symptom scales) and grouping; comparator(s); biological outcome details (assay type, specimen, timing, pre-analytic controls); neuroimag ing/EEG acquisition and preprocessing (scanner/model, sequence, motion control, head motion thresholds, multiple-comparison corrections); neurocognitive task parameters; covariates/confounder control (e.g., age, sex, IQ, SES, adverse childhood experiences, motion); statisti cal models and effect estimates with confidence intervals; and funding/COI. One reviewer took out all the entries, and a second checked them. Risk of bias assessment Two reviewers used design-specific tools on their own. RoB 2 was used in randomized and quasi-randomized studies [53]. Non-randomized intervention and analyti cal observational studies utilized ROBINS-I (Sterne et al., 2016). The Joanna Briggs Institute checklist [54] was used to evaluate purely cross-sectional analytic designs. Domain-level and overall RoB judgments informed the synthesis by guiding the interpretive weighting of find ings, with greater confidence placed on studies with lowto-moderate RoB, while results from higher-risk studies were interpreted more cautiously. When feasible, sen sitivity analyses highlighted findings from studies with lower RoB and adequate control for key confounders such as age, sex, IQ, medication status, and motion. Synthesis approach Meta-analysis was not planned due to the heterogene ity of populations, exposures, and outcome metrics. The review followed Braun and Clarke’s method: (1) getting to know the corpus; (2) coming up with initial codes based on biological and neurological concepts (for exam ple, HPA-axis profiles, cytokine/tryptophan pathways, amygdala/cerebellar morphometry, cortico-striatal–cer ebellar connectivity, reward-related ERPs, executive-con trol performance); (3) developing themes across studies while keeping in mind age band (child vs. adolescent), ODD status, and assay/modality differences; (4) review ing themes against study quality and context; (5) defin ing and naming final themes; and (6) writing an analytic narrative that connects signals from lower-risk stud ies and explains differences by design, measurement, or confounding [50]. When authors provided effect sizes or model coefficients, these were extracted to facilitate structured, tabular comparisons across modalities and age strata. Managing review-level bias and deviations Before database queries, the protocol laid out plans for eligibility, screening, and analysis. We used dual-reviewer processes for screening, RoB, and extraction. Reasons for exclusion were documented and are illustrated in the PRISMA diagram [48]. Grey literature was deliberately omitted to preserve the integrity of peer-review quality control; the possibility of publication bias is addressed in the Discussion. A planned quantitative synthesis for executive-function outcomes was not conducted due to incompatible measures and statistics, as stipulated by the Cochrane Handbook [51]. Characteristics of included studies Across the 26 sources, nine studies employed crosssectional neurobiological or neurocognitive case–con trol designs to compare ADHD-only, ADHD + ODD (and occasionally ADHD + CD), and healthy controls, primarily during childhood/adolescence. These stud ies included amygdala-seeded rsfMRI/DWI with care giver ratings [55], structural morphometry in adolescent boys [12], cerebellar VBM with resting-state connectiv ity [13], resting-state fNIRS ALFF [56], serum trypto phan–kynurenine profiling [57], cytokine panels pre/post

Two additional cross-sectional clinic samples exam ined family and temperament correlates [62], and clini cal executive function and irritability differences among DMDD, ADHD, ODD, and DMDD+ADHD, utilizing both performance-based and everyday executive func tion measures [63]. Two longitudinal studies were con ducted: a one-year cross-lagged panel network analysis involving high-risk Chinese children with ODD and/or ADHD [64], and a follow-up study from preschool to age 8 examining reward-related inhibitory control, approach motivation, and autonomic reactivity as predictors of subsequent ADHD, while considering ODD and callous– unemotional traits [65]. Two experimental/physiological challenge paradigms were incorporated: a naturalistic, single-dose methylphenidate attention task in drug-naïve ADHD individuals with and without ODD [66], and an ERP guessing task assessing reward positivity with mod eled interactions among CD/ODD symptoms, irritability, and CU traits [67]. Three extensive neuroimaging/model ing studies utilized ABCD baseline data: a bifactor ver sus alternative factor modeling of externalizing behaviors using emotional n-back fMRI [68], a resting-state fMRI sample-entropy analysis of cool/hot executive function networks in individuals without comorbidities of ADHD and ODD and in those with comorbid presentations [69], and an amygdala-volume brain-chart methodol ogy correlating subcortical volumes with ADHD risk and symptom severity, excluding comorbidities such as ODD [70]. A study in adolescent psychoneuroendocrinology examined the association between dimensional ADHD and diurnal cortisol, incorporating prevalent comorbid symptoms and, in sensitivity analyses, replacing ODD with CD [71]. A clinical psychology study compared ADHD with ADHD + CDS and ADHD + ODD regard ing family, emotion regulation, and executive function indices [72]. The collection also included a translational editorial/review that summarized the structural findings from the ENIGMA scale and the task-fMRI effects linked to stimulants, along with notes on ODD/CD [73], as well as a registered mixed-methods pharmacokinetic proto col for supervised cannabis as an adjunct to stimulants in youth exhibiting ADHD and ODD characteristics [74]. In total, there were at least 13 studies that were crosssectional case–control with biological or neurocognitive endpoints [12, 13, 19, 55–63, 71], two were longitudinal [64, 65], two were challenge/experimental [66, 67], three consisted large-scale ABCD imaging/modeling [68–70], one was an editorial synthesis [73], one a mixed-methods protocol [74], along with one a clinic-based EF/irritability comparison including ODD as a diagnostic cell [63]. There were clear sampling frames and group definitions in more than twenty studies, and most of them had three or four arms. A large clinical study compared 2,015 chil dren with ADHD to 745 typically developing controls in terms of emotional lability and monitored the develop mental trajectory of ADHD symptoms and oppositional defiant disorder (ODD) symptoms [8]. Imaging cohorts were stratified by modality and age: rsfMRI/DWI com prised 354 ADHD-only participants, 161 ADHD + ODD participants, and 100 controls, with an imaging subsam ple of 209 [55]; VBM/rsFC analyses utilized ADHD-200 subsamples of 27 ADHD-only, 27 ADHD + ODD, and 27 controls aged 9–14 years [13]; adolescent morphom etry matched 36 ADHD-only boys, 26 ADHD + ODD/ CD boys, and 30 typically developing boys aged 11–17 [12]; resting-state fNIRS included 165 medication-naïve children aged 7–15 years across ADHD, ADHD&LD, ADHD&ODD, and controls [56]; hyperscanning fNIRS consisted of 72 mother–child dyads, 35 ODD and 37 healthy controls, during free-play and valenced discus sions [64]. Biological assays were conducted in prepu bertal or medication-free cohorts: serum kynurenine metabolites in 46 ADHD-C, 43 ADHD-C + ODD, 33 ADHD-C + CD, and 50 controls [57]; cytokines at 09:00 before and after ~ 4.6 months of methylphenidate in 31 prepubertal inattentive vs. combined ADHD screened for “ODCD” and anxiety [58]; hair cortisol and skinconductance in 98 medication-naïve ADHD and 107 healthy controls with DSM-5 comorbidity assessment [19]. The methylphenidate challenge included 53 drugnaïve individuals with combined-type ADHD (26 with ADHD + ODD and 27 without ODD), all possessing an IQ of 80 or higher and excluding other neurodevelop mental or psychiatric disorders [66]. The ABCD-based samples were substantial: 11,878 9-year-olds for the bifactor/task-fMRI model (Perlstein et al., 2024) and 61 individuals with comorbid-free ADHD, 38 with ODD, 48 with OCD, 833 with comorbid presentations, and 269 matched controls for the rsfMRI-complexity study [69]. The cross-lagged panel network monitored 263 highrisk children aged 6 to 13 years over the course of one year, creating two cross-sectional networks and a CLPN [64]. A community school sample was utilized to match ADHD and non-ADHD groups by sex (50 boys and 58 girls per group; ages 6–15) for the purpose of compar ing ODD/CD/anger [61]. A clinic-based developmental cohort commenced at preschool (mean age 58 months) and was re-evaluated at approximately 8 years (mean age 101.4 months) for ADHD outcomes, while also docu menting ODD/CU symptoms [65]. A child psychiatry outpatient sample examined DMDD, ADHD, ODD, and DMDD+ADHD in relation to everyday executive

The modalities and measures encompassed structural and functional neuroimaging, neurophysiology, cogni tive and behavioral phenotyping, and peripheral biol ogy. Structural MRI with FreeSurfer produced indices for total gray matter, surface area, and cortical thickness, identifying a thicker right rostral middle frontal cortex in individuals with ADHD and ODD/CD [12]. VBM iden tified diminished anterior cerebellar gray matter volume (Cerebellum_4_5) exhibiting hyperconnectivity to execu tive function and default mode network regions in indi viduals with ADHD and ODD [13]. Amygdala-seeded resting-state functional MRI (rsfMRI) and diffusionweighted imaging (DWI) measured subnetworks and streamline density in conjunction with the Child Behav ior Checklist (CBCL) and the Behavior Rating Inventory for Executive Function (BRIEF) [55]. Discussion The results of this systematic literature review (SLR) pro vide significant insights into the neurobiological, neuro cognitive, and endocrine characteristics of ADHD, both with and without comorbid ODD. The central assertion of this systematic literature review is that oppositional ity in ADHD is rooted in limbic–striatal circuitry, com plemented by distinct cerebello-cortical and executive overlays. This aligns with and refines conclusions from previous global reviews. Extensive meta-analytic and mega-analytic evidence has associated fronto-striatal– limbic systems with ADHD, characterized by diminished subcortical volumes (amygdala, accumbens, caudate, putamen) and modified task-evoked responsivity [18, 44, 77, 78]. This synthesis enhances the existing literature by comparing ADHD-only with ADHD + ODD. The fact that ADHD-only has stronger amygdala–striatal–frontal cou pling than ADHD + ODD and higher streamline density in projection and callosal pathways goes against a simple “dose–response” externalizing account and supports topology shifts with comorbidity. This aligns with ODD/ CD-focused imaging meta-analyses indicating amygdalacentric abnormalities that are not congruent with ADHD [1], and with bifactor studies attributing reduced right amygdala fear reactivity to general externalizing while associating ADHD with ventral-striatal activation [68, 77]. Recent normative “brain-chart” analyses that identify amygdala morphometry as an ADHD-risk correlate con textualize the present findings within population-based trajectories rather than clinical convenience samples [70]. The pattern aligns with hierarchical dimensional frameworks (HiTOP/p-factor), wherein ODD variance is associated with antagonistic/disinhibited spectra that overlap, yet are not identical to, ADHD [79–81]. Cerebellar contributions in ADHD + ODD, particu larly diminished anterior lobule volume coupled with

Simultaneous findings of diminished resting-state signal complexity within cool/hot executive function networks correspond with systems-level analyses indicating default-mode dys regulation and extensive network instability in ADHD [44, 83]. The current review posits that ODD does not merely exacerbate ADHD-related dysconnectivity but rather reconfigures it. This perspective effectively reinter prets previous null contrasts in prefrontal hemodynam ics between ADHD with and without ODD on fNIRS as indicative of potential measurement-modality limitations rather than an actual absence of effect [56]. The executive-function theme combines different pri mary studies with two consistent signals from larger SLRs: medium-sized, general EF deficits in ADHD that get better with age [84, 85], and disorder-specific impair ments in ODD/CD across “hot” EF (decision-making, emotion recognition) [86]. The current systematic litera ture review (SLR) indicates a more pronounced execu tive function (EF) impairment in adolescents with both ADHD and ODD compared to those with ADHD alone, aligning with previous meta-analyses. In contrast, small, medication-naïve cohorts exhibiting minimal ODD increments underscore prevalent threats to precision, including underpowered tasks, construct impurity, and task impurity confounds. Parallel emotion-processing syntheses indicate that emotion-recognition deficits in ADHD are identifiable yet heterogeneous, likely influ enced by task demands and bottom-up response require ments [84], thereby reinforcing this review’s focus on irritability as a transdiagnostic amplifier of EF-adjacent dysfunction. Endocrine and autonomic findings suggest that lower morning and cumulative cortisol levels associated with ODD-symptoms, alongside diminished sympathetic reactivity in boys with ADHD and comorbid ODD or CD, align with a broader framework of reduced electrodermal and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) responses in disruptive behavior [87, 88]. These findings also update ADHD-specific meta-analyses that indicate minor and inconsistent cortisol variations when comorbidity is not differentiated [26]. Recent systematic literature reviews (SLRs) converge on hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis alterations in pediatric ADHD, yet they cau tion that effect sizes depend on sampling, assay timing, and adversity covariates [88], the very moderators this SLR addressed by modeling adverse childhood events, resulting in persistent sympathetic effects, but not cortisol effects. This selective robustness bolsters the assertion that autonomic blunting serves as a superior biological marker of oppositionality in ADHD compared to tonic cortisol. Peripheral immune-metabolic evidence is still not final. The current synthesis accurately categorizes tryp tophan-kynurenine shifts as ADHD-broad (rather than ODD-specific) and cytokine variations as sensitive to presentation and comorbidity. This position corresponds with systematic reviews that identify slight, inconsistent inflammatory increases in ADHD [28, 89–91], and cau tion against heterogeneity among assays and case-mix. It is biologically plausible that methylphenidate normalizes comorbidity-linked IL-1β/IL-13 differences, as evidenced by stimulant-related network normalization observed in fMRI studies [92], however, causality remains uncertain in the absence of randomized biomarker-stratified trials. The family/temperament and dyadic-synchrony theme is a notable strength, connecting individual neural indi ces with interpersonal regulation. Decreased parent– child neural synchrony in ODD dyads enhances existing synchrony reviews [93, 94], by linking effects to symp tom-network nodes and augmenting SLRs that outline family-system risk pathways for ODD [95]. Alongside EF/irritability findings, the multilevel perspective aligns with developmental network models that suggest fam ily context influences the interplay between emotionregulation systems and oppositional behaviors over time. Treatment-responsivity as a biological readout is astutely contextualized. The diminished attentional enhancement to methylphenidate in ADHD + ODD aligns with fMRI meta-analysis indicating that stimulants predominantly enhance inferior frontal/insula inhibition and timing net works [92], suggesting that disruptive comorbidity may reflect persistent network dysfunction less responsive to catecholaminergic modulation alone. The immune devia tions associated with ODD/CD diminish with stimulants, suggesting a hypothesis and promoting the development of multimodal biomarker panels. However, previous pharmacological systematic literature reviews indicate that neural changes do not consistently correlate linearly with symptom improvement [44], thus, the identified effect modifiers (irritability, CU traits, family processes) should be prospectively stratified. Lastly, the symptom-network and heterogeneity architectures combined here fit perfectly with modern dimensional nosology. Longitudinal network analysis identifying “annoy,” “blame,” and “vindictive” as bridge nodes parallels extensive ADHD/ODD network research highlighting the centrality of oppositional and cognitivedisengagement characteristics [96, 97]. Additionally, the current bifactor evidence resonates with the p-factor lit erature, attributing fear-related amygdala hypo-reactivity to general externalizing behaviors while distinguishing

This dual ity elucidates the minimal separation observed in certain imaging contrasts (e.g., resting prefrontal ALFF) between ADHD and ADHD + ODD [56], in contrast to cortical thickness or entropy metrics that indicate comorbiditysensitive deviations. Methodologically, the SLR is unique in that it (a) sepa rates ADHD-only from ADHD + ODD across modalities; (b) triangulates task fMRI, resting connectivity/com plexity, morphometry, ERP, peripheral biomarkers, and dyadic neurobiology; and (c) interprets findings within dimensional models. The remaining limitations, which are also present in previous SLRs, encompass task and pipeline heterogeneity, limited medication-naïve sam ples, motion/resolution confounds in pediatric imaging, cross-sectional inference for developmental assertions, and potential publication bias in EEG/ERP and cytokine literatures [98–100]. The most defensible translational message is not that ODD “adds more of the identical” but that it remodels ADHD’s neural and physiologi cal landscape toward altered limbic–striatal coupling, cerebello-cortical compensation, broader EF and emo tion-regulation burdens, and reduced autonomic reac tivity within a general externalizing architecture. Future trials should utilize these insights to examine mecha nism-guided combinations (stimulants combined with irritability-targeted cognitive-behavioral therapy/parent training) and to assess biomarker-defined subgroups. As the number of studies included was very heteroge neous, especially in methods used to diagnose ADHD and ODD, sample sizes, and the nature of neurobiological and psychological outcomes measures, a formal quanti tative synthesis or subgroup analysis was not possible in the review. Methodological recommendations imply that these types of analyses need fairly similar study designs and standard outcome measures that would generate valid and interpretable findings [51, 101]. As a result, an inductive narrative synthesis was used to support the diversity in methodology and to give a wider interpre tation of the neurobiological patterns of ADHD-ODD comorbidity. Though narrative synthesis can be per ceived to be inappropriate in cases where evidence is heterogeneous and inappropriate to use in meta-analysis, it is regarded as a suitable method when the evidence is heterogeneous and that cannot be utilized in the context of meta-analysis and can be used to build a basis upon which future studies can use more standardized methods and have a similar dataset [101, 102]. Despite significant findings, the present study is limited to include studies that are mostly based on cross-sec tional research design. Although these studies can have good information in terms of neurobiological correlates, it limits the possibility of establishing causal relationships as well as the manner in which neural changes occur in various stages of development. Since the progression of ADHD and ODD has dynamic developmental dynamics, future studies ought to focus on large-scale longitudinal studies to monitor neurobiological indicators, as well as individual changes in behaviors and cognition. These lon gitudinal designs would aid in clarifying the leads up to the presentation of comorbid symptoms or occurring as an outcome of them thus beefing the causal interpreta tion and addressing the formulation of more specific and developmentally sensitive intervention plans. The wide area of the question of the review was care fully chosen to include the complex and multifactorial nature of ADHD in the presence of comorbid ODD. In spite of the sound complaint that the reviewer made about the incorporation of several biological, neurologi cal and neurocognitive domains, current studies indicate that ADHD and ODD comorbidity should be viewed in an integrative framework involving multiple interact ing neurobiological mechanisms, as opposed to single working mechanisms. Research has demonstrated that dysfunctions, which overlap both emotional regulation, executive functioning, and reward processing parts of the brain, mostly in the prefrontal cortex, amygdala, and frontostriatal loops, are involved in both ADHD and ODD, indicating the necessity to adopt a cross-domain approach [1, 103]. Moreover, neurocognitive aspects, including impairment of inhibitory control, emotional control, and decision-making have been observed to have common underlying neurobiological mechanisms in children with ADHD and disruptive behavior disorders (Matthys et al., 2013). The synthesis of evidence in these areas allowed the current review to determine deeper patterns and converging processes that can lead to the emergence and continuation of ADHD ODD comorbid ity. However, it is admitted that future researches can be facilitated by taking particular domains in biological or neurocognitive areas and using domain-related metaanalytic techniques to shed some more light on these associations. This review presents a thorough overview of the existing evidence base despite the limited scope of its conceptualization and shows the significance of combined methods in comprehending the multifaceted mechanisms of the comorbidity of ADHD and ODD. Recommendations This systematic literature review supports a biologi cally grounded, multidomain framework of opposi tionality in ADHD, characterized by limbic–striatal signatures (amygdala–striatal coupling, caudate-linked network simplification), cerebello-cortical modifications, increased executive demands, and selective autonomic/ HPA dysregulations. In clinical practice, evaluation should transcend mere symptom enumeration to include dimensional profiles of irritability, fluctuating executive

Page 22 of 26 Shah et al. BMC Psychology (2026) 14:882 functions, and familial systemic influences, supple mented—when possible—by scalable biomarkers (e.g., amygdala–striatal reactivity indices, resting-state com plexity metrics, and electrodermal responsivity). Treat ment planning must consider diminished stimulant response in the context of ODD and should integrate pharmacotherapy with parent training/CBT focused on irritability, emotion recognition training, and family communication/problem-solving modules. The findings advocate for the early identification of at-risk dyads (char acterized by diminished parent–child neural synchrony and heightened irritability) and the implementation of stepped-care pathways that incorporate both behavioral and pharmacological interventions. Before deciding on a medication, you should get multimodal baselines (clini cal + EF batteries + autonomic readouts) and then check them again after titration. Programs should use measure ment-based care dashboards to keep track of things like attention levels, irritability, and family communication. These dashboards should have set levels for when to add more support (for example, parent training or schoolbased support). At the systems level, funding should be provided for integrated clinics that can conduct neurobe havioral assessments alongside family interventions. Limitations The evidence base is limited by the diversity of imaging pipelines and tasks, small medication-naïve samples, insufficient power for sex and developmental stratifica tion, motion artifacts in pediatric neuroimaging, incon sistent assay timing in endocrine studies, and probable publication bias in EEG/ERP and cytokine research. Most studies included in this review are cross-sectional, which limits the ability to determine causal relationships or understand the developmental progression of neuro biological changes associated with comorbid ADHD and ODD. Because both conditions evolve across develop ment, future research should prioritize large-scale longi tudinal studies, preferably pre-registered, to track neural changes alongside symptom trajectories over time and to provide stronger evidence regarding causality and long-term outcomes. Clinic-based sampling and not enough low- and middle-income settings make ecologi cal validity worse. The research that comes next needs to be Things that are important include: (1) pre-registered, multi-site longitudinal groups that separate ADHD-only, ADHD + ODD, and disruptive subtypes, with harmo nized tasks (inhibition, timing, affective decision-mak ing) and prevalent imaging/physiology pipelines; (2) biomarker-stratified randomized trials testing combined stimulant + irritability-focused behavioral packages, with mechanistic mediators (limbic–striatal connectivity, cer ebello-cortical coupling, autonomic indices); (3) norma tive modeling and network methodologies that connect symptom bridge nodes (“annoy,” “blame,” “vindictive,” “angry”) to neural and physiological edges over time; (4) developmental windows and sex-specific moderators; (5) the integration of genetics, adversity, and family-level moderators through causal mediation/instrumentalvariable techniques; and (6) high-frequency, real-world phenotyping (EMA/wearables) to assess generalization beyond the laboratory setting. Oppositionality in ADHD is not simply an exacerbation of symptoms; it represents a reconfiguration of neural topology and physiology that impairs executive and socio-emotional regulation and alters treatment responsiveness. Anchoring care to dimensional, multimodal profiles and testing mech anism-guided combinations presents the most cred ible approach to achieving sustainable, developmentally appropriate enhancements. Conclusion This review illustrates that ODD comorbidity signifi cantly alters the neurobiological and functional charac teristics of ADHD across neuroimaging, neurocognitive, endocrine, autonomic, and immune–metabolic domains. Oppositionality was consistently associated with modified limbic–striatal signaling, cerebello-cortical compensation, diminished executive-network com plexity, and unique patterns in the HPA-axis and sym pathetic systems. These convergent findings suggest that ODD+ADHD constitutes a neurobiologically dis tinct phenotype rather than merely a severity variant of ADHD. Clinically, this underscores the imperative of amalgamating stimulant therapy with emotion-reg ulation, parent–child relational, and behavioral inter ventions. Subsequent longitudinal and mechanistic investigations are crucial to elucidating developmental trajectories and enhancing precision-tailored care. To view a copy of this licence, visit ​h​t​t​p​:​/​/​c​r​e​a​t​i​ v​e​c​o​m​m​o​n​s​.​o​r​g​/​l​i​c​e​n​s​e​s​/​b​y​-​n​c​-​n​d​/​4​.​0​/​.​ Abstract Background Adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are at risk for problematic digital use (PDU), which is better characterised by loss of control and functional impairment than by screen time alone. The present study investigated problematic internet, social media, and gaming use among adolescents with ADHD, focusing on impulsivity, obsessive-compulsive (OC) symptoms, and perceived cognitive flexibility. Methods This cross-sectional case-control study included 132 adolescents aged 12–18 years (69 treatment-naive adolescents with ADHD and 63 healthy controls) recruited from a tertiary child and adolescent psychiatry outpatient clinic. Participants completed self-report measures of problematic digital use, impulsivity, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and perceived cognitive flexibility. ADHD diagnoses were confirmed using the Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age Children–Present and Lifetime Version (K-SADS-PL). Adjusted binary logistic regression models included participant age and biological sex. The primary within-ADHD regression and moderation models included the Conners ADHD Index. Results Problematic internet use and probable problematic social media use were more frequent in the ADHD group and were associated with higher odds of ADHD group membership after adjustment for age and biological sex. Within the ADHD group, impulsivity and obsessive-compulsive symptom severity were independently associated with problematic internet-use severity. For gaming symptoms, impulsivity remained a significant independent correlate, whereas the OCI-R main effect was not statistically significant. A preliminary OCI-R × CFS interaction was observed for gaming symptoms after adjustment for parent-rated ADHD symptom severity (B = 0.024, SE = 0.008, 95% CI [0.007, 0.040], p = .004; ΔR2 = 0.087). Conclusions Adolescents with ADHD showed higher frequencies of problematic internet use and probable problematic social media use than healthy controls. Impulsivity was a consistent dimensional correlate of problematic digital use. The interaction involving perceived cognitive flexibility should be considered preliminary and hypothesisgenerating and requires replication in larger independent samples.

Page 2 of 11 Altun Varmış et al. BMC Psychology (2026) 14:1232 ​Background Digital media are integrated into adolescents’ daily lives, and most use is functional. However, a minority develop patterns characterised by loss of control, unsuccessful efforts to reduce use, persistence despite negative con sequences, and impairment in everyday functioning. The umbrella term problematic digital use encompasses related but non-equivalent manifestations, including problematic internet use, problematic social-media use, and gaming-disorder symptoms [1–3]. Because screen time alone does not distinguish normative engagement from clinically meaningful difficulty, symptom-based indicators of impaired control and functional conse quences are particularly important [2, 4–6]. Adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) may be particularly vulnerable to problematic digital use. ADHD is characterised by devel opmentally inappropriate inattention and/or hyper activity–impulsivity and is commonly associated with difficulties in self-regulation, inhibitory control, reward processing, and executive functioning [7, 8]. Digital envi ronments frequently provide immediate feedback, vari able rewards, continuous content, social reinforcement, and easy access. These features may interact with ADHDrelated reward sensitivity, impulsivity, and difficulties delaying gratification or disengaging from rewarding activities [9–11]. Consistent with this rationale, children and adoles cents with ADHD show higher levels of problematic digital-media use than typically developing controls [11]. Meta-analytic evidence also indicates a substantial asso ciation between ADHD symptoms and gaming-related difficulties [12]. Longitudinal evidence suggests recip rocal temporal associations between ADHD symptoms and digital-media use. Baseline ADHD symptoms have been prospectively associated with later high or prob lematic digital-media use, whereas baseline digital-media use has also been prospectively associated with later ADHD symptom levels [4]. These associations have been observed more consistently for problematic-use indica tors than for screen-time measures, although their mag nitude and direction vary across studies [4]. Two transdiagnostic constructs relevant to addic tion-like behaviours are impulsivity and compulsiv ity. Impulsivity is defined as rapid responding to obtain reward without sufficient deliberation, whereas com pulsivity is defined as repetitive, inflexible, or perse verative behaviour that continues even in the face of negative consequences [13]. Impulsivity is a core clinical feature of ADHD and may amplify sensitivity to digital environments through reward-seeking behaviour, poor inhibitory control, and difficulty delaying gratification. OC symptoms (here defined as a dimensional mea sure of OC symptom burden rather than a diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder, OCD) may contribute via repetitive checking, difficulty terminating sessions, ordering or completion tendencies, and persistence in platform-specific goals [14–16]. More recent meta-ana lytic work supports the view that impulsivity is a consis tent correlate of gaming disorder symptomatology [17]. A useful framework for understanding how personlevel vulnerabilities interact with digital cues to produce problematic use through affective, cognitive, and execu tive processes is the Interaction of Person–Affect–Cogni tion–Execution (I-PACE) model [18]. Within this model, impulsivity may be more closely related to reward-driven initiation and escalation, whereas compulsivity-related features may be more closely related to recurrent use, checking, completion, and difficulty disengaging [18, 19]. However, to date, there has been little research on how comparable or dissimilar internet, social media, and gaming indicators are in clinically assessed ADHD populations. Perceived cognitive flexibility and ability-based cogni tive flexibility are related but non-equivalent constructs. Performance-based tasks assess observable set-shift ing or task-switching under standardised conditions, whereas the Cognitive Flexibility Scale assesses individu als’ subjective appraisal of their ability to generate alter natives and adapt their responses in everyday situations [20–23]. The CFS was selected because the present study concerned perceived adaptability as a person-level factor potentially relevant to digital engagement, rather than objective executive-control performance. This distinction may be particularly relevant in adolescents with ADHD, whose difficulties with self-regulation and disengagement occur in everyday, highly reinforcing contexts. Accord ingly, CFS scores were interpreted exclusively as indica tors of perceived cognitive flexibility. Within the I-PACE framework, perceived cogni tive flexibility may shape how OC symptom burden is expressed in digital environments [18]. Perceived adapt ability was not assumed to be uniformly protective. Gam ing environments require strategic adjustment while also providing structured goals, progression systems, repeated challenges, and completion contingencies [19, 24]. Among adolescents with greater OC symptom bur den, perceiving oneself as able to generate alternative strategies may therefore be associated with continued optimisation or completion-oriented engagement rather Keywords ADHD, Problematic digital use, Internet gaming disorder, Impulsivity, Obsessive-compulsive symptoms, Perceived cognitive flexibility, Adolescents

Accordingly, the hypothesis-driven moderation analysis focused on whether perceived cog nitive flexibility modified the association between OC symptom burden and gaming symptom severity. Never theless, analogous interactions for problematic internet use and problematic social-media use were examined as parallel exploratory analyses to assess whether a similar pattern was present across other digital-use domains. This proposed pathway is context-dependent and hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as an established mechanism or as a reflection of objective executive functioning. The present investigation was motivated by three gaps. First, few studies have examined ADHD in rela tion to multiple problematic digital-use indicators in a clinically assessed, treatment-naive adolescent group. Second, the separate contributions of impulsivity and OC symptom severity within ADHD have not been sys tematically examined while controlling for parent-rated ADHD symptom severity. Third, although there is a need to delineate perceived flexibility from performance-based executive function, perceived cognitive flexibility has rarely been investigated as a moderator of the association between OC symptoms and gaming symptoms. Three hypotheses were tested. First, compared with healthy controls, adolescents with ADHD would be more likely to show problematic internet use, problem atic social media use, and probable internet gaming dis order. Second, robust associations would be observed between impulsivity and OC symptom severity and problematic digital-use indicators within the ADHD group, which would remain significant after entering parent-rated ADHD symptom severity into the model. Third, perceived cognitive flexibility would moderate the association between OC symptom severity and gam ing symptoms, such that OC symptoms would be more strongly linked with gaming severity at higher levels of perceived flexibility. Given the cross-sectional design, all results were considered as associations rather than causal processes. Methods Study design and participants This cross-sectional case-control study was conducted in a tertiary child and adolescent psychiatry outpatient clinic. Both ADHD and healthy control participants aged 12–18 years were recruited by convenience sampling from the same clinic. No individual matching, frequency matching, or stratification was performed between the groups; group characteristics were compared statisti cally. The final sample consisted of 132 adolescents (69 treatment-naive adolescents with ADHD and 63 healthy controls). The ADHD group was initially screened with 100 ado lescents. After the structured diagnostic interview, 30 were excluded because of concurrent psychiatric diag noses and one was excluded because of incomplete ques tionnaires, resulting in a final ADHD sample of 69. The control group initially included 70 adolescents, of whom 7 were excluded because of incomplete questionnaires, resulting in a final control sample of 63. At study entry, all participants underwent the Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for SchoolAge Children–Present and Lifetime Version (K-SADSPL) [25, 26], administered by experienced child and adolescent psychiatrists. In the ADHD group, the inter view was used to confirm a DSM-5 diagnosis of ADHD and to assess current psychiatric comorbidity. Inclusion criteria for the ADHD group were: (1) age 12–18 years; (2) a DSM-5 diagnosis of ADHD confirmed using the K-SADS-PL; (3) treatment-naive status, defined as no previous pharmacological treatment for ADHD; and (4) absence of any current comorbid psychiatric disorder. Accordingly, adolescents meeting criteria for a current depressive, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive and related, trauma-related, eating, tic, disruptive-behaviour, or other psychiatric disorder were excluded. The ADHD group comprised 31 adolescents with the predomi nantly inattentive presentation and 38 with the combined presentation. Inclusion criteria for the healthy control group were age 12–18 years and absence of ADHD or any current or lifetime psychiatric disorder according to the K-SADSPL. Thus, an adolescent meeting criteria for current major depressive disorder or another current psychiatric disorder was not included in either group; any lifetime psychiatric disorder additionally precluded inclusion in the healthy control group. Additional exclusion criteria for both groups were intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, psychotic disorder, substance-use disorder, use of any psychotropic medication within the previous four weeks, and chronic neurological or other medical con ditions that could affect neurocognitive or behavioural outcomes. The healthy control group consisted of adoles cents presenting to the same outpatient clinic for routine evaluations, such as health reports for sports or school, or for mild and transient developmental concerns, such as minor peer conflicts or mild academic stress. The K-SADS-PL comprises an introductory interview, a screening interview, and diagnosis-specific supplements assessing current and lifetime psychopathology across major diagnostic domains, including mood, anxiety, psy chotic, attention-deficit/hyperactivity and disruptivebehaviour, substance-use, eating, and tic disorders [25, 26]. Statistical analysis Analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics and jamovi. Continuous variables are presented as means and standard deviations and were compared between groups using Welch’s independent-samples t tests. Categorical variables, including biological sex and the categorical digital-use indicators, were expressed as frequencies and percentages and compared using Pearson’s chi-square tests. For probable internet gaming disorder, a two-sided Fisher’s exact test was used because one observed cell count was small. The descriptive comparisons reported in Table 1 were unadjusted; no ANCOVA was performed. Multivariable binary logistic regression models esti mated odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for ADHD group membership associated with each problematic digital-use indicator. Participant age and biological sex were included as covariates. Maternal and paternal age were examined descriptively but were not included in the adjusted models. No measures of family functioning, parental monitoring, or parenting practices were available for inclusion as covariates. Pearson prod uct–moment correlations between CFS, OCI-R, and BIS11-SF total scores and the three continuous digital-use outcomes were calculated in the full sample and sepa rately within the ADHD and healthy control groups. The Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction was applied separately to the nine total-score correlation tests within each analysis set, using pairwise-complete obser vations. A descriptive Pearson correlation matrix for the principal continuous study variables is presented in Sup plementary Table S1. Within the ADHD group, ordinary least-squares mul tiple linear regression models examined BIS-11-SF and OCI-R total scores as simultaneous correlates of YIATSF and IGDS9-SF scores. The primary models included the Conners ADHD Index as a covariate; correspond ing models without the Conners ADHD Index were retained as unadjusted secondary analyses. Moderation analyses were conducted using observed-variable linear interaction models corresponding to a simple modera tion model [41] and estimated by maximum likelihood, with coefficient inference based on two-sided Wald z tests and model-based 95% confidence intervals. The pri mary hypothesis-driven IGDS9-SF model included the Conners ADHD Index; the corresponding unadjusted IGDS9-SF model was secondary, and parallel unadjusted YIAT-SF and SMDS models were exploratory. The interview was used for diagnostic assess ment and was not treated as a separate quantitative mea sure of social functioning. Measures All measures, unless otherwise specified, were self-reported. Sociodemographic characteristics. The sociodemo graphic variables included in the present analyses were participant age, biological sex, maternal age, and paternal age. These variables were recorded using a researcherprepared information form. Birthplace, family eco nomic condition, parental educational attainment, and broader family-level characteristics were not available for analysis. Problematic internet use was assessed using the Young Internet Addiction Test–Short Form (YIAT-SF) [27, 28]. Scores > 30 identified the problematic/high-risk cate gory, and scores ≥ 37 defined a higher-severity range for descriptive and sensitivity reporting. These cutoffs were used as potential risk indicators, not as clinical diagnoses. Gaming symptoms were measured by the Internet Gaming Disorder Scale–Short Form (IGDS9-SF) [29, 30]. A total score ≥ 32 indicated probable internet gam ing disorder. Problematic social media use was measured by the Social Media Disorder Scale (SMDS) [31, 32]. The presence of ≥ 5 symptoms suggested probable problem atic social media use. Scale-based categories were used as probable indicators and not as diagnostic categories. Impulsivity was evaluated using the Barratt Impulsive ness Scale-11 Short Form (BIS-11-SF) [33–35], which yields attentional, motor, non-planning, and total scores. The severity of OC symptoms was measured with the Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory–Revised (OCI-R) [36, 37]. OCI-R total scores were interpreted as dimensional indicators of self-reported OC symptom burden and not as evidence of a clinical diagnosis of OCD. The Cognitive Flexibility Scale (CFS) [20, 38] was used to measure perceived cognitive flexibility. The CFS is a self-report measure of perceived flexibility and per spective-taking. It does not assess performance-based executive function, neurocognitive set-shifting, or taskswitching capacity. Findings involving the CFS were therefore interpreted as relationships with self-perceived flexibility, not with objective cognitive control. The severity of parent-reported ADHD symptoms was measured with the Conners Parent Rating Scale–Revised Short Form [39, 40]. The Conners ADHD Index was included as an a priori covariate in the primary withinADHD regression and moderation models.

Results Sample characteristics The sociodemographic and symptom-scale characteris tics of the groups are presented in Table 1. The sample included 132 adolescents (69 with ADHD and 63 healthy controls), of whom 50.8% were male. The mean age of the full sample was 14.27 ± 1.82 years. The ADHD group was younger than the healthy control group (13.91 ± 1.85 vs. 14.67 ± 1.71 years; p = .016). Biological sex distributions did not differ significantly: 37 adolescents with ADHD (53.6%) and 30 healthy controls (47.6%) were male (p = .491). Maternal age was lower in the ADHD group than in the healthy control group (40.54 ± 5.91 vs. 43.89 ± 6.43 years; p = .002), as was paternal age (44.41 ± 5.65 vs. 46.95 ± 6.51 years; p = .019). Parent-rated ADHD symp tom severity was higher in the ADHD group (Conners ADHD Index: 26.46 ± 6.83 vs. 10.38 ± 6.41; p < .001). Adolescents with ADHD also had higher BIS-11-SF total and subscale scores. CFS awareness and willingness scores did not differ significantly between the groups (p = .230 and p = .354, respectively), whereas CFS self-efficacy and total scores were lower in the ADHD group. OCI-R total scores also did not differ significantly between the ADHD and healthy control groups (22.04 ± 12.01 vs. 22.95 ± 13.96, respectively; p = .690). In the primary model adjusted for the Conners ADHD Index, the OCI-R × CFS interaction for IGDS9-SF scores was statistically sig nificant (B = 0.024, SE = 0.008, 95% CI [0.007, 0.040], p = .004). Parallel exploratory unadjusted models did not identify statistically significant OCI-R × CFS interac tions for YIAT-SF scores (B = 0.004, SE = 0.009, 95% CI [− 0.013, 0.022], p = .640) or SMDS scores (B = − 0.0009, SE = 0.0022, 95% CI [− 0.0052, 0.0035], p = .696). Among the three outcomes examined, a statistically significant interaction was observed only for gaming symptom severity in the present sample; however, the interaction coefficients were not formally compared across out comes. Given the relatively small ADHD subgroup, the IGDS9-SF interaction and ΔR2 estimates should be con sidered preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Discussion This study examined problematic digital-use indica tors in adolescents with ADHD, focusing on impulsivity, OC symptom severity, and perceived cognitive flex ibility. Four findings merit emphasis. First, problem atic internet use and probable problematic social media use were more frequent in the ADHD group and were associated with higher odds of ADHD group member ship after adjustment for age and biological sex. BMC Psychology (2026) 14:1232 probable internet gaming disorder was more frequent in the ADHD group in the crude comparison, although an adjusted binary estimate was not reported because of sparse cells. Third, within the ADHD group, impulsiv ity was independently associated with both problematic internet-use and gaming-symptom severity, whereas OC symptom severity showed an independent main effect for problematic internet use but not gaming symptoms. Fourth, a preliminary OCI-R × CFS interaction was observed for gaming symptoms, including after adjust ment for parent-rated ADHD symptom severity. Elevated odds of problematic digital use in ADHD The between-group findings are consistent with previ ous evidence indicating elevated problematic digital-use indicators among adolescents with ADHD [11, 12]. The strongest signal concerned problematic internet use: crossing the problematic/high-risk threshold was asso ciated with higher odds of ADHD group membership, and the more stringent higher-severity threshold yielded a comparable result. Probable problematic social media use was also associated with higher odds of ADHD group membership, although the magnitude was smaller. This pattern is consistent with a broad but not unlim ited view of digital risk in ADHD. The findings do not imply that all digital platforms are equally harmful, or that screen-time quantity alone explains the associa tion. Loss of control, repeated unsuccessful attempts to cut down use, and impairment in daily functioning are more likely to be the clinically meaningful signal [2, 4]. This is consistent with existing PUI frameworks that view problematic online activities as related indicators under a broader umbrella rather than independent constructs [2, 3]. Gaming symptoms warrant a more nuanced inter pretation. In the crude categorical comparison, prob able internet gaming disorder was more frequent in adolescents with ADHD. Within the ADHD group, gam ing severity was positively correlated with impulsivity, whereas its bivariate association with OCI-R score was not statistically significant. The regression and modera tion results likewise suggest that OC symptom burden was not associated with gaming severity through a uni form main effect; rather, the association varied according to perceived cognitive flexibility. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the overlap among the digital-use indicators and the relatively small ADHD subgroup. Impulsivity and OC symptoms as clinically relevant correlates Impulsivity was consistently associated with problematic digital use. This is consistent with transdiagnostic models that emphasise reward-seeking, poor inhibitory control, and rapid cue-reactivity in addiction-like behaviours [13]. Impulsivity is a core diagnostic feature of ADHD [9, 18], and digital environments that provide instant feedback and a variety of rewards may be particularly difficult to disengage from. The persistence of associations between impulsivity and digital-use indicators after adjusting for parent-rated ADHD symptom severity suggests that impulsivity carries clinically relevant dimensional infor mation that is not reducible to either diagnostic status or global ADHD severity. OC symptom severity showed an independent asso ciation with problematic internet-use severity within the ADHD group. The absence of a between-group difference in OCI-R total scores does not preclude such dimensional within-group associations, particularly because adoles cents with current psychiatric comorbidity, including OCD, were excluded. For gaming symptoms, however, the OCI-R main effect was not statistically significant; the observed association varied according to perceived cognitive flexibility. These patterns are compatible with the possibility that repetitive checking, completion ten dencies, ordering, and difficulty stopping may be relevant in some digital-use contexts, but they do not establish a direct compulsivity mechanism [14–16, 19]. OCI-R scores were interpreted as self-reported dimen sional indicators of OC symptom burden rather than evidence of clinical OCD. This distinction is important because the OCI-R is a symptom measure, whereas cur rent psychiatric comorbidity was assessed using the K-SADS-PL [36]. Perceived cognitive flexibility and gaming symptoms The between-group CFS findings were not uniformly null. Adolescents with ADHD had lower CFS self-effi cacy and total scores, whereas awareness and willing ness scores did not differ significantly between groups. This pattern may indicate that differences in perceived cognitive flexibility are facet-specific rather than global. Because the CFS assesses subjective appraisal of adapt ability rather than performance-based set-shifting, the absence of differences on individual subscales should not be interpreted as evidence of intact objective cognitive flexibility. Conversely, the present study cannot deter mine whether discrepancies between self-perception and objective performance contributed to these findings because no performance-based flexibility measure was administered. The preliminary interaction finding may help gener ate hypotheses regarding gaming-related processes in adolescents with ADHD. The OCI-R × CFS interaction accounted for an additional 8.7% of the variance in gam ing symptom severity in the primary model adjusted for parent-rated ADHD symptom severity and 7.6% in the corresponding unadjusted secondary model. Although

BMC Psychology (2026) 14:1232 these estimates indicate incremental explanatory contri bution beyond the main effects, they were obtained from a relatively small ADHD subgroup and may be sampledependent. Accordingly, the interaction should not be interpreted as evidence of a stable or clinically estab lished moderating mechanism. In the unadjusted condi tional-effects analysis, higher OC symptom severity was associated with greater gaming severity only at high lev els of perceived cognitive flexibility. One possible, speculative interpretation is that adoles cents who perceive themselves as highly adaptable may remain engaged in gaming environments that reward planning, goal achievement, and strategic adjustment. Among adolescents with greater OC symptom burden, this perceived adaptability may be associated with a more repetitive or completion-driven pattern of gaming engagement and greater difficulty disengaging. However, the present cross-sectional findings cannot establish such a mechanism. Self-perceptions of adaptability may have context-dependent associations [24]. The conditional pattern should not be interpreted as evidence that perceived cognitive flexibility is clinically harmful or lacks a protective role. Parallel exploratory models did not show statistically significant interactions for problematic internet-use or social-media-use scores, but the interaction coefficients across outcomes were not formally compared. Replication in larger samples using longitudinal designs, objective usage measures, and performance-based measures of cognitive flexibility is required. Clinical implications The findings suggest that clinical assessment of ado lescents with ADHD should not be restricted to screen time. Relevant signals include loss of control, unsuccess ful efforts to reduce use, functional impairment, and repetitive or completion-driven engagement. Impulsivity may help identify broad vulnerability across digital-use domains, whereas assessment of dimensional OC symp tom burden may help characterise patterns with a more repetitive, rigid, or completion-driven quality. These interpretations do not establish an OCD diagnosis or a specific causal mechanism. The present interaction finding is not sufficient to sup port specific treatment recommendations concerning flexibility-oriented interventions. Rather, it identifies a preliminary question for future clinical and longitudinal research regarding how perceived adaptability and OC symptom burden may jointly relate to persistent gaming engagement. Family-level assessment may also be infor mative, given that family functioning has been linked to PUI severity in youth [42] and that parental monitoring and digital norms were not directly assessed. Strengths and limitations Strengths of this study include the use of a treatmentnaive sample of adolescents with ADHD, comprehensive structured diagnostic assessment, simultaneous exami nation of multiple digital-use indicators, group-strati fied correlation analyses, and inclusion of parent-rated ADHD symptom severity in the primary within-ADHD models. Several limitations should also be noted. First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal infer ence, including conclusions about whether ADHDrelated vulnerabilities contribute to problematic digital use or whether problematic digital use contributes to later ADHD symptom severity. The use of self-report measures may also inflate shared method variance, and the digital-use categories represent probable indicators rather than clinical diagnoses. Second, perceived cogni tive flexibility was assessed by self-report and should not be generalised to performance-based executive function ing. Third, although the incremental variance explained by the OCI-R × CFS interaction was quantified using ΔR2, the moderation models were estimated in a rela tively small ADHD subgroup; the interaction and effectsize estimates may therefore be unstable and should be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Johnson–Neyman regions were not examined. Fourth, the three digital-use outcomes were intercorrelated, indicating shared vari ance, although they were analysed as separate outcomes and should not be regarded as interchangeable con structs. Fifth, maternal and paternal age differed between groups and were not included as covariates, so residual family-level confounding cannot be excluded. Birthplace, family economic condition, parental educational attain ment, family functioning, parental monitoring, and par enting practices were not available for analysis. Finally, sample-specific internal consistency coefficients could not be calculated because item-level responses were not retained in the analytic dataset. Conclusions Adolescents with ADHD showed higher frequencies of problematic internet use and probable problematic social media use than healthy controls. Within the ADHD group, impulsivity was independently associated with problematic internet-use and gaming-symptom sever ity, whereas OC symptom severity showed an indepen dent association with problematic internet use but not a uniform main effect for gaming symptoms. A prelimi nary OCI-R × CFS interaction was observed for gaming symptom severity and accounted for incremental vari ance beyond the corresponding main effects. This finding requires replication in larger independent samples and should not be interpreted as evidence of a stable or clini cally established moderating mechanism.

metadata_title: Prevalence of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder/hyperkinetic disorder of pediatric and adult populations in clinical settings: a systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression
pages: SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OPEN Prevalence of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder/ hyperkinetic disorder of pediatric and adult populations in clinical settings: a systematic review, meta-analysis and metaregression Simon Johnson 1, Eric Lim 2,3, Peter Jacoby4, Stephen V. Faraone 5, Benjamin Minche Su 6, Marco Solmi 7,8,9,10, Benjamin Forrest11, Bethany Furfaro12, Kiri von Klier 13, Jenny Downs 4,14,20 and Wai Chen 13,15,16,17,18,19,20✉ © Crown 2025 BACKGROUND: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)/Hyperkinetic Disorder (HD) is linked to increased risks of morbidity, comorbidity and mortality, with higher prevalence in clinical populations. The differential prevalence of ADHD/HD across adult and pediatric clinical populations, influenced by factors such as time trends, sex, age, geographic regions, and comorbidities, has not been systematically assessed. METHODS: MEDLINE, CINAHL, Embase and PsycINFO databases were searched from inception to 1st August 2023 for eligible fulltext papers published in English, and reviewing reference lists of identified studies and review papers. Studies reporting ADHD/HD prevalence in adult and pediatric clinical populations were included. Meta-regression evaluated the effects of geographic region, year of publication and sample size. RESULTS: From 30,740 citations, we reviewed 521 full-text articles, yielding 311 studies for inclusion (including 653,558 pediatric and 43,311 adult participants). Overall, worldwide pooled prevalence of ADHD/HD in clinical settings for pediatrics was 32.4% (95% CI 31–34%), and in adults 21.4% (95% CI 20–23%). Prevalence was higher in outpatient settings than inpatient settings. Prevalence based on rating scales was higher than studies using diagnostic interviews or clinical record review. Prevalence varied significantly across subspecialist settings for children and adults. No significant time trend was detected between 1981–2023. Pediatric prevalence appears influenced by geographic region but not year of publication or sample size. For adults, larger sample sizes were associated with lower prevalence estimates. CONCLUSIONS: ADHD/HD prevalence in clinical populations is 8-9-fold higher than community estimates. With these patients at risk for many adverse outcomes, our findings underscore the critical importance of resource allocation for screening, diagnosing and treatment. Molecular Psychiatry (2026) 31:576–586; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41380-025-03178-8 INTRODUCTION Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by age-inappropriate levels of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity, associated with persistent and pervasive impairments across the lifespan (DSM-5-TR) [1]. The World Health Organization (WHO) [2] conceptualizes a similar condition as hyperkinetic disorder (HD) in ICD-9 and ICD-10; however, in 2022, ICD-11 revised and renamed HD as “attention deficit hyperactivity disorder” (without the slash between “attention deficit” and “hyperactivity”) [2]. While there are nuanced differences between ICD-11 and DSM-5-TR versions of “ADHD” as reviewed elsewhere [3], these different versions can be collectively captured by the term “ADHD/HD” [4]. ADHD/HD is a common condition, with a worldwide pooled prevalence estimated at 3.4% in child populations [5].
