Collaborative frameworks involving neuroscientists, clinicians, ethicists, educators, and families will be essential for shaping responsible and socially informed research trajectories. In sum, psilocybin represents a powerful experimental tool in contemporary psychiatry, with particular relevance for stressrelated—and potentially developmental—neuropsychiatric conditions. Its greatest near-term value may lie not as an immediate treatment for ADHD, but as a mechanistic probe for understanding how neuroplasticity, E/I balance, and stresssensitive circuits can be modulated after vulnerability or dysfunction has emerged. Within this framework, psilocybin is best conceptualized as a candidate intervention for secondary and tertiary prevention, aimed at attenuating symptom progression, restoring cognitive and emotional regulation, and limiting long-term functional impairment rather than preventing initial disease onset. If pursued with scientific rigor, clinical restraint, and ethical responsibility, psilocybin and related compounds may ultimately open new avenues for developmentally informed interventions that target not only symptoms, but the underlying neurobiological mechanisms contributing to ADHD and related disorders. metadata_title: Dynamic relationship and pleiotropic loci of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with sleep traits
pages: ARTICLE OPEN Dynamic relationship and pleiotropic loci of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder with sleep traits Yujuan Zu1,2, Tao Pang3, Lingxue Luo3, Chao Liufu3, Zixuan Xu3, Luxian Lv 1,2, Wenqiang Li 1,2✉and Suhua Chang 1,3✉ © The Author(s) 2026 Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder modulated by genetic and environmental factors. Approximately 20–55% of individuals with ADHD experience concurrent sleep disturbances, yet the dynamic relationship between the two and their shared genetic mechanisms remain unclear. This study analyzed 11,288 participants (52.1% male) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study using the Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children. We found a robust positive correlation between ADHD and sleep traits, though ADHD medication weakened this relationship. Latent growth curve modeling revealed that ADHD symptoms significantly impacted sleep traits with a lag effect. Polygenic risk score analyses showed significant but very small associations (explained variance ~0.28–0.30%). Pleiotropic analyses identified two loci associated with ADHD and excessive somnolence (implicating 30 genes), and cross-cohort comparisons with UK Biobank insomnia data uncovered 12 additional pleiotropic loci (98 genes) enriched in brain tissue. Functional enrichment analysis highlighted excitatory and inhibitory neuronal subtypes in visual and frontal cortices, suggesting roles in synaptic transmission and neural circuit development. Protein-protein interaction network analysis identified 10 hub genes involved in cell growth regulation and neurodevelopmental processes. This study demonstrates robust ADHD-sleep associations, with medication moderating this link, and provides preliminary insights into their shared genetic architecture. Translational Psychiatry (2026) 16:423 ; https://doi.org/10.1038/s41398-026-04166-4 INTRODUCTION Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder in children [1], characterized by symptoms such as inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. It typically emerges in childhood and can continue into adolescence and adulthood [2]. Globally, epidemiological data indicate that ADHD affects approximately 5% of children worldwide [1] and 6.5% of children in China [3]. The disorder is associated with significant challenges in daily functioning, disciplinary behavior, substance use, mental disorders, and sleep disturbances [4]. Metaanalyses [5–7] indicate that children with ADHD report significantly more subjective sleep problems than non-ADHD controls and also exhibit some objective sleep alterations, as measured by actigraphy or polysomnography. Furthermore, a meta-analysis by Cortese et al. demonstrated that these alterations are not attributable to comorbid psychiatric disorders or ADHD medication [5]. Specifically, children with ADHD often struggle with insomnia, excessive daytime sleepiness, and delayed sleep phase syndrome [8]. They also tend to exhibit higher rates of snoring, nighttime awakenings, and restlessness compared to their peers without ADHD [9]. On the other hand, sleep problems can impair cognitive functions such as attention, memory, language skills, emotional regulation, and behavioral control, potentially worsening ADHD symptoms [10]. Interestingly, research has shown that improving sleep quality can lead to a reduction in symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity symptoms [11]. Therefore, understanding the dynamic relationship between ADHD symptoms and sleep patterns is essential, as it has important implications for both clinical practice and public health. In recent years, numerous observational studies have explored the relationship between sleep traits and the clinical diagnosis or symptoms of ADHD at the behavioral level. Cross-sectional studies have shown that the severity of ADHD symptom is associated with sleep disturbances throughout the lifespan [12–15]. For example, one study investigating the link between early-life sleep and ADHD in adolescents found that sleep disturbances may be a stronger predictor of ADHD than sleep duration or sleep patterns over time [16]. Longitudinally, Shen et al. found that ADHD symptoms were associated with sleep disturbances across one or more follow-up assessments [17]. In another longitudinal study, sleep disturbances at an average age of 13 were found to predict increased ADHD symptoms 5 years later [18]. However, much of these research relied on cross-sectional or case-control designs [19], and while some longitudinal studies exist, they often suffer from limitations such as limited follow-up time points [17] or small sample sizes [18]. Building on previous findings, we recognize that understanding the relationship between ADHD and sleep must extend beyond the group level to incorporate long-term Received: 29 December 2025 Revised: 8 May 2026 Accepted: 3 June 2026 1Henan Collaborative Innovation Center of Prevention and Treatment of Mental Disorder, The Second Affiliated Hospital of Henan Medical University, Xinxiang, China. 2Henan Key Lab of Biological Psychiatry, International Joint Research Laboratory for Psychiatry and Neuroscience of Henan, Henan Medical University, Xinxiang, China. 3Peking University Sixth Hospital, Peking University Institute of Mental Health, NHC Key Laboratory of Mental Health (Peking University), National Clinical Research Center for Mental Disorders (Peking University Sixth Hospital), Beijing, China. ✉email: lwq781603@163.com; changsh@bjmu.edu.cn www.nature.com/tp Translational Psychiatry 1234567890();,:

assessment and analysis of individual differences, which is crucial in developmental neuroscience. Specifically, in the context of ADHD and sleep problems, it is crucial to better understand how sleep problems evolve over time in individuals with ADHD and whether this trajectory is influenced by variables such as ADHD medications. By distinguishing between time-invariant (betweenperson) and time-varying (within-person) effects, Latent Growth Curve Modeling (LGCM) offers a robust and flexible analytical framework for testing an array of developmental hypotheses [20]. Twin studies have demonstrated that ADHD has a heritability of approximately 74% [21]. The most recent ADHD genome-wide association studies (GWAS) identified 27 genome-wide significant loci, and single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) accounted for 14% of the heritability [22]. Previous research has indicated that the relationship between ADHD and sleep traits is shaped by both genetic and environmental factors, though the underlying mechanisms and causal relationships remain unclear [23]. Individuals with ADHD may be more susceptible to sleep disorders due to the combined influence of genetic predispositions. Twin studies [24] and ADHD GWAS have revealed a positive genetic correlation between ADHD and insomnia [25]. Additionally, Liu et al. found that insomnia is closely associated with the future development of ADHD [12]. A Mendelian Randomization study further supported a causal relationship, suggesting that insomnia, daytime napping, and short sleep duration contribute to ADHD [23]. Although the hypothesis proposed by Hvolby that shared neurobiological mechanisms contribute to both ADHD and sleep disturbances [26] is supported by evidence implicating the monoaminergic system in the pathophysiology of ADHD [27] and the regulation of sleep-wake cycles [28], the genetic underpinnings of this relationship remain poorly understood. A critical gap exists in the identification of pleiotropic SNPs or shared genetic risk factors mediating the ADHD-sleep association, precluding comorbid mechanistic insights and identify potential therapeutic targets. This underscores the need to characterize their genetic overlap and common pathways. Hence, in this study, we aimed to explore the dynamic relationship of ADHD symptoms with several sleep traits using longitudinal data and model, and to analyze whether this correlation is influenced by factors such as ADHD medications use; then we further identify shared genetic pleiotropic loci between ADHD and sleep traits to try to explain the tight associations by investigating the biological functions of these pleiotropic genes (Fig. 1). MATERIALS AND METHODS Data sets For the phenotype and dynamic correlation analyses, we utilized data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study. The ABCD Study is an ongoing longitudinal and observational research initiative designed to explore brain development and child health. It includes children recruited from 21 sites across the United States (https:// abcdstudy.org/study-sites/). The study began with a comprehensive baseline assessment (T0) of 11,880 children aged 9 to 10 years, followed by follow-up assessments at 1 to 3 years (T1, T2, T3). We included data from the ABCD Study data release 5.1. Measures ADHD symptoms and diagnosis of ADHD in ABCD. The Achenbach’s Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) is a key tool for identifying problematic behaviors in children. In this analysis, we used T-scores from the ADHD DSM-5 Scale (CBCL_ADHD) as ADHD symptom data and a binary variable for ADHD diagnosis, based on parent reports from the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (KSAD-S). ADHD patients were defined as those meeting diagnostic criteria without comorbid conditions (Supplement Methods), while controls had neither ADHD diagnosis nor comorbid conditions. continuous CBCL_ADHD T-scores. Detailed sample information is presented in Table 1. Sleep traits in ABCD. We evaluated sleep traits in children using the Sleep Disturbance Scale for Children (SDSC), a 26-item parent-rated questionnaire based on the child’s behavior over the preceding six months, which utilizes a 5-point Likert-type scale for responses. The SDSC comprises six subscales that assess different sleep-related issues [29], i) disorders of arousal or nightmares (SDSC_DA), ii) disorders of initiating and maintaining sleep (SDSC_DIMS), iii) disorders of excessive somnolence (SDSC_DOES), iv) sleep breathing disorders (SDSC_SBD), v) sleep hyperhidrosis (SDSC_SHY), and vi) sleep–wake transition disorders (SDSC_SWTD). Additionally, we included the total score (SDSC_TOTAL) as a measure of overall sleep disturbances. Higher scores indicate greater clinical severity of sleep disturbance. Details provided in the Table 1 and Supplementary Materials. Other relevant variables. Household income was categorized into three levels (<$50 K, $50K-$100 K, >$100 K). Medication use for ADHD and sleep disorders was assessed via the PhenX Toolkit [30]. A weighted daily screen time score was derived from self-reported weekday and weekend usage (details provided in the Table S1 and Supplementary Materials). Genotype data and ADHD PRS calculation. Genomic DNA from biospecimens in the ABCD database was genotyped using the Affymetrix NIDA Smoke Screen Array [31], with rigorous quality control applied to SNPs and individuals, utilizing PLINK for data processing (Supplement Methods). We computed polygenic risk score (PRS) of ADHD based on the recent ADHD GWAS [22] for each sleep trait using PRSice-2 [32]. The associations between the PRS and the target phenotypes were examined in linear regression models with age, gender, and genetic principal component (PC) 1–10 as covariates for each P-value threshold (Supplement Methods). Statistical analysis Phenotype correlation analysis. We used Pearson’s correlation to assess relationships between ADHD symptom scores and SDSC subscales/total scores at baseline and follow-up (1–3 years), with significance set at FDR < 0.05. T-tests was used to compare SDSC scores between ADHD and non-ADHD groups, using the same FDR threshold for significance. To examine the potential moderating role of ADHD medication in the relationship between ADHD symptoms and sleep problems, we performed multiple linear regression analyses. The models included sleep problem scores as the dependent variable and the interaction term between centered ADHD symptoms (to mitigate multicollinearity) and medication status (a binary variable) as the independent variable of interest, adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, household income, screen use time, and sleep medication use. We validated the baseline findings using first-year followup data and conducted sensitivity analyses stratified by sex to assess the associations separately among children with and without ADHD medication. Prior to statistical testing, normality of distribution was examined using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Some variables showed right-skewed distributions. Given the large sample size of this study, parametric tests (Pearson correlation, independent samples t-test, and linear regression) were still employed based on the central limit theorem. Latent growth curve model analysis. The latent growth curve model (LGCM) used in this study consisted of fixed and random effects to analyze sleep trait trajectories using the R package lavaan [33]. We evaluated model fit with RMSEA, SRMR, CFI, and TLI, aiming for good fit criteria. Sex, race and ADHD PRS were included as time-invariant covariates, while age, BMI, household income, sleep medication use, and ADHD symptoms, ADHD medication, and their interaction were served as time-varying covariates at four time points. This approach facilitated the disentanglement of between-person and within-person effects, allowing for a nuanced assessment of the lagged effects of factors such as ADHD symptoms and medication use on sleep. Genetic correlation analysis. We conducted PRS analysis to investigate the genetic correlation between ADHD and sleep traits. ADHD was used as base to get the best P-value threshold to predict the sleep traits (six subscales and a total score scale at baseline). Permutation n = 10000 was used to get empirical P-value. Empirical P < 0.05 was considered as significant. Identification of pleiotropic loci. We performed GWAS on SDSC traits using PLINK, adjusting for age, sex, and 10 PCs. Pleiotropic loci between ADHD and sleep traits were identified using pleiotropic analysis under the composite null hypothesis (PLACO) [34]. This approach is based on the hypothesis that a genetic variant is associated with either none or only one of the examined traits. We utilized meta-analysis summary statistics for ADHD and three GWAS summary statistics datasets for SDSC to identify shared common SNPs. Genetic variants exceeding a predefined significance threshold (single-trait p-value > 10 −4) for any trait were excluded to estimate the correlation coefficient (ρ) between Z-scores. Notably, PLACO demonstrates versatility by accommodating both independent traits and correlated summary statistics across studies, following Z-score decorrelation. To enhance power, we incorporated the GWAS summary data of insomnia data from UK Biobank (GWAS sample size N = 440,422), calculated its PRS associations with sleep traits in ABCD, and pleiotropic loci with ADHD using PLACO. Bayesian colocalization [35] (PP4 > 0.9) was used to validate the shared loci. Details are in Supplement Methods. Functional analysis of the pleiotropic loci. To characterize the function of pleiotropic loci shared by ADHD and sleep from PLACO findings, we clumped SNPs within a ± 250 kb radius and linkage disequilibrium (LD) threshold of r2>0.6 using FUMA [36]. Loci were annotated based on proximal genes, expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL), and chromatin interactions. Tissue enrichment analysis for the mapped genes was conducted with MAGMA, considering Bonferroni-corrected P < 0.05 as significant. Gene set enrichment was analyzed via Metascape with FDR < 0.05 for significance. Additionally, Web-based Cell-type Specific Enrichment Analysis of Genes (WebCSEA [37]) was used to assess the celltype specificity across 1355 human tissue-cell types with significance set at Bonferroni-corrected P-value <0.05. Furthermore, we examined the enrichment of brain cell types by using single-cell transcriptomic data from three brain regions (Lake et al., 2018). Then, the protein-protein interaction network involved by the mapped genes were obtained from String (confidence score >0.4) and the hub genes were identified from this network using the Maximal Clique Centrality (MCC) algorithm. RESULTS Phenotype correlation and effect by ADHD medication Our analysis firstly verified the fundamental phenotypic associations between ADHD symptoms and sleep traits. We observed significant positive correlations between CBCL_ADHD scores and both the total sleep score and subscales at baseline (Fig. 2A), which were consistently maintained throughout the follow-up period (Fig. 2B). This initial analysis served not only as a quality control measure, by replicating well-established effects, but also streamlined our subsequent analysis by identifying four key sleep subscales for further investigation. To quantify the differences in specific sleep traits between individuals with and without ADHD after excluding comorbidities, we conducted between-group comparisons on the four key sleep subscales (SDSC_DIMS, SDSC_DOES, SDSC_SWTD, and SDSC_TOTAL). The results confirmed that the ADHD group scored significantly higher on all these measures, with Cohen’s d values indicating strong effects (Figure S1A-D). regression models. The analysis revealed significant associations between ADHD symptoms and all four key sleep traits (SDSC_DIMS, SDSC_DOES, SDSC_SWTD, SDSC_TOTAL, Table 2, Fig. 2C). Notably, the associations for DIMS, DOES, and TOTAL sleep traits were significantly moderated by an interaction between ADHD symptoms and medication use (SDSC_DIMS: β = −0.05, FDR q = 0.007; SDSC_DOES: β = −0.04, FDR q = 9.97 × 10−4; SDSC_TOTAL: β = −0.13, FDR q = 2.29 × 10−4), indicating that the association between sleep problems and ADHD symptom severity was attenuated in medication users. These findings, including the moderating role of medication, remained consistent in one-year follow-up data (SDSC_DIMS: β = −0.05, FDR q = 2.59 × 10−3; SDSC_DOES: β = −0.03, FDR q = 0.01; SDSC_TOTAL: β = −0.09, FDR q = 2.30 × 10−3, Table S2, Fig. 2C), demonstrating their robustness and temporal stability (Table S2). Sex-stratified analyses revealed that the main associations between sleep phenotypes and ADHD symptoms were significant in both boys and girls. However, the moderating effect of medication use differed by sex. In boys, a significant interaction between ADHD symptoms and medication was observed only for the SDSC_DOES subscale (SDSC_DOES: β = −0.03, FDR q = 0.03, Table S2, Fig. 2C). In contrast, among girls, this moderating effect was significant across three phenotypes: SDSC_DIMS, SDSC_SWTD, and SDSC_TOTAL (SDSC_DIMS: β = −0.11, FDR q = 2.32 × 10−3; SDSC_SWTD: β = −0.07, FDR q = 3.60 × 10−3; SDSC_TOTAL: β = −0.22, FDR q = 7.31 × 10−4, Table S2, Fig. 2C). However, it should be noted that both ADHD symptoms and sleep characteristics were assessed using parent-reported instruments, which carries a risk of reporting bias. Longitudinal Dynamic relationship of ADHD and sleep traits To investigate whether the moderating effect of interaction on the relationship between sleep traits and ADHD exerts an impact on the subsequent year (whether a lag effect exists), we examined their dynamic relationship using latent growth curve model. We incorporated sex, race and ADHD PRS as time-invariant covariates (TIVs) in the LGCM to evaluate their influence on ADHD symptoms and sleep traits, thereby assessing between-person differences. Model fit indices were satisfactory (Table S3). Higher ADHD PRS significantly predicted the initial levels (intercept: i) of SDSC_DIMS, SDSC_DOES, and SDSC_TOTAL, suggesting increased sleep difficulties in individuals with greater ADHD genetic risk (Table S4). ADHD symptoms, medication use, and their interaction term were included as time-varying covariates (TVCs) in the model to investigate their lagged effects on sleep characteristics at the within-person level. The analysis revealed that CBCL_ADHD scores from T0 to T2 significantly predicted the four sleep traits at timepoints T1 to T3 (Fig. 3A–D, Table S4), indicating that prior ADHD symptom levels have a stable predictive value for subsequent sleep outcomes. Furthermore, the interaction term exhibited a significant lagged effect for the SDSC_DIMS and SDSC_TOTAL subscales, suggesting that ADHD medication weakens the association between ADHD symptoms and sleep problems in the subsequent year. Genetic correlation of ADHD and sleep traits At the basis of phenotype correlation, we further investigated the effects of PRS for ADHD on the risk of three sleep subscales and sleep total scale (i.e. SDSC_DIMS, SDSC_DOES, SDSC_SWTD, SDSC_TOTAL) from the ABCD database. Pleiotropic loci of ADHD and sleep traits We investigated the pleiotropic loci between ADHD and sleep traits (SDSC_DIMS, SDSC_DOES, SDSC_TOTAL) based on genetic correlations identified in the PRS analysis. Firstly, GWAS revealed 2, 4, and 3 significant loci for SDSC_DIMS, SDSC_DOES, and SDSC_TOTAL, respectively, mapping to 64 genes (Figure S3A-C, Table S5). Then, PLACO analysis of the GWAS summary data showed 0, 2, 0 significant loci for ADHD and SDSC_DIMS, SDSC_DOES, SDSC_TOTAL, respectively (PPLACO < 5 × 10−8). The lead SNPs for the pleiotropic loci were rs7942482 and rs1790123. Notably, rs1790123, a key pleiotropic locus on chromosome 12, mapped to 30 genes by positional, eQTL or chromatin interaction (Table 3), including 7 genes mapped by cis-eQTL SNPs who influence gene expression levels, 27 genes mapped by 3D DNA–DNA interactions, and 7 genes were annotated by both eQTL mapping and chromatin interactions (Fig. 4C), though it did not reach significance in the original GWAS (P > 5 × 10−8). Due to the small sample size of the ABCD database, we further used the GWAS summary data of insomnia from UK Biobank for PLACO analysis. Given inherent differences in age, phenotype definition, and cohort design between pediatric sleep phenotypes in ABCD and adult insomnia GWAS data from UK Biobank, the following results should be regarded as exploratory. Firstly, PRS analysis showed significant positive correlations between UKB insomnia PRS and SDSC_DIMS/SDSC_TOTAL (Figure S2E-F), while LD Score regression revealed a strong genetic correlation between ADHD and insomnia (P < 4.8 × 10−37; rg = 0.32, s.e.=0.03). Then, we explored shared pleiotropic loci between insomnia and ADHD using PLACO, identifying 14 lead SNPs across 12 genomic risk loci (Fig. 4B, Table 3). Among these, two loci were significantly associated with ADHD and insomnia in the original GWAS, two with only ADHD, three with only insomnia, and seven with neither. These loci mapped to 98 genes through positional, eQTL or chromatin interaction analyses (Table 3), including 27 ciseQTL SNPs, 74 chromatin interaction genes, and 14 genes from both methods (Fig. 4D, Figure S5). Bayesian colocalization tests were conducted on the two ADHD and SDSC_DOES pleiotropic loci and fourteen ADHD and insomnia pleiotropic loci (Table 3) from PLACO results. Function of pleiotropic loci of ADHD and sleep traits Following pleiotropic locus analysis, exploratory tissue enrichment analysis using MAGMA revealed that ADHD and SDSC_DOES PLACO results were enriched in the pituitary (Figure S6A). These observations align with previous reports that dysregulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical axis and circadian rhythms may be relevant to sleep regulation and attention [38]. GO enrichment analysis showed significant associations with translation factor activity, negative regulation of organelle, centrosome, transcription coregulator activityand mitotic cell cycle (Figure S6B). Enriched tissue-cell types included myeloid and erythroid progenitors, hematopoietic stem cells, and plasma cells, all crucial for immune function and linked to sleep [39] and ADHD [40] (Figure S6C). As an exploratory extension, pleiotropic loci analysis for ADHD and insomnia revealed enrichment in brain-related tissues, particularly the brain cortex, frontal cortex (BA9), and anterior cingulate cortex (BA24) (Fig. 5A). GO enrichment analysis highlighted pathways potentially relevant to synapse organization and regulation of growth (Fig. 5B). The 98 mapped genes were significantly enriched in Lake_2017_VisualCortex_Ex5a, consistent with a potential involvement of excitatory neurons in the visual cortex, a region previously associated with for ADHD [41] and sleep [42] (Figure S6D). To explore potential functional themes among the 128 genes shared between ADHD and sleep problems (SDSC_DOES and insomnia), we performed exploratory analyses using brain transcriptome data to define their enrichment patterns across diverse neural cell types [43]. The results revealed a significant enrichment of these genes in eight cell types in the prefrontal cortex (six excitatory and two inhibitory neurons), seventeen in the visual cortex (eleven excitatory and six inhibitory neurons), and one microglial cell (Mic) in the cerebellum (Fig. 5C). Furthermore, we constructed a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network for the 128 shared genes. Genes with literature evidence of association with neurodevelopmental diseases or sleep related traits were marked with different colors (Table S6). Using the Maximal Clique Centrality (MCC) algorithm, we identified 10 hub genes. Functional enrichment analysis indicated that these 10 hub genes are involved in growth-related pathways, specifically regulating cell growth (Fig. 5D). DISCUSSION At the descriptive phenotypic level, this study revealed a significant positive correlation between ADHD symptom scores and sleep scale scores over time, particularly for SDSC_DIMS, SDSC_DOES, SDSC_SWTD, and SDSC_TOTAL. Children with higher ADHD symptom scores associated with more severe difficulties in sleep initiation, maintenance, excessive daytime sleepiness, and sleep-wake transitions. These findings are consistent with prior research demonstrating that ADHD, as one of the most extensively studied neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), is frequently associated with significant alterations in sleep patterns, including difficulties in falling asleep, impaired sleep maintenance, frequent nocturnal arousals, and daytime lethargy [44, 45]. Building on these descriptive phenotypic observations, we further conducted sex-stratified multiple linear regression analyses to examine the relationship between ADHD and sleep, particularly the moderating role of medication. As expected, ADHD symptoms consistently demonstrated a robust positive association with sleep problems. Interestingly, we found a significant negative interaction between ADHD symptoms and medication use, indicating that medication attenuated the association between ADHD symptoms and sleep. This indicates that although the medication itself may have some side effects on sleep (as shown by its significant β), it moderates the association between ADHD core symptoms and sleep problems. more pronounced in girls (Fig. 2), despite literature suggesting that girls with ADHD are less likely to receive pharmacological treatment [46, 47]. This finding may potentially stem from the instability inherent in the identified subgroups. Of note, the outcome measures in the present study are not objective sleep phenotypes, nor do they represent clinically defined sleep disorders. Building on these longitudinal lagged association analyses, we used LGCM to investigate the temporal dynamics of ADHD symptoms on sleep traits. A key strength of this approach is its ability to distinguish between-person effects (time-invariant factors) and within-person effects (time-varying factors), which allowed us to examine sex differences, genetic influences, and associations with ADHD medication use in a manner not commonly applied in previous research. In the model incorporating time-invariant covariates (i.e. sex, PRS_ADHD), significant sex differences were observed at the between-person level. Girls showed significantly higher initial levels (intercepts) of disorders of initiating and maintaining sleep (SDSC_DIMS, Table S2) and disorders of excessive somnolence (SDSC_DOES, Table S2) than boys. Consistent associations were also detected between ADHD polygenic risk score (PRS) and baseline intercepts for SDSC_DIMS and SDSC_DOES. Therefore, we hypothesize that genetic susceptibility to ADHD may influence an individual’s baseline level of these specific sleep problems. Regarding within-person effects, consistent and significant lagged associations were observed across time points, such that ADHD symptoms, ADHD medication use, and their interaction on subsequent sleep problems. These longitudinal associations support temporally ordered relationships but not causal effects. Building upon exploratory post-GWAS analyses, we further investigated pleiotropic loci to generate hypotheses regarding the potential shared biological mechanisms underlying ADHD and sleep traits. Our analysis identified 30 genes associated with pleiotropic loci linking ADHD and SDSC_DOES, along with 98 genes associated with ADHD and insomnia. Enrichment analysis across neural cell types (Fig. 5C) revealed diverse excitatory neuron subtypes in both the visual cortex (VC) and frontal cortex (FC), including deep-layer subtypes Ex5a, Ex5b, Ex6a, and Ex6b. Notably, these deep-layer excitatory neurons are critical for long-range corticocortical and corticofugal projections [48] involved in executive control and arousal regulation, core neurobiological domains disrupted in both ADHD and sleep disturbances. Notably, we identified VC-specific subtypes Ex3b, Ex3c, and Ex3d in the VC, corroborating previous findings [43]. These VC excitatory neurons highly expressed markers such as SLC17A7 [49], which are associated with synaptic signaling and visual perception. Within established frameworks of circadian and visual pathway regulation of sleep, the visual cortex serves as a key relay for photic input to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) [50], and aberrant excitatory signaling in this region has been proposed to disrupt circadian entrainment and sleep–wake timing frequently observed in ADHD [51]. Furthermore, NREM sleep modulates neural synchrony in the visual cortex, thereby influencing cognitive performance [52]. Our analysis revealed significant enrichment of inhibitory neurons in the frontal cortex and visual cortex. Notably, the In6 subtype was prominently enriched in the visual cortex. The In6a subpopulation specifically encircles layer 4 [43], which is the primary target of thalamic visual inputs and, as noted earlier, is functionally implicated in synaptic neurotransmission and sleep [53]. Enrichment of inhibitory neuron subtypes such as In6a points to disrupted regional E/I balance as a shared cellular substrate for both ADHD pathophysiology and sleep dysregulation [51]. Prefrontal and visual cortical E/I imbalance is known to impair topdown inhibitory control and promote cortical hyperarousal, both of which contribute to attentional deficits and difficulties initiating and maintaining sleep [54]. Following the pleiotropic locus analysis, and through comprehensive literature review and database analysis, we determined that 58 of these genes have established associations with neurodevelopmental disorders, psychiatric conditions, sleeprelated phenotypes, or immune system functions (Table S6). Protein-protein interaction network analysis using the STRING database suggested a complex network comprising 97 genes, with several functionally significant modules potentially emerging (Fig. 5D). The primary module (highlighted in blue) comprises the 10 hub genes identified by the Maximal Clique Centrality (MCC) algorithm, which may point to enrichment in growth-related pathways that could imply relevance to neurodevelopmental processes. The gene NPRL2 encodes a critical component of the GATOR1 complex, which serves as a key negative regulator of the mTOR signaling pathway in the central nervous system. Together with DEPDC5 and NPRL3, NPRL2 contributes to fundamental neurodevelopmental processes such as neuronal maturation, circuit formation, and synaptic plasticity [55]. Loss-of-function mutations in NPRL2 are directly linked to Sleep-related Hypermotor Epilepsy, suggesting a potential genetic link between mTOR pathway regulation and the pathophysiology of this sleep-specific neurological disorder [56]. CACNA2D2, a candidate gene for neurological disorders including developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, ataxia, and cerebellar atrophy [57], is linked to early infantile epileptic encephalopathy. Given its role in calcium channel function and neuronal excitability, CACNA2D2 may represent a hypothetical candidate for disrupted synaptic transmission and neural circuit stability that might underlie ADHD and sleep disturbances. SEMA3F, a member of the semaphoring III family involved in axon guidance during neuronal development, has been linked to autism [58]. Its role in neural circuit formation raises the hypothesis that it may contribute to ADHD and sleep comorbidity by affecting the development of brain regions involved in attention and circadian regulation. HYAL1 and HYAL2 play pivotal roles in nervous system development, neural function maintenance [53, 59], and sleep-related disorders. Of particular relevance to sleep medicine, HYAL1 is associated with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) [22, 60, 61]. Together, these genes form an interconnected network that functionally integrates key biological processes—such as neurotransmitter regulation, synaptic function, and neurodevelopment—which are linked to the pathophysiology of ADHD and sleep physiology. Previous research has conceptualized neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) as “synaptopathies” or “connectomies” and exploring their relationship with sleep and circadian rhythms [62]. “Synaptopathies” potentially contribute to sleep disturbances [63] and “connectomies” associated with cognitive, behavioral, and sleep-related dysfunctions. These observations generate testable hypotheses for future mechanistic studies. Our study employed a longitudinal, multi-layered analytical approach. Our phenotypic findings extend previous research [17, 18] by systematically examining this association across multiple time points, subpopulations, and under varying medication statuses. By employing LGCM and incorporating phenotypic factors, we were able to model developmental trajectories while distinguishing between-person differences from within-person changes. This strategy enabled an integrated investigation of ADHD, medication use, and their interaction on sleep traits in the ABCD cohort, providing a potentially useful framework for future longitudinal studies. Evidence suggests that sleep-targeted interventions improve sleep quality and broader symptom profiles in NDDs [64]. In the genetic component of our study, we identified pleiotropic loci and risk genes associated with both conditions. These findings add to the existing understanding of the genetic architecture link ADHD and sleep disturbances. Collectively, our phenotypic and genetic analyses provide a perspective on the interplay between ADHD and sleep. Our study has several limitations. First, the predominantly European sample limits generalizability to more diverse populations. Second, while we used the parent-reported SDSC to assess sleep traits as a continuous variable, this approach does not capture clinically defined sleep disorders nor objective sleep parameters, and both ADHD symptoms and sleep problems were derived from parent-reported measures, introducing substantial risk of shared informant bias and shared-method variance that may inflate observed associations. Therefore, future studies should incorporate objective measures such as actigraphy or polysomnography to validate these findings. Third, our post-GWAS analyses combined child sleep phenotypes from the ABCD cohort with adult insomnia GWAS data from the UK Biobank. Although this strategy was employed to enhance power by leveraging large-scale adult sleep GWAS for exploratory pleiotropic mapping, it introduces considerable heterogeneity in age groups, sleep phenotype definitions, and cohort characteristics. Sample size limitations and age differences between datasets may hinder the identification of pleiotropic loci and their biological functions. Accordingly, these cross-cohort genetic results are regarded as strictly exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory evidence. Lastly, the longitudinal analysis is constrained by the short time span and lack of data during adolescence, potentially affecting generalizability. The brief follow-up period fails to capture the full developmental trajectory of ADHD and sleep problems into later adolescence. Missing data across this key maturational stage limits our ability to assess whether observed associations change with age or pubertal development. As a result, the generalizability of our temporal and developmental findings to older adolescent populations remains unclear. These limitations highlight the need for future research with more diverse populations, extended timeframes, and clinical sleep disorder assessments to better understand the ADHD-sleep relationship. CONCLUSION Our findings suggest that ADHD medication mitigates the association between ADHD symptoms and sleep problems. The identified pleiotropic loci offer hypothesis-generating insights into the shared biological underpinnings of this comorbidity, which may provide directions for future research into clinical approaches for comorbid ADHD and sleep disturbances. Comparing qualitative thematic analysis and machine-based topic modelling in the analysis of autistic and ADHD young people’s accounts of emotions Steve Lukito 1,13, Lifang Li 2,3,13, Susie Chandler 1, Myrofora Kakoulidou 1,4,5, Georgia Pavlopoulou 4,6, Maciej Matejko 1, Isabel Jackson1, Beta Balwani1, Tiegan Boyens1, Dorian Poulton 1, Luke Harvey-Nguyen 1, Amber Johnson 1, Daniel Stahl 2, Angus Roberts 2,14, Edmund J. S. Sonuga-Barke 1,14 & the RE-STAR Team* Systematic analysis of interview data can provide important insights into how young people experience and interpret their emotions. Both human-led qualitative (e.g., thematic analysis) and machine-driven quantitative (e.g., natural language processing [NLP]) analytical approaches are available, but their solutions are rarely compared. Interview responses by 57 neurodivergent adolescents to questions about their emotions, previously analysed using reflexive thematic analysis (RTA), were submitted to Topic Modelling (TM). Topic labels were developed in collaboration with neurodivergent co-researchers to ground their meaning in the lived experience of neurodivergent communities. Topics were mapped to RTA themes or subthemes to examine their proximities. Topicbased cluster analysis was used to identify participant groupings with similar topic distributions. TM revealed 10 interpretable and meaningful emotion-related topics – some closely overlapping with and others differing from the RTA themes. TM topics differentiated the young people’s emotional experiences at school from those in other settings. TM and RTA resulted in overlapping and different insights into the meaning of neurodivergent young people’s accounts of their emotions. Our findings demonstrate the potential use of TM in interview analysis and might suggest a potential complementarity between the TM topics and RTA themes, to be further explored using more advanced algorithms and a more sophisticated NLP implementation. Keywords Autism, ADHD, Reflexive thematic analysis, Topic modelling, Emotional regulation Neurodivergent young people who are autistic and/or have attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are at an increased likelihood of mental health difficulties, compared to neurotypical peers1–4. Among these groups, the experience of strong negative emotions and emotional responses5–7 are common and have been shown to mediate the emergence of depression [8–10, e.g.,11]. The RE-STAR (Regulating Emotion – Strengthening Adolescent Resilience) research programme has taken a participatory research approach and placed the neurodivergent young people’s experiences at the heart of its inquiry. We interviewed autistic secondary mainstream school pupils and/or those with ADHD about their emotional lives using a semi-structured interview schedule co-produced with neurodivergent young people. We first explored the young people’s insights into their emotions by using reflexive thematic analysis (RTA)13. RTA is an approach to qualitative analysis where researchers actively construct patterns of meaning, or themes, within texts, while emphasising self-awareness and critical reflection, and acknowledging their positionality14, which can play multiple important roles in translational research15. Our RTA of the above young people’s interview scripts revealed themes relating to: (1) the nature of upsetting events that bring negative emotions in young people, and (2) the sorts of activities or supports that help the young people manage these emotions16,17. These provided a basis for the development of a new self-report measure of emotional burden associated with schoolbased upsetting events18. In this paper, we contrast this with a quantitative machine-learning approach called topic modelling (TM). TM is a statistical technique used to identify hidden themes or ‘topics’ in large collections of text. It works by analysing vocabulary and topic distributions across documents, typically in a large collection19,20, allowing the algorithm to group related terms and to assign separate topics to each document. TM is one of many techniques used in natural language processing (NLP) – the computational analysis and representation of natural language text for various applications21. Machine learning and modern NLP are data-driven, deriving outputs from the empirical evidence in the textual input, rather than from a theoretical understanding of the text. TM uses an unsupervised machine learning technique, in that it applies an algorithm to generate a statistical model of text from previously unseen data, without the benefit of training, prior data labelling, or supervision from humanlabelled examples of similar textual data. Unlike primarily human-led qualitative analysis, which can be a prolonged and iterative process, especially during the coding stages leading to the derivation of themes, TM can be applied to large datasets with relative ease, forming topics with a high degree of replicability, which can then be interpreted and labelled by humans to ensure that they are contextually meaningful22. Despite these strengths, TM does have the disadvantage of requiring large quantities of text for optimal performance, e.g., those derived from discourses in online forums or social media [e.g.,23–25], but its potential use in conjunction with qualitative research, typically conducted with fewer participants, has been proposed recently [see e.g.,26–28]. Notably, drawing a degree of equivalence between topics and themes, Gillies and colleagues26 outlined several possible workflows for combining TM and qualitative research, including, among others, the use of TM topics as a seed or starting point for thematic analysis or the use of qualitative themes derived from a subset of data as a seed for running a subsequent topic model on the remaining data26. While TM’s potential in qualitative enquiry involving a high volume of free-text qualitative datasets (e.g., > 500 participants), too large for a qualitative researcher to manage, has been demonstrated23,24, this is less obvious in studies involving verbal interaction like interviews, which typically have considerably fewer participants, e.g., between a minimum of 12 and as many as 50–60 individuals29–31. Only a few TM studies involving this kind of data currently exist in the literature. For instance, Bastiaansen and colleagues32 compared qualitative themes with TM topics from unstructured interviews with 13 young people about their experiences as siblings of neurodivergent adolescents, while Miyaoka and colleagues33 compared themes generated from a ‘pure’ and TM-augmented thematic analysis on focus group conversations of 16 teachers about students’ experience using maths technology. Both found overlaps between qualitative themes and topics or themes generated or augmented by TM, as well as unique output from the respective analyses, although outputs from TM were typically less nuanced than the human-generated themes. Both studies involved data derived from a relatively small sample. Similar exploration involving a larger sample size, where qualitative analysis is more effortful but leads to greater thematic nuances and diversity, could serve as a useful contrast. The larger participant sample size also enables more sophisticated quantitative explorations than in previous studies32,33. Considering the potential overlap and unique contributions from each methodology, we designed a study to investigate the similarities and differences between the TM topics and reflexive themes following the RTA investigation. Using responses from interviews with 57 autistic young people and/or those with ADHD, we conducted an exploratory study investigating similarities or differences between the TM and RTA approaches. We asked: (i) if we could extract meaningful topics from the interview transcripts from these young people using TM; (ii) whether these topics could be relevant clinically, for instance, whether they are associated with the young people’s diagnosis or contextual background, and (iii) how the TM findings compared with the conventional RTA methods. We first applied TM to the young people’s responses to interview questions to generate topics and inspect their contents for clinical relevance. We further investigated whether the distribution of such topics among participants clustered them in a way that was associated with their diagnosis and other characteristics. Finally, we examined how these topics relate, or map, to the RTA themes and subthemes. Methods Study design This study utilised TM in secondary analyses of semi-structured interviews from “My Emotions and Me” study, which explored the emotional experiences of autistic young people and/or those with ADHD16. Interview schedules were co-produced with autistic young adults and/or those with ADHD aged 18–25 years, members of RE-STAR Youth Researcher Panel (Y-RP)34 and were administered in school-aged students to explore: (1) what provokes negative emotions in everyday life, and (2) what helps young people to manage the emotions. Each interview took place online with an experienced post-doctoral level researcher (MK/SL) for approximately 90 minutes. The study received ethics approval from UK National Health Service Research Ethics Committee (22/NI/0017) and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Participants Participants were 57 mainstream secondary school students aged 11 to 15 years (Mage ± SD = 13.0 ± 1.36 years; 19 female) and with sufficient use and understanding of spoken English to complete the interviews. Nine participants (15.8%) were on free school meals, 14 (24.6%) were non-white. Twenty-one had a diagnosis of autism, 24 had ADHD, and 12 had autism + ADHD. Thirty-two (56.1%) received at least one medication. Psychostimulants were the most common, taken by 20 (35.1%) participants with ADHD or with autism + ADHD (Table 1). The participants were recruited through autism and ADHD charities, social media, and the South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust. Reflexive thematic analyses The RTA was fully described in a separate publication16. Briefly, individual interview accounts were transcribed and analysed using NVivo 1.6.1 (QSR International Pty Ltd). The analysis steps consisted of researchers’ familiarisation with the interview transcripts, development of codes related to the research questions, and the generation of interview subthemes and themes, along with their nuances based on Y-RP input13. These were further checked by a subset of participants, reflecting our commitment to participatory rights-based research35. RTA yielded shared themes across the diagnostic groups (i.e., autism, ADHD, autism + ADHD) around everyday upsetting experiences including: (1) ‘under-/over-stimulation and sensory mismatch’, consisting of the subthemes ‘over-stimulated’ and ‘under-stimulated’; (2) ‘social dislocation, alienation and conflict’, consisting of the subthemes of ‘stigma, conflict and victimisation’ and ‘a mismatch of salience’, i.e., the mismatching of expectations or perceptions of events between others and the young person; (3) ‘experience of hiding one’s true self, the need to mask’, consisting of the subthemes ‘efforts to protect others from my feelings’ and ‘a constant need to protect self from others’ reactions’; and (4) ‘self-doubt, loathing, embarrassment’, consisting of the subthemes ‘being invisible and dismissed’, and ‘guilt and embarrassment when help is needed’16. Furthermore, responses to the question of what helps to manage negative emotions revealed three broad themes: (5) ‘what helps prevent experiences from becoming upsetting’, consisting of the subthemes ‘connections and acceptance over rules and expectations to fit in’ and ‘self-care as protective practice’; (6) ‘managing emotional responses during periods of upset’, consisting of the subthemes ‘affirmation by and “check-ins” from others’, ‘self-directed regulation: autonomy and action during distress’ and ‘letting it out: physical and emotional release’; and, finally, the theme (7) ‘leveraging own strengths – drawing strength from “within”’, i.e., using the strengths that individuals possess to be self-reliant and resilient17 Topic modelling and cluster analysis plan TM commenced after preliminary RTA themes were generated to minimise the influence of the TM on our primary qualitative analysis. TM analysis consisted of four steps (Fig. 1). The first two steps were led by an independent computer scientist (LL). The remaining steps were led by the first author (SL), who participated as a coder in the earlier part of the RTA. Inputs were sought from Y-RP members at different stages (Fig. 1). Step 1, data preparation, comprised several pre-processing stages applied across documents. Following Bastiaansen and colleagues32, a single document was defined as an interviewee’s response to a question or an utterance instead of the entire interview. We chose this approach to improve the stability and interpretability of the topic model despite the limited number of participants by TM standards. The pre-processing stages were conducted using the Python package Sklearn36, and involved: (i) Tokenisation, i.e., dividing text from each interview response into a collection of single words (tokens); (ii) Case conversion, i.e., transforming all words into lower cases; (iii) Stop-word removal, i.e., removing common English words that were not useful for TM, (e.g., prepositions, numbers as identified using the Python nltk library), extended to include additional terms identified in the data: “um”, “oh”, “okay”, “mhm”, “ah”, “uh”, “yes”, “get”, “yep”, “yeah”, “no”, “hm”, “wow”, “.”, “?”, “-”, “-”, “:”, “mm”, and “oop”; (iv) Lemmatisation, i.e., generalising the text data by mapping all words to their base form (e.g., ‘walked’ or ‘walking’ becomes ‘walk’); and (v) Creation of a Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) model, in which words are assigned a frequency adjusted according to their capacity to exert influence in the document, based on both their frequency in an individual document and across all the documents37. Following previous approaches, we removed terms with less than 1% and more than 50% frequency in the documents [see e.g.,38,39]. In Step 2, TM was performed across all documents, i.e., responses to questions, blind to the RTA themes. The unsupervised Bi-term TM (BTM) was carried out using the Python package bitermplus40]. The BTM algorithm was selected instead of the traditionally used Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA). The BTM typically outperforms LDA when modelling short text in microblogging posts (e.g., tweets) with sparse word co-occurrence40,41, which are comparable in length to our young people’s verbal utterances/responses. coherence from open-ended forms of such posts, including consumer surveys and disaster-related tweets, than the LDA42,43, with higher efficiency41 and accuracy44. Unlike the LDA, the BTM models the co-occurrence patterns of (unordered) word pairs instead of looking at single words, and across the whole set of documents, which is assumed to contain a mixture of topics, instead of focusing on separate documents. Each word pair or bi-term is assumed to be drawn from a specific topic, and the BTM can process overlapping and hierarchical topics, offering a greater flexibility to modelling topics in this context compared to the LDA40,41. The decision of how many topics were optimal per individual and across the dataset was informed by their perplexity and coherence scores, calculated by the bitermplus package45,46. The number of topics associated with the overall lowest perplexity while maintaining coherence was tested in 2 to 14 plausible numbers of topics. In Step 3, we explored whether topics might be associated with participant clusters with meaningful characteristics such as their diagnosis. This was performed using R 4.1.1 on the RStudio 2023.12.1 using the package Cluster47. We first performed a cluster analysis to explore groups of individuals with similar distributions of topic frequencies or “topic profiles” (i.e., the counts of each topic divided by the number of counts of all topics across documents in a participant’s interview). The cluster analysis was performed blind to the participants’ identity. We used the k-medoids clustering or partitioning around the medoids (PAM) due to its robustness against outliers48, and since it produced replicable clusters when tested using simulated data with a well-defined group partition (Supplements). Based on the literature demonstrating differences in the emotional expression and regulation difficulties in autistic young people and/or those with ADHD7,16,49, we explored a potential emergence of k = 2 or 3 clusters among the participants. The participant grouping into k = 2 clusters could, for instance, reflect distinctive emotional experiences of autistic adolescents or those with ADHD, where the autism + ADHD group has combined features of the two clusters. In contrast, k = 3 could reflect three distinct clusters of emotional experiences distinct to each diagnosis [see also50,51], although other predictors could also explain the clusters. Before the cluster analyses, topic frequency data were scaled by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. They were subsequently transformed towards normality using the Yeo-Johnson transformation. We thus clustered the participants based on their scaled and normalised topic frequency data. The mapping of cluster memberships in the two- and three-cluster solution was explored using cross-tabulation. The degree to which clusters were well defined was assessed using the Silhouette and Caliński-Harbasz (CH) indices52,53. To evaluate the robustness of the clusters, we performed bootstrap resampling with 1000 iterations and computed both adjusted rand index (ARI) and normalised mutual information (NMI)54,55 for each resampled solution. Following the cluster formation, we further explored whether cluster memberships were predicted by participant diagnosis or other potential explanatory variables such as age, sex, medication status, and the identity of the researcher interviewing the participant. This was performed using Chi-square analysis for categorical predictors, or logistic regression for continuous predictors. We first predicted cluster memberships using the predictors separately. Then, to examine the specificity of association between predictors and clusters, the significantly associated predictors with cluster memberships in the first stage were entered simultaneously in a single model to predict clusters in a second-stage analysis. Model fit was assessed using McFadden pseudo-R256. To further characterise the clusters, we compared the frequencies of each topic across them twice, adjusting for the interviewer’s identity in the second comparison. In this explorative study, we did not correct for multiple comparisons across the topics57, but post-hoc comparisons among clusters were adjusted using Bonferroni correction. Since the association between clusters and diagnosis was confounded by the interviewers’ identity, we also conducted cross-tabulation and a chi-square test post-hoc for the association between these variables. In Step 4, in line with the participatory research framework, academic researchers and Y-RP members collaborated as domain experts to label topics, thus incorporating the authentic voice and neurodivergent positionality in this process. The topic labelling involved collaborative examination and interpretation of topics in three 1-hour sessions. The first session focused on generating topic labels from the top 20 words and the word co-occurrence network representing each topic (Fig. 2). Labelling exercise continued to the second session, alongside discussions of the topics’ potential relations with the RTA preliminary themes. Topic labels were refined further by academic researchers through close reading of documents informing each topic58. In the third session, academic researchers and Y-RP members discussed the final labels and the interpretation of findings. Once the topic labels were decided, as an additional exploration, academic researchers examined the mapping between topics and themes to better understand their similarities and differences by assigning one RTA theme to the documents informing each topic. We then qualitatively inspected each topic distribution across themes, focusing on themes consisting of more than 14.3% of documents from each topic, the chance level for a document to be distributed across the seven themes. Topics and themes The ten topics were labelled: (1) ‘Sensory stimulation and experience’, (2) ‘Struggle to maintain focus and interest’, (3) ‘Engaging in learning and leisure activities’, (4) ‘After-school relaxation or obligation’, (5) ‘Stressful situations at school’, (6) ‘Experience and expressions of emotions’, (7) ‘Navigating around friendships and peer relations’, (8) ‘Time, changes, and emotional experience’, (9) ‘Struggle to decide under pressure’, and (10) ‘Managing annoyance, frustration and anger’. Example topic documents are in Table S3. TM topics and labels, RTA themes and subthemes, and the percentages of topic documents reflecting each theme are shown in Fig. 3. Within each topic, documents were related to at least one theme above the chance level of 14.3% among the documents. Topics 1, ‘sensory stimulation and experience’; 2, ‘struggle to maintain focus and interest’; and 9, ‘struggle to decide under pressure’ stood out in their relations with the theme ‘under-/ over-stimulation and sensory mismatch’. Furthermore, Topics 1 and 9, which described the feeling of being overwhelmed, aligned with the RTA subtheme ‘over-stimulated’ (Table S3a, i), while Topic 2, which was related to classroom boredom, aligned with the subtheme ‘under-stimulated’ (Table S3b). In addition, Topics 1, 2 and 9 were related to a few other themes, albeit to a much less extent: Topics 1 and 9 contained documents reflecting the theme ‘managing emotional responses during periods of upset’, while Topic 2 contained some documents reflecting the theme ‘leveraging own strengths’, reflecting conversations about hyper-focusing (Table 3a). Both Topics 3, ‘engaging in learning and leisure activities’, and 6, ‘experience and expressions of emotions’, relate more strongly to ‘what helps prevent experiences from becoming upsetting’ and ‘managing emotional responses during periods of upset’ than other themes. Topic 3 documents appeared related to ‘what helps prevent experiences from becoming upsetting’ more strongly than ‘managing emotional responses during periods of upset’—it also related to a lesser extent to ‘self-doubt, loathing and embarrassment’, whereas Topic 6 documents showed a reverse pattern. Perhaps learning and leisure occurred more likely in the absence of upset, or to have a preventative role against upset, instead of as a way to manage emotions during upset. Contrastingly, emotional expressions were more likely experienced while managing upsets, and less so when they were prevented. Topics 4, ‘after-school relaxation or obligation’, and 5, ‘stressful situations at school’ differentiated between school and after-school settings (e.g., home) in relation to the young people’s emotional experience. Topic 4 was related strongly to ‘what helps prevent experiences from becoming upsetting’ and ‘managing emotional responses during periods of upset’, suggesting a restorative/supportive role of after-school settings for the young people. To a lesser extent, Topic 4 was also related to ‘social dislocation, alienation, and conflict’, reflecting the conflicts associated with parent-imposed obligations (Table S3d). Topic 5 was related primarily to ‘social dislocation, alienation, and conflict’, aligned with the subthemes ‘stigma, conflict and victimisation’ and ‘a mismatch of salience’; and to a much lesser extent with the theme ‘what helps prevent experiences from becoming upsetting’, reflecting the predominantly hostile experiences at school (Table S3e). Topic 7 ‘navigating around friendships and peer relations’ was related to ‘social dislocation, alienation, and conflict’, ‘self-doubt, loathing and embarrassment’, and ‘what helps prevent experiences from becoming upsetting’, denoting the ambivalent role of peers in young people’s lives – some were sources of upsets and self-doubts, while others helped prevent them. Topics 8 ‘time, changes and emotional experience’ and 10 ‘managing annoyance, frustration, and anger’ were related primarily with ‘managing emotional responses during periods of upset’. Topic 8 highlighted the dynamics of the experiences, such as their lengths and changes. Both topics also contained documents expressing ‘social dislocation, alienation, and conflict’, reinforcing their proximity to upset. Discussion We explored the similarities and differences of outputs from TM and RTA used for analysing transcripts of semi-structured interviews with 57 autistic adolescents and/or those with ADHD, considered a large sample for qualitative interviews29,30 although relatively small for TM. As a secondary data exploration, TM was performed independently from, and commenced after, the generation of reflexive themes that have been published elsewhere16,17. We identified ten TM topics, some closely mapped with, and others unrelated to RTA themes or subthemes. The topics appear associated with diagnostic status, related to a high proportion of participants with ADHD in one cluster, although this was potentially confounded by the study interviewers’ identity. Topics identified through TM generally represent broad concepts comparable to the RTA themes. Some topics map well to the RTA themes or subthemes. For instance, the topics ‘sensory stimulation and experience’, ‘struggle to decide under pressure’, and ‘struggle to maintain focus and interest’ are part of the RTA theme ‘under-/over-stimulation and sensory mismatch’ and its subthemes. and anger’ resembles the theme ‘managing responses during periods of upset’, and its subtheme ‘letting it out: physical and emotional release’ resembles the topic ‘experience and expressions of emotions. These resemblances are interesting, especially since the chosen TM algorithms are ignorant of our research questions about everyday upsetting experiences and what helps manage them in neurodivergent young people. Indeed, topics like ‘after-school relaxation or obligation’, ‘navigating around friendships and peer relations’, or ‘managing annoyance, frustration and anger’, for example, include a mix of themes related to both questions, rather than being structured around each one separately. Such mixtures might relate to the reduced nuance of the TM topics compared to the RTA themes, which have been discussed previously32,33. This highlights the need for more sophisticated algorithms, or the inclusion of additional steps in our methods, to separate documents relevant to each research question before beginning the TM process. Some TM topics explicitly reveal the role of settings and temporal dynamics in the emotional experiences of the young people. The topics ‘stressful situations at school’ and ‘after-school relaxation or obligations’ particularly illustrate a contrast between the predominantly negative experiences of neurodivergent young people at school and the more balanced challenges outside school, where supportive influences are more present. This positions school as a particularly challenging environment for neurodivergent young people, aligning with the frequently reported school-related distress among the student subpopulation59–61 and providing post facto support for the RE-STAR team’s focus on understanding the emotional burden of neurodivergent young people at school18,62. Our topics differ from the RTA themes that focus on the phenomenology of the experience but do not emphasise the distinct patterns of supportive and negative emotional experiences across settings, suggesting a potential complementarity of the two outputs. The themes ‘experience of hiding one’s true self’, ‘self-doubt, loathing, and embarrassment’, and ‘leveraging own strengths’ bear no resemblance to any topics. The topic-theme map also shows relatively infrequent occurrences of these themes across topics. This could be because, first, terms underlying the themes were discussed less frequently during the interviews, and consequently, the topics were ‘drowned out’, and second, especially for the theme of hiding or masking, its expression might be more implicit and use more varied terms, of which the semantic connections are lost to the machine. In these instances, human positionality and/or interpretations — shaped by the literature63–65 and the lived experiences of the young people in this study — have surpassed our inadequately trained machine algorithms in capturing the full richness of the neurodivergent experience. This was partially mitigated in our novel approach by incorporating neurodivergent positionality during topic labelling and results interpretation. Topic labels co-constructed by academic researchers and neurodivergent youth co-researchers from reduced data (e.g., word co-occurrence and top 20 representative words) and subsequent closed reading of the interview response documents are imbued by the reflexivity of the young people who are familiar with the context, therefore crucially, foregrounding the topic interpretation on the lived experience of the neurodivergent community. Exploratory attempts to quantify relations between topics and clinical diagnoses yielded inconclusive but interesting findings. The two-cluster solution had better separation and offered more parsimony—although both solutions demonstrated similarly modest cluster structure with resampling. The two clusters were predicted, with moderate fit, by diagnosis but also confounded by interviewer identity and thus should not be overinterpreted. The confounding influence of interviewer identity arose because quantitative topic modelling was a secondary analysis, and the study was not originally designed for this purpose. Our post-hoc analyses showed that one researcher interviewed more participants with ADHD alone, while another significantly interviewed more autistic participants by coincidence. It should be noted, however, that controlling for interviewer identity led the diagnosis-cluster association to just miss the significance threshold, indicating that we were potentially underpowered to differentiate between the clinical groups. A future mixed-methods study testing the usefulness of TM should balance participant diagnoses across interviewers or randomise interviewer allocation and could consider increasing the sample size or including neurotypical students as an additional comparison group to aid contrast. The latter would also ensure that experiences from all students are captured. Based on the emerging differences of the finally labelled topics from the themes generated in the previous RTA (e.g., some labelled TM topics have highlighted the distinct influences of school compared to home/ community, and these were not explicitly present in the RTA themes or subthemes; see Fig. 3) and the inherently distinct processes leading to these, we suggest that TM and RTA exhibit potential complementarity, whereby each method can be used to elaborate on, enhance, illustrate, or clarify the results of the other66,67. How these outputs, or the processes leading to them, may influence each other and are integrated in a truly mixed-method study is beyond our scope, and remains to be formally tested, ideally within a convergent parallel design where data are analysed separately yet concurrently using these distinct approaches68. Indeed, our experience suggests that TM and RTA are best conducted separately, allowing each method to engage fully with its own paradigmatic and philosophical foundations. Within a research team employing a mixed-method approach, one group of researchers using RTA generates themes through iterative, reflexive, interpretive, and context-sensitive processes, while another group using TM derives topics through replicable computational procedures, which are later labelled and interpreted by humans. Importantly, although the processes leading to topics and themes differ across these methods, both theme generation and topic interpretation and labelling are ultimately human-led and rely on critical examinations of the researchers’ assumptions and positionality. Integration or synthesis of findings may be considered once outputs from the respective analyses are finalised—although see other ways for integrating methods and/or outputs between qualitative and quantitative research69–71. This requires openness, curiosity, and an appreciation of methodological plurality15. Tensions between researchers using the two methods may arise during integration and should be acknowledged. For example, the above interview content variability across interviewers may be perceived by machine-learning approaches as noise, while it is considered a source of richness and diversity in qualitative research. Ideally, integrating knowledge from the two methods would leverage the distinct strengths of each13,14. Most importantly, Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:4615 10 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-34570-7 www.nature.com/scientificreports/

insights derived from one method should not be used to “validate” or “verify” the findings of another. Instead, the emphasis should be on fostering dialogue among researchers, exploring the complementarity of findings, and producing new knowledge. One strength of this study is its methodological innovation in modelling topics. This includes treating interview responses instead of the entire participant interview as a unit of analysis to enhance the stability and interpretability of topics, therefore bringing the method closer in practice to qualitative logic. The novel incorporation of neurodivergent voices during topic labelling and interpretation of findings infused reflexivity and neurodivergent positionality into topics, which could be further expanded. One major limitation affecting the cluster analysis in this study was the coincident association between interviewer identity and specific diagnoses, which could be addressed by balancing participant diagnoses across interviewers or randomising interviewer allocation in future mixed-model studies. Another potential limitation is that topic labelling and TM interpretation were conducted after the generation of RTA themes, to prevent TM findings from influencing the primary RTA processes. Thus, the topic labelling and interpretation might be influenced by the RTA, exaggerating the overlapping findings. Ultimately, our in-depth study of topics and their comparisons with the RTA themes was confined to a specific strand of NLP, i.e., topic modelling. Future comparisons and formal examination of the complementarity between thematic analysis involving more sophisticated strands of NLP such as generative artificial intelligence and large language models, which has been claimed to have the potential for supporting an NLP-augmented qualitative analyses64,65, would be useful. Our study has provided an additional example in the sparse literature on the potential use of TM in analysing interview data. Based on the differences shown by the finally labelled topics from the themes generated in the previously published RTA, and the inherently distinct processes leading to TM topics and RTA themes, we have suggested a potential complementarity between the two methods. Our proposal on how this could be further investigated, incorporating the views of youth researchers as domain experts in TM, may be implemented using advanced algorithms and more sophisticated NLPs.
