Evaluation of the relationship between vitamin levels and symptom severity in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder Demiryürek Esra1 & Kocayiğit Havva2 This cross-sectional study aimed to compare serum vitamin B12, 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25-OHD), ferritin, and iron levels between adults diagnosed with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and healthy controls, and to evaluate the relationship between these biochemical markers and the severity of ADHD symptoms. In this cross-sectional study, a total of 35 adults with ADHD and 36 age- and sex-matched healthy controls who presented to a psychiatry outpatient clinic in Sakarya in 2024 were included. Participants’ demographic data and clinical characteristics were collected through interviews, while laboratory findings were examined using blood samples taken at the time of inclusion in the study. The severity of ADHD symptoms was assessed using the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) and the Wender–Utah Rating Scale (WURS). Serum vitamin B12 and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels were significantly lower in the ADHD group compared with controls (p < 0.001). No significant differences were observed in ferritin and iron levels (p > 0.05). Vitamin B12 and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels showed moderate-to-strong negative correlations with symptom severity. For example, vitamin B12 levels correlated with ASRS inattention (r = − 0.54, p = 0.00009) and WURS inattention (r = − 0.56, p = 0.000002), while 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels correlated with ASRS hyperactivity/impulsivity (r = − 0.53) and WURS depression (r = − 0.54). These findings indicate that lower serum vitamin B12 and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels are associated with greater ADHD symptom severity in adults. The results underscore the potential relevance of biochemical factors in adult ADHD and suggest that assessment of vitamin status may be considered in future clinical and research contexts. Keywords ADHD, vitamin B12, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, ferritin, iron Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition that begins in childhood and may persist into adulthood. Adult ADHD can lead to a marked reduction in quality of life due to symptoms of inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity. The prevalence of adult ADHD in the general population has been reported to range between 2 and 5%. While neurotransmitter systems such as dopamine and norepinephrine are central to its pathophysiology, nutritional and biochemical factors involved in the synthesis and metabolism of these neurotransmitters may also play a contributory role1,2. Recent studies have demonstrated that vitamin D, vitamin B12, ferritin, and iron levels play important roles in neurodevelopmental processes and cognitive functioning. Accordingly, deficiencies in these micronutrients have been proposed as potential contributors to ADHD pathogenesis. Meta-analyses conducted in child and adolescent populations have shown significantly lower serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels in patients with ADHD compared with healthy controls3. Randomized controlled trials in children have also reported that vitamin D supplementation may lead to partial improvement in attention and hyperactivity symptoms4,5. Similarly, there is robust evidence indicating reduced ferritin levels in individuals with ADHD. A metaanalysis found that ferritin levels were significantly lower in pediatric ADHD patients compared with controls (SMD = − 0.40; 95% CI = − 0.66 to − 0.14), whereas findings for serum iron levels have been inconsistent4,5. 1Private Clinic, Sakarya, Türkiye, Turkey. 2Sakarya University, Sakarya, Türkiye, Turkey. email: esraozdil09@gmail.com OPEN Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:9329 1 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-41493-4 www.nature.com/scientificreports

Studies on vitamin B12 have likewise suggested that B12 levels may be lower in children and adolescents with ADHD6,7. Despite robust associations reported in pediatric populations, these findings cannot be directly extrapolated to adult ADHD. The clinical presentation and underlying neurobiological mechanisms of ADHD evolve substantially across the lifespan, and evidence derived from children and adolescents may not fully capture the pathophysiology of the disorder in adulthood. Accordingly, the number of large-sample or prospective studies examining micronutrient-related parameters specifically in adult ADHD populations remains limited. In addition to core dopaminergic and noradrenergic dysfunction, accumulating evidence suggests that micronutrients involved in neurotransmitter synthesis, neurodevelopment, and neurometabolic regulation may contribute to ADHD symptom expression. Vitamin B12 plays a critical role in one-carbon metabolism and methylation pathways essential for neuronal integrity, monoaminergic neurotransmission, and cognitive functioning; deficiency has been associated with attentional impairment, cognitive slowing, and neuropsychiatric symptoms8,9. Vitamin D is increasingly recognized as a neuroactive steroid that modulates dopaminergic signaling, neuroimmune processes, and neurotrophic factors, with experimental and clinical evidence suggesting its involvement in executive functioning and attentional regulation10,11. Iron-related parameters, including ferritin and serum iron, are of particular relevance given iron’s role as a cofactor in dopamine synthesis, dopamine transporter regulation, and myelination. Importantly, peripheral iron indices reflect different aspects of iron metabolism and neurobiological functioning, warranting the assessment of both ferritin (as an index of iron stores) and serum iron12,13. However, findings regarding iron-related biomarkers in ADHD have been inconsistent across the literature. Meta-analytic evidence, largely derived from pediatric populations, has reported lower ferritin levels in some individuals with ADHD, while results for serum iron have been variable14. In adult populations, the relationship appears to be more complex and may depend on the clinical and hematological characteristics of the sample. For example, Demirci et al. (2017) reported higher ADHD symptom scores and an increased prevalence of ADHD diagnoses among adult women with iron deficiency anemia compared to healthy controls, suggesting that ironrelated alterations may be more evident in the context of clinically manifest deficiency15. In contrast, findings in non-anemic adult ADHD samples have been less consistent. Lopez et al. (2019) reported that while iron deficiency may be observed in certain adult ADHD subgroups, such as individuals with comorbid restless legs syndrome, associations between ADHD and peripheral iron parameters are not consistently observed across broader non-anemic adult ADHD populations16. Consistent with these observations, the present study—which excluded individuals with a history of anemia—did not identify significant differences in ferritin or serum iron levels between adults with ADHD and healthy controls. Taken together, these findings support the assessment of both ferritin and serum iron to provide a more comprehensive evaluation of ironrelated biomarkers, while suggesting that in the absence of overt anemia, peripheral iron indices may not show a robust association with ADHD symptom severity in adults. In line with integrative perspectives highlighted in the literature, including work by Rucklidge and colleagues, multiple micronutrients may interact to influence brain function and behavioral regulation in ADHD, supporting the investigation of combined micronutrient profiles rather than isolated biomarkers17. Collectively, these neurobiological and biochemical considerations provide a strong rationale for examining serum vitamin B12, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, ferritin, and iron levels in relation to symptom severity in adult ADHD. Previous research examining serum vitamin and iron parameters in adult ADHD populations remains underexplored and methodologically heterogeneous. A small number of studies have reported associations between adult ADHD and altered peripheral biomarkers such as ferritin, homocysteine, and oxidative stress parameters; however, these investigations often focused on selected biochemical markers, included heterogeneous clinical samples, or lacked well-matched healthy control groups18,19. Existing adult ADHD studies have primarily examined ferritin levels or oxidative stress markers, with variable consideration of symptom severity and limited control for confounding factors such as anemia, comorbid medical conditions, or psychotropic medication use18,19. Moreover, few studies have simultaneously assessed multiple micronutrients—particularly vitamin B12 and 25-hydroxyvitamin D—using standardized laboratory methods while directly correlating biochemical findings with validated ADHD symptom scales. In contrast, the present study employed strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, excluded individuals with anemia, systemic illness, or psychotropic medication use, and utilized age- and sex-matched healthy controls, enabling a more controlled evaluation of serum vitamin B12, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, ferritin, and iron levels in adults with ADHD. Additionally, by assessing symptom severity using both the ASRS and WURS and obtaining biochemical measurements on the same day as clinical evaluation, this study aimed to provide a more comprehensive and methodologically rigorous examination of the relationship between micronutrient status and symptom severity in adult ADHD. Although ADHD is classified as a neurodevelopmental disorder with onset in childhood, its clinical presentation and underlying etiological mechanisms may differ between pediatric and adult populations. While childhood ADHD is predominantly driven by genetic vulnerability and early neurodevelopmental alterations, adult ADHD appears to be influenced by a broader range of factors, including age-related neurobiological changes and cumulative environmental, lifestyle, and biological influences across the lifespan1,2. These distinctions suggest that etiological factors identified in pediatric ADHD may not fully explain symptom persistence and expression in adulthood, highlighting the importance of investigating biochemical and nutritional correlates specifically in adult ADHD. In light of these considerations, comparing serum vitamin B12, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, ferritin, and iron levels between adults with ADHD and healthy controls, as well as examining the relationship between these biomarkers and symptom severity, is clinically relevant and addresses an important gap in the current literature. Materials and methods This cross-sectional study aimed to compare serum vitamin B12, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, ferritin, and iron levels in adults diagnosed with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) with those of a healthy control group, and to evaluate the associations between these biochemical markers and the severity of ADHD symptoms. Participants were recruited between January and December 2024 from a private psychiatry outpatient clinic in Sakarya, Türkiye. Thirty-five adults diagnosed with ADHD by a psychiatrist according to DSM-5 criteria and 36 age- and sex-matched healthy controls were included in the study. Individuals aged 18–65 years with normal cognitive functioning and no history of anemia were eligible for inclusion. Exclusion criteria included comorbid neurological disorders, chronic systemic illnesses, current psychotropic medication use, pregnancy, obesity (to reduce potential metabolic confounding effects on vitamin D and related micronutrient levels), or active infection. Demographic characteristics (age, sex, years of education), socioeconomic variables (marital status, living conditions, occupation), and detailed psychiatric history were obtained for all participants through clinical interviews. Psychiatric history assessment included information on childhood ADHD symptoms or diagnoses, history of other psychiatric disorders, past use of stimulant or other psychotropic medications, and family history of psychiatric conditions. Participants with current psychotropic medication use or comorbid psychiatric diagnoses were excluded from the study. Clinical reasons for referral and current psychiatric status were also evaluated. Participants reporting current use of vitamin B12, vitamin D, or iron supplements were excluded from the study. All participants were free from psychotropic medication at the time of blood sampling; prior stimulant exposure was assessed during clinical interviews but was not an exclusion criterion. Symptom severity was assessed using the Wender–Utah Rating Scale (WURS) to evaluate retrospective childhood ADHD symptoms and the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) to assess current symptom severity. The Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) and the Wender–Utah Rating Scale (WURS) are widely used standardized assessment instruments in ADHD research. Turkish validated versions of both scales were used in this study, and their use for research purposes does not require additional formal permission. Venous blood samples were collected in the morning after an overnight fasting period on the same day as the clinical assessment to minimize potential diurnal and dietary effects on biochemical measurements. Serum vitamin B12, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, ferritin, and iron levels were analyzed using standardized laboratory procedures at the Sakarya University Training and Research Hospital Biochemistry Laboratory. Ferritin and vitamin B12 levels were assessed using chemiluminescent immunoassay on the ABBOTT ARCHITECT i2000SR analyzer; 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels were measured using the ChromSystems-based Architect 25-OH Vitamin D kit on the same platform, and serum iron levels were evaluated photometrically using the ABBOTT ARCHITECT c16000 device. The study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki, and informed consent was obtained from all participants. The study protocol was approved by the Health Sciences Scientific Research Ethics Committee of Sakarya University School of Medicine (Approval No: 635; Document No: E-43012747-050.04-543041). Statistical Analysis Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 27.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA; https://www.ibm.com/products/spss-statistics). The distribution of continuous variables was assessed using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. Normally distributed variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD), and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Between-group comparisons were performed using independent-samples t-tests for continuous variables and chi-square tests for categorical variables. Although some variables approximated normal distribution, ASRS and WURS scores are derived from ordinal Likert-type items, and biochemical variables (particularly vitamin B12 and ferritin) showed skewness and outliers. Therefore, Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient was preferred as a more robust non-parametric measure of association. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Because multiple correlation analyses were conducted between biochemical markers and numerous symptom subscales, false discovery rate (FDR) correction using the Benjamini–Hochberg method was applied to reduce the risk of Type I error. A post hoc power analysis was performed using G*Power software, Version 3.1.2 (Heinrich-Heine-University Düsseldorf, Germany; ​h​t​t​p​s​:​/​/​w​w​w​.​p​s​y​c​h​o​l​o​g​i​e​.​h​h​u​.​d​e​/​a​r​b​e​i​t​s​g​r​u​p​p​e​n​/​a​l​l​g​e​m​e​i​n​e​-​p​s​y​c​h​o​l​o​g​i​e​-​u​n​d​-​a​r​b​e​i​t​s​p​s​y​ c​h​o​l​o​g​i​e​/​g​p​o​w​e​r). Based on the observed between-group differences in vitamin B12 and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels, effect sizes were large (Cohen’s d > 0.8), and the calculated statistical power exceeded 0.95, indicating adequate power for the primary biochemical comparisons. Post hoc power analysis for ASRS and WURS scale comparisons also demonstrated very large effect sizes (Cohen’s d approximately 1.7 to > 6.0), with corresponding power values greater than 0.99. However, the study may have been underpowered to detect small effect sizes, particularly in correlation analyses and for biochemical parameters such as iron and ferritin. Results Comparison of demographic characteristics between the 35 adult ADHD patients and 36 healthy controls revealed no significant differences in age, sex, marital status, employment status, or years of education (all p > 0.05). Demographic characteristics of the participants are presented in Table 1. All ASRS subscale and total scores were significantly higher in the ADHD group compared with controls (p < 0.001). Specifically, ADHD patients had significantly elevated ASRS inattention (31.37 ± 3.19), hyperactivity/ impulsivity (24.57 ± 6.29), and total scores (55.94 ± 8.72) relative to controls (13.78 ± 3.37; 5.75 ± 3.67; 19.53 ± 6.20, respectively). Correlation analyses demonstrated significant negative associations between serum vitamin B12 and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels and both ASRS and WURS subscale and total scores. Lower serum levels of these vitamins were associated with increased severity of inattention, hyperactivity/impulsivity, and behavioral symptoms. After applying false discovery rate (FDR) correction for multiple comparisons, the majority of these negative correlations remained statistically significant (e.g., ASRS inattention vs. vitamin B12: r = − 0.45, adjusted p = 0.00009; WURS inattention vs. vitamin B12: r = − 0.53, adjusted p = 0.000002), indicating robustness of the findings despite multiple testing. Given the modest sample size and cross-sectional design, these associations should be interpreted as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. No significant correlations were found between iron or ferritin levels and any symptom scores (all p > 0.05). These findings suggest that lower serum micronutrient levels may be associated with ADHD symptom severity. Discussion This study examined serum vitamin B12, 25-hydroxyvitamin D, ferritin, and iron levels in adults with ADHD compared with healthy controls and evaluated their associations with ADHD symptom severity. The main findings indicate that adults with ADHD had significantly lower vitamin B12 and vitamin D levels than controls, whereas ferritin and serum iron levels did not differ between groups. In addition, lower vitamin B12 and vitamin D levels were significantly associated with greater ADHD symptom severity, as assessed by both ASRS and WURS scores. The observed reductions in vitamin D levels are broadly consistent with previous literature, which has predominantly focused on pediatric ADHD populations. Meta-analyses and randomized controlled trials in children and adolescents have reported lower serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels in individuals with ADHD and modest improvements in attention and hyperactivity symptoms following supplementation3–5,20. Rather than reiterating these well-established pediatric findings, the present results extend existing evidence by demonstrating that similar associations between vitamin D status and symptom severity are also evident in adult ADHD. Given vitamin D’s involvement in dopaminergic signaling, neuroimmune regulation, and neurotrophic processes10,11, low vitamin D levels may contribute to attentional and executive dysfunction across the lifespan. Evidence regarding vitamin B12 in ADHD remains more limited. Nonetheless, low vitamin B12 status has been associated with impaired one-carbon metabolism, disrupted methylation pathways, alterations in monoaminergic neurotransmission, and reduced neurocognitive functioning8,9. Prior studies examining vitamin B12 in ADHD have largely focused on pediatric populations and have suggested lower B12 levels in affected individuals7. Consistent with these observations, our findings suggest that lower vitamin B12 levels may also be relevant to symptom expression in adults with ADHD, supporting the possibility that shared neurobiochemical mechanisms extend beyond childhood. In contrast to findings reported in children, we did not observe significant differences in ferritin or serum iron levels between adults with ADHD and healthy controls. Meta-analytic evidence indicates reduced ferritin levels in pediatric ADHD samples, whereas findings for serum iron have been inconsistent14,21. Adult evidence appears more heterogeneous, and associations between iron-related parameters and ADHD may depend on clinical context. Prior studies have suggested that iron-related alterations are more evident in specific adult subgroups, such as individuals with iron deficiency anemia or comorbid conditions including restless legs syndrome, whereas findings in broader non-anemic adult ADHD samples are less consistent15,16,18. In the present study, exclusion of individuals with a history of anemia may have reduced variability in iron indices and limited the ability to detect group differences, potentially contributing to the null findings for ferritin and serum iron. These results suggest that peripheral iron parameters may be less informative in non-anemic adult ADHD populations. This study contributes to the limited literature examining multiple micronutrients simultaneously in adults with ADHD. By focusing on an adult sample, employing strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, and using two validated symptom scales (ASRS and WURS), the findings highlight the potential relevance of vitamin B12 and vitamin D in adult ADHD symptomatology while suggesting a more limited role for ferritin and serum iron in non-anemic individuals. These results are consistent with integrative perspectives emphasizing the interaction of multiple micronutrients in influencing brain function and behavioral regulation in ADHD6,17. Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. The relatively large variability observed in serum vitamin B12 levels, particularly in the control group, may reflect inter-individual differences in dietary intake, absorption, and subclinical nutritional status commonly reported in adult populations. The unusually high variability in control-group vitamin B12 levels (SD = 126.99 pg/mL, representing approximately 42% of the mean) also constitutes a methodological constraint that may limit the interpretability of our findings. Although statistically significant differences in serum vitamin B12 and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels were observed, the present study did not aim to classify participants according to categorical deficiency or insufficiency thresholds; therefore, the clinical relevance of these differences should be interpreted with caution. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and it remains unclear whether lower vitamin levels contribute to ADHD symptom severity or reflect behavioral and lifestyle factors associated with ADHD, such as dietary habits or reduced sunlight exposure. Multiple potential confounders—including dietary intake, vitamin supplementation, seasonal variation and sunlight exposure, physical activity, smoking status, and body composition—were not systematically assessed. Although obesity was excluded to reduce metabolic confounding, this may limit generalizability, as obesity is common in adult ADHD populations and influences vitamin D metabolism. In addition, exclusion of individuals with a history of anemia may have constrained the evaluation of iron-related biomarkers. The relatively small sample size represents an additional limitation of this study. Although large effect sizes were observed for the between-group differences in serum vitamin B12 and 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels, the statistical power may have been insufficient to detect weaker associations, particularly in multiple correlation analyses. Therefore, very small p-values should not be interpreted as evidence of large clinical effects, but rather as statistical findings that require confirmation in larger and independent samples. Although false discovery rate (FDR) correction was applied, the correlation analyses should be interpreted cautiously due to multiple testing and their exploratory nature, and residual Type I error risk cannot be completely excluded. Finally, although prior psychotropic medication use was assessed, lifetime exposure and its potential long-term effects on nutritional status could not be fully quantified. In conclusion, this study suggests that lower serum vitamin B12 and vitamin D levels are associated with greater symptom severity in adults with ADHD, whereas ferritin and serum iron levels may not differ in nonanemic adult populations. Assessment of vitamin status may be considered as part of a comprehensive evaluation in adults with ADHD; however, given the cross-sectional design, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Longitudinal and interventional studies are needed to clarify causal relationships and to determine whether changes in micronutrient status are associated with clinical outcomes in adults with ADHD. Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:28707 1 www.nature.com/scientificreports | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-54609-7 OPEN Machine learning-based screening model for Tic disorders comorbid with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in children and SHAP value interpretation: a retrospective observational study Zilin Chen1, Xu Wang2, YuXin Chai1, YuChen Hu1, Ru Jia1 & Fei Han1 Tic disorders (TD) are common neurodevelopmental conditions in children and adolescents, characterized primarily by motor and vocal tics, with heterogeneous symptom presentations and significant fluctuations. Concurrently, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a highly prevalent comorbidity of TD, often exacerbating academic and emotional difficulties. However, due to the potential masking of ADHD symptoms by TD manifestations and insufficient awareness of comorbidities, ADHD diagnosis is frequently delayed. This study aimed to develop a machine learningbased classification model to identify children with TD who have a higher model-predicted probability of ADHD comorbidity, thereby potentially aiding diagnostic accuracy and treatment planning. The research was conducted by the Pediatrics Department of Guang’anmen Hospital, China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences, from October 2023 to October 2024. A retrospective cohort of 1,364 children with TD was included, comprising 889 with TD alone and 475 with TD comorbid with ADHD. The dataset was divided into a training set and an independent test set using a stratified 7:3 split, with the random seed fixed at 42 to ensure the balance of baseline characteristics between the two groups. 10-fold cross-validation was used for hyperparameter tuning and preliminary performance evaluation within the training set, and the final model performance was verified on the independent test set. Twenty-eight clinical features were collected, encompassing general information, family factors, academic performance, medical history, emotional status, and sleep quality. Core variables were selected using Lasso regression, and five distinct machine learning models were constructed. Feature importance was interpreted using SHAP analysis. Ultimately, seven key features were identified for algorithm development: learning initiative, guardian type, academic performance, allergic rhinitis, irritability, adenoid hypertrophy, and sleep quality. The random forest algorithm emerged as the optimal model, achieving an AUC of 0.780 (95%CI: 0.742–0.818), accuracy of 0.793, recall of 0.793, and F1-score of 0.753 on the test set; the Brier score was 0.18, indicating good calibration of the model. SHAP analysis elucidated the contributions of specific features to the model’s prediction of TD with ADHD, with learning initiative (mean |SHAP| = 0.07) and guardian type (0.05) identified as the most influential predictors, followed by academic performance (0.04), allergic rhinitis (0.03), irritability (0.03), adenoid hypertrophy (0.02), and sleep quality (0.02). These findings may provide preliminary references for future screening research and support further investigation into early identification of comorbidity, pending independent validation. However, external validation is required before any clinical implementation. This is a single-center retrospective study without external validation, and the generalization ability of the model needs to be further verified.

Epidemiological data indicate that the prevalence of TD in children is approximately 0.3% to 1%, with a significantly higher incidence in males than in females (male-to-female ratio about 3:1). Symptoms typically first appear between 4 and 6 years of age, peak around adolescence, and may persist into adulthood in some patients2. The pathophysiological mechanisms of TD have not been fully elucidated. Studies suggest that TD may be correlated with aberrant neural transmission in the cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuit3, and dysregulation of the dopaminergic system is considered one of the core mechanisms4. Attention-deficit/ hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is another common neurodevelopmental disorder of childhood, characterized primarily by persistent inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity5. Globally, the prevalence of ADHD in children and adolescents is approximately 8.0%, with the rate in boys (10%) being twice that in girls (5%)6. Individuals with ADHD often experience academic difficulties, social impairments, and emotional dysregulation7,8. These challenges not only affect their daily lives but are also associated with an increased risk of various psychiatric disorders during the transition from childhood to adulthood9. Numerous clinical studies have demonstrated a significant comorbidity between TD and ADHD10. Epidemiological investigations indicate that approximately 50%-60% of children with TD also have comorbid ADHD, while the prevalence of TD in ADHD patients is significantly higher than in the general population11. This comorbidity not only associated with more severe clinical symptoms in affected children, such as learning difficulties, emotional dysregulation, sleep disturbances, self-injurious behaviors, and elimination problems12, but is also linked to poorer long-term outcomes, including impaired social adaptation and reduced quality of life13. However, in current clinical practice, the recognition and diagnosis of TD comorbid with ADHD remains delayed. On one hand, the tic symptoms in children with TD may mask the core manifestations of ADHD14; on the other hand, insufficient understanding of the comorbidity mechanisms among some clinicians may result in underdiagnosis or misdiagnosis15. The high heterogeneity of clinical phenotypes further increases the difficulty in identifying TD-ADHD comorbidity and the risk of diagnostic delay, highlighting the necessity of developing a prediction model based on multi-dimensional clinical indicators16. Given the multifactorial and heterogeneous nature of TD-ADHD comorbidity, traditional statistical methods may be limited in capturing complex, non-linear interactions among risk factors. Machine learning has emerged as a powerful tool for developing predictive models in psychiatry, capable of integrating high-dimensional clinical data to improve diagnostic accuracy and risk stratification for neurodevelopmental disorders17. For instance, ensemble learning algorithms such as Random Forest and Light GBM have been successfully applied to model complex clinical phenotypes, demonstrating superior performance in identifying patterns within multifaceted data18. Furthermore, interpretability methods like SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) have enhanced the transparency of these “black-box” models, facilitating the identification of key predictive factors and their directional contributions, which is crucial for clinical translation19. For instance, in predicting Tourette Syndrome (TS), researchers have developed a gradient boosting machine model based on blood biochemical markers (e.g., β2-microglobulin and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D3), with SHAP interpretation highlighting the key roles of these biomarkers20. Similarly, in screening for ADHD, comparative studies of algorithms such as logistic regression, classification and regression trees (CART), and neural networks have demonstrated that the CART model can achieve relatively high discriminatory performance21. However, these studies have primarily focused on single disorders and often rely on laboratory tests or specialized assessments, which may limit their feasibility in primary care settings.

Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:28707 3 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-54609-7 www.nature.com/scientificreports Therefore, we have developed a machine learning-based classification model to predict ADHD comorbidity in children with TD, specifically aiming to distinguish between TD alone and TD comorbid with ADHD. A total of 28 clinical features were collected, and diagnoses were assisted using the Yale Global Tic Severity Scale (YGTSS), Conners, and Swanson, Nolan, and Pelham-IV Rating Scale (SNAP-IV). These indicators were selected not only because the 28 clinical features comprehensively cover multiple dimensions including general information, family guardianship patterns, academic performance, medical history, allergic predisposition, emotional status, and sleep quality, but also because they systematically capture potential associated factors of comorbidity, making them particularly suitable for early predictive classification of TD comorbid with ADHD. The core innovations of this study include: (1) developing a model with potential relevance for future screening research in primary care settings based on multi-dimensional clinical indicators that can be easily obtained in routine outpatient clinics; (2) integrating LASSO feature selection, multi-algorithm comparison, clinical utility evaluation and SHAP interpretability analysis to form a complete clinical prediction model construction process. This study aims to develop and validate an interpretable machine learning-based prediction model for identifying high-risk groups of TD children complicated with ADHD, providing data support for early clinical screening. Overall, the study included 28 clinical features of 1364 TD children, screened core indicators by Lasso regression, constructed 5 machine learning models and compared their performance, and finally used SHAP analysis to explain the prediction logic of the optimal model, providing tools and basis for early screening of TD complicated with ADHD. The TD with ADHD group consisted of children diagnosed with both TD and ADHD, while the control group comprised children diagnosed with TD only. A descriptive summary of the demographic and clinical baseline characteristics of the study population is provided in the Supplementary Table S1. The exclusion criteria included patients with other severe psychiatric disorders, neurological diseases, or systemic conditions affecting cognitive function, as well as cases with incomplete clinical data. Ethical statement This retrospective observational study was conducted in strict accordance with the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Guang’anmen Hospital, China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences (Approval No.: 2023-211-KY-01). All legal guardians of the participants were fully informed of the study’s purpose, procedures, and their rights, and provided written informed consent. All collected information was strictly anonymized and stored in a secure environment to ensure participant privacy and data security. Diagnostic criteria The Western medical diagnostic criteria for both TD and ADHD strictly adhered to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5). To enhance objectivity and consistency in diagnosis, standardized scale-based assessment tools were employed as supplementary measures for both conditions. The YGTSS is a widely used clinical instrument for evaluating the severity of TD. It provides a comprehensive assessment across multiple dimensions, including tic frequency, intensity, complexity, interference, and overall functional impairment. The total YGTSS score is interpreted as follows: <25 indicates mild severity, 25–50 indicates moderate severity, and > 50 indicates severe severity. The Conners’ Rating Scales, completed by guardians, are behavioral assessment tools primarily used to support the diagnosis and severity evaluation of ADHD. Scores are classified as follows: 0–10 falls within the normal range, 11–19 suggests mild abnormalities, 20–29 indicates moderate abnormalities, and ≥ 30 signifies severe behavioral abnormalities requiring further clinical evaluation and intervention. The SNAP-IV, revised based on DSM-IV criteria, is a commonly used tool for screening ADHD symptoms and assessing their severity. The total score is interpreted as follows: ≤13 is within the normal range, 13–17 indicates mild abnormalities, 18–22 suggests moderate abnormalities, and 23–27 indicates severe abnormalities. Collection and selection of clinical features Our study systematically collected electronic medical record data to comprehensively document multidimensional clinical information from children with TD. The collected data encompassed the following categories: General information (sex, age), Birth history (parity, mode of delivery, difficult labor, preterm birth, birth asphyxia, resuscitation history, low birth weight), Family factors (parental guardianship, parenting style), Academic performance (learning initiative, academic achievement), Medical history (history of common cold, febrile seizures, head trauma), Precipitating or exacerbating factors (parental discipline, poor exam performance, high stress, fright, prolonged smartphone use, extended television viewing), Constitution-related factors (frequent colds, chronic pharyngitis, chronic rhinitis, asthma history, adenoid hypertrophy), Allergic disease history (allergic rhinitis, allergic conjunctivitis, allergic purpura), TD clinical symptoms (persistent episodes, eye movements, nose movements, mouth movements, facial movements, head and neck movements, shoulder movements, upper limb movements, trunk movements, lower limb movements, throat sounds), Comorbidities (e.g., comorbid allergic rhinitis), Emotional and behavioral characteristics (irritability, timidity), Lifestyle and somatic status (dietary habits, sleep quality, bowel and urinary habits). From a clinical definition perspective, “allergic rhinitis” is classified by etiology, “chronic rhinitis” is classified by disease course, and “comorbid allergic rhinitis” is a comorbidity diagnostic label. These three are distinct clinical concepts with independent clinical significance. From a statistical perspective, the core advantage of Lasso regression is its ability to automatically handle statistical redundancy between variables through regularization. In this study, Lasso ultimately retained only “allergic rhinitis” as a core feature, verifying that this method can effectively screen out the most predictive variables. To ensure data quality and consistency, we implemented standardized protocols for feature collection: (1) Parental factors (parental guardianship, parenting style) were assessed via structured questionnaires completed by legal guardians during the initial clinical visit, utilizing standardized response options (e.g., “biological parents as primary guardians” vs. “other relatives/guardians”; “authoritative” vs. “permissive” parenting) to ensure objectivity. The standardized questionnaire used in this study is a routine clinical assessment content of the outpatient clinic for neurodevelopmental disorders in the Department of Pediatrics of our hospital. All included children are required to complete this set of questionnaires by their legal guardians during the initial diagnosis, which is used to assist clinical diagnosis and baseline assessment of the condition. The questionnaire data will be simultaneously entered into the electronic medical record system. This study is a retrospective analysis, which directly extracts the existing routine assessment data in the electronic medical record, and does not carry out additional data collection work for this study. (2) Variables related to prolonged smartphone use and extended television viewing were operationally defined as ≥ 2 h of daily screen time, consistent with clinical guidelines22. These were extracted through a dual-verification process: primarily from guardians’ structured behavior reports (integrated into the routine clinical assessment form), and secondarily cross-referenced with physicians’ documented observations in the electronic medical records. (3) Crucially, all aforementioned variables were collected through structured data entry templates, not via subjective interpretation during retrospective chart review. Trained research assistants provided uniform instructions to guardians for questionnaire completion, and physicians verified the clinical consistency of the responses. For the minimal cases with incomplete structured data (affecting < 3% of the total sample), the variables were excluded rather than inferred, thereby preserving data integrity and avoiding bias. All data were uniformly collected and organized by trained professionals to ensure accuracy and completeness.

To avoid data leakage, Lasso feature selection adopts a nested cross-validation strategy: We used a stratified 70/30 train-test split. All feature selection and hyperparameter tuning were conducted only within the training set using 10-fold cross-validation; the test set was kept untouched for final evaluation. A Lasso regression model was constructed, and the regularization parameter λ was optimized through 10-fold cross-validation. The optimal λ value was determined based on maximizing the Area Under the Curve (AUC), thereby identifying predictive variables significantly associated with TD comorbid with ADHD. Notably, non-discriminatory variables (e.g., isolated history of common colds) were automatically excluded during the Lasso selection process due to their minimal contribution to model performance. For variables such as academic performance, we explicitly distinguished between “baseline academic performance prior to TD symptom exacerbation” and “academic difficulties secondary to ADHD symptoms” through retrospective medical record review. The “academic performance” and “learning initiative” indicators included in this study are all baseline data before the aggravation of TD symptoms. The time node is clearly earlier than the clinical diagnosis of ADHD through the course records in the electronic medical record, avoiding the circular argument of “using functional impairment caused by ADHD to reversely predict ADHD”. This distinction avoids circular reasoning, as we focused on pre-existing academic functioning rather than ADHD-induced impairments (Table 1). To further interpret the model and evaluate feature importance, we utilized SHAP value analysis. A positive SHAP value indicates that the feature contributes to the model’s prediction of a higher probability of comorbid ADHD, while a negative value suggests it contributes to a prediction of lower probability. Model development and evaluation Feature selection was performed using the Lasso regression algorithm to effectively mitigate overfitting. Ultimately, seven core features were identified for predictive model development. Five distinct machine learning algorithms were employed to predict the probability of being classified as TD comorbid with ADHD: Random Forest, Light Gradient Boosting Machine (Light GBM), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), Logistic Regression. The adoption of a multi-model comparison approach facilitated the evaluation of each algorithm’s performance, thereby identifying the most effective technique for predicting comorbidity risk. To ensure robust model evaluation while maintaining computational efficiency, we implemented a holdout validation approach with internal cross-validation for hyperparameter optimization. The dataset was first split into a training set (70%) and an independent test set (30%) using stratified random sampling (random seed = 42). Within the training set, we employed 10-fold cross-validation during Bayesian optimization to tune hyperparameters for each algorithm. The independent test set was held out from all model development and tuning processes and served exclusively for final performance evaluation, providing an unbiased estimate of model generalizability. AUC, accuracy and F1 value are model performance quantitative indicators, which are used to directly compare the predictive ability of different algorithms; PRC, DCA and calibration curve are clinical utility evaluation frameworks, which are used to verify the applicability of the model in actual clinical scenarios. This study uses the Youden index to determine the optimal classification threshold; to address the imbalance in sample size between the TD group and the comorbid group, a class weight adjustment strategy is adopted during model training to reduce the dominant effect of majority class samples. For logistic regression and MLP, continuous features are standardized by Z-score; tree models (random forest, LightGBM, XGBoost) do not require standardization. All binary variables are coded with 0/1; there are no multi-category variables in the core features. Bayesian Optimization is used for hyperparameter tuning, the optimization target is AUC, and the search range is determined based on literature reports and pre-experiment results. For the calculation of 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for all performance metrics, we implemented a non-parametric bootstrap resampling approach with 1000 iterations. This method involved repeatedly sampling with replacement from the test set, recalculating the performance metrics for each bootstrap sample, and then deriving the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as the lower and upper bounds of the 95% CI. The reliability of the models was comprehensively evaluated using four core metrics: Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC), PrecisionRecall Curve (PRC), Decision Curve Analysis (DCA), Calibration Curve. Furthermore, performance metrics including accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score were thoroughly compared and analyzed. Statistical analysis Data in this study are presented as median and interquartile range [M (Q1, Q3)]. Normality of continuous variables was assessed using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Group comparisons for normally distributed data were performed using independent samples *t*-tests, while the Mann–Whitney U test was applied for non-normally distributed data. Categorical variables are expressed as frequencies and percentages, with group comparisons conducted using chi-square tests or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. All statistical analyses were performed using R language (version 4.2.1) and relevant statistical packages. A P-value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The statistical tests described in this section are only used for descriptive comparison of baseline characteristics of children in the two groups, providing clinical basis for subsequent feature screening; the core conclusion of this study is based on the prediction performance indicators of machine learning models, rather than the P-value of traditional hypothesis testing. To justify the sample size, we performed a post-hoc power analysis for the primary outcome (AUC of the Random Forest model). Assuming a moderate expected AUC of 0.75 under the null, a two-sided type I error of 0.05, and a power of 0.90, the required minimum number of positive cases (TD with ADHD) was calculated to be approximately 190 using the method of Obuchowski and McClish. Our study included 475 positive cases, which exceeds this requirement. Results Data processing and feature selection A total of 1,364 children with TD were included in this study, comprising 889 cases in the TD-only group and 475 cases in the TD with ADHD group. The data processing and feature selection workflow are illustrated in Fig. 1. Ultimately, 1,364 children were included in the analysis. No significant differences were observed between the two groups in most baseline characteristics, such as sex, mode of delivery, preterm birth, birth asphyxia, or resuscitation history (P > 0.05). However, significant differences (P < 0.05) were identified in the following 14 features, suggesting their potential association with the model-predicted probability of comorbidity (Supplementary Table S1): Children in the TD with ADHD group were significantly younger and exhibited significantly higher proportions or incidences of difficult labor, inadequate parental supervision, poor learning initiative, low academic performance, history of febrile, precipitation by fright, chronic rhinitis, adenoid hypertrophy, allergic rhinitis, lower limb involuntary movements, vocal tics, irritability, and poor sleep quality compared to the TD-only group (P < 0.05). Subsequently, we defined the binary outcome variable as the presence or absence of ADHD comorbidity and included 28 clinical features as initial predictive variables. To identify the most predictive variables and mitigate overfitting, Lasso regression was employed for feature selection. The regularization parameter λ was optimized via 10-fold cross-validation, with the optimal λ value (λ = 0.012) determined by maximizing the AUC (Fig. 2A). The Lasso regression path analysis showed that as λ decreased, features significantly associated with the outcome were gradually incorporated into the model (Fig. 2B). Ultimately, Lasso regression identified seven core features significantly associated with TD comorbid with ADHD: learning initiative, guardian type, academic performance, allergic rhinitis, irritability, adenoid hypertrophy, and sleep quality. The importance of these features within the LASSO model was quantified by the absolute values of their coefficients (|β|), yielding the following ranking: Learning initiative (|β| = 0.326) > Guardian type (|β| = 0.271) > Academic performance (|β| = 0.218) > Allergic rhinitis (|β| = 0.185) > Irritability (|β| = 0.179) > Adenoid hypertrophy (|β| = 0.103) > Sleep quality (|β| = 0.098) (Table 2). At the optimal λ, the LASSO model itself achieved an AUC of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.78–0.86) in 10-fold cross-validation, confirming its robust performance for comorbidity prediction. Sensitivity analysis To assess the robustness of our findings, we conducted several sensitivity analyses (Supplementary Table S3). First, a feature coding sensitivity analysis was performed by reversing the binary coding of all seven core features (e.g., setting 1 = passive, 0 = active for learning initiative). The Random Forest model retrained on the reversed coding achieved a test set AUC of 0.775 (95% CI: 0.738–0.812), representing a ΔAUC of 0.005 compared to the original coding (0.780, 95% CI: 0.742–0.818). This negligible change indicates that the model’s predictions are not materially affected by the choice of binary encoding. Second, to evaluate the impact of class imbalance, we separately applied SMOTE oversampling and random undersampling to the training set before model retraining. The resulting test set AUCs were 0.772 (95% CI: 0.735–0.809) for SMOTE and 0.774 (95% CI: 0.737–0.811) for undersampling, corresponding to ΔAUCs of 0.008 and 0.006, respectively. All AUC differences were below 0.02, confirming the model’s stability under different class‐balance handling strategies. Third, we estimated the uncertainty of SHAP‐based feature importance rankings using bootstrap resampling (1000 iterations). For each iteration, the Random Forest model was refitted on a bootstrap sample of the training set, and mean |SHAP| values were recomputed on the out‐of‐bag observations. The 95% confidence intervals of the mean |SHAP| values for the seven core features are presented in Supplementary Table S3. Although minor overlaps of the confidence intervals were observed between adjacent features (e.g., guardian type and academic performance), the ranking order of the seven features remained completely stable across all 1000 bootstrap iterations, with learning initiative and guardian type consistently identified as the top two predictors. Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:28707 10 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-54609-7 www.nature.com/scientificreports Discussion The core conclusion of this study is based on the clinical correlation analysis of machine learning models, aiming to identify high-risk groups of TD complicated with ADHD, rather than revealing the causal mechanism of the disease. TD are neurodevelopmental conditions characterized by sudden, repetitive, non-rhythmic motor movements or vocalizations. These symptoms typically emerge during childhood, most commonly between the ages of 5 and 10, with a higher incidence in boys than in girls23. In addition to tic symptoms, individuals with TD may exhibit sensory features, specifically premonitory urges and heightened, persistent sensitivity to non-harmful external or internal stimuli24. These distinctive perceptual and emotional regulation responses often significantly impact patients’ daily lives. Furthermore, TD patients may present with various behavioral comorbidities, including ADHD, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and autism spectrum disorder (ASD)25. Current clinical scale assessments indicate that children with TD frequently present with comorbid ADHD. Although TD and ADHD often co-occur, the nature of the relationship between their symptoms remains unclear14. Early identification of ADHD comorbidity in children with TD continues to pose significant challenges in clinical practice. Given these diagnostic difficulties, establishing reliable clinical prediction models is crucial for improving the accuracy and timeliness of comorbidity recognition. To address the diagnostic complexity of TD-ADHD comorbidity, this study leveraged the capability of machine learning to integrate heterogeneous clinical data by developing a predictive model for ADHD comorbidity in children with TD. Specifically, we employed Lasso regression combined with 10-fold crossvalidation for feature dimensionality reduction and selection. Seven core features were ultimately identified as key predictive features for the model’s classification of TD comorbid with ADHD: learning initiative, guardian type, academic performance, allergic rhinitis, irritability, adenoid hypertrophy, and sleep quality. Through systematic comparison of five machine learning algorithms (Random Forest, Light GBM, XGBoost, MLP, and Logistic Regression) across performance metrics including ROC curves, precision-recall curves, decision curves, and calibration curves, the Random Forest model was determined to be the optimal predictive model. SHAP summary plots and bar charts highlighted the substantial contributions of features such as learning initiative and guardian type to the model’s predictions. Notably, features such as learning initiative and academic performance may reflect shared underlying constructs related to executive function and motivation. The simultaneous inclusion of both in the model should be interpreted with caution, as their individual importance might be influenced by this conceptual overlap. Nonetheless, from a predictive standpoint, both contributed to model performance, and their combined effect is clinically meaningful for screening purposes. The strong concordance between the feature importance rankings derived from LASSO regression and SHAP analysis (Spearman’s ρ = 0.92, P < 0.001) underscores the robustness of our core predictors—such as learning initiative and guardian type—in identifying TD comorbid with ADHD, irrespective of the interpretative method. More importantly, SHAP analysis provided critical added value beyond the linear, global summaries of LASSO. Specifically, SHAP (1) captured nuanced non-linear relationships and threshold effects (e.g., for sleep quality), (2) offered individual-level explanations that clarify risk attribution for specific cases, and (3) delivered intuitive visualizations that enhance model interpretability for clinical practitioners. Thus, while LASSO confirmed feature selection stability, SHAP significantly extended our understanding of the model’s decision logic, thereby improving its clinical translatability and utility in personalized assessment. One notable finding is that the YGTSS total score was not selected by LASSO regression as a core predictive feature. This suggests that, within our cohort, the severity of tic symptoms per se does not independently discriminate between children with TD alone and those with TD comorbid with ADHD. Instead, the model captured behavioral, emotional, environmental, and allergic comorbidity factors. This is consistent with clinical observations that ADHD comorbidity in TD is driven more by shared neurobehavioral dysregulation than by tic severity. Thus, the model should be understood as capturing phenotypic correlates rather than tic-specific clinical features. The model identified family guardianship patterns and learning behavior characteristics as the most influential predictive features for distinguishing children with TD and ADHD from those with TD alone. Our model identified parental guardianship as a key predictor, indicating that parental guardianship is a key predictive feature in the model; children with parents as primary guardians had a lower model-predicted probability of being classified as having ADHD comorbidity. This should be interpreted as a model-based association rather than a causal protective effect. This association may be explained by more stable emotional support and a structured environment, which are theorized to be conducive to better behavioral regulation. Conversely, we observed that insufficient parental involvement or frequent family conflicts are associated with increased ADHD manifestations, which may be related to neurochemical imbalances and psychological stress26–28. Additionally, TD children with high learning initiative and strong academic performance were associated with a lower model-predicted probability of being classified as comorbid with ADHD29,30. Baseline data further indicated that in the TD with ADHD group, 45.3% of children exhibited poor learning initiative and 41.7% had below-average academic performance—significantly higher proportions than those in the TD-only group (23.1% and 22.5%, respectively). This underscores the close relationship between academic performance and comorbidity risk. Furthermore, high-quality family interactions, such as parent-child reading activities, have been shown to positively modulate the relationship between tic severity and quality of life31. Although the socially constructed predictors identified in this study (such as guardianship type and learning initiative) are subjective indicators, they can be quickly assessed through standardized questionnaires. In the future, these indicators can be integrated into the routine screening scale for children’s neurodevelopmental disorders to form a comprehensive screening tool combining ‘objective signs + subjective behaviors’, thereby improving the efficiency of comorbidity identification32. The core predictive indicators identified in this study can provide reference directions for clinical screening, and the intervention value of these indicators needs to be verified by prospective studies in the future.

Scientific Reports | (2026) 16:28707 11 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-54609-7 www.nature.com/scientificreports Moreover, our findings suggest that allergic conditions such as adenoid hypertrophy and allergic rhinitis are important predictive features supporting the classification of ADHD comorbidity in children with TD. While our study did not measure biological markers to elucidate the underlying mechanisms, the observed associations are consistent with previous hypotheses implicating immune dysfunction and neuroinflammation in neurodevelopmental disorders. For instance, literature suggests that adenoid hypertrophy is linked to chronic hypoxia and sleep-disordered breathing, which could theoretically compromise prefrontal oxygen supply and dopamine metabolism, potentially contributing to impaired executive functions33–35. Similarly, allergenactivated mast cells are thought to initiate neurogenic inflammation and release pro-inflammatory cytokines, processes which have been theorized to dysregulate key neurotransmitter systems including dopamine and norepinephrine, thereby potentially exacerbating attention and behavioral regulation deficits36–40. The predictive correlation between indicators such as allergic rhinitis and adenoid hypertrophy and comorbidity may be related to neurodevelopmental abnormalities caused by chronic inflammation. This hypothesis needs to be verified by prospective studies combining biological markers. Our results demonstrate that sleep quality and emotional dysregulation serve as significant clinical predictive features for ADHD comorbidity in TD patients. Studies have shown that the prevalence of insomnia in TD patients (32.16%) is significantly higher than in the general population (13.70%), with ADHD comorbidity being one of the key drivers of sleep disturbances41. From a pathophysiological perspective, sleep deprivation and fragmentation are hypothesized to exacerbate impulsive behaviors and emotional dysregulation by impairing prefrontal-limbic circuit functionality and reducing serotonergic neurotransmission42,43. Meanwhile, irritability, as a core predictive symptom in our model, is known to interact bidirectionally with tic symptoms in TD. This interaction is thought to involve abnormal amygdala connectivity and deficits in cognitive flexibility44,45, with approximately 20%-40% of TD patients potentially experiencing severe anger outbursts46. Notwithstanding the satisfactory predictive performance of our model, this study has several limitations. First, its retrospective, single-center design based on electronic medical records is susceptible to potential biases, including selection bias and information bias due to inconsistent data recording. This study adopted a singlecenter retrospective design. Some subjective indicators relied on guardians’ recall, which may lead to recall bias. Future prospective studies can adopt real-time recording methods to reduce such bias. Second, machine learning models are inherently stochastic; although we used cross-validation, the reported performance and feature importance may exhibit variability. Third, the identified feature importance signifies association, not causation. The predictive features should not be interpreted as direct causal risk factors, as their relationships could be confounded by unmeasured variables. Moreover, several key predictive features—including learning initiative, academic performance, irritability, and sleep quality—conceptually overlap with core or associated symptoms of ADHD. Although we attempted to distinguish baseline academic functioning prior to TD exacerbation, some overlap is inevitable in a retrospective design. Therefore, our model should be interpreted as a clinically informed screening and classification tool that identifies children with TD who are likely to have concurrent ADHD based on currently manifested behavioral patterns, rather than a purely prognostic model for future risk. This distinction is important to avoid circular reasoning. Future studies can include more biological indicators unrelated to ADHD to further optimize the independence of the model. Fourth, the observed slight performance drop in the test set (AUC = 0.780) compared to the training set (AUC = 0.810) may indicate a degree of overfitting, despite our use of feature selection and cross-validation to mitigate this. Fifth, the current model is not intended to replace standard diagnostic procedures. It should be used only as an exploratory screening support tool to help clinicians identify children with TD who may benefit from further ADHD evaluation. Definitive diagnosis must follow DSM-5 criteria and comprehensive clinical assessment. Sixth, and crucially, this model was developed and validated within a single-center retrospective cohort without external validation. The generalizability and transportability of our findings, particularly for the family and social variables, across different healthcare settings, regions, or populations remain uncertain. Therefore, the predictive model developed in this study should serve as an ancillary tool to be integrated with comprehensive clinical assessments. It cannot replace the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria and clinical scale evaluation. The final diagnosis needs to be determined by specialists based on the comprehensive clinical manifestations of the children. It should be emphasized that these findings are derived from a single-center retrospective study without external validation. The proposed model currently serves as a research tool with potential clinical relevance, not a ready-to-use decision aid. Prospective studies in diverse populations are necessary to confirm its utility. Conclusion In summary, we have successfully developed a machine learning model based on clinical practice data to distinguish children with TD comorbid with ADHD from those with TD alone. Among the five machine learning algorithms evaluated in this study, the Random Forest model demonstrated the most outstanding performance. By applying the SHAP method for model visualization, we not only clearly illustrated how various features contribute to prediction outcomes but also effectively determined feature importance. SHAP analysis identified seven key features contributing to the model’s prediction probability of TD comorbid with ADHD: learning initiative, guardian type, academic performance, allergic rhinitis, irritability, adenoid hypertrophy, and sleep quality. This comprehensive research approach provides valuable insights into the clinical correlates associated with this comorbid condition, although the model requires external validation before being considered for routine clinical use.
