Hutchins2 , and Amanda Phillips Martinez1 Abstract Objective: The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends behavioral therapy as first-line evidence-based treatment for young children with ADHD, and in combination with medications for children ages 6 years and older. However, a significant percentage of young children are receiving medication treatment for ADHD rather than behavioral treatment. There is limited research capturing parent experiences of barriers to implementing behavioral health services for young children with ADHD diagnoses. This paper seeks to fill this gap by exploring these perceived barriers among parents of children diagnosed with ADHD. Method: Parents of children with ADHD diagnoses (N = 29) were invited to participate in four focus groups to discuss their experiences with accessing treatment for their child. Focus group participants were recruited from one Southeast city through an ADHD parental support group and nationally from parents attending a conference on ADHD. Results: Three themes emerged as perceived barriers that impact ADHD treatment. Parents reported barriers that can be conceptualized as (1) misconceptions and stigma; (2) availability of financial and time-related resources; and (3) treatment messaging and provider coordination. These barriers may be more pronounced for parents of young children with ADHD living in the Southeast. Conclusion: Parent responses about perceived barriers in this study suggest a need for better coordinated care of ADHD across places of service, providers, and families. These findings may inform future efforts to improve access to and utilization of evidence-based treatments for ADHD in the Southeast and nationwide. (J. of Att. Dis. 2026; 30(9) 1091-1103) Keywords ADHD, behavior therapy, parent, barriers

1092 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(9) from 2007 to 2011 to 2012 (Visser et al., 2014) and has remained stable or declined in recent years (Board et al., 2020; Danielson et al., 2023, 2024; Davis et al., 2020). Use of behavioral therapy has remained stable between 2016 and 2022 despite increasing prevalence of ADHD, which may indicate possible continued gaps in access to treatment (Danielson et al., 2024). Most children diagnosed with ADHD receive some type of services and support to help with their behavior during their childhood (Danielson et al., 2018). Examples of support include individualized education programs (IEPs) and 504 school programs, but the best evidence is for behavior therapy, delivered as individual or group child therapy, or family therapy (Evans et al., 2018; Wolraich et al., 2019). Parent training in behavior management is evidence-based as the first treatment option with preschool age children with ADHD diagnoses (Bussing & Murray, 2014; Wolraich et al., 2019), has strong evidence up to age 12 years in combination with medication, and may also be beneficial as part of behavioral intervention for adolescents (Evans et al., 2018; Wolraich et al., 2019). Parent training is a key recommendation from practitioners, especially for parents with symptomology of ADHD (Halperin & Marks, 2019). Children who receive behavioral therapy, including parent training and behavioral classroom management, experience better academic, social, and familial outcomes (Daley et al., 2014; Pelham & Fabiano, 2008). However, a significant percentage of young children are receiving medication treatment for ADHD rather than behavioral treatment (Bannett et al., 2021; Visser et al., 2014, 2016), and only about one third of parents reported ever receiving parent training (Danielson et al., 2018), thus treatment is not aligned with the best evidence-based practice. Barriers to behavior treatment are experienced by many families, can be unique to the child’s environment and family context, and can range from individual level factors such as knowledge, beliefs, attitudes, perceived needs and stigma, to factors affecting the social network, or the larger community (Kappi & Martel, 2021). Parents report a lack of knowledge about available behavioral parent training or other parenting program advertising for their preschool aged children (Smith et al., 2015). Some studies have reported positive perceptions of the effectiveness of behavior therapy (or non-medicated approaches) from parents and adolescents (Krain et al., 2005; Lu et al., 2022). Stigma associated with ADHD diagnosis and treatment also impacts parental decisions to initiate treatment (dosReis et al., 2010, Kappi & Martel, 2021). Qualitative studies highlight increased familial and social stress from receiving unsatisfactory support for their child’s experiences with ADHD (Leitch et al., 2019) and medication use as treatment (Charach et al., 2014). Before initiating treatment, parents of preschool children report reservations to initiating medication for their children (Hart et al., 2018), and perception of behavior treatment can affect initiation and participation in parent training (Chako et al., 2017). Structural factors including service systems and insurance and administrative factors can also restrict access to treatment (Eiraldi et al., 2006). Financial barriers to treatment are a significant factor and were higher among families with children diagnosed at an early age (Nasol et al., 2019). Access to ADHD diagnoses and treatment in the U.S. varies by state and region, with states in the south having higher prevalence of ADHD diagnoses among children ages 3 to 17 years but less initiation of behavioral health treatment compared to those in the western states (Danielson et al., 2022; Visser et al., 2014). Further, parents’ engagement in treatment is affected by their prior experience with healthcare providers (Taylor et al., 2021). Lack of knowledge is a significant barrier documented in research (Kappi & Martel, 2021), and parents may depend on healthcare providers for receiving such knowledge. Some providers may not follow clinical guidance to provide referrals for parent training (AlRasheed et al., 2021; Bannett et al., 2021). Extensive data exists to highlight the efficacy of available treatment options for children with ADHD diagnoses (Wolraich et al., 2019); however, gaps still exist in the literature about parent experiences with managing options and uptake of ADHD treatment, especially in early childhood (McKenna et al., 2023). This study investigates experiences with behavioral health services in a sample of parents of children diagnosed with ADHD, including a subset of children diagnosed between ages 2 and 7 years. The study aims to highlight parent-perceived barriers to seeking and receiving behavioral health services. Given that behavior treatment is evidence-based and recommended as the primary treatment for young children but continues to be used less often than medication treatment (Danielson et al., 2022), the study especially focused on behavioral therapy such as parent training, for their children with ADHD, including both logistical barriers such as access and social/ emotional barriers such as attitudes and perception. Methods This study was reviewed and approved by the university’s Institutional Review Board. All participants provided written informed consent prior to participating. Parents or caregivers (hereafter referred to as “parents”) of children with ADHD diagnoses were invited to participate in one of four separate focus groups to discuss their experiences accessing treatment for their child, with a focus on behavioral treatment. Two focus groups were held in a major city in the Southeast with subjects recruited from a local ADHD parental support group with assistance from the group leader, and two focus groups were held with participants attending a national, ADHD-themed conference with

Taylor et al. 1093 support from conference marketing and registration staff. Participants were recruited through flyers and e-mail blasts requesting attendance of parents of children diagnosed with ADHD who were either (1) between the age of 2 and 7 years old at the time of the study, to focus on children who were identified with ADHD in the early years, before adolescence, when behavioral treatment should be offered first before medication, or (2) had received their ADHD diagnosis in the last 5 years, regardless of age, to focus on families whose child received their diagnosis more recently and who could best remember their initial diagnosis and treatment experiences. All participants received a light meal or refreshments and were compensated $40 for their participation in the focus group. Data Collection In sum, 29 parents participated across the four separate focus groups. Thirteen parents participated in one of two focus groups held in the Southeast. One of the Southeast focus groups included seven parents with children who were aged 2 to 7 years and the other group included six parents of children diagnosed with ADHD in the last 5 years (regardless of age). Two focus groups were held nationally with 16 participants that lived predominately in the Western geographic region of the U.S. Of these 16 parents, 1 parent had a child aged 2 to 7 years, and 15 parents had a child who was diagnosed with ADHD in the last 5 years. Seventeen participants across all four focus groups broadly identified themselves as the children’s parents, while 11 participants identified themselves specifically as mothers. Because the location and context of the focus groups (national conference versus local support group) may have influenced the type of participant, we heretofore will label the two locations as “National focus group” and “Southeast focus group.” All four focus groups were conducted in-person between May 2015 and November 2016 and lasted approximately 60 to 90 min. To provide background information about the sample, prior to the focus group discussion, parents were administered a brief survey that included child demographics, diagnosis, and medication treatment (see Table 1). The focus group guide covered topics to ascertain the varied and multifaceted experiences with accessing ADHD treatment options, with a focus on behavioral treatment. Question topic areas included: accessibility and availability of services; experiences with behavioral and medication treatment for their child; motivations for implementing behavioral therapy; and expectations about services received. Focus group facilitators did not have any conflict of interest or relationship to the focus group participants. All four focus groups were audio recorded and transcribed verbatim. Names of participants and their children were deidentified to protect the identity of participants. Qualitative Coding The codebook was designed using an iterative process following Template Analysis, a form of Thematic Analysis (Brooks et al., 2015), that balances a high degree of structure with the flexibility to adapt to the needs of the study and what arises in the data. The first step in designing the codebook was to identify and include important concepts and themes in the focus group guide; deductive codes were identified during a review of the available literature and guided by initial research questions. The next step included further refinement based on an initial read of all transcript data; this involved confirming relevant codes, identification of new inductive lower-level codes related to diagnosis experience, organization of codes and themes into meaningful clusters, and clarifying meaning by providing definitions for the codes. A set of researchers skilled in qualitative research (C.S. and L.F.) independently coded approximately 10% of the sample focus group data. Coding between the two researchers was compared to assess for a standardized application of the codebook to the dataset and increase reliability. Standardized application of codes meant both coders were assigning the same codes throughout the chosen 10% of the sample from the transcripts. When discrepancies in coding were identified, these discrepancies were discussed, and the codebook was further refined to ensure clarity. Following confirmation of the codebook design and the subsequent standardization exercise, focus group transcripts were coded using Atlas.ti by the independent coders (C.S. and L.F. for the Southeast focus groups and C.S. and A.H. for the National focus groups). Data Analysis Data analysis of the four focus groups involved a rigorous application of thematic analysis (completed by B.T. and A.D.). Thematic analysis is a widely utilized qualitative method for organizing or highlighting recurrent themes, patterns, and connections between interview or focus group data (Braun & Clarke, 2006; Kiger & Varpio, 2020; Nowell et al., 2017). The application of thematic analysis for this study involved an in-depth review of the coded transcripts (by B.T. and A.D.), identifying generalized, emergent themes, and organization of defined themes across the four focus groups (see Table 1). Emergent themes were identified and refined inductively and informed by available literature on recommended ADHD behavioral intervention therapies and barriers to evidencebased treatment (Wolraich et al., 2019). An inductive approach occurs when themes are derived from the actual data, as opposed to identified a priori (Kiger & Varpiro, 2020). This inductive process included regular meetings with the research team (B.T., A.D., A.S., and C.S.) to

1094 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(9) organize and confirm emerging themes. Saturation in both data collection and analysis largely depends on how the organized themes are connected to (1) the codebook design, (2) the framework used to support the research question, and (3) contributions to the field (Constantinou et al., 2017; Morse, 2015). The inductive, iterative approach applied to all four focus groups supported the identification of emergent themes to answer the research question. A point of saturation was reached when new themes were no longer emerging in the analysis. Participants’ responses across the four focus groups indicated sufficient commonalities and uniqueness in treatment experiences. Themes common across groups and those most relevant for the Southeast versus the national groups were noted. Themes were consistent among the two Southeast focus groups (with one focus group including children 2–7 years of age and one focus group with children diagnosed in the last 5 years, regardless of age). Results Descriptive Characteristics Twenty-nine parents reported on 32 children with ADHD, as some parents reported having more than one child with an ADHD diagnosis in their household. Ages of children and length of time since diagnosis varied across all focus groups. The median age of participants’ children was 10 years, with 62% of children between the ages of 6 and 10 years. Fifty-three percent (n = 17) of children were given an ADHD diagnosis between the ages of 2 and 7 years. Seventy one percent of children were identified by the parent participant as male (n = 23). Perceived Barriers to Receiving Behavioral Health Services for ADHD Following the thematic analysis of both deductive and inductive codes, multiple themes emerged as perceived barriers to seeking or receiving behavior treatment for children with ADHD diagnoses, regardless of child’s age when diagnosed. Parents also discussed medication treatment, but for the purpose of this study, the analyses focused on behavior treatment. Parents of children aged 2 to 7 years from the Southeast focus groups more often reported barriers to ADHD diagnosis and behavior treatment compared to parents in the National focus groups. These barriers can be conceptualized as (1) misconceptions and stigma regarding ADHD; (2) access and availability of behavioral treatment; and (3) coordination and messaging. Misconceptions and Stigma Regarding ADHD When parents reported their first observations of ADHD symptoms, hesitancy around “knowing” and misconceptions around age-appropriate behaviors sometimes preempted – or even delayed – a clinical diagnosis and treatment. These observations were based on witnessing their child’s behavior or reports from others (such as their child’s teacher). Apprehension and related misconceptions regarding ADHD were reported by parents in both National and Southeast focus groups. One parent in a National focus group described her and her husband’s initial denial of their child’s behavior being attributed to ADHD, saying, So my husband and I were sort of in denial but we knew . . . I mean, I knew in my heart that there was something going on. (National focus group) A parent in a Southeast focus group attributed their child’s hyperactivity to stereotypes based on masculine and feminine expectations, dismissing a possible diagnosis. One parent noted, Um, but, yeah—we, for a long time, we figured, ADHD. He’s a boy. He’s young, you know what I mean? We really didn’t, I guess, acknowledge it. (Southeast focus group) Another parent in a National focus group recalled how his son showed characteristics of hyperactivity, and assumed his behavior was warranted due to age. He stated, Um, at daycare, when my 11-year-old who is diagnosed with ADHD was about 5 – actually, 4 – there were lots of concerns about his impulsivity, inability to stay focused, and we just sort of let it . . . thought it was age-appropriate behavior . . . (National focus group) Parents in both of the Southeast focus groups reported a negative reaction to the ADHD diagnosis. These parents identified feeling uncomfortable or saddened by their child’s diagnosis, especially with fears of societal stigmas. (Southeast focus group) One parent discussed the presumed stigma of parental blame associated with her child’s diagnosis and struggle to seek assistance. And then, sometimes, to be honest, people don’t realize it, don’t wanna admit it—sometimes it’s reflecting on you, is what you’re feeling like. (Southeast focus group) Access and Availability of Behavioral Treatment When discussing the ability to seek out and receive treatment for their child, parent responses indicated barriers related to access and availability of treatment that stemmed from the lack of financial resources and time needed for treatment. Insurance coverage and the cost of treatment were reported as financial barriers to accessing treatment; many parents’ insurance plans had a finite number of allowed visits for behavior treatment. One parent recalled, And it almost makes it impossible, now, because, now my insurance is changing . . . depending on how they’re gonna bill it, won’t be able to afford to take her if she needs to go, because you know, you’re dealing with co-insurance, you’re dealing with co-pays, and then you’re also dealing with medicine . . . And like, my insurance only allowed so many visits. (Southeast focus group) Another parent spoke about how they felt their insurance was a barrier to treatment, as well as feeling a sense of isolation rather than support from their child’s psychologist. She noted, But you’re basically out there . . . our insurance paid a little but we paid a significant amount of money for it and then she’s [child psychologist] like, ‘I can’t treat you. Sorry’ . . . so it’s like you really are on your own to navigate the system, to see what else is out there. (National focus group) Parents also spoke about the increased cost and time challenge that comes with behavioral therapies that require family engagement. When asked about integrating behavioral therapy, a parent in a Southeast focus group said, “we haven’t been able to afford that so that hasn’t been an option.” Family engagement and training is considered the foundational component to behavioral treatment, especially for young children. Parents expressed frustration with the limited amount of time available in the day to attend family therapy with their child or to integrate tools at home during limited evening hours after school and work. One parent in a National focus group likened the time challenge that comes with treatment management, particularly with navigating various treatment while the child is at school, as “a nine to five job of just advocating and busting down doors.” Another parent in the Southeast expressed the time challenge being a barrier to their child’s treatment even when treatment was working. She noted, . . .Once a week, both parents had to be present for quite a while. So we had to [use] sick leave or what-whatever leave from work. It required 30 minutes driving to the place. And then, respectively, driving our son back to school and going in the opposite direction to go to work. And we diligently did it for a year, and . . . it help [sic] him . . . at one point we decided it was really too much because the stress level in the family was great . . . it was really impossible. There was a toll. (Southeast focus group) This parent described satisfaction with behavioral treatment services yet could not continue due to consistent conflicts with work and time spent attending appointments. Navigating time off from work became an undue burden that the family felt they simply could not sustain. A parent in a National focus group summarized the access and availability-related burdens in a similar way: So the decisions that you’re making have a large consequence on your home life and how you’re going to pay for all of it because you have no support to do it. (National focus group) Treatment Messaging and Provider Coordination One National focus group participant identified ADHD treatment as a “decision-making matrix,” highlighting how parents may perceive multiple directions and entryways for treatment that often intersect with one another, and reported that determining the most appropriate form of treatment proves difficult. Another National focus group parent said, “ . . . you need an integrated way to treat your child but there is nothing in place . . . there’s no instruction manual or roadmap.” Inability to access necessary information about available treatment options was noted as a consistent, logistical barrier for parents. This was often described as a lack of appropriate information about available treatment options. Parents reported a lack of communication or support from their place of service, such as schools or their health providers. Other parents discussed long wait lists for appointments

Taylor et al. 1097 to see psychiatrists or psychologists for evaluations. One parent expressed her frustrations with the lack of consistent options after receiving a diagnosis from a psychiatrist. This parent reported that she did not feel as if she had access to information about the correct direction to take post-diagnosis. She noted, . . . I had never – where is this supposed to be happening? So, that was my experience with it. I was very frustrated. And I’m still frustrated that, as a parent, when you hear this, what are you supposed to do? (National focus group) Many parents described feeling as if they were educating themselves on available behavioral treatment options, as opposed to information and education being readily available from their place of service (POS). One parent went as far as to enroll in a psychology course to educate herself on treatment options for youth with ADHD and attended an ADHD conference but still reported frustration. She said, I jumped into trying to learn everything I could. Went to CHADD2; read all the materials. And I kept seeing these references to you need to do medication plus behavioral therapy . . . what CHADD seemed to be referring to was more along the lines of helping parents and teacher, but parents in particular to use behavior modification techniques. And what I found very frustrating was, it’s like, yes, but, who, but where . . . (National focus group) Parents described that the lack of coordination is often further heightened due to aforementioned financial costs, communication issues with providers, or lack of overall support. One participant noted, The financial implications of it all and then the stress of it having to feel that you’re making the right decision for your child, while trying to wade through what felt to me like an overwhelming amount of information and points of view. (National focus group) Parents also described a lack of communication between the systems of care, which may impact treatment efficacy. A parent from the National focus group stated, “ . . . it’s the types of things that fall into this behavior group [that] become really difficult because it involved multiple systems but none of those systems talk to each other.” Another participant likened access to therapy as a “multi-problem approach,” describing that her child required varied solutions to treat co-occurring behavioral and mental health issues. She noted, So we have to- parents have to piece it all together. I don’t know whether to go to a psychologist, a psychiatrist, a pediatrician, a neurolo[gist]–I don’t know who to go to to start. And so, you get all these little fragmented pieces and you just try to patch it all together for the remedy. (Southeast focus group) Another parent in a Southeast focus group described care coordination among providers as the “missing piece” to help connect the best treatment options for her child, and said, I think that’s part of the piece that’s missing is . . . all of the different providers working together. I found this ADHD coach that worked with a psychologist, a psychiatrist—they all worked together. Every week they’d talk about her patients and how we can help them . . . there’s not much of that around. And the ones that are around, they don’t take insurance. (Southeast focus group) One participant noted how treatment and care for children with ADHD are not triaged like other diagnoses. Comparing available treatment plans to more acute care, one parent stated, It’s not like there’s a diagnosis and a treatment plan, like cancer . . . you check after so many months, after so many years. There’s not – no size fits all. (National focus group) Parents of young children with ADHD diagnoses in the Southeast reported similarities in lack of direct referrals for treatment options, including upon diagnosis and while attempting to access different treatment options for their child. When asked if any health providers, pediatricians, or other medical professionals provided any direct referrals for services, parents in one Southeast focus group answered with a resounding “no.” Discussion This study sought to highlight parent experiences and perceived barriers to behavioral health services for children diagnosed with ADHD. Responses from parents are consistent with prior research on barriers to ADHD treatment experienced by parents in the United States, including stigma, overall awareness and knowledge of ADHD, issues locating support and services, and logistics related to managing and navigating care (McKenna et al., 2023). In addition, our study also noted barriers with messaging and coordination from providers regarding behavioral health treatment (Mofokeng & van der Wath, 2017). Our study expands on the small number of previous qualitative studies on treatment barriers; our findings confirmed themes for barriers of behavioral service access that had emerged from studies of broader ADHD treatment access (McKenna et al., 2023). Despite being a treatment recommendation, major barriers exist to implementing behavioral treatment for young children diagnosed with ADHD as part of the evidence-based treatment protocol for children of all ages (Kappi & Martel, 2021). Parents described a need for providers – and places of service – to promote a more cohesive and unified treatment plan for young children diagnosed with ADHD. While major strides have been made with

1098 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(9) increased representation and access for ADHD treatment options, stigma was a main barrier reported by parents. Misconceptions and stigma connected to an ADHD diagnosis often preempted parents’ decision-making related to treatment, which has been identified as a theme in the literature (dosReis et al., 2010; McKenna et al., 2023; Paidipati et al., 2022). Parent responses in the current study illustrate the sociopsychological effects of misconceptions and stigma associated with receiving a health diagnosis (Goffman, 1989). Parents reported an initial awareness of their child’s symptoms (i.e., hyperactive and emotional) without acknowledging it as deviant or impairing; they described how this further influences their decision-making by seeking available treatment. This process follows a similar pattern where parents of children with ADHD initially engage in normalization and hesitation, followed by concerns about fear and stigmatization (Spencer et al., 2021). Healthcare professionals as well as education professionals can provide information and education about when behavior is normative and when it is a cause for further evaluation to increase the likelihood that parents seek timely diagnosis and treatment. Further, professionals can address concerns regarding stigma and labeling to promote collaboration between parents and professionals on the treatment plan and to assuage anxieties and frustrations reported by parents (Wolraich et al., 2019). Parent responses also highlight the amount of time required to participate in recommended behavioral therapies, consistent with prior research identifying time and other logistical challenges as prominent barriers to accessing treatment (McKenna et al., 2023). The added time requirement adds stress to their ability to provide care for their families. Parents described a time burden from navigating behavioral treatment options that result in missed time spent with family and career responsibilities. Participating in recommended behavioral therapy services for ADHD becomes an added stressor on parents in addition to being a possible solution to behavioral challenges. Additional treatment options, such as offering online parent training, may decrease barriers for some families (DuPaul et al., 2018). Considering most parents involved in the focus groups were women, more research is needed to identify whether these responses were further influenced by maternal stress (Blum, 2007) and whether there are unique barriers to treatment for mothers of young children with ADHD diagnoses. Additionally, parents of children diagnosed with ADHD between 2 and 7 years of age in the Southeast alluded to more stigmatized experiences than parents in the National focus group. Parents in the Southeast particularly addressed concerns with stigma related to the child’s behavior and to the ADHD diagnosis. Parents in the Southeast focus groups more often reported extensive issues navigating the requisite systems of care to determine the best treatment options, including lack of availability and access to appropriate treatment and referrals. These parents described feeling like pieces were “missing” regarding how to access treatment options. This aligns with national data pointing to higher prevalence of ADHD diagnoses in the states in the south of the U.S., but lower initiation of behavioral health treatment compared to the western states (Danielson et al., 2022; Visser et al., 2014). However, the fact that the Southeast focus groups were conducted in a community-based setting and the National focus groups were drawn from parents who attended a national conference on ADHD limits the generalizability of these differences. Ultimately, parents described lack of information about their child’s treatment as a barrier, regardless of their child’s age. Parents reported having concerns about their child’s behavior at the onset of a diagnosis but were unsure how to implement the appropriate treatment options. Parent training in behavior management is recommended by providers as the primary treatment option for preschool children, but many parents reported needing multiple treatment options to best fit their child’s needs, consistent with prior research (Lu et al., 2022). The high burden and low support described by parents in the focus groups are particularly problematic given the chronicity of ADHD and the need for long-term treatment, specifically for children who experience symptoms at a young age (Loe & Feldman, 2007). The subcommitte on children and adolescents with attention-deficit/ hyperactivity disorder within the American Academy of Pediatrics (Wolraich et al., 2019) identifies ADHD as a long-term condition for children that requires careful monitoring and ongoing support. In addition to facing issues with access to providers, parents also noted issues with a lack of coordination of care and described how the lack of consistency with treatment plans can cause ADHD treatment to become a “multi-problem approach.” ADHD treatment approaches may benefit from having more robust and intentional treatment plans that include collaborations among providers and referrals to specialists for needed care, as well as collaboration with the schools, to develop treatment plans that are unique to their patient’s lived experience (Leslie et al., 2007; Lu et al. 2022; Wolraich et al., 2019). Behavioral therapy is recommended for ADHD, yet clear and accurate messaging, education, support, and guidance regarding these treatments and how they may be integrated with medication where appropriate were largely reported as absent; the lack of consistent communication and coordination were described as frustrating for both parents and their children (Mofokeng & van der Wath, 2017). Pediatric care providers may benefit from additional training to address these barriers. Limitations Key limitations to this study are related to convenience sampling of focus group participants, the age of the data,

Taylor et al. 1099 the inclusion of parents with older children with ADHD diagnoses, and the small number of participants recruited, resulting in limited, non-generalizable participant responses. Focus group participants were recruited from select groups of parents of children with ADHD (ADHD parental support group and ADHD-themed conference), which introduces sampling bias and significantly limits the generalizability of these findings. Parents recruited from both locations may have increased knowledge of ADHD treatment options or be more attuned to navigating care or seeking support. This limits generalizability and may have led to underestimation of barriers, as other parents who are not already connected to ADHD education and support may experience additional barriers. Future research that recruits both parents with presumed access and parents lacking access to a support group or ability to attend a conference may provide a more representative sample. The eligibility criteria for focus groups were also expanded beyond those in the focal age group (diagnosed between the ages of 2–7 years) to increase the pool of eligible participants while focusing on the treatment options offered to parents when receiving an initial ADHD diagnosis. This resulted in a sample of parents where over a third (43%, n = 11) of children were 11 years of age or older. Factors that enable engagement in the select groups from which participants were recruited, and/or factors associated with agreeing to participate in this study, may also have been related to experiences accessing evidence-based treatment for their children in ways that prevent extrapolation of study findings to parents of children with ADHD more broadly. While many key themes emerged (both across parent responses in the two Southeast focus groups and between the National and Southeast focus groups), a larger sample size may be more conducive to generalizability and would support a better understanding of how certain factors influence diagnosis experiences. A more representative sample of parents of children with ADHD throughout the United States (outside of the Southeast) may lead to different conclusions. Additionally, not all participants in this study had children with the same length of time since diagnosis; parent recall with diagnosis or treatment experience may be a contributing limitation. Race and ethnicity of children and parent participants were not captured at the time of the focus groups. While the research questions were not developed with the intention for across-group analyses based on race or ethnicity (or to identify differences with care), this is a limitation given that children of color are disproportionately impacted by misdiagnoses and face additional and markedly different barriers to receiving and maintaining care (Kamimura-Nishimura et al., 2023; Morgan et al., 2013, 2015; Zablotsky et al., 2020). Incorporating these demographic markers in future research would contribute to the literature on childhood ADHD diagnosis experiences across race, the potential misdiagnoses (and dual diagnoses) of ADHD among children of color (Ballentine, 2019), and potential additional barriers to receiving and maintaining ADHD treatment due to negative healthcare experiences. Increasing the sample size to allow and prioritize inclusion of children and parents of color would enable an understanding of their lived experiences and the barriers to receiving and managing ADHD treatment. Finally, the age of the focus group data (2015) is a potential limitation. However, given that findings support and build on themes in the literature, our study findings are applicable in the current context. Conclusion The parent responses presented in this paper can provide a deeper understanding of perceived barriers to behavioral health services for young children diagnosed with ADHD. Our study contributes to current literature by highlighting barriers parents experience when attempting to initiate behavioral health services. The key themes identified in parent responses have implications for enhancing coordinated care of ADHD treatment options across places of service, providers, and families. Training of healthcare providers and educators, along with school-based intervention, may be viable options to improve both access and communication between services and parents, as well as decrease negative educational outcomes (Loe & Feldman, 2007; Wolraich et al., 2019). Addressing these barriers may further improve the alignment between current clinical practice and best practice for treatment of ADHD, particularly among young children. Further, parents from the two Southeast focus groups in particular reported barriers to access especially navigating appropriate care. The parent experiences and perceptions documented in this paper may also inform future efforts to improve access to evidence-based treatments for ADHD in the Southeast and nationwide. Observational Study 1 Medicine ® The association between asthma and ADHD in children and adolescents An observational study and a meta-analysis of Mendelian randomization studies Xiaohui Lan, MDa, Ni Zhong, PhDa, Zixi Tang, MDa, Zebin Tang, MSb, Jiajie Liu, MSa, Xinxin Leng, MSa, Junneng Huang, MSc, Jichao Sun, MDd, Jun Ai, MDe,* Abstract Observational epidemiological analysis and a meta-analysis of Mendelian randomization (MR) were used to investigate the association between attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and asthma in children and adolescents. Based on data from the 1999 to 2004 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), an analysis was conducted to evaluate the association between ADHD and asthma in children and adolescents aged between 4 and 19 years. ADHD and asthma were defined based on self- or parent/guardian proxy-reported physician/health-professional diagnoses from the NHANES Medical Conditions Questionnaire. After analyzing ADHD genome-wide association study data from the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium as instrumental variables, we performed two-sample MR analyses based on genome-wide association study data from 5 studies to examine the causal relationship between genetically predicted ADHD liabilities. In addition, we summarized the results of the inverse-variance weighted method using a random-effects meta-analysis. Asthma prevalence was higher among participants with ADHD than those without ADHD (10.2% vs 5.9%). ADHD was associated with higher odds of asthma (odds ratio = 1.64, 95% confidence interval = 1.36–1.98), and the pattern of results was broadly consistent across subgroups. In contrast, the MR meta-analysis did not support a causal effect of genetically predicted ADHD liability on childhood asthma (odds ratio = 0.94, 95% confidence interval = 0.84–1.05, P > .05). According to data from the NHANES, ADHD and asthma are significantly associated in children and adolescents. A meta-analysis of the MR data did not reveal a causal connection between genetically predicted ADHD liability and childhood asthma. This paradoxical finding illustrates the complex interplay of genetic and nongenetic mechanisms in the ADHD-asthma association. Introduction Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is one of the most common neurodevelopmental disorders in childhood and is associated with substantial functional impairment and comorbid conditions. Asthma is a prevalent chronic respiratory disease in children and adolescents.[1–5] Increasing evidence sug gests that ADHD and asthma may co-occur more often than expected.[6] Prior observational studies have reported associations between asthma and ADHD, but findings have not been fully consistent across populations and study designs.[7–9] Proposed explanations include shared genetic susceptibility, environmental exposures, psychosocial factors, and inflam matory pathways.[10–13] Mendelian randomization (MR) has been used to assess potential causality between ADHD and asthma, yet published MR results remain mixed, likely due to differences in datasets and analytical approaches.[14–16] Two-sample MR leverages genetic variants as instrumen tal variables (IVs) to estimate the effect of an exposure on an outcome and can help reduce confounding and reverse causation.[17] Therefore, we conducted a cross-sectional analysis using National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) to evaluate the association between ADHD and asthma in children and adolescents, and a meta-analysis of 5 two-sample MR studies to examine the effect of geneti cally predicted ADHD liability on childhood asthma risk. We hypothesized that ADHD would be associated with higher odds of asthma in NHANES and that genetically predicted ADHD liability would increase the risk of childhood asthma in MR. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Observational epidemiological analysis Three NHANES cycles (1999–2004) were selected for the study, as these cycles which data on diagnosed with ADHD in children and adolescents was available. Initially, 11,782 subjects aged 4 to 19 were identified in NHANES 1999 to 2004. Following the exclusion of 12 subjects with missing or indeterminate asthma status data were excluded, 24 subjects with incomplete ADHD data, and 1325 subjects with missing covariates (age, sex, race, poverty-to-income ratio [PIR], smoking status of household members, body mass index Z-score [BMIZ], total energy intake in 24 hours, and total fat intake in 24 hours), 10,421 subjects were deemed eligible for inclusion in this study’s analysis. As illustrated in Figure 1, the screening process for participants is a multifaceted procedure. 2.2. Assessment of ADHD and asthma outcomes In NHANES, asthma and ADHD were ascertained from the Medical Conditions Questionnaire (MCQ) module using self- or parent/guardian proxy-reported physician/healthprofessional diagnoses. The diagnosis of asthma was made by answering “yes” to the following question on the NHANES Family Questionnaire (MCQ: MCQ010): “Has a doctor or other healthcare professional told you/the study participant (SP) that you/SP has asthma?” To assess ADHD, in our study, ADHD was diagnosed by answering (MCQ: MCQ060) “Yes” to the following question: “Has a doctor or health profes sional ever told you/SP that you/he/she/SP has attention deficit disorder?” Figure 1. Study population selection flowchart. ADHD = attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, NHANES = National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.

Other covariates We identified potential confounders based on clinical insights and previous studies,[18–24] including age, sex, race, PIR, smoking status of household members, BMIZ, total energy intake over 24 hours, and total fat intake over 24 hours. PIR categorizes poverty status into 3 categories: 1.30, 1.31 to 3.50, and 3.50. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated as weight in kilo grams divided by height in meters squared (kg/m2). Due to the lack of pre-calculated BMIZ data for the NHANES 1999 to 2004 cycles, BMI Z-scores were calculated based on age and sex using 2 distinct methods according to age groups: For children aged ≤59 months, BMIZ was calculated using the WHO Anthro Survey Analyser Online (https://worldhealthorg. shinyapps.io/anthro/), following the tool’s instructions and based on the 2006 WHO Child Growth Standards. Input parameters included age (in months), sex, standing height, and weight. BMIZ values outside the biologically plausible range of −5 to +5 standard deviations (SDs) were flagged as potential errors; in this study, no such extreme values were identified, and all calculated BMIZ values were retained for analysis. For children and adolescents aged >59 months, BMIZ was calculated using SAS software (version 9.4; SAS Institute Inc.) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)- provided SAS source code program (cdc-source-code.sas), which implements the CDC 2000 growth reference. This program uti lizes age (in months or days), sex, height (in cm), and weight (in kg) to compute age- and sex-specific BMI Z-scores. Similarly, BMIZ values outside the range of −5 to +5 SDs were considered biologically implausible; no such extreme values were found in our dataset. The age cutoff of 59 months (approximately 4 years 11 months) was strictly applied to determine the calculation method. Children aged 4 to 5 years are classified according to the 2006 WHO child growth standards,[24] while children and adolescents aged 5 to 19 years are classified according to the 2007 growth reference values.[25] Children’s weight status was subsequently categorized as: normal weight (BMIZ < +1 SD), overweight (BMIZ ≥ +1 SD and <+2 SD), and obesity (BMIZ ≥ +2 SD). Smoking status among household members was assessed using the NHANES household questionnaire (SMQFAM: SMD410). Dietary intake data for two 24-hour periods were used to determine participants’ energy (kcal) and fat (g) intakes. An average of the total energy intake and total fat intake over the 2 recall periods was calculated; if only the first day’s data were available, the first day’s value was used instead. Among covariates, PIR had a skewed distribution, median imputation of missing values was performed using Empower stats software (X&Y Solutions, Inc.). For all covariates except PIR, the individual was excluded if any covariate was missing. In the final analysis, the data of all 10,421 people were complete. Because PIR was right-skewed and served only as an adjustment covariate, we imputed missing PIR with the median (a robust measure for skewed distributions) to preserve sample size and statistical power. 2.4. Sources of two-sample MR This two-sample MR study aimed to investigate the causal effect of ADHD on the risk of childhood asthma. Genomewide association study (GWAS) data for ADHD were obtained from the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium (PGC).[26] A total of 225,534 people were included in the study, includ ing 38,691 ADHD patients and 186,843 controls. Singlenucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with ADHD at genome-wide significant levels were selected, and this study used P < 5 × 10−8 as the screening threshold for exposure factors and selected independent SNPs with r2 < 0.01 and clump distance ≤5000 kb to avoid the influence of linkage disequilibrium on the results. In addition, we assessed the strength of the exposure factor using the F-statistic value calculated as follows: f = β2/SD2, where β denotes the effect value of SNPs on exposure and SD denotes the standard deviation. SNPs with F-statistic values <10 were excluded to avoid bias due to weak IVs.[27] The final 26 SNPs associ ated with ADHD were retained as IVs for subsequent MR analyses. Table S1 presents further information regarding the exposure and outcome datasets. A comprehensive over view of the SNPs associated with ADHD can be found in Table S2. Childhood asthma GWAS summary statistics were drawn from 5 large, publicly available datasets (FinnGen, UK Biobank, and 3 published GWASs) to maximize statistical power and to assess robustness across independent resources, prioritizing predominantly European-ancestry samples to reduce population stratification.[28,29] Potential sample over lap between the PGC ADHD GWAS and each asthma GWAS dataset was evaluated based on reported cohort composition; no overlap was expected. Methodological work indicates that, if overlap were present in a two-sample MR with weak instruments, the resulting bias would tend to move estimates toward the confounded observational association, whereas complete non-overlap yields conservative bias toward the null.[30] 2.5. Statistical analysis NHANES uses sampling weights, strata, and primary sam pling units. In this study, regression analyses were conducted without applying NHANES sampling weights or survey design variables; therefore, estimates should be interpreted as associations within the analytic sample rather than population-representative estimates. In observational epi demiologic analyses, we grouped participants according to the presence or absence of asthma, and descriptive analyses were performed for all participants. We expressed baseline characteristics as mean ± SD for continuous variables and as percentages for categorical variables. Stratified analyses were performed to assess the associa tion between ADHD and asthma within predefined subgroups (sex, age, race, PIR, BMIZ, total energy intake, total fat intake, household smoking status; see Table 2). A significant interaction (P < .05) indicates that the strength of the association between ADHD and asthma differs across the levels of the stratification variable. Statistical analysis using logistic regression was performed to assess the association between ADHD and asthma. Three models were constructed: Model 1 (unadjusted model), Model 2 (sex, age), and Model 3 (age, sex, race/ethnicity, PIR, smoking status of household members, BMIZ, total energy intake over 24 hours, and total fat intake over 24 hours). P < .05 was con sidered statistically significant. The strength of the relationship was determined by calculating odds ratios (ORs) and 95% con fidence intervals (CIs). In MR, genetic variation determines the causal relationship between an exposure factor and an outcome. To analyze the causal relationship between ADHD and asthma in children and adolescents, we adopted the following methods: inversevariance weighted (IVW), MR Egger, weighted median, simple mode, weighted mode, and MR-PRESSO.[31] Cochran Q test was used to estimate heterogeneity. EmpowerStats software (www. empowerstats.com) and R (version 4.3.1; https://www.r-project. org) were used to analyze all data. The IVW results from the 5 two-sample MR analyses were combined using a random-effects meta-analysis method. The I2 statistic was then used to assess the heterogeneity of each outcome from the different data sources. I2 values of <25%, between 25% and 75%, and >75% indicate low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. A random-effects model was

Epidemiological observation and analysis Finally, a total of 10,421 patients were included and divided into an asthma group and a non-asthma group, with 1665 patients (16.0%) in the asthma group and 8756 patients (84.0%) in the non-asthma group. There were signifi cant differences between the asthma group and the nonasthma group in terms of gender, race, BMI Z-score, and ADHD prevalence (P < .001). In the asthma group, 54.7% were male, 40.1% were non-Hispanic Black, and the BMI Z-score distribution was skewed toward to higher inter vals. Total fat intake was slightly higher in the asthma group than in the non-asthma group (P = .029). Notably, the ADHD prevalence rate was 10.2% in the asthma group, significantly higher than the 5.9% in the non-asthma group, suggesting a potential association between the 2 conditions (Table 1). Stratified analyses (Table 2) generally showed a positive asso ciation between ADHD and asthma across demographic, socio economic, and metabolic strata. The magnitude of the association varied across subgroups (e.g., sex, age group, race/ethnicity, PIR, BMI category, dietary intake, and household smoking status), and interaction testing suggested effect modification by income (P for interaction < .05). Table 3 shows the results of logistic regression analysis. ADHD was significantly and positively associated with asthma in all 3 models. The results showed that after adjusting for all covariates, the association between ADHD and asthma remained significant with an OR of 1.64 (95% CI = 1.36–1.98, P for trend < .01). 3.2. Results of MR analysis The results of the MR analysis of ADHD on childhood asthma are shown in Table S3. Following our defined screen ing criteria (P < 5 × 108, r2 < 0.01, F > 10) and after exclud ing potential confounding factors associated with asthma, 26 independent SNPs significantly associated with ADHD were selected from the PGC dataset as genetic instrument vari ables for ADHD. The childhood asthma dataset from FinnGen Database included 8402 cases and 259,839 controls, all from a European pop ulation. Funnel plot analysis did not reveal significant bias (Fig. S2A), and sensitivity analy sis using the leave-one-out method indicated that remov ing any SNP did not significantly alter the results further supporting the robustness of the findings (Fig. S3A). The dataset from Sakaue et al’s study[32] included 27,712 cases of European ancestry, 411,131 controls of European ances try, 547 cases of East Asian ancestry, and 161,803 controls of East Asian ancestry. Meta-analysis results This meta-analysis identified significant heterogeneity (I2 = 83.9%, P < .0001) across studies, necessitating a randomeffects IVW model. The pooled OR (OR = 0.94, 95% CI = 0.84– 1.05, P > .05) across FinnGen, UK Biobank, and prior studies (Sakaue et al, Ferreira et al, and Zhu et al) demonstrated no significant causal relationship between ADHD and childhood asthma risk (Fig. 3). 4. Discussion This study examined the association between ADHD and asthma in children and adolescents using observational analy ses and MR. Observational analyses indicated an association between ADHD and asthma, whereas MR did not support a causal effect. This apparent discrepancy highlights the complex interplay of genetic and nongenetic mechanisms underlying ADHD–asthma comorbidity. Because the NHANES component is cross-sectional, these observational findings should be inter preted as associations and do not establish causation. In con trast, MR evaluates the effect of genetically predicted ADHD liability on asthma under instrumental-variable assumptions. We observed a positive association between ADHD and asthma, consistent with previous studies.[34,35] For example, a case–control study in adults reported a significant association: asthma prevalence was 9.7% among individuals with ADHD, significantly higher than in those without ADHD.[34] In addition, a meta-analysis suggested that children with ADHD are more likely to develop allergic diseases, including asthma.[35] Stratified analyses indicated that the ADHD–asthma asso ciation was stronger in females, suggesting that sex may modify mechanisms underlying comorbidity. For ADHD, pedi atric clinical studies report a male-to-female diagnostic ratio of ~4:1,[36] whereas population-based studies often report a ratio closer to 2:1.[37] Females with ADHD more often present with Figure 2. ESR signaling has been implicated in sex differences across psychiatric disor ders, suggesting that hormonal factors may modulate ADHD pathophysiology. Notably, the same variant (rs6930355) has also been associated with obesity-related traits (e.g., waist cir cumference and BMI),[41] highlighting its broader involvement in metabolic and neurodevelopmental pathways. Animal stud ies provide further insight into sex-specific mechanisms. Male ESR1-knockout mice showed reduced airway hyperresponsive ness after allergen exposure (P < .05), whereas no such effect was observed in females.[42] This finding suggests that ESR1 regulation of airway hyperresponsiveness differs by sex, with males exhibiting a more pronounced airway response to aller gens. Further research is needed to determine whether hormone fluctuations across developmental stages influence the cooccurrence of ADHD and asthma. Age-stratified analyses showed a significant association between ADHD and asthma among participants aged 6 to 19 years, consistent with prior epidemiological evidence.[43] Intriguingly, the <6 years age group (N = 957) showed the high est point estimate of risk (OR = 2.43, 95% CI = 0.74–7.99, P = .144), though statistical significance was not achieved, potentially due to limited power from the small subsam ple size. However, children of different age groups have dif ferent immune levels[44] and sex hormone levels, especially during puberty, which is an important developmental period marked by hormonal, metabolic, and immune changes,[45] with hormone-driven gender differences gradually becoming appar ent.[46,47] In the future, it will be important to conduct further longitudinal studies. Race/ethnicity-stratified analyses indicated a stronger ADHD–asthma association among Hispanic participants, par ticularly in other Hispanic subgroups. Differences in educa tional resources, socioeconomic gradients, parental stress, and cumulative adverse childhood experiences exist across racial groups,[48–52] which may simultaneously increase the likelihood of ADHD and asthma in certain racial/ethnic groups. We also observed that the association was strongest in low-income households. Studies have reported that each 10% increase in household income during childhood is associated with a 0.6% to 1.7% increase in asthma medication use and a 2.5% decrease in psychotropic medication use.[53] Economic stress may act syn ergistically through exacerbating psychosocial stressors (such as strained caregiver-child relationships[54]) and environmental triggers (such as homelessness[55]), thereby increasing the risk of neurodevelopmental disorders and allergic diseases. Stratified analyses by BMI Z-score (BMIZ), total energy intake and dietary fat intake indicated stronger associations among overweight/obese participants and those with highcalorie, high-fat diets. Although ADHD co-occurs with obe sity,[56] and obesity is associated with asthma onset,[57,58] ADHD and overweight/obesity in the general population may also reflect psychosocial factors (e.g., overcrowded living conditions and parental separation).[59] High energy intake may influence both ADHD and asthma.[60,61] For example, high consumption of artificially sweetened beverages has been linked to hyper active symptoms.[62] In addition, early use of stimulant medi cations (e.g., methylphenidate) may increase susceptibility to sugar reinforcement, thereby increasing the risk of obesity.[63] Notably, interactions along the gut–brain and gut–lung axes have been proposed as possible pathways linking neurodevelop mental and respiratory phenotypes, primarily through immune modulation and microbiota-related processes.[64–69] Both ADHD and asthma have been reported to be associated with low-grade inflammatory activity, and cytokines such as interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor-α have been discussed as candidate correlates rather than confirmed drivers of co-occurrence.[70] High-sugar/high-fat dietary patterns can alter gut microbiota composition and intestinal barrier function and may influence systemic inflammation.[71] In children with ADHD, differences in gut microbial profiles and related metabolites (including shortchain fatty acids) have been observed, and SCFA-related immune effects have been suggested to be relevant to allergic disease and asthma.[72–75] However, these gut–brain/lung pathways remain hypothesis-generating, and longitudinal or experimental studies are needed to establish directionality and causality. The association between ADHD and asthma was significant regardless of the presence of smokers in the home. Previously, exposure to secondhand smoke in the home has been investi gated as a potential risk factor for ADHD associated with aller gic diseases.[76] Harmful substances from smoking (e.g., nicotine and tar) may increase the risk of ADHD and asthma through multiple mechanisms, such as affecting fetal development and influencing the function of the immune system in children.[77,78] The results of the stratified analyses in this study suggest that factors such as gender, age, race, household economic status, weight, and dietary habits may influence the association between ADHD and asthma through different mechanisms. These find ings provide important directions for future research, suggesting the need to further explore the specific roles of these factors in the mechanisms of ADHD and asthma. However, observational studies are vulnerable to confounding, including unmeasured factors such as maternal medication use during pregnancy and maternal disease history. Genetic studies have found that paren tal asthma, particularly maternal asthma exacerbation, is asso ciated with an increased risk of ADHD in offspring.[79] However, there is limited evidence and conflicting results regarding a causal relationship between ADHD and asthma. In order to assess the causal relationship, we used MR and meta-analysis of MR results. The results of 5 two-sample MR analyses were inconsistent, and this discrepancy may be attributed to differences in popu lation characteristics and sample sizes across the datasets.[80,81] ADHD in childhood is highly heritable and primarily driven by familial factors; however, its heritability appears to be lower in adulthood, though this remains a topic of ongoing debate.[11] A study in Turkey observed that the prevalence of asthma among children with ADHD was similar to that of their siblings.[82] Some studies have separated ADHD into hyperactivity–impul sivity (HI) and IN dimensions and examined each in relation to asthma.[83] They found that the association between childhood asthma and HI may be mediated by genetic overlap or envi ronmental factors, while no significant association was found for IN.[84] Future studies could refine phenotyping by analyz ing HI and IN separately and by classifying asthma into clini cally relevant subtypes (e.g., cough-variant asthma), to test for subtype-specific causal relationships. Although MR can reduce unmeasured confounding and reverse causality, ADHD and asthma are influenced by both genetic and environmental factors,[84,85] and MR primarily cap tures effects mediated by genetic instruments. Secondly, limita tions of IVs are also a possible reason for this discrepancy, and despite the stringent screening criteria we used (P < 5 × 10−8, r2 < 0.01), the IVs (SNPs) may still suffer from pleiotropy,[86] which affects the accuracy of causal inference. The present study included a dataset sample of mainly children of European origin, which may have reached different conclusions from previous observational studies due to differences in genetic background. Meta-analysis suggested a high degree of heterogeneity between studies (I2 = 83.9%), suggesting that different populations, envi ronments, or genetic backgrounds may have contributed to the differences in effect sizes. 4.1. Significance and limitations of the study Our study integrates data from multiple annual cycles and specifically targets children and adolescents aged from 4 to 19 years. MR studies reduce confounding bias and reverse causality

8 Lan et al. • Medicine (2026) 105:21  Medicine bias. We also performed a meta-analysis to combine associa tions estimated from independent data sources. Providing mul tidimensional evidence for comorbid ADHD and asthma, this approach ensured adequate statistical power and robustness of the findings. As the main study population was children and adolescents aged 4 to 19 years, some covariates (e.g., smoking status, alcohol consumption, mental health problems) were incomplete, thus preventing correlation analyses and confirmation of whether these covariates played an interaction role in this study. Our assessment of ADHD and asthma relied solely on parent/guard ian self-report in the NHANES family questionnaires. Although this approach is practical for large-scale surveys, it is susceptible to misclassification. Self-reported diagnoses may underestimate the true prevalence, particularly for milder cases that do not seek medical attention or where the diagnosis was not com municated or recalled.[87,88] Furthermore, differential reporting tendencies or healthcare access across racial/ethnic groups and socioeconomic strata could introduce bias in the observed asso ciations.[89,90] This non-differential misclassification would likely attenuate the observed associations towards the null, meaning our reported ORs might underestimate the true strength of the link between ADHD and asthma. While MR offers advantages over observational studies in minimizing confounding and reverse causality, several inherent limitations of the MR approach warrant careful consideration when interpreting our causal null findings: MR primarily captures the component of the causal effect mediated by the genetic predisposition to the exposure (ADHD). Both ADHD and asthma are complex multifactorial disorders influenced by intricate interplay between genetic susceptibil ity and environmental exposures (e.g., air pollution, early-life infections, psychosocial stress, and diet). Our analysis cannot incorporate direct effects of environmental factors or geneenvironment interactions (G × E). For instance, the genetic risk for ADHD might only translate to increased asthma risk under specific environmental triggers, a pathway invisible to standard MR. Asthma is a highly heterogeneous condition. Our MR anal yses primarily utilized broadly defined “childhood asthma.” Crucially, ADHD genetic liability might be causally linked only to specific asthma endotypes or phenotypes, such as allergic asthma or severe asthma, rather than asthma as a whole. The aggregation of diverse subtypes in the outcome GWAS could dilute or obscure genuine subtype-specific causal effects. Future MR using GWAS data on well-defined asthma subtypes is needed. Therefore, our MR meta-analysis, while not supporting a consistent direct causal effect of the genetically proxied risk for (largely adult-defined) ADHD on broadly defined child hood asthma, cannot rule out: environmental effects or G × E underlying the comorbidity; a causal effect specific to childhood ADHD genetic factors or specific asthma subtypes; or import ant indirect causal effects mediated by ADHD-driven behavioral and lifestyle changes. 5. Future research directions In the future, multi-omics analyses combining genomic, epig enomic, and transcriptomic data should be performed to reveal the molecular mechanisms underlying the co-morbidity between ADHD and asthma. Longitudinal studies should be designed and prospective cohort studies should be conducted to assess the long-term association and dynamic changes of ADHD and asthma. Asthma is a heterogeneous disease, and different sub types (e.g., allergic asthma vs nonallergic asthma) may be dif ferently associated with ADHD. In addition to the traditional classifications of ADHD into hyperactive-impulsive, inatten tive, and combined (ADHD-C) subtypes, ADHD can also be categorized into familial and nonfamilial forms.[91] These sub type classifications exhibit distinct developmental trajectories and clinical outcomes.[92] Large-scale stratified analyses are cru cial for resolving subtype-specific heterogeneity and identifying potential causal pathways. 6. Conclusion Using observational and MR analyses, we found a positive ADHD–asthma association in NHANES but no causal effect in MR, with heterogeneity across asthma GWAS datasets. These results suggest complex genetic and nongenetic contributions. Clinicians should consider integrated management for chil dren with co-occurring ADHD and asthma, and coordinated pediatric care may improve outcomes and reduce healthcare utilization. Observational Study 1 Medicine ® The relationship between problematic social media use and psychological factors among university students with evaluation of ADHD, social anxiety and self-esteem Gamze Gürcan, MD, MSca,* , Latife Büşra Çokaslan, MDa Abstract Problematic social media use (PSMU) has been increasingly associated with various psychological vulnerabilities; however, findings remain mixed, particularly among university students and in non-Western contexts. This study aimed to examine the associations between PSMU and psychological factors including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms, social anxiety, and self-esteem among university students, as well as to explore the role of selected sociodemographic and usagerelated characteristics. This cross-sectional study included 179 university students aged 18 to 25 years. Participants completed a sociodemographic and clinical information form, the Social Media Addiction Scale–Adult Form, Adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Self-Report Scale, Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale, and Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale–Short Form. Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS v22.0. Spearman correlation analyses and group comparisons were performed, with statistical significance set at P < .05. Mean daily screen time was 352.29 ± 156.41 minutes, significantly higher than the global average. Social media addiction scale scores positively correlated with ADHD symptoms (r = 0.412, P < .001), social anxiety (r = 0.395, P < .001), and low self-esteem (r = 0.221, P = .03). Participants who found it easier to communicate on social media exhibited higher social anxiety scores. The use of social media with hidden identities or fake accounts was associated with increased screen time, social media addiction severity, and social anxiety. The findings indicate that problematic social media use among university students is closely associated with psychological vulnerabilities, particularly ADHD symptoms and social anxiety, whereas the role of self-esteem appears more nuanced. These results support the conceptualization of PSMU as a multidimensional phenomenon influenced by individual psychological traits and usage-related behaviors rather than by time spent online alone. By providing data from a non-Western university student population, this study contributes to the cultural generalizability of existing literature and highlights the importance of considering multiple psychological domains when addressing problematic social media use. Abbreviations: ADHD = attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, ASRS = Adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder SelfReport Scale, LSAS = Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale, PSMU = problematic social media use, RSES = Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale-Short Form, SMAS-AF = Social Media Addiction Scale-Adult Form. Keywords: ADHD, PSMU, self-esteem, social anxiety, social media 1. Introduction The exponential growth of digital technologies has led to a marked increase in global internet usage, with over 62.6% of the population actively engaging with social media plat forms as of May 2024.[1,2] Despite its ubiquity, the empirical literature on problematic social media use (PSMU) remains underdeveloped relative to broader research on internet and smartphone addiction. Internet addiction presents in various subtypes, including social media addiction, gaming disorder, cybersex addiction, and compulsive online shopping.[3] While the detrimental effects – such as social withdrawal, financial distress, familial conflict, and deviant behavior in minors – are well documented, the nosological status of internet-related disorders remains contentious. Competing paradigms situate these behaviors within the frameworks of substance use dis orders, obsessive-compulsive spectrum disorders, or impulse control disorders, reflecting significant diagnostic ambiguity.[4,5] Consequently, terminological inconsistency persists, with over lapping labels such as “problematic internet use,” “internet addiction and “internetomania.”[6,7] The authors have no funding and conflicts of interest to declare.
