2 Gürcan and Çokaslan • Medicine (2026) 105:38  Medicine Andreassen and Pallesen define PSMU as excessive preoc cupation with and compulsive use of social networking plat forms, impairing psychosocial functioning.[8] Other terms used to describe this condition include “Social Media Use Disorder and “Networks Use Disorder.”[9] While usage alone may be neu tral or modestly linked with mental health outcomes, PSMU – defined by compulsive, addiction-like behaviors (e.g., preoccu pation, withdrawal, tolerance, loss of control) – has emerged as a more clinically relevant construct.[10] Excessive social media use, similar to excessive internet or smartphone use, has been linked to various issues, including sleep quality,[11,12] symptoms of anxiety,[13,14] depression,[13,15,16] reduced psychological well-being,[17] diminished self-esteem[13] and psychological distress.[18,19] Nevertheless, alongside evi dence of adverse psychological effects, some studies highlight potential benefits, including enhanced quality of life, improved social support, greater well-being and decreased stress.[20,21] Problematic social media use refers to patterns that mirror behavioral addiction, characterized by compulsive engage ment and an inability to reduce usage despite negative con sequences.[22] Like heavy usage, problematic use has been associated with mental health problems, including increased symptoms of depression and anxiety, lower well-being, and reduced self-esteem.[23-26] A focused meta‐analysis of 53 studies revealed a robust positive correlation between social anxiety and PSMU.[10] Studies have demonstrated a positive correla tion between problematic social networking site use and atten tion deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).[11,27] Further studies suggest links to major depressive disorder, obsessivecompulsive disorder, eating disorders, and substance use.[28] A study on personality traits found a positive correlation between impulsivity and social media addiction, while selfesteem served as a protective factor.[29] Notably, social media can be beneficial for individuals with low self-esteem and self-confidence by providing support and facilitating commu nication within their social circles.[30] Recent research has increasingly examined the relationship between ADHD and social media use, highlighting both fre quent and problematic patterns of engagement.[31,32] Studies across various digital domains, including television and internet use, suggest a temporal association between early media expo sure and later ADHD symptoms, though these studies often lack clinical ADHD samples.[33] Meta-analyses reveal modest links between ADHD traits and digital engagement, especially internet addiction, but do not support strong causal infer ences. Empirical findings further differentiate between intensity of use – frequent use not necessarily indicating dysfunction – and problematic use, which more consistently correlates with ADHD symptoms.[34-36] Adolescents with ADHD tend to use social media more intensely, hold more accounts (also more fake accounts) and exhibit higher distractibility and impulsivity online.[37-39] The studies found an association between PSMU and ADHD characteristics. In a large survey, adolescents reported an association of addictive social media use with hyperactivity.[40] A study showed that, users with ADHD have significantly dif ferent posting behaviors, such that they posted more tweets and used more swear words.[41] The studies mostly focused on the Facebook and Twitter as social media channels.[42] Social anxiety is widely recognized as a significant risk fac tor PSMU.[43,44] Individuals with high social anxiety or social deficits may overuse social media to compensate for offline social difficulties.[45] Social media provides a comfortable virtual environment, potentially replacing real-world social interac tions. PSMU acts as a coping mechanism to fulfill unmet social needs among those with elevated social anxiety.[46-48] Conversely, socially skilled and extraverted individuals also engage inten sively with social media, thereby increasing PSMU risk, indi cating that the link between social anxiety and PSMU is not straightforward.[49-51] Empirical studies report positive correla tions between social anxiety and PSMU, but effect sizes vary substantially, with some studies finding no significant associa tion.[10] Gender differences remain inconclusive: some research indicates males are more prone to PSMU. Some studies have even suggested that the relationship between social anxiety and PSMU may be stronger in females than in males, whereas other studies suggest minimal or even stronger effects in females.[52-54] Age as a moderator is also unclear, and cultural factors also play an important role.[49,55] The studies suggested that low self-esteem and PSMU are consistently correlated, but the causal direction of their rela tionship remains unclear.[56] Two dominant perspectives exist. The first one suggests that low self-esteem contributes to PSMU. Individuals engage with media to fulfill psychological and social needs.[57] Personal traits – such as self-esteem – influence sus ceptibility to internet-related behavioral addictions. Individuals with low self-esteem often experience social difficulties and a weak sense of self, making them more likely to seek affirma tion through social media. This behavioral pattern may lead to PSMU as users increasingly rely on digital interactions for social validation and identity reinforcement.[58] Conversely, the second perspective contends that PSMU may negatively impact self-esteem.[30] Frequent social media use encourages individuals to experiment with multiple online personas, weakening their sense of a coherent identity.[59,60] Furthermore, upward social comparisons, common on networking platforms, can intensify feelings of inferiority, contributing to lower self-esteem.[61] Most research in this area relies on cross-sectional data, lim iting conclusions regarding directionality rather than causality, and has predominantly focused on adolescent samples.[56,62] Although university students are often classified as late adoles cents, they represent a distinct developmental and contextual group characterized by increased autonomy, reduced parental monitoring, and greater exposure to academic and social stress ors. Research examining the associations between problematic social media use and psychological factors specifically among university students, particularly in non-Western countries, therefore remains relatively limited. This study aims to exam ine the associations between problematic social media use and psychological factors including ADHD symptoms, social anxi ety, and self-esteem among university students. In addition, the study explores the role of usage-related characteristics (screen time, communication preferences, and anonymous account use) in relation to problematic social media use. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Participants This study was conducted at the Department of Psychiatry, TOBB University of Economics and Technology, and received ethical approval from the local ethics committee (Ethics Committee No. KAEK-118/134). The study included 179 university stu dents aged 18 to 25 who met the inclusion criteria and pro vided informed consent. A convenience sampling method was used. Participants were recruited through announcements on the university’s official faculty communication platform. After receiving ethics approval, a brief explanation of the study, the informed consent form, and a secure survey link were sent to eli gible students. Inclusion criteria were being within the specified age range and willing to participate. Exclusion criteria included reluctance to participate, incomplete participation, or expecta tion of financial benefit. Data were recorded anonymously. 2.2. Procedure This study was designed as a cross-sectional one. The partici pants were assessed with a sociodemographic and clinical form, the Social Media Addiction Scale- Adult Form (SMAS-AF), Adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Self-Report

3 Gürcan and Çokaslan • Medicine (2026) 105:38  www.md-journal.com Scale (ASRS), Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale for Adults (LSAS), Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale- Short Form (RSES). All proce dures performed in studies involving human participants were in accordance with the ethical standards of the institutional and/or national research committee and with the 1964 Helsinki declaration and its later amendments or comparable ethical standards. Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study. 2.3. Instruments Participants were assessed using the following instruments: The Sociodemographic and Clinical Information Form: Sociodemographic data (age, gender, social environment, income status), screen time, anxiety level when unable to access social media, and social media use patterns were collected. Anxiety level when unable to access social media was assessed via self-report using a visual analog scale ranging from 0 (no anxiety) to 10 (extreme anxiety). The Social Media Addiction Scale-Adult Form (SMAS-AF): The validity and reliability of which was made by Şahin and Yağcı,[63] is a scale consisting of 2 sub-dimensions and a total of 20 items. The score for each question is rated from 1 to 5, “1-Not suitable for me at all,” “2-Not suitable for me,” “3- Undecided,” “4-Suitable for me,” “5-Very suitable for me.” Negative expres sions were reverse coded. The virtual tolerance sub-dimension consists of items 1 to 11, and the virtual communication subdimension consists of items 12 to 20. The lowest score that can be obtained from the scale is 20, and the highest score is 100. The Cronbach α internal consistency coefficient for the overall scale was reported as 0.94. Adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Self-Report Scale (ASRS): This scale was developed by the World Health Organization to detect attention deficit and hyperactivity dis order in adults. The validity and reliability study was con ducted by Doğan et al., and the Cronbach α was 0.8.[64] It is an 18-item self-report scale consisting of 9 items each, with 2 subscales: attention deficit (A) and hyperactivity/impulsivity (B). The score of each question is rated from 0 to 4 (never = 0, rarely1, sometimes = 2, often = 3 points, and very often = 4 points). A score of 24 or above on either of the 2 subscales is indicative of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. The use of the ASRS in this study reflects its suitability as a screen ing tool for assessing ADHD symptoms in non-clinical pop ulations. However, it should be noted that the scale does not provide a clinical diagnosis, and the results should therefore be interpreted as reflecting symptom severity rather than con firmed ADHD. The Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale for Adults (LSAS): The scale, developed in 1987 by Michael Liebowitz, consists of 24 items and 2 subscales. The 24 items are first rated on a Likert scale from 0 to 3 on fear felt during the situations, and then the same items are rated regarding avoidance of the situation (Fear: none = 0, mild = 1, moderate = 2, severe = 3 points/ Avoidance: never = 0, occasionally = 1, often = 2, usually = 3 points). The total scores for the Fear and Avoidance sections provide an overall score with a maximum of 144 points. The validity and reliability study was conducted by Dilbaz and Güz.[65] The Cronbach α was 0.98. Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale-Short Form (RSES): The scale, which is considered a reference in self-esteem measurement, was developed by Morris Rosenberg in 1963. The reliability and validity studies of the scale in Turkey were conducted by Çuhadaroğlu (1986), and the Cronbach α was 0.71.[66] The scale consists of twelve subdomains, and the first ten items mea sure self-esteem. Items 1, 2, 4, 6, 7 are positively coded, while items 3, 5, 8, 9, and 10 are negatively coded. A low score in the scale indicates high self-esteem; a high score indicates low self-esteem. 2.4. Statistical analysis Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS (Statistical Package for Social Sciences) version 22.0 for Windows. Mean ± standard deviation and median (minimum–maximum) were used as descriptive statistics for quantitative variables, and the number of people (percentage) was used for qualitative vari ables. Normality of distribution of the numerical variables was examined by the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, and the homoge neity of the variances was examined by the Levene test. When data were not normally distributed, nonparametric tests were applied. Spearman correlation analysis was used to examine relationships between numerical variables. Participants were categorized into 3 groups based on how they compared social media with face-to-face communication (more difficult on social media, no difference, easier on social media) and into 2 groups based on whether they used social media with a hidden iden tity or fake account. The Mann–Whitney U test was used for 2-group comparisons, and the Kruskal–Wallis test was used for comparisons of more than 2 independent groups. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test. The signifi cance level was set at P < .05. 3. Results 3.1. Discussion While previous studies have often examined ADHD, social anx iety, or self-esteem in isolation, the present study contributes to the literature by simultaneously examining these psychological domains within a single framework. This integrative approach allows for a more nuanced understanding of how multiple vul nerabilities may coexist and interact in relation to problematic social media use. An additional contribution of this study lies in the examination of specific social media usage patterns, such as preferences for online versus face-to-face communication and the use of hidden identities or fake accounts. These behav ioral indicators are rarely examined alongside standardized psychological measures and may serve as clinically relevant markers of problematic social media use risk. The mean daily screen time of 352.29 ± 156.41 minutes and the mean SMAS-AF score of 55.40 ± 11.97 indicate a high level of social media engagement in this population. This usage exceeds the reported global average of 2 hours and 20 minutes per day,[2] may indicate that PSMU is more common among uni versity students, particularly those aged 18 to 25, than the general population. This could be attributed to the voluntary nature of the study, potentially attracting students with higher social media usage. Whereas previous studies predominantly focused on plat forms such as Facebook and Twitter, our study yielded a different result.[42] Instagram, an application emphasizing visual content, was the most frequently used platform. The evolving content and features of social media platforms suggest that studies on PSMU need to be continually updated to reflect these changes. Specifically, SMAS-AF scores were positively associated with both the inattentive and hyper active/impulsive subscales of ASRS, suggesting that both symp tom domains of ADHD may contribute to compulsive social media engagement. These results align with prior studies indi cating that individuals with ADHD traits may be more suscepti ble to PSMU due to difficulties with self-regulation, higher levels of distractibility, and a greater tendency to seek instant gratifi cation.[31,34,35] In a large survey, participants reported an associ ation between addictive social media use and hyperactivity.[40] These findings align with previous research demonstrating simi lar associations.[11,27,31,32] In our study, screen time was positively correlated with the ASRS-A score (attention deficit symptoms); however, it was not associated with hyperactivity/impulsivity (ASRS-B). This suggests that while hyperactivity may be a risk factor for PSMU, it is not directly related to increased screen time. The participants were evaluated according to their compar ison between communication on social media and face-to-face communication and were divided into 3 groups. There was a statistically significant difference in terms of the total score of ASRS and ASRS-A, and the group that found it more difficult to communicate on social media had lower scores. Although the literature consistently demonstrates a positive association between PSMU and ADHD, the findings of the present study offer a noteworthy observation: individuals exhibiting ADHD symptoms – particularly those characterized by inattention – appear to perceive face-to-face communication as more chal lenging compared to communication via social media platforms. However, the limited sample sizes across the groups may have reduced the statistical power and generalizability of these find ings. If participants had been categorized into binary groups (e.g., yes vs no) rather than 3, different results might have emerged. It was found that adolescents with ADHD tend to use social media more intensely, hold more accounts, and also more fake accounts.[37-39] In our study, a statistically significant difference was observed in only ASRS-A scores between the groups divided due to hiding identity/using a fake account or not. However, no significant differences were observed in total ASRS and ASRS-B scores. Studies focusing on PSMU and ADHD often lack clinical ADHD samples.[33] As in our study, there are existing studies that screen for ADHD symptoms; however, there is a growing need for future research that compares individuals with a clin ical diagnosis of ADHD to matched control groups. Consistent with the inherent limitations of cross-sectional designs, our study cannot determine the directionality of the observed asso ciations. Specifically, it remains uncertain whether problematic social media use contributes to the exacerbation of ADHD symptoms, or if individuals exhibiting ADHD-related traits are more susceptible to developing problematic usage patterns. In line with the existing literature, this study also found robust positive associations between social anxiety and PSMU.[43,44] Participants with higher LSAS scores, reflecting elevated levels of both social fear and avoidance, were more likely to report higher SMAS-AF scores and greater screen time. This is congruent with the hypothesis that individuals with social anxiety may overutilize social media as a compen satory strategy to navigate social interactions that they find challenging in offline contexts.[44,45,47] The virtual environment offers a sense of control and reduced risk of negative evalu ation, potentially fostering a maladaptive reliance on online communication. Differences in PSMU severity across groups, categorized by their comfort levels in online versus face-to-face communication, further support this situation. Participants who found online communication easier than face-to-face interaction demonstrated significantly higher levels of social anxiety, underscoring the possibility that psychological vul nerabilities may influence communication preferences and exacerbate problematic engagement with social platforms. At the same time, those using social media by hiding their identity or using a fake account, as expected, had higher social anxiety scores. While the current findings reveal a significant association between PSMU, screen time, and social anxiety, they do not ade quately elucidate the directionality or underlying mechanisms of this relationship. It is conceivable that individuals with height ened social anxiety may turn to social media as a compensatory strategy due to impaired face-to-face communication, thereby increasing their susceptibility to problematic use. Conversely, sustained engagement with social media and prolonged screen exposure may further entrench social anxiety symptoms by reinforcing avoidance behaviors and reducing opportunities for real-world social interaction.[49-51] The cross-sectional design of the study limits the ability to determine the directionality of the observed associations. It is plausible that these relationships are bidirectional, whereby psy chological vulnerabilities such as ADHD symptoms and social anxiety increase susceptibility to problematic social media use, while excessive and maladaptive use may further exacerbate these symptoms over time. Interestingly, the relationship between self-esteem and PSMU was less pronounced. While there was a modest correlation between SMAS-AF and RSES scores, no significant association was observed between screen time and self-esteem, and virtual communication subscale scores did not significantly correlate with self-esteem. These findings suggest that although selfesteem may play a role in the development or maintenance of PSMU, it may not be as central as ADHD symptoms or social anxiety. This is partially consistent with the dual-pathway hypothesis in the literature, which posits that low self-esteem may either predispose individuals to excessive online engage ment or be negatively impacted by it due to mechanisms such as upward social comparison or identity fragmentation.[58,60] Gender differences were observed in both PSMU and social anxiety, with female participants exhibiting significantly higher scores on SMAS-AF and LSAS. This finding aligns with several studies that report higher social media use and social anxiety symptoms in females,[53,54] though the directionality of these associations remains a matter for further investigation. Females may engage in more emotionally driven use of social media, including seeking social support and validation, which may place them at greater risk for experiencing negative psychologi cal outcomes when these needs are unmet or inconsistently ful filled online. Dam et al reported that women generally use social media for more than 2 hours per day and more frequently than men, which contrasts with the findings of our study.[6] In our study, there was no difference between women and men in terms of screen time. This suggests that while men and women may spend similar amounts of time on social media, women may be more susceptible to developing social media addiction. The presence of hidden identity or fake account usage was associated with higher SMAS-AF, LSAS, and ASRS-A scores, as well as longer screen time. This behavioral pattern may reflect a tendency to experiment with alternative self-presentations due to underlying social insecurity, impulsivity, or attempts to avoid judgment in online interactions.[46-48] Such behaviors are increasingly common and may serve as an important clinical marker for PSMU risk, particularly in populations with ADHD and social anxiety traits. The findings should also be interpreted within the sociocul tural context of Turkey. In a society where interpersonal rela tionships and social connectedness play a central role, social media may serve as an important extension of offline social interactions. High levels of social media penetration and wide spread smartphone use may further amplify both adaptive and maladaptive patterns of engagement. These cultural factors may influence the observed associations and should be considered when generalizing the findings to other contexts.

8 Gürcan and Çokaslan • Medicine (2026) 105:38  Medicine This study has limitations, including its cross-sectional design and reliance on self-report measures, which may be subject to recall bias and variations in usage patterns. The reliance on self-reported ADHD symptoms rather than clinically confirmed diagnoses may limit the clinical interpretability of the findings, as ASRS scores reflect symptom severity rather than diagnos tic status. Although participants were not recruited via social media platforms, the voluntary nature of participation and the use of convenience sampling may still have introduced selec tion bias. Individuals with greater interest in or engagement with social media may have been more likely to participate. Furthermore, the large number of statistical tests conducted increases the risk of type I error, and the findings should there fore be interpreted with caution. Future research should employ longitudinal designs and consider more objective measures of social media usage, although social media addiction differs from other internet and internet-related addictions due to its unique characteristics. 5. Conclusion This study has several strengths, including the use of wellvalidated instruments, a relatively large and gender-diverse university student sample, and the simultaneous examination of multiple psychological domains. The findings highlight the importance of psychological traits – particularly ADHD symp toms and social anxiety – in understanding problematic patterns of social media use among university students. While self-esteem was also associated with problematic social media use, its role appeared weaker and more nuanced, suggesting that its influ ence may be moderated by other psychological or behavioral factors. Overall, the results support the conceptualization of prob lematic social media use as a multidimensional phenomenon shaped by individual vulnerabilities and usage-related behaviors rather than by time spent online alone. By providing data from a non-Western university student population, this study extends existing research beyond predominantly Western and East Asian contexts and contributes to the cultural generalizability of find ings in this field. Given the pervasive role of social media across multiple domains of modern life, further interdisciplinary and longitudinal research is needed to clarify underlying mecha nisms and to inform prevention and intervention strategies tar geting vulnerable populations. From a clinical perspective, these findings suggest that prob lematic social media use may be particularly relevant among university students presenting with ADHD symptoms and social anxiety. Incorporating screening for problematic social media use into routine mental health assessments in university set tings may be beneficial. In addition, interventions targeting selfregulation, social skills, and healthy digital habits may help reduce the risk of problematic use and its associated psycholog ical difficulties. pages: © 2026 Nigerian Postgraduate Medical Journal | Published by Wolters Kluwer - Medknow 496 Original Article Introduction Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is the most commonly identified childhood neurodevelopmental disease.[1] The characteristics of ADHD are problems such as lack of attention, hyperactivity and impulsiveness.[2] Inattention, impulsivity and hyperactivity are three main symptoms seen in a child who has ADHD. Lack of concentration, fidgetiness, easily distracted, forgetting or losing things a lot and difficulty in coping with others are the signs and symptoms usually exhibited by a child with ADHD.[3] If a child with ADHD is not taken care of properly, it can have several consequences throughout their life, such as academic underachievement, criminality and problems with personal relationships.[4] World Health Organization conducted a survey which included 20 lower-to upper-income countries and revealed that the United States has the highest ADHD rate amongst children and adolescents. According to a national survey of parents using data from 2016 to 2019, an estimated 6.8% of children in the United States are diagnosed with ADHD. According to What Predicts Attention‐Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Literacy in Primary Schoolteachers? Jemy J. Jome, Vidya Prabhu, Varalakshmi Chandra Sekaran, R. Vani Lakshmi1 Departments of Global Public Health Policy and Governance and 1Applied Statistics and Data Sciences, Prasanna School of Public Health, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, Karnataka, India Background: Attention‐Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition affecting children’s learning and behaviour. Teachers play a pivotal role in early identification, yet little is known about factors predicting their ADHD literacy in India. Aims: This study was conducted to evaluate the Mental Health Literacy (MHL) of primary schoolteachers regarding ADHD and to identify the predictors of MHL among teachers. Methods: A cross‐sectional, quantitative study was conducted among 303 primary schoolteachers. The study period was from December 2023 to June 2024. The study was conducted in Varkala and Attingal educational subdistricts of Thiruvananthapuram district. There are a total of 110 schools in both Attingal and Varkala subdistrict. A stratified cluster sampling technique was used to recruit the participants. Data were collected using a semi‐structured validated questionnaire. Furthermore, the Knowledge of Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (KADDSs) was used. Descriptive and inferential statistics were used to assess knowledge and compare across socio‐demographic characteristics. Binomial logistic regression was used to identify the predictors of MHL. Results: The majority of participants (56.8%) were in the age group of 35–50 years, with 94.4% being female. Most teachers (38%) had more than 10 years of teaching experience. The study found that 98.7% of teachers had a low level of knowledge related to ADHD. The mean knowledge scores showed significant association with socio‐demographic characteristics such as marital status (P = 0.01), status of work (P = 0.004), type of school (P < 0.001), teaching hours per week (P = 0.005), medium of instruction (P = 0.03) and average class strength (P < 0.001). The school area and average class strength were significant predictors influencing the MHL of teachers (adjusted odds ratio [AOR]: 3.40, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.22–9.44; AOR = 2.38, 95% CI: 1.37–4.15, respectively). Conclusion: Findings show that most teachers have low ADHD knowledge, influenced by socio‐demographic factors, with school area and class strength significantly predicting MHL. This highlights the need for targeted training to improve teachers’ ability to support students with ADHD. Jome, et al.: Predictors of ADHD literacy in primary schoolteachers Nigerian Postgraduate Medical Journal ¦ Volume 33 ¦ Issue 4 ¦ July-August 2026 497 data from both the National Survey of Children’s Health and the National Health Information Survey, boys have a higher chance of getting diagnosed with ADHD than girls.[5] An umbrella review of meta-analyses reported that the global prevalence of ADHD amongst children and adolescents is approximately 8.0%.[6] Primary schoolteachers play a pivotal role in the early identification of ADHD because symptoms often emerge during the early developmental years when children begin formal education. Teachers are the first individuals to identify the problem and send them for treatment. At this stage, teachers observe foundational behaviours such as attention span, impulse control and social interaction core areas affected by ADHD. Given that the students spend half of their waking time in school, interacting with their teachers, teachers may act as Gateway Providers for mental health services. Teachers, as relatively neutral observers, may be better positioned than parents to identify subtle behavioural changes in children at an early stage. This is because parental observations can be influenced by emotional involvement, preconceived expectations and familiarity with the child’s typical behaviour, potentially obscuring emerging symptoms.[7,8] Enhancing teachers’ knowledge about ADHD promotes better mental and educational outcomes, which is linked to the objective of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG-3 (Good Health and Well-being) and SDG-4 (Quality Education).[9] Mental health literacy (MHL) advances SDG-3 by increasing awareness, reducing stigma and promoting early intervention.[10] Few research studies have highlighted gaps in teachers’ knowledge about ADHD, which may contribute to misinterpretation of symptoms, stigma and missed opportunities for timely support and referral.[11,12] In India, ADHD remains underdiagnosed and often misunderstood in school settings due to limited awareness, lack of formal teacher training and cultural stigma surrounding behavioural disorders. A meta-analysis of 19 Indian studies reported an ADHD prevalence ranging from 6.3% to 11.3% amongst children.[13] Although some studies have assessed teachers’ knowledge of ADHD, research specifically evaluating ADHD literacy among teachers is scarce.[14-16] To address these gaps, this study was conducted to assess the ADHD literacy of primary schoolteachers and to identify predictors of MHL related to ADHD. Conceptual framework MHL related to ADHD in this study was assessed using a multi-method approach, incorporating knowledge of causes and treatment (via Knowledge of Attention Deficit Disorder Scale [KADDS]), recognition (via case vignettes) and behavioural indicators (training attendance, identification, referral and information-seeking behaviour). Jorm’s MHL framework served as the theoretical basis for the study design[17] includes components such as problem recognition, knowledge of causes and treatments, help-seeking attitudes and information-seeking behaviour. Independent variables were grouped into two broad categories: • Socio-demographic variables (e.g. age, gender, marital status, education level and teaching experience) – hypothesised to influence baseline knowledge and attitudes towards ADHD • Teaching- and work-related variables (e.g. school type, status of work, school area, teaching hours, medium of instruction and syllabus) – expected to affect exposure to training, access to resources and opportunities for identification and referral. These variables were analysed to determine their association with ADHD-related MHL, providing a comprehensive understanding of factors influencing teachers’ capacity to support students with ADHD. Methods Study setting and design The study was conducted in Thiruvananthapuram district, Kerala, India. The schools in Thiruvananthapuram district are divided into 12 different educational subdistricts. The study was conducted in Varkala and Attingal educational subdistricts of Thiruvananthapuram district. There are a total of 110 schools in both Attingal and Varkala subdistricts. A cross-sectional study design was employed, and data were collected between December 2023 and June 2024. Study population and sampling technique The study participants were primary schoolteachers who are teaching from grades 1–7 and those teachers who are currently employed in Thiruvananthapuram district. Special education teachers are excluded from the study. The cluster stratified sampling technique was adopted. Schools were stratified into government, aided and private schools. Schools were randomly selected from each stratum, and sampling from each of these strata was performed using the probability proportionate to size [Figure 1]. Sample size Considering 20%[18] amongst teachers with relative precision 6%, 95% confidence interval and design effect of 1.5, accounting for 20% attrition, 303 teachers were enrolled in the study. Ethical considerations Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional Ethics Committee (IEC 672 - 2023). Permission was obtained from the Director General of Education (DGE), Deputy Director of Education, Kerala and respective Assistant Education Officers. Written informed consent was obtained from the participants. Study tool A semi-structured validated questionnaire was used to collect the data. The questionnaire comprised four sections. Sociodemographic variables, identification of adolescent mental health problems through case vignette (a brief, hypothetical scenario that describes an child with ADHD

Jome, et al.: Predictors of ADHD literacy in primary schoolteachers Nigerian Postgraduate Medical Journal ¦ Volume 33 ¦ Issue 4 ¦ July-August 2026 498 symptoms), KADDS and general questions regarding mental health practices amongst teachers. The KADDSs is a validated, structured questionnaire comprising 39 items designed to assess teachers’ knowledge of ADHD across three key domains: symptoms and diagnosis, treatment and general information (such as its causes and courses).[19] The permission was obtained from the author to use the questionnaire. Each correct response was scored as 1, whereas incorrect or ‘don’t know’ responses were scored as 0, with a total score range of 0–39. The KADDS score was categorised into high, moderate and low scores. Based on Bloom’s cut-off, those with >80%, 60%–79% and <60% are considered to have high, moderate and low levels of knowledge, respectively.[20] Data collection methods Data were collected using a self-administered questionnaire. Administrative permission was obtained from the headmasters/ headmistress of the respective schools before starting the data collection. After getting written consent from the participants, the questionnaire was distributed to participants and collected back after checking the completeness of the questionnaire. Data analysis Data were entered in Microsoft Excel, cleaned, coded and imported into Jamovi version 2.3.28[21] (The jamovi project, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia) for analysis. Descriptive analysis was done to find the frequencies and percentages. One-way analysis of variance, Mann–WhitneyU-test and Independent Samples – t-test are done to find the statistical association of mean KADDS score across the socio-demographic variables. Binomial logistic regression was done to find the predictors of MHL amongst teachers regarding ADHD. Results Socio-demographic characteristics of the participants. Table 1 shows the socio-demographic characteristics of participants. Most of the participants were in the age group of 35–50 years (56.8%). Most participants were female (94.4%) and aged 34–50 years (56.8%). Most participants (47.5%) had a diploma degree in education. About 38% of participants had more than 10 years of teaching experience. The majority of the participants had more than 10 years of experience. Most educators (88.8%) were permanent employees, with 72.3% working in government institutions. 51.2% of participants taught in classes with an average strength of <30, whereas 56.8% taught for more than 10 h. Case vignettes About 108 (35.6%) of participants could recognise the condition as ADHD based on the case vignette. About 247 (81.5%) participants perceived that the student needed help. Out of 247 participants, about 167 (55.7%) participants opined that the student needs help from a mental health professional. Mental health literacy on attention deficit hyperactivity disorder The maximum score for the KADD scale is 39. The univariate analysis was carried out to assess the significant differences in the variables across groups [Table 2]. At the 5% significance level, no statistically significant difference was observed in the mean ADHD knowledge scores across age groups (P = 0.68), gender (P = 0.45), family type (P = 0.09), education level (P = 0.45), teaching experience (P = 0.16), school area (P = 0.21) and syllabus (P = 0.06). Statistically significant differences were found in relation to marital status (P = 0.01). Similarly, status of work (P = 0.004), type of school (P < 0.001), teaching hours per week (P = 0.005), medium of instruction (P = 0.03) and average strength of class (P < 0.001). All the variables with P < 0.25 from the univariate binary logistic regression are taken into the multivariate regression analysis.[21] They included age group, status of work, school area, teaching hours per week and the average strength of the class. It was found that the school area and average strength of the class were the predictors of ADHD knowledge. The participants from the urban school predicted higher odds of identification of ADHD as compared to participants from rural school (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 3.4 [1.22, 9.44], P = 0.01). The SDG-3 and SDG-4 also focus on improving teachers’ MHL and highlighted the importance of enhancing students’ mental health and well-being in educational settings.[30,31] On comparison of the mean knowledge scores and the sociodemographic characteristics of participants, it was found that marital status, status of work, type of school, teaching hours per week, medium of instruction and average strength of class are statistically significant differences in the mean knowledge score. The study conducted by Sharma and Kunwar in Nepal also found the association between knowledge of ADHD and duration of teaching.[32] On assessing the predictors of MHL, it was observed that teachers from urban areas had better MHL on ADHD as compared to teachers from rural areas. This might be because overall health literacy in urban populations is higher than that of rural populations.[33] It was also found out that teachers who taught the classes with a strength of 30–40 had better identification of ADHD as compared to teachers who taught smaller class strength. This might be because teachers can more effectively engage with their students without being overwhelmed when the class sizes are moderate. Strength and limitations of the study This study is one of the few in India, and specifically in Kerala, to assess ADHD-related MHL amongst primary schoolteachers, thereby addressing a major gap in the literature. A multimethod approach was employed, incorporating validated tools such as the KADDS, case vignettes and behavioural indicators, which enabled a comprehensive assessment of MHL beyond knowledge alone. Furthermore, the relatively large sample size (n = 303) with diverse socio-demographic and schoolrelated characteristics enhanced the representativeness and robustness of the findings. Limitations The cross-sectional design of the study limits the ability to infer causal relationships between teacher characteristics and MHL levels. In addition, since the study was conducted in a single state (Kerala), the findings may have limited generalisability to other regions of India, where teacher demographics and cultural contexts may differ. Considerations for future studies Future research could use longitudinal or interventional designs to assess the impact of teacher training programmes on ADHD-related MHL. Incorporating qualitative methods, such as interviews or focus groups, may provide deeper insights into teachers’ attitudes, cultural perceptions, and challenges in supporting children with ADHD. In addition, studies should explore the effectiveness of policy-level interventions, including the integration of ADHD and MHL training into pre-service and in-service teacher education curriculum.[34] TRIVANDRUM EDUCATIONAL DISTRICT ATTINGAL EDUCATIONAL SUBDISTRICT VARKALA EDUCATIONAL SUBDISTRICT Government Total schools=44 Aided Total schools=15 Private Total schools=6 Government Total schools=31 Aided Total schools=10 Private Total schools=4 Total teachers = 12 Included =4 Total teachers =99 Included =23 Total teachers= 151 Included=100 Total teachers = 28 Included =13 Total teachers = 118 Included=44 Total teachers = 240 Included= 119 Total collected =303 Figure 1: Sampling Design of the study

The teachers who did not attend formal training related to mental health issues were not able to identify ADHD. This highlights the importance of incorporating formal training programmes for primary schoolteachers regarding childhood mental health issues. Early identification of children with mental health issues and timely referral are essential to ensure appropriate interventions and support. The findings emphasise the importance of integrating ADHD and broader mental health training into both pre-service and in-service teacher programmes. pages: https://doi.org/10.1177/10870547251404197 Journal of Attention Disorders 2026, Vol. 30(5) 677–693 © The Author(s) 2025 Article reuse guidelines: sagepub.com/journals-permissions DOI: 10.1177/10870547251404197 journals.sagepub.com/home/jad Article Introduction Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder marked by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, typically emerging in childhood and often persisting into adulthood (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). Its global prevalence is about 8% in children/adolescents (Ayano et al., 2023) and 2.58% among adults (P. Song et al., 2021). ADHD negatively impacts academic performance (Jangmo et al., 2019), social functioning (Nijmeijer et al., 2008), and emotional regulation (Stern et al., 2020). Additionally, research has linked ADHD to an increased risk of suicidal behavior (K.-L. Huang et al., 2018) and substance use disorders (Lee et al., 2011). Inhibitory control deficits are a core cognitive mechanism underlying impulsivity and executive dysfunction in ADHD (Barkley, 1997). Email: ysy77@163.com Effects of Exercise on Hyperactivity/ Impulsivity and Inhibitory Control at Behavioral and Electrophysiological Levels in ADHD: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Zeping Zhang1 , Xuanyu Bo2 , Kun Liu3 , Jiangdi Su1 , Yongfei Zhu4 , and Suyong Yang5 Abstract Objective: This study aimed to assess the impact of exercise on hyperactivity/impulsivity, inhibitory control, and inhibitionrelated event-related potential (ERP) components in individuals with ADHD. Method: A systematic search identified relevant studies, and methodological quality was assessed using the Revised Cochrane Risk-of-Bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2) and the Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I), with data analysis conducted using Stata software. Results: A total of 36 studies (38 comparisons) were included, comprising 10 acute and 26 chronic exercise interventions. Exercise yielded a small-to-moderate improvement in inhibitory control but showed no significant effects on hyperactivity/ impulsivity or inhibition-related N2 and P3 components. Subgroup analyses of inhibitory control revealed significant moderating effects of age (children/adolescents), intervention type (chronic interventions), frequency (three sessions per week), control condition (sedentary or no-intervention groups), and study quality (studies with moderate or high risk of bias). Conclusion: Exercise enhances inhibitory control in individuals with ADHD, with the effect being especially pronounced in children and adolescents. Chronic interventions and a frequency of three sessions per week appear to be most beneficial. However, it shows no significant effect on hyperactivity/impulsivity or inhibition-related N2 and P3 components. The impact of exercising should not be overestimated. (J. of Att. Dis. 2026; 30(5) 677-693) Keywords attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, exercise, inhibitory control, behavioral performance

678 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(5) external distractions, with two subtypes: response inhibition (suppressing automatic motor responses) and interference control (avoiding distractions from irrelevant stimuli) (Diamond, 2013). Impaired inhibitory control is closely linked to hyperactive and impulsive behaviors, such as restlessness, excessive talking, and frequent interruptions (Johnstone & Clarke, 2009). Behavioral studies show that individuals with ADHD have higher error rates in tasks like Go/No-Go (Uebel et al., 2010), Flanker (Marquardt et al., 2018), and Continuous Performance Test (Doehnert et al., 2010), indicating difficulty suppressing impulsive responses and filtering out irrelevant information. At the electroencephalographic (EEG) level, the event-related potentials (ERPs) closely associated with inhibitory control are N2 and P3. The N2 component refers to a negative deflection in the frontocentral region occurring within the 250 to 400 ms time window after stimulus presentation under No-Go or incongruent conditions, with its primary neural source located in the anterior cingulate cortex (Gang & Tie-jun, 2010). It reflects the process of conflict monitoring (Groom & Cragg, 2015; Randall & Smith, 2011). The P3 component related to inhibition appears as a positive deflection in the central region within the 300 to 600 ms time window after stimulus presentation, with its primary neural sources located in the inferior frontal gyrus, precentral gyrus, and supplementary motor area (J. L. Smith et al., 2013). It is considered a marker of both cognitive and response inhibition (J. L. Smith et al., 2008). Neurophysiological evidence supports these findings, with reduced N2 and P3 amplitudes in No-Go trials among individuals with ADHD, suggesting impaired conflict monitoring (Broyd et al., 2005; Johnstone et al., 2009) and inhibitory processing (Chmielewski et al., 2018; Zarka et al., 2021). A neuroimaging meta-analysis revealed reduced volume and function in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex/insular-striatal regions in ADHD (Norman et al., 2016), which may contribute to the core neurocognitive deficits commonly observed in children with the disorder. Exercise has gained attention as an ADHD intervention due to its cost-effectiveness, accessibility, and non-invasive nature. Regarding hyperactivity/impulsivity, some studies suggest yoga alleviates ADHD symptoms in children (Luo et al., 2023), while others do not confirm this effect (Benzing & Schmidt, 2019; Bustamante et al., 2016; F. Sun et al., 2024), highlighting inconsistencies. Inhibitory control improvements have been observed in children with ADHD following aquatic exercise (Chang et al., 2014), ball games, and aerobic exercise (Memarmoghaddam et al., 2016), with further benefits from aerobic exercise combined with cognitive tasks (Liang et al., 2022), exergaming (Benzing et al., 2018), and table tennis (Pan et al., 2016). These effects may be mediated by brain changes, increased serotonin, dopamine, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and enhanced neuroplasticity (Berwid & Halperin, 2012; Chan et al., 2022). However, some studies report no significant effects on inhibitory control in children with ADHD (Geladé et al., 2017; Ludyga et al., 2023; F. Sun et al., 2024). Similarly, findings in adults with ADHD have also been mixed, with some studies failing to demonstrate consistent benefits (K. Fritz & O’Connor, 2022; Kouhbanani et al., 2023). These inconsistencies call for systematic reviews and meta-analyses to better evaluate exercise interventions and identify moderating factors. Although previous meta-analyses have examined the effects of exercise on ADHD symptoms and executive function in children (H. Huang et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2021; Seiffer et al., 2022; W. Sun et al., 2022), several limitations remain. These studies often treat executive function as a unitary construct, with moderator analyses focusing on overall executive function and not isolating specific subdomains like inhibitory control. Inhibitory control, a core component of executive function linked to impulsivity (Bari & Robbins, 2013), has been insufficiently addressed. Additionally, most studies focus on children, neglecting adults with ADHD. Most research also relies on behavioral data, with limited electrophysiological evidence, restricting understanding of the neural mechanisms of exercise interventions. Finally, the dose-response relationship between exercise and inhibitory control is unclear, hindering optimal intervention development. This study aims to assess the effects of exercise on hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms and inhibitory control at behavioral and electrophysiological levels in ADHD, explore the dose-response relationship, and identify potential moderators, providing a foundation for optimizing exercise-based interventions. Methods This study adhered to the PRISMA guidelines (Liberati et al., 2009) and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42025637758). Eligibility Criteria Inclusion criteria were: (a) ADHD diagnosis based on the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) or the International Classification of Diseases (ICD), with no age restrictions; (b) interventions involving exercise or physical activity, with no restrictions on type, either alone or in combination with usual treatment; (c) control conditions included medication, neurofeedback therapy, psychoeducation, sedentary activities, waitlist control, and regular physical activity; (d) outcomes including hyperactivity/impulsivity symptom questionnaires, behavioral tasks on inhibitory control, and corresponding event-related potentials (ERP); and (e) study design including randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled trials (Non-RCTs), and crossover designs (CRD). Exclusion criteria were: (a) crosssectional studies, (b) non-peer-reviewed articles (e.g.,

Zhang et al. 679 theses), (c) studies in languages other than Chinese or English, (d) conference abstracts, and (e) studies with unextractable or unconvertible outcome data. Literature Search This study conducted a literature search in PubMed, Web of Science, EBSCOhost, Embase, Cochrane Library, PsycINFO, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), covering all records from each database’s inception to January 12, 2025. We used a combination of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms, including “Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder,” “Exercise,” “Physical Activity,” “Inhibitory Control,” “Response Inhibition,” and “Interference Control.” Search strategies were tailored to each database’s requirements. In addition, the reference lists of all included studies and relevant reviews were manually screened by two researchers to identify additional eligible studies. Any disagreements regarding the inclusion of additional studies were resolved through discussion with the first author. The full search strategy, including Boolean operators and database-specific adaptations, is provided in Supplemental Material 1. Screening and Data Extraction The first author imported the relevant literature into EndNote 20 and created a reference library. Duplicate articles were removed, and two researchers independently conducted an initial screening by reviewing titles and abstracts. Full texts of the articles that passed the initial screening were then downloaded, and the final inclusion of studies was determined, along with the extraction of relevant data. Data extracted included study characteristics (i.e., author, publication time, country, and study design), participant details (i.e., age, sample size, diagnostic criteria, ADHD type, and medication usage), interventions (i.e., program, exercise session, frequency, duration, and exercise intensity), outcome measures (i.e., types of questionnaires, behavioral tasks, and ERP components, and key quality assessment elements. Literature screening and data extraction were independently conducted by two researchers. Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion with the first author. Risk of Bias Assessment The risk of bias in included studies was assessed using the Revised Cochrane Risk-of-Bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2), the RoB 2 tool for crossover trials, and the Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I). Two independent researchers conducted the assessments, with disagreements resolved by discussion or consultation with the first author. For randomized controlled trials, RoB 2 was used to evaluate bias across five domains: randomization, deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, outcome measurement, and selection of reported results, with studies classified as having low risk, some concerns, or high risk (Sterne et al., 2019). For crossover trials, the adapted RoB 2 tool incorporated additional considerations such as carryover effects (The Cochrane Collaboration, 2021). For non-randomized studies, ROBINS-I evaluated bias across seven domains: confounding, participant selection, classification of interventions, deviations from intended interventions, missing data, outcome measurement, and selection of reported results, with studies categorized as low, moderate, serious, or critical risk (Sterne et al., 2016). Statistical Analysis The meta-analysis was performed using Stata SE 14.0 with the following treatments: (1) Inhibitory control at the behavioral level was assessed using key measures like No-Go error rates in the Go/No-Go task, converting accuracy to error rate when necessary; (2) In ERPs, inhibitory control is assessed through inhibition-related components, including the amplitudes of N2 and P3 in the fronto-central region under No-Go or incongruent conditions; (3) For RCTs with three study arms, the sample size of the control group was split equally (1:1) following Cochrane recommendations to minimize unitof-analysis bias; (4) If symptom questionnaires were completed by both parents and teachers, all outcomes were included; (5) If both response inhibition and interference control were assessed, all relevant outcomes were included. The pre-to-post change in mean and standard deviation (SD) was calculated using the formulas: meanchange = meanpost − meanpre; SDchange = square root [SDpre2 + SDpos2 – (2r × SDpre × SDp os)], where the correlation coefficient (r) was fixed at 0.5 (H. Huang et al., 2022). A random-effects model was used for the pooled analysis. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Q statistic and I2 statistic. The standardized mean difference (SMD) was estimated using Hedges’ g, with effect sizes interpreted as large (≥0.8), moderate (0.5), and small (≤0.2), as defined by Hedges (1981). Subgroup analyses were conducted based on the following moderators: subject age (children/adolescents, adults), domains of inhibitory control (response inhibition, interference control), study design (RCT, CRD, non-RCT), exercise intervention type (acute: a one-time, short-duration exercise session; chronic: repeated and regular exercise training over an extended period of time), exercise duration (<12 weeks, ≥12 weeks), exercise frequency (2 times/week, 3 times/week, 5 times/week), exercise session length (≤50 min, >50 min), exercise intensity (moderate, moderate-to-vigorous, vigorous), motor skill type (closed-skill, open-skill), control group type (sedentary activity/no treatment, traditional aerobic exercise,

680 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(5) neurofeedback training), and study quality (low, moderate, high risk). Sensitivity analysis was conducted by sequentially excluding individual studies to assess the robustness of the meta-analysis results. Funnel plots and Egger’s test were used to examine publication bias, with Egger’s test applied only when more than 10 studies were available. When publication bias was detected, trim-and-fill methodology was applied for correction. Results Screening Results The study selection process is shown in Figure 1. A total of 4,218 records were identified through electronic databases and manual searches. After removing 1,499 duplicates, 2,595 records were excluded based on title and abstract screening, leaving 124 studies. In age subgroup analysis, exercise intervention showed a small-to-moderate effect in children and adolescents with ADHD (g = −0.46, 95% CI [−0.70, −0.21], p < .001) but no significant effect in adults (g = −0.52, 95% CI [−1.31, 0.27], p = 0.196). Chronic interventions had a moderate-to-large effect (g = −0.57, 95% CI [−0.89, −0.24], p = .001), while acute interventions had no significant effect (g = −0.26, 95% CI [−0.52, 0.00], p = .051). Exercise frequency of three times per week showed a significant moderate-to-large effect (g = −0.76, 95% CI [−1.17, −0.35], p < .001), while twice (g = −0.30, 95% CI [−0.93, 0.33], p = 0.351) and five times per week (g = −0.43, 95% CI [−1.27, 0.41], p = 0.317) showed no significant effects. Exercise interventions had a moderate-to-large effect compared to sedentary/no-intervention groups (g = −0.52, 95% CI [−0.79, −0.24], p < .001) but did not differ from regular physical activity (g = −0.13, 95% CI [−0.52, 0.27], p = 0.537) or neurofeedback training (g = −0.36, 95% CI [−1.35, 0.63], p = 0.473). Subgroup analysis by study quality revealed a significant effect for moderate (g = −0.34, 95% CI [−0.64, −0.05], p = .023) and high-risk bias studies (g = −0.61, 95% CI [−1.01, −0.21], p = .003), but not for low-risk studies (g = −0.13, 95% CI [−0.48, 0.21], p = 0.445). However, no moderating effects were observed for inhibitory control domains, study design, exercise time (min/session), exercise duration (weeks), exercise intensity, or motor skills. Detailed results are presented in Figure 8. Sensitivity Analysis Sensitivity analysis using the leave-one-out method revealed that the 95% confidence intervals of the pooled effect sizes for hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms, behavioral performance of inhibitory control, and the N2 and P3 components of ERP remained largely unchanged, indicating that no single study substantially influenced the overall results. Publication Bias A visual inspection of the funnel plots (Figure 9(A) for hyperactivity/impulsivity, 9(B) for behavioral performance of inhibitory control, 9(C) for the N2 component, and 9(D) for the P3 component) suggested potential asymmetry. However, Egger’s linear regression analysis revealed no statistical evidence of publication bias for behavioral performance of inhibitory control (p = 0.167). Egger’s tests were not conducted for hyperactivity/impulsivity, N2, and P3 due to the inclusion of fewer than 10 studies in each case. Discussion To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review and meta-analysis evaluating the effects of exercise interventions on inhibitory control in ADHD across three levels: questionnaire assessments, behavior, and electrophysiology. Synthesizing 36 studies (38 comparisons), we found a small to moderate significant effect of exercise on behavior performance of inhibitory control, supporting its efficacy in ADHD management. No significant effects were found on hyperactivity/impulsivity or inhibitory control-related ERP components. The forest plot shows some effect sizes on the right of the null line, potentially contributing to the non-significant result. Possible reasons include small sample sizes (Converse et al., 2020; Jensen & Kenny, 2004), reducing statistical power and increasing variability. Sun et al. (2024) noted that studies conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic faced intervention period restrictions due to public health policies, potentially reducing intervention efficacy. Although our overall analysis did not detect significant effects, individual studies observed positive impacts of exercise on hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms, necessitating further research to clarify these findings. Behavioral Outcomes of Inhibitory Control Our findings align with previous studies (H. Huang et al., 2022; Liang et al., 2021; Welsch et al., 2021), suggesting that exercise enhances inhibitory control in individuals with ADHD. In addition, a recent umbrella review also reported that exercise significantly improves inhibitory control in children with ADHD, with this conclusion supported by a high level of evidence (Dastamooz et al., 2023). Previous research mainly examined the effects through moderator analyses, whereas our study focused on inhibitory control as a single dimension and included more studies. Sensitivity analysis confirmed the robustness of our results, with no evidence of publication bias. Several moderators were identified, including participant age, exercise type, exercise frequency, control group type, and study quality. Subgroup analysis showed exercise interventions were not significantly effective in adults, likely due to more stable inhibitory control from neurodevelopmental maturation. In contrast to children and adolescents, adults demonstrate lower impulsivity scores in tasks like CPT-AX, reflecting superior inhibitory control. Additionally, No-Go N2 amplitude declines with age (Jonkman, 2006), suggesting that adults may have already attained mature inhibitory control, influencing exercise intervention effectiveness. Nevertheless, this finding should be interpreted with caution, as it may be partly attributable to the small number of studies included in the adult subgroup. Acute exercise interventions did not show significant effects, possibly due to their transient impact on neural processes rather than sustained behavioral performance (Mehren et al., 2019). While acute exercise can enhance cerebral blood flow (Mulser & Moreau, 2023) and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Borror, 2017), these

688 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(5) short-term changes may not yield lasting behavioral improvements. Chronic exercise, on the other hand, also increases gray matter volume (Tarkka et al., 2019), optimizes neurophysiological functioning (Meijer et al., 2020), and modulates neurotransmitter systems (Chan et al., 2022), leading to more substantial and sustained improvements in inhibitory control. Three sessions per week produced significant effects, supporting the inverted-U hypothesis, which suggests moderate intervention frequency optimizes outcomes. Both insufficient and excessive frequencies may hinder efficacy. Exercise interventions did not outperform regular physical activity and neurofeedback training, both of which have been shown to enhance inhibitory control. However, exercise interventions showed more significant benefits when compared to passive control groups (e.g., sedentary conditions or no-treatment controls). Studies with a low risk of bias did not demonstrate significant improvements. Notably, the low-bias-risk category included two RCTs that implemented rigorous randomization and blinding procedures, minimizing expectation effects from both researchers and participants. Consequently, effect size estimates in these studies were likely more objective and conservative. In contrast, studies with moderate or high risk of bias, which exhibited methodological limitations such as inadequate control conditions or randomization procedures, tended to report larger effect sizes. No moderating effects were found for inhibitory control domains, study design, exercise duration per session, total intervention duration, exercise intensity, or motor skill level. Electrophysiological Measures of Inhibitory Control The N2 component, a negative deflection linked to conflict monitoring, reflects response inhibition in the Go/No-Go task (Groom & Cragg, 2015; Randall & Smith, 2011). A more negative value indicates greater improvement. Among the three studies, one (Ji et al., 2023) showed an effect size on the right side of the null line, comparing exergaming and cycling. While no significant pre-post changes in No-Go N2 amplitude were found, the exergaming group showed a significant increase in Go N2 amplitude, suggesting that exergaming may enhance response execution rather than directly improving response inhibition. The P3 component, a positive deflection associated with inhibitory control (Gang & Tiejun, 2010; Groom & Cragg, 2015), attentional resource allocation, and context updating (Polich, 2007), serves as an index where greater positive values indicate improved performance. Three studies (four comparisons) used Go/No-Go and Flanker tasks. Two studies (Ludyga et al., 2023; S. D. Smith et al., 2019) reported effect sizes to the left of the null line. In the study by Ludyga et al. (2023), the judo intervention did not yield significant improvements, which may be attributed to the participants’ relatively low motor skill levels. Figure 9. Similarly, S. D. Smith et al. (2019) observed no significant effect of exercise on P3, possibly due to the study’s small sample size and limited intervention dosage. Although no significant effects of exercise interventions on N2 and P3 components were observed, these findings do not rule out their potential benefits for inhibitory control. Future research should use neuroimaging to explore the neural mechanisms underlying exercise-induced improvements. Limitations This study has several limitations: (1) Many studies reported only total symptom scores, limiting subgroup analyses on hyperactivity/impulsivity; (2) The small number of EEG studies may have reduced our ability to detect significant effects, and future research should integrate neuroimaging techniques for more comprehensive evidence; (3) Few studies were classified as lowrisk, and future RCTs should follow CONSORT guidelines for greater transparency in study design, randomization, and blinding; (4) Some studies lacked detailed diagnostic criteria and intervention parameters, limiting subgroup analyses. Future studies should provide comprehensive methodological details for better reproducibility and comparability. Conclusions This meta-analysis shows a small-to-moderate beneficial effect of exercise on inhibitory control in ADHD, significantly moderated by age, intervention type, frequency, control group type, and study quality. However, exercise did not show significant effects on hyperactivity, impulsivity, or inhibition-related N2 and P3 components, suggesting that its impact should not be overestimated. These findings underscore the necessity of implementing chronic exercise interventions and maintaining a moderate exercise frequency from childhood to promote the development of inhibitory control. Future RCTs employing neuroimaging techniques and following CONSORT guidelines are needed to clarify the mechanisms of exercise and verify its effectiveness in ADHD management.
