metadata_title: Optimizing exercise interventions for motor skills enhancement in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: Evidence from meta-analysis
pages: Optimizing exercise interventions for motor skills enhancement in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: Evidence from meta-analysis Yuxuan Zhang1,*, Xiaoman Che1,*, Zhenghao Dong2, Jiaxing Shen1, Ye Tao3, Bo Cui4 and Feilong Zhu5 Abstract Objective: This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate effects of physical exercises on gross and fine motor skills in children and adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and to explore the influencing factors and dose–response relationships for optimizing exercise parameters. Data sources: Six electronic databases were searched from inception to 20 June 2025, with an updated search performed on 27 January 2026. Methods: The effect sizes were estimated using Hedge’s g within three-level random-effects modeling frameworks. Subgroup analyses were performed to examine potential moderators, while restricted cubic splines were employed to characterize dose–response relationships. Results: Twenty-one studies with 850 participants were included. Physical exercises showed moderate positive effects on both gross motor skills (Hedge’s g = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.48–0.76) and fine motor skills (Hedge’s g = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.54–0.90). Significant improvements were observed in subcomponents of gross motor skills (locomotion, object control, body coordination, and strength) and fine motor skills (manual dexterity, hand-eye coordination, and handwriting). Moderator analyses indicated that longer session durations (>45 min) and higher frequencies (≥3 sessions/week) were associated with greater benefits. Fine motor skills (∼1350 min) appeared to require greater cumulative exercise exposure than gross motor skills (∼810 min) to achieve substantial gains. 1School of Clinical Medicine, Yangzhou Polytechnic University, Yangzhou, China 2The Affiliated Xuzhou Rehabilitation Hospital of Xuzhou Medical University, Xuzhou Rehabilitation Hospital, Xuzhou, China 3Department of Physical Education, Sejong University, Seoul, Korea 4Yangzhou Guangling Bai Xingtang Traditional Chinese Medicine Clinic, Yangzhou, China 5School of Sports Medicine and Rehabilitation, Beijing Sport University, Beijing, China *Yuxuan Zhang and Xiaoman Che contributed equally to this work and share first authorship. Corresponding author: Feilong Zhu, School of Sports Medicine and Rehabilitation, Beijing Sport University, Beijing 100091, China. Email: zhufeilong1559@163.com Original research article Clinical Rehabilitation 2026, Vol. 40(9) 1177–1194 © The Author(s) 2026 Article reuse guidelines: sagepub.com/journals-permissions DOI: 10.1177/02692155261428944 journals.sagepub.com/home/cre

Conclusion: Physical exercise is an effective intervention for improving motor skills in children and adolescents with ADHD. However, the effectiveness of interventions appears to be moderated by motor subcomponents and dose parameters. Tailored programs, specific motor skill targets and dose parameters, should be integrated into clinical and educational practices to maximize outcomes. Keywords Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, physical exercises, children and adolescents, motor skills Received: 16 August 2025; accepted: 16 February 2026 Introduction Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, affecting approximately 5.3%–7.2% of children worldwide.1 Beyond these behavioral manifestations, up to 50% of children with ADHD exhibit impaired gross and fine motor skills, including difficulties in coordination, balance, object control, and manual dexterity, which often limit participation in physical activities, hinder social integration, and reduce quality of life.2–9 Pharmacological treatments are the most common intervention for ADHD but are associated with side effects (e.g., decreased appetite, sleep disturbances).10 Nonpharmacological approaches, such as psychological and behavioral therapies, are often costly, less scalable, and have limited efficacy for motor deficits.11 Physical exercises has emerged as a promising alternative, as it is easy to implement and has shown benefits for motor proficiency. For instance, studies have demonstrated table tennis and aquatic training can improve locomotor and object–control skills.12–14 However, findings remain inconsistent, particularly regarding fine motor skills and handwriting.12,15 These discrepancies likely stem from variations in exercise parameters (type, frequency, intensity, duration) and differences in the specific motor components assessed. Recent meta-analyses have explored exercise effects on ADHD-related outcomes but leave critical gaps. Our previous work focused on symptoms and executive functions, with limited analysis of motor skills.11,16 Prior syntheses either combined ADHD with other neurodevelopmental conditions, omitted fine motor subcomponents such as handwriting, or did not examine dose–response relationships or moderators (e.g., session duration, frequency).15,17 Consequently, the field lacks a comprehensive, domain-specific evidence synthesis to guide intervention optimization. Therefore, this study aimed to systematically analyze the effects of physical exercises on both gross and fine motor skills in children and adolescents with ADHD, with three key innovations: (1) disaggregating motor outcomes into specific subcomponents (e.g., locomotion, object control, manual dexterity, and handwriting) to identify which skills are most responsive to exercise interventions; (2) conducting moderator analyses to identify optimal intervention parameters (e.g., session duration, frequency); and (3) modeling dose–response relationships separately for gross and fine motor domains to inform intervention dosing. This study was essential for advancing the field of ADHD interventions and improving the quality of life for children and adolescents affected by this disorder. Methods This meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA).18 Additionally, the protocol of this study has been registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; ID: CRD420251064443). The search strategy was formulated according to the patient Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome (PICO) framework. We searched the 1178 Clinical Rehabilitation 40(9)

following electronic databases, including PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Embase, SPORTDiscus, and CNKI, for relevant studies. To avoid the risk of missing relevant studies, additional articles were searched manually in Google Scholar and bibliography of previous published relevant reviews. We used a combination of Medical Subject Heading terms with free text terms as follows: ADHD, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, children, adolescents, physical activity, exercise, sport, motor, motor ability, movement skill, motor skill, gross motor, fine motor, motor development, motor proficiency. In each database, key words were used the Boolean operations “AND” and/or “OR” to combine connections. We searched all databases from their inception to 20 June 2025, and no language restrictions were applied. We conducted an updated search on 27 January 2026, and no additional studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified in this update. The detailed search strategies are given in Supplementary Material Table S1. Studies were included if they met the following criteria: 1. Participants: Children and adolescents aged 5–20 years who had received a formal diagnosis of ADHD based on standardized criteria, with no restrictions on gender or ADHD subtypes. 2. Interventions: Any structured physical exercise program lasting ≥3 consecutive weeks, with no restrictions on frequency, intensity, duration, or modality. 3. Comparator: Control conditions included passive control (e.g., no intervention, waiting-list) and active control (e.g., routine school activities). 4. Outcomes: The outcome measures included at least one objective and validated measure of motor proficiency/skills, including gross motor skills (e.g., locomotion, objective control, body coordination, balance, strength, flexibility) or fine motor skills (e.g., manual dexterity, hand-eye coordination, handwriting). 5. Study Design: Randomized controlled trials, quasi-randomized controlled trials, and nonrandomized comparison studies published in any language. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) interventions combining physical exercises with additional therapeutic components (e.g., pharmacological treatment, cognitive-behavioral therapy, or dietary modifications) where the independent effect of exercise could not be determined; (2) singlesession or acute exercise interventions; (3) noninterventional study designs, including protocols, reviews, cohort studies, case–control studies, conference papers, and book chapters; (4) studies lacking sufficient statistical data (e.g., means, standard deviations, or sample sizes) required for effect size calculation in meta-analysis. The study selection process was conducted independently by two reviewers using predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Any discrepancies between the reviewers were resolved through discussion, and a third reviewer was consulted if consensus could not be reached. The consistency between reviewers during study selection was quantified using Kappa coefficient, computed with IBM SPSS Statistics 25.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL). Consistency levels were categorized as follows: excellent (>0.75), good (0.60–0.75), fair (0.40– 0.59), or poor (<0.40).19 A standardized data extraction form was used to capture relevant data from each included study, including bibliographic information (authors, publication year), study design, participant characteristics (sample size, sex ratio, age), intervention details (type, frequency, duration, intensity, and length), comparator information, and outcome measures. Data extraction was performed independently by the two reviewers, and any discrepancies were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Data from each study were extracted and converted into a format suitable for meta-analysis. We extracted pre- and postintervention means, standard deviations, and sample sizes from all studies. The difference in means was calculated as20: Mean difference = Meanpost- Meanpre For studies employing reverse-scored measures (where higher values represented poorer outcomes), Zhang et al. 1179

we inverted the scale by multiplying group means by −1. The standard deviation of the difference (SDdiff) was calculated using the formula20: SDdiff =  SD2 pre + SD2 post −2 × 0.5 × SDpre × SDpost  When standard deviations were unavailable, we calculated them from standard errors, confidence intervals (CIs), t or p values.20 For unreported data, we made at least three email attempts to contact corresponding authors. Graphical data were extracted using GetData Graph Digitizer (v2.20) when numerical results were only presented in figure format. The Risk of Bias version 2 (RoB2) tool was employed to evaluate the quality of the included studies.21 It comprehensively evaluated the RoB in the included studies from five key domains, namely the randomization process, deviations from the intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. The RoB in each domain was judged and classified into three levels: “low risk,” “high risk,” and “some concerns.” The methodological quality of evidence was systematically evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations approach.22 Through this standardized framework, we assessed five domains that may downgrade evidence quality: (1) RoB (study limitations), (2) inconsistency (heterogeneity), (3) indirectness of evidence, (4) imprecision, and (5) publication bias. The evidence was categorized into four quality levels: high, moderate, low, and very low. Given that many studies reported multiple effect sizes, we employed a three-level random-effects model to more accurately account for the correlations among effect sizes. The model parameters were initially estimated using the restricted maximum likelihood method to ensure robustness. For continuous outcomes, we utilized the standardized mean difference as the effect size measure. Considering the relatively small sample sizes of most included studies, we adopted Hedge’s g, which is based on an exact formula and adjusted for small sample bias, as the effect size indicator. The magnitudes of effect sizes were categorized as follows: 0– 0.2 for trivial, 0.2–0.5 for small, 0.5–0.8 for medium, and >0.8 for large. Heterogeneity was assessed using tau-squared (τ2) and I-squared (I2) statistics. The interpretation of I2 was as follows: 0%–25% indicated low heterogeneity, 25%–75% indicated moderate heterogeneity, and >75% indicated high heterogeneity. To evaluate the robustness of the results, sensitivity analyses were conducted, including leave-one-out analysis and changes in model structure, such as traditional two-level model and robust variance estimation (RVE). Additionally, subgroup analyses were performed based on different subcomponents of motor skills (gross motor skills, e.g., locomotion, objective control, body coordination, balance, strength, flexibility; and fine motor skills, e.g., manual dexterity, hand-eye coordination, handwriting), as well as control group type (passive control, active control), age group (younger age group: 5–8 years; older age group: ≥9 years), intervention frequency (<3 sessions/week, ≥3 sessions/week), duration (≤45 min, >45 min), period (≤8 weeks, >8weeks), and total volume(≤720 min, >720 min). Since most studies did not report intervention intensity, no analysis was conducted on this variable. The total intervention volume (in minutes) was defined as session duration × frequency × period. Publication bias and small-study effects were detected using funnel plots and Egger’s regression test. If publication bias was detected, the trim-and-fill method was used for adjustment. To model the potential nonlinear dose–response relationship, we employed restricted cubic splines (RCS) rather than standard linear meta-regression, as preliminary visual inspection of the data suggested a nonlinear trend (e.g., diminishing returns at higher volumes) and RCS can capture complex dose–response patterns without a priori specification of functional forms. The relationship between the total intervention volume (defined as session duration × frequency × period, in minutes), a pragmatic indicator of cumulative exposure time used due to the frequent lack of reported intensity data, and effect size was calculated. The RCS model was specified with 3 knots, which is consistent 1180 Clinical Rehabilitation 40(9)

with standard practice in meta-analytic dose– response modeling for small-to-moderate sample sizes. The knots were placed at the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentiles of the total exercise volume distribution, a strategy that balances flexibility (to capture nonlinear relationships) and stability (to avoid overfitting with limited data points). The RCS model was embedded within the three-level random-effects framework (used for the primary meta-analysis), which accounts for two levels of heterogeneity: within-study variance (between effect sizes from the same study) and between-study variance. Importantly, these dose– response findings, including the approximate thresholds, must be considered exploratory, given the inherent limitations of pooled analyses across heterogeneous exercise modalities. All statistical analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.2.1). Results A comprehensive search was conducted across electronic databases, yielding 1365 records. An additional six records were identified through manual reference screening. After removing duplicates, 962 unique records remained for title and abstract screening. Two independent reviewers performed the screening process, demonstrating good agreement (κ = 0.70, 95% CI: 0.60–0.82). Of these, 34 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Thirteen studies were excluded for the following reasons: (1) involving non-ADHD populations (n = 2), (2) reporting irrelevant outcomes (n = 3), (3) providing insufficient data (n = 3), (4) employing nonclinical study designs (n = 2), or (5) having inaccessible full texts (n = 3). Inter-rater agreement during full-text review was excellent (κ = 0.88, 95% CI: 0.72–0.99). Ultimately, 21 studies met the predefined eligibility criteria and were included in both qualitative synthesis and quantitative meta-analysis. The study selection process adhered to PRISMA guidelines, with details provided in Figure 1 and Supplementary Material Table S2–S3. This systematic review and meta-analysis incorporated 21 studies (11 randomized controlled trials and 10 quasi-experimental studies) published between 2012 and 2024. A total of 850 participants were included across the studies, predominantly male (85.8%), with ages spanning 5–14 years. The studies were conducted primarily from Asia (n = 11), followed by Europe (n = 7), and North America (n = 3). Notably, only two studies specifically recruited children with ADHD without taking medicines. Of those studies, the most common comparator was a passive control with no intervention or waiting list (n = 15), followed by active control with routine school activities (n = 5). The physical exercise interventions spanned 3–24 weeks (median: 8 weeks), with session durations ranging from 15– 90 min and frequencies of 1–6 sessions/week. Thirteen studies did not report exercise intensity, while the remaining eight studies employed moderate-to-vigorous intensity. Motor skill assessments were conducted using standardized tools, with gross motor skills evaluated in 18 studies and fine motor skills in 14 studies. The predominant assessment instruments were: Bruininks–Oseretsky Test of Motor Proficiency, 2nd Edition, Test of Gross Motor Development-2/3, and Movement Assessment Battery for Children-2. Detailed study characteristics are provided in Table 1. The RoB assessment for included studies is summarized in Figure 2. Overall, 38.1% of studies demonstrated a low RoB, while 57.1% were rated as high risk, and 4.8% raised some concerns. Ten studies (47.6%) failed to adequately describe randomization procedures, introducing potential selection bias. One study (4.8%) was flagged for high risk due to excessive participant attrition (>20%), compromising data completeness. All studies satisfied criteria for outcome measurement and selective reporting, indicating consistent endpoint assessment and transparency in result presentation. Effects on gross motor skills The meta-analysis examining the effects of exercises on gross motor skills in children with ADHD included data from 16 studies, comprising 46 effect sizes and a total of 613 participants. The results indicated a moderate and positive effect of exercises on improving gross motor skills in children with ADHD (Hedge’s g = 0.62, 95% CI: 0.48–0.76, P < 0.001, I2 = 32.61%). To assess the robustness of the results, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by Zhang et al. 1181

sequentially excluding individual studies, which the effect size Hedge’s g ranged from 0.59 to 0.64. Additionally, we compared the results using a traditional two-level model and a RVE method, which the traditional two-level model yielded a pooled effect size of Hedge’s g = 0.60 (95% CI: 0.48– 0.73), while the RVE method resulted in Hedge’s g = 0.62 (95% CI: 0.48–0.76). The meta-analysis revealed differential effects of exercise interventions across specific subcomponents of gross motor skills in children with ADHD. Results revealed exercise significantly improved locomotion skills (Hedge’s g = 0.53, 95% CI: 0.19–0.87, P = 0.002, I2 = 0%), objective control (Hedge’s g = 1.20, 95% CI: 0.48–1.92, P = 0.001, I2 = 64.19%), body coordination (Hedge’s g = 0.58, 95% CI: 0.21–0.96, P = 0.002, I2 = 20.33%), and strength (Hedge’s g = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.24–0.77, P < 0.001, I2 = 0.01%). Effects on balance (Hedge’s g = 0.37, 95% CI: −0.10 to 0.84, P = 0.124, I2 = 0%) and flexibility (Hedge’s g = 0.50, 95% CI: −0.16 to 1.16, P = 0.139, I2 = 62.25%) were not significant. Figure 2. Effects on fine motor skills The meta-analysis investigating the impact of exercises on fine motor skills in children with ADHD encompassed 13 studies, 45 effect sizes, and 553 participants in total. It revealed a moderate positive effect (Hedge’s g = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.54–0.90, P < 0.001, I2 = 49.71%), suggesting that exercises significantly enhanced fine motor skills in children with ADHD. To evaluate the stability of the results, a sensitivity analysis was conducted by sequentially excluding each study, which revealed that the Hedge’s g varied between 0.69 and 0.76. Furthermore, the robustness of the results was verified through comparison with both a traditional twolevel model (Hedge’s g = 0.78, 95% CI: 0.64–0.92) and a RVE method (Hedge’s g = 0.72, 95% CI: 0.54–0.90). The results are shown in Figure 3B and Supplementary Material Figure S8. The meta-analysis revealed differential effects of exercise interventions across specific subcomponents of fine motor skills in children with ADHD. Results demonstrated that exercises significantly improved manual dexterity (Hedge’s g = 0.66, 95% CI: 0.08–1.25, P = 0.026, I2 = 73.34%) and hand-eye coordination (Hedge’s g = 0.57, 95% CI: 0.25–0.88, P < 0.001, I2 = 24.34%). Additionally, handwriting skills showed a particularly significant improvement (Hedge’s g = 0.86, 95% CI: 0.68– 1.04, P < 0.001, I2 = 6.13%). The detailed results are presented in Figure 4G–1 and Supplementary Material Figures S9–S11. Moderator analysis The moderator analyses revealed significant differential effects across intervention characteristics. For gross motor skills, exercise demonstrated substantially greater benefits when compared to passive controls (Hedge’s g = 0.65, 95% CI: 0.49–0.81) than active controls (Hedge’s g= 0.25, 95% CI: −0.19 to 0.70). Notably, session duration emerged as a critical moderator (P < 0.001), with interventions >45 min showing nearly double the effect size (Hedge’s g = 0.75, 95% CI: 0.60–0.90) of shorter sessions (Hedge’s g = 0.34, 95% CI: 0.17–0.52). Frequency of ≥3 sessions/week yielded larger effects (Hedge’s g = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.64–1.04) than less sessions (Hedge’s g = 0.49, 95% CI: 0.29–0.62). The detailed results are presented in Table 2. For fine motor skills, exercises demonstrated substantially greater benefits when compared to passive controls (Hedge’s g = 0.87, 95% CI: 0.74–1.00) than active controls (Hedge’s g = 0.05, 95% CI: −0.48 to 0.58) and session duration of >45 min yielded larger effects (Hedge’s g = 0.81, 95% CI: 0.62–1.00) than less session duration (Hedge’s g = 0.40, 95% CI: 0.04–0.75). The detailed results are presented in Table 2. Publication bias The funnel plot asymmetry and Egger’s test (P < 0.05) for gross motor skills indicated the presence of publication bias and small-study effects. Trim-and-fill analysis adjusted the effect size downward to Hedge’s g = 0.44 (95% CI: 0.29–0.59), suggesting an overestimation in the original analysis. Similarly, fine motor skills outcomes demonstrated funnel plot asymmetry with significant Egger’s test results (P < 0.05), primarily reflecting smallstudy effects. The trim-and-fill adjusted effect size remained robust at Hedge’s g = 0.68 (95% CI: 0.52–0.83), indicating relatively stable estimates despite potential bias. The detailed results are provided in Supplementary Material Figures S12–S13. Quality of evidence Pooled analyses yielded moderate-quality evidence for both gross motor skills (limited by RoB) and fine motor skills (limited by RoB). However, quality of evidence for specific subcomponents of motor skills ranged from very low to moderate (Supplementary Material Table S4). Dose–response relationships The effect size for gross motor skills showed a trend (β = −0.01, 95% CI: −0.43 to 0.40) of increasing with the total dose up to approximately 810 min, 1186 Clinical Rehabilitation 40(9)

after which the curve plateaued (Figure 5A). For fine motor skills, a significant positive dose– response relationship was observed up to a cumulative dose of approximately 1350 min (β = 0.18, 95% CI: 0.03–0.34), beyond which further gains appeared to diminish (Figure 5B). Discussion This systematic review and meta-analysis comprehensively evaluated the effects of physical exercises on motor skills in children and adolescents with ADHD, focusing on both gross and fine motor skills and their subcomponents. The results demonstrated moderate positive effects on both gross (Hedge’s g = 0.62) and fine motor skills (Hedge’s g = 0.72), with significant improvements observed across specific subcomponents. Notably, exercise interventions exhibited differential efficacy based on skill type, intervention parameters, and control conditions, underscoring the importance of tailored approaches in clinical and educational settings. The meta-analysis revealed that physical exercise interventions significantly improved gross motor skills in children with ADHD, with notable enhancements in locomotion, object control, body coordination, and strength. These improvements can be attributed to the structured and repetitive nature of exercise interventions, which provide opportunities for motor learning and skill acquisition.30 In contrast, balance and flexibility did not show significant improvements. This may be due to the specific nature of the exercises included in the interventions. Balance requires precise control of the vestibular and proprioceptive systems, which may not be adequately targeted by the general exercise programs reviewed in this meta-analysis. Flexibility, on the other hand, is often improved through specific stretching and mobility exercises, which were not a primary focus of the interventions included in this study. The lack of significant effects on these Figure 3. Forest plot for change in gross motor skills (A) and fine motor skills (B). 1188 Clinical Rehabilitation 40(9)

subcomponents suggests that future interventions may need to incorporate more targeted exercises to address balance and flexibility deficits in children with ADHD. Additionally, the heterogeneity in the types of exercises and the varying durations and intensities of the interventions may have contributed to the inconsistent effects on balance and flexibility. The observed improvements in fine motor skills, particularly handwriting, represented a critical finding. Unlike gross motor skills that primarily impact physical activities, fine motor deficits directly impair essential daily functions from self-care tasks like buttoning shirts to academic performance through handwriting difficulties. The robust effects likely stem from shared neural circuitry between fine motor control and the executive functions impaired in ADHD. Handwriting gains may reflect enhanced integration within the cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit, which coordinates motor precision and cognitive control.24,40 Exercise-induced neuroplasticity, including striatal and prefrontal dopamine upregulation, improved cerebellar connectivity, and parietal lobe adaptation could underpin these changes.11 Similarly, gains in manual dexterity and hand-eye coordination suggested optimization of the dorsal visual stream pathway, crucial for translating visual input into precise movements. Importantly, these improvements may create a virtuous cycle: fine motor tasks inherently train executive functions through demands on working memory and inhibitory control, while enhanced cognitive functions in turn support better motor learning. This bidirectional Figure 4. Forest plot for change in different subcomponents of gross motor skills (A–F) and fine motor skills (G–I). Zhang et al. 1189

relationship underscores why targeted fine motor interventions could address both the motor and core cognitive symptoms of ADHD, offering a comprehensive therapeutic approach that extends beyond conventional symptom management. Moderator analyses indicated that higher intervention frequency (≥3 sessions/week) and longer session duration (>45 min) were associated with greater motor skill gains, and improvements in fine motor skills may require a longer period of accumulated Figure 5. practice (∼1350 min) than gross motor skills (∼810 min)beforeplateauing.Thisdiscrepancylikely reflects distinct neurobiological demands. Fine motor control depends more heavily on the integration of prefrontal-executive and sensorimotor networks, which are particularly impaired in ADHD due to reduced dopamine availability and weaker frontocerebellar connectivity.41 While gross motor skills may benefit from general physical activity through basic neuromuscular adaptations, fine motor tasks (e.g., handwriting, buttoning) demand precise coordination between cognitive control (e.g., working memory for letter formation) and hand musculature —a process requiring repeated, focused practice to induce cortical reorganization in the primary motor and somatosensory cortices.42 Previous meta-analyses have similarly shown that executive functions (closely linked to fine motor control) require longer intervention durations todemonstrate improvement, suggesting that the extended dose requirement for fine motor gains may reflect their shared dependence on frontostriatal circuit plasticity.43,44 These findings underscore the importance of sustained, frequent exercise protocols when targeting fine motor deficits in ADHD, as the neural systems supporting these skills appear to need greater cumulative stimulation for meaningful change. Therefore, tailored exercise programs that consider individual motor skill profiles and integrate specific motor training goals may be more effective in clinical and educational settings.Weemphasizedthat the dose–responserelationships are modality-agnostic and should be interpreted as “general cumulative exposure thresholds” rather than modality-specific prescriptions. For example, dynamic sports (e.g., table tennis, swimming) may achieve gross motor skill improvements at a lower volume due to their inherent focus on locomotion/ object control, while precision-based exercises (e.g., perceptual-motor training) may require similar or higher volume for fine motor gains. This study had several limitations. First, the high RoB in many included studies, often due to inadequate description of randomization, may affect the validity and precision of the pooled estimates. Second, inconsistent reporting of intervention details, particularly exercise intensity, which limited moderator analysis and the specificity of exercise prescriptions. Third, generalizability was constrained by the underrepresentation of participants not taking medications, limiting applicability to untreated populations. Fourth, evidence for specific motor subcomponents was of low or very low certainty due to imprecision and heterogeneity. Additionally, the dose–response analysis, based on cumulative exercise volume, did not account for unreported intensity or modality-specific demands, so the derived thresholds should be viewed as exploratory rather than prescriptive. Future studies should prioritize high-quality randomized controlled trials with standardized intensity monitoring, include medication-free cohorts, and further investigate effects on specific skill domains and underlying mechanisms. In conclusion, this meta-analysis provided moderate evidence that physical exercises are an effective intervention for improving gross and fine motor skills in children and adolescents with ADHD. The benefits vary across different motor subcomponents, highlighting the importance of tailored exercise programs. Notably, fine motor skills appeared to require greater cumulative exercise exposure than gross motor skills to achieve substantial gains, suggesting that exercise intervention protocols should carefully consider dose parameters. These findings support the integration of structured physical activity into clinical and educational interventions for ADHD; however, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to the methodological limitations and confounding factors of the included studies. Clinical messages • Physical exercise programs should be designed to include longer (>45 min) and more frequent (≥3 sessions/week) sessions to maximize benefits on motor proficiency. • Interventions should be specifically tailored to target different motor skill components. pages: https://doi.org/10.1177/10870547251408127 Journal of Attention Disorders 2026, Vol. 30(6) 765–772 © The Author(s) 2026 Article reuse guidelines: sagepub.com/journals-permissions DOI: 10.1177/10870547251408127 journals.sagepub.com/home/jad Article Introduction ADHD is one of the most common neurodevelopmental disorders of childhood characterized by hyperactivity, inattention, and impulsivity (Sharma & Couture, 2013). According to DSM-5 diagnostic criteria, the prevalence of ADHD is 11.3% in children under 12 years of age and 12.7% in adolescents aged 12 to 18 years (Salari et al., 2023). In a study conducted in Turkey, the prevalence of ADHD among primary school children was 12.7% (Ercan et al., 2015). Its etiopathogenesis has been reported to involve dopaminergic dysfunction, particularly in the mesocortical, mesolimbic, and nigrostriatal pathways (Del Campo et al., 2011; Sonuga-Barke, 2005). It is thought that dysfunction in the mesocortical dopamine pathway is associated with cognitive impairment, and that hypoactivity in the mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway plays a role in the motivational impairment seen in ADHD patients. The mesolimbic pathway is also an important part of the “reward” circuitry that is impaired in ADHD (Mehta et al., 2019). At the same time, the striatum is the largest source of dopamine in the brain, suggesting an important role for dopamine in attention. Connections to the striatum are a major source of dopaminergic synapses and have been suggested to play a role in ADHD (Dougherty et al., 1999). ADHD is increasingly seen as a syndrome of dysconnectivity rather than a disorder defined by changes in specific brain regions (Cortese et al., 2021). Study of functional connectivity in ADHD suggests that dopaminergic functional connectivity is a potential prognostic factor in ADHD (Zaher et al., 2024). Email: hhilalozturk@gmail.com Increased Serum Netrin-1 Levels Among Children Diagnosed With ADHD Hümeyra Hilal Öztürk1,2 , Selen Sezen1 , Elçin Çağlar1 , Serenay Elgün Ülkar1 , and Sadettin Burak Açıkel1 Abstract Objective: ADHD is a common neurodevelopmental disorder of childhood characterized by altered projections of dopaminergic neurons and connectivity issues in various brain regions. In our study, we aim to investigate the potential effects of axon guidance molecules, Netrin-1 and Semaphorins 3A, 4D, and 7A, on these connectivity problems by examining the levels of these molecules in the peripheral blood of children with ADHD compared to healthy controls. Methods: A total of 43 children with ADHD and 40 healthy controls 6 to 12 years of age were included in the study. The K-SADS-PL was administered to exclude any additional psychopathologies (excluding ODD in the ADHD group). The Revised Child Anxiety and Depression Scale was provided to the children, while parents completed the revised Conners’ Parent Rating Scale (CPRS-R), the Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS), and the Behavior Rating Inventory for Executive Functioning (BRIEF). Additionally, teachers of the ADHD group were given the Conners’ Teacher Rating Scale. Furthermore, the WISC-4 was administered to assess the IQ profile of 35 children in the ADHD group. Results: Netrin-1 was found to be statistically higher in the ADHD group. When the R-CADS scores were recalculated taking the covariate into account, the significant increase in the ADHD group remained. There was no statistically significant difference between the two groups for semaphorin 3A, 4D, and 7A. The positive correlation of Netrin-1 with the hyperactivity subscores on the CPRS-R and the Global Executive Score on the BRIEF scale is noteworthy. Conclusion: Netrin-1 may play a role in the etiopathogenesis of ADHD. Further studies are needed to clarify the relationship between Netrin-1 and ADHD. (J. of Att. 766 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(6) variability in the cingulo-temporal, cingulo-parietal, frontotemporal, and fronto-parietal networks compared to typically developing children (Misra & Gandhi, 2023). Netrin and Semaphorins are molecules that regulate the connectivity of neurons in the brain, have important roles in axon guidance and therefore may have an effect on the etiology of ADHD. Netrin was first discovered in the 1990s as a vertebrate homologue of the laminin-associated UNC-6 protein found in Caenorhabditis elegans (Serafini et al., 1994). Netrins are categorized into two families of receptors: The DCC (deleted in colorectal cancer) family, which includes DCC and neogenin, and the UNC5 family, which includes Unc5a, Unc5b, Unc5c, and Unc5d proteins (Engelkamp, 2002; Leonardo et al., 1997; Livesey, 1999). In the central nervous system, netrins influence cell and axon migration and have been demonstrated to facilitate axon arborization and synapse formation during neural development (K. L. W. Sun et al., 2011). Additionally, they are known to promote cortical axon branching (Dent et al., 2004). Beyond axon guidance, netrins are involved in synaptic plasticity, synaptogenesis, cell migration, cell survival, and axon regeneration (Boyer & Gupton, 2018; Glasgow et al., 2021; Kefeli et al., 2017; K. L. W. Sun et al., 2011). Studies indicate that netrin-1 may be implicated in the function, plasticity, and peripubertal reorganization of mesocorticolimbic dopaminergic systems (Manitt et al., 2010). In animal models, the presence of netrin-1 has been shown to restore dopaminergic axonal projections in the striatum, whereas its absence is linked to dopaminergic cell loss in the substantia nigra (Jasmin et al., 2021). Moreover, netrin-1 has been found to maintain the integrity of the blood-brain barrier, mitigate neuroinflammation by reducing chemokine secretion from central nervous system endothelial cells, and exert an anti-inflammatory effect on the blood-brain barrier in response to cytokine-induced disruptions (Podjaski et al., 2015). Semaphorins (Sema) constitute a large, evolutionarily conserved family of proteins that function as both secreted and membrane-associated guidance cues (Alto & Terman, 2017). Research has demonstrated the essential role of semaphorin signaling in accurately directing specific subsets of afferent projections within the nervous system to their designated targets (Tran et al., 2007). Other functions in the central nervous system include facilitating synapse formation (Inoue et al., 2018; McDermott et al., 2018), contributing to homeostatic synaptic plasticity (Orr et al., 2017), promoting axon terminal branching (Cioni et al., 2013; Jung et al., 2019), enabling axonal pruning (Liu et al., 2005), influencing dendritic morphogenesis and arborization (Danelon et al., 2020; Yamashita et al., 2014), and aiding in the removal of ectopic synapses (Mohan et al., 2019; Tran et al., 2009). Among the various semaphorins, Semaphorin 3A has been extensively studied, revealing numerous functions within the central nervous system. The interactions between Semaphorin 3A and neuropilin are pivotal for the migration of striatal and cortical interneurons (Marı́n et al., 2001). Furthermore, Semaphorin 3A has been associated with the inhibition of neurogenesis in the subventricular zone (T. Sun et al., 2016) and has implications in neuroprotection during neural stress (Majed et al., 2006). Sema4D is a biologically active molecule in both its membrane-associated and soluble forms (Smith et al., 2015) and is expressed by oligodendrocytes by oligodendrocytes, where it plays a role in inhibiting axon regeneration (Moreau-Fauvarque et al., 2003). Semaphorin 7A is unique as the only glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored semaphorin identified to date, expressed in both glial and neuronal cells in the adult central nervous system (Xu et al., 1998). It is suggested to facilitate not only axon guidance and neuronal migration but also the inhibition of neurogenesis in the hippocampus (Jongbloets et al., 2017; Pasterkamp et al., 2007). Additional roles of Semaphorin 7A include involvement in glial scar formation and maturation following spinal cord injury (Kopp et al., 2010) as well as contributions to gliosis (Gutiérrez-Franco et al., 2016). These various functions suggest a potential role for Semaphorin 7A in neurodegenerative processes (Gutiérrez-Franco et al., 2016). The objective of this study is to explore the potential roles of netrin and semaphorin guidance molecules in the etiopathogenesis of ADHD, with a specific emphasis on their impact on the development of dopaminergic pathways and neural connectivity. The primary hypothesis posits that dysregulation of netrin-1 and semaphorin signaling contributes to the abnormal formation of dopaminergic circuits and synaptic plasticity that underlie the cognitive, motivational, and behavioral deficits observed in individuals with ADHD. Given the connectivity deficits associated with ADHD, our study will examine the blood levels of netrin-1, an important factor in dopamine axon guidance, as well as semaphorin 3A, 4D, and 7A, to investigate their roles in the etiopathogenesis of ADHD. Materials and Methods Participants Children aged 6 to 12 years who were admitted to the outpatient clinics of Ankara University Faculty of Medicine, Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, between June 2023 and February 2024 were included in this study. Informed consent was obtained from all children and their families who participated. The ADHD group comprised 48 patients who had recently received a diagnosis of ADHD and did not have any comorbid psychiatric disorders, aside from oppositional defiant disorder (ODD). In contrast, the control group consisted of 42 healthy participants who did not meet any psychiatric diagnostic criteria. The exclusion criteria for both groups included: known systemic illnesses, presence of any psychiatric diagnosis (aside from ODD in

Öztürk et al. 767 the ADHD group), regular medication use, infection-related illnesses within the past month, and illiteracy. Approval from the Ethics Committee at Ankara University Faculty of Medicine was secured (11.05.2023/I05-291-23). A total of 133 children were invited to participate in the study, including 56 for the control group and 77 for the ADHD group. In the control group, 14 children declined participation and were subsequently excluded from the study. In the ADHD group, 18 children either refused to participate or withdrew during the study; these participants were also excluded. Additionally, 11 children who provided blood samples but did not complete the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children Fourth Edition (WISC-4) were excluded from further analysis. Ultimately, 42 participants were included in the healthy control (HC) group, while 48 participants were included in the ADHD group, all aged between 6 and 12 years. Seven children (five from the ADHD group and two from the HC group) were excluded from the analysis due to missing blood values. Procedure The assessment of the children was conducted by the researcher using the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age ChildrenPresent and Lifetime Version (K-SADS-PL-DSM-5Turkish). The parents of all participants completed the Revised Conners’ Parent Rating Scale (CPRS-R), the Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS), and the Behavior Rating Inventory for Executive Functioning (BRIEF) parent report. Additionally, teachers of children in the ADHD group completed the Conners’ Teacher Rating Scale (CTRS). All participants were administered Turkish version of the Revised Child Anxiety and Depression Scale (RCADS) to screen for anxiety and depression scores. Additionally, the intelligence quotient (IQ) of children in the ADHD group was evaluated using the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children Fourth Edition (WISC-4). All participants underwent screening for anxiety and depression using the Turkish version of the Revised Child Anxiety and Depression Scale (RCADS). Furthermore, the intelligence quotient (IQ) of children in the ADHD group was assessed using the WISC-4. The CPRS-R is a widely utilized tool for evaluating ADHD and related behavioral concerns in children and adolescents, offering insights into inattention, hyperactivity, and oppositional behaviors based on reports from parents, teachers, or self-reports (Conners et al., 1998). The BRIEF is a standardized assessment tool that evaluates executive function in children and adolescents, measuring aspects such as working memory, emotional regulation, and cognitive flexibility through reports from parents, teachers, or self-reports (Baron, 2000; Gioia et al., 2000). The RCADS is a self-report questionnaire employed to assess symptoms of various anxiety disorders and major depressive disorder based on DSM criteria (Chorpita et al., 2000). The SRS is a standardized measure that evaluates the severity of social impairments associated with autism spectrum disorders by assessing social communication, interaction, and restrictive behaviors across multiple contexts (Constantino et al., 2003). Biochemical Examination For laboratory analysis, blood specimens were collected from all participants at 8:00 and 10:30 AM after a fasting period of at least eight hours. Blood samples collected in biochemistry tubes were centrifuged at 4000 × g for 10 min; the resultant sera were stored in Eppendorf tubes at −80°C until analysis. Serum samples were analyzed in the research laboratory of the Department of Medical Biochemistry at Ankara University, utilizing ELISA kits for these markers. The levels of Netrin-1 (Ntn1), Semaphorin 3A (SEMA3A), Semaphorin 4D (SEMA4D), and Semaphorin 7A (SEMA7A) in the serum samples were assessed using a sandwich ELISA method. The blood neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) was also evaluated as an inflammatory parameter, derived from complete blood counts. While age, gender, and measurement methods may influence NLR values, a serum NLR ratio of approximately 0.7 to 3.5 is considered within the normal range (Forget et al., 2017). Therefore, children with an NLR ratio exceeding 3.5 were excluded from the study. Statistical Analysis Given the absence of comparable studies in the literature, the effect sizes proposed by Cohen (1988) were utilized to determine the appropriate sample size (Cohen, 1988). Assuming an effect size of 0.8, a type I error rate of 0.05, and a statistical power of 95%, the required sample size was calculated to be 84 participants, with 42 in each group (Cohen, 2013). Statistical analyses were performed using the SPSS 25.0 software package. Descriptive analyses were conducted to examine demographic data, and the relationship between categorical variables between the two groups was analyzed using the chi-square test. Comparisons of biomarker levels and scale scores between the two groups were assessed using the t-test if the data met the assumptions of normal distribution; otherwise, the Mann-Whitney U test was employed. The relationship between scale scores and serum levels of biomarkers was analyzed through correlation analysis. To account for potential psychiatric confounders affecting biomarker levels between the two groups, anxiety and depression scores were included as covariates in an ANCOVA analysis. A p-value of less than .05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses.

768 Journal of Attention Disorders 30(6) Results A total of 43 participants were included in the ADHD group (comprising 25 boys and 18 girls) and 40 participants in the healthy control group (including 22 boys and 18 girls). The mean age of participants in the ADHD group was 8.34 years (SD = 1.53), while the mean age of the control group was 8.85 years (SD = 1.64). No statistically significant differences were observed between the groups regarding gender (p = .773) or age (p = .150). Demographic data for the participants are presented in Table 1. When comparing the R-CADS subscale scores between groups, no significant difference was found for the Total Anxiety score (p = .096). However, the Depression score (p = .004) and the Total Internalizing score (p = .039) were significantly higher in the ADHD group. Additionally, all subscale scores of the BRIEF were significantly elevated in the ADHD group compared to healthy controls (p < .001), and the total score of the SRS was also significantly higher in the ADHD group (p < .001). Among the CPRS-R subscale scores, all but the Perfectionism score (p = .140) were significantly higher in the ADHD group compared to the healthy control group, including scores for Psychosomatic (p = .003) and other subscales (p < .001). Serum Netrin-1 levels were significantly higher in the ADHD group compared to the control group (p = .016; refer to Table 2). Even when recalculated with covariates, the significant elevation of Netrin-1 levels in the ADHD group remained evident (f = 5.392, p = .023). Conversely, no significant differences were found between the two groups for serum levels of Semaphorin 3A, 4D, or 7A (p = .446, .099, and .676, respectively; Table 2). The serum NLR ratios are also summarized in Table 2. Positive correlations were found between serum Netrin-1 levels and levels of Semaphorin 3A, 4D, and 7A (in the ADHD group: Sema3A, 4D, and 7A p < .001; in the healthy control group: Sema3A and 4D p < .001, Sema7A p = .004). Additionally, serum Netrin-1 levels were positively correlated with the CPRS-R subscores: Hyperactivity (r = .512, p = .001), DSM-4 Hyperactivity-Impulsivity (r = .396, p = .017), and DSM-4 Total score (r = .353, p = .037) in the ADHD group. Moreover, serum Netrin-1 levels were positively associated with various subscale scores of the BRIEF in the ADHD group, including the Inhibit score (r = 0.408, p = .007), Emotional Control score (r = .407, p = .007), Working Memory score (r = .371, p = .014), Organization of Materials score (r = .330, p = .031), Monitor score (r = .315, p = .040), Behavior Regulation Index score (r = .391, p = .010), Metacognition Index score (r = .334, p = .029), and Global Executive Score (r = .367, p = .015) . Additionally, a significant positive correlation was observed between serum Netrin-1 levels and the total score of the SRS in the ADHD group (p = .040). Discussion In our study, we found that levels of the axon guidance molecule Netrin-1 were significantly elevated in children diagnosed with ADHD. In contrast, we observed no significant differences in the levels of other axon guidance molecules, namely Semaphorin 3A, 4D, and 7A. Netrin-1 is a key axon guidance molecule that plays a crucial role in neuron migration and in determining the trajectory of growing axons and dendrites during the embryonic development of the nervous system (Huber et al., 2003). It is particularly important for the development of dopaminergic neurons extending to the striatum, continuing through puberty, as well as for the proper formation of the mesocorticolimbic pathway (Hoops & Flores, 2017). Dysfunction in axon guidance molecules has been implicated in various neurological disorders (Wang et al., 2022). Alterations in brain connectivity are also documented in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease (Conti et al., 2022; Y. Sun et al., 2014). Notably, a study found that serum Netrin-1 levels in patients with Alzheimer’s disease were significantly lower compared to healthy controls (Zhang et al., 2021). Moreover, research by Ahn et al. (2020) in a Parkinson’s animal model demonstrated that processes leading to decreased Netrin-1 levels may induce apoptosis in dopaminergic neurons. The findings of our study, which indicate elevated Netrin-1 levels, contrast with reports from Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease research. This discrepancy may be attributable to the inclusion of younger participants in our study. Previous studies suggest that the striatal and cerebellar regions are capable of modulating behavior, refined through experiential learning, during childhood development. Such modulation may occur via afferent and efferent pathways to the prefrontal cortex (Amso & Casey, 2006; Nigg & Casey, 2005). Furthermore, research by Nigg and Casey (2005). suggests that these pathways might be less robust in children diagnosed with ADHD, potentially affecting their behavioral regulation. Costa Dias et al. (2013). provided evidence that the nucleus accumbens (NAcc) exhibits atypical connectivity with various cortical regions in children with ADHD. Öztürk et al. 769 abnormal patterns of spontaneous neural activity in individuals diagnosed with ADHD. The abnormal regional connections and activity patterns observed in ADHD may result from increased Netrin-1 levels leading to excessive neuronal connections. In essence, while Netrin-1 facilitates the guidance of altered dopaminergic neurons in ADHD, it may also induce aberrant axonal connections through various mechanisms. The increased plasma levels of Netrin-1 observed in our study may represent a compensatory response to impaired axon connectivity. Moreover, we found that Netrin-1 levels were positively correlated with all BRIEF subscales, except for Plan/ Organize, Initiate, and Set Shifting. The brain regions involved in executive functions include the prefrontal cortex, striatum, and hippocampus. Netrin-1 may influence the connectivity of prefrontal neurons through the DCC receptor, with potential effects on executive functions such as working memory. Additionally, Netrin-1 may enhance memory processes by increasing synaptic plasticity of hippocampal neurons (Glasgow et al., 2021). While lower levels of Netrin-1 are associated with impaired memory and hippocampal function (López-Huerta et al., 2013), our findings suggest that elevated Netrin-1 correlates with executive function impairments. This indicates that maintaining Netrin-1 levels within an optimal range is essential for proper neural remodeling. Furthermore, our results indicated that serum Netrin-1 levels were positively correlated with hyperactivity and DSM-IV total scores on the CPRS-R. These findings underscore the significance of Netrin-1 in brain regions, such as the prefrontal cortex and NAcc, which are integral to behaviors associated with hyperactivity in ADHD. ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder with an incomplete understanding of its etiopathogenesis, which remains an area of active investigation. In our study, we propose that axon guidance molecules, previously overlooked in the context of neurodevelopmental disorders, may contribute to the etiology of ADHD and warrant further research. Currently, there are no biomarkers available for diagnosis or treatment monitoring in neurodevelopmental disorders. Thus, we sought to identify a biomarker that could assist clinicians in diagnosis and treatment. Axon guidance molecules, particularly Netrin-1, may be valuable in this regard. Future studies may enhance clinical practice by comparing plasma levels of Netrin-1 with treatment responses, especially as changes in Netrin-1 within the NAcc can influence the efficacy of stimulant medications. The strengths of our study include its status as the first investigation of axon guidance molecules in children with ADHD within the existing literature and the exclusion of additional clinical and psychiatric diagnoses in ADHD participants. However, our study has certain limitations, including its conduct at a single center with a clinical sample derived from outpatient settings, as well as the assessment of these molecules using peripheral blood samples. Additionally, our reliance on parent-report questionnaires without incorporating cognitive tests presents another limitation. In the analysis phase of our study, we did not observe any significant differences between groups for non-netrin markers. Therefore, to avoid the false discovery rate, we did not perform further analyses on these markers. Selen Sezen, MD, graduated from the Department of Biochemistry, Ankara University Faculty of Medicine. Her research focuses on biochemical markers and their role in health and disease. Sadettin Burak Açıkel, PhD, Associate Professor, graduated from the Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry at Necmettin Erbakan University, Meram Faculty of Medicine.
